texts.speaker: Michael Peter Farley
texts.profession: Group Chief Executive Officer, Persimmon Plc
texts.text: We're also particularly pleased about Space4. We've worked long and hard on Space4 now. And we're now seeing  it up to over 3,200 units of production. And that equates to nearly a third of our house completions. It's a very  energy-efficient production method, and also it obviously adds a speed of construction on site. And I think we will  see that business continue to expand in the future.

texts.speaker: Michael Peter Farley
texts.profession: Group Chief Executive Officer, Persimmon Plc
texts.text: So where are we to be focused in the shorter term. As I say, opening those 60 new sites in the first half, giving us  that pent-up demand, building on that 9% increase in our forward order books is our focus. Doing a bit more with  Space4, because with the new building regulations that's coming forward, that becomes more cost-effective option  for us and focusing on putting more houses on our land bank rather than apartments and around 13% is probably  a sort of percentage we'll target for the future.

texts.speaker: Michael Hugh Killoran
texts.profession: Group Finance Director, Persimmon Plc
texts.text: Looking at the land holdings of the business, just over 63,000 plots owned and under control at the end of 2011. I  think a key indicator for the future is that cost to revenue percentage, 18.5% land cost percentage there, to my  mind, is a very low percentage. And I have looked back over the last 15 to 20 year history of Persimmon. And I  think that is the lowest cost to revenue percentage in a long, long while. You'd have to go back to the 1980s, I  think, to get anywhere near that.

texts.speaker: Michael Peter Farley
texts.profession: Group Chief Executive Officer, Persimmon Plc
texts.text: We have reinvested some capital. We were able to acquire some additional equipment for the factory, so we're  now processing the fourth line there. So we can take volumes up to around 8,000 if required. So we're building in  plenty of long-term capacity. We think that it will be the future as government regulations change, as we move  nearer to the zero carbon, et cetera, Space4 will come more into its own. So we think it's a good product and we'll  continue to let it grow. But we're going to grow it naturally.

texts.speaker: Michael Peter Farley
texts.profession: Group Chief Executive Officer, Persimmon Plc
texts.text: And I think the other aspect – a key aspect which really you try and put your finger on is the land replacement  cycle. Because what we're trying to do is make sure that we replace quality with quality in terms of input cost of  the land, which is obviously – it defines the ultimate outcomes considerably. So what we're trying to do is bring  through as much strategic land as we can to increase the quality of the inputs into the business and minimize the  development costs as a result of that, to produce the best quality outcomes in terms of margins and cash  generation. And obviously, the bigger the volume that you're delivering, it becomes more demanding to do that.

texts.profession: Group CEO, Executive Director & Group MD

texts.profession: Group CEO, Executive Director & Group MD
texts.text: So as long as we've got that good spread of developments across the UK close to home, all of these things are key  issues for the workers. texts.speaker: Jeffrey Fairburn
texts.profession: Group CEO, Executive Director & Group MD
texts.text: So it does vary quite significantly but I don't think it's really changed significantly over the years apart from we  have heard the debates about the bigger garden city type situations which have still got a long way to run. texts.speaker: Jeffrey Fairburn
texts.profession: Group CEO, Executive Director & Group MD
texts.text: I think there's a number of factors going on there, [ph] Kevin, (01:21:00) to be honest. texts.speaker: Jeffrey Fairburn
texts.profession: Group CEO, Executive Director & Group MD
texts.text: So it's not necessarily an impact. texts.speaker: Jeffrey Fairburn
texts.profession: Group CEO, Executive Director & Group MD
texts.text: But for the longer term sustainability of our business, to underpin the individual companies that we've got for the  volumes they're producing it's a great way of getting sustainability. And yes, we're being opportunistic. As I say,  there's less competition for those bigger sites and we can enjoy some very good terms on those. So for us, at this  moment in the cycle, it's absolutely the right thing for us to do in order to manage our business going forward.

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: And in regard to your first question, I'm happy, more than happy, that you placed the question because, as you  know, we have repeatedly, since August last year, said that we have three main reasons for why we upgraded our  earnings with DKK 125 million in August for the full year. texts.text: Let us begin and please turn to slide 2. I'm pleased to present the annual results for 2015 and a performance,  which is better than we expected at the beginning of the year. texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So we have with us today Peter Sharpe, who is our Executive Vice President for Wells, and he will be joining Andy  in that panel. And we have Istvan Kapitany, who is in charge of Shell's 43,000 retail sites around the world. He  will be joining John Abbott. And then, we have Steve Hill, and some of you may know Steve from his days in BG.  Well, he can talk an awful lot with you about LNG trading. So he will join Maarten in the panel there.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: The downturn in the oil prices, obviously, had an impact on Shell and the industry around us. And this chart here  looks at some of the lights and the important trends that we are going to be witnessing in the energy sector, but  also in society at large. And this, I think, will shape the industry and, therefore, Shell in the next decade or even  longer. Now, of course, on top of the chart, you will see a pretty familiar driver, so growing population. We will go  from 7  billion people to 9 billion people by mid-century. But at the same time, hopefully, we will also see a much  higher quality of life for many of them. And they are incredibly powerful drivers that inexorably will drive for  more energy demand in the future.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: At the same time, governments, businesses, and society at large expect that this increased energy will also come  with less CO2. So this results in a tricky robust demand outlook for oil and gas and over the longer term, also, the  transition of the energy system to a much lower carbon intensity.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Now, simultaneously with this, we also see strong demand for petrochemicals, petrochemicals that are the  building blocks of many of the things that people take for granted in modern life and also building blocks that, in  many ways, will be the enablers of the carbon intensity reduction that modern society expects.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: And within all of this, traditional value chains between LNG suppliers and customers are also seeing considerable  change and, in some cases, actually quite a bit of disruption, driven by factors such as energy storage, the digital  world, which altogether leads to much more choice by customers. And this will not only impact how energy gets  consumed, but it will also impact where investment in energy is made and by who.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: While all of this is happening, we are also seeing a era of sustained volatility that we have entered. A part of this is  the result of OPEC policy, the advent, of course, of very large oil and gas resources and shales, the speed of  information flows and trading, the inevitable need for large scale resource developments. And each category of oil  supply that I've just mentioned here has different response times to price signals. And it's, therefore, making it  very hard for market forces to provide price stability against these three types of response times. Now, our  traditional role in developing more complex projects, of course, is impacted by the Shell's plays and by the lower  oil price generally. And, therefore, we must make sure that our cost structure, that our portfolio choices, and our  business models are adapted to allow us to thrive also in this particular setting.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Now, let's make some comments first on the energy supply mix, a lot of interest in this, particularly, of course,  following Paris in December. So, today, oil and gas and coal supply over 80% of primary energy worldwide. We all  know that renewables is growing, it's growing fast, but it's growing from a very small baseline. So renewables also  get a supply around 4% of primary energy today. And two-thirds of that 4% is hydro. So less than one-third is  wind, solar, and other renewables that we know.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Now, Shell strongly supports the agreements that had been made in Paris to limit global warming to 2 degr ees C  compared to pre-industrial temperatures. But we're also concerned at the same time that the commitments that  were made at COP21 will actually not go far enough to meet those supporting goals. We also think that we can  thrive in a 2 degree C world, and we have a strategy that will allow us to do so, whatever will play out here.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: And if you look at the 450 bpm scenario, the International Energy Agency, which is essentially diversion of the 2  degree C scenario that we all hope to see, which is a pretty ambitious change in the energy mix and a demand  picture for oil and gas that is lower than what we are predicting in the – or that we are looking at in our scenarios,  there is still quite a bit of running room in oil and particularly in gas investments for decades to come. And that is,  of course, alongside very substantial growth potential in renewables that we also expect to see. And that is the  context for Shell's sustained investments in oil and gas today and for putting more focus also on new business  models and renewable, going forward. We'll talk about that in a little bit more detail later on.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: But there are other areas that we want to focus on, too, and think of these as an integral part of the investment  case. First of all, I want Shell to be more relevant, a more valuable company, which means a large market  capitalization and a more valued company, which means that we are listened to. We are respected for the things  that we do and the things that we say. It means reducing Shell's carbon intensity. This is inevitable, and it's  something we are working hard on today. And we will continue to put strong emphasis on reducing our carbon  intensity. But we also need to establish, beyond any doubt, that Shell as a company provides sha red value, that we  are a force for good in society. It's very hard to express that in clear metrics, but it's also very, very hard to get it  right in the minds of society.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: But there is also more upside as we are using the BG transaction as a platform to reshape the company. I talked  about it before, a springboard for change. And of course, there's some further value potential, also, if oil prices  turn out to be higher than the average market participants' outlook had on the 15th of February. So all in a ll, we're  pretty pleased with the deal. The BG acquisition was, of course, the largest change that we had in the last few  years, but it wasn't the only one. It was just one element in a much broader transformation that was already under  way at Shell. And this transformation includes over 500,000 barrels per day of profitable new production; it  includes the restructuring, remember, of our products and Upstream, covering some $91 billion of capital  employed. It – a measured and a thorough rationalization and reduction of the option set that we were working  on, which should mitigate altogether around $45 billion of capital spending, and we delivered $22 billion worth of  divestments already in the last few years.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: But thirdly, we also need to focus right now on selective future opportunities that will provide us with material  growth and material cash flow per share in the next decade and beyond when the energy transition is playing out  and opens up new areas for us. And running through all of this is our intention to be in fundamentally advantaged  positions, which all have resilience and running room. You can imagine that in doing so, asset  sales have an  important role to play as well in all of these strategic themes as well, of course, as the investment decisions that we  make. And I'll talk about it in a moment.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Up to 10% of our oil and gas production is earmarked for sale at the moment. That includes around 5% to 10%,  depending a little bit on how things will play out, total country positions that we will be exiting and, of course,  quite a significant number also of midstream and downstream positions that we will be divesting. And let me s ay  again, this is a value-driven program. This is not a time schedule-driven program. It's an integral element of the  portfolio re-shape and the shareholder proposition that we made in December when we issued the prospectus.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Let's look back a little bit. Shell's free cash flow in the last three years was $35 billion, cumulatively over the last  three years. And we had around 8% return on capital employed. So, essentially, we covered the dividends and the  buybacks here. But this was a period when, on average, the oil price was $87 a barrel. Of course, high prices in  2013, pretty good prices in 2014 and, of course, declining prices in 2015. But the cash flow is working – was  working as it was supposed to do.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: But at the same time, I have to be really frank here and say that it has worked well when the oil price was high.  And operating performance wasn't always as good as we wanted it to be, particularly in 2013. And really, the asset  sales as well as turning on scrip on the dividend have been important elements of the overall free cash flow of the  Company and how we have been covering the dividends.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So we have made a lot of improvements, including the turnaround in oil products, restructuring in shales. But it's  also fair to conclude that we have to do more. We cannot rely on a recovery back to a higher oil price to balance  the financial framework. So we have been, and you have been seeing us, reducing systematically our capital  investment levels in a steady and measured way over the last few years. And this is to rebalance the financial  framework for lower oil prices, of course, to become more selective of which projects will be the final investment  decision, and to establish also a more predictable spending profile.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: We've made changes in the way we allocate capital in the Company. And I would like to give you also a little bit  more visibility on our spending plans, going forward. So we are planning to spend between $25 billion and $30  billion each year until 2020. And we see $30 billion as the ceiling, which is all about, of course, reducing debt,  following the BG deal, about meeting our intentions for shareholder distributions as well. And at the bottom end  of the range, at $25 billion, I think that reflects the spend we believe we need to maintain a medium -term growth  in the Company. But if need be, we can and will go below that level, if oil prices warrant it. But, of course, the final  outcome for each given year will be determined by the pace and development of the portfolio, overall affordability  considerations within that year. And at the moment, of course, we are seeing oil prices at a level where we clearly  want to ramp down investment levels towards the bottom end of the range. After 2016, we expect to be coming out  at $29 billion or less.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Now, the BG deal, of course, has very much a large conventional oil and gas business here. So here now, we need  to high-grade that strategic theme to the point that it offers really high returns, it offers strong free cash flow, and  also has still very significant running room. And this means, of course, asset sales, but it also means an increased  focus on Heartlands exploration, especially near-field exploration to improve the resilience of this portfolio, but  also to sustain it well into the 30s. Integrated gas is now also a cash engine, and I'll touch on that in a moment,  actually.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: If you look at oil products, we've been restructuring the strategic theme probably for more than a decade by now,  but we're getting to the end of this, restructuring that is. The oil products business did very well last year. It shows  that it can deliver strong double-digit returns. But it now will also need to demonstrate that it can do this at all  points in the cycle.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Oil sands is now also a cash engine. Previously, we talked about this as a future opportunity, but it needs to deliver  free cash flow now, and it can. As a matter of fact, it can deliver more so than any of the other cash engines, but  dollar of cash invested in that business. And, of course, it is a business that offers a lot of upside to oil prices as  well.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Let's talk about integrated gas then. So as I've mentioned, that's now also a cash engine. And that's a change  because, previously, we saw this as a growth priority. And now, it needs to be generating a  growing cash surplus  and it needs to provide very strong returns. So integrated gas has a global footprint. We've a leading position of all  the international oil companies in this area. The BG deal pretty much accelerated the strategy that we had before.  That doesn't mean now that this is a cash engine that we will stop investing in new projects, of course. But it does  mean that if this business is roughly one-third of the capital employed of the entire Shell Group, it better be  delivering very, very strong returns, very strong double-digit returns, and with relatively low capital maintenance  compared to some of its upstream peers. I expect this business also to be a major, if not the major contributor to  our free cash flow, going forward. So those were the cash engines.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: And for chemicals, it means investing in fundamentally advantaged feedstock projects such as low-cost ethane in  the United States. And you will have seen that this morning that we took a final investment decision on a 1.5  million tonne per annum Pennsylvania project today. Now, both of these businesses, Deepwater , Chemicals, first- class businesses in their own right, have very significant growth potential ahead of them, and that's simply  because we have a large inventory of ready projects to undertake or because the theme supports tremendous  growth in this sector.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: And let me give you an impression of the scale of growth that we are looking at here. And here is a slide with  volumes. The volumes, of course, are also a proxy for value. Let's first have a look at Chemicals. With t he  investment decision that we made today on the new cracker in Pennsylvania and the brownfield project that we  already have underway in the Gulf Coast and in China, we should have 8 million tonnes per year on stream at the  start of the new decade. That's a 30% increase of where we are today. And secondly, if I look at Deepwater, pretty  much driven by Brazil, of course, and the Gulf of Mexico, we expect to see production of at least 900,000 barrels a  day early in the new decade. And let me stress that all the growth that I'm talking about here is from just  discovered established position, so not something that we are still dependent on exploration success for or  business development. This is already within the Company. It's a matter of activating and deliver ing it.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: And in New Energies, of course, we have been investing in renewables such as wind and biofuels for many years.  We even have a small solar business, not well known to many of you. But New Energies contains more than these  traditional renewables. The theme also encompasses the digital revolution, so more electrification, especially in  transport, more customers with a wider choice in the energy mix. And we've made the decision that we will build  on our existing foundations in these renewable areas and that we will pay a lot more emphasis on New Energies,  going forward.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: And we've really identified three areas in this space as good opportunities for our competency set. First of all, new  fuels for mobility, think here of biofuels but also hydrogen, where we are still one of the leading companies;  integrated energy solutions, so for example, wind and solar energy, which can partner very well with natural gas to  tackle intermittency issues; and completely new business models for energy, connecting customers with  digitization and decentralization of energy systems. And Maarten will cover this in a bit more detail in one of the  subsequent sessions.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: And first of all, over the last few years, and then also you can see where we expect to be in the first part of the next  decade. Now, let me say again, maybe against better judgment, that these are not targets. The chart show the  possible shape of the Company, and this is at a modest recovery in oil prices. So we're looking at $60 oil here. And,  of course, the environment could play a very different – could play out very differently than what we are expecting  and presenting here today. But around the end of the decade, we expect to have reduced debt by this time, of  course. And the free cash flow that you see here should be part of the dividend and the buy back program of the  Company.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: The cash engines would have stabilized in their portfolios. The main divestments and ramp -ups are behind us.  The growth priorities, Deepwater, delivering free cash flow; Chemicals still in the tail-end of the growth mode that  it will be in. But it will have a $3 billion per year or more free cash flow potential [indiscernible] (32:18) a little bit  further out. And you will see the shales and the new energy portfolios ready for more substantial growth  investment if we decide, indeed, to take up that step.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Now, it's important to recognize that we have substantial essence at our hands today to deliver all of this. So we're  not dependent on new developments here. As some of you may say, 2020 is a long way away. And some of you  may emphasize that the reality is that we are still in an oil market downturn and we are. And, therefore, I think it's  also important that we update you on our plans for the nearer term, for the financial levers that we are pulling for  the Company today. And Simon will update you on this next as well as on the details of the integration with BG.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: The strategy, the financial framework, they are designed to manage through a multi-year macro price cycle. That  can be a short-term cycle, but we have a multi-decade investment and returns program. We have to balance near- term affordability and the cost trends that we see with the fundamentally much longer term nature of the industry  that we're in. Our financial framework is and will remain a key element of the overall strategy. It is embedded in it.  The balance sheet must support the dividend and the reinvestment through the low point in the oil cycle, which  closes where we are today, and conversely the strategy must support the balance sheet.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: The strategy that Ben just outlined defines our intention to generate sufficient free cash flow of the lower end of  the oil price cycle to cover the cash dividend. We should not be dependent on anything more than a normal level  of divestments to meet this objective. And the portfolio Ben just spoke about, numbers you've seen, should deliver  this outcome by the end of this decade.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: We must set investment levels accordingly for the foreseeable future. That means between $25 billion and $30  billion a year, or lower level that the oil price remains at the current level for some time. It is an eight -month high  today, by the way, if any of you have noticed.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: The return on capital across the totality of the portfolio needs to be double digits at the lower end of the cycle and  in the mid-teens average through the cycle. And the three-year average free cash flow, including divestment now,  that should exceed cash dividends, whatever the price is. We have to go with the environment as it is, not how we  like it to be, or how we might have planned it to be.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So following an acquisition with an enterprise value of some $67 billion, and in a low oil price world, clearly, these  metrics are different, the metrics I just outlined is the historical framework, they are different from the recent  history, but they are as we expected.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So turning now to the financial framework. There's no change in the priorities for cash flow that we set following  the announcement of the BG acquisition, which were actually a change on the previous comment: reducing debt,  paying the dividend, followed by a balance between capital investment and share buybacks. We committed to at  least $25 billion of buybacks in the period 2017 through 2020, subject to debt reduction and some recovery in oil  prices. We aim to use in the shorter term extra cash reduction to strengthen the credit metrics to the desired  levels. And while these are complex, gearing around 20% on the balance sheet is a reasonable proxy. And once we  get there or see our way through 2020, then we will most likely turn the scrip off first. We then, and this is  sequential thinking, are likely to move to buybacks. We will not let investments exceed $30 billion before we've  executed a material part of that buyback program. This is going to take some years overall. But as we've said  before, we will do whatever it takes to have a sustainable financial framework in whatever the actual oil price  environment is, and we will stick with these priorities.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So we're pulling all levers to manage the financial framework through this downcycle. And fundamentally, much  of this is really important opportunity, and it turned out to be maybe a bigger opportunity than we thought to  improve our own underlying competitive performance, irrespective of oil prices. We are focusing on four  levers:  asset sales, capital spending, operating cost reduction, and delivering the new projects from both portfolios that  will add significant cash flow. Of course, there is a fifth lever that's not on the slide, and that is the oil price, which  we don't control. But now, a $10 move annually on the oil price can drive the cash flow up or down by $5 billion.  That sensitivity should and probably will increase over time, very strong leverage. What we're actually planning on  within the Company and underpinning with the messages and the data we share today is a low $40s oil price this  year, $50 next year, and the mid $60s by 2018.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: I'll now run through the levers in a little more detail before closing. Firstly, on the asset sales. We're using the  sales as an important element of the strategy to reshape the company not just by reducing debt but remember  growth to [ph] 7 5% (46:09). Up to 10% of Shell's oil and gas production is earmarked for sale, including several  country positions. Y ou see on the slide 5 to 10 country positions and selected midstream advanced stream assets.  This is a value-driven not a time-driven divestment program. And, of course, it's an integral element of Shell  portfolio improvement plan, underpinning the shape Ben has just shared.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Asset sales are an important part of starting to reduce the debt, and the timing of the divestments does depend to  some extent on oil prices and, hence, the external asset market. But we're not planning for any asset sales at  giveaway prices. Don't think you can come and get a distressed asset from us. So there's no reason today to think  we can't deliver the $30 billion. But if it takes a bit longer to preserve shareholder value, then so be it.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Then moving on to project flow. We see this is, perhaps, the underappreciated lever that will make a difference.  Delivering the oil and gas, because it's all we actually do as part of our – which is our core business model and it  does drive new cash flow and free cash flow over time. The portfolio is geared to give an improvement in  production and, most importantly, to cash flow from operations and free cash flow in 2017 and beyond. That's  pretty much what Shell was prior to the BG deal.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: By 2018, so that's the year when we want to see some recovery in the price, start-ups since 2014 or anything we've  started up last year or later in the BG plus Shell portfolio, should be producing around 1 million barrels of oil  equivalent per day, 1 million barrels. And more importantly, a generally high-margin barrel with price upside. So  great opportunity set, and it's been considerably enhanced by the BG acquisition. This also [indiscernible] (48:54)  earlier delivery.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So as an indication for you, and you might like to include this in some of your modeling, we expect to see an  average cash operating cost in these projects, 1 million barrels, around $15 per barrel of oil equivalent, probably  reducing as we ramp up as well. And then average statutory tax rate of around 35% from the growth profile. Now,  that compares to maybe around 50% on average for Shell. And I think this quality of barrel is sometimes missing  in the market valuations.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Exploration spend. Essentially, we are embedded in these numbers amounting to substantial reduction in the  exploration spend, but also a change in the priorities. Going forward, we'd expect spends around $2.5 billion a  year on the combined Shell and BG portfolio. And that's a reduction of around $3 billion or 50% from last year,  just from 2015 alone. What's driving this is focus on lowering costs, embedding the BG synergies, many of which  were made choices between the two portfolios, which high-grades the portfolio but also, of course, the exit from  the Alaska offshore activity within Shell. There's also a shift in the spend that we will make in emphasis towards  producing basins, growing out from where we're already in a strong position.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Within that totality of looking at new opportunity, the BG acquisition and our own recent exploration find, they  just mean simply that we rely less on exploration in the near term, medium future than we have did in the past.  The exploration that we do spend will be around 80% targeted on the Heartlands, the basins we're already  present, including Deepwater. The program is essentially rightsized for the combined portfolio. We're reducing  the major Frontier exploration spend, not just Alaska, but we are keeping very selected positions, where we have  the geological insight and retaining options of low cost elsewhere where we're able to do that.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So a little bit more detail on the capital investment. And Ben has already set out the framework. We will manage to  $25 billion to $30 billion per year up to the end of the decade. We will improve capital efficiency, and we aim for  more predictability in the flow of projects. This year's investment, 2016, expect it to be $29 billion. That's 35%  lower already than the pre-deal period of 2014, if we combine Shell and BG. In the current prevailing low oil price,  we will continue to drive the capital spending down towards the bottom end of this range. But in a higher oil price  future, we'll cap the spending at the top end of the range. So the bottom end is price -sensitive, the top isn't. So it's  an absolute limit.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: The track record here demonstrates we can respond quickly to the macro by reducing investment. And as Ben  explained, between $25 billion to $30 billion per year is sufficient to maintain the portfolio with a mo derate  growth potential and does assume that we can deliver some material capital efficiencies. If we need to go lower, we  will. We can do that through further supply chain reduction [indiscernible] (53:44) linked to lower oil prices, but  also by deferring or cancelling further projects, if we need to.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So just as a reminder, some 40% of our total operating costs are direct staff-related costs. There are significant  reduction programs already underway here still to deliver to the bottom line. These are tough. These are difficult  leadership and management actions, but the whole of the organization is doing a great job in terms of delivering  this in an effective and respectful way.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So this final slide from me just summarizes the potential from the levers that we're pulling. And let's just not  forget the impact that the oil prices can also have. Last year in 2015, the oil price was $52 on average. The  combined companies, you just do pro forma combination, together delivered some $11 billion of free cash flow  before dividend in that 12-month period. That figure is coincidentally, but basically, the same as we would expect  for the combined cash dividend in 2016. So we cover the cash dividend at $52. There's no doubt 2016 is a  challenging year, more challenging than last year as the oil price is lower despite today's recovery. So including all  the deal effects and the reduction in the cash flow that we saw in the first quarter, that was partly oil price, $34,  and negative working capital effects, it's going to be a tough year.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: With that, let me pass you over first to John on the Downstream, followed by Andy on the Upstream, and then  Maarten on the Integrated Gas. John?

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director
texts.text: Thank you very much, Simon, and it's good to be able to update you today here on the Downstream in Shell. Our  priority remains the improvement of our financial performance, and we have to remind ourselves that the  Downstream is an intensely competitive sector with fundamentally very narrow margins. And as Ben indicated  earlier on, we have been restructuring our portfolio in the Downstream now for some time, and the nature of the  asset market has meant really that that process could not be instant. But we have made some $12 billion in  divestments over the last five years. And in the last decade, we exited from 22% of our refining capacity. That's  900,000 barrels per day.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director
texts.text: The improvements I've just described has helped Downstream to deliver more than $9 billion of clean earnings,  $11 billion of cash flow from operations, $7.5 billion of free cash flow, as well as 19% retu rn from the Downstream  over the last 12 months. Our marketing activities are providing a resilient and steadily increasing stream of  earnings. And whilst Refining & Trading, which are intrinsically more volatile, are working well together as an  integrated business, they are also enhancing our returns and cash flow.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director
texts.text: Restructuring our underperforming parts of the company is an important lever to improve our financial  performance, and I'd like to talk about that now. As you can see on this slide, we have already had substantial  successes in this area. Despite a refining footprint that is smaller by 20% on crude intake and the marketing  footprint that is reduced by 30% in volume since 2007, the Downstream clean earnings have improved by $1.5  billion, and this is 23% higher. And we picked a timeframe here where refining margins were almost identical  during those periods.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director
texts.text: Shell premium fuels such as V-Power are the world's most widely sold premium grades. They're available in 68  markets globally. And Shell's premium lubes, which are marketed under the Helix, Pennzoil or Rotella brands  continue to show very strong returns and increasing market penetration.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director
texts.text: Chemicals is now a growth priority for Shell as you've already heard. And petrochemicals is the fastest growing  hydrocarbon demand sector, with an annual growth of 3.7% over the last 10 years and we expect this to continue.  And Shell's chemical strategy focuses on activities with a clear competitive advantage. We optimize returns from  using different feedstocks, investing in our existing first-class footprint and continuing to focus on enhancing our  customer relationships and also our customer services.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director
texts.text: The global chemicals portfolio now offers both a regional balance and a balanced exposure to both gas and liquids,  as well as exposure to many different value chains. And this ensures that we can capture good value and  good  margin conditions in a range of volatile market conditions.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director
texts.text: With a competitive edge in chemical feedstocks underpinned by strong product portfolio and proprietary Shell  technology, the business is entering a new period of growth. And let me give you some examples of that. For  example, in the Gulf Coast, we've decided to expand our Chemicals footprint at the manufacturing site in Geismar  in Louisiana, making the site the largest alpha olefins producer in the world.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director
texts.text: And in China where Shell and CNOOC took the final investment decision in the first quarter this year to expand  the existing petrochemical complex. This project will increase ethylene capacity by more than 1 million tonnes a  year, about double the current capacity which we have in that location. It will become the largest petrochemical  site in China offering a platform for continued future growth with CNOOC as a major strategic partner for Shell.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director
texts.text: And today, we are excited to announce the final investment decision of our petrochemicals project in  Pennsylvania, in the U.S. This site will use ethane from the lowest cost shale gas basin in North America to  produce polyethylene at world scale. The new facility will generate 1.5 million tonnes of ethylene capacity per year,  which, of course, is converted into polyethylene. It will be the most cost competitive polyethylene producer in the  U.S.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director
texts.text: And you have three components of competitive advantage over the U.S. Gulf Coast investment. And let me  describe those to you. Firstly, we will use locally sourced ethane with a very significant supply cost advantage.  Secondly, a location advantage as it sits right in the demand center of U.S. polyethylene. More than 70% of the  North American polyethylene market sits within a 7 00-mile radius of Pittsburg. And customers will benefit from  shorter supply chain with more dependable supplies compared to the options in the Gulf Coast.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director
texts.text: And the third competitive advantage is economic development, job creation and investment incentives from the  State of Pennsylvania, as the project adds new growth and of course jobs to that region. Main construction will  start in about 18 months time as we manage capital affordability in the current low oil price environment. And  commercial production is expected to begin hopefully in the next decade.

texts.speaker: Andrew Brown
texts.profession: Director-Upstream International
texts.text: The conventional oil and gas business is a cash engine for Shell. It's a legacy portfolio of assets. Think of more  traditional businesses like in the North Sea, Nigeria, Malaysia, Oman and Brunei, as well as the more recent  positions such as in Iraq and Kazakhstan. These are positions that need to deliver resilient and attractive returns  and free cash flow.

texts.speaker: Andrew Brown
texts.profession: Director-Upstream International
texts.text: And it's here in particular where we have opportunities for asset sales in the enlarged Shell-BG portfolio to high- grade this portfolio. Deep water is one of our company's two growth priorities. It contains distinctive and  advantaged assets and acreage positions in the Gulf of Mexico, Brazil, Nigeria and Malaysia. The strategy here is  to develop a material, attractive and resilient business over the coming years. Ultimately, deep water should  become a cash engine. And thirdly, shale in the Americas. Today, this is a restructured and more competitive  portfolio. And we're maturing it into a new growth priority for the 2020.

texts.speaker: Andrew Brown
texts.profession: Director-Upstream International
texts.text: The financial results you see in the Upstream reflect the very different stages of maturity in these three themes. Oil  sands are in these numbers too, which we report in Upstream is governed by John. Conventional oil and gas is  typically a business with a large cash flow and higher returns. Deep water and particularly shales have generated  low earnings as you would expect in growth-orientated portfolios with relatively high unit depreciation charges.

texts.speaker: Andrew Brown
texts.profession: Director-Upstream International
texts.text: The low oil price is a significant opportunity for us in Upstream to drive change throughout the organization,  delivering lower costs through operational excellence and also leveraging the supply chain. We have reduced  Upstream costs by $1.2 billion in 2015 or 8%. This includes a job reduction of at least 5,000 staff and contractors.  In 2016, we expect to absorb BG's costs with no increase overall against the 2015 total, and a further underlying  reduction of $2.3 billion or 15%.

texts.speaker: Andrew Brown
texts.profession: Director-Upstream International
texts.text: I also want to make clear that particularly following the BG deal, we're having a very close look at the tail of the  conventional oil and gas portfolio. This means dilutions and asset sales from this portfolio, which is third part of  this $30 billion divestment plan for the company.

texts.speaker: Andrew Brown
texts.profession: Director-Upstream International
texts.text: Now, let's look at the three themes in more detail, starting with shales. Now this is a portfolio that's really been  built up since 2008 through a series of acquisitions and land deals or by a period of drilling and early production,  which is basically the shale's equipment of exploration.

texts.speaker: Andrew Brown
texts.profession: Director-Upstream International
texts.text: Now over the last two years, we've seen significant portfolio reduction, cost savings, and performance  improvements in these North American [ph] shale provinces (01:19:11). Today, we have around 12 billion barrels  of resources and potential. This is over 750 million barrels more than in 2013 despite the fact that more than half  the number of plays we're in. Today, we're focused on continuing to increase the profitability of this business by  further reducing cost and proving recovery factors. We have achieved a 70% re duction in direct overhead costs  since 2013 and a 50% reduction in drilling and completion costs for liquid-rich shales, again since 2013. We're  working hard to further enhance our performance and take full advantage of the sweet spot areas where we can  harvest the potential of these assets through increased investments, through into the next decade.

texts.speaker: Andrew Brown
texts.profession: Director-Upstream International
texts.text: Now, turning to our growth priority, deep water. Shell has an advantaged portfolio and a strong track record in  deep water. Our new projects are resilient across the cycle and competitive on the cost curves.

texts.speaker: Andrew Brown
texts.profession: Director-Upstream International
texts.text: On the development side, we're continuously driving down breakeven cost in deep water projects, both on projects  under construction as well as pre-FID projects. [indiscernible] (01:20:37) costs which have historically accounted  for about 50% of total project costs have come down significantly as we are drilling wells faster and with lower  spread rates. For example, in Bonga, in Nigeria, over the past two years, we delivered 21 wells with savings of over  $1 billion.

texts.speaker: Andrew Brown
texts.profession: Director-Upstream International
texts.text: And we now see average breakeven point in our pre-FID projects which are lower than the current oil price. Think  of an average breakeven level of $45 per barrel, and Shell's deep water volumes could grow to over 900,000  barrels a day by the early 2020s. This is not growth for growth's sake, but we expect these deals to deliver resilient  returns and free cash flows once they ramp up, and to make a considerable contribution to Shell's bottom line.

texts.speaker: Andrew Brown
texts.profession: Director-Upstream International
texts.text: One of them, Cidade de Saquarema, is on its way to its offshore positions on Lula, as planned, and will start  producing shortly. The reservoir performance in the pre-salt is exceeding our expectations, with the top 10  individual wells flowing at over 35,000 barrels a day on average per well. Across all the wells producing of the  seven FPSOs, the average well rates are around 25,000 barrels per day. That's the average well rate for those wells  across those seven FPSOs with production steady. And in the pre-salt projects under construction, we see  breakeven prices under $40 on average, as a result of this significant well flow rates and competitive project  delivery and operating costs.

texts.speaker: Andrew Brown
texts.profession: Director-Upstream International
texts.text: Now if I turn to Gulf of Mexico. In Q1, Shell had over 270,000 barrels a day on-stream here, and our production  continues to grow in the Gulf of Mexico by ramping up Mars B and Cardamom. We're working hard to reduce  operating costs and improve uptime in the Gulf. For example in 2015, we restarted four shut -in wells in the Mars  Basin, which has since delivered 0.5 million barrels of oil equivalent.

texts.speaker: Andrew Brown
texts.profession: Director-Upstream International
texts.text: And on the project delivery front, Stones, our first FPSO in the Gulf, is scheduled to start up in the second half of  2016. And Appomattox which was sanctioned last y ear will come on-stream towards the end of the decade.  Beyond this, we continue to see considerable potential to tiebacks such as North Kepler into Na Kika, Kaikias into  Ursa and new hubs such as Vito and more exploration. I think there's great potential for Shell remaining in this  high-margin province.

texts.speaker: Andrew Brown
texts.profession: Director-Upstream International
texts.text: Let me now update you in the conventional oil and gas portfolio, one of the Shell's cash engines. There's a large  range of assets here ranging from selective growth positions such as in Kazakhstan and West of Schiehallion in the  UK to late like positions like places like the North Sea or New Zealand or Gabon. Our growth project in  conventional oil and gas should add some 250,000 barrels per day of production in the next few years. This  combined with lower spend should improve our performance in free cash flow and returns. Conventional oil and  gas is as much about costs, uptime and portfolio management as it is about competitive growth projects.

texts.speaker: Andrew Brown
texts.profession: Director-Upstream International
texts.text: Exploration is an important element of Upstream and we have added 6.5 billion barrels of contingent resources  over the last six years, including 1.5 billion from deals with a finding cost of around $4 per barrel and an average  success rate of 44%. Most of these barrels are within Shell's Heartlands where we have infrastructure and detailed  sub-surface knowledge facilitating early monetization. Shell's recent successes, especially in the Gulf of Mexico  and Malaysia, demonstrates there's still running room in the producing basins of our Heartlands where large,  high-value discoveries can still be made.

texts.speaker: Andrew Brown
texts.profession: Director-Upstream International
texts.text: In the GOM, more than 60% of the 1.2 billion barrels of oil equivalent discovered in the last six years is already  post-FID and 10% is already on production. And following the BG deal and our exit from Alaska, exploration  spend has reduced to around $2.5 billion per year on our combined Shell and BG portfolio. We have reset the  strategy. The majority of our exploration dollars will be focused on sustaining our Heartland positions with near  field targets and selected wells aimed at new geological plays with material potential, both in the Heartlands but  also a few in the Frontier basins.

texts.speaker: Andrew Brown
texts.profession: Director-Upstream International
texts.text: Let me sum up. There are three very distinctive elements in the Upstream business today with different time scale  to profitability. Running through all of this is a major performance drive focusing on costs, uptime and breakeven  levels. We're aiming at a breakeven level which is lower than $45 in the new deep water fields, 50% or more of  reduction in liquid-rich shale well costs with breakeven prices now falling fast and opportunities for drilling and  sweet spot increasing, and a major drive to reduce cost and sell tail end positions in the conventional oil and gas  business.

texts.speaker: Andrew Brown
texts.profession: Director-Upstream International
texts.text: I'm looking forward to talk to you more about this later in the day. And now Maarten Wetselaar will talk about  Integrated Gas and New Energies. Maarten, over to you.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thank you, Andy, and good afternoon. It's good to be here and talk to you today about the Integrated Gas  business, and particularly how we are changing the priorities in that business to focus on growing free cash flow  and growing returns going forward.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Shell is the IOC leader in LNG and gas to liquids. The acquisition of BG underpins our leading role as the – both  the leading producer and the leading marketer of LNG amongst all independents. It also accelerates the growth  strategy that would otherwise have taken into the next decade to put the energy business up to scale. Today, Shell  is present across the full value chains that the energy business covers globally, and what is still the fastest -growing  sector of the natural gas market.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And in gas-to-liquids, we take gas to the full value chain again into our oil products business as you saw John with  GTL into lubricants, attracting an increasingly growing premium over the oil price.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Going forward, our primary focus now shifts to growing our free cash flow and growing our returns, and to  creating and serving new premium gas demand. Whilst at the same time, we moderate our capital spending,  spend it wisely and moderate a base of new FIDs. And in so doing, we will optimize for growing free cash flow and  our returns.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We've also established a new growth opportunity called New Energies in Shell, that will explore and invest in new  low carbon energy opportunities, that in many ways complement our Integrated Gas business. It's an exciting and  fast moving landscape. We put a lot more emphasis on the options in this business going forward. And I'll go into  details, in bit of detail in the business a bit later on.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Winning through all of these, we have a major drive including with the BG synergies to push down the cost and  optimize the margins in our business. Let me talk first about the recent financial performance of Integrated Gas.  On this slide, you can see the earnings and return profile. And the impact of the lower oil and gas prices are clearly  visible in the trends. But it's also visible within the last 12 months, with oil price averaging $48, this business  generated $8 billion cash flow, and a 6% clean return on capital employed which illustrates the resilience of the  business model and the portfolio that we hold and most of it is pre-BG of course.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: With BG in the fold, the Integrated Gas capital employed now stands at approximately $90 billion, which includes  about $20 billion of capital under construction not yet generating earnings or cash. And indeed with $90 billion,  this now stands at about 30% of Shell's balance sheet.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, we expect to deliver a robust and competitive cash flow and returns from that substantial balance sheet. And  we will build one strong legacy of operational performance in our Shell LNG plants that typically operate at  availabilities in the top quartile range of our industry, when we look at benchmarks.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Let me now turn to LNG supply and demand dynamics before we turn into the Shell portfolio. The global LNG  market is growing and continuous to grow and diversify, with more and more countries importing LNG, new  customers in existing importing countries choosing LNG, and LNG accessing more market sectors such as  transport.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In fact since 2000, LNG demand has grown by about 6% per year every year, last year reaching 250 million  tonnes. 30 countries now importing LNG with about 20 exporters, and this is expected to grow to 50 and 25  respectively early in the next decade. With these trends in mind, we expect global LNG demand to double from  today by 2030 to 500 million tonnes, assuming there is sufficient investment and supply to meet the demand.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Those are the long term trends. But as for the nearer term, where I think a lot of the interest and attention in the  room will be focused, we expect the LNG market to be supply driven for the rest of this decade, into the early parts  of the next. And this is down to more than 100 million tonnes of LNG liquefaction volume under construction or  recently coming on-stream, coming into the market primarily from North Africa – North America and Australia.  And despite that most of this volume has been contracted either to end user or to portfolio players, this is leading  to a near term softening of the LNG market.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Let me now update you on the LNG portfolio that we in Shell have today. As I've mentioned, the acquisition of BG  further strengthens our lead in this global LNG market. [ph] I think GE did (01:33:11) Shell plays an aggregator  role whereby on top of our own liquefaction volumes we buy third party volume under long term contracts often  from other joint venture partners. And we market it to our worldwide customer base. We also purchase and sell  spot LNG volumes to further optimize our business through logistics and market optimizations.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Y ou can see on this chart that the gap between the LNG that we liquefied ourselves and the LNG that we sell has  grown over the last two years and the trend increases with the BG in our portfolio, the difference between the red  and the yellow line. It emphasizes the increased importance of providing flexibility to secure new market positions  in this growing market. This is a business that benefits from scale and diversity of source end market positions as  it increases the number of options that we can trade around and optimize globally.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Turning to pricing, here's a snapshot of the LNG contracts that we have in place in 2015. The vast majority of Shell  and BG combined LNG is currently sold on long term contracts here defined as between two years and 20 years  duration, linked to oil and gas prices, 75% oil, 25% gas, as you can more or less see on the right hand of this slide.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, some volumes are sold on a short term basis or spot sales. They are mostly offset by spot purchases, an  optimization game that we play. Now remember that this is not a deep or liquids spot market, like you see in oil or  other liquids markets or commodities. Most of these spot volumes actually originate are the retails of LNG cargoes  originally delivered in the long term agreements between suppliers and customers.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: As of today, looking forward to 2020, our portfolio five years away is about 10% unsold. So we will pursue new  long term sales agreements or keep that volume available for spot trading and we have a choice to make that.  Now, the fundamentals of this market are changing, but remain robust. LNG producers continue to look for long  term off-take from credit worthy buyers to independent financing of their projects. And LNG buyers are looking  for competitive and reliable supply constructs that provide increasing flexibility and different pricing constructs  that Shell is very, very well positioned to supply into this market.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And let me also stress that in this short term market, Shell has sold almost all of its LNG portfolio already on long  term contracts. So we have limited exposure to this softening spot price that we see in the market.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: On to developing new gas demand, at Shell, we actively develop and secure new gas markets and outlets for our  gas. We already have capacity rights of around 40 million tonnes in 10 re gas terminals around the world, and we  are targeting new terminals particularly in the emerging LNG markets.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now as well as pursuing further classic long-term sales agreements with big customers, we're also going further  down the value chain behind the terminals, securing new gas demand and using our marketing and power trading  capabilities in order to increase our market.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We're also part of the creation of a new segment for LNG, of LNG to transport. LNG for transport, particularly  heavy trucking and the shipping market is a very promising and potentially material segment that Shell is well  placed to serve as we know most of the customers through John's business.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, turning to our portfolio of new supply options. We have a very rich and diverse level of opportunities for  both greenfield and brownfield LNG growth. Here's an overview of the combined BG and Shell portfolio. Our on - stream LNG sales are in the [ph] mid-50s in terms of (01:37:55) million tonnes per year comprising of about 31  million tonnes of LNG that we liquefy, about 18 million tonnes of long-term supply contracts and the balance in  spot trading, if we look at last year.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We've slowed down the pace of new investment decisions in this business and we're redesigning projects to offer  even better returns. This in order to help manage Shell's affordability overall, but also to make sure that we  remain competitive in evolving LNG market, and that we only add the most competitive supply positions to our  portfolio.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In the last year, we've already delayed more than 3 million tonnes of LNG, FIDs. And our plan is to continue to  slow down the pace of new investment. And a strategy to improve free cash flow and returns from  Integrated Gas.  But it will take time to rebalance this mix, with several projects already underway post-FIDs and some important  investment decisions coming up quickly. But the intention here is clear.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, before I close, I want to make some comments for the New Energies business. Shell's capital employed in  new energy activities is around $1.7 billion today, mostly in biofuels. And we are currently spending around $200  million a year on research, development and very selective investment in low carbon o pportunities. We think that  a position in low carbon opportunities or renewables will be very important for Shell and its shareholders in the  long term as the energy transition unfolds in years and decades to come.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now we are determined to be winning company in that transition, and believe energy – new energies will play an  important role in that. But it will take time. Our focus will be largely on asset light plays that share adjacencies  with our current business such as location, adjacent value chains, maybe existing relationships or ease of fit with  existing infrastructure where we already have an energy business. And all these elements that Shell already have,  can be a key source of advantage, of competitive advantage for a new energy business in Shell compared to  specialist investor in this industry who doesn't have these adjacencies.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: With new fuels, we've already invested in third-generation but also second-generation biofuels made from non- edible plants and crop waste. We've also invested in hydrogen as a transport fuel with a joint venture in  [indiscernible] (01:40:25) and options in the U.S.A. and UK. As for Integrated Energy solutions, Shell has interest  in wind business on-shore in the U.S., offshore in the Netherlands, there is a major renewables power trader in  North America.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We're also exploring ways to deploy solar technology into our operations, lowering the carbon intensity of our  operations, but also helping broaden our offering in Downstream gas and power markets. Natural gas can of  course be a perfect partner to the solar and wind power generation opportunities as we aim to deliver non- intermittent power to customers.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Director-Integrated Gas and New Energies, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And finally, the third leg is that we aim to deliver [indiscernible] (01:41:10) and customer reach to maximize the  opportunities that are offered by the increased digitalization and decentralization of energy offerings. So there's  some interesting opportunities we've developed here but it will take time, and we will manage the pace of  exposure to this business in accordance with our financial framework and the opportunities we find.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Okay. Simon, why don't you take the first one, and let me talk a little bit first about the second one. You're  absolutely right, Jon. This is going to be transformation. I hope the numbers will speak for themselves. If we are  indeed able to generate this type of financial outcome at a $60 oil environment at the end of the decade, this will  be a company that is financially a lot more resilient, a lot more attractive, and indeed a world-class investment  case.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So how much CapEx is going in to sustain versus growth. At the moment, you see from the slide it's around $10  billion, $11 billion a year plus exploration plus effectively what's going into the shale business is a couple of  billions, $2.5 billion exploration; a couple of billion on the shale.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: This strategy as we go forward, in part, is aiming to reduce that number, not so much on the shale and exploration  but on the stay in business CapEx. Remember, quite a large part of that is John's in the Downstream on the  refineries, distribution terminals, et cetera. So the divestment program has helped there. In the Upstream, a  similar approach will also help.

texts.speaker: Oswald Clint
texts.profession: Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you very much. Oswald Clint at Sanford Bernstein. Y eah, I guess a high level question first, Ben, please. The  CapEx ceiling comment, so I guess can you just clarify or confirm that you're really saying that no matter where  the oil price goes to, $30 billion is that cap and what is the process for maintaining that? I guess the skeptic will  think of higher oil prices and that number reaching that level at least if we look back through history. So maybe  give us some confidence in what's happening there to keep that at $30 billion on a go -forward level?

texts.speaker: Oswald Clint
texts.profession: Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: And then secondly, maybe a question for Maarten but I'm sure Simon has the numbers. But you spoke about the  scale benefits – the synergy benefits with LNG, trading benefits and transportation benefits, any idea, any ballpark  numbers that you can start to provide us for the LNG business joining up with BG please? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So now it becomes a matter of how quickly do cost deflate because that will still continue to happen. So if you see  continuous low oil prices, cost will continue to deflate and we will be able to trend it much more to the $25 billion  end of the range, and we probably will have to also for affordability reasons. We probably will have to go beyond  the $25 billion to lower numbers if we are looking at oil prices as we are having today, but we will be able also  there to get more bang for the buck. Capital intensities will improve at lower oil price levels as well.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Y eah. If oil prices will go up, of course we will have plenty more opportunities knocking at the door and say, I am a  competitive prospect, please sanction me. And then it will be all down to not only our willpower to stay at $30  billion, that's easy enough to just say, this is what we're going to do, but also how do we then sequence the  opportunities in such a way that we will preserve as much possible. It's not just a matter of discarding a  competitive shift that we just don't want to do an investment decision on, but making sure that we smooth out the  capital problem so that we indeed cap at $30 billion and have that extra free cash flow available to fulfill the other  commitments that were part of the deal.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Thanks, Ben. The LNG opportunity, just briefly in terms of background. BG tended to build their LNG value chain  from the market backward to the supply and Shell historically built from supply forward into market. But over the  last few years, as it was laid out, Shell has been a bit more market-driven as well. So we've actually put together  now a fantastic portfolio of supply point market demand. And some level of flexibility and perhaps to join the two  and that is the core of the potential value that you note.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Thanks, Irene. Let me give Simon some time to work out the numbers there. Yeah. In principle, you're right. So we  have to see more from that Downstream portfolio. And I think we can. But it's also good to decompose the two  components of Downstream. So in oil products where we have a much lower investment load and a much more  sort of long-ranging business, yes, we should be able to get to strong double-digit returns at the bottom of the  cycle as well.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: They have to do with increasing standards of living. They have to do with trying to reach to two degree C world  warming target. A lot of it has to do with basically lowering carbon intensities, better insulation materials. You  heard John talk about alpha olefins. A lot of you may not know what alpha olefins are. Well, they are the stuff that  certain detergents that actually work also at very, very low temperatures. So it's these sort of things that will  continue to drive the growth for petrochemicals in the segment that we are invested in.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Thanks, and you'll all go home now and think about why your washing machine works at 40 degrees, not 140  degrees.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So one of the reasons we don't target proved reserve replacement, there's this every new barrels worth $10 and  every old one was worth $5, I only need to replace half the barrels for the same value. $15 cash was on those  projects effectively named projects that come on stream by 2018. Now, total average is just about $20 or has been  just about $20. It's coming down anyway. If you read the small print, in one of Andy's slides, I think, Andy, the UK  came from $60 a barrel to around $30. Sorry?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Now $20, now that's over the last week or two. So that's the pace of the progress that we're actually seeing. So the  whole portfolio is coming down from $20, the new barrels starts at $15 and should come down. The new barrels  again to be per quarter, also the portfolio may be between 25%, 30% of the portfolio. And it's likely that we divest  some of the higher unit cost activities as well.

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: Y eah. Hello. I wanted to ask you about few things. First of all, it's not a number that was mentioned today. But if I
texts.text: remember correctly, the total number of sort of planned job losses stands at 12,500. And if you look at Shell  altogether, the vast majority of the company works in the Downstream. But it makes sense given how low oil  prices is that the majority of this 12,500 will be in the Upstream. But if you start to put these numbers together,  you could see that the percentage job losses in the Upstream could be rather large. And I was wondering whether  if this is indeed correct, also what that means for the capabilities of the organization and how you managed the  associated risks that come with that.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Maarten, as he will look at developing his new Energy business, looking after how we do large scale wind projects,  or integrated solar and gas projects, will have the same pressures. We cannot work in the same sort of technical  assurance regime as we have on a deepwater level. So there will be new methods and new ways of working that  will have to come in. It's fantastic that we are doing it at the moment on the back of this integration that we are  seeing. Did I answer your second question?

texts.speaker: Iain Reid
texts.profession: Macquarie Capital (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Hi. It's Ian Reid from Macquarie. Just a question about disposals, I remember going back to the presentation in  November, you seemed to be quite bullish about your ability to do $30 billion. I think you said you have coverage  in terms of the people expressing interest of more than $30 billion. And you talked there about the potential of the  Midstream and infrastructure disposals. I kind of get the impression that you've got a little bit more cautious on  that. Obviously, the Upstream environment has done a bit of that, talking to potentially people who are buying  assets off you, they seemed to be telling us that we're not getting very far in talking to Shell about buying  Upstream assets. But also, what's going on in the kind of Midstream area, because that seems to be only area  which has got no other [indiscernible] (02:07:44).

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: And the expectation number is indeed $20 billion to $25 billion free cash flow at $60 oil. On top of it, whatever  number we think is reasonable for divestment, say another five, and that's probably even conservative, we have to  do a significant amount of ongoing portfolio maintenance also on a high graded portfolio. So I think indeed it is a  very, very robust number that we are looking at under very conservative circumstances.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
