In the USA, we are further down the track of  establishing a large power demand position, and we increasingly see opportunities for differentiated and branded  customer offerings, a game that Shell has a proven track record in.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Integrated Gas & New Energies Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Demand will drive our investment in generation capacity and storage capacity for low carbon source of power like  wind, solar, but also gas. Equity supply will be complemented with third-party supply. Capacity ownership will be  selective with the intent to create reliability and flexibility in our portfolio, and in the middle between our supply and  demand positions – between increasingly intermittent supply of renewables and increasing intermittent demand of  customers powering cars and homes, we will drive extra value through optimization of a portfolio of positions with  embedded optionality and flexibility. We will leverage our existing scale and expertise in this area to deliver value  and enhance our returns.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Integrated Gas & New Energies Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: But we also see Shell as being part of the response to energy poverty, one of the world's biggest energy  challenges. We aim to define and scale up a commercial solution to the problem that so many of the world's  citizens lack access to power. This is an emerging field with many technologies and business models starting to  deliver affordable off-grid solutions to a market of more than 1 billion people. We believe we can make a real  difference in this area and create shareholder value in the process.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Integrated Gas & New Energies Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, let's talk about capital and returns. We will only invest in New Energies where it makes sense and that is  commercial sense. Capital investment in New Energies will be between $1 billion and $2 billion a year for the rest  of this decade, part of which is likely to be inorganic to build positions. We will be focused and selective with this  investment and build a base from which to turn this business into a growth priority in the 2020s. We expect the  largest part of our investments in [ph] new energy (01:49:05) to go into power, where we will invest to gain  customer access and selectively pursue generation capacity ownership in solar, wind, and gas to create  integrated positions. Returns will be a key selection criteria, already in this emerging phase. For new fuels, we  expect downstream-like returns in the high teens. For power, we are seeking 8% to 12% equity returns with stable  and ratable cash flows.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Integrated Gas & New Energies Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We are stepping up our efforts in New Energies, an emerging opportunity that we target to turn into a growth  opportunity in the 2020s. We will be selective, disciplined, and commercial in our investment decisions, leveraging  the adjacencies with our existing businesses and existing competitive advantages and capabilities. We aim to  build a new value chain for Shell, leveraging our current strengths, acquiring new capabilities in the process, and  building a business that will help Shell thrive through the energy transition.

texts.speaker: Thomas Adolff
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: The second question maybe a quite random question. Is there an ideal balance between the size of the company  and the internal capabilities? Is it 85,000 people, 60 million in LNG supply, 3 million in refining capacity et cetera?  What is the right balance, if there is a balance?

texts.speaker: Thomas Adolff
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And finally, just on the IMO regulation, is this a net benefit financially to the organization? Now, the question  maybe not just on refining, in refining, you may be processing more sour crude, therefore, it's a positive in  upstream. I don't know what happens to the realization. And in LNG, are you shifting away from JCC because  JCC is sour [ph] and it's not going (01:52:17) for Brent indexation? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In terms of IMO, yeah, we expect that to be a net benefit for some time. But we also believe, by the way, that the  market will quite rapidly respond to the shifts that you will see in the different refining cracks. And, as a matter of  fact, any sort of big differential between fuel and diesel will probably quickly close in the years to come. But there  will be some transient effects. It's factored into some of our forward-looking economics, but it's not a major effect.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: What I do believe though is that increasingly also, you will see shipping sector go to cleaner fuels like natural gas,  and the opportunities that Maarten mentioned in terms of penetrating LNG into shipping, but also in land  transport, I think has probably a bigger effect than the effect IMO will have on our refining footprint.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I think what we have been doing, and I think this is what I said earlier on in my part of the presentation as well,  and I hope it came through when my colleagues talked about different businesses. We have worked incredibly  hard on improving the clarity for each of the businesses that we have. And the first step in that of course was to  sort of clearly delineate what are the main strategic themes of the company and what purpose do they have in the  overall framework of running the company. And of course, running an oil products business is different than  running a deep-water business, it's different again than chemicals and certainly New Energies.

texts.speaker: Theepan Jothilingam
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane BNP Paribas
texts.text: Yeah. Hi. It's Theepan from Exane. Just a follow-up on the trigger for the buyback. I think in the past, you've  talked about line of sight for the Scrip removal. I just want to understand how do we see that trigger precisely in  terms of – is it 20% AA rating then we can see a buyback in place? And your free cash flow above a certain oil  price gives you that buy back.

texts.speaker: Jon Rigby
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd.
texts.text: The second question is just on the Downstream, I'm not expecting you to tell me like an oil price you do in the  Upstream. But can you at least triangulate where you think things like refining margins are going to be visibly  maybe the last two or three years? We can actually get some idea about the operating environment that you're  assuming in terms of the cash flow generation.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Okay. If you don't mind taking the financial questions, I will talk a little bit about refining margins. Jon, I always  say, I don't want to predict the oil price because, I will end up looking like a fool. I think predicting refining margins  is even harder. I think there is going to be considerable volatility still in refining margins to come. We've seen  indeed bit of a good run and it may well be indeed that we will see another downward lag in the years to come.  Much of course is, again it's a supply and demand picture or an availability of refining capacity picture versus  demand. Demand, of course, has been growing strongly. Low oil prices has meant that oil products demand has  gone up quite considerably, particularly also in emerging economies. Think of place like India seeing tremendous  amount of growth in diesel and gasoline but also in other emerging markets.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And we see that is sort of the big growth wave of refineries coming on stream. [indiscernible] (02:08:12) is sort of  coming a little bit to an end as well but not entirely. So, you could argue that maybe in the sort of near term,  there's a slight tightening and high utilization levels of refineries. But then again, you have to overlay on top of  that, how the energy transition is changing things too.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And altogether, that makes for almost and equally unpredictable mixture of where things will go. And the other  thing to bear in mind, of course, is that a lot of it will also be driven by how quickly will refineries go out of fashion  for people who own them. And quite often these are long, difficult, painful processes, quite often of course, with  government intention sitting behind them as well. So, altogether, hard to predict where it will go. But what we have  said, our refining footprint needs to be resilient in whatever the outcome is. It's a bit like the overall story for oil  and gas prices.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The second point on the ROACE piece, for each of our businesses, we look at it at the business level because  that's more appropriate. So, we look at chemicals. We look at integrated gas. We look at deep-water. And we're  looking for those businesses to generate the most competitive returns for their sector. The 10% is the average.  That's important, but I think it's more important in terms of how we're trying to drive returns is ensuring that we get  the most competitive returns from each of our businesses.

texts.speaker: Oswald Clint
texts.profession: Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Yeah. Thank you very much. Oswald Clint of Bernstein. I want to maybe ask a question about LNG, please.  You're speaking about advising governments of a gas policy, talked about the coal in China. And so that's clear  you believe in gas demand in China. [indiscernible] (02:17:03) give us a chart on the lack of FIDs within the LNG  space. I mean do you have the confidence to start moving forward with some of those LNG project sanctions  earlier than the kind of the rest of the group, the rest of the industry, given your insights into Asian gas demand.?

texts.speaker: Oswald Clint
texts.profession: Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: And also kind of linked to that, I see comments here about buy versus build when it comes to LNG. So, is this also  a bit of a move here where you're willing to start buying more and more LNG rather than building it, kind of  connect it?

texts.speaker: Oswald Clint
texts.profession: Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: And then secondly, just on the power or the New Energies' perspective, the 8% to 12% returns in power, I mean  I'm not a utility expert but normally we think of lower levels of returns in power. Can you maybe walk us through or  explain how you could get to 12% return when it comes to these investments in power? Please. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Okay. Let me take the returns question. Would you like to comment on the energy a bit?

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Sure.  Ben van Beurden  Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc  A  I think, Oswald, it's very important to – I'm sorry for picking on some of your word choices, it's very important to  recognize what it is that we try to do in new energies. We don't try to be utility. We like to be an integrated power  player and part of that means, if you have to, in the build generating capacity as well, probably not entirely  covering the shorts that we will have in the overall power market. But the value that we are going to reap from this  business is not just a utility return that you will have like your boring old utility that your parent used to know.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And therefore, the returns that we like to have from that integrated power chain are indeed going to be 8% to 12%  return on equity. I think that is absolutely doable. Can you get that by just holding a portfolio of PPAs? Probably  not. But that's also not what we endeavor to do.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So, in terms of the LNG market, I think you've heard we're very bullish on the market. We believe in the  fundamentals of what will drive the growth of LNG. We expect it to essentially double by 2030. We have a suite of  great options for new supply. Maarten pointed those out around the globe.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The other piece is indeed timing it with the market. So, there's a lot of supply that's come onstream the last year,  which the market has absorbed. There's more coming onstream. So it's really about when does the world need  more LNG going into the 2020s.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I would expect in the next couple of years, we would be seriously looking at an FID in that space. And indeed we  do also engage in the market. That's strategically driven and commercially driven. So given the strength of our  portfolio, we can engage commercially in ways that others can't. We can take risks that others can't. You can  have examples where a customer may not want to buy Henry Hub-indexed LNG for one reason or another. We  can bring that into the portfolio and then offer them something else.

texts.speaker: Thijs Berkelder
texts.profession: Analyst, ABN AMRO Bank NV
texts.text: Thanks. Thijs Berkelder, ABN AMRO. Thanks for the clear commitments on the Paris Agreement. A question  related to that. Looking at your capital employed ambition for 2020. This is more or less unchanged from the  current capital employed. That means either that you indeed return all excess cash to shareholders, which is  more like $50 billion than $25 billion, or does it mean that you really identify Shell as a company which is taking  new energies serious and then stopping in growing in fossil fuels. That's, I think, not the messages. Message is,  CapEx is clearly, including expansion CapEx, so why is capital employed not growing in the coming year?

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I don't know, Thijs. I'm not sure whether this would be a forward-looking statement or not, the number of refineries  that we would have. I think we will have, in 10 years' time we will not have a refinery, it doesn't make sense. And  that's the only thing I can say about it. And I think, we have shown a very strong track record of cleaning out asset  portfolio when we see the running rumors is not there anymore or it loses its ability to make sense to hold it for  marketing purposes or whatever else. A lot will depend of course also on how the energy transition will play out.  But we – I would imagine, we will be in many of the geographies where we operate, we will be the last – not the  last, but we will be one of the core refining positions left, that makes a lot of strong sense.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And of course, increasingly, you can also see, we will also build, next to a very strong and high quality Upstream  business, we will also build a business that has a volume component but not your traditional volume component  of barrels [indiscernible] (02:26:13) or whatever else. So, as we double our Chemicals business, and maybe triple  it towards the end of next decade, we'll come free of barrels. New Energies is the same thing. And of course, our  Marketing business is – yeah, they have barrels but not sort of barrels that you're interested in but in terms of  production.

texts.speaker: Irene Himona
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA (UK)
texts.text: Thank you. Irene Himona, Société Générale. I have two questions please. Firstly, Andy spoke of the materiality of  your 2P and 2C resources today. And you are the first major to introduce a material reduction to your carbon  footprint. In your speech you mentioned you accept the risk that some resources will become stranded in this  energy transition. I wonder if we assume you deliver the first target, which I think is a 20% reduction to your  carbon footprint by 2035, what do you assume happens in terms of resources being stranded. So what proportion  of your resource would be stranded in that scenario? My second question and apologies I'm coming back to the  detail, the increase of $5 billion in the free cash flow by 2020. Can you please clarify two things? First, how much  of that incremental change comes from outside the Upstream? And secondly, for the Upstream, what do you  assume happens to new barrels? The previous level was 1 million barrels of startups contributing $10 billion of  cash flow from ops in 2018. Within your $5 billion increase in free cash flow, what happens to the production  side? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Irene. Let me take the first one and maybe you can talk about the second. So the ambition that we set for  reducing our carbon footprint is the carbon footprint of the products that we sell. Very important to bear that in  mind because quite often it is forgotten how it all works. We sell twice as many products as we refine, roughly.  And we refine twice as many barrels as we produce. So in the end, the only thing that really matters for society is  that the energy products that we put into customers' hands to enrich their lives with need to have overall a lower  carbon footprint over the entire life cycle of where that amount of energy came from. And that I believe is in the  end also what society needs to deliver on the back of the Paris commitments. And we have put our ambition in  place to be in line with society. And as a matter of fact, that means that we have to run a bit harder in society  because our current product mix is very much dominated by oil and gas type energy products. So that's again a  bit of the clarification of what I said.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: What does it mean in terms of stranded assets? Well, there's not necessarily a correlation between one and the  other because still going forward certainly towards the end of the next decade or even after that, there will be a  need for oil and gas in that mix. As a matter of fact, there will be a higher need for oil and gas investments in that  mix because no matter how hard the world will continue to drive to a lower carbon energy system, lower carbon  footprint; the rate at which existing resources will deplete is much faster. So the world will need to invest  continuously in new oil and gas projects. And therefore, there is still relevance for a business model that relies on  investment in these resources. Now, of course, some resources will be better placed than others. And what Andy  has been doing and Michael for that matter as well is continuously find our way to the best part of the creaming  curve. So the lowest cost assets that will continue to be competitive and also those projects that are, what I said,  climate-competitive. So very low carbon footprints. Because ultimately, even if we get to a 50% reduction by 2050  in the carbon footprint of the energy products; we will still need to have investments in oil and gas. And again, it's  a bit like the last person standing story with refining. If you have the best positions to enjoy, you will be enjoying  delivering that portion of oil and gas that society is inevitably still going to need.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: ...the CFFO growth that's going from new projects. And then there's the $5 billion from free cash flow growth that  we've increased from [ph] 25 to 30 (02:32:34). Both of those reflect growth happening across our portfolio. So I  think that's important. It's not just Upstream; it's not just Downstream; it's not just Integrated Gas. But we're seeing  growth across the portfolio. That will come from Appomattox starting in the Gulf of Mexico. That will come from  Prelude starting in – LNG projects starting in Australia. It will come from our chemicals projects that are starting  up. So it's really across the portfolio. I wouldn't say it's overly weighted to one portion of the portfolio or another. I  think it's a relatively balanced portfolio in terms of what's driving that growth both in CFFO and free cash flow.

file: RDSB - Investor Day Downstream 21March2018 630 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 21-Mar-18.pdf

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So our Downstream business, I believe is a unique platform to allow Shell to lead through the energy transition  both in Oil Products and in Chemicals. My leadership team today will take you through their plans and aspirations  and we'll make new disclosures to substantiate the resilience of their businesses and for Marketing and  Chemicals their growth aspirations. In Refining and Trading, we'll disclose indicative margin and cost parameters.  And in Marketing, a segmentation of how our current and future value will be delivered.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now before we start, let me highlight the disclaimer statements which many of you will be familiar with. But now  let's get onto the key messages. So the key messages to take out of this presentation today are as follows. Shell  and Downstream is a key contributor to the world-class investment case, in general and to the 2020 free cash  flow outlook in particular. We anticipate to deliver $6 billion to $7 billion per annum of organic free cash flow by  2020. A $9 billion to $12 billion per annum by 2025 and that's $60 a barrel and mid-cycle Downstream conditions.  The variability by the way comes from the Chemicals CapEx choices which of course we have when once we get  into the 2020s.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: On Oil Products, our cash engine delivered $6.5 billion in earnings with Chemicals, a growth priority delivering a  further $2.6 billion in CCS earnings excluding identified items in 2017. And as I mentioned earlier, as we look  forward by 2020, we expect to deliver that $6 billion to $7 billion per annum organic free cash flow, $9 billion to  $12 billion per annum by 2025 at mid-cycle industry conditions from our Downstream.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now Lori and Andrew, Refining and Trading respectively. Our Refining portfolio is well balanced and the strategic  placements of our assets in trading hubs and advantage markets makes refining resilient. Andrew runs one of the  largest energy trading operations in the world and you saw and heard from the video, it's a central nervous  system for Downstream, bringing trading capability, deep market knowledge and global portfolio and end-to-end  integration together all in one unit.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Graham, Graham van't Hoff runs our Chemicals business, which is a growth priority for Shell. And Chemicals has  delivered a solid performance and returns averaging 15% over the last five years. And Bjorn Fermin, our  Executive Vice President of Downstream Finance, and Gerard Penning, our Executive Vice President of  Downstream Human Resources will be joining us on the stage later on this morning to, to take questions.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The value chain starts at the customer end and the investments in the rest of the value chain are only made, if  they are required to deliver and realize incremental value. Now take the example of Refining. We own about 3  million barrels a day of refining capacity whereas we sell more than 6 million barrels a day of products to our  customers. It's our Refining and Chemicals sites, we are managing a joint P&L with our Marketing and Trading  activities.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: To our knowledge, none of our IOC competitors run Downstream in such an integrated manner with such highly  skilled and motivated people. We see that as a real competitive advantage translating into higher cash generation  and improved resilience. Of course, the integration goes further into our Upstream and Integrated Gas  businesses, but of course, that's not the main focus of today's discussion.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And as you know, we are looking at the future of the energy landscape through many different lenses and  scenarios. And as you will well appreciate knowing this business, these scenarios have very different drivers and  outcomes that they all have a common conclusion.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Total oil demand is higher in the 2013s than today. The reason is that there are some key sectors for all demand,  in particular, road freight, aviation and petrochemicals that have both strong underlying demand growth, but also a  slower rate of transition away from oil. Another very widely recognized trend is the growth of Chemicals, the GDP  plus rates. And the outlook for Chemicals demand has tremendous fundamentals, primarily, of course, related to  GDP growth, but also to the requirement for more chemicals materials for the delivery of cleaner energy solutions.  And many of those you'll be familiar with, the chairs you're sitting on today, the insulation in buildings, lighter  components, which substitute the steels and metals in transportation vehicles.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: But we do recognize that the energy transition will impact our industry and Shell is already a willing and able  player in this transition as we seek to decarbonize our offerings and products. We see commercial opportunities in  participating in the global drive to provide more and cleaner energy solutions and Shell's Downstream business is  taking a lead role in navigating Shell through that energy transition as we refine and evolve our products and  service offerings in response to the changing needs of customers and society at large.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We plan to be leading through the energy transition. One example of this, which I'd like to share with you is the  penetration of electric vehicles and its implications for our business. So, let's take a look at that. The accelerated  penetration of EVs is a reality, but it's also an opportunity. We're adjusting our offer to meet this new demand and  both István and Huibert will talk more about that with you later on.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Another reality though is that the most credible scenarios for the development of EVs still predict an absolute  growth in the number of internal combustion engine vehicles in the next two decades. Now, let me remind you of  how Downstream fits in to the world-class investment case that we shared with you as an executive committee  last year.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So what is our Downstream strategy here in Shell? And I would summarize it as follows. Starting with the  customer, our Marketing value growth strategy is driven by leveraging the number one global brand and our  technically innovative differentiated fuels and lubricants and growth in our base markets and new markets as well  as sectors resilient to the energy transition. And we've been reshaping Refining and Trading portfolio to focus on  and enhance our large complex highly integrated and competitive sites in our three main hubs, our three main  trading hubs of the Gulf Coast, Rotterdam and Singapore. And that rationalization is nearing completion.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And in Chemicals, we're growing from a very focused portfolio which relies upon advantage feedstocks,  proprietary technology with growth as I've explained supported by the energy transition, all enabled by customer  connectivity and increasing levels of digitization which I will talk about more later on.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And Refining and Trading are working extremely well together as an integrated business to also enhance those  returns and cash flow. And we announced at Shell's Management day last November that we would be allocating  an extra $1 billion of capital investment to Oil Products to support the profitable growth of this business.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So in total, we're planning to allocate $4 billion to $5 billion per year to Oil Products with a directional 50-50  allocation between Refining and Trading and Marketing, and $3 billion to $4 billion per year to Chemicals.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, as you've heard me say resilience is a key feature of our Downstream business, and I'd like to highlight  some of the key resilience factors of our business not only today, but as we move into the future. And as you  know, GDP is a key growth driver for most of our Downstream businesses. Therefore, a balanced geographic split  of our business is important to balance the exposure to regional economic cycles.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In Chemicals, we're making our business more resilient by actively balancing feedstock types like liquids and gas  across the portfolio and across the regions. For Marketing, we balance B2B with B2C and our growth drivers are  also well diversified looking at attracting new customers, developing new sources of revenues and also increasing  our revenues from resilient sectors like the industrial and commercial sectors themselves.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now in my view as well, resilient should also be considered through the lens of the energy transition and the  associated disruptions which will inevitably occur in Downstream. And let's be honest, nobody really knows  exactly how the energy transition will play out in the Downstream sector and how first trends like those we're  seeing across mobility will really gain materiality and significance. But one thing we do know is that our  Downstream business is a unique platform to capture those opportunities as they emerge.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We recognize that society's carbon footprint needs to reduce. We want to reduce the net carbon footprint of our  energy products. One of the ways we can achieve this is through offering our customers a choice of energy  products, including low carbon options and as part of our net carbon footprint ambition, we also want to reduce  the emissions from our assets.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In Refining and Trading, the key to resilience is to continue to improve the competitiveness of each of our sites.  Certainly from a cost point of view, but also from a complexity point of view anticipating disruptors like the new  IMO sulphur regulations or demand for lower CO2 fuels. And as we think about long-term competitiveness, we're  also positioning our businesses to win by proposing innovative solutions for our customers.

texts.speaker: István Kapitány
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Retail, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: When you put these numbers in comparison to some other major retailers and you see the major retailers in the  middle bar, together, it represents less than this number. Or even if you just stick to the more traditional  international oil company competitors, in this case, you can see Total and BP. They have significantly fewer sites  than us even if you combine them. Of course, a very important and key success factor for us is our people. John  talked about the 0.5 million service champions in 75 countries who are serving our customers every single day.

texts.speaker: István Kapitány
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Retail, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now moving to the other big differentiator, we have our iconic brand, the Shell brand. There you would – as you  can see from the chart significantly higher than other international brands like Coca-Cola or Nike and our  traditional competitors you can see on this chart.

texts.speaker: István Kapitány
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Retail, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So, let me provide you now a bit more details on two critical levers that further reinforce our differentiation. The  first one is Shell V-Power, our premium product that 20 years ago changed the belief that all products are the  same, that all fuels are just commodities. We, Shell, established a new category, and as you can see it is an ever  growing story from 2013, reaching about 20% penetration from our fuels in 2017, and we are planning to grow this  further. Other international oil companies and regional players, now also play in this area.

texts.speaker: István Kapitány
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Retail, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Looking at the graph on the – on the right-hand side – on the bottom right-hand side in the UK for example Shell's  share of the premium fuel market is close to 60%, while some of our competitors achieving significantly smaller  shares with the premium fuel offer.

texts.speaker: István Kapitány
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Retail, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Shell V-Power is a product, we eco-engineer with Scuderia Ferrari. You might have seen a Ferrari car out there  that is a very strong reason for that of course. An interesting fact around this cooperation and innovation  partnership with Ferrari, which dates back actually 60 years is that the V-Power unleaded fuels that we are selling  to our customers on the road contains at least 99% of the same compounds, what Ferrari using on the track. This  is a unique differentiation, the premium our customers like and importantly are willing to pay for.

texts.speaker: István Kapitány
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Retail, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: A good example of this, you see it on the chart on the left-hand side in the bottom is the U.S., the largest premium  fuels market in the world. There the street price of our premium fuels is higher than that of our major competitors,  and I already talked about the penetration before.

texts.speaker: István Kapitány
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Retail, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Then other important, very successful, but perhaps less known part of our Retail business, and the differentiating  activity is our fleet solutions business. We are the only energy major that has a dedicated global organization  focused on this business. We serve close to 2 million business customers worldwide daily and growing and we  expect fleet solutions to be very resilient to energy transition, because it is focused on commercial transport and  high mileage fleets. And of course, we offer new fuels like LNG, services like tolls, maintenance and telematics.  We are currently turning over $2 billion in road services in Europe alone.

texts.speaker: István Kapitány
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Retail, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So, our global scale and the direct customer relationship allow us to evolve and adapt. For example, we  introduced CO2 offsetting solutions to our customers. We will talk about later on a bit more, but we also very  happily started with e-charging, but also digital mobility solutions like [ph] Tap Up (00:34:07) also in the B2B area.  Connected car, connected freight and we work with many ride-hailing companies like Didi and Grab in Asia.

texts.speaker: István Kapitány
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Retail, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We expect to deliver $400 million additional net earnings through convenience retail alone by 2025 compared to  2017. Another example is our ambition for 20% of our fuel's margin that our company decides to come from, low- emission energy solutions by 2025 from around 7% today.

texts.speaker: István Kapitány
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Retail, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, we are very, very active in this area, I hope you know, in fact including Raizen, our Brazilian joint venture,  we are one of the biggest blenders and distributors of biofuels in the world. We are at the forefront of hydrogen  development in Germany, the United Kingdom and the United States. And on electric mobility, Shell is really  paving the way. We recently opened more than 20 Shell recharge stations in London and in Netherlands and  together with IONITY, a very strong consortium of European engine manufacturers, automatic manufacturers, we  will offer more than – we will offer more than 500 charge posts in 10 European countries alongside the European  motorways in the next two years. And of course, our recently announced acquisition of NewMotion, one of the  biggest European electric charging networks along with our acquisition with first – of First Utility allow us to extend  our offer to our customers, not only at the Shell service stations, but also at home and at work.

texts.speaker: Huibert Vigeveno
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Global Commercial, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Let's start with aviation. We have a significant global market share and we are present at approximately 850  airports. We fuel one aircraft every 14 seconds. This is a growth industry. Specialties is made up of our bitumen  and our sulphur businesses. We supply enough bitumen to pave 450 kilometers of road every day, and we're also  one of the largest marketers of sulphur worldwide. And then lubricants, our largest business in Global Commercial  and main earnings contributor, which I will focus on today.

texts.speaker: Huibert Vigeveno
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Global Commercial, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In lubricants, we are the global number one player and have been for the last 11 years. Lubricants is a truly global  business. We sell about 5 billion liters of lubricants every year, one-third which goes roughly into passenger cars,  two-thirds which goes into industrial and heavy duty use. A key competitive differentiator here for us is the way we  integrate with other parts of Shell, both across Downstream, but also with our Integrated Gas business.

texts.speaker: Huibert Vigeveno
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Global Commercial, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So, how do we integrate? The two main components of lubricants are base oils and additives. We buy an  important share of our base oils from Lori's refineries. We also have a unique differentiator in technology with  PurePlus. Our base oils made from natural gas, which we sourced from Shell's Pearl gas-to-liquid facilities in  Qatar.

texts.speaker: Huibert Vigeveno
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Global Commercial, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Lubricants is the largest driver of future growth in Global Commercial, so I'll focus on that part of our business  today, so how are we winning in lubricants. Our first strength is our Shell brand. Ipso talked around the power of  the pecten to Retail. Well, it matters to lubricants as well. We have the highest global brand share of preference in  several markets around the world for both passenger cars and heavy-duty engine oils. Our focus on value has  driven premium penetration to above 40% in passenger car motor oils and we see significant room for further  growth here. Premium products contribute significantly higher margins. We lead the market by volume share in  the most resilient sectors; industrial and commercial. These sectors are strongly linked to GDP growth and are  likely to be less sensitive in the medium term to the onset of electrification.

texts.speaker: Huibert Vigeveno
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Global Commercial, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We have three main competitive differentiators. First, we add significant value to our key accounts through co- engineering of new lubricants. We spend more than $100 million per year on research and development, and a  significant part of that investment goes towards co-engineering new lubricants with our global customers. Then  we offer car manufacturers the most cost effective way to deliver fuel economy benefits and lower emissions –  lower carbon emissions by supplying them with ultra-low viscosity grades of lubricants, using our propriety  PurePlus technology.

texts.speaker: Huibert Vigeveno
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Global Commercial, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Finally, we can help our global partners by providing insights based on data about the preferences of our 52  million loyalty customers. None of our competitors can come close to providing this level of insight. One of the  primary growth drivers in recent years has been the sales of our premium synthetic lubricants, which we have  grown at the rate of twice the market. We see strong growth across our global key accounts, as more companies  internationalize and build out their global supply chains. Of course, this planned growth will take place against the  backdrop of the energy transition and changes in the digital world. Over the coming decade, we see significant  growth in many sectors around us. From industrial production to cars powered by internal combustion engines,  shipping and aviation.

texts.speaker: Huibert Vigeveno
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Global Commercial, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The bitumen business is very resilient to the energy transition. No matter how your car is powered, it will need a  road to drive on. In lubricants, we expect continued growth in the attractive industrial segments where we can co- engineer products with our customers. And finally, digital and services is a new area with exciting prospects and  new revenues. It won't be material by 2020 but it will be by 2025.

texts.speaker: Huibert Vigeveno
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Global Commercial, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I'll now hand over to Lori and Andrew, who will talk to you about our Refining and Trading capabilities. Lori,  Andrew?

texts.speaker: Lori Ryerkerk
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Manufacturing, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Huibert, and again welcome everyone. I'm Lori Ryerkerk and it's my privilege to lead the nearly 15,000  Shell employees who operate our Refining and Chemical facilities around the globe. I've been with Shell for only  eight years, but I have spent a total of 34 years working in the oil, gas and power sectors. Refining is the heart of  our Downstream business, with 14 refineries in eight countries. We produce enough fuel every day to power 2.1  million cars, 650,000 trucks, jet fuel for 335 commercial airplanes and 250 large containerships. Our Refining  business is tightly integrated with Trading and Supply.

texts.speaker: Andrew Smith
texts.profession: Executive Vice President-Trading & Supply, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Hi. I'm Andrew Smith. I count myself as the luckiest man in Shell. I've work for Shell for about 32 years in just  about every part of Shell; I've stacked the crisps in the service stations; I've looked after building LNG plants and  spent a decade in the Trading business as well. As John mentioned, I run one of the largest energy trading  businesses in the world and Trading and Supply is indeed the central nervous system for Shell. We have a global  refinery footprint, a large freight portfolio, as well as commercial knowledge and highly talented people with the  right experience and these are clear differentiators for us. We're active in all global markets and use the  knowledge and expertise from these to build third-party businesses.

texts.speaker: Andrew Smith
texts.profession: Executive Vice President-Trading & Supply, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The physical flows from Shell enable us to make compelling offers to other producers and marketing companies,  and we use the insights from those flows to unlock further option value for Shell. It's a virtuous circle. You can see  this in our Trading volumes where we trade almost three times the amount of physical crude that our refineries  process. And we sell 6 million barrels of refined product to the market, which is more than twice what our refining  system makes. This gives us a real advantage of scale and reach. It allows us to make compelling offers for both  Shell businesses and the third parties we work with.

texts.speaker: Lori Ryerkerk
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Manufacturing, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The focus on high grading our portfolio are as we like to call it trimming the tail has improved our competitive  position, moving from an average site capacity of 150,000 barrels per day to more than 230,000 barrels per day  while increasing our solemn complexity. This is shown on the chart on the bottom right hand side of the slide. This  shifts our portfolio yield structure to higher value products and provides greater processing flexibility, a flexibility  that will be an increasingly advantage for us as we move through the energy transition.

texts.speaker: Andrew Smith
texts.profession: Executive Vice President-Trading & Supply, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Further, [ph] downstream (01:03:35), we also work closely with our Marketing businesses to provide cost  competitive supply as well as into new markets and high grade our portfolio. Shell's depth of commercial,  technical and analytical capabilities and our scale and understanding of the global hydrocarbon markets enable  us to adapt and respond to a changing market and industry conditions in a highly dynamic way. This allows us to  see value in crudes that others can't, which mean that we make decisions that will deliver the highest value  across our integrated global system. This also enables us to effectively mitigate unplanned refining or supply  events by utilizing the flexibility of the refining network, logistics facilities and optimizing around our portfolio of  sales and supplies contracts. We'll talk more about this integrated optimization and the value it enables us to  create both for Shell and our global customers next.

texts.speaker: Andrew Smith
texts.profession: Executive Vice President-Trading & Supply, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: For example, to supply our Marketing businesses, we can make finished fuel grades in the refineries, we can sell  refinery components separately to other manufacturers and buy quality finished fuels from the market or we can  use some refinery streams and blend them with other components from the market. This make, buy, blend  optimization is key to creating value. It allows us to constantly adapt to market conditions and hydrocarbon supply  and demand positions.

texts.speaker: Lori Ryerkerk
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Manufacturing, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: A second example illustrates the upside of being an integrated refining and chemical facility, as it enables us to  take advantage of both Chemical and Refining margins. With the most recent Motiva separation and a 100% Shell  ownership of our Norco refinery, Shell has been able to dramatically increase the Norco integrated value, by  operating the asset as a refinery with a chemical cracker versus the historic operation as a refinery and a  separate chemical cracker.

texts.speaker: Lori Ryerkerk
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Manufacturing, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Using integrated economics, the site was able to immediately unlock additional value by capturing Chemicals  margins through a change in refinery operations. We expect even further opportunities to be unlocked through  eliminating some of the operating constraints with this integrated value in mind. We anticipate this approach will  unlock more than $70 million per year of additional margin for Shell. The foundation for our Refining and Trading  business though is a safe and reliable operation.

texts.speaker: Lori Ryerkerk
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Manufacturing, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Our safety performance in both personal and process safety has been improving. The uptick in 2017 for Tier 1  and 2 incidents that you see in the left graph is primarily related to Hurricane Harvey flooding, and the related  start-up and shutdown issues in the Gulf Coast, and the addition of our Norco and Convent to our portfolio.

texts.speaker: Lori Ryerkerk
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Manufacturing, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: 2017 was our best year in personal safety, as shown in the top right graph. As we continue to focus on Goal Zero,  no harm and no leaks. Refining utilization is also continuing to improve with a step change made in 2014. This  change is a result of improved reliability, a focus on optimization and economic utilization coupled with Trading  and Supply value chain optimization. By working increasingly closely together, our Refining and Trading  combined unit cost has reduced significantly. And work is continuing with a view to reducing this even further in  the coming years, both through ongoing efforts on the same business drivers and through focus on all key  integrated value creation and cost levers. We expect that by 2020 our combined unit cost will be approximately  20% lower than in 2013.

texts.speaker: Lori Ryerkerk
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Manufacturing, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The integrative – indicative margin is a new disclosure and supplements the industry standard margins. The  integrated indicative margin shown here in the bottom graph is a calculated, anticipated margin based on a  representative configuration and complexity of our portfolio inclusive of Trading. This integrated indicative margin  historically follows our gross margin very well and has been very robust over time. It is a good indicator of our  capability going forward. The forward view is the average of the last 10 years equaling $10.40 per barrel. The  band of air is one standard deviation and shows that volatility despite being present has been limited to that range  more than 75% of the time in the last 10 years. This is a key point. Margins are volatile. But the integrated nature  of our business between Refining and Trading ensures that we are better equipped to capture shifts in profitability  and limit the impact of volatility and that integration increases the resilience of our business.

texts.speaker: Lori Ryerkerk
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Manufacturing, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So looking to the future, it is clear that the world needs more and cleaner energy in a range of forms. We  recognize that the energy transition in which electrical and increasingly renewable energy will take up a growing  share of the total energy demand will impact our industry in a broad sense. But, at the same time, oil product  demand is foreseen to be increasing for many years to come. Our response is to both strengthen our core  business and develop new solutions to adapt to a changing energy world.

texts.speaker: Lori Ryerkerk
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Manufacturing, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Pipelines have been completed connecting the Norco and Convent refineries to allow for feedstock optimization.  The [ph] fluid ice cap (01:15:26) cracker at Convent scheduled to be shut down this year will extend its operations  following a mid-year turnaround in order to capitalize on market conditions, conditions which we continually  evaluate. Together, our crude trading and refining teams are continuing to open up a range and flexibility of crude  and feedstock supply options to our assets, both to optimize the value potential today and to create new  opportunities for the future in response to market, regulatory or competitive opportunities guided by our unique  market insights.

texts.speaker: Lori Ryerkerk
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Manufacturing, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We are busy unlocking potential in our U.S. Gulf Coast assets following the successful restructuring of our  business and our asset base in the U.S. after the Motiva separation. We are further expanding our options in  Rotterdam and Singapore through selective investments and operational improvements. We are also investing in  our logistics facilities to increase our integrated flexibility and value creation potential. We are further expanding  our products make, buy, blend capability and preparing ourselves for the forthcoming changes in the bunker fuel  specifications in 2020.

texts.speaker: Lori Ryerkerk
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Manufacturing, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Refining is also piloting advanced technology to produce green hydrogen at Rhineland and solar power at  Moerdijk.

texts.speaker: Lori Ryerkerk
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Manufacturing, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: These technologies combined with traditional approaches such as cogeneration and robust energy efficiency  initiatives, combined to help us achieve our aim to lower CO2 footprint of our facilities. Our preparations for the  change in the IMO bunker fuel specification in 2020 is another great example of how Refining and Trading work  together to optimize our offerings to the market and maximize our value potential. The new IMO specification  promises to be a significant disruption across the downstream industry, but our preparations are well advanced.  We also continue to grow significant activities in low carbon fuel solutions and services. Our carbon trading,  power trading and biofuels blending activities are all significant in industry terms already today and are expected  to play a growing role in responding to the evolving needs of our customers and regulatory developments in the  future. Andrew and I look forward to discussing these activities with you further later today.

texts.speaker: Lori Ryerkerk
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Manufacturing, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I now will turn it over to Graham who will talk about Shell's chemical business.

texts.speaker: [01S48D-M Graham van't Hoff]
texts.text: Thanks, Lori. You might have to work my way out of here. Very good. Good morning, everyone. I'm Graham van't  Hoff and I look after Shell Chemicals, which, as John mentioned, is a significant global player and a growth  priority for Shell. I've been in Shell for just over 33 years, much of which has been in the Chemical business and  I've led this business for the last five years. I must say, it's nice to see a number of you were from the Chemicals  investor event that we hosted in October last year.

texts.speaker: [01S48D-M Graham van't Hoff]
texts.text: As someone who started life as a chemist, I'm incredibly proud to run this business that produces and sells high  quality petrochemicals across the world. After all, petrochemicals are vital to the modern life that so many of us  lead and so many others aspire to. In our homes, cars, at work or while we relax, from furniture, appliances,  packaging, shampoo ingredients, clothes to mobile phones and computers, we often use products that began life  as petrochemicals. These petrochemicals, such as ethylene, propylene and aromatics are made from crude oil or  natural gas.

texts.speaker: [01S48D-M Graham van't Hoff]
texts.text: Shell Chemicals is building scale both in existing value chains like cracking and styrene in China or alpha olefins  in the USA and adding new 100% equity production in others, for example, Pennsylvania Chemicals.

texts.speaker: [01S48D-M Graham van't Hoff]
texts.text: We are one of the top 10 chemical companies in the world and among the leaders in base chemicals. We have a  strong advantaged feed position, as well as a global balance between liquid and gas-based feedstocks.  Compared to some of our peers, we participate more in the bulk chemicals and cracker [ph] plus one (01:21:04)  space. This plays to our strengths in integration and refining which Lori has explained so clearly.

texts.speaker: [01S48D-M Graham van't Hoff]
texts.text: Let me explain to you some of the key components of our strategy. First, advantaged feedstock. We leverage  advantaged feedstock with internal integration across Upstream and Downstream, processing NGLs from  Upstream, and leveraging refinery integration on feedstock, flexibility and optimization with Trading. We will  continue to use the natural advantage that we have as being part of a global, integrated energy company.

texts.speaker: [01S48D-M Graham van't Hoff]
texts.text: Co-locating with Shell's refineries and working with Shell's natural gas business means we can secure access to  the best raw materials and can have world-scale facilities. Collaborating with Andrew's global trading organization  creates unique commercial opportunities. As you've heard from my colleagues today, this high level of integration  creates significant value and is difficult to replicate.

texts.speaker: [01S48D-M Graham van't Hoff]
texts.text: Finally, and crucially, excellence every day and attention to health safety and environment. Our chemical plants  and our people are part of communities and we take our responsibilities to those communities seriously. We do  everything that we can to ensure our processes and our operations are safe. We've seen significant  improvements in this area since 2014 and 2015 and our robust delivery framework is improving every day. All of  this is underpinned by leading proprietary technology that provides long-term advantages and sustained  competitiveness.

texts.speaker: [01S48D-M Graham van't Hoff]
texts.text: Technology is a key enabler and differentiator for Shell Chemicals. We have a long history of petrochemical  process and technology development all the way since 1929. And we've established some key petrochemical  technologies that enable us to lower the cost of production and to manufacture products which only a limited  number of suppliers are able to produce. For example, we're number one in styrene monomer and higher olefins.  We are number two in detergent alcohols. We're number three in propylene oxide derivatives and polyols. And in  monoethylene glycol, or MEG, we're a leader in catalyst and licensing provision, and have a major position in the  market.

texts.speaker: [01S48D-M Graham van't Hoff]
texts.text: More recently we've developed a new technology for diphenyl carbonate, the critical precursor for the  polycarbonate chain. We're progressively working on the technology and bringing our ability to start  commercialization. This technology has fundamental cost advantages, and is safer than the main alternatives.

texts.speaker: [01S48D-M Graham van't Hoff]
texts.text: On financial performance, we've shown that we are performing and delivering competitive returns across a range  of crude and gas prices. And our 2017 results were a record for the Chemical business. The improvement of  feedstock and asset footprint has been a key enabler for the turnaround achieved between 2008 and 2011.

texts.speaker: [01S48D-M Graham van't Hoff]
texts.text: In 2014, 2015 and 2016, while the portfolio showed underlying resilience to changing oil and gas differentials,  financial results were depressed by some key operational outages, which we've worked hard to correct, and since  the beginning of 2017, all units are operational again, and the financial performance is back to the expected level.

texts.speaker: [01S48D-M Graham van't Hoff]
texts.text: The business has achieved a concentrated core footprint with strong underlying performance. 15% ROACE and  CCS earnings excluding identified items of more than $2 billion. This demonstrates the resilience of the portfolio  across the cycle, as the profitability of gas-based feedstocks has declined in North America and the Middle East,  liquid-based feedstock margins in Europe and Asia increased correspondingly. These show that our focus on  performance and delivery is working.

texts.speaker: [01S48D-M Graham van't Hoff]
texts.text: And now onto growth. Global demand for petrochemicals is expected to grow at 3% or more each year as people  raise their standards of living. As economies move from agricultural to industrial and then as people afford a first  refrigerator and a first smartphone and part of this demand growth will come from the increased pool from  consumers and societies for lower carbon and sustainable solutions. To meet this growth in demand, we're  investing to add supply.

texts.speaker: [01S48D-M Graham van't Hoff]
texts.text: Right now, Shell is expanding its site in Geismar, Louisiana in the U.S. with our joint venture partner, CNOOC,  we're expanding our site in Nanhai in China. And we're also building a major new plant in Pennsylvania where we  will produce polyethylene. We're making good progress on the construction for all three of these major projects.

texts.speaker: [01S48D-M Graham van't Hoff]
texts.text: We expect to start up the Geismar AO facility in the second half of 2018 and the cracker in Downstream units at  Nanhai are expected to start during 2018. We began the main construction phase at the Pennsylvania Chemicals  Project in late 2017 and work continues at pace with start-up still expected early next decade. All of these projects  show that Shell is committed to Chemicals.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And our customer base has diversification as well from consumers who can enjoy István's offers from non-fuels  retailing or to commercial and industrial customers who rely on the more traditional fuels and lubricants. This will  ensure resilience through the energy transition. And Downstream is helping the whole of the Shell Group thrive  during the global shift to that lower carbon energy system. And as the energy system evolves, our Marketing and  Chemicals business will be agile platforms to really meet the changing needs of our customers to which we are so  closely attuned.

texts.speaker: Lori Ryerkerk
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Manufacturing, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I would just say no one really knows what's going to happen with IMO. I mean if you look at all the different  players in the industries' forecast, some predict light heavy will get very large, some predict sweet-sour will get  very large. I think the answer is we don't know. So our strategy is to be able to supply our customers with the fuel  that they want, whether that's marine gas oil, heavy sulphur fuel oils for those ship owners that choose to invest in  scrubbers, light sulphur fuel oil for those that choose not to or LNG for those who would like to transition to an  entirely new energy. We are prepared to provide the fuel in all four of those scenarios for our customers.

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: Thank you. And thanks for the disclosure and improvement today, we appreciate it. My question – two questions if
texts.text: I can relate to slide 42 and if I can refer to a couple other charts, and just firstly I guess in terms of looking at you  referred to high-grading of the tail. So, I can see that you still got sort of six to nine refinery assets out of your 14  that looked to be on that tail. Can you just make a comment on terms of the integration you needed, because of  geography or are there some government requirements?

texts.speaker: Lori Ryerkerk
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Manufacturing, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Yeah, thanks. So, yes in fact we have been cutting the tail. Our strategy is to locate our largest most complex  refineries around our three trading hubs and in those areas where they integrate with Chemicals, but there are  few what we call choice refineries we also have, so just to give you a few examples. So, for – for example in the  Philippines, that would be a tail refinery, our Tabangao Refinery. Its small, but it serves a local market in the  Philippines, which is hard to serve in other ways because of legislation, because of terminal import restrictions et  cetera. So it's a choice, it supports a very robust marketing strategy that we have there.

texts.speaker: Lori Ryerkerk
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Manufacturing, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So, I mean your observation is right. We've really moved from probably being less complex and less big than  many of our peers and we've now moved to where I'd say, we're close to equivalent to our peers. And that's why  our efforts continue and the $2 billion to $3 billion a year that we're investing are really aimed at further increasing  our complexity probably not our size as much if you look long-term at our industry, but increasing our complexity.  So, things like the SDA, the solvent deasphalter unit in Pernis, things like the hydrocracker expansion, we finished  in 2016 in Scotford that increased its capacity to 20%. So, we will definitely be moving to the right on this chart but  we probably won't be moving up much on this chart – in terms of size.

texts.speaker: Jon Rigby
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd.
texts.text: The second is around Trading. I've seen some reports in the media over the last few days about the difficulty of  generating profits in oil trading these days versus historic experience. And I also noticed a report from Cargill  talking about how the ability to trade around hard assets now in [indiscernible] (01:50:50) is much more difficult  than it used to be. And I just wondered whether the analogy could be drawn with your oil and product trading. And  in that context, what degree of sort of speculative trading is taking place in that business to the extent that you  can comment? Thanks.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Okay. So in terms of our growth plans and aspirations, let's say you do have to look back at the Shell Group's  strategy and how we fit into those strategic themes. So Oil Products is a cash engine and Chemicals is a growth  opportunity. So it's very clear the direction in which we are heading.

texts.speaker: Andrew Smith
texts.profession: Executive Vice President-Trading & Supply, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I think the other thing that we do maybe differently from some others is this focus on customer. So, Lori spoke  about IMO and that preparation. So we have one team that is dealing with the shipping industry and we'll happily  sell gas oil, low sulphur fuel oil, LNG through the one customer team, and that generates opportunities back into  the rest of the Trading and Supply business. So there is quite a few differences between their trading and supply  business and how we integrate with the rest of the Shell and some of the people we compete with.

texts.speaker: István Kapitány
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Retail, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So you have an impact on your own destiny. So, when I talk about V-Power, there is a reason why we picked V- Power, clearly in 15 minutes, you cannot talk about the whole portfolio. 20% of our fuel sales is now V-Power. 20  years ago, if I would have said to people that we will have 20% of our portfolio, V-Power, they would have said  are you serious, how would we believe. As you've also seen that chart which we put up there for illustrative  purposes and as a third-party external information is the price levels in the United States for premium fuels. And  in that sense, you could see that this is a Marketing activity, so this is not selling a commodity, it is a Marketing  activity trying to find the customer segment is satisfied.

texts.speaker: István Kapitány
texts.profession: Executive Vice President Retail, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So we believe that we don't see the cyclical nature of this business, we haven't seen it in our own results,  particularly not going forward, because the mosaic of fuels what we are selling is now expending. So with energy  transition, we're now not going to be selling electricity, we're going to be selling hydrogen, we're going to be  selling LNG and it's giving us an opportunity also to find other customer segments that we didn't have before. The  last piece I would say, a significant part of our profitability, of course, growingly will be coming from non-fuel  retailing activities like fleet solutions services I mentioned, or convenience retail, the coffee and the food that you  had. And there the margin situation is very different I must say than in hydrocarbons.

texts.speaker: Alastair R. Syme
texts.profession: Analyst, Citigroup Global Markets Ltd.
texts.text: ...Refining and Chemicals.  John Abbott  Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc  A  Okay, fine. Let me answer the question on the oil sands business. I mean, I'm obviously not going to go into the  contractual terms of that divestment, but what I can tell you is the way that that has been negotiated is in such a  way that we protect the value in the value chain. As you know that was a mine, it was in the upgrader sitting with  a refinery in a Chemicals facility and the Downstream Marketing businesses.

texts.speaker: John Abbott
texts.profession: Downstream Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So, indeed, it is not surprising therefore that you start to see growth in the earnings from our Marketing  businesses, probably lending yourself to the – response to the second question is that a lot of that growth is in the  likes of Indonesia and China and India and Mexico and Russia, those are the countries. And what we are  concerned about is that we get competitive and sustainable cost of supply into our Marketing businesses. And if  that means that – and you've heard how we get that from China, if we feel that that is impaired in any way, we will  go further up the value chain, but it is driven from a customer perspective. But that does not mean we're not  investing in Refining and Trading, getting returns from that. And you've heard from Lori some of the investments  to ensure that we remain highly competitive in Refining because ultimately if you believe the energy transition and  the impacts that may have in 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 years' time, it is very important to have very competitive Refining  and Trading business, which we believe we have and we will strengthen that.
