texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Firstly, could you take a moment just to read the definitions and the cautionary note. Our CCS  earnings, current cost of supply earnings, excluding identified items for the quarter were $4.8  billion. That’s an earnings-per-share increase of some 61% from the first quarter 2009. Our results  have stepped up from last year, and profitability has certainly increased from the low levels that we  saw in the fourth quarter of 2009.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: This year-over-year improvement has been driven by higher oil prices and higher chemicals  margins, but that’s combined with increased sales volumes and that’s as a result of our operating  programs – our operating performance and our growth programs. These are better results from  Shell, but we’re not relying on economic recovery or seasonal effects from here on in. The macro  environment will be what it will be. We continue with our focus on growing our cash flow  underpinned by new projects and lower comps.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We had successful startups at two new projects in the quarter, deepwater oil and gas production at  the Perdido platform in the Gulf of Mexico and new ethylene capacity came onstream in Singapore.  We’re delivering on the downstream asset sales in what is still a difficult environment with an  agreement to sell our New Zealand position. And we’re making good progress against our target to  reduce costs by $1 billion in 2010. We are embedding a culture of continuous improvement,  commerciality and cost control in our day-to-day activities.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Looking to the longer-term, we’re building on our 2009 exploration success with new discoveries.  We’ve taken up new gas positions in China and Australia, a new Brazil biofuels joint venture, which  includes of course more downstream potential.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: So, overall it’s a good start to 2010. Now let me give you some details on performance in the  quarter, and I’ll start with the macro environment. If you look at the macro picture compared with  the first quarter last year, the oil prices were significantly higher than the $44 a year ago. Brent  averaged $76 a barrel. The natural gas prices increased in most regions but were slightly lower in  Europe. The industry refining margins were significantly lower than the year ago levels and that’s in  most regions, although refining margins did improve from the fourth quarter ‘09 and they were  supported in this by high levels of industry downtime for maintenance in the first quarter.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Now let me talk about the individual business performance in a bit more detail. Firstly, on the  upstream, the upstream earnings increased by 132% to $4.3 billion in the first quarter of 2010. The  higher oil prices, the higher oil and gas production and the higher LNG sales volumes were the  main drivers in the upstream results, and these are partly offset by the lower realized gas prices in  Europe.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Some of you have asked to see our gas realizations, including our large affiliate company in the  Netherlands, the NAM. So we have now included the NAM realizations in the European information  in our supplementary tables for you to use, and hopefully this helps you with your modeling and on  that basis you will note that the European price went down year-on-year.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The upstream production increased by 6% first quarter to first quarter, and we reached some 3.6  million barrels of oil equivalent per day. If you set aside what we call uncontrollable factors, things  like the OPEC quota, the weather, and look at the underlying performance and the barrels from the  new fields and the ramp-ups contributed some 200,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, and that  more than offset the 150,000 barrels a day impact from the natural field decline.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Our LNG sales volumes grew by 38% first quarter to first quarter and over 4.2 million tons in the  quarter; that’s our highest volume ever. That’s driven by increases from Sakhalin II in Russia and  from Nigeria LNG, where we had a limited restart at the Soku gas plant and that improved the gas  supply picture for Nigeria LNG.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Looking into the second quarter, while the weather-related gas sales added some $200 million to  Q1 earnings comparison; this is unlikely to repeat of course in the second quarter. Let me also  remind you that the Athabasca Oil Sands project in Canada that produces between 70 and 80,000  barrels a day for Shell, that went into a planned shutdown and significant turnaround in mid March  and that will restart again in June. We’re also expecting some Q2 downtime in the Gulf of Mexico  on a planned basis – that was in April – and some operational issues in Nigeria.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: So, overall in the first quarter, a much better earnings performance from the upstream. But we’re in  a delivery window, particularly for the Group, with a sequence of 13 new projects, 12 of which are in  the upstream, and they’ll come onstream in 2010 and 2011. These projects underpin the cash flow  and production growth targets for 2012 that we discussed back in March, and last year’s start-up  Sakhalin in Russia and BC-10 in Brazil deepwater, they’ve both had very successful ramp-ups,  contributed to Q1-to-Q1 uplift of around 120,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day. And both of these  projects are currently producing above the planned expected levels.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In the last few weeks, we’ve had a successful startup at Perdido in the Gulf of Mexico. A reminder  that Perdido is the industry’s first production from the lower tertiary reservoirs in the Gulf of Mexico.  This star development is expected to produce around 100,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day in  some 2.5 kilometers of water depth. This really is a high-tech first development with many industry  firsts incorporated in the design. And more importantly, I expect this to be a highly profitable hub  development with additional growth potential in the future as we’ve now developed that new  infrastructure in the region.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 3 The next suite of start-ups includes the mine expansion in Athabasca in Canada and our two gas  projects in Qatar. These projects remain on track and they will underpin our growth across 2011  and 2012.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: So, starting for a change with chemicals. The chemicals earnings have improved from a loss  making position a year ago. This is due to the shift to more flexible feedstocks, i.e. gas, in our Gulf  Coast portfolio and to more favorable market conditions worldwide. In Singapore, the new  chemicals plant, which is integrated with the Bukom refinery, came online in November last year  with the monoethylene glycol production, and the main ethylene cracker production started there at  the end of March this year. The first quarter 2010 chemicals earnings were pretty close to the full  year performance in 2009 and it’s good to see that.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We reduced Shell’s underlying operating costs by some $2 billion in 2009, and we’re on track to  deliver a further $1 billion of underlying cost savings in 2010. This will come from head count  reduction, around 2,000 positions in 2010-’11, in addition to the 5,000 staff reduction that we saw in  2009. It’ll also come from simplifying and standardizing our activities that help to reduce the supply  chain costs that form such a large part of our total cost base. So, we made progress here and there  is clearly more to come.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 4 successful appraisal on the 2009 Vito discovery, all of this in the Gulf of Mexico. 2009-’10 drilling to- date has delineated over $350 million barrels of oil equivalent resource for Shell in the Gulf of  Mexico, and we continue to evaluate these discoveries. We’re looking at options to fast track the  development of the – these exciting new finds with over 150,000 barrels per day of oil equivalent  production potential.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Elsewhere in the world, we built up new gas potential in the Asia-Pacific region with tight and shale  gas acreage additions in China and a bid for the coal bed methane to LNG play at Arrow Energy in  Australia. This is a joint bid with PetroChina, and still obviously subject to final approval. In the  downstream, we announced potentially a $12 billion Memorandum of Understanding with Cosan, a  Brazilian company, to create the joint venture for our Brazilian activities; that is both downstream  and ethanol – sugar to ethanol – and we will work with Cosan on biofuels growth.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry>: Thank you, Michele, good question and the two answers related, as you  might expect. Nigeria in Q1, yes good performance; offshore we are running at relatively  sustainable levels that we expected. Onshore, we did well operationally in two areas. One was the  Soku gas plant, where we have been up and running for most of the first quarter, and we also  brought onstream the shallow water slightly offshore EA producing unit as a floating vessel. texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 2010 production guidance, just to remind, our actual production in 2009 was 3.15 million barrels a  day of oil equivalent. Our stated guidance was to be broadly flat in 2010. We obviously take into  account the fact that our production is obviously quite seasonal; Q1 and Q4 are typically highest  production quarters, largely driven by European gas demand when it’s cold. texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator

We also have had a few weeks out in the Marversa corridor for  planned maintenance in April, so quite a few factors already affecting the second quarter  production. It is true of course that having 3.6 million barrels a day in the pocket from Q1 is a help,  but given the uncertainties I’ve just run through, it’s a bit early to be projecting that we’ll end up  ahead of our expectation for the year. texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The last factor worth noting is that stocks typically remain relatively high, particularly stocks of  distillate, and Shell in particular has a refining configuration that is distillate heavy. And that’s  something we need to work the stocks out of the system.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator

Of course it does come down to the lifetime of a project  as you prove up more reserves associated with a given the project. And yes, you’re absolutely  right, the fact we added three plus billion barrels of reserves – proved reserves at the end of 2009  has a direct arithmetic impact on our depreciation rates in the year. As we go forward I’ll be able to  give you a very specific forecast going forward, but Q1 is relatively clean in that respect in terms of  the depreciation in the upstream. What we will say, of course, as we bring, for example, Perdido  online, the Athabasca Oil Sands online, it’s likely to go back up again.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry>: That’s a good question, Irene. I might put the question to the Board, but  fundamentally we set the new policy – of course we aim to grow earnings and cash flow through  the cycle and the dividend to grow accordingly. There are clear issues over the next one to two  years that we talked about in March, where if refining, gas pricing and oil prices were to be at the  lower end of the cycle, we are spending more than we are earning. And in those circumstances, it’s  probably not prudent to be increasing the dividend. So, fundamentally, we will as I think you  probably recall, we indicated 2010 dividend flat. We also talked about the potential introduction of a  scrip dividend. And we will review as we go forward and see the big projects deliver. I really think  trigger will be big projects kicking off, ramping up, showing that production growth towards 2012.  And of course the big machines won’t really be ramping up until next year, which is why we gave  that indication for 2010. So, it will really be successful project delivery will be the straight answer.  A short burst of higher prices will probably not do it. It’s the underlying cash flow that really matters.  Hopefully that’s good guidance.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Joseph Tovey>: Good morning, brilliant results for the quarter, which you don’t need me to  tell you; absolutely delighted. I was rather wondering given that your company is relatively more  exposed to natural gas than some of your competitors, does the increase in unconventional gas in  the United States and the application of some of that technology to Europe and possibly other  areas put any question on or in the forecast with respect to LNG growth and the margins in LNG?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry>: Thanks Joseph. Thanks for the acknowledgment and good strategic question  for the long-term in terms of the positioning. The U.S. growth in unconventional gas has  undoubtedly changed that market from being potential import of LNG, where LNG may have been  linking U.S. gas prices to the rest of the world, we see that as an island market, but still a very  attractive one. So, we have built a very strong position onshore in the U.S. to play that. We talked  about 20 Tcf and very significant growth potential in our March meeting. There are 4 to $6  breakevens on the portfolio we’ve got. Good business, potential to make it better. Your question I  think is primarily about the rest of the world.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry>: Yes, there is potential for unconventional tight or shale gas in Europe. We  don’t see it developing as quickly in Europe for a variety of reasons. One is just the infrastructure;  there are 65 onshore rigs I think operating in all of Europe at the moment compared to the  thousands that you can rustle up in a few phone calls in the United States. So, that plus pipeline  infrastructure plus planning and environmental and the fact that, to be honest, we don’t see the       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Elsewhere in the world, we would say China and of course coalbed methane in Australia are the  two areas that we are interesting two of. In one of them, we are established as a player now,  coalbed methane to LNG, the bid for Arrow Energy with PetroChina, clearly is an aim to play that  into the LNG market. And the fact we’re doing it with PetroChina, although we’ve not confirmed, it’s  quite likely we will take some of those LNG volumes to China and a very good business opportunity  for us.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The unconventional gas opportunities in China, we do see as potentially very significant, which is  why we’re delighted to get the two 4,000 square kilometer each blocks in China in partnership with  PetroChina for exploration and appraisal. So, we do think it will impact the overall gas market. But  medium and longer term, we still see strong demand for LNG long-term contracts into, amongst  other places, China as well, but Japan and Korea, the typical customers, still strong interest, and  we are negotiating out the volumes of LNG supply that we potentially have particularly from  Australia at the moment. So, it’s a factor, not that big in Europe; we don’t see 5 to 10 years, but  further out, the balance in Asia will be largely driven by Chinese gas demand where we see all the  signals being fairly positive. Hopefully that covers the market.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q>: First question on the gas prices Europe, which apparently held up quite well in view of the  strong winter, also that happened in Asia. How do you see gas prices going forward the rest of this  year, as also in the view of the ratio between spot prices and contracts? And the second question is  about your Iraq efforts in Majnoon. Will you count, I understand you’re already started there, and  we will have some production next year or so. Will you show those production figures in the total  production?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry>: Okay. Thanks, Bert. The gas pricing in Europe, I’ll basically reiterate what I  said in March; there’s not a lot to update. Typically we’re 60% oil price linked, 40% spot price in       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 10 Europe. The particular market conditions in Q3-Q4 last year plus the fact that the contracts have  some inherent flexibility, meant that in Q4 we switched more to 40% oil linked and 60% spot, and  that carried on through most of the first quarter. We – the one thing that is relatively new is we have  been re-looking at the – any renegotiation clauses with quite a lot of our longer-term customers.  And we’ve done several deals which confirm that most customers are very interested in longer term  linkage to oil prices and contract volumes as opposed to spot volumes and so we traded off longer  or extensions in the longer term that are oil price linked against greater flexibility to spot prices in  the short term. So you will have seen that. Actually spot prices in Europe were reasonably firm,  mainly because of the very cold winter during the quarter. And so it worked in our favor in that  sense.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Majnoon, good question; what we are currently focusing on is that first commercial production. We  have to get the production up to 175,000 barrels a day from its current 45, before we really get any  return, volumes or cash. Thereafter, we will be looking at a major field development plan, which  would consume significant investment, but also produce significant cash flow back to Shell as a  result. As we get to the point of recovering our expenditure, i.e., beyond first commercial  production, we will, we do expect to recognize production, and that will be done effectively like a  production sharing contract. We divide the, our commercially available share of revenues by the  prevailing oil price to get the number of barrels produced. It’s very similar to a PSC. A small amount  was included in the 2012 target, because we do expect to reach our target by 2012. Looking out  beyond, it’s very difficult to say how much volume we’re talking about, because we haven’t yet  defined the scope and particularly the pace of the second level of the major field development. We  should take the field itself up above 1 million barrels a day of production. Relatively small spend in  the first couple of years, no volume till 2012. We will recognize volume thereafter, but it will depend  on the pace of the development. So, hopefully that’s clear.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q>: Great, thanks very much. Very small follow-up on the gas one. Do I basically understand that  you have a sort of 20% of flexibility between spot and fixed contracts, long-term contracts?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Jason Kenney>: On the LNG business, which accounted for I think over $300 million of the  beat in earnings today, still a bit of black hole for forecasting. And I was just wondering if there was  a case for increased disclosure or better guidance on EBITDA in the LNG business? I know from  your full-year results that the producing activities in the upstream give one number, and you have a  reported upstream number and there was some implication that gas and power in midstream  activities obviously make up the rest. But are you not at risk of having the LNG business  undervalued if we don’t see better disclosure?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry>: Well, I think perhaps we’re the only one of the majors to actually split out the  LNG business, so, in this kind of way to show the integrated earnings. And I think also, as we we’ve       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 11 only really been doing this for two to three quarters, I do fully understand some of the challenges  that you guys may have, and also 38% volume increase is not something that you may have  projected. I think all of those factors play into the improvement that you see. The one other thing is  that some – if some of our LNG businesses are actually cost dividend again because we’re left with  a 20% shareholder and you get – some quarters you got the dividend, some quarters you don’t.  And finally there is in the integrated gas business, in some businesses, such as Sakhalin, there is  some liquid. We don’t try and separate out obviously the liquids production contribution in Sakhalin;  it would be a bit meaningless. And so all of those factors are playing into the ability of the analyst  model, but I think over time you will see significant growth in this part of the business. You will see  the Qatar volumes coming in there, and it will settle at a level which you’ll see is not only  strategically very, very relevant, but also gets easier for you to model over time. Okay.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry>: No, I think you – we’ve put 5 billion into working capital; we could always take  some of that back out again. That’s one of the factors, and the oil price and gas price are the  others. And we’re not talking anywhere near the top end.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Mark Gilman>: All right, thanks. Simon, good afternoon. Just a couple things. Could I ask you  to clarify your comment I believe just a minute ago as to whether Sakhalin liquids volumes are  included within your integrated gas reported earnings?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 12 transparent, but I won’t repeat it here. And as long as the oil price is high enough, there is a pretty  rapid recovery of the sunk costs and thereafter your recovery is on a quarterly basis virtually,  because there is a lot of volume and lot of available revenue to recover the cost, even though the  CapEx cost will be quite high. So there is not a big cash sink in Iraq. There is going to be quite a lot  of cash going in and coming out.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Mark Gilman>: Okay, and then finally just one more: you stated your Asia-Pacific gas  realizations fairly significantly. Could you discuss what that restatement was about?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry>: Northwest Shelf essentially; in the past because we have an EP and a GP  business, we have what is, in effect, an artificial transfer price between EP and GP, because the  Northwest Shelf, like Sakhalin, is a fully integrated project. So the change is primarily Northwest  Shelf, but it gives us a much more realistic basis going forward. The gas realizations in Northwest  Shelf are LNG. Of course Sakhalin and Qatar are also fully integrated, and basically the rules that  you would expect applied from the way we choose to report them. Okay, hopefully that’s clear.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Theepan Jothilingam>: Yeah, afternoon Simon; two questions please. Firstly, Could you tell  us what type of activity you’ll be doing around the China shale gas and tight gas in 2010? And the  second question, just on FIDs; perhaps if you could give us a little bit of color on what FIDs you  might take this year and when you expect to take them? Thank you

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry>: Thanks Theepan. Good afternoon. The line went a little bit on the first  question, but I think you’re asking about this year’s 2010 tight gas, shale gas activity.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry>: In China, we’ve taken on two 4,000 square kilometer blocks in joint venture  with PetroChina. They will operate as PSCs. They are exploration blocks. So it’s acreage we know  is prospective. We know there’s gas there. What we don’t know is what’s the quality of the  reservoir, very much similar to an early North American play. We need to explore, learn from the  initial wells, do the seismic, look for the sweet spots, get into the reservoir, do the frac jobs, look for  the productivity, have we got the commercial development. We will do early activity on both of the  large blocks this year. It’s probably a two-year program before we know we’ve got, so unlikely  before 2012 that we’d be looking at a major FID. We may do some pilot work before them.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In the FIDs, back in March we gave a really full list of the 2010-2011 potential list, but the two key  ones we’re looking at at the moment, obviously [inaudible] second platform in the [inaudible] basin  and [inaudible] floating LNG in Australia. You mentioned tight gas as well, of course. We don’t take  quite the same kind of FID, but the level of spend on our tight gas, shale gas positions, particularly  in the Haynesville and in Canada, we look at at the moment as to what’s the appropriate level of  spend in the current market on both the cost and the revenue side. So, they’re the key I think  investment decisions in the next 6 to 12 months.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Jon Rigby>: Hi, couple of questions. Just on the gas pricing. If we stand now and assume oil  prices remain at the current levels, how long would you estimate before your European portfolio,  nation portfolio, would catch-up with where the oil price is now? And also within that, is there  something we should sort of take into account with the way that NAM works as high price gas that  you’re going to sell more off in the winter than the summer? And then the second question, just to  come back on your depreciation comment. As I understand it you depreciate over proved  developed reserves, so can you just talk about whether that’s on a field-by-field or a region-by- region basis or whatever, just so I can get a feel for how that depreciation charge could move with  the bookings?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry>: Our stocks are back-in-work with proved developed reserves drive  depreciation at a field level. It’s certainly economic unit level, if you can identify cash flow  associated with a given reservoir, that’s the real, the level at which you calculate depreciation. So,  even within a basin you can get quite different rates of depreciation, and hence it’s sometimes a bit  difficult to be completely unequivocal about the direction of movement. On gas pricing lags, we  typically, on average, about a five-month lag, but within that there are anything between about three  and six-month lags, and that applies to both LNG and the way that oil price linkage is structured in  a European contract. So, if you’re meaning today’s oil price, mid 80s, how long to catch-up with  that? Well it might be sort of late Q2, early Q3 before you get close and maybe mid Q3, late Q3 to  average that amount.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Jon Rigby>: Will it be fair to say you’ve also got some upside on mix effect sort of if you were  to normalize out your spot to oil price linked mix as well?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry>: Difficult to project really what the gas demand in particular in Europe is going  to do. I will say while the cold winter has been good for demand, it’s not been very good for demand  projections. We’re not – we’re just not able to separate out what was weather driven and what was  commercial industrial recovery driven. And that was the big drop in Europe, 15-20% down in some  markets in ‘09 versus ‘08. So we really don’t see real indicators of sustainable demand recovery  yet, and if that stays low, stocks are reasonably okay and reasonably high, then gas pricing will still  be under pressure during 2010.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Our CCS earnings, current cost of supplies excluding identified items were $6.3 billion in the first  quarter. That was an earnings per share increase of 29% compared with the first quarter of 2010.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 2 During the quarter, we started production at two new projects, Schoonebeek Heavy oil project in  the Netherlands and Qatargas 4 LNG project in Qatar, which together would add 90,000 barrels of  oil equivalent per day for Shell when they are both at their peak production.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We continue to crystallize new investment options for the medium term and exploration success  and enter into the Chevron operated Wheatstone LNG project in Australia.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: So let me move to a few more details on the result starting with the macro. If you look at the overall  macro picture compared to the first quarter a year ago, oil prices and our gas realization increased.  However, the spread between oil and natural gas realizations remains relatively wide and North  American gas prices actually declined.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We switched to margins based on dated Brent which is a blend of North Sea crude rather than that  pure Brent price for the European refining margins and we’ve switched to a [ph] mass (4:10) coking  margins for the Gulf Coast rather than WTS.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Turning now to our earnings. The headline CCS earnings of $6.9 billion for the quarter included  identified items of $0.6 billion. The CCS earnings excluding identified items was $6.3 billion, the  clean earnings.  The underlying EPS increased by 29%.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The quarter saw higher earnings in both upstream and downstream. So let me talk about the  business performance in a bit more detail. Firstly, the upstream. Excluding identified items, the  upstream earnings increased by 8% to $4.6 billion in the first quarter and that compares with the  first quarter last year. The main drivers in these results were higher oil and gas prices and higher  dividends from an LNG joint venture. These postives were partly offset by increases in costs  relating to the start up of new projects, increased feasibility study cost and higher taxes. Earnings  were also impacted by weaker natural gas trading results, divestments and maintenance downtime.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Upstream production at 3.5 million barrels of oil equivalent per day and that declined year-on-year  by a headline of 3%. We saw reduced demand for gas in the quarter some 50,000 barrels oil  equivalent per day. We had 90,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day of maintenance downtime  impacts. And the divestments had an impact of 85,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day. However,  the underlying performance were better and volumes were flat on year ago levels excluding only  the impact of the asset sales.       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: LNG volumes increased by 4% to 4.4 million tonnes reflecting higher volumes from Nigeria and the  start up in Qatar and production overall from new fields and field ramp up was around 230,000  barrels of oil equivalent per day, higher than it was a year ago and that more than offset the  underlying field declines at around 160,000 barrels a day. All reflecting the medium-term plan for  production and cash flow growth where the key targets are of course next year 2012.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: As you know, and will know, the UK government announced during the quarter a tax increase for  the upstream. That is a negative impact of some $60 million from this in our first quarter results on  a clean basis. To give you an idea of the forward impact at current oil prices we’re expecting a  further $150 million charge for the rest of 2011, and then an increase to around $100 million per  quarter for 2012. In addition to these charges, we’re expecting to take a one off $500 million charge  for the tax change relating to the deferred tax provision on abandonment cost once the legislation is  actually enacted. We think that’s most likely in the first quarter of 2012.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Turning now to the downstream. Excluding identified items, the downstream CCS earnings  increased substantially from first quarter last year to some $1.7 billion. Refining made a small profit  compared to the year ago losses. That was the first profit for a couple of years. Refining earnings  also improved from the fourth quarter of 2010 where we had impacts that we advised from the  downturn from the catalytic crackers at Port Arthur in the U.S. and Pernis in the Netherlands, and  both these came back on line during the first quarter.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Cash generation on a rolling basis, a 12 month rolling basis was $46 billion. That includes $10  billion of disposal proceeds and over that period the Brent oil price averaged $87. This combined  with the ongoing capital spending program. This resulted in a slight reduction in the balance sheet  gearing in the quarter to 14% and that compares with the 17% we saw at the end of 2010. And also  it fits very well in the 0% to 30% range that we look out for the company in the overall financial  framework.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We will continue to watch the cash position and the balance sheet very careful, and I’m pleased to  see this quarter the inflow and outflow rebalancing to a surplus, albeit assisted across by higher oil  prices and the asset sales.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The sale proceeds for the quarter were $3.2 billion. Upstream, we concluded $2.4 billion of these.  That covered 60,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day in production with a prime transaction being  the exit from the South Texas tight gas production.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Turning now to the growth. I mentioned, we started two new projects in the quarter, part of a  sequence was over 20 new projects in the full-year 2011-- 2014 timeframe. In the Netherlands, we  restarted production at the 20,000 barrel a day Schoonebeek heavy oil project. Schoonebeek is  actually a rather old field, already produced 250 million barrels since 1947 when it first came on  stream.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: With the field was shut in for economic reasons in 1996, but we looked at it again to find ways to  extract more oil from it. With our value-added technology, the new steam flood scheme is expected  to produce a further 120 million barrels over the next 25 years, and that’s an enormous 50% uplift  on recovery.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In Qatar, I’m delighted to confirm, we had a very successful start-up so far at the 7.8 million ton per  year Qatargas 4 LNG project.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: That train is now running at full capacity and has been from the beginning of April. It delivered, it’s  first LNG cargo only on the 19th of February to Hazira in India. So very quick ramp up. Later this  year, Qatargas will start deliveries to Dubai and China in line with the long-term contracts.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Staying in Qatar, and I am sure you all have an interest in this. We also achieved first gas from the  offshore into the Pearl GTL project. This is an important milestone for Pearl out of the GTL Train 1  start up sometime in the middle of this year.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We’ve actually now started to make syngas in the first bank of reactors at Pearl in the first train.  This is our Shell proprietary technology. The next step is to take that syngas into the GTL reactors  to make the wax. After that, we take the wax into or you may recall the refinery conversion units at  the end of the train before we produce that first product sometime in the middle of this year.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Worth also I think an update on Canada growth. In the oil sands, we are making good progress  starting at the expansion project. The mine production is gradually increasing, and we are actually  using some spare capacity in the original Scotford upgrader to process this bitumen. The  construction of a new upgrader, the expansion, was completed in the first quarter. We’re now in  early commissioning stages and we should be fully operational by the end of the second quarter as  planned. So overall, particularly on those big three projects, good progress bringing them on stream  on track growing the company towards 2012.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Looking ahead a little bit longer beyond 2012, we’ve also made progress crystallizing some of the  longer-term options. Just to remind you we are planning to take final investment decisions on some  10 new projects in 2011, 2012, these include Prelude Floating LNG in Australia, debottlenecking       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 5 the Athabasca Oil Sands Project and deep water oil and gas developments at the Cardamom  discovery in the Gulf of Mexico.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In Australia, we’ve just included our share in recent gas discoveries in the Carnarvon basin. We  included that into the Chevron-operated Wheatstone LNG project. So now in that project, we have  an 8% stake in the unitized gas fields for upstream production and a 6.4% stake in the liquefaction  facilities to produce LNG. Wheatstone is being designed, the two train 8.9 million tonnes per year  LNG project.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Oswald Clint – Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.>: Hi. Good afternoon. Maybe just a question on  Asian gas. And I’m just wondering with strong Asian gas demand and the Japanese events of the  quarter, how you’re thinking about demand in that region and is there any thoughts around Sakhalin  II in terms of that being expanded. Is that something that could be done? Is it something you’re  thinking about and would you have sufficient gas in the region to think about the third train there?  And the second question just on your European gas production in the quarter it was down quite  significantly. You mentioned some reduced demand there. Could you just say if that was actual  production declines or was that a pure demand phenomena? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry – Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director>: Thanks, Clint. I’ve seen  some of your research covering this subject, Asian gas. So thanks for the question. The Asian gas  demand, short-term yes has been impacted by the Japanese situation. We’re diverted I think  around 11 cargoes either swapped or diverted into Japan to try and help with the power situation  there. We’re basically putting it in a normal contract price. It has an impact, but essentially, it’s not  making a big event on earnings.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We think that could be taking up to a million tonnes a month for some time, which actually adds up  to the more than Sakhalin production if it were to continue in that level for a year. Medium and  longer term, we’ve always seen Asian gas demand as a the prime driver of that strategy. About a  third of the demand, global gas demand growth in total comes from China and close to another  third from Asia and/or Middle Eastern markets. So about two thirds overall and we didn’t see any  reduction if anything is potentially an increase.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: What we have certainly been able to do over the past three to six months is take all spare gas of  course Qatar is producing earlier and faster than we had expected. So we have had spare gas, but  it’s -- the Qatar has been able to market that away from North America and into the higher-value  markets in Asia and Europe.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We continue to look at that opportunity with Gazprom, it would almost certainly require us  accessing more gas in the Sakhalin III area, which is under Gazprom control, but we have no real  progress to report on that. So yes, we’d be interested. No we don’t have concrete milestones on  that. Our main growth in gas production to supply the Asian markets will come from Australia, the  multiple projects that we have there.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: On the European gas production, I mentioned 50,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day reduction,  that’s about 300 million scuffs. That’s nearly all in Europe and primarily driven by the weather. It  was colder last year, very cold last year in Europe. It was actually unseasonably warm this year, so  quite a big difference. And many thanks for the questions Oswald, hopefully that’s okay.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry – Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director>: Potentially, it’s a good  question, Jon. It’s actually the first profit I think since the last quarter of 2008 in refining. But it’s so  small, it’s not material. So nearly all the [ph] oil products earnings (23:05) came from marketing and  trading sector.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry – Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director>: Another challenging  question. Thank you, Alastair. The oil products, cash from operations does benefit by definition, it  includes the [ph] coser (25:23) adjustment. So there’s maybe $2 billion in there for the quarter that  essentially is a one-off impact that goes up and down. So the underlying delivery is somewhat less.  No we are not there, yet.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry – Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director>: Thanks, Lucy. We don’t  split out the trading results. Partly for the reason I just stated. Our trading activity is not a separate  desk. It is the way we optimize value through the integrated hydrocarbon value chain. So there is  an uplift in trading. It was a more volatile quarter. But it’s only possible because of refineries and  stock positions and marketing around which we can trade. So, overall marketing was back above  $1.1 billion, marketing and trading together. I think back in the fourth quarter, it was more like $400  million or so. So it’s quite a significant uplift overall. And that reflects both -- a pretty strong  marketing performance too.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Liquefaction in the U.S. I think we said around the strategy presentation time. Yes it’s something  that we could be interested in. Are we actively pursuing a project at the moment, no. It’s a question  of getting the capital cost down to a level at which it makes sense relative to the alternative means  of monetizing gas. And there are -- oh -- sorry I’m thinking a little bit about gas to liquids, but in  principle, LNG and GTL and gas to transport, or even gas to chemical, they are all different ways of  monetizing gas against liquids prices.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Yes, we are interested in LNG and looking actively, but it would more likely be in Canada than the  United States. We’re still not convinced that the U.S. has thought through the potential and the  security issues around export of gas from the lower 48.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: On GTL, gas to chemical, gas to transport, these are all more ideas for the medium to longer-term if  in fact gas to oil arbitrage opportunity remains as strong as it is today.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Lucy Haskins – Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.>: I think you’ve quantified in the past that  GTL probably is a goer if you don’t see gas prices much above 6, but starts not to hang together  above 8, do you have -- can you give some order of magnitude in terms of liquefaction?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry – Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director>: Well, in terms of GTL, I  think we said that the current gas to oil differential will probably make it attractive. We’re not sure  that this trend will sustain for a period long enough and sustainably enough to make that kind of  investment. What we need to do is continue the work on the catalyst development and on getting  the capital cost down. We will learn a lot from our own project in Pearl, in Qatar that will help us on  the potential future efficiencies that will help us to answer that question better. But clearly, there is  potential in the much longer-term and it would require significant investment to help convert some  of the gas exposure to liquids.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And then my second question on upstream performance, clearly it was weak versus expectations  but also versus your own price sensitivities. Is the gap mostly the start-up costs in which case what  should we anticipate for the rest of the year? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry – Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director>: Thanks, Irene. Good  question around the CFFO. Your first point, your arithmetic is absolutely correct. $36 billion, rolling  12 months, $87 a barrel, still something of a gap -- $6 billion, $7 billion. You may recall that we’ve  always said Qatar was about a third of the uplift or around $4 billion at $70 oil price. So neither of  the Qatar project is yet actually contributing anything material in the first quarter.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Theepan Jothilingam – Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc>: Yeah. Hi, Simon.  Actually just following up on that question, [ph] E&P (34:46). Could you just talk about perhaps the  delta on OpEx and increased royalties you are experiencing with the higher oil prices? And then  just going forward through the year, I mean as you’ve had quite a lot of high margin barrels off for  maintenance. I guess in particular with Nigeria, Bonga, do you expect that to come back on?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The changes in OpEx, there is a lot of talk about cost inflation coming back into the industry. We  don’t actually see that yet and when we go to market, maybe it will come. If it comes it will likely  have more impact on CapEx than OpEx. So, our OpEx increases we will see increased OpEx as  we go through the year as we start to incur, OpEx in for example oil sands and Qatar. The unit  OpEx -- once all of those projects are online, we expect to go down a bit, because actually and  particularly in Qatar, OpEx is relatively low.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Jason Gammel – Macquarie Capital (USA), Inc.>: I wanted to follow up on a comment that  you made earlier about your LNG portfolio. Having three projects in Australia that essentially would  fulfill future market demand. Have do you go about prioritizing the marketing of those three  projects? And would any of them be more appropriate say for just taking into your own portfolio  versus a long-term contract with a single buyer or a group of buyers?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry – Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director>: Thanks, Jason. Good  question. The three projects you talk about are Gorgon which is already under construction.  Prelude, which hopefully is close to a final investment decision, that’s the floating LNG project. And  the third one is the CBM to LNG project coal bed methane or coal seam gas, which is in the Arrow  project, which is a 50-50 joint venture with PetroChina and Shell’s share of production in all three  projects is between 3 and 4 million tonnes. And so we have about 10 million tonnes in total of  Australian LNG to market.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: All of those volumes are effectively to be sold from the project to Shell and Shell will then market to  customers. So in practice we are and have some contracts we are seeking in more that are not  source or destination specific, where we sell to the customer and they are indifferent to the source  of the LNG. So we are effectively taking them into Shell’s portfolio and that’s why the Australian  projects make such a big difference to our overall portfolio. Because by and large the majority of       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The BC-10 Phase II project is progressing. We will be doing more drilling there. And we have a  couple of other wells being drilled on our behalf by Petrobras that we have. It’s a exciting time  offshore for us in Brazil this year. Raizan JV reports on Rubens’ pay package. This is Rubens’  compensation not his remuneration. It’s an effectively from the joint venture. He was a major  shareholder or is a major shareholder of Cosan a big obviously supporter of the deal, not a Shell  employee. No decision yet. Either it’s not necessarily -- it’s not really a decision for Shell. This is a  decision for the joint venture. That’s all I can say really.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 12 one of the large three oil service providers is focused keenly on improving their margins  significantly. And just wondering how you see your costs escalating over the next year? And then in  the long run, what are your expectations with natural gas kind of on a global basis? Do you see  prices -- more of a global price, or do you see kind of pockets where there will be dislocations  based on supply and demand in that specific geographic region?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Gas prices longer run, clearly we’re gas becoming a company, probably will produce more gas than  oil this year. So a very important question for us. Three different markets North America will remain  diverse from oil, pricing it will be driven by supply demand and alternative uses, also basically we  believe at the top end alternative sources of fuel for power. We plan on the basis of a range of gas  prices $4 to $8 per million cubic feet Henry Hub. And will the [ph] global (44:54) gas market develop  well not to the core, that’s not our expectation, at the margin there will be movement to molecules  from and may be both directions from North America to Asia. But the Asian market, we see medium  and long-term remaining quite closely linked to oil prices.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And in between Europe that market has shifted already from what used to be 60% oil liquid related  contracts and now is more like 40%, with the rest being sort or hub priced. That trend may  continue, there is still a market for longer-term oil price linkage depending on the customers’  wishes. But of course spot and hub price in the past quarter alone were 1.3 times higher than the  Henry Hub price. So the fact that spot and hub prices may become the norm, does not necessarily  mean they will be a lot lower. It’s just a question of what kind of volatility and what kind of price  arrangement does the customer want. So we see three markets. LNG will arbitrage between them,  but probably more at the margins than it will do structurally. It’s a complex situation. My pleasure.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry – Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director>: I’ll tell you there is not Iraq,  but in essence it’s basically higher LNG realizations. We’ve got every other area that you can think  of it being a sway from Africa through Middle East through to Russia. So yes it does include Russia.  But it will include the LNG from the Middle East, also from Nigeria. So that’s really what’s driving it.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry – Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director>: Thanks. It’s a good  opportunity to -- just reiterate to where we are in the Gulf. We have eight applications in including  new exploration plans. We’ve had two of those exploration plans now approved, one approved and  one accepted as complete. The approved one is Cardamom and the Appomattox plan has been  accepted as complete is now in the consideration period. They are the only once so far to have  reached that complete stage. So that’s for new wells. The Cardamom first drilling permit was  issued. We started drilling three weeks ago.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: So we are actually drilling exploration wells in the Gulf of Mexico at the Cardamom prospect which  is good news. Separately, we’ve also had approval – one of the Perdido development wells which  we’re also about to drill. We’ve got five floating -- drilling units and we are drilling off some platforms  work such as workovers and recompletions. Of the floaters that we’ve got, three of them are  already new regulation ready and one is close.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Iain Reid – Jefferies International Ltd.>: Two quick questions. The provision you made for  UK tax seems pretty small in relation to your size. And certainly a lot smaller than your UK  competitor announced yesterday. Is there some sort of tax relief there or kind of different treatment  do you think which you’re applying there. And secondly on Qatar, I just wondered if you could  remind me of what percentage of the LNG volumes are long-term contract linked to oil from that?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Uk tax provision, it’s interesting one. We had to work a bit on this. We haven’t taken a provision yet.  The provision that we take, the big change will be next year in the first quarter. The reason we  haven’t taken the provision is basically the impact is a deferred tax liability that we carry as a result  of capital allowances being different to depreciation. And the deferred tax asset that we carry, that  reflects the future decommissioning liability. If those two are of a similar size, which in our case they  are, the change in tax have no or little or no net impact, which is the case for us.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry – Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director>: I’ll reserve judgment on  whether it’s realistic. We will have to try quite hard I guess to spend on that rates in organic.  Particularly the other point that you arise on US GAAP. We have stated in the past, we’ve got the  portfolio expense somewhere between $3 billion and $5 billion per year on this activity. Typically  our investments, the strategic plan looks at something in the middle of that range. It’s likely or  certainly as early planning is more at the bottom end of that range, while the gas price stays at $4.  But there’s still some quite potential on the liquids, the more liquids rich part of the portfolio. And  just on the FID, things like Prelude, Cardamom, the two UK projects [indiscernible] (55:41) and the  Athabasca debottlenecking. They will start to take up the slack fairly quickly as we get into the  second part of the year.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Mark Gilman – The Benchmark Co. LLC>: Simon. Good afternoon. I had a couple of things.  I think one of the slides indicates that in the first quarter you acquired some additional Rockies and  Marcellus acreage. Wondered if you could quantify that both in terms of acreage and cost? We will  also appreciate some commentary on what the Americas unconventional gas production looked like  in the quarter and how it compared to prior periods?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry – Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director>: Thanks, Mark. We picked  up a little bit more acreage in the Marcellus and around the North American plays. But it’s not been  that material in terms of what we were picking up relatively underdeveloped shall we say, we are  not paying top dollars. And the unconventional gas production, during last year, we grew to 1.2 Bcf  a day by the end of the year. Of course we are now seeing the impact of the investment in South  Texas. So we were back just above a Bcf a day or 180,000 barrels a day oil equivalent. So it’s a  dropped back again, but we expect that figure to grow as we go through the year, particularly at the  Haynesville, [ph] Grand Birch (57:19) latterly out of Marcellus.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Sergio Molisani – UniCredit Bank AG Milan Branch>: Yes. Good afternoon to everybody.  Two questions if I may. The first one on the Pearl GTL, on the occasion on the Qatar trip you gave  a sort of guidelines for the operating cash flows expected from Qatar based on a price scenario of  $50 to $70 per barrel and if I remember well the guidance was $3 billion to $4 billion more or less  until 2020. Can you give us an idea of what would be this cash flow on an $100 per barrel oil price  scenario. And the second question is on CapEx. Your US$28 billion guideline, includes or is gross  or net of the circa $1 billion of start up costs that you guided for. Considering if I understand well,  these are start-up cost or investments that you are not allowed to capitalize pending the start up of  this project? Thank you very much.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry – Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director>: Thanks. I’ll take the last  question first. $1 billion is OpEx is not part of the CapEx. So it’s the $28 billion is separate and is  genuine investment activity. On Pearl GTL, you are absolutely right in your memory. $3 billion to $4  billion or $50 to $70. All we had is $70 is $4 billion of cash flow per year and that’s both projects,  not just GTL but Qatargas 4 as well. We’ve not given any update at higher oil prices, mainly  because we don’t necessarily expect to stay $120 for long enough for it to be a sensible discussion.  So I can’t really to be honest give you an additional factor. But hopefully it’s good that we can  confirm the $4 billion at $70.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Underlying oil and gas production increased by 4% in the quarter. We've started up new projects in upstream and  now in the Downstream for further growth and we continue to mature new options mostly of course in the  upstream, with successful drilling in the Gulf and new exploration acreage in the quarter. So this continues  progress we made on the new options in 2011, for example, the Abadi floating LNG project in Indonesia and the  additional liquids rich shale positions.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Give you some more details starting with the macro environment. Now if you look at the macro picture compared  to the first quarter last year, oil prices are higher. There is an increase in the differential between Brent and WTI.  Our overall global natural gas realizations, they increased from the first quarter 2011, while – though, of course,  the U.S. Henry Hub related prices declined quite sharply.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Our overall refining marketing and chemicals margins were all weaker for Shell year-over-year. Currently, we're  seeing a very mixed picture on energy demand. Oil prices have been supported by geopolitical events, despite a  market which, in our view, is fundamentally well supplied. We've seen LNG demand increasing year over year, led  by Asia.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In the U.S., a combination of improving economic conditions and low gas prices are now stimulating gas demand.  But European gas demand remains weak, due to the weak overall economic conditions and basically price  competition with coal. In oil products, our underlying volumes were flat quarter-one-to-quarter-one. Demand is  being eroded in developed markets by high prices. Our volume is flat in Europe and the U.S., firm demand for  branded fuels in Asia.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So, moving onto the earnings. Current cost of supplies, CCS, earnings for the quarter including the identified  items were $7.7 billion, excluding identified items the earnings were $7.3 billion. Earnings per share increased  15% compared to 2011. On a quarter-one-to-quarter-one basis earnings in Upstream were higher and Downstream  lower.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Just let me talk about the business performance in a little more detail. Upstream earnings excluding identified  items were $6.3 billion in the first quarter, and that's an increase of 35% versus the same quarter last year. The  earnings were of course driven by higher oil and international gas prices, but also by volume growth from high  margin new projects, particularly in Qatar, and also a positive environment for gas trading. There were some  offsets from higher cost and depreciation and lower U.S. Henry Hub gas prices. The headline oil and gas  production for the first quarter was 3.6 million barrels of oil equivalent per day. That is an increase of 4%  excluding asset sales exits and price impacts.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In addition, we had some 80,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day of entitlement loss from profit sharing  contracts, as a lower entitlement kicked in at contracted milestones and high oil prices moved some PSCs out to  cost recovery mode. The LNG sales volumes grew by 17% quarter-one-to-quarter-one and not reflect basically  growth from Qatargas 4 and Nigeria LNG.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The year-over-year planned maintenance impacts were negligible in the first quarter at Upstream and  Downstream. So during the second quarter of 2012 looking forward, there will be higher levels of planned  maintenance activities on offshore fields in the Americas, in Asia-Pacific and in Europe. This is expected to lead to  a production impact, a negative impact of some 50,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day across second quarter and  that's compared to the second quarter in 2011.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In Qatar, the Pearl gas-to-liquids project continues to make good progress. We're on track to reach full capacity in  the middle of 2012, as always planned. We are running planned maintenance on sections of both the Pearl Trains  during the second quarter. These pit stops, they are part of the startup phase of the project, clearly impact  production. The three large startups last year: Qatargas 4, Pearl and the Athabasca Oil Sand Project in Canada, are  all capable of producing 450,000 barrel equivalent per day at their peak production or capacity.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Turning now to the Downstream. Excluding identified items, the Downstream CCS earnings were $1.1 billion, and  numbers in chemical. In aggregate, refining, marketing and trading margins were all weaker compared to Q1 2011,  some uplift from the Raízen joint venture in Brazil and from lower operating costs. However, we did see an  improvement in refining chemicals and trading conditions compared to the fourth quarter 2011, which was a  particularly quarter. Although marketing margins were weaker sequentially, this was due to continuing rising oil  prices in a weak demand environment.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Turning to cash flow. Cash generation on a 12-month rolling basis was some $50 billion, including $6.8 billion of  divestment proceeds, with an average Brent price across that period of $115 per barrel. Both the Upstream and the  Downstream segments generated surplus cash flow after their own investment and, as a result, the gearing at the  end of the first quarter sat at 9.9%. And that compares with 13% at the end of the fourth quarter and, clearly, we're  moving lower in the zero to 30% range as, of course, you would expect in strong oil price conditions.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And I'm particularly pleased in this quarter to welcome new strategic partners into our Prelude floating LNG  venture in Australia, where Inpex of Japan, KOGAS of Korea and CPC of Taiwan have now joined us. This  partnership monetizes some of our own Shell optionality at an early stage and are part of Shell's plans for new  growth in global gas.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Let me update you in progress on the growth portfolio. Production has now commenced at the Caesar-Tonga  project in the Gulf of Mexico and the Pluto LNG project in Australia is now – has reached ready-for-start-up  status. Together, the two upstream projects are expected to add a total 40,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day  and 0.9 million tonnes per annum of LNG.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: On the Downstream side, we've just started processing crude in the Port Arthur refinery expansion project. That  will create the largest refinery in the United States. There's some 600,000 barrels a day of overall total refining  capacity. These three projects are all part of the diverse portfolio of some 26 projects we previously discussed that  Shell is developing worldwide today. We're driving the targets that we set for cash flow and production.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Earlier this week, we announced an intended cash offer for Cove Energy plc in the UK and this was recommended  by Cove's board. This is part of a strategy to build up our presence in East Africa and Cove would mark our entry  into Mozambique gas and also new exploration potential in both Mozambique and Kenya. Now the cost – total  cost for Shell is expected to be just below $2 billion. That includes the price to Cove's shareholders and an  estimate of the capital gains tax charge. So, good progress on the growth portfolio.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now oil prices have almost doubled since 2009, whereas refining margins and the U.S. natural gas price clearly  have remained low or got lower. We as a company must look through the short-term volatility when we plan for  dividends and we take decisions on a long-term policy basis. There is no simple mechanical formula. The  resumption of the measured affordable dividend growth that we've confirmed today reflects the improving  underlying financial position of the company and the delivery of our strategy in line with policy.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So, just let me summarize before we go to questions. First quarter earnings have increased from the year-ago  levels, driven by operating performance, new projects and strong oil prices and this is despite the continued  challenges for our industry in the downstream and in North American natural gas pricing. With $2.4 billion of  divestments in the quarter, we're increasing the divestment target for the year to over $4 billion. Our underlying  oil and gas production increased by 4% in the quarter, starting up new projects in upstream and downstream for  further growth. The dividend for quarter one will increase, with our strategy delivering sustainable financial  growth and we continue to mature growth options and growth mostly in the Upstream, so making good progress  against targets to deliver a more competitive performance.

texts.speaker: Theepan Jothilingam
texts.profession: Analyst, Nomura International Plc
texts.text: Yeah. Afternoon, Simon. Thank you for your comments. Two questions please, firstly, a very good number in  integrated gas. I'm being greedy but is there anyway to disclose the split between GTL and LNG? Or put it another  way, could you give us maybe the delta quarter-on-quarter for LNG? And some comments on whether you think  this result is sustainable going forward.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Theepan. Thanks for the comments. Integrated gases indeed the main driver of the improved Upstream  earnings performance and cash flow. It is of course the strategy playing out in action. We've being saying for  sometime this is core to Shell strategy. So there's increase of $1.35-or-so-billion dollars in the earnings, Qatar,  both projects are responsible for about 60% of that. The remainder is split roughly equally between additional  volumes ahead of Nigeria and Russia, better pricing and better opportunities from cargo diversions, simply  because we have more LNG to work with and, of course, the market's been fairly tight in the quarter.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So it is strategy coming into action, so in the same macro, then, yes, it would be basically sustainable. It's also  fairly robust, given that, as you're probably aware, the majority of the LNG volumes and obviously the GTL  volumes are oil price-linked, so very little exposure, by definition, in the integrated gas segment to lower prices,  for example, in U.S. or spot prices in Europe.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: 8.5% remains perhaps a little low for a Shell presence in what hopefully will be quite a large LNG development  and we are and will remain interested in increasing from that level of involvement. I really can't comment on  whether we have or will hold discussions with individual members in the existing consortia, either in that area or  elsewhere. I just confirm that, yes, of course, we're interested but one step at a time; we must close the Cove deal  first.

texts.speaker: Theepan Jothilingam
texts.profession: Analyst, Nomura International Plc
texts.text: Okay. Can I just come back to your comment on LNG and Q1? You talked about it being a tight quarter. Do you see  that going into Q2 and beyond for 2012 please?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In general. yes, although it is a big seasonal. So the demand can come off a bit across the summer, it depends on  how warm it is in countries with lots of air conditioning. And so, in general, the demand is higher than it was a  year ago. We will see Pluto coming on and there's a couple of other smaller projects likely to come on during the  year, but most of the volume's already sold into long-term contracts. There are various Chinese regas terminals  opening up capacity expanding. India is fairly strong in its demand for LNG at the moment. So as we look across  the variety of markets, we do expect the market to stay pretty tight.

texts.speaker: Jon Rigby
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: The second is just on your commentary at the end on the dividend and the balance sheet; I think you brought that  in. Is – I take your point about where oil prices are. But, as you said, is -Downstream's not great. And you're  generating a kind of level of cash flow now which is pretty similar or inline with the kind of number that you  aspirationally want to do at mid-cycle. So, what are you thinking about how you'll deal with what is very  impressive level of free cash flow generation that you're now starting to throw off? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Iain S. Reid
texts.profession: Analyst, Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: And secondly, on U.S. gas, is it possible to say how much of the U.S. gas you're producing at the moment is non- liquid related, i.e., pure dry gas? And what's your plans for investment in growing that number whilst the – while  Henry Hub is at these sort of levels?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And U.S. gas percentage and LRF. We have not a lot of production in the liquids-rich shales at the moment.  Almost all of our U.S. gas is, in practice, dry gas production. The liquids-rich shale and associated production at  the end of the quarter was just over 10,000 barrels – at the end of the fourth quarter, sorry, at the end of the year.  At the end of the quarter, it was around 40,000 barrels. So we are growing that quickly in the Eagle Ford area.  That figure does include the gas that comes with the liquid.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So our aim as we go through the year, we were 240,000 barrel or so in terms of the first quarter onshore  unconventional activity production, gas on liquids. We expect that to grow through the year, but we are basically  still in the process of switching drilling activity from dry gas to wet gas or liquids. And difficult to project exactly  what the outcome is but the net impact is probably less volume in 2012, more we believe in 2013. I'll give you an  update more specifically, I expect later in the year.

texts.speaker: Martijn P. Rats
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Yeah, good afternoon. Two questions, if I may, the FAS 69 disclosure in the 20-F shows that in the Upstream  production costs, excluding taxes, went from broadly $11 on a per barrel basis to roughly $13.5. So they went up  23% from 2010 to 2011. I was wondering whether you could comment on what is driving the change? I already  seeing significant cost inflation coming through there mix effects going on and driving that OpEx per barrel figure.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Martijn. You've been doing some good homework there. Production increased 11% to 23% and  fundamentally there are some mix effects there. For example, the Oil Sands comes on stream. You saw the first  cost coming in Qatar and our cost per barrel in, for example, the onshore activity that I just talked about, the  onshore gas is this fundamentally higher and there's also some foreign exchange impact.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So all of those put together are really driving the cost up and plus having there was a bit – there was somewhat  less deepwater production from pretty much the same cost base and that was a Macondo related issue. So all of  those things lifted the unit cost, but also I need to recognize that almost everything I've just said are in areas  where fiscal treatments are relatively attractive as well. So we have more access to the price upside. So cost is only  one side of the margin question.

texts.speaker: Michele della Vigna
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International Ltd.
texts.text: I just had a very quick question, you mentioned Alaska. I was wondering what the key thresholds are for you to be  able to start the drilling there? And what kind of potential size you're looking for the exploration targets?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Michele. This is possibly the most important single milestone of this year. That's what does it take to  drill? Well, there are three things we're working on. One is operational, second is regulatory and the third is the  legal or the litigation access. Operationally, we plan two rigs and around 35 other vessels, which will provide all  the support and logistics, including, of course, the oil spill response. All of that fleet, including the two rigs, is  either on-station in Alaska or on its way to Alaska at the moment. So it's a huge logistical exercise but likely via a

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And the second point, regulatory permit. A significant number of permits are required, everything from  exploration [inaudible] (36:34) to air quality permits. All regulatory permits are either achieved and in hand or we  expect to receive in good time to be able to start drilling in the third quarter. And on the last comment, we have an  expected size of prospect but we have actually invested around $4 billion to-date in Alaska.
