So you can be fairly  sure that we're looking for something big enough to justify that level of investment and the persistence that we've  had to show over the five, six years in which we've been preparing to drill.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Alast. The financial framework around Mozambique [indiscernible] (39:05) initially in the strategic  years basically, to 400 million tonnes per annum and there are a significant number of projects already filling that  gap. But we expect growth beyond that, potentially to 500 million tonnes per annum and beyond as a result of our  assessment of the gas market in countries that are likely to import LNG. It's a huge market, it is growing. Our  current capacity is 21 million tonnes per annum. Our amount under construction is 7 million tonnes per annum  and we are looking at 15 million tonnes per annum, excluding Mozambique, of new potential projects.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: If we're successful in entering Mozambique and the project goes ahead, then we would be looking at ranking that  against other LNG opportunities. We can't do everything I've just talked about, but we will do the better ones. So it  actually provides a bit of diversification in the portfolio away from Australia, for example, where all our projects  under construction today are actually in Australia, although many of those we're looking at are not, such as  Canada, Indonesia and, hopefully, now Mozambique.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In pricing and returns, there's no reason why Mozambique should not be as good if not better than our current  LNG projects. Clearly, the entry cost is only going to be a small part of the overall investment because a large LNG  development has huge capital investment associated. Now we don't have a figure for that, you'd need to ask the  operator. But they took a 17 Tcf to 30 Tcf and potentially 30 million tonnes per annum of LNG, so it would be  significant the investment that we need to rank against several alternatives.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: At Port Arthur, it's – some of the downstream units are working already with finished product, the distillation unit  has crude cycling at the moment, the hydro cracker will start up by the end of the quarter. Collectively, probably  not a huge impact on the second quarter; should start to see some contribution in the third quarter. Please just do  remember, it's actually embedded at a 50-50 joint venture with Saudi Aramco. So we just see the equity share of  earnings in Motiva joint venture. At the moment the margins are maybe not that attractive in the Gulf Coast, but  over the cycle we expect Port Arthur to be a significant contributor to the Downstream earnings.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Gulf of Mexico exploration, we talked specifically about Appomattox doubling the potential resource there up to  500 million barrels. But it's worth just reflecting, we are bringing Caesar-Tonga on stream. Well, in fact, Anadarko  brought it on stream for us in March. We are building Mars-B, Cardamom and also BC-10 phase 2 in Brazil. And  we have three opportunities in the Gulf, of which Appomattox is actually the largest, but Stones and Vito are the  other two that we're currently appraising ahead of, hopefully, FIDs in the not too distant future.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Appomattox is the largest; it's also probably the most uncertain because it's in that new East Gulf area in the  Jurassic play. We are appraising – we will – we have just appraised, that's the driver of the doubling. We will drill,  hopefully, another couple of wells in the area. And we already have the Vicksburg discovery also in that area. We  have 75% or 80% Shell working interest in quite a bit of acreage in the area and we're fundamentally aiming to  appraise and understand that area while we progress all three of those prospects towards FID.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Our aim generally in the Gulf is to create the production line of assets, where we design one, build many in terms  of the surface and subsurface facilities. We are doing everything we can to bring investment decisions forward, but  Appo is so potentially large and uncertain that we're probably several years away from investment decision.

texts.speaker: Peter W. Hutton
texts.profession: Analyst, RBC Europe Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Hi, Simon. Yeah, a couple of quick questions, actually, both in the U.S., one in the upstream, one in the  downstream. The profitability in the U.S., it's below $10 a barrel operating. Now you had talked about reducing  the investment in tight gas. Are we seeing any of that impacting the volumes yet? And what else might be – is in  those numbers that might be affecting these quarters? I wonder whether any of the costs associated with Alaska is  showing as operating costs or is that fully treated as CapEx at this stage?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I'll try and help, Peter, thanks. The oil products is – I'll start at the back end – demand products. An interesting  fact there, the Rhine River, it hasn't rained enough. It was low, therefore it was difficult to move product, therefore  we sold considerably less than one might have hoped to do in both commercial and trading in the supply sense.  But at some point it was beginning to threaten supply security. Fortunately, it started to rain again but had quite  some impact in the quarter. So that explains Europe against the United States. Our own volumes in the U.S. being  generally maintained, but the market is flat. It's not clear, is it going up or is it going down, we'll see as we go into  the driving season.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And profitability Upstream in the Americas, you're absolutely right that it is somewhat less than we might have  wished for. And, yes, there is some of the Alaska spend going into OpEx; we don't capitalize until we drill. But  other factors that were quite significant in the quarter, we had quite some significant maintenance activity in the  Oil Sands in Canada. We are seeing higher depreciation and amortization, partly as a result of early production in  the onshore gas or liquids-rich shales carried quite significant unit depreciation because we are quite slow and  conservative to actually recognize proved reserves there.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Clearly the gas prices, the natural gas prices had quite an impact. And in Canada, in particular, the WTI discount  has an impact on crude realized prices. So all of those factors are keep going the Americas earnings low, which is  unfortunate but hopefully not all sustainable issues as we go forward. We are switching out of gas into liquids-rich  shales. That is having, as I've mentioned earlier, not too much volume impact now. It may have 20,000, 30,000  barrels a day impact by the end of the year relative to where we might otherwise have been.  But as we switch into what is essentially an appraisal activity on the liquids-rich opportunities in Canada and the  U.S., we won't replace it with liquids production this year but it will create the potential for liquids production  next year. S, it will be a value upgrade assuming like-for-like drilling activity. So we're just managing this within  the overall capital and also our operational capability. We're running about just under 40 rigs at the moment of  which we're shifting probably more than half towards the liquids opportunities. And so hopefully that covers  everything. Thanks, Peter.

texts.speaker: Kim A. Fustier
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Yeah, hi, Simon. Good afternoon. I had a couple of questions if I could. Firstly, could you just give us an update on  your latest strategy in North American gas, particularly your plans to build a large scale GTL plant in Louisiana?  And how that would compare to economics on LNG exports? I mean, clearly you're bullish on the LNG market  long-term. Is that something you're eventually going to consider?

texts.speaker: Kim A. Fustier
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And, secondly, could you comment on your latest thinking in Australian LNG? Again, there's some headlines  saying you're prepared to cooperate with other players on Queensland coal-bed methane. And how the economics  there would compare to Mozambique? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Kim. And North American gas strategy and fundamentally we're looking at 40 Tcf plus of gas which in a  $2 world we probably would prefer to monetize on something other than natural gas. So we're looking at four  different ways of doing that, of which LNG and GTL are two. The other two are gas direct-into-transport, LNG  uses fuel for trucks, ships or rail, or gas-to-chemicals, which essentially is an ethane play in the Pennsylvania  region.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Gas-to-liquids, yes, we are looking to replicate what we've done in Qatar on the Gulf Coast, not necessarily in  Louisiana, we're looking in Texas as well as Louisiana. Essentially looking for Brownfield opportunities, exiting  infrastructure, access to the gas network and looking at what have learned in Qatar that can bring the costs down,  increase the yields, increase the efficiency? It will take some time, a year or two, to work that through and then  several years to construct. So we're some time away from making a decision on gas-to-liquids, and more likely  towards the end of the decade before we get production. It does look attractive.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: How does it compare with LNG export?  Well, it depends of course on the answer to what will be the cost be and  what will the yield be. But there's not a lot of difference there we'd say at the moment. LNG export, we would  expect and are giving priority to exports from Canada, from the West Coast to Asia and we're working with our  is primarily on Canada. Out of the U.S. it's possible, but looks a little expensive in terms of getting access to  facilities. So focus on Canada.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: CSG, coal seam gas, or CBM in Australia. Just to reiterate, there are four projects planned, three under  construction plus our Arrow LNG project, where the LNG is in the feed process, potential FID maybe the end of  next year. But, clearly, CSG is not like Sakhalin. We've started up Sakhalin on a handful of wells and it runs at full  capacity on nine wells. To run big LNG and on the CSG basis you may need several thousand wells, which you  can't just start and drill and start up on day one. So it is clearly a challenge for all the projects to have enough gas  available to run the trains economically.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: What I said this morning, I've not seen what's actually has been reported, was that we have plenty of gas for our  two-train project, where we're prepared to choose our timing of FID to minimize the potential impact of inflation  and, in the meantime, if and as we develop production capability, we're open to discussion with other projects on  provision of gas into other people's facilities. That doesn't mean it's going to happen, but we were open for  discussion.

texts.speaker: Lucas O. Herrmann
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Prime Brokerage)
texts.text: Simon, thanks, afternoon. Just a couple of points of clarification perhaps. Athabasca Oil Sands, can you just  expand on the maintenance comments and give us some indication of when you might perhaps be moving towards  new capacity on that project?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I presume, Lucas, the second question is about the liquids-rich shales?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Yeah. Okay. Many thanks. In the first quarter in Canada, in the Oil Sands, we have unplanned maintenance  events. We're still learning a bit about managing some of these assets and it did contribute to some of the numbers  I talked about earlier in terms of the potential value left on the table. We are, however, improving. When we will  be at capacity? Well, we've shown every individual piece of the value chain works at capacity, in fact, the upgrade  is work above capacity.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: It's typical, just for your information, for mine sites to be built for some reason with a target reliability and  availability in the low 80%. And given that we manage better than that in most of the rest of our portfolio, that's  what we've been working on over the past two to three years and we are steadily lifting that towards 90% and  beyond.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And acreage purchased in the U.S. and Canada, liquids-rich shales, although we tend to look at globally, as much  as just North America, but specifically in North America we've picked up acreage obviously in the Eagle Ford,  which we're drilling. And that's the most advanced; it's the only one that has material production for us. And – but  we have acreage also in the Mississippi Lime and several plays in Canada, including the Alberta Bakken and the  Duvernay play, which is of the geological name, rather than the company.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So we are currently operating nine rigs in appraisal and development and another four in exploration. We expect  that to increase over the coming months. We – and those are the areas that we're focusing on. We have other  acreage that we may not get the rigs to as quickly and – but we are certainly pushing the boundaries of all our  existing acreage to the extent we can to produce wet gas.

texts.speaker: Lucas O. Herrmann
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Prime Brokerage)
texts.text: And, Simon, when you talked earlier about 40,000 barrels a day from the Eagle Ford gas and oil. Can you give us  some sense as to what the proportion of that 40,000 comes from liquids?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: No, it's not just Eagle Ford, by the way, the 40,000 [barrels] but it'll depend on how the plays play out. Just one  comment worth making on the LRS plays. They're not the same as each other; they're not even the same if we're  drilling wells a kilometer apart. We're getting quite different results and that's exactly the same as the rest of the  industry. This is an immature activity. It is not as mature as the gas and it's very difficult for anybody to project  specific outcomes based on what we know about reservoirs and that includes the Williston Bakken as well.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Raízen materiality it's, hopefully, several hundred million dollars per quarter. It is being driven or helped at the  moment by good sugar and ethanol prices. So far, we have had a very successful operational start-up. Ventures are  not always easy bringing together two cultures, but we found very good strategic alignment. Cosan is a good  partner and we're seeing more synergies, more opportunities than we'd originally envisaged in the operation,  which has been good so far.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Longer-term, of course, the Cosan's interests are basically for them to determine and you to talk to them about,  but if their interest are in the energy sector development in Brazil, the clean energy sector development, these are  the statements they make, then Comgás is not only well placed being in São Paulo State and close to a lot of their  current activities there, it has potential longer-term percentages with Raízen but there are no current plans to  merge or take the strategy together.

texts.speaker: Irene Himona
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA (UK)
texts.text: Okay, thanks. Can I just very quickly ask about going back to the point on the potential for GTL in the U.S.  Obviously, the life of such a project is 30-years plus. It is a free market; the project's economics too depend on the  oil to gas price differential. Isn't it a little bit of risky to sort of bet that the current differential remains in place for  that time period?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Fair question but I would push back on, it doesn't actually depend on the differential, it depends on the difference  between oil price and cost of gas, if we're producing our own gas. It only depends on the differential if you're  buying the gas. What you give up if the Henry Hub gas price were to go to $10, $11 again, would be the  opportunity cost of course. So what it does actually, it de-risks the portfolio from just being pure natural gas by  converting some of the natural gas to oil. So it's really play on what do we see the long-term oil price, as long as we  got low-cost gas in our own portfolio. So that's how we think about it. So the question we need strategically to  consider, which is being considered.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: But if I had an answer, I'd probably be looking to share with you in a strategy discussion. What is the proportion of  the total gas resource base on which we want to effectively develop liquids-related pricing exposure? And it's not  necessarily 100%, but I don't know what the number is. But the priority we're giving at the moment, as I  mentioned earlier, Canadian LNG and we're looking at GTL. That may not use a whole significant demand to the  40,000-plus [barrel] Tcf that we actually have but something that will – on which the strategy will evolve, as we  see – get a better view of the costs, and the economics, and the relative attractiveness.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Alaska, or Arctic more generally, our focus clearly is in the U.S. on Alaska and Greenland, where we will do some  further study work this year, looking to drill in the not-too-distant future, we hope. Russia, as a whole, big  country, lot of acreage, some of the acreage being taken up. We're always open to discussion with Russian partners  but it needs to be – we need to be able to find an outcome that suits both their needs and our needs and that's not  yet been possible for us. But we have good relationship with both Gazprom and Rosneft and maybe that will  ultimately lead to further opportunity. But in the short and the medium-term, we have quite a lot of Arctic  exposure, quite a lot of Arctic experience and that's where we'll be focusing our efforts.

texts.speaker: Hootan Yazhari
texts.profession: Analyst, Merrill Lynch International (United Kingdom)
texts.text: Hi there, Simon. Just a quick question regarding gas pricing in China, given your unconventionals position there,  I just wanted to see if you could give us a sense as to how much the Chinese are using that to promote gas-on-gas  competition in the country? And whether that's beginning to affect LNG prices and the sorts of levels that you're  beginning to – or that you're achieving on new contracts that you're signing out there?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Hootan, it's a good question, but you're probably slightly ahead of the game in terms of an answer I can  give you. Just to be clear, the Chinese energy policy, at the moment, in the 12th Five Year Plan is clear. They  expect to grow gas as a share of primary energy demand from 4% in 2010 to 10% or higher by 2020, so probable  trebling or more of the total gas demand in country, as a result of needing to meet energy demand – the demand  that is growing, but also for a cleaner form of energy. So, it's got quite strong support already in the policy and that  policy was predicated mainly on imports either pipeline or LNG.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: LNG, typically, is setting marker prices on the coast. Further inland, the prices tend to be a net back against those  coastal prices. There has been a policy to raise prices from their current levels, which are certainly higher than  North American at the moment anyway, towards the import parity over time, essentially what you say the gas-on- gas competition. But prices are set differently for different consumers as well. So everything you say – you ask  about is very valid, but all of the answers come not from Shell but from the government. And I'm sure that they  will be taking into account, exactly what is the potential in shale gas? We don't know that yet. That's what we are  trying to help establish together with PetroChina, at least in the acreage we're working together there. So we  completed 11 wells last year, we hope to complete quite a few more this year, maybe around 25.

texts.speaker: Quirijn Mulder
texts.profession: Analyst, ING Bank NV (Broker)
texts.text: Okay, thank you. Hi, Simon. One question: with regard to selling 32% of your Prelude 100% stake to some Asian  partners, what are your intentions there for the future?  Are you trying to accelerate the exploration efforts there  in that area? And also with regard to further FLNG projects starting up there, like a concert or something like  that?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks. There are three partners have come in Inpex, KOGAS and CPC. Now two of them are clearly LNG  customers for Shell and interested in LNG supply back to their home base. And so, for us, that's a typical way of  de-risking an equity LNG project, where we started at 100% bringing in customers. The Inpex is slightly different.  You'll note that in Q4 2011 we agreed to enter a body floating LNG project in Indonesia, which is an Inpex project.

texts.speaker: Quirijn Mulder
texts.profession: Analyst, ING Bank NV (Broker)
texts.text: And the book value of $500 million I think in the project, is that – this part of construction, et cetera, what has  been done on FLNG?

file: RDSB - Q1 2013 Earnings Call 2May2013 830 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 02-May-13.pdf

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So far this year, we've seen the growth impact of recent startups with underlying volumes up 2%, and we've taken  four additional final investment decisions during the quarter with new investments announced in petrochemicals  in Singapore, in deepwater in Nigeria, and in LNG for transport capacity in the North America. This should all add  new value for shareholders.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And we've made further portfolio moves recently, such as the plan to sell down part of the Downstream portfolio  or positions in Italy and Australia. Of course, we have the agreement to buy Repsol's global LNG portfolio, which  has LNG supplies in Latin America, in Trinidad and Peru.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Oil prices have fallen recently, and this kind of volatility is a fact of life in our industry. And we are implementing a  long-term, consistent strategy against what is and will continue to be a volatile backdrop.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Let's just move on to the macro environment. You can see just from the lines on the chart the volatility we faced. If  you look at the macro picture compared to the first quarter 2012, the oil prices were lower than the year-ago. And  there was an increase in the differential between Brent and WTI to $18, and between Brent and West Canada  Select or WCS, $45 per barrel discount.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Our global natural-gas realizations increased from the first quarter a year ago. That includes the higher Henry  Hub price levels in North America.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We've also refreshed how we define identified items – difference between headline and adjusted for identified  items – clean earnings. We've got more clarity on definitions and we've removed the old $50 million threshold.  That's because that threshold did lead to sometimes rather binary outcomes, and that was out of step with the  peer group. We're moving to be more easily comparative.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The CCS earnings for the quarter including the identified items were $8.0 billion. Excluding the identified items,  the earnings were $7.5 billion, and that's an earnings per share increase of 2% over last year.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Our growth projects, such as Pearl Gas to Liquids, had a positive impact on the Q1-to-Q1 results, with some uplift  from gas prices. We also had positive year-over-year impact from tax, from LNG trading and from inventory  effects.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Our Upstream Americas business returned to profit in the first quarter, compared to the losses sustained in the  second half of 2012. This was driven by higher volumes, higher price realizations. However, earnings were lower  than one-year-ago levels, due to lower oil prices, higher costs, and a higher depreciation charge.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Our Downstream results excluding identified items and on the CCS basis were $1.8 billion. That's higher than  year-ago levels and they – and supported by higher oil products and chemicals results.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The headlines: oil and gas production for the first quarter was 3.6 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, about  2% up on an underlying basis. The volumes were supported by growth from Pearl Gas to Liquids, a Pluto LNG  project in Australia, and both of these effectively are now fully ramped up. And also supported from North  America liquids-rich shale plays where we produce 52,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, and that compares to  only 7,000 barrels per day a year ago.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Maintenance, especially in the North Sea, took around 30,000 barrels oil-equivalent a day from production year  on year. And the worsening security picture in Nigeria, that reduced our share of SPDC volumes onshore by  30,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, again, relative to last year.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: LNG sales volumes globally were flat Q1 to Q1. The growth from Pluto in Australia was offset by reduced loadings  in Nigeria where it appeared gas supply was disrupted by attempted theft on the gas pipelines.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And if you look at the underlying trends, we saw lower chemicals and oil-products sales than one year ago. Europe  and North America oil-products volumes declined. We did see some growth, led by retail, in Asia.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now looking forward to the second quarter of 2013. We are expecting, relative to last year, 20,000 barrels oil- equivalent per day of negative impact from the North Sea and Gulf of Mexico maintenance activities. And those, of  course, are high-margin barrels.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now we've restarted production at Port Arthur's crude expansion project and the refinery in Texas in the  Downstream. In the Upstream, we started up the first of the oil-sands de-bottlenecking project in Canada. We  started up the Amal enhanced-oil-recovery project in Oman. And we started yesterday operations in the Basra Gas  Company in Iraq, which will capture and commercialize the gas currently being flared in Southern Iraq.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We saw four new final investment decisions in the quarter. 60,000 barrel oil-equivalent per day in Nigeria  deepwater, on a 100% basis, that would be. And 500,000 ton per annum of integrated gas in the gas-to-liquid  fuels or transport fuels in North America.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We also launched new polyols and ethoxylation investment in Chemicals at the Jurong petrochemicals facility in  Singapore.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We added new exploration acreage worldwide. We found new gas reserve in Australia discovery, and had  continued near-field drilling success in our upstream engines.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now looking at new potential final investment decisions, we've had real progress in two areas in the last few days.  We were very pleased to be chosen by the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company to participate in a 30-year joint  venture to develop Bab sour gasfield with a 40% stake in that joint venture. And this could be up to 0.5 Bcf per day  for sale gas, or around 90,000 barrels a day oil-equivalent.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And in Canada, we've been granted regulatory approvals for the Carmon Creek in situ heavy oil project. And that  could come to final investment decision in the next 12 months and eventually be an 80,000-barrels-a-day project.  And currently, that's 100% shale project.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Acquisitions and acreage purchases in the quarter totaled $0.6 billion. That includes the increased stakes at Beryl  and Schiehallion in the U.K. where we already had an equity holding. Divestments were also $0.6 billion,  primarily proceeds from dilution of the Prelude floating LNG project in Australia to a strategic partner.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: There has been quite a bit of progress on our integrated gas portfolio. So I'll just give you oversight there.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Firstly, in Australia, the operator of Browse LNG, the potential project, the operator is Woodside. They announced  that the project will not go ahead with the original on-shore design that had been studied in FEED, and it will not  proceed, due to the high expected cost level. We fully support that decision, and the operator will now assess  alternatives, including floating LNG, which Shell believes is a viable economic alternative for this important  resource. 16 tcf of gas there, so it's a very potentially interesting resource for future development.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Elsewhere, we've taken FID on two new LNG for transport projects in North America. Brings our total capacity  there for transport LNG to 0.75 million tonnes per annum.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We also, in the U.S., formed a joint venture with Kinder Morgan for an LNG export facility at Elba Island in  Georgia. This is planned to be built using the same small-scale modular liquefaction facilities that we used in the  gas for transport. We'll build Elba Island in two phases for an expected total 2.5 million tonnes per annum with  Shell offtaking 100% – all of the LNG gas.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And we also reached an agreement in the quarter with Repsol to purchase their LNG business. 7.2 million tonnes  per annum of sale agreement, including the support from 4.2 million tonnes per annum of Latin America  liquefaction capacity.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, we're already a leading LNG trader, clearly, and we can add value to Repsol's positions through that trading  capability. We see up to $1 billion per year of cash flow potential from these Repsol assets, once the deal closes.  And we expect that to be later this year or early 2014. A lot of detail to work through.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So pretty good progress overall on the integrated-gas portfolio. And I have to point out one important fact here for  you. The new positions – Elba, gas for transport, Repsol LNG, and the Basra Gas joint venture – they'll all bring  good future cash flows, growth, returns to Shell. But collectively, they don't add a single barrel to our reserves or  production. And this is just symptomatic of – reflects our long-standing emphasis on value creation ahead of  volumes. I must reiterate, any production target is only a proxy for financial growth, and you can see in this choice  of projects precisely what that means.

texts.speaker: Theepan Jothilingam
texts.profession: Analyst, Nomura International Plc
texts.text: Just coming back to Australia, could you just talk about the other options still in the Shell portfolio, particularly  around Arrow LNG. And also the stake in Woodside on the latter. How you think that sort of adds value to the  Shell Group?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The Arrow joint venture, 50/50 Shell, PetroChina, is developing the Upstream. Looking potentially at early sale of  ramp-up gas to domestic or export customers. And we are preparing or progressing in parallel, both the  Greenfield LNG option and potential cooperation with the existing projects. There are three projects under  construction there.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And we deliberately delayed our own LNG project because of cost inflation. And there are three projects ongoing  in a country which is basically short of welders. So you can see what the underlying impact is on the project. We're  not in any particular hurry to make a final decision. We want to get the economics right.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We also have other floating LNG options. We've talked about Sunrise previously. We have other discoveries on the  Exmouth outer – or the outer Exmouth Shell, and in Evans Shoal. And we're still doing exploration. We've got a  big well going down, Shell only, 100% at the moment.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So very significant gas province. And it is important for us that we develop the right projects at the right  economics at the right time in terms of cost. But Australia remains an attractive country in which to do business  for LNG.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Woodside. As a result of all of the above, we said a couple of years ago that Woodside was no longer really a  strategic necessity for Shell, in terms of executing our LNG strategy in Australia. And we did sell down part of our  shareholding.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The liquids-rich shales in the U.S., 52,000 barrels oil-equivalent per day at the moment. That's basically the  Permian and the Eagle Ford. We've got 12 rigs in both – in the two in total. And we're also drilling out other  liquids-rich opportunities in Canada, in particular. So right around 20 rigs at the moment on liquids-rich activity.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We won't see quite such a step-up as we've recently seen because the 52,000 barrels oil-equivalent is – about a  half of it is in the Permian, which was an acquisition in the fourth quarter. But we do expect to see some growth  over the rest of the year.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Just as a benchmark, the average on-shore shale production was about 260,000 barrels oil-equivalent through the  totality of 2012, and we're at about 320,000 barrels oil-equivalent in Q1 2013. So quite some step-up, and that's  helped in the turnaround of the Upstream Americas results.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I can't give an absolute figure because it does depend on drilling results. And overall, you may recall, we've scaled  back our absolute activity in the onshore drilling for now, just to get the right balance and the right capital  discipline into the system.

texts.speaker: Jon Rigby
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: And secondly, just on the Canadian stuff, you referenced a small expansion and debottlenecking, and also talked  about Carmon Creek. As you look at your Canadian position, are you able to run – effectively run all the future  potential production from the oil sands through Scotford, and therefore sort of avoid, to some degree, some of the  problems that the rest of the industry is having in terms of differentials? Although clearly still affected in some  degree? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Canada. Debottlenecking is relatively small, the first one. It's 6,000 barrels a day, Shell's share. But this is –  remember, this is a series of relatively small projects that, over time, should get to 60,000 barrels a day, Shell's  share. And Carmon Creek is 80,000 barrels a day, Shell's share at the moment.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Can we run it all through Scotford? I'm afraid the answer is no. We would need to move some to Sarnia, some  potentially to Puget Sound, and some to the Gulf Coast. That is the intent, always was the intent. Clearly will  depend on access to appropriate pipeline capacity. And we can only really talk about that at the point at which it's  established. Particularly Keystone is an important indicator for the industry, although it's not the only way of  moving heavy oil down there from Canada.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And the one thing I would point out is that there's an ethane stream currently not seeing too much value, because  you can't actually stick it through the Fischer-Tropsch process. And that ethane stream is being allocated in future  into the chemicals projects that we're now working on with Qatar Petroleum. The Al-Karaana project.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So over time, additional investment helps add further value to the hydrocarbon streams in Qatar. And also, we  hope to spud shortly the new exploration well in Block D with partners PetroChina. So Qatar remains an area of  potential growth for us, looking good.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And throughput in Port Arthur, I don't have a specific number. It's not 100% on the 320,000 barrels new  expansion project, but it's close to 300,000 barrels. Not a lot of earnings impact in the first quarter, as we're still  ironing out some of the product flows, but it's actually performing pretty well. So it's about 80%, 90% of its  capacity on the distillation unit. So it's looking good, but not making a big impact on the bottom line just yet.

texts.speaker: Irene Himona
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA (Broker)
texts.text: Firstly on gas and the Basra Gas Company. Can you comment on whether the economics of that project would be  conditional on a future LNG export project, or whether you can actually deliver a return – an acceptable return  selling the gas domestically to power stations?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Irene. Yes, Basra Gas started yesterday. The economics are certainly not conditional on future LNG  exports. In fact, it's almost the other way around. The LNG economics would need to – I suspect they'll require  quite some work, both on the costs and the value-chain piece.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So the upfront activity is, basically we collect the gas; we strip the liquids; we put dry gas back into power, for  which there is a fee. And there is some access to the NGL revenue that we take out. And that's what underpins the  returns. So they're reasonably attractive. Better than the oil.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Exploration. We've got $4 billion going into conventional exploration, and $3 billion into unconventional. So  unconventional first. The most exciting is some of the LRS in – liquids-rich shale in Canada, in Argentina. And on  the gas side, we are, first well in Ukraine, and we have 10 rigs operating in China. Not all on exploration. Some are  in [indiscernible] (40:57). And China and Ukraine on the gas. Argentina and Canada on the liquids.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: You also hopefully have picked up the Gazprom Neft agreement, where we're looking at opportunities in the  Bazhenov shale in Russia, which we would expect to be liquids-rich, as well. So that could be of interest. Whether  we'll get to drill it this year or not, we do not know yet.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: But I just mentioned [indiscernible] (41:33), which is a gas prospect in [ph] the Prikov (41:39) that we will spud  shortly. We have two wells in [ph] Benine and Gibbron (41:42). Deepwater new plays. We have – the Australian  well at the moment is the Pulte. We're, interestingly, drilling in Albania on land for oil. And we have a fair few  wells in more mature areas, both the North Sea and Malaysia in particular, that could be certainly of interest.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: As we go forward, there are quite a few other areas such as Nova Scotia and the other Guiana and Columbia  deepwater and the Latin American trend. Greenland. And New Zealand that we may get to drill in 2014. So the  next two years is quite interesting in terms of the major plays.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So we will drill dry wells. They will not all be dry. And so let's see how it progresses. Some of the most exciting –  it's the most exciting set of wells we've had in conventional exploration for a very long time, I think.

texts.speaker: Jason D. Gammel
texts.profession: Analyst, Macquarie Capital (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And then just within that, could you address how having incremental Pacific basin volumes from Peru will help  your trading business, in light of a lot of those volumes already being committed in the Manzanilla. And I guess  really what I'm getting at is would you have other solutions for getting gas into Mexico that would allow you to re- route the Peruvian LNG to other Pacific Basins markets?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So mature as a region. But all those projects attractive. Four of them are oil projects. Clair, Schiehallion, Val  d'Agri, and Tempa Rossa.

texts.speaker: Iain S. Reid
texts.profession: Analyst, Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: Hi, Simon, good morning. Could I ask a couple of questions about Asia-Pacific LNG?

texts.speaker: Iain S. Reid
texts.profession: Analyst, Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: Firstly on Sakhalin, it looks like your partner there is interested in building a southern LNG facility down at  Vladivostok. And also Rosneft are talking about a facility in the region. Does this effectively mean that expansion  of Sakhalin, your Sakhalin plant, is kind of off the table for the moment?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Iain. Asia-Pacific LNG, well Russia specifically, as I mentioned, hopefully you all picked up the Gazprom  Neft announcement on Bazhenov shale, and arctic opportunities together with Gazprom Neft, signed in the  presence of the President and also Alexey Miller, the Chief Executive and Chairman of Gazprom.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The Train 3 option at Sakhalin continues to be worked. We have work ongoing in terms of the design. It is one of  the options available to Russia Inc. and Gazprom in particular to expand and enhance their LNG market presence.  It's our view, of course, that it is both the cheapest and by far the quickest way of achieving that. But there will still  – still decisions ahead of us.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: PNG, better be careful what I say because I was quoted out of context a year ago. So there is an InterOil process.  Clearly we've taken a look from a distance. And I can't really comment any further, other than to say I think I  started on the Australian project portfolio in LNG. We are known to be working the Abadi floating LNG project  with our partners at Inpex, who are also the operators, of course, in Indonesia. We are working Canada LNG very  actively at the moment and we announced the Elba Island export facility, plus of course the Repsol volumes.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The whole LNG business is progressing at quite a rate at the moment for us, and any new opportunities would  have to look pretty attractive to displace the ones that I've just talked about. So that's about all I can say, really.

texts.speaker: Iain S. Reid
texts.profession: Analyst, Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: You can't comment on whether you're actually part of the InterOil process?

texts.speaker: Lydia R. Rainforth
texts.profession: Analyst, Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: And then secondly, if I could, on the U.S. [ph] oil gas to transport (53:40) section, how big do you eventually see  that ending up being? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Gas to transport. Good question. When we started, we may have had certain aspirations for this market. What  we're essentially doing is producing LNG in small scale, and selling it to trucks, fleet operators, and to shipping.  Small fleet operators in shipping, or large enough to justify the investment, anyhow.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We have been surprised at how quickly this is coming together. We have many manufacturers now looking at this.  Cummins and Westport are the main ones in North America. But just in China alone, I think there are around  Guangdong 17,000 trucks and busses running now on LNG. That's growing fast; Chinese manufacturers. We're  seeing appetite for LNG barges running down the Rhine in Europe. We acquired Gasnor, which is an LNG for  shipping provider in Norway last year. So potential is multi-million tonne per annum.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Much of this will not necessarily be provided from our own Upstream gas production. It will depend basically on  the logistics close by. But we see the take-up of the various parts of the value chain accelerating in an attractive  way. And it's – our challenge and opportunity is to ensure that we can find an offer for the customers, the right  pricing, the right distribution that helps us develop a leading position there.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So it could be very substantive globally over a period of time. And we see North America and China in particular as  growing this as a major part of the transport fuels mix.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We're currently progressing Stones towards FID, which will be a floater – floating production storage unit. That's  a 3 billion-barrel resource remember as well in the lower tertiary. So it won't be a major development upfront  because it'll be more an early production system. But that will be the next one.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And costs – that's not that much of an issue in the Gulf yet. It could be, if the projects all take off, of course. And  just back on the shales, costs actually on the drilling and the activity, not too much inflation there at the moment.  It's more on the administration – how on earth do you manage across the 14 basins that we're in at the moment?  And you may recall, I talked about the $28 billion on the balance sheet three months ago.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So we're still working our way through that. We rebalanced the drilling activities, I said before, with most of it now  on liquids-rich plays. And a lot of that is still exploration and appraisal. So we need to work our way through that,  towards full field development and projects that we can see, and work out effectively how that $28 billion finds its  way to the profit and loss statement. And that's something that will play out and we'll talk about in quarters going  forward.

texts.speaker: Alejandro A. Demichelis
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane Ltd.
texts.text: In terms of the buyback, you mentioned in the $4 billion to $5 billion for this year, and clearly that you're not  prepared to increase debt to meet this. Should we assume that if for whatever reason oil prices were to drop in the  second half of the year, that $4 billion to $5 billion may not be there?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: That's a fair question. I'm looking more at what we've already delivered from free cash flow than what we're about  to deliver from free cash flow. If the oil price dropped to 70, we may look at the buyback program, but for now, we  don't see a problem with that.

texts.speaker: Kim A. Fustier
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Firstly on, Alaska, I was hoping you could give us some color on the drilling program there, which was postponed I  guess two months ago. Basically what are the next steps? And any color as well on the accounting treatment of the  cost for this year?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The same is essentially true of the remaining balance, which relates about $700 million to the capitalized cost of  the wells that we have drilled to-date, and the rest is basically the capital cost of the containment barge and the  Kulluk drilling rig, which obviously are ongoing, valuable assets.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And Nigeria. 30,000 barrels a day was essentially comparison between Q1 last year and Q1 this year. The absolute  loss is higher. It's more like 60,000 barrels a day. And similar [ph] to that (1:07:04) in the first quarter I  mentioned was attempted theft from a gas line which unfortunately you can't steal. And also took us down in the  NLNG volumes, so quite valuable production loss.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Going forward, we have, in April, closed the Nembe Creek Trunkline simply because the theft is so high and the  environmental damage potentially is so high, it's no longer sustainable. And we need to go and remove all of the  theft points. And of course, the thieves just move to the next pipeline. And I believe Eni have also shut down  facilities in country.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So it's quite a difficult situation. It's not getting any better. I don't have a figure, other than that if both pipelines  were to be shut down, it's quite a significant materiality in earnings terms. It may be up to $100 million a month,  if both of the major pipelines were to be down. One is running at the moment. One is taken down, out of service  for repair work. So it's an uncertain environment.

texts.speaker: Fred Lucas
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: There's another big diesel machine ramping up in the Middle East. It's ARAMCO's Jubail refinery. 400,000  barrels a day, of which more than half the product slate is diesel. What effect do you think that it will have on the  profitability of Pearl GTL over the coming months?

texts.speaker: Fred Lucas
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: And if I could squeeze a third one in, it just needs a numerical answer. Can you put a number to how much of your  oil sands output doesn't make it into the Scotford upgrader? So for every 10 barrels, per se, how much doesn't?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The first one's relatively easy. Big diesel machine. GTL profitability is underpinned by base oils and special  products, and being purely clean diesel. So unless the Saudis can produce completely clean and sulfur-free diesel  from crude oil, they will not be impacting the markets where we are seeing premium pricing.

texts.speaker: Fred Lucas
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: Out to 2017, 2018 to get to the 4 million barrels a day?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Well, the 4 million barrels a day, I think there was a clue in what I said earlier that we will invest in at least four  projects now that have no value volume associated with them at all, but will lead to equivalent cash flow growth.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And again, I could give you any growth or cash flow I want to, merely by drilling shale out in North America. But  we're only going to do that when it makes sense to make money at competitive returns.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Last point. Oil sands production to Scotford. The upgraders basically will process everything out of the mines.  Some of the debottlenecking we're doing at the moment will increase the upgrading capacity. We're not able to –  the upgraders, of course, only produce syncrude. They don't necessarily a lot of finished product. Because we  brought that into the Scotford refinery.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And the refinery is smaller than the upgraders. So we're actually moving upgraded crude to, for example, Sarnia  and the West Coast. Some of it's going by rail to the West Coast. And ultimately it will be the most likely some  synthetic crude, but also some just basically straight bitumen – diluted bitumen – that will go to the Gulf Coast.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: But at the moment, everything can be upgraded, bar the 10,000 barrels a day coming out of Peace River, which is  not of a quality that can go through the upgrader. And in the future, we will not – it's highly unlikely we'll build  new upgraders, if and when we grow the heavy-oil production further. Our aim will be to take it into our own  refining network.

texts.speaker: Guy A. Baber
texts.profession: Analyst, Simmons & Co. International
texts.text: Thanks for taking my question. I was just hoping you could address the environment for asset divestitures right  now. But your guidance this year is I believe just $3 billion, which would be the lowest total in a couple of years for  you all. And last year you ended up doing a little bit more than twice what the original guidance was.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Previously we had slightly higher targets because we had a major Downstream program in progress for about five  years. That major program is now basically running out. And we talked about Italy and the refinery in Australia, et  cetera. But these are not major factors.

texts.speaker: Guy A. Baber
texts.profession: Analyst, Simmons & Co. International
texts.text: Yeah, my follow-up was on U.S. gas production. But production very strong this quarter, presumably on some  Marcellus ramp. But just hoping you could provide for us the framework for how you plan to manage production  through the balance of the year, and activity levels, in light of some of the major variables. So Marcellus, some of  the improvement we've seen in spot gas pricing, but also just considering how materially you've cut the capital  budget there for gas this year.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Okay. Most of the current gas activity is actually in West Canada in the Groundbirch. More than Marcellus. We've  got twice as many rigs there.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And we're also producing some gas in the Eagle Ford along with the liquids. So that's helped some stronger gas  production.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Prices now are $4.30 I think in gas terms. Even at that price, it's probably still more attractive to keep the rigs very  much on the liquids-rich shale appraisal activities, as much as production, as well. And to ensure that we're  drilling out, for example, the China Ukraine exploration opportunities.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So we're not actually planning or aiming to ramp back up again in a material way in North America in gas at this  point in the market.

texts.speaker: Hootan Yazhari
texts.profession: Analyst, Merrill Lynch International (United Kingdom)
texts.text: And then going forward, just to get a clear idea of you how you're thinking about project planning, et cetera, how  are you looking at projects that add value to Downstream in the United States versus your growth targets for 2017  and 2018? Is there a case to start to push up the – some of the potential LNG, GTL, GTT, et cetera, projects up the  chain, and thereby displace some of the growth there? Or do you feel that – or would you be more willing to re- lever the balance sheet up and include everything? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And projects Downstream in the U.S. Actually there are quite a few opportunities. Everything ranging from buying  rental cars to LPG exports to tweaking the refineries to process the crudes that are available. All being thought  about and progressed, and not just by us, as well, of course, at the moment.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In absolute materiality terms, not yet that significant. It will help to grow CFFO or protect current CFFO. So very  much part of the thinking, as is the same thinking around gas, where all the gas get moved within the continent.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The big projects to monetize. We've already talked about Elba and the gas-to-transport projects. These are what  we might call the medium-size projects committed [ph] on those (1:21:21) export LNG.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Big projects – Canada LNG is pretty much highest priority. That we do need to get moving, because of the good  partners we have there, getting that gas to Asian markets.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Gas to liquids, gas to chemicals, very much in the mix, in terms of optionality. Unlikely to see a whole lot of CapEx  in that period up to 2015.

texts.speaker: Jason S. Kenney
texts.profession: Analyst, Banco Santander SA (London Branch)
texts.text: And then maybe secondly, on the gearing at 9.1%, have you got a view of where gearing might exit 2013, if Brent  oil price stayed at $100?

texts.speaker: Lucas O. Herrmann
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Prime Brokerage)
texts.text: First, just chemical. If you could talk a little about more about the performance. Doesn't seem the environment's  changed dramatically, but the profit performance certainly appears to have.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In Asia-Pacific, it's good place to be in some of the more specialist products. The intermediate products. Mono- ethyl glycol – the MEG, and ethylene oxide.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So just generally well-positioned business. And benefits compared to, say, four, five years ago fundamentally from  the switch to ethane feed in the United States.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: You mentioned the deepwater projects. Yes, Mars B, Cardamom, and BC10, together with in 2015 definitely we'd  like to see Gorgon producing. Those big projects will certainly make a difference, where you're talking multiple- billion uplift there.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: But fundamentally the challenge today for the next 12 months is primarily steady progress Downstream and  Upstream, taking the extra dollars out of the flow of the hydrocarbons that we're involved in.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: But the Americas, I shied away from production forecasts. But we are established now our 320,000 barrels of  production a day on-shore. We're about 190,000 barrels a day in the Gulf, the deepwater offshore.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: That 190,000 barrels a day was a bit below trend. Some planned maintenance, some down time in the Auger  platform. We are ramping up still production in Great White, Perdido.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The major projects are next year. That's Mars B and Cardamom in particular. And when we report Upstream  Americas, we include Brazil. So the BC-10 and Bijupirá and Salema both have additional production coming on  next year.

file: RDSB - Q1 2014 Earnings Call 30April2014 700 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 30-Apr-14.pdf

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We are repositioning the company for changes in the industry landscape, particularly in Oil Products and the  North America shale plays. The impairments that we announced today in the Downstream reflect our updated  views on the outlook for refining margins where there are substantial pressures on the industry. We are also  taking hard choices across the portfolio, with some $4.5 billion of asset sales announced in the quarter that  included Wheatstone LNG in Australia and Downstream position exits from four countries.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Our investment strategy is delivering at the bottom line. The first quarter has seen new profitable production from  the deepwater Gulf, a ramp-up Iraq, together with the new LNG from the acquisition of Repsol's portfolio. And  we're maturing new options, with front end engineering and design or FEED decisions on deepwater and in the  LNG business. And this is part of the project flow that will continue to drive further financial growth from us for  many years to come.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Turning to the results and I'll start with the macro. But if you look at the picture compared with the first quarter  2013, the Brent crude prices were some $4 per barrel lower, and we saw narrower differentials between Brent and  the North American market. Our liquids realizations declined from the first quarter last year, but we saw an  increase in the gas realization. The North American winter was especially cold, with milder condition year-on-year  in Europe, and we saw that both in the gas pricing and the volumes.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Turning now to the earnings. Earnings for the quarter, including a $2.9-billion identified item predominantly in  Downstream – I'll say more about that in a moment – but excluding those identified items, the underlying current  cost of supply, or CCS, earnings were $7.3 billion for the quarter. That's a 2% decrease in earnings per share from  the first quarter of 2013. A slight decline in Downstream earnings, broadly flat in the Upstream.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So looking at the moving parts in the results. Environmental factors such as the prices, Downstream margins, in  aggregate a slight positive, some $300 million Q1 to Q1. Security picture remains difficult in Nigeria, although it  has improved from the very tough conditions a year ago, where you might remember the disruptions to the gas  supply to LNG, as well as the ongoing effect of crude oil.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Looking at the Integrated Gas business. The Upstream results included $3.3 billion of underlying earnings from  this segment of the business, and that's LNG and GTL. This was a record result for this piece of business and a  30% increase year-over-year, balancing growth and return.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So let me be clear that there were some effects in this result that may not repeat, such as around $90 million of  exchange rate gains and $170 million of higher dividends from the Malaysian LNG venture. That's both Q1 against  Q1. And we also saw a strong LNG trading environment. That's quite normal in the first quarter. However, over  time, we are seeing the impact of the steady improvement in plant availability also.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: This is also the first quarter where we consolidated the LNG portfolio that we acquired from Repsol at the end of  2013. All of that helped drive the strong first quarter earnings and the cash flow shown on this slide and Repsol  alone adding a few hundreds of million to earnings and CFFO in the quarter.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We believe we are on track for the up to $1 billion per year cash generation potential from that acquisition. And  that comes from both the base offtake and also the enhanced trading opportunities that we've achieved from  combining the two portfolios, Shell and Repsol. Now, Integrated Gas is profitable and it's growing, and we  continue to be the leader amongst the IOCs in this business.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Overall, the Upstream earnings, on an underlying basis, were $5.7 billion, pretty much the same as a year ago. The  earnings were supported by higher contributions from Integrated Gas but also from trading, as well as higher gas  realizations overall, which offset the lower oil prices and the increased costs, depreciation and exploration  charges.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, we've given you the split of the exploration charges on the chart here at the top right, and I hope you find  that useful. You see that in some quarters, the scale of the exploration activity in Upstream Americas, for example,  can dwarf the overall results there. Americas results were in profit compared with losses in the last several  quarters. This in part reflects higher Henry Hub gas prices and better associated gas trading results in the cold  snap. The volume effects were neutral on a Q1-to-Q1 basis in the Americas, and we're looking forward to  continued ramp-up in the Gulf of Mexico later this year.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Oil and gas production overall for the quarter, 3.2 million barrels of oil equivalent a day, and that's the headline  decline of 9%. That's a large movement. But the earnings impact Q1 to Q1 was negligible, with much of the  reduction being in low-margin barrels. This figure in total includes 180,000 barrels oil equivalent a day of  negative impacts for license expiries, including Abu Dhabi, production sharing contract effects, the year-on-year  difference in Nigerian security, and also in the Netherlands, the gas production reduction related to the  earthquake mitigation. Excluding all of the above effects, the production volumes declined by around 4%.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Production was impacted by warm weather in Europe and also by some 60,000 barrel oil equivalent per day of  maintenance impacts and asset replacement dominated by South East Asia, the Canadian oil sands and the Gulf of  Mexico.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Looking forward into the second quarter, LNG sales volumes are expected to be higher than the year ago, driven  by the volumes from the acquisition. The ADCO license in Abu Dhabi expired in January this year. That will  reduce our production by over 155,000 barrels a day going forward, but it is a low-margin contract.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In the Upstream, we are expecting continued impacts from the Nigerian operating environment. But you may  recall we had particularly difficult gas constraints in the second quarter last year, and we also saw the start of the  blockade on the LNG plant itself. Compared to the last year second quarter, we are expecting an offset from lower  maintenance activities and increased exploration costs and the higher depreciation charges all on Q-to-Q basis; a  mixed bag of comparative movements.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: As we indicated earlier, we've reviewed the balance sheet values for the Oil Products portfolio and we've taken a  $2.6 billion impairment charge today. And this basically reflects an updated view on the industry landscape, in  refining in particular. We see continued pressure on margins from the growth of liquids-rich shales in North  America, from a stronger demand growth for diesel products ahead of and compared with growth for gasoline,  and continuing significant overbuild in refining capacity especially in Asia and the Middle East. Now, the  impairment today represents about 14% of the total PP&E fixed assets in refining. We're continuing to refocus the  Downstream portfolio with divestments of non-core positions underway in four countries out of a total of some 70  countries and, of course, further reviews underway.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now looking back to the second quarter of 2014, we are expecting higher chemicals availability than second  quarter last year but lower refining availability due to planned maintenance.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The final tranche of the acquisition for Repsol's LNG portfolio, some $2 billion, was booked to capital investments  in the first quarter of 2014. Our gearing at quarter-end sat at 15.6%, and that's a slight reduction from the position  at the end of last year.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now let me update you on the portfolio activity, another busy quarter. We've added new opportunities during the  quarter, started up new production and announced further asset sales, all part of positioning the company for  profitable future growth. And you can see the details on this chart by strategic themes. We completed the Repsol  acquisition. We made new oil and gas discoveries in Asia Pacific. We added new exploration acreage in Namibia,  in Norway and Russia.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
