texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The world is in an era of important geopolitical transition, strong volatility, and intensified economic cycles.  Emerging nations like China and India are going through rapid development and OECD economies have financing  challenges. All of this comes at a time when access to low cost oil and gas is more difficult and there are questions  in society around environmental impact. This is a complex and volatile landscape for the energy industry and an  opportunity for Shell.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Our Q2, 2011 CCS earnings, excluding identified items, were $6.6 billion, an earnings per share increase of 52%  year-on-year. This improvement comes despite pressure on refining margins and low North American natural gas  prices. Underlying Upstream volumes were good, up 2% and we are continuing to work on our costs.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Looking into the medium-term, we have launched some exciting new projects this year, with 9 new FIDs final  investment decisions, and we have finalized the Raízen downstream joint venture in Brazil, which is a leading  biofuels player.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So, overall good progress on our plans in 2011. Let me give you more details on it. Continuous improvement is  embedded in our operations and activities here at Shell. This is all about smaller, incremental initiatives to  enhance our performance and commerciality. It is things like simpler structures and standardization, for example,  in contracting and procurement. The opportunities in total run to billions of dollars of potential.  Again, let me give you an example here. Shell drilled over 200 tight gas and CBM wells worldwide in 2010. So how  do we work on costs there? We are establishing a 50-50% joint venture with CNPC, China's Natural Petroleum  Company, which we expect to substantially improve our competitive cost position in onshore gas drilling. The JV  is intended to develop and own, standardized and automated drilling equipment, sourced from low cost suppliers,  for drilling and completing new onshore wells. This is intended to be used for high density drilling projects, both  in Canada and in other countries in the future.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Three of these new projects, oil sands in Canada, LNG, liquefied natural gas, and GTL, gas to liquids in Qatar, are  now on stream. These three projects alone, at peak, should reach over 400,000 BOEs per day for Shell or over  10% of 2010 production.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: These start-ups reflect some of Shell's unique strengths in the energy industry today: innovative technology,  integration across value chains, and creating long-life returns for shareholders. So these are exciting times on the  growth side.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Prelude Floating LNG is the largest of these new developments. This is an innovative development solution for  smaller-sized, stranded gas fields and a first in our industry. Taken with our other interests in Australia, we now  have some 8.3 million tonnes per annum of LNG under construction there. Another 40% step on top of our  worldwide capacity of 20.5 million tonnes per annum on stream today.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So when you combine our 2011 progress on new projects with the five investment decisions we took in 2010: Mars  B, BC-10 phase 2, North American tight gas, we've matured over 400,000 BOE per day of new production in the  last 18 months.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So, 400,000 barrels per day of new capacity coming on stream in 2011 and another 400,000 barrels per day going  into construction. This is all about sustained investment for growth and shareholder returns.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now let me turn to Downstream growth. In Downstream, let me highlight that our Brazil joint venture with Cosan,  which is called Raízen, went live in June this year. We have merged our Brazil marketing operations with Cosan's  portfolio and the JV will have about 4,500 retail sites combined, a top three player in Brazil.  All of these will be branded as Shell sites and offer Shell's distinctive suite of fuels products for customers. To give  you some perspective, Brazil on a 100% basis is now about 10% of our retail network worldwide and one of our top  three retail countries.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Raízen also marks Shell's first move into substantial biofuels production. The company is the number one  bioethanol player in Brazil and it could more than double in scale in the next five years.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thank you, Peter. I'll start with the macro environment. If you look at the macro picture compared with the  second quarter of 2010, oil and gas market prices have increased from year-ago levels, with broadly similar Henry  Hub.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The discount of WTI to Brent widened to $15 in the second quarter, and that compared with less than $1 in the  second quarter 2010. And this, of course, impacts our oil realizations.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Turning now to earnings. Our CCS earnings for the quarter, included identified items, were $8 billion. Excluding  those identified items, the CC earnings were $6.6 billion, and earnings per share increased by 52%, and that's  compared with the second quarter of last year.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now let me move on to the business performance in a little more detail. Firstly, the Upstream. Excluding the  identified items, Upstream earnings were $5.4 billion in the second quarter, and that's an increase of 66% against  the same quarter in 2010. The earnings were driven by higher prices and higher oil and LNG volumes, and they  were partly offset by lower natural gas demand, higher taxes and increased operating expenses, these largely  reflecting the start-up of new projects.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Headline oil and gas production for the second quarter was 3 million barrels of oil equivalent per day. That's an  positive impact from growth barrels; they more than offset the natural field decline. There were also negative  impacts from asset sales, maintenance and demand. However, the underlying performance is good here.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: LNG sales volumes grew by 14% in the first half of 2011 compared to the same period in 2010. It's probably worth  reflecting that the comparative figure against 2009 first half is 55% growth, just showing what the portfolio can  do. And that, in this particular quarter, does reflect the successful ramp-up of Qatargas 4 as well as higher  volumes from Nigeria LNG.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And now turning to cash flow. Cash generation on a rolling 12-month basis was $50 billion, including $10 billion  of divestment proceeds and the average oil price over that 12 months has been $96 for Brent.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Both the Upstream and the Downstream segments are generating surface cash flow, after investment. We're  watching the cash position very carefully and I'm pleased to see our inflows and outflows are now moving to a free  cash flow position, albeit, of course, assisted by higher oil prices and the asset sales.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Turning now to capital spending and the balance sheet. The improving free cash flow position, combined with our  capital spending and dividend program has resulted in a decline in balance sheet gearing. At the end of the  quarter, the gearing sat at 12%. That's compared with 14% at the end of the first quarter, continuing to move lower  in our 0% to 30% range. Now, you would expect that is in strong oil price conditions, of course.

texts.speaker: Lucy S. Haskins
texts.profession: Research Analyst, Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Good afternoon. I'd like to ask on the integrated gas contributions for the quarter, was very strong. Could you give  some [ph] theory (19:00) in terms of how much of that was coming from – we're seeing the volume  improvements; we're seeing in margin improvements. How much of the margin improvement was just the lags in  sort of oil price effect coming through? How much of it was arbitrage opportunities you were able to exploit during  the quarter? and how much of those arbitrage opportunities do you think could be sustainable now you're building  perhaps a little bit more flexibility into your LNG portfolio?

texts.speaker: Kim A. Fustier
texts.profession: Research Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Yes. Hi, good afternoon, gentlemen. Just a couple of questions, please. Firstly on Iraq, could you please comment  on the Basra gas deal that was initialed a couple of weeks ago? What are the next steps from here? And when can  you start thinking about LNG? My second question is on China Gas. Could you maybe give us an update on your  Shell Gas drilling activities, especially in the Sichuan Basin? Have you fractured the wells and tested them for flow  rates? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Yeah, thanks for the question. I take Iraq and then Simon can do China. Yes, we are very pleased of having signed  the contract on South Iraq gas, there's still more hurdles to go. I think the prime objective in the near-term is,  clearly, to actually capture [ph] flare  (22:07) gas and make it available domestically and then over time as  production ramps up, obviously, you go into potential export schemes. I would say they are a few years down the  road and I think that planning would still take place a little bit later.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So I think we will concentrate first on getting the deal over the line and once we have it then we will capture that  gas and as it ramps up, I'm sure we will talk soon about exporting gas then as well. With that, over to Simon on  China gas.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Peter. China overall, just to reiterate the overall program there, we actually have, of course, the one  operating concession, Changbei. We have two large or one type, one shale gas concession 4,000 square kilometer  reach in Sichuan province and we have two CBM activities further north in Shaanxi Province. So over that, that  whole portfolio, the plan was to effectively spend over $400 million drilling this year 15 to 17 wells.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks Peter. And in total, we've currently received, what, three exploration plans, a development plan, a couple  of additional well permits. The exploration plans typically include some drilling permits as well. We are, or we said  we'd be, up to 50,000 barrels a day short on production relative to what we otherwise would have been for this  year. That level of permitting and drilling means that we can basically confirm that; that we were 50,000 short of  where we might have been.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: What we're likely to produce in the Gulf, subject to hurricane activity of course, is around 200,000 barrels a day  this year, so it should have been 250,000. And that's quite a significant impact on all of our earnings, the way that  you do the analysis. And that's down from 2010 and 2009. 2009, the last year pre-hurricane was 270,000. So you  can see quite some impact.  As we go forward, we expect to make up some of the gap. The comparison against what we would otherwise have  achieved becomes rather like meaningless as we go forward. As we adjust our drilling plan to the opportunities  that are currently available to us. But we should certainly make up in areas like the [ph] Dido (26:51) and ensuring  we're working over wells on the operating platforms. So we should see some narrowing of that gap in 2012 built-in  already to the projections that we've been making, even though we made the original projections before the  moratorium.

texts.speaker: Jon Rigby
texts.profession: Research Analyst, UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: And then the second question is just on Chemicals, which seems to be having a remarkable renaissance over the  last couple of years. And I just wondered how much of that was down to the U.S. business? And is there something  sort of structural around profitability in the U.S. Chemicals business that will stick around until [indiscernible]  (28:16), until U.S. gas prices close on sort of international oil prices? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I think on the Chemical side I'm very pleased with how the Chemical business has turned around, specifically in  the United States for us, because they're really moving us away from a competitive disadvantage of being liquids- driven in the [ph] crackets (29:34) to actually being ethane-driven, has really made a big turnaround for us.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We also have improved clearly the cost base, not just in the United States, but across the world. So I think we are  structurally much greater positioned now. And given where the gas prices are, et cetera, et cetera, I think you can  expect a good performance and a strong continuous performance out of the U.S., obviously, depending on pricing  structures in the market, but the underlying operating performance is very strong.  Now, based on that, I just take a little bit of wider view on this. As we said previously, we also are looking now at  how we can actually use the chemicals stream and linking that back to our tight gas and unconventional gas  positions, which we have in the United States. So we're also looking into that and how we can add further value  further down the road. But I'm talking about a few years down, really down the road. So very pleased about the  strategic and the operational shift, which we have made in the U.S. in chemicals.

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: Hello. Yes. Two questions, if I may, first, on the acquisition of the 30% of the Abadi Floating LNG. Can I just check
texts.text: how that fits into the portfolio of other LNG profits you've got in Australia heading in the same direction? 2018,  does that sort of jump up ahead of some of the others that you've got? And, for example, is it likely to come ahead  of Arrow? And does it use Shell generic technology?

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Okay, Peter. And then your first question, I think first of all, we are very pleased with our progress in Indonesia  together with Inpex to buy into that LNG project. So very pleased about that and they are the operator but I think  we can bring some help and some advice and skills to that.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We have – on your Australian question then, I think we are concentrating on Prelude as we have taken [ph] a five- year. (33:00) This is our strong, strong kind of focus on. Now as you know we have many of other – of the other  projects there like Sunrise where we have already agreed with a list of partners that we will use our technology.  And we are also, obviously, working on Arrow where we have said that we will actually target LNG fee in 2011. And  I think we are talking there around the first phase which should be two trains and 8 million tonnes per year LNG.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Yeah. Thanks for the questions. On your first one, no, there's really no change to that. We have said in $60 and in  the $80 where they 50% up or at least 80% up between '09 and 2012. That really means that we are aiming at the  $43 billion at the higher end and $36 billion on the other side, if you'll take a lower – the lower amount, so no  change to that. It's also reflecting the production targets which we have given, which is 3.5 million barrels per day.  And this is all what we are working for in – at the moment and then into 2012. So on the capital employed, I give  that to Simon.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So we're effectively more productive, but not yet producing at the full whack. And exactly, as Peter said earlier, the  production we've only got 170,000 barrels to add to the 400,000 barrels on the three big projects and on the  earnings. Very little cash flow and these projects together in Qatar alone were projected at close to $4 billion at  $70 a barrel and another $1 billion in Athabasca at $70 a barrel. So there's still quite a lot to come there.

texts.speaker: Fred Lucas
texts.profession: Research Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Ltd.
texts.text: No. Hi. It's Fred Lucas at JPMorgan. Good afternoon, guys. Couple questions. Recently visited Rumaila in Basra  Province, Iraq and there seems to be some confusion there as to what actual rights the Basra gas deal might give  you with respect to the gas that's currently being [ph] fled by Rumaila, (36:40) which is very significant. I wonder  if you could clarify that point.

texts.speaker: Fred Lucas
texts.profession: Research Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Ltd.
texts.text: And the second question relates to the LNG projects, especially Prelude. I think Malcolm Brinded has indicated  cost there of around $3,500 a tonne which would point to total CapEx north of $12 million to recover just over 0.5  billion barrels. So it looks quite expensive reserve recovery at over $20 a barrel. Should we expect projects like  that to make a return on the first project? Or does it need the boat to move on to a second project to make an  adequate return?

texts.speaker: Fred Lucas
texts.profession: Research Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Ltd.
texts.text: And then finally, on your coalbed methane to LNG project in Australia, today, we saw – the FID saw AP LNG so  that leaves you fourth in the queue. Don't you think that's quite a precarious position to be in, given emerging  inflationary pressures in Australia, more generally upstream?

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I think I leave the Floating LNG to Simon. I'll deal with Arrow, which was your third question. I think we said  from the beginning that we are not in a rush here. We will develop this. We see the rush into quite a few FIDs by  others. That is our opinion will drive costs up, and I think we are quite happy to go later into feed and then FID  and be already behind some of the others because we think that gives us a cost advantage.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Let's also remember, we have floating LNG. We are working on it to divert other projects in Australia at the same  time. So our annual spend will most will be in the $3 billion to $4 billion in Australia alone, over the years to  come. And I think let's work carefully our way into that.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And then I'll pass on to the financial performance, et cetera, questions on FLNG to Simon.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks Peter. On Floating LNG, Prelude's 3.6 million tonne per annum project. What we said, Malcolm said was  $3,000 to $3,500 per tonne of capacity. What we have not done is given any specific CapEx for this project. What  we have indicated is its economics are similar to other large LNG projects, greenfield ones, in Western Australia,  for example, Gorgon, or in fact, the CBM projects, prior to the inflation that you just mentioned, of course, Fred.  And the returns, therefore, are good.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We will use this particular vessel to produce the Prelude field and likely two other fields close by. Thereafter, we  will have probably a couple of decades of useful life left, after which we will already have got a very attractive  return. Also $20 of barrel, I'd just point out, isn't such a bad cost and they're relatively attractive. Fiscal  environments and $115 oil; it's pretty good at $70, as well.

texts.speaker: Irene Himona
texts.profession: Research Analyst, Société Générale SA (UK)
texts.text: And my second question on cash flows. I think Simon mentioned the rolling four quarter $50 billion operating  cash flow on an oil branch of $96, so obviously, the oil price is well above your planning range. I don't know if it's  possible to adjust, but can you give an indication of what the gap is at your planning range versus the target,  please? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The other thing, of course, is we had said the 2012 target, expected I think a better refining environment than  we've seen in the past 12 months, and they were originally premised at a $6 North American gas prices, which is,  of course, higher than today. And you can take your own view of what that's like for next year. We are, however,  committed to meeting the cash flow generation targets next year.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Yeah, thanks Simon. And I think actually indirectly absorbed quite a bit of barrels, which we have filled and still  achieved the $3.5 million barrels also gives us another additional challenge. But as Simon says, we are well on  track to achieve it. Thanks, Irene. Next question.

texts.speaker: Lucas O. Herrmann
texts.profession: Research Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Prime Brokerage)
texts.text: And secondly, I just wonder if you could just talk around North American gas production and the seeming lack of  progress in terms of growth there. I'm not sure to what extent it's influenced by the divestment of the [ph] big  spherical (45:09) of Texas assets, but Canadian production doesn't seem to be moving north either. Is it just,  again, what's actually happening in terms of drilling spend and intention at the present time relative to the targets  that you set out in November last year?

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I know this is difficult for you guys to do because we don't give you those numbers, but just be assured that we are  actually taking a full integrated look at all of this and we see our supply and trading and the refining business like  that. With that then over to North American gas I give that to Simon.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Peter. The actual onshore gas volumes there are then, yes, from about 1.2 Bcf to 1.3 Bcf a day; this is  basically the reductions driven by the divestment of the [ph] Taft (49:09), Texas volumes. The program this year is  pretty much on track, although, we're in the lower end of the intended investment range, simply because the price  is in the $4 range at the moment.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We are there investing to produce in the Haynesville, in the Groundbirch. We're doing a fair bit of appraisal work  in Marcellus and Eagle Ford. In both Groundbirch and Haynesville, there's quite a bit of drilling leaving gas  behind pipe as we have not yet brought the infrastructure online.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So drilling is running a bit ahead of the production in the year-to-date, so we're overall still very much on track for  that medium-term target across the Americas, building up, in effect, a much better understanding of what is  required to mostly economically develop Groundbirch and Marcellus, in particular, because they're the big  drivers.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks. Entitlement over time, Mark, we've given in the past reasonably clear projections at different oil prices  about entitlement to production and entitlement to cash flow. They were actually at $50 and $70. And basically,  we have quite a significant cash flow, while we are in full cost recovery phase. That takes about seven to eight  years. That's at $70, obviously, a lot less if we were to stay at $117.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I take the two portfolio things. Let me start with the retail one, Mark. I think these are stations which are  predominantly in the midlands and the southeast of England. They fit very well into our network, which we have.  We get to 1,150 stations in total. We see great potential with our differentiated fuels offering, which we have in our  lubricants offering. I think these are all stations in prime markets, filling gas which we have, and therefore it does  really fit well into the UK and the overall retail strategy on a global basis.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And have met all the normal, rather stringent profitability criterias, which we have in Downstream, specifically for  marketing assets. So I'm pleased with the deal. On the AOSP side, I think you need to look at this in a wider sense,  that we are going for developments or debottlenecking of various, let's say tranches of the 30,000 to 40,000  barrels, 30,000, 35,000 barrels.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Okay. On the first one, I think the 30K, we reckon it will be around on the – on the oil sands will be around $2  billion. It will be offset, which gives you a breakeven below 50K, and if you take some of the tranches within that  package, they will be quite below the 50K, but on average it will be 50K.

texts.speaker: Oswald C. Clint
texts.profession: Senior Research Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Yes. Hi. Thank you. I guess is this sort of net income or the earnings per barrel was a bit – was higher than I was  expecting, also higher than your long-term trend relative to the commodity, just for the Upstream business. Is that  primarily, do you think the LNG businesses, Nigeria, that the Qatar volumes coming on that could be pushing that  up? Or is there anything else going on there?

texts.speaker: Oswald C. Clint
texts.profession: Senior Research Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: And then secondly, it's just the divestment, I understand you may have exited the Swedish Alum shale that you  were testing. I just wanted to know if you could give us any rationale behind that? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I think you're – as well, you're right that the LNG volumes and strong performance there realized prices is an  effect. There is a tax mix as well. If you think – and we've been saying for sometime it's beginning to start to come  through. We've been shifting fundamentally the portfolio towards countries with more attractive fiscal regimes. So  once you start to get Australia, Canada and Qatar and the United States contributing and maybe less for higher tax  countries, such as Europe, you might see a better income per barrel going forward as well.

texts.speaker: Sergio Molisani
texts.profession: Research Analyst, UniCredit Bank AG Milan Branch
texts.text: Yes. Good afternoon to everybody. Two questions on the potential gas re-export from North America, if I may. The  first one is can you give us an update on your re-export LNG project at Prince Rupert in Canada in terms of  authorization status and an investment at different timetable? And what are the main factors currently under  scrutiny, such as pipelines, location, competition, contract agreement and so on?

texts.speaker: Sergio Molisani
texts.profession: Research Analyst, UniCredit Bank AG Milan Branch
texts.text: And the second question is potential GPL in North America. You have related in the past that the car rental oil and  gas price differential justified such decision. But what could make you actually and definitely confident on the  long-term economics of these initiatives?

texts.speaker: Sergio Molisani
texts.profession: Research Analyst, UniCredit Bank AG Milan Branch
texts.text: And the last question is that the Pearl GTL is a wet gas project. I suppose that the potential GTL in North America  is likely to be a dry gas project. How this difference could affect the cost per barrel of the new project in North  America, compared to the $6 per barrel we saw at Pearl GTL? Thank you very much.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Yeah. Sergio, thanks for the three questions. I think they're all a little bit in the box of future strategy, which we  are, obviously, pursuing in terms of looking at our very strong gas position, which we have across North America,  and how we can actually monetize the molecules with, let's say, the lowest element of Henry Hub exposure and the  highest element of maybe liquids or other market exposures or LNG exposures.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So I think I most probably give you a really one answer to the three. So we are working on all the issues you have  said like LNG exports in China, gas to liquids in the United States, also potentially gas to chemicals. So there are  more things which can come in here.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I think what you need clearly on the LNG side is an export into the Asian markets, which gives you a different  pricing exposure. Therefore, it is also for Canada differentiated in terms of not having only one market close to  them, which is the U.S. It gives them a market opener somewhere else. So that's one driver. And I think we are  progressing there. You have mentioned all the elements you are working on, but I'm not going to go into details at  this stage.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: On the gas-to-liquid side, I think what you need is gas abundantly available, you need gas which has a reasonable  low breakeven – cash breakeven costs and you need to have a big liquids market. And I think in that sense, the  U.S. obviously has all these elements and that could make a GTL possibility.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now we are through Pearl, through our early investments into being tooled in Malaysia. We are the company with  the best and the divided experience in this field, so I would just say, we are looking at it and we'll update whilst we  are going forward. Any specifics on the economics, like gas quality and what that means I think is for later on.  Thank you, Sergio, for the future strategic questions. So that brings the Q&A to an end today.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Obviously you know the drill on this one. Let me start with the overview, the global economy and the energy  markets are likely to see continued high volatility. This is really an interplay between structural growth in energy  demand and on the other side some unprecedented geopolitical events, such as we see playing out in the Eurozone  at the moment, Arab spring comes to mind and others.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So this is a very complex landscape for us in the energy industry and in highly interconnected world. Therefore we  see a lot of opportunities for a global integrated company like Shell. We're on track for our cash flow targets of up  to $200 billion for 2012 to 2015, which as you know is some 50% higher than the previous four years. And we're  also on track for oil and gas production of 4 million barrels of oil equivalent per day in 2017 and 2018, the  outcome of our investment decisions and financial targets.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now this is an ambitious program and we have got lots to do. So let me, over the next few minutes update on  where we are with our progress in all of this. Our Q2 2012 CCS earnings, excluding identified items, were $5.7  billion or $13 billion for the first half. Now in the second quarter, we had a lot of planned maintenance actually as  some of it we have indicated and we also had some timing issues on dividend payments. That really was roughly  $500 million, which you need to take into account when you look at our clean earnings.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We're also working hard to get choice in to our portfolio, with new exploration acreage and new integrated gas  opportunities crystallizing in 2012. And I'll come back to that with a slide later on.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: There's clearly more to come here, but we've seen so far a very positive trend, with actually the first half  unplanned downtime at historically low levels and a top quartile industry performance. The Port Arthur refinery  expansion project on the Gulf Coast, which had crude distillation unit damage shortly after start-up, is not yet in  the figures on this chart. The Motiva joint-venture, which runs this plant, expects the crude unit restarts to be  delayed into 2013. Now let me just be clear, we're not happy with this and we're investigating and we're working  hard to turn this around and actually learn out of the incident.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: On the Upstream side, we're coming to the end of the ramp up of the three large projects; we have been working  for the last six years or so. Qatar LNG and GTL and Canada oil sands and I think many of you have had a chance  to visit these assets. Large-scale, taking low upstream volumes into end-user products and markets, major  investments in infrastructure and technology. These are all the themes where Shell adds a lot of value.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now Qatargas 4 LNG achieved full production in 2011 and it has already delivered 9.8 million tonnes of LNG in 11  countries. AOSP expansion one in Oil Sands Canada has been operating at ore-quality adjusted design rates in the  second quarter. Pearl gas-to-liquids has already produced 4.5 million tonnes of NGLs and GTL products and both  trains have run at 90% to 100% of design rates. This is a great achievement and Pearl is one of a kind of an asset  and some of you are, or most of you have seen it as well.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now we have already learned a lot about this facility, which gives us new opportunities for continuous  improvements. Maintenance started in the second quarter will continue during the third quarter, impacting  production, with minor modifications, as we get both GTL trains and the utilities running as a single integrated  asset. This is all building to the final slate and marketing the higher value products on what I call the Downstream  side of the project, essentially a gas based refinery.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now I want to change the emphasis here. The last six years have been all about the construction and ramp up  phase of these exciting projects. Going forward, on these three, it's all about safe and reliable production  operations, getting more out of the assets from things like debottlenecking of oil sands for example, catalyst  improvements, more product placed in high value specialty markets, and petrochemicals opportunities in Qatar  and maximizing commercial returns in the integrated value chains on all of these projects. So you might hear less  about them in our presentations but they are going to be important drivers of the results.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now asset sales are part of our business model. We have sold $31 billion of assets in the last five years, which is a  rollover of nearly 15% of our capital employed. At the same time, we're recycling some of that capital into new  growth positions, for example exploration and LNG options.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We're driving our resources growth with exploration and bolt-on deals. We have been reloading our exploration  portfolio in the last few years, with a buildup of frontier exploration acreage, tight gas and shale plays, as well as  maintaining an active drilling portfolio in our more matured heartlands.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We've had three successful offshore wells so far in 2012, all in the Gulf of Mexico. Two oil appraisal conforming  the 500 million BOE resources at Appo and at the recent Vito appraisal, now confirmed as 300 million BOE  resources. Now these should – both should actually be adding to our bottom line in the second half of the decade.  We have drilled some 50 exploration in the appraisal wells worldwide in liquids rich shales and tight gas in the  first half of the year. And you can see actually some of the names on the chart. So well results in China Gas and the  North America liquids-rich shale are encouraging but more work is needed to demonstrate commerciality.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now let's just look at Alaska for an update here. We're getting ready to spot new wells offshore in Alaska this  summer. A great deal of planning has gone into this program with over 20 vessels to cover the drilling and  contingencies. Ice conditions will dictate how long the drilling seasonal will last, with a slower start due to the  heavy ice conditions. We're planning for two exploration well completions this year, with potential for drilling top- hole section on further locations, which we expect to drill next year. Now this is an important step for us in Alaska  in what could actually become a substantial, although long-term, province for Shell.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now before I pass you over to, Simon, let me make some comments on North American gas. On the gas drilling  side, we're continuing to spend at the low end of our potential range with around 160 exploration and  development wells in the first half of this year. This is similar to last year, focusing on acreage retention and the  lowest cost plays across the continent. We're working on a series of integrated gas options, where I think Shell has  a very strong credential. We have 0.3 million tonnes per annum of LNG for transport under development in  Canada and we're working on two similar projects in the United States, which we expect to launch shortly. You  may have seen, we recently signed the memorandum of understanding with TravelCenters of America to sell  liquefied natural gas to heavy duty road transport customer in the U.S. This is at about 100 sites nationwide.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: On the LNG export side, we're working with strategic partners on a 12 million tonne per annum LNG project in  Canada. The gas supply for this project could include resources from Shell's Western Canadian gas position. This  includes Groundbirch, where resources have increased from 6 Tcfe in 2008 to potentially more than 12 today  through drilling programs in recent years. We have doubled the resources potential here since we actually  Duvernay. Now we have further natural gas value chain options on the drawing board. This is LNG. This is gas to  chemicals but also gas to liquids. We will say more about those in the future but I think there is a very strong  opportunity set emerging here for Shell.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So overall good progress on the strategy, the development project flow and broadening out of our pre-FID option  set.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Thank you, Peter and good afternoon. As I've said before, quarterly results are very relevant but good or bad,
texts.text: So I'll just start with the macro-environment. If you look at the macro compared with a year ago, second quarter  2011, oil prices and the global natural gas realizations declined from a year ago, and this change reflects some  easing of the geopolitical pressures that were actually boosting the oil prices a year ago. In North America, the  Henry Hub natural gas price has essentially halved due to the supply bubble from shale gas. Outside of North  America, the natural gas realizations they were broadly unchanged Q2 to Q2, some regional differences, but  supported by of course time lagged oil price linkages where gas prices don't yet reflect the fall in the oil price.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Thank you, Peter and good afternoon. As I've said before, quarterly results are very relevant but good or bad,
texts.text: Industry refining margins were higher in Europe and they fell in the U.S. and in Singapore, particularly in Asia  Pacific. Industry chemical margins rose in the U.S. on the back of tight supply. In Europe, they're underpinned by  the falling naphtha price. But in Asia-Pacific again, they remained low due to weak demand. The overall trading  environment for oil and gas has been softer than a year ago with overall weak demand but also lower daily price  volatility than we saw last year. So the basic message is: we continue to see a very mixed picture on overall energy  demand and the consequences for results.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Thank you, Peter and good afternoon. As I've said before, quarterly results are very relevant but good or bad,
texts.text: So oil demand in total did increase year-on-year, and LNG demand remains strong. But European gas demand  remains weak due to the weak economic conditions, price competition with coal. In fact, we're seeing coal  substituting gas at the moment for power production, particularly in the UK. And in the Downstream, we do see  evidence of a slowdown at the end of the second quarter, and that's as we effectively enter the third quarter with  softer industry refining margins in the U.S. and in Asia-Pacific. So still very mixed.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Thank you, Peter and good afternoon. As I've said before, quarterly results are very relevant but good or bad,
texts.text: Turning now to the earnings in the quarter itself. CCS earnings, current cost of supplies were for the quarter,  including the identified items were $6 billion. Excluding the identified items, the CCS earnings were $5.7 billion,  and the earnings per share decreased by 13% as compared with the second quarter 2011.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Thank you, Peter and good afternoon. As I've said before, quarterly results are very relevant but good or bad,
texts.text: So let me talk just a bit more about business performance firstly on the Upstream. The Upstream earnings  excluding identified items were $4.5 billion in the second quarter, and that's a decrease of 17% versus the same  quarter 2011. Weaker oil and gas prices, weaker gas trading conditions, they were the main drivers of the decline,  and that's about $700 million of the quarter two to quarter two impact. We did see positive earnings momentum  from growth projects.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Thank you, Peter and good afternoon. As I've said before, quarterly results are very relevant but good or bad,
texts.text: The deferral of the second quarter dividend payments into Q3 by one of our LNG joint ventures combined with  planned maintenance that we did highlight back in April of 50,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day greater than  we were seeing a year ago. They took around $500 million off the earnings on the Q2 to Q2 comparison. A lot of  that 50,000 was oil rather than gas.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Thank you, Peter and good afternoon. As I've said before, quarterly results are very relevant but good or bad,
texts.text: For the first half oil and gas production in total was 3.3 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, and that's an  underlying production increase for the half of 4%, same as the quarter compared to last year. And the growth  comes as a result of a multi-year investment in new oil and gas fields and the programs to increase the production  uptime, both of which Peter referred to.  So comment on Upstream for the third quarter. During the third quarter, looking ahead there will continue to be  planned maintenance mostly now in Asia-Pacific and Europe, and relative to Q3 last year, that's about 25,000  barrel a day oil equivalent impact.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Thank you, Peter and good afternoon. As I've said before, quarterly results are very relevant but good or bad,
texts.text: Three recent large start-ups that Peter showed, Qatar and Canada, they produced 360,000 barrels a day oil  equivalent in the second quarter 2012, and we expect similar production from these assets in the third quarter,  same as the first quarter as well.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Thank you, Peter and good afternoon. As I've said before, quarterly results are very relevant but good or bad,
texts.text: Turning now to the Downstream. Excluding identified items, the Downstream CCS earnings were $1.3 billion and  that is slightly higher than year-ago. Oil Products numbers were slightly higher; slightly lower numbers from  chemicals. So Oil Products earnings reflect an improvement in the overall refining margin environment, slightly  lower marketing and trading results although overall market and trading was basically in the expected band.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Thank you, Peter and good afternoon. As I've said before, quarterly results are very relevant but good or bad,
texts.text: Cash generation on a 12-month rolling basis excluding working capital was some $47 billion, and that included  $7.3 billion of disposal proceeds, and over that 12 month period the average Brent price has been $112 per barrel.  The cash flow generation has been underpinned by strong oil prices clearly, and by the ramp up of new projects,  some support from the timing of dividends declared across the 12 month period, and by our equity affiliates. The  Upstream generated surplus cash flow after investment. The Downstream was broadly cash neutral before any  payment to the dividend. It's good to see the cash flow that we've been generating, but we are looking for more  from the company here. As you know, this is a core part of our strategy and medium term target set.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Thank you, Peter and good afternoon. As I've said before, quarterly results are very relevant but good or bad,
texts.text: Turning now to the balance sheet. Firstly, gearing sits at 8.1% at the end of the quarter. That compares with 10%  at the end of the first quarter, continuing to move lower in the zero to 30% range. Now you would expect this in  the oil price; even though it came down, still above $100. We continue and intend to continue paying competitive  and affordable dividends. We've got a great track record on dividends, and they are our main route to return cash  to yourselves, the shareholders.

texts.speaker: QUESTION AND ANSWER SECTION
texts.profession: QUESTION AND ANSWER SECTION
texts.text: My second question was on exploration. You highlighted a large number of prospects that you're drilling in the  second half. Could we perhaps focus on the Chinese shale gas opportunity? You have made some discoveries. You  sound quite excited about that. How can we think about the timeframe of commercializing that? And also longer  term, the potential impact of that on your LNG business. I'm thinking here about the threat to the oil price linking  your Asian LNG contracts? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Okay. Thanks for your questions. I think, I take the LNG and I'll take the first one. And Simon is working with me  on China, he can take the shale gas one. On your first question, I have to – in a very strong way pushback on your  actually that, you, A) learn out to it, you know what it is and you make absolutely clear that, over the years you're  actually improving your operational, your asset, your safety and your integrity performance. We've worked very  hard on that the last six years to eight years. And we have clearly improved and all of our stats which we also make  available in our sustainability report, they're all trending in the right directions, which is a strong improvement  over the last 10 years.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: On the second one, I start with the macro-picture on the LNG and then actually, Simon, can give the details. On  the LNG forecast, which we see across the world and specifically in Asia, we see a kind of a doubling of the LNG  consumption between now and 2013. This is driven, a lot is driven by China but also by other countries who are  now starting to import LNG. Most of these countries, we still have a very low percentage of actually gas in their  energy mix, so there is quite a huge potential there still. And in China itself, there's only 4% in the energy mix is  gas at the moment. And I think the more domestic gas we actually find, the more we will see a switch from other  energy sources into gas and into LNG. So we don't see actually the demand slowing down.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now let me also just be clear on this discussion about oil price linked or not linked. I think the market at the end  will determine the price. And if you take a three year or let's take $4 Henry Hub that gives you $11, $12 landed in  Tokyo. If you're not in the spot market dealing at the movement which is $14, $15 in a normal price environment  there is actually not much of a difference between an oil price linked, what they call and a Henry Hub delivered  into Asia. I think the customers in Asia, they're very keen on long-term reliable supply. And if they actually get the  LNG from big infrastructure projects like an LNG plant that's actually what they want and what they look for. And  therefore I think you will have a return for those who build these things and that's expressed at the moment in an  oil price linked type of formula because what we are replacing is mainly oil exposure in industrial oil and hence  actually to have the same formula for them is quite interesting. I think we should change our talk and really start  to talk about gas prices landed in Asia and then even a cheaper Henry Hub is actually no longer that far away. And  I think that's the way you approach it. And then the other thing is how we're actually optimizing the gas in North  America and we can talk about that later. There is plenty to be done there. Some results from China.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Peter. This is strategic play, so I'll talk about maybe the overall picture and then specific results. Few  years ago, the first development, Changbei, we got up and running with PetroChina. As a result of that good  opportunities within China, initially with PetroChina but you will have seen, hopefully yesterday's press release,  we announced a great deal with CNOOC, which are obviously offshore deals, one in China and one in Gabon. So  Changbei was our first, yesterday we announced an extension of the, the nature of the license in Changbei and not  just in time but in scope. So additional barrels, different development horizons that will build out potentially  additional resources and additional production from our existing main operated activity. Couple of years ago, we  started to look at the onshore tight gas and shale gas activities. As Peter says, the two of us spend quite a bit of  time on aeroplanes to Beijing.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So far, we've had a range of outcomes on wells good, bad, some interesting not quite what was expected but  usually in that sense better than expected. We don't know yet the full answer to your question. In a year's time we  will. We'll share it as we go forward. There is definitely great potential there. It's a question of how to make it  economic. We've not stopped looking for further acreage even. There are several other opportunities in the  country and including potentially wet or more liquids oriented opportunities. And if we're able to achieve mature  those, we'll tell you about it.

texts.speaker: Iain S. Reid
texts.profession: Analyst, Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: Iain Reid from Jefferies. Couple of questions about your North American gas assets. We started to see some  companies write down the value of dry gas assets in the U.S. And I'm just wondering how comfortable you feel  about your carrying values, given the acquisitions you've made in the past that future gas prices you see on the  screen?

texts.speaker: Iain S. Reid
texts.profession: Analyst, Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: And secondly, on LNG export, there's quite a big queue of proposed facilities in advance of anything you might put  in there. And if you add up the numbers, you get quite a big number in terms of what could be exported from the  U.S. I wonder how much comfort you'd have from the U.S. government about if you go in there, the tail end of  this, whether you'll get approval for an LNG export scheme of whatever magnitude you're thinking of, to deliver  few years down the line. What's the U.S. government thinking about this because obviously you don't want to go  ahead if you don't really going to have the capacity approved?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The question's really about the carrying value of the North American gas assets that we've acquired over the past  few years and we talked about $17 billion. It's a bit more than that now. We've been investing further in them on  the 40 TCF asset base. We do an impairment review, value erosion review every third quarter. So we're about to  enter this year's program. We've been using $4 to $6 for that the same way that we talk about investment  decisions that we make. Last year everything was fine. What will change this year is not so much the pricing  outlook I suspect, it's what's the drilling program outlook. Because we shifted the drilling now 20 rigs onshore in  North America now on liquid rich activity, it was I think five or six a year ago and that's halved the gas drilling  activity. We're doing very little for example in Wyoming or in Louisiana at the moment. Only gas drilling is in  Canada and Marcellus. I don't know what the outcome will be. We'll just do the normal work, looking forward  long-term gas prices for the Q3 results and we'll let you know at the time. But I can tell you that in the second  quarter, despite the current gas prices all our basins are actually operating on a cash positive basis.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: If we then move southwards I think the base assumption here is there will be LNG in export. The question then is  how much. If I take it from a very strategic point of view, I think you will see in North America, specifically in the  U.S. that they have got an energy situation now which could bring them pretty close to energy independence over  the next 20 years, if the Gulf, if Alaska, if liquids rich shale, if the gas actually takes off and is kept in the country,  replacement of coal driven power generation through gas et cetera, et cetera. But on top of it, it could also actually  bring a lot of manufacturing industries back into the county, petrochemical industries back into the country  because you have a cheap source of feedstock, and that all equals jobs and revenues in the U.S. So I think, whoever  is in charge of the energy policy, [indiscernible] (48:19) you will get in the U.S., [indiscernible] (48:20) get also  one in Europe at one stage, will look at this as on the one side as a pure energy policy but on the other side also  about jobs and revenues and actually having, let's say, industries back home.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So therefore, I think, you could think of a very high number of LNG exports. I think the market will actually drive  the right number at the end from a export point of view on the gas side, but also from a demand point of few  inside the country. Governments will give you most probably incentive schemes, tax incentive schemes to invest in  the United States. So therefore I think there will be a natural kind of cap most probably not enforced by the  government, but because of measures they take, it will get to one.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Therefore I think, I would agree with you, if you have got 10 or 20 in the pipeline, you most probably need to be in  the earlier half rather than in the second half in order to have some certainty of that. Now we are working on LNG  projects also in the United States. We will inform about that going forward. But we are looking at that, and I'll  make it to you very clear, we are looking at that not just somewhere in the country but also at the Gulf Coast. And  we're looking at whatever opportunities we have there, and we'll see how we can actually link that into our very  well developed gas chain strategy, which we are pursuing with LNG in transport to liquids, to chemicals, LNG  export, and we'll then determine how we move actually molecules around. One from the web.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Some shorter term impacts, we see in Canada oil being produced, but they realized bitumen and synthetic crude  post upgrading prices. The bitumen was about $65 and the synthetic crude about $80. So an additional discount  to WTI of around $15, and that's widened from more like $5 a year ago. Some of that is a short term issue, some  logistics constraints in the Chicago area, getting that crude out of Canada and into a refining network. And some  of it is a medium-term issue because its WTI linked, but long term, it's less of an issue because those distribution  systems will even themselves out.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We did see increased depreciation in the quarter. A significant amount of this is to be expected. It's new  production coming on stream, for example in the Gulf. And early on in a project, particularly deepwater project,  you do see higher unit cost depreciation. That unit depreciation goes down as you prove up more reserves as data  on the reservoir comes through. The same happens onshore. It's not too dissimilar; it's just a lot more wells.  Smaller numbers, but they add up to material impact. We are moving those rigs from gas to liquids rich shale.  We're therefore not proving up as much reserve in the gas activities as we might have hoped to at pace. And that  has led to high unit depreciation, not only on the gas, but also on the early liquids production. So you're seeing  probably for the next year or two high unit depreciation until that settles out, as we recognize more reserves  through more drilling in the basins we focus on.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We've then got more exploration and more feasibility expense, more seismic expense and more feasibility expense  on the project. Peter just talked about LNG, GTL, gas to chemicals; you can't do the study and the design work  without spending some money. That's all coming through in the same quarter. It's not one off. It won't go away,  but it is good leading to future opportunity. So a combination of all of those things, and if each only take $50  million, $100 million out relative to expectations, that's what leads to the results you see. So fundamentally, it's a  cash positive business. You can see the cash flow coming through – and it is a business in a strategic transition. It  was a quarter in which most of the wind blew in the wrong direction. Hopefully that helps, Jon. Peter?

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Simon. On the Downstream, we have worked on the Downstream over the last few years in order to get to  a portfolio which we see as a portfolio to go forward. That included significant downscaling of refineries, so we  sold significant barrels there or we closed them and changed them into depots. Some are still in the making, and  we have talked about them. Some will change over the next 12 months to 24 months or 30 months. We have also  significantly actually purified our marketing portfolio, sold out of smaller countries where we have no economy of  scale in order to actually take costs out and capital out.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now if you take that integrated value chain, quite clearly in the second quarter, we saw that, compared to last  year's second quarter, where there was a lot of volatility in the oil market, in the product market because of Libya  for example, this was different this year. Therefore we added less value by using our refinery molecules into the  system. We had, obviously, a decreasing pricing environment. Whilst we kept prices, the volume at the same time  was coming down. So Q2 was a quarter which where we adjusted from a high to a lower oil price with not a lot of  volatility around it from a trading point of view.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Upstream Americas you have to think of it as not one business, each of the different activities has different profile.  The heavy oil is now solidly profitable, solidly cash generative. And the return on capital is okay, it can improve  some of the programs Peter talked about. But it is improving. Unit cost of $10 a barrel lower today than they were  a year ago. So we're down below $40. We're at benchmark top quartile levels in that mining activity. We've got  debottlenecking opportunities. We have opportunities to the steam assisted Carmon Creek to grow. But we won't  be putting a lot of capital into that business relative to the rest.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The deepwater business just talked about will hit low hopefully at 180. That has significant growth potential from  the things I talked about. Again it's solidly profitable, good returns, high oil price up side. So the issue is not  everything across the Americas, it's primarily the onshore activity. That was also the main driver of the production  the Gulf of Mexico profile, we're pretty much on target for what we said in 2010. The big difference is onshore,  gas, and liquids rich shales. And in fact, liquids rich shales didn't really feature in the discussion back in 2010.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So we've cut back, I would say, we were planning by now 50 to 60 rigs on gas drilling alone on rapid development  of gas. We've now dropped below 20 and then – and even in that, there's less of it going into development than  still on to appraisal, which is preparation for a recovery in gas prices, no point in producing now, if you can  prepare, sit on and produce in the future. So our actual level of activity is about a quarter of what we expected in  the gas. But the molecules are still there. Most of them are in Marcellus and Western Canada and the breakeven  there is at or heading towards $3 economic breakeven, cash breakeven is more like $1.50 once you're up and  running.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: To switch to liquids rich shales, now we're in immature basins relatively other than Eagle Ford. So we're up about  10,000 barrel a day production there now, but it will take some time to come through. We'll only see momentum  there in 2013. How much momentum will depend on how successful the exploration appraisal work that we're  doing. And most of the basins were named on the earlier exploration sheet but basically it's in Western Canada, in  or around Duvernay and the Canadian piece of the Bakken, it's in Mississippi Lime, in Kansas, in the Utica and in  Eagle Ford in the United States. We will have drilling later this year in the Neuquén in Argentina and the Vaca  Muerta play. And in general on gas and drilling activity, we've also shifted some emphasis outside the U.S. So  Ukraine, China, South Africa, the big gas players is where we may well and we've only got so many drilling  engineers as well so it will be less in the U.S. it will be more developing.

texts.speaker: Alastair R. Syme
texts.profession: Analyst, Citigroup Global Markets Ltd.
texts.text: It's Alastair Syme from Citigroup. Can I – I'm probably just asking actually quite a similar question. If you look at  the $50 billion of cash flow. I know I'm sort of giving you round numbers 2012 through 2015 at $100 oil and you  try and sensitize that for sort of $3 gas and $15 Canadian discounts. Is there a big delta that we need to be building  into our assumptions because we're kind of at $39 billion today? So I'm trying to reconcile those numbers in my  head.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The $39 billion, yeah, thanks Alastair. The $39 billion is a 12 month period, in which we're still ramping up. Gas,  there is a sensitivity, but it's not many, many billions. And deepwater Gulf of Mexico is probably much more  significant in terms of will we or won't we deliver the projects we spoke about earlier. The Canadian one it  and we're taking part in some of those whether it's reversal of pipelines in the U.S. or the construction of new  pipelines from Canada further south. So by the middle of the decade we'd expect that all the discounts to have  compressed. Question is how quickly will they compress. And it's not hugely material factor, but it's one we need  to manage carefully. Peter, I don't know if there's anything else you would?

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I think more in a general way, we have the $200 billion or if you divide by four then you have a rough number at  $50. We have clearly said that from a gas point of view, we would expect to be in the range of 4 to 6 somewhere in  2015. That may not happen that's what Simon just said. And where the refinery margins will be, we will see by  then. But I don't think – I would still say we're on track to deliver that. There are some challenges in there, but  that's fine but we are on the way to deliver this. And as you know cash flow is the key target, which we have across  the company and that's where the focus is. So we are on these targets, some challenges that we are exactly two  quarters in at the moment. So there is another few years to come.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Okay. Thank you very much Jason. I take both of them. Russia, we delivered so far the only subarctic LNG play.  We are very happy with Sakhalin. It's going very well, producing more and generating more cash. [indiscernible]  (71:32) with Gazprom and our Japanese partners. We also have Salym producing, that's also with Gazprom Neft  now. And we have been very open that we would not be against further investments in some projects where Shell  can add value. There are various ways of doing that, and therefore we always look at options. But I guess as you  would expect, I will not confirm the questions regarding Shtokman. I will confirm that we are interested in further  investing in Russia and recent changes in the tax systems or in the tax schemes either Arctic or tight oil or tight  gas. And that's obviously gives some more leverage, some more opportunities. And the clear drive from the  President Putin to more investments in Russia may also open up some avenues.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In totality, the LNG projects which we have across the world, if I start to list them, you will see that we have plenty  of them. So we already talked about those in Australia number, Canada we talked, we also have obviously in  Indonesia we have Abadi. So there is plenty of things already, and plenty of things, which we are still evaluating.  Now East Africa is an interesting province. It's a big resource, needs obviously skills, which can do Upstream,  Midstream and Downstream; therefore is an interesting environment but the valuation has to be right, and that's  what where we took a view on Cove. We took a view on the valuation but we also took a view on the process itself,  and therefore we will look at other opportunities if they come along. And if not, I think we have a rich portfolio  already so we'll see what we do. Any questions inside now. I said back there first and then there is one, I think  more on the right.

texts.speaker: Hootan Yazhari
texts.profession: Analyst, Merrill Lynch International (United Kingdom)
texts.text: Hi. It's Hootan Yazhari from Bank of America Merrill Lynch. Just coming back to your U.S. business. There's  much talk of shifting the focus. as many people have. away from dry gas to liquids rich acreage. But there doesn't  seem to be a lot of talk about how NGL liquids are really suffering on the pricing side. and realizations there  continue to come down. I mean is there any chance of this derailing your plans or indeed pushing you towards  more capital intensive moves down there, to actually really realize value from that portfolio as in moving more  into petrochemicals, more into GTL, more into sort of LNG distribution onshore, anything like that. I mean, love  to hear your thoughts on that?

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Yeah. Thanks for the question. Quite clearly, the way I would describe our strategy at the moment is: we have got  some liquids rich shale but we have a lot of gas and we have got the stuff which is in between. What we're looking  is actually to change the exposure we have to some cheap prices into exposure higher up the value chain. And  there you have got various ways of doing that. And we are firmly already in the business of pushing LNG into  transport. And in Canada, we are doing that in the U.S. and by the way we do the same starting in China, we are  starting in Europe on the same. So that's a business model which is coming, which really brings Upstream and  Downstream together, because you need the customers on the one side, because we know them from the retail  business and from the B2B business and you bring them together with Upstream. So that's really taking advantage  of the differential between Henry Hub and diesel at the end of the day. That's one, so we're driving that.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And the same in that similar area is actually for shipping. So we're running bigger projects already in other parts  not in North America, but we are also looking into that at the moment, where the shipping industry will replace  diesel engines with LNG – with gas engines, so that's another area.  Then the next one which we're looking into in Pennsylvania is to take that gas into chemicals. So this is clearly a  cracking route which gives us higher exposure from a value point of view. We are looking into that, and we are –  have identified a site, now it is the scoping exercise, et cetera.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The next one, we talked already which will be LNG export and LNG consumption in other areas inside the U.S.  And then the last one will be gas-to-liquids. That's what we just built in Qatar; can we do the same in the U.S.,  where would we do it, how big it will be, how are the economics, how expensive will be building something like  this, because one of the issues you have always in the U.S. now, it could lead to a cost explosion, let's say, for  example, around the coast, because everything has been built there. And therefore we take a view on that and we  will also take a view on how we time this.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Okay. I think on, the first one really goes into portfolio management and you're using Prelude as an example, and  we brought INPEX for example in to Prelude, and INPEX brought us in to Abadi in Indonesia. Both are floating  LNG developments, most probably you can add one-on-one to get why this has happened. And so clearly, we are  looking at these type of things.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, you have to be careful on the oil sands, because in oil sands there is always a capacity issue depending on  which ore grades you're actually digging through in your oil sands and that's why we normally say that's the  capacity you can reach depending on what oil percentage you have there. But there we are talking about a few  thousand barrels rather than 100,000 barrels. So I think in second half of this year we'll see all of these three  projects then becoming really and fully operational and we will optimize the products later on an ongoing basis.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: PNG, there is gas. There is an intent for LNG projects from the government. The government we have been talking  to for a couple of years now.
