They announced last year that we're a preferred partner because of the capability they  want to bring into the country, large project developers, people who can develop markets and local capability. So  yes, we've had discussions with PNG government. We had discussions with InterOil from time to time and I can't  say too much about where those discussions are at the moment. Yes, we're interested in project. Yes, it must meet  exactly the criteria that Peter laid out to compete with other LNG options. We don't actually know yet whether  that would be the case. There is new government election process in progress at the moment in the country. As  they commence with that, confirmation of fiscal opportunity and where InterOil fits in the government thinking  will enable potentially a project to go ahead there. It is very difficult for us to say more because it's still quite  uncertain at the moment. It's an attractive play in the same effective geological trend that we're in Australia and  now in Indonesia. So, it's one we think we can add a lot of value to, provided the other conditions are right.

texts.speaker: Richard I. Griffith
texts.profession: Analyst, Oriel Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Sorry, good afternoon. Richard Griffith, Oriel Securities. Just coming back to 4 million barrels a day target, you  talked about by 2017, 2018. Throughout the course of the afternoon in the Q&A, you've mentioned quite often  issues of costs whether it's Australia, reconsidering the FID of some of those big projects. You've mentioned, costs  around the Gulf of Mexico, you mentioned rig availability. So at what point does these issues accumulate to a  point where your project FIDs then effectively push your target our or it becomes eroded? And the second one is  just coming back to the Downstream issue and the improvements of the operational side of it. I mean, how much  of this is related to say, a structural issue or an age-related issue and how much are you going to have to spend to  get those 1% improvements and availability?

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Okay. Let's start with the ice, that's the one thing which we don't control too much and normal really season which  start mid July in Alaska, this year it's late, so we expect the ice to gone most probably within the next two weeks.  And on the permitting sides, on the – there's some certification of the containment system, which we are working  at the moment, so that's together with the Coast Guard. These has more to do that this is a containment system,  which is barrier number four or five and it's the first of its kind which has been build in the world, which stretches  is also the Coast Guard a little bit from a permitting certification point of view and we are working together there.  So I think we are working our ways through there. So as that is delayed, we have got that time, then I think  typically to wind would be – it's a little bit shorter on the Chukchi because the ice comes earlier back in that since  compared to the Beaufort. That's one thing to consider and then there is also on the Beaufort we have to stop  drilling somewhere for when the whale hunting is ongoing, but that's a concession which we made with the local  communities.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So having said all of this, we are aiming for the two wells to be drilled and maybe some others to be prepared for  next year. We have already applied for more so that we can actually continue next year to drill. So, we should not  go through the same permitting process because we already have applied them. Some of the permits you need to  renew yearly. I think we are on the right track. We have done everything, great cooperation resulted regulatory  bodies and we are now just getting to the end of the certification and all the rest of the vehicles and I always say to  Marvin he is now also the captain of an armada out there because he has more than 30 ships up there and in order  to actually drill the two wells which are as you know there's shallow water low-pressure that's actually not the  most difficult thing to do but we have all that prepared. And so I think that's how it is working at the moment, drill  this year and should drill next year in that sense. It's the thickest ice which we have had for the last 10 years. And  that has delayed it somewhat now but otherwise it's going okay.

file: RDSB - Q2 2013 Earnings Call 1August2013 830 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 01-Aug-13.pdf

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Let us start with the disclaimer first. Firstly on the results. Our second quarter 2013 underlying CCS earnings were  $4.6 billion and cash flow from operations was $12.4 billion. Higher costs, exploration charges, adverse exchange  rate effects and challenges in Nigeria have hit our bottom line.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We don't have oil and gas production targets. We have retired our outlook statements on production today. Our  recent portfolio moves make a production target less and less relevant. New plays like the Repsol LNG and the  [indiscernible] (2:56) don't have any production entitlements for example. And overall, we are targeting financial  performance at Shell.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We are 18 months into the financial program we set out last year and there is no change to those targets. $17 5  billion to $200 billion of cash flow from operations for 2012 to 2015 combined in a $80 to $100 oil price scenario  and we have delivered $7 0 billion of CFFO in the first 18 months of that program.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, before Simon takes you through the numbers, let me just make a few comments on Nigeria. We have seen a  marked escalation in security problems and theft in Nigeria in 2013. The SPDC joint venture has had shuttings on  major oil pipelines and the gas pipelines that feed the Nigerian LNG plant due to sabotage. This has all been  compounded by tax disputes between the Nigeria LNG joint venture and the Nigerian Maritime Administration  and Safety Agency, which resulted in a blockade on exports from NLNG for 23 days, ending on July 13. Oil theft  and sabotage in Nigeria are resulting in substantial revenue loss for the Nigerian government and widespread  environmental damage.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: On an annual basis, this could actually be an earnings loss of $12 billion for the Nigerian government and society.  For Shell we had a second quarter 2013 shortfall of around 100,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, 150,000  tonnes of LNG and at least $250 million of lost earnings, as a result of all of this. Now Shell and our partners are  all working with the Government of Nigeria as well as foreign governments on solutions to what seems to be an   endemic issue. Now, we at Shell will play our part, but we cannot solve this on our own.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Peter and good to talk today. I'll start with the macro environment. If you look at the macro picture  compared to the second quarter 2012, Brent oil prices were $6 lower year than a year ago, narrower  differentials  between Brent and the North American markets. Our own realized liquids prices declined by around $10 per  barrel, Q2 to Q2, so that's more than the market. However, our natural gas realizations increased from a year ago.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Our quarterly results are important and this is a phrase you'll recognize after the first quarter. Whether they're  high or low, but they are really just a snapshot of performance in the volatile industry and we are implementing a  long term through cycle strategy. The second quarter CCS earnings, current cost of supply, excluding the  identified items were $4.6 billion, earnings per share decreased by 21% from second quarter 2012.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Our reported CCS earnings included $2.2 billion of identified items and these were for downstream in Italy where  we announced the intention to sell assets, but much more substantially in the upstream Americas business with an  impairment with some of our liquids rich shale positions, that reflects the latest insights from drilling and  production data, and in a lot of ways this is similar to an exploration write -off.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The clean depreciation in the quarter was $3.9 billion and that's $2 billion higher on an annualized basis  compared to 2012 due in part to IFRS 11 effects, but also new project ramp ups and the amortization rate on the  resource plays.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The ongoing depreciation will not be significantly impacted or decreased by the second quarter impairment  because we've also increased the amortization rate for the non-productive leases as we go forward in the North  American resource plays. Now this reflects increased subsurface uncertainty following the recent drilling results,  and that effect offsets the reduction in depreciation on the impaired assets. For the second quarter 2013 DD&A  also included an impact of $80 million for catch up effect in nonproducing lease amortization, that was not taken  as an identified item.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The headline oil and gas production for the second quarter was 3.1 million barrels of oil equivalent per day. That's  an underlying increase of 2% excluding the impact from Nigeria, from PSC price effects and from divestments.  Volumes were supported by growth from Pearl Gas-to-Liquids and the Pluto LNG project in Australia. But the  Nigeria security problems reduced production by some 65,000 barrels per day on a relative Q2 -to-Q2 basis. We  had some 40,000 barrels a day of Q2-to-Q2 maintenance and performance impacts, that's negative and that was  spread across a number of assets such as oil sands in Canada, the UK North Sea and the Brazilian Deepwater.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: This chart shows you the main drivers of the results this quarter compared to 2012 Q2. The macroenvironment  overall was broadly neutral, looking at upstream and downstream margins and the uplift from the LNG joint  venture dividend receipts. So the results we're impacted by a series o f external environment factors that we're in  aggregate a $0.7 billion negative for shareholders, that's the lost revenues in Nigeria due to the sabotage and the  blockade of NLNG, but also an increase in the deferred tax liability, which is a foreign exchange effect due to the  weaker Australian dollar.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Operating expenses increased by 9%, primarily in the upstream and that's with increased costs for maintenance  and for growth in the portfolio in general. The feasibility study costs for the new opt ions such as Carmon Creek,  gas monetizations options in the Americas, Majnoon in Iraq, Abadi  Indonesia and Bonga Southwest in Nigeria.  They totaled around $400 million pre-tax in the quarter.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now you might remember that the bulk of our Alaska spending is being expensed this year, rather than capitalized  simply because we're not drilling. Now this charge, around $90 million post tax this quarter, this comes through  as an operating cost. Now you will see some pointers for the third quarter on this slide too. So let me highlight that  in the upstream, we are expecting similar exploration charges to the second quarter of about $1.3 billion, and that  our continued impacts from the Nigeria security and LNG blockade. We're expecting 35,000 barrels a day of  higher margin maintenance and asset replacement impacts Q3 versus Q3, these include the Auger platform in the  Gulf of Mexico where there's a hookup underway for the Cardamom tieback, but also at the BC-10 project in Brazil  and several North Sea fields, now this is normal planned turnaround activity, but higher than last year.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We saw 30,000 barrels a day lower volumes from the highly profitable deepwater, around 10,000 barrels a day  reduction in heavy oil, some 60,000 barrels per day higher production from the shale. So the net result is higher  volumes overall, but with growth in lower margin production.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: That's resulted in a shrinking contribution from the high-margin deepwater build in the Gulf where production in  2009 was around 250,000 barrels oil equivalent a day. It was 17 7 ,000 barrels oil equivalent per day in this  quarter.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now the Gulf of Mexico volumes are likely to remain low in the second half of 2013. However, this trend should  reverse during 2014 and 2015 with the new growth from Mars B and from Cardamom and later on from Stones.  The three projects alone are a total of around 17 0,000 barrels a day at peak for Shell. This is an important  earnings and cash flow driv er for us.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Looking at heavy oil, also currently profitable. But with less near term top line growth, the focus here is as we've  said before, current operating performance, debottlenecking capacity and controlling the costs. Resources plays at  the shales, we are seeing the impact of low gas prices, but also the start-up cost, the exploration charge and the  effect of the higher lease amortization. And it's not unusual or unique to Shell to see this kind of financial profile  in the growth business.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Feasibility cost category mainly covers pre-FID options such as integrated gas projects, particularly, Alaska. These  are basically the options for the future. Under the current macro conditions, we expect the Upstream Americas  business to remain in a loss for at least the second half of 2013. As resources plays losses and the ongoing feas-ex  outweigh the profit we expect in the deepwater and the heavy oil. The growth in the oil production, which should  come from deepwater and from the liquid rich shales should drive a return to profit in 2014, although Upstream  Americas is in and will remain in a growth mode, so this will fundamentally be a cash flow story for Shell, rather  than earnings for quite a while to come.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Well, let me update you on the progress with the portfolio in the quarter. Now, we've made more progress with  accessing new investment opportunities and we're working the portfolio hard to drive capital efficiency. In the  upstream engine, we were selected to develop the Bab sour gas fields in Abu Dhabi. We're adding new options and  equity in integrated gas, and we've made new discoveries and taken new FIDs in deepwater and in Nigeria this  quarter. In July, we announced the final investment decision for BC-10 Phase 3 deepwater project in Brazil and  the redevelopment of Bijupirá/Salema in the same country.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, Peter will give you more details in a moment, but we have also launched strategic reviews of our Nigeria  onshore and our North America resources or shale portfolio, both of which should lead to more div estment  income and more focused investment spending going forward.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Turning now to the financial framework, our business strategy aims to grow cash flow on a sustainable basis  through the macro environment cycle. We have clear targets for financial growth underpinned by consistent and  appropriate capital investment that is subject to strict investment hurdles all aimed to add value for shareholders,  and the balance sheet itself underpins this overall financial framework.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We've taken on incremental new projects this year, where we see good oppor tunities above what were our base  plans, and these include Elba Island, LNG export in the U.S., the gas to transport project also in the U.S. We're  investing in projects offshore like Stones, which is effectively now on a 100% basis rather than that a lowe r  percentage.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In addition, we're making good progress with the Repsol transaction, which could close in the second half of this  year, and that's earlier than we had expected. Putting all of this together, we are expecting net spending for 2013  to be around $40 billion. And this figure includes around $3 billion of non-cash items such as the FPSO and LNG  ship leases.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In May of this year, we took final investment decision on another deepwater field, which is Stones and Simon has  mentioned it. This is Shell's second lower tertiary development in the Gulf and our first FPSO there. Stones has  substantial upside potential from the application of innovative technology. The field is estimated to contain more  than 2 billion barrels of oil in place. The first phase of development is for 50,000 barrels per day from more than  250 million barrels of recoverable resources.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now let me update you on the resources plays in North America shales. We are making some important decisions  on what I'm convinced is going to be a success story for Shell. Exploration in shales is a dynamic activity with  production at an early stage of the cycle. We have built a substantial position here with some $24 billion for North  American resources plays on the balance sheet. We are now entering a period of focusing our portfolio down to  our best liquids plays whilst maintaining key dry gas assets for longer-term integration value. We have some nine  operational theaters in North America. I think you can take it that this will reduce to about half that number over  time as we focus down this portfolio while growing our business.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We expect to see a step-up in asset sales for North American resources plays in the next 18 months. Now we have  reduced spending overall in this theme with less activity on dry gas and more in liquids-rich plays. There may be  some further small acreage build around our core assets or areas to achieve our desired scale, but the major  acreage deals are behind us now.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So let me turn to our long-term plays in Iraq, Nigeria and Kazakhstan. We are pleased to update that the Basrah  joint venture in Iraq is up and running. This JV uses associated gas that would otherwise be flat, from oil fields  and converting it to LPG and natural gas for local customers.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In Nigeria, this remains a complex and difficult environment for the international o il companies. SPDC's new  investments has been focused on pipeline upgrades to reduce sabotage and theft, flares and flares reductions, feed  gas for LNG and some selective oil projects. SPD has been – SPDC has been divesting part of its onshore portfolio,  concentrating its operations into a smaller more contiguous area and supporting the government's policy of  encouraging investment by indigenous companies.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Since 2010, Shell has sold its 37 ,000 barrels per day interest in eight SPDC licenses for a total of $1.8 billion. We  have recently launched the review of Shell's interest in SPDCs licenses in the Eastern part of the delta. This could  result in divestments of some 80,000 barrels to 100,000 barrels per day Shell's share of production as we  continue to refocus the portfolio.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now let me turn to Kazakhstan. We are expecting first oil production from the Kashagan field in the second half of  2013. Now this is a giant field. 3 billion BOEs are being developed in Phase 1. This is a two train development that  will be ramped up over a two year period to the designed capacity with an average 300,000 barrels per day  production plotted.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now I'm not going to go basin by basin, what goes and what stays on. I think you will understand it is  commercially interesting for us to keep that to ourselves, and we will drive it that way. But all in all, I think we are  seeing very positive areas for us. We are driving those and that's where the investments go – will go in. Just to give  you some investment numbers, we had $9.9 billion of CapEx last year. This year, it's around $5.7  billion, and it's  roughly 60% LRS and 40% is dry gas. So, that's how we are driving the change from gas into LRS, quickly  assessing, moving away when it is not to our scale and focusing on those which we want to keep.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Simon explained and how this is fits together with the financial framework and in that sense, we are driving  around a $30 billion net capital for the four years. We are very careful of letting the right project comes through  for the post 2015 growth area. Now the one thing I've learned over the last four years to predict CapEx three, four  years out, that is always quite a challenging thing to do because it has a lot of macro and other impacts and oil  price and gas price impacts et cetera.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And returns are slowly beginning to edge up there. The Deepwater, the integrated gas, they are growth areas, but  they already have good returns, 15% plus. The aim there is to grow and maintain the returns at that level. The  future opportunities, the Iraq, Nigeria, Kazakhstan, heavy oil; at the moment the returns are re latively low there,  but there is a program in place or projects coming on stream that will make a difference there.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So, unconventionals first, China, we progress, we can see, beginning to see line of sight to economic developments,  requires costs to come down a bit. Better knowledge of the production rates in the reservoirs and a clear view on  the gas price, but progress is positive.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So some of it has not been successful, but some have. Obviously, you will see development there going forward. On  the conventional side, we've had successes so far, we've talked about Australian gas and Vicksburg in the Gulf of  Mexico, which will certainly help the economics of the Appomattox development.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Second half, coming up, we have Albania where we are on production tests at the moment. We are drilling in  Qatar for gas on the [ph] Queen (49:30) and Corinth wells in the Gulf of Mexico that have oil targets. We're about  to spud I believe in Benin deep water and the rig there will then move on to Gibbon deepwater in the second half,  that's the sub-salt prospect, West Africa. Those are the key prospects with a potential high impact as we are  headed forward through the year. There is more also in Australia, in both Brunei and Malaysia and we've just  taken new acreage in the North Sea, so it's a very full program over the next couple of years and we look forward to  sharing with you the outcome. Thanks, Jon and thanks, Irene. Now, the next question operator.

texts.speaker: Hootan Yazhari
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: Good afternoon, gentlemen. I just wanted to focus on the North American business if we may. First of all, I just  wanted to understand whether there had been any price reviews in your impairments with regards to North  America? And given where we are with liquid-rich shale pricing, if you haven't looked at pricing, whether there are  any risks when you undertake any reviews there for further impairments? The second thing I wanted to see is  really how the asset disposal program in the North American on-shore business will interact vis-à-vis your on- shore strategies in the downstream i.e., with regards to gas, the transport, LNG and GTL? Whether you're having  to accelerate any decisions there to get more clarity and what assets you can sell and the like there? Any clarity  there would be much appreciated. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Peter. The pricing expectations for gas have changed, but mainly that was an impact in 2012. Q3 we took  smaller impairment, $500 million, $600 million in Colorado and Louisiana that reflected a lower expectation for  gas prices. The recent impairments – the current impairments, they are driven more by understanding of the  asset, based on drilling results, both what it tells us about the sub-surface but also the production rates that we've  been seeing and where they have not matched – mapped out to expectations then that's had an impact on  potential development projects.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: On the second one, I think you need to distinguish in the divestment strategy between gas and LRS. So what we  are announcing today is much more focused on LRS rather than gas. The integrated projects which you are  pursuing, which is gas to chemicals potentially gas to liquids and gas in transport and also LNG export. Some of  them are already under design, construction, which is more on the LNG and the gas to trans port side. They  continue as normal. We are looking at – or moving forward on gas to chemicals and gas to liquids at the normal  pace, so no acceleration, we just do that, which is by the way one of the drivers of the higher feasibility  expenditure which we have in the Americas.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Then once we take those integrated project decisions, then we will look at the gas molecules again, we'll decide  how much is third-party, how much is own gas molecules, which we will use. And then we take it from there in  terms of upstream assets. If nothing goes forward then we will have another close look on what we do with our  own gas assets in [ph] that sense (54:29). So that's pretty much our strategic theme at the moment and we'll get –  we are moving forward on all of these for the time being and we'll get to a decision point over the next 12 to 18  months. Thanks for the question. Next one operator?

texts.speaker: Peter W. Hutton
texts.profession: Analyst, RBC Europe Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Hi, thanks for question. Can I just ask on the status of two areas really, Pearl, that was ramping up and I think is at  full capacity for the quarter, gas volumes in MENA were up 33% now as we understand it. Those volumes of  MENA gas are amongst the higher margins particularly in Pearl, but we saw profits per barrel down. Were there  any specific costs relating to the final start up of Pearl or is this underlying profitability in Q2 as we would expect  to see that going forward?

texts.speaker: Jon Rigby
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Hi. Thank you. Two questions actually. First is, on your cash flow targets that you've got now, can you perhaps just  go back into them and tell me what needs to go right and what needs to go wrong materially around the risking,  going forward, to meet what you need to, i.e., what are the sort of big leavers are still left? And then second, just  going back to the removal of the production target, you referenced the fact that you've made choices,  value choices  to go into things like Iraq and the Repsol LNG that didn't have production attaching to them, which is fine, but  can you maybe turn it around the other way, and say what in the last 18 months have you chosen not to invest in  in the upstream would have contributed to make that 4 million barrel a day target in 2017 -2018? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Jon. I start with the second one on the production target side. I think apart from having invested in a few  areas like you have mentioned, like Repsol, like gas. We also have as you've heard today, increased our potential  divestments, which will have an impact in that as well. I think over the last 12 months, we have not made the  choices which, obviously, would have put the target on the risk. But we have clearly slowed down in a few areas.  We have actually also accelerated in a few other areas. But I think what comes to mind is where we took very  tough decisions on postponing or getting out of projects like Arrow, we postponed because of the high prices. We  took a slower kind of development in some of the North Sea projects, for example, one in Norway and another one  further down there.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So we have actually slowed down projects in order to not spend into the high areas. They would have had  production but we had other things coming through which would have delivered the cash flow because,  remember, we said it's a proxy for cash flow growth, quite clearly. We have invested in LNG and transport, which  we see as a long-term business, which again will give us mainly margin and cash flow rather than the other things  like production volumes.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The last one I would like to mention is we have clearly taken the decision to move from gas to LRS. We made it  very clear therefore we have deliberately slowed down the gas side, which would have delivered a lot of gas  volumes over the years to come. We switched into an exploration appraisal strategy on the LRS. We have now  taken even some further pace out of that by focusing more and that obviously also has an impact, and that was  again, it was an economic choice behind it and there is also rationalization going on there.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: On production, internally production will still be a key figure which we are looking at. As I said, we are value - driven, and not absolutely top-line driven. So I don't have you a kind of a matching production number, that's not  the way I look at this. We will look at the best projects with the best NPVs, the highest IRRs, the best long -term  type of returns you can expect and we slice it, as Simon said, we look portfolio – for portfolios. So the strategic  things like deepwater, integrated gas and how we optimize those returns. And then that will give you as an  outcome, then, the production which we are managing. I think I'll leave it at that rather than to try to have a  number here, so...

texts.speaker: Robert A. Kessler
texts.profession: Analyst, Tudor Pickering Holt & Co. Securities, Inc.
texts.text: Hi. Good day, gentlemen. I'll try and make this fit as two questions. The first one being clarification on North  America's shale write-down and the asset sales corresponding to that, how much of this was triggered by moving  assets to a held for sale categorization? It just seems like you need an event to tr igger a broad based review for a  write-down unless it's just your annual review process?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We haven't given any indication of specific assets and partly that's for commercial reasons. There will be portfolio  actions and it's not in our interest to talk about individual assets, but by and large, the Canadian assets, I think  we've said before, the gas assets look in good shape, this is not a gas play, and most of the LRS activity on the  radar screen has been in the U.S. So I can't say more than that really. And, yes, some of it might impact as we go  forward, when we sell, it may impact production, which, of course, would not only impact production, but might  have an impact at the margin on cash generation. But I would stress it's probably going to be at the mar gin in the  period that we're talking about.

texts.speaker: Michele della Vigna
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: Good afternoon. Thank you for taking my question. With the Repsol LNG business and Basrah Gas, you have  added upstream assets with no associated production. I was wondering if you could quantify how much cash flow  you expect from these businesses on a timeframe of three to five years?

texts.speaker: Alastair R. Syme
texts.profession: Analyst, Citigroup Global Markets Ltd.
texts.text: Y eah, good afternoon, Peter and Simon. Can I ask firstly about – again about the CFFO delivery? I mean you're  promising growth, but equally, you did promise growth in cash flow in the past and I think if you – if you look at  first half 2013 pre-working capital and disposal proceeds, you're running at about $5 billion lower than you did in  the first half 2011 in a very similar Brent oil price scenario. So can you help me explain the difference and  particularly what you think has happened to the contribution from Pearl and Athabasca? And secondly, just a very  quick question, has anyone approached to you on assets in North America or assets held for sale in North  America?

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Okay. Thanks, Fred. I think on the first one, there are a lot of moving parts, but the simplest way to look at this is  $33 billion didn't include actually the Repsol deal, which has a kind of a $6 billion plus ticket against it, of which  some is cash and some is not cash, that's an easy way to get to close to your $40 billion. And we have said there  are a few moving parts around new projects which have come in like the Elba, and the gas to transport and I think  that's the rest of it. To be very transparent, we don't know yet how much the Repsol deal will be at the end, so we'll  see that. But I think with around the net $40 billion, it's – that's the right number to take with.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: It's a good question, Jason. And the potential answer is yes, but the good news for you all is it won't make much  difference in the next one or two years, not Basrah Gas, nor the other gas-to-transport or monetization  opportunities that we talked about. So the only I can say is that as we go forward and we br ing them on stream  and they start to have a material impact. We will need to find a way that will help, transparently, to understand  where the value is being created. A lot of it will show up in the integrated gas. I expect that you see the earnings of  today, but your point is well made and we will need to think about that as we go forward, but it isn't going to make  a big difference to the next year or two.

file: RDSB - Q2 2014 Earnings Call 31July2014 830 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 31-Jul-14.pdf

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So we're taking firm actions to improve our capital efficiency by selling selected assets and making much tougher  project decisions. And we've continued to ramp up production at Mars B in the Gulf of Mexico, which is part of  Shell's industry-leading deepwater portfolio. And our exploration program is delivering with new finds in the Gulf  of Mexico and Malaysia.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We've set clear priorities for 2014 and beyond to – consistent with Shell's long-term strategy, and at the same time  we are sharpening up in a number of areas. As you know, we've implemented a series of new performance units in  the company for a more robust appraisal system. There's about 150 of these, which are clusters of assets, markets,  or value chains, such as integrated refineries, or groups of oil and gas fields in similar geology and tax regimes.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, turning to the results, and Simon will give you a bit more detail in a moment, our second quarter 2014  underlying CCS earnings were $6.1 billion and cash flow from operations was $8.6 billion. On a 12-month rolling  basis, which for me is a more meaningful measure than a single quarter, we've delivered some $21 billion of  underlying earnings and $39 billion of CFFO. Free cash flow, which is the cash generation after investment, the  money available for pay out and debt pay down, has been on a rising trend in the last few quarters, as our  acquisitions and divestments turn to a net positive.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, turning to the North America resources plays, excluding divested assets, such as Eagle Ford, we have some  260,000 barrels of oil equivalent today of production on stream. Around 80% of this production base is gas. This  is a major long-term growth opportunity for Shell shareholders; however, Upstream America's resources plays  remained in loss for the first half of 2014, about $400 million loss. And although, this does represent a positive  earnings swing of some $900 million, on the first half to first half basis, reflecting higher gas prices and the  improvement plans that we have on the way.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We have updated our view on portfolio and strategy, both for dry gas and liquid rich shales. Major divestments of  noncore liquid rich shales positions are now complete, totaling some $800 million of proceeds in 2014, and  around 60% of our near term resources plays investment in North America will continue to be directed at liquid  rich shales acreage. And this will be in appraisal drilling and, potentially, material liquid rich positions in the  Permian and Western Canada.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In gas, Western Canada acreage has the resources and potential to underpin a large scale LNG project, and we  have a 12 million ton per annum scheme in front-end engineering and design at Kitimat processing the remaining  potential for Shell in Lower 48 gas, including expiration. And as we work through the portfolio, there could be  further asset sales and impairments there. Okay, so that's an update on some of the steps we are taking to improve  our financial performance.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Turning, then, to the second priority of capital efficiency, Shell is opportunity rich and capital constrained, and  this is driving the hard choices in the portfolio. So this involves moving ahead with growth projects, such as LNG  Canada and Appomattox in the Gulf of Mexico, where we are in front-end engineering and design, and at the same  time being more selective on new FEEDs with a routine in place, now, where I review FEEDs with $500 million or  greater cost implications with my colleagues on the executive committee.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Turning, then, to the third priority of project delivery, Mars B, which started up six months ahead of the original  schedule in February of this year is still on track for ramp-up to its 100,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day plateau  in 2016. And Mars B averaged around 38,000 barrels a day in the second quarter of 2014. So our overall Gulf of  Mexico production increased from some 177,000 barrels to 231,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day on a Q2 2013 to  Q2 2014 basis, an important profitability driver for us.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now let me update you, then, on conventional exploration, where we are spending around $4 billion in 2014. So,  very long-term plays, like Arctic and other frontier basins, could deliver really substantial new oil and gas fields;  but, at the other end of the spectrum, near field drilling can add high value barrels in a short timeframe. We  expect to continue to add new discoveries in our Heartland basins, where basic geology and technical risks are  well understood.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, regarding Alaska drilling, at the moment, as you know, we are blocked by the U.S. courts and we are not  prepared to commit to a drilling campaign there unless those issues are resolved. However, we continue to work  with local stakeholders on logistics and on permitting to keep the option to drill there safely in the future.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So in the Gulf, the Rydberg discovery in 2,300 meters of water is our third find in the Norphlet play. Rydberg  takes the [ph] headlined (11:49) discovered potential in the Appomattox area to 700 million barrels, and we are  assessing if Rydberg will be developed as a tie back to Appomattox or as a standalone project.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And in Malaysia deepwater, the new Rosmari discovery is the latest in a series of new gas discoveries which could  potentially feed into existing LNG schemes there. And Rydberg and Rosmari are both examples of where Shell is  adding value – material value for shareholders with the drill bit in our Heartlands. And looking into the second  half of the year, we have some important wells coming up in Albania and, of course, the Libra field in Brazil  subsalt.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Ben. Good to talk to you all today. I'll start with the earnings. Our reported current cost of supply, or CCS  earnings, included a negative $1 billion of identified items. That included impairments of some $2 billion,  predominantly related to the dry gas properties in the U.S., partly offset by divestment gains of $1.4 billion mainly  related to the sell down of Woodside and Wheatstone, both in Australia. The impairments in the U.S. come  primarily as a consequence of reduced intended development spending on the Lower 48 dry gas properties. That  leads, in turn, to reduced production and cash flow expectations in the near term.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Turning now to the business in more detail. Upstream clean earnings for second quarter 2014 were $4.7 billion.  That's an increase year-on-year of $1.2 billion, or 34%. Integrated gas and Upstream Americas both showed  robust earnings momentum on a second quarter to second quarter basis. I do need to flag, we had a positive year- on-year impact in the Upstream from an increase in the deferred tax liability in Australia due to the stronger  dollar there, $100 million positive effect in the quarter. A year ago it was a negative $400 million.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: On the flip side, recognition of the second quarter dividend to Shell from one of our LNG joint ventures slipped  into Q3, paid early July. That was around $200 million. The headline oil and gas production for the second  quarter was 3.1 million barrels of oil equivalent a day. That's an underlying increase, adjusting for divestments, et  cetera, of 4%. The volumes were supported by ongoing ramp-up at the Mars B platform in the Gulf of Mexico and,  particularly, in Majnoon in Iraq. We also saw new volumes from revamping older fields in deepwater Brazil and  the Gulf. A year ago, production was reduced by high levels of maintenance compared with what we saw in the  recent quarter.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Our LNG, liquefied natural gas, sales volumes were up 28% Q2 to Q2. That was driven by the acquisition of  Repsol's Atlantic and Peru LNG business, but also a much improved feed gas supply into the Nigeria LNG unit.

texts.speaker: Theepan Jothilingam
texts.profession: Analyst, Nomura International Plc
texts.text: Yeah, afternoon, Ben, Simon. Just two topics, please. Firstly, just on the Arctic, do you think it's – how do we go  about thinking about the cost? How long can you continue to have an expense in the Arctic without really having  much sort of activity levels or well results from that? And I'm thinking is there a possibility to tone down that  spend in the context of overall exploration spend? And secondly, more strategically for the Group, I think you've  talked about reducing costs, particularly in North America, but could you talk about now what the opportunities  are more at wider corporate level? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Cost in North America, absolutely, you're right. If I take North America here as shorthand for unconventionals, we  have, of course, been focusing very much on the cost take out. Take out overhead costs. Take out costs very much  – equipment costs that the well had. Gas processing plant cost is the next phase that we are focusing on. It's an  absolute must for us to be cost competitive, together with being in the sweet spot in order to be able to have a  profitable business there. That will continue to be a drive going forward.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Yeah. Thank you very much, Thomas. Let me take the Oil Products question; Simon will talk to the buybacks.  Yeah. Let me just correct you slightly, it is actually the Downstream as a whole you're talking about, so Oil  Products and Chemicals combined. And we said we would indeed expect a $10 billion cash from operation at a  10% to 12% return. That would be against the sort of macro conditions that we were seeing in 2013. So there is an  upside on that, of course, as macro conditions could also improve, because we still consider 2013 to be not exactly  a cycle average year.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We will continue to look at where some of our aspects in the portfolio simply cannot get there and, therefore, I  don't rule out portfolio action in the somewhat weaker parts of our Oil Products portfolio. Chemicals portfolio is  pretty much where it needs to be in terms of robustness.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Ben. Just note, on the Oil Products cash generation we're about $8 billion over the last 12 months; $8  billion in the previous years as well, but as you can see, the actual performance is a little bit better this year. So a  lot of the improvement we're starting to see from the work that we're doing ourselves, because the environment  this year has not been any better than it was in earlier years. And also on the buyback, $7 billion to $8 billion,  we've already completed as of last night $1.8 billion. We're about 150 million shares short of offsetting the  cumulative impact of the scrip, which is about 2% dilution.

texts.speaker: Oswald C. Clint
texts.profession: Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Yes. Thank you very much, gentlemen. Good afternoon. First question was really maybe on your comments about  long-term LNG ambitions in Canada using your unconventional portfolio and kind of exporting it from there. I  just wonder how that – those ambitions may or may not have changed given the kind of Russian pipeline gas deal  into China. It could appear that a large part of the demand may just have been absorbed by that pipeline deal. And  I wonder if that's affected your long-term views on Canadian LNG exports?

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Okay. Thanks, Oswald. I'll take your first question. Yeah, I think our long-term LNG ambitions are just that: long- term LNG ambitions that haven't really changed. Our LNG business is an incredibly important business for us. It's  a huge opportunity to continue to grow in a reliable way. It's a very, very material business, as you know, already  producing very, very strong returns. And we will be looking at advantaged LNG projects to take that business  further.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I think Canada LNG is an advantaged LNG project, if you consider the fact that it's still aimed at what, at this stage  and in the future, will remain to be an advantaged market – one of the strongest market, the North [ph] Asian  (34:28) markets, as well as the fact that, of course, Canadian gas is slightly more challenged to get to markets than  gas in the Lower 48. So, therefore, there is, in principle, the largest value arbitrage available in the market.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Of course, the Chinese deal with Gazprom will take care of a significant amount of gas demand in China. But if you  look at the volumes and if you look at the prospects for China to grow, bearing in mind that gas demand in China  is 5.8% of the LNG mix at the moment, there's a huge amount of demand growth still available for us. And no  matter how we analyze it, we see there will be room for a number of LNG projects to get in there.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So, therefore, the prospects that we see for LNG Canada, possibly even for a follow-on investment, are still very  strong and very much there. And, therefore, we continue to move forward with it.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Sure. Thanks, Ben. You're absolutely right, Clint, that the U.S. liquids production has improved year-over-year,  primarily driven by the deepwater performance. We've also got an uptick in Brazil. I mentioned other projects, but  both BC-10 and Bijupirá/Salema had new well activity come on stream this year, which has given some uptick in  the Upstream Americas result, overall.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Some of it is sort of taking advantage of the availability of advantaged crude and other feedstocks; of course,  without the very much a heavy feedstock machine, so therefore not necessarily, you could argue, suited for the  light crude that tend to be in abundance at the moment. But nevertheless, we can put in there some residues and  other feedstock to make sure that we load up the units fully.

texts.speaker: Iain S. Reid
texts.profession: Analyst, BMO Capital Markets Ltd.
texts.text: Hi, gentlemen. Just a question on the Lower 48 gas, we can characterize as hold or divest. I'm just wondering  what is going to push you in either of those directions, Ben? Is there a macro driver there? Presumably there is in  terms of have you changed your long term [ph] hub assumption (43:10). Or is there a more technical analysis  required of the individual assets in order to make your mind up on that?

texts.speaker: Iain S. Reid
texts.profession: Analyst, BMO Capital Markets Ltd.
texts.text: And the second question is on your MLP initiative, now you call these utility style assets. You've got a huge  amount of these sorts of assets elsewhere in the world, particularly LNG production assets, et cetera. Is it your  intention to put this philosophy to work elsewhere in the world?

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And then, it's a matter of deciding whether that is indeed good enough to develop in its own right against the  prevailing gas prices that we see, whether we have the capital to dedicate to it, whether that indeed is the best use  of our capital, or whether we can find that this is better developed by somebody else and we basically get the value  of the position at the sort of gas prices that we would see going forward or better. So there is – it is going to be  purely a value play, and, of course, very much a value play that has a precondition that we need to understand a  little bit better what is there. So there's still some appraisal activity to be carried out. It is not part of a larger  strategic integrative play, much like the Western Canadian position integrated with LNG Canada. On the MLP,  Simon, to you.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: On P&T, let me first of all say that P&T, of course, very important and very crucial part of our organization. The  very fact that we have put that capability together and have really high-graded it and made it a very prominent  capability represented at the executive committee level has really helped us to make sure that we get very, very  focused on the key things that they do: the [indiscernible] (49:42) performance, project delivery, hydrocarbon  maturation as well as a number of other things that sit in that, technical IT, contracting and procurement, et  cetera, et cetera.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Okay. Thanks, Jon. Good questions. Yeah. On the Lower 48 – or rather, your $4 billion of conventional  exploration, is that enough to replace the hopper? No. It's not. We know that. We will need a mix of finding  hydrocarbons by the drill bit and getting them through to [ph] MBD (52:26) activities that we will develop a good  enough funnel to continue to replace and grow the business, give us enough opportunities to have a rich set of  choices. And then, we can always balance these two if we have a very, very successful run of exploration results.  The pressure to do deals is less. And vice versa, if we run into very, very good opportunities, quite often – you've  seen us do that with Libra, we will try and find the money for that in a sensible way out of our exploration budget,  without, of course, cannibalizing the opportunity set. But it will always be a two-legged strategy to make sure that  our hopper or our opportunity funnels for all the different investment themes are adequately filled.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Sure. Thanks, Jon. It gives me a chance, I think, to maybe reiterate some messages I've said before. Clearly, 10  years ago the industry was in a different place. It was, in my humble opinion, living off the fruits of the legacy. In  our case, we basically opened up one new province since the 1980s, I think, which is the Deepwater Gulf of  Mexico. And we had, as an industry, been hugely under-investing. That's why the oil prices are $100 today, not  $20 as it was 12 years ago. And, of course, returns were higher. But that is not a sustainable situation. You can see  that for everybody. Oil price rises, costs rise with it.

texts.speaker: Irene Himona
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA (Broker)
texts.text: Thank you. Good afternoon. My first question concerns Russia. You have about 5% of your production there. I  wonder if you could share your thoughts on the potential threat that the current sanctions being implemented,  specific to the oil industry, may pose to shareholders. My second question is on LNG. A very good second quarter  thanks to the Repsol acquisition, but, actually, spot prices did collapse in the quarter. We can see that in the  numbers. Was there an effect on your business? And what do you think drove such a dramatic decline? Do you  think it's sustainable or reversible? And I'd say, what is the impact on the underlying Shell business? And my final  question, very briefly, Ben, you referred to the challenging refining environment in Europe. Exxon has recently  announced a fairly sizeable upgrade in their European refinery. Does that impact the Shell view of the challenges  of European refining? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Okay. Thanks, Irene, very good questions. Let me take the first and last one, and then Simon will talk to the LNG  pricing. So Russia, yeah, I find it very hard to make sort of definitive pronouncements on a day like today when  there is so much still uncertain happening as we speak. So we have, of course, a pretty good idea conceptually  what sort of sanctions are being proposed, but the devil will be in the detail here.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: If you look at the oil and gas technology sanctions that are being proposed, you could look at it and say, "Well, it's  very much sort of oil targeted," of course, for reasons that also the E.U. wants to protect its own gas supply  security from Russia. So you could on the one hand argue that, of course, investments that we have in Sakhalin  should be spared, if you like, from sanctions. But at the same time, of course, we have to in the end see in detail  what these sanctions will entail, particularly also the financial sanctions, which look like financial instrument  sanctions but there can be quite some devil in the detail on how that looks as well.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Sure. Just overall, the integrated gas result was very strong again. The primary drivers year-on-year were actually  gas-to-liquids at its highest-ever capacity utilization to date, and the total LNG volumes being quite a bit higher,  more than a bit, million tons higher in the quarter, three-quarters of which came as a result of the Repsol  acquisition. Most of the rest is Nigeria.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In pricing terms, first quarter we were seeing spot cargoes at $20; in the second quarter, some at $12 or lower.  However, the vast majority of our sales are linked to long-term oil prices. We had slightly fewer diverted cargoes,  which can mean – or link to spot. We had slightly fewer in the second quarter than we had in the first quarter, but,  overall, our exposure to that spot market remains limited. So the uptick is primarily GTL and the total volume. Of  course, going forward the spot prices are very driven by short-term effects, which include weather. Around the  world, gas demand has been quite a bit lower because of the weather, but also some of the choices, particularly in  Europe, made around the constituents of the power mix. So, therefore, more coal, less gas and, therefore, more  carbon dioxide seems to be the European energy policy. And that does reduce the number of cargoes going into  Europe.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: If we project and see a fall in prices – remember $10 is roughly $3 billion of cash generation per year – so a $10  move in the crude oil price. If we see weakness there, we do need to think about investment levels at the margin  and also the impact that fall in revenue or commodity prices usually has on capital cost, the unit cost of capital as  well as the total amount of activity, and negotiating effectively with suppliers around some level of flexibility in  that. And then, we do have some of that in place in terms of contracts that adjust to changes in market rates.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So we'll have to look more through cycle at the investment level if we start to worry about the commodity price.

texts.speaker: Michele della Vigna
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: Good afternoon. Thank you for taking my question. You have worked a lot on refocusing your shale exploration  over the past year, year-and-a-half. I was wondering if you could give us an update on what level of resources or  potential you see in your liquid rich shale portfolio in the Permian and in West Canada, and also if you could give  us an update on your international shale strategy? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Michele. Resource level in the Permian and West Canada, we've talked, small number of billions. It's still  appraisal. Still some exploration to do, but we have quite large positions in both. And we'd hope to see in liquids  rich shale development quite significant resource bases over time. We've not yet pulled the trigger on a major  development program, but we are seeing growth, for example, in the Permian. We're about 13,000 barrels a day  shale share ahead of where we were a year ago. And that's without actually pulling the trigger on a development  program. So we would hope to be able to build that portfolio into several billion barrels equivalent.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And around the world, the shale program, there are several countries, small countries, where we've looked, tried  and we're thinking about, well, what's the long-term exposure in countries such as, say, Tunisia and Turkey. We  have already stepped back in a couple of countries onshore or stepping back, for example, in Latin America. So the  major plays outside North America are now China and Argentina, in terms of the activity that we are embarking  on today.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: China, as we said before, remains a geological challenge. We can see the hydrocarbon, but actually producing  economically – we are still working on a couple of plays in Sichuan with our partners. We're not at the point where  we can define a development program there just yet, and we are exploring and appraising acreage in the Vaca  Muerta play in Neuquen Province in Argentina at the moment. The other plays that I'm sure you're aware we've  been involved in, in Russia and Ukraine, I think I can add very little to Ben's earlier statements about the  uncertainty going forward there and the fact that we are effectively, de facto, temporarily suspended operations in  the Ukraine.

texts.speaker: Christopher Kuplent
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: Thank you. Good afternoon. Just two questions. Your announcement regarding the longer term recycle rate of $5  billion annual disposals, are you announcing that today because, given the success you had already this year in  your asset disposal program, you want to make clear that we shouldn't wait for the next $20 billion disposal  program announcement next year? And, Simon, I know I'm only teasing you, but does that mean you also have a  longer-term ambition of a annual $5 billion M&A budget? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Thijs Berkelder
texts.profession: Analyst, ABN AMRO Bank NV (Broker)
texts.text: Second question relates to – not to LNG pricing, but to European gas pricing. European gas prices have decoupled  from the old price. And also, your realized gas price in Europe is clearly lower than we've seen in the past. What is  that meaning in terms of strategy for you as a company, looking at European gas assets?

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Thijs. Simon will deal with the European gas pricing question. Let me say a little bit about the divestment  program. Yes, $12 billion announced, $8 billion in the bank. I think you should focus on the $8 billion in the bank,  not on the $12 billion announced. Yeah? Because that's, in the end, what we want to do. We want to deliver the  cash, not announce future arrival. So is it almost finalized? I don't think that's necessarily the way of – to look at  it, yeah?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Ben. European gas price, indeed, the spot prices, the hub prices at the moment are probably at a three- year, four-year low. That has been primarily driven by weather conditions, which has both reduced demand but  also ensured that stocks have remained high. They're not necessarily related to the medium or longer-term  supply/demand situation, which is perhaps more driven by politics and the relative economics of gas as a source  of fuel for the power sector.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The politics driving the current demand, and in practice, I think, any of you who follow the power sector, it's at  nearly 60 gigawatts of gas capacity in Europe currently not being used. Two gigawatts is roughly equivalent to 6  million tons of carbon dioxide a year, which ultimately is currently being replaced by coal. So there's a massive  disconnect at policy level, which we can't see pertaining or sustaining, at least not with politicians retaining any  level of credibility on the subject.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So gas demand, we do think, will grow in Europe. That will have an impact on price. But strategically, quite a few  things have already happened. Fundamentally, we've moved away from oil-linked pricing. It's much more hub,  spot, and a little bit of oil now; some long-term contracts, but there has been a move towards shorter contracts.  We've reflected that in the amount of both trading activity, the amount of investment we make in new European  production, and fundamentally not looking, certainly in the medium-term, to be making any investment or  strategic push towards bringing LNG into Europe. As and when the policy unwinds itself in a more rational  fashion, then we will be well-placed to do that, particularly given the additional LNG volumes that we now have in  the Atlantic Basin. But our focus, primarily in gas markets, is on North America and Asia-Pacific, and developing  new LNG markets in emerging economies, such as Southeast Asia and Latin America.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: What is the best operator? So what should the cost be if we wanted to be at base setting level? And the targets that  we have set ourselves, the targets that we are very much going after and are meeting in quite a few categories. So I  just want to, I wouldn't say, ignore it, but I want to put to one side the argument that we cannot be cost  competitive. Now having said that, of course, the whole cost competitive question, as I said earlier on, is much  more important in dry gas. And in dry gas, of course, you also have to ask yourself the question, how can I access  more value, because it's not necessarily a good game to just be the most competitive operator in a cutthroat  market where supply is very, very long and pricing is being set in a very, very liquid market.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So, therefore, the focus on gas is very much bifurcated into two areas. One is Western Canada where I do think we  hold a very strong position, can be a very cost competitive operator, but we will integrate it with our Canadian  LNG position to make sure that we maximize the integrated value and, therefore, look at – for our dry gas position  as part of that integrated value chain. And the Lower 48, yeah, we just have to have top acreage, and we have to be  a top producer and a top operator, and we have to see gas prices that will make it worthwhile to invest in it. And if  you can't see all of that, then these positions will be under review – will continue to be under review or we will see  whether somebody else with a different outlook or a different appetite will be a better owner of it. And that's  basically the strategy that we have chosen and that is playing out. Exploration, Simon?

texts.speaker: Bertrand Hodée
texts.profession: Analyst, Raymond James Euro Equities SAS
texts.text: And the second question is you've had also good performance on Mars B, already reaching around 40,000 barrels  of oil equivalent per day. Earlier comments from Simon, if I recall, were – pointed to quite a slow ramp up at Mars  B before reaching plateau of 100,000 barrels a day. Do you still expect this plateau of 100,000 barrels a day to be  reached by early 2016 or before that?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Mars B, slow ramp? Well, we've only got, I think, three wells on at the moment. That's entirely normal for a facility  of this scale and complexity. We bring them on one at a time. There is an element of waterflood associated with  the activity, both on Mars B into the Mars A reservoir and vice versa. So there's quite a complex interplay between  the two platforms over time, and very important that we do this safely, reliably and in a way where we get to  understand the reservoir as quickly as possible so that we can maximize the future production in the most reliable  way.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So yes, it's still effectively some time away, the full capacity. I have to say, we brought it on six months before we  expected, and the ramp-up of the first two wells, in particular, was pretty trouble free compared to what could  have happened. But we cannot project – this is the subsurface. Things happen. We can't project, really, any  differently than we previously have. So if 38,000 is 100%, 24,000 is ours in the second quarter. So it's pretty good  progress so far given this only came on-stream in March. But let's see where we get to by the end of the year.

file: RDSB - Q2 2015 Earnings Call 30July2015 900 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 31-Jul-15.pdf

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Quickly, the disclaimer slide, which you are familiar and then let's get going. So, our integrated business model  and our performance drive that we've had for some time now are really helping us to mitigate t he effect of lower  oil prices on our bottom line. We delivered $3.8 billion of underlying CCS earnings in the quarter and $16 billion  over the last 12 months. And our results today also showed that we are successfully reducing our cost and our  spending.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So, we have to make sure that our company is resilient in a world where oil prices remained low for some time.  And of course, we have to also keep an eye on potential recovery which, we believe, will indeed eventually come.  So, the three priorities that I put in place in early 2014 remain unchanged. So, it's financial performance, it's  capital efficiency and it's delivery of projects, all underpinned by a rigorous approach of performance unit  appraisal.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Now, at the same time, we are making good progress with the combination with BG which should enhance our  free cash flow. It will create one of the LNG and deep water leaders in the IOCs. And very crucially, it will be a  springboard for change in Shell into a much simpler and much more profitable company. So essentially, what we  are doing here is grow to simplify. Of course, they are very challenging times in the industry, but I also feel they're  very exciting times in my company.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: The health and safety of our people and neighbors and, of course, the environmental performance, they remain  the top priorities in Shell. And I believe, we have the right safety culture in place, and our track record is  improving and I think very competitive. But we will continue with the safety drive, which we call Goal Zero to  further improve wherever we can.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: The oil price downturn that began in late 2014 is triggering some very significant changes in our industry, and  today's oil price downturn could last for several years. Of course, we also don't have a crystal ball here, but our  planning assumptions reflect today's market reality. So, we're planning on a prolonged downturn, although we  continue to believe that the fundamentals will reassert themselves in the medium term. So, we are responding  with urgency and with determination.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Now of course, our results are lower with the lower oil price. But our integrated business model is offsetting that,  at least some of it. And Downstream is delivering a strong and much improved performance, supported, of course,  by industry margins but also by self-help programs, including non-core asset sales, cost reductions, improved  commerciality, and also significantly improved uptime.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: In Upstream, where margins are under pressure from oil prices, our unit operating costs were around $19 a barrel  in the quarter, and BG's portfolio has the potential to sustain or even further reduce this overall production cost.  So, the performance drive that we launched in 2014 is helping at the bottom line and there's more to come there,  and the balance sheet gearing remains low despite the downturn.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Safety and environment, of course, remain top priorities also for P&T, but we want to drive better value for our  capital project design and execution and from the associated supply chain. And we expect this year $1.5 billion of  capital efficiency gains, but there's more to come here.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: And the recent investment decision that we took on Appomattox in the Gulf of Mexico is a good example where we  took out some 20% from the cost, went ahead with a project with around $55 oil price breakeven on a go -forward  basis. And as I expect, there will be much more to come out of the projects and technology organization to update  you on later in the year.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So, the results, excluding identified items, the underlying CCS, current cost of supply earnings, $3.8 billion for the  quarter. That's a 37 % decrease in the earnings per share from a year ago.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Upstream, obviously impacted by the significant decline in the oil and gas price.
