texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: For 2011 we are currently expecting around 220,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day production in  the Gulf. That’s around 40,000 barrels a day lower than it would have been had the moratorium not  been in place. There could be further impacts into 2012. We just don’t know yet.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Turning now to the downstream, excluding the identified items again, the downstream CCS  earnings increased substantially from the third quarter ‘09 to some $1.5 billion in total. texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: So moving on to the portfolio, we made good progress with portfolio development in the quarter.  We’ve now started up five as of the 13 new projects that coming online in the two year period for  2010 and 2011. texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The production in Jackpine will ramp up in 2011 as we also bring on the new capacity at the  Scotford Upgrader plant, and that will come on stream early next year and that processes the  heavy oil into the more valuable lighter products.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Now, having two mines in service now means that we can start to reduce the unit costs from the  synergies we see from the scale we now have there. So we now expect to reduce the cash  production costs by over $3 per barrel for the entire oil sands project.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Looking out now beyond 2012, we’ve made progress with crystallizing some of our longer term  options. We have recently taken the final investment decision, what we call FID, on two deepwater  projects.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Firstly in the Gulf of Mexico, we launched the 100,000 barrel a day Mars B development, that’s in  the Mars basin. And in deepwater Brazil offshore, we’re now going ahead with the second phase of  the BC-10 project.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The acquisition of East Resources takes our North American tight gas potential resource base to  some 40 tcf or well over 6 billion barrels of oil equivalent. texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And of course in the downstream we signed binding agreements with Cosan to form the marketing  – downstream marketing and sugarcane-based biofuels joint venture in Brazil. texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Exploration program, we are in the process of the first wells on the BMS-54 block. This is now 80%  Shell, 20% Total, Total just farmed in. texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator

texts.speaker: Operator

texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: CapEx, the first part of the CapEx is relatively low. It’s essentially facilities to capture gases already  being put together. Over time, though, we will move, first of all, to capturing and stripping the LPG  and potentially exporting LPG, and then finally, if there is excess gas beyond the domestic gas  requirements, there is potential for LNG export from the country. That is – there are effectively three  distinct stages or potential phases of investment. So the upfront CapEx is relatively low. And we’ll  update as soon as we know what we’ve actually agreed with the government there.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Jack Moore>: I was wondering if you could just comment on natural gas in North America  specifically and just the recent transactions with people farming in on acreage and what your  thoughts are there? And then also just the notion that a lot of production is being – a lot of drilling is  being done to hold acres, and where you see gas over the next, say 18 months or so going, and  how you expect to react to that?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Against that, many companies have hedged their production, which made it just about economic,  but those hedges are now beginning to run out. So we see – it was always our premise that by the  end of 2012 a lot of that drilling to hold acreage by production would have reduced, that the hedges  would have run out, and that the supply/demand position would move the price more to the  marginal cost, which we think is a bit higher than what the gas price is today. We’ve seen,  interestingly, in the last few days, a few announcements which suggest we might have been right in  that. So we do think that supply and demand will begin to reassert themselves over the next 12, 18  months. And that prices will move to levels which will make our acreage, where we believe we’re  heading for lowest unit cost in each of the basins, it will make our acreage look pretty attractive and  the returns equally attractive.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q>: Great. And maybe one final follow-up, if I may. You have, of course, your joint venture in  Sichuan in China for the shale gas. Now, I saw that recently the Chinese have decided to give more  licenses to the domestic operators. Is your view that this is a one-only involving a foreign company  like Shell or do you see chances for further licenses there?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry>: Yes, you’re right. In Sichuan, we have two 4,000-square-kilometer licenses  for production sharing contracts with PetroChina. We’ve also got a coal bed methane license  elsewhere, and we’re working on further acreage with PetroChina. China is a big country. 8,000  square kilometers may sound a lot, but perhaps more so in the Netherlands than China. So there is  quite a lot of potential.

file: RDSB - Q3 2011 Earnings Call 27October2011 930 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 27-Oct-11.pdf

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Our share buyback program restarted in August with $800 million done in the third quarter. Underlying oil and  gas production increased by 2%, and that's driven by the continued progress in Qatar and in Canada. And we're  maturing new projects for medium-term growth with exploration success in French Guiana, Australia, and also  launching new Upstream development projects.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So we are making good progress against our targets to deliver a more competitive performance from Shell. So let  me give you a few more details starting with macro environment.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: If you look at the macro picture compared with the third quarter of 2010, oil and gas marker prices have increased  from year-ago levels, although Henry Hub price is broadly similar. The discount of West Texas Intermediate  (WTI) to Brent widened to $24 per barrel in the third quarter, and that compares with less than $1.00 a year ago.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Our natural gas realizations increased from the second quarter in 2011, whereas the oil realizations actually  declined sequentially. Industry refining margins diverged in the quarter with improved margins in the US West  Coast, but declines in all the other regions. In Chemicals, industry margins increased from year-ago levels,  especially in the US, although we did see a decline in margins in Asia. We saw signs of a slowdown in demand at  the end of the quarter in several of our Downstream businesses.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Turning now to earnings overall. The CCS earnings, current cost of supplies, for the quarter including identified  items were $7.2 billion. Excluding those identified items, the CCS earnings were $7.0 billion, and earnings per  share increased by 40%.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now let me just talk a bit more about the business performance in a little bit more detail, firstly, the Upstream.  Excluding identified items, Upstream earnings were $5.4 billion in the third quarter, and that's an increase of 58%  versus the same quarter in 2010. These earnings were driven by higher oil and gas prices and also a very positive  environment for LNG (liquefied natural gas) trading.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Our Upstream earnings were similar to the previous quarter, to second quarter 2011, despite the $3.60 decline in  the Brent price. Natural gas and LNG were an important part of that good performance, where gas is priced  primarily on lagging oil markers. Shell's LNG business did very well in the quarter with growth in a good  marketing environment. Our integrated gas earnings, which is essentially the LNG business, have more than  doubled from year-ago levels.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The Headline oil and gas production for the third quarter was 3.0 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, and  that's an increase of 2% excluding the asset sales impacts. The LNG sales volumes grew by 12% Q3 to Q3, and that  mainly reflects the successful ramp-up in Qatargas 4.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So those are the overall earnings. Turning to the cash flow. The cash generation on a rolling basis, a rolling 12- month basis, was $53 billion; that includes $11 billion of disposals proceeds. And that's against an environment  with an average Brent oil price of $106 per barrel. Both the Upstream and the Downstream business segments  generated surplus cash flow after investment.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And that gave us a free cash flow position, which combined with – a positive free cash flow position – which  combined with our capital spending, dividend, and buyback programs has resulted in a decline in the balance  sheet gearing. Gearing in the end of the quarter sat at 10.8%. That compares with 12% at the end of the second  quarter, moving lower in the 0% to 30% expected range. Of course, you would expect this in the strong oil price

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: There are further asset sales in the works, for example, Downstream business in Africa and the gas pipelines in  Norway. These should complete across the end of this year or early in 2012. Asset sales will continue as part of the  overall strategy; however, the pace will probably slow down from here after what's been a very active period in the  last couple of years.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Before we close, let me update you on progress with the growth portfolio in the quarter. We have more than 20  new project start-ups planned for 2011 to 2014, the four-year period. Those projects will deliver some 800,000  barrels of oil equivalent per day of new production. These are the new projects which underpin our cash flow and  production growth targets.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In Canada, the Athabasca Oil Sands Project, the first Expansion, has ramped up and it should now stabilize at its  plateau rate in the near future. In Qatar, at Pearl Gas-to-Liquids, it's a similar story. Train 1 has now pretty much  ramped up, and we're working to reach sustained plateau rates. Train 2 should start up as planned before the end  of this year.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The two growth projects in Qatar – that's Qatargas 4 and GTL – and the Athabasca Mine Expansion in Canada,  they added some 190,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day for Shell in the third quarter. That compares with the  total expected peak production from the three projects of some 400,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, still  some way to go of course for that. These start-ups reflect some of Shell's unique strengths in the energy industry  today: innovative technology, integration across value chains, and creating long-life returns for shareholders.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now we've also made progress with maturing new projects for medium-term growth delivery during the quarter.  In Australia, the Arrow coal bed methane LNG project entered detailed design, what we call FEED, for an 8  million ton per annum, 2 train LNG project. Arrow has made an offer to acquire Bow Energy in Australia with  further gas resources in this play that could increase the size of the LNG trains by more than 10%.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Elsewhere we announced two final investment decisions on two non-operated developments: the Clair Phase 2  development in the UK; and the Wheatstone LNG project in Australia. Together these two projects are expected to  add around 40,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day for Shell at their peak production level. We've also gone ahead  with an innovative LNG scheme in Canada called the Green Corridor that will take onshore gas production into  small-scale LNG. That LNG will be  used for fuel in the trucking industry on long-distance routes.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: On the exploration side, we had good progress in our frontier exploration portfolio. We have new acreage  positions onshore in the Americas and in the Ukraine, and offshore in New Zealand and Tanzania. In our actual  operations we had a gas discovery offshore Australia and the Zaedyus oil discovery in French Guiana.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Theepan. The start-up costs in Qatar and Oil Sands, basically the start-up costs already are now behind us  in Oil Sands. And in Qatar LNG, up and running now, there's still some costs particularly associated with the  start-up and ramp-up of Train 2 and the GTL ahead of us. It's really only of the order of a few hundred million  dollars still to go. Difficult to separate out what has happened in the past from the future, but overall, there being  that reduction as we go into next year, but it's only a few hundred million dollars, and that's pre-tax as well.

texts.speaker: Kim A. Fustier
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Two questions, if I may. First of all in Alaska, I think the US EPA has recently issued clean air permits. Could you  just comment on where you stand at the drilling process? And beyond these clean air permits, are there any other  milestones that we need to watch out for?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Kim. Alaska. Yes, it was good to see that the clean air permits were issued. We're now in permitting sense  further than we've been before. You could say we're in uncharted territory. And we have been working to a  timetable in terms of approval and various permits, and we're pretty much keeping to the timetable that would  enable drilling up to three wells next year.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Reizen. Just a reminder for those who don't know, Reizen became effectively operational in April this year, so  second quarter of operation. It's a $12 billion joint venture with Cosan, a Brazilian company, 50/50. The world's  largest sugar-to-ethanol producer and also the owner and operator of just under 4,500 retail gas stations in Brazil,  a fast-growing market, over 20% market share in the country.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In the third quarter we did see a positive earnings contribution of around just under $200 million, which is good  to see. We expect generally to get a positive earnings contribution from Reizen. It's operating in a market we know  well in the Downstream. And at the moment, sugar and ethanol prices are both reasonably attractive. Both of  them happen to be a little bit volatile there, so we do expect some volatility in earnings coming from Reizen. But  so far so good, up and running, great growth prospects.

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: All right. But given the situation in the Gulf of Mexico earlier in the year, I think you didn't spend as much as you
texts.text: were planning in the Gulf. And also with low gas prices in the United States, I thought your investments in tied gas  projects in the United States would be less. And obviously if you spend less now, you'll produce less later. I mean, I  was wondering what the impact would be of that? It seems pretty much a US question, actually, now that I think  about it.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: On the gas side there's quite a bit of back-end of the year production, so by the end of the year, our production will  be around about where we projected on the gas. But the average for the year has effectively come out at a lower  level because of the phasing of the spend.  So likelihood is, in both cases it doesn't make the target in 2012 any easier, but they were built in to projections  that we've made. And just to be clear overall, assuming we get back up to speed in those areas, we are going to be  back up at the top end of the range of that CapEx spend next year; that's my expectation.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Qatar ramp-up, we have potentially some tens of thousands of barrels to come just from Train 1 ramp-up. Train 2  isn't likely to have much impact. It's more likely to come in towards the end of the quarter. And Qatar and  Athabasca won't – Qatargas 4 and Athabasca may add a little bit of volume in the quarter, but there's not too  much more there in the fourth quarter.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: There is a bit of upside, but the main factor for fourth quarter production, as always, is the weather in Europe.  And fundamentally, our gas production is tied quite closely to the temperature. So far, it's not been particularly  cold. It was a relatively cold quarter last year, I think, so that's the main factor outside our control. Hopefully, that  helps give you some indication of the things to watch for.

texts.speaker: Robert Arthur Kessler
texts.profession: Analyst, Tudor Pickering Holt & Co. Securities, Inc.
texts.text: It looks to me like you've got at least four options in front of you for exploiting the BTU discrepancy in North  America between accrued or liquids or refined products on the one side and natural gas prices on the other. You've  got what seems to be a brewing potential for liquids-rich shale transactions, you and everybody else, which might  speak to the potential price points or lack of attractiveness there, depending on the base, and I understand you  want to be quiet about that.

texts.speaker: Robert Arthur Kessler
texts.profession: Analyst, Tudor Pickering Holt & Co. Securities, Inc.
texts.text: You've got Western Canada export of LNG potential, which you've clearly done in the past outside of North  America, northeast ethane cracker, and then, now a US Gulf Coast-based GTL plant. Can you rank those options  for me?

texts.speaker: Robert Arthur Kessler
texts.profession: Analyst, Tudor Pickering Holt & Co. Securities, Inc.
texts.text: And as it relates to GTL plant, it seems as though it might be a pretty capital-intensive option. I know you've done  well with Pearl, but is the cost of construction not perhaps higher on the US Gulf Coast versus Qatar? And even  though the shale gas keeps seeming to get better as a feedstock, it seems tough to meet the bar set by the North  Field at Qatar from a cost of supply standpoint. Any thoughts on that?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Robert. You've done your homework. Unfortunately, you missed one; it was the Canadian Green  Corridor, the gas to LNG effectively [ph] strengthens the plans (36:46)

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Into liquids transport. So priority is a question of two things: one, overall economic and strategic attractiveness;  and secondly, the timescale of doability. Clearly, that one is doable more quickly, and therefore the liquids-rich  shale gas falls in that category as well. And yes, we are active, although so far minimal impact on results. So those  are the top two in the short term; direct access to the, effectively, the liquids pricing in the North American  market.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The other three, the export of LNG from British Columbia to Asia; ethane, potential ethane cracker in  Pennsylvania; and potential gas-to-liquids on the Gulf Coast are all viable options economically, but none of them  are going to happen in the short term, and they're all capital intensive.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The most progress is essentially the LNG export where we're looking at land, pipeline, and production together  with three Asian partners, PetroChina and Japanese and Korean partners. And it's still early stages, but that's  generally an agreement in place and looking to put together the full value chain. Clearly attractive to take forward  all our gas to Asia, where the price in the last quarter was around $15, so quite an arbitrage to support the  investment.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The other two, the ethane cracker and the US Gulf gas-to-liquids, it is a question of two things: one, the cost of  development; and secondly, for how long do we think that the gas-to-liquids price differential will be sustained at  a suitable level. At $4 gas and $100 oil, roughly $110 oil, today's price, both of them are economic, and whether we  projects [ph] down (38:51), because we'd like to be robust against an environment rather less attractive than a $4  gas and a $100 oil.

texts.speaker: Robert Arthur Kessler
texts.profession: Analyst, Tudor Pickering Holt & Co. Securities, Inc.
texts.text: What would be the earliest possible date you'd see GTL products on the US Gulf Coast?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I think the Qatar project took five years construction; 2006 was the  investment decision. Mind you a little bit  more quickly in the US, but we'd need to go through a FEED process as well, so 18 months you can add to that, 12,  18 months. And we're not yet at the point where we'd go to FEED. We are doing some design work, potential  design work, and we've identified a couple of possible sites, but you're at least six, seven years away even if we  took a decision tomorrow.

texts.speaker: Jason D. Gammel
texts.profession: Analyst, Macquarie Capital (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you. Simon, I had a couple of questions about the trading environment in 3Q and its sustainability. First of  all, your Downstream numbers look to handily beat the consensus, and that's actually been a fairly consistent  pattern with your peer group. I was wondering if the large drop in crude prices over the course of the quarter,  which obviously have subsequently rebounded, led to any outsize trading profits that would have shown up in the  Downstream business?

texts.speaker: Jason D. Gammel
texts.profession: Analyst, Macquarie Capital (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And then secondarily, the LNG trading environment was obviously strong in 3Q. Spot prices in Asia appear to  actually be on the incline. Would you expect that the LNG trading environment gets better for you?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: LNG trading, it was a good quarter, very much so. We actually had 26 cargo diversions; that's nearly double where  we were a year ago. Partly that's driven by Asian demand, and partly it's driven because we, today, have access to  more LNG on our own account to do that type of activity. Fundamentally, we're moving cargoes that were maybe  initially planned for North America into higher value markets.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In Europe where average realized gas price have been at $9, Asia around $15 for the quarter, so generally a good  quarter of opportunity and demand for short-term delivery following the Fukushima accident earlier this year,  and some of the choices in European energy policy has been quite good. And you need to look at both Downstream  and Upstream trading as substantive, sustainable, and very important strategic value levers for Shell. They are not  opportunistic and they are not short-term.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: See how long the first one takes, Lucas. UA profit's relatively simple. You had some downtime in Oil Sands. The  bitumen realized price in some weeks was in the $50s, as opposed to what you might have expected closer to WTI.  And we had a lot of downtime in the Gulf of Mexico, mainly BP-operated assets in the [ph] Aqeeq (44:33),  Holstein. And we did have some shut-in time, planned shut-in time, in Mars and Auger. So it had some temporary  effects on the oily-over-liquid type activities.

texts.speaker: Lucas O. Herrmann
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Prime Brokerage)
texts.text: So as the operator's fully up and running, the bitumen discount should negate, though, no? By year?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So, for the upgrade in margin. So the Upstream is taking some of the apparent pain for the low bitumen price.

texts.speaker: Lucas O. Herrmann
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Prime Brokerage)
texts.text: So, Simon, when you say a couple of hundred million, that's for LNG and GTL?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And so refining out an improvement would help that, plus some of the differentials in Europe work in our favor.  So we're a heavy diesel relative to the market diesel producer, and that's basically what helped. Plus, the  availability was up at a much better level, and the non-availability on an unplanned basis was down to a more  acceptable level. So it was one of our better quarters in terms of operational performance, but that's basically it.

texts.speaker: Iain S. Reid
texts.profession: Analyst, Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: Firstly, is it possible that you can tell us the 800,000 barrels a day of production you're bringing on between '11  and '14, how the cash margins of that compare with the existing cash margins of your base business?  And secondly, another topic. On exploration CapEx and well drilling, could you tell us what you think you're going  to be spending and drilling this year in terms of numbers of wells, and how that compares to what you're  expecting to do next year?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: On average, it's better. And that's what drives, for example, our 11% production increase between '09 and '12,  2009 to 2012, driving 50% more cash flow. It's fundamentally because the unit cash flows of the new production is  better than the old. And the underlying driver, typically fairly clear, a lot of the new production is big iron. It's  large capital investment, but go forward, low operating spend, operating cost spend, and quite limited future  capital requirements in projects such as GTL, any LNG, or Ormen Lange or the Oil Sands.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So the fundamental nature and shape of the portfolio has changed. They're all, you probably realize as well, they're  in basically lower or more stable fiscal environments, and fiscal environments which have less of a creaming at  higher oil and gas prices. So those are strategic choices which we're now seeing playing through in today's  margins, and they will play through increasingly up to 2014.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: What I would say is we're actually in the middle of some, or a beginning of some, exciting activity at the moment.  We're still completing; we're sidetracking in French Guiana. We are – we just farmed into the Petrobras  opportunity in Tanzania, 50% there. We are drilling Appomattox, appraisal well in the Gulf of Mexico. We just  spudded BMS-54, which is the 80% shale block in the pre-salt in Brazil. We are, hopefully, getting in a position to  drill in Alaska. We are drilling in China onshore. And there's a lot of onshore activity in North America. So it's  quite an exciting time and if anything we'll be looking to increase the level of activity next year.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: No. Seriously. What I can tell you is the ratio of liquids to gas is higher now than it will be as we ramp-up. The bait  worked out particularly liquids rich and in the lower ramp up phase. Good idea to call IR later on that one, I think.  Sorry, Mark.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: $670 million in the quarter, the best ever quarterly result. They clearly are benefiting structurally, because it's not  necessarily top of the chemical cycle at the moment. They're benefiting structurally from that switch we talked  about earlier in terms of gas feedstock in the US. We are continuing to do a little bit here, a little bit there in terms  of investment and work-around work to ensure we're maximizing that opportunity in the US, which we're  definitely benefiting from today in the manufacturing side; still seeing reasonable margins in the market there.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Definitely up against a year ago, and up against the second quarter overall on the grounds that there's a lagged oil  price in here, so we're still benefiting from the rise of the oil price earlier in the year. Slightly offsetting that is  quite a few of the diversions will be going into Europe. Now it's obviously better than sending them to North  America, but on average is less good than into Asia. Those are the trends, but it's up in both cases.

texts.speaker: Oswald C. Clint
texts.profession: Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you very much, Simon. Just a question on Arrow and down in Australia, I'm wondering if you're also  looking at potentially some tight sands that are down below the coal seams across your joint venture there, your  acreage?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Sure. Thanks for that, Oswald. Arrow, we basically have two CBM or CSG, coal seam gas, positions. One in the  Surat Basin; it's close to Brisbane. And one in the Bowen Basin, which we've just [ph] added, took (56:31) with the  acquisition of Bow. In both cases our prime focus is on the coalbed methane rather than on gas and the tight  sands. There is some in the area but that's not our prime focus.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Jeff. Port Arthur is 90% complete in terms of construction. We're already working on some of the units  and due to warm them up and bring them in, but effectively won't have any impact on production until early next  year. There are a multiplicity of units there. We're going from 325,000 barrels a day to around 600,000 barrels a  day with full upgrading capabilities. So it's a very large activity. So we're warming up the utilities at the moment.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Tanzania farm-in, quite excited about it; could be a good prospect. It's, as you're probably aware, a gassy play, so  it's gas that we'd be looking for. Can't really give details on the target size. Hopefully, we will know more by the

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The Gulf has declined. We're around 220,000, 230,000 barrels a day at the moment. We would hope – Perdido's  now up at 70,000 barrels a day and hopefully rising because drilling those development wells. We would hope to  pick up at some point during the year, not clear exactly when, you need to operators to see the Tonga chute come  online, and we've quite a bit of drilling to help sustain production over at  Auger, and Mars still to come.
