texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Shell's underlying current cost of supplies, or CCS earnings, were $4.5 billion for the quarter. That's a 32%  decrease in earnings per share from the third quarter of 2012. Cash flow ge nerated from operations was $10.4  billion and that's an increase of 10% year-over-year. There were a number of negatives for us in the quarter. We  were impacted by weaker industry refining conditions globally. Our industry is facing considerable headwinds  from those low refining margins and we saw continued challenges in the operating environment in Nigeria.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now we have a strong project flow in place for 2014 and beyond. We've started up a series of new oil and gas  projects in the last few months in deepwater in Brazil, in integrated gas in Australia and in the longer term plays  such as Iraq. Now these are all part of the project flow that'll drive our cash flow in 2014 and well beyond, of  course. But that comes alongside what we expect will be a significant reduction in net spending next year as we  work through the series of the 2013 acquisitions and we increase the pace of divestments.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Move on to details starting with the macro. Now, if you look at this picture compared with the third quarter of  2012, Brent oil prices were some $1.00 per barrel higher than year-ago levels, but with narrower differentials  between Brent and the North American market, particularly WTI. Our upstream overall realizations did decline  slightly from the third quarter a year ago. On the downstream side, the refining margins weakened in all regions,  particularly the U.S. and Europe.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Turning now to earnings. First, the regular disclaimer. Quarterly results are important, clearly, high or low. But  they are only a three-month snapshot of performance in what is a volatile industry. And where we're  implementing a long-term strategy, that has both investment and performance, their criteria looks at a much  longer wavelength than three months. The third quarter CCS earnings excluding identified items were $4.5  billion, with compared to last year, lower contributions in both the upstream and the downstream.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In aggregate, macro and environment factors were a $1 billion net negative  for us on a Q3 to Q3 basis. That  includes the lower margins in refining, but also a $200 million relative reduction from a double dividend payment  in LNG in last year's results, just the one payment this year. We had $300 million earnings reduction year -on-year  for Nigeria, where the operating conditions continue to be challenging and uncertain. The upstream portfolio  growth was overall positive in these results, adding around $500 million year -on-year, particularly driven by Pearl  gas-to-liquids project in Qatar, and that despite an offset there from higher maintenance.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Turning now to operating performance. The headline oil and gas production for the third quarter was 2.9 million  barrels of oil equivalent per day. The deteriorating Nigeria operating environment resulted in some 65,000 barrels  of oil equivalent per day reduction, and that's on a Q3 to Q3 basis, but also removed 280,000 tons of LNG from  the quarter. But excluding oil price production sharing contract effects, the effect of the Nigeria environment and  divestments made in the last 12 months, the underlying oil and gas production actually increased by 1% and LNG  volumes increased by 4%.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The underlying production volumes are supported by the growth projects, and the operating performance there  overall was good. There were offsets to that, with some 60,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day from maintenance  activities, including downtime in the U.K. North Sea, where we are replacing the Sakhalin FPSO, and in the Gulf of  Mexico where the 30,000 BOE per day Auger field was shut down for maintenance. Now, we took advantage of  that downtime opportunity at Auger to do some of the work on the future Cardamom tie -back. Auger should be  back online in Q4 and the 50,000 barrel a day Cardamom discovery is scheduled to come on stream next year.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In the downstream, refinery and chemicals availability improved from year-ago levels, and that benefited from  lower planned and unplanned downtime. Overall, a good performance. Excluding accounting changes, the oil  products sales volumes were broadly unchanged Q3 to Q3, and the underlying chemicals volumes increased due to  trading activity. Now, you'll see some indications on this particular slide about the fourth quarter. We are  expecting a heavy quarter for maintenance overall, some 60,000 barrels oil equivalent per day in t he upstream,  Q4 to Q4 reduction. That's in production at high-margin assets, such as the U.K., in deepwater Nigeria and in  Brunei.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: There will be planned maintenance in Pearl gas-to-liquids during the fourth quarter, and LNG volumes in general  will be reduced by around 900,000 tons. That's around 17 % to 18% of total, by maintenance programs in a  number of facilities. Exploration charges should remain relatively high in the fourth quarter and the operating  environment in Nigeria remains challenging and uncertain.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Three months ago, in the second quarter results we announced strategic reviews of our Nigeria onshore and our  North America shale resources portfolios. We are now marketing assets from both of these areas, whereas I expect  more to come.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now just let me highlight four new project start-ups. In deepwater Brazil, we commenced production on the  second phase of the BC-10 development. This should add 35,000 BOE per day, 100%. We recently launched the  construction of phase three development for BC-10, and that is for a further 28,000 barrels oil equivalent per day.  This is a highly successful development for the field overall.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In Australia, Woodside has started production at the North Rankin redevelopment project. And that provides new  gas supplies to the Northwest Shelf LNG project. In Iraq, we've restarted the Majnoon field, and we're now  focused on reaching the first commercial production target of 175,000 barrels a day. That's the point at which we  will start to recover costs.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In Kazakhstan, the North Caspian Operating Company commenced production at the Kashagan field in  September. The field is currently shut in, not producing, following the discovery of leaks on the gas pipeline. Shell  and KazMunaiGas, or KMG, who will ultimately be the joint venture operators of Kashagan, they are ready to  manage production activities at Kashagan on behalf of the joint venture as and when the facilities are ready for  hand-over.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In the deepwater, commissioning is now underway in both Mars B in the Gulf of Mexico, the Olympus platform,  and Gumusut-Kakap in Malaysia, making good progress on both of those Shell-operated projects. Now, we're  making good progress closing out the purchase of Repsol's LNG business, and that will bring some 7 .2 million  tons per annum of LNG volumes into Shell's overall portfolio, representing long-term off-take agreements. We  still expect the acquisition to close by the end of this year.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, looking further into the future, just let me highlight two exciting new oil plays for Shell. Firstly, in Canada,  heavy oil, and secondly, deepwater Brazil. We have taken final investment decision announced today on the  Carmon Creek development in the Peace River area in northern Alberta. This will be a steam plug development,  two phases, 40,000 barrels a day each. The bitumen will be exported by pipeline to east Canada, already  committed capacity. And from there onward to refineries for processing, for example, on the Gulf Coast in the U.S.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: For 2013 we have announced some $10 billion of acquisitions, already announced, so nothing new here. They  include the Rexall LNG business, the pre-emption rights for BC-10 in Brazil, the Petrobras share which was for  sale, the signature bonus for Libra just mentioned, and the bulking up earlier in the year of the North Sea  upstream positions. That means that our net investment spending we expect assuming closure of all of the above  to be around $45 billion in 2013. The final outcome will depend on the timing of closure.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Overall, I'd like to stress that quite clearly we are managing to a $130 billion net spending program 2012 through  2015. That's a four-year program in the $100 oil price scenario. There are many moving parts in that intent and in  that investment program, not just investments, but asset sales, acquisitions, new final investment decisions. We  manage all of this on a multi-year basis, not annual and certainly not three months.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We've built up substantial new options for the company in the last few years and a much larger exploration  portfolio. I think we've reached critical mass maybe beyond 2015 and beyond investment options right now. So  there will be decisions to make in the next few quarters on which options to take through to final investment  decisions and which projects we drop or defer out beyond that period. And that particularly applies to our global  integrated gas business.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We have a series, an embarrassment of riches, of high-quality opportunities for new LNG gas-to-liquids and in  downstream gas-to-chemicals. We can't do all of these. Some of these potential projects are reaching critical  planning milestones over the next few months and each project is potentially individually material. So we are  expecting to make choices in the near future, part of capital discipline embedded in our management process.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now moving on, just to summarize before the Q&A. Underlying CCS earnings, $4.5 billion for the quarter. Strong  project flow, we believe the best in the industry for 2014 and beyond. We can see the transparency of what gets  delivered now over the next one to two years. We've already started up a series of new oil and gas projects in the  last few months, none of which were on the big five list, but each of which is material, and that being in deepwater  and integrated gas in the longer-term plays like Iraq. They are all part of a project flow that drives Shell's cash flow  into 2014 and beyond. It will come alongside a signific ant reduction in net investment spending next year,  particularly helped by increased divestment.

texts.speaker: Alejandro A. Demichelis
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane BNP Paribas
texts.text: Y eah, good afternoon. Alejandro Demichelis from Exane BNP Paribas. A couple of questions here. The first on is  you mentioned the lower net investment into next year. Maybe you can give us some kind of indication of how we  should be thinking about the growth CapEx or the organic CapEx into next year? And then the second question is  maybe you can give us a bit of an update in terms of what would be your net cost of Carbon Creek now that we  have the FID there?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We are able to finance that level of investment and the growth in the dividend as we deliver the cash flow growth.  So there's no spin or one-off or headline attempt here. This is sustainable investment activity through cycle in  pursuit of long-term strategic intent. The organic level of CapEx, a lot of next year is already committed. We will  be looking, obviously, for opportunities either to effectively look for partners and investment that's ongoing, or  where we bring new projects in, such as the Carbon Creek, look to offset that with the divestment program. So I  can't be more specific than that because it will to a certain extent depend on actual transactions, some of which are  only in early stages of development.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: At Carbon Creek, just to say a couple of words about that, it is a project that will produce a decade. This is a multi - billion-barrel resource. The first two phases we announced today. There are further phases potentially available to  take advantage of the resource. It's one of the longest-lasting potential resources in the Shell Group. It will  produce 80,000 barrels a day for many decades. It is a break-even price, well below the bottom of our range of  testing for investment capability. And in practice, the up-front investment in facilities lasts for many years, but the  drilling continues for many years beyond that. So even if I was predisposed to give an individual figure for single  investment, I wouldn't because the drilling takes place for the best part of 20-odd years.

texts.speaker: Hootan Yazhari
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: Hi there, Simon. Two questions, if I may. Starting with how you're thinking about your aggressive divestment  program in 2014 and 2015, it would be great if you could give us some c olor around the sorts of assets that you're  looking for inclusion in the divestment program, whether it be producing assets, whether it be upstream,  downstream, whether you'd look to sell-down some of your integrated gas portfolio? Or is it just too early to say?

texts.speaker: Hootan Yazhari
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: The second question I had was regarding the North American portfolio. Obviously, in the second quarter you took  some write-downs after an extensive geological assessment of your assets in North America. I just wanted to see  going into the end of the year whether that process would continue or whether you had substantially finished that  and whether the valuation of your U.S. portfolio could be impacted by any re -pricing of assumptions that you have  on U.S. natural gas? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Hootan, thank you very much for that. Two important questions. The divestment program, give you a couple of  specifics and then the general intent. The specifics are clear, Nigeria and the onshore shale portfolio that we talked  about in Q2, they will happen. The general intent in divestments always, and this is an ongoing program, will just  be slightly more aggressive I think as we go forward, is mature, mid-life or late-life assets in the upstream are  always potential divestment candidates because of the just – other people have a different approach. They have to  generate value and may be better owners than Shell. So that's always formed part of our sales.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The other type of assets in the upstream is at the other end of the maturity curve, it is exploration or early  development-type assets, where we have de-risked, we've created an opportunity, created value and either it's not  strategically or economically attractive for us to develop it and better for somebody else or where we can bring in  partners, such as we did for example on the Prelude floating LNG project. So that type of asset or those two types  of assets in the upstream will I think form the bulk of the activity.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: North America, if you want the total North American portfolio, I think the question is really about shale and the  unconventional gas and liquids rich. The process c ontinues and the process is exploration and appraisal rather  than continually looking for impairments. So the reason that there were impairments in the second quarter is that  exploration activities did not lead to a potential development in the assets that were impaired. We have $25 billion  still on the balance sheet. Some of that remains exploration. It's less than half, but it's still a significant potential  number.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The exploration appraisal continues in the third quarter, maybe in the fourth quarters. I t's still too early to tell.  The rest of the portfolio is either being developed or we see a clear path to development. We're already producing  320,000 barrels a day. Expect that go down a bit from divestments and up as we focus our investment on the  better opportunities. So it's a huge portfolio, it's a great resource, it will be very valuable for Shell over time. It's  not something we'd change around overnight. And as for the second quarter, I cannot and will not rule out any  future impairments. But they are of the nature of an exploration write-off, they just happen to be in an accounting  sense defined as impairments. And hopefully that's clear.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Theepan. Iraq, Majnoon, remember this was essentially a greenfield development, unlike the first wave of  Iraq developments, such as West Qurna or Zubair. So it's built on some old facilities, but essentially it's greenfield.  So, we took the brownfield down and we're now bringing the greenfield facilities up. The new facilities we are  running well above the first commercial production target of 175,000 bbl/d. We're running today well over 10%  above that. However, we have to sustain that on average for 90 days out of 120 days. So to meet that original  requirement, we need to sustain the performance level. Looking good at the moment with a bit of a fair wind  behind us. Because it's not simple operations, we should get there by the end of the year, which then enables us to  get cost recovery.

texts.speaker: Jason D. Gammel
texts.profession: Analyst, Macquarie Capital (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Thanks very much. Simon, I want to come back to the North American portfolio. I'm trying to put my arms around  what we should think about it in terms of the rate of return on the liquids-rich shale venture here. And I believe  you spent about $10 billion on essentially unproved property acquisitions in the U.S. over the last three years.  Now, we would expect to see proceeds coming in from the property sales that you've talked about in Niobrara,  Mississippi Lime, et cetera. But can you really talk about where you think you staked out c ore positions in liquids- rich shales? Is the Permian an area that you think is scalable and economic? And are there any others that you  find scalable and economic outside of the Marcellus and the Duvernay?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Jason. The portfolio question is easier than the rate of return. The portfolio is the scalable position is the  Marcellus and the Grand Birch in the gas, potentially the Haynesville, which is already fairly mate rial. It's just at  the higher end of the cost curve in Louisiana. On the liquids-rich, yes, Permian. For us, most likely no Eagle Ford.  That's one of the assets that's for sale. And, again, West Canada in general in more than one area. So those are the  areas we would expect to scale up in North America.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We are drilling in the Vaca Muerta in Argentina, which looks good. Early days, but we're two rigs down there. And  of course, in the rest of the world, in China, Ukraine, we are drilling. In Russia, there is some activity through our  joint venture with Salym Petroleum. So there are plenty of basins around the world that offer opportunity. But for  now, it's West Canada and Permian that are the main liquids-rich. And development with Argentina, probably the  next one.

texts.speaker: Jon Rigby
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Second question is the Scrip. I think where people for the industry as a whole get concerned is around assurances  on capital discipline. Of course, one of the methods of giving some sort of assurance around that is the availability  of a buyback. Has there been any discussion or is the board – does the board appreciate that the Scrip dividend  itself actually blocks you out from doing a traditional share buyback, if I understand it correctly? And has there  been some sort of abandoning the Scrip just to give yourself the availability of doing a traditional share buyback  rather than just an anti-dilution share buyback? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And, yes, clearly if we divest more and it happens to be particularly cash generative, it will have an impac t.  Probably worth noting that on the full-year cash generation overall, there is not only behind us some challenges  on the operational performance, such as Nigeria or the operational downtime we've had in the UK and the Gulf.  But looking forward, Nigeria doesn't get any better. We are doing slower investments in the shale. And we are –  the divestments are likely to have an impact. And the refining macro, the gas price in North America both look  considerably worse than we might initially have hoped for.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So hopefully in 12 months' time you can ask me the same question, Rahim. We'll have some divestments behind  us, we'll the have the proof points on the growth, and the discussion at the board will be precisely what to do with  that excess cash. At the moment, it's about the confidence at delivery and the choices that we make to ensure that  we remain in charge of the choices irrespective of what happens in the macroenvironment and recognizing the  clear and legitimate interest of the shareholders and the rating agencies, for that matter. Thanks, Rahi m. We'll  come back to that subject I'm sure in the future.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Michele. The Gulf of Mexico refining, we are not set up to process light sweet crud e. Our refineries are  designed and configured for heavy sour. In fact, they're designed to process just about everything up to old tires,  and unfortunately that is not the feed stock that is most attractive at the moment. We can take some. We're  looking to maximize what we can take, but that is not the basis of design.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The balance of the 24 rigs that are drilling, two-thirds of them are on LRS acreage. Some of it, development in the  Permian, the rest is rapid appraisal in Canada. And we would expect that we have about 40 wells awaiting hook - up in the fourth quarter, maybe more as the drilling continues during the quarter. So I would expect to see the gas  declines that we're clearly seeing because they're not drilling offset by LRS production coming in over the next  three months to six months.

texts.speaker: Lucas O. Herrmann
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Prime Brokerage)
texts.text: On the other hand, you've got an integrated gas business where you're grown your invested capital by broadly $24  billion. Y ou've driven your returns from 12% to 23%. Y ou've driven your profit from $3 billion or $4 billion to $10  billion. Y ou've got clear competitive advantage. It's a market that is moving in your direction, yet everything that  you have in that business suggests it's going the right way for you. And the decisions on Repsol were absolutely the  right ones to take. And then I listen to you talk about hard choices, and the integrated asset, the integrated gas  opportunities that you indicate you're going to sell – that you indicate you're selling down. Now, I appreciate you  can't take everything, but the allocation of capital here over the last five years is in many respects beyond belief.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I've talked about the shale gas. The shale gas we've created a large portfolio. It is losing money at the moment, still  losing money. In earnings terms, we're slightly cash positive. It needs to become rather more cash positive and  returns positive based on the strategic moves we're taking, and that is one thing, in fact, both the things we've just  talked about, both the downstream and the shale business and where we are heading on exploration, those are the  things that we will definitely cover [indiscernible] (54:15).

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The rest of the business, the oil family is performing well. Reliability imp roving. It's profitable. It's cash  generative. The challenge there is the de-bottlenecking and the ensuring that the ongoing maintenance CapEx  does not get too close to the cash generation from the asset, so the de -bottlenecking, et cetera. We'll grow that  business over time. Carmon Creek is an in situ heavy oil play. It is not stranded because we have the access of the  bitumen to the East Coast. In fact, it's most likely to be a fully integrated play with the solvent required to move  the bitumen coming from our own liquids-rich activities. And Carmon Creek is essentially a gas-to-oil arbitrage,  because there was a very significantly gas going into the project, which will go into effectively CHP schemes to  produce the steam and export electricity.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So we're creating a core piece of energy infrastructure that will make money for many, many years to come. It's  also the major player in in situ, it's our only major player in in situ, but it's an asset we've worked for many years.  So as a stand-alone material piece of business, it could double from the initial 80,000 barrels a day, it is very  much worth having in the portfolio. So it's wrong to look at the Americas only through one lens. I didn't talk about  Brazil, but that has a separate potential if anybody will wish to go there.

texts.speaker: Martijn P. Rats
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Y eah, good afternoon. I'll leave it at one question. I just wanted to ask, during the quarter, there's been some  newspaper coverage of a large GTL facility in Louisiana. I was wondering if you could comment on where we stand  with that project? And at the same time, that also includes the chemical cracker which I believe is scheduled for  Pennsylvania and the project for energy exports. In those sort of three types of investments, what do you expect in  terms of FIDs over the next couple of quarters?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Well, over the next couple of quarters none, because none of them are anywhere close to FID. But I'll give a  broader answer to that, Martijn, thanks. Those three opportunities are all large -scale investment. LNG Canada  will be the LNG I think that you mean. They're all approaching what we call the conceptual action stage before we  go into final front – the engineering design, front-end engineering feed stage before the final investment decision.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We're already doing some of that detailed design in LNG in Canada, but we're not there yet, though it's early on  the other two. When I talked about choices in the integrated gas portfolio and the funnel and deciding which ones  we take forward, that's precisely what I was referring to. We cannot afford to take all three together at once. And  even if we could, I'm not sure we have the engineers and the project managers to do so. So we will need to make  choices which go forward. At the same time, just on North America overall, we are investing in the Elba Island  export facility, which is small, modular, rapid and highly profitable.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The gas to transport scheme is a go-ahead. There are three of those, also small and modular, a bit more risk on the  profitability on those projects because we're looking to create a new market, but all of those and, as I mentioned,  Carmon Creek are in effect plays on gas price, a low gas price, high oil price arbitrage opportunity so quite  significant value potential for Shell. We don't have to do all of these at once. We will not do all of these at the same  time. Hopefully that helps.

texts.speaker: Peter W. Hutton
texts.profession: Analyst, RBC Europe Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: And thesecond area is you said Alaska drilling is effectively a binary option. There will be big oil there or there  won't and we will find out soon. Can you confirm that you are planning to drill in the summer window in 2014?  Thanks very much.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Peter. Exploration, yeah, we did actually give an indication this will be higher for Q3. It ended up being  slightly higher than even we expected. The [ph] Porter well (1:03:03) was around a of couple hundred million. We  also had write-offs, one in the Gulf of Mexico, in Qatar, in Norway, in Kazakhstan. That's not in the Kashagan  concession, it's elsewhere. In French Guiana. And we also had some of the shale gas developments in the JQ  activity in China. Interestingly, nothing really in LRS in this particular quarter. So more exploration is a good idea  to build a portfolio. Unfortunately, it was a particularly unsuccessful six months really because not all those wells  were actually drilled in the third quarter.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So we have the two rigs. We need to go through – and the intent clearly is to drill in 2014. But first of all we have  to ensure that all our own equipment, all 25 or so vessels that need to be in the theatre are ready and permitted to  operate and we'll be sure about that some time in the first quarter. And then we need the exploration plan and all  the associated permits in place before we start to drill. The clear focus is o n the Chukchi, the Berger Prospect. And  just to close the loop strategically, Libra, Carmon Creek and Alaska are all multi-billion barrel prospects. Just the  Berger prospect alone matches our potential share in Libra or higher.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Go back to Q1. We were miles ahead of the market's estimates. So our view is and will remain we've given you the  guidance. There will be updates during the quarter on anything that's relevant, such as issues in Nigeria, which is  a perennial, you see the gas prices yourselves, and it's highly unlikely that we would have a profit warning ahead of  results just because market estimates are not where they are. Warnings are only against statements we've made,  not statements made by analysts or anybody else it happens it be that guess at what our earnings might be. And to  be honest, both of the last quarters were not that different from the guidance that I'd given in the  previous  quarter. I just acknowledged that our exploration write-offs were higher. But they're not, in the bigger scheme a  really big issue.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Stephen. The production in the third quarter is about 320,000, which about 55,000 or so of which was  from liquid-rich areas. That was about 340,000 at the beginning of the year, so we've been running down the gas  basically and replacing it with liquids, but not quite at the same rate. The going forward, the 55,000 will go down  by something around 25,000 as and when we are able to sell the Eagle Ford asset, give or take. But we'll go up as  we invest in Permian and West Canada.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The gas is likely to decline for a bit because we are not drilling at really at replacement rate and we are reducing  our investment there pretty much to the lowest level that is appropriate to staying in the major basins. So I can't  give a number because I don't actually have a number, but those are the trends. And perhaps the more important  thing from the financials is getting the cost base right on both the operating costs and the capital cost of drilling  those wells, driving it down so that everything we're drilling is okay at $4 and the prices that we're s eeing realized  in the NGLs and the condensate. So that's where the focus is really. It's not a production thing, it's a financial  outcome driven strategy and hopefully that is something we'll be able to return to with more positive news over  the next few quarters.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Moving on to the priorities. The results today show we are delivering on the three priorities we set out the start of  this year both our financial performance and enhanced capital efficiency and continuing strong project delivery.  We aim to grow cash flow through the cycle and at the same time deliver competitive shareholder returns. We're  making good progress with restructuring in North American resource plays, essentially completing the asset sales  program there and we're continuing with the costs and the portfolio reductions in Oil Products.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Now the recent decline in oil prices is very much part of the inherent volatility in our industry. We've planned our  strategy around an expectation of such volatility. The portfolio needs to be attractive and resilient in a wide range  of circumstances. It underlines the importance of our drive to better performance management, to keep a hold on  costs and spending, to improve the balance between growth and returns, and to improve our capital efficiency.  The proceeds from asset sales so far this year total almost $12 billion with further disposals ongoing. The new  projects are delivering benefits to the bottom line now. Overall production volumes were lower but margins are  higher as this strategy of investing in profitable projects with or without equity production pays off. We've  continued to mature new investment opportunities in the quarter and we've added quite a few new barrels with  the drill bit.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Turning to the results, starting with the macro. Shell's liquids and natural gas realizations declined from the third  quarter 2013. The Brent oil price was some $8 per barrel lower than year-ago levels with similar differentials  between Brent and WTI. Of course current prices today are still below this level and are squeezing revenues  further. On the Downstream this was a quarter characterized by higher leve ls of industry and refinery downtime  which led to a year-on-year uptick in margins in all regions, although Singapore margins and Asia Pacific in  general remained in negative territory. Industry base chemicals margins increased on the back of reduced feed  stock costs with tight supply conditions; however, intermediate margins declined in challenging market  conditions.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Now turning to our earnings. Excluding identified items, Shell's underlying current costs of supplies, or CCS  earnings, were $5.8 billion for the quarter. That's a 30% increase in earnings per share from the third quarter a  year ago. On a Q3-to-Q3 basis, we saw higher earnings in both Upstream and Downstream. Earnings were  supported by a range factors. In the Downstream, the industry margins were higher and the operating  performance and the capture of those margins improved. In the Upstream, we benefited from new higher margin  production, local exploration expenses and higher integrated gas results. Return on average capital employed,  excluding identified items, was 10.1%.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: The Upstream Americas and Integrated Gas businesses both showed positive earnings momentum on a third  quarter to third quarter basis. Now we've benefited from new high margin production offsetting the effect of lower  oil prices and lower volumes overall. And this is the result of a strategy to invest for profitability; not simply  volumes and not something simply started a year ago. It's something that was effectively a strategic choice seven  years or eight years ago. And of course some of our recent projects such as Iraq gas and the Repsol LNG deal came  with financial uplift but no, zero equity production volumes.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Headline oil and gas production for the third quarter was 2.8 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, a n  underlying increase of 2% supported by the ongoing ramp up at Mars B in the Gulf of Mexico and Majnoon in  Iraq. Now we also saw some new volumes from existing fields in Deepwater Brazil and the Gulf and lower levels of  maintenance compared with the third quarter a year ago. The LNG sales volumes were up 16% Q3 on Q3. That's  strong growth and that's driven primarily by the acquisition of Atlantic and Peru LNG.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Y ou'll see some pointers for the fourth quarter on this slide covering production and some financial items. Now  just let me note that some 65% of Shell's worldwide production revenue is linked to oil prices and a $10 per barrel  move in Brent equates to some $3.2 billion of earnings impact on an annual basis for 2014. Now that sensitivity is  likely going to grow and be higher in 2015. Let me also note there is a four month to six month time lag between  LNG prices moving or between spot oil prices moving and LNG prices that are oil price linked moving after that.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Now I think you're all aware, we don't take a particular view on near-term oil prices. We have a strong balance  sheet, and we take a longer-term view on financing and project economics. But as you would expect from Shell,  we're keeping the pressure on the spending and the operating costs, and the current environment may actually  give us opportunities to get better value from the supply chain here. So that's a round up on the results. Just let  me update you on the portfolio.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: The asset sales program is making good progress, around $12 billion of proceeds in the bank so far this year.  Announcements we made over the summer on the lower 48 onshore gas essentially marked the completion of the  major portfolio reduction in North American resource or shale plays. That's with around $3 billion of disposal  proceeds announced 2013 and 2014.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Once these deals and license expiry effects have all been completed we'll have exited around 11% of our 2013 oil  and gas production and some 6% of refining capacity. That means we enter 2015 with a more focused and efficient  portfolio and balance sheet. But of course there will be a reduction to headline production and re serves.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Turning now to project delivery, we've had a strong year in portfolio development. We had first oil at Gumusut - Kakap in the quarter in Malaysia, and that completes the last of four Shell-operated Deepwater startups that we  planned this year and it's great to see these fields all making an impact now on the bottom line. There have been  some well publicized delays in some non-operated projects in our portfolio, and this, combined with the 2014  divestment program and license expiries, collectively mean that headline production has been falling.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Looking to the longer-term, we have a highly competitive set of fields under construction for startup, particularly  in the 2016 through 2018 timeframe. For example Prelude Floating LNG still in the Deepwater Gulf, Carmon  Creek heavy oil in Canada. But we also have the non-operated developments such as Gorgon, LNG Australia, Clair  and Schiehallion in the U.K. North Sea and eventually Kashagan in Kazakhstan. And we've made a lot of progress  in 2014 on maturing new opportunities with front end engineering and design feed underway in some very  substantial plays such as Appomattox and Vito, deepwater in the Gulf of Mexico that could drive production well  into the next decade there. And LNG in Canada, where we can leverage our leadership in integrated gas.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: And also now, I'll slightly update you on exploration in the quarter. We've announced four interesting new  discoveries in the last few months and also continued with the highly successful this year near-field exploration  program. In the Gulf of Mexico, the Rydberg and Kaikias oil discoveries, they could add new barrels in the  Appomattox and Mars Ursa areas, both with tie-back potential to existing oil planned hubs. In Deepwater,  Malaysia the Marjoram gas line is one of a series of new hubs and near-field discoveries that could feed into  existing LNG schemes. And I'm very pleased to confirm that we've found gas in Deepwater Gabon with a subsalt  exploration well called Leopard-1. We are going to appraise this one with at least one more well potentially next  year. And we're also assessing the further exploration potential in this area. It is essentially a new  play for us and  potentially the industry.

texts.speaker: Lydia R. Rainforth
texts.profession: Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: And then secondly, and this is just more on the numbers, in terms of the Integrated Gas line, given the Repsol  acquisition, how much of that actually comes from the Upstream Americas these days as opposed to the  International part of that? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Thanks, Lydia. On the macro, I think I've been saying for two years or three years now that the oil price probably  was defying gravity and that's perhaps coming through in the way that the underlying supply and demand  fundamentals would indicate at the moment.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: The gearing range we say we would expect to see us through such periods, such volatility is 0% to 30%, currently  11% – just over 11%. I am well aware that the rating agencies in particular, and quite possibly the equity markets  too, would get a little nervous if we hit 20%. One of the reasons being the inclusion of off-balance sheet liabilities  as well, and therefore before we would get nervous, another 10% gearing, roughly $20 billion of additional net  debt, that's equivalent to effectively,  think about it, $30 for a couple of years off the oil price.

texts.speaker: Lydia R. Rainforth
texts.profession: Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: It was just about the proportion of the Integrated Gas business from the Americas.

texts.speaker: Theepan Jothilingam
texts.profession: Nomura International Plc
texts.text: Hi, Simon. Two questions, please. Just firstly on, you talked about the deepwater projects that Shell have started  up and are an operator of and the 300,000 barrels per day plateau. So I was just wondering what the contribution  of those four assets were in Q3 and when you might expect to reach plateau? And the second  question is just  following up a project delivery. Could you give us an update on Corrib, please? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Project delivery, Corrib, a bit of a forgotten project in some ways. But we're essentially pretty  much mechanically  complete but we need to start moving into the commissioning phase, which means us going back to some wells  which have been down for quite some time, et cetera. So we're not planning on any contribution really until  towards the end of next year. But the tunneling is done and most of the mechanical pieces are all in place. Many  thanks, Theepan.

texts.speaker: Thomas Y. Adolff
texts.profession: Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Hi, Simon. I have two questions as well, please. For a company like Shell, which is exposed to in essence every  type of upstream projects and I'm aware of what you said earlier on, on strategy and planning. But say we get to  the stage where you have to manage your CapEx slightly differently, which area or areas are the most likely  impacted first? Is it shales, exploration in your base in terms in terms of work overs, in-field drilling, deferral of  operated projects? In essence how is Shell's portfolio CapEx managed in a slightly lower oil price environment?

texts.speaker: Thomas Y. Adolff
texts.profession: Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: The second one is just a quick one on Basrah Gas. It's a bit of a black box. If you can possibly quantify what sort of  contribution you expect from the project? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Thanks, Thomas. I'll start on Basrah Gas first. As you may recall it's essentially processing wet gas, stripping  liquids. The dry gas goes back into the effectively the Iraqi Power chain for which where Ba srah Gas receives a fee  and can sell the liquids. So no equity production but we're now processing around, getting close to 600 million  standard cubic feet of raw gas at the moment; collected from – it's basically associated gas. It's a reduction of  flaring. So it's doing a great job there for the environment as well as the Iraqi Power sector. The actual  contribution at the moment is relatively small but cash positive. The next question for us is investing in expansion  in some of the LPG handling and so far, so good. The operation is very, very well managed. We have 5,000  employees there, all Iraqi, and working well. Over time it can be quite a material contributor.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: I'm not sure we're exposed to everything but we certainly do have a diverse portfolio of investment opportunities.  Going forward, let's look at it in different tranches, what are we spending on the big projects, the headline  projects, which is only around a third of the total spend. We will complete, finish what we started there. We will  think carefully about the timing of big new decisions going forward, but we do as I mentioned in the speech, Appo,  Vito, LNG Canada, there are some really great interesting and exciting projects ahead, even Libra in Brazil even,  the early work there. So that's the big projects.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: We have probably not dissimilar amounts going into asset integrity, small project type of activity as well. So the  asset integrity comes first, the smaller projects clearly they are likely to be in practice either attractive or necessary   to sustain the operation as it is today. So while there is some flexibility possible, there are consequences for cutting  that back in the short term. We then have about a quarter in the longer term which essentially is exploration and  the unconventional spend and if you like pre FID feasibility or late feed work. That has a bit more flexibility. That  is something that we take a close look at but not really willing to eat our own seed corn particularly when we've  made some pretty informed choices around portfolio priorities in the unconventional areas.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So we're not going to jump to any rapid decisions to stop, cut or slash anything because that in the short term will  only destroy value. Having said, that, we are not immune to the environment and I would like to think there's a  very constructive discussion about priorities, phasing and in this environment looking again at the supply chain  and the way that we deal with our suppliers as we're placed in a period of lower revenues. So it's not a single  outcome that we're looking for and quite a few levers that we need to balance.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Those events include amongst other things weather in terms of the windows for moving the facility out and  commissioning. That would be 10 years from original discovery, which we think is pretty competitive given the  nature of the project. It's a challenging project but looking good in the yard. We  were there quite recently to visit  and very confident that we'll have a great project there.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: On the next wave of projects, the slide only shows the feed decisions this year really. There's quite a few other  projects. The big projects at the moment that are through feed, all of which are operated by us are LNG Canada,  Appomattox, and Vito in the Gulf. We are pretty much ready to pull the trigger on Bonga South West Deepwater  in Nigeria as well. But that actually needs quite a lot of broader stakeholder support as well.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: On non-operated projects, remember Browse is not Shell operated. It's Woodside operated. I would have to defer  you to Woodside. Clearly it's an interesting project and would be a very large project for Shell with the  shareholding we have 26% or so. And I can't really add anything to the statements made by Woodside. Thanks,  Alastair.

texts.speaker: Fred Lucas
texts.profession: JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: And if I may just a quick question around your application to suspend operations in North American Arctic. If  your request is denied by the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement, where does that leave you? Do  you see the acreage recycled and then having to rebid fo r it or do you cease operations there altogether? Thank  you.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: The clean DD&A you're absolutely right has gone up and down. Another factor that is there this year and will  probably come down a bit next year is Majnoon, a lot of the cost recovery effectively slows thro ugh the DD&A. So  the current clean DD&A is around $3.5 billion Upstream third quarter or $14 billion for the year. That will come  down a bit with Majnoon reaching full cost recovery roughly the end of this year, but will go back up a bit as  effectively the deepwater production goes up because the unit DD&A there is pretty significant in the early phases  of production.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Similarly, linking back to your first question on which projects, FID startups, et cetera, if possible we start to ramp  up some activity in for example the Permian and the West Canada liquids-rich shale next year. That's one over  which we may have some flexibility, of course pending the oil price and that usually comes with pretty high early  unit depreciation as well. We will start up Corrib. There are a series of small activities, but primarily the boost next  year is coming from full year of operation of this year's start-ups plus the variety of small projects around the  world.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So all of those flowing through will have quite an impact on volumes. The underlying volume delivery will depend  a bit most likely on the rate of progress on the unconventionals. So the underlying decline at the moment is  actually about 3% year on year, which we're looking to offset. So all of those factors combined, production will be  lower, we'll aim to keep the unit margins up, notwithstanding the movement in the oil price and very much a focus  on the dollars and not the volumes.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Well you might be right on the latter, let's wait and see. But the big ones but most likely we have Appomattox,  which is an 800 million barrel now in the Gulf of Mexico Deepwater. A potential chemicals plant in Pennsylvania,  let's not forget the Downstream. There's a couple of smaller ones as well in Singapore and Rotterdam in refining  terms as well but they're small relatively quick payback, a few hundred millio n. And the LNG Canada maybe not  next year but let's see quite where we can get to.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: I can't really comment on some of the non-operateds such as Browse or Abadi. I think in the environment they  may get pushed further out.

texts.speaker: Iain S. Reid
texts.profession: BMO Capital Markets Ltd.
texts.text: Just listening to what you were saying about production there and just kind of taking a step back, it wasn't very  long ago that you were sitting there or standing there I think and telling us that Shell had a target of 4 million  barrels a day. And I know you don't target production anymore but you're now down to about 2.8 million barrels a  day and guiding lower. And I'm just wondering for a company the size of Shell, what sort of critical mass that you  think you'd need to have in terms of volumes, not to support all the earnings but to support the kind of  infrastructure in terms of people, project teams et cetera?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: And just anecdotally of course, just compare the Abu Dhabi impact with the Gulf of Mexico impact, a few  thousand barrels, tens of thousands is replacing 160,000 barrels a day with a net positive impact on the bottom  line. And Repsol, Basrah Gas likewise. So that's how think about it. It's really the certainty of the underlying  growth and I think you will find in terms of where the cash flow generation is we very much still are second and  over time let's hunt them down.

texts.speaker: Iain S. Reid
texts.profession: BMO Capital Markets Ltd.
texts.text: Could I just ask one quick follow up? On the refining impact you've given, does that include the potential shut  down of a train in Singapore?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: We've not made final decisions, but we're certainly looking at the – I'll tell you what, we did certainly look to close  the base oil plant in Pernis for lubricants as a means of improving the flexibility of crude supply into the refinery,  and we're already seeing early benefits from the lower crude cost that's enabling us to fulfill the demand for fuel  throughout the value chain.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: The downstream result, we're up about $900 million. We're up at the y ear-to-date quite significantly. It's not easy  to be very specific here about environment versus actual underlying structural improvements because ultimately  one of the improvements is capturing the opportunities from a volatile environment. But it's about  50/50,  Martijn.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: When we've talked about return on capital improvement, it's to a competitive position but not necessarily an  industry-leading position because we think there is a trade-off between growth and returns. And obviously the  actual return we achieve is, to an extent, oil price linked. Are we happy with 10% returns at $110 per barrel? No, of  course not, so we would expect to improve the returns by a few percentage points. But not necessarily deliver 20%  returns at $110 per barrel.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So if I said Downstream, I would not expect that to increase but it depends on what choice we make with  Chemicals. It may at least stay at a similar level. I expect Integrated Gas and Deepwater in particular to grow  strongly. And the rest of the portfolio, well let's see. Though they will be choices based in part on capital and in  part on returns, but very much also in part on what's the ongoing investment commitment and the potential  growth.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Exploration charges, Q4. And you're absolutely right, it was $1.7 billion and it was lar gely driven by high  exploration write-offs, which unfortunately don't come along regularly, or you could say fortunately this year they  haven't come along at all, really. And we had more than our fair share of them last year. The ongoing rate is about  $800 million to $900 million per quarter with a small number of, or contributions from write-offs. We have a  couple of wells going down now; I think we have are one or two that [ph] may place (53:52) into the write-offs. I  don't actually have a feel yet for the success rate likely in the quarter and which wells will reach TD. In fact several  of the big wells at the moment won't reach TD until first quarter. So there's not many that have a big exposure in  Q4 and may run over into 2015.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Sure. I agree it gets confusing because actually we've said very little about this. Just about everybody else has;  buyers, sellers, government and banks. So while the facts are we have four onshore licenses and one related  pipeline activity. All the activity is basically oil, associated with the Nembe Creek trunk line environment,  evacuated through the Bonney oil terminal. The potential production in that space is 80,000 barrels a day to  100,000 barrels a day, Shell's share, that's 30% of it. And current production is more like 30,000 barrels a day to  40,000 barrels a day because remember this is the area that is very subject to sabotage and theft. So it's a big area,  it's got big reserves, and the figure of $5 billion that has been quoted strangely is approximately correct, but that's  for the Shell, Eni and Total's share. NNPC is not selling and in fact, actually has preemption rights on the sales,  and were they to choose to exercise that right.

texts.speaker: Lucas O. Herrmann
texts.profession: Deutsche Bank AG (Broker UK)
texts.text: Y eah. Where does that leave you with the rest of your onshore, by the way, which isn't gas? Because I mean my  impression would be that the prices you're able to command seem pretty attractive relative to the troubles that the  positions entail?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Fundamentally, the remaining piece that is not gas is just to the east of that blocks that we're selling. It includes  the well-known Ogoni block, although we don't operate within that particular area, and is associated with the  Trans Niger pipeline. So there's another pipeline system associated with it. In this particular process, this block is  not actually included. And that doesn't mean, I wouldn't exclude necessarily future consideration, but it's one step  at a time. To the west of these blocks is essentially the gas-producing acreage, which

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: we are investing in at the moment to grow the production there and ensure that both domestic gas and production  grows and that we keep the LNG plant full. And we also have some shallow water offshore blocks which are  operated by the joint venture as well. So it's still a major operation in addition to Gas and Deepwater. Hopefully  that gives you a feel. Now a lot of the oil reserves are associated with the blocks that are for sale and that one  particular big block in the Trans Niger pipeline area.

texts.speaker: Jon Rigby
texts.profession: UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Hi, Simon. Can I ask just one question, just one clarification? Can you just update on what you're thinking around  LNG Canada? I noticed earlier this week a competitor project was sort of being backed off a little bit, and I guess  there is a process where you need projects to get shaken out rather like we saw in Australia. So, can you sort of  characterize where you stand on this project and where you think it is in terms of its maturation?

texts.speaker: Jon Rigby
texts.profession: UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: And then just going back to the discussion around Nigeria and the onshore. If I follow what you were saying, look  at what SPDC was producing over the course of this year, I think 100,000 barrels a day in the first two quar ters  and a little lower in the third, are you effectively saying that the remaining liquids production in SPDC to you will  be probably order of about, I don't know, 60,000 barrels a day to 70,000 barrels a day liquids?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: It does actually include EA. Y es, you're correct, which is shallow water offshore, for those who that are not as  familiar. And there is also further growth potential, shallow water offshore by the way, but we're not growing there  at the moment. LNG Canada, there is 17  projects applied for permission to export. It's even more crowded than  the Gulf of Mexico at the moment in terms of notional projects. If all of the North American projects went ahead  by the way it would be 400 million tons of export capacity, which c ompares to today's entire market of 250 million  tons.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: We don't think that they're all going to go ahead, let's put it that way. To make these projects happen takes quite a  long time, particularly for the first at a greenfield environment, or at least part of it greenfield, to bring together all  the stakeholders. We've been working extremely hard for the past two to three years to ensure that we have not  only the land to build, which is clearly in place now in Kitimat. It's a brownfield site, non-greenfield, so we're  already over quite a lot of the hurdles in what is an environmentally sensitive area.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: We have great partners, both for the midstream but also the upstream gas production and the downstream LNG  markets in our Chinese, Japanese and Korean partners. We have the best pipeline operator, TransCanada,  contracted to build a pipeline from the Montney area, and our Groundbirch gas development. So all the pieces of  the value chain are in place. We've been working very hard also with the First Nations tribe s, I think we've got 28,  29 tribes or peoples that are either at one end of the physical value chain as well. And last but certainly not least,  the British Columbian government, particularly in terms of the fiscal regime.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Thanks, Irene. $140 million is the answer to the second question, of which again is roughly half and half. And  although in their case it's more like 60/40 environment and operations. And Majnoon, good question. We are one  year into now production with remuneration. We had to meet the original first commercial production target of  175,000 barrels a day. Remember this is the first greenfield bid, or oil license that was on offer. The previous fields  [ph] West Clair and Arrow (1:02:04) actually they were brownfield. So we needed to take time to set up some of  the processes and the relationships, particularly the government, on cost recovery for example for greenfield,  which is one of the reasons we've been a bit later to hit the first commercial production.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: We have not yet agreed to full field development, either what the concept would be and the objective and the  production levels. If and when we do so, that would effectively add CapEx that is recovered typically within three  months. Now we have a very high cost recovery rate, close to 100%, having taken a lot of time upfront to get  agreement and build the levels of trust that are required in a new environment. So again a bit like Canada LNG,  we would think that in the longer term the upfront investment in stakeholders, the relationships, it does pay off.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: We also have of course the Basrah Gas which is contributing. I t's actually contributed a bit more than Majnoon,  even at the moment and certainly in the longer term. Absolutely the decision to grow Majnoon will do better. I  think that covers it I think, Irene.

texts.speaker: Richard I. Griffith
texts.profession: Canaccord Genuity Ltd.
texts.text: Good afternoon, Simon. I was intrigued by a comment about your liquids-rich shale and whether you might or  might not take decisions next year on the back of where we are in the oil price. And I was just wondering what do  you see as the cash breakeven for LRS from your point of view but also from the industry point of view in North  America and also if possible by basin?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: I wish I knew, Richard because that's one of the things that will drive the decision. Because it's not independent of  the oil price, the costs do tend to adjust but maybe not enough. We're in the middle to late stages of appraisal in  both the Permian and West Canada. We're seeing some great wells and we've had quit e a significant number of  wells at the 1,000 barrels-plus initial production rate, which is when you're talking sweet spots, something that is  going to work. Clearly 1,000 barrels a day and multiple millions of dollars of barrels when you're only spending  somewhere between $5 million and $10 million to drill and complete a well, then you're going to do okay.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: But what you need to know is what's the average going to be when you decide to drill 100 wells or 200 wells across  a particular rollout where you're building infrastructure, et cetera. That's where it's too soon to say. We're not that  far away but we may not pull the trigger on a development for what we call a common value area, sooner rather  than later as we take a view on what the oil price actually is. That's Shell's perspective. We would hope to be able  to develop at oil prices with a breakeven below today's level. I doubt we would take a positive decision if we  couldn't do that.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: For the industry, it's a great question. We're watching what others say, people who have more direct experience.  But actually the thing that is of interest to us is the fact that so much of the drilling to date has been financed by  the capital markets or the banks, $250 billion or so that we can see has be provided by debt o r from debt providers  into that industry. And very little of the drilling has been financed from owned cash flows. And the way that one  plays out with lower oil prices will be interesting to watch.

texts.speaker: Christopher Kuplent
texts.profession: Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: Good afternoon. Simon, I just wanted to ask you about dividend growth. You've got this $30 billion or more than  $30 billion number in your press release or you've had that for some time now for this year and next year. I don't  know whether my calculations are right but I think you can get there without having to raise the $0.47 quarterly  rate. Does that mean you're sort of leaving yourself a little bit of flexibility depending on CapEx budgets, oil prices,  how do we think about that more than $30 billion becoming $35 billion over the next few years? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Why would we be interested? Well, there's an awful lot of hydrocarbon in Abu Dhabi and the Emirates and the  surrounding regions. Some of it is approaching the maturity where advanced technology -- I think it's well known  we're also looking at a project, the sour gas project on the Bab field. So there are other opportunities both in the  Emirates and in the region where Shell's technology, Shell's ability to project manage and to take product to  market could be able to create quite v aluable good returns. And if the extension of the ADCO contract forms part  of that overall portfolio of activities, that will be a good outcome. But we're still waiting to take – well not waiting,  but in progress on all of those opportunities. But we won't be chasing it just for the headline barrels, We need a  good return also.

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: Y es. Hi, Simon. From [ph] ING, Kuram Muller (1:15:46). Two questions. One is of course with regard to
texts.text: divestment program. You're progressing so fast now. Are you considering to raise the target there given the fact  that you have $15 billion for 2015 or is that the end of the low-hanging fruit now? And the second question is on  Alaska. We heard some environmental players saying that you were trying to get your license, which in my view is  quite logical. Are you progressing there or is there something, a standstill at this moment in the d iscussion with  the government on the license?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Okay, thanks, divestments we've done $12 billion, you're correct. Progressing perhaps a little bit quicker than  might have expected against the $15 billion two-year target. We have in progress and still to conclude the MLP is  effectively $1 billion. We have conclusion of the Haynesville onshore gas asset, which is another $1 billion, and we  have the Nigerian deal, which is about $3 billion. So that's $5 billion in progress, plus a couple of smaller ones. So  I would hope just from that portfolio we can get to the $15 billion. Having said that, we are now going forward  looking at a much more difficult environment to divest those. So it's good that we have moved quickly and  achieved good prices. We are seeing some challenges in one or two smaller deals that we're looking at, as to  whether the buyers can finance and take through to conclusion the deal.

texts.speaker: Oswald C. Clint
texts.profession: Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you, Simon. Hi. Just the first question maybe on the Upstream per barrel kind of earnings. Good to see the  Americas picking back up again, but could you just talk about Europe in terms of net income per barrel? It seems  to be deviating away from the rest of the regions over the past fo ur or five quarters. Is that just the oil barrels  falling out of the mix or is there something else happening there?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Thanks, Oswald. By and large it's aligned with demand on the second question, but we also sold Australia, so we  lose the Australian volumes. The earnings per barrel oil equivalent in Europe, well quite a lot of what w e do in  Europe is gas, so we've seen weaker European gas prices, partly because it's been so warm, and we've seen a  decline in the unit margins in Denmark, which is partly higher costs. Obviously we're now seeing the oil price  coming down, and I think we'v e spoken before about challenges on the operational performance in the United  Kingdom, particularly on the Central North Sea assets where asset integrity spend, maintenance costs and  declining production, or at the very least the availability, the reliability of production have all been challenges. So  it's a combination of all those factors in Europe. And I think that probably is all I can say about that without  speculating further. Thanks, Oswald. Next question?

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: Hi, Simon. Thanks very much for your extensive answering of all the questions. I have one major and one follow -
texts.text: up question. The major question is the gas pricing. I believe spot prices in the Far East are about $13, Europe $6.  In the past you once said that you had about 60% on contract and 40% on spot. Is this still actual? And how are  you looking to going forward? Would you sort of enlarge your spots to wait for better contract p rices in the future  when prices would go up again? That's the first question. And a small corollary question is LNG volumes went up  16%, mainly Repsol. What do you figure without Repsol, what's autonomous growth in LNG volumes?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Okay. I don't have a specific number on the second question, although there is some growth because Nigeria LNG  suffered operational challenges last year. And most LNG plants run full, remember that. It's quite difficult  to grow  other than by either buying or building. The gas pricing, you're about right in terms of where spot prices have  been. They've picked up a bit in Europe. Now they're at $9 or so in the U.K. NBP. We and the whole industry has  shifted progressively in Europe in particular towards a much greater proportion that is spot linked. Now spot  means that usually a combination of the hub price, not just the U.K. but Antwerp or elsewhere. So we're doing  better than $6, and then the realized price is probably closer to the $9 at the moment. But there are few new long- term gas contracts that are directly and solely oil price linked, quite often there's a bit of a mix.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Asia Pacific, I mean fundamentally our LNG, 90% or more of the volumes are on long-term contract, which are oil  price linked one way or another. And 70% of the actual contracts, of those contracts themselves are directly linked  with oil. So the majority of our LNG business and probably around 40% of our gas in total has some kind of oil  price linkage. I can't really be too much more specific on that because there are a lot of moving parts out there at  the moment and in particular in Europe. The evolution of the market has certainly been one way, and the majority  will not be solely oil linked going forward.

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: Right. Thank you. Of course, indeed I was referring to the shifting landscape, especially in view of the well let's say
texts.text: the rumors of the prices the Chinese pay for Russian gas, more in the order of $10 or $11. So I was wondering  whether clients indeed are sort of trying to get away from long-term contracts and preferring the actual lower  prices.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: I think most of the long-term customers, remember that doesn't include very many in Europe, so Asia Pacific,  they're looking for a mix of pricing basis.
