texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q>: Hi, Peter. Hi, Simon. A short question about your Shell gas position in the U.S., can you give  some – shed some light on the acreage or your production targets, et cetera?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 19 Pinedale, South Texas and Haynesville. We have got the Deep Basin, Pinedale and South Texas  already operational. The others are actually kind of in development phase.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Peter Voser>: On the second question, the conventional/unconventional, I think again we will  talk a lot about that in March, but let me just be very clear that the unconventional side, so we are  actually looking at, let’s say Shell at – from time to time as an unconventional company. But let me  just be clear, we have a very low percentage of unconventional production, and you know quite  clearly from my earlier talks, I don’t consider GTL as a unconventional, it’s pretty much a refinery  and the gas upstream.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry>: Thanks, Peter. Theepan, the CapEx flexibility within 28 billion is pretty  limited, given that the big projects, which is Qatar, Canada, Kashagan, and now Gorgon, of course  do absorb quite a significant demand. And therefore the only flexibility at the margin is typically in  that North American gas program, we just refer to under shale gas where we do have a bit of up  and down flexibility and separately in the exploration program where there can be choices made  but we believe it’s in our interest to continue at the reasonably high level around the $3 billion.

texts.text: <Q – Christine Tiscareno>: Good afternoon. Thank you very much. How would that change your strategy or  is that something that we talk about in March?

texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Peter Voser>: We will certainly talk about – thanks for the question, Christine, certainly talk  about the long term gas market, etcetera and the project in March, but let’s just be clear. We are  investing for the longer term here for the next 20, 30 years and therefore we look at the long term  positioning of the gas and that as I said earlier on, this remains positive. That’s where we see the  growth, so clearly LNG will be key in our thinking going forward, the rest then in March.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Firstly, take a moment to read the disclaimer. The world is in an era of important geopolitical  transitions, strong volatility and intensified economic cycles. Emerging nations like China and India  are going through intensive developments. The recession interrupted the oil and commodity price  boom but it may well return. This is a complex and volatile landscape for the energy industry and an  opportunity for Shell.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: I am pleased to say, that we have made good progress on all of these themes in 2010. Our 2010  CCS earnings excluding identified items were $18 billion and earnings per share increase of 56  year-on-year percent.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: This improvement comes despite pressure on downstream margins and natural gas prices. We  have taken out $2 billion of costs and we sold $7 billion of non-core assets with exits from 12% of  our refining capacity. We increased our upstream production by 5%.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We made eight new discoveries and made strategic acquisitions in unconventional gas and  biofuels. Project delivery is going well and I will update you on that including Qatar in a moment. So  overall good progress on our plans in 2010.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: So let me now turn to gross delivery. We have a sequence of new projects for 2010 and 2011 start  up that underpin our production and cash flow targets for 2012. We’ve made good progress in ‘10  with six new startups. Let me give you an example. In Nigeria, the Gbaran-Ubie gas project has  ramped up well and is on track for its peak production of some 250,000 barrels or BOEs per day.  This adds to Nigeria’s LNG supply capacity and we will feed electricity supplies for local  communities. Now our most recent startup in early 2011 was in Qatar. Let me say more about that  with the next slide.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 2011 is going to be an exciting year for Shell in Qatar. We have two projects there, both due for  startup this year, Pearl GTL and Qatargas 4 LNG. Together, these projects which will cost about  $20 billion for Shell and will add some 350,000 BOEs per day to our production, which is over 10%  of our current production worldwide today. The first of these, Qatargas 4 LNG is now in the start up  phase. We started to produce LNG at Qatargas 4 in the last few days and we’re expecting the first  shipment of LNG in the next few weeks. Our second project in Qatar Pearl GTL is also making  good progress. Major construction on both trains is now complete. This was a mammoth  undertaking, 52,000 workers at the construction peak.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Safety performance has been excellent and we have set new records in 2010 with 77 million  working hours or hours worked on-shore without the lost time incident. During the fourth quarter of  2010, we made considerable progress on commissioning. More than half of the roughly 2,000 Train  1 systems we need have been brought to what we call ready for startup status. We have completed  our Train 1 steam blowing. We have started our first air separation unit, imported gas, oil and  condensate to do the live commissioning and load the catalyst in over half of our Train 1 reactors.  So overall, a very satisfactory performance for what is a large and complex facility.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Now let me update you on progress with longer term options. We are working hard to turn  exploration success into commercial production. In 2010, we took final investment decision on two  new deepwater projects in the Gulf of Mexico and Brazil. And we’ve made good progress with new  exploration and appraisal with eight new finds and further operational success. Now we are  studying all of these results and will update you on the resource potential during our strategy  presentation in March, like in previous years.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 2010 was also a busy year for new deals. We have added new acreage positions in 2010, some  53,000 square kilometers. The focus here has been on building up new plays for Shell. We have  also made progress on Iraq Oil and in our downstream of biofuels joint venture in Brazil.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Shell has a long history of successful partnerships with national oil companies. I would like to  highlight the new momentum that we have built with NOCs in 2010 including deals with Petronas in  Iraq, in Qatar, where we are in talks for a new petrochemicals plant in Saudi Arabia going forward  in the [inaudible] quarter; other is China. We have concluded a series of deals with the Chinese  NOCs in 2010.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: This included an upstream partnership in Syria, the joint acquisition of Arrow, the CBM-LNG play in  Australia, gas exploration in China and exploration in Qatar, linking Shell QP and Chinese NOCs.  Finally on NOCs, last – late last year we signed a new MOU with Gazprom looking at joint  expansion of our upstream activities in Russia, so [inaudible] invests in the new international  partnership.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 3 Macondo was the largest ever deepwater blowout and the largest peace time oil spill for 100 years.  We can all talk about causes and make all kinds of explanations, but the reality is that the picture  has changed for the deepwater industry. There will be increased regulations and more public  scrutiny on safety. To put it simply, our industry needs to rebuild trust with the communities we work  in.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Shell has a good track record in deepwater and we always look for ways to improve. We have  completed an initial review of the Presidential Commission Report into Macondo and we agree with  the majority of the findings. In particular, we shared a conclusion that the U.S. regulations and the  risk management practices of some companies in the Gulf of Mexico do lag behind the standards  set by other companies and set by regulators in other countries. We support the Commission’s  recommendation to introduce risk-based standards specific to the relevant activities, similar to the  safety case approach in the North Sea.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Let me also update you on the near term drilling outlook in the U.S. offshore. In the Gulf, I’m  pleased to say that Shell is the first company to have successfully submitted the plans for  exploration drilling three wells in the Auger area in accordance with the new [inaudible] standards  for the Gulf. These permits are now with the authorities for review.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Our plans for drilling in 2010 were put on hold following the BP Macondo blowout. Despite our best  efforts, critical permits continue to be delayed and the timeline for getting these permits is still  uncertain. Therefore and regrettably because of these uncertainties we have decided not to drill in  offshore Alaska in 2012 and stop the spending for these activities. We need urgent and timely  actions on permitting and regulations in order to go ahead with 2012 the drilling program and we  are working towards that.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Simon Henry, Chief Financial Officer  Many thanks, Peter and I’ll just take you through the fourth quarter numbers and give you a heads  up on some of the key figures for 2011. First on the macro, if you look at the macro picture  compared with the fourth quarter of 2009, the oil and gas prices have increased from a year ago  levels, although, actually in North America the gas prices did decline. Refining margins increased  from a year ago levels and chemicals margins increased in the United States, but they declined  slightly in the other regions.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Turning then to Shell’s fourth quarter earnings, the headline current cost of supply earnings at $5.7  billion for the quarter, they included identified items of $1.6 billion, primarily gains on asset sales,  mainly Woodside. Excluding the identified items, the CCS earnings were $4.1 billion and that’s an  earnings per share increase from Q4 2009 of 49%. Cash flow from operations for the quarter was  $5.5 billion. And the dividend for the fourth quarter was announced at US$0.42 per share. And we       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Now let me turn to the business performance in a bit more detail. Firstly, the upstream, excluding  the identified items the upstream earnings increased by 25% to $3.4 billion in Q4. And that was  driven primarily by higher oil prices, higher realized gas prices outside of North America, and by the  5% increased volumes.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We had overall another good quarter for production. The upstream production increased by around  5%, Q4 on Q4. And LNG sales volumes increased by 11% for the quarter. Through the full year,  the production averaged 3.3 million-barrels of oil equivalent per day. Output from the new field and  field ramp-ups was 170,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day and that more than offset the natural  field decline.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Production this year was also boosted by external factors such as colder weather, particularly in  Europe and North America and improved security situation in Nigeria. And therefore production was  ahead of our original guidance for the year. Having said that, the growth was typically from lower  margin barrels.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: For the full year the LNG sales volumes grew by 25%. That was underpinned by increased volumes  in Nigeria LNG, largely increased supply from new projects and better security but also by the full  ramp-up of Sakhalin LNG in Russia which has been producing above nameplate capacity for  basically all of 2010.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Turning to the U.S. upstream where the whole of our industry, of course, is being impacted by the  BP Macondo blowout; and Peter talked about the longer term implications and I’ll focus on the  financial impact. So we didn’t actually receive any permits for new exploration or development  drilling during Q4.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: As a result, we took a $70 million identified charge in the fourth quarter for the cost of the idled rigs,  the four deep water floaters that we have in the region. This combined with the charges in the  earlier quarters, Q2 and Q3, and the production shortfalls that led to an earning loss for Shell in the  full year of $260 million. The equivalent was 10,000-barrels of oil equivalent per day of lost high  value production, mainly liquids.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: By the year end that was a run rate approaching 30,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day. And we  actually had to postpone around $700 million of planned investment in exploration and  development during the year.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: For 2011, we are expecting around a 50,000 barrel a day impact against the plans that we had prior  to the moratorium and that’s an increase in the guidance for the loss we’ve previously had around  40,000. So recognizing the slow pace of any likely restart in the Gulf and the lack of any permits  being issued to-date.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Turning now to the downstream. Excluding the identified items, the downstream CCS earnings,  they increased from the fourth quarter 2009 at around $482 million. Within this number the       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 5 chemicals earnings increased substantially. This is driven by industry margins, lower costs and our  actions to enhance the portfolio to improve the structure of the margins including conversion to gas  feed.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And the chemicals margins did fall at the end of the quarter reflecting higher naptha prices following  the crude price up. And that will impact on into the first quarter of 2011. I should also update you  that we have substantial planned downtime in the Singapore chemicals plant in the first quarter of  2011. So both factors will play a part.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: But trading overall saw a less favorable environment and a less positive contribution. Marketing  margins and underlying volumes did decline compared to the third quarter of 2010 and that was  mostly driven by the steady increase in oil prices although that was also impacted by some of the  weather conditions we saw in the U.S. and Europe. So those are the earnings.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In 2011, we will see spending rates decreasing in some of the plays like Qatar and Canada heavy  oil that have dominated recent spending but we will step up in areas such as Australia, Iraq and of  course there is the $2 billion to complete the Brazilian biofuel deal. So within this mix, I expect  exploration spending of around $3 billion again this year. And our overall North American tight gas  spending, where you will recall we talked about quite a wide range of possible spend, we’d expect  that to be around $3 billion again this year. So both exploration and the tight gas spending of  around $3 billion, similar to 2010 levels, excluding acquisitions of course, because around $6 billion  of last year’s acquisitions were actually in that area.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We increased our operating production by 5%, made new discoveries and made strategic  acquisitions in unconventional gas and biofuels. So overall, good progress on our plans in 2010  and Shell is back on track for growth. Thank you very much. Back to the operator for the Q&A  session.       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In the upstream, around $450 million income impact from startup costs, higher taxes and royalties  and that’s on the income statement, not just paid. And that’s partly revaluation of deferred tax  assets in Brazil and also lower contribution from gas trading. The market is just less volatile. And  most of that in the upstream showed in UA. So it’s $450 million there.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We obviously keep earnings in mind. But that’s really how we are driving it and I’m pleased to the  way they are performing on the gas side in terms of optimizing cash costs and costs in general. I’m  pleased with the progress on total costs related to the rest of the portfolio.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: For example on east resources, lease bonuses and some of the acquisition premium we do  amortize anyway. Because it’s in North America that amortization before we actually produce does  impact the results. So if there is an impact there that drives earnings down but has no cash flow  impact in our upstream America result. That piece of capital becomes active as we bring the assets  into production. So the piece in the gas, particularly the unconventional gas, as we develop and  produce, east resource acreage for example, that will reduce and returns will increase. So quite  closely linked answers and I don’t know where that $19 to $20 billion will go. I hope we continue to  acquire new acreage going forward as a similar level for that which we have done recently.

texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 10 think we are well on track there. The majority of our cost savings actually is coming out of  downstream and a good proportion is coming out of the refining. We have these outages and relatively  high turn around work in the fourth quarter, but clearly there is more to be done on the refining side.  But we have all of that at hand or in hand as we are moving forward to that. As I’ve said in previous  calls and previous talks, a strategy update in March will be kind of the next use of downstream, how  we take it forward.

That’s where we have got quite sizable square kilometers of  acreage which we had actually at the end of the fourth quarter, we started to actually reach the  exploration, so we are very excited about those. Two blocks for shale gas, tight gas and the one  block for CBM and we think that China has got quite a bit of potential in that sense and we’ll report  back on that once we are further in the exploration phase. Thank you.

texts.profession: Operator

texts.profession: Operator

texts.speaker: Operator

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Jason Gammel>: First of all, with the Gulf of Mexico and Alaska now, I guess more or less  off limits for the next two years from an exploration standpoint. Can you talk geographically about  where you could have high impact exploration? And then secondly, given the huge discrepancy on  a BTU basis between natural gas and liquid product globally, would you be looking to invest  incrementally in gas to liquids projects?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And on Alaska, I have said clearly, it’s again – it’s not two years, it’s for 2011. We are preparing the  permits so that we can actually drill in 2012. I just don’t want to spend the money as we still have  uncertainties, and you would have to spend $100 million to $150 million between now and getting       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Jason Gammel>: Just given the large discrepancy in pricing on a BTU basis between natural  gas and the liquid products, would you consider incremental investments in gas to liquids?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry>: I’ll start. Exploration expansion is getting tricky to actually report now  because the unconventional gas activity becomes exploration or development almost well by well  depending on exactly where it’s drilled in terms of recognized reserves. So I was thinking in more  general terms, the amount allocated by budget just over $3 billion in 2010 and again in 2011 for --  through exploration activity, that’s seismic and drilling, about half of that is spent on drilling. So  there is no real increase. What actually gets reported as expenses does vary for that reason in  unconventional gas. Abu Dhabi -- I’m so sorry, I will leave Abu Dhabi for Peter. The key...

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 17 support $25 billion to $27 billion of net investment and $10 billion of dividend. The big drivers of that  cash flow growth together factor that. We like the equilibrium positions of the projects. As we go  through this year the big three projects that drive the cash flow, the two Qatar projects and the  Canadian oil sands should ramp up. That’s what we expect as and when they come on stream.  That, plus the balance sheet, plus the ongoing oil price development will drive the discussion about  dividend growth. Peter?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Neill Morton>: Good afternoon. It’s Berenberg actually. Two quick numbers questions,  please. Firstly could you perhaps say how much of this 5% increase in production in 2010 was due  to colder weather year-on-year. I think Simon you may have given us a profit impact on that as well;  that would be useful. And just secondly, could you quantify your expectations of production growth  from new field startups and ramp-ups in 2011 versus the 170,000 barrels that you achieved in  2010? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry>: Thanks. There were a couple of impacts that side there, control in terms of  OPEC demand constraints and the weather -- basically 1,000 barrels a day increase year-on-year  2010 versus 2009. If you remember it was very cold not only in Q4 but also Q1. It’s a lot warmer  this year is all I would say on that. Sorry, could you just repeat the second question. I didn’t...

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry>: Well, we would hope it would be higher in principle because we should get  the better part of a year out of oil sands and we should see the impact of full year for example of  [inaudible] of -- hopefully we will get back from Perdido and the Gasoil projects will start to ramp-up.  I wouldn’t want to give a [inaudible] production forecast for 2011. We said broadly similar but with a  -- quite a wide range of potential outcomes both positive and negative, depending on for example  the weather, Nigeria and security and the rates of those ramp-ups. So, broadly similar plus or  minus.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q>: Yes. Good afternoon, it’s good to be back. Three quick questions, if I may. First, on the tight  gas, if I understand well you are guiding for the low part of the three to five year dollar billion CapEx  indicated on the occasion of the North American slip fleet. If I’m correct, what is the read across we  may take from this decision in term of gas spot price you expect for 2011 and 2012?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Simon Henry>: Thanks Peter. Does the low end CapEx indicate low gas prices? Well, initially  to some extent, yes. We are drilling where we need to hold acreage and where we’ve already got  the costs down to the point where we can make money at $4 and that’s what driving us. If the gas  price goes up, well we will see where we go because it’s relatively easy activity to ramp-up.  BMS-54 exploration just a reminder, is an 80% Shell block now with 20% Total in.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We have two prospects to drill. We drilled one late last year. We hope to drill roughly the middle of  this year the second prospect. There are two reservoir horizons in both prospects. We are currently  evaluating the first well. It looks prospective and we have indicated – this is not a multibillion barrel  prospect.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: But it looks very interesting at the moment. We need to drill the second well, do the appraisal work  before we can really say anything further. 2011 production, yes the statement is broadly similar but  with a wide range of -- a relatively wide range of outcomes. We actually increased our production in  Nigeria onshore. We are now 100,000 barrels a day, or over 100,000 barrels a day in ‘10 versus  ‘09. In the current security environment and with the Gbaran-Uble, the gas project up and running  we could do that or better again in 2011. But there is an election in Nigeria this year and that’s a  level of uncertainty.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Our aim and expectation for 2012 because we control most of the main drivers of 2012 is to deliver  the 3.5 million barrels a day target, even though the divestments we’ve done will in fact reduce  production in 2012 by around 80,000 to 100,000-barrels a day compared to what we had originally  projected.
