texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: You know this page. The global economy and energy markets are likely to see continued high volatility. This is the  interplay between robust structural growth in energy demand and unprecedented geopolitical events, such as the  Arab Spring, the Eurozone crisis or the Japanese earthquake.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, let me start with safety and reliable operations. That's at the heart of everything we do. Our HSSE key  figures are trending in the right direction. For example, 2011 TRCF and the numbers of spills are broadly similar  to 2010, and our fatalities numbers have declined. However, we still had fatalities and other incidents last year,  and operational spill volumes increased and so we have more to do here.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, let me look at the overall development. Rapid economic development in non-OECD countries is driving  sustained and long-term demand growth for all forms of energy. Demand for oil and gas overall could rise by 40%  by 2030 and this growth will be kind of equal or equivalent to 7 North Seas, which will require huge industry  investments. But with many traditional basins actually in decline, the challenge is much larger, replacing declines  on the one side, as well as reaching demand growth on the other.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Regulatory and political uncertainties, combined with challenges in the debt markets, are adding to price and cost  volatility in this longer-term trend. And we are seeing local pressure points from things like excess refining  capacity in the Atlantic Basin, and a supply bubble in the North American gas market.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, in Shell, we are dealing with this by staying focused on the longer-term trends. Shell activities provide  affordable safe and reliable energy supplies for our customers worldwide. We use conservative ranges and long- term assumptions for project assessments. We plan inside a $50 to $90 range for oil and $4 to $6 for U.S. gas.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: On climate change, we see mitigation opportunities in energy efficiency and CO2 capture and storage, as well as  investing in themes like biofuels, which have CO2 advantages. On the financial side, we are planning for a balance  between attractive payout for shareholders today and investing for shareholder value in the longer term.  So let me have a look at the performance since 2009. Our underlying CCS earnings have increased by some 115%  since 2009. And cash flow from operations, excluding working capital movements, has increased 80% versus  2009 to $43 billion. We have been investing for new growth and selling down non-core positions in Upstream and  Downstream.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Underlying oil and gas production has increased as we deliver our growth plans, and the refining capacity has  come down by net 15% due to asset sales. And for shareholders, our total shareholder return was around 70% over  the last three years, a sharp increase over the period and a competitive performance by Shell.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, as you can see, on the next slide, the portfolio has developed tremendously in the last few years. And we will  show you how this fits together in a moment. We started up three really substantial projects last year, and you  know them, it's LNG in Qatar, GTL and Oil Sands and we went ahead with biofuels in Brazil. And we took FID on  the floating LNG in Australia. This is all part of a large sequence of start-ups and portfolio moves in recent years.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Our free cash flow, before the dividend payment, was $23 billion in 2011, $16 billion after the injection into  working capital. And we declared $31 billion of dividend over the last three years. Our project delivery in the last  two years has gone very well, and combined with the higher oil prices, that's helped us to rebalance the financial  framework to free cash flow last year. And that underpins the dividend increase that we announced earlier today.  So we've worked hard to generate new options, and we've launched new projects for medium-term growth.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: A few words on the quarter. The current cost of supply earnings, CCS earnings for the quarter, including identified  items, were $6.5 billion. Excluding the identified items, which were primarily gains on asset sales, the CCS  earnings were $4.8 billion, earnings per share increase of 16% as compared to the fourth quarter 2010.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: On a Q4-to-Q4 basis, we saw higher earnings in Upstream, but weaker results in the Downstream. The earnings,  of course, were impacted by higher oil prices and cyclical pressures in the industry downstream margins. We also

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Since 2009, our Upstream underlying earnings have increased by $12 billion. The Upstream cash flow, excluding  working cap, has increased by $15 billion. Of course, that's underpinned by a $50 per barrel increase in the oil  price. We have had higher gas realizations as a result and we've also seen profitable production from the new  growth projects. And the contribution from new projects like Pearl gas-to-liquids continued to grow or will  continue to grow in 2012. So feel good about what we've achieved, the underlying performance and the underlying  potential in the Upstream just for 2012.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Refining, however, remains a very difficult segment for the industry and, if anything, we entered a down cycle  across the board in refining again in quarter four. Now, we have restructured the Downstream portfolio quite  considerably in the last few years. We've brought in some selective growth, for example, in chemicals and biofuels.  And I think that puts us in a lot more competitive position, a more robust portfolio in Downstream overall than we  were a few years ago.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In the Upstream, we've sold 120,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day of Upstream positions where we see others  can add a lot more value. And at the same time, we've made $15 billion of acquisitions, and that includes new  resource positions and growth markets where we have either a technology, infrastructure synergies or other  advantages that can add value for our shareholders. These are deals like the North American resource plays and,  for example, Brazil biofuels.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: A few words on resources. We will report our SEC reserves position in detail in the 20-F return as usual in the  middle of March. However, we'd expect to see the headline reserves replacement ratio, all-in on an SE basis, to be  around 100% and the replacement ratio, on an organic basis, just the additions during the year, of around 120%  when we take account of the impacts of acquisitions, divestments and changes in oil price and the allocation of  resource in production-sharing contracts.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, in addition to reserves, of course, we look at resource as a broader definition, and that's what we use to  manage the business. Now, we have a substantial oil and gas resource base in Shell. This chart shows you just the  subset of the total resources position that is in active maturation today. That's around 32 billion barrels of oil  equivalent or about 27 years of current production. And this is where we put the focus of activity in the Upstream.  We look to commercialize these barrels and we turn what was exploration or negotiation or technology success  into production and cash flow.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Shell now has some 12 billion barrels of oil equivalent of resources on-stream producing today. That's an increase  of 20% in only 12 months. It's the big projects coming on, but it's also 3 billion up and 30% up over the last three  years, during which time we've produced 3.5 billion barrels. And today, we have a further 20 billion barrels of oil  equivalent of resources either under construction or in development design options, and they, as we mature them,  will drive the cash flow further from the middle of this decade onwards.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Looking at our targets for 2012. We've made good progress on both the key targets, production and cash  generation. We are on track for an increase in production in 2012. The precise outcome for the year, of course, will  depend on external factors like temperatures, the Nigerian security situation and the pace of investment in our  onshore tight gas activities, particularly in North America.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, if you put together the divestments, the Gulf of Mexico and the onshore effect, those impacts together, since  2009, equate to around 200,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day of production or, in fact, 100,000 barrels a day  since we last spoke to you in March of last year. So that effectively means we're substantially ahead of the targets  that we set ourselves, both on an economic basis and underlying production basis, although the headline figure  may be somewhat lower, as you can see.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: However, of course, the macro picture is very different today compared to the environment we envisaged in early  2010. Oil price is higher, downstream and the U.S. gas price are in the down cycle. So we are moving on from  these 2012 targets, setting a new outlook for the company longer term and they reflect the new realities.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Capital efficiency is a key part of Shell's strategy, and we expect some 250,000 BOE per day of asset sales and  license expiries over the 2012 to 2017/2018 timeframe. We look at operating metrics such as oil and gas  production on a very long-term basis. And you can see the potential here if these impacts play out; an increase of  25% from 2011 levels to 4 million barrels per day, absorbing the 250,000, which I explained beforehand.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Just as one example, our Q4 unit operating costs at our Canadian oil sands have fallen by $5 a barrel compared to  the same period in 2010, with continuous improvement initiatives, as well as our start-up of the Expansion-1. We  expect to take out another $3 to $4 per barrel in the oil sands over the next two years.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So let me give you some more details on the portfolio that is driving the next tranche of growth from Shell. This is  all about more energy in Asia Pacific, more deepwater and tight gas in the Americas and more investments in  traditional and oil and gas plays.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I think if you look at Shell's growth profile in the last few years, the investment profile was really dominated by  three large projects, which was Qatargas 4, Pearl and the Oil Sands expansion. There is an important shift in our  project flow here now these three are on stream, with 26 projects under construction, which will open up another  wave of production growth. I think this is one of the most competitive portfolios of projects under construction in  our industry today.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So let me update on some of these new projects. Shell continues to be the leading IOC for integrated gas, that's  LNG and GTL, and I expect to hold onto the position to at least the middle of the decade. We have delivered new  projects in Qatar, as you know, in 2011 and our energy capacity is now 20 million tons per annum.  The next tranche of energy growth for Shell is coming from Australia with 8 million tons per year under  construction, which is expected to lift our capacity by 40% by 2017. Prelude FLNG, which is an industry first, is  progressing well. The Crux field will provide part of the gas supply for Prelude, and we are discussing with Nexus  to take an 80% stake in Crux and develop an FPSO there to commercialize the liquids content. We have entered  the Abadi FLNG project in Indonesia in 2011, with a 30% stake and we have bought Bow Energy, which will allow  us to increase the train size in Arrow LNG. Overall, Shell has around 50 million tons per annum of new LNG  options under study.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We have also made progress on LNG sales, with contracts for 6 million tons per annum of LNG sales signed in  2011, linked to oil markets and valued at $100 billion at today's prices. These are portfolio deals. That means the  gas isn't linked to any particular supply project.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, turning to the deepwater Gulf of Mexico. This is an important region for Shell. We are one of the largest  player in the industry here. The moratorium announced in 2010 after the spill did bring delays industry wide. The  moratorium ended in 2011 and the new safety standards in the regions are pretty similar to the ones we have at  Shell. The slowdown in the Gulf is still having an impact on our drilling program, but we are really regaining  momentum here.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, let me turn to our heartlands. We have some large projects underway in Shell's traditional heartlands. These  are plays like new oil in the U.K. Atlantic Margin, and new gas investments in Asia Pacific for Shell's LNG joint  ventures there. Much of this investment is non-operated. It's an important part of maintaining Shell's cash flows  from these profitable and long-life basins.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So when you put all of this together, we expect to see attractive growth in Upstream in the next few years. I look  for financial growth here, not simply chasing the barrels. You can see the impact this is having on our production  mix, with growth in the Americas in resource plays and deepwater, and growth in the Middle East and Asia Pacific  integrated gas.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Some 80% of our capital investment is going into Upstream, but we're also investing in very selective growth in  Downstream as well. As you all know, Port Arthur refinery expansion in the Gulf Coast is coming on stream  during the first half of 2012. We are also working on new potential chemicals capacities in North America and in  Qatar, which would be integrated with the upstream gas for feedstock.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We're investing in selective growth in oil products, for example, in China, and continued momentum in Brazil  biofuels. I think overall, we will continue to have a measured approach to Downstream manufacturing, relatively  small stakes in new manufacturing assets, building just one or two at a time and positioning for low-cost  advantaged feedstocks and market growth potentials.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: But the nature of exploration is changing, with onshore resources plays in tight gas and liquid-rich shales, which  are driven by land acquisitions and drill-out, alongside more traditional offshore activities. We made a series of  resource-based deals in 2011, including liquids-rich shales in several countries.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, here you have got two examples of exploration appraisal progress in 2011. French Guiana, this discovery  tested an entirely new oil play. This oil discovery is a stratigraphic trap. It means that defining the edges of the  reservoirs is complicated, and this will need some careful appraisal. We think that in French Guiana, the well  confirms now over 300 million BOEs. We are printing two wells in this block in 2012, which have the potential to  increase these estimates as we explore this new exciting play.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: As mentioned, in Australia, we have continued to find new gas there, with three successful wells in 2011, which  could be part of future expansions of the Gorgon LNG project.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Shell has a long track record in adding new oil and gas resources through exploration. Exploration has added  around 15 billion BOEs in the last 10 years. Now, exploration is still the lowest cost entry into new oil and gas, and  Shell has a global exploration program underway.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We focus on large prospects in proven hydrocarbon plays, high-value near-field wells, resource plays like liquids- rich shales and tight gas, and we make selective moves into frontier acreage positions with, as said, higher  risk/reward trade-offs.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We stepped up our exploration spending in 2005 with positive results, and we are increasing our commitment to  exploration again in 2011 to 2012. So we expect to see a 35% increase in core exploration spending in 2012 to $5  billion, as we drill up our new acreage and continue to build new options. Now, this increase includes a step-up in  drilling in liquids-rich shales and continued investment in tight gas and CBM.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, setting aside these resource plays, we expect to drill 20 to 25 key wells in 2012, compared to 18 in 2011. The  drilling plan covers both wildcat activities on the one side and then high-value near-field prospects. So that's  where we are on exploration.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We have been working hard to build up Shell's portfolio in tight gas, and we have moved rapidly into liquids-rich  shales. These are exciting themes for our industry, unlocking large resource positions, using advanced drilling  technologies. In liquids-rich shales, which is a relatively new play for us, we are looking into our existing licenses  across the world, where we can produce oil from what the industry used to see as source rock.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: What's increasingly clear is that controlling our supply chain is going to be critical in tight gas and CBM. The wells  joint venture we have formed with CNPC in China is making good progress. We expect to build nine new rigs  together in 2012 and, ultimately, to deploy about 40 rigs and support services like fracking on a worldwide basis

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: This is very much a story of drilling up and commercializing the portfolio, building a longstanding and profitable  gas supply business, with interesting integration opportunities and building up liquids production.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I expect to see total spending in these plays to be some $6 billion on a worldwide basis in 2012. Development  spending in North American tight gas will be around $3 billion in 2012, which is similar to 2011, and at the low  end of our spending range of $3 billion to $5 billion per year, reflecting, obviously, the weak pricing environment.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We are moving to develop our Eagle Ford liquids-rich position following successful appraisal there in 2011, part of  just over $1 billion of development spending on the liquids-rich shales in 2012. We will also spend some $2 billion  on exploration and appraisal in these themes this year, with a focus on maturing our new liquids-rich portfolio,  which you have seen on an earlier slide.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We have quite some flexibility in how much we spend in developing tight gas and shales, and spending could be in  a range of $5 billion to $6 billion per year on a worldwide basis over the next few years, including exploration, of  which $3.5 to $5 billion would be in North American gas plays. The precise annual spending levels will depend on  near-term pricing and, obviously, on our capital allocation choices overall.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, some of you may know this, we have been looking at ways to leverage Shell's strong resource position in  North American tight gas into value-added products. So Shell is assessing at the moment options for LNG exports,  for GTL, for gas-to-liquids and for LNG to transport. These are value chain projects, which will very much play to  Shell's strengths as an integrated player.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Let me just stress, these are early days. We are looking into various value chain opportunities and it's just too soon  to say which one, all of them or none of them will go ahead. The precise timings and how we balance the  opportunity between spot gas exposure and integration will come.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, the one that we have launched is actually a small scale 0.3 million tons per year LNG to transport project in  Canada, which is called the Green Corridor. We are installing a gas liquefaction plant at our Jumping Pound gas  plant and LNG fuel dispensing equipment at the Shell/Flying J joint venture truck plazas throughout Western  Canada. We are, at the same time, maturing similar projects worldwide. For example, we are looking into LNG for  shipping fuel out of Rotterdam and LNG for trucks in China.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Finally, on options, let me update you on Iraq. In Iraq, we are continuing with the development of the giant  Majnoon field. Now let me be here very clear. Majnoon is a greenfield project. Basically, we started from scratch  and rather different from the brownfields awarded to some companies in the first round.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We signed the final agreement for our gas commercialization joint venture in Southern Iraq at the end of last year.  This is a midstream gas deal, so no production entitlement, and we plan to supply subsidized domestic gas to local  power companies and sell LPG and NGLs at international prices.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The early stages of the JV are all about upgrading and expanding the existing facilities. In the longer term, we are  starting a 4 million tons per annum LNG project, likely to be a floating LNG, to avoid congestion on what is a  short coastline.  As we mature this portfolio, we should be taking some 15 new FIDs in the next two years, all part of a strong  pipeline of new projects to drive our financial performance into the medium term. We are maturing these and  other options, and we will launch new projects according to portfolio fit, profitability of these projects and  affordability, which, of course, is partly linked to the development of oil prices and downstream margins.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We've also taken on new portfolio options in 2011 and they will have an impact on CapEx too, in plays like  exploration, the Iraqi gas, liquids-rich shales. This will increase our feasibility expenditure costs, for example, in  the new LNG and chemicals options. And you can see the main investments on this chart and we're putting the  priority on a series of large themes, investment themes, where we get economies of scale through technology or  contracting and procurement, and overall in the portfolio, we get the right diversity of political and technological  risk and overall, we get the right size of portfolio, the material projects that we need to impact our own bottom- line growth.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, the returns on these projects are attractive for Shell and they are attractive for shareholders. About 80% of  the investment is Upstream and, of that, 60% is in Australia and North America. The portfolio of projects that we  have underway has an oil price break-even on a net present value basis of less than $60 per barrel and, over time,  as these projects come on stream, we're expecting that these attractive full-cycle returns will translate into a much  more competitive return on capital employed for Shell.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, our cash flow from operations was $136 billion over the past four years, 2008 to 2011, during which, the  average oil price was $87. We're expecting cash flow from operations, measured on the same basis, but $80 to  $100 range, to be some 30% to 50% higher than the last four years. That's, in aggregate, around $175 billion to  $200 billion at the two price extremes.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Today's downstream in U.S. gas markets are clearly in a downturn. So, in these figures, we've assumed a return to  mid-cycle downstream conditions and a $5 Henry Hub in the outer years to give these projections. But we have  got more conservative assumptions in the short term.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, we look at the free cash flow very carefully. And there is no simple formula for what we choose to do with it.  I expect incremental CapEx, debt management and payout to the shareholders will all play a part, although I want  to be clear that we see share buybacks primarily as a tool to offset the scrip dilution rather than as a primary route  to return cash to shareholders.  Also, I would like to be clear that we look at oil and gas production levels, they're an outcome of the investment  decisions that we make on a long-wavelength basis, over multiple years. They're not a primary strategic driver for  the company. Capital efficiency is an important part of the strategy. And we're expecting, over the coming years,  around 0.25 million barrels a day of license expiries and asset sales. If those impacts all play out, then we would  still expect to have production to average 4 million barrels of oil equivalent per day 2017 and 2018. That's 25%  higher than the 2011 levels.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, we have been focusing our spending in Qatar and North America in the past few years, and we're expecting  substantial production and cash flow growth from these regions as a result; ramp-up of Pearl, Canada oil sands  driving this.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, going forward, we expect to see sustained high spending levels in the Americas. That now includes the build- up of a deepwater at the Gulf of Mexico, liquids-rich shales, and that's offsetting a slowdown in investments in the  oil sands.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In Asia Pacific, we will be building up in Australian LNG and continuing to invest in the traditional heartlands  such as Malaysia and Brunei. So cash flow there should continue to grow more quickly than production.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The spending levels that we see this year and into the future, they will be driven by the choices we make and the  macro environment. And oil and gas prices themselves are an important driver of industry costs as we see. Of  course, we can afford more flexibility on our spending levels in the up cycles. We must keep a conservative balance  sheet to underpin through-cycle spending. And the dividend, as per the policy, is linked to the underlying financial  performance.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Our financial position gives us room to announce a measured increase in both our investment levels and cash  term, with over 60 projects and options maturing, 20 billion BOEs of new resources, and all of this is underpinned  by new cash flow targets for the next four years; the sum could be up to $200 billion, as Simon said, for the four  years depending on the oil price or 30% to 50%.

texts.speaker: Theepan Jothilingam
texts.profession: Analyst, Nomura International Plc
texts.text: Secondly, just, Simon, you mentioned major start-ups and you've got about 150,000 barrels per day to go in terms  of – from 2011. Can you give us any indication of what the cash flow from Qatar and the expansion in Athabasca  has contributed so far?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks. The three big projects, what we have said on the production potential is total, and this includes the first  phase of Athabasca as well, is 450,000 barrels a day. In the third quarter, we were around 300,000 barrels a day –  fourth quarter 300,000. So there's 150,000 more to come from that activity. That's about 180,000 in Qatar,  115,000 or so in Athabasca. We had some downtime on the first part of Athabasca. Expansion was running okay.  GTL was about 110,000 barrels a day. So steady ramp-up, still you can see quite a lot to come.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: What we've said on the cash flow side, contribution, at $70 a barrel, those three projects would deliver $5 billion  of cash in a given year because the oil price was higher, but we actually delivered about just under $2.5 billion  from those three projects last year, about $800 million in the fourth quarter. I'm being kind with you in terms of  granularity at the moment. We're not going to give this information every quarter as we go forward. But it is  important in terms of the ramp-up and you can see the potential we still have to come.

texts.speaker: Iain S. Reid
texts.profession: Analyst, Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: Hi. It's Iain Reid from Jefferies. Peter, you showed the production breakdown by theme earlier of your 4 million  barrels a day. I just wonder of that, how much is North American dry gas? And I wonder if you can give us a  sensitivity, if, for instance, North American gas prices remain at these sorts of levels, how much would you cut off  that 4 million barrels a day of what you announced there?

texts.speaker: Iain S. Reid
texts.profession: Analyst, Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: And secondly, just coming back on the dividend. You say that a dividend's not for Christmas. But a share buyback  can be, in the sense that you could turn it off and on to reflect the environment. So I wonder why you're not – you  said earlier that share buybacks are not your preferred methodology apart from wiping out the scrip dilution. I  wonder why it's not the case because your peers in North America use that very extensively. So it seems strange  that you've kind of taken that one off the table.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Yeah. I think on the gas side, as we have said, we have a certain framework between, let's say, $3 billion to $5  billion on what we could spend going forward. At the moment, we're spending at the lower end. We expect a  certain price recovery later in the period, as we said, to Henry Hub $5 in the order of magnitude $15. This all will  drive our investment levels and therefore, will drive our production outlook for 2017 and 2018.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I would say today, if the price recovers in the way I have just described, I think you will not see an impact on the 4  million barrels. I would also say, if you lower actually the gas, the tight gas and shale gas investments, we will most  probably switch some of that money either into the liquids-rich shale where we get more oil exposure, let's say,  60% oil exposure, 40% gas, and therefore, we would add barrels through that. Or if you have more money being  freed up, which we don't want to spend in the U.S., with the options which we have in the funnel, and we have  deliberately more options that we think we can actually do ourselves, some of them we will have to monetize, we  could actually then develop that.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So I think in the way I look from a macro picture, I think we will manage to those 4 million barrels in whatever  shape or form. The only thing I'm not going to do is it's exactly X gas because I don't know how much gas it will  be, but we will go for the 4 million barrels.  Simon P. Henry  Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc  A Thanks. A couple of words on buybacks. Just to reiterate. It is our policy to use buybacks to offset the scrip  dividend. That means that the current rate of scrip takeup, around $3 billion per year. We're not like our  American friends in that there are some restrictions on how quickly we can do this. We can only buy back B shares  as a result of withholding tax restrictions around the A shares, and we can only buy back a quarter of the liquidity  on any given day.

texts.speaker: Jason S. Kenney
texts.profession: Analyst, Banco Santander SA (London Branch)
texts.text: And then the second question would be the sustainability of the integrated gas result, which was quite special in  the fourth quarter. I mean you'd spoken about Qatar already. But are you willing to guide a bit more on integrated  gas earnings for the next year or the medium term?

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Okay. I'll leave the mid-cycle to you. I do the integrated gas earnings, so go ahead.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: What is a reasonable rate of return? Well, we've previously talked we have to get above cost of capital return on  capital at the bottom of the cycle. We're not there today. Our actual return was around 7% on a FIFO accounting  basis. So we know we need to do better. Some of the things we've talked about today are what we expect to help us  Peter R. Voser  Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc  A Thanks, Jason. I pretty much know – you know that I will not give you guidance in terms of numbers for the  integrated gas. But I think it is – you can really see the strategy coming to life with clearly bringing the integrated  gas projects on stream, not just Qatargas, bringing all the others on stream, running the LNG business on a 90%  long-term contract basis, with roughly 80% oil price linked. And I think these are parts of our strategy, which you  now will see obviously the earnings coming in.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And then don't forget, GTL is coming into that line as well. And therefore, you will see growth in that line.  Assuming the oil price stays roughly at the same level, you will see growth because GTL will just come more in into  2012. But very pleased about the strategic drivers there, and it's really something which we push, as you have  heard from the presentation.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: But I think this will be – we will play over time and we will see how it develops. I think with the cash flow outlook  which we have given, we have enough buffer in there to actually deliver the growth and we will have now, for the  first time, and that's what I said, previously we had three big projects driving our spend. Now we're looking at  much more and more flexibility. So we can react also faster, hence, typically in the past I said, when you go into  these big projects, you need an 18 months, 24 months kind of timeframe before you actually see lower costs  coming into your capital expenditure. So that should happen a little bit faster. And if you are in a lower oil price  world, you need to balance that.

texts.speaker: Paul Spedding
texts.profession: Analyst, HSBC Bank Plc (Broker)
texts.text: Paul Spedding from HSBC. You commented earlier about seeking capital efficiency. But if we take your financial  framework, it seems to me that at the high end of oil prices, you are probably going to be in a net cash position  towards the end of your planning period, with cash earning probably 0.5% maximum or low risk, bonds earning  maybe 1% or 2%. That doesn't seem to be a particularly good return to shareholder.

texts.speaker: Paul Spedding
texts.profession: Analyst, HSBC Bank Plc (Broker)
texts.text: The area that you do seem to have some flex on CapEx appears to be American dry gas, which, at current prices, is  probably also a zero return business. And it's also very a short lead-time business. You commented that the  buyback you're sort of prohibited or find it difficult because of the restrictions with your share structure.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Can we do more? Most probably, yes. Will the world change and costs will go up over the next three, four years? If  you are constantly on a $100, $110 oil price could also happen, but I think then our cash inflow will also change.  So I think this is a dynamic framework, which I just don't want to go into giving you long-term projections at this  stage, so, on the CapEx side. Do want to add anything?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: No, not really. Other than the oil price does determine the unit CapEx cost through the cycle. So oil price stays at  $110, then you may have to spend a bit more to get the same outcome.

texts.speaker: Robert Arthur Kessler
texts.profession: Analyst, Tudor, Pickering, Holt & Co. Securities, Inc.
texts.text: And then the third question would be of the $6 billion 2012 Downstream budget, how much of that is associated  Simon P. Henry  Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc  A Completion of Port Arthur. Port Arthur, how much?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: It was quite a bit higher because there's a lot of acreage acquisition. If you just said of actual activity, it was  probably about the same. So it was $400 million or so in China, the rest in North America. But with a significant  shift of what the activity is from gas to liquids rich. And in last year, in particular, quite some significant spend  acquiring the acreage that Peter's referred to.

texts.speaker: Jason D. Gammel
texts.profession: Analyst, Macquarie Capital (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Jason Gammel, Macquarie. Given the prominence of tight oil in the capital spend program moving forward in the  Eagle Ford in particular, I was hoping you could let us know what the existing production was in the play and how  much acreage you have in the Eagle Ford, if possible, broken down between black oil condensate, rich gas and dry  gas?  And if that's too much detail, I'll just get Marvin afterwards.

texts.speaker: Jason D. Gammel
texts.profession: Analyst, Macquarie Capital (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Then, second of all, on the Motiva expansion, we know what the incremental distillation capacity is. You should be  able to share what the hydro cracking and coking capacity that's being added at Motiva are.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Yeah. Eagle Ford, overall, most of our liquids activity today is on Eagle Ford. There's a little bit elsewhere, Utica  and in Canada, but most of it's Eagle Ford. We've got 13 rigs, quarter of a million acres, 250,000; about 60% of it  is condensate rich. And that's where we're focusing the activity this year. About right, Marvin? Thanks. I'm sorry  on Port Arthur, I can't you give you the hydro cracking, not the specific capacity.

texts.speaker: Jon Rigby
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: And then if I look at – I think you quoted some costs of resource ads, which I think was a mix actually of  acquisition and exploration. But if you do a quick bit of mathematics, it would suggest that you can probably self- support yourself at $5 billion on resource adds organically. Is that true or is that an aspiration internally to do  that?

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Okay. I think on the – you take the second one. I'll try the first one. So yes, indeed, it was the nature we did  acquisitions in the explorations. We have always said where we can and we want to some niche acquisitions were  part of the game. I wouldn't rule that out going forward. The pipeline and having the right people, having actually  the structure, we reviewed this extensively in 2011. In order to make sure that if we step up the spending, like we  have done a few years ago in 2005, today we have the people but we also have then actually people to mature the  barrels through the hydrocarbon maturation funnel and that's exactly what we have now tested and checked. And  I think from that point of view, we could go on and do this.

texts.speaker: Martijn P. Rats
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Yeah, hello. It's Martijn Rats from Morgan Stanley. Two questions, one really to production. You're talking of 4  million barrels a day, it's obviously a very encouraging one, but at the same time, the industry has a history of  missing that, right.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So we know, and we've been saying for some time, you need to judge us quarter by quarter as the current projects  come on, show the quality of the current projects, and believe that the new projects, the Gorgon, the Prelude, the  onshore gas, the deepwater, are going to be as good as the current wave. And then you've got to believe we can  replicate it and grow over time with the new opportunities.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So it's not an easily covered dividend in the event that the price comes off and we need to – the balance sheet's in a  better place but the rating agencies are also a little bit tougher than they once were. And that AA rating means a  lot of us. So it's all of those things we balance. And I wouldn't want to give an oil price case, but you know we look  at $50 to $90 on the range. I'm not sure we see it right at the bottom of that one over the next 12 months, but we  Peter R. Voser  Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc  A Good. Come to you and then go back somewhere there, yeah?

texts.speaker: Oswald C. Clint
texts.profession: Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: And then, secondly, I guess, related to the 4 million barrels per day in 2017, maybe if you could talk about the  decline rates in the base production that's embedded with that. And maybe put that in context of today's decline  rate, what it will be in 2017, and maybe actually what it was five years ago. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So the shape of the portfolio is changing over time. Today's unconventional production's less than 10%. It could  grow towards 20% and then what I've just said starts to make a much bigger impact on decline overall.

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: Hi. Good afternoon, everyone. Thanks for taking my questions. First question is on Iraq. Could you elaborate a
texts.text: little bit on the economics of the Basrah Gas project? And, in particular, will it be profitable only thanks to the  LNG part of the project, or will the domestic gas part will be profitable on its own as well?

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: On the Iraq side, I think we look at this project in two stages. And therefore, we look also at two profitabilities and  both parts are profitable. So the first one is what we are doing now, which is the domestic gas. It's the export of  LPG, et cetera. And then the second one, there could be longer term an LNG play. But the longer term is quite a  few years down the road. And from that point of view, we have been clearly focusing on the first part and that first  part had to go and pass through our profitability hurdles, which we have internally in the company. So we are now  looking at one big project whereby one part is really an option for the very, very longer term. And thanks for the  question.

texts.speaker: Iain Armstrong
texts.profession: Analyst, Brewin Dolphin Ltd. (Investment Management)
texts.text: Iain Armstrong, Brewin Dolphin. Do you have an implicit assumption that there's going to be a well established  export market for LNG in the U.S. given that you're putting so much more money into shale gas? Because it strikes  me that everyone's trying to do this. You're putting money into a market which is already in surplus, with the  assumption that the gas price is going to get higher. Are you making some assumption that U.S. GDP's going to  Peter R. Voser  Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc  A No. I do agree there is too much gas around at the moment. And I think that's why we say we look at possibility to  change, to [ph] have enough exposure into (1:37:45) liquids exposure and I gave you a few examples. I think I  would also distinguish between the U.S. and Canada. So, if I look at Canada, I would see the export of LNG  through the Western Canadian side as something which will happen and we are working on that with our  partners, CNPC, Mitsubishi and Kogas. So I think that's an option.

texts.speaker: Iain Armstrong
texts.profession: Analyst, Brewin Dolphin Ltd. (Investment Management)
texts.text: I think we will also see some exports coming out of LNG of the U.S. But I still believe that this is going to be  limited, given the fact that there is potential to generate actually more out of that gas locally, so gas-to-liquids,  gas-to-chemicals, which will actually use the gas and produce the energy inside the Americas, less dependent on  imports, more job-generating capabilities.

texts.speaker: Iain Armstrong
texts.profession: Analyst, Brewin Dolphin Ltd. (Investment Management)
texts.text: And I think whilst I can see that some energy plans will go ahead, I wouldn't think that these exports will be at  such a magnitude that A, they will have an impact on the global market, point one; and point two, I think, it will be  limited in capacity, because I think the more value chain integration will actually happen in the U.S.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Okay. You can take the second. I'll take the first. I think your question was about the Downstream portfolio or  overall the whole company?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So expect to see it more in the areas that Tullow clearly has that expertise. Elsewhere, we have many other  partners around the world. This is not uncommon in the oil and gas industry that you have partners for  exploration in particular basin areas.

texts.speaker: Peter R. Voser
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Yeah. Mark, on the Malaysia EOR one, which potentially could be the first EOR offshore project by using  chemicals as well. Very excited about it, 30 years extension of the license, together with PETRONAS. And I can  only say as much as the terms which we have received for these extensions are attractive for the technology and  the innovation we bring into the project from our side. But also attached to it, there is actually joint R&D going to  happen between the two parties for the longer term to develop more. So very attractive terms there.

texts.speaker: Colin S. Smith
texts.profession: Analyst, VTB Capital Plc
texts.text: Thank you. It's Colin Smith from VTB Capital. Your chart sort of implies, I think, that you're looking for about 1.5  million barrels a day of production out of the Americas come 2017, 2018. And that looks like it's up about 1 million  from where we are today. If you go through the major projects, I add up 300,000, 350,000 barrels a day, which  leaves a pretty big gap. And there is quite a lot on the projects under construction, but it does kind of feel like an  awful lot of that is going to have to come from shale or unconventionals of one sort or another. And I wonder if  you could just comment if that's sort of roughly right...

texts.speaker: Colin S. Smith
texts.profession: Analyst, VTB Capital Plc
texts.text: And I will drive it and I think we have driven it the last three years. Projects are on stream. It's coming through.  Yeah, we didn't forecast that Q4 2011 was warm and the whole production came down. That's fine. That's one  quarter. We look a little bit long term quite clearly, and we will drive it.

texts.speaker: Colin S. Smith
texts.profession: Analyst, VTB Capital Plc
texts.text: So like I said before, you will not get a gas number in North America, because that one will change. But I have  enough in the portfolio to get to the 4 million including the 250,000 which we take out through the sales and the  licenses. So I'm happy to take the challenge.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Well, Marvin's here, so I don't want to tie him to the math too much. But if you think, the Americas is where the  growth potential is. There's still another 100,000 to come in the oil sands. We've already said that. 250,000 we  talked about liquids-rich shales, that's from zip.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And we have set up 3 Bcf gas before. Obviously, the balance of those two will need to be considered. And we've just  said there's another 150,000 plus to come in the Gulf of Mexico. So there are some real projects driving real  growth. There is potentially more to come in the Arctic. So he's got the assets, he just has to deliver it. Sorry,  Marvin.

texts.speaker: Jean-Pierre Dmirdjian
texts.profession: Analyst, Oddo & Cie SCA (Broker)
texts.text: My second question's regarding the licenses expected to expire in 2017. Can you give us a sense at all for those  licenses expected to expire and their contribution in terms of proven results in 2011?  And my last question is regarding the mix between oil and gas in 2017 and what may be this mix compared with  the current oil and gas mix? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Didn't quite catch the second question. I think it was about proven reserve contribution. But basically, there were  three main areas of contribution in 2011. They were in the Groundbirch activity in Western Canada, in the Oil  Sands expansion and in Prelude in Australia. They were the three main additions, but they added up to less than  half of the additions. The rest were spread right across the portfolio. Overall, quite a significant contribution  coming through now from the unconventional activity.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Oil and gas mix in 2017. Well, 2011 was 52% oil, 48% gas. We have said for some time 2012 is the inflexion year.  We will produce more gas than oil this year, whatever the circumstances I think. And we expect the share of gas to  grow. How quickly it grows will depend on the growth in the onshore gas. By the middle of the decade, and  certainly contributing to 2017, 2018, we'll have more big LNG coming on stream, so Prelude and Gorgon will make  a difference. And we hope, of course, that we'll have various other gas developments, but offset by liquids-rich  shales, deepwater, maybe the Arctic.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So while it will probably increase from low 50s, it will not go to 60% and beyond in terms of the gas oil. And we're  saying, of the gas production today, about three-quarters of it is actually priced against oil exposure. So our total  exposure in terms of the price exposure is very much oil linked not gas.
