texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So let me recap on my thinking of strategy and performance and the priorities as I see them for Shell. Firstly on  HSSE. The health, safety of our people and our neighbors and our environmental performance remain the top  priorities in Shell. We're heading in the right direction over time, as you can see, but this is an area that a company  can never be satisfied and never be complacent. I believe we have the right safety culture in the company, and our  track record is improving and competitive. But we did regrettably have safety incidents in 2013. So we will  continue our safety drive, which is called Goal Zero to further improve here.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And although our operating performance has been satisfactory overall, our earnings and cash flow have slipped in  some areas. There are several factors here. For example, changes in the industry environment such as low refining  margins, low U.S. gas prices, and the security picture in Nigeria. We can't influence that and we are looking  carefully at where we need to adjust our strategy and our exposures. And on the Shell side, we've been hit  with  high levels of maintenance and exploration charges in 2013, which have reduced our results.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Let me highlight two areas of the company that we are restructuring, North American resources plays or shales  which lost over $2 billion, excluding identified items in 2013 and global oil products where our returns at 4% in  2013 are simply too low.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now Shell has a substantial capital employed in these two areas of the business, nearly $80 billion combined at  end 2013. And both have been impacted by weak industry conditions, like a fall in the U.S. gas prices, low refining  margins both triggered by oversupply, which should be or could be a permanent structural change. And we are  restructuring both of these portfolios with asset sales and, potentially, further impairments. And we are going to   be a much more selective on growth opportunities here. We'll give you more information on all of this in our  March Management Day and this is clearly going to be a focus for us in 2014 in what is going to be a multi-year  program to address these issues.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: For example, we recently halted design work on a large scale gas-to-liquids project in Louisiana, and we  postponed FID on the Arrow LNG project in Australia. We didn't like the economics and the inflation risks on  these proposals. We sold our Wheatstone LNG stake in Australia, which was simply too small to be material for  Shell. Shell's focus in LNG is to deliver Prelude, Elba and the non-operated Gorgon project and, of course, to be  capital efficient in progressing the next wave of LNG options like Abadi, Canada LNG, Browse and Arrow. And we  are not expecting any major FIDs in Asia Pacific LNG in 2014.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The growth priorities, deepwater and integrated gas are where Shell has leadership positions in the industry. And  in integrated gas, we have a very rich funnel of development opportunities, maybe a little too much. And this is an  area where we have been trimming our portfolio more recently. And at the same time, we are building on our  deepwater funnel, new exploration and deals like Libra in Brazil.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The longer term category covers potentially very large positions for Shell in the future, but where we need to be  careful not to over-invest at too early a stage. And this includes politically complex place like Iraq, Kazakhstan,  Nigeria and also sensitive environments like the Arctic and oil sands. So we've put resources plays in this long - term category as well. I believe we got a little ahead of ourselves in some of these longer term plays, and I want to  moderate our investment base here.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now turning to projects. We started up seven large projects in 2013 that have some 180 ,000 barrels of oil  equivalent a day potential when they are fully onstream. And we have four major startups in 2014. Three of these  are deepwater fields operated by Shell, and at Mars-B, which is a 100,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day tension  leg platform, we are expecting startup of early production very shortly. And the fourth one, of course, this year is  the Repsol LNG acquisition, and we are busy integrating that into our LNG portfolio. So substantial portfolio  additions coming online in 2014.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Many thanks, Ben. Welcome, everybody. It's great to see so many here today. I hope that means an upturn in  interest in the sector. As Ben said, we had a busy year in 2013, so let me just summarize some of the highlights.  Current cost of supply earnings, CCS, excluding the identified items, $19 billion, details shortly. We had some  substantial new field startups such as Iraq onshore, Majnoon and gas, and in the deepwater in Brazil. We  announced a series of acquisitions of $10 billion in total, adding assets in areas where we already have leadership  positions, deepwater and LNG.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Buried in today's results announcement was the expectations for the SEC reserves. Final volumes reported in the  2013 Annual Report, we expect additions of 1.6 billion barrels of oil equivalent, that's a headline replacement ratio  of 131%. So this chart shows the step-down of all the factors that has underpinned the reduction in earnings both  for the full year and the fourth quarter.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In aggregate, the macro picture, oil and gas price, downstream margins, Nigeria security impact, they were  negative for us for the full year and also for the fourth quarter. The volume and mix effects within the upstream  production were up positive for earnings in the full year. However, in the fourth quarter, we did see a significant  fall-off in volumes had a large negative impact on the results of around $300 million quarter -on-quarter.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And overall, we saw uplift from the growth projects, but that was more than offset b y around $500 million  negative from a high maintenance asset replacement cost compared with the fourth quarter. And they were  actually reducing the high value oil and gas volumes in regions such as the Gulf of Mexico from the Auger  platform, Nigeria deepwater Bonga, and in the North Sea.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We had LNG sales volumes down, as noted in the third quarter call, [ph] Gatar in (20:54) Australia. Our  exploration charges increased. They rose in the year from $3.1 billion a year ago to $5.3 billion in 2013. And those  charges built up in the second half of the year. Y ou saw them impact in Q3, Q4. So the net impact was around $1.4  billion in the fourth quarter alone, and that compared to the previous year was around $500 million of change in  the after-tax income. Now this was clearly driven by the higher level of exploration well write-offs quarter-on- quarter, particularly in French Guiana where we effectively took several wells at once, and also in the resource of  the shale plays globally. Unfortunately, in both cases, very limited tax shield against those losses increasing the Q- on-Q impact.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Moving on, operational performance. Headline oil and gas production for the fourth quarter, 3.3 million barrels  oil equivalent per day, and that's an underlying decrease 3%, but that 3% excludes the Nigerian impact and  divestments.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now volumes were supported by the growth from the liquids-rich shales in North America, from Iraq and ramp- ups elsewhere. However, this was more than offset by the field decline and the 95,000 barrels of oil equivalent per  day of maintenance impact, which is higher than we had indicated three months ago. Our LNG sales volume,  maintenance activities down 10% quarter four to quarter four.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now just let me highlight, the upstream, we are expecting continued impacts from Nigeria operating environment,  in the fourth quarter is $54 million of income, 40,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day of p roduction versus the  2012 quarter.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In Abu Dhabi, the ADCO license expires this month. It will reduce the production as of now by 155,000 barrels a  day or by around 4% of production. It is a low margin contract, so the financial impact will be considerably  less  than that. And if you've traveled from the Netherlands today, you'll be well aware that the Dutch government has  announced a gas production curtailment for the NAM joint venture in the north of the Netherlands in which we  hold 30%. The impact in the first quarter year-on-year against 2013 will be 60,000 barrel a day equivalent. And  that's partly because it was so cold a year ago, we had a very high production there a year ago. The average impact  for the year is likely, we estimate, to be around 20,000  barrels oil equivalent across this year versus 2013.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We are expecting around 50,000 barrels a day of maintenance impacts versus Q1 last year in the high margin  plays, it's still North Sea, a little bit in the Gulf. That's about half of the maintenance im pact that we've seen in the  previous quarter.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Exploration charges will be higher Q1 2014 versus Q1 2013. Upstream depreciation charges will also increase in  2014. The underlying DD&A, $15 billion last year. There will be some step-up this year on top of the $15 billion  related to the Repsol acquisition. It's around $400 million and expecting maybe around $1.2 billion step -up from  the Majnoon project operating in 2014, assuming current oil prices of around $100 oil price.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now the macro effects, higher oil prices, actually, they were broadly neutral for us over the last two years  compared to original expectation despite the high headline Brent price. Nigeria security, outside our control,  impacted the bottom line by around $1 billion. Our own operational performance has fallen short of initial plans  including uptime from facilities that are onstream and from new startups and, in aggregate, over the two years,   we've delivered around $5 billion less than we had expected. The issues include, inter alia, project delays in Iraq,  Kazakhstan, the downtime in the North Sea we've spoken about quarterly, the startup of the Motiva refinery in  Port Arthur, and the additional costs incurred in Alaska in 2013.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So overall, we expect further underlying CFFO growth over the next two years – we need to deliver that – driven  by the startups and the four new projects that Ben outlined this year, deepwater and Repsol LNG.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So a few words on the portfolio. It's a busy year. Working from the left to right on this chart, it explains how we fill  our development funnel within the strategic themes, and how we bring new oil and gas onstream. And we made  some strategic acquisitions during the year. We announced divestment, redesigned in certain positions or  opportunities where we were not meeting our own strict investment criteria.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Explorers have four good discoveries and appraisal successes with the drill bit and we're assessing the potential  from those finds. We'll update you on that, the overall progress at a later stage. Good year on investment  decisions. We took final decision on nine new projects, the largest of which was the 80,000 barrel a day Carmon  Creek project, heavy oil, in Canada. We started up seven new developments, which should add some 180,000  barrel of oil equivalent per day at peak production potential. Now this includes some large Shell operated projects  such as Majnoon in Iraq and the second phase of the BC-10 deepwater development in Brazil.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now the largest acquisition we made last year, in fact, for some years was the purchase of Repsol's LNG portfolio.  Now these assets fill a supply gap in our LNG portfolio and that's the geographic gap in t he West Atlantic and the  East Pacific. We bought 4.2 million tonnes per annum of equity LNG capacity, 7 .2 million tonnes per annum of  sales volumes. That compares with the market around 250 million tonnes per annum and our current share of  around 23 million tonnes per annum, 24 million tonnes per annum. So, significant growth.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We can add value to this portfolio supplying already contracted customers from a more diversified supply base,  e.g., shorter shipping routes, optimizing gas quality, and by combining the Repsol's supply positions with our own  global trading business. Remember we made $9 billion last year and the year before in our integrated gas  business. So this acquisition is cash flow accretive for our shareholders today. It's only got very minor o ngoing  CapEx requirements, expected less than $50 million a year and we said before and we still believe there's potential  for up to $1 billion of CFFO per year back to Shell. So we're very pleased with the transaction, traders particularly,  and I think it's a great addition to our portfolio.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The growth priorities, deepwater, integrated gas, both allocated $6 billion each this year. That's a reduction in the  deepwater, about level in integrated gas. The resources or the shale spending will be reduced across the Americas  and the global portfolio, coming down from $6 billion to around $5 billion, of which $4 billion is in the Americas,  that's a $1 billion reduction there. And on the future resources, developments such as Carmon Creek will drive a  slight increase in spending to around $6 billion, an increase from last year. So basically, it's $5 billion times $6  billion and a $5 billion, a very fair equitable allocation across the different strategic opportu nities.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Embedded within those numbers is the exploration spending capitalized and expensed, and that was around $7   billion in 2013, will be similar in 2014. There's a 60-40 split between conventional, mostly deepwater, mostly  drilling, and shale plays which will continue to be mostly drilling.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Y eah, thanks, could be a parsimonious CFO looking forward on the dividend, of course, with a slightly more  optimistic belief in the delivery. Right, where is the CFFO growth coming from? Maybe a few comments. The two  points I've just made are a big driver. The biggest shortfall actually, in net terms, against what we previously  expected is in oil products, it's not the upstream, it's oil products. And that's what Ben was really working hard on  and we still hope to see significant better performance from our oil products business.

texts.speaker: Jon Rigby
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: And the second question is a question I think I've asked about three times or four times over the last couple of  years. I'll ask it again because it looks like there's a change here. I've asked about the performance of oil products,  and your predecessor, I think, has said it on a number of occasions that it was performance not portfoli o. But it  looks to me that you are indicating it's at least a bit portfolio from the sort of restructuring announcements or  indications that you're saying. So could you just talk, particularly with your background, about what – in a bit  more detail about what you're thinking about where oil products goes from here?

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Y eah, okay. Y eah, I think in terms of balancing the portfolio, in terms of risk, yeah, we have to take a view on how  you spread attractiveness and risks and you have indeed seen a shift certainly with the significant focus on North  American shales investing into OECD. I think what we have to do there is just to make sure that portfolio that we  have now is high-graded to the right properties that we can add value to, simply because we have integrated  opportunities, gas to LNG, or we happen to sit on very, very strong acreage positions with good sweet spots in it  or, in general, we have quite a good leverage, cost-wise and also decision process-wise to get some of these assets  into good productive profitable use.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: It doesn't just apply to oil products, it certainly also applies to shales. As a matter of fact, it applies to the entire  portfolio, but the focus will be very much on oil products and on the unconventionals to get that piece right. This  is the way we started it in oil products when I was Downstream Director for nine months and basically, this is  what I've done in chemicals, so I know it works.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Okay, exploration question first. Indeed, $7 billion, that's a step up, not from last year, but step up that we have  done a few years ago. Y ou have to bear in mind the things that we explore for quite often result either in a  deepwater projects and integrated gas project. Quite often, the whole maturation process between an actual  discovery and bringing something onstream could be as long as a decade.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The other tends to be a combination of increased decommissioning restoration provisions, that sort of thing, that  doesn't necessarily fall easily in the different categories, some of which have tax implications. So there's again,  there's no single bullet, it's a large complex portfolio. Each of these factors worked in that direction, some of them  will and are being targeted to move back in a positive direction over the co ming years.  Ben van Beurden  Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc  A  Okay, good.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I'll start backwards. Majnoon, 60,000 barrels a day at the same oil price. We're producing over 200,000 barrels a  day there, but it's not all our share. So it should stay like for best part of a year and a half until we fully cost  recover, then our share drops down. The earnings is in the tens o f millions, the cash flow is in the hundreds of  millions. Overall, we've got a couple of billion to recover and that will take us best part of two years overall. But it's  going very well at the moment. Our other Iraqi ventures are also effectively either c ash neutral or positive at the  moment.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Exploration $7  billion is actually investment, it's not all to the P&L. So it's typically about $1 billion or so,  [indiscernible] (01:02:46) and seismic, that does go straight to the P&L. Almost, I guess, over $5 billion of drilling,  that only goes to P&L if it's unsuccessful, and it's primarily deepwater and shale, that's where it's going. Quite a lot  of the deepwater, the offshore is frontier basins, so we're drilling in Benin and Albania, and we'll be back in Brazi l.  So there's quite a lot that remains risky and will come through to the bottom line in a relatively short period of  time. Some, we hope, will work.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The other one, the two projects that you mentioned, yes, they are opportunities that we are pursuing. So the Qatar  petrochemicals project, they are in the middle of feed Sakhalin Train 3, you've seen the announcement. So we  basically decided together with Gazprom to get into the next step. Again, when there is a next milestone to  announce, we will announce that, but they are definitely the sort of opportunities that we want to have in our  funnel.

texts.speaker: Thijs Berkelder
texts.profession: Analyst, ABN AMRO Bank NV (Broker)
texts.text: Thank you. Thijs Berkelder, ABN AMRO. Two questions. In your presentation, you talked about, let's say, maybe  slowing down in heavy oil, can you give an explanation there? Secondly, last year, you clearly made a shift in  Browse to floating LNG from onshore LNG, you're selling out of Wheatstone. Can we expect more divestments in  onshore LNG?

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I can't remember having said that we were slowing down heavy oil, but we said we would take a very hard look at  the sort of long-term opportunities. Heavy oil is one of them of course, it's in that bucket of opportunities that are  just longer term and they are longer term because they are more complex, for whatever reason, they are more  risky. All we understand – we don't quite understand yet how we're going to make it work, but they do have  fundamental potential and attractiveness.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The view that we take we need to balance that particular bucket against the two other buckets, which is basically  cash now, how do I keep that healthy and cash tomorrow, how hard can I step on the gas for both integrated gas  and deepwater, and is basically rebalancing these three categories. I think if you look at what we have in that high  risk, high complex longer term category, I think you have to ask yourself the question is that, is that too much?  How much do I want to do right now? Do I want to pace some of that into the future? And indeed, have you  [indiscernible] (01:15:44) into that category? But actually, it was one of the investments decisions that we to ok in  that field, Carmon Creek. The next one, yeah, we will have to balance that in terms of how that fits into that overall  balancing picture.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The next question actually can be quite – shorten it and I'm sure Simon will have something to say on floating  LNG and [indiscernible] (01:16:10) onshore LNG, but basically, we're not commenting on anything that we might  do portfolio-wise. You will have to see what happens there. What I did say in my speech, though, LNG, very, very  important, very rich opportunity set, so there's plenty to pick from and plenty to monetize.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks. Just comment – the earlier question about OECD, which reminds me in this question, Canada, Australia ,  United States, top three countries is half the CapEx. So it's not a switch away from OECD at all. Part of that's  heavy oil. LNG is a about $6 billion, it's all in Australia at the moment, but a little bit in the U.S. on Elba Island.  But the next phase of LNG, there are four main opportunities, Browse, Abadi, a potential floating opportunity in  Indonesia, Arrow LNG in Australia, and Canadian LNG, British Columbia.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We can't do all four at once, so that's part of the way we're looking at it at the moment, w hich of those goes  forward and in what order. Maybe we will do all four, but maybe not all at the same time. Floating LNG is basically  a competitive advantage for us. Prelude looks a great project; Abadi, most likely the first stage is a floater; and  Browse, we've gone from the onshore to the offshore, and Woodside is the operator there. So we're not at liberty to  say much further than that. But the partners all agree, the priority at the moment is to look to create a floating  option that is attractive to all of us that we will invest in.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now those four that I mentioned, they're all huge resources, huge gas resource. The question is cost to develop  and quality of the market that you will then service. But LNG [ph] retail (01:17 :56) business made $9 billion last  year earnings and the year before, so it's pretty good business, sustainable. And we've got Gorgon, Prelude and  Elba on their way through as well. So this is the core of Shell in the 2020s and for a lot longer than that, the nature  of the business assets that we're developing.

texts.speaker: Lucas O. Herrmann
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Prime Brokerage)
texts.text: The second question and more conceptual, Ben, is fantastic job. Congratulations. I wonder to what extent – you  walk into that job and you say, my God, this is a complex organization. You're running the better part of seven to  eight different business models across unconventional gas, LNG, mining, conventional oil, marketing, refining, et  cetera, et cetera, it's an awful lot. It's an awful lot for you and indeed it's an awful lot for a board to get their head  around and really understand, and if they really believe that they're going to be able to maximizing value for  shareholder out of all of them.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: But the integration where I can say, hey, if I take offshore gas in Qatar and I can actually get that into premium  lubricants in North America, and I can capture a huge value arbitrage and I can do that with technology, but it's  kind of hard to distinguish whether it's upstream or downstream, that is actually quite valuable. I f I look at oil  sands and we can integrate it all the way into our North American markets and capture the value wherever it goes  and I can tell you, it goes up and down the value chain an awful lot, that I think is valuable integration that gives  you robustness.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: If you look at our existing asset base and then you superimpose on it the capability to trade around it and  therefore add extrinsic value to our operations, that's hugely important, hugely valuable. If you look at new value  chains from upstream into chemicals, where we can do things that basically next of us, there's only one other  company that I know that can do this, actually one of very, very few players with the proposition to major resource  holders to bring value to their resource, to get access to it that nobody else can. That's very valuable integration.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Chemicals piece is sorted out, we have some great pieces in that oil products portfolio that are very strong. And we  just need to be very granular, very disciplined to sort out the rest. So then you have a very, very strong core  business in the downstream that can actually play a larger part in the integrated company, integration being  different for what it used to be in the 1950s.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Henry
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Ben. If we go trading in biofuels, I think [indiscernible] (01:23:24) trying to think...

texts.speaker: Peter W. Hutton
texts.profession: Analyst, RBC Europe Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: And the second one, which is partly linked to that one, in Alaska with no drilling in 2014, can you give an  indication of what the underlying costs will still be in there, if there are any. Are there any cost savings? What you  do with it? The two rigs that you were going to deploy one to drill and one to hang around, what happens on there  is this an opportunity or is this a sunk cost?

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So look at Upstream Americas, I think we've said quite a few times, it is actua lly quite a number of different  businesses in there, right. Let's be very clear, we have a very, very successful, highly cash generative, profitable  deepwater business with some startups later in the year, one of which is imminent. So therefore, the story on  deepwater will be a good story for 2014.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We have a heavy oil business, some of which is integrated into our downstream business, which is again a pretty  good story, it being, I think we can say with great confidence and pride that we have leading cost performance.  When it comes to heavy oil, we have great integration forward, which actually protects us in terms of netbacks to  the mines, so also then heavy oil, I think, a pretty solid business.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now once you have done that, you then also have to say, well, how much superior return can I make in that  business really? So you pick out the bits and pieces of the business where we can really integrate it into higher  value outlets rather than just pipeline gas and getting Henry Hub exposure. Or you just have to say, listen, this is  such an attractive opportunity, my resource position is so good that actually the underlying resource gives me a  privileged return, a strong return. Everything else is basically an opportunity to high-grade away from. And the  details on how we will do that, and the focus that we will have on that, I'm afraid you'll have to wait for March.  Also Marvin will be here to talk about it.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: On Alaska, I think I said it in the speech. It's also very clear in the press release, so the decision on Alaska is a very  recent one. It is – we have been working for years to understand how we develop this very, very complex resource,  complex in terms of its logistics, complex in terms of the conditions that we face there, weather condi tions, but  also, of course, more technical risks that we see. We now have on top of it legal issues and basically, at some point  in time, you have say, listen, this complexity that we have here, which is creating a lot of cost, added with the  uncertainty that we have, it doesn't justify at this point in time going ahead. So the decision was very clear in my  mind, we have to pause this for 2014 and see what we're doing. Financial treatment, you want to say something  about that, Simon?

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: So we're leaving today without any explicit targets from the company. I think you've said that your goal is to
texts.text: improve your ROACE, and that you target to be better than your peer group. I'm wondering if we're going to get  any more explicit targets in your Strategy Day in March. And also, it's great to give us the target of we can have a  better ROACE than our peers if you're talking to people who are only investing in a pool of integrated oil and gas  companies, but in reality, the market is struggling to understand whether or not this industry is an attractive one.  So I'm wondering if you can give us any guidance around that today or in March.
