texts.text: And I've noticed that in terms of reserve replacement, reserve life, your growth and future opportunities, those  three remaining buckets don't really contribute, whether it's chemicals, shale, or New Energies. So would it be fair  to say that you are increasingly comfortable with not your 1P but your 2P reserve life as you look at the future and  go you know what, even deep water, even LNG now is a cash engine? So just wanted to see whether you could  broadly put that into context how you're thinking about the next decade?

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Chris. I think I've said it here before, and it's not because I do not have a reservoir engineering  background but I am somehow less obsessed with reserves and reserve life than perhaps others might be,  including some of you. For me it's all about the longevity and the running room in the business from a cash  perspective. Of course, it is very important to understand how much do we have to work on. So like for instance  on the deep-water business that you've referenced, it is important for me to understand when is the stock of  opportunities that we have in the pipeline, when is that going to run out and when will this business go and decline  unless I do something about it. Well we just actually did a very detailed strategic review of the deep water  business in the board yesterday, so I can use the numbers that are current. But our business, our deep-water  business, will be at the level where we will get it to by the end of the decade, well into the next decade. And by  2026, you will see that if we have no success nowhere and don't add to it, this business will go into decline.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: You're absolutely right also by noting that's we're not a pure E&P company. We have a very significant part of our  cash flow, free cash flow, come from non-opportune activities, whether it's oil products, whether it's chemicals. I  think in 10 years' time we'll be standing here hopefully saying a large part of our New Energies cash flow is  meaningful as well, and that gives another form of resilience. It may not give you the massive upside and  downside to oil price movements, but it's very, very good free cash flow with relatively limited capital maintenance,  which is what I like about that business as well. So I think we have the right approach, we have the right strategy.  I don't think we are sort of unhelpfully, myopically obsessed with metrics that are meaningless, and that's the way  I like to run the business anyway.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So indeed competition is strong for capital with new organizations, and I think that will continue for the coming  years. I think we're fortunate for the suite of opportunities that we have in all of our businesses. So all of them are  consistently coming to the executive committee and asking if they can grow more, with most if not all having I  think good opportunities. In terms of what's committed of the $25 billion of spend, I think it depends what question  you're trying to answer. So I think we've tried to give an indication the composition of that. So if that's what you're  interested, an important part of that is asset integrity. There's another piece of that, which is kind of small projects,  kind of easy growth options that you have within an asset. And then you have kind of the next generation of truly  kind of greenfield new projects. Most of our spend is kind of the first couple categories, and kind of a smaller  portion of that $25 billion is that kind of true greenfield new project opportunity for us.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Important decisions that are on the horizon for us with no preference, because that's not appropriate, but we're  looking at things like our Vito project in the Gulf of Mexico. LNG Canada, another important decision for us in the  next couple of years. Our marketing business, which Ben mentioned, we're growing in Mexico, China, India; these  are either new or expanding markets for us. Relatively low but those are decision points in terms of how we're  growing our business.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: What we would like to do also, and our thinking is reasonably advanced on that, is to see whether we can really  accelerate the development of this. Typically, if you look at developments in the Gulf of Mexico, we have been  looking at between discovery of first oil for more than decades. We have set ourselves a target to significantly  reduce the timeframe. Also to significantly reduce our unit development cost, and I think you saw some of that in  the slides that Jessica showed, the ambitions that we have. The Whale project will be a great test bed to see how  fast we can go and whether we can indeed take advantage of certain replication ideas to just really bring this into  a fast-track development. So fast-track development, in this way will not be a tie back but a new development but  on a really rapid pace.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So a lot of good underlying delivery that's translating to that lower cost basis. There's also some one-off helps in  there. So speaking to your point around how sustainable it is, and I think it's – an important piece in there is a lot  of reduction in our D&R in the year. If you looked at our balance sheet, our D&R provisions went up from $25  billion to $20 billion over the year. Some of that flowed through the OpEx as well. Great story, so the same  impacts we've had with our P&C organization, reducing cost in places like the Gulf of Mexico and our  unconventionals business. We've applied this similar thinking to our decommissioning and restoration, and that  value is coming through both in terms of our balance sheet exposure but also in the OpEx.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And let me reassure you that Jessica is not the only who thinks that there are more opportunity in OpEx. I think  that is completely shared not only by me but also by our business directors. Let me just remind you with a few  dates before we close. And first of all, thank you very much for all your questions. I know there are a few more  questions in the room, so we will be available of course after this presentation outside as well, but just a few  dates. On the 26th of February, we will have the LNG team present to you here in London the outlook for supply  and demand. I know that LNG is still very much a topic on people's minds, how is that playing out, and maybe  less so than a year ago, but it's still very important and instructive to come listen. And then we have the  Downstream leadership team that will host a Downstream open house for investors on the 21st of March, also  here in London. And then of course we have our Q1 results on the 26th of April, and Jessica will be presenting  those, so I'm sure you're looking forward to them.

file: RDSB - Q4 2018 Earnings Call 31January2019 900 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 31-Jan-19.pdf

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Before we get to it though, let's take another quick look at our disclaimer with which I'm sure you are intimately  familiar. A reason why Jessica and I have been looking forward to today is that we can now, with the full year  results, declare that 2018 was another year of great delivery against our strategy. And as you know, our strategy  is to deliver a world-class investment case, to thrive through the energy transition, and to maintain a very strong  societal license to operate. And where we have made some promises in line with that strategy, we have delivered  in 2018 and I believe we have established a track record of delivery now.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So we have shown that we are a company that delivers against the commitments that we make. And with our  recent commitment to set short-term targets to reduce the net carbon footprint of the energy products that we sell  in a world that is going through an energy transition, we have also shown leadership as a responsible company,  preparing for changing customer and market preferences as this transition unfolds.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now let me talk about some of the 2018 highlights first, after which I will take you through the HSSE performance  and provide you with a closer look at our actions related to the energy transition. Then I will talk you through the  Shell delivery and our outlook for 2020, and then Jessica will talk in a bit more detail about the fourth quarter  results.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, as I promised, first some more detail on 2018. It will not have escaped you that 2018 was another year of oil  price volatility and in spite of that, we saw all of our businesses deliver. And that translated into a current cost of  supply earnings, excluding identified items, of over $21 billion. We delivered free cash flow of more than $39  billion. And return on average capital employed for the full year was 7.6%, that's 2 percentage points higher than  2017 and brings us closer again to our outlook for 10% in 2020.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: But there is a fact, one thing that is even more important. It is something that comes before anything else at Shell  and that's our Health, Safety, Security and Environmental performance. We all know that safety is critical for us to  achieve our strategic ambitions. We must all be safe if Shell is to be a world-class investment case. We must all  be safe if Shell is to thrive through the energy transition and we must all be safe if Shell is to maintain a strong  societal license to operate.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Next, operational spills. Although we achieved a decline in the number of spills in 2018, that fell by some 8%, the  volume of material spills actually went up. There're fewer spills but, on average, they were larger. Now in other  areas our HSSE performance was more encouraging. So we continued to reduce flaring. For example, this was  driven by, a large measure, by our decision to exit Majnoon in Iraq, but we also reduced flaring in Nigeria, in Qatar  and in the Permian. And process safety was another area of improvement. And I'm glad to report that in 2018, we  achieved our best ever process safety performance. But clearly, our work is not done. We must achieve Goal  Zero and that means that we must continue to focus and get the performance to that level. Now just as society  expects Shell to operate safely, its expectations of Shell to act in the face of climate change are only growing  stronger.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, we have taken a number of steps over the past year to show that we are a responsible corporate citizen to  lead the industry and to get ahead of the changing market and customer preferences to deliver commercial  opportunities that also will come with the energy transition. So, for example, we announced plans to establish  short-term targets as part of our long-term ambition to reduce the net carbon footprint of the energy products that  we sell. And this will be in step with society's drive to meet the goals of the Paris Agreement and we will link these  targets to executive remuneration. We developed this approach through extensive collaboration with institutional  investors working together on behalf of Climate Action 100+. And we recognize that we have an important role to  play as part of society's response to its needs for more and cleaner energy. The actions we've have taken on a  net carbon footprint position us for the future and enable the execution of all three strategic ambitions.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I'm also pleased to say that we are making progress in a number of areas in support of our ambitions. And just to  highlight a few examples, in Nigeria for instance, we have been able to reduce the flaring intensity year-on-year  by some 70% over the last 10 years. And of course, we are also developing our New Energies business which  seeks out the commercial opportunities that the energy transition will bring. And last year we invested $800  million, including investments in areas such as solar and wind, as part of our New Energies business. And we are  looking to scale up this business in a very disciplined manner, spending $1 billion to $2 billion on average per  annum on commercial opportunities with competitive returns.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And we started the divestment program back in 2016. You will remember the oil prices below $40 a barrel and  market conditions for executing a program of this scale were challenging to say the least. But we managed to  execute the deals and to do so using diverse deal constructs, so you saw us announcing traditional asset  divestments, packages of assets, IPOs, having raised cash through our MLP

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And the sales of our Woodside and Canadian Natural Resources shares were some of the largest block trades in  any sector and they were pretty well timed. Geographically, we exited business around the world, such as oil  sands in Canada, downstream in Argentina, downstream in Japan, upstream in Ireland and in Gabon, and  integrated gas in Thailand and New Zealand. And we simplified our operations in many more countries on top of  that. But even where we exited in a number of places, we have put in place trading arrangements, offtake  arrangements and brand licensing arrangements. And importantly, of course, we delivered all of this with  attractive valuations. We generated the cash we needed to strengthen our balance sheet and to improve our  credit metrics.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And through our transactions we have sought to also high-grade the margins in our portfolio and improve the risk  profile by reducing country risks, business operational risks and financial risks. So for example, we have removed  around $5 billion of decommissioning and restoration liabilities from our balance sheet. And crucially, of course,  we ended the program with a stronger portfolio which was the main design. And we will continue to high-grade  this portfolio with divestments. So expect to do more than $5 billion in each of 2019 and 2020.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now as you can see on this slide here, we've made a lot of progress delivering these projects and there is more to  come as not all of these are operating at full capacity yet. So, take for example, recent FPSO in Brazil that has  come on-stream in late 2018 and it's expected to be at peak levels towards the end of 2019. And additionally, we  are developing smaller projects. Those that are expected to start up in 2019 should produce more than 150,000  barrels of oil equivalent per day at peak levels and that's more than offsetting decline in the period. And beyond  this, we expect an additional $5 billion in cash flow from operations by the end of 2020. And this, we feel, is very  heavily de-risked. And this incremental cash flow will be realized with continued ramp up of the projects already  on-stream, the delivery of Appomattox and ongoing investments in the Permian.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So let's talk about some of these key projects that will help us realize this extra cash flow in a bit more detail. First  of all, as you know, Chemicals, a growth priority for Shell, part of our strategy to thrive through the energy  transition, global population growth, rising living standards are likely to drive petrochemical demand for years to  come.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now early in 2018, we started up a new ethylene cracker in Nanhai in China. And then in December, we started  up the fourth alpha olefins unit at our Geismar facility in the U.S. Gulf Coast. This investment increased capacity  at the site to some 1.3 million tonnes of alpha olefins per year, making it the largest alpha olefins site in the world.  Alpha olefins, you may have come across them every day, but in fact you do because they are needed in  everyday products like soap, synthetic lubricants, low temperature detergent, all projects – products that save  energy and reduce CO2 emissions.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And then we have Australia where we opened four of the seven wells at Prelude. We are now progressing with  the commissioning and start-up of the rest of the Prelude facilities. And at the same time, we are producing  condensate, preparing for the first condensate cargo and later the first LNG cargo. And once fully operational,  Prelude will produce 3.6 million tonnes of LNG and 1.7 million tonnes of natural gas liquids per year.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Let me show what we are working on in 2019 and 2020. Appomattox will be a key asset in the Gulf of Mexico. We  expect some 175,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day from the Norphlet play when operating at peak production  levels. This will bring a step change to our cash flows with high margin barrels delivering cash for Shell for years  to come. The teams are now working to commission and safely bring Appomattox on-stream later this year.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: With our Permian acreage which produces some 145,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, you have seen a 200%  increase since January 2017. And we continue to dedicate around 50% or more of our shales capital to the  Permian. We've also matured an inventory of resources in excess of 1 billion barrels of oil equivalent in the  Permian with forward-looking breakeven prices of less than $40 per barrel. So we expect to deliver continued  growth through 2020. But our delivery doesn't stop there, as you would expect, we are developing options in our  portfolio that will start generating cash in the 2020s.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: When we announced the Whale discovery last year, I said we were looking to accelerate the development cycle  and bring the project on-stream faster. So I'm pleased to announce that we are ready, already assessing the  results of the exploration and appraisal wells that we have drilled at Whale. In parallel, we are assessing  development options and at the heart of these discussions is standardization, replication and incorporating the  learnings from Vito. And this should allow us to accelerate timelines and depending on the outcomes, of course,  we could take a final investment decision as early as next year.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Let's just stay with our growth priorities, but now looking at our Downstream business in the U.S. So our  Pennsylvania Petrochemicals Complex, it's under construction at the moment and is expected to deliver  commercial production early in the next decade. Pennsylvania will produce 1.6 million tonnes of polyethylene per  annum. Polyethylene is a petrochemical product used to make many finished products, from automotive  components, sports equipment, household furniture, and consumer electronics. So these are just two examples,  but our project funnel is strong, and we have options across all of our strategic themes to support the company's  cash generation far into the future.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: At the end of Q4 2018, earnings on a CCS basis, excluding identified items, amounted to more than $5.7 billion.  ROACE reached 7.6%, 2 percentage points higher than in the same quarter last year. We are demonstrating  progress towards 10% ROACE by the end of 2020.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Net debt decreased almost $26 billion since 2016 and around $9 billion since the last quarter. The net debt  reduction in Q4 is supported by a large release of working capital linked to the drop in oil prices as well as  reduced inventory levels.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The impact of working capital from inventory movements alone, with the combination of lower prices and  inventory levels, contributed to a release of $7 billion. While this may partly reverse based on recent positive oil  price movements, the underlying trend on gearing is moving in the right direction. And we are progressing  towards our 20% target.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, let me run through some of the portfolio highlights of the quarter. In addition to the projects Ben spoke about  earlier, we had the start-up of Clair Phase 2 in the North Sea, which will produce up to 120,000 barrels per day.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In December, we announced our final investment decision on Assa North in Nigeria, a gas development to  support domestic needs.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And I also want to mention that as part of our power portfolio in the New Energies business, we acquired offshore  wind leases off the Northeast Coast of the U.S. These have the potential, if developed, to provide peak power  generation capacity of 4.1 gigawatts, enough power to supply some 1.7 million homes.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Shell is well-placed to develop these opportunities, combining our offshore capabilities from our Upstream  business and our wind experience, along with the experience of our partners.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Let us now have a look at the earnings this quarter. Our Q4 2018 CCS earnings, excluding identified items,  amounted to $5.7 billion, which is almost $1.4 billion or 32% higher than in Q4 2017.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In our Integrated Gas business, earnings, excluding identified, items were $2.4 billion or 44% higher than in the  same quarter last year. Integrated Gas benefited from higher realized oil, gas and LNG prices, as well as higher  contributions from LNG trading. These were partly offset by movements in deferred tax positions.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Total production volumes were largely unchanged compared with the fourth quarter 2017, while LNG liquefaction  was some 3% higher, mainly due to lower maintenance and increased feed gas availability partly offset by  divestments.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Earnings, excluding identified items, in Upstream were approximately $1.9 billion or some $200 million higher  than in Q4 2017. This is driven by higher realized oil and gas prices, as well as lower well write-offs. This was  partly offset by movements in deferred tax positions being less favorable.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In Downstream, CCS earnings, excluding identified items, were $2.1 billion or 53% higher than Q4 2017.  Downstream benefited from increased contributions from crude oil trading and stronger refining and marketing  margins, but these were partly offset by higher operating expenses and lower base chemicals and intermediate  margins.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And in Upstream, derivatives related to our Denmark divestment saw a similar help from the recent decline in oil  prices and generated a $350 million cash inflow. These derivatives may have an impact on our cash flow until  deal completion, which is expected in 2019. Both of these were then partially offset by smaller movements on  foreign exchange derivatives. We have included additional details on the movements of cash, derivative  margining and working capital in the appendix.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: For example in the Mars corridor, volumes are up almost 50% since 2016. This was done with infill drilling, well,  reservoir and facilities management and near-field development. Our unit development and operating costs have  been steadily decreasing year-on-year and are now below $10 per barrel in our deepwater operations. We're  getting better at our turnaround including using robotic non-intrusive inspections.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Turning to reserves, our SEC proved reserves at the end of 2018 were 11.6 billion barrels of oil equivalent, which  is a decrease of around 600 million barrels from the end of 2017. Our reserves replacement ratio for 2018 is 53%.  This is due to divestments and impact of Groningen which we previously disclosed. Reserves replacement,  excluding Groningen this year is estimated at 98%. Our three-year average reserves replacement ratio stands at  an estimated 96%.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Our strategy is working, and we are delivering. The cash flow generation for the company has improved  materially. For 2018, we were able to deliver free cash flow of around $39 billion, of which $31 billion was organic.  Again, more organic free cash flow delivery at lower oil prices. This covered our buybacks, cash dividend and  interest expense. And based on our outlook, we believe we have the free cash flow to deliver on our strategy, to  grow cash flow, reduce debt and increase shareholder distributions.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now with that, let's have some Q&A. We are fortunate to have Maarten with us. As many as you know, Maarten  runs our Integrated Gas & New Energies business, a very important quarter for that business, so we thought it  would be good for him to join us.

texts.speaker: Lydia Rainforth
texts.profession: Analyst, Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: And then sorry, just a very quick follow-up one on the reserves replacement number. If I look at adding back the  Groningen and the divestments, is it right that it is actually over 100% for this year, so the 112%?

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Yeah, I think the returns, of course, are partly a function of history, the capital employed, and we will take some  time to work off a very capital-intensive period, which we had during the high oil price world, but also, of course,  the capital that we had to put in the balance sheet after the BG acquisition. That will work its way through. We will  continue to improve. And of course, it's a function of oil prices as well and gas prices.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So I think that the reference conditions that we have set, $60 real term 2020, I think 10% is, I mean it'd be doable.  That can be – have higher returns or will we get to higher returns as we will continue to invest in projects that are  fundamentally and intrinsically more returning than the projects that we tended to do in the last 20 years? Yes, we  should, yeah. But then of course, that also takes into account certain assumptions on oil price.

texts.speaker: Christyan F. Malek
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: And third, and apologies for the third question, your cash breakeven this year is $60. That's where the oil price is.  Are you comfortable with that in terms of managing a dividend cover in what is an increasingly volatile oil market?  Thank you.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So the way we look at reserves life or at the sustainability of the business, because that's what this is all about, is  to look specifically strategic theme by strategic theme, how we see things evolve over the next 10 years-plus.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: For each of the businesses, we have very clear views on how to do that. And we have very strong funnels that we  believe are adequate to see us all the way through into the second half of next decade. And then of course, we  are working on strengthening the funnels to see us through into the 2030s. We think that is the only sensible  approach that I know to manage the company going forward.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: But then I also need to again tell you that there are accounting effects in reserve life that are distorting these  things. So for instance, we have issues with proved and undeveloped reserves. If you look at our LNG Canada  project, for instance, it booked zero reserves on that. And that is simply because SEC booking guidelines for LNG  project require you to actually have offtake contracts for LNG before you can book the reserves associated with it.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We have an offtake contract with ourselves, because that is our business model for the LNG business. So  therefore, strictly speaking, we cannot book a single tcf or single cubic feet even, which doesn't mean that we  have built this and – that we are going to build this LNG project without the prospects of the gas being there. It is  simply the accounting treatment that we have to follow by the SEC rules. And we are sticklers for that.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The other thing is deepwater, we have said that before as well. We have a very large deepwater business with  significant issues when it comes to booking as well. When analogs are not available, we need to be conservative  with the bookings that we can make. And, therefore, we book relatively few barrels with our deepwater FIDs.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So these things are distorting effects. Because we are the largest integrated gas player and a very large, if not the  largest, deepwater player, we are hit by it disproportionately. It doesn't mean that our position is uncompetitive.  And it definitely does not mean that we cannot sustain this business throughout the 2020s. Jessica?

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So perhaps building on what Ben just said, we're very comfortable with our development funnel for our Upstream  business, but also the funnel of opportunities we have to grow our Downstream business and our Integrated Gas  business. And again, we're focusing on growing value for the company, growing cash flow for the company. And  we don't feel any anxiety around our reserves level.

texts.speaker: Irene Himona
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA (UK)
texts.text: Thank you. Irene Himona, Société Générale. In your very large Asian-oriented LNG business, but also perhaps in  the Downstream, are you seeing any signs at all about the Chinese economic slowdown, which has so scared  global stock markets?

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Integrated Gas & New Energies Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Yeah. Trade wars and Chinese economic growth, to the extent that it drives global GDPs obviously has an impact  on, let's say, some of the important profit drivers for all of the company, because it drives oil price trends, et  cetera.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Integrated Gas & New Energies Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: But when it comes to gas demand in China, actually, the drivers are a bit different, or at least the main driver isn't  actually economic growth. We've seen 2018, which was indeed mixed in terms of economic growth in China, the  gas markets still grow by 16% because domestic production isn't going so well. The energy imports into China  grew by 40%. So that's a disappointing year in China, don't know then [ph] low may last (01:04:04) in terms of the  gas market.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Integrated Gas & New Energies Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And it is because it is very much policy-driven. It's around their quality, it's around displacing coal. And we see the  growth of gas in China very much into industry and into heating, not so much into the power sector. So, we  believe it is quite a resilient demand for gas and still we are well below the 10% penetration of gas in the energy  mix in China. So, we believe there's still a lot of replacement of coal displacement scope to go.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Integrated Gas & New Energies Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And elsewhere in Asia, we see a similar trend in India. It's earlier days and policies are not yet as well matured  and implemented as we see them in China, but it's starting. So in India you saw a 4% gas market growth and  leading to 10% LNG import growth. So, I do think these markets still have a lot of resilient growth ahead of them,  that is, to a large extent, actually decoupled from their exact economic performance because of the displacement.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And then on the share buybacks, when we made the commitment, and consistent with how we framed it since, it  is of course subject to macro environment and the price environment and our ability to continue to deleverage the  company. We've, I think, been very prudent, if that's quite the right word, but measured in each step that we've  taken as we've gone through the last couple of years, and meeting each of the commitments because we want to  do this in a sustainable way.

texts.speaker: Jason Gammel
texts.profession: Analyst, Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: Second question very specifically on LNG Canada, thus far, you have only sanctioned, essentially, the  downstream component of the project and when it's fully operational, it'll be a 2 bcf a day consumer of gas. When  do you think you need to make the decision on whether to proceed with your own equity gas and when you need  to start drilling versus just buying the gas off the grid?

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And of course, you can imagine that if we have an affordability challenge with low oil and gas price environments,  yeah, of course, we will be more at the bottom of the range. And if we have no affordability issues, we know we  can go all the way up to $30 billion, but how that exactly will play out is something that I don't want to necessarily  sort of box myself in right at the beginning of the year. We will just do what is right by the company, doing, as  Jessica says, a number of things at the same time, growing the company, deleveraging the company's balance  sheet and improving shareholder returns. And having a little bit of room to maneuver in the capital is actually quite  helpful.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Integrated Gas & New Energies Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Yes. The short answer is not yet. But important to say is we only have 40% of the LNG Canada, of course, so we  don't quite need to get up to 2 bcf, but we do need to produce more gas. We have a fair amount of gas on-stream  as we speak actually in Canada that we sell into, largely, the local market, attracting fairly for netbacks. To some  extent, LNG Canada will finally give an outlet to that gas that is much more advantaged than the AECO price. So  to some extent, it is just placing current production or current wells or current sustaining programs into a better  value chain. We will need to invest in some more gas gathering and compression facilities to get all the way up to  the volumes we need to fill the trains, and we will probably make that decision in about two years from now.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Integrated Gas & New Energies Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: It also depends a little bit on how we see the market, because if we see AECO be as weak as it's been, then we'll  probably look to procure more of the gas and not drill all of it ourselves, which is one of the interesting elements of  LNG Canada, we can actually kind of play the Canadian upstream market and decide just how much do we want  to drill, how much are we very happy for other people to drill and sell it to us at what is currently a very depressed  local gas price. So that will all go into we will manage it carefully and we will want to keep some optionality to  optimize, let's say, the last 20%, 25% of our gas needs.

texts.speaker: Thomas Adolff
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And the second question is for Maarten, I think your estimate is that global LNG markets will double by 2035. So  when we think about Shell in LNG, should we think about Shell maintaining the current size or growing in line with  the market, or the reality is somewhere in between? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Integrated Gas & New Energies Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: First, let's say – we don't obviously have a market share target in LNG, that will be a wrong thing to have. But we  do think that our current scale in absolute terms, but also in relative terms, brings us advantages that give us  returns on our businesses that others will struggle to copy. So, essentially, I think it's reasonable to say that as the  LNG market continues to grow, we will want to grow with that market. So, I would not want to sacrifice our current  position of strong leadership in that market. And whether that means what exactly percentage at the moment,  we're somewhere between 20%, 25% of the market in terms of delivered LNG. Where in that range we would sit  depends a bit on – is a bit opportunistic. But more importantly, how we get there will really depend on the build  and buy decisions that we take every time we come across an opportunity.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Integrated Gas & New Energies Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So in the case of Canada, we clearly decided to build to put our capital down ourselves and to go full value chain.  But in quite a lot of other instances, we're quite happy for other people to put our capital on the ground and be the  off taker of the LNG, because we have advantaged market access over almost anybody else. And as long as we  continue to pull these two levers, I think there's quite an affordable pathway to having an Integrated Gas business  that is a lot bigger than what we have today as long as the markets continues to grow in line with that vision.

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: Ben, it's an interesting year and you've got much better visibility on the opportunities that may be coming through
texts.text: than we do. But if I think to what's potentially on offer this year, Qatar gas for LNG; Brazil, sizable acreage on  offer; Permian, U.S. onshore, look, you're associated with a number of things and I think you're clear in terms of  your comments around your own interest in having greater optionality, whatever, in that area. And then obviously  New Energies is also a priority and something that you're intent on growing and expanding in.

texts.speaker: Jessica Uhl
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Yeah. It's the same every year. And so what we do at the beginning of the year, and we look at the capital  program, we say listen, let's just give ourselves a little bit of room so that we can understand when opportunities  do come up, whether we want to do them, yes or no. It's pointless to begin the year with a plan where we are  trying to figure out how on Earth do we get below $30 billion. Of course, we will manage it, because we by now  have the discipline, the processes and everything else to do what it takes to get within the range that we need to  be at. But it's a whole lot easier if you just say, well, there's a few things that we can do during the year, let's see  how they play out, let's see where they actually do play out. Let's take a really good look at it, and let's make  some choices. And indeed, there will be a few things that we will have to regret.

texts.speaker: Jon Rigby
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd.
texts.text: Yes. Jon Rigby from UBS. Can I just have a look – I'll get you to look at the strategic themes table and the cash  flow evolution. And I think you sort of signaled that in overall aggregate terms, you're pretty close to the bottom  end of that $25 billion to $30 billion free cash flow. But if we sort of disaggregate it, it looks like the Upstream and  the shales, looks like they've got work to do, especially if you correct for oil price as well. So I just wondered  whether you are able to give some insights in what has to happen over I guess the next 24 months to hit those  2020 targets. Is it all portfolio or is there something else that has to happen?

texts.speaker: Jon Rigby
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd.
texts.text: And flipping around the other way and Maarten's here. So it's also evident that Integrated Gas is ahead of your  2020 target. Is that something that is just unusual to the 2018 market and may reverse? There's a bit of super  normal profitability in there. I'm clear, obviously, you've just spoken about Prelude coming on this year, so that  would, on the face of it, improve your performance further into 2020. So I wonder whether you could talk a little bit  about your segment's performance in the context of that target. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Yeah, I think, Jon, you're right, there is some more work. We said there's $5 billion of cash flow yet to come from  projects that are going to ramp up further and still start up. So the big one that's still has to start-up is Appomattox,  that will start up somewhere this year. But then there's quite a few projects in Upstream that still need to ramp up.  So we have still ramp up facilities that have started up in Brazil, we have two more FPSOs to come on-stream in  Brazil. We have the Permian, of course, which is not necessarily one single project, but we are still in a very  significant ramp up phase there as well with new production coming on-stream in 2019 and then again in 2020.  So yeah, there is more work to do. But as I said earlier on as well, it's heavily de-risked because [ph] it's either  already there (01:27:45) and just needs to get to [ph] next cap (01:27:48) or it is about to come on-stream and we  are in the final phases of delivering it. Integrated Gas, do you want to talk a bit more about that?

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Integrated Gas & New Energies Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Yeah, Thanks, Jon. And it is good of course to be there, although we're there at $71 per barrel not at mid-$60s.  So corrected for price, we're not above the range we're in. Of course, with Prelude coming on and with Elba  coming on later this year, which of course is not in our projects list, because it's a Kinder Morgan investment, but  it will be 100% Shell offtake. We will [ph] have to mix (01:28:21) our gas potential and the cash flow coming in  from these assets. There's also a few that we sold of course, so Thailand where Thailand was still partly this year  and we had New Zealand until December. So there'll be some offsets but of course they're smaller than Prelude  and Elba. So I think we feel pretty good about our ability for Integrated Gas to be well into that range.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Integrated Gas & New Energies Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Even if you take out, there's been some dislocations in the global LNG market in 2018 that we were very well  prepared and positioned for and that we managed to exploit. In the next 10 years, we'll have multiple of these  events and we will be again well-positioned for them.

texts.speaker: Martijn Rats
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Yeah. Hello, it's Martijn Rats at Morgan Stanley. I wanted to ask you, if you could talk a little bit about the  announcement from early December on carbon. I guess I have to say I don't feel I, like, fully understand it. The  metric of net carbon footprint, the way that you sort of talk about it, that is an intensity measure, not a sort of total  tonnes of CO2 equivalent number, right?

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Okay. Thanks, Martijn. That's a really good question. Let me explain first again what the net carbon footprint is,  why we have it, and then what the difference is from having an ambition to now having a target.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So what we've always said, we want to be a responsible company that remains relevant through the energy  transition. If you look at what the world will need to do in order to meet Paris, it will have to decarbonize the  energy system. So in other words, energy being consumed will have to have a lower carbon content.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: The world on its way to less than 2 degrees C will have to reduce the carbon intensity of the energy it consumes,  and forgive me for using some engineering units here. There are around 40 grams of CO2 per megajoule of  energy consumed.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: We in Shell are at the moment with our portfolio roughly at 80 grams. Of course, we have predominantly  hydrocarbons in our portfolio. The world itself is probably close to 72 grams, but that's because the world in total  has lots of hydro and nuclear and biomass, et cetera, which we don't have in our portfolio.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So we have said if we want to be relevant and if we want to be with society on a path of less than 2 degrees C or  1.5 degrees C, we have to be at 40 grams by 2050 as well. So effectively, it means that we have to have the  carbon intensity of the energy products, not the assets, the energy products that we put into society.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And why do we talk about products? Well, because that's the real impact we have on society. We have on society  impact because we provide energy products that people use and that in their use produce greenhouse gases.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I think it's insufficient and wholly inadequate to say we are going to make the production of hydrocarbons less  carbon-intensive. Really? Why would that be somehow compatible with Paris? So it's about the energy products  that we sell and reducing the carbon intensity of these energy products to be in line with what society needs to do  to meet Paris.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: It's a complicated description, but I think it's the only thing that will keep us relevant, if you want to remain relevant  as a company throughout this energy transition.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now then, how are we going to do that? We're not going to do that by, as I said earlier on, somehow making our  refineries more efficient and LNG plants more efficient. But we have to do it as well. We have to show that the  charity starts at home, we do the right sort of things. But it is just not going to move the needle enough.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: In the end, we have to change the makeup of our product portfolio. So that means that we'll have to introduce  more low carbon energy solutions. So therefore, renewable power, more biofuels. And also indeed, you will have  to put offsets, mitigating effects, because many of our customers will continue to use hydrocarbons well into the  second half of the century. And therefore, if you want to have a net zero energy system, society will somehow  have to find offsets for that.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And if you want to offset the emissions of a plane or the emissions of a ship or even emissions of cars that are not  electric, you will have to have things like reforestation to make it happen.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: So the main levers that we have to reduce the net carbon footprint of our energy products are just that as well.  Yeah, of course, it's more gas because gas is less carbon-intensive than oil, as of course, less heavy oil, more  light oil, et cetera.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: But again this is all marginal. It is mainly more renewable power, it is nature-based solutions, and it is more  biofuels. We think we can get there by 2050, but of course we can only get there if society as a whole gets there.  We can't do it on our own.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I've said this many times before, it sounds a bit flippant, but it is absolutely true. I cannot fill up a car with  electricity if it doesn't have a battery in it. So if our customers tend to come en masse with internal combustion  engines, that's going to be a problem if you want to have more electricity in your product output. But anyway, we  think we can get there.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Now, the ambition that we have set for 2050 is just that. We want to meet that ambition. And of course, many of  our shareholders but also many of our critics have said, why don't you make it a really high target, come what  may, you go half your net carbon footprint?

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I said, well, that's a bit unfair, because I may not be around by 2050. And secondly, you need to have a little bit of  flexibility to see how things will play out. But I'm okay to talk about targets if you talk a little bit more near term. So  we have a trajectory that we know we have to travel. And I'm quite okay to talk about what are we going to do  three years from now, five years from now.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And I'm also okay just to make sure that you really understand we mean business that I'll link my salary to that.  So this is not some sort of fancy thing that we can talk about and nobody worries what really happens in 2015  (sic) [2050] (01:35:45). No, we commit to link our remuneration through the long-term incentives program to the  reduction in net carbon footprint that we can achieve in that sort of timeframe that you typically have long-term  incentives. And that's the way we have operationalized an ambition by making hard targets.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: How does it constrain us? Well, it really doesn't. The only thing we have to do is to change the makeup of our  portfolio. It doesn't mean that I cannot sell or produce oil and gas anymore. It just means that the mix has to be  lower carbon.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And that is actually quite in line with what we want to do. We want to have a portfolio that is much more balanced.  So we have oil and gas, and we have petrochemicals, and we have power. At the moment, the oil piece is more  than two-thirds, the gas piece is more than a quarter, and chemicals and power is less than 10%.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: If you think about what the world will have to do, it will probably have to build five more electrical systems of the  same size as the one that we have built in the last 135 years. So the opportunity that is associated with that is  enormous, because we're not going to somehow subsidize four or five more of these things. There will have to be  real business behind it, otherwise, it's just not going to happen.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: I'm quite confident that Paris will be delivered, because there is a very significant societal push behind it. And if it  has to be delivered, it has to delivered through business, and I intend to fully benefit from that. Sorry, for the long  answer. [ph] Feel out? (01:37:37) There's a question from the line, isn't it?

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Integrated Gas & New Energies Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: No, there's no unusual pricing support in Oman, so the business has run well. PDO has had a very strong year in  terms of its oil production, but it captures the normal price advantage and fiscal structures that it attracts every  year. So there's not been an unusual – in the earnings...

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Integrated Gas & New Energies Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: Yeah. Well, first of all, I know that there are all sorts of speculations in the market, let me just not add or subtract  from them. There is nothing that I have to announce or to fuel or pour cold water on, other than to say we are  extremely committed to our capital discipline, and that includes inorganic investment.

texts.speaker: Maarten Wetselaar
texts.profession: Integrated Gas & New Energies Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: And there is a tremendous amount of value in that. If you look at the dislocations that's currently happened in gas  prices, which are of course massive, but also in NGLs. But even in oil, there is a tremendous amount of value  optimization that can be done by companies that are competent integrated players, have a trading and  optimization capability and visibility into how the hubs play out, can take positions around it that nobody else  have. And the Permian is I think the sort of almost archetypal play for these type of integration challenges. So  yes, absolutely, we have that as a key priority, certainly already over, 2018, and 2019 we will continue to focus on  that, because ultimately, if you don't get it right, there's just too much value that leaks away to probably somebody  but not to us.

texts.speaker: Ben van Beurden
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Royal Dutch Shell Plc
texts.text: As already hinted at, we have quite a few events coming up in the next few weeks and months. So first of all, we  have the annual LNG Outlook that is scheduled for February 25, and Maarten will be hosting that. And then as  already mentioned and filled by a few of you also, we have something to say about IFRS 16 and what it all  means. Our Group Controller will talk you through it on March 28.

I’d like to ask you, is this proposal going to go ahead? If it  does, do you know what impact it might have on your current outlook under this business plan  you’ve presented today? Thank you.

Electricity is very adaptable to the needs of our society, which has a high demand  for information and knowledge, and people are living more and more in towns and cities, which also  means that we’ve got a high concentration of energy consumption by surface units in town.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: Red Eléctrica's strategy continues to focus on operational excellence. Our key strategic initiatives are development  of the infrastructure program, establishing system investment requirements to 2016, and integration of our  recently acquired transmission assets. Another important component of our business strategy is to facilitate the  cost-effective and reliable incorporation of renewables into the generation mix and the rollout of demand in  ancillary services within the electricity system here in Spain.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: I think that it's worth highlighting that in the current economic climate, despite the company's significant  investment over the last decade, the transmission contribution to the overall cost of running the power system  continues to go down.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: Our CapEx program calls for investments totaling €4 billion for the years between 2011 and 2015. It's based on a  conservative interpretation of the investments approved in Spain's Energy Infrastructure Plan. It also includes  significant and growing investment in the non-mainland transmission grid at around about €150 million a year as  of 2012.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: At the end of 2010, the Spanish government published a revised version of its infrastructure plan for 2008 to 2016  in which it deferred certain demand contingent investments, but reiterated its annual investment spend excluding  non-mainland systems of €900 million. In 2011, the government published a first draft of the new infrastructure  plan running up to 2020. This contemplates stable investment. We expect the plan to be reviewed such that there  will be postponement of some investment projects depending on the demand and updated generation mix targets.  And we don't think this will have to modify the company's CapEx plans here in Red Eléctrica.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: 2011 marked a new milestone in uploading renewable energies to the Spanish grid. We reached 16% of total power  energy took place without in any way jeopardizing operational excellence. The government has reiterated the  2020 renewable power capacity targets, and the trend in demand allows for a – room for maneuverability in the  implementation of these facilities. To date, the government has reiterated its existing remuneration commitments  of approximately 10% with respect to capacity in 2011.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: The specific characteristics of this energy source mean that the transmission network is a vital component of its  integration into the national grid. Red Eléctrica is working on this basis. Elsewhere, the network development has  led to a significant drop in transmission losses.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: In conclusion, let me say that we plan to continue to focus all our efforts on creating value for our shareholders at  Red Eléctrica while preserving our solid capital structure and working tirelessly to guarantee high quality and  efficient power supply.

texts.speaker: QUESTION AND ANSWER SECTION
texts.profession: QUESTION AND ANSWER SECTION
texts.text: Victor Peiro Pérez  Analyst, Bankia Bolsa Sociedad de Valores SA  Q Good morning; Victor Peiro from Bankia Bolsa. Now, I'm going to break the ice with a difficult question. Can you  give us any indication of how you see regulation of the electricity sector? What changes will take place in the next  few months? I know this is a complex issue, but can you highlight what is going to affect your company the most?  Thank you.

texts.speaker: Luis Maria Atienza Serna
texts.profession: Chairman, Red Eléctrica Corp. SA
texts.text: I'll go ahead and answer that. Well, quite honestly, it's not up to me to answer for the regulator on this matter. I  mean, all I can say is that Red Eléctrica isn't a keystone in the debate about future regulations. And as you've seen  very clearly, it's not something that's contributed to the imbalances within the sector or within the economy. And  we can't really contribute to the solution, either. You've seen the contribution that transmission cost made to the  entire system. The contribution, and I underline this word, the contribution to the savings because of the  reduction in our losses is extraordinarily relevant when evaluating the importance of the investments in the  transmission grid.

texts.speaker: Jorge Alonso
texts.profession: Analyst, SG Securities Services (Spain)
texts.text: And then the last question, excuse me, has to do with your big CapEx projects. Taking into account the current  situation of renewables in Spain, do you think that there could be changes in your CapEx plans over the next few  years?

texts.speaker: Esther Maria Rituerto Martínez
texts.profession: Director General-Finance & Administration, Red Eléctrica Corp. SA
texts.text: I'll take that question, the question on the average cost of debt. For 2012, we have a hypothesis of an average debt  of 4%. And in the future, since we have covered most of our refinancing needs for 2013 and 2014, we expect rates  that are very similar to that cost. Our work in process – the work in progress that appear at the end of the year are  all investments in transmission. All of those investments will be remunerated in the future once these installations  come on stream.  Now, let me answer your question on the CapEx, the – when I said that a possible revision of the infrastructure  plan which might postpone some projects that we are contemplating to be more in line with the way demand  develops and the displacement of some of our capacity for renewables that have been installed throughout this  decade, I said I don't think that this would affect Red Eléctrica's CapEx because our investments are focused as –  from a very conservative perspective in terms of the infrastructure plan.

texts.speaker: Esther Maria Rituerto Martínez
texts.profession: Director General-Finance & Administration, Red Eléctrica Corp. SA
texts.text: As you know, investment projects in transmission are projects which have a very long life. And so, you have to  think of them as long-term projects. That means that there is a margin for revision of the infrastructure plan,  which – and if it does happen, this will not affect our investment plans here at Red Eléctrica over the last – the  next four years.

texts.speaker: A
texts.profession: So, let's go to the questions from the webcast. The first one is from Javier Suarez. And who wants to know: how
texts.text: long does the company believe it will have double-digit growth? And there's a second question and that is: if this  year, any regulatory measures have been reviewed, when do you think the government will introduce, or will  announce, its new infrastructure plan? The Minister has indicated that electricity costs are high. How can Red  Eléctrica contribute to reducing those costs?

texts.speaker: Luis Maria Atienza Serna
texts.profession: Chairman, Red Eléctrica Corp. SA
texts.text: Nonetheless, I'd like to repeat; the transmission grid throughout Europe is showing extraordinary growth in  investment because of the change in the generation mix and the speeding up in investments started here earlier,  because we were rolling out our renewable energies plan, especially with wind power, which demands a lot of  transmission capacity precisely because of the circumstances. Not because of the volatility of the input, but  because you get some more at night time than during the day, and it tends to all come in at once as well,  throughout the national territory.

texts.speaker: Luis Maria Atienza Serna
texts.profession: Chairman, Red Eléctrica Corp. SA
texts.text: So, we can't say what rate of investment we'll have in the long term. I think it will continue to be significant,  because the transmission grid is a fundamental part of the European electricity system. And the generation mix  that we're moving towards, it's part and parcel of that. So it's going to be an emerging rather than a mature  industry, which is what it's been considered to be for the last two decades. So, we haven't brought in any changes,  or rolled forward our business plan. We've kept the horizon at the end of 2015. Looking at earnings per share  throughout that period, it's over 12% a year.

texts.speaker: Luis Maria Atienza Serna
texts.profession: Chairman, Red Eléctrica Corp. SA
texts.text: And you ask about the regulatory changes? Well, nothing's really been changed for the moment. Well, certain  standards have been updated automatically, or the automatic updates, but not real changes. And as I said, we  don't know what the schedule is for rolling out the new infrastructure plan.

texts.speaker: Luis Maria Atienza Serna
texts.profession: Chairman, Red Eléctrica Corp. SA
texts.text: The high prices that you talk about, high electricity prices? Well, I'm not going to argue about pricing levels.  Throughout Europe, we're seeing a big increase in prices. And that's due to the targets established for renewable  energies, incorporating more and more renewable energy throughout Europe in other countries as well, and that  does put up the prices of the generation. But, anyway, as you've seen, if you look at the total cost for the system,  really the transmission grid is only 4.8% of the total; so the contribution of the transmission costs to any changes  in the final price to the consumer are going to be marginal.

texts.speaker: Luis Maria Atienza Serna
texts.profession: Chairman, Red Eléctrica Corp. SA
texts.text: And you can look at things on scales and say, okay, savings, which we are getting in reducing energy losses, that's  on one side. And then you have to look at the impact on the generation costs from having no grid constraints or  resist because otherwise, we put out the cost throughout the system in generation. So, we've got the transmission  costs and they contribute to bringing down the cost in the system, paradoxically, because they're reducing the  losses and they're improving the generation without any restrictions once it gets onto the grid. And you asked  about our plan after 2016, for the reasons that I've given you, looking at the generation mix and how it's going to  perform in the future.

texts.speaker: Luis Maria Atienza Serna
texts.profession: Chairman, Red Eléctrica Corp. SA
texts.text: And above all, if you look at the percentage of wind energy, which is the renewable power source that's currently  most cost-efficient as an alternative when we are looking at the CO2 emissions. Well, given the percentage of wind  power in the total mix, I think that we can expect investments to continue to be quite high. But obviously, we  should wait until the infrastructure plan is actually published, the 2012 to 2020, before we say anything about  that.

texts.speaker: Luis Maria Atienza Serna
texts.profession: Chairman, Red Eléctrica Corp. SA
texts.text: Yes, we can give you some information, but I don't know how reliable it's going to be. As I've said on many  occasions, how come? Well, our network is very meshed, which means that most of our assets, or at least a big  chunk of our investments, are multifunctional. That means that we can use them to manage the variable flows  because of our generation mix changing all the time impacted by weather conditions all the time throughout the  main part of the grid. But also, we can feed into the network for the high-speed train and help to offload bits of the  generation that's coming in from renewable energies in certain areas.

texts.speaker: Luis Maria Atienza Serna
texts.profession: Chairman, Red Eléctrica Corp. SA
texts.text: So, if you look at the transmission grid, when it so highly meshed it means you have to be very careful when  planning in it. What we do when we're planning is to look at possible bottlenecks. That's really what we're focusing  on.

texts.speaker: Luis Maria Atienza Serna
texts.profession: Chairman, Red Eléctrica Corp. SA
texts.text: What are the weak points in the grid? Under a certain scenario, with respect to the mix – the generation mix and  the demand. What we can do, however, is to allocate things for an infrastructure project which will have to be  done as a function of certain wind farms coming online or some high-speed train project. What we do is to  estimate the distribution, of course, and we say, okay, 35% of this meshed grid -- another 35% will be for  reinforcing the distribution network for transport and trains, and then we have the international link-ups as well  and we can say this amount is for offloading wind power. But we're talking about the basic infrastructure or the  ones that are functionally going to be used for offloading wind power without having to reinforce the grid in order  to bring in more wind power or anything. We can say, okay, 5.6% for combined cycles, 5% for the high-speed  train, and nearly 8% for interconnection for their cables between the islands because you know that our biggest  cable under the sea is already online in the Balearic Islands.
