texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Our strategy for the period 2016-2020 focuses on value and resilience, seeking to harness the group's increased  scale and balanced portfolio to create value even in a low oil price environment. Through increased efficiency and  flexible portfolio management, we are aiming for a more competitive and leaner company, adding value by  avoiding unnecessary complexity. We will reduce our organic free cash flow breakeven, after CapEx, dividends,  and financial costs, below $50 a barrel by the end of this plan.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: For 2016 and 2017, our objective is to divest €3.1 billion. We are not in a hurry, but we have already accomplished  €1.6 billion through the partial disposal of our Piped LPG business in Spain transaction that will be closed on cash  in 2016, the dilution of our position in Alaska and the sale of our stake in CLH. We will initially divest assets  whose value is not linked to the oil price. The aforementioned sale of part of our Piped LPG business for a multiple  close to four times EBITDA shows how Repsol keeps a wide range of assets with hidden value that can be divested  in the near term, achieving great multiples without penalizing the company ability to generate cash.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: In our Strategic Plan, we have established a $6.4 refining margin reference. I'd like to clarify that figure which has  raised some controversy among the oil and gas analysts. The base Repsol crack margin indicator used for the plan  is $2.7 per barrel, which would compare to the margin of an average European refinery. This figure is 25% lower  than the average base margin of the last 10 year cycle, where we had periods of low, medium and high margins.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Turing now to the market environment and outlook for the full year 2015. During the quarter, the weakness in oil  price together with a strong dollar continued. Brent crude prices averaged $50.5 per barrel, more than $11 lower  than the previous quarter, and less than half the average price in the third quarter of 2014.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: In relation with gas prices, they were also weak during the quarter. Henry Hub averaged $2.8 per million Btu, a  figure that compares with the $2.6 of the previous quarter and with the $4.1 seen in the third quarter 2014.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: In refining, we saw a year-on-year increase in margins from $3.9 to $8.8 per barrel due to the strengthening of the  products and light-heavy spreads. On top of the lower energy cost derived from the efforts in efficiency  undertaken in the past years, the margin premium, thanks to our refinery upgrades, has averaged $3.8 in the  quarter.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Utilization rate of the distillation capacity was 94.5% during the quarter, while conversion continues to run at full  speed. In our marketing activity, we have experienced a 1% growth in gasoline and diesel sales in service stations,  and 4% growth in the wholesale segment. Based on the current price environment, Repsol estimates CCS adjusted  net income for the full year 2015 will be in the range of €1.6 billion and €1.8 billion, with an estimated net income  in the range of €1.25 billion and €1.5 billion.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Now let me move to the third quarter 2015 earnings performance and operational highlights. Third quarter CCS  adjusted net income was €159 million, 62% lower compared with the same period of last year, and 49% lower than  in the second quarter. Operating income stood at €511 million, in line with last quarter.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Average production in the quarter stood at 653,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day. This figure is 79% higher  year-on-year, and 24% higher than in the second quarter of 2015, which includes less than two months of  production from Talisman assets. In October, daily production has averaged 685,000 barrels of oil equivalent per  day.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Year-on-year, performance excluding the impacts and results of Libya's and Talisman contribution is explained as  follows. Lower crude oil and gas realization price had a negative impact at the operating level of €464 million.  Taxes had a positive impact of €185 million due to the lower results, partially offset by the impact of the  devaluation of the local currencies, mainly in Brazil. Higher exploration expenses lead to a decrease in the  operating income of €70 million.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Turning to our Downstream division, CCS adjusted net income in the quarter was €682 million, significantly  higher than the €190 million of the third quarter of 2014, and €243 million above the result of the second quarter.  Adjusted net income for the first nine months of the year was €1.7 billion, 158% higher year-on-year. This  improvement in earnings is mainly driven by better refining and petrochemical margins and an enhanced  performance in the commercial and trading businesses, partially offset by lower results in gas and power.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Moving to gas, power and trading, these businesses increased their joint operating income by €65 million.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: With regard to Gas Natural Fenosa, the €103 million adjusted net income in third quarter of 2015 was higher  year-on-year mainly due to the contribution of CGE-Chile that offset the lower results from gas commercialization  and lower contribution from the gas and power distribution businesses in Latin America.

texts.speaker: Brendan Warn
texts.profession: BMO Capital Markets Ltd.
texts.text: Yeah. Good afternoon, and thank you. Thanks for taking my question. I'll keep it to one considering we've had the  strategy update. But I was going to say, Miguel, could you just talk through the sort of the 307,000 barrels a day  contribution from Talisman and seeing this is their first full quarter?

texts.speaker: Flora Trindade
texts.profession: Banco Português de Investimento SA (Broker)
texts.text: And then secondly, on Downstream, the performance of the Chemicals business has been outstanding. What part  of this do you believe is sustainable? So what would be a reasonable level for next year, for instance?

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: And in relation with the Downstream performance, especially in the Chemical business, I would say that  approximately 60% of the improvement comes from the market conditions and 40% is all the homework that has  been done in the business in the last, I would say, two or three years in which we have modified the structure of  the business. We have downsized it. We have changed the feedstock of the whole business, and additionally  including extraordinary measures to be energy efficient. So, I would say that 40% of the improvement is  permanent and then the rest will be on the market. Did I answer you, Flora?

texts.speaker: Filipe Rosa
texts.profession: Haitong Bank, S.A. (Broker)
texts.text: Hola. Good morning to everyone. So, three questions from me as well. The first one in terms of CapEx outlook. So,  I know that you have just done your Strategic Plan, but the Brent price continue to drop. The natural gas price in  U.S. continues to drop versus I think like three, four weeks ago.

texts.speaker: Filipe Rosa
texts.profession: Haitong Bank, S.A. (Broker)
texts.text: And my question relates to 2016, what will be your flexibility to lower your CapEx if the oil price and the Brent in  the area stay at the current level? And what could be – if you could provide some guidance for the output in 2016  and what could be the risk associated to the need to lower CapEx because that CapEx would not be profitable at –  to the current level of the Brent and the – of the area. That would be my first question.

texts.speaker: Filipe Rosa
texts.profession: Haitong Bank, S.A. (Broker)
texts.text: Sorry. But just because – but in U.S., you have some flexibility. You have some flexibility because you're saying  that you are now about breakeven if – and the oil price in Q2 was higher than – sorry, in Q3 was higher than it is  now, the area was also higher than it is now, so you'll probably lose more money if you continue to invest there. So  could you, for instance, cut your CapEx in U.S. if there is this persistently low oil and gas prices?

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: If the prices, and you are looking at scenario totally different from around the $50 we are in today, for sure, we  will modify that. But I was thinking more in this $50 oil in which we have projected our figures. But I mean you  are right in a sense that if it goes to a really low, low level, we'll take measures.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Okay. Starting with the second one. The Mayan spread has opened up to $14 and it's really, really aiming the – an  important part of the margin in this quarter. We have moved from the driving season into the, I would say, winter  season and the – I think that we are going to depend much on the temperatures for the year-end in relation with  the spread about the diesel.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Right now, the whole margin is more or less at the same level we had in the third quarter with a small reduction  during October due to the contango situation of the diesel, but it has recovered quite well. So it's difficult for me to  assess a percentage of it and I'll say an important part of it has been due to the increase in the spreads on heavy  and light, okay?

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: In relation with the drilling, Ángel is telling me that 33% of improvement in drilling costs per foot is what we have  obtained from 2014 full year to this quarter in 2015. I don't know if that's much help or not, okay?

texts.speaker: Biraj Borkhataria
texts.profession: RBC Europe Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Hi, guys. Thanks for taking my questions. I've got two. First one on the Downstream, conversion utilization  remains above 100% and has been for a few quarters now. So, I was wondering what number is baked into your  plan and how you – what number should that be on a sustainable basis going forward?

texts.speaker: Thomas Y. Adolff
texts.profession: Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Hey, thanks. Sorry, I missed your strategy update. So I do have a few questions. The LPG assets, you've got some –  you sold assets, very good valuation. Aside from those, I wondered how much more of the EBITDA you consider  non-core in the LPG business.

texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Remember that we sold in 18%. I mean the assets sold implied an 18% of the total EBITDA generate by the LPG  other than the pipeline, so I considered the rest as core business. So, we'll keep the unit the way it is without the  pipelines.

texts.speaker: Thomas Y. Adolff
texts.profession: Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Thanks. Just a good quick one on the LPG again, just to clarify. You said apart from what you've announced so far,  you're not going to sell more of the LPG business or you said there is going to be another 200,000 contracts to be  sold?

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: I will say that, yes, we are going to sell the rest of the contracts of – linked to the pipelines.

texts.speaker: Lydia R. Rainforth
texts.profession: Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: If I take out Talisman, if I just back to what you would have had just the stand-alone Repsol without Talisman. And I'm just wondering, if there's a particular area that concerns you, be it  Venezuela or one of the other areas or whether there was anything unusual during the quarter?

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: And if I have to mention areas of concern, I will say those that are more sensitive to the oil and gas prices. In that  sense, I would say Trinidad, Venezuela are areas of higher sensitivity, that Southeast Asia to say something. But,  on the quarter, I didn't foresee. I mean, if I move the figures through the operating results, I see more or less a  similar behavior from both the assets of Talisman and those of Repsol. Okay, Lydia.

texts.profession: UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Just one other follow-up if I could. So on a previous question, I think we discussed the Angolan commitment wells  at first quarter, I think you said then that the final well was at the sort of partner's discretion to drill. Is that still  the case, and is it absolutely certain that you have to drill the final well?

texts.profession: Tudor, Pickering, Holt & Co. International LLP
texts.text: All right. All right. Sorry about that. Just one question on the operational side in the Upstream in Brazil. Just  wanted to know if you can give an update on the situation at BM-C-33. So, just wanted to know about  your updated thoughts of the discovery over there and if that impacts any potential timing on the FID. That will be  it. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Taking into account the size of the project, timing is not an issue, first comment. So we'll see and we have to agree  with our partners where to go. I think that there was a lot of condensates, we're talking something like close to  200 barrels or 180 barrels per million standard cubic feet of condensate, so we don't see a major problem there.  Though it's true, your comment that the discover was gassier and we have to think of it. In front of us, we have at  least two years of appraisal before taking any final decision about Campos 33.

texts.speaker: Irene Himona
texts.profession: Société Générale SA (Broker)
texts.text: Hi, Ángel. Thank you. Miguel, I had two questions, please. Firstly, obviously, the CCS adjusted tax rate is a little  bit complicated by the effects of the currency devaluations. I just wondered if you can give us your sort of best  estimate for full year 2015 CCS adjusted tax and then perhaps for 2016, 2017 under your $50 scenario.

texts.profession: JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: Second, more a clarification, this is in relation to divestment target of €6.2 billion. Is it fair to say that you still see  potential to meet this target even under your $50 oil price scenario, given that you suggest that you'll rely on non- oil assets if oil price remains low? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: So for the rest €4 billion, I really have a – I mean, it's not that difficult to really fulfill the €6.2 billion. And if you  look at the past you will see it clearly. I mean in the last three years, for different reasons, we divest more than €10  billion, €4.5 billion in the LNG business in a good moment, and €6.3 billion from Argentina. And even without  starting the 2016-2020 period, we already have €2 billion. So I don't see any problem at all to really obtain the  extra €4 billion that are needed...  Nitin Sharma  JPMorgan Securities Plc  Q  Perfect. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: Thank you, Paul, and thank you to those online for attending this conference call on our third quarter 2016 results.  CCS adjusted net income was €307 million and €1.2 billion for the quarter and the first nine months of 2016,  respectively.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: In the third quarter, Brent crude averaged $46 per barrel, flat quarter-on-quarter, and lower than the $50 per  barrel witnessed in the third quarter of 2015. Crude oil prices fluctuated within a $40 to $50 range for much of the  quarter, with news from OPEC meeting in Algeria, helping oil price to close in September near a year-to-date  high.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: In the U.S. gas price recovered materially in this quarter. With Henry Hub averaging $2.8 per million BTU, 40%  higher than the second quarter and comparable to the third quarter of 2015. The average refining margin indicator  declined in the quarter to $5.10 per barrel versus $8.80 per barrel last year. Despite the decline in margin and  lower year-on-year commodity prices, the business generate an EBITDA of €1.1 billion in the quarter, a €130  million higher than in the third quarter of 2015, demonstrating our capacity to outperform in the lower part of the  cycle.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: Now, let's focus on the main operational highlights for the quarter. Starting with the Upstream division, production  averaged 671,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, marginally lower than the second quarter of this year, when  volumes averaged 697,000 of oil equivalent per day.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: Third quarter volumes were impacted by the cessation of production in the Varg field in Norway and by planned  maintenance mainly in Trinidad and Tobago, Malaysia and Vietnam. Production was also impacted by planned  outage in the UK and in Trinidad and Tobago due to development projects. Year-to-date, average production for  the first nine months of the year is 694,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, 36% higher than in the same period  in 2015.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: Thanks to the contribution of the acquired assets, the ramp up of Cardon in Venezuela and Sapinhoa in Brazil  and higher production in Peru. We are expecting start up of Lapa in Brazil and the ramp up of production in  Trinidad and Tobago in the fourth quarter. Average production for the full year is still forecast to reach 690,000 up  to 700,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day in line with our prior guidance.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: Moving into the Downstream division. In Refining, our margin indicator averaged $5.10 per barrel in the quarter.  Impacted by the weaker product demand and a tightening of light to heavy spreads, compared to earlier in the  year. The return of Cartagena and Tarragona refineries to full operation was planned maintenance, improved our  distillation and conversion utilization, increasing our total volumes and allowing us to generate a real CCS margin  of $5.80, a material premium to the indicator.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: Moving into financial results. Third quarter 2016 CCS adjusted net income was €307 million, a €148 million higher  than the third quarter of 2015. CCS adjusted net income year-to-date was €1.2 billion, €175 million lower than the  same period of last year, primarily due to the positive effect of exchange rate positions entered in 2015. In the  Upstream, adjusted net income for the quarter was €367 million higher than in the same period of 2015 at  negative $28 million.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: Year-on-year, third quarter variances in Upstream are primarily due to the following. Lower realized oil and gas  price, net of royalties, had a negative impact on operating income of €121 million. Lower exploration activity and  lower amortization of dry wells increased operating income by €157 million, excluding the impact of exchange rate  movements. Third quarter results include the write-off of two wells that were previously under evaluation. Lower  depreciation amortization charges principally as a consequence of a lower amortization rate in North America  increased operating income by €88 million.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: Third quarter balances in the Downstream are primarily due to the following: in Refining, lower margins and lower  utilization rates reduced operating income by €289 million. This was due to narrower middle distillates, gasoline  and light-heavy crude spreads, partially offset by the lower energy costs.

texts.speaker: Haythem M. Rashed
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: And then secondly, I just wonder if you could provide us an update with your recent discussions with the rating  agencies, whether given the delivery time you have so far, given where the environment is, how comfortable they  are with your plans, whether there are additional requirements here? How are you thinking about your different  financing options to hybrid debt? Are there any other sort of further measures that you might want to think about  taking? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Jason S. Kenney
texts.profession: Analyst, Banco Santander SA (London Branch)
texts.text: Good morning. Well, good afternoon, sorry. Are you able to comment on the Black Sea oil discovery offshore  Bulgaria at all? And by the way, I was looking some guidance on the possible exploration effects going into the  year-end where what do we got left to look for from exploration?

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: Well, in relation with the discovery in the Black Sea in Bulgaria, it's definitely an oil and gas discovery, is an  Oligocene play, it's commerciality has not been proven and we need to appraise as to really know where we are.  In relation with the second question, about the guidance for exploration in the year-end, I think we're not going to  be really much impacted at that limit. I would say, $120 million, $140 million would be the figure of the impact in  P&L. And all year round, it's going to be around $700 million what we have been invested in 2016 for the  exploration.

texts.speaker: Bruno Almeida da Silva
texts.profession: Analyst, Banco Português de Investimento SA (Broker)
texts.text: Hello. Good morning. I have just two small questions pending. The first one, and I'm not sure, if Miguel has  addressed this or not, I couldn't hear. Regarding the gas realization price discount, it has widened significantly. I  don't know if you could enumerate the key drivers for this evolution and what would be a reasonable estimate for  the coming quarters?

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: In relation with the first question, Gas Natural – gas price realization, I have the same question when I look at  other figures because Henry Hub was moving up and our realization price was going down. The point there has  been that despite a positive impact of basically Marcellus of $0.2 per million BTU, there has been an adjustment  in Trinidad and Tobago, prices coming from prior periods that has penalized the realization price of our gas in 0.3  – $0.30 cents per million BTU. So on average despite having a better scenario, our price realization, finally price  has been lower due to this adjustment made in Trinidad and Tobago.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: Estimate gas realization price for the next quarters, I think that we have to go along with the split we have,  basically 33% for gas is linked to the Henry Hub and the rest 20%s and 25%, respectively are linked to oil price  and to fixed price. So it's going to be aligned with the evolution of the barrel in one hand, 25% ,and the Henry Hub  in the other, 33%. Is that okay, Bruno?

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: That's correct. I mean we have adjusted – it's an adjustment one-off in the third quarter, due to previous  discussion about prices of our gas there, okay?

texts.speaker: Thomas Adolff
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And in relation with the KPIs, you know the profile of our COO. So he is going to keep pushing, pushing and  tighten the objectives for next year, no doubt on that. CapEx reduction, I'd say partially it's a CapEx reduction by  itself. And partially it's also a lack or a delay in some of the programs. I mean for the future, we have three basic  large projects which are [ph] Campos, Sacarias (44:11) and Alaska. And we are going to lay those, steal the  moment in which we feel that the price deck is sustainable enough to return good returns to our shareholders.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: The first one is that our growth has come a) because of the acquisition of Talisman, we have doubled our size.  And I will say second, if you remember the 10 projects for former Repsol, they are either full invested or almost as  Lapa that will come on-stream by the end of this year and Reggane that will produce their first gas next year.

texts.speaker: Alastair R. Syme
texts.profession: Analyst, Citigroup Global Markets Ltd.
texts.text: Hi, Paul and Miguel. Thanks very much. Can you talk a little bit about decommissioning, because you have quite  a lot coming ahead of you. You took a €28 million post-tax charge on Varg and Yme this quarter. I mean just to  confirm that, that's closure cost rather than decommissioning cost. Are we going to [ph] see that the closure cost  regulates through (01:00:36) business in the coming periods? And I guess also related to that, as you go out into  the market and get bids on the decommissioning of these asset, are they in line with what you provisioned in  aggregate?

texts.profession: Analyst, Macquarie Capital (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Yeah, good afternoon. Thanks for taking my question. I have three questions. One, Miguel, again on production  for 2017, so you can't give an indication of where you see production because you are still waiting to see the  CapEx projection for North America. If we assume that rig count stays flat there, it's where we – and assuming no  further divestments, where do you see production for 2017 going? Second question is when I look at Upstream,  Europe operating profits, it's higher than the reported EBITDA, just trying to reconcile there what type of FX you  have had impacting? Third one is on Latin America. You had quite a big drop in your profitability there in  Upstream. Just wondering if it's entirely related to reduction in gas prices, was there on other items we should  consider? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA

So this is the other factor that has reduced the results in  LatAm. Okay?

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: Let me now go into detail in the main operational highlights for the quarter. At the macro level, we saw an  improving trend in oil prices that continue to build on the recovery experienced by the sector during the year.  However, this was partially offset by weaker U.S. dollar. The disruptions caused by Hurricane Harvey in Gulf of  Mexico had a significant impact on production and refining capacity in the region, resulted in inflated global  refining margins for part of the quarter.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: In the Upstream division, production averaged 693,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, a 2% increase quarter- on-quarter. Up to September, accumulated production has averaged 688,000 BOEs per day. Quarterly volumes  were positively impacted by the ramp-up of new projects, higher production in Libya and the normalization of gas  sales in Indonesia. Production in Libya averaged around 25,000 net barrels per day, despite being interrupted for  17 days in the quarter. Accumulated volumes in Libya to September have averaged around 23,000 barrels per  day, net to Repsol.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: Flyndre and MonArb in the UK North Sea reached an average production of 7,000 net barrels a day in the  quarter. In Trinidad and Tobago, Juniper achieved first gas in August, as expected providing an additional 5,000  boes of net average production during the third quarter. Kinabalu in Malaysia delivered first production late in  October. Development work continue at Sagari in Peru and we expect to achieve first production later in this  quarter. We now expect Reggane in Algeria to start production around year end.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: In total, the sum of MonArb, Juniper, Kinabalu, Sagari and Reggane will more than offset anticipated natural  decline over the next 12 months. Development work has continued at Red Emperor in Vietnam and Buckskin in  Gulf of Mexico, following the FID's taking earlier this year. Both projects have a breakeven below $50 a barrel and  are expected to start production in 2019.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: Now, continuing with the Downstream, good performance across all business lines, delivered another quarter of  strong cash flow generation. In Refining, our margin indicator averaged $7, supported by strong middle distillates  and gasoline spreads, steady demand and the positive impact from capacity disruptions across other operators.  Completing all of our major planned maintenance in the first half of the year has allowed us to run our refineries at  very high distillation and conversion factors, thereby benefiting from the positive environment during the quarter.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: Moving now on to the financial results, I will briefly summarize the principal outcomes for the quarter. Third  quarter 2017 CCS adjusted net income was €576 million, €269 million higher than in the same period of 2016.  The EBITDA CCS stood at €1.6 billion, an increase of more than €400 million year-on-year.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: In the Downstream, CCS adjusted net income was €502 million, €107 million higher than in the third quarter of  2016, principally due to better margins and higher utilization, together with better results in Chemical (sic)  [Chemicals], Trading, Marketing and LPGs.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: Let me now finish with some thoughts on guidance for full-year results. Starting with our efficiency and synergy  program by the end of the year we expect to fully deliver our €2.1 billion target of final cash savings accelerated  by one full year, our original objective for the end of 2018. The acceleration of our efficiency program, together  with the higher margin barrels coming on stream is allowing us to continue reducing our cost base and lower the  overall breakeven of the Upstream portfolio. In fact, the breakeven for Upstream in the first nine months of 2017  dipped below $60 per barrel. We expect that lower investment needs, supported by more effective optimization  and overall lower cost will allow us to reduce our full-year group CapEx to around €3 billion, without impacting  production volumes over the coming years.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: Considering accumulated production to-date, we expect to end 2017 with an average production of around  690,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, subject to fluctuations in Libya.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: Up to September, the accumulated refining indicator has averaged $6.8 per barrel, well above our long-term  target of $6.4.

texts.speaker: Flora Trindade
texts.profession: Analyst, Banco Português de Investimento SA
texts.text: And then just a small question on something that was in the press in Spain mentioning that you are studying  investments in renewables on top of the OGCI funds that you are investing. So can you tell us just what kind of  investments are you looking at? Thank you very much.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: And in relation with your third question, renewable. I'll have to say that I think that right now all the industries  looking at which to transition to a lower carbon emissions world would be. Probably, we were the first company  that has the concepts of energy, not only the concept of oil company; and in that sense I may remember that we  have been in Gaznat for more than 20 years, which was always an optionality to whether or not we should move.  Other than that, we are involved in a net throughout Spain of electric charge in our service stations. We are  working also in a project on batteries for motorcycles in Catalonia. We are also investing in floating windmills in  Portugal. So, we have always been around there. So, basically I'd say it's part of a game that we have been in for  20 years. It's only that probably others have been moving lately and with more noise than ours, but basically it's it.  I think it's continuity in our concern about the carbonation. Did I answer you, Flora?

texts.speaker: Thomas Adolff
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Secondly, just on your Upstream portfolios. Obviously, it's kind of young in nature today and also more gassy,  therefore your portfolio decline rate today is quite low. And I wondered at what point do you expect decline rates  to accelerate from today's portfolio which then obviously will require to invest a little bit more or do you see many  new tie-back opportunities that actually can keep the portfolio decline rate at current rates for many years to come

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: In relation with the second question, it's true that our Upstream portfolio, it's – our production is two-thirds is gassy  and our reserves are three quarter gassy, so decline rate is lower than probably other companies. And right now  with the data I have, I may say that till 2021, 2022 and without any of the five largest projects would be able to  keep the production a little above the 700,000 barrels a day. This is what I can tell you. So, we are quite confident  and more focused on value per barrel than number of barrels. Also think that we are – I mean, two years ago, we  were a company of 320,000 barrels a day of production; so somehow, the growth has been there and right now  with a CapEx figure between €3 billion for the whole company or €3.5 billion, would be able to keep that  production steady around 700,000 BOE per day.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: In relation with the – and it's becoming almost popular, the [ph] AC/DC plus 1 (24:40) which is Sagitario. I would  say that the first oil, first gas – well, in CP-9, we are already producing, but the new project probably will reach  plateau and show its strength by 2021.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: Alaska. Well, probably, by the end of 2022-2023, would be the year in which Alaska will deliver their first oil.  Campos 33 will come a year later, probably by 2024 and finally Sagitario the day after; so basically the run [ph] is  to already (25:35) producing that will be ramping up shortly; and then Alaska, 2022-2023, Campos 33 in 2024,  and finally Sagitario by 2025. Okay, Brendan?

texts.speaker: Hamish Clegg
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: My second question is, I wondered if you could tell us a little bit more about your new partner in Alaska,  Nanushuk, who kind of been suggesting to the market its breakeven oil price of around $45. Could you tell us  what's being done on the block to kind of establish some slightly better economics?

texts.speaker: Biraj Borkhataria
texts.profession: Analyst, RBC Europe Ltd.
texts.text: Hi. Thanks for taking my questions. I have two, please. Just to follow-up on the CapEx and you're running well  below the previous guidance and you've obviously reduced that. Can you talk about – can you just give a bit more  detail about what is driving that reduction and how investors can be assured that you're not necessarily under  investing in the Upstream business?

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: Right now, we have 13 exploratory wells ongoing. So, it's that we reduced from the €3.6 billion initial figure to this  €3 billion that could end €3 billion, €3.1 billion, but most of this reduction has been achieved through cost savings.

texts.speaker: Lydia Rainforth
texts.profession: Analyst, Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Hi, Paul and good afternoon. A couple of questions, if I could? The first one, just on the cost savings.  [indiscernible] (32:06) been doing very well on that. I mean, do you think that continues into next year now or is it  pretty much everything you wanted to be done on that? And then the second one, was just on the Refining  business, which obviously did very well this quarter. Those conversion rates of 104% utilization and distillation  utilization of 99%, is that really this maximum that you can get to in any given quarter?

texts.speaker: Anish Kapadia
texts.profession: Analyst, Tudor, Pickering, Holt & Co. International LLP
texts.text: Hi, good afternoon. The first question was – I was wondering if you can give some idea of any potential negative  impact for oil prices increasing from $50 to $60 on the Downstream? I assume you have some negative impacts  from higher energy prices and feedstock prices, and then some impact on the marketing margin. So if you could  kind of just give us some idea of a sensitivity of any negative impacts you've seen from that higher oil price from  the Downstream.

texts.speaker: Anish Kapadia
texts.profession: Analyst, Tudor, Pickering, Holt & Co. International LLP
texts.text: And then the second question was, I was wondering if you can kind of give some idea of the contribution from a  kind of earnings cash flow standpoint of Bolivia? And the reason I ask is you've seen Argentina talk about  becoming self-sufficient for gas towards the end of the decade. Brazil's got a large amount of gas production  coming through from the Brazilian pre-salt. So, it seems like there's some risk that Bolivian gas exports will have  to fall at the end of the decade and beyond which might impact your exports. So, just wondering kind of your  opinion on that, and then if you can give some idea of your exposure? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: Well, to the first one. Well, it's not precisely a positive approach. I mean negative impact of an increase on Brent  prices – I mean I would love increasing Brent prices as a base, okay? Negative impacts? For sure, there would be  some but would be minor in comparison with the advantage of having higher prices. For sure, cost base will  increase with some lag but the service companies will increase price, because the sector will increase the drilling  and will increase the activity. And in relation with the Downstream, probably chemicals which is the most anti- cyclical business we have with the Upstream will be the one that suffers.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: So, basically I would say it's positive. But it will have some minor, counterparts, which are basically cost increases  and some impact in the Chemicals, but I don't see more than that if Brent prices goes up. And in relation with  Bolivia, I'll say that Argentina – let me, Argentina is a country that is absolutely gasified and that gas consumption  is really high, so I don't see the first, the hypotheses of Argentina exporting gas or being self-sufficient is going to  happen at least in the short-term. So I think that the impacts that we have suffered this year comes more from El  Nino the year – the hydraulic year in Brazil, which has been really good and this has reduced the number of  exports from Bolivia to Brazil. But other than that, I don't see short-term an issue being Argentina self-sufficient.

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol SA
texts.text: A different thing is the cash generation. And in relation with Chemicals, I think that earnings moving next year is  going to be absolutely linked to the oil price, I mean in a reverse situation. If the barrel really moves up, for sure  Chemicals will have some pain. But having said so, EBIT would be between €500 – around €500 million next year  with the data we have today in $59, $60 scenario. For sure if the conditions change, the Chemicals would be  affected. But as of today, the figure should be around €500 million EBIT level.

texts.speaker: Tristan de Jerphanion
texts.profession: Analyst, Kepler Cheuvreux SA
texts.text: Secondly, on CapEx, you said €3.5 billion would be a sustainable run rate in the medium-term. Could you please  give us a bit of details regarding the Downstream run rate CapEx for 2018 and beyond?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Let me recap on this. In upstream, production and reserve figures were both in line with our plans  targets. Our production recorded 3% organic growth, with a better production mix, reaching 42% in  liquids versus 40% in 2009. Reserve replacement ratio for the year achieved 131%, almost all  organic.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In downstream, we continued to make progress toward the start-up of the Cartagena and Bilbao  refining projects, set to come onstream in fourth quarter ‘11. At year-end we had to spend 71% of  the total investment budget. Both projects continue to be on track and will be onstream below  budget. In YPF, local prices for liquids continued its strength towards international parity. Dollar  increases reached 14% in gasoline, and 19% in diesel over the year.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Moreover, we proved that oil decline could be contained with the right economics in place. Even  though BOE productions declined 5.4%, it was only 1.6% in crude oil, versus more than 5% in the  previous year. These two improvements in product prices and oil volumes explain how what we call  the hidden value is flourishing and positively impacting our profit and loss account book.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In addition to these wells, we also achieved good results in the deeper formation at the current  producing structure in Rio Grande, Bolivia. That could haul 1 Tcf and which could be developed  rapidly since the facilities are already in place. We also continue with our seismic intensive  campaign and are adding exploration acreage in the Gulf of Mexico, Norway, Canada, Indonesia  and Peru.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: At the beginning of 2011, we were also awarded three exploration licenses in Angola. Regarding  our upstream development operations, let me share with you the status of the different projects. In  Brazil, further discoveries were made in 2010. We reported to the E&P, the presence of  hydrocarbons at Creal B within the Albacora Leste block in Brazil deep offshore Campos Basin.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In Peru, we continue with the appraisal activities in the Kinteroni field. In January 2011, Kinteroni-2  proved positive and large, the initial resource estimations. A second appraisal well, which is  scheduled, busier, and progress is being made, so that the first gas production comes onstream in  2012 as originally planned.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The award of Carabobo in Venezuela is a strategically important, since the access to this large  reserve was secured, heavy oil supply for our Spanish refining system. The project is progressing  as expected and the consortium is working on a plan to accelerate production in this scenario.       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 3 The first oil from this field could be onstream in 2013.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Also in Venezuela, the Ministry of Energy & Petroleum approved the Carbon IV Appraisal Plan.  Perla 2 and 3 wells were drilled in 2010 and Perla 4 also proved positive and extended the field  north.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Recoverable resources are estimated at 9 Tcf, although after this well, further upside is expected.  The first gas production will come onstream in 2014. In Bolivia, the Final Investment Decision for  the first phase of the Margarita project was made in 2010. Incremental volume production will be  exported to Argentina at a price linked to oil prices. The first gas output of Phase 1 remains to come  onstream in 2012.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In the Gulf of Mexico, the drilling of Buckskin-2 appraisal well was suspended after having drilled  125 meters. The resumption of Buckskin drilling has not been authorized yet, despite the fact that  the moratorium was lifted in October. In Shenzi, we were able to restart drilling operations, but only  for water injection. We believe that Shenzi’s average production through this year will be slightly  below to that of fourth quarter 2010, due to the delay of planned development wells. In the  meantime, we are contemplating our review of operating procedures and management system to  comply with the new legal framework. On February 8, we presented the first exploration plan to the  authorities.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: So in regard to LNG, Peru LNG, the second of our growth projects in this business line successfully  started operations in the month of June. Since then and until December, 20 cargos were shipped  from the liquefaction plant to different locations. As a consequence, Repsol’s LNG volumes  narrowly increased. Repsol and Kogas had recently signed an LNG supply agreement that will  involve the shipment of 1.9 bcm of gas equivalent to Korea. We will ship the LNG from the Peru  LNG terminal where we have the entire offtake rights. Also, Repsol’s role as an LNG supplier to  Argentina continued, providing a total 8 cargoes during the year.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: At YPF, on top of the two drivers, pump prices moving to import parity, and crude oil decline  mitigation. I would like to highlight from the operational standpoint, two significant events that  supported the progress achieved in Argentina. On the one hand, the reserve replacement ratio has  been the highest in recent years, with oil replacement fuel reaching 100%, due to the effort aimed  at improving the recovery factor.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: A one point of increase in the crude oil recovery factor implies around 250 million barrels more than  2.5 years at current production level. On the other hand, the progress achieved in relation to non- conventional resources, let me elaborate on this topic. On the tight gas side we concluded a four- well program that enable us to access a 4.5 TCF reserve base in Loma La Lata field. We are  developing the first phase, based on a contract signed with Vale do Rio Doce. Vale will initially  invest up to US$150 million, and will have the right to receive sharing operating costs, 50% of the  1.6 million cubic meters a day estimated production.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: On shale oil and gas, we have drilled several vertical wells as part of the exploration work to prove  the existence of this type of resources in the Neuquén Province.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The three fracture wells reveled that the Vaca Muerta formation presents similar conditions to shale  oil and gas of those found in Bakken and Eagle Ford Basins in the United States. We are currently  drilling a horizontal well to gather additional data and evaluate final potential of our production well,  while estimating final recovery. The records obtained in the drilled wells make us optimistic and the  progress achieved is encouraging.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: All the drilled wells have been vertical ones so far and production levels under natural flow. We will  start another well this week. To finish with unconventional reserve potential in Argentina, in late  November we were awarded the 13 available licenses in the Neuquen Province tender round. The  interest of their formation potential in the area was confirmed by the fact that some of the major  players in the sector, Total, Apache, Exxon, et cetera joined us in all the areas.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Net income, including inventory effects and non-recurring items reached €4.7 billion, mainly due to  the Sinopec transaction. CCS-adjusted net income was €2 billion, 57% higher than 2009, while  fourth quarter was €499 million, 107% higher.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In 2010, we reached a CCS-adjusted operating income of €4.7 billion, 71% higher than the year  before, while fourth quarter reached €1 billion, 41% higher year-on-year. The improvement in our  variables explained the good performance, both for the quarter and for the year as a whole,  compared to last year, higher international oil and gas references, a stronger dollar against the  euro, superior integrated refining and marketing margins, better results in the chemical segment  and an overall improvement in Argentina.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Let me go now into the main effects in fourth quarter and 2010 results business-by-business. In  upstream, adjusted operating income was €361 million versus €225 million in the same quarter  2009. The increase in our oil realization prices has been inline with the increasing conventional  references. Furthermore, our gas realization prices in the year increased 17% more than the 10%  increase of Henry Hub prices. These had a positive €122 million impact on operating results year- on-year. At the full year level, reaching almost €1.5 billion upstream-adjusted operating income,  was 67% higher than the €884 million posted last year, mainly as a consequence of higher average  oil and gas prices and higher volumes.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Moving to LNG, enhanced performance was mainly driven by higher LNG margins and volumes  following the start-up of Peru LNG. In the downstream business, CCS-adjusted operating income  was €164 million in the quarter, 73% up year-on-year.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: For the entire year, CCS-adjusted operating income in the downstream business as a whole  reached €977 million, 51% higher than a year ago, mainly explained by the higher refining margins  due to the wider spreads in light and the heavy crudes, and in medium distillates, as well as rate of  recovery shown in the Chemical business.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Moving on to YPF, adjusted operating income in the quarter was €371 million, higher than the €331  million posted in fourth quarter 2009. The most significant variations continue to be driven by higher  domestic prices in dollar terms and higher international prices. Higher gas volumes and prices,  particularly in the Industrial segment also had a positive impact on operating income.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In Gas Natural, operating income in the quarter was 60% higher than in the same period in 2009.  The increase is mainly attributable to the cold weather in Spain in fourth quarter, the better results  of the power distribution businesses in Spain and the greater contribution of Latin America gas  distribution activities.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: For the full year, adjusted operating income at Gas Natural was €849 million, in comparison with  €745 million posted a year earlier. The 14% rise is mainly due to the inclusion of 100% of Unión  FENOSA’s results as of 30 April 2009 in the results of Gas Natural SDG.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In Perla, after drilling three wells we have exceeded size original. The increase in size will mean  higher total investments, but lower on a per barrel basis. The ministry has assigned a US$3.69 per  million Btu price, securing a good return on our investment. We have also great expectations on  Guara, where the consortium has already contracted the FPSO and the project remains on  schedule to be onstream in early 2013. We also added two projects not forecasted in last year  presentation.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: First, our Albacora Leste Deep or Creal B discovery, a project that will be adding production during  the strategic period since tests will be performed in 2013, 2014. Second, the 2009 Lubina  Montananzo discovery in the Spanish waters was a new corporation. Despite the real size it is a  very profitable project due to oil quality, existing facilities and the physical framework in Spain. We  are currently in the process of obtaining authorizations.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Therefore, I can assume that the regional production targets of 3% to 4% compounded average  growth per annum for the period 2010, 2014, and reserve replacement ratio greater than 110%  could be achieved, despite the dilution of our 40% stake in our Brazilian subsidiary. Looking ahead,  consolidating our LNG position is just a matter of doing what we know best, applying operational  efficiency and optimizing to these assets. To achieve these goals, we will leverage our trading and  marketing strength, the quality of our assets, our know-how, [inaudible] to give us privileged access  to premium markets, Korea and Mexico. Flexibility is the key regarding LNG and we could benefit  from our position as a global operator and privileged market access.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Our main goal in the downstream business is to finish the projects on time and consolidate our  leadership position by marketing the regional upcoming volume from these investments. A  continued recovery in macro conditions and the widening of the differentials will support the start-up  of these projects. And our current refining margin conditions with these projects onstream had  increased the company-refining margin by $2 per barrel. The three targets for the business stated  in our strategic update remain in place; increasing distillation capacity, improved the middle  distillate yield by 25% and then increase the Conversion Index by 47%. The conversion projects will  enhance Repsol’s position in the European downstream. Once the two projects come onstream, we  will run first position in the European Union in middle distillate yields. Therefore, the downstream  business will be a net cash generator and will support the growth of the company.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In Argentina, strategically speaking, we will focus on the one hand on non-conventional resources  and on the order on conventional crude oil production by further improving in the recovery factor,  while managing the P&L and cash generation. Provided that we have achieved a sound financial  position, and we are now more comfortable to face next capital requirements, we could consider  Gas Natural as a long-term value. Not only this investment provides a good dividend yield, but also  enhances our energy business through the synergies between the two companies.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Regarding new energies, we are working now on the development of the business unit and  strategic plan based on five potential areas: bioenergy, renewable generation, mobility, CO2 and  energy efficiency. We will keep a smooth, but continued pace, investing in research and becoming  involved in risk control projects. Although we believe that the challenges we face in 2010 will  remain in place in 2011, this will be softened by the continued global recovery.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In relation with our CapEx plan, we plan to invest ex-Gas Natural, around €6 billion in 2011.  Corporate tax in 2011 is estimated at around 41% and the final figure will depend on the evolution  of macro variables and the performance in the different business and companies where we  operate.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The second question, going back to North Africa, the impact you have already mentioned and also  considering your subsidiary issues with Sonatrach, you have also mentioned that in the case of  Gas Nat is now perceived as a long-term investments, considering the synergies in LNG. My  question is actually trying to understand, after diluting your provision in Brazil for the reasons you  presented at the time, if Gas Nat is perceived as a priority project for yourself and therefore you  would never sell it and would rather prefer continue to dilute your exposure in some areas of the  E&P business?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In relation with your second question about Gas Nat, Sonatrach in North Africa, we are not saying  that we will never sell Gas Nat. What I’m saying is that Gas Nat is a good stake for us. We don’t  have a financial operation today. It’s good to think that we keep that, the stake, that can be liquid in  a very short period of time, but at the same time since we don’t need it, it could add a lot of value to  us in terms of LNG, in terms of couple of synergies et cetera, et cetera.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And lastly, which is my main concern today is in LPG. You know that the Spanish authorities  changed by the end of 2009, the way to price LPG, the regulated LPG, based on a formula that in a  growing market, in a growing raw materials market, kill the profits and therefore now we are just  having, that we have gone to the core, we have asked everyone to change their formula, because  in a continuous trend of the world, moving up the price of oil and therefore the price of propane and  butane we will suffer in LPG. And that’s not what we want. It’s a regulated business. By law, we  have to be regulated for being in the regulated business. And I think that sooner than later, we will  have to see a change in the ruling. But this quarter, because of the increase in the price of the  propane and butane, we have to suffer. These are minor reasons that all of them added makes a  [inaudible] your conclusion.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Anish Kapadia>: Hi, good afternoon. I’ve got three questions, if I can. Firstly, just on your  balance sheet, it looks quite comfortable at the moment. The question is what you can look to do  with your cash that you generate over the next few years, and are you going to look to go back to a  10% per annum increase in the dividend or are you going to look at acquisitions? And secondly, on  the LNG side of the business, can you give some guidance in terms of your earnings at 2011? So it  appears like you are buying gas from Peru at Henry Hub pricing, this is all uncontracted. So you got  the ability to sell this at spot gas prices, which are significantly higher. Can you just give some idea  of what that means for your earnings this year?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Anish Kapadia>: Just one clarification on that. So if current spot LNG prices stay where they  are, what’s the upside to that forecast?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Antonio Brufau Niubó>: Okay. Henry Hub for us is not critical. I mean that we have a  netback. In case of Manzanillo, in 2012, would be the formula give us, I will – I don’t remember  exactly $0.60 of dollar after paying everything. Therefore, two-thirds of the production will go to  Manzanillo. Obviously, the formula is linked to Henry Hub, but for us it seems $0.60 per million Btu.  2011, we will not go to Henry Hub. Obviously, we’ll go to Korea, we go to Spain, we go to Europe,  we’ll go to the Toulon, to the UK, and to Argentina. Remember, in Argentina, they are paying -- not  Henry Hub, they are paying $9, $10 per million Btu through the LNG floating terminals. Therefore  we try to move around the world and forget about Henry Hub. Henry Hub is a nightmare for us. And  we don’t like Henry Hub.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Irene Himona>: Good afternoon. I had three questions please. So first, Libya, can you please  clarify how much of the 3% to 4% targeted production growth rates in the upstream is Libya? In  other words, if we assume zero, what happens to that 3% to 4%? Secondly, in your five-year plans  to 2014, given your scenario on oil and gas prices, what dividend growth rate can we anticipate and  what do you think you can afford? Are we looking at double-digit growth rates? And my third  question concerns costs and YPF. You present on slide 13, for example, the reduced decline rates  of YPF output, but then equally, if I look at YPF upstream CapEx in 2010 it was up 57% year-on- year. With cost inflation in the country, have you got any particular initiatives to control cost, any  particular targets and what happens to your spending as we progress through the next few years?  Thank you.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In connection with -- in relation with the oil and gas prices and the volatility we see today and  obviously that’s impacting our P&L and therefore having an impact in our dividend policy. Today,  maybe it’s the worst day in this year, to answer this question, now, because from 8’O clock in the  morning to tonight, I don’t know how many dollars per barrel we have bid. $7 per barrel no, and  tomorrow I don’t know what’s going to happen. Let say that this year it’s very important for us to be  very prudent, very – we’ve got very strong discipline, financial talking.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Obviously, if we add Gas Nat, I was thinking, Gas Nat is 6.5. For the next few years I think that it  will move between 6 and 7 provided that the downstream CapEx will be significantly reduced to the  levels of €0.5 billion. Therefore, we will free something like €1 billion of downstream CapEx to  finance upstream CapEx.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In Argentina, you may be surprised with this level of CapEx, but Argentina is CapEx and reward. I  mean the payback of this CapEx, and we have proven that this year, 2010, is that investing in new  drillings, enhancing oil recoveries et cetera, the tight and the shale gas, all the exploration, all the  drilling activities that we have in Argentina will give an immediate reward in terms of reduction in the  declining ratios, increasing production et cetera, et cetera.       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – James Hubbard>: Thanks. Just two questions please. You mentioned the slide $200 to $400  a day coming from – in oil coming from these tight reservoirs in the Mexican Basin. I’m wondering  what are your plans to -- I’m assuming that’s inherently more attractive than the 4.5 Tcf of tight gas,  just given the local oil prices on a like-to-like basis so much higher. So what are your plans to  appraise and develop these types of oil horizons? It sounds like you have only done vertical wells  so far, so I assume you are going to try horizontal and I assume you are going to try to fracture it.  So, yeah, what is the outlook there, what is your plan?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Antonio Brufau Niubó>: Okay, the first question of Shell oil or Shell Gas Company with tight  gas. In Shell Oil, we are planning now to drill something like 20 wells. Shell Oil, 20 wells, this year  and the year to come. I mean in 2011, 2012, in order to value, to assess the Guara, and we see a  tremendous potential and the results are very good. Still now we are just doing vertical drills and we  haven’t started with horizon drilling. Therefore, we are very optimistic. And all the other majors       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 14 there, all the other companies are going there together with us. We see a tremendous potential. But  one thing about tight gas. Tight gas by itself is not good, because you cannot get [inaudible], but if  you do a deal, like our case, through [inaudible] with Vale do Rio Doce, that’s a good business, I  mean because Vale is paying for the first $150 million of investment, of CapEx. Then thanks to that.  And after that investing half and half, paying $7 per barrel of million Btu and then going together.  Why are they are keeping 50% of their production and thus selling to Vale at that price, the  remaining 50% production. Therefore, I’m not too sure this is not a good business, tight gas,  although, obviously, we see more and more in the shorter, in a closer manner, the shale oil  production, because we see the results and they are very, very good as of today.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Daniel Ekstein>: Thanks. A couple of questions, both on Argentina actually. Firstly, on the  Petróleo Plus, which seems to have made a fairly material contribution to YPF’s earnings this year.  It looks achieving the baseline of 250,000 barrels a day of oil in ‘11, could be difficult. Are you going  to be able to renegotiate the baseline, I would say, at a lower level? And do we need to worry about  the sustainability of that part of white gas profitability? And secondly, this is a difficult question, I  know, we’ve got the Argentina final elections coming up in October. And I’m just wondering what  you guys are thinking about how this could impact the process of price liberalization in that country?  And could you elaborate on your hopes and fears, I suppose? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Antonio Brufau Niubó>: Okay in relation with Petróleo Plus, which we agree with you, it has  made a very good contribution to our P&L. We have a different point of view, this strike that we  suffer, last quarter, will damage us. No way. And to restart at the same level of production is  something that we are not so sure that’s going to happen. Therefore, I think that we have doubts,  personally have doubts, that we will be able to get the first quarter Petróleo Plus subsidy. We’re  sure that we are going to work to get the second, third and fourth quarter. First quarter will be  difficult, and we’ll do our best in order to get the second quarter. But having said so, I mean that  even if we don’t get the Petróleo Plus this semester, the first semester, the P&L of Argentina looks  very good, by the way. They got price increases et cetera, are huge. Obviously, Argentina is  suffering elections in October and all of us suffer elections, but in Argentina you have elections  every year. And every year those elections become the most important elections for their country.  It’s the same in Spain or in U.S. et cetera, but I don’t think that the authorities today in Argentina  are not aware of the need to clarify prices. I don’t think so. I mean, it could be the reality three or  four years ago. But today, they know for sure that the best thing they can do to have a very good  energy sector is to have prices at the level to make CapEx and investments to appear, and in my  opinion, some prices will increase. Gas prices will increase, not at the level of the distribution at the  retail level, but at the level of the power plants, industries, et cetera. And that’s life. I mean it’s  nothing to do with price. I mean it’s a country that is breakeven today that we have to import natural  gas, we have import products, we have to import crude, and therefore, playing with prices it’s not  anymore the game and the authorities are very serious today, in my opinion, and I have discussed  a lot of time with them, they need to clarify the whole situation and the reaction that they get from  them is always a very serious reaction and a very positive reaction. It’s just a matter of time.

I mean, right now in relation with this Petróleo Plus program, the total situation we had  when the government and the Energy Department of Argentina modified a ruling was that we have $105 million of  grants that were already accepted by the government and signed by the Energy Department. Apart from those, we  have $170 million that we have presented the papers to the administration, but was pending on their approvals,  okay? Both were receivables and the $170 million with the announcement they made, they decided that they were  not going to sign any more grants. So, we have to write it off. That's $170 million.

texts.speaker: Daniel Ekstein
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: From the other $105 million, there was a note sent by the Ministerio de Planificación Federal, Inversión Pública y  Servicios signed by the Secretary of Energy in Buenos Aires the 6th of February in which in the last paragraph,  they indicate that those grants that were authorized priorly will be perfectly valid. So, we have basically write-off  all the grants we deserve, but were not signed by the government, $117 million. Okay?

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol YPF SA
texts.text: Thomas, well, basically in relation with the U.S.A. production, mill is included in the guide we gave you for 2012,  okay? In relation with the second one, you are totally right. I mean, the destruction of demand is being massive in  future and we think that after 20% fall in demand in the last four years. We have still a way down move. Well, at a  given moment for sure, we'll be exporting. But I think that we already have suffered the most of the crisis over  here in relation with diesel consumption.

texts.speaker: Thomas Y. Adolff
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Miguel, just a quick follow up on the upstream production. So you said, nothing is included from the  Mississippian and Russia. So, if you were to actually include Mississippian and Russia, how would the production  profile look instead of the 335,000 you're giving here?

texts.speaker: Miguel Martínez San Martín
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Repsol YPF SA
texts.text: I mean, Russia – I mentioned, the Mississippi, it's zero. Well, it's actually something around 1,000 barrels.
