texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Moving on to copper on slide number seven, underlying earnings increased and that reflects the higher price  driven by a steady increase in copper demand and that's all you know continued tightness in the supply side of  last year and those in particular the mature pits in [ph] mostly (0:06:27) coppers, these are pretty predictable in  cycle, up and downs, this was a cycle down for 2011 and we do expect a recovery in 2012 as those grades do pick  up again.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: And looking further ahead, we'll deliver new production, which will be timely into the tight markets from Oyu  Tolgoi project in Mongolia from about 2013. Construction is going well at OT with nearly a third complete as of  the June 30, 2011. And while development in OT continues to be on schedule, OT will require an agreed power  solution sale schedule to deliver first commercial production in 2013. We've approved further funds at resolution  United States. We completed the 50% of the 30 kilometer drilling program at La Granja in Peru. We are also  progressing brownfield options at KUC and Northparkes.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Turning to the energy group on slide eight, earnings were impacted by severe bad weather particularly at our  Queensland coal mines during the first quarter. Operations are recovering well although we are not yet at full  production rates. Hunter Valley mines were affected to a lesser extent although we did see some additional rain in  the second quarter particularly in June. Expansions are progressing with additional port capacity now secured for  the 8.5 million ton per year proposed Mount Pleasant thermal coal project.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Moving onto slide number nine, I would like to say a few things about Riversdale. An important highlight of this  half, was the transformation of our energy group growth portfolio through the acquisition of Riversdale given the  fact that the number of Tier I company coal development projects in Mozambique. On Monday we completed the  compulsory acquisition process and we now own 100% of Riversdale.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: As we move to the slide number 10, demand for borates and titanium dioxide feedstock continued to strengthen in  the line with improved global market conditions. Market conditions for rough diamonds also strengthened in the  first half of 2011, as demand from India and China continued to grow with a moderate recovery from the U.S.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: There's been quite a bit of focus on TiO2 prices over the course of this year, and of course you have seen quite a bit  of strength and I think recognition that there are some structural issues with TiO2 supply which will benefit the  producer. For the time being though our exposure to swap prices is really relatively limited as our multi-year  contracts mature over the course of the next couple of years, they are being replaced by contracts with alternative  pricing mechanism, which will provide increased exposure to current market pricing.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: I would like to now talk about prices and cost structures and move to slide number 11. It should come as no  surprise the primary driver of our performance has been price, partially offset by the impact of the currency  movements, notably the stronger Australian dollar. As previously highlighted, volumes were impacted by  extraordinary weather disruptions in the first half and lower copper and gold grades in the first half. The effect of  higher exploration and evaluation costs reflect the greater levels of investment in the forward look of the business  and what we would consider to be a good cost. The increase in cost was significantly influenced by uncontrollable  factors in the first half 2011 including adverse weather and lower grades, higher input prices and also the raw  materials and general inflation.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: And this is well demonstrated by the fact that China's Central and Western provinces continue to experience far  lower GDP per capita and metals intensity rates than their Eastern neighbors. I was in Central China just last  month and judging by the construction crane count, we were talking with mayors and senior – senior leaders,  certainly the expectation will be that, that cities like Chengdu and provinces like Sichuan will be growing at even  the higher levels of rate than you'd see overall within China and this will certainly have a positive effect on the  overall demand for our products.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We'll keep our eyes on the landscape, of course you would expect that we'd keep our eyes on the landscape. But we  have to look at that in the backdrop of having what we believe to be the single best set of iron-ore expansion  opportunities in the sector. I think that the copper projects we have are some of the best of the organic growth  opportunities in the sector, particularly in Oyu Tolgoi, particularly in the near term and things like now with  Riversdale, I think we have pretty attractive suite of coking coal growth options to look out for the future.

texts.speaker: Tony Robson
texts.profession: Research Analyst, BMO Capital Markets Corp.
texts.text: Okay, thank you. Second question would be on the operational level, I thought, and at the ton level your costs in  the Pilbara [indiscernible] (22:52) were really quite good. Obviously keeping costs under control there, but I was  rather surprised by what I thought was a [ph] blood (22:56) in the cash costs for ton levels for Queensland and  [indiscernible] (23:02) for coal even taking into account the wet weather in quarter one. Is Queensland also facing  very high labor inflation rates and input costs even as bad as or worse as the Pilbara?

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Yeah, I think first of all, thank you for your comments on the Pilbara. I will pass them on to the team in West  Australia because I want them to do a better job next quarter, but I think that when we look at the challenges we  faced in WA, with people, with contractors etc., I would agree that they're doing everything they can, in what was a  challenging weather environment, to deliver the goods and – but we are looking for them to do a better job in the  second half.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: I think in Queensland, we have two issues. First of all Queensland actually has a challenging labor market in the  coal fields that you would see in WA, you have quite a bit of turnover, quite a bit of mobility, increasing use of fly  in, fly out. So we are seeing as much labor pressure in Queensland as we do in WA, and that was definitely then  further hampered by the weather related items.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Guy [Elliott] in his presentation would have presented a pie chart showing how we would see the $1.2 billion of  cost increase being distributed and there was a big chunk of it which was weather-related, about $245 million, I  think almost all of that would have been in Queensland. So that just gives you a sense that we had not only a  increase on the cost side of $245 million in Queensland. I hope it's just a one-off weather-related factor, but we do  have those other factors in Queensland to deal with

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: And Tony, as I look forward into the future and I talk to people say in the gas business, there seem to be further  pressures both in WA and Queensland on skills. So I think if we are challenged today, we're going to be even more  challenged in the next year and the coming years as we see not only mining projects beginning to ramp up but a  number of these very, very large gas projects both in Queensland and in WA also ramping up. They will all be  competing for the same people.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: What I just wanted to say that I have been out to Simandou about a couple of times over the past couple of  months, last visit was in May, with the chairman of Chinalco, he was incredibly excited with the quality of the ore  when you look at some of the road cuts you see basically it's blue and it's just blue hematite and the whole  mountain is like the blue hematite. It gives you a sense of the quality of what's there.

texts.speaker: Tony Robson
texts.profession: Research Analyst, BMO Capital Markets Corp.
texts.text: Tom, thank you again for taking my question. In terms of what I'd have to say is your rather heroic target of a 40%  EBITDA margin in your aluminum business by 2014, do you have any price assumptions on that, top line realized  price assumptions or are you really looking at those three factors in terms of cutting costs and rationalizing your  portfolio a little bit?

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Yeah, I think well again these are big resources, some would be out there throwing a date up there and so we'll  worry about it when the date comes but we do have, I think a pretty good track record, is not overpromising. We're  trying to give you a sense of what the issues are there, both clearly world class resources, part of the recent copper  prices are so high now is that a lot of the new discoveries that have been made, actually they have a range of issues  that prevents them from getting to market earlier, which is again I think in everyone's mind. By the way, that also  reinforces the competitive advantage that Oyu Tolgoi brings to the table. Operator, anything else?

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Well. I think I'd say that given sort of what people are worried about when look at their computer screens or look  into CNBC or anything else like that, the physical demand has been remarkably resilient in China. If anything, I  think over the past, just the past week or so we've seen strengthening iron ore pricing while some see a product  that are weak and maybe some increase in stocks I'd say on balance the steel markets are doing well, particularly  the rod and stuff that goes into the residential market. I think if you look at what I would call some of the  inventory movements and say some of the premium I haven't been fussed about the copper and aluminum.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So, I believe our business, particularly given the fact that, our iron ore is almost entirely priced on a four-month  lag, and it's a quarterly pricing. But what I see that's in the first quarter this year, it gives us essentially pricing of  iron ore now, until early part of December, so we've got a pretty good idea that we obviously sell into those  markets, what our year looks like for iron on pricing.

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: Sure, it appears as though the company earned $6 billion from iron ore out of the $7.5 billion. And the iron ore
texts.text: segment is very well and all the other businesses added together are about the same as the first half of a year ago  costs. Do you think the performance of the company aside from iron ore was non recurring events due to weather  and grade, do you perceive any of these issues is a problem, such as a combination of one penny or dollar or  decline in grades and could you just sort of elaborate and framing this to simplify it or too harshly

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: John, I think you have captured pretty well sort of comparative performance at a high level, I do want to  emphasize that iron ore and coal and uranium and the diamond business in our goal and our bauxite and  aluminum production were all affected by quite extraordinary weather event in the first half, and I wouldn't hope  to see those repeat themselves next year and I think I still remember the pictures in newspapers where Brisbane  was flooded we had at one point 1,600 of our employees without offices to go into, because all six buildings were  under water.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We had levels of water in [ph] Emerald (42:37) in the coal mining area that those levels not seen for sixty years  and also we had quite exceptional sea swell events and rain event in [ph] Billborough (42:48). I wouldn't want to  be seen impacting again, and again I think that was – these were series of one offs that effected a wide range of  businesses and certainly dampening overall performance and showed up in both volumes that are inside. Again as  I said Queensland cost variances in sort of half on half. I think also in terms of your point about the currency, well,  that has been a headwind. Frankly that headwind has been part of the natural hedge with the commodities, so  with commodity strong we're taking some of that off with currencies. I think what we've seen and this is not just  seen in the past few years as back to a decade and these commodities were to soften, we would certainly see the  opposite move on the currencies take place. So, that again is a natural mitigating factor.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Okay. Thank you very much and I appreciate all of you taking the time. We've had the pretty good audience today.  Again, I think, everyone's probably either thinking about what's going on in Washington DC and what's going on  in Greece or Italy, or what's going on the beach right now. So, the iron ore may not be the highest thing on  people's general agenda, but from our perspective, we are continuing to draw a strong market. We are continuing  to see those in – and anticipate continuing to see those over the coming months. Our operations have recovered  quite well from the difficult weather conditions and as we move in to the second half, I think, again we are seeing  some of the things that we want to see beginning to take place.

file: RIO - Q2 2012 Earnings Call 8August2012 430 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 08-Aug-12.pdf

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: Many of our high-quality projects are getting close to completion and will start to generate returns over the next  12 to 18 months. By the end of 2013 we'll have 50 million tonnes of new capacity at Pilbara, taking us to 283  million tonnes. The second phase taking us to 353 million tonnes by mid-2015 is also underway. Commercial  production for Oyu Tolgoi will start in the first half of 2013.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: These integrative and innovative technologies are delivering returns now and they'll allow us to transition to a  much higher capacity of business in the near future. Our underlying iron ore earnings were the second highest for  a first-half period. And this was achieved despite lower prices, as the market came off historic highs. Of course  even in these challenging markets, we realize an average price for a Pilbara Blend fines product of US$133 per  tonne. Our results were boosted by first half production, leading to increased sales volumes as we increased  annual capacity by 5 million tonnes to 230 million tonnes.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: We are setting the stage for the whole of the sector with our focus on productivity improvement and cost  management to our Mine of the Future program. This is delivering real performance improvements on the ground  as we speak. But it's also setting us up for our planned growth in annual capacity of 353 million tonnes in 2015  and for further major debottlenecking gains beyond that level. So once again we've delivered an outstanding result  in iron ore. It is a good place to be.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: As expected our copper production was lower in the first six months of 2012. At Kennecott Utah Copper the  relocation of the in-pit conveyor at the mine and the 26-day smelter shut down were scheduled to coincide with  the period of lower grades. Both were successfully completed in the first half.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: At Escondida, copper grades began to improve with mine copper production 29% higher half-on-half. During the  period we approved projects that are Tier 1 brownfield assets to maintain production into the future. At Kennecott  Utah Copper we're extending the life of the mine by another 10 years to 2029. And at Escondida a new mill will  replace Los Colorados and allow access to higher grade ores.  In addition to brownfield volume growth we will see first commercial production coming from Oyu Tolgoi in the  first half of next year. After acquiring our majority stake in Turquoise Hill, we agreed to support the  comprehensive financing plan and nominate a new team of Rio Tinto management, led by Kay Priestly. After over  two years of construction I'm looking forward to seeing Oyu Tolgoi coming on-stream in the very near future.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: Moving on to aluminum, our aluminum business is better positioned compared to its industry peers, but we have  experienced increasingly challenging market and operational conditions. I am confident that we are pursuing the  right course with our focus on EBITDA improvement, concentrating the portfolio on Tier 1 assets and completing  strategic investments in modernization projects. But we do need to do more and particularly to aggressively  achieve further cost reduction and EBITDA improvements. This will require us to take some tough decisions  across the global aluminum portfolio with these businesses that continue to lose cash in the current environment.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: Global economic concerns continue to weigh on the LME price, with aluminum now trading about $1,820 per  tonne. At these prices, combined with continued elevated raw materials costs, approximately 25% of the smelting  capacity outside of China is in a loss-making position. Some smelter closures have been announced, but we've also  seen local governments, both in and outside of China, providing incentives to ensure loss-making smelters  continue to produce. This is preventing the rationalization of high-cost capacity that's required to balance the  industry. Given these circumstances we will continue our proved projects, including at Kitimat, AP 60 Phase 1 and  ISAL, but we'll be deferring further allocation of capital to aluminum smelting and refining projects for the  foreseeable future.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: The net result of higher prices, higher raw material costs – or lower prices, higher raw material costs and  favorable currency movements was to reduce EBITDA by about $600 million compared to the first half of 2011.  EBITDA was further reduced by approximately $100 million as a result of the lockout at Alma. This was resolved  in July when employees ratified a new collective labor agreement. The new agreement will provide RTA with the  flexibility required to implement cost and productivity improvements into the future. The adverse impacts were  partly offset by further progress on business improvement initiatives and the recovery from abnormal flooding  that we saw in Queensland back in 2011.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: Delivering on the business improvement initiatives outlined last year remains a top priority and we've now  achieved a run rate of $250 million of annual EBITDA improvement. However, in the current environment, we  are prioritizing our efforts and delivering further cost reductions. To the late, we have delivered improvements  from better terms on bulk site sales, reductions in corporate costs and capacity creep at the Canadian smelters. In  the second half, further cost savings will be delivered from reducing site and support costs, in addition to  productivity gains from the ramp up at Alma.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: Another driver in the transformation of our aluminum business is delivering on strategic investments in the  highest-quality assets. During the first half, the expansion of Yarwun, the first of these projects was completed.  The expansion more than doubles capacity to 3.4 million tonnes of alumina per year and is expected to ramp up to  full capacity by the third quarter of 2013 and will deliver unit cost improvements, moving our alumina production  firmly into the second quartile of the cost curve.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: Our Energy group has also seen a tough environment recently. Excess seaborne thermal coal supply has been  driven by growth from all the major producing regions as well as an increase in seaborne supply from the U.S. due  to low domestic gas prices. Thermal coal prices have now fallen to levels that are putting pressure on producers at  the top end of the cost curve. The current environment of excess supply, coupled with rising Australian costs, is  likely to be with us for some time. Despite these global changes in the Energy sector, we continue to see continued  growth in demand for seaborne thermal coal over the long term. As recent blackout events in India have

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: The coking coal market has been affected by increased supply from Australian and other regions at a time of  weaker demand from the steel industry. We are under no illusion about the scale of these challenges and we'll take  strong action to return to acceptable levels of profitability. All of our Australian coal operations are actively  looking for ways to reduce costs through ongoing business improvement and asset management programs.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: In Mozambique we achieved a key milestone with the first delivery of coking coal to an Indian customer. We do  expect Benga Mine to produce and rail more than 400,000 tonnes of coking coal this year. Meanwhile we're  continuing exploration activity with promising results. Early indications are that the exploration potential is far  higher than anticipated just a year ago and beyond that of coking coal. Significant additional tonnes may be  delivered, however, it is likely that it will take longer to develop this infrastructure than previously planned due to  the timing approvals and internal constraints on our capital. Discussions continue with the Mozambique  government on a range of future infrastructure solutions.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: Turning now to diamonds and minerals, we'll see a portfolio shift to this product group over the coming years. In  particular our late-cycle TiO2 feedstock business is just starting to see the benefits of growth in demand from  China and other emerging markets. Earnings did more than double over the period as the group benefited from  higher prices across the minerals portfolio. In particular, we saw significant momentum for the prices achieved in  titanium dioxide feedstock, as long-term contracts continued to unwind.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: Markets for both TiO2 and zircon did soften in the first half compared to late last year. And this is in line with the  current economic cycle, following inventory build by consumers and weaker demand growth this year. However,  we do remain positive on the mean-in-term outlook for TiO2 feedstocks and demand will strengthen in line  urbanization in the emerging markets.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: We also enjoyed a healthy increase in TiO2 product with record half-year production at RTFT and year-on-year  growth at QMM in Madagascar, following successful implementation of dry mining and other improvement  initiatives. RTIT is the world's leading producer of TiO2 feedstock and has many options to enhance shareholder  value through expansion and investment.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: We are excited to be doubling our stake in Richards Bay Minerals, which is expected to be complete in the second  half of this year. This is a significant Tier 1 asset and will give us increased exposure to the growing market, where  China now represents 30% of global TiO2 feedstock demand.  The outlook of the diamonds industry is attractive and strong demand growth in the world's emerging economics,  coupled with lack of new supply, means that it has some good prospects. However, given the relative scale of our  Diamond business within the broader Rio Tinto group and the capital intensive nature of the industry, we may be  able to create more value through a different ownership structure.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Lower sales volumes reduced earnings by $584 million, largely due to temporarily lower copper and gold grades at  Kennecott, as expected, and no metal share from Grasberg. This was partly mitigated by record iron ore and  higher coal volumes in line with recently completed thermal coal expansions and less severe weather conditions.  These boosted earnings by $366 million compared with the first half of 2011.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Industry-wide cost pressures continued in 2012, notably in some of the mining hot spots in which we operate. The  impacts of inflation and higher energy costs lowered our first half earnings by just over $170 million. Higher cash  costs reduced earnings by a further $388 million, of which the majority related to an increase in operational  readiness and site transition costs connected with the Pilbara expansions. I'll return to this in a moment, but  overall I would say that we've had a good cost performance during the first half.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In 2012, we've seen quite a significant increase in exploration and evaluation costs, notably at some of our more  advanced projects, including Simandou, Resolution, La Granja and Mozambique coal. Given progress made,  Simandou evaluation costs are now being capitalized from the 1 of April this year. These higher exploration and  evaluation costs are shown net of the gains on disposal of various exploration properties, notably our interest in  Kalahari Minerals and Extract Resources. Their total impact, together with other movements, including interest  and non-cash, was to lower earnings by just over $100 million. This brings us to our underlying earnings of $5.2  billion.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Now let me touch briefly on net earnings. The Australian government introduced the Minerals Resource Rent Tax  or MRRT on the 1 of July this year. We've recognized a deferred tax asset of just over $1 billion within net earnings  in relation to this. This is a non-cash accounting item. It reflects the deductibility for MRRT purposes of the  market value at the 1 of May, 2010, of our considerable past investment in our Australian iron ore and coal assets  to the extent recovery is considered probable. This is clearly a highly technical accounting area, but it has no  bearing on our underlying business performance, and so it's excluded from underlying earnings. So overall, net  earnings came in at $5.9 billion.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: While we would expect these costs to continue as we prepare for commissioning, they will be offset by higher sales  volumes and unit cost efficiencies through improved productivity in the future. We've also highlighted an increase  in stripping rates at Rio Tinto Coal Australia, which is a phenomenon that we would expect to reverse over the  shorter term. And we incurred some additional one-off costs, in particular the impact of the Alma lockout, which  we've shaded in this chart. Last year we suffered significantly higher costs from exceptional weather events. These  have had a lesser impact in the first half of 2012, creating a positive variance.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: For some time we've been taking a phased approach to many of our project approvals, such as our decision in  2009 to expand the Pilbara in two distinct stages. This phased approach allows us to commit capital in a risk- measured way, balancing our CapEx commitments with the market environment and other potential uses of cash.  In the Pilbara it has not only reduced risk, but has created embedded options. We've also enhanced the overall  value of the project by increasing its scope from 100 million tonnes to 133 million tonnes of annual capacity by  identifying and eliminating bottlenecks.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Our approach to investment will shortly be rewarded, as we bring these new projects on stream. Over the next 18  months we will see first production from Yarwun 2, Oyu Tolgoi and the first phase of the Pilbara expansion. And  any new project approvals will only get the green light should market conditions be favorable.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Alongside investment to create – to generate superior returns, we're also continually reviewing the portfolio to  ensure that it remains aligned with our strategy. We're, of course, aware that iron ore has come to dominate our  earnings in recent times. This reflects the superb quality and performance of that business.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Looking specifically at steel demand, the urban population will typically reside and work in high-rise buildings,  own at least one car, have a myriad of home appliances, including computers, et cetera, and depend on supporting  infrastructure such as metro, rail, elevated roads, bridges, power and water to sustain an urban lifestyle.  Construction will continue to drive steel demand in this decade before consumer demand begins to take over  beyond 2020.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Our top-down and bottoms-up analysis indicates that Chinese annual crude steel production will peak at around 1  billion tonnes toward 2030. And you can see from this chart that our projections are modest compared to some of  the most other reputable industry analyses.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In addition, and as we've been saying for some time, resource nationalism is elevating risk and reducing available  capital, leading to reduced supply. A range of emerging stakeholder issues is also leading to greater pressure on  permit approval processes. The cumulative effect of all these factors will continue to lead to less supply coming to  market than envisioned just several years ago. And this is not just a feature of the iron ore industry. It's also  affecting copper, coking coal and a number of other key commodities.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Our track record of delivering iron ore expansion projects in Western Australia on time and on budget is  unrivaled, as demonstrated by this third party study. Our Pilbara expansion project will be amongst the first to  market, taking advantage of conditions created by other project delays. I am confident that this is the best iron ore  project in the sector today and will generate high returns for shareholders under any probable macroeconomic  condition.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We are making great progress with the expansion of our Pilbara annual capacity to 283 million tonnes, due to  come on stream the second half of next year. And in June we approved the next stage of phased growth from our  global iron ore business. Approval has included the port and rail elements of the 353 million tonne per year  capacity project and funding for other detailed studies, early works and long lead items, for a continued  development of the Simandou project in Guinea with our partners, the IOC, Chalco and the government of  Guinea.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Not only are we delivering projects on time and on budget, but we can hold our product quality for the longest  single traded iron ore product, our Pilbara Blend fines for the next 30 years. And this is an unrivaled position in  the sector.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Our product portfolio will also be enhanced with high grade and high quality Simandou iron ore in 2015, as  construction in that project continues. While we have options for further expansion of the Pilbara beyond 353  million tonnes, as I've said before, it's unlikely – it's likely at that time we will pause for breath. And our intention  is that we will redirect our engineers toward debottlenecking, with a plan to have a larger stated capacity than the  current name plate objective of 353 million tonnes at that time. These efforts will be focused on a combination of  normal business improvement plans and taking full advantage of the integration on automation of the Pilbara,  through our Mine of the Future program. We'll cover this in more detail later in the year.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: These next few slides show pictures of the progress we're making with our Pilbara growth programs. At the port  we've now completed, ahead of schedule, dredging for not only the 283 million tonne expansion project, but also  that required for the ramp up of production, 353 million tonnes. We're also on schedule with the sinking of pylons  for the phase A wharf and jetty, which is now almost 85% complete. And you'll see in the quarterly production, it's  progressively ramping up new mine capacity at some of our existing mines in anticipation of this infrastructure  expansion.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Moving to the rail system, we are in the process of fitting out all ore cars, Electrically Controlled Pneumatic  brakes. This will improve braking efficiencies and reduce the risk of breakaways and derailment, and work  progresses on fitting out the same technology on our locomotives to further increase speed at which our trains can  safely travel. Overall, the 283 million tonne expansion program is now about 55% complete and on schedule for  the ramp up to commence at the second half of next year.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: As you know, we are ahead of the industry in developing and using innovative technologies. As I've said, we're  already seeing the benefits of the Mine of the Future program in the Pilbara. Integrating these technologies at the  Pilbara iron ore operations is helping us hold the line on costs. Automation in the operations center are bringing  greater efficiencies and in the near term, there will be more benefits from further debottlenecking in the Pilbara  supply chain.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The Mine of the Future is much more than just automation. It's things like faster underground tunneling, better  mineral recovery and an airborne gravity gradiometer that will help us find future Tier 1 ore bodies, all of which  we're starting to trial.

texts.speaker: Lyndon Fagan
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities (Australia) Ltd.
texts.text: Hi there. I've just got a question on impairment charges. I noticed there wasn't any major impairments for the  aluminum division, yet your net asset value is still quite high compared to market valuations. Just wondering if  perhaps you can shed a bit of light on that. And then just a second question, can you perhaps talk a little bit more  about the iron ore market, and your take on where iron ore prices are sitting at the moment relative to marginal  costs, and whether you've seen any material production cuts to Chinese domestic ore? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Maybe, Guy, you can focus on the impairment question. I'll focus on the iron ore markets.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In terms of our business, we are continuing to see a full sales and full order books, and again our sales are really  more affected by operational performance than anything else. As we certainly recognize that the margins are very  thin within the steel industry. We've seen some buildup of inventories, but frankly if you look at overall  inventories, whether at sea or in stock piles or at the steel plants, they've been relatively flat over the past year and  – in say weeks of consumption or days of consumption purposes. I think in talking with steel makers, they are  watching very closely these Chinese stimulus programs, and what affect that will have on their business. So I think  actually seeing metal consumed on the ground, we would be seeing some changes in the overall balance of steel  markets and steel inventories.

texts.speaker: Myles Allsop
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Hi. It's Myles Allsop, actually, from UBS. Just another couple of questions. First of all on your sort of Chinese steel  production, looking at Sam's [Sam Walsh, Executive Director] iron ore investor briefing back in April, you were  talking about China production reaching 1 billion tonnes by 2020. Now you're saying by 2030. Should we read  that you're getting slightly more cautious on the longer-term outlook for sort of Chinese steel consumption in  China? And then secondly just could you remind us with the sort of target 40% EBITDA margin for aluminum,  sort of when we can get there? What is realistic in the current pricing environment?

texts.speaker: Paul D. Young
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Australia)
texts.text: First on your growth in the Pilbara, you, clearly you have skeptics, [ph] still deride (47:37) that expansion, that  seems to be apparent to 353 million tonnes and beyond, and if your view is that global seaborne demand will  increase by that 80 million tonnes to 100 million tonnes over the medium term, and combined with the fact that  your global peers appear to be really rethinking their future expansion plans. And surely this presents a massive  opportunity to Rio Tinto, and therefore the question, shouldn't you be trying to accelerate your expansions from  this point in time?  And on Oyu Tolgoi, can you just give us some clarity or some information on when you think you'll approve more  CapEx to the underground or Phase 2 and can you comment on when you'll announce a review of Ivanhoe's – I  think it was $11 billion CapEx estimate for the Ivanhoe, the block cave, and the plant expansion. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Yeah. I think on, first of all on iron ore expansion, and I do appreciate your views that we are well positioned to go  beyond 353 million tonnes. I think in the context of our view of the markets, but also recognizing the need to find  this balancing between how we expend our funds, also cash returns to shareholders and a strong balance sheet, it's  probably better for us to be prudent, get 353 million tonnes built, recognize the 353 million tonnes. We would  have had a massive expansion from the 200 million tonnes level to get to that point, and we should by the nature  of that have opportunities to create debottlenecking. And I think we'd be best served in terms of value creation to  put some efforts in, probably for a couple years, to get the maximum debottlenecking at that level.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So I think if we talk about value creation, I think anything we can do to create low capital intensity,  debottlenecking opportunities over and above 353 million tonnes at the end of the current phase of the Cape  Lambert work, will be best for shareholders.

texts.speaker: Heath R. Jansen
texts.profession: Analyst, Citigroup Global Markets Ltd.
texts.text: Guys, I'm sorry to harp on about aluminum again, but you sort of made the comments that you said you were  going – or willing to take strong action on aluminum. Does that sort of mean that you are going to shut in  capacity? And just on that, what percentage of your ali capacity and aluminum capacity now is cash negative and  potentially would be in a shutdown situation?

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Yeah. I think, first of all, I think that it is quite important to recognize that every plant manager in the aluminum  very real risk of plant closures. And whenever we consider whether to keep an operation running or not, we look at  the cost of the closure and cost of re-startup against that. I'd say even in the current market, that virtually all our  facilities are holding their head above water. We have shut down some facilities, and we have been permanently  closing down some facilities, as you know, and we've done that with all the proper stakeholder consultation.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In the smelter area, I'd say that businesses are basically holding their own, even in the current environment.  Although I think some are quite stressed, and in some cases, we have been reducing capacity, say not rebuilding  pots as we've gone through to protect cash. The area probably in the aluminum business that would be probably  most in the position of losing cash in the current market would be the Gove refinery, and that is basically affected  by not only the weakness in the aluminum markets but also the high cost of fuel required for the steam for the  refining process.

texts.speaker: Jason R. Fairclough
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: Yes. Good morning, gentlemen. Just two quick questions on pricing, if that's okay. The first one is on TiO2  feedstock. Perhaps you could discuss the extent to which you're now exposed to the spot market versus still selling  on these longer term contracts. And I guess as part of that, how are you setting prices for your TiO2 products now?  And then second on iron ore, to what extent are you exposed to counter party risk? We do remember 2008, 2009,  where we had mass reneging on contracts. Is there a risk that the iron ore that you think is contracted isn't  actually, because clients decide they'd rather buy it at a lower level?

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: I think it's important to recognize in TiO2 that even though the current spot market is actually weaker for  pigments now, or I'd say the underlying market is weaker for pigments now than it would have been six months  high grade feedstocks in particular that are matched for their particular pigment production configuration. So  we're very well positioned in that space, and as we see these contractings wind down, it's generally been a positive  effect on our overall business performance.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In the Chinese market we've seen, I think a case, as you say correctly in 2008, and I think some recent events  which would show that longer-term contracts have the risk of being gamed in a short-term drop in the price. And  progressively you've seen the Chinese steel markets moving to shorter, shorter contracts, either spot or some type  of monthly actual or quarterly actual, where frankly, there's less incentive to create a counterpart risk  environment in those contracts, because as suspect, effectively not much of a difference between those contracts  and what would be a tradable spot market.

texts.speaker: Jason R. Fairclough
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: Tom, could I just push you back a little bit on the TiO2? So perhaps could you give us a little bit more color on how  you're actually setting prices for these new TiO2 products that are available to deliver into some kind of a spot  market? What's the price discovery mechanism there?

texts.speaker: James F. Gurry
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: All right. Thanks very much, guys. I just want to pick you up on the debottlenecking of the iron ore operations in  Western Australia. Is it too early to be thinking that by the first half of 2015, you will actually have capacity a step  higher than 353 million tonnes if you're going to do 5 million tonnes per annum of debottlenecking between now  and then? Or when does that 5 million tonnes per annum of the debottlenecking start?

texts.speaker: James F. Gurry
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And just also on CapEx approvals, there's a huge step down in non-iron ore CapEx spend, based on your currently  approved projects next year. Is it a concern of yours given that over 90% of earnings is coming from iron ore at the  moment; more volume growth is coming in the future; how do you look at being a diversified mine and now given  the fact that even iron ore is a huge strength at the moment?

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Now I would just remind you that moving from 225 million tonnes to 230 million tonnes on reflection was as  obvious as just increasing tug capacity. That was the bulk of that. It seems that obvious in reflection, but actually it  was a lot of hard work to actually find out where those pinch points were that could be actually debottlenecked on  an efficient basis.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Does that mean we're moving away from a diversified strategy in the long term? Not at all. I mean if you just think  about the quality of the assets that we have outside the Pilbara and outside of iron ore. If you think about what  Oyu Tolgoi is going to be in terms of future producer of copper. You think about the quality of our interests in  Escondida or ownership in Kennecott Utah Copper, you think about the emerging quality of what will be the  Moatize Basin in terms of the next big coking coal business, and you think about the quality of what our TiO2  business will be as we move off these contracts and China continues to march up the consumption curve.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Your next question comes from a Des Kilalea from RBC. Please go ahead.  Des G. Kilalea  Analyst, RBC Europe Ltd. (Broker)  Q Thank you very much. Tom, I just wondered about strategy, there. Two of your divisions have faced sort of what  could be kind of major changes. The gas threat to thermal coal and what you see for price, maybe you could talk to  that? And then also in aluminum, the persistence of production continuing at a loss and whether this is going to  be something you see as a long-term problem? And what it might do to the way you think about those two  divisions? And then finally are there any changes in Oyu Tolgoi's power tariff from the Chinese? Or is that all  secure now?

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Okay. Thank you. I think on strategy, let me talk about gas, then aluminum and then I'll say something on OT,  although frankly I think it's probably more appropriate for Turquoise Hill to get into the specifics of how that  math is evolving. I just want to say on OT power, I do – I am confident that when the commissioning of the mine  needs their power, that we will have the power at that point. And it's going to be something that it's going to be  seen to be commercially competitive.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: I think on the gas and thermal coal, we've been spending quite a bit of time with Doug Ritchie and his team asking  ourselves the broad question about the global energy sector, because I think that the energy sector globally has  actually had more change in the past two years than it's seen for the prior 20 years. When you think about the post  Fukushima world, and the effect on nuclear, when you think about the changing and evolving nature of carbon  and whether it's going to be priced or not, and certainly when you look at what has been a phenomenal boost into  the U.S. economy in terms of moving from being almost an energy importer to being almost an energy exporter,  that has consequences in terms of the markets and how we see the business long term.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We have looked quite a bit at what this means for seaborne thermal coal. We have asked the question and we've  tested quite a bit with experts outside our industry in terms of what would be the likelihood of the propagation of  shale gas outside the U.S. market and to what extent that shale gas will play into traditional markets for thermal  coal.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: And I think on balance, I'm convinced that thermal coal for at least the next 10, probably the next 20 years, maybe  into the 2020s, maybe 2030, will still be seen as the cheapest source of a BTU in terms of – or a, say, kilowatt-cost  basis. It's still going to be the cheapest source of electricity. You've seen in India what happens when you don't  have the electricity and it doesn't grow at the rate of the population or the development: things get difficult quite  quickly. Each government, consuming government will make trade-offs between energy security versus energy  cost versus the ancillary issues of carbon versus nuclear safety. And I think that thermal coal will play well into  that into the long term.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Of course we have made some strategic decisions ourselves over the past couple years. I think they were the right  ones. Three years ago we said, let's focus on thermal coal business, just on the seaborne markets and we chose to  divest, for a variety of reasons, from our coal business in the U.S.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: That was the right decision on reflection. We did that partly because of our concerns about carbon and how  carbon will be basically priced via regulation, rather than being priced via market. And also the fact that we've had  this long-standing issue with the rail carriers basically carrying the economic value. And subsequent to that, of  course, shale gas has made that market much more difficult, so that was the right decision.  We'll always keep our eye on that, but for the foreseeable future I think that in the long-term the thermal coal  seaborne market will have a robust demand environment. It will also have a robust supply environment, because  people will have come up with new thermal coal.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In terms of aluminum, we are continuing to see production at a loss. We are – though we have to ask ourselves,  how permanent that situation is, because some of the subsidies you are seeing, not just in China, but also you've  seen them in Australia, you're seeing them to some extent in Europe. Are they permanent subsidies? Are they just  going to be something that basically represent a transition to a closure?

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In China today I think we are seeing probably some smelting capacity being carried at a loss but we're also in a  weaker Chinese economic environment where we're also seeing power generation not being as stressed as it is  when times are tougher. What we'll all be watching is as the Chinese economy gets boosted by the stimulus, and  say overall power generation is no longer in surplus like it is right now, will they continue to carry that aluminum  at a loss?

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: And, again, these are questions that certainly we're keeping a close, close watch on, and they do have an effect on  how we think of the business, but frankly we should remind ourselves, we have first tier assets. Late last year we  talked about a strategy which is going to be basically curtailing capital on the air – parts of the business that are  most exposed to, as you say, the smelting capacity issues, but also being ready to focus more of the business on  those parts of the sector which are benefiting from that, particularly bulk site feeding into the Chinese market.

texts.speaker: Abhishek Shukla
texts.profession: Analyst, SG Asia Holdings India Pvt Ltd.
texts.text: Hi. Good morning. I would like to ask two questions if I may. First is what do you make of the recent fall in the  prices of steel, iron ore, coking coal, et cetera? Is it just a question of lower demand or is it also an element of  destocking or higher supply in it?

texts.speaker: Abhishek Shukla
texts.profession: Analyst, SG Asia Holdings India Pvt Ltd.
texts.text: Second, could you please just remind us of your guidance for how much coal you expect to export out of  Mozambique over the next two years and what is your likely unit cash cost of production on FOB basis?  And third, could you please let us know roughly how much MRRT you expect to pay in 2013 if all commodity  prices and exchange rates, et cetera, stay where they are? And am I right in assuming that given your high level of  CapEx, it will be a very small amount? And in the long run, if iron ore prices fall to something like $75 a tonne,  you may actually be a net beneficiary, because you will pay little MRRT, and you may actually end up benefiting  from higher depreciation. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Thank you, Abhi. I'll try with the first two questions and maybe ask Guy to talk about MRRT. I think as we've been  seeing and you correctly point out, we've seen a fall in steel pricing, both finished steel and also rebar pricing.  We've seen falls in iron ore pricing, although to a lesser extent than we've probably seen steel and coking coal.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: I think we are seeing, as the Chinese economy has slowed its GDP growth from say the 9s% to something closer to  mid-7s% in terms of GDP growth, we've had probably over capacity of steel in China that has created an excess –  an increase in steel inventories, although it's not been extreme, there has been an increase in inventories and a  drop off in prices. I think that there are probably others that are better positioned to talk about where that price is  going to go on steel, but let me just focus on iron ore and coking coal.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: As we've said before we do see iron ore pricing generally driven by the cost of iron ore at the margins. And in the  current environment of where seaborne supply sits right now, our view is, and I think the market's view is that the  floor has been somewhere about $120 per tonne, and that's essentially the marginal cost of Chinese consumption.  We're now probably two, three weeks into a period of time when prices have been below $120 per tonne, albeit not  a big level. And I think everyone's going to be asking, how does that support get tested in this environment or do  we break through that support?

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: And to some extent, I think coking coal is following that same basis. I think coking coal has the added feature that  the Chinese market probably has more self-sufficiency in coking coal and less of a reliance on the seaborne market  than you would see overall in terms of the iron ore space.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: I think in Mozambique we have flagged that we would expect about 400,000 tonnes of production of coking coal.  It's been a good quality coking coal that we've been delivering so far this year, and I think as we've been saying, we  will want to be ramping that up. But to be realistic, our own imposed constraints on capital spending will mean  that we'll probably be a slower rate of ramp up than we probably would have envisioned 12 months ago. But the  potential for that ramp up exists. If anything, I'd say the work we've been doing over the past 12 months indicates  we probably have more potential in total as we go forward. And again, this is truly a world-class basin deposit.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In terms of costs, I think realistically as you are working at lower levels of production you're not going to get the  full benefits of higher costs, but I would say the Mozambique asset does benefit from a much lower stripping ratio  than we see from traditional coking coal provinces around the world. So that will be a mitigating factor.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Guy R. Elliott  CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc  A Let me finish on the MRRT. Look, what I would say is, as I mentioned earlier, we're a very big taxpayer. In  Australia we paid about AUD$7 billion last year, and under the MRRT, we do expect to pay the MRRT. I'm not  going to give you guidance though, as to how much we're going to pay, and I would discourage you from trying to  calculate from the deferred tax asset any number, which you might expect, reflects the likely cash payments that  we'll be making in October and early next year. And the reason for that is that there are a lot of moving parts in  this calculation to do with iron ore prices, coal prices, volumes of both, foreign exchange rates, costs, et cetera.

texts.speaker: Clarke Wilkins
texts.profession: Analyst, Citigroup Global Markets Australia Pty Ltd.
texts.text: Hi. Yeah, just a couple of questions around CapEx, just in terms of sort of the 2013, where would you sort of  expect CapEx to come out based on the current approved projects and given you do have some major projects sort  of coming to an end outside of iron ore? I think Guy sensed earlier that CapEx wouldn't go any higher, but without  approving additional projects, would you actually think that the CapEx essentially drop next year?

file: RIO - Q2 2013 Earnings Call 8August2013 500 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 08-Aug-13.pdf

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In aluminium, we've been focused on improvements for quite some time, as you know. We have simplified and  improved the portfolio by divesting or curtailing of 15 assets; 15 over the past five years. It's now clear we can't sell  Pacific Aluminium for value in the current market, so therefore we're bringing these assets back into our  aluminium product group.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We do have a way to go to improving the performance in the aluminium business and its returns. Let me be clear,  there is no straightforward easy solution here, but we are making progress in aluminium, including continuing  success in reducing our cost base where we've achieved a cost improvement of around $200 million so far this  year.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: And finally, we're delivering results by completing our major projects and divesting of non-core assets. So far this  year, we started the commissioning of four major projects, including the open pit mine and concentrator at Oyu  Tolgoi. And we're about to commission a major expansion of our Pilbara iron ore business to 290 million tonnes a  year of annual capacity. These are significant milestones.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Turning to prices, so far this year, the iron ore spot price has ranged between $110 and $160 per tonne delivered  to China. On average, our achieved prices were $137  a tonne in the first half, $5 lower than the same period last  year.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Coking coal prices have weakened substantially due to strong supply growth from major seaborne producers and  ongoing weakness in import demand. And the copper market has been in modest surplus resulting in a 7 % price  decline. Overall, lower average prices led to a $1.3 billion drop in underlying earnings compared with 2012.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Let me make just a few comments of that some of the good efforts starting with our aluminium division. A major  cost driver for this business is raw materials where we've achieved cost reductions well-ahead of market prices by  renegotiating pricing mechanisms, securing new sources of supply, and standardizing our product qualities. This  has led the cost savings of $37  million across our raw material spend in the first half compared to last year.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Another example comes from our energy group, where we're targeting a reduction of over 60% in the number of  contract to companies we engage, in addition to negotiating reduced rates in order to drive the material reduction  in contract to spend levels. This is forecast to deliver over $100 million of cost savings for the full year of 2013.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We've also seen a number of adverse influences on our costs. The major flood in the Gladstone area in  Queensland, Australia has severely disrupted operations at QAL and Y arwun, and we continue to incur additional  operation readiness and ramp up costs in the Pilbara as part of our growth plans. Despite these headwinds, we  have delivered solid operating cost reductions of $97 7  million.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Over the past decade, our geologists have discovered nine Tier 1 resources, which is an excellent achievement. Our  investment in exploration will ensure that we continue to have an industry -leading pipeline of Tier 1 growth  options that we may choose to develop over the years to come.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The slide was a defining moment in 110-year history of the Bingham Canyon mine and the employees of Kennecott  have rallied as part of the recovery efforts. We're delivering approximately 100,000 tonnes of ore per day to the  concentrator from the pit. And this is being supplemented by ore from a lower grade stockpiles. Concentrator  throughput has recently been close to full capacity which is a solid achievement after such a significant event.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Cleanup of the slide has begun. A major piece of work here is to reestablish a heavy equipment access road which  we expect to have completed by the first quarter of 2014. This will enable additional ore production along with the  remediation and waste removal. There does remain a significant amount of slide material to move which we  expect to continue until the end of 2015.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Replacement equipment importantly is already operating and four of the 13 damaged ore trucks have been  recovered and they're back in service. As you'd expect, our operating cost will also be affected in the second half of  2013 driven by recovery costs, the purchase of concentrate to meet customer commitments.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: However, the team continues to pull cost out of the business and align to the changed environment including the  removal of a number of wells. The business interruption and equipment loss insurance process is also underway.  Near and medium term production is being limited by being able to physically access the ore. In 2013, we expect  to produce around 150,000 tonnes of copper with further improvements as per the slide in 2014 and 2015.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: At Oyu Tolgoi, we've reached a major milestone in July making the first delivery o f concentrate to our customers.  Their completion of this $6 billion greenfield project, the largest ever private investment in Mongolia, is a truly  remarkable feat. And thousands of people who've contributed to our success here should all be proud of what's  been achieved.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Now, back to Australia and our Pilbara iron ore expansion program. We're making great progress towards the  commissioning of the next stage of growth, which will see us add 53 million tonnes to reach 290 million tonnes a  year of annual capacity. We remain on track to deliver first ore from the expansion in September, in line with the  accelerated schedule that we announced in February.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In April, we achieved a key milestone with the delivery of the shiploader, which is now installed at Cape Lambert.  All of the coastal infrastructure for 290 is now in place, and the first train was unloaded by the new Car Dumper  on the 20th of July. Also between July and October of this year, four new trains will be delivered which will help  us to steadily ramp up shipments over the next 12 months. This highly valuable project will deliver excellent  returns for years to come.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The Phase 2 expansion of the port, rail and power infrastructure to 360 million tonnes a year as you know was  approved in June last year. And as I previously mentioned, there are multiple pathways for bringing on new mine  capacity. We could choose to develop new mines to ramp up quickly and deliver tonnes or we could fill some  capacity with incremental tonnes from existing mines at lower capital intensity before we bring the new mi nes on.  But I can assure you that we'll always be focused on getting the most out of our existing and newly expanded  business. And we've already demonstrated our ability to grow our production through low cost incremental  productivity improvements.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Our Pilbara expansion project, as you know, has grown from 320 million to 360 million tonnes a year as we've  progressively found debottlenecking opportunities. So we have options to grow from 290 million to 360 million  tonnes with flexibility around the timescale and capital intensity. The decision on which path we'll actually choose  will be made, as we've previously said, at the end of the year.

texts.speaker: Menno G. Sanderse
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Y eah, good morning. It's Menno Sanderse at Morgan Stanley. Two questions, one on aluminium and one on the  capital allocation. It's clearly good to hear that capital allocation is going to change and you mentioned a number  of measures and metrics you're using. But the problem still remains, garbage in, garbage out, and clearly in  Mozambique's case, you could argue that it wasn't the best stuff that went in. So how have you changed the  company to make sure the data going into this is not over optimistic as it has been for the industry as a whole, in  the last 10 years? And secondly, on aluminium, I take your point, there is no easy solutions, but you would think  that the easiest solution was to bring your own cost down and close the high cost assets. So why are  you slowing  down Kitimat, which should be a very low cost asset when it's finished and not taking quicker action on the higher  cost ones?

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: I think the best way I can describe it is that there are things that need to be worked through in the middle of an  organization. You can't actually determine these from the top of the organization. Y ou need the subject matter  experts. The investment committee can't make decisions as to whether there's been enough infill drilling. They  can't make decisions as to whether – the hydrology model, right, or the geotechnology. They've really got to rely  on the middle level experts to do that. We had weakened that process. Chris and I have reinforced the basic  systems that we operated really since the establishment of Rio Tinto. Those systems work. We know that they  work. The organization gets it; they understand how they work. So that has helped us get the discipline back. Of  course, we've created an environment of "scarce capital" and that also ensures that – you're putting a priority on  only the best projects. It's not every single project that gets through and pass muster.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In relation to aluminium, look, I think there's been – there has been some very good work in terms of reducing the  costs of the aluminium business. If you compare our business to other western aluminium producers, hey, we're  doing pretty well. But of course the whole segment has been impacted by low aluminium prices and the rate of  growth of aluminium, particularly in western China. But we have reduced our costs. We have taken off 600,000  tonnes of smelting capacity. We have either curtailed or sold 15 of our aluminium assets. And you can see in our  costs and our improved results in our aluminium business that, hey, we are making a difference there. Now, am I  satisfied with where we are? No, I'm not. There is clearly more work to  be done. But we've got that business and  we've got the broader business focused on improvement, focusing on cost.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In relation to Silvergrass, Silvergrass is of our options. Silvergrass and Koodaideri are the two major options in  relation to the new mines associated with 360 million tonnes and that'll be a part of the review that the board  undertakes in the latter part of this year. We may or may not announce Silvergrass at that point in time depending  on what is the logical and most rational order to develop, taking into account the productivity improvements I  mentioned.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Y eah. Look, in relation to the 290 million tonnes ramp up, on any acceleration there has – relates to the fact that  originally we were going to bring on that mine – or that process towards the latter part of this year, we're now  bringing it forward to September. And as I provided you some details, some granularity, it's getting very close,  which you'd expect, if you're going to start the full commissioning in September.

texts.speaker: Abhishek Shukla
texts.profession: Analyst, Societe Generale Global Solution Centre Pvt Ltd.
texts.text: Hi, good morning. I would like to ask three set of questions. First on Pacific Aluminum, roughly how much  EBITDA and EBIT did you make in the last six months? And is there a good part and a bad part to the business? I  mean is there half of the Pacific Aluminum which is maybe free cash flow positive and other half whi ch is  negative? This will really help us understand the business better. Second, on Bingham Canyon, how much money  do you expect to recover from the insurance? And third, on the titanium dioxide, when do you think the  destocking will end, and when do you expect a pickup in the market? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In relation to the TiO2 market, titanium dioxide, look, the market – if you look at the medium to long-term, the  market is good for this product. These projects are hard to bring on. They're not easy and there are not a lot of new  projects that are in the hopper. So I think the prognosis for titanium dioxide is good going forward.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: At the moment, we're going through adjustments. At the moment we're going through processes of uncertainty.  We've seen with these products that they're on a different cycle to the rest of our portfolio. TiO2 used in paint and  other applications, it tends to be well, you've built a building, you're now going to go in and maintain it or repair it  or whatever. So it has a different cycle, but all of our products have a cycle and it will have its time in the sun.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: With regard to other good and bad assets, yes, and a couple of them between that as well. So – in the mine, this  business right now the better – the closer to the dirt you are the better, and bauxite is probably the strongest part  of the PacAl assets. But the other assets are being dramatically improved and some really good work underway  there, and you may have seen the announcements regarding the NZAS contract by the way of example which is a  big change from what that contract would otherwise have delivered. So some very  good value delivered there.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Y eah. Look, firstly, in relation to iron ore market and 360 million tonnes. I mean there are more than two options  in relation to 360 million tonnes. There is an option of moving ahead full steam. There is an option of not doing it  of course, but there are other options in the middle as I've tried to describe in relation to productivity  improvements, incremental mining, existing improvements, and bringing on new mines. So I mean there we have  got the ability of developing 360 million tonnes in a range of ways lot of flexibility.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
