texts.text: 360 million tonnes will happen. It will go ahead now. Now, the issue is timing, the issue is the way that we bring it  ahead and so on. But it's a robust project, it's a good project, and the market will need the iron ore that comes  from this. Remembering that we are the low cost producer. Remember that Pilbara is the closest delivery point or  shipping point in relation to China. There has been a lot of controversy. In fact there is a lot of instan t experts on  iron ore and iron ore process and so on. In relation to tradeoffs of volume and price. And there has been some  people who are worried that in our analysis, we don't take into account our existing iron ore portfolio when we  look at that the additional tonnes that we're bringing on.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Well, let me to show you all. We look at the title picture, we look at the total valuation of the business in terms of  our trade off there between price and volume. But importantly, what will drive that expansion wil l be what the  market demands physically need. Glyn, I can remember back in sort of the early 2000s where people said well,  you're bringing on more than tonnes than the market needs. Well, we relied on the very detailed analysis that our  marketing people do on the ground looking at supply and demand, looking at potential steel projects, looking at  what the demand for steel is going to be, looking at potential iron ore supply opportunities, and so on. And by  taking all that into account, we've made decisions with hindsight pretty darn good decisions. That process is still  in place. That process will actually evaluate in great granularity as to what the market demand is going to be for  the product and how we physically bring it forward.

texts.speaker: Ian Rossouw
texts.profession: Analyst, Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Hi, good morning. It's Ian Rossouw from Barclays. Just a bit of details on the cost saving targets you're talking and  what you've achieved in the first half. The $977 million on the operating side. In the waterfall chart you gave some  details on the grade. I just wanted to – well, it's unclear how much you've banked from unit cost reductions from  volume improvement and I was just hoping if you could quantify that?

texts.speaker: Paul D. Young
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Australia)
texts.text: Thanks, gentlemen. I have a few questions on the aluminium restructure. It appears that most of the savings to - date are from efficiency gains rather than cost-cutting. And I know that divestment or closure of three smelters  during the half will show benefits in the December half, but clearly, more work needs to be done on reducing  overheads. So the question is, specifically, what progress have you made in reducing overheads in Canada? And  are the government agreements and commitments from 2007 an impediment? And lastly, are you reviewing the  closure of other low margin small smelters such as Edea, Sorel, and Bell Bay? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Thanks very much, Paul, for that. In relation to aluminium, we're looking at every area of the business whether it's  efficiency, whether it's management overhead, whether it's actually the day -to-day how we operate, what we're  doing in house, what we're doing outside and so on. And reducing overheads is an important element of that.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In relation to decisions regarding our aluminium assets, as recently as yesterday, we made a decision to curtail  Shawingan, 50,000 tonnes immediately and 50,000 tonnes in the latter part of this year. So it is an active process  that we have underway. What we need to do is compare our improvement projects versus how prices are tracking  versus how an actual operation is tracking. But we've not stopped. We're going to continue to improve that  business. And I think what you've seen in the results for aluminium in the first six months, it has changed. We are  injecting additional improvement and we'll see additional benefits flow through.

file: RIO - Q2 2014 Earnings Call 7August2014 500 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 07-Aug-14.pdf

texts.speaker: Mark Shannon
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So, if I could just start off by asking you all, as always, to turn off your mobile phones, please, or turn them to  silent. There is no planned trial of the fire alarm today. So if you do hear a fire alarm, it is a real event. In those  circumstances, you should go out of the same doors that you came in through. Immediately after that, there is an  entrance to a fireproof stairwell.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So, let me turn to some of the highlights in our half year performance. Our underlying earnings were $5.1 billion,  up 21% over the same period last year. We have achieved $3.2 billion of sustainable cost reductions, exceeding the  $3 billion target that we had set and achieving this six months ahead of schedule.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Copper earnings were up by over 70%. A strong operational performance saw mine copper production increase by  23%, following the recovery in grades at Kennecott Utah Copper and the continuing ramp up of shipments at Oyu  Tolgoi.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In Energy, thermal coal prices declined at the lowest level since October 2009 during the first half. However, the  exceptional work of the team to reduce costs and increase productivity at our thermal coal operations has helped  to mitigate this impact. In Diamonds & Minerals, underlying earnings were down, reflecting lower prices for  zircon, titanium dioxide, feedstocks, borates and metallics. We continue to reshape these businesses to ensure that  they're matching production to demand. We're minimizing cost and are well-positioned to take advantage of  future price increases.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: One of the key headwinds we've faced this year is lower iron ore prices with a spot price averaging 20% less than  in 2013. But the quality of our business, together with our marketing leadership is ensuring that we continue to  deliver significant value. Demand for iron ore remains strong, but steel production in China are expected to grow  by 3% to 4% year-on-year in 2014. Most of this increase has been driven by domestic consumption. We're seeing  growth in steel consuming sectors like infrastructure, machinery and transport, offsetting weaker activity in  residential construction.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: As anticipated, this has been a period of growth in seaborne supply of iron ore and a commensurate exit of high  cost supply with around 125 million tonnes of capacity expected to leave the market this year in response to lower  prices.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We've already seen significant curtailments of iron ore supply from the Chinese domestic sector, as well as  reductions from non-traditional suppliers such as Indonesia and Iran. We are better placed to thrive in this  environment than any other iron ore producer, given our industry-leading cost of production, the quality of our  Pilbara Blend products and our strong marketing capabilities.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Pilbara Blend products, introduced by Rio Tinto in 2007, are the base feed and largest consumed product by  Chinese steel mills. Pilbara Blend sets the industry standards, so to speak. While much of the industry growth in  seaborne supply over the past six months has been lower quality material, leading to increased discounting by  some producers, the focus of our expansions has been on our Pilbara Blend products. These now represent  approximately 70% of our current Pilbara portfolio. We continue to experience high levels of demand for these  products across varying market conditions.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: As an example, you can see from the chart that Pilbara Blend fines spot sales achieve on average a premium above  the Platt's 62% iron ore index. Over the whole of our Pilbara sales portfolio, we achieved an average realized FOB  price of $99 per wet metric tonne in the first half. Furthermore, the relative value of our non-Pilbara Blend  products has remained consistent in the first half of 2014 compared to prior years.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Turning from revenue to cost, we've beaten our cost reduction targets, with $3.2 billion of sustainable operating  cash cost improvements. This is a great result, six months early and reflecting the determined efforts of our  employees across the business. And based on our planning for the rest of this year and next year, we're expecting a  further $1 billion of sustainable cash cost improvement by the end of 2015.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: What's truly impressive about our cost reductions is that our assets already had well-positioned cost structures.  Almost half of our revenue is generated by businesses with EBITDA margins in excess of 60%. And those assets  that are not currently generating such high margins are, in general, low cost producers in their respective industry  sectors, poised to benefit from price recoveries. For example, our Aluminium business realized on average an  EBITDA margin of around 20% in the first half. But these assets are low cost and any price improvement will flow  through to the bottom line. In fact, a 10% change in the LME price for aluminium leads to a $444 million earnings  impact. We're now starting to see some improvement in the aluminium prices as a modest supply deficit opens up  outside of China.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We're confident that these levels of CapEx will provide future options for long-term sustainable growth, whilst at  the same time maintaining the strength of our balance sheet and the conservative price assumptions. We expect to  achieve significant volume growth of more than 8% a year on a copper equivalent basis from 2012 to 2015.  Increased volumes are coming on-stream in iron ore, copper, coking coal and diamonds.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Further ahead, we have a strong suite of potential future projects across the groups, including in bauxite with  South of Embley; in copper, with Oyu Tolgoi Stage 2; and in thermal coal with the Mount Pleasant Project.  However, these projects will compete with other uses for cash, and only the highest quality projects will attract  capital.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: And in the first half of this year, we reached our run rate capacity of 290 million tonnes a year, two months ahead  of schedule. And we're making great progress with a next-stage expansion of our infrastructure capacity, to 360  million tonnes a year. We've already completed the necessary rail duplication and track work, and we're on  schedule to complete the automation of our Pilbara rail operations. This technology will be in full operation in  2015 and will unlock further productivity gains.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The Copper group is focused on its 4 + 2 strategy with the immediate objective of improving the quality of its  earnings and its cash flows. And during the first half, the team continued to prioritize three key areas. Firstly,  enhancing productivity at all Copper operations; secondly, reducing costs; and thirdly, optimizing the portfolio  around four Tier 1 assets while building a pipeline of attractive growth projects.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Strong progress is being made in simplifying the Copper portfolio this year with the divestment of three non-core  assets announced. The Copper group is delivering strong operational and financial performance in the first half  with underlying earnings growing by over 70%, and this was achieved despite lower prices and was driven by  another exceptionally strong operating performance at Kennecott Utah Copper. At Kennecott, the team are  continuing to oversee the recovery of the mine from the pit wall slide last year and in doing so importantly they  have realized record productivity improvements and sustainable cost reductions.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We're continuing to focus the business on the highest quality assets. We're recording strong results in our cost  reduction program with over $800 million of savings from the Aluminium group. And overall we've increased  EBITDA from Aluminium by 26% to $1.1 billion in the first half.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: At Gove in the Northern Territory, we're well-advanced in the transition to our bauxite export business. This is  already operating and the export capacity is six million tonnes a year and will grow to around eight million tonnes  a year by the end of 2015. The expansion of Weipa through development of the South of Embley project is a truly  Tier 1 growth opportunity and is expected to deliver a very attractive return on investment. And the team is now  completing the study work with a focus of leading – or producing the lead time to bring this world project into  first production.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Yes. Hi. We're getting a little bit ahead of ourselves, but I mean this will be a decision made by the board and  clearly the board will review options. For delivery of our dividends, special dividends, buybacks, that is approach  that I would expect that they would consider. And, clearly, the board will take into account where we sit at the end  of this year, but let me assure you that all of our modeling and forecasting is pretty robust. But of course, I'll take  into account forecast for exchange rates and commodity prices and energy prices and so on. And, obviously, that  will determine the quantum. Chris, I don't know if you wanted to add anything perhaps to that.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Perhaps, Jason here in the front row – second row.  Jason R. Fairclough  Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch International (United Kingdom)  Q  Jason Fairclough, Bank of America Merrill Lynch. Just maybe a little bit of color on some of the changes to CapEx  for this year because that certainly got people's attention. Just wondering could you talk a bit about the extent to  which the $2 billion reduction is a permanent reduction or just a deferment – a deferral of the CapEx. And I guess  more generally then if we look at Pilbara 360 and how low the capital intensity is. If we look further down the  road, are we setting ourselves up for a big catch up CapEx build later on because you're just working with these  existing assets so hard?

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In relation to the question about Silvergrass in the Pilbara, Iron Ore group are putting forward their plans in  relation to the mine capacity associated with its move to 360 million tonnes a year. You would have picked up that  a large majority of that has actually been through squeezing harder existing mines and that work is proceeding  quite well. In relation to Silvergrass, specifically I'm not exactly sure of what the timing would be for that project,  but it will be there to meet the ramp up.

texts.speaker: Clarke Wilkins
texts.profession: Analyst, Citigroup Global Markets Australia Pty Ltd.
texts.text: I guess so, it's okay. The question is just on the Kitimat side in terms of the CapEx there. $4.8 billion the  modernization, yes, I think the increase is probably $1.5 billion is a bit more than expected. Is that the cost of  building only smelters now in the western world or what went wrong with that project considering that that's  almost a 50% increase in the budget that was originally improved and sort of double what it was when it was  originally proposed back in 2008.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We have significantly strengthened the management on site. And, Alf Barrios, who is now running the Aluminium  group, is responsible for the handover from construction to operations. And he is actively involved, ensuring that  there will be a smooth handover of the 256 systems associated with the smelter as they'll ramp up progressively  through to June next year.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In relation to your question about the operating cost reductions, look, it's been across the board in relation to the  organization. Thousands of projects, real momentum gathered. I mentioned during my comments about the $800  million that Aluminium had reduced out of their costs. So we also saw significant reductions both in the Energy  group and the Copper group of around the same dimension.

texts.speaker: Lyndon Fagan
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities (Australia) Ltd.
texts.text: And then, the second question is just on Grasberg, can you perhaps clarify whether you've got to contribute to the  cost of building a smelter there? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In relation to Grasberg, the settlement that Freeport announced about Grasberg has been done by them. We've  indicated for some time that we're not going to be a party to a smelter project at Grasberg. I visited the project  couple of months ago. I've got to say they're doing some very, very good work in terms of the underground  development and it's a very impressive operation. I don't take too many visitors for some reason, but it is  something that's worth looking at. They're doing some good work there.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Yes. I mentioned back in February that Chris and I were not interested in setting a top-down target for cost  reduction going forward. We need to make sure that the savings are sustainable. We need to make sure that the  savings are not going to cut into the muscle or even worse, cut into the bone.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Sam, I think perhaps two points. One is that your comment about the low hanging fruit is absolutely right. I think  in addition to that, we have got some known events in the second half of this year. An example of that is the  Kennecott smelter outage coming up, so we know that it's going to be that much harder there.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Yes. Yes. And the short answer is yes, we do think we can rein that in during the second half. It's an area that we  probably had a slightly artificial reduction at the end of last year. We're doing a lot of work now to negotiate to  extend those payment terms on the way out. And we're making sure we're collecting on the way in. We're also  reducing inventories. So, I think we've got a good line of sight. Actually, we've had a team working on this and  working on it from a basis of what's the optimal working capital rather than sort of targeting a 5%, 10% reduction,  it's really about what do we actually need in the business.

texts.speaker: Glyn Lawcock
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Securities Australia Ltd.
texts.text: Hi, Sam. Just two questions, firstly just a little bit more detail on the costs. Aluminium, $800 million; Energy,  almost $800 million; they're good numbers, but a year ago, you said you'd get over $1 billion out of Energy, close  to $900 million in Aluminium by the end of calendar 2014. Have you stretched yourself a little too far and can you  actually get the numbers? Because I mean, the energy market, obviously coal, uranium prices look tough unlikely  to lend you any support. Just wondering whether you can still get those costs out in those two divisions.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Look, I'll let Chris comment on franking credits in a moment. But you were spot on, in relation to the cost  reduction targets, Energy group were targeting $1 billion. They're still targeting $1 billion, and Aluminium were  targeting $900 million.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: But now we are looking at it. We are looking in for ways to see whether there is a way that we can liberate them to  get them to be more value in the hands of their shareholders. But it's not easy and I guess we've had probably  every bank on the planet sort of come and talk to us about it. But rarely do the proposals that they sort of come up  with have appeal that would be fair and equitable to shareholders and that's really the challenge in this.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The second privileged position really relates to the quality of the product and with increased focus on pollution,  when we talk about the environment, we're generally focused on climate change or greenhouse. When the Chinese  mentioned that they're focusing on smog, they're focusing on actual pollution. And at the China Development  Forum that I attended earlier this year, a small group of CEOs met with the Premier of China and he indicated that  it's probably the biggest problem they have and the most difficult to solve, but they are committed to solving it.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: This has actually meant that there's been a shift in relation to the product that the steel mills are using as they are  focusing on improving their environmental performance. And the shift to higher quality ore which has reflected in  terms of, obviously, the attractiveness of our product but also the significant discounts, the 15% to 20% discount  that the low grade junior suppliers have had to offer to make their product even attractive to the mills.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So, there's a range of factors there in terms of how we see. We are seeing steel prices improve a bit. We're seeing  steel stocks reduce. We're also seeing port stocks of iron ore reduce. And we've seen some 85 million tonnes of  China's domestic product come off the market. We're expecting that that will be around 125 million tonnes  through this year. So, there is a change in the dynamics. There is a restructuring underway there.

texts.speaker: Heath R. Jansen
texts.profession: Analyst, Citigroup Global Markets Ltd.
texts.text: Yes. Morning, Sam. Just a related question in terms of iron ore ramp ups. I mean you're still giving a range of  potential ramp-ups in the order of 20 million tonnes a year to 30 million tonnes a year or the next couple of years.  And I think you said before your results, that was really subject to market conditions. So, I'm interested in terms  of how you're thinking about that now, as you said you've knocked out potentially 125 million tonnes of domestic  production and the price has come down.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So, we are in a very good place in relation to this and now is not a time for the best iron ore producer in the world  to take a step back. Now is the time for others to really feel the consequence of the price against their operating  costs and for them to make decisions.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Yes, thanks, Sam. I think probably two things. One is around that number would definitely have included Pilbara  sustaining mines. Back at that time I don't have the specific data in front of me at the minute but that would be  one issue. The second one and sorry to address that point given the expansion program that's underway in the  Pilbara, the concept of Pilbara sustaining is sort of – is a lower number today. But look I think we have applied the  same rigor and discipline to the sustaining capital as we have to other forms of growth. And I think part of that is  showing up in some of these numbers. I think the climate for the cost of capital construction and capital sort of  works is also has moved on a cyclical basis in our favor in some ways.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: And I have mentioned the cost reduction. Look, there is a need for us to further streamline the operations as we go  forward. But we are making the tough decisions. We are refocusing the business. And I would remind you that –  correct me, Mark, if I'm wrong – 80% of our metal is produced using highly competitive hydropower, so "not only  is the power source low cost, it's also green".

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So, it's a good place for us to be. Alumina continues to be tough and we are continuing to focus on improving our  costs in the Alumina side of the business which right now, and we're not alone, is probably the toughest part of the  business, bauxite, with bauxite selling in the spot market for around $60 a tonne, with 5 billion tonnes of bauxite  sitting in our portfolio, it's a good place for us to be. And I've already hinted as strongly as I can about the South of  Embley project.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: And I've said before, if you were to look at an example of that, well, look at Japan. Japan used to have a very  vibrant Aluminium smelting industry. Today, there's none. It's all gone. And I suspect that we'll see a similar, if  not exact, but a similar shift in China as this currently trapped power is either opened up through transmission  lines and increasing the grid or direct use of that power in those communities to drive their consumer goods.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We've done a lot of the pre-work in the last 6 months to 12 months, it has been targeting about what these ideal  levels should be. And I think we've got two bodies of work going, underway, one is around what's the ideal level of  inventory that we need to sustain our various operations and you'll see some of the things like Oyu Tolgoi now  starting to ship in excess of what they're producing in the open cut. We have got some of the iron ore that's been  held up at the mine site that we can now have a better opportunity to get it down the infrastructure change in the  port. So, there's opportunities like that.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: But thinking about it more about what the ideal levels are rather than some sort of target of 5% or 10% reduction  is far more meaningful, but it's a bit slower but more sustainable. So, that's it. That's our ambition. We're  confident we can achieve it.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Chris will go through, in a moment, the results in detail, but let me first point out a few of the highlights. Today,  we're reporting underlying earnings of $2.9 billion. Our cost saving initiatives, along with positive currency  movements and lower energy costs, have offset almost 40% of the $3.6 billion of price decline.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Non-Executive Director
texts.text: There's a modest benefit from higher volumes, which we expect to continue in the second half of the year as we  ramp up our completed infrastructure project in the Pilbara, and increased output from the modernized and  expanded Kitimat smelter.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Non-Executive Director
texts.text: Underlying earnings were $2.9 billion for the first half. Net earnings were $806 million, $2.1 billion below  underlying due to impairments and non-cash exchange movements. This compare with $4.4 billion of net  earnings in the same period last year. Impairments of $421 million booked in the period related mainly to the  carrying value of Energy Resources of Australia. This was flagged on the 11th of June following a decision made by  the ERA board not to proceed with the final feasibility study of the Ranger 3 Deeps project.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Non-Executive Director
texts.text: Adverse prices impacted the underlying earnings of the Copper & Coal businesses, which you'll recall were  combined earlier this year. This combination has created additional opportunities to improve cost and  productivity, and the product group achieved total savings of $150 million in the first half. Underlying earnings  decreased to $393 million during this half. However, operating EBITDA margins rose to 36 %, which is an  impressive achievement in a declining price environment. Our Australian coal mines are amongst the lowest cost  in the industry and continue to generate positive cash flows.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Non-Executive Director
texts.text: We started this year with a cost saving target of $750 million. In the first half, we've achieved $641 million, $551  million of operating cash cost reductions and about $90 million from reduced exploration and evaluation, which  brings us to 85% of the full year target. We're now increasing our full year 2015 target to $1 billion. Our cost  reductions have been achieved across the business with Copper & Coal delivering about $1.9 billion and Iron Ore  and Aluminium each delivering around $1 billion since the program began in 2013.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Thanks, Chris. Over the course of the first half, we improved our safety as measured by all injury frequency rate.  However, tragically, we've had three fatalities. One at our operation at QMM in Madagascar, one at our Canadian  titanium dioxide business, and one at our coal operations in South Africa. My thoughts and prayers are with their  family and their friends.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: This half, our Iron Ore assets and the team running them have again demonstrated their exception al capability.  During the half, we've increased production in the Pilbara compared to the same time last year, despite late  cyclones which saw us lose 7 million tonnes in shipments. The operations benefited from the weaker Australian  dollar and lower energy costs, but also management delivered a significant cost savings of $244 million for the  half, taking their cumulative cost savings to almost $1 billion since the beginning of 2013.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: This business continues to deliver an FOB EBITDA margin in excess of 60% in the first half. It's a remarkable  outcome considering there's been a near 50% decline in the average index price. Even with the impediment of  weather that I've just talked about, our Pilbara assets still remain the lowest cost producer delivered into China  with C1 cash costs of $16.20 per tonne. However, at today's currency and energy prices, this is $15.20 a tonne. It's  a stunning achievement from Andrew Harding and his team, and there's more to come.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Operating and commercial excellence is a core skill for Rio Tinto and critical for success in this environment. So,  let's look at a few examples of this from across the group. Achieving maximum efficiency from our equipment and  infrastructure allows us to simplify our processes and lower unit costs, and this can be seen in reducing iron ore  rehandling in the Pilbara or redesigning our railcar unloading system at Kennecott to handle tolling.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: As well as efficiency saving, we also look for ways to increase production through incremental improvements in  the way that we use our assets. And this allows us to get additional throughput without additional equipment. For  example, increasing the conveyor speed at Gove, our bauxite operation in Northern Territory, and fitting dovetails  to the trucks at Oyu Tolgoi in Mongolia, these have both contributed to improvements in utilization and  throughput.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Having achieved production at this cost, our aim is then to sell the product at the best price. Our Iron Ore sales  continue to achieve a price premium over the index, demonstrating the deep capability in our marketing team. In  Aluminium, our focus on value-added products has reduced the need for some of our customers to remelt  material. And this has delivered additional average product premiums of $259 a tonne.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: In every area of our business, we look for continual improvement, greater efficiency, lower cost and higher prices.  I personally believe that there are always opportunities to improve a business. The group has a pipeline of  exceptional near-term projects. The 360 Mt/a infrastructure project in the Pilbara is largely complete, which will  enable us to deliver global sales in line with the guidance of 340 million tonnes of iron ore in the full year. We  optimized the value of our 360 Mt/a infrastructure. Our future Pilbara investment will be focused on maintaining  the quality of the Pilbara product.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: In bauxite, we have the high-quality and large-scale resource at South of the Embley, where we anticipate  completing the feasibility study by the end of 2015.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Our Aluminium product group, it is a truly world-class business. In May, we announced the signing of the  Underground Plan of Oyu Tolgoi. And we're now carrying out a refresh of the feasibility study, we're  finalizing the  project financing, as well as obtaining the necessary permits. Along with our increase in our share of copper metal  from Grasberg, we'll see a significant increase in future volumes of our Copper product group in the years to come.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: As I mentioned during my comments, if you look at the way that we're delivering projects in terms of much  greater focus, weakening Aussie and Canadian dollars, reduced energy costs and gas costs and, quite frankly,  reduced contractor costs and input costs, we are seeing that we're able to maintain our growth.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Of course, key projects for us are the 360 Mt/a project, the OT Underground, as you mentioned, and  South of the  Embley. But we have other projects that are in the pipeline. Alan has the Diavik A21 Diamond project, but he also  has the Zulti South titanium dioxide project.

texts.speaker: Myles L. Allsop
texts.profession: UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Myles Allsop, UBS. Just a couple of questions, one following up from a – the previous question. If it was February  today, when you got 21% net gearing, you've got less than $6 billion of CapEx next year, when iron ore prices are  $55. Would you be recommending to the board that you should sustain the buyback?

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: I mentioned during my presentation that we're expecting that during this year, 120 million tonnes of capacity will  come off with a further 45 million tonnes of got the wobbles. If you look at what we 're expecting in terms of supply  to come off – come on, including our share, that's actually 110 million tonnes.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Now, we invest for the long term. We're not investing for what's happening right now. On behalf of you, we've  been investing in our iron ore over the past 10 years. We now have the infrastructure in place. And we're bringing  on brownfield mine expansions.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: With a unit cost of $16.20 a tonne, all converted to today's exchange rate and energy cost, $15.20 a tonne,  compared to an iron ore price of $55 a tonne, we're doing okay, the margin is all right. And for me, sitting here  today, thinking that I'm going to sacrifice net margin so that someone else somewhere in the world can bring  capacity back on, to me, it just doesn't make sense.

texts.speaker: James F. Gurry
texts.profession: Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Thanks, Sam. It's James Gurry from Credit Suisse. Just a follow-up on Myles' question. Can you confirm that the  350-million-tonne target for 2017 for the Pilbara is still valid?

texts.speaker: James F. Gurry
texts.profession: Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And secondly, just on – I'm thinking about the portfolio. Clearly, iron ore is in the bottom quartile. 80% of the  aluminium smelters are in the bottom quartile as well, and that's where you need to be. Can you talk about the  copper portfolio and how you see that developing over the medium term? Because I think we would have thought  that OT might have got going a little bit quicker in terms of the underground development now that the agreement  is finalized.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Our guidance for iron ore for 2017 has not changed. We're focusing on 350 million tonnes there for the Pilbara  operations.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Copper, copper is going to be tough going forward. There aren't enough projects that are coming on stream. The  projects are tough because the ore bodies are complex. They're deeper ore bodies, lower grade in a number of  cases, and the approval cycle is extended.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: I jumped for joy when our people successfully received approval of the land swap resolution in Arizona as a result  of an act that went through Congress and President Obama signed. I didn't say it was probably going to take six  years or eight years to get environmental approvals.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: But whether you look at us or whether you look at our competitors, it is seriously tough bringing on these future  projects and, well, if you step back from it, it bodes well for the copper industry. It means that we will see copper  moving into short supply going forward.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Can we have a question from thin air, from the phones?

texts.speaker: Lyndon Fagan
texts.profession: JPMorgan Securities (Australia) Ltd.
texts.text: Thanks very much. Sam, couple of questions. The first one is on the South of Embley. Can you perhaps give us an  update on how you're thinking on the scope of that project? Initially, you sort of talked about a 22.5 million tonne  mine. But with all this additional Malaysian supply, does that influence the way you're thinking about bringing on  that project? And perhaps if you could give us some color on how you're thinking about the bauxite market going  forward.

texts.speaker: Lyndon Fagan
texts.profession: JPMorgan Securities (Australia) Ltd.
texts.text: And then I guess the next question is on iron ore, whether you could give us a bit more detail around Silvergrass  and the delays there. Obviously, you've done a good job managing the depletion or sort of deferring the ultimate  depletion, but when we think about sustaining mines, is it still a new 50 million-tonne operation every five years  or has it been worked on to sort of improve that outcome? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Okay. Look, why don't I handle South of Embley and, Chris, if you could comment on iron ore, which will be a  change. South of Embley, our basic scope for volume hasn't actually changed. However, we are looking at the  capital aspects of the project, and I'll flag this to you for a number of times that in line with the comments I have  made earlier about the impact of a weakening Aussie dollar, energy prices, input prices, contractor prices and so  on, the aluminium group and the projects group have been looking for how we, in fact, optimize that project.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Chris, perhaps, if you could cover off on iron ore and how Silvergrass and the brownfield expansions all come  together.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Non-Executive Director
texts.text: Okay, Sam. And, I guess, the oddity of this is that you're not talking about it, rather than I am. I guess I do get to  talk about it quite a bit in the one-on-ones. But given Mr. Iron Ore and all that type of stuff, so – but anyway,  Andrew and the team were able to develop a more brownfield response to the capital expansions or the capacity  expansions. And that resulted in a significant reduction in the capital expenditure part. Clearly, though, it puts a  little bit more pressure on managing the quality to the Pilbara Blend for the 62% iron and the like.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Non-Executive Director
texts.text: And when we get there, it will be primarily worrying about maintaining that quality issue and making sure that  that's in as good a shape as we can get it for the process going forward. So, Silvergrass will come in 2016, and it  will be down in that part. But the brownfield path was largely designed about could we get to the same sort of  capacity at a lower capital expenditure rate? That carries with it other challenges, of course, but that's been  successfully deployed, and the guys have done a really good job on that.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Non-Executive Director
texts.text: So, there's an opportunity here now that we've got a path now through. We've had a brownfield process to -date.  We've got a couple of these, Silvergrass is one, Koodaideri can come later, but the processes are in place now for –  it's almost time for Silvergrass to come. So, it's well-heralded, it's well-prepared, and I'd expect we'll see it  somewhere during 2016.

texts.speaker: Clarke Wilkins
texts.profession: Citigroup Global Markets Australia Pty Ltd.
texts.text: Hi. Thanks for the question. Listen, just in regards to Silvergrass, I think the capacity is a bit over 20 million  tonnes. So, if you maintain a target for sort of 350 million tonnes in 2017 basically from the  brownfield  expansions, does that inherently mean we're getting debottlenecking capacity beyond the 360 million tonnes? And  what scope is there to really push the capacity, the infrastructure in the Pilbara?

texts.speaker: Clarke Wilkins
texts.profession: Citigroup Global Markets Australia Pty Ltd.
texts.text: Next question just in regards to the CapEx reduction. How much of that reduction sort of for 2015 and 2016 is  currency versus delayed projects versus just a cooling the environment. I don't know  whether you can provide a  breakdown on that, and what does that mean for projects like Silvergrass and also  South of Embley, et cetera?

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Look, let me just add some color on Silvergrass. What we're seeing there is that Silvergrass would  supplement/replace some of the brownfield projects that we put on. But the primary driver for it is, as I have  mentioned, to retain the integrity and the quality of the Pilbara Blend. It is a very important source of iron ore for  our customers. And maintaining the Blend through 2030 and beyond is an impo rtant element of our iron ore  strategy.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Debottlenecking, because, as I mentioned during my comment, I personally believe that there's always room to  improve the business. And I'm sure Andrew and his team will be looking at, well, how can we improve the  business. However, I would comment that the primary driver for it relates to quality of the Pilbara Blend, not to  drive further tonnes through the system.

texts.speaker: Andrew T. Driscoll
texts.profession: CLSA Research Ltd.
texts.text: Hello, gents. Look, a very strong results But when I look at the earnings bridge, I'm surprised that energy and  inflation only contributed a $79 million uplift to first half earnings. Y ou've improved prices. We're down now  about 50% year-on-year in the first half. Can you talk a little bit about that and whether we can expect more  benefits to flow through perhaps as inventory is being worked through? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Non-Executive Director
texts.text: Y eah. Well, it is one that will require a bit of work to get through to hone down to an exact number, but the key  issue is really around how much inventory of – as the price falls, we get a bit of a lag with regard to how it goes  through into the cost structure, that's one issue. Second one is a lot of our energy inputs are self-generated. In  many cases, if you take the smelting system by way of example, we generate 50% of our own energy there and a lot  of hydropower there as well. So, not all of our energy is obviously in the oil sector.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Non-Executive Director
texts.text: But if you look at it on a full year basis from where we are today, at about the $6 0 mark. It's roughly about in the  mid-$80s million for an overall impact on the cost structure. In terms of about $80 million, if it was – it would  vary by about 10% of the current sort of levels of pricing. So, clearly, it takes some time to work its way through,  but – which is a good thing because I think the oil prices are probably here for – well, they look pretty solid at  these sort of levels. So, we look to take advantage of that.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Non-Executive Director
texts.text: We don't count it in our cost reductions as such. We sort of put it to  the side with the prices when we take account  of the reduction in our commodity prices. We also don't give ourselves credit for a lower oil input cost.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: And we've seen the reductions flow through, not only in relation to cost reduction, but also in capital, in sustaining  CapEx. Two-and-a-half years ago, when I sat here and talked to you, we were talking about $5 billion of sustaining  CapEx. Today, we're spending $2.5 billion. My head office, it was 600 people. It's now 250 people. And everything  that used to happen happens.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Y eah. Look, those are two good questions and Alan Davies, who runs both of those operations, is sitting here in  the front row. And I'm sure you two, over a cup of coffee, could talk more about it. But in relation to uranium, we,  following a decision from ERA, Energy Resources of Australia, issued a press release to say that we did not   support further development of the Ranger 3 Deeps underground operation at ERA.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: We don't believe that the ERA project will be progressed and, of course, the ERA board needs to explore further  options. And further options could be an alternative development plan. It could relate to Jabiluka. Time will tell  with that. At the moment, we'll continue through 2018 to process the low-grade stockpile. Then clearly through  2025, we will complete the rehabilitation work.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Y es, there's a possibility of an extension to the lease. We're not really working on the basis that that will come to  pass. The project is highly controversial in Australia, and we're seeing nuclear power here as a solid underpinning  of power production. In Australia, there is only one very small nuclear plant, which is basically a prototype plant,  and it's something that, as I say, is controversial.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: It's interesting even with the CapEx in Japan, we're still receiving some orders for uranium from Japan which sort  of, in a way, is counterintuitive, but it's also showing that the uranium companies – or sorry, the nuclear  companies, they're expecting that there'll be a need to bring back nuclear reactors in Japan that actually meet all  the safety standards and all of the changes that have come through. Meanwhile, we're seeing in China and  elsewhere, commitment to further nuclear power stations. And even here in the UK, there's a commitment to  another nuclear power station.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: In relation to 1 billion tonnes by 2030, yes, we are holding that. And I think the greatest difference between us and  other forecasters, I think there's alignment in relation to the domestic demand. I think export is, as you point out,  the area where there's the greatest difference and we look at exports of finished steel product. But we also look at  export of the levered manufacturers and capital equipment and so on. And it's that where we're seeing that we  differ from other forecasters.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: But we're continuing – let me assure you that our economics department has come under great focus thanks to all  your articles and those of the press and what have you. They're holding the line. They've done quite a bit of  research and analysis and they feel confident that that 1 billion tonne figure will continue to hold. Now, if you step  back from it, to achieve 1 billion tonnes of crude steel production by 2030, that's 1% growth a year. I think we'll be  all right there.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Non-Executive Director
texts.text: So, in the short term, I think we do benefit slightly from the fact that there's been a fair bit of re cent expenditures.  So, by way of example, if you take the Kitimat smelter as a stand-alone issue, we shouldn't need to spend a hell a  lot of sustaining capital on that in the near term. If you go to the refineries at Gladstone, you'd probably get the  opposite case there where it's a bit like your grandmother's ax where she's had four new handles and a new blade  every 25 years sort of thing.

texts.speaker: Peter O'Connor
texts.profession: Shaw and Partners Ltd.
texts.text: Hi, Sam. Congratulations on a great result. Just a question on the Energy portfolio. It's a portfolio that really has  been long for many decades, both in coal and uranium. And following up on your further – the recent answer for  coal and uranium, is where do you see Energy in the portfolio going forward? I ask that with a sense of what's  been happening in the headlines lately, a bit out of the U.S. with what Obama's announced. A lot of media in  Australia are pushing back on energy, particularly coal-fired. And does that change your view of the mix going  forward or does it change the business model going forward?

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: In relation to the Energy business, I think I mentioned at the results in February that we've been fairly arbitrary in  terms of the rejigging of the Energy group into the Copper group, Copper & Coal, and into Alan's group, Diamonds  & Minerals. And that was really to pull out the product group overhead. The group's done a great job of pulling  $800 million of cost out.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: In relation to climate change, in relation to greenhouse gas, that is an important issue for us. And if you look at  our greenhouse gas performance over the past five years, on an intensity basis, we've reduced our greenhouse gas  by 16%. Clearly, we have further targets to improve it. And yes, that is a combination of things. It's a combination  of energy efficiency. It's a combination of technology. It's a fact that we have closed or divested of high -energy  businesses, high greenhouse-producing businesses. So, we are very focused on the comments that President  Obama and other world leaders are making on this topic. And I suspect that there'll be further comments coming  out of COP21 in December in Paris.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: In relation to our Coal business, we do produce cleaner coal there than elsewhere in the world. Coal is going to  continue to be part of the energy equation probably for the next 50 years. And clearly, there is no substitute for  coal in the mix in terms of power production in the moment. Y es, there are a number  of alternatives that are  coming along, but they're going to need to substantially reduce both their capital cost and their operating cost to  be truly attractive to the market. We continue to run both of those businesses, the Coal and Uranium business.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Non-Executive Director
texts.text: I reckon the only way that that could occur, it's possible that there's a difference in the – if you take aluminium by  way of example, we're not shipping much of that into China as you can expect so – and it had a price increase  where if you compared – a lot of the product going into China had price decreases. There's probably a little bit of  that in there, but I don't want to take that as a factual answer. It's just – it's in my mind so that would be...

file: RIO - Q2 2016 Earnings Call 3August2016 500 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 03-Aug-16.pdf

texts.speaker: John Smelt
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations
texts.text: Morning, everyone. My name is John Smelt, Head of Investor Relations at Rio Tinto. Thank you all very much and  welcome to our 2016 Interim Results. Couple of bits of housekeeping. First of all, in terms of fire alarms, there's  no practice alarm set for this morning. So if it does go off, it is a genuine alarm. It's voice activated. The fire exits  are either through that door and to the right or out through the back and to the left, very clearly marked, and there  will be wardens here. If you could at least turn your mobile phones on to mute. Off would be great. But if you can't  cope with that, mute would be good.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive-Copper Business
texts.text: The Energy & Mineral group under Alan Davies include some solid and well-established businesses, such as [ph]  borate (8:10) and some potential rising star. There are also challenged businesses in this portfolio, but Alan and  his team are focused on cash generation via cost and productivity improvement. The group has managed to  increase operating EBITDA margin to 23% against the backdrop of lower prices.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: In February, we announced a cost reduction target of $2 billion for 2016 and 2017 combined. During the first half,  we've delivered more than half of this year's target, and costs have reduced by $580 million. This takes our total  cost reductions since we've launched this program, I guess, 2012 cost base, to almost $6.8 billion. And has  assisted us in delivering an EBITDA margin of 33%.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: As always, it's important to note that this excludes the impact of exchange rates, in particular in Australia and  Canada, and changes in oil and energy costs. We've continued to make good progress due to the cost culture  that's now embedded throughout the organization. All of the product groups and central functions have  contributed to this success.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Late last year, the Aluminum group set out their target of $300 million for 2016. And during the first half, they've  actually reduced their cost by $223 million. Iron ore have delivered pre-tax operating cost savings of $138 million,  further reducing their operating unit cash cost to $14.30 a tonne. This is actually an increase, though, on the  second half of 2015, due largely to seasonally lower volumes and a stronger Australian dollar. The Energy &  Minerals group have contributed $152 million of operating cost reductions during the half, taking that group's total  to $1.2 billion since 2012.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: As operating cost reductions are measured on a unit cash cost of production basis, the impact of lower volumes  from Escondida means that the contribution from the Copper & Diamonds group is minimal this half. We'll  continue to find opportunities and capture greater value in all of our businesses.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Turning to CapEx, we're maintaining our CapEx guidance through to 2018. We continue to find ways of achieving  the same outcome at lower cost. But spending is also reduced with the completion in 2015 of the iron ore  infrastructure expansion and the Kitimat project.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: We expect our overall spend to be second-half weighted, with CapEx of just $1.3 billion this half. During the  period, we have progressed the Amrun bauxite project, which was approved in December of 2015, and so far  spent about $100 million on initial construction of accommodation, roads, and river terminals, yeah. It should be  noted that approximately 70% of the $1.9 billion approved for this project is expected to be spent in 2017 and  2018. In May, we approved the $5.3 billion underground project at Oyu Tolgoi in Mongolia. Activities have started,  with the EPCM contract awarded, and mobilization is in progress.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive-Copper Business
texts.text: Let me give you some examples. Our Pilbara assets are not just low cost, they deliver a product of exceptional  quality. In Aluminum, our position in bauxite mining and aluminum smelter is sector-leading. Our smelters keep  improving their cost position, and their low carbon footprint makes our aluminum attractive to customers.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive-Copper Business
texts.text: In Copper, we have interest in three of the largest and highest quality copper deposits globally, Escondida,  Grasberg and Oyu Tolgoi. The Energy & Minerals group has a world-class thermal coal asset and a significant  TiO2 business. This group can act as an incubator for smaller businesses and new commodities.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive-Copper Business
texts.text: The third P is really about building distinctive capabilities to enable a step-up in our delivery. And at the core of it  are people. Excellent commercial capability is key to quality returns. Let me give you some examples. In iron ore,  we have a strong track record of achieving a premium on our Pilbara blend spot sales. During the first half of this  year, this translated into a $0.80 per tonne premium over the average Platts price for the period. In Aluminum,  more than 50% of our products are value-added, allowing us to charge an additional premium. In Copper, we  have taken advantage of the underutilization of the Kennecott smelter and processed over 600,000 tonnes of  third-party concentrate since 2014, generating a margin on every tonne.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive-Copper Business
texts.text: In thermal coal, we have increased the premia achievable to benchmark following the development of the  [indiscernible] (25:23). Clearly, there are real benefits derived from spreading marketing and commercial best  practices for the group, and our people are key to delivering both commercial and operational excellence.

texts.speaker: James F. Gurry
texts.profession: Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Thanks very much. It's James Gurry here from Credit Suisse. Congratulations on a solid set of results. Just in  terms of the most important business for you, can you give us your view on the long-term outlook for iron ore and  for steel production in China, and when you think it will peak, or if it has already peaked?

texts.speaker: Lyndon Fagan
texts.profession: JPMorgan Securities Australia Ltd.
texts.text: Thanks very much. Yeah. Look, the first question I've got is on AutoHaul. Clearly that looks responsible for the  2017 guidance downgrade, can you talk about whether that 10 million to 20 million tonne downgrade is all  AutoHaul, or whether there are other things driving that, and maybe an update on how that's going, and when you  might get to 350 million tonnes?

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive-Copper Business
texts.text: Now, before you ask the question is, we are – and I think Chris mentioned it in his speech, we are – we will  deliver on those $2 billion cost saving commitment over 2016 and 2017, and the $580 million that we have  delivered in the first half of this year is an important good step against this $2 billion target.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive-Copper Business
texts.text: On iron ore, we did revise the guidance a few months ago in relation to Pilbara, and the guidance as it stands is  330 million to 340 million tonnes for next year. There was several drivers why we had to revise the guidance, and  one of them is AutoHaul. AutoHaul is a complicated project. It's a combination of infrastructure and software, and  we are working our way through it in a very safe and structured way. But today, as we are standing here in  London, we maintain our guidance for next year of 330 million to 340 million tonnes.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive-Copper Business
texts.text: In relation to the next question you asked about, when do we get to 360 million tonnes? And thanks for ask ing the  question. I'm going to restate what I said a few months ago. The iron ore strategy is not about volume, it's about  value. Okay? We have the infrastructure for 360 million tonnes at the port level. We have the capacity, more or  less, on the mine. We don't have it today in terms of railway.

texts.speaker: Clarke Wilkins
texts.profession: Citigroup Global Markets Australia Pty Ltd.
texts.text: Great. Thank you. Sorry to go on about iron ore, but just in regards to the iron ore cost. We saw them rise, as  Chris pointed out, in the first half this year on that [indiscernible] (43:54) sensitivity. We've seen, from one of your  peers in the Pilbara, that as they continue to push costs lower in that first half of the year despite those factors.  So, what is the potential, I suppose, for further cost reduction in the Pilbara, and can Rio maintain its position as  the lowest cost total producer, given the threat from Fortescue's pushing down to that $12 to $13 per tonne?

texts.speaker: Anna Mulholland
texts.profession: Deutsche Bank AG (Broker UK)
texts.text: And secondly, what place does coal have in your portfolio, specifically thermal coal? Obviously, you've been  selling some of your thermal coal assets.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive-Copper Business
texts.text: On thermal coal, which was your second question; first of all, I would like to say that we are really pleased with all  the good work of our teams in the coal business. It's one of the safest business we have across the group, and it  is free cash flow positive, including take-or-pay obligations.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive-Copper Business
texts.text: As I said, if anybody in this room wants to make any offer on any asset of Rio Tinto, you know my number, and  you know his number as well. We'll look at it, all right? Today, the coal are in the portfolio. Tomorrow, if somebody  knock on the door and offer a good price, we will look at it. It is what it is. In the meantime, we will run them as  best as we can, safety being the priority number one and free cash flow being number two.

texts.speaker: Myles L. Allsop
texts.profession: UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Myles Allsop, UBS. I managed to get the mic. Just following up on a couple of the earlier questions. With the  Pilbara production, is there a scenario, if demand's soft, softer than everyone expects, doesn't get to your million  tonnes of steel production in China so that you never get to 360 million tonnes, and you have to approve  Koodaideri to get to 360 million tonnes, is Silvergrass largely maintenance? Just to give a bit more clarity as to  how aggressive you'll be on the value over volume strategy.

texts.speaker: Paul D. Young
texts.profession: Deutsche Bank AG (Australia)
texts.text: I [ph] can't rush those. (62:15) Apologies. So, firstly on OT, J-S. Glad to see the approval of the underground.  Quite a bit disappointing to see the CapEx estimate [indiscernible] (62:24) despite industry-wide CapEx deflation.  So, can you discuss the scope for any CapEx reductions? Also, the possibility for bringing forward first production  from the current 2020 target. So that's the first question.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive-Copper Business
texts.text: Well, I can start with the aluminum. As Alf said last year is, we have a clear target, $300 million. We are already  making good progress against the full year target. Are we going to stop there? The answer is no. We believe  there is still room for improvement. And we'll go after it, that's the exact thing that you know. We need to start  somewhere. As you said, lots of improvement has been achieved already, but we're not going to stop there. We'll  just keep going, we'll continue to keep going to improve our cost position, not only with our smelter part, but the  alumina as well, and look at the turnaround of the alumina refineries.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Okay. The sound quality coming through is pretty poor there, but let me have a crack at it, as I sort of think I heard  it. The key with CapEx is that, in the Pilbara especially, we have completed the bulk of the infrastructure spend for  the 360 million tonnes for the full capacity and so on and – during 2015. And so, this year has been a relatively  modest spend. Our overall CapEx for the total corporation has been $1.3 billion, and about $700 million of that  was sustaining capital. The Silvergrass approval that was approved yesterday is the remainder of the Silvergrass  project. So, if you think about the Silvergrass complex in total, you can talk about the Nammuldi Incremental  Tonnes 1 and 2, and then this latest spend, the $338 million that was approved yesterday. If we were talking 6 to  12 months ago, we would have had probably just shy of $500 million allocated to what was yesterday approved  for $338 million.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So, I think there's some efficiency in there, and it also goes to Paul's earlier question, there is still pricing pressure  on capital projects in Australia, given that the general climate has slowed down considerably. That's particularly  true in Gladstone, where the gas projects...

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive-Copper Business
texts.text: All right. So, there are a few questions here, is – our understanding today is that, year-on-year, the iron ore  production in China has reduced, okay? If you look – compared to where we were a few years ago, we're at –  ahead of 400 million tonnes. We must be below 250 million tonnes today. It could be even 230 million tonnes, 240  million tonnes. But there is – China, it can be a slightly complicated picture, let's put it this way. As I said earlier  today is, good steel demand in the first half, if you look at the run rate for Q2 it was much, much higher than what  it was for the full year of 2015.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive-Copper Business
texts.text: Then the second part of your question, Glyn, I think you and I already had this conversation two or three times.  So, the Energy & Minerals group is not a South32 or 33 or 34, whatever number you want to pick. You have some  stars in the portfolio. I mean, look at the borates, the borate business has been there for more than 100 years,  generating lots of good cash flow. It's a real Tier 1 asset. If you look at, in the TiO2 space, Richards Bay in South  Africa is a Tier 1 asset. The way we have organized ourself is to make sure that iron ore is really focusing on the  Pilbara, that aluminum is focusing on the aluminum asset. That copper and coal are really trying to build this  capability in Russia, to underground, that will be critical for us going forward. And the portfolio of Alan, and the  mission of Alan and his team, is really to run the smaller assets in a more aggressive way, to drive cash on one  side. And, the second mission is really to act as an incubator for new commodities or new businesses we would  like to build there.

file: RIO - Q2 2017 Earnings Call 2August2017 500 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 02-Aug-17.pdf

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We delivered our $2 billion cash cost saving program six months early, and momentum is building on our  productivity drive. We already had the strongest balance sheet in the sector. At the end of June, our net debt was  $7.6 billion. We continue to strengthen our portfolio of assets. As you know, we announced the sale of our thermal  coal business in Australia for $2.7 billion which is expected to complete this quarter.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We realized a strong first half iron ore price of $67.80 a tonne, 40% higher than the same period last year  reflecting the well-placed product portfolio. Copper prices increased 23% compared to the first half of last year  reflecting strong demand from China and some supply disruptions during the period. However, this was partially  offset by continued supply additions from Peru and increased scrap volumes.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Aluminum prices improved compared to the first half of 2016 with an increase of 22% reflecting strong demand.  We believe this also has been driven by news flow around China's supply-side reforms that they've announced  earlier in the year, yet to take effect because their winter – their actually wintertime measures.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The coking coal price spiked as a result of weather disruptions in Australia and has now dropped back to prices  seen in the first quarter. This chart shows the striking recovery in prices from the first half of last year. As you can  see, inflation, energy cost and exchange rates have remained relatively stable. Volumes were generally lower  compared to the first half of 2016.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In the Pilbara, shipments were impacted by wet weather in the first quarter and accelerated rail upgrade in the  second. Hard coking coal also suffered from adverse weather in the first half following Cyclone Debbie in late  March, which impacted both rail and pit access at Hail Creek.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: These lower volumes were partly offset by record production in bauxite and increased production of TiO2. The  14.9 million tonnes of third party sales of bauxite were a first half record. On cost, we also delivered a further $300  million of cash cost savings, or $0.5 billion pre-tax.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In February 2016, we set a $2 billion cash cost reduction target for 2016 and 2017 combined. As I mentioned, we  have achieved $500 million in the first half, which together with last year's $1.6 billion means we've now achieved  our target some six months ahead of schedule.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: This takes our total reductions against the 2012 cost base to $8.2 billion. This excludes the impact of exchange  rates, inflation and changes in oil price and energy costs on the way through that. This is an ongoing journey and  we don't intend to stop.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In June, shareholders approved the disposal of our Australian thermal coal business to Yancoal for consideration  of $2.7 billion. This is a much improved offer compared to the one made in January including $500 million more  cash on completion. The transaction is expected to close this quarter.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Including Coal & Allied, we've now announced divestments of almost $8 billion in the last four years, but we still  retained flexibility in our portfolio. Some of our assets are smaller, but they're valuable and highly cash generative.  We'll continue to exit any assets or projects that don't fit our requirements and where we can realize attracted  value to shareholders.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Separately to AutoHaul, we've brought forward upgrades to the Pilbara railway network. This had another solid  impact on iron ore shipments in the second quarter. The CapEx for this work is already included within our CapEx  guidance. The upgrade work will continue during the year and ultimately along with AutoHaul create a far more  flexible system.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
