texts.text: So now, let me focus on the steel industry in China. It is today both healthy and profitable. Order books are full.  As a result, demand for high-grade iron ore has been strong and due to productivity should continue in the  foreseeable future. This creates opportunities for us, Rio Tinto. So, the outlook is stable but price volatility will  remain a feature of the market.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We have more than 800 trucks which we can use more effectively. We have around 50 processing plants, which  today are not fully loaded. We are investing to upgrade our railway infrastructure in the Pilbara. This will give us  greater flexibility to extract value from our iron ore asset base in WA, Western Australia. We will be generating an  additional $5 billion of free cash flow over the next five years and the run rate of $1.5 billion of free cash flow per  year by 2021.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Two weeks ago, Chris and I were at our $1.9 billion Amrun bauxite project in Queensland. Key construction  activities and fabrication of the process plant have started. And we are on schedule for first production in the first  half of 2019.

texts.speaker: Menno Sanderse
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: If I look at slide 11 on here, where you showed the bridge very helpfully. If I combine volume, inflation, and energy  on one hand, and I combine the cost savings on the other hand, you basically stand still as a company. And that's  clearly not a bad outcome given where you are in the cycle. But is that going to be the Rio Tinto of industry we  need to look at for the next three, four or five years until more projects come to fruition, or can you actually do  more than that?

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: What is absolutely clear, and you saw it because you've done your homework already. You saw that there is  some cost inflation coming back, and I think a good example is aluminum where you see caustic soda cost  picking up and so on. And you see it in the margins as well and so forth, right?

texts.speaker: Lyndon Fagan
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Australia Ltd.
texts.text: Thanks very much. A couple of questions from me. The first one is just on aluminum costs, particularly for the  Primary Metals segment. I noticed they have gone up about $0.10 a pound to around that $0.74-type level half- on-half. I'm just wondering if you could sort of talk a bit more about that, and whether that's the new base going  forward or whether there are some one-offs there?

texts.speaker: Lyndon Fagan
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Australia Ltd.
texts.text: And then, the next question is just on the lithium project. Could you talk a bit more about what the scope is, what  the likely CapEx is? Is there anything more you can sort of shed some light on that given you put an  announcement out, but there really wasn't a whole lot in there. Thanks.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Okay. I'll do the lithium. Okay. So, we made the announcement. We signed an MoU with the government of  Serbia 10 days ago now. The assessment is underway. There are couple of parts which are pretty obvious, one is  the marketing study about lithium, about the attractiveness of the lithium industry, clearly on the back of electrical  vehicles, batteries and so on and so forth.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: You want to pick up the aluminum piece and the increasing costs, Chris?

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: On the ali costs, where the input costs into aluminum this half versus the same half last year are about $320  million higher. So, that's a significant headwind that's all market related, but it goes to caustic soda, the coke and  pitch inputs into the smelting system, and also the energy costs, particularly in the Australian smelters.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So, basically, caustic is about $150 million, coke and pitch about $115 million, and energy is the bulk of the  remainder. So, it actually accentuates the point about the power of those Québec smelters and the hydropower,  where we're in the first costs decile, and that difference. Also get a bit of the benefit for the green aspect of  aluminum in Québec with the hydro as well.

texts.speaker: David Pleming
texts.profession: Analyst, HSBC Securities (South Africa) (Pty) Ltd.
texts.text: Good morning. Thanks very much guys. Just two questions. Just with respect to the Coal & Allied sale, I  wondered if you could give us some insights in terms of if there's any tax payable on that sale, and what is the  actual book value so one can ascertain the impact on the earnings?

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Yeah. With regard to the Coal & Allied proceeds, we do have carryforward losses in the Australian jurisdiction, so  anticipate very, very low, if any, may well be zero tax payable on that so it's – it'll be a pretty clean transaction.  We'll utilize pre-existing tax losses – capital losses.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Thank you. Amrun, bauxite, Queensland that would be another one. Oyu Tolgoi, copper, Mongolia that would be  another one. The one we just mentioned about smelter in Canada where the aluminum smelter are not in the first  quartile of the cost curve, but the first decile of the cost curve are world-class. I think I gave you already a pretty  good sense of which asset we regard as world-class.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: But couple of points is, we're not going to do a fire sale, okay? We've sold $8 billion of assets in the last four  years, and if you look at the valuation we did extract Northparkes or even Coal & Allied, we did extract more than  full value for those assets. So for sure, I want to clean up the portfolio as quickly as I can, but at the same time  there will not be a fire sale. So, that's where we are.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: But I think just build on this one before I pick up the second question, Paul, is, and you know better than anybody  else that the weather was pretty bad this year. And in Queensland where we are building Amrun during the wet  seasons, you can't do anything at all. That's pretty simple. The mud is pretty significant. So, the weather – a  couple of weeks ago now. Three weeks ago? Two weeks ago with Chris. Now you can see clearly, physically a  pickup in terms of activity. So, I'm very confident that the ramp up of activities in Amrun will translate into  additional CapEx in the second half. And the second element, as an example, is clearly Oyu Tolgoi is still ramping  up. And therefore, commitment – capital commitment will translate into cash expenditure and so on and so forth.  So, we won't get to $5 billion maybe, but I think there will be a clear step up of CapEx between H1 and H2.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Moving on to the question on the Pilbara. It's absolutely clear. We are totally transparent on the fact that there  were operational issues in the first half in the Pilbara. A big chunk of it is weather related and you'll see it with  some of our peers as well. But we took the decision to accelerate the upgrade program on the railway in order to  make sure that we can enable further productivity improvement in the coming years. So, you know, the results are  what they are in the first half.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So, [indiscernible] (40:03) it's actually broader the question here. I had the opportunity to meet with the, for  example, Chairman Xiao, who is the Chairman of SASAC who controls all the non-financial SOEs three times the  last 12 months. I've got no doubt in my mind that the government of China is serious about restructuring this  industry, but restructuring the industry doesn't mean a drop in output. So, they're taking out the old polluting  capacity and they are concentrating on newest. And for them to be able to produce the same output, and you've  seen from the start that the output, this year's output – this year has been very, very strong in China. They need to  have better raw material, starting with iron ore.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: You've got Silvergrass now coming through, which is going to be conveyor rather than trucks, so it takes the cost  down, but there's a CapEx involvement to put it in. We'll probably spend more on retrofitting some of the trucks for  AutoHaul or new AutoHaul trucks.

texts.speaker: Clarke Wilkins
texts.profession: Analyst, Citigroup Global Markets Australia Pty Ltd.
texts.text: Good morning, gentlemen. Just a couple of questions on the unloved children, so to speak. The Australian  aluminum asset, we're seeing a lot of pressure on electricity prices here in Australia. Yeah, I understand you have  a long-term contract for power supply, but we're already seeing curtailment of some capacity. Have you looked at  the sort of longer-term implications of that in retesting the current carrying value of those assets, or is that  something that should have been done at the sort of full-year result?

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Pick up the energy one. I mean, I'm on public record saying that you know, there is a serious situation in relation  to energy in Australia. It's not only about Rio Tinto. It's across the patch, all right. What we want as a company is  a source which is affordable and reliable of power in Australia. And today, that is not the case. And it's not  because of a lack of capacity. It's about the regulatory framework and how it's working at the state level.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So, the only thing I can say is please fix the problem because otherwise when I look at the plan, either at the state  level or the federal level in Australia where people want to develop more manufacturing activities, if the industry  can't have access to reliable and affordable source of power that will not work.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: However, where – and I hope I'm wrong. I really hope I'm wrong. Where I'm very cautious is when people say that  in winter they will switch on and switch off product lines. Coming from the aluminum industry I've got my doubts  because when you switch on switch off, you destroy your product lines as simple as that, okay? That's the piece  and, as I said, I hope I'm wrong. So, in the short term, I'm very cautious.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: I know the market is saying something else, which is great because we enjoy those higher prices year-on-year.  I've got my concern in the short term. Medium and long term, no doubt about it that they will do what they said  they will do. And in this context, having aluminum smelter in Canada, hydro-based where they are not in the first  quartile of the cost care but in the first decile of the cost curve, is a fantastic advantage. So, we have no issue on  this one in the medium and long term.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Okay. That's the answer for the first question, no change. We want to have a robust balance sheet, but having a  zero net debt is not one on the agenda.

texts.speaker: Sergey Donskoy
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA (UK)
texts.text: The restructuring of the steel industry, my sense, is moving in the right direction. The key source of uncertainty is  really about two things. It's the volume of domestic production in China. Remember a few years ago, they  produced around 400 million tonnes, roughly 235 million tonnes last year, first half. We believe they are back to  275 million tonnes. And as and when somebody is going to say enough is enough, I've been sitting on the loss  and I'm going to clear the deck on the stockpile.

file: RIO - Q2 2018 Earnings Call 1August2018 500 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 01-Aug-18.pdf

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Turning to capital allocation. As I mentioned today, we announced a record interim dividend and a top-up to our  existing buyback programs. We also continue to improve our world-class portfolio, announcing divestments for a  total of $5 billion in the first half of this year. Overnight, we closed the sale of our remaining Queensland coal  assets for around $4 billion. The post-tax proceeds from our divestments will be returned to our shareholders. Our  strong balance sheet with a net debt of $5 billion positions us well for the future

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Thanks, J-S. These are another strong set of results. But let's have a look at the numbers in more detail, starting  with the commodities. In iron ore, benchmark 62% prices declined by 9% versus last year. This was driven by  slightly lower demand, stronger-than-usual first half seaborne supply, and some destocking of inventory at the  ports, mostly in the second quarter. However, lower iron ore prices were offset by higher prices across the rest of  the group.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Copper prices in the first half of 2018 were 20% higher than the first half of 2017, primarily as a result of strong  demand from both China and the rest of the world. China's environmental policies also curtailed the importation of  scrap, which created increased demand for concentrate and cathode. Copper prices sold off in the last month or  so as markets became concerned by the noise around potential trade wars.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: As I've just discussed, pricing has been broadly positive across the commodities with higher pricing in most of our  products, more than offsetting slightly lower iron ore prices. Overall, there was an improvement of $600 million  compared to the first half of last year.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Price improvements during the period could have been about $200 million higher for the group, but for the impact  of legacy alumina contracts. These contracts are for the supply of just over 2 million tonnes of alumina per year  and are linked to the primary metal LME price have ended into first half in 2003. We're likely to see the same  impact in the second half should prices stay high. The impact of unfavorable exchange rates, energy costs and  measured inflation, have had a combined negative $400 million impact in this period. This brings us to flexed  underlying EBITDA of $9.2 billion.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: During the period, we've seen input costs in both our Aluminum and TiO2 businesses, negatively impacted by  about $300 million. Other cash costs have had a negative impact of $200 million. This includes additional  exploration and evaluation activity, as well as spend in Information Systems & Technology, and further investment  to support the group's mine-to-market productivity program. These were partially offset by improvement in the iron  ore cost base, further enhancing our productivity gains.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We started to see cost increases in 2017, initially in the Aluminum group. As you can see here, the indexed price  of caustic, coke and pitch remain well above the first half of 2017. And as a bell-wether for input costs, average oil  prices rose approximately 28% to $68 a barrel during the first half. We'll continue to fight against rising inflation  across the business. And I'll now discuss how our productivity program has assisted in offsetting some of these  increases, and allowed us to keep our EBITDA margin broadly in line with the first half of 2017.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: For 2020, we're raising our guidance to around $6.5 billion. This $0.5 billion increase partly reflects the timing of  spending and additional capital required for some of the replacement production in the Pilbara and increased  CapEx expected in that year on the Oyu Tolgoi power station. In each of those years, the expectation is that  sustaining capital will be between $2 billion and $2.5 billion. In 2018 and 2019, we'll continue to spend CapEx at  Amrun. At OT, we're spending around $1 billion in each year to develop the underground mine, and from 2019,  we'll also start spending CapEx on the power station.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In the iron ore business, we'll need to spend around $3 billion on sustaining CapEx over the next three years.  We'll also spend about $2.7 billion on replacement mines over the same period. And starting in 2019, we expect  to see spend coming through for the Koodaideri Mine. The increase that we're seeing in the Pilbara replacement  mine spend is due to a combination of increased capital costs from revised scopes for some of the projects and  the fact we're bringing forward some of our 2021 spend into 2020. The feasibility study for Koodaideri is ongoing.  And yesterday, the board approved $150 million of early-works funding for this project. One of the advantages of  a strong balance sheet is the ability to invest in the business through the cycle and to drive future returns.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: During the first half, we've announced $5 billion of divestments from our coking coal assets in European  Aluminum smelters. We've now received $4.1 billion pre-tax proceeds from the disposal of our coking coal assets,  Hail Creek and Valeria, Kestrel and Winchester South. The bulk of this was actually received overnight, pretty  close timing.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In addition, China's policy changes have had a significant and enduring impact on several industries, including the  mining sector. Supply side reforms and pollution controls have resulted in capacity reductions, which are  unprecedented. This is particularly the case in steel making, the outcome of which is higher capacity utilization  and improved profitability.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The change in industry structure has also led to a shift in iron ore demand, which in turn has given rise to a  significant premium for higher quality product. And that is absolutely good news for Rio Tinto.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Resource nationalism is not the new feature of the mining industry. But there is no doubt that many stakeholders  want a greater share of the wealth created by minerals development. There is also an increasing emphasis on  how we operate and our impact on the world around us. This is why we believe our license to operate is a make  or break for the industry.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Yesterday, the board approved around $150 million, $146 million exactly, Chris, for early works and studies at the  Koodaideri mine. This will be our first fully-autonomous mine. We also have an extensive pipeline of additional  replacement and growth options in the Pilbara. Oyu Tolgoi and Resolution are two of the largest Copper projects  in the industry, long life, low cost and close to our customers in China and in the USA.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Our Canadian Aluminum smelters are in the first quartile. Long term, as demand grows, we will strengthen these  assets through continued productivity gains and potentially, brownfield expansions. These smelters are already  the greenest in the industry. And the new technology joint venture between Rio Tinto, Alcoa and Apple to create  carbon free smelting will mean an even more attractive product for consumers and the further reduction in  operating costs.

texts.speaker: Jason Fairclough
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: No. You mentioned the quality premiums being paid in iron ore right now. Could you talk a little bit about how the  organization thinks about the sustainability of those premiums...

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: All right. So, you asked me the same question last year? Okay. So, one of your colleagues did. So, we believe  that the shift between high grade and low grade in iron ore in China is becoming more and more structural, all  right. We have the opportunity to meet again with [indiscernible] (33:53) months ago and there is no doubt that the  restructuring of the steel industry is here to stay. That the push for environmental better performance is there as  well, and therefore, they will continue to reduce capacity. That doesn't mean they will reduce production. And you  saw the latest stats on the production, steelmaking is still – steel production, sorry, is still increasing in China. And  therefore, for them to continue to produce, we will reduce capacity you need higher grades. So, we believe that  the spread, the difference, the discount, the premium, call it whatever you want between high grade and low  grade is here to stay. That's the first point.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: And the metrics have not changed. $10 of price is worth $2 billion of free cash flow after tax for Rio Tinto. So, we  do this optimization every year. And at this point in time, we are comfortable with the guidance of 330 million  tonnes to 340 million tonnes for this year. We'll provide a new guidance at the end of this year. And then we have  updated our guidance in terms of CapEx for the next three years where you see some slightly higher replacement  CapEx for iron ore.

texts.speaker: Paul Young
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Australia)
texts.text: Hi, J-S. Hi, Chris. J-S, two questions for you actually. The first one is on the bauxite market. I noticed a statement  in the results about there being significant uncertainties around the direction of the bauxite market. That appears  to be new. You had a decent increase in realized price during the half, but based on what you're seeing in  Guinea, in Guinea supply, how's this changed your view on long-run fundamentals and pricing? And second  question, J-S is on Oyu Tolgoi underground development since you're progressing very well, but I'm interested in  the exact CapEx requirements for the power plant and the benefits of actually on the cost side. And also your  view on the current government study around this implementation of the investment agreement. Thanks, J-S.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: On Oyu Tolgoi is – do you want to pick up the power stuff, Chris?

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: I'm sure there will be further announcement including potentially a power station in the second half of this year. If I  can take another question from the phone and then I'll come back. Is now there somebody?

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Today, we don't have any problem whatsoever. Remember, you need to look at it through the lens of a consumer  in the U.S. If you are a consumer in the U.S., you want to have access to a low-cost, reliable source of Aluminum.  You could argue some of them wants to have a green access to sources, to have access to a green Aluminum as  well. And the best Aluminum we can think of is coming from our smelters in Canada. I mean they are not in the  first quartile of the cost curve. They are in the first decile of the cost curve. They are hydro-based.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: And then on top of it, when you think of the joint venture we signed with Alcoa and Apple to develop the  [indiscernible] (48:59) technology, we are few years away from having a purely green product there. So, at the  end of the day from a consumer standpoint in the U.S, I've got no doubt because the supply chain is so integrated  between the U.S. and Canada that there will be – that common sense will prevail.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Yes, well, the K, the year-on-year increase is about $200 million. But – and your question was really about, going  forward, I really can't give you any better guidance and probably maintain the same sort of basis into the second  half. They seem like they're stabilizing and leveling off, but time will tell. It's primarily the inputs of caustic, pitch  and coke. They are the main inputs into that mix. And you see that across our peer group variously as well with  those same items coming through. And the carbon material is also a factor for us in the TiO2 business  [indiscernible] (55:26) But I don't think I can give you much better than that, really.

texts.speaker: Paul Gait
texts.profession: Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Thanks very much. Paul Gait, Bernstein. A couple of quick questions. Could you – you alluded to supply side  reforms in China in terms of steel capacity, but we've also seen that in terms of the iron ore, domestic iron ore  production in China has come down quite markedly year-on-year. Just wondering if you could give us some  thoughts about what you're seeing there.

texts.speaker: Paul Gait
texts.profession: Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Second of all, in terms of the Pilbara Blend and, of course, Koodaideri feeding into that, but how long can you  actually maintain the quality of the Pilbara Blend in sort of roughly today's specifications, given the reserve base  that we've got or that you've got?

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: On the iron ore in China, we have 200 people in Shanghai and we have a big team in China and part of their job  is to find out about it? If you go back a few years ago, our understanding was the local domestic production of iron  ore was around 400 million tonnes. They dropped to, at some stage, to 225 million tonnes. We believe in the first  six months of this year, post-winter cut, we back – there is some uncertainty but if I had to pick a range between  235 million tonnes and 245 million tonnes, maybe slightly below 250 million tonnes if you want to be on the top-ish  side.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Interesting enough, our understanding is primarily a lot of it is underground and not open pit because of pollution,  environment concerns and so on and so forth. So, there is compared to the question asked one year ago, two  years ago, we have full confidence that the iron ore production, domestic iron ore pollution will continue to reduce  because it's high cost, but more importantly the environmental concerns are very significant, hence my comments  about open pit versus underground. So, that's the best views that we have today.

texts.speaker: Myles Allsop
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd.
texts.text: And then secondly, maybe with Pilbara iron ore kind of unit costs, I mean, doing a good job first half of this year.  As we look forward with AutoHaul with the volume increase, can we – kind of is the potential for unit costs to go  down on a two year view despite inflation or is it best case stay where we are?

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Yeah. So, iron ore is not immune from the threat of inflation, what our challenge is is to offset that. So, that's  where we'll be targeting with the productivity agenda. Obviously, things like the oil price showing pretty healthy  sort of increases over the course of last year. And we will have – we will be entering more below water table-type  mining as well. We're going to have longer haul distances. So, we do have some challenges coming our way,  which is important that we get the productivity agenda in full run there.

texts.speaker: Clarke Wilkins
texts.profession: Analyst, Citigroup Global Markets Australia Pty Ltd.
texts.text: And also, just in regards to iron ore, like the comments around the sort of grade discounts being more structural,  we've obviously seen recently impurity penalties rising quite significantly and given your comments around China  domestic supply continuing to fall, is there a chance or is there a potential to defer impurity penalties in the market  are also going to be more structural and is bringing forward the sort of caveats at Koodaideri a potential way to  sort of adjust the quality of that Pilbara Blend?

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: On the iron ore pricing is, without getting into the detail too much, the impurity is already priced. So if you look at  the pricing formula, it's not only about the Fe content. There are adjustments for alumina for us and so on and so  forth. So, the pricing exists already there to adjust for those impurities. But your question is absolutely spot on is,  it is – our experience is the – because of the pressure from SASAC and the government in China in relation to  environment, the management of the burner and of the blast furnaces is becoming more and more important. And  last summer I went there and I met with some of the engineers or some of the people at our customer sites, I can  tell you I've never seen. And I've been traveling to China for many, many years in the context of steel. Remember,  I used to work in the steel business before joining Rio Tinto.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: I've never seen our customers knowing how well to manage their burner, how well to run their – the performance  of their blast furnaces and so on and so forth. So, it is absolutely clear that all customers in China are becoming  closer to the customer we have in Japan, very aware of how you optimize your blast furnaces and I'm sure that  the question about the impurities the first, for example, in alumina will become something which could be a  feature. But the point is, the pricing already account for those adjustments and so on and so forth. So, that's  where we are.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Having said that, we are looking at option that we've done forever to expand the capacity of aluminum smelter on  the back of brownfield and on the back of creeping because that is productivity and so on and so forth. But before  we take a decision to build a brand new 0.5 million tonne smelter in Canada, we see it a few years away. And I  invite you to open this smelter, Chris, when it happens.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Tom Albanese, Chief Executive  Thank you, operator, and good morning to everyone on the conference even though they are  probably sitting in snow or maybe at home waiting for the snow to melt. You should all have a slide  pack titled North American conference call available from our website.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Production has exceeded the employed capacity with Pilbara since the second quarter and we’re  now set  full year production and sales records despite severe weather and poor market conditions  at the start of the year. The Operations Centre in Perth continued to enhance performance as it  neared the final stages of construction and ramp up. We remain active across a range of sales  mechanisms with our Asian customers and in late 2009 we made the first delivery of iron ore to  India.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Our iron ore business in the Pilbara is currently expanding beyond its 220 million tonne per year  capacity. This will be achieved by first injecting a new incremental capacity of 10 million tonnes per  year and then looking at further stage development to take us to 330 million tonnes per year by the  end of 2015.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Moving on to slide number nine. Earnings at the energy group were study with higher volumes  compensating for weaker prices. Demand for the Clermont thermal coal, particularly from China  increased in the second half and China also emerged as a significant met coal important in 2009.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: U.S. coal earnings reflected higher prices in contracts and the impacts of divestments. At our  uranium businesses, ERA production was strong and continued to benefit from higher realized  prices as legacy contracts continued to expire. At Rossing, lower market prices resulted in lower  revenues.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: I would like to add, well on uranium, that my view uranium is an increasingly important part of our  energy portfolio as we move progressively toward a carbon-constrained world.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Lower energy cash costs from reduced spending on evaluation and exploration improved the  earnings further. At 6.3 billion, 2009 full year underlying earnings were 2.4 billion higher than 2.8  once adjusted for the effect of movements in traded and non-traded prices and exchange rates.  Our total cash costs declined by 5.6 billion between 2008 and 2009 as shown in slide 14. Setting  the under controllable costs aside and excluding the impact on costs of changes in production level  between the two years, we reduced our pre-tax cash operating costs by 2.6 billion. This exceeds  the target we set for ourselves one year early.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Energy will complete the Clermont and Grasberg projects, with first call from Clermont expected to  be shipped on time and on budget in the fist quarter of this year and at full capacity by 2013. And  we have had one of the best portfolios of undeveloped copper projects in the world highlighted by  our Oyu Tolgoi Investment. Construction planning is underway for the target of first production in  2013.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Anthony Rizzuto>: Tom in the last couple of days we’ve heard BHP Billiton and Vale talk  about a more – adopting a more flexible pricing structure in iron ore, and we’ve also heard talk  about met coal too. But do you believe that the spot market is becoming a more accurate indicator  of the supply/demand in the market? And if so, could we see you guys adopting more flexible  structure with regard to your negotiations?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: So I do think that what we’re seeing now which is strong demand for steel and basically an increase  in steel production on a global basis now leading to stronger demand for iron ore which is now  leading to higher spot prices for iron ore. We’re certainly taking that noted as we look at 2010 and  the period ahead. And just to emphasize, our demand for iron ore today has never been stronger.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Anthony Rizzuto>: Okay. Just if I could segue over to kind of portfolio management activities  that you guys have done. Obviously, you’ve got net debt down very, very substantially and you’ve  recapped your balance sheet. Just a question, we see your competitors obviously becoming very  active in the fertilizer area and even though you have sold potash assets in Argentina and Canada,  how do you feel about the fertilizer business for the long term? Is it something that you think is well  positioned?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Tom Albanese>: Well, Tony, I was the project champion that got us into the PRC project in  2001, so I’ve been following potash for most of the last decade. There are three fertilizers, minerals,  macro-minerals and there is a bunch of micronutrients. Of those three I think that potash has  number of very strong attributes and also very closely aligned with the mining industry. It’s  geologically fairly scarce and restricted to certain types of deposits. And it’s also something that is  not easily substitutable by say, other feedstocks. So if you look at say phosphate for example, there  is lots of phosphate around the world and lots of alternatives for phosphate consumers, and  besides that you’ve got to take phosphate through a fairly capital intensive DAP process after that.  Nitrogen, there are some natural nitrate minerals but most of the nitrogen comes as the byproduct  of the oil and gas industry, so it’s not playing to our strength.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Phosphate, it’s a mineral product, not a lot of downstream processing to put it on the soil, that’s a  good news. The bad news, of course, as you know that potash and potassium tend to be banked   in the soil so that if a farmer has a bad year, they will basically continue to put on the nitrogen and  the phosphates but they’ll basically reduce their consumption or eliminate their consumption of  potash in that given year. So when you have a global financial crisis like we’ve had, every farmer  around the world stops applying potash at the same time. So it is subject to some fairly high swings  and volatility that the industry needs to be aware off.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In our – looking at the potash market and the PRC project, I think we recognized from the beginning  that that was predominantly a feedstock and naturally the feedstock for the Brazilian markets. And I  think in the course of our discussions with Vale last year, they had – they saw a strategic  advantage and there’s probably some government support Brazil for self-efficiency in that ag  sector. So they had some strategic imperatives to get into that particular business particularly an  Argentinean potash producer.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: So I think we saw the value. We like that value. It was very, very helpful for us as we were needing  at that particular period of very difficult economic conditions to bring down our debt and that was  the right transaction. Longer term, I do think potash is a place to be. In our decade of being  involved with potash we discovered the world. We have a pretty good idea of where there be some  additional basin and I’ve told our geologists to go out and find some potash.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Tom Albanese>: Yes, Sayan, we have very concrete growth plans for 2010. Let me just walk  through them in some detail. We had already said we’re running in excess of a 220 million tonnes  per year run rate, and we had flagged in the results seminar last autumn that we were looking at  two smaller, but incremental expansions really debottlenecking the Dampier port to take that 200 to  225 by early next year, and then 230 by early 2012.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q>: Thank you for being available once again. Two questions. First, BHP disclosed that they sold  46% of their iron ore on spot or quarterly or outside the benchmark system in the half year. And I  think 27% of their metallurgical coal. If you could tell us how much of your sales are outside the  system, that’d be helpful in assessing the health of the system or the benchmark.

texts.text: As Tom mentioned earlier, the aluminum group achieved further controllable cost savings in 2010  of at least $300 million in addition to the $1 billion realized in 2009. This demonstrates the  transformation which is underway in our aluminum business. These cost improvements have been  achieved through the cumulative effect of many different initiatives. Our continued focus on  procurement has supported further caustic soda and coke cost savings. We continue to focus on  identifying further sustainable and significant operating cost improvements in the business.

texts.speaker: Jan P. du Plessis, Executive Chairman
texts.profession: Well, let’s start then. Good morning, everyone, here in London and good evening to those of you
texts.text: Elsewhere, we did see some upward pressure on costs. Adverse weather, higher strip ratios and  lower yields led to higher costs at our Australian coal operations. In New South Wales, part of this  increase in waste removal is in order to prepare for a ramp up of production over the next two years  to utilize latent capacity. It’s likely that strip ratios will increase slightly in 2011 before falling  modestly in 2012.

texts.speaker: Jan P. du Plessis, Executive Chairman
texts.profession: Well, let’s start then. Good morning, everyone, here in London and good evening to those of you
texts.text: As I’ve said before, a stable investment climate is critical to allow commitments of this size. We’ve  worked in consultation with the Australian government’s Policy Transition Group on the proposed  mineral resources rent tax. We acknowledge that the PTG’s recommendations are an important  step towards ensuring that the design and principles of the heads of agreement entered into with  the government are carried through to the final MRRT legislation.

texts.speaker: Jan P. du Plessis, Executive Chairman
texts.profession: Well, let’s start then. Good morning, everyone, here in London and good evening to those of you
texts.text: Rio Tinto has announced the investment of almost $9 billion in Australia since the MRRT was  proposed. This includes our iron ore expansion plans in the Pilbara, which is the largest mining  project ever undertaken in Australia. This investment underlines our confidence that the MRRT deal  will be honored. We will work constructively with the government and the proposed implementation  group in 2011.

texts.speaker: Jan P. du Plessis, Executive Chairman
texts.profession: Well, let’s start then. Good morning, everyone, here in London and good evening to those of you
texts.text: There’s two primary projects in differing phase of evaluation and development and the key features  of these properties based upon Riversdale reports are set out in the table below. Both projects will  produce about 60% hard coking coal and 40% thermal coal. If successful, this acquisition would  provide Rio Tinto with a substantial development pipeline in the emerging Moatize Basin in  Mozambique, in line with our established strategy.

texts.speaker: Jan P. du Plessis, Executive Chairman
texts.profession: Well, let’s start then. Good morning, everyone, here in London and good evening to those of you
texts.text: I’m a great supporter of investment in new innovative technologies through our Mine of the Future  programme. We now advance programmes in a number of areas. Our focus ranges from  exploration to rapid underground mine development, advanced mineral sorting and autonomous  equipment. We are now moving these technologies from proof of concept to pilot to implementation  across our product groups.

texts.speaker: Jan P. du Plessis, Executive Chairman
texts.profession: Well, let’s start then. Good morning, everyone, here in London and good evening to those of you
texts.text: In iron ore, as I’ve said, the Operations Centre has been a resounding success. We’ve also been  trialing automated equipment in the Pilbara at West Angelas. We’re also seeing greater efficiency  and lower production costs as well as improved health, safety, and environmental performance.

texts.speaker: Jan P. du Plessis, Executive Chairman
texts.profession: Well, let’s start then. Good morning, everyone, here in London and good evening to those of you
texts.text: In copper, we’re actively responding to the challenges of deeper and lower-grade ore bodies.  Technologies for rapid underground mine construction will allow us to develop future mines more  quickly, more safely and at lower costs. Advanced mineral recovery techniques will enable us to  turn low-grade deposits into future tier one assets. And as competition for tier one resources  increase, competitive advantage in exploration and technology will continue to deliver great value.
