texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So let's now turn to 2011 results. We achieved record underlying earnings, record EBITDA and record operating  cash flows. This was despite the severe weather conditions in the first half and the fall in commodity prices we saw  through the second half. Our Pilbara iron ore business broke annual production and sales records and shipped  record volumes in the fourth quarter, not – of course, as Jan said, not all our divisions are enjoying those same  tailwinds. At our November seminar, we outlined our refocused aluminum strategy in response to the uncertain  and evolving macroeconomic conditions.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We're advancing our industry leading portfolio of growth projects, and it's worth highlighting that Pilbara has the  highest quality iron ore expansion in the global sector. Pilbara at 283Mt/a is now fully approved and on track to  months, raised them to 20 million tonnes to 353 million tonnes per year. Subject to board approval, we will reach  this capacity in the first half of 2015.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: This is in stark contrast to the broader iron ore industry trend, which has seen some projects subject to significant  delay and increased capital intensity. We've successfully completed a number of acquisitions through the year,  which complement our organic pipeline and give us further growth options.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We now have significant Tier 1 resources in coking and thermal coal in Mozambique, and uranium in Canada. And  earlier this year, we moved to majority stake in Ivanhoe Mines, further demonstrating our commitment to a safe  and successful development of the Oyu Tolgoi copper-gold mine.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: On the supply side, we estimate that about 45 million tonnes of iron ore was removed from the market in 2011 due  to adverse weather in the Pilbara, lower than expected Brazilian exports and rising export tariffs in India.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We exceeded our production targets for 2011 and increased our annual capacity in the Pilbara to 225 million  tonnes, completing our first debottlenecking project on time and on budget in the first quarter last year. This  incremental capacity together with the continued productivity improvement from our industry leading operations  center helped us achieve these records.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: It is important, of course, to – remember, we're currently in the middle of the cyclone season in Western  Australia, and already this year, we've seen some disruption and we'll a keep careful eye on all of the weather  forecast.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: At Cape Lambert, all the dredging for the expansion of 283 million tonnes is complete and engineering is at 82%.  We've just approved the construction at Amaldi Mines, and so this 283 million tonne expansion is now fully  authorized. And, of course, studies are progressing well and are accelerated and enhanced expansion to 353  million tonnes. We've already ordered the long-lead items, and just this week we approved $1.2 billion for further  early works. Cape Lambert, as shown in the picture here, continues to be the best expansion opportunity in the

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We continue to drill out the resource base in our Tier 1 Pilbara ore bodies and over the next five years, we plan to  drill another 600,000 meters per year to add to our 2.9 billion tonnes of iron ore reserve in line with our multi- decade mine planning. And our global growth options are not limited to the Pilbara. At our Canadian operations,  the first stage of concentrate expansion project is currently being commissioned. And at Simandou in Guinea,  solid progress has been made, early works construction is ramping up, including the construction of roadworks  and the development of early trucking options.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In China, aluminum prices have historically traded at a premium to the LME and have been less volatile. Despite  experiencing a rising cost of electricity, higher margin cost smelters in the coastal and central provinces are able to  take advantage of this higher Shanghai price premium. This has also led to a further expansion of smelting  capacity at the remote but coal-rich provinces in the West, particularly in the Xinjiang province.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Outside of China, we estimate roughly 2.5 million tonnes of smelting capacity is at a loss-making position at the  current prices and input costs. Further capacity reductions are necessary to move the aluminum market to a more  balanced state.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Looking further ahead, we continue to believe in our long-run outlook for aluminum demand growth. But Chinese  output of primary aluminum is still tracking internal demand. Production has shifted more towards the  Northwest, where stranded coal is being used to generate cheaper electricity.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Programs are underway to deliver $1 billion of incremental EBITDA from business improvements. And we are  focusing investment on the high return creep and modernization projects. We'll be longer in bauxite and alumina,  taking full advantage of our exceptional Tier 1 bauxite resources, and with have a portfolio of modern hydro-based  smelters supported by leading industry technology.  This is absolutely the right strategy, but it has required us to relook at the value ascribed to aluminum assets. As a  result, we have recorded an impairment charge this year, which Guy will speak to in more detail.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In 2011, the copper market was in deficit with the shortfall of supply met by drawing down supplies mainly in  China. We expect the market to continue to be finally balanced in 2012. New global copper mine supply is  expected to come online in 2012. However, experience has shown that project delivery and ramp-up timelines  have taken longer, globally, than expected.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Just a few weeks ago, just shortly after the expiry of the standstill agreement with Ivanhoe, we – our shareholding  Ivanhoe increased to a majority 51% interest. The project itself has made good progress. But as you know,  discussions continue on security of power source for the project, we still needed to remain on schedule. I have a  feasibility study to Phase II to develop the underground block cave mine continues to make progress.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We're also, of course, moving forward on other Tier 1 copper projects. La Granja received prefeasibility funding to  evaluate a three-staged phase development using conventional milling and leaching. The feasibility study at  Kennecott Utah Copper to extend the mine life to 2028 is expected to be complete in the first half of this year. And  again at Escondida, project approval for OGP1 is targeted for the first half of 2012.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So again, now let's turn to our Energy group. In 2011 coal markets were volatile with both global supply and  demand disruptions occurring at different times throughout the year after cheering near-record prices in January  2011, following Indonesian and Australian supply side disruptions, global thermal coal markets experienced broad  price declines through the remainder of 2011.  This decline reflected weaker global economic activity and strong supply growth, however, prices remain well  supported. While the uranium market is likely to be subdued over the next few – five years, uranium will continue  to form an important part in the overall energy mix, with long-term demand expected to be driven by strong  growth in China.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Our Energy operations in Australia recovered well from the effects of significant wet weather that occurred  extensively in Queensland, New South Wales and the Northern territory in the first quarter of 2011. Disruptions to  the supply of explosives in Eastern Australia has impacted overburden removal for some of our New South Wales  operations as it has in the rest of the East Australian mining sector, with the consequential effect to the level of in- pit inventories.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Though there was no overall significant impact to the Australian coal production in 2011, there will be some  impact in the first half of 2012. As part of our continuous program to improve our portfolio, we just completed  joint acquisition of the minority interest in Coal & Allied in December in partnership with Mitsubishi. And this has  resulted in a simpler ownership structure with greater flexibility and access to funds for growth.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: At ERA, extreme wet weather caused the prolonged suspension of operations in the first half, but the operations  did recover well in the second half. AUD 500 million rights issue was completed in December, which will allow  ERA to fund its strategic water management plan, closure obligations and the Ranger 3 Deeps exploration decline.  At Rössing, grade will progressively improve over the next two years as we access lower benches in the mine.  Meanwhile, work continues on excavation drilling to extend mine life beyond 2023.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Our Energy group is now entering a new phase with many prospects for value-adding growth in the near term and  beyond. At Australia, our target has increased annual coal capacity to 73 million tonnes per year by 2015. This  growth will be underpinned by the development of new mine at Mount Pleasant in the Hunter Valley, which is  currently in feasibility study.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In the short term, we're increasing capacity at existing operations, such as the Clermont Mine and the brownfield  expansions into Hunter Valley, Mount Thorley Warkworth and at Bengalla. These will lead to an increase of about  15% to 20% in total Australian coal production in 2012. The Kestrel Mine extension is well advanced and is  scheduled to start production in 2013 with incremental annual production of around 1 million tonnes.  Infrastructure will be a critical factor in the delivery of this growth, and our position for the future continues to  strengthen.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In New South Wales and Queensland, investment has been made in the coal supply chain to meet this increasing  demand. During the first half of the year, we completed the acquisition of Riversdale, which has now been  renamed Rio Tinto Coal Mozambique. There's a good photo of it in the upper side of the plant and under  construction at present. This does provides a substantial Tier 1 coking coal development pipeline in the emerging  Moatize basin. Initial production from the Benga project is scheduled for the first half of this year.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Following the Riversdale transaction, we completed the acquisition of Hathor in Canada, and these encouraging  uranium exploration development opportunities are one of the highest grade uranium basins in the world. With  the forecast demand for energy and steel production over the coming decades, I have real confidence the high  quality growth projects being pulled together by the Energy team, will deliver excellent results over the long term.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Turning now to diamonds and minerals. Demand for borates and titanium dioxide feedstocks held up well despite  ongoing market volatility. 2011 saw a continued tightness in TiO2 feedstock supply, which is expected to continue  over the medium term. Diamond prices were strong in the first half of 2011, but the second half did see lower  new diamonds and further potential for diamond growth in China and India. Diamond production did decline  15%, overall, due to heavy rains we saw due to flooding at Argyle early in the year and maintenance shutdowns  that we saw at Argyle in the fourth quarter in the processing plant.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The impact of the record wet season in Argyle, coupled with the continued strength of the Australian dollars, did  result in a further $500 million of capital be improved – being approved to complete the Argyle underground  project. And we would expect to experience lower grades until the underground mine is at full production by 2014.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Earnings for Iron & Titanium business did double in 2011 as we continue to replace these multi-year sales  contracts with alternative pricing mechanism, increasing the business' exposure to market prices for TiO2  feedstocks.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: At QMM and Madagascar, production steadily increased due to successful dry mining operations. Full capacity is  expected to be reached over the next two to three years. As you know, we sold our talc business in August and have  created new opportunities in potash through a joint venture agreement in Saskatchewan, home to nearly half the  world's potash reserves.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: And finally, just last week, we announced we'll be doubling our stake in Richards Bay Minerals on Tier 1 asset that  we've been managing for many years, actually, many decades.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Let me start by taking a look at how our record underlying earnings were achieved. It will come as no surprise that  the primary driver has been price, increasing earnings by $6.7 billion. By far, the largest benefit came from iron  ore prices, although, copper and hard coking coal increases were also significant. These benefits were partially  offset by the impact of currency movements, notably, the stronger Australian dollar. These collectively reduced  our underlying earnings by nearly $1 billion compared with 2010.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: As previously flagged, lower copper and gold grades at Kennecott Utah Copper, Escondida and Grasberg have led  to lower sales volumes, which reduced our earnings by just over $0.5 billion. This was partially offset by record  volumes from iron ore as increased port capacity was brought online.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Continued cost pressure is evident throughout the industry and we are not immune. The impacts of inflation and  higher energy costs reduced our 2011 earnings by over $600 million. And more importantly, higher cash costs  reduced earnings by a further $2.1 billion, which I'll return to in detail in a moment.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The exceptional weather experienced in the first half of the year also impacted our volume and, as a consequence,  increased our unit cash costs. And we've also incurred additional cost due to our investment in operational  readiness as we prepare to bring online a number of major growth projects, in particular in the Pilbara.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Purchases from China include coke, caustic soda, rail cars and other supply. And we will also continue to mitigate  some of these cost increases through our industry leading investments in technology. This will lead to increased  automation and improve productivity across many of our operations in years to come.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The industry, as Guy says, does continue to face challenges with the supply side, from rising raw material and  labor costs as well as industrial action and weather events. And projects, as you've heard, will becoming  increasingly difficult to finance for some, and the capital intensity for both projects is continuing rise. Resource  nationalism and long processes for permitting, stakeholder engagement improvals also have the effect of reducing  supply growth. Of course, geologically, the deposits are becoming more difficult to find and, technically, more  difficult to develop. And all these factors will continue to put pressure on the supply side within the environment  of this increasing demand. This development, of course, will go through periods of volatility such as what we're  currently facing right now.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Over in the Exploration group, work has led to the finding and developing of the next generation of ore bodies,  from bauxite in Brazil through the potash in Saskatchewan, new projects across the globe are delivering promising  results.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: First of all on OT, we have two things that are being done that will need to be done on the power. The first is the  construction of the power line on the Chinese side of the border between power generating capacity and the OT  operations. And second would be the power supply agreements. While we have continued to, I think, make good  commissioning process to be ready by 2013. We're well within that window now and I'm very pleased with the  work that's going on the ground, actually on both areas. I think that part of it will be engineering, engineering  activities on the ground. The actual construction, which again, is something that is measurable and definable and I  think there are actually good efforts and I'm confident are underway as we speak.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: You mentioned Argyle, actually, I mean although currency contributed to that, there were a number of other  features to that overrun. The first being that we slowed the project down in the global financial crisis and that had  a whole lot of demobilization and then remobilization effects. And on top of that, we have the effect of the weather  last year, which certainly has led to some difficult conditions, which had safety implications within the mine. So  we had to slow things down. So there were a number of other features in the case of Argyle. But anyway, to  reassure you, we are looking at it and if we make a change, we will tell the shareholders.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Well, thank you, Jason. I'm going to talk about iron ore and our longer term view of iron ore. Frankly, we're – we  probably have some similar ideas of where we might have a different approach from BHP. Our view on steel  demand in China is that we are moving toward a point, which you would expect of deceleration of steel  consumption growth in China, and that's nothing that would be surprising. I think all modelers and econometric

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: And we're in that stage that you're moving from steel consumption leading GDP to steel consumption beginning to  lag GDP, while GDP growth begins to moderate but from a much larger base. And just as a reminder of that larger  base, we had very, very rapid steel consumption increases in 2007, which we had been flagging. It's slowed down  since then but the overall level of steel consumption in China is more than 40% higher than 2007. So it's slowing  down from a much larger base.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Meanwhile, the Chinese domestic iron ore production is not getting any better. It's not getting any cheaper. It's  not getting any more efficient. It's actually rising in terms of its overall cost levels. You have expansions flagged in  Australia in Brazil and in lesser extent, in West Africa but you also have production coming out of the market  likely on a trend basis from India. So we had to look at all these individual balances when we map out what levels  of capacity is there in the seaborne market.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: And the final step, I think, is capital intensity. I'm very, very pleased with the capital intensity comparative to the  rest of the sector, although I'm concerned about the fact that capital intensity in general has increased, which  probably has just increased the reason why we do need to phase in some of these next tranches.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Now in addition to Pilbara, of course, we have IOC, which is basically has added an even smaller bites with these  various smaller expansions, especially in concentrate capacity, we have the magnetite resource, it's just a matter of  developing the concentrating, the gravity separation, the magnetic separation, so we can increase concentrate  production.

texts.speaker: Jason R. Fairclough
texts.profession: Analyst, Merrill Lynch International (United Kingdom)
texts.text: In iron ore, I think it's fair to say that you guys got dragged kicking and screaming to the spot market, could you  talk a little bit about price discovery for titanium dioxide and how that's going to eventuate?

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Now in terms of TiO2, I think that the structure of the TiO2 market, which is not as big as iron ore obviously, but  we have a very big part of it, has been one of contracts on a business-to-business basis. And I think these contracts  have served Rio Tinto iron and titanium well over the past 20 years, during a period of time when the sector had  been, I think, a mature sector, primarily driven off of North American and European building construction and  painting seasons and sort of the conventional attributes of the pigment sector. What we've seen – we would have  seen in it coming, but it's finally happened, is that the Chinese are beginning to play into these industrial minerals  that are more consumer oriented.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Yeah. Thank you, Myles. If I look at the uranium markets and I talk with our team in Rio Tinto Energy, my view is  that uranium's going to be probably one of the least exciting one of our markets for at least the next five years. And  the way we could plot that out is the fact that you can really see plants, either they're in construction or they're not  in construction, take many years to get built. And we've seen with – certainly with the post-Fukushima world,  some countries deferring projects, some countries leading policies, right or wrong, that basically are trying to be  moving away from nuclear power.  And with that being said, there continues to be, especially in China, but I think elsewhere in the world, a need for  large central sources of power, a large and – distributor systems, the environmentalists might think, that's all you  need, is windmills on every house, but that's not going to work. You're going to need large central systems. You've  got options of basically hydro and that's not an easily expandable power source. You've got options of nuclear,  you've got options of coal and increasingly, there's more and more pressures on future generators to think about  something besides coal. And that's even more the case as we see the markets for carbon beginning eventuate, and  of course, natural gas. So I guess I think natural gas will probably one in the post-2020, which would go more  head-to-head with nuclear. But for those countries that don't have natural gas or they're not conveniently situated  for LNG or just LNG is fairly expensive by then, nuclear power looks quite attractive.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: And I think in China and elsewhere, in the post 2020 environment, I do see nuclear power and uranium to be a  growing part of the global energy mix. I would not be surprised if by post-2020, global energy requirements are  actually higher than what people are forecasting for the same reasons that we're looking at higher steel  consumptions and higher copper consumption.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So for that – what it means for our strategy is essentially be prudent, at least for the next five years in terms of  what we're are investing in the sector, no big bets. We have some house-cleaning to do at our ERA business. We  have to move from open-pit to underground over the next year. We have to deal with the water issues from a  series of what were record-high rainfalls. And then we will be well-positioned, I think, in that post-2020 period  with options at that point.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: And then finally in Canada, we should remind ourselves that the Athabasca Basin contains, by an order of  magnitude, some of the highest quality and highest grade uranium ores in the world. I mean this is – materially,  you have to actually dilute before you could put it in the mill, it's so rich, it's 100 times higher in grade than the  grade at Rössing. So great grade does make a lot of sense in this business if you can get good grades. Our  geologists basically they look around at all sorts of opportunities and all sorts of sectors and our geologists were  quite excited about this opportunity that came to us.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: As you know, I've listened to geologists in the past. We've had some pretty good hits, Oyu Tolgoi being one of  them, and they said this is a place to look. And I was ready to back the Energy group and the geologists for Hathor.  I'm quite excited about what that will deliver. But again, it's not going to be a five-year place. So again, what we've  got to do in our sector is we've got to look out past the next five years, and we have to set aside the options for the  future generations of Rio Tinto so we can actually create great businesses. And that's where I think we can go with  uranium.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And then I guess the second part of the question is we've heard quite a bit in relation to the phased approach to  capital which certainly gives you benefits relative to some of your peers. Can you just elaborate on that a little bit  in relation to the aluminum assets, perhaps particularly Kitimat, given the magnitude of the spend there?

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: I will – maybe I'll tackle through the first part of aluminum, but I think, Guy, if you can add to that, and then I'll  say something about Kitimat. On aluminum and these markets with a – really a strained LME price and higher  input cost, I think it's fair to say that every plant manager of every smelter in Rio Tinto and in the global sector is  paying very close attention to their own marginal cost of production versus the LME price. And we should remind  ourselves the marginal cost for aluminum capacity is somewhere in $2,300 to $2,400 per tonne range or even  higher. So there is a fair amount of global capacity that's probably running in the red as we speak.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So that's something you've seen us do, frankly, you've seen most others in the sector do, and I would say that every  plant manager knows just that, and it's in their best interest, basically, to find a way to run their businesses in this  environment of lower LME and high input prices. Guy, if there's anything else you want to say about aluminum  first.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So we looked at the various options. We did push on whether we could create a smaller starting point, but we also  have a very large – very low cost source of power. I think it's in the first decile in terms of power cost at Kitimat.  And we have so much power that actually – you have more power that you can actually distribute down the  transmission lines. So you've got to find a market for them. I think Kitimat, as we designed it and as we proved it  in the December, took into account both our objective for phases, but frankly, we also had to taking into account  the fact that we had some of the most attractive, most competitive power anywhere in the world but sitting with  some of the oldest technology anywhere in the world.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: I think that when we look at our cost increases – I'll give you some numbers which are year-on-year as opposed to  half-on-half. And the reason I'm going to do that is that last year was a complicated one to analyze because of the  effect on unit cost of whether that harmed the first half, and also because of grade, which also reduced volume in  the Copper group. But if you exclude royalties, freight and the trading activities, which go on in aluminum to save  transport costs, the overall increase in our unit cost was 14.6%. Now that included what we consider to be mining  inflation and input price increase of about 8.4% and the effects of weather, which we computed just under 4%.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So I think that when we look at this, we feel that – I mean, of course, it's much too high a level of increase, we're  tackling it in the various ways which we described during the presentation, but I think that breaking it down by  half is distorted by that weather and – particularly that weather effect.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In 2015, I hope to see half the tonnes we move in the Pilbara being moved with driverless trucks, and that's where  I come about looking at shifts between capital and labor. So I hope that BHP is right that only 20% of these cost  increases are structural, but I think we'd actually have to work harder to keep that from getting worse.

texts.speaker: Paul D. Young
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Australia)
texts.text: And also on your cash flow forecast, can you actually build all these projects at once and then a question on your  aluminum division, I mean Alma, which is [ph] Australian mine (01:13:25) numbers, the most profitable and  valuable smelter in your fleet that's running at 30% output. Are there any sort of one-off costs that we should be  aware of? Can you give us an update on the industrial action there?

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Now that does put us in a position we probably have excess water, it will affect the supply chain, and we made  moves accordingly, but it has led to us having excess hydro capacity. And so that's allowed us – so that's very low  incremental power cost with that, and so we have diverted some of that into restarting two of the lines at  Shawinigan, which will run as long as that makes economic sense to do that.

texts.speaker: Peter O'Connor
texts.profession: Analyst, Merrill Lynch Equities (Australia) Ltd.
texts.text: Tom, just a thought on your latent capacity in your system. Guy walked through the copper issues of low grade at  Escondida, Kennecott and also at Grasberg, I'm just wondering, compared to the tonnage you put out in 2011,  what could we reasonably expect in terms of copper units would come back over the next couple of years? And  similarly with weather in iron ore and weather in coal, what low capital latent capacity do you have that's available  over the next one, two, three years?

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Now a lot of latent capacity one would argue is because of weather, and I wish I could – I can predict the weather,  but we're no better at it than they were a thousand years ago. So we have – I mean you've seen that we can run the  Pilbara, for example, at 240 million tonnes per year, and people say, well, if you do that in the one quarter, why  can't you do for the whole year? And I do have to remind you that these cyclones do come through and I have been  assured and certainly in past several years have seen evidence of this that the cyclonic activity in  Western/Northwestern Australia is actually the most unpredictable cyclone activity of any hurricane, cyclone,  typhoon system in the world. And these things do literally turn on a dime, so it's very difficult to make any kind of  prediction.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: All we could do is basically derate our capacity during these summer wet seasons and then just hope for the best.  And then during the dry season, hope we can make up for whatever the gaps were. We had two weather systems  that came through the Pilbara. In January, one hit – all over Pilbara, hit land and probably made an effect across  the board. The second one didn't hit land but also created some sea swells and also impacted production.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Because with these cyclones, you have three things that could drive the outcome, one is the wind effects and  basically, you have to tie down and protect the plants from wind damage. And the wind effects with winds at over  200 kilometers an hour can be quite enormous, so you have to actually shut down facilities and spend lots of days  of prep and un-prepping. The second would be rain, and again, so you have not only the rain hitting the site but  more likely, because you don't have mature river systems in the Pilbara, you have washouts and you have large  valleys that flood with water and that could have the effect on rail capacity and do quite a bit of damage to rail  systems.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: And the third would be, which is probably the least noticed, is sea swells, and that is that if the storm's hitting off  the coast and it's creating sea swells, and I think the last system is we saw sea swells of three meters in the port,  you've got to actually – you've got to take the ships out to sea, so you can't load during those periods.

texts.speaker: Tom Albanese
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Unpredictable, I wish I could predict them but I wouldn't have called that latent capacity. I think we got to build  our own overall assumption of capacity, making the presumption that we will have a weather factor and we'll try  to calculate that as best we can.

texts.speaker: Peter O'Connor
texts.profession: Analyst, Merrill Lynch Equities (Australia) Ltd.
texts.text: Tom, could I follow on Coal & Allied. And first to congratulate you, after four decades of trying, you've only got  there last year. Where did that business go? And how quickly can you make that business actually work?

texts.speaker: Peter O'Connor
texts.profession: Analyst, Merrill Lynch Equities (Australia) Ltd.
texts.text: Hi. Congratulations on your Coal & Allied deal, which is four decades in the making so – well done, finally.

texts.speaker: Richard J. Hatch
texts.profession: Analyst, RBC Europe Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Thanks, Richard Hatch, RBC. Just a quick question on your CapEx. So your aluminum CapEx and your copper  CapEx is around about the same sort of money in total. Given the fact that copper's contributing more than  aluminum, could you put more money into copper than – sorry, given that copper is putting – contributing more  money than aluminum, would you push more money into your copper assets than your aluminum?

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Well, we don't really do it in a way that you're suggesting, in other words, just putting money into things that are  making money today. We try and take a long-term view of all the capital projects that we do. We're not  deterministic. In other words, we're not trying to create a particular percentage portfolio for copper and  aluminum by 2020, let's say.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So Kitimat, the big investment that we're making is actually, as Tom was explaining earlier, a very good project  indeed, the best probably in the aluminum industry by far. So we have no regrets about that project. And I think  that the other point to make is although we – it looks as if we're spending quite a lot on aluminum, much of it is  just finishing Yarwun, which is, after all, going to be in production in August. So most of that capital has actually  already been spent. So the big one, as I've said, is Kitimat and it's a good project as our copper projects, they are  also good. And by the way, finding new copper projects to put money into at the moment is problematic. That is  part of the bull case for copper. There just aren't very many opportunities that are available in the short term.  We'd very much like have more of them and we're putting money where we can, but there is a limit.
