texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: These write-downs are deeply disappointing. In particular, the substantial impairment of our Mozambique coal  business is unacceptable. There clearly is a need for greater discipline, in particular in the way we allocate and  manage capital at Rio Tinto. I believe Sam is ideally placed across a fisheye over how we address the challenges  and opportunities in the business. He's a highly experienced and capable executive who has already made a  significant contribution to Rio Tinto, not only as an executive, but as a director of the company.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Putting it very, very simply, this means individuals will have clear targets and will be accountable for their  performance. It also means we'll strengthen our management and approval systems, bringing greater rigor to  internal debate and having more effective checks and balances and clearer lines of sight to critical business issues.  We will deliver on our cost-saving targets. We will see an annual run rate improvement of $3 billion a year by the  end of 2014. And Guy will talk us through this shortly.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Thank you, Sam. We've reported underlying earnings of $9.3 billion and cash flows from our operations of $16.5  billion. Whilst lower than last year, principally due to lower commodity prices, these results demonstrate the good  performance and healthy position of our underlying business. As we flagged in January, we've recognized an  impairment charge of $14.4 billion, mainly related to our aluminium and Mozambique coal assets.  The aluminium market deteriorated further in 2012, while the Australian and Canadian dollars remained strong.  These factors, coupled with high energy and raw material costs, reduced market valuations substantially.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In Mozambique, we had planned to barge coal along the Zambezi River. This has not received formal approvals,  but we remain actively engaged with the government of Mozambique on all transport options.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We've revised down our estimates of our recoverable coking coal, which necessitated a reassessment of the overall  scale and ramp-up schedule, resulting in the impairment. The impairment charge has been partly reduced by a  deferred tax asset of $1.1 billion, following the introduction of the MRRT in Australia last year. We recognized net  gains on the consolidation of Richards Bay Minerals and Turquoise Hill of around $800 million. So, overall, we  recorded a net loss of $3 billion.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: It was a tale of two halves for iron ore prices in 2012. The first half of the year was relatively stable. The second  half was highly volatile, with prices falling to as low as $89 per ton before recovering to the mid-$150s in early  2013.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In aluminium, we continue to face challenging market conditions. The 16% decline in the LME price lowered  earnings by just over $940 million. It was also a difficult year for coking coal, driven by a combination of a  recovery in supply from Australia and a weak macroeconomic environment.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In 2012, copper markets moved from a net deficit to a slight surplus. The 10% decline in the copper price lowered  our earnings by just over $300 million. On a more positive note, the unwinding of legacy contracts for titanium  dioxide feedstocks resulted in $270 million of additional earnings. This sector will become an even more  important driver of our earnings momentum, as repricing of legacy contracts continues.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Turning now to volumes, volume increases enhanced earnings by $634 million. Just over half of this came from  rising iron ore sales following the debottlenecking projects in the Pilbara. Other significant gains included higher  copper volumes at Escondida and at Northparkes, in line with a recovery in grades.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Raw material cost inflation continued, particularly in our aluminium business, where higher coke, pitch and  caustic soda prices persisted. Offsetting these cost increases was less weather disruption than we experienced a  year earlier.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So, by the end of 2014, we will have achieved sustainable reductions of $3 billion in our operating cash costs  compared with our 2012 cost base. For context, in 2012, our net operating cash costs were $35 billion, around $6  billion higher than just three years ago. This is not a sustainable trend, so we're taking decisive actions to reverse  it.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Let me explain the rules we will apply in measuring performance against this target. We're assuming constant  including inflation, currency movements, the impact of input prices linked to quoted metal prices and major one- offs, such as a significant weather event.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Performance against this target will be measured by pre-tax unit cash cost improvements, shown in our earnings  variance analysis. Productivity gains that reduce unit cash costs will be reflected in our performance against the  target. Equally, any increases in unit costs as a consequence of operating conditions, such as greater haul  distances, will need to be more than offset. All earlier cost reductions that we've talked about are included in our  new target. This includes the cost savings from our aluminium transformation program and from our service and  support cost review.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: However, our planned reductions in exploration and evaluation spend of $750 million and further reductions in  sustaining capital are in addition to this target. Nearly two-thirds of the $5 billion cumulative savings will come  from our aluminium and energy businesses. These have experienced the highest cost increases over recent years.  Central service and support costs also make up a substantial part of the reduction.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: What sorts of initiatives are we taking to get there? Well, a few examples may help explain. In our energy business,  we've implemented a salary freeze, which will result in a real terms cost saving. We're also improving labor  sourcing strategies. We've recently completed the first round of our service and support cost review, which  included significant head count reductions and the downsizing of a number of high-cost city offices. And we're  now reviewing our central office locations and are aiming for substantial savings through further relocations,  outsourcing and offshoring.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Beyond our cost reduction programs, we're also taking action at some of our higher-cost operations. For example,  at Gove, we're working closely with the Northern Territory government to finalize agreements for gas supply and  are advancing plans to convert the refinery from high-cost fuel oil to gas.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We will be looking at existing projects with a fresh pair of eyes and considering alternatives. These include  continuing with the current plan, slowing down, introducing partners or canceling projects altogether. For  example, we have slowed down the development of Kitimat over the winter period, given the aluminium market  conditions. And we've deferred work at the Argyle underground project not required to bring first production  onstream. And we're looking at options for reducing the capital we've invested in shipping, including novating two  existing new ship orders to a third-party provider of freight services.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Rio Tinto is a company that's always focused on the longer term. Here, our view is unchanged. But over the course  of the next two decades, billions of people will move from rural to urban areas, driving up consumption of the  metals and minerals that we produce.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The aluminium industry is likely to face challenging market conditions for some years to come. A structural shift  has occurred, driven by the decoupling of the supply chain for bauxite, alumina and aluminium, and continuing  growth in the Chinese smelting industry. We have seen some smelter closures and they've been announced, but  we've also seen local governments across the globe providing incentives to ensure that loss-making smelters  continue to operate. These actions are preventing the rationalization of the high-cost capacity that's required to

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Secondly, our energy group also gave disappointing performance in 2012. And under Harry Kenyon-Slaney's new  leadership, I expect significant new steps to be taken, costs to be cut, and underperforming operations to be closed  or divested. Harry's already taking tough decisions to turn that business around. So, as I said, there's a lot to be  done.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Now, turning to our investment program, we have a number of projects at varying stages of completion. We're  focusing on delivering our major capital projects on time and on budget. In Queensland, Yarwun 2 was completed  in mid-2012 and we've ramped up at an unusually fast rate to 90% of capacity. New tons are also being delivered  from our Australian thermal coal operations following the completion of brownfield expansions in 2012. And in  British Columbia, the Kitimat modernization is expected to deliver first metal by the end of 2014.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Looking further ahead, we continue to make good progress at Simandou. In 2012, we formed the joint venture  with Chalco, received a $1.3 billion earn-in, and we also focused on the social and environmental impact study.  We anticipate further progress once project financing has been put in place and approval is granted by the  government of Guinea for work on the ground.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In Western Australia, our Pilbara expansion project will see us grow annual iron ore production from 237 million  our annual capacity from 230 million tons to 237 million tons, with minimal capital investment. And today, Guy  mentioned that we've brought forward the completion of the 290-million-ton-a-year project from the fourth  quarter of this year to the third quarter of 2013, delivering value faster. As a result, our global iron ore production  will grow to around 265 million tons in 2013 on a 100% basis.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: And in 2014, we'll have a full year of operating at this higher capacity, delivering further year-on-year growth. This  will be quickly followed by an additional 50 million tons of annual capacity by the end of 2014 and a further 20  million tons by the end of the first half of 2015 to reach an annual capacity of 360 million tons per annum.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We've also saved $1 billion of capital by removing the wet plant at Brockman 4 from the expansion project. So,  this means we'll be able to maintain a capital intensity in the Pilbara of mid-$150 per annual ton, despite facing  some of the highest inflation rates in the industry and major headwind from the strong Australian dollar.  Importantly, this is an achievement unmatched by any other developer of a major iron ore project. We run a  highly efficient, fully integrated mine, rail and port network in the Pilbara. And I welcome last week's decision by  the Australian Competition Tribunal regarding third-party access to our rail. This protects the value of the system  that we've created over decades of investment.

texts.speaker: Rob B. Clifford
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Prime Brokerage)
texts.text: And thirdly, the changes you're talking about require some significant cultural change from the last few years.  Have you got the skills within the leadership team across the levels to deliver? And specifically, the two big  divisions, energy and aluminium, you talked about the fact there's a lot of changes already in energy, but  aluminium has been looking for these changes for some years. How can they do things differently to get the  outcome that you require?

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Yes. I mean, I would comment that the business is broader than iron ore, and as I mentioned in relation to  Yarwun 2 coal, Oyu Tolgoi, I mean, we have a range of projects that are in the portfolio. And we are diversified,  importantly, and different parts of our business go through different parts of the cycle, and they have their time in  the sun.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In relation to iron ore, I mentioned Chinese GDP growth increasing greater than 8% this year. I mean, that's an  important indicator. Also, in January, I made comments about the fact that we're expecting volatility in iron ore  prices. We had seen a ramp-up of prices surrounding potential weather effects in the Pilbara, in fact, elsewhere in  iron ore production. Also, we'd seen destocking. We've not seen that restocking take part at the pace that we  expected.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The iron ore stocks at the major Chinese ports is hovering around 70 million tons. It used to be around 95 million  tons to 100 million tons. So, there is restocking that's required. But we're seeing continuing investment in  urbanization. We expect that that will flow to industrialization sort of during that three to five-year period that  you meant.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We'd also seen in India, we've seen steel capacity there come on, and we've not seen commensurate increase in  iron ore mining. That's been as a result of a number of factors that are relating to land access, relating to  infrastructure and relating to power. And these are issues that are slowing down expansion of iron ore. And India  has made the decision to drastically reduce their exports of iron ore.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So, those things are helping produce an iron ore market that's a bit stronger. Iron ore prices are currently $155 a  ton CFR for fines. Will prices remain at that level? I suspect not. But I think that they'll still remain relatively  robust, particularly when I look back and think that I can remember when prices were $25 per ton. It's certainly –  I think it's a good outlook for iron ore, notwithstanding the fact that we'll expect volatility during 2013,  notwithstanding the fact that we expect that iron ore prices will come back a bit.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: IOC has brought on its Concentrate Expansion Project 1. It's working through the second flows of that. Step two,  Concentrate Expansion Project 2. But they've had a difficult year in relation to those projects and in terms of  weather events. And we're working with the IOC team in terms of what more we can do in relation to that business  in terms of generating value for shareholders.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So, let me come back to the fact that we are a diversified, we are a portfolio company. Iron ore is important and it's  got its time in the sun today but I'm very encouraged by the work that's happening in other areas.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Look, firstly, Clarke, on your question about volatility, look, I think the entire industry would prefer a scenario  where we had reduced volatility. But the old days are past. We won't see a return to annual prices, and quite  frankly, both customers and iron ore producers are moving to even more frequent pricing reviews, whether it be  monthly or, in fact, daily.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: This is no different to what we do with other traded commodities, no different to aluminium and copper. And it  reflects, to an extent, the vagaries of weather that I've just mentioned. It reflects seasonal factors. It reflects  holiday seasons. It reflects a whole raft of issues. And we need to sit back and we need to look at, overall, at the  trends that we can see with iron ore.  And importantly, this urbanization and industrialization that I talked about is going to continue, certainly in  China. But then, we'll see the benefit of this flowing forward in terms of India, Indonesia, Vietnam, Philippines,  Thailand, Malaysia. We're seeing it in South America. We're seeing it in Eastern Europe. And if I want to really  stretch your imagination, it'll happen in Africa, too. We're seeing growth there. And we'll see a time when there are  actually more people in Africa than there are in China. There's already 1 billion people in Africa. All of these are  building blocks, the building blocks of developing economies. And we're very fortunate to be in a position where  we're providing the fundamentals that provide these building blocks.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Yes, we do take a tough stance in relation to that. And yes, if we didn't get gas, we would have, in fact, waffled at  that plant. But through a process of very healthy engagement, working with both governments, we've moved to a  situation where, not only for the people of Nhulunbuy and the Northern Territory in Australia, but also for Rio  Tinto, we've got the best possible outcome. We'll have an asset of PacAl that is an integrated aluminium business,  bauxite, alumina and aluminium. That's important to maximize the value of the sale.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: But importantly, it will – the gas will enable us to move that operation into the lower area, the second quartile,  cost quartile. That is physically important.

texts.speaker: Fraser R. Jamieson
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities (Australia) Ltd.
texts.text: Thanks, Sam. It's Fraser Jamieson from JPMorgan. Really, a question around the cost-saving targets, the first part  of which is, could you just confirm that that $5 billion number is not relying on disposals to be reached?

texts.speaker: Fraser R. Jamieson
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities (Australia) Ltd.
texts.text: The second part, could you just remind us about the existing targets that are already feeding into that? I think  we've got $1.6 billion of EBITDA improvement in aluminium, of which about 50% is cost-related. Could you just  remind us what else is in there?

texts.speaker: Fraser R. Jamieson
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities (Australia) Ltd.
texts.text: And then the third part is just around Guy's comments on absolute and productivity-driven costs. Is it – if we look  at the pie chart, is it reasonable to say aluminium and energy division is not growing, not scheduled to grow much  over the next couple of years; therefore, we should think of those cost savings in absolute terms and the central  cost, whereas iron ore and copper, you're obviously going to get the benefit of higher volumes, so therefore, they're  more productivity and fixed-cost leverage related?

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Yeah. I mean, I think we're trying to make high-quality, sustainable cost reductions here. So, if we make a  disposal, which we may do as we've discussed just now, it will have to be deducted from both the starting point  and the endpoint. So, we'll have to make an adjustment for that.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Also, as you say, aluminium and energy aren't really expanding and we're having to look elsewhere. And I gave  some instances of it, but to give a little bit more color to this, we're looking very hard, for example, at  procurement. Can we achieve better deals negotiating hard with those who supply us? Can we really reconstitute  the areas on which we spend money? Can we eliminate whole areas of cost as well as reducing the price of the  things that we're buying? We want better visibility and KPIs on all our costs. And on top of that, of course, there  are all the labor productivity benefits that we're looking for. And this applies everywhere, but especially in those  two divisions.

texts.speaker: Guy R. Elliott
texts.profession: CFO & Senior Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So, that gives a bit more texture to it. And when we next get together in August, I'm hoping that we will have some  flesh to put on these bones.

texts.speaker: Glyn Lawcock
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Securities (Australia) Ltd.
texts.text: And so – and then secondly, I'm just trying to understand the mineral sands cuts that you've announced today,  just if you had any feel for if that's just for a year, or you haven't really thought it through this far yet? Thanks very  much.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Yeah. Thanks very much, Glyn. Look, in relation to Gove, there is no government handout. This is physically the  government of the Northern Territory making available gas. There is no cost to them. And in fact, they've got take- or-pay obligations that will be removed. So, there's actually a benefit to the Northern Territory in there. But there  are no handouts by the government.

file: RIO - Q4 2013 Earnings Call 13February2014 330 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 13-Feb-14.pdf

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We have achieved record production in bauxite, thermal coal and iron ore despite operational and weather-related  challenges we've a more accountable and disciplined business. And we've strengthened our systems and our  processes. Importantly, we've delivered strong underlying earnings and improved cash flows against a  backdrop  of weaker commodity prices.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: As I mentioned, our financial results demonstrate the very real and significant progress that we've made. With  sharp focus on every dollar we spend, we've improved cash operating costs by $2.3 billion. By focus ing on our  exploration and evaluation spend, we've reduced these costs by $1 billion – a further $1 billion. And at the same  time we set new production records in bauxite, thermal coal and iron ore. Across our total group production grew  by 9% in 2013 on a copper equivalent basis.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We've also delivered on our major growth projects. Of note, expansion at our Pilbara iron ore assets to 290 million  tonnes a year was commissioned $400 million under budget and four months ahead of schedule. We completed  the first phase of the Oyu Tolgoi copper/gold mine in Mongolia, and shipped first concentrate in July.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Underlying earnings were also impacted by the effects of commodity prices during the year. Overall, lower  commodity prices reduced earnings by $1.3 billion. In particular, lower coal prices reduced earnings by $530  million as supply increased and onerous take-or-pay freight contracts in Australia incentivized uneconomic  supply  to remain in the market.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In aluminum financial deals continue to lock up substantial amounts of metal in the LME system. Although we  saw strong growth in demand for aluminum in 2013, and therefore increases in regional premia for physical  delivery, this was not enough to offset an overall 9% decline in the LME. And in the copper market supply  increases resulted in a fall in prices of 8%.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Within this generally weaker price environment iron ore prices stood out with average spot prices higher in 201 3  than in 2012.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: I'll return to our cost reduction program in more detail shortly. But adding together our cash cost improvements  and lower exploration and evaluation spend, you can see this has boosted earnings by over $3.3 billion pre -tax or  $2.1 billion for the year on a post-tax basis.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Overall our group average unit cash cost has been reduced by 10% before the further impacted exchange  movements. These improvements can most clearly be seen in the unit cost reductions at each individual business.  By way of example Kennecott Utah Copper has reduced gross cash costs by $1,500 per tonne. Primary aluminum  in North America has reduced its cash costs by $300 per tonne, and Rio Tinto Coal Australia has achieved a $30  per tonne unit cost reduction.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: While the bulk of the operating cost savings have been realized in aluminum, energy and copper, all of the product  groups have contributed and will continue to do so. Each of the product group CEOs gave examples of the work  underway in their businesses at our December investor seminars.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: However let me walk you through a couple of initiatives being implemented in 2014. In September of last year our  Hail Creek Mine in Queensland ran a two-day trial, producing saleable thermal coal from reject product. It was so  successful that this process will continue throughout 2014, leading to an additional 7 50,000 tonnes of annual  production, largely using existing equipment and available capacity.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Fuel usage at our coal operations in Australia is another area which will be targeted this year. Through engine  calibration, reduced revolutions during idling, and component upgrades for older trucks, we estimate that we can  save over 4 million liters of fuel without affecting production. And in iron ore our competency-based approach to   training will free up 200,000 man hours, the equivalent of more than 90 full-time staff.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: As you can see with thousands of cost saving projects underway across the group, the focus on cash and running  the business for value continues. And we're confident that we'll achieve our 2014 targets.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We're comfortable that this is a level which will allow us to continue to develop a robust pipeline of future options.  Right now we're progressing 30 projects across 10 different commodities, with a particular focus on the La Granja  and Resolution copper projects, together with our ongoing central exploration program.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The iron ore team has recently shown a clear example of this with a breakthrough pathway for expanding the  Pilbara operations, which was announced in November. This new pathway to 360 million tonnes per annum is  planned at a substantially reduced capital intensity of between $120 to $130 per tonne, and $3 billion less than  the previous forecasts. This shows that CapEx can be reduced whilst delivering exciting value -adding growth. And  we're adopting the same mindset to our sustaining CapEx, which reduced by around $2 billion i n 2013.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: 2013 was another landmark year for our iron ore business. In the Pilbara we completed and began operating the  new facilities at Cape Lambert. Ramp up of mine capacity to 290 million tonnes a year is underway. And as  mentioned we've completed expansion four months ahead of schedule and $400 million under budget.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We've achieved record production in shipments at our Pilbara operations in 2013, up 5% compared to 2012.  Importantly we took advantage of delivering these additional tonnes into the strong iro n ore market. The  infrastructure expansion project is on track to increase annual capacity to 360 million tonnes a year in the first  half of 2015.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The breakthrough development pathway announced last year will maximize the value of our resources. Additiona l  tonnes from low-cost brownfield mine growth and productivity gains will feed the expanded infrastructure as it  comes online. We'll be extending the lives of some of our existing mines, as well as adding additional resources  into the system.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In copper we focused the business around a 4+2 strategy. This is a clear roadmap to position the copper group as a  first quartile, low-cost producer and leader in its sector. The 4 of the strategy are our Kennecott Utah Copper, Oyu  Tolgoi, Escondida, and Grasberg.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: At Kennecott the recovery from the slide which occurred in April is well underway. The heavy haul road was  completed ahead of schedule, which allowed further waste movement to provide access to all. Work on the  Cornerstone Project, which extends the life of the mine also, continues. The recovery from the Manefay slide is a  remarkable achievement after such a major event. And I would like to congratulate the Kennecott team on the way  they've responded to this challenge.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The 2 of the 4+2 strategy represents two world-class greenfield projects. These are Resolution in the United States  and La Granja in Peru. Both are exciting and prospecting copper growth options, which will develop in a stage  manner in the years ahead.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: During the year we continue to rationalize our aluminum portfolio. We sold Saint-Jean, we closed the Shawinigan  smelter, and announced the suspension of the Gove alumina refinery.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: At the same time we're seeking ways to maximize value from the Kitimat asset. We recently sold assets to acqui re  or lease a parcel of land near our Kitimat operations to a Shell-led joint venture. And whilst the financial terms are  confidential, this agreement has the potential to generate meaningful value for Rio Tinto.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: And in energy we've made real in-roads into addressing the challenges of the economic outlook facing the energy  sector. The team has pulled significant costs out, and we have driven an aggressive transformation agenda. I'm  confident that we'll achieve the targeted 2014 cost reduction in our energy business of $1 billion compared to  2012.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So to sum up, 2013 was a year of delivering on our commitments. We achieved underlying earnings of $10.2  billion, up 10%. We exceeded our cost reduction targets, whilst we set production records. And we significantly  increased our operating cash flows, whilst reducing our net debt. At the same time, we have reduced capital and  completed projects, such as Oyu Tolgoi Phase I and the Pilbara 290 [million tonnes] expansion.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In relation to our Canadian operations, look, it's a tough market. And I think in a falling LME to deliver a result  that has taken our earnings from $54 million in 2012 to $557  million this last year, it's an impressive  performance. And it's evidence of the work physically on the ground. Clearly, Kitimat I'm very disappointed in. It's  the impact of LNG projects underway in that area, shortages of labor leading to cost escalations to the project.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: I've got to say, though, that there is some prospectivity in the business. Sooner or later as China moves to a  consumption-led economy, people are going to be buying refrigerators, TVs, and air conditioners. And they're  going to want to be able to turn them on, and they'll need power. And in the same way that Japan had to  restructure its aluminum industry, I'm sure that China will have to do the same.

texts.speaker: Heath R. Jansen
texts.profession: Analyst, Citigroup Global Markets Ltd.
texts.text: Good morning, it's Heath Jansen here from Citigroup. Just in terms of the iron ore slide you presented in terms of  a range of ramp up. And it seems like you've got a high and a low scenario that sort of 25 million to 30 million  tonnes. I'm just wondering whether you'd talk through that a little bit more? I mean is that subject to market  conditions or market price or infrastructure? Should we read into this that you're willing to sort of balance the  market much more than we've seen in the past? And if the prices c ome down you'll take off production?

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: I guess another piece of information there relates to China's focus on the environment, which actually relates to  pollution, rather than necessarily greenhouse, although that's obviously an issue. And as they are looking to  improve environmental performance, they are moving to higher-quality product. So for example, demand for our  overall product, but we're seeing in direct charge product where you bypass sinter plants and coke batteries, we're  seeing higher premiums for lump product and for pellet product, which comes down to the mills aiming to  improve their efficiency, reduce their production of slag, and can be better off fro m an environmental viewpoint.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In relation to the ramp up, look, obviously the team will be working to ramp that up as quickly as they can. We've  been impacted there by a cyclone at the end of last year and the flow through of water through the Pilbara aqu ifer  has been significant. We've also had a tropical low come down there last week, which dropped a lot of water on the  operation, so you can say it's a conservative buildup, but I'd rather a situation where we are very focused on the  delivery, match the market, and not do anything silly in terms of overreaching ourselves.

texts.speaker: Fraser R. Jamieson
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities (Australia) Ltd.
texts.text: Are you still very focused on portfolio rationalization, given that certain markets are impro ving? Is there the  opportunity for some stuff that was considered previously and abandoned to come back? And specifically with  respect to your comments around Chinese environmental or the focus on the environment there and increasing  lump premiums, how is that influencing thinking around iron ore of Canada?

texts.speaker: Adrian P. Wood
texts.profession: Analyst, Macquarie Securities (Australia) Ltd.
texts.text: And second, just looking at the pressure or the focus on sustaining cost reductions, if I look at the slide 14, the  2015 CapEx guidance implies something in the order of around $2.50 per tonne in sustaining capit al in the  Pilbara. Can you just give some sense as to how sustainable that is and how long that could last, given that  Silvergrass and Koodaideri of course, those mine developments are now going to be classified as sustaining?

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: At the halfway mark the one-offs I think were around $50 million. That it remains a relatively modest part of the  cost reductions. An important job we've got in 2014 is locking in those savings, ensuring that they are sustainable  as we go forward.

texts.speaker: Lyndon Fagan
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities (Australia) Ltd.
texts.text: Thanks. The first question is just on iron ore, I wanted to drill down a little bit more into the guidance, which  looks a bit soft relative to the September site visit material. And I guess are you still targeting 290 [million tonnes]  by the end of May as a run rate? Or has that weather interruption pushed it out? And if so can you perhaps talk  about the individual mines that it might have affected, i.e., is the Nammuldi project ramp -up now slower?

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Look I'm confident about the project. It's a good project for the government and people of Mongolia. It's a good  project for Turquoise Hill and for Rio Tinto. We need to cross the Ts, we need to dot the Is. But the OT  underground is the next copper development project. We just need to ge t the fundamentals right.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Now work – you're right. The work is continuing on La Granja and Resolution, but these are more longer -term.  There are a number of things, including a land swap at Resolution, the drilling work that we're doing in Peru, that  needs to be done before we bring that project on.

texts.speaker: Menno G. Sanderse
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: And secondly, you talk a lot about 4+2 in the copper strategy. But also in your slides you only talked about 2+2. So  what do you think fundamentally about your position in copper, where you only really control two projects, which  are the ones that are not performing as well as maybe as Escondida is?

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In relation to 4+2, it is 4+2. I spoke about our managed operations and projects, pure and simply because they are  the ones that we do operate. But Escondida there, we're continuing to invest there, the power proje ct and the  water project last year are part of taking that project forward. It's a great business. We have a good partnership  with BHP and Mitsubishi there. And yes, we have people involved in the technical committee and how that  operation goes forward, but it is an non-managed operation.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Grasberg. Look, there are a range of challenges there, and Richard Atkinson and I had a very long chat the other  day. From a safety viewpoint, it was a very sad year for Grasberg with the tunnel collapse and then a string  of  fatalities.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: But aluminum, no easy solution but the results aren't bad. They're better than consensus expected. They're a  significant improvement on last year.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In relation to the prioritization of projects, I think as you know our projects go through a series of stage guides,  order of magnitude, pre-feasibility study, feasibility study, decision to proceed. We have three central functions in  our business, which Chris and I have strengthened. The economics group, which provides the economic  assumptions, the exchange rates, commodity prices, energy prices and so on; the business evaluation department  that looks at the commercial aspects of a project; and the technical evaluation group, which looks to technical  aspects.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In answer to your question, yes aluminum has got to compete for a dollar against the other product groups,  against iron ore and against copper. We are committed to investing in the best projects across our portfolio.  So it  actually means that in the areas of aluminum, energy, and the diamond and minerals portion of Alan's group,  we're not expecting any significant investments in those areas.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Our next telephone question comes from Paul McTaggart of Credit Suisse. Please go ahead.   Paul McTaggart  Analyst, Credit Suisse (Australia) Ltd.  Q  Hi gentlemen. I just want to follow up on coal, a pretty good effort at getting costs down $30 a tonne. But clearly  you sold at least one coal asset. Y ou've been talking about sort of exiting others.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: How do you feel about coal at the minute? Is this a business that is really going to form part of the long -term Rio  Tinto portfolio? Or are you feeling somewhat lukewarm on the business? I just want to get an update really on  how you see coal at the moment.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Y eah look, Paul, energy is tough. And as I say it's not just coal. It's also uranium business is facing some pretty  tough times. We have Harry Kenyon-Slaney and his team have done a great job in terms of refocusing the costs.  And yes we did divest of Clermont last year.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: There is no easy solution in relation to energy for the long term to actually provide an alternative for coal and in  fact uranium. Y es in the EOS there has been advances there with fracking, I suspect that it's going to be much  slower coming on elsewhere. Clearly there has been a range of issues as it's physically developed.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So I think in terms of both coal and uranium, I think they will get their time in the sun. When is that going to  happen? Well time will tell. In the meantime we need to focus on improving the business. That's exactly what  Harry is doing and delivering.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: But if you look at the long-term view for diamonds and for industrial minerals, the outlook is good. The outlook is  strong. We're happy with our investment in Richards Bay Minerals and the doubling down. It will get its time in  the sun.

texts.speaker: Unverified Participant
texts.text: There are no scheduled fire alarms for today. So if you do hear any announcements, then please make your way to  the nearest exits. Nearest exits are out the two doors to your front and turn left or right and follow the green  running man signs. Once you're out of the building, we've conveniently placed a fire assembly point via easily  recognizable landmarks. So if you head towards St. Paul's and as you get there, there'll be some members of the  staff sporting the latest fashion in high visibility jackets; and if you'll just muster there, and you'll be given further  instructions.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: There were impairments relating to overruns of the Kitimat modernization project, which were recognized at the  half year, and the write-down of the Moly Autoclave project at Kennecott. These were partially offset by the  reversal of a previous impairment taken on the PacAl assets. This reversal reflects improved pricing in the  industry, but more importantly is driven by our successful work to improve the efficiency and cost  competitiveness of the PacAl assets.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Losses on disposal mainly relate to the divestment of our interests in Rio Tinto Coal Mozambique in October. And  following the repeal of the Minerals Resource Rent Tax, or MRRT, in Australia in the second half of last year, we  wrote off the deferred tax asset to the tune of $362 million.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Iron Ore prices declined significantly in 2014. On average, the price of 62% iron declined by 30% from the prior  year. Notwithstanding this, our Iron Ore business' underlying earnings were $8.1 billion, a reduction of only 18%.  We increased our sales with 90% of our expansion tonnes going into our premium Pilbara Blend product. And in  addition, continued cost reduction efforts and the favorable effect of the weaker Australian dollar partially offset  the price decline.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: This year, as promised, you will have seen that we've split out the revenues, EBITDA, and earnings of our  bauxite  and alumina businesses. This enhanced disclosure reveals that our bauxite business is generating strong margins,  but also that more work needs to be done in the alumina refineries. We've set some tough targets for 2015, so we  expect that alumina's profile will steadily improve.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Our Copper product group delivered an 11% increase in underlying earnings. This was despite a 7 % reduction in  average copper prices and reflects the efforts of our team there in reducing costs and boosting productivity.  Improved volumes from OT and reduction in cash unit costs and exploration and evaluation were the main  reasons for the improvement.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Our Energy business faced a very tough year and generated a loss of $210 million at underlying earnings. This is  down from a $33 million profit in 2013. Lower prices across the coal sector reduced earnings by $433 million, but  not all of this could be offset by cost reductions of $170 million. Rio Tinto Coal Australia was profitable at $21  million, but ERA incurred a loss of $119 million; and Rio Tinto Coal Mozambique, a loss of $93 million before it  was divested in October of 2014.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Compared with the 2012 base, we've now reduced our operating cash costs and evaluation and exploration  expenditure by $4.8 billion, but we're not stopping there. When we announced at the half year that we had  achieved $3.2 billion cash unit cost reductions, beating the $3 billion target six months ahead of schedule, we  were keen to ensure that the momentum in the business was maintained and the focus on reducing these costs  continued. We, therefore, set an additional target of a further $1 billion of sustainable cost improvements by the  end of 2015.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Since the end of 2012, we've now delivered over $3.6 billion of operating cash unit cost savings, beating our  original $3 billion target by about 20% by then end of 2014. As you can see from the chart, we've achieved  significant cost reductions across our portfolio with around $900 million coming out of our Copper group, $800  million from each of Aluminum and Energy, and $700 million from Iron Ore. The remaining $300 million came  largely out of Diamonds and Minerals, other operations and the head office cost reductions. Additionally, we've  saved $1.2 billion over the past two years by reducing our exploration and evaluation activities, focusing only the  highest-value projects.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: We continue to deliver greater operating and commercial efficiency in our unrivalled Pilbara assets. In 2014, our  cash unit cost was $19.50 per tonne. But if you take current oil currency rates, our estimate for Q4 unit cash cost  would be equivalent to about $17 a tonne.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Our average realized price for our Pilbara Blend products was $84.30 per wet metric tonne for the full year of  2014, equivalent to about $91.60 per dry metric tonne; and our spot sales continue to be consistently above the  Platts 62% Fe benchmark. The combination of low cost and sound marketing has led to consistent and attractive  margins.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: And we'll further expand our bauxite business at Gove and the South of the Embley project where we recently  approved capital to complete the feasibility study this year with first production expected in 2018. And we have  further growth options also in the Cape Y ork Peninsula, which we'll seek to develop in line with market demand as  we continue to develop our product as the seaborne bauxite of choice.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Aluminum has grown into a significant contributor to group earnings and cash flows. Jean-Sébastien and his team  in Copper have delivered some impressive cost improvements and they've also restructured the Copper division,  preserving EBITDA margins of 42% year-on-year. And there's a continued focus on our Copper portfolio. We  exited Pebble in 2014, and we're in the process of exiting South Gobi. Ramp-up of Oyu Tolgoi continues; and  Kennecott will have a year of preparation as we work towards higher output in 2016.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: In Energy, and a pretty difficult industry environment, Harry and his team have worked hard to maximize  efficiencies and reduce costs. Our Australian coal operations continue to generate positive earnings and positive  cash flows.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: A key focus for 2015 will be progressing the Hunter Blend project. This is a plan to operate our  Hunter Valley  assets as a fully integrated network of mines, rail and port; and the strategy will be underpinned by the Integrated  Operations Center, which is expected to open in Singleton early this year, and the Process Excellence Center which  is already operating in Brisbane.

texts.speaker: Jason R. Fairclough
texts.profession: Merrill Lynch International (United Kingdom)
texts.text: Jason Fairclough, Bank of America Merrill Lynch. Maybe a simple question, Sam. Y ou mentioned your colleagues  in minerals and how they're doing some work to sort of match capacity production with the market demand for  that product. Maybe the bigger question for Rio Tinto is iron ore. Y ou're one of the world's largest producers. To  what extent do you feel a responsibility to play a role in balancing supply and demand with iron ore?

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: If you look at supply and demand for iron ore, it really hinges on the marginal producer; and we've seen that  prices have dropped substantially during 2014. If you look at 2015, we're expecting that about 100 million tonnes  of new capacity will come on. There will be growth in demand of about 20 million tonnes; and there's around 80  million tonnes of capacity that is likely to come off, if you look at the cost reduction and their ability to respond,  they're underwater.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Beyond that 80 million tonnes there is about 80 million tonnes that we would describe as being at risk. Now these  are people that are currently underwater, but they've got the option of reducing costs and making the  improvement to keep their business afloat. Now, I know there are some people hanging on by their fingernails and  some of them are burning the furniture and reducing expenditure on maintenance and sustainin g CapEx and  firing Board members and all sorts of things. You can only do that for a certain time, and sooner or later you've  really got to recognize the reality of life.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: As we just mentioned during the presentation, if you take the current spot exchange rate and the spot energy price  into account, then the Iron Ore business costs are running at around $17 per tonne cash cost; and as compared to  the selling price today of $62 a tonne. So there's a significant margin there for us.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: And guess what happens when you take 100 million tonnes off, well, the price goes up and all those people that  went out of the market come back into the market. And guess what the price gets back to where it was, and wacko  we'd be down 100 million tonnes. That's not in the best interest of our shareholders. So whether you like it or not,  there's no OPEC in iron ore. Its independent producers making their independent decisions; and the decisions  that we make are in the best interest of our shareholders. That's very, very important.

texts.speaker: Jason R. Fairclough
texts.profession: Merrill Lynch International (United Kingdom)
texts.text: So as a low-cost producer, you don't feel any responsibility to balance supply and demand in iron ore?

texts.speaker: Menno G. Sanderse
texts.profession: Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Good morning. It's Menno at Morgan Stanley. Two brief ones. First on corporate, you talked a lot about creating  options for the Board, but the options in corporate seem to be quite long-dated or progressing very slowly. Is there  anything you can do to push that business a bit harder or make it look differently because 2015 is clearly going to  be quite a tough year to say the least? And then, secondly, on steel consumption in China. Rio Tinto has always  been very resilient or confident, some would say stubborn, in its views that $1 billion of steel is, or...

texts.speaker: Menno G. Sanderse
texts.profession: Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: ...2 billion tonnes of steel is going to be consumed in China. What gives you that continued resilience despite last  year being quite a tough year for steel consumption?

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Y eah. In relation to copper, of course, we have our existing operations. We have Kennecott Utah Copper. We  have  the OT open-cut operation, which some people forget is operating and operating well. We have our tonnes at  Escondida; and the availability of tonnes out of Grasberg, depending on their production. And we've got the OT  underground project; La Granja and Resolution are all in the hopper.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: OT underground, we put our best and final offer to the government of Mongolia in November; and they're  currently considering that. There have been some positive moves in relation to a number of shareholder issues.  There's been resolution of some operating constraints, for example, in relation to water availability for the project.  Also, the provision of third-party power into the project. So there is progress. We are patient. It is a long-term  project. We need to get it right. We're not about to rush this and jeopardize the long-term future of the project.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Resolution, the land swap, which went through the U.S. Congress just before Christmas, that was a significant  move for that project; and it provides us with full optionality in relation to how we develop that project. Yes, it's  going to go through a range of environmental and other governmental approvals, but work on that development is  continuing as with La Granja.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: In relation to 1 billion tonnes in China, that is still our forecast that China will reach 1 billion tonnes of production  by 2030. That requires 1% growth per annum; and we believe that that is imminently possible. When you look at  the fact that China is currently – urbanization is around 54%,and we expect that it'll move to 70%. And everything  that we're hearing from China indicates that that urbanization process is still under way.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Now, importantly, growth in construction is continuing in the Tier 1 cities. In the lower tiers, yes, we've seen a  surplus of real estate; and a lot of people are focused on that. But the demand for high-grade iron ore continues.  And not only is the issue of urbanization, industrialization an important issue for us, but also the issue of  improving pollution in China. This is particulates, this is smog, this is an increasing issue for the people in the  major cities in China. And improving the grade of iron ore is actually going to help improve the efficiency of their  anti-pollution measures. Do we have a question on the phone line?

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: If you can get the full flow through, the full effect of exchange and oil prices, then that accounts for about $450  million of the reduction. The balance of the reduction is actually looking at timing, streamlining projects, value  engineering work, which is underway with South of the Embley and Zulti South and OT and other projects. So  part of that exchange effect will actually flow through, assuming exchange rates stay where they are, in subsequent  years.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So there's a couple of factors there and, of course, we're always looking at improving the way that we actually  develop our projects and recognizing that we're seeing a whole range of input costs, labor, and materials that have  actually also reduced. It's one of the things that flow through from, I guess, people being more focused on capita,  but you actually see capital cost go down. And certainly we're seeing it not only in the minerals industry, we're also  seeing it in oil and gas that the heady days of all these projects is coming to an end. And it's important – we take  the benefit of that as we go forward.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So we're saying it's not just a resources issue, it's across the board. And if you go to the oil and gas industry, I think  you're going to see some fairly significant reductions in that area pretty quic kly. And just probably the U.S. shale is  probably the most obvious example there where the response can be a bit quicker than perhaps the routine  offshore oil.

texts.speaker: James F. Gurry
texts.profession: Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Thanks, Sam. It's James Gurry here from Credit Suisse. Just want to talk a little bit about Aluminum. You're  actually earning more EBITDA and net earnings from Aluminum than you are from Copper. The Aluminum  group's never been worth more to you now as a group than since you bought it. How sustainable do you see the  earnings within the Aluminum portfolio? And what do you think the dynamics are of expanding your bauxite and  alumina exports into China? And at the same time, China is recently exporting a significant amount of Aluminum  products to the rest of the world. Does that have the potential to potentially harm the earnings at the smelter  portfolio?

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: We've taken 7 00,000 tonnes of metal out of our production. We've shut, curtail, sold businesses. We've  renegotiated our contracts; a whole raft of activities. If you look at the metal business, when Kitimat comes on  stream, the Kitimat modernization expansion, whatever you want to call it, around 80% of our businesses will be  in the first-cost quartile. That's a very strong position for us to be in metal.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So a lot of focus, big spotlight, and we're working to improve that business. We did take action last year to curtail  the Gove refinery; and action like that is actually improving the bottom line of the alumina business. In relation to  bauxite, bauxite continues to be a very prospective business for us with the increase of export capacity from Gove,  from around the 6 million tonnes to 8 million tonnes of export.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: It's infrastructure; that means we're having to ramp that up during this year with new conveyors and handling  systems and what have you. The South of the Embley  project, we've approved the study funding recently for the  full feasibility study. And we're expecting that the full project will come into the investment committee and the  Board later this year.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: In relation to the trade-off of – do you supply bauxite, or do you hold back and hope that that will mean that China  and elsewhere will reduce their exports? Well, our view of that is that one way or another the bauxite will be  supplied. And we're in an ideal position with proximity to China or out of Weipa to actually supply that material to  them. If we don't, it will come from somewhere else.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: But let me just sort of close this item off by saying, look, you've also got to look at the long-term prognosis for  aluminum in China, that currently they're using a lot of stranded power; and what better than right now build an  aluminum smelter, and that'll provide jobs and provide other business opportunities and what have you.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: But as China moves to a more consumption-led economy, and during the past year they've moved from 34%  consumption to 48% consumption, which means that households are buying refrigerators, and washing machines,  and air conditioners, and every electrical gadget known to man. They're going to need that power. And there will  certainly be a huge draw on that power as the middle class in China increases. And having bought their fridge,  they want to actually be able to turn it on.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So there is a shift there. And for those of you that say, well, Sam, you're all dreaming; just have a look at what  happened in Japan. Japan, prior to the 1970s, had an aluminum smelting industry; and exactly the same thing  that I'm talking about happened there. Today, there's not an aluminum smelter in Japan. So over time, the same  thing will actually happen there. So there will be a transition and that will limit their ability to domestic  requirements of aluminum. So they can put it actually into their refrigerators and washing machines and  everything else. Another question in the room, we have one just here. I hope everybody will get a chance. Sorry,  second row.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: With regard to working capital, the cash released from Diamonds and Minerals, so it's not just diamonds it's  Diamonds and Minerals business, it has been significant. But they did have quite high inventories relative to the  scale of their business. We've been actively working to reduce that. Alan and his team have been on that for some  time now. And that sort of activity – the opportunity varies across the patch. But we've still got – for instance, in  Iron Ore, we've still got product up at the mine end of the infrastructure chain which has been bulked out. But  once we've got capacity to be able to move that down the infrastructure chain and get it available  to a port, then  that can be further reduced by way of example. If you go into the smelting businesses, probably less opportunity in  there in the aluminum smelters side of the house.

texts.speaker: Myles L. Allsop
texts.profession: UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: And then finally, just on Iron Ore and supply discipline. Obviously you're adding 50 million tonnes of the 100  million tonnes. So you're kind of the biggest contributor this year. But I think the more interesting side is IOC  because at current prices I suspect is not generating a huge amount of cash flow. Are you prepared to take action  there if it moves into a cash flow-negative situation? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: I think in relation to growth, our intention is that our growth would be continuing at the indication that we gave of  5% copper equivalent growth. Clearly, again, moving parts in relation to what does happen with the exchange  rates and energy prices; and, as Chris mentioned, what happens with capital equipment and so on. But we are very  focused on getting the balance right between shareholder returns, future growth of the business, future value to  shareholders. And our feeling is that 5% is getting it about right. Certainly, when we raised it in November,  December with shareholders, shareholders accepted it. That's pretty reasonable. That's pretty fair. That ensures  that you've got ongoing growth. On the last question, my pen ran out of ink, so...

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: And I think that with the reductions that I guess the iron ore business in Canada has seen in relation to Wabush,  in relation to Bloom Lake, Millennium, you name it, we're seeing a community there, we're seeing suppliers, we're  seeing a workforce that is actually far more attuned to the realities of life.

texts.speaker: Paul D. Young
texts.profession: Deutsche Bank AG (Australia)
texts.text: And also, considering the PacAl assets performed pretty strongly, have you completed your portfolio  simplification or rationalization for Aluminum? Then also on bauxite, I noticed that the spot bauxite price has  increased by about $15 a tonne over the last 12 months, yet it looks like your realized bauxite price was flat year on  year, if I look at it on a CIF or a FOB basis. So wondering when you expect higher bauxite prices to start flowing  through? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: In relation to bauxite prices, we do have some legacy contracts. We also have some internal transfers. But, Chris,  beyond that I can't think of why that increase in bauxites may not be flowing through. Do you have any feel?

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Well, we had the Gove effect of – we're now selling more direct bauxite rather than processing it through Gove  over the last year-and-a-half or whatever. And I guess not all bauxite is fungible. Depending on the characteristics  that present in the bauxite depends on what the audience is for that particular bauxite, is it high or low  temperature and so on.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So there are so many idiosyncrasies about bauxite. It's one of the reasons why we'll continue to treat – we'll give  you the data about bauxite and alumina separately, which we've done now and hopefully that will be appreciated  for more transparency on that data. But from a business and accounting point of view, we'll continue to see that as  one, what we call, cash generating unit on the basis that we still have a relatively balanced system in the aggregate;  and not all bauxites can go to all refineries. A refinery has got to be set up to receive a particular type of bauxite, if  you like.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So we've got to be a little bit careful about translating across a headline number to every particular tonne. They're  not all the same, and they'll attract different prices depending on how big the audience is for that particular type of  bauxite.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: In relation to our Iron Ore prices, you're actually seeing a couple of effects here. You're seeing the effect of the  balance of our sales portfolio between quarterly lagged and monthly lagged and spot, plus as you quite rightly say,  the lump premium. We have seen a stronger premium than we thought, which comes back to my comments  earlier about the Chinese mills trying to improve their environmental performance, and they are coming under a  significant pressure to do that. But, look, it's a very volatile world out there, and I'll leave the market to determine  where the price is going to be going forward. Do we have – Heath?

file: RIO - Q4 2015 Earnings Call 11February2016 330 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 11-Feb-16.pdf

texts.speaker: John Smelt
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations
texts.text: Good morning and welcome to Rio Tinto's 2015 Full Y ear Results. My name is John Smelt. I'm the Head of  Investor Relations at Rio Tinto. First of all, on safety, there are no scheduled fire alarm test today, so if the alarms  do go off, please listen to the announcements and follow the instructions. In the event of an evacuation, the  assembly point is over by St. Paul's Cathedral and the Stock Exchange team will be on hand to assist. The nearest  fire exits are these two doors to either side of me. If you go out of here, you can go either left or right and the exits  are in the same direction. So, behind where we are standing and they're indicated by the standard green signs.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Further outcome of our actions has been margin stability. Tier 1 assets with tight operational control assure that  we continue to generate strong cash flows and to protect margins and profitability. The success in the Pilbara has  been remarkable. The second half of 2015, we reduced our C1 cost to $13.80 per tonne, which, of course, includes  the benefit of weaker Australian dollar and lower oil prices but a lot of action by the team on the ground.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: If we use spot prices at the end of January, this $13.80 would be equivalent to $13.20 per tonne. And I should  highlight that C1 cost is an all-in measure, which includes SG&A. EBITDA margins at our aluminium business  increased year-on-year to 31%. I believe the statistics show it that we have the best aluminium business in the  world. Their performance was assisted by further portfolio optimization and cost reduction.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: First, our price volatility continued to be the dominant theme, and it's taken – the impact of declining prices on  our earnings continued in the second half and led to a significant reduction of $7.7 billion for the year. There was  some offset from currency but the impact of energy costs and inflation was relatively modest. This brought us to  the flexed 2014 earnings of $3.8 billion. There was a benefit from higher volumes, mainly from the Pilbara and  increased bauxite exports from Weipa and Gove, but this was partly offset by lower volumes at Kennecott and in  titanium.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Further impairments of $684 million relate mainly to the carrying value of Energy Resources of Australia,  following a decision by the ERA board to not proceed with the final feasibility study on the Ranger 3 Deeps  project. We also impaired the Roughrider uranium project in Canada following completion of an order of  magnitude study.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Over the past three years, we've delivered $6.2 billion in cost savings. Obviously, it's getting harder. But we  continue to find opportunities to reduce costs and have been able to maintain strong momentum. All product  groups have contributed to this impressive achievement, with Copper & Coal delivering $1.9 billion and Iron Ore  and Aluminium each delivering about $1.1 billion of cumulative savings.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Signs of recovery in industrial demand are yet to emerge, and a prolonged downturn brings increased risk.  Housing sales in China stabilized during the second half of 2015, but we're yet to see a turnaround in China's  construction activity. The transition to a less commodity-intensive and slower growth path, often referred as the  new normal, is further compounded by these soft industrial trends. The recent decline in oil prices has wide  repercussions. Even though we benefit from it, a lower oil price clearly has a negative impact on many  governments and their economies. The volatility in global financial markets reflects concern over the strength of  global manufacturing and global trade, and we can see this impact on emerging equity markets.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: The iron ore market dipped below $40 per tonne towards the end of last year, representing an 80% fall since its  peak in 2011. Domestic steel consumption in China fell by between 4% and 5% in 2015 due to its exposure to  property and investment.
