China's iron ore demand, however, was more stable due to a combination of higher steel  exports and lower scrap use.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: For some time, we've been highlighting the iron ore exits. At the start of 2015, we anticipated cuts for the year of  around 85 million tonnes. We actually saw 130 million tonnes cut from high cost production, and this was on top  of the 125 million tonnes of exits that occurred in 2014. So high-cost supply is leaving the market.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: In 2016, we estimate that around 75 million tonnes of new supply will come on to the market from seaborne  producers. This will be more than matched by exits. But it's not just iron ore prices that have been impacted by  recent market turmoil. Prices for aluminium, thermal and met coal are at levels preceding the China boom or only  briefly seen during the depth of the Global Financial Crisis.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: In each of these cases, strong Chinese supply and slow curtailments have exacerbated global market imbalances.  As a result, prices are cutting deep into cost curve, despite significant reductions in cost, weaker currency and  lower energy prices. We've also seen a gradual erosion of the copper price with rising expectations of continued  supply growth, coupled with weaker demand.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: We continue to look to ensure that our balance sheet is robust and that returns are based more on profitability.  Our 2015 underlying earnings were $4.5 billion. Now while this is simplistic, if we adjusted that number with the  current consensus iron ore price alone, today's earnings would've been around $2.7 billion. And as before taking  into account any other commodity prices or premia that we're seeing in the markets today.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: In the Pilbara, we've essentially finished the infrastructure build and are now looking at a much smaller spend on  the Silvergrass project. And this primarily provides product quality for the Pilbara Blend. It's now expected to  come in below $500 million.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: The Amrun project team are working hard to find alternate ways to finance key infrastructure components as well  as re-phasing expenditure. And at OT, the feasibility study continues and we expect that to be completed in the  first half of this year.

texts.speaker: Jason Fairclough
texts.profession: Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: It's Jason Fairclough, Bank of America Merrill Lynch. Just a sort of more general question on the  sustainability of  the business, and you've talked – Chris, I think I heard you three times – doing this from a position of strength. If  we look at the dividend you're talking about for 2016, it still looks pretty close to 100% payout ratio for 2016. Now  maybe that's a bridge year, but that still doesn't feel that sustainable to me. If I then look at what you're spending  in terms of CapEx, it's much less than depreciation, particularly if I look at your sustaining CapEx. So, I guess the  question is, do you feel like the business is stable here? Do you think it's sustainable as you've set it up today?

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Y eah. Thanks, Chris. And I mean, just to wrap up on that, in terms of sustainability, that's really the basis of  everything that we're talking about today, to ensure that we maintain the strength of our balance sheet and the  robustness of the business.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Look, perhaps if I'll let Chris pick up the first and third question and if I pick up on long-term demand for iron  ore. But, Chris, perhaps on the 2017 dividend and washing machines and so on.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Y eah. It's always going to be a board decision and I guess we have given guidance now further than the 2016  transitional arrangements. But the – so, I think it's highly unlikely.

texts.speaker: Clarke Wilkins
texts.profession: Citigroup Global Markets Australia Pty Ltd.
texts.text: Good evening, Sammy. Listen, just in regards to the iron ore side, just with Silvergrass, that $500 million, I think,  was mentioned as what the sort of updated CapEx coming under. Is that – that's in the sort of the growth projects  rather than the stay -in-business CapEx? And also just in terms of stay-in-business CapEx for the Pilbara, on a $1  per tonne basis, where does that sort of sit after the cost reductions?

texts.speaker: Clarke Wilkins
texts.profession: Citigroup Global Markets Australia Pty Ltd.
texts.text: And finally, just in regards to sort of with Silvergrass, where does that get you towards selling up your  infrastructure capacity of 360 Mt/a and how does the sort of current thinking about when Koodaideri's required  to keep that running at 360 Mt/a in the future?

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Oh, that was a good half-a-dozen questions. Let me perhaps pick up on those. Silvergrass, I think, as you know, we  have actually already started Silvergrass in a trucking operation through to the Brockman 4 plant. It was  nicknamed by the iron ore folk NIT 2 and Nammuldi incremental tonnes 2, and it's actually a trucking of  Silvergrass product, around 10 million tonnes into Brockman.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Silvergrass is all about maintaining the Pilbara Blend and retaining the specification, quality, whatever you want  to call it, grade of the Pilbara Blend product. Pilbara Blend is critical to us in terms of optimizing our products. As  you're aware, we blend 13 of our products to produce Pilbara Blend to optimize iron content, phosphorus, silica,  alumina and so on. And that enables us not only to provide a base for the foundation of burdens for steel blast  furnaces. But also it underpins the price establishment in the spot price being such a major element in the iron ore  seaborne trade.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So, it's an important element, but let me emphasize that bringing on Silvergrass is aimed at maintaining spec, not  bringing on extra tonnes. And although we have announced that we now have 360 million tonnes of infrastructure  capacity rail and port in the Pilbara. At this stage, we're not taking full usage of that. And this is  really phasing the  implementation to more match the market for iron ore.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: In relation to cost per tonne, Silvergrass will be highly competitive against our existing operations and in fact the  project has a very, very good return. In relation to Koodaideri, Koodaideri is a future prospect for us. The iron ore  team are looking at exactly when we should implement Koodaideri with the view to continuing to push that out for  as long as we can.

texts.speaker: Lyndon Fagan
texts.profession: JPMorgan Securities Australia Ltd.
texts.text: Thanks very much. Just with the dividend cut, there's obviously a lot more available free cash flow, yet the Pilbara  isn't running at 360 Mt/a, which is what your infrastructure capacity is. Given the cost reductions in the Pilbara  and the attractive margins there, why not accelerate a bit of that production to sort of utilize that lightened  infrastructure? That's the first question.

texts.speaker: Lyndon Fagan
texts.profession: JPMorgan Securities Australia Ltd.
texts.text: Then the next one's just on coal. You've obviously saw Bengalla and now Mount Pleasant. Should we expect  further exits of coal assets or are you committed to retaining a presence in coal? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: With regard to coal, we did – as you rightly point out, we did have the two disposals that have been in the market  recently, the Bengalla and then the Mount Pleasant Project, circa $800 million of value recycled out of the balance  sheet. Other than that, we've now got pretty much the best thermal coal assets in Australia or if you want to call  them a good house in a bad street, that's probably not a bad description of the state of the market at the moment.  But – so we're going to run those for optimizing cash flow and earnings. And it's important for our team that they  get focused on making sure that they optimize those operations.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: I don't think anybody in this room actually predicted that commodities – oil and gas, so on – would be where it is  today. More importantly, it's that we take proactive action that, in a way, you can say we're taking a leadership  action, but we're taking proactive action to ensure the strength of the business going forward. And having a strong  balance sheet is fundamental to what we do.

texts.speaker: Luc Pez
texts.profession: Exane BNP Paribas
texts.text: Hi, gentlemen. Thanks for taking my question. One question, maybe when you discussed M&A and your focused  on Tier 1 copper assets, do you mean by this that you're more attracted by existing producing assets, so would you  also consider Tier 1 projects or, let's say, does the experience of Oyu Tolgoi [ph] has (1:09:04) somehow cooled  your appetite for such large projects?

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: I think our focus with acquisition would be primarily looking at operating assets that are generating cash flow.  And of course, we have our own development projects in the pipeline, as you mentioned correctly, Oyu Tolgoi  underground. But also, the Resolution project and the La Granja project are two further copper development  projects that we have in our portfolio.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Y eah, you're right, Hayden, in relation to our iron ore products in the Pilbara. We certainly have Pilbara Blend, we  have Y andi, and we have the Robe Valley product. With Y andi, there are certainly further options for us beyond  the life of the existing projects. And that's certainly things that we'll be looking at down the track. They're not  immediately in the pipeline but of course, with our evaluation work, we're continuing with our infill drilling and  exploration work around existing operations. The world is a very different place when you're producing about 1  million tonnes a day coming out of the Pilbara, and we need to ensure that we are, in fact, frontloading the system  with this drilling program.

texts.speaker: Paul D. Young
texts.profession: Deutsche Bank AG (Australia)
texts.text: Y eah. Hi, gentlemen. Hi, everyone. Chris, a few questions for you. And now that I know JS is in the room, this is  pretty relevant. Just on your CapEx guidance, your $2 billion drop in 2017, that's huge. That's a big number. Part  of this is FX, part is lower contractor rates, and I understand that. And you've given a lower number for  Silvergrass. But have you seen any savings on the OT underground due to the lower CapEx environment? That's  question number one.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: With regard to Escondida, here on the site visit, we weren't permitted to go on that site visit, not quite sure what  the dialogue was. But, look, I think the rapid drop in the price on copper over the last period has obviously had an  effect. And JS, would you have any particular granularity about?

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Well, I mean, obviously, the capital as put forward by management has the projects that we see necessary to  continue growth. And if you look at the three projects, A, they do have very good return. If you look at  Amrun,  South of the Embley, half of the project is actually replacement tonnes. As we move to the end of the life of East  Weipa, we do need to have replacement tonnes.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: The optimum, the best option for that is South of the Embley, Amrun. And to operate that, you need to put in new  infrastructure. You need to put in a new port and other infrastructure facilities. Once you do that, with the  expectation of growth in the bauxite market, the export tonnes become very, very attractive. So, Amrun, as I've  said many times to you, is one of our very best projects. But it's also required to actually maintain the replacement  tonnes for East Weipa.

texts.speaker: Samuel Maurice Cossart Walsh
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: We do, as you know we have finding commitments from some 25 banking institutions for the project finance for  the project. And our view is looking at copper going forward and looking at the difficulty that people have bringing  on copper projects, that OT underground is going to be a very important part of copper supply going forward. So  it's really a combination of those factors that the board has taken into account.

file: RIO - Q4 2016 Earnings Call 8February2017 330 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 08-Feb-17.pdf

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: I've been very pleased with our cost reduction program. We delivered $1 billion in the second half. This comes in  addition to the $580 million in the first half. So, we are well on track to deliver on our promise of $2 billion in cost  savings across 2016 and 2017.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In 2016, we further strengthened our portfolio as we said we would, again, not just talking, but delivering. We  announced disposal of more than $1.3 billion in the year, closing the sale of Lochaber in the UK in December.  And last month, we announced the divestment of our thermal coal business in Australia worth $2.45 billion which,  subject to approval, should complete later this year.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The Copper & Diamonds product group had operating EBITDA margins of 35% and continued to develop our  world-class resources including Oyu Tolgoi. And Energy & Minerals match production with market demands,  generating significant free cash flow in 2016 due to improved prices in some commodities including coal. I am  delighted with the strong performance across the group and with the hard work and commitment of all our  employees around the world.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Thanks, J-S. These are another strong set of results. Let's have a look at the numbers in more detail starting with  the commodities. Prices were depressed at the start of 2016. However, we saw an improvement during the year  in most of our main commodities. Iron Ore started the year at around $40 a tonne, ended the year around $75 a  tonne. The average price was $53.60, which was 6% higher than 2015. Copper prices were, on average, 11%  lower than 2015, notwithstanding a 25% increase during the year. Aluminium ended the year 20% higher. But the  average was 3% below 2015, but market premia also fell. For example, the Mid-West premium declined by 40%  to $162 per tonne in 2016.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Higher sales across most of our commodities were offset by lower copper and byproduct sales and there was a  lower attributable share of coal arising from the restructure of the coal in Allied Group and the sale of Bengalla.  We delivered a further $1.6 billion of unit cash cost savings in 2016, which equates to $1.2 billion post tax, but we  maintain our target of $2 billion of cost savings over 2016 and 2017 combined.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: As always, it's important to note that this excludes the impact of exchange rates and changes in oil and energy  costs. This takes our total reductions against the 2012 cost base to $7.8 billion. A strong culture of cost cont rol is  required to assist in further cost reductions, especially where many of the easier wins have already been taken.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: I'm sure that each of our businesses will apply the same tenacity to our new target of increasing free cash flow  through productivity improvements by $5 billion over the next five years. J-S has already mentioned the  outstanding work that we've seen in the Aluminium group this year where cost reduction targets have again been  beaten, delivering a further reduction of $481 million. Aluminium found a total now of $1.6 billion of cost  reductions since 2012 and a program of more than 1,250 initiatives is still being worked on.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The Energy & Minerals group also reduced costs further, taking out an additional $342 million in 2016 and  bringing its cumulative total to $1.4 billion. And Copper & Diamonds took out $278 million in 2016 despite lower  volumes.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The growth projects are progressing well under the oversight of our Growth and Innovation group. The Silvergrass  project in the Pilbara will deliver high-grade low phosphorus ore for the Pilbara Blend and give us operating  benefits.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Our work and expenditure on this project is ramping up now and we're on track for production in the second half  of 2017. At the $1.9 billion Amrun bauxite project in Queensland, the access road is now complete and we'll have  the river terminal operational this quarter. As previously guided, most of the project spend will be over the next  two years, with first production in the first half of 2019.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We continue to refine our portfolio to ensure that we make the most efficient use of our capital. In 2016, we  announced $1.3 billion of divestments. We closed the sales on our Bengalla mine and the Mount Pleasant  thermal coal project. We announced the sale of the Lochaber's aluminium smelter for which we received slightly  more than half the proceeds in 2016 with the remainder to be received later this month.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Two weeks ago, we announced that we'd agreed the sale of Coal & Allied for up to $2.45 billion plus potential  royalties. This sale is subject to a number of conditions, but the transaction should close in the second half of this  year.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Including Coal & Allied, we have announced divestments of more than $7.7 billion in the last four years, but we  retained flexibility in our portfolio. Some of our assets are smaller, but they're valuable and highly cash generative.  We'll continue to exit any assets or projects that don't fit our portfolio and where we can realize attractive values.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Let's look at the iron ore market. Recently, the market has been much stronger than expected by many observers.  There are four key drivers that will continue to impact the iron ore supply/demand balance in 2017. The first is the  health of the Chinese economy, which I've just covered. Next, the Chinese domestic steel market is looking to  drive out high-polluting production. This is a clear opportunity for us as we will see demand switch from low-grade  ore to high-grade product we offer. The third, the additional supply from seaborne iron ore producers, we expect  about 40 million tonnes of new capacity in 2017. And last but not least, the domestic iron ore production in China  is a key source of uncertainty and could keep the balance.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Now, going forward, in the future, you will see an increase in terms of sustaining CapEx. That is absolutely clear,  and this will be combined as well, especially in the context of the Pilbara, as you see it on the graph, that we  would have to spend more and more money in relation to replacement CapEx because when you move 330  million, 340 million tonne per annum, at one stage, you need to open up some new mine. So, today, are we  comfortable with the level of sustaining CapEx? The answer is yes. But in the coming years, it will increase.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: You mean you don't have the answer or you...  Christopher J. Lynch  Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc  A  No. No. No. No. But anyway, we can talk more about that later. But the issue on this one is really about  international competitiveness, and we talked about, J-S mentioned Indonesia and [indiscernible] (37:48). But  throwing changes into an environment like that actually and targeting two companies only, unilaterally or whatever  the right word is for two, target the two, just isn't a big statement about what the country risk or the investment risk  is in those sort of jurisdictions there.

texts.speaker: Paul Young
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Australia)
texts.text: Yeah. Hi, J-S and Chris. The first question is on the Aluminium division. Cost performance continues to be pretty  impressive. Division did most of the heavy lifting for the group in 2016. My calc show that your primary metal unit  cost dropped to $0.66 a pound in the December half, so great performance. Question is how much further can  you reduce primary metal unit cost through overhead reductions and production creep? And really interested in  what the contribution of the Aluminium division is to the $5 billion free cash flow target. That's the first question.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: All right. So, I am going to pick the Grasberg one. You pick the other one, Chris. So, the question on Grasberg is  the following. We were – all of us taken by surprise by the new change or the changes of regulation that occurred  three weeks ago. That was – first of all, it's across the entire mining business. It's not only targeted at Grasberg  per se, for the first point.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The other thing to keep an eye out there for in the smelters is they will have a few headwinds as well with costs.  And just think about the carbon material side of the business for the coke and pitch and the like, that will go in  there. So, we expect them to be a healthy contributor to productivity gains. They'll be under the same sort of  internal pressures as everybody else will be, and they have made great progress on the cost structure thus far.  There's more to come, but I think you should expect, I think it was Myles' earlier question, that is getting – the low- hanging fruits have been well and truly harvested here. So, we are getting to the stage where incremental  improvements there are getting more and more difficult. So the productivity drive is important, and it's important to  get the focus not only on cost but also on the top line aspects of that as well.

texts.speaker: Anna Mulholland
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG
texts.text: And in terms of the ongoing investigations at Simandou and on the Mozambique coal site, in your statement this  morning you've spoken about a potential material financial cost. At what point do you have to provision for that?

texts.speaker: James Gurry
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Yeah. James Gurry from Credit Suisse. Just hopping on a little bit more about copper and options. It's a little bit  unusual for a diversified miner to have zero percent of earnings coming from the Copper & Minerals division. So,   does it concern you that it is quite small? And obviously the copper market could tighten in the coming months  because of production disruptions at two mines that you've got a stake in? So, are there any other ways to  heighten the contribution of copper to the portfolio that you're looking at maybe on acquisitions, smart acquisitions  or other greenfield opportunities like the Resolution Copper Project?

texts.speaker: Clarke Wilkins
texts.profession: Analyst, Citigroup Global Markets Australia Pty Ltd.
texts.text: Yes, that's Clarke here. Just a couple of questions. First off, just in regard to the additional sort of rehabilitation  costs that go – quite significant increase. We've seen that happen, I suppose, with the Ranger at ERA. Is that  being looked at and applied across the other closure provisions across the other assets given the potential risks  we've seen across the industry for closure costs to be underestimated?

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The question about closure provisions -- the Gove issue is – we curtailed the refinery at Gove. We're still  continuing to mine there and we continue to do that for some time, but it's really around the refinery and the  residue dams pertaining to the refinery.

texts.speaker: Hayden Bairstow
texts.profession: Analyst, Macquarie Securities (Australia) Ltd.
texts.text: And then just on the presentation on page three, I noticed you had a picture of an electric car. I mean, are we to  take from that the Jadar lithium project is moving along quite nicely in the feasibility stage?

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So, I'll take the car definitely. I mean, the electric car is made of aluminium, copper, lithium for the battery and  even high-strength steel in some of them. So, don't draw any conclusion. But I can confirm that we are studying  very, very carefully the Jadar project and the study is underway. And when we have something else to share to  the market, we will do it. So I think it's a broad range of product here.

texts.speaker: Hunter Hillcoat
texts.profession: Analyst, Investec Bank Plc
texts.text: Hi. It's Hunter Hillcoat from Investec here. There's a lot of clever people around who think iron ore is going to be  $55 by the end of this year. I'm not one of those people. But...

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Now, what is important for us and that's – when we talk about value over volume, in the context of iron ore, one  dimension is really around making sure we produce the right product for the right customers, okay.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: And back to the point I mentioned today, as and when the government restructure the SoEs in China because of  pollution issues, and as they want to increase the productivity of their best blast furnaces, mainly on the cores, by  the way. In order to increase the productivity of your blast furnace, you need to improve [ph] to abandon (1:03:26)  your burden. And that's where you're going to need higher coking coal quality and that's where you're going to  need higher iron ore quality. So, we see lots of opportunities in that space, so that's where we are.

file: RIO - Q4 2017 Earnings Call 7February2018 330 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 07-Feb-18.pdf

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In 2017, we also further strengthened our portfolio, generating $2.7 billion of proceeds from our divestments,  including Coal & Allied. We will continue to exit any assets or projects that do not fit our strategy. Let me give you  an example. Last month, we received a binding offer of $500 million for the sale of our Aluminium Dunkerque  smelter in France. So, in summary, we are in good shape, we have the very strong set of results, and we are well  positioned for the future. But let me be clear, I can assure you we are not becoming complacent at all.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Now, I will cover some of our operational and product group highlights, starting with safety. Safety comes first at  Rio Tinto. Our ambitions remain the same: all of our employees and contractors must return home safely at the  end of each and every day. Sadly, you will remember we lost a colleague in a tragic incident at our Kennecott  operation in October. Albert Lozano died following injuries he suffered after SO2 exposure. I was on site at the  time and I can tell you that Albert's loss was deeply felt by his family, friends and all over Rio Tinto. We are  working very hard to try and ensure this never happens again.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Let's take a look at our product group performance. Every part of the business is focused on maximizing cash  through driving productivity from mine-to-market. In Iron Ore, we delivered free cash flow of $7.3 billion and  EBITDA margin of 68% as customers demanded our higher-quality product, driven by the need to improve  environmental performance.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Copper prices increased 27% compared to last year, reflecting strong demand from China and supply disruptions  during the period. Tighter Chinese environmental policies curtailed the importation of scrap which has created  increased demand for concentrate and cathode.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Realized hard coking coal prices were 42% higher on average compared with 2016. Impacts from Cyclone  Debbie in Queensland saw prices spike in the first half. And whilst these have come off from those levels, strong  demand from China and a tight supply chain have meant prices have remained strong compared with 2016.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: With the aluminium business, we have the hydro-powered Canadian smelters, which are in the first quartile and  even first decile of the cost curve. And we have the exceptional bauxite assets in North Queensland. Having high  quality Tier 1 assets with attractive commodity offerings is key to delivering higher margins through the cycle.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Underlying earnings are up 69% on last year. This chart shows clearly the recovery in prices in 2017 across our  commodities, with prices increasing earnings by $4.1 billion versus 2016. As you can see, energy costs and  exchange rates, whilst increasing, have only had a modest negative impact.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In the first half of the year, Pilbara shipments and hard coking coal production was impacted by significant  cyclonic weather. And our copper division saw disruptions from labor negotiations at Escondida. The strong  second half, particularly in the Pilbara and the Australian bauxite operations, meant that we were able to recover  volumes for the year, and production finished pretty much in line with 2016.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We've achieved cost savings which more than offset raw material cost increases of around $200 million,  particularly for input prices in aluminium which we mentioned in December. There was a one-off impact to  underlying earnings of $176 million as a result of the strike at Escondida. The completion of the Coal & Allied  disposal on the 1st of September reduced thermal and semi-soft coal volumes in 2017. So, overall, delivered  underlying earnings of $6.8 billion (sic) [$8.6 billion] (00:12:49).

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: As before, the cash cost variance excludes the effects of inflation, energy costs and exchange rates. All other  costs are being taken on the chin. For example, the current headwinds on input prices for coke, pitch and caustic  have not been forgiven. We have adjusted for tax. On a post-tax basis, the total productivity improvements,  including what was achieved in the first half of this year, amount to $0.5 billion.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Capital spend for the year was $4.5 billion, of which $2 billion was sustaining our current operations and $2.5  billion on the compelling growth projects. During the year, we completed the $338 million Silvergrass project with  commissioning occurring in the fourth quarter. The mine will continue to ramp up. It's currently delivering around  10 million tonnes of low-cost additional capacity, supporting our highly valued Pilbara blend product.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The Amrun bauxite project in North Queensland is on track to deliver first ore in the first half of 2019. During the  year, we installed both the wharf and the plant beneficiation modules. At Oyu Tolgoi, we saw a ramp up in spend  in 2017 as we continue to mobilize contractors. We've recently completed this sinking of Shaft 2 and lateral  development is on track. An annual project review was completed during the year and we remain on track to  deliver first drawbell production in 2020.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In 2018 and 2019, we'll continue to spend CapEx at Amrun; and at Oyu Tolgoi, we're spending around $1 billion  in each of these years, including plant funding for a power station from 2019. Both of these projects are highly  value accretive.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In the Iron Ore business, we'll need to spend around $3 billion on sustaining CapEx over the next three years  including spend on rail. We'll spend about $2.2 billion on replacement mines over the same period, and starting in  2009, we expect to see spending coming through for the Koodaideri mine.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: One of the advantages of a strong balance sheet is the ability to drive future returns. When we make capital  allocation decisions we ensure that we only fund the best projects. During 2017, we reduced our net debt to $3.8  billion, a 60% reduction from the end of the previous year. Two things we want to point out here that are factored  into our thinking. The first is $1.9 billion on market Rio Tinto plc-share buyback program announced in September  2017 following the Coal & Allied divestment. This portion of that buyback will be completed by the end of this year.  There's $1.9 billion to spend there.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: And then we did the off-market buyback in Rio Tinto Limited of $0.6 billion related to the Coal & Allied proceeds.  That was also completed in November of 2017. The $2.5 billion supplementary buyback was split between Rio  Tinto Limited and plc on the weighting of the DLC as you'll see on the next slide. $1.9 billion of that remains to be  completed this year.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The Party Congress restated its focus on environmental performance starting with the steel industry. This has  resulted in high premiums for our product such has our Pilbara blend. Longer term, the Belt Road initiative will  create further opportunities in the infrastructure and construction space.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Let's take a look at steel fundamentals in more detail. This chart shows that we can expect to see around a 5%  reduction in steel capacity in China due to supply side reforms in 2017 and 2018. In addition, further reductions in  capacity will occur over the winter period as a result of environmental policy impacts. This is good news for Rio  Tinto's Pilbara blend, which meets the high-quality requirements of our Chinese customers.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Let's turn to Aluminum. We remain very positive about demand. We see annual growth of around 4%, and we  expect this trend to continue over the next 15 years. This is underpinned by growth in the transport sector with the  uptake in electric vehicles.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: More significantly, over the medium-to-longer term, we expect China to be broadly balanced in aluminium, which  creates significant implication for supply from the rest of the world. This could be a turning point for the aluminium  industry, for which we are uniquely positioned with our 2.3 million tonnes hydro-powered Canadian smelters. And,  of course, we remain optimistic about copper because of constrained supply and rising demand from  electrifications.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Our position in both sides provides attractive growth options which we can trigger when there is market demand.  Our first-quartile smelters in Canada are the most profitable and energy-efficient in the industry, with attractive  brownfield options. In Copper, we have large high-quality expandable resources at Oyu Tolgoi and potentially  resolution. Copper is the primary area of focus for exploration teams. And the high-quality energy and minerals  portfolio has already shown its capability to increase supply into a growing market.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: OT is one of the few copper growth projects in the world. The Underground Project is 18 months into a five-year  program and is well on track. I saw it for myself last month and the progress is pretty impressive. I spent time with  the Prime Minister and we're working with the government of Mongolia to strengthen the relationship.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: And then the other one is the buybacks that were already in the market. So, we had the proceeds from Coal &  Allied, $1.9 billion remaining to spend on that that was in the balance sheet but already committed to pay out this  year.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The main impact last year was in aluminium, but we expected – if you take a three- or four-, five-year perspective,  it's going to come back. And that's why our mine-to-market productivity, the $5 billion of additional free cash flow  that we are targeting in the next five year is so important. It's not a nice to have, it's a must have in order to offset,  as a minimum, the inflation. So, that's the reality of it. We acknowledge it. Oil prices are going up. Steel prices are  going up and so on, so forth. And I expect, at some stage, the [ph] wage (00:36:56) to go up as well, all right? So,  mine-to-market is the way forward.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So, the power station is part of the agreement. If you want to be very detailed, its clause 7.2, 7.3 and 7.4 of the  investment agreement signed in 2009. It was in the CapEx. It's I think $250 million every year from 2019. So that's  in the forecast. Yeah. So, there is no change from that perspective.

texts.speaker: Clarke Wilkins
texts.profession: Analyst, Citigroup Global Markets Australia Pty Ltd.
texts.text: Good morning. Just in regards to the [indiscernible] (00:42:48), I think Chris said only the best projects get  approved. How far away are the Canadian sort of brownfield expansions in the hydro aluminium away from being  those best projects and how much further improvement in price would we need? And it's also, just in returning to  the CapEx guidance, is there any CapEx for studies or growth options in the 2019, 2020 numbers?

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: I'll pick up the aluminium; you pick up Grasberg, please, if that's okay. So, on aluminium it's clearly the assets we  have in Canada are world-class because of the hydro-based energy base. We have multiple growth options. We  will pursue for obvious reason all the creeping options, the low-capital intensity creeping options that they are  already in the plan. But above and beyond that, we could have further brownfield expansion, but here I've got to  restate what I said is, we could be at a turning point in relation to the aluminium industry in China, okay?

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: It's early days. If China really restructure the aluminium business, then that could create significant opportunities  for us. So, what we want is to being option-ready that if we're absolutely comfortable that there is a market there  then we can trigger those options. So, yes, we're doing the studies. There is money earmarked in terms of E&E in  our budget and so on and so forth. But we are not there yet. We are watching the aluminium situation in China  very, very carefully and I put it on the slide.

texts.speaker: Paul Young
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Australia)
texts.text: Hi, J-S. Hi, Chris. A couple of questions on your aluminium business, just an observation on, first of all, cash cost  in aluminium. It was pretty good performance actually, $0.77 a pound in the December half versus $0.75 a pound  in the first half. And I understand you guys probably don't have these numbers in front of you but – and that was  despite higher aluminium prices. So I'm just curious about that lack of sensitivity to aluminium price, lot of its  shuffling profits of course. And also, are we yet to see the big flow-through of higher coke and pitch prices? And is  that coming this year?

texts.speaker: Paul Young
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Australia)
texts.text: And then on bauxite, just an observation, you've had now four halves of flat realized pricing at around $40 a tonne  that for the last couple of years. So, I presume that's due to your longer term contracts. I'm just wondering how  long is the realized price going to sit around that $40 mark.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Thank you, Paul. So, I'll pick up the aluminium, you pick up bauxite. I think there is no doubt that we had a  massive cost increase in terms of [indiscernible] (00:46:52) in aluminium last year, as you said, Paul, and it will  continue this year, all right. And that's why the mine-to-market which the way it translates in aluminium for us is  there are too many drivers. One is creeping, trying to extract more aluminium from the existing assets every year.  And we target depending on the year between 1% and 2% improvement year-on-year, so that's going to be a big  element that you offset it. The second element is to push harder on the value-added products for which we have a  better margin. So, that is the reality of the market.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: With regard to bauxite, Paul, it's really about – in terms of realized prices for bauxite, it's more about what the  Chinese have been able to do with bauxite coming out of Guinea and the speed at which they're able to do it and  also the cost structure. So, there's been a pull-through of Guinea bauxite into China that probably diluted or  dampened down the bauxite price a little bit on the seaborne trade. So, that's something that we are keeping a  very close eye on, but we do take a transfer price for the calculations here. We take a transfer price of bauxite  through our refineries, and then again a transfer price of alumina through to the smelters. But the primary mover  in bauxite was really the amount of bauxite that was able to be sourced out of China – Indochina rather primarily  out of Guinea.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: To be clear, Paul, today, we don't have any issues to place our tonnage from more bauxite mines. I mean,  everything is sold out. But, once again, back to the aluminium question, we've got multiple growth options above  and beyond Amrun. We've got version 2.0, 3.0, 4.0. What we want is to be option-rich and option-ready, and  depending on the development of the market then we will add capacity as appropriate. But for us, it's really about  creating value. We want to have the options. We have the options and then depending on the market conditions  we trigger those options at the right point in time.

texts.speaker: Alon Olsha
texts.profession: Analyst, Macquarie Capital (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Hi. It's Alon Olsha from Macquarie. Just one question on Iron Ore. As you pointed out in the fourth quarter you  achieved 360 million tonnes annualized shipments. Is that a number you think can be achieved over the course of  an entire year once AutoHaul is up and running? And if so, when and how should we think about AutoHaul in  terms of capacity versus availability?

texts.speaker: Fraser Jamieson
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: Actually, a couple more on Iron Ore. So through your presentation, you kind of implied the very high steel margins  were what has driven the premium of 62% versus 58%. There's definitely some evidence out in the market that  though people are viewing those actually as a bit more structural rather than cyclical. So, could you just sort of  explain what your view is on that and what you're hearing from your customers? How should we be thinking about  this in terms of sort of structural versus cyclical?

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Yeah. I think maybe just one observation on the inflation. The other area we haven't talked about with regard to  the labor inflation, but – currently, what we've seen so far is some spot inflation on – we talked about those input  prices for the alloy business. But in copper, this year, there's something like 28% of the world's copper capacity is  coming up in a price agreement negotiations and that type of thing. How that comes out is another matter.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So, we've got to be real to it and alert to it, but that's – and then the structural versus the cyclical I think what  you're seeing with regards to that is that the environmental play in China is also coming across a series of  products and notwithstanding steel. So, you are seeing a demand for the higher-quality raw material inputs  coming through there.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: I think there is no doubt that last year, they did shutdown some capacity, the induction furnace and so on and so  forth and some of the smaller blast furnaces, but that didn't mean, if you look at the stats, a drop in terms of output  of steel.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So, with the reduced capacity, the only way to produce more is by driving the productivity of your blast furnace in  a harder way to increase the scrap ratio in your steel plant, and so on and so forth. And that's what we're  experiencing in the marketplace, all right?

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So, all the indications are moving in the right direction; the environmental policies, the fact they're making money,  they're trying to produce more with the reduced capacity and, therefore, the need for higher-quality product. Our  sense is we are moving close to a structural change, but we are always very cautious.

texts.speaker: Christopher J. Lynch
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: It is and it's warm as well. So, there's a long way to go on Resolution. There's probably five years of permitting  process still to go. So, what we're approving with regard to Resolution are really milestone-based lumps of  money. We're not capitalizing it, it's going into – we're expensing it. But the key issue really is around making  sure. So, for instance, right now we're focused on extension of the shafts, we need two points of egress before we  want to have – so we want that to be common. And then – but there's a lot of work to go with regards to getting  into the ore body and determining how we think the cave would ultimately work as well. So, we're a long way from  being in a position to give a notice to proceed on that project. It's very much rudimentary at this stage, so...

texts.speaker: Lyndon Fagan
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Australia Ltd.
texts.text: And then the second question, just in terms of – you've spoken about China a fair bit. China domestic iron ore  mines have usually been the source of elastic supply. Are you still seeing the market that way or are you seeing  the environmental restrictions limiting the reaction of Chinese supply to what are now very attractive prices?  Thanks.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: One is you mentioned it is environmental permits for some of those mines are much more difficult to get, mainly  because of dust. And the other element that we just mentioned is if you believe in the structural change and the  need for higher-quality iron ore to drive the productivity of your blast furnaces, a lot of those mines are low grade,  all right? So, it's going to be more and more difficult for them to make money. However, if I go back to the 400  million tonne I just mentioned, half of them were SOEs and half of them were privately owned. There has been lot  of stickiness in the SOE sector to be restructured, all right?

texts.speaker: Paul J. Gait
texts.profession: Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Thanks very much. Paul Gait, Bernstein. Just sort of shifting commodities, lithium, you mentioned electric  vehicles. I was just wondering how you're thinking on the lithium market. I know Jadar is long-dated, but how your  thinking on the lithium market's evolved over the course of the year, what your thinking is around electric vehicles  and any kind of numbers that you might sort of be able to put around Jadar in terms of your thinking there.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: All right. I think if you go back to the slide of Chris, I don't know if you can go there, you know the washing  machine, we are very clear about the capital, the disciplined capital allocation cycle that we have and we do it  twice a year. The main time is in February for the board we had this week. Are we going to return all the cash  from divestments? I can't tell you yes or no. It will be part of the allocation, the process. We did an off-cycle last  year on the back of Coal & Allied proceeds, but you can't take any comfort that we will do off-cycle. I want to be  very clear on this one. Our process is very clear, we do it twice a year with the main time in February and that  we've just done. That's one aspect.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The second driver is about organic growth. We are already underway at Oyu Tolgoi. We are already underway at  Amrun. We have growth options in aluminium and bauxite. We talked about it earlier today. We want to be option- rich, but we will trigger these options only if the market conditions are right and we make money out of it, okay?

texts.speaker: Tyler Broda
texts.profession: Analyst, RBC Europe Ltd.
texts.text: Yes. Tyler Broda at RBC. You mentioned the structural change that you see potentially happening in China  around aluminium. How does this change your views around Rio's position in the alumina market? And then  secondly...

texts.speaker: Tyler Broda
texts.profession: Analyst, RBC Europe Ltd.
texts.text: Yeah. Yeah, yeah. [indiscernible] (01:08:50) in terms of the [ph] overall historic (01:08:51) as well. Yes. And then,  how do you see the changes around your view about Pacific Aluminium within Rio in this environment?

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Okay. No worries. Thanks for the question. I think we believe that if you got aluminium smelters, especially like in  Canada, where you got on the back of hydro-based, you make a lot of money and that creates value for  shareholders. If you have bauxite, these typical mining margins, we like it as well. Alumina is in between. There is  not a lot of liquidity in the market, okay? So, we have to be integrated from a supply chain standpoint, but we try  to be integrated as little as we can because alumina is something in between and you don't create a lot of value.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Now, having said that, you can see that all our alumina refineries are making a lot of money today because the  team are working hard. But in terms of capital allocation, first of all, to go back to your question, the capital  allocation is across all commodities and all assets; it's not earmarked by product group. But, today, if I were to  look only in the aluminium supply chain, if I were to allocate money, I would put it in the smelters first, I would put  it in the bauxite first, and alumina would come at the back end of the list, all right? So, that is the reality of it.

texts.speaker: Tyler Broda
texts.profession: Analyst, RBC Europe Ltd.
texts.text: Structural change that you see potentially happening in China, potentially change structurally where Pacific  Aluminium fits with Rio Tinto?

file: RIO - Q4 2018 Earnings Call 27February2019 330 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 27-Feb-19.pdf

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In summary, we generated $18.1 billion of EBITDA with a strong merging of 42%, and we delivered cash of $11.8  billion from our operations. We achieved $8.6 billion in assets sales, the divestment of coal and Grasberg adding  to our sustainability credentials.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Today, we are the only large mining company with no coal or oil and gas in our portfolio. And we also invested  $5.4 billion in a world-class portfolio. We generated a return on capital employed of 19%. AutoHaul is now  running. We have progressed Oyu Tolgoi and Amrun, and we found a promising new mineralization – copper  mineralization that we knew in Australia. More on that later on.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Now, let me turn to safety and sustainability. But before I talk about Rio, I would like to acknowledge the sad loss  of life at Minas Gerais in Brazil. This is an absolute tragedy and also a dark moment for the entire industry. It's the  responsibility of everyone in this industry to do better. At Rio Tinto, across 32 operations, we have 100 tailing  facilities and 36 that are no longer active. We take management of all of them very, very seriously. Since 2015,  we have had a global tailings standard, which is regularly reviewed. This standard applies to every Rio Tinto site  worldwide.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The second level of protection to the Rio Tinto standard is through business conformances audit and technical  reviews supported by our Surface Mining Centre of Excellence. And then the third level includes an external audit  program. If you like more details, they are available on our website including our standards and our guidance  notes.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Sustainability is absolutely vital in the 21st century where we must be part of the solution. In 2018, we progress  our sustainability agenda. For example, today, we published our first climate change report, which outline the  risks and opportunities to our business in the transition to a low carbon future. The materials we produce are  essential to this transition from the aluminum in your phone, cars and in airplanes to the iron ore in the buildings  we see every day.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: We continue to take steps to reduce emission from our oil footprint as we innovate with customers to develop  greener products like what we are doing with our new technology partnership for aluminum with Alcoa and  supported by Apple. And we have a portfolio free of coal and oil and gas. We are well-positioned to thrive in the  world that values sustainability more and more.

texts.speaker: Jakob Stausholm
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The iron ore price was supported by robust demand from both inside and outside of China. China steel production  reached a record level of 930 million tonnes last year, and we saw a particularly strong demand in China for  higher quality iron ore such as ours, driven by environmental policy and steel sector reforms.

texts.speaker: Jakob Stausholm
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Global seaborne supply was essentially flat year-on-year as producers experienced higher levels of disruptions  that we haven't seen for a number of years, in total, around 40 million tonnes. And so we saw stable iron ore  pricing, 4% lower than in 2017.

texts.speaker: Jakob Stausholm
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In copper, we experienced good price conditions in the first half of the year, but a weakening price environment in  the second half as supply outgrew demand. This was mainly because the major copper producing assets  generated a better output than what we have seen for many years. Unlike iron ore, there barely were any  significant supply disruptions, 3% against the historical average supply percent. Despite that second half, on  average, copper prices were 6% higher in 2018 than in 2017. So in summary, a quite benign pricing environment  in 2018.

texts.speaker: Jakob Stausholm
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The volumes and product mix added $0.9 billion. Energy prices went up significantly last year and raw materials  prices went up even higher, particularly for aluminum. But because of our growth, we could absorb these cost  headwinds to deliver strong and consistent earnings.

texts.speaker: Jakob Stausholm
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Excluding our coal assets, we generated EBITDA of $17.2 billion at a margin of 41%. Strong EBITDA turns into  strong underlying earnings of $8.8 billion after primarily deducting depreciation and tax. Our IFRS net earnings  was $13.6 billion, equivalent to 30% return on capital employed. That, of course, also includes profits from our  divestments. Our effective tax rate of our underlying result was 29%, in line with our earlier guidance of 30%.

texts.speaker: Jakob Stausholm
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Also, for our world-class assets to continue to deliver at their full potential, we must invest in them. This means  investing both in sustaining CapEx and replacement projects, such as the recently approved $2.6 billion  Koodaideri project, which will add 43 million tonnes capacity in phase 1 and open up a whole new prosperous  area in the Pilbara.

texts.speaker: Jakob Stausholm
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Now to Aluminium. Despite higher prices and stable operations, the performance our Aluminium business was  squeezed by inflation in raw materials and energy cost of $0.5 billion. And we also had the impact from our legacy  contracts of another $0.45 billion.

texts.speaker: Jakob Stausholm
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: External events such as China's environmental policy changes and restructuring of the aluminum industry  resulted in a reduction in supply. Also, the potential for trade tariffs and proposed sanctions created considerable  uncertainty and unusual price movements.

texts.speaker: Jakob Stausholm
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Despite all of this, we have some of the best aluminum assets in the industry and the most integrated ones with  bauxite mines, refineries and smelters. This is reflected in our industry-leading EBITDA margin.

texts.speaker: Jakob Stausholm
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: In 2018, we actually strengthened our aluminum portfolio. We made great progress at Amrun project six weeks  ahead of schedule and below budget. We also divested Dunkerque and land at Kitimat at attractive prices. Our  focus in 2019 will be on delivering additional free cash flow from improved productivity.

texts.speaker: Jakob Stausholm
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: The outlook for 2019 is production of 550,000 tonnes to 600,000 tonnes of mined copper. The top of the range is  similar to 2018 when you exclude the divested Grasberg asset. The reason for the lower guidance is because we  do expect to see a lower grade at the open pit at Oyu Tolgoi and at Kennecott.

texts.speaker: Jakob Stausholm
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: During 2018, we made good progress on our underground project at Oyu Tolgoi. And we closed 2018 by meeting  our commitment to agree a power solution for the mine, which we are now focusing.

texts.speaker: Jakob Stausholm
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: As we learn more about the rock mass around and under the orebody, we continue to encounter geotech  challenges. This is a complex project. And we have indicated a further delay to the main production shaft. And we  will continue to assess the mine plan and design.

texts.speaker: Jakob Stausholm
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Our E&M group went through significant changes in 2018. We divested our remaining Australian coal assets for  over $4 billion. And let me just repeat what JS said, for the first time in 60 years, we have not taken coal out of the  ground. We are the only major miner no longer involved in extracting fossil fuels. We also agreed to sell our share  of our Uranium business in Namibia. With these divestments, we will now have a more simplified business with  really high-quality assets.

texts.speaker: Jakob Stausholm
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Due to strong cash flow and the $8.6 billion of cash received from divestments, primarily coal assets and  Grasberg, our balance sheet moved to a net cash or $0.3 billion at the end of 2018. However, we should  acknowledge that some cash has already been allocated. And from the beginning of January 2019, we recognize  an additional $1.2 billion of net debt related to operating leases with the changes to IFRS 16. Hence, the pro  forma net debt is around $8 billion. This is still a low level. And that has been recognized only three weeks ago  when Moody's upgraded us to A2 that complements our A rating from Standard & Poor's.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Turning to our value-over-volume strategy, it's about portfolio, performance, people, partners. Portfolio is about  world-class assets. Here, we will focus on delivering on average of 2% growth per annum over the next five years.  Performance is about operating and commercial excellence. We will focus first and foremost on safety. We will  drive greater productivity and exit 2019 with $1 billion run rate from our productivity program. This is an additional  $600 million of free cash flow. And we will make sure the benefits of our commercial [ph] excision (00:30:26) are  fully realized. People, it's about developing industry-leading capabilities. We will focus on building our technical  skills and engaging with our workforce. And partners is about long-term relationships. It's about sustainability with  a strong focus on engaging host governments, communities and employees will all hear the agenda including  climate change.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Before I close, let me cover one of our priorities in more details, growth. As you've heard, we have been investing  in our existing business and we have exciting growth projects already underway in iron ore, in copper and in  bauxite. We are progressing other options. For example, on Resolution, our copper project in Arizona, we are  spending $368 million in infrastructure as we progress the permitting process. We are on track to complete the  EIS in 2020. In exploration, which is the upstream part of our pipeline, we have over 50 projects underway. We  have activity in over 8 communities and 16 countries. We plan to spend around $250 million in exploration this  year only.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Copper remains the bulk of our exploration spend, and we have a number of exciting opportunities. One of them  is Winu that I mentioned earlier. It is early days, and we have more work to do. But the initial results from the first  phase of drilling are pretty encouraging. We just disclosed the results of the first 24 drill holes that you can see on  this slide. As you can see, there is copper, there is gold, there is silver. And I'm really looking forward to the  second phase, and we will keep you updated.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Our recent track record speaks for itself, with $29 billion return – being returned to our shareholders over three  years, including $13.5 billion declared for 2018 only. We have a world-class portfolio, well-positioned for a low  carbon future. We have the strongest balance sheets in the sector, and we are progressing exciting growth  options. We will continue to deliver on our promises day in and day out.

texts.speaker: Jakob Stausholm
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Last year, we saw very significant increases in energy costs and in raw materials prices. We hope to see less of  that this year. But there are inflationary pressures, particularly in the areas where we operate in Western Australia  and Québec, et cetera.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: But a second element is really about building the mine, the infrastructure, the drill point, the extraction drive and  so on, so forth. And that's clearly on the back of the information we have in terms of geotech that we need to look  at, where do you put the infrastructure? So where do you put the extraction drives? Depending where the faults  are. Where do you put the air ventilation? Where do you put [ph] out-passes (00:42:47)? And so on, so forth, in  order to make sure that as and when you initiate the cave, then you have the right ground conditions and so on,  so forth.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So the work is underway. Anyone who's got any block cave technology or experience should know that it happens  pretty often. So when you have the geotech issue, you have to upgrade the model. And that's what the team is  doing. And as I said, sometime during the year, we'll update the market accordingly. But as I said, where I started  this, the cave is going to cave.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: One, is the fact that last year in the context of Energy & Minerals, we had a series of issues, the strike on IOC for  example. And the second piece is three of our furnaces were down, and we're going to restart a couple of them  this year.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So year-on-year, you have an uplift in terms of volume. And the other element just to build on this point is last  year we were highly impacted by the cost environment, price cost squeeze in Aluminium because of raw material.  And today, we don't see further increase in terms of raw material.

texts.speaker: Menno Sanderse
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Yeah, morning, it's Menno at Morgan Stanley. Just on the projects again, if even Rio Tinto cannot deliver with all  the knowledge and skills on a project like this, and does it lead you to review, first of all, greenfield, brownfield  projects and Rio Tinto's desire to do them firstly? And secondly, does it lead you to review how much existing  assets are worth that may or may not be out there to buy in copper specifically first?

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Our view has not changed. I mean, ideally, if you have an option – if you have two options, one is in brownfield  and one is in greenfield, you go always for the brownfield first. I mean, there is no change whatsoever. So that's  the first element. The second element is our strategy has not changed in terms of [ph] ally (00:45:34). I mean,  Jakob said it, we keep a watching brief on it. If there is a case to look at a transaction, we will look at a  transaction. But at the end of the day, it's about creating value for shareholders and so on and so forth. So, today,  when I look at the organic pipeline, we will deliver around 2% per annum growth in the next five years, which, I  think, in the context of GDP 2.5% to 3%, is pretty okay. At the macro environment, you step back. If you grow  between 2% and 2.5% per year, you fundamentally maintain market share in terms of copper equivalent. So,  there is no change in strategy from that perspective.

texts.speaker: Menno Sanderse
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Okay. And, secondly, on Aluminium, clearly, it looks for a moment that things were going to improve. It all ended  in tears again, they were back to where – the disaster situation that we were in 2016. And you've always been a  bit skeptical about Aluminium and you said it's going to be medium term. Has this sudden turn for the worse  changed your view again about the optionality in that business?

texts.speaker: Myles Allsop
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd.
texts.text: So, going back to Iron Ore, are you capped at 350 million tonnes this year because of AutoHaul. So, for markets  there, do you think there is potential to go beyond 350 million tonnes? And also – I mean we've had now had a  month or so since the tragedy. I'm sure you've been running the numbers. And what do you think the impact on  Brazilian iron ore supply is going to be? I mean, obviously, it's still kind of a moving feast, but what's your initial  sense?

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: So, there could be some substitution here. If you go back in time, as you know, was it four, five years ago, there  were around 400 million tonne of production in China. It did drop to 235 million tonnes, 225 million tonnes last  year. It's winter. I know that it doesn't look like it in London today. But it's winter in China, so the old question is  going to be coming out of winter, are some of the smaller mines in China are going to restart and so on and so  forth. So it would be – I'm not saying it's the base case, but it's easy to see a scenario, you have – if you start from  a baseline of 245 million tonnes last year, potentially increasing by 25 million tonnes this year and so on and so  forth. So that's one element.

texts.speaker: Jakob Stausholm
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: That's your job and your models. But the guidance I can provide you. I mean, you've got your production guidance  and you can see right now, you look at last year, we had 19% return on capital employed. We're coming in with a  very strong business. And yes, right now, we have seen a hike in the iron ore price. But who knows how long time  that will carry through and that's where you have to make some assumptions. But, obviously, looking at last year,  from a strong point, take away the divestments that you kind of deal with on a more kind of ad hoc basis. But the  underlying business is strong. We're coming strong into the year with the increased prices from iron ore. And then  I think you'll have to do the exact math yourself.

texts.speaker: Hayden Bairstow
texts.profession: Analyst, Macquarie Securities (Australia) Ltd.
texts.text: Yes. Thanks, JS. Just a question on further asset sales, I mean, you had the climate change document you put  out, that was pretty interesting. But with OT, obviously, being powered by coal, I mean do you feel that the  portfolio needs further adjustment? Does that comes online with a coal-fired power station or are you sort of  happy with the bulk of where you sit now on – particularly on with those carbon emissions out of IOC and Pacific  Aluminium? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rio Tinto Plc
texts.text: Then, on the question on the OT and the power station, a couple of points, today, we're buying the electricity from  China in Mongolia, which is coal-fired power, okay? That's what it is about. So, that's the first element. The  second element is when the investment agreement was put in place in 2009 is one of the clause is about, and you  can understand from a government standpoint is when you're sitting on massive coal field to have a fire power  station in [ph] one (00:54:05) country, remember, the last fire power station that was built in Mongolia was from  memory, 50 years ago, okay, by the Russians at that time. So, you can understand that if you are in this country  and you really want to uplift 3 million people out of poverty, at some point in time, you want to have a coal-fired  power station in contract. However, what the team is looking at, and the government is supportive, is to have  ideally a hybrid solution, where we have an element of coal fire in order to deliver very base load, very low cost  source of power. Remember, the underground is we're going to put people 1,000 meter underground, all right?  And I want to be able to extract those people if there were to be any issues whatsoever.

texts.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Jacques
