Latin America is predominantly an oil and gas market for us and  continues to be challenging.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Turning now to the divisions. Controls performed well in the period. Order intake was up 18.7% or 6.3% on an  OCC basis. Improvements in the water, power and industrial markets and upstream oil and gas drove a 14.1%  increase in revenue or 2.2% OCC. Underlying gross margins have improved 60 basis points, reflecting material  cost savings initiatives. At an adjusted operating profit level, OCC margins were 30 basis points lower as the  inflationary increases in staff costs offset the gross margin improvement.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Asia grew due to investment in downstream in China and growth in the power market. North America and the  Middle East were positive due to upstream oil and gas. Europe was more mixed, with strength in industrial offset  by lower oil and gas sales, and Latin America remained challenging.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: There is growing interest in our CK product range for the power and water markets, which will support our focus  on this growing area. We also see good opportunities for Controls products in the growing HVAC and industrial  markets

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Fluid Systems is the division with the highest proportion of oil and gas sales and has seen order intake up 17.8%  or 5.3% on an OCC basis, as activity has increased primarily in upstream oil and gas in the Middle East, Africa  and Eastern Europe. Reported revenue increased 10.2%, but on an OCC basis decreased by 1.8% as the  improvement in order intake takes time to flow through to revenue.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: The power and industrial markets made modest progress with the biggest growth in water. The Americas and  Europe both grew with Asia and Latin America up as well. We continue to leverage the Mastergear additions t o  our portfolio both through strengthening existing relationships with customers and developing relationships with  new valve makers. Our global brand with local support is becoming increasingly important to customers as our  innovative solutions such monitoring fugitive emissions and gathering information on how the valve is operating.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: We saw a double-digit growth across the water, power and industrial markets. Asia and North America was strong  and accounted for just under 50% of Instruments sales in the period. Each of the Instruments businesses  continue to expand their product ranges and new products – with new products and variants of existing products  across the wide range of end markets that Instruments sells in to.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: We're seeing several common trends across the divisions. The North American and Middle East regions are  active across each division, particularly in upstream oil and gas where positive sentiment in the U.S. and activity  in the Middle East has provided some support for new onshore drilling activity.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: We're starting to see stabilization across the oil and gas market. Midstream oil and gas is still expected to exhibit  modest growth in the medium term, mostly arising from incremental investments in new gas pipelines and  territories such as Eastern Europe and Asia.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Downstream activity will be driven by emerging markets, low raw material costs, and new environmental  legislation such as the demand for lower sulfur content. The need to cut the cost of production is driving a  requirement for increased reliability and plant efficiency. The ability to understand how equipment in the plant is  performing is critical to this. Asset management and data analysis provide the customer with insights to the  performance of the plant and can help to reduce unplanned shutdowns. There is a trend to extend the life of  plants wherever possible and an improved understanding of plant performance facilitates this.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: The board has ambition to return in time to the mid- to high-single digit growth enjoyed prior to the oil and gas  downturn, and to the higher margins associated with that. And it seeks to deliver that growth without an ex pressed  reliance on a material upturn in capital spend in the oil and gas market.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Now, this ambition requires a fresh perspective on our approach to our business. And such an approach is likely  to include a material increase in the investments in our new product development activity. And a significant  expansion of our service activity. Both represent fertile territory for Rotork with oil and gas customers, for  example, demanding much greater innovation from their supply chain as they seek to regroup around the new  $50 a barrel norm.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: I guess in terms of the new Bath site, it's got a program that sees us moving in some point towards the back end  of next year. So, it doesn't really, fully get picked up in terms of operating costs until 2019 I suppose. But the site  is housing the same number of people that we currently have in Bath, the facility itself will be more energy  efficient and modern. But whether that has any significant impact on the operating cost I think is – it will be  marginal. Clearly, there will be a cost of moving and transfer, but that's a quantifiable number we can give you by  the time [indiscernible] (27:46) takes place.

texts.speaker: Mark Davies Jones
texts.profession: Analyst, Stifel Nicolaus Europe Ltd.
texts.text: Hi. It's Mark Davies Jones from Stifel. Can I ask a question about visibility? You say you've got reasonable  visibility. Clearly, orders have trended a bit better, but one thing we're hearing a lot in terms of the oil and gas  contracting market is delays, push-outs, differences in timing relative to earlier expectation.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Yeah. I think we've always talked about projects slippage both in terms of order receipt and in terms of delivery.  And that's always been a feature of all of the projects we work on. Not just the oil and gas ones and I don't think  anything has particularly changed. I suppose as we went through some of the more recent years, we're talking  about extended delays and extended slippage.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: There's a lot of very impressive things about those businesses, as well as things we can improve upon, but from  my experience in the oil and gas sector and other businesses, private equity business, this business has done a  phenomenal job particularly on the Controls side and defending its pricing practices in the market, which is a  measure of just how well established the brand is and how many applications are truly critical in nature. And I  think I could turn to other markets and other parts of this supply chain and I can point to 20% to 30% pricing  compression over the last two or three years. And they've done a terrific job here in defending that, which gives  you a lot of comfort around the quality of the brand and its standing.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: And it's quite interesting, as you think about how does the market deal with a new norm of $50 a barrel instead of  $100 a barrel. And one of the ways customers are dealing with it is to put enormous pressure on the supply chain  in terms of price compression, which is okay in the short term but is not sustainable longer term. The supply chain  will suffer hugely in that environment and it can't go on, which is why real innovation in the supply chain, finding  smarter ways of performing the same job for a lot less money is the crucial requirement for this sector and is  something that Rotork needs to invest a lot more heavily in. And we've got lots of ideas as to how we're going to  do that. Yeah, Andy.

texts.speaker: Andy Douglas
texts.profession: Analyst, Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: Secondly, in Controls, you talked about HVAC and industrial markets being more important. I think over the years,  we've also had water and waste water. Can you just double check and of course, confirm for us about how's the  similar margin profile to oil and gas? So we can just make sure that Controls margin doesn't come in a bit of  pressure.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Of course, if one spends that money and doesn't get the returns, you're not going to like the results very much.  But just to give you a sort of flavor for the sort of areas that you might be thinking about, I mean, again, if the  supply chain in oil and gas is to innovate and itself become profitable at $50 a barrel instead of just being clouted  on pricing and margins, it has to look at what's [ph] requirement. (34:57)

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: So, if you think about energy consumption in a lot of oil and gas facilities, particularly shale plants, for example,  where they actually use a lot of the depleted, but when these shale plants get slightly older and the pressures  deplete, they're using a lot of that gas pressure to run compressors, to run the energy requirements of the site.  And they become uneconomic, unviable fairly quickly. If you could find a way of literally having a zero-power  actuation site using solar, using clever solenoid and actuated technologies, then you extend the useful life of  those plants for many, many years. This is an area that we're spending a lot of time on. We think about smart or  what I call power-to-weight ratios in the industry.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: So, for example, lots of equipment is designed around peak loading and excised around peak loading. Very often  that peak loading might only occur for 5% of the time. So there are smarter ways of looking at that, using the  accumulators, using reservoir technology, so that you can still meet peak needs by storing up energy over time,  but run everything else on much smaller scale, equipments and plant, a smarter way of taking cost out of the  business.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: So, by getting smarter about the supply chain, we can find the way, I am sure, of taking a much larger share of a  smaller capital equipment budget over years to come. And for people who say, well, surely you should be moving  away from oil and gas in this sort of environment given the lower growth. I'd say quite the contrary, there's some  serious opportunities here for us to extend our reach within oil and gas in a market that we know well where we've  got great branding and great positioning and we know how to get to the customers.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: So, that's just one example of how we might look at innovation. You talked about the water market. There's some  fantastic things going on in the water market. There's SmartWater, for example. And having sat on the board of a  public utility for a long time and being involved in water business in the U.S., it is remarkable how dumb so many  of our water networks are and how they could certainly benefit from much greater intelligence in the sector.  Things like, for example, soft-closing and soft-opening for valve.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: So many valves are straight on/off in our water maze. It creates huge hammer in the system, huge vibration in the  system, all the pipes vibrate and shatter over time, and a simple Rotork actuator on the top of these valves  providing soft-opening and soft-closing would change all of that. It would also give them proper intelligence about  what's going through the network, the quality of the water, and give them the opportunity to reroute water very  quickly in the event of leakages to ensure no interruption to supply.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Huge opportunities in water to upgrade and make a smarter network. Things like desalination. Huge parts of the  world don't have access to potable water. I say places like Africa, but I also mean places like California. Hey, you  know, what is happening around the treatment of brackish water and sea water. The big issue is always energy  cost. That is what makes desalination expensive, if you can find a way of reducing that energy costs and it opens  up huge opportunities.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: And things like Rotork actuators combined with solar power to ensure that you're optimizing the positioning of  solar power panels for maximum efficiency is enormous opportunities for us. Things like water reuse, I mean I  know nobody likes the idea of water reuse, but it's common and we're going to have to get our heads around it.  And the opportunities for Rotork actuators in these multiple recycling processes, where you need smart control  and close control are enormous.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: I think I've probably talked a little bit about R&D, HVAC and industrial markets. Are the margins lower in those  markets at the moment? Yes, they are. Do they need to be lower in the longer term? Well, maybe not. If we're  going up the value curve and we're getting into things like SmartWater, water reuse, solar power, then there's no  reason why we shouldn't extract proper value for money from that innovation.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: That whole piece will be part of the innovation review. I think it's a fabulous opportunity in our service business.  And when we talk about service business growing regularly, even through the downturn which is absolutely true,  and we talk about asset management within service, and again, the opportunity to go into say an LNG plant  where there might be as many as 500 or 600 Rotork actuators on the plant and say, look, 30% of those are  critical, you need to make sure that those 30% of those 600 actuators never fail. And the ability to put in smart  feedback systems that enable you to deploy predictive maintenance and ensure that those don't fail and sell a  guarantee, and a contract that guarantees uptime against those critical application is a very powerful value  proposition. Our problem at the moment is we've probably got less than 5% of the available market currently sold  into those contract arrangements. It should be higher clearly.

texts.speaker: Jack O'Brien
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: Good morning. It's Jack O'Brien from Goldman Sachs. I just want to delve into the downstream oil and gas portion  a little more deeply. So, firstly, just interested in what you're seeing by region and the sort of sequential run rates  in terms of order intake.

texts.speaker: Jack O'Brien
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: Secondly, just whether you've got the scale within downstream oil and gas in this new sort of $40 to $50 oil  environment and whether there's been any ramifications from the Emerson and Pentair tie-up.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: If we take it on an OCC basis, then I don't think there was – downstream was across the board fractionally lower.  So, it's relatively consistent in that at least.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: In terms of scale and where we are and where the opportunities are coming and can we capitalize on the  emerging market ones, and then certainly we are well spread in terms of sales network and in terms of  manufacturing footprint to a degree in the emerging markets through India, through China which are two of the  areas where we are expecting there to be downstream oil and gas investment. And, indeed, China is an area that  we are seeing projects coming through which haven't yet impacted revenue but would be expected to as we go  forward. So, the – but – sorry, you're going to add?

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: And also, if you think of what's happening in terms of lower sulfur levels, for example, and the requirements to  reduce sulfur content from 3.5% to 0.5%, that has some pretty serious implications for capital investment in  refineries. In some refineries, it will be more expensive to adapt to those lower sulfur obligations than the viability  of the refinery itself. It might actually accelerate the closure of one or two refineries, but it will provide  opportunities for new expansion and new capacity in emerging markets. So, it's hardly a – refinery and  downstream is hardly a dull sector at the moment. There's a lot going on.

texts.speaker: Jonathan Hurn
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG
texts.text: And second one was just coming back to – or not coming back, but just on water. Obviously, you saw good order  intake in that. How much of that is a – or how much of it is market driven? And how much of it do you feel that  you're taking market share with your new water product? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: In terms of water intake and where that is and how that's driving it, one of the big improvements in water was in  China in the first half. So, that was one of the markets where we saw an improvement in the water market, and I  think that is about taking some degree of share. And also, obviously, we've got the CK product which is a water- targeted product, which is still gathering momentum. It's a slow process as some of these product launches often  are. But I think those are the two items that are connected, but not always overlapping. Some of the expansion in  China in water is around Gears, not just around electric actuators.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: In terms of the water market, more generally, it's a very exciting market right now. And there's not many markets  that are exhibiting 4% to 6% compound annual growth over probably the next decade or so. And that's why  there's a lot of interest in the water market right now, and there's a lot of investments in it. So, it's a good space for  Rotork to focus its attention.

texts.speaker: Stephen Swanton
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Just interested to know what will happen there. And the second question is a little more long winded, but it's  probably quite easy for anyone, us or investors to think that change is needed because your sales have fallen,  margins have fallen, and the oil price gone from $100 down to $50. But this was 2014, and hypothetically the oil  price were to stay at $100, is it your view that Rotork could have run into difficulties from a growth or market share  perspective or indeed from a margin perspective due to a complex cost base and the inflationary pressures from  that, they would eventually run into trouble if they stayed on kind of slower strategy as you alluded to?

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: In respect to what would have happened to Rotork had it still be in a $100 a barrel, and had the supply chain  continue to enjoy what frankly was a fairly complacent approach to cost control, particularly in the oil and gas  industry, well, what can I say? I can say, now looking at 20% margins and all the upside opportunities that one  can see, it's a great place to start. I'm used to starting at 5% or 6%. So, starting at 20% is a great place to start. I  can say that if we drive some revenue increase in this business, it drops to the bottom line beautifully, particularly  in Controls, at 40% to 50% to the bottom line. So, one can see how those margins can move upwards.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: I accept there may not be the same burning platform for change when you're $100 a barrel and 25% margins, of  course not. I mean, maybe the change might not have happened under that scenario. But the whole supply chain  has been woken up and said, look, you have to adapt and you have to find a way of innovating around this new  norm.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: ...in terms of the Instruments' margins, Bifold is part of the story there as well. In terms of product mix within  Bifold, we've seen a switch of products within that business from their traditional sort of hydraulic areas which is  often subsea or subsea related that has actually declined further this year. So, there's been a mix issue there.  There's also been some elements of material cost pressure on some particular areas in the Far East in YTC.  Those are the two biggest drivers really around that decline.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: [ph] in these (01:13:00) systems, which is one of their big areas. So, all the electro-hydraulics and things like that  would typically be emergency shutdown. CPs, GPs, the big pneumatic hydraulics.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Yeah. Well, oil and gas is interesting. I don't expect $50 a barrel, if it is that, of course, it'll be $100 next year when  you're talking to me. But I mean, I don't expect it to show 5%, 6% compound annual growth rate. I expect it to be  a GDP or there or thereabout – maybe slightly lower than GDP growth end market. But that belies the key point  which is the supply chain requirement to innovate and enable the whole industry, not just the oil and gas majors,  but the whole supply chain to make handsome returns in that environment. And that's where I will see great  opportunity for more innovation and a bigger share of a smaller wallet, if you like, over time.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: So, I think we need to be prudent and reasonable about where we think oil and gas markets are going, but not  despondent about it. There're plenty of opportunities.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: I think water, as we've said, is an attractive market. I can see 4% to 6% compound annual growth rate in that  water market. We're not as big in water as we'd like to be and we've got to change that, but I can see it.
