texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Despite continued difficult trading conditions in the oil and gas market in the second half, the results we are  delivering today are in line with the revised guidance we provided in September. We acted swiftly to mitigate the  challenging environment with an accelerated cost management program, we announced this at the half year  results in August, and it has delivered greater than anticipated annualized savings. Continued cost management  will remain a key focus in 2016 and we are taking further actions as regards material, overhead, and  manufacturing cost, which I'll come on to later in my section.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Executive Director & Group Director-Finance
texts.text: Thank you, Peter. As you can see from the slide, all key measures were impacted by deteriorating oil and gas  market conditions. Order intake of £526 million was 11.7% lower than the prior year. On an organic constant  currency basis or OCC, order intake was 15.2% lower, with the second half 17.7% lower than the second half of  2014. Order intake in the fourth quarter was 3.2% higher than the third quarter on an OCC basis.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Executive Director & Group Director-Finance
texts.text: Order intake for Gears was marginally higher than the comparative period, 0.4% up on an OCC basis. H2 was 2%  higher than H1, but on an OCC basis H2 was 2.6% lower. Revenue was also lower in the second half compared  with the first half, 3.3% down as reported or 7.8% lower on an OCC basis. For the year as a whole, revenue grew  just over 1% with the currency headwind, a very similar value to the contribution from Roto Hammer.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Executive Director & Group Director-Finance
texts.text: Instruments results are heavily influenced by acquisitions with the full year contribution from YTC and Midland  for the first time in 2015, as well as the M&M, Bifold and Eltav acquisitions during the year. Whilst reported order  intake is 43% higher, on an OCC basis, it declined 9.1% as some of the slowdown experienced by Fluid Systems  impacted Instruments customers. The revenue comparison is similar with the reported 46.5% increase reversing  on an OCC basis to a 5.8% reduction. The reduction in revenue resulted in a 50 basis point reduction in gross  margin on an OCC basis, with the reduction increasing to 250 basis points with the addition of the acquisitions.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: During 2015, the oil and gas market continued to be impacted by the weakness in the oil price with all sectors;  upstream, midstream and downstream being affected. Oil and gas contribution as a percentage of t otal revenue  declined in the period to 53%, down from 57%, with midstream and downstream declining as a percentage of  revenue, and upstream remaining at 15% of revenue despite the absolute reduction in the oil and gas sector.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Total revenue in the power market was also down. Our strategy, as we've said many times, is to have a diverse  product portfolio and end market focus. And this provided resilience as we saw a positive progress in the global  industrial and mining and water end user market.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Looking in more detail at the divisions, Controls had a difficult year, with sales to the oil and gas markets being  the most heavily impacted with reduced revenue across upstream, midstream and downstream applications. The   division's market exposure to oil and gas reduced to 48%.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Despite the challenging market conditions, North America continued to grow across most end user markets,  including oil and gas. The Middle East also saw growth in the oil and gas sector and also p ower. The gains in these  markets were not sufficient to offset the reduction in revenue in Asia, which remains the largest market for the  Controls division, and where all end user markets, apart from water, showed a decline.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Centork is the new actuator for the water, power and industrial markets. The final variants of this product range  are being launched in the first half of 2016, which will enable Controls to better leverage direct valve maker  business.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Fluid Systems is the Rotork division with the largest exposure to oil and gas. However, the division's exposure to  this end market reduced once again in 2015 with revenue down from 72% to 68% with all segments experiencing a  reduction. Oil and gas did, though, continue to provide opportunity for the division in some areas. For example,  North America saw a modest growth. Within other end markets, results were mixed. Industrial market grew the  fastest and became the second largest market for Fluid Systems, and most of this increase came from Western  Europe.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: The nuclear, marine, power, LNG and HVAC end markets are all potential sources of market expansion and  growth in 2016. Products like the SI3 take time to gain traction in the market, but we expect to see positive  momentum in the second half of the year. There is a significant opportunity for Fluid Systems to collaborate with  the Instruments division to deliver solutions for our customers. And Fluid Systems will start to see the benefit of  our new world-class manufacturing facility in Lucca as production ramps up and as the offices are completed in  the second quarter.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Now, turning to Gears. Western Europe was the division's best-performing region and remains its largest end  destination market representing 31% of sales, up from 28% in the previous year. In terms of end markets, Gears  saw growth in power, industrial and water markets. Oil and gas remained the division's largest end market, but  reduced from 57% to 50% of sales. The Roto Hammer acquisition in September adds a new product line to the  Gears product range and increases its presence in the important U.S. market.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: In August, we completed the acquisition of Bifold for up to £125 million. This is the largest acquisition completed  by Rotork to-date. Bifold was established more than 100 years ago and has operations in Manchester and Taunton  in the UK. It manufactures pneumatic and hydraulic instrument valves for the oil and gas industry and  wider  industrial markets with expertise in a number of niche sectors such as subsea and wellhead control systems.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: The difficult short-term conditions in the oil and gas market are likely to remain for some time. However, we  believe the longer-term trends remain intact in all our markets. The IEA, for instance, still forecasts oil demand to  grow at an annual average growth rate of 1.2% from 2015 to 2020. This is only 0.5 percentage point below the  previous comparable time period from 2009 to 2015. Global gas demand is also projected to grow 2% per year on  average from 2014 to 2020, slower than the 2.3% averaged over the previous 10 years.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Total CapEx on water, wastewater and desalination is forecast to grow by 6% from 2015 to 2019. As we know,  growth will be driven by global megatrends such as urbanization, the growing global population and emerging  market growth. These will drive the long-term demand for new infrastructure. However, aging infrastructure is  also likely to drive further investment.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: As well as external drivers, we continue to review our own project tracking system. This should only be seen as an  approximate leading indicator, as it reflects projects that are visible to our sales organization, and does not try to  anticipate the date of order. As you can see, during the period, project activity was down in oil and gas and power,  up in water and steady in industrial. Activity levels remain steady in the Americas, but was down in other regions.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Chairman
texts.text: Thank you.  Mark Davies Jones  Stifel Nicolaus Europe Ltd.  Q  Hello. Mark Davies Jones at Stifel. Could you talk a little bit about your upstream oil and gas  business, which  seems to stay relatively stable as a proportion of revenue, which I guess is a surprise, given that that's where the  CapEx cuts would be most fierce? Is there any of that which is timing-related in terms of when that impact comes  through to you, or is there anything else that explains that?

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: A couple of things that explain that. I think the acquisition of Bifold in the end of year is more upstream related to  that, supports that and adds to that. But in North America, we are still seeing – even in shale and those areas,  we're still seeing some continued investment in some of the fields although not at the same level, but that work is  ongoing. And then you've got your maintenance and your replacement activity work that is ongoing.

texts.speaker: Jonathan P. Hurn
texts.profession: Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And thirdly, just in terms of the actual order book, can you just give us a feel of the mix there, where we are? Are  we seeing more orders within the order book towards water, for example? That would be helpful. Thanks.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: But, obviously, there is sometimes movement when it's in the order book because we received it as order intake, so  it's sitting in our order book, there are sometimes when there is delays in project. So, that's normal anyway.  Projects, when you're building a refinery or you're building a tank farm or a power station, there often can be  delays in a project. And so, that would push deliveries out.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: But you also need to explain to the customers the importance of your product as well and not lose sight of what is  the differentiator between us and the competition. Because our products are still mission critical. If they don't  work, the impact to the customer, whether it's a water authority or it's an oil company, can be significant in terms  of penalties. And so quality, on-time delivery, local service, all that support, innovation, that is really still key and  we need to keep that in focus. So I think we're doing very well in managing the pricing pressure that we are seeing  at the moment. But it is there and we have to keep on within focus.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: And in terms of RFS in momentum, I think, there's a couple of point there. One, we can see quite a few projects  around. I mean, RFS would see the benefit of larger projects more than most, and there are still a number of large  oil and gas projects around the world that are happening and still planning to happen. There are a number of  pipelines especially gas pipelines, LNG still active. There are certain countries that are quite still very focused on  production and if you look at like Saudi and places like Iran.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So there are opportunities. We are seeing those opportunities and we see the positive momentum in this. But you  still have to win it and it's a competitive landscape. So we see that positive opportunity. We're well placed on a  number of projects. We are well placed and we do well with LNG projects. We won a number that we announced  last year, some of the LNG projects in the Gulf Coast region in America. America was very active in LNG. And for  some of those, we haven't started delivering yet. That will be delivered in the second half of the year and that will  help the results and help the positive movement.

texts.speaker: Chris R. Dyett
texts.profession: Investec Bank Plc (Broker)
texts.text: And you're confident your team understands that when a big oil company cut CapEx by 25%, you know it's quite  the same pattern and therefore you take them out of the system.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Y es. I'd like to think that it was completely accurate, Chris, but I would imagine there'll be one or two areas within  that. But generally, yes is the answer. That's what we're focused on, that's what we're following. But it's not just oil  and gas and it's not just projects, even some of the projects will be delayed, so they'll announce delays, so that is  not happening at the moment. So there is a time when that might still remain in our project tracking, because it's  not been cancelled. It's not completely dead, but it's not happening this year, they might stay back and it might be  happening in the future that would remain in our numbers, but – even if we haven't got the date when it's going to  happen. So that's why that you got to take it, there is some sort of safety warning on the indication.

texts.speaker: Chris R. Dyett
texts.profession: Investec Bank Plc (Broker)
texts.text: Sure. Here comes the third tricky question. Obviously, you've made assumptions in your planning around what  2016 is going to look like. Y ou obviously made cost decisions and how much you can save. On that basis, can y ou  give us a flavor on what you think 2016 looks like, based on those cost saving assumptions?

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Inventory reduction initiatives are ongoing and on an OCC basis, inventory is 15.8% lower than the start of the  year, and now represents 14.6% of sales compared with 16% last year-end. Trade receivables are 5.7% lower on  an OCC basis. And debtor days have reduced by 1 to 61 days. The EU referendum result and its impact on bond  yields has affected the pension scheme deficit, which has risen to £58.5 million, a funding level of 75%.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: At an adjusted operating profit level, lower volumes have a greater impact, and OCC margins are 60 basis points  lower despite a 2.5% reduction in the absolute value of overheads. Lower activity in midstream and downstream  saw total sales from oil and gas reduced from 48% to 45% of the division sales. Water and waste water sales  grew and increased as a share of the division sales to 18%, with the U.S. the largest contributor to this.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Sales in Power declined 8% in constant currency terms and reduced to 21% to the division sales. Whilst the  Americas saw a positive water market, this was more than offset by the decline in oil and gas. The Far East,  where power and oil and gas are the most significant end markets, also saw lower revenue compared with 2015.  The Middle East grew supported by a positive oil and gas market with Europe, Africa, and Southeast Asia also  making progress.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: The breakdown of sales by end market is remarkably consistent between 2015 and 2016. Oil and gas has  increased by 1% to 69% with the delivery of the LNG projects in the year increasing midstream, slightly more than  the decline in upstream and downstream. Midstream was the only end market in Fluid Systems which saw growth  in constant currency terms.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: On an OCC basis, oil and gas would have reduced from 35% to 34% of the division sales. M&M has increased  the value of sales to the industrial markets and this remains 17% of sales. Each of the Instruments businesses  continues to expand their product ranges with new products and variants of existing products, and many have  been launched during the year across the wide range of end markets that Instruments sells into.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Right. As in previous years, I've tried to summarize the business on a couple of slides. All of these slides are on  an as-reported basis. All of the divisions except RFS grew with RFS impacted by the continued slow down in the  oil and gas market, which accounts for 52% of Group revenue.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Actually, this can be seen in the chart in the bottom right, all of the markets with the exception of other were up on  the prior year. Oil and gas was lower for Controls and RFS, but Gears saw an increase in its oil and gas business.  Instruments benefited from the acquisition of Bifold. And as most of you are aware, it's predominantly focused on  the oil and gas market, and especially the upstream sector. This helped to show growth overall in the oil and gas  market.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Water was actually up in every division, except RFS. And they saw results flat year on year in this particular end- market. Power was flat, too, down in each division, with only Instruments showing growth and supporting the  overall result. Controls performed well in the industrial sector and Instruments also grew.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: In terms of geography, we had positive performances in North America, Europe, and the Middle East. North  America saw positive activity in the midstream oil and gas area, water and power markets. Europe was up in the  oil and gas and industrial markets, but benefited from acquisitions. As part of our strategy, we have continued to  strengthen our presence in the Middle East, and this is having a positive impact with all end-markets up in the  region. Asia was down and is related to oil and gas activity with water, power, and industrial, all higher than the  prior year.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: If we look at our main markets to see the near-term drivers, upstream oil and gas, the recent OPEC agreement,  and positive sentiment in the U.S.A. has provided some support for new onshore drilling activity and this brings  with it an element of market stabilization. Our own product development and recent acquisition also provides  support to this market.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Midstream oil and gas is still expected to grow with new pipelines planned. However, the market still believes that  all pipelines will be slow with growth coming from gas pipelines. Downstream activity will be driven by emerging  market and low raw material cost, although this market is not anticipated to be growing strongly in 2017.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Automation and control in water is anticipated to grow at a rate of 7% compound annual growth rate until 2020. 1  in 10 people still lack access to clean water, and 1 in 3 lack access to improved sanitation. In power, there is a  change going on in power with renewables growing fast with investment in clean coal, gas, and nuclear. Despite  this, there is still over 1 billion people with no access to electricity. Industrial is becoming an important market for  us, and industrial automation is increasing as we see opportunities in commercial vehicles and life sciences and  process control.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: If we now look by division, we see the trend for controls is that we are seeing more project activity. However, the  size of orders are smaller, and this relates to some extent to the fact that we are seeing more water projects that  are often smaller in size than oil and gas opportunities, especially in downstream. China and the Middle East are  seeing positive activity.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: The development of our CK brand for the power and water markets will support our focus in this growing area.  Broadening or extending our product ranges, such as the IQ3 and IQT3, remains a key part of our strategy, and  often provides us with an improved competitive offer for our customers. And developing our sales channels and  strengthening our local presence is another important part of developing these relationships, providing us with the  ability to increase our aftermarket service support.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: For Rotork Fluid Systems, the oil and gas market has seen some stabilization. But there remains uncertainty  around key projects. However, these is a market trend for increased reliability and plant efficiency driving our  customers purchasing decisions, with the Middle East and North America, an important market for us.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: A stable oil and gas sector will bring confidence back to the market and encourage further investment. We're  starting to see signs of this now, but it's still too early to say when or if the market will return to the previous levels.  But we are monitoring this closely. For this reason, we continue to broaden our market exposure for our range of  pneumatic and hydraulic actuators. Markets, such as marine and HVAC, provide those opportunities.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Gears continue to provide the valve industry with a competitive solution for their gearbox needs in a growing  regulatory market, meaning that a customer looking for a global brand with the support and necessary approvals  is becoming more important in this area. As in Controls, Gears are seen in active water and in industrial process  market, with the U.S.A., China, and Europe, important geographies for us.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Instruments now serves the widest variety of end markets out of all of the divisions. And so, the trends in each of  them vary a lot. But there is a general increase in automation, a drive for lower energy use and a general  reduction in the environmental impact of plants. The developing brand and broad product portfolio provides a  strong platform, but we need to continue to build out by expanding the product range further and developing the  sales channel for the division, including further integration and synergy with the Rotork organization. The  acquisition of Bifold provides a catalyst for a number of new product development, and the technology  collaboration across Rotork Instruments and the Rotork Group.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: We anticipate that any near-term growth in energy markets will remain modest. Our focus will remain on providing  our customers with innovative, high-quality products and services, reducing their cost of ownership and improving  plant efficiency. Cost management will remain a priority in the current year as we look to mitigate any inflationary  pressure through our highly flexible operating base.

texts.speaker: Alexander Virgo
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: Thanks. Morning, everybody. Alex Virgo, Bank of America Merrill Lynch. Peter, wonder if you could elaborate a  little bit on your pricing and what you're seeing in terms of sequential development, particularly what you're seeing  in the oil and gas end markets. And I wonder if you wouldn't mind just quantifying the organic constant currency  decline in oil and gas for us in terms of orders and revenue. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: And the other one was organic constant currency for oil and gas. So basically, on an organic basis upstream  would've shown still some growth, and also midstream. It was downstream that was down overall. So that  would've – organically, would've shown oil and gas slightly down on the prior year, but upstream was up, but that  really was the benefit of Bifold, the acquisition and so on helping that.

texts.speaker: Mark Davies Jones
texts.profession: Analyst, Stifel Nicolaus Europe Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you. Mark Davies Jones from Stifel. One little one and one broader one. The small one, you've mentioned  on Fluid Systems that there was some LNG business in there driving some strength in the midstream. Is that  related to contracts from sometime back and is that completing as a source of strength or is that one area where  we could see some incremental weakness in 2017?

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: So on the LNG, yeah, you're right. These are projects that we'd won sort of 2014 and 2015, actually, that we're  working out, out of the order book. So we're pretty much past that now, so – and in 2016. So there is a little bit  left, but actually we are seeing some weakness in the LNG area. So that will be something that is a – one of those  things that we have to find a way of finding other business to fill that little hole that is there. And so that's taking  into account – into our thinking. And so we know where we are with that.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: There are other things that are positively impacting there, that's helping. So LNG will be down. We're anticipating  that in this year. And in terms of downstream MRO, we are seeing more activity levels in terms of our servicing  capabilities, customers asking us for repair. So that's starting to see an increase, which is why we've been  increasing our service personnel or part of the reason we've been increasing that. And we see that will continue.  Not enough, I don't think, to offset the downstream activity levels being down in that level, but it will be supportive.

texts.speaker: David Larkam
texts.profession: Analyst, Numis Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Dave Larkam, Numis. Just look at the first half with the order book where it is, down 13% organic, does that mean  the first half organic is likely to be a little bit softer? And then, secondly, can you talk about water? It sounds like  that was pretty good in the year, particularly sort of North America. Is there a trend going on there that we should  know about? Is there a lot more investment coming through? Any programs?

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: On the water front, I'll just take that first. Most of you, I think I've sat in lots of different meetings over the years  talking about the opportunity of water. And actually, I'm not saying that we've turned that corner, but we – other  people are talking about water as well now. So, it's not just me. So, we're spreading the love. And so, we are  starting to see some activity levels in water. And I think we've now got product portfolio that will allow us to take  advantage of some of that activity in water.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: So, it's a slower burn in terms of – because of often it's government investment that is required for water  investment. So, it does take a little bit longer. But activity levels are improving. So, I think water will be – will  continue to be an important market for us and a growing market for us. And as I said, there are still a lot of people  without access to clean water and sanitation. So, there is a demand definitely for that.

texts.speaker: Jack O'Brien
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: Morning. It's Jack O'Brien from Goldman Sachs. First question is as some of the non-oil and gas sort of  exposures and components grow, should we think about an impact on the sustainable group margin, i.e., is there  lower margins there? Secondly, there's been some consolidation in the sector, notably sort of Emerson-Pentair.  Are there opportunities there or – and any threats? And third point is China, obviously an important market for  you. I think 12 months ago, everyone was thinking that there could be a hard landing perhaps in 2016. It didn't  really come through. But could you just sort of point to what you're seeing in that significant market?

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: And China, we've had different things going on, different market activities in China. There's positives and  negatives going on. So, we started to see a positive trend in all industries. There is some question mark on power  in China at the moment, which is a recent sort of announcement that came out, where there's some concern on  some of the – I was going to say the dirty power stations and closing them down or not going ahead with some  projects. So, that is working its way through.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: However, on the other side, they'll be doing more clean because they still have need of more power-generating  capacity. So, they'll be looking at clean fuels and other things to offset that. So, it's just a mixing, or the  uncertainty will maybe delay some projects that we were anticipating or things may change. But overall, China  seemed a more active market and – than a year ago.

texts.speaker: Andrew J. Wilson
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: Thanks. It's Andy Wilson from JPMorgan. Just a few, hopefully, quick ones. Just a question on the order books,  following up I think on David's question, because you had – presumably you don't have these big LNG sort of  long-dated projects in there, can we expect the order book to be a bit more the kind of standard sort of three to  six-month delivery profile in terms of looking forward, and therefore it's not that we've got orders which are going  to come through in kind of late 2018 or is it?

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Yeah. I think there are – some of that will be seen. But I think actually, you've got other things that come in to  order books. So, I'm hoping this year, we'll have a bit more nuclear business that will come into the order book, for  instance. And that is likely to be longer in the order book than LNG. So, the benefit of having a broad end market  is that you get these lumps of different things going on.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: And normally, there's always a different lump happening at different times. So, actually, the profile will remain  fairly similar, but it will be for something completely different reason. And so, at the moment, what I would say is  LNG was a big lump that we have to replace. But there are other things that may replace that, and we can see on  the horizon that could do that job. So...

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: And Project Energise, yeah, that is – it is an important project, is Project Energise because – actually, it's a  competitive world out there. And what we're trying to do is make sure that everything that we do, we're getting  advantage of that. So it's our self-help program to increase those volumes. As I've said a few times, we've got  these margin pressures, but it's volume who's going to drive it.

texts.speaker: Wasi Rizvi
texts.profession: Analyst, RBC Europe Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Hi. It's Wasi Rizvi from RBC. Just a couple left for me. Just starting – just turning down onto the mix question. We  think about Controls specifically. That's one where you're flagging that water is going quite well and might be quite  good in the next year. So do we need to think differently about drop thorough in a scenario of modest growth in  Controls specifically, water with sort of cost pressures and inflation?

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Certainly, in terms of the different end markets and their different margin points, yes, we've talked about before  that there is potentially a headwind if the business were to shift dramatically to water. But as ever, project  businesses, there is good projects and bad projects within – margin-wise within any of the end markets. So it's  more like to be a marginal headwind than a tailwind, a shift towards water.

texts.speaker: Wasi Rizvi
texts.profession: Analyst, RBC Europe Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: All right. Okay. And then, just putting together what you've said, I mean, if I look at your outlook, it talks about  modest growth, but then specifically on your energy markets. And then when I think about what you've said about  water and industrial, sounded like they're a bit better. So I mean, would it be fair to say that the overall Group  picture is perhaps a little bit better than you might read just from reading the outlook? I mean, what that means in  numbers, I guess, is a separate discussion, but modest versus a bit better than modest. But is that a fair  conclusion?

texts.speaker: Wasi Rizvi
texts.profession: Analyst, RBC Europe Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: That'd be a specific [ph] reference to energy, haven't you, (01:01:00) and then the rest of the portion does seem  to be a bit better.

texts.speaker: Robert J. Davies
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: The second one is just around pricing. And pricing by sort of vertical, can you give us some, kind of more color of  what you're seeing in the different sort of water versus industrial versus oil and gas dynamics of pricing? And  then, finally, just around what customers are saying by sub-segment of oil and gas or their CapEx outlook for  2017? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: It's not necessarily our product that we're giving the information on because this could be to do with the valve. The  valve needs to be maintained, which often these things do need to be done. Or it could be that they can see that  there is a leak in the pipe or something like that. So, that's having an impact. So, the pressures drop or – and  they're taking that information. So, it's information that will help the customer be more efficient with their plant and  ultimately save them money is what we're trying to get to. So, we are working with the customer on that basis. I  think the – what we're seeing – was it kind of the pricing pressures in water and industrial and that sort of thing.

texts.speaker: Peter I. France
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: So, I think in pricing, we see more activity in industrial. So, it's a very competitive marketplace, as is water. So,  we're not seeing anything different really within those markets. They are competitive markets and remain so. So, I  don't think anything's really changing there. And then, the CapEx outlook into oil and gas subsectors, I think what  we're anticipating at the moment is upstream to be better; midstream, patchy; and downstream, potentially still  less active than we would like is a kind of – based on the information from all of the oil companies that we've  analyzed and looked at so far as a rough guide.  Wasi Rizvi  Analyst, RBC Europe Ltd. (Broker)  Q  Great. Thanks.

file: RORL - Q4 2017 Earnings Call 6March2018 445 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 06-Mar-18.pdf

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Back in August, we announced a change in the leadership for the business and an ambition to return Rotork to  previous levels of growth and margins, irrespective of any cyclical recovery in oil and gas markets.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Now turning to the operational review. This slide summarizes the group's key markets and geographies. These  slides are on an as-reported basis. Revenue grew in each division and all end markets were up on the prior  period. Oil and gas was a lower percentage of group revenue, due to the faster growth in other end markets.  Upstream and downstream markets were positive but midstream was significantly lower than last year,  predominantly due to comparatively lower levels of LNG activity. Industrial was the fastest growing of the other  end markets with power the slowest, up 25% and 5% respectively.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: North America, Middle East and Africa, and Eastern Europe grew due to investment in upstream, whilst growth in  Europe was from industrial process. In Asia, the water market grew most, but other markets grew slower than  Controls as a whole.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: The CK range developed to support the water market grew particularly in China. We continue to see growth in  HVAC and industrial markets across most geographies, but particularly in North America and Europe.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Fluid Systems is still the division with the highest proportion of oil and gas sales, but it's seeing the share of sales  from these markets reduce in the year. Order intake increased more in Fluid Systems than any other division, up  11.7% on an OCC basis. Revenue decreased 2.8%, as the improvement in order intake takes time to flow  through to revenue. Underlying gross margins improved 100 basis points, as a slight improvement in the pricing  environment compared with 2016, and material cost savings more than offset any inflationary cost pressures.  Adjusted operating profit increased £2.8 million to £9 million for the year, a 6% margin, 150 basis points  improvement in the year.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Within the overall oil and gas market, the Middle East and Eastern Europe saw positive activity from upstream,  whilst the U.S. and Asia were impacted by lower midstream activity. This was a combination of pipeline projects  being generally smaller than last year and several LNG projects completing in 2016. Downstream in China and  India was positive, and we're looking to indigenize some of our core RFS products in both countries. Korea also  saw growth in downstream, but the Middle East declined.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: The water and industrial markets both grew, increasing their share of RFS sales. The growing presence of the  division in India and China is supporting a move to more low-cost sourcing, which together with value engineering  initiatives will help mitigate the continuing tough pricing environment and commodity cost pressures. During the  year, we continue to consolidate operations in Italy, relocating two businesses into the main RFS facility in Lucca  and ceased production in Germany.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Work continues to ensure the broader product range created with the Mastergear lines is fully adopted and being  sold wherever appropriate. New product ranges with greater connectivity and intelligence, such as the Fugitive  Emission Gearbox and Smart Position Indicator, are helping Gears to differentiate their products.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: We saw double-digit growth across the water, power and industrial markets. Asia and North America remain the  fastest-growing areas, and we are now more than 50% of Instruments sales. Each of the Instruments businesses  continued to expand their product ranges with new products and variants of existing products across a wide range  of end markets that Instruments sells into.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Thank you, Jonathan. Activity levels within the oil and gas markets in smaller to midsized projects are picking up  following the sharp downturn over the last two to three years. This reflects a return to more normal investment  patterns around maintenance and upgrades, and is most visible in our Controls division.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Larger project investments in oil and gas is still materially lower than historic levels and remains patchy, albeit  there are signs of increased quotation activity, as project viability improves on lower engineering costs. This is  most visible within the RFS division.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: The North American and Middle East regions are active, particularly in upstream oil and gas. We expect this to  continue throughout 2018. While we expect midstream oil and gas to remain flat in the short term, we see some  growth opportunities in the medium term, mostly arising from incremental investments in new gas pipelines in  territories such as Eastern Europe and Asia.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Downstream activity will be driven by emerging markets, low raw material costs and new environmental legislation  such as the demand for low sulfur content. We expect this sector to exhibit some growth in 2018.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Our analysis is focused on a number of significant market drivers impacting one or more of our end markets. In  broad terms, they relate to underlying changes in the drivers of market demand. The accelerating economic  pressures for cost reduction and the efficiency, the growing demand for real-time data and adoption of digital  automation, and the ever increasing impact of regulatory and environmental change.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: But I would not underestimate the opportunities arising from smart innovation, particularly in the oil and gas  sector. It will be all too easy to say, look, overall levels of oil and gas expenditure over the next 10 years are going  to be lower than over the last 10 years. That may be true, but the opportunity for innovation in that space as our  end customers look to try to get more efficient smarter solutions to bring down the break-even point are very  considerable. And furthermore, given that it's oil and gas, those applications tend to be mission-critical. They do  require higher added value technology, and that's where Rotork excels.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: So, it wouldn't surprise me if oil and gas remains by some measure our largest single market. It's around 50% of  our revenue today. It wouldn't surprise me if it was still around 50% of our revenue in five years' time.

texts.speaker: Mark Davies Jones
texts.profession: Analyst, Stifel Nicolaus Europe Ltd.
texts.text: Good. That sort of brings me onto the second question, which is the mix issue within margin. Obviously, one of  the issues for Rotork over the last few years is that you've moved away from – perhaps the extreme oil and gas  dependence and from Rotork Controls dominating revenues. The other segments, the other product lines and  divisions have not had the same margin structure. So, you don't think oil and gas will continue to decline or you do  think you can grow the basic profitability in the other business lines?

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Look, I think we've come through the very significant decline in oil and gas over the last two or three years. As we  said in the presentation, the smaller project activity particularly around maintenance and upgrades has returned to  what we would call the more normal buying patterns. And I think part of the revenue growth that you're going to  see in 2018 reflects just that. We've not seen an increase in a lot of the big ticket expenditure yet in oil and gas,  although I have to say there are signs of increased quotation activity.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: So, subsea, for example, which was a very important part of the Bifold product portfolio, obviously, had a pretty  tarried time over the last two or three years. But quotation activity in that space is increasing, that's yet to be  converted to orders, but most market commentators out there would talk quite positively about that in 2020 and  beyond. So, the important point to say about that is all of those end markets, LNGs and other ones require very  high added value, high-tech technology.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: They are in critical applications where the consequences of failure are very significant indeed, and that's where  we excel. So, it wouldn't to surprise you to know that a very significant chunk of the incremental R&D is going in to  those oil and gas areas in support of those drivers. So, the good news about it is that that is margin positive. The  mix margin impact of more investment in oil and gas in the critical areas we serve is a positive development for  the group.

texts.speaker: Michael Blogg
texts.profession: Analyst, Investec Bank Plc
texts.text: Could you tell us, please – sorry. It's Michael Blogg from Investec. Could you tell us please whether there's a big  drive towards value engineering, particularly in products designed for the oil and gas sector, and whether that's  having a deflationary impact on the revenue line in currency terms?

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Clearly, all of the end – oil and gas majors are working to try to reduce the breakeven point for any new  investment. So, they are looking for the whole supply chain to optimize their solutions. They don't particularly want  things oversized. They don't want things over complicated. And Rotork has an important role to play in that. And a  lot of the value engineering work we've don't over the last two or three years has been a feature of Rotork's  investments over the last two or three years, has been put in place in response to that.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: I don't see that going away, Michael. I think that is the part of the ongoing commitments of the business. And we  have got good quality value engineering team set up to do that. It's also an important piece of work in response to  commodity inflation which is around, so it won't have escaped you to see what's happening with steel prices,  aluminum prices over the last 18 months. They need to be offset and the value engineering work that we've done  has helped us to do that.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: In terms of M&A, I think unsurprisingly we've not been particularly active over the last six months or so. We said  that back in August that we were focusing on other things. It won't have escaped your notice that we're virtually  debt free now in Rotork. It's also true to say that a lot of the end market work that we've been doing in terms of  plotting the future direction for oil-and-gas and our other end markets is helping to shape a much more strategic  view of where we want to compete and where we don't want to compete. That's important not only from a new  product perspective and the money we're putting to that, it's also important from an M&A perspective.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Power, I think we've got a variety of sort of drivers within the power market obviously reflecting the different  sources of that power generation. I think obviously we talked, I think around about this time last year, about  changes in China to strategy on coal-fired power stations as coal as a source of generating capacity. We've still  seen activity in coal through this year in China, but it's no doubt it is a diminishing part of that business, but one  that does use a huge amount of actuators.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: So, our power sort of market is shifting, and I think we are likely to see more spend within gas as a generating  sort of area, which tends to mean larger number of smaller power stations, but still opportunities for us to  participate. It's not likely to be the strongest growth market going forward. It is in that kind of switch over phase  from different sources.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: In terms of RFS lead times, we talked typically about conversion times in the Fluid Systems for most of the  products around about sort of 12 to 16 weeks, I guess. It's the longest lead time part of the business. That's  assuming the customer wants the product as soon as we could deliver it, often it's not. So, because Fluid  Systems is more oil and gas focused than our other divisions and tends to have lumpier projects, they are often  the longer lead times. So, it's not uncommon. And if you go back to the LNG projects that we completed in 2016,  some of those were received in 2014.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: I think just picking up on Jonathan's point on power and gas-fired combined cycle plant in particular, you're going  to see a lot of investment in that area versus other areas over the next sort of five or six years. I will say more  about this in the sort of innovation showcase towards the end of the year. But one of the features of that is they're  looking for quick response. These are peaking or cycling plants where we are trying to manage intermittent load.  That needs very quick response actuation. So, again, the focus on faster, more reliable, quicker responding  actuation, which is good for us is a part of that investment thesis over the next five years, and it won't surprise you  to know that a chunk of our R&D budget is going into that sort of area. And it's that sort of color that we'll provide  for you later in the year.

texts.speaker: Alasdair Leslie
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA (UK)
texts.text: Yeah. Hi. Good morning. Alasdair Leslie from Soc Gén. Just a couple of questions. Firstly, just on kind of  innovation, maybe if you could just give us some examples where you expect to have a quick payback on  innovation, normally what we – product lifecycles or product innovation cycles, development cycles can be quite  long, particularly in your core markets oil and gas customers can be quite conservative, which obviously gives you  that barriers to entry. But do you see that sort of changing as well in terms of the approach of oil and gas  customers that's going to allow you to accelerate innovation?

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: On some of the other areas that we're investing in, obviously we've talked before about these things, but ultra-low  power actuators may be solar powered, which are really important longer term because not only do you  dramatically reduce energy cost and the efficiency of those plants improve there, you also reduce significantly  infrastructure costs. If you're having to take power to remote locations, the infrastructure cost of laying all that  cabling and power supply is significant. That's a key area of work and focus for us, but that's not going to give as  a payback in the next one year or two years. Clearly, that is going to be a longer-term payback. I'm not talking 10  years, I'm talking a three to four-year payback in that sort of activity.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: There is a big focus on things like emissions. There's no doubt there is increasing environmental focus on things  like CO2 emission, methane emission, and again, there is significant opportunities for us to work on technology,  which would dramatically reduce that, again, over a sort of three to four year payback.

texts.speaker: Alasdair Leslie
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA (UK)
texts.text: Thank you. I just had a second question on IMO 2020 as well, I was wondering if you could just update us on the  outlook for refinery investment there because I think we sort of see momentum I think pick up over the last couple  of quarters, a number of shipowners, for example, are talking about how they won't adopt scrubbers as a kind of  solution for the sulfur regulation. So, I don't know whether you've seen a pickup in quotation activity. I noticed  again, there was a reference in your statements.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Yeah. Obviously, this is about taking the sulfur levels down from 3.5% to 0.5%. I always wonder with these things  how much teeth is there in the legislation, and will it actually happen. It does appear, so it is happening and  shipowners are responding to that.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: So, we have seen, I think as Jonathan mentioned in his script, a pickup in downstream quotation activity, as  facilities look to be able to deal with this. I think you'll also see a pickup in LNG. LNG at the end of the day is  virtually 0% sulfur content, and I think will become an increasingly important fuel supply in transportation.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: I know there was a lot of investments in LNG 2013 through 2016. One of the reasons why our midstream was  down in 2017 versus 2016 because we have those big orders back in 2015 and into 2016. But most  commentators would say that there is a capacity gap opening up in 2020 and beyond as LNG increasingly  becomes the fuel of choice. And I think you'll start to see increased activity around LNG over the next two to three  years, which is good for us.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: I mean, I think what we're seeing at the moment in the oil and gas market is a return to more normal buying  patterns, in the sort of maintenance and small upgrade market where even that, as you know, is being pushed off  and deferred a year ago or two years ago. So, the improvement in the oil and gas market that you're seeing at the  moment is more a nature of resetting that than all of a sudden a major change in the dynamics in the market.  When we start to see big project activity pick up again that might mark a return to what we might think of as the  normal oil and gas markets of 2012, 2013.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: As you know I'm pretty cautious about that. We're designing a game plan for Rotork that does not rely on that that  thinks about a $60 barrel price as the long term average in this market and all of our plans are assuming that. If  we do get a pickup and a return based on higher oil price, however from long period, short period of time that  might be that is clearly an upside opportunity for the business, but not that one we're going to rely on.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: It hasn't done it. So, anywhere near the same extent of the power industry is done, all the general industrial  automation industry is done. So, it's playing catch up and there is no doubt that most of our competitors in this  space, particularly the bigger ones see this as an area of focus. It's also therefore extremely important that Rotork  puts a significant chunk of investment to work in those areas.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: We are confident. I mean, oil and gas has always notoriously been a very conservative industry. It's been quite  slow to adopt new technology, and that's why it's materially behind the power sector and other process industries  in terms of digital. But $60 a barrel is a real burning platform here. I mean, it's focused everyone's attention on the  fact that it's not going back to $90 to $100. The industry has to find a leaner, more efficient way to manage, and  this is a really important part of that. It's been trialed in other industries. It's been successful.

texts.speaker: Martin James Lamb
texts.profession: Executive Chairman, Rotork Plc
texts.text: But if you thought that the gas market was going to grow at 3% or so a year over the next period of time, power is  probably near at 2%. Water, certainly, the smart water aspects of that are probably near a 4% or 5%. LNG is  probably near a 5%. Once we get through 2019, there's a lots of moving parts, Robert, but it won't be unfair to  say, overall, end market growth is probably half our overall growth ambition.

file: RORL - Q4 2018 Earnings Call 4March2019 330 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 04-Mar-19.pdf

texts.speaker: Kevin G. Hostetler
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Let's take a look at our full year highlights. Once again, we've delivered a strong set of results driven by  management actions against the backdrop of macroeconomic conditions that became more uncertain as the year  progressed. Our business was supported by increasing activity within our oil and gas markets, notably evident in  smaller to midsized projects such as retrofits and upgrades.

texts.speaker: Kevin G. Hostetler
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: In the first half of 2018, we also experienced several major project wins, principally in Asia, which we delivered  upon in the third and fourth quarters. We saw hesitation in the release of similar larger projects in the second half  of 2018, largely due to significant fluctuations in oil prices and increasing uncertainty on a variety of economic  fronts. Additionally, I'll highlight the significant progress made in our penetration of the Industrial process  segments driven by our increased focus on these markets coupled with a continuing increase in general  automation.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Redundancy costs in respect to a number of locations which have downsized as part of product rationalization  changes or through efficiency improvements or where roles have disappeared as we've reorganized the  management team. At the same time, disposal or closure of the three businesses resulted in a loss of £0.7  million. Other restructuring costs include R&D write-offs on discontinued product lines and asset write-offs in  respect of the footprint rationalization program. We are anticipating around a £5 million charge in respect of these  items in full-year 2019.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Now, turning to the operational review, this slide summarizes group's key markets and geographies. These slides  are on an as reported basis. Revenue increased in all divisions and in all regions except the Middle East and  Africa. Oil and gas increased from 50% to 54% of group sales. Its fastest-growing end markets were downstream  oil and gas, up 30%, and industrial which grew 14%. Midstream grew in line with group revenue, so remained 9%  of group sales whilst upstream and water markets grew but at a slower rate than the group.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Power sales fell by 11% as sales in the Far East declined and projects in the Middle East and Africa in 2017  weren't repeated in 2018. This was one of the contributors to the lower sales in the Middle East and Africa where  upstream also declined after an active 2017. All other regions reported higher revenue with a strong downstream  oil and gas growth being instrumental in the growth of the Far East, which was the fastest-growing region and  increased from 28% to 32% to group revenue.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Controls oil and gas exposure is greatest in downstream. The growth in that market up 35% in the year has  therefore benefited the division and boosted its sales particularly in the Far East and to a lesser extent North  America. Upstream and midstream were broadly flat overall, but within this, upstream was positive in Eastern  Europe but declined in the Middle East. And midstream was positive in the Far East as a result of improved  pipeline sales.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Power declined due to lower activity in the Middle East and Africa and Far East with the Far East also reporting  the largest reduction in water. Industrial process including HVAC and marine grew as a result of positive  performances in Europe and the Far East.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: The downstream growth came in the Middle East and Far East, where some of the projects are the same as  those seen in Controls division. Upstream saw a positive North America and Far East region, offset by a decline  in the Middle East. Whilst water and industrial grew in line with the division as a whole, power declined. The  reduction in power was in the Middle East, following a large project there in 2017 and the sale of the Hiller nuclear  actuator business at the half year.

texts.speaker: Jonathan M. Davis
texts.profession: Finance Director & Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Overheads reduced in the year and were also improved by the closure of the Valvekits facility, resulted in an  adjusted operating margin only 70 basis points lower than 2017. Midstream and downstream sales drove the  increase in overall oil and gas sales from 52% to 54% of divisional sales, with activity in the Middle East, Far East  and North America most positive.

texts.speaker: Kevin G. Hostetler
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Jonathan. Now, let me begin this section by saying a few words about our outlook for 2019. So, firstly, we  do welcome the recent stabilization of the oil prices. And our view is the current CapEx forecasts for the oil and  gas sector are now coming in at between 4% and 6% year-on-year. Having said this, it's important to remember  this growth rate varies dramatically between sub-segments of the market, between geographic regions and  between the specific application sets.

texts.speaker: Kevin G. Hostetler
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: The midstream segment for Rotork is largely about pipelines and LNG. We see pipeline expansion in the U.S.  shale market and pipeline expansion specifically related to LNG, as well as a general LNG-related expansion  beyond pipelines on a global basis.

texts.speaker: Kevin G. Hostetler
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Lastly, the pillars we've discussed are supported by our strategy, portfolio and product line assessment activities.  In 2018, we previously announced the planned exits from three businesses: The nuclear island actuation  business, the valve adaptation business and a small regional engineering center. These exits are now complete.  Additionally, we initiated a detailed product line review identifying a number of product lines to be withdrawn from  production over the next 18 months.

texts.speaker: Kevin G. Hostetler
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: I'll close out by making a few comments on the outlook for this year. 2018 began with very strong oil prices, which  supported expansion in larger programs and stimulated the return of small to midsized maintenance and upgrade  programs throughout the oil and gas spectrum.

texts.speaker: Kevin G. Hostetler
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Towards the end of 2018, we saw a high degree of oil price instability causing some of the larger programs to  pause for what we believe is a short term. We've said it many times over a particular price in a barrel of oil, say  $55 to $60, the stability in the price of a barrel of oil is more important than the overall discrete price levels.  Despite a slowing global economic environment and these dramatic fluctuations in oil prices witnessed in our  fourth quarter, we continue to execute on our specific growth initiatives to drive our results.

texts.speaker: Kevin G. Hostetler
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: I think we're still very positive on subsea. I think we're still very positive on LNG. The core spending seems to be  holding up in terms of the maintenance and upgrade spending. That's still I think it's just some of the larger  upstream and some larger downstream are still – those are the projects that are kind of in-hold in the short term.

texts.speaker: Kevin G. Hostetler
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: I think on supply chain, supply chain, lots of opportunities. But, I think, we're tempering this year to that £5 million  number simply because of the inventory reduction program that we have, right? So, you have two opposing goals,  one, generate additional cash, reduce inventory, which may then reduce the overall purchases required this year  to get to our target. So those are kind of those programs.

texts.speaker: Kevin G. Hostetler
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: Let me unwrap a few of those questions. So, typically, in the application set that we're playing in, in particular in  the Far East, again, we're in the critical application. Our strength is in the explosion-proof electric actuators. Those  are critical applications with critical high value fluids and gases. And therefore, it's not the type of application set  where you're going to go out and cheapen out on price.

texts.speaker: Kevin G. Hostetler
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rotork Plc
texts.text: When we're in meetings with those companies, they will draw a very clear distinction between what they call the  Tier 1A pieces of the project and then others that maybe – so maybe on some of the water circulating around a  facility for cooling water, it may not be as critical to them as the application set with the pipeline having the gas,  right. And they're very clear about these sites having kind of a two-tier strategy of having Rotork, A, level up here  on all critical applications. texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rotork Plc

texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Profits to-date are more or less as we expected and compared to previous guidance we will see a small effect from  the nuclear disaster in Japan that has caused some disruption to our supply chains and delayed deliveries into the  factories and also delayed some overall activity and that's going to cost us about £10 million or thereabouts over  the full year. texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc

texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Turning to the last of the four divisions, Energy. We continue to invest to improve products in new businesses  such as nuclear, fuel cells, and tidal power. texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc

texts.text: Second, CapEx and intangibles reflect continued investment to meet the rising load of delivering 2,000 Trent  engines over the next five years.
