The  remaining balance of about £130 million related to higher development and certification costs. Expect CapEx to  be about £100 million higher in 2013.

texts.speaker: Mark Morris
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: In offshore, there continues to be encouraging signs of recovery driven by high oil prices. You can see this is in the  rising order intake and we expect this to continue in 2013.

texts.speaker: Mark Morris
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Finally, to our Energy business, there's some big percentage movements here but remember, the absolutely  numbers are small in the context of the group. Similar to Marine, Energy revenue performance has been subdued  by lower OE deliveries due to less volume and customer delays, partially compensated by good growth in services  revenues.

texts.speaker: Mark Morris
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Importantly, the level of bid activity has risen both in our oil and gas and power generation businesses. We have a  well-established oil and gas business that makes up around 2/3 of the revenue and nearly all the profit in our  Energy segment. The four less mature businesses of power generation, civil nuclear, fuel cells and tidal, have  suppressed financial performance with continued investment.

texts.speaker: Mark Morris
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: As you're aware, we have now sold our tidal business and a 51% stake in our fuel cells business as we focus on the  areas we want to grow. We'll carry on investing in the civil nuclear business where we see significant opportunities  ahead.

texts.speaker: Mark Morris
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Me again? Sure. I mean firstly, we don't measure things in halves. So I just don't think we have the granularity to  pick up trends over from one half to the other. I mean I think, as both John and I have alluded to, when we talk  about our four C's, cost and cash are big drivers of those, and clearly, unit cost reduction is a key part of that.  And of course now, as we're large and we have far more larger share our ability to leverage our supply chain and  deploy far higher levels of TCA contracts in terms of the amount of capture we take, which enables us to schedule  how we do overhauls and the work scope, all of that, helps us with efficiency and therefore, cost improvements as  well.

texts.speaker: James Guyette
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer of Rolls-Royce North America Inc., Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Now, two things. One, is the sequester and two is a continuing resolution. Whether or not there is a sequester or  not, a continuing resolution or not, I think we all know that budgets in the developed world for defense are going  down so, we have that kind of challenging environment.

texts.speaker: James Guyette
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer of Rolls-Royce North America Inc., Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: What makes this much more difficult for us is a sequester because a sequester – and by the way, our opinion, not  necessarily is going to be fact, but our opinion is it will kick in on March 1. That will bring with it a lot of chaos,  chaos because the Department Of Defense and the various Service Chiefs have no ability to move money. They  can't change the priority. All they can do is simply take a cut.

texts.speaker: James Guyette
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer of Rolls-Royce North America Inc., Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: So to sum it up, yes, I think sequester will take effect. It's unfortunate. We'll go through the chaos. It will be  painful. But I think we're all going to have to come to our senses after the fistfight is over and resolve it. Now, the  question you didn't ask me is have we baked some of this into our assumptions? Yes, we have as best we know  how.

texts.speaker: Mark Morris
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: And then of course you talked – you've raised the issue about RB211 and again, some of the older fleet, as it starts  to come out, two things to remember in our total aftermarket which includes time and material and spare sales is  that our older engines, we typically have a far lower level of TCA penetration sort of 40% to 50%.

texts.speaker: Mark Morris
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: And although engines may sort of grow in a sort of much more predictable pattern, when we look at retirements of  engines, they don't typically sort of just go at a straight line. It depends on where the fleets are and what people  are doing with them. So two things are happening, if you don't have the level of TCA capture on old product which  we don't and you start to get some lumpy retirements which we're starting to see in 524 which is totally expected  by the way.

texts.speaker: Celine Fornaro
texts.profession: Analyst, Merrill Lynch International (United Kingdom)
texts.text: My second question is on the Energy division. I thought we had a £26 million charge in 2011 related to an  industrial trend. So actually the improvement in margin in 2012 is actually probably slightly lower than  anticipated. Is that a fair point?

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Okay. Why don't I ask Mark to start on the – at the R&D and Colin to make a few comments about what we're  actually doing in terms of research and development. Mark, you may want to comment on Energy and then I'll  maybe pick up the 787 and Jim, add a few comments on that as well.

texts.speaker: Mark Morris
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Right, Energy. So, as I said in the presentation, we look at Energy and profit and margin progression. The oil and  gas business really drives this business and the other businesses continues to sort of take in investment and  therefore, drag its financial performance. As we've said, we've removed two of those so the R&D and associated  things we'd expect to go down and the associated investment with that will start go down.

texts.speaker: Mark Morris
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: We continue to see price pressure in the oil and gas business. But a lot of good inroads are being made on cost  reduction. So, we do expect some progression in profit and margin for next year. But again, it's just worth  remembering that these are of small numbers and the Energy business has low volumes, relatively expensive  packaging. And so if something slips over the year, the ability to sort of move the numbers can be a bit more  extenuated than it can on other businesses. But certainly, we are expecting both revenue and profit growth during  2012.

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Yeah, let me just add what I said last year, the financial performance of the Energy division is not acceptable. We  know that. We're taking steps to address it. You've seen some of the steps we've taken during the course of 2012.  We continue to work on that.

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: In terms of concentration, I think if I take the kind of things that I've been concerned about, I think the evidence  around getting sharper on that is what do we do and what don't we do, and tidal and fuel cells would be examples  of what we decide that we're not going to do those. But that never really goes away. I think the nature of the  business that we have and the kinds of people we employ who are naturally curious, inquisitive, are looking to do  – trying to make them focus on – what we really want the focus on is always going to be a challenge. So it will  probably remain one. But I would say some progress there with the evidence I've given you.

texts.speaker: Mark Morris
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Okay. So let's just remind ourselves, so Engine Holding's is the vehicle, the joint venture through which Rolls- Royce and Daimler have sought to acquire Tognum. We have also put in our Bergen diesels business that went in  from effectively our Marine and Energy businesses into Engine Holding's.

texts.speaker: Gordon R. Hunting
texts.profession: Sales Associate, Fiske Plc (Broker)
texts.text: At the moment, all your big engines are three-shaft. On the premise that two-shaft engines less likely to have  dangerous oil leaks, are you going to switch over to carbon blades and also to two-shafts for your 777 replacement  engines? And are you already doing R&D for the 777 replacement?

texts.speaker: Colin P. Smith
texts.profession: Executive Director & Technology Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: The simple answer, Gordon, to the first question is no, we're really comfortable with the three-shaft concept, for a  whole host of technical reasons that I could bore the ears off you, but I won't in the interest of time. We have put  an offer into Boeing with a engine that's based on the technology we've been developing, which does include  carbon fiber fan blades as I think we've discussed in the press. And all engines have oil in the middle of them and  all engines have a propensity to leak and each person resolves that in their own way but I know what you're  alluding to.

texts.speaker: David H. Perry
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International Ltd.
texts.text: No, hopefully this isn't – I think you said at the last meeting you'd give us an update on your plans for fixing power  gen. Can you just give us some detail on that, please?

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: What I would say is the Energy business in total we've sort of talked about. You break it down as Mark has done. It  had the five parts. Fuel cells we've dealt with. Tidal we've dealt with. Civil nuclear is a business we're investing in.  Oil and gas is doing well, power gen is a challenge for us in a number of ways.

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: I've learned a few lessons but that's certainly one of them. Look no, I'm absolutely sure I never said that we would  come back by year-end. The progress that we made in the Energy in total is the ones that we've talked and we have  made some progress on some issues in power gen. I'm not going to get hung up on a timetable for this, because  that undermines some of the things that we may or may not want to do.

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: But we're well aware of the issue, and as I said, we're well aware of the financial performance of the Energy  division in total. It's not where it needs to be and we need to address it.

file: RRL - Q4 2012 Earnings Call Fixed Income 14February2013 845 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 14-Feb-13.pdf

texts.speaker: Mark Morris
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: I think the first thing to say is that I believe it's been a good year for us. We certainly delivered on our guidance,  the order book is up at £60.1 billion against the backdrop of relatively uncertain macro economic climate and, of  course, the order book is what gives us the visibility and confidence to continue investing to meet the rising load.

texts.speaker: Mark Morris
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Nonetheless, I think the Defence landscape looks pretty uncertain as we look forward into 2013. Lots of budget- free constraints and sequestration and so forth, and of course, accordingly, we're not immune from that. We  expect to see lower opportunities and we expect to see lower flying hours. And of course, on the back of that we've  guided the profits will reduce slightly, although from a higher base on which most of the market was starting from.  Energy, I think just briefly, I mean, this is a business where we have really a very good oil and gas business. And it  generates about two-thirds of the turnover, and almost all of the profit. But its performance is then dragged down  by the investment we have in less mature – in immature technologies that we've had in power generation. Civil  nuclear as we seek to build that up. And our Tidal and Fuel Cells business, both of which now – the Tidal business  has been sold, and we sold 51% stake in our Fuel Cell business as we seek to focus on the key areas that we do want  to grow.

texts.speaker: Mark Morris
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: So, as we look into 2013, we expect the Energy business to perform better, obviously less drags from having two  businesses effectively having been removed, lower R&D from those parts as well. But of course, we'll continue to  invest in civil nuclear.

file: RRL - Q4 2013 Earnings Call 13February2014 400 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 13-Feb-14.pdf

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: So while we need to keep investing in gas turbines and we also – we'll also look for opportunities to expand in  reciprocating engines, both to maintain balance in our portfolio and to generate the cash required in the much  longer cycle gas turbine business. Back in 2011, we invested in Tognum to add scale, reach and capability to our  reciprocating engine business. This is an important business and has proved a good investment. I spend a good  deal of time there, most recently last week.

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Unit cost is down in Marine, Energy and Power Systems, although slightly higher in our aerospace divisions. We  are building new, more efficient facilities and capacity that will support a doubling in production of Trent engines.  We are moving production away from high cost countries, negotiating terms with our suppliers and consolidating  our supply chain. We are improving productivity and designing cost reduction into our engines.

texts.speaker: Mark Morris
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Next, let's take a look at our Energy business. We've seen good growth in the order book, with a £1.1 billion order  intake for the year, predominantly in oil and gas, which provides good visibility for 2014. We have a well- established oil and gas business that makes up around two-thirds of the revenue, and more than all of the profit in  our Energy business. Revenue increased 9%, driven by higher OE volumes in our oil and gas business. Profit  increased £7 million, reflecting higher volumes, partially offset by pricing pressure, and continued investment in  our civil nuclear business. In 2014, we expect further good growth in revenue and profit, but as you can see, the  margins remain poor in this business, and this is an area we continue to work on.

texts.speaker: Mark Morris
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Tognum had a tough first half and a good second half, exactly as we said. Our strong performance in the second  half was driven by sales in marine and agricultural markets that included the effect of customers buying ahead of  new emissions legislation that came into effect this year. Revenue was broadly flat. We saw good growth in our  marine and industrial markets, offset by lower revenue in oil and gas, mining and lower aftermarket sales. Profit  was also broadly flat after a strong second half recovery, which is helped by unit cost reductions too. In 2014, we  expect modest growth in revenue and good growth in profit, driven by marine engines and land power systems.

texts.speaker: Mark Morris
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: So, now before talking about our guidance for 2014, it's worth highlighting that we've created two new reporting  segments: Aerospace and Marine and Industrial Power Systems which we call MIPS. This reflects our two strong  technology platforms of gas turbines and reciprocating engines. Aerospace will comprise our Civil and Defence  businesses, while Marine Power Systems and our Energy business will now sit in MIPS. Our Energy business will  now be called Energy & Nuclear and will include our nuclear submarines business which transfers from Marine.

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: So what I would say is as we look at the business – and again, it shouldn't be a great surprise, we look at it in terms  of the gas turbines and the reciprocating engine businesses. We've got those two platforms, and they have some  similar characteristics in terms of the fact that they are complex integrated power systems in the sense of an OE  and an after-market. And they're also, I think, important in terms of the balance that they bring to the group in  terms of the different nature of the financials and the industries that they're in, with shorter cycle, longer cycle,  earlier cash generation, longer cash generation, more capital-intensive, less capital-intensive. So there is a mix  there that I think is important. It's important to get that balance right.

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: In terms of the medium-speed, as we look at our portfolio, marine, which is a strong portfolio in terms of what we  can offer to marine, an area that I think we need to strengthen is our medium-speed diesel portfolio where we are  relatively small. So if you look at the medium-speed diesel, the big players, clearly Wärtsilä is a big player there.  And if we look at our Marine business, an attractive part of that portfolio that we need to strengthen is medium- speed and it's important in terms of pull-through of other products.

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Okay. The next, the front again. We'll start on the front on this side and kind of wind our way a little bit up and  come back. I know Sandy likes to be at the end.

texts.speaker: James Guyette
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer of Rolls-Royce North America Inc., Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: So, this year, it's now manifesting itself in OE and I'll cover that in just a second. But I'd like to provide a couple of  other points that might be helpful to you. If you look at the U.S. for a moment, last year, I provided a tutorial on  sequestration. My colleagues have asked that I don't do that again this year but we can do it later if you would like.  We do have a defence budget for the first time in several years in the U.S. and that's good news.

texts.speaker: James Guyette
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer of Rolls-Royce North America Inc., Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: The other good news is that for this one year, it put aside the effects of sequestration only for one year. The other  good news is that it is a $12 billion improvement over where sequestration would have been. The bad news is the  defence budget is $40 billion less than the president requested. So, again, a little bit of gain here but not as much  as the defence department thought it needed to run its business.

texts.speaker: James Guyette
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer of Rolls-Royce North America Inc., Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: The other point that I would raise is this is a year of midterm elections. So, every member of the House is up for  reelection, a third of the Senate. And I think it means that there is probably less room for political mischief. People  are going to be on their better behavior. Now, what does that mean for sequestration next year? Don't know, but I  suspect again better behavior.

texts.speaker: James Guyette
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer of Rolls-Royce North America Inc., Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Now, what we do is upgrade the engine and what it provides to the customer is somewhere between a 10% and  15% reduction in fuel. And so, with a small investment, there's a big gain. So, we're looking for every opportunity  again to help those customers that we have do more with less in a budget-constrained environment. So, I  apologize for a long answer, but I do think that since defence was kind of a headline item that, perhaps, it might be  helpful to handle it in a comprehensive way. To answer your direct question, yes, we saw it coming, reflected in  order book declining.

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: And it isn't just about marine, there's a land power part to it as well. So we need to make sure that you understand  that business, I think, much more clearly than you do, and we recognize that that's something that we haven't  been particularly good at doing. And to clarify that point, Tognum is sort of the high-speed diesel engine company  rather than a medium speed. So, if you look at reciprocating engines in simple terms, you've got three speeds: low,  medium, and high.

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: So, as an acquisition, I am comfortable that that was a good acquisition and a good plan. In terms of medium  speed though, it doesn't address some of the issues that I think we have, we think we have in terms of marine and  the growing land power business. So, irrespective of what was understood or said in the past, to be clear, we  believe that we need to strengthen our medium-speed diesel engine businesses.

texts.speaker: Mark Morris
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: On launch pricing on XWB, look, we're not going to sort of get staked out in the sun program by program in giving  you the guidance from 2014 and then what I call a bit of figure painting for 2015. We've factored that in into our  thought process. And again, ditto on sort of Trent 500 net debtor, it's a small contribution to the overall net  debtors. As you know, the Trent 500 as a four-engine aircraft is not doing as well given the higher fuel price  environment. Again, that's factored into our calculations but I'm not going to break it out specifically, but again,  it's reflected in the total rise in net TotalCare debtor that I gave you for 2014.

file: RRL - Q4 2013 Earnings Call Fixed Income 13February2014 900 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 13-Feb-14.pdf

texts.speaker: Mark Morris
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: It's just worth remembering that we are a high technology Power Systems business and we invest in two strong  technology platforms, being gas turbines and reciprocating engines. And those products take us to the various  markets in which we play: civil, defense, energy, marine and industrial power. £

texts.speaker: Mark Morris
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Now in terms of our 4Cs, customer, on-time delivery improved, which has been really, really great work from our  civil large and particularly our – and Corporate Jet business as well. The Trent XW powered A350: it's on its first  flight and there's now over 1,600 Trent XWs being sold. Our first Environship on the Marine side set sail with [ph]  Holden (03:26) engines and propulsion reducing CO2 emissions by 40%. And the MT-30 MTU power packs have  been selected to power the U.K.'s new Type 26 Frigate.

texts.speaker: Mark Morris
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Costs, at a group level the pace of progress has been slower than we would have liked. Aerospace actions have  been taking time to feed through. But we are, in terms of the new efficient factories that we're getting, we're still  not in terms of the benefit of the ramp-up. So we've got some what I'll call under recovery occurring there. A lot of  work going on with both our supply base and low cost [ph] country (04:03) sourcing, and it's a continuing  journey. But it just takes a little more time because in most cases when we design or manufacture new parts it  requires that it's been re-certified, and of course that takes time. But we've made good progress in our Marine and  Energy and Power Systems business on unit cost reduction, but more to do.

texts.speaker: Mark Morris
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: On concentration, which we really refer to as where we invest and where we choose not to invest, as I've sort of  laid out before, we continue to look at how we grow our gas turbines and reciprocating engines. We made a  number of smaller acquisitions last year, predominantly technology acquisitions which were really s ort of CapEx  style. But these are continued little fill ups that we fill in to ensure that we get the technology or additional  products or roots to market.

file: RRL - Q4 2014 Earnings Call 13February2015 500 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 13-Feb-15.pdf

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: As you know, we've been reshaping the company. And during the course of the year, we completed the sale of our  Energy gas turbine and compressor business to Siemens. This was an issue that needed to be addressed, and we've  dealt with it. We also completed the acquisition of Power Systems, so all the challenges have been substantial.

texts.speaker: David Smith
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director
texts.text: And of course, the turbines in our gas turbine engines, so they're operating – small instruments that are operating  at temperatures that exceed the melting point of the metals of which they're made and have to be cooled with  microscopic air systems. And that cooling air is still at 700 degrees. It's just amazing technology.

texts.speaker: David Smith
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director
texts.text: They look very closely to our credit rating. It also gives us the flexibility, for example, to return the proceeds of the  divestment of our Energy business to shareholders through the share buyback, and that's currently underway.

texts.speaker: David Smith
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director
texts.text: And unfortunately, these negative factors more than offset actually some good progress that was made in the  business on cost, both on product cost and indirect cost. We lost about 300 people last year. Clearly, since  September, October, our oil prices have halved. And that will create additional further pressure in many of our  markets. And I'll come back to that issue a little bit later.

texts.speaker: David Smith
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director
texts.text: Turning finally to the Nuclear & Energy business, which for the final time is reflected in our numbers. That was  sold to Siemens on December 1. As you can see, I've actually excluded that business from the analysis to give you a  better understanding of the drivers in the retained business.

texts.speaker: David Smith
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director
texts.text: In Defence, we expect further progress on costs and margins. In Land & Sea, however, this is where I'm really  more cautious, as I think we can expect continued further pressure from the external environment. And there is  more uncertainty here, both around the duration of the oil price impacts, but also pricing and adverse mix  pressures. Of course, that doesn't mean that we're not going to be really focused on improving operating  performance to try and offset some of those external factors, but they are there. So, that completes my review of  the key numbers.

texts.speaker: David Smith
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director
texts.text: In fact, I was in Friedrichshafen a couple of weeks ago, going around the Power Systems facilities there. And I was  very, very impressed with the work they're doing on lean manufacturing. It's as good as anything I've ever seen in  the automotive industry. We must and will do more, however, in all of our businesses. But in doing that, we must  also be realistic. This will take some time.

texts.speaker: David Smith
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director
texts.text: Second is the focus we have on life cycle costs. This is hugely important as product life costs can be three, four  times the OE cost of an engine. And our focus here is really delivering. And there are recurring and non-recurring  benefits. You can see that within the £150 million charge. But actually, the benefits that we're delivering are  greater than that. They will come through in future years as well. And so, the progress, I would say, is ahead of our  expectations.

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: For example, SmartMotor is a world leader in permanent magnet technology that we apply to our marine  thrusters. HyperTherm has increased our knowledge of ceramic matrix materials that are critical in improving gas  turbine efficiency. Individually, not all these transactions are especially significant, but taken together, they  represent a focusing of the group on technologies and markets where we're confident of long-term profitable  growth.

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Just a few areas in which we have world-leading expertise: a fluid dynamics that has a broad application from the  development of fan blades and water jets, to understanding coolant flow in nuclear reactors; 3D printing and hot  isostatic processing, manufacturing techniques that improve design, reduce cost and shorten delivery time; safety  critical engineering processes developed in our Nuclear and Aerospace businesses that are being applied across  the group to meet our customers' increasing requirement for safety and reliability.

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Strategically, our two divisions address markets where our long-term growth is underpinned by expanding  population, increased affluence, and environmental regulations. Both Aerospace and Land & Sea markets offer  attractive returns and play to our strengths.

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: As you're all aware, we're progressing our next generation of aero engines, Advance and UltraFan engine. We have  flown a test engine with carbon/titanium fan blades and we're building a new test facility for power gearboxes in  Dahlewitz.

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: In our reciprocating engine portfolio, we are investing in technology to further improve fuel efficiency and  emissions. These are all necessary investments in the future which brings us to the third element of our strategy,  profitable growth.

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So the fundamentals that underpin our business and provide opportunity for long-term profitable growth are  strong. Of course, in the short-term, the pace of economic growth in individual markets were fluctuating. The  price of commodities may be volatile. The most obvious example at the moment is the oil price which has halved  in the space of months. This should, of course, help growth across the world, but has pluses and minuses for Rolls- Royce.

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: In Civil, there is limited short-term impact, although it helps airline profitability which, in the medium and longer  term, could translate into more orders. In Land & Sea, reduced CapEx from the oil majors has a more immediate  impact on our revenue, forcing us to focus even more on cost. So in the long term, we will be leaner and more  efficient.

texts.speaker: Christian A. Laughlin
texts.profession: Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you. Christian Laughlin from Bernstein. Just one question from me. Kind of from – taking a step back at a  high level, the steep decline in oil price obviously was, clearly, a big surprise to everyone in 2014 and knock-on  effects are still working their way through the system in various adjacent businesses. John, has this changed the  way you view the attractiveness of this end market versus last year at this time or when you took over as CEO?  And might it change or influence decisions to further invest in the short cycle businesses that are heavily geared  towards energy exploration and production, either organic or inorganic investments over the, say, medium term?

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Thanks for the question. I think I've tried to address that, I think, in my set piece in a sense that we see the longer- term growth in these markets being substantial; the longer-term growth driven by population, driven by  urbanization, driven by the increase in demands of power. I'm certainly not well-placed to forecast oil prices, and  I'm not even going to try. There are other people who are better placed to do that, so I'm not even going to try.

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: But we believe that the mega trends, as I've described them, of the population, urbanization that will drive  demand for power are really strong in the long run and that's what I'm looking at. In the shorter term, the issue is  addressing the impacts that we see in our – particularly in our Marine business that is impacted most directly by  cutbacks in CapEx from the oil majors. And that means focusing intently on costs.

texts.speaker: Gordon R. Hunting
texts.profession: Fiske Plc (Broker)
texts.text: Gordon Hunting from Fiske. Singapore, are you finding it much more difficult to start production out than you  were anticipating particularly as the temperature is about 80 degrees Fahrenheit and the humidity about similar  figure of 80%. Is this going to be a problem? And did you anticipate that when you started moving XWB  production across to Singapore?

texts.speaker: John F. Rishton
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Okay. The shorter answer, and I'll give a short answer, is we were fully aware of the temperatures in Singapore.  Production has ramped up very successfully particularly on the fan blade side. The issue that we have in Singapore  is unrelated to temperature. It's the speed with which we fill the facility, which is geared to build Trent 1000s and  Trent 900s. We're ramping that up slowly over time.

texts.speaker: David Smith
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director
texts.text: So, on the second question around consensus, I mean I think you've rightly picked up that I've – in setting the  consensus – I still have the kitchen sink with me, by the way. But I haven't tried it out quite yet. But I am more  cautious in certain areas and I think, particularly, Marine is a clear one. Power Systems is not so much just about  the oil price. It's actually more about my caution around general economic factors at the moment. So, what's  happening in slowdown in China, what's happening in the Eurozone?

texts.speaker: David Smith
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director
texts.text: We're also getting incremental benefits now from the engine health monitoring system. So, we have a process of  converting that information now back to give us a much more accurate view on what the lifetime usage of parts is  going to be in the replacement requirements.

texts.speaker: A
texts.profession: Okay. I've got a question from Rob Stallard, RBC. On inventory levels, particularly in Civil Aerospace, how much
texts.text: further do you think you have to go in terms of optimal inventory terms and how long do you think it would take  to get there? And also what sort of assumptions have you built into 2015 to 2017 plan regarding build rates on  Trent 700 engine production for the A330ceo?

texts.speaker: Rami Y. Myerson
texts.profession: Investec Bank Plc (Broker)
texts.text: And lastly, of course, on the Land & Sea businesses, can you talk a little bit about pricing pressure? We have heard  some of the customers, they're talking about requiring price decreases from their suppliers?

texts.speaker: Lawrie J. Haynes
texts.profession: President, Land & Sea
texts.text: On the Marine original equipment, we are – about 60% of our supply is into the oil and gas industry, the offshore  industry. So, yes, what we're seeing at the kind of top level, the top tier is rippling into us, so we're having kind of  considerable discussions with a number of our customers on the OE side. And on the services side, a number of  our customers are de-stocking. They're actually using their existing stock and which, of course, they're putting  pricing pressure onto the Marine side.

texts.speaker: Lawrie J. Haynes
texts.profession: President, Land & Sea
texts.text: We're also seeing on the – at the Land side, a number of our customers are taking advantage from the lower oil  price but at the same time, they're using that oil price to pressurize oil suppliers on price. So, I'm afraid it's a  uniform view across the market.

texts.speaker: David Smith
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director
texts.text: We've guided a little bit lower on the Marine and Power Systems sides of the business, and that really reflects, I  think, the uncertainty around the oil price at the moment. Marine in particular has a reasonable exposure to the  oil and gas sectors, particularly in the offshore markets. And we have seen already, and we expect probably to see  further deferrals of orders, and particularly, I think around the servicing of equipment in that sector, a reduction  in discretionary spend.

texts.speaker: David Smith
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director

texts.speaker: David Smith
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director
texts.text: So thank you for your patience. I know that was a longer presentation. In conclusion, the full-year results were in  line with our earlier expectations, albeit at the bottom end of the range. That reflected the challenging oil and gas  markets and the transition effects in civil aerospace. Both of these we see continuing throughout this year.

texts.speaker: David Warren Arthur East
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: So I'll start on the left-hand side of the slide with the first of the three strategic themes. Now, the first one is  engineering excellence. texts.speaker: David Warren Arthur East
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: To drive the cost competitiveness, yes, there are certain parts of the business where we need to really focus on  driving the cost competitiveness. And strengthening  our routes to market, we're already seeing examples of that happening and being reflected in the order book in our  Power Systems business.

texts.speaker: David Perry
texts.profession: JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: Secondly, as a broader question, if I take the shorter-cycle businesses, and I would include in that the oil and gas  piece of Marine, a lot of what Tognum does and business jets, it feels like the world has changed quite a bit since  November 2015, for the worse in all those markets. texts.speaker: David Smith

texts.text: In terms of the macro environment, I would agree with you. texts.speaker: David Smith
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director
texts.text: On your RRPS question, this unfortunately is one that you have to go into a bit more detail because of the mix of  businesses, so some of the shorter-order book and longer-order book contracts. Things like power generation, for instance,  which aren't necessary longer contracts that have replaced some of the governmental business we saw.

texts.speaker: David Smith
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director
texts.text: Power Systems has got an order book over quite a wide variety of end sectors. That area of power generation is  certainly a positive one for us at the moment. So – and as I said, oil and gas is actually quite a small part of their  business at the moment, so the commodity exposure is quite low. So, I think, yes, their absolute number is about  the same, but we are actually quite positive that we'll see some revenue and profit growth in 2016.

texts.profession: Investec Bank Plc (Broker)

texts.speaker: David Smith
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director
texts.text: Y eah. I'd just add. I mean, clearly, the area that we have seen the most pricing pressure was on the A330 CO. And  we talked about that. So, that's clearly an area where we have – but I think on the A350 perspective, Trent 7000, A330neo, I don't see  any evidence of that at the moment.

texts.speaker: David Smith
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director
texts.text: On CARs, so interestingly, the CARs growth last year was a combination of Trent 1000, which is actually about  half of it and a smaller number on XWB and some Trent 7 00, obviously, because of the lower pricing that we got  on the COs coming through. So, we will see, as I think was mentioned on the slide, about the same level of CARs  growth in 2016 of slightly higher. So, it's a combination of higher volume but actually better unit cost, so the two  are beginning to mitigate.

And we're – also, numerous  other examples of what we're doing to leverage our installed base.

texts.profession: Director-Investor Relations, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: So we will benefit from the cycle improving and we will continue to win business as indeed we are winning  business today in adjacent applications and particularly around new technologies, such as all-electric ships. texts.speaker: David Smith
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: For Marine, overall, the outlook has to remain very cautious, with revenue down further in 2017 and losses at a  similar sort of level. We expect that market will continue to feel the impact of low oil prices for some time, and the  general overcapacity in several segments will take time to reach equilibrium. So we're continuing to sustain our  cost reduction program, focused on manufacturing, supply chain, and overhead costs in order to deliver a more  competitive business.

texts.speaker: David Warren Arthur East
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Yeah. The conceptual question about the nuclear reactors, I mean, clearly, Toshiba is a potential partner,  potential customer for our civil business in Nuclear. I think if you  back off it a little bit and say, actually, these really big nuclear projects are quite challenging and they're quite  challenging to finance. And this is one of the reasons why we are keen to promote the small modular alternative.

texts.speaker: David Warren Arthur East
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Yes, there's the technology piece, which is a little bit different. And so, conceptually, it's an opportunity for us, because we can play a larger  role there than we can with just our instrumentation and control and waste management systems around the big  reactors.

texts.speaker: David Warren Arthur East
texts.profession: Chief Executive, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: In fact, when I go around and talked, when I first joined the business, I talked to lots of people around Rolls-Royce  and asked them about what's Rolls-Royce really all about. texts.speaker: David Warren Arthur East
texts.profession: Chief Executive, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: So, for example, in our Power Systems business, there is an awful lot of electrification. texts.speaker: David Warren Arthur East
texts.profession: Chief Executive, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: We take that system expertise in one direction and we map it into a domain expertise from Aerospace in the other  direction. And so, that's what championing electrification is all about. texts.profession: Chief Executive, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc

texts.profession: Chief Executive, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc

texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Looking a little bit further forward, UltraFan. The UltraFan, we had a great year in terms of hitting the milestones  on our UltraFan architecture development. texts.speaker: David Warren Arthur East
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Looking a bit further forward, we said we're championing electrification. That's manifesting itself in a few  electrification programs in aerospace. texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Looking forward for Power Systems, and just coming to that order book point, there's more than a 20% increase  in the order intake year-over-year, better order cover ratio than the prior as well. texts.text: And on the sort of situation in Power Systems, I mean we highlighted a couple of things and Stephen said, 15%  growth last year. texts.speaker: David Warren Arthur East
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc
texts.text: Okay. Volumes of large engines. Look, when we put up our projections of volumes, it is our best estimate at the  time. texts.text: On climate change, I just want to make a couple of points. texts.speaker: Andrew M. Ransom
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rentokil Initial Plc
texts.text: The factors that we believe are relevant to the development of the hygiene market are: changing demographics  and population growth, rising middle classes, an aging population and more women in the workplace, increasing  hygiene compliance and regulation, particularly in areas such as food retail and production, rising consumer  expectations, with businesses much more aware of the risks of poor hygiene standards, the impact of social  media now driving businesses to invest in brand protection, sustainability with clean air a major topic around the  world, but particularly so in Asia, and the importance of brand experience, with organizations investing in the use  of scent and design as they seek to differentiate themselves in the market.

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Rentokil Initial Plc

texts.speaker: Andrew M. Ransom
texts.profession: Chief Executive, Rentokil Initial Plc
texts.text: How much of that is correlated to the hot weather? texts.profession: Chief Executive, Rentokil Initial Plc

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: What else for the highlights in the first quarter of 2010? On April 14, we commissioned the new  CCGT in Lingen. This is the first large generation project of our total program of approximately 12  gigawatt of gas and coal-fired power plant that we will bring online by 2013. Also in April, we took a  further step according to our motto, the energy to lead. RWE Innogy started a new cooperation with  26 municipal utilities and regional electricity companies. This joint venture is called Green GECCO.  It will invest approximately €1 billion in renewable projects by 2020. The first projects are already  underway.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Last weekend, we signed an agreement with E.ON to purchase 4.8 terawatt hours generation rights  from their decommissioned Stade nuclear power station for our Biblis A nuclear plant. With this, we  are making sure a point of no return is not reached before the energy plan and the reversal of the  nuclear phase-out scheme have been presented by the government. With the good start to the  year, we are confident that we will achieve our set of targets for 2010 despite some uncertainties,  especially in the gas market.       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: On to our divisional performance, let me start with RWE Power. Its operating result improved by  11%. Slide 5 gives you the individual value drivers as usual. Since the beginning of the year, we  have included the regular adjustment of nuclear and mining provisions, the so-called [inaudible] in  the operating result, which is in line with the industry standard. In the past, it was part of the non- operating result. We have not adjusted the previous year’s figures. The effect in Q1 this year was  plus €51 million.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: As the provisions were originally built within the operating result, there is no reason to exclude the  reg adjustments from this line. However, there is only one item with respect to nuclear and mining  provisions. In total, we had a negative impact of minus €103 million in Q1 compared to the previous  year. Extraordinary items in the future however would of course be reported as part of the non- operating result. We expect the positive trend at RWE Power to continue during the rest of 2010.  The high availability of our Biblis nuclear power plant and lower costs for fuel and CO2 emission  certificates will be the main reasons for this.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Let’s have a quick look at the sketches of our German forward selling. We have sold for 2010 more  than 90%. We have sold for 2011 more than 80%, for 2012, more than 30% and we have started  selling volumes for 2013. Average realized prices are still above €6 per megawatt hour, which in  principle corresponds to a mix of approximately a 90% base and 10% peak. However, we already  see that this split might develop towards 80% to 20% or even above in the future, due to our  changing power plant portfolio and the increase in renewables in the overall system.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Our sales and distribution network business area closed up 2%. The cold weather supported our  gas sales volumes. This was offset by low electricity margins. The German Distribution Grid  business was hit by the refunding of excess proceeds, the Mehrerlösabschöpfung. I explained the  background in February.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: On the other hand, the cold weather led to lower maintenance work and hence reduced  maintenance costs. This will lead to increased activities and costs in the rest of the year. For 2010,  we expect the operating result to be up. This will be mainly due to improved earnings in the  electricity and gas sales business, but/or because of the absence of one-off costs caused by  negative gas-to-oil spreads incurred in 2009. In the distribution grid business, we expect that a  negative impact of refunding excess proceeds will be partly compensated for by lower costs for grid  losses.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Now onto our new Netherlands/Belgium division. The numbers for 2010 are substantially affected  by consolidation effects. Let me remind you of the most important ones. The €100 million operating  result in Q4 last year included €141 million from Essent and 39 million from RWE Energy  Nederland, REN. The Q4 2009 figure for REN was disproportionately high and may not be  extrapolated for full year. Essent itself in 2009 still included the wind and the trading activities.  Since January of this year, we have been reporting the wind activities within the renewables  division and the trading – as part of the trading in a midstream division. Since REN is now fully       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The performance of the Netherlands/Belgium division in Q1 was supported by higher gas sales due  to the cold weather. Please don’t extrapolate Q1 for the full year. Essent’s profit was  disproportionately high. In the first quarter, Essent typically counts for more than half of a full year’s  earnings. In addition, we expect lower generation spreads for the rest of the year, but due to the  consolidation effect, the division is expected to be significantly above last year.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Let me continue with RWE npower. Its operating result improved by 18%, adjusted for FX effect, it  was by 15%. Earnings in our retail business were the main driver for the improved performance.  Margins in our gas business improved on the back of lower purchase costs. As we lowered our gas  tariffs at the end of March this year, this trend will not be sustainable for the rest of the year. On the  other hand, we suffered from declining electricity margins after our price cut in March last year.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The performance of our generation business was down, driven by reduced spreads and lower  income from the short-term markets, while its commercial availability remained high. In contrast,  costs for purchasing CO2 certificates declined by approximately €20 million due to fuel switch from  hard coal to gas. We expect that lower spreads will also influence the performance of our  generation business for 2010 as a whole. This will be partly offset by the commissioning of our new  power plant at Staythorpe in the second half of 2010. On the other hand, we will digest the first  upfront costs of our U.K. nuclear program.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We expect retail earnings to benefit from slightly lower purchasing costs, but in this fiercely  competitive market, this will be offset to a large extent by the electricity and gas price reductions  implemented in March last year and March this year, respectively. In addition, we expect burdens  from higher electricity network charges. Our focus will remain on efficiencies to ensure a  competitive cost base. The €100 million program initiated last year will be turned into a sustainable  improvement and we are working on additional measures. Overall, we should see a moderate  increase in RWE npower’s operating result.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Operating earnings at our Central & Eastern Europe division climbed by 39%. One major factor for  improved margins in our Czech gas sales business, mainly since Q4 last year. But this made up for  lower margins in earlier periods. On the other hand, trend of revenues and volumes were lower. In  addition, we had a positive contribution from improved electricity sales margins in Hungary and  Poland. This was supported by positive FX effects.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We anticipate that earnings generated by this division would decline this year. And the main reason  is that margins in our Czech gas sales business, as well as in the Hungarian electricity sales and  generation business, are expected to come down again. On the other hand, we will see higher  earnings contributions from our regional Czech gas grid business.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Our renewables division posted a steep increase in operating result of 50% of it coming from a very  low bases. The first-time consolidation of the Essent wind assets contributed €6 million to earnings.  This is less then originally expected, as Germany and the Netherlands had a quarter with  disappointing very low wind levels due to the cold winter. The first time consolidation of Danta de  Energias in Spain in May last year, as well as the commissioning of the 90 MW Rhyl Flats wind  farm late last year also had a positive effect on our earnings.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Upfront costs for our large investment programs still dampened the development of Energy’s  operating result. As regards 2010, we are quite positive for RWE Energy. We will see further results  of our growth investment program. But upfront costs for our projects are still offsetting most of this.  In addition, Energy will benefit from the first time consolidation of Essent’s wind activities. The  earnings improvement will accelerate in the coming years, as you know.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 4 Upstream Gas & Oil reported a 20% increase in operating earnings. This is mainly a result of higher  oil prices, as well as lower royalties and production costs in the drilling business. In addition,  exploration costs in North Africa were down. On the other hand, they have suffered from lower gas  prices and production volumes. Compared to the very weak 2009, we see significant upside  potential for 2010. RWE Dea expects to see improved oil prices, this will be partly offset by lower  gas prices and volumes.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Operating results in our Trading/Gas Midstream division fell by 76%. Please bear in mind that the  first quarter of last year was extraordinarily high. The mark-to-market performance of the trading  business was as good as last year. On top of this, we benefited from the first time consolidation of  the Essent trading activities. They contributed €86 million in Q1 this year. This is a  disproportionately high number and may not be extrapolated for the full year.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The steep decline is mainly related to our supply activities. This is because of two major effects.  First, in 2009, the supply business realizes an extraordinarily high profit in the first quarter. Second,  the fall in gas market prices led to a write-down of our Czech gas storage inventories. In 2010, we  expect the division to close significantly below the previous year’s record level, despite the  integrations of Essent’s trading activities. Though our trading margins compared to the  extraordinarily high level in 2009, and the absence of the special items in 2009 are the major  reasons.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In Gas Midstream, we are exposed to risks from oil-indexed gas contracts. You know our gas  position from our February presentation. [inaudible], we see Trading/Gas Midstream to show a  positive gas margin for 2010, despite negative effects from the gas-to-oil spread. On the other  hand, we still see some various prospects regarding the gas market for the mid-to longer term. We  see that the Czech gas market becomes more competitive, which might lead to further burdens for  future years. However, as outlined in February, we actively used the given instruments in our  contract to mitigate this asset.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The split of non-operating results looks a bit different than in the past. To further increase  transparency, there’s a new line for the earnings impact of commodity derivatives. We reported this  number last year as part of restructuring, other, as you may remember. These are typically effects  stemming from derivative hedges for gas forward sales in our sales and distribution business area  and Trading/Gas Midstream division.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: While the derivative has to be valued mark-to-market, the underlying business transaction is still  accounted for our own use. Since the beginning of the year, there’s also been additional impact  from the German gas portfolio. The amount and liquidity in the gas market allows us to actively  manage our purchase contracts and thereby make use of opportunities and limit associated risks.  Accordingly, in 2010, we started accounting for these contracts at fair value instead of on use. All  the numbers we shown in this slide are purely timing differences.
