Just sort of update  on your latest feeling around the nuclear life extension debate and what’s happening and what  might happen in the next few weeks and months? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Dr. Rolf Pohlig>: Please understand I will not give you that detail, I would not say something  extra. But we still recover that – what we did not get during the course of some part of last year.  With respect to nuclear, yeah, of course there was some kind of disappointment. But I think we  have seen this ups and downs over the last six or seven months. I think we were all a little bit  enthusiastic on the morning after the general election in September. Monday morning this week, we       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 8 were a little bit disillusioned. But I think we still have a lot to do on this, but we are still working on  this and we are still rely on what the coalition parties to the Berlin government have agreed upon in  September, October last year. That means to broker a nuclear lifetime extension within the great –  larger context of a new energy policy for Germany overall.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: I know that some people are making the argument that there is a necessity that not only the lower  house of the Berlin Parliament, i.e. the Bundestag, but also the upper house, Bundesrat, should  approve the lifetime extension and based on the North Rhine-Westphalia election, the Berlin  government does not have any more of a majority in the Bundesrat. However, that is still not that  crystal clear. I think that is our analysis that there are ways to have a lifetime extension of nuclear  power stations without needing the approval by the Bundesrat. So technically, that should be still  open, but it’s still hard work to work on that.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Dr. Rolf Pohlig>: To be very frank, no, because there are so many factors impacting that. I  think it’s quite obvious, yes, we made some extra money in the gas sales business, especially to  retail customers, especially in the situation where we could buy additional gas volumes at relatively  low prices in the wholesale market. Yes, that is the case and that is the case, I think, at most of our  retail gas business in the several countries in which are involved.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: On the other side, I’ve also mentioned that, that same harsh winter meant that we had a stable area  of high pressure in the Northern European weather system, which at the same time, meant that,  there was only very low wind. So we had a real dampening effect on the wind business at Energy.  And I mentioned that this was also really a disappointment. I think it was a 30 years low in wind in  Northern Europe. Quite in contrast to Southern Europe, where in Spain, there was much more wind  than usual. So I’m not in a position to give you a real hard figure on that. Nobody can tell me what  is the impact of weather at the spot market prices on power and other commodities and I’m not in a  position. Other people might be in a position, I am not in that position.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q>: Yeah. Good afternoon. The first question is on the efficiency enhancement and cost  reductions. You aim at efficiency enhancement amounting to 700 million in the current fiscal year,  which part of that have you been able to achieve in the first quarter and how does the breakdown in  terms of the divisions is looking like? Secondly, on CO2 certificates, would you please shed some  light on your expectations of the price development in the mid term and are you currently already  buying your two certificates for the third ETS phase or are you considering to do so in the short  term?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Dr. Rolf Pohlig>: I will not share with you in detail our price expectations for CO2. But I think  we have told market for some time that gas, as you just assumed, we are buying CO2 certificates  beyond our normal hedging pattern for the third compliance period as – at prevailing current prices       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 9 are attractive for this purpose. But please understand that we will not share in more detail our price  expectations for CO2 in the future.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: So what I can tell you, share with you is that we are still on track to achieve this goal for the full  year. This as you most likely remember, does include a lot of efficiency enhancement in our grid  business, but also the availability of our power stations in Germany and abroad and all that adds up  then to this efficiency enhancement process. So it’s not purely a cost reduction program. It’s at the  same time making some investments to increase the availability of our power stations.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q>: Thank you, good afternoon. First question, please can you quantify the positive impact of the  deal with E.ON on the nuclear, because I assume it will boost your operating profit in 2010  compared to your initial guidance, even if it may have negative impact at the EPS level? And  second point, question on the change in the way you account for the changes in nuclear and mining  position. Can you indicate an estimate of by how much your operating income will be revised,  would you boost it by this on the full year 2010 level, is it 1, 2%? Can you confirm this part of your  5% growth guidance? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: With respect to Stade, the generation rights we bought from E.ON, this will not have a significant  impact on our earnings for this year. You see, we did this transaction not to maximize profits. Of  course, we are doing all this to maximize profit. But what was much more important for us here is  that we will not reach this point of no return with respect to our Biblis A power station before the  government has made up a final presentation of their new energy policy, including nuclear lifetime  extension. So that is much more important than a couple of millions.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: So, I think that has proven perfectly correct and that has helped. And in addition to that, the cold  weather in the first quarter helped, because that’s led to a nice increase in the gas retail business of  Essent in the first quarter.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Vincent De Blic>: Two questions, please, on RWE Power. You don’t seem to have hedged a  lot more in the Q1 for 2012 according to your slide. I was just wondering whether you could share  some thoughts on the latest development in the power price? And whether you have seen any       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: With respect to 2012, yes, overall, I think we’re all excited that prices increased over the last  several weeks after we have assumed a significant downturn in prices until the end of the first  quarter. So that is helpful. With respect to customer behavior, I’m not aware about any significant  change in customer behavior – in looking for longer-term contracts. And by the way, you know that  by far, the bulk of these forward sales is done by the power market and not with individual  customers.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Ashley Thomas>: I’ve got a question on upstream, where you are now guiding for gas  volumes to be down year-on-year. So I just wanted to confirm that you’re still comfortable with the  guidance given in January that total production volumes would increase in 2010? And if not, could  you perhaps elaborate on what the issues on gas are, is it focused on full depletion or is it on new  production ramp up?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Dr. Rolf Pohlig>: Oh, I think the liquefaction ramp up, that issue we had last year, I think that  was in Norway that case, but I think that has been solved. I am thinking about whether it is in the  North Sea, I think that could – we have to double check this. I have it not in my mind. Can you give  us a minute, we will come back in a minute to that.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q>: Hi, good afternoon. I have a question on the nuclear extensions. Could you remind us if your  medium-term guidance assumes nuclear extensions for Biblis? Also, could you also guide us  whether similar to the Stade transaction, are there other opportunities to buy extra hours? And like  in 2009, would you consider putting the plant on an extended maintenance to buy more time?  Thank you.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q>: And any possibility of buying hours from another nuclear plant for Biblis B?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Dr. Rolf Pohlig>: What I said is that buying generation rights is important for us from a  strategic point of view, to still have the option of – technically the option for making use of lifetime       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 13 extension. But otherwise, the sub-generation rights have a price and that price is connected to the  market price of power. So I think it is not a sustainable business in itself to buy generation rights  from other people, irrespective of whether other people would be prepared to sell.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q>: Hi, good afternoon. Just with your kind of apparently negative free cash flow and also given  your guidance, it seems that your credit ratios will still be fairly stretched with the Moody’s rating.  What actions are you prepared to take to defend that rating? And then secondly, could you tell us  how much capital you have invested in clean development mechanism projects? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And the second is with this commissioning now the Lingen plant. Just in terms of competitiveness  of this plant in the market, are you able to give us an idea at least if you are in the position to  purchase a significant part of the gas needs in the spot market for this or do you have to revert to  long-term contracts for these plans?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Dr. Rolf Pohlig>: No, I think it’s important to have in mind that the original business idea for  Lingen was to buy gas in the spot market and make use of that relatively cheap gas then to  produce peak power. But remember that Lingen is in the unique situation that five major gas  pipelines are crossing nearby and enough storage facilities are available. So that is the very idea,  but how successful that will be, we will see then over the next several months. You remember that  it is just in the process of being technically and commercially in operation. With respect to the  refunding of the excess, I think we said that we will do it relatively short timeframe. I think you can  expect that the bulk of that will be done within two years.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Tanja Markloff>: Yeah, good afternoon. I have a short follow-up question on Lueder’s  question on the Essent generation margins. I would like to ask whether you sell power from Essent  on the more short-term basis compared to the way you sell power in your German portfolio?

file: RWE - Q1 2011 Earnings Call 12May2011 900 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 12-May-11.pdf

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Stephan Lowis, Vice President, Investor Relations  Thanks. Good afternoon ladies and gentlemen, and welcome to our conference call. We are living  in turbulent times. After the domestic event in Japan, the public debate about nuclear energy in  Germany is dominated by motions rather than facts. Therefore let’s turn to facts with our Q1  conference call. And Rolf over to you.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Rolf Pohlig, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer  Thank you, Stephan. We are indeed living in turbulent times. Last February, I was discussing with  you the four major challenges for German utilities – that is, low commodity prices for Germany, the  fuel tax, negative gas storage spreads and tighter CO2 regime from 2013 onwards.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: These challenges are still relevant. However, on top of this, we have a new debate about the future  of Germany’s nuclear power plants. More about that in a minute.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Let me first begin with the positive aspects of Q1 2011. Better [indiscernible] (0:01:15). As we  expected, EBITDA, operating result, and recurrent net income couldn’t match the record high  numbers of the previous year. The strong cash flow as well as the successful disposal of  Thyssengas and our stake in the Rostock hard coal power plant were the main reasons why we  could reduce our net debt to €27.5 billion.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Despite the negative impact from the three-month nuclear moratorium in Germany, we confirmed  the guidance we gave in February. But please let me emphasize, at the current point in time, we  can only comment including the effect of the three-month moratorium. We will have to reassess our  expectations especially in case of further burdens depending on the decisions of the German  government.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The earnings declines we recorded in Q1 this year is less than we expect for the rest of the year.  This is based on three main reasons. Firstly, performance in our German generation business will  not show the same strength as we have seen in Q1. Secondly, our UK business had a  disproportionately successful first quarter. And thirdly, we expect further burdens in our Trading  /Gas Midstream division mainly driven by the negative gas storage spread.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Before I guide you through the Q1 numbers, let me give you a brief overview of where we stand  with regards to the moratorium for the nuclear safety review in this country. This should help you to  get a better understanding of the current political situation in Germany. Altogether, five stages have  to be gone through before we see decisions on future energy policies in Germany.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Slide four gives you the details of this process and the major milestones. By mid-June, the  government wants to implement a new framework for nuclear energy in Germany. Within this  process, the government has set up an Ethics Commission to evaluate the role of nuclear energy in  our society as well as transition to new energy and how much risk the German public is willing to  accept.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 2 The parameters of this very narrow time [indiscernible] (0:03:43) is extremely ambitious so that  some delays might occur. As you know, we have filed a suit against the forced interim  decommissioning of our biggest power stations. Let me once again emphasize that we don’t want  to cause a confrontation with the German government. We’re open to any kind of discussion, but  we think it’s important to clarify whether the order of the Hessian authorities to shutdown was based  on valid legal grounds.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Before I provide you with more details on the performance of each of our divisions, let me give you  a brief overview of the group’s key performance indicators. External revenue was up 3% among  other things because of higher oil prices.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: EBITDA and operating result were down 4% and 5% respectively. This is mainly due to the  performance of our Trading/Gas Midstream division. The non-operating result improved as a result  of having higher capital gains from the sale of assets and the lower burden from the earnings  impact of commodity derivatives.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Now, on to our divisional performance, starting with RWE Power. Its operating result improved by  2%. Slide six gives you the individual value drivers. Performance of plus 2% in Q1 was much better  than our expectation for full fiscal year 2011. This is mainly due to the fact that we have not yet  been burdened by the nuclear fuel tax, which we expect to reach €300 million to €400 million in  2011.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In addition, we expect higher fixed operating and maintenance costs, which were another major  issue in Q1 and higher depreciation charges associated with the commissioning of our new lignite  plant in Neurath later this year. Please bear in mind that there is still a lot of uncertainty against the  backdrop of the current nuclear moratorium.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Chart seven gives you our usual update of the hedge position of our German electricity generation.  At the end of March, we have sold more than 90% for 2011, more than 70% for 2012 and more  than 20% for 2013. In other words, the output position for the year 2012 was already sold before  the strong increase in electricity prices resulting from the moratorium on nuclear power plants in  Germany.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: A large portion of the output position for 2013 was also sold. Therefore, we received a full positive  impact from higher electricity prices in the year 2014 and thereafter if the current price level  prevails.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Our Sales and Distribution Network business area closed 9% below the previous year. This is  mainly due to the development in our distribution network business. Normalized weather conditions  led to lower volumes, especially in the gas segment. Furthermore, higher burdens resulting from  the feed in of renewable energy could not yet be passed on completely to the transmission  operators.       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: However, income from investments improved and cost for refunding excess proceeds were lower  than last year. Earnings in our sales business declined mainly due to lower gas volumes on the  back of normalized weather conditions. Also for full fiscal year 2011, we expect the operating result  to fall below the previous year. This is mainly a result of higher OpEx for improving the quality of  our distribution network business. The cost for refunding excess proceeds will be slightly lower than  in 2010. For the sales business, we expect lower gas volumes assuming normalized weather  conditions. Last year, we benefited from a colder-than-average winter.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Now on to our Netherlands/Belgium division. The numbers for 2011 are substantially affected as we  now report part of the gas midstream business in Trading/Gas Midstream. In addition, the division  recorded lower gas margins as a result of normalized weather conditions. Furthermore, the  performance was negatively affected by decline in generation margins. However, the division  benefited from efficiency improvements and synergies from the integration of Essent into the RWE  Group. The effects we had Q1 will also drive down fiscal year 2011 significantly.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The performance of our generation business was supported by higher production volumes due to  our new CCGT at Staythorpe and a positive one-off impact following the settlement of claims  relating to major investment projects.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Operating earnings in our Central Eastern and South Eastern Europe division were nearly on par  with the last year’s record figure. Adjusted ForEx effect, the division was down 5%. Earnings  suffered from slightly lower income in our Hungarian business and weather induced lower gas sales  in the Czech Republic. This was partly compensated for by a high income in our Czech gas  transport business.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: For 2011, we expect the operating results to be down significantly year-on-year compared to the  exceptionally high number in 2010. In the Czech Republic, we expect gas sales margins to come  down. The contribution from our Hungarian electricity activities is also expected to fall behind last  year’s level. However, we expect to see higher electricity network margins in Poland.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The operating result of our US division more than doubled to €68 million. Increased earnings were  partly driven by our growth CapEx program and improved electricity prices. In addition, we received  liquidated damages relating to the Greater Gabbard project. However, the liquidated damages  replaced lost revenues and profits due to delays in commissioning.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Upfront cost for large investment program, including higher staff costs are still dampening Innogy’s  operating result. For 2011, we expect RWE Innogy to post a strong earnings increase. We will see  further results of our expansion program. Higher electricity prices will have a positive impact as  well.       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In addition, we assume improved wind levels compared to the very weak conditions in 2010,  although still not returning to normal levels. Upfront costs for projects including our staff costs are  still offsetting some of the positive effects.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Upstream Gas & Oil reported a 38% increase in operating earnings. The main positive factors were  rising oil and gas prices, higher oil production volumes and lower exploration expenditures.  However, gas production was down. In addition, production costs increased and royalties in the  German gas business were higher. We expect the earnings trend of Q1 to continue during the rest  of the year. Therefore, we see significant further upside potential for full fiscal 2011.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The operating result in our Trading/Gas Midstream division turned into a significantly negative  number in the first quarter of 2011. On the one hand, the developments in our trading business  suffered from the unforeseen effects on commodity prices caused by the events in Japan and  Northern Africa. In addition, our supply business is under pressure from the negative gas storage  spread. From our February conference that we are in negotiations with all our suppliers and don’t  expect major solutions in 2011. On the other hand, the division benefited from gas midstream  margins, which have previously been reported in the Netherlands/Belgium division.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Ladies and gentlemen, our guidance for 2011 remains unchanged. I already mentioned that this  statement can only take into consideration the current status of the German nuclear moratorium.  The final outcome is still unclear and it is not unlikely that further short-term burdens might result  from political decisions relating to the future of nuclear energy in this country.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Although from a macroeconomic point a view, the politically motivated phase-out of nuclear energy  is a disadvantage for German industry, it still has to be seen how utilities will be affected. On the  one hand, there will be lost margins, although these margins had already been squeezed by the  nuclear fuel tax and required investments for the lifetime extension. On the other hand, the  tightness of generation capacity has led and will lead to rising electricity prices, which increases the  value of the residual generation fleet, especially our lignite plants.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And the second thing is there again, following what your friends said yesterday, there was a slightly  more positive message coming out of E.ON on the gas contracts, some form of renegotiation and a  feeling that maybe you could actually reach some form of agreement at least on a temporary basis  by the end of the year. Should this optimism as well apply to you at the current stage of your  negotiations?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: With respect to gas, I have no insight what our Düsseldorf based friends are doing. But with respect  to ourselves, I can only tell you that we are not looking for temporary solutions, but that we are  more looking for longer-term and permanent and structural solutions. And insofar our current  forecast does, as we told you already in February, not include any solutions in the current fiscal  year 2011, but only in the following years.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Patrick Hummel>: Excuse me. Yeah, it’s Patrick. Sorry for that. Two questions, please, also  on nuclear and gas. On nuclear, could you maybe elaborate a bit if Biblis has to kept shut or has to  be mothballed what the earnings burden would be on the provisioning side, or extra costs occurring  regarding the decommissioning that may have not been provisioned yet?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And a second question, also on gas, just to understand your renegotiation strategy. I mean it  seems your competitors are doing a two-way approach with a quick fix, which they apparently have  been partially successful with, plus a structural ongoing renegotiation. You’re telling us – you’re just  looking for a structural adjustment, but if you can have both don’t you lose money in the meantime  compared to what your competitors are doing? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: No, I think, we would not lose any money in the meantime. We would later on  get a higher repayment from the other sides. So I think that is not the issue. With respect to Biblis, I  think the main issue you should have in mind is that in case the lifetime extension would finally be  cancelled then we would have to adjust the existing provisions simply due to the timing affects, via  discounting these provisions because then actual decommissioning would start earlier and that  would then have an impact on the provisions. But with respect to figures, it’s too early. We will still  have to see the outcome of the government debates and decisions.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Lueder Schumacher>: Good afternoon, two questions. One is just on the legal challenge  you have against the costs of the moratorium and, I suppose, whatever other nuclear issues there  to come. Can you run us through the process? Is it a bit like [indiscernible] (0:24:50) where you got  – in the end maybe end up with a theoretical claim that you theoretically can – I don’t know, may or  may not get in years to come? Or would it actually stop any implementation of what the government  intends to do? Just if you could shed some light on this whole legal process.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 8 that you’ve sold somewhat above 20% of your 2013 power. I just wondered if you could give us an  indication in terawatt hours of how much more 2013 power there remains to be sold, particularly  outright power.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And then, secondly, on the potential impact going forwards of a permanent shutdown of the Biblis  plant from 2011 onwards. If we had a scenario where there was no compensation, no change in the  methodology that the German government was using in respect of the nuclear tax, what would you  have to do in respect of your €8 billion disposal program in order to meet the balance sheet targets  that you have? And would there be any risk that you might ultimately have to seek recourse to  equity, which, of course, you’ve dismissed in the past? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: With respect to the first question that is highly depending on the question what  further nuclear volumes will be available and that is depending on the outcome of the government  decisions. So, I think we can give you a much clearer answer only when we know the outcome of  that government debate. With respect to the second question, I’m not quite sure whether I got this. I  think – correct me if I’m wrong, Martin but you’re saying, what happens if the nuclear text gets away  to our disposal program?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: Martin, what is important in the context of the government decision to us is, on  the one side exactly as I just described, what will be the lost volumes, but on the other side we will  see what here is the additional price impact on the other side, as I just mentioned. And we have  seen already a significant price impact which will really come through then in our financial figures  starting in 2013 and then the full impact in 2013. But on the other side, there is also debate in this  country about the nuclear fuel tax, and then of course in case we cannot reopen Biblis, and there  would not be anymore the additional retrofit measures necessary. So, only when we know all the  details of the government decision package, then we can give you a more detailed comment, but  you have to have all these factors in mind when, then, making a calculation later on.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: No, that is too simple, because it’s really the balance of the nuclear fuel tax,  retrofit measure and lost volumes and price impact. And only the bottom line of that tells you then  whether it really becomes tougher in immediate years.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Benjamin Leyre>: Yes, thank you, good afternoon. One question, please, on the rating  agencies. I wonder if you could share with us where your conversation stands with rating agencies  and your negative credit watch at the moment. Are you comfortable that the cut of your rating would  be only by one notch? And second point, can you also confirm that you still expect 2012 to be  worse than 2011 at current regulation and given the recent rise in power prices? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: Here the point is that, we confirm the 2011 guidance with the caveat depending  on the further outcome of the government decisions. With respect to 2012 and ‘13, we usually  would update you only in February next year and we only have to see what will be the outcome of  the government decisions on nuclear energy in this country.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Matthias Heck>: Hello. My two questions are, firstly, as far as your 2013 outlook is  concerned. You have mentioned in your closing remarks the increase of power prices and also the  potential absence of the Biblis A plants – Biblis A and B plants, which are probably the most  important changes in your assumptions you took in your 2013 outlook in February. Now what’s  happening to that outlook? Can you confirm that on today’s basis or do you put that under review  again as you did with your initial outlook last summer again already?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Second question is in – also in February you mentioned that around 8 gigawatt of thermal  generation capacity in Germany is out of the money at the level of February market conditions. Now  we have seen a material increase in power prices and also in generation spreads. Could you  please update us here where we stand right now? Do you still expect these 8 gigawatts to be out of  the money right now here, i.e., do power prices have to increase further to keep these plants alive?  Thank you

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: I’m not quite sure if those were actually two questions. I think there were two  complexes with a couple of sub-questions. With respect to the first one, with respect to 2013 as  already mentioned, we usually update you – it’s only in February this year, and if the necessity  would arise to update you in between that can only then be an issue after we know the full effect   of the government decisions. And once again, you have really to have look on the full picture that is  the price impact, that is the nuclear fuel tax, that is retrofit measures and then potential lost  volumes. And it is not that easy calculation as you just are trying to make it.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: With respect to the 8 gigawatts, which we mentioned are close to/or being out of the money. But  first of all, everybody should remind that via the moratorium I think 8.4 gigawatts were forced out of  the system, so that was forced out of the system by the government. I think with respect to the  spreads, we have some more details.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Stephan Lowis>: Just to – with respect to the spread, it depends on what efficiency you  assume, but the spreads – the clean dark spreads in Germany haven’t moved significantly. So they  moved from €3 to €5 to €6, which means the pressure on these old inefficient hard coal plants are  still there.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Matthias Heck>: Okay. So if you assume, potentially, the seven plus one nuclear plants to be  permanently shut down, it could be necessary to keep this 8 gigawatt of older inefficient plants to  keep them alive. In other words, you would expect further power price increase or at least  increases in the clean dark spreads?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: Matthias, I think the market has overall given the answer, the market has led to  increase of power prices as in under forward markets from €52 per megawatt hour, which was the  level before the March 15 decision to €59 almost €60, which is currently the forward prices for 30       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Peter Wirtz>: Hi, good afternoon. I have two questions. The first one is again on nuclear [ph]  provisioning (0:39:14). Yesterday, E.ON was very cautious in terms of permanent shutdowns with  respect to one-off costs to be included in the 2011 figure. So the company has given a very wide  range regarding that subject between €100 million and below €1 billion. You seem to be much more  relaxed. Is it a statement for you to say keep relaxed on that one-off cost here? And a second  question regarding an option to invest in new gas power stations. Is it an option for you, or do we  have to have a new legal framework, which means capacity payments before you can think about  that option?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: With respect to one-off costs, there is a broad potential spectrum, and  predominantly is an issue of adjusting the decommissioning provisions, and then via the  discounting affect that might then have an impact. And that is not only referring to potential nuclear  power stations to be shut down relatively shortly, but also cancelling lifetime extension has an  impact on the present value of the decommissioning provisions. So one has to have really then an  understanding of the details of the government decisions.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: With respect to new gas, I think we have total market for some time that based on our calculation  the new entrant power price for a new gas-fired station is in the €80 per megawatt hour range. So  totally if somebody is convinced or is persuaded that in longer-term they will see on a permanent  basis also power price in excess of €80, it makes sense for him or her to take a fine investment  decision on gas.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Alexander Karnick>: Yes, hi. Good Afternoon. Alex Karnick, Deutsche Bank. Just two  questions. In your Q1 statement, you mentioned several times in various regions increasing  competitive pressure in the gas resale market, I think Germany, Eastern Europe  – basically just a  “reflection”, just a reflection of your less competitive pricing at the moment where the spot? And       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: With respect to the competitive situation in the gas resale business, I think we  also mentioned that in Germany we could actually increase the number of residential customers in  the gas sector, but I think overall it’s fair to say that new entrants, which rely only on purchases in  the gas wholesale market, have some advantage compared to people who have also the burden –  at least the current burden of oil-indexed contracts. That may be one reason for that.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: With respect to the disposal program, I think nothing what I can really comment in detail. I think it’s  well known in the public that we are prepared to sell our 25% stake in Berlin waterworks to the city  of Berlin, but of course not at any price. And also is the rumor that we are in talks with institutional  investors so that they will become shareholders in our high-voltage, power transportation business  in Germany to bear the burden of all the necessary investments to upgrade the German high- voltage system. That’s the only comments I can make today.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Ingo Becker>: Yes, thank you. Good afternoon. I had a question on the system. The  chairman [indiscernible] (0:44:05) decision after Fukushima was pretty quick in announcing that  they think they can – the system can cope with the moratorium simply buying increasing loads on  the prevailing fossil fleet.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And you’ve been mentioning the higher level of imports here to date. I was wondering what your  view is how the system from here and going forward and also under the assumption that the  moratorium plants remain shut for good would cope with [indiscernible] (0:44:30) say, for the next  two years? Ongoing high imports, or do you think that, given the existing capacity and the capacity  with commission for the next two years and others would basically be higher fossil-fired output,  keep the system in balance?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And another question in general would be, looking beyond that, after even yesterday and also  looking forward what you might say on that. How do you think the German system should develop,  given that we decide to exit nuclear here?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: Let me start with the, is there enough capacity available. Let me start with one  remark. I have in the standard presentation why I tried to educate people about the load  development during the course of the year. And I usually tell people that in the month of May and  early June, we see lowest demand in the country. So I think the real test will not be May, June, but  in November, December, January this year, and we will have to see what will happen then. In the  short run, the system could cope with that via more fossil at power stations being in the money and  being in the system and also with higher importations.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: But to give you the figure, the overall installed capacity in this country by late last year was 453  gigawatts. Out of that, there is a significant portion of photovoltaic meanwhile, 17 gigawatts; winds,  about 28 gigawatts; biomass, 4 gigawatts; Hydro, 4 gigawatts; comp storage, 5 gigawatts. So  conventional nuclear capacity is 95 gigawatts. But out of these 153, we subtract or the unsecured  capacity, and that is almost all – well, it’s 100% of photovoltaic. It’s I think 90% or so of winds. It’s  some portion of Hydro, and of course also of conventional nuclear capacity. The secured installed       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 13 capacity is not 153 but only 97. And out of this 97, typically 7 gigawatts needed for the balancing  market.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: So before the moratorium nuclear shutdown, the country overall had roughly 90 gigawatts secured  store capacity. Minus the 8.4 gigawatts which were affected by the moratorium, leads to a secured  available capacity of roughly 80 gigawatts. The peak demand in this country is – sorry 82 gigawatts,  the peak demand in this country is 80 gigawatts. So let’s see what will happen over the further  course of this year, and to what extent imports can then really make up for it.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: By the way, when making this argument, we are relying on the assumption that there’s already a  European-wide copper plate available. And I think, meanwhile, people are discovering that this is  not the case, that we have also some good issues when we are reshuffling the generation portfolio  in this country.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Ingo Becker>: And your view on how the system should be developed, having – if we have to  accept that nuclear now greater will phase-out, what kind of technologies or additional measures  would you want to see being developed?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: At this point in time, I have no definitive answer to that. I have only given the  remark or made the remark that for gas fired power stations and lot of people assuming that gas  fired power stations could make up of this difference or the shortfall, there is a need for our  wholesale power prices in excess of €80 per megawatt hour. So currently there is no incentives to  build these power stations even if they are physically needed.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And then the second question relates to your carbon management program that you set out a year  or so ago. Some of the physical measures in there are related to extending the lives of Biblis A and  Biblis B. And from memory, they were a reasonably material piece of that strategy. I know that you  don’t have clarity as to what will happen to the lifetime of those assets. But as you sit and work  through that strategy today, how would you kind of manage for the loss of the lifetime extensions?  And what other measures could you take to mitigate your carbon exposure?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: Perhaps Stephan will then, in a minute, take the first question that is with  respect to – are there any further delays in the power plant portfolio, which we have under  construction. With respect to carbon management, that’s absolutely right, what you just mentioned  that one the assumptions in the program, which we communicate to the market was nuclear lifetime  extension. But I think with respect to what is needed to adjust that overall program, we’ll really have  to understand the details of any government decision.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And that is not only of Biblis A and/or B but it’s also a question to what extend we can use our other  nuclear power station, and also to what extend other people can use their nuclear power station,  because as you all know that has an impact then also on CO2 prices. And the argument we made  in the past that our average CO2 intensity was already below the marginal CO2 intensity of the       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 14 system, we have then to update that calculation whether it’s still valid then in this potentially almost  likely changed environment.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Stephan Lowis>: Coming to your second question, on this – are we on schedule. I would say  generally, yes. As you would know, we have in our company presentation a slide which gives the  overview about the conventional power plant new-build program. The next one – the next plant is  the BoA plant, which the first part of this will be online in June this year. And then, the total BoA will  be in January 2012. The online will hit slightly later than we indicated on the chart. And also  Eemshaven is indicated to be fully online in 2014, and that is also a slightly later we indicated that  on the chart with only one part of that, but it seems to be that the full plant is fully available in 2014.  So there are some slight delays, but for 90% we are on schedule here.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Vincent De Blic>: Yes, good afternoon. My first question is on your hedging ratios. I’m not  too sure I understood what you said in your introduction. But could you give us the percentage for  outright power. I mean, nuclear and lignite for both 2012 and 2013, or I guess based on the current  regulatory environment for nuclear? That’s the first question.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And the second one, you mentioned that what happened in prices because of the moratorium was  good for lignite, which is clear. What do you see as the long-term prospects for this fuel in  Germany, given the CO2 targets for 2020, which would become even more stretched without some  of the current nuclear fleet? Thank you, very much.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: Once again, I will start with the second question, and Stephan will then take up  the first question. Yes, overall, we think that the position for lignite has improved by this  environment, because we have seen an increase in power prices. Yes, we have also seen an  increase in CO2 prices, but by far not in let’s say magnitude, so the competitive position of lignite  as a baseload fuel has improved, and we also expect this to continue beyond 2020. With respect to  the hedge ratios, Stephan.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 15 the nuclear part and then the lignite part. So that gives you an indication that the nuclear part is  more or less sold, and then we are now in 2013 selling the lignite part of all production.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Vincent De Blic>: Okay. So it’s nuclear, lignite, then spread here.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Tanja Markloff>: Yes, good afternoon. I have one question on arbitration. I thought you could  give us an idea of the timeframe when we could expect first news flow on the outcome of any of  your arbitration cases, and the gas contract arbitration. And the second would be on the  Netherlands-Belgium Division, whether you could give us an idea how large the consolidation effect  was of the gas midstream business.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: I think volatility is actually loved by our traders, but what we have seen in  Northern Africa, and especially then after a decision by the German government on the nuclear  situation in this country and also some increase in gas demand for Japan, that was a real event risk  and that was not foreseen. So volatility itself is good for the trading business, but not to say events  driven. And with respect to the lawsuit, if at the very end so the court in this country decide that the  decision by the government had no valid legal basis, then of course we can look getting  compensation for the damages we had based on this behavior by the Hessian administration.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: You see, last year, we had also an adjustment of the nuclear decommissioning provisions, because  we could, via the discounting impact, lower some of the nuclear decommission provisions. And that  has not been adjusted for in your account net income. And so far, from today’s perspective, I would  not see that it is adjusted for when we are making the calculation for the current net income. But  really have to see what are the ingredients may be in the government package.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Andreas Thielen>: Yes, just one follow-up. You were pointing to the price levels which are  needed for gas. Obviously, at the moment, the market is not giving this price signal. Are you aware       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 17 of any discussion for let’s say renewed subsidies on gas business, as on the political side everyone  seems to point to the necessity and the wish to expand gas generation in Germany again?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: With respect to the levy I think, not only we but the industry, the nuclear  industry overall has taken a position that the levy was based exclusively on nuclear lifetime  extension, and to the extent there is no lifetime extension, there is no room for any levy. And  perhaps you remember that based on this, the four of us, the four nuclear operators, decided to  stop any prepayments in this new energy fund, which is an element of this contractually agreed  upon levy. With respect to fuel tax, I remember that in late summer last year, when the government  started to debate about lifetime extension, the government on the one side mentioned that the fuel  tax is a separate law, separate fund on lifetime extension law. On the other side, it was also  communicated that there is a political connect between the nuclear fuel tax and lifetime extension.  So to the extent that there is no lifetime extension any more, then there shouldn’t be any room for  nuclear fuel tax. But we have to see what will be the outcome of the government debate.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: The short-term burdens, that is relatively easy. Biblis B was planned to resume  operation by May 22. So if the moratorium will then lead into permanent shutdown of Biblis B, we  would lose the volumes for Biblis B in the second half of this year. In addition to that, we might then  see an adjustment of decommissioning provisions, and that really depends on further details of the  government decision.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Please bear in mind that our results in 2011 were heavily affected by the events at Fukushima and the following U- turn in German energy policy. However, these burdens largely materialized only after the first quarter 2011.  Therefore, the development of the first quarter this year is within our expectations.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me quickly mention some important steps we have taken during the last few months. The renegotiation of our  oil-indexed long-term gas contracts, again, led to positive results. We were able to further structurally change  several smaller contracts to gas wholesale market indexation with major gas suppliers. We can now fully  concentrate on the remaining three big suppliers to also proceed with our structural solution.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me now come to the headline figures for the Group. External revenue was slightly down by 1% mainly as a  result of the deconsolidation of our TSO business, Amprion. I have already mentioned our decline in EBITDA and  operating result. Declining generation spreads and high burdens in the gas midstream business were determining  factors for the decrease in the operating result. I'll come to the details in a minute.  The non-operating result fell below last year's figures by about €200 million. One reason is the decrease in capital  gains compared to the first three months in 2011, which included the sale of Thyssengas and our minority stake in  the hard coal power plant in Rostock.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: As you know, working capital can be very volatile especially over the course of the year. One other fact is in  relation to the deconsolidation of Amprion. In 2011, we reported a temporary increase in liquidity at Amprion  resulting from the renewable energy allocation levy. The other fact is in relation to our trading business resulting  from the fact that payments in connection with purchases and sales fluctuate significantly over the course of the  year.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Before explaining the drivers for the operating results of our individual divisions, let me give you a quick update  on the gas-to-oil spread situation. You might recall that in March we reported that during 2011, we reduced the  volume of our oil-indexed gas contract by 4 bcm to 20 bcm. The net exposure, which includes our oil-indexed  sales to end customers, fell by 2 bcm to 18 bcm.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Over the last couple of weeks, we have been able to make further progress. We have successfully adjusted  additional contracts to gas wholesale price indexation. As a result, our gross exposure fell by another 1 bcm to 19  bcm and our net exposure to 70 bcm.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Slide six gives you an impression of how we have been able to reduce our future gas-to-oil spread exposure as a  result of our renegotiations compared to our original maturity profile. We are still renegotiating six out of our 17  contracts and are optimistic that we will reach a conclusion by 2013.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Our main focus now lies on the negotiations and arbitration proceedings for the remaining contracts with three  major oil and gas companies. Our main objective is to implement structural solutions for these contracts in order  to eliminate future earnings risks by either terminating them or referencing their prices to trade it against  wholesale market prices by recovering as much of our overpayments of the past few years as possible.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me now explain the development of the operating result in each of our divisions. The operating result in our  Power Generation division came down by 12%. The division suffered from lower realized spreads compared to the  first three months of 2011. The forced closure of our nuclear power plant at Biblis has an impact on the results. A  positive contribution resulted from the trial run of our new lignite plant BoA 2&3 at Neurath. We plan to have the  plant fully commercially operational in the next couple of weeks.  Before I move on to the other divisions, let me spend a minute on the development of the generation capacity in  Germany. As I understand, this is a burning question for you. From our side, you may recall our announcement in  February of 2011 that we would not extend some of the power contracts which we have with Steag. These contracts  have a total volume of 1.4 gigawatts in capacity and will expire at the end of this year. We've also decided not to  extend the additional Steag contracts with a combined volume of another 0.4 gigawatts. These contracts would  also expire at the end of this year.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: In March, I told you about the close of our remaining 12 coal and 150 megawatt lignite blocks by the end of this  year. Furthermore, we must close one gas-fired block at our gas-fired plant with a capacity of 355 megawatts in  spring.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Our Dutch business, Essent improved its results by 4%. Cost cutting and price increases improved margins. The  start of the commercial operation of our new gas-fired power plants Moerdijk 2 and Claus C also contributed  positively to the performance, despite overall lower margins in the generation business.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: RWE npower's operating performance fell by 29% to €291 million. The main reason is the deterioration of the  generation margins. In addition, the division suffered from the outage of our converted power plant at Tilbury due  to the fire in a biomass bunker. Last year, Tilbury still contributed to earnings as a hard coal plant. Furthermore,  last year's first quarter results benefited from one-offs relating to claim settlements.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Our Central Eastern and South Eastern division reports a reduction in operating results of 28%. Lower gas sales  margins in our Czech distribution business and decline in generation spreads and retail margins in our Hungarian  business are the attributing factors. In addition, we see some negative ForEx effects.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Our Renewables business benefited from increased generation volumes and more favorable wholesale prices. Our  wood pellet plant at Georgia in U.S. also contributed to the positive result.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Our upstream business strongly increased its operating result by 37% to €241 million. Higher gas and oil prices  and depreciation of U.S. dollar over the euro are main drivers.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: In our Trading/Gas Midstream division we see an improvement of 20% compared to the first three months of  2011, yet the division still reports a loss of €220 million. We had continuously faced the burdens from the negative  gas to oil spread. However, the performance of the trading business has considerably improved. Please bear in  mind that we will not know whether the gas losses are real losses but only temporarily effect until we have  completed the ongoing negotiations and arbitrations.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Finally, I would like to come to the Group's outlook for 2012. Today, I can confirm the outlook for 2012 that we  provided to you at the beginning of March. We expect EBITDA, operating results and recurrent net income to be  in the order of 2011 despite the lower than originally expected performance of our UK business. We will certainly  benefit from the commercial operation of our new plant. For instance, our lignite plant BoA 2&3 at Neurath. In  addition, it will not be affected by last year's negative effect resulting from the U-turn in German energy policy  except for the nuclear test.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: On the downside, we'll still be suffering from the negative gas storage spread despite our further successful steps  in reaching commercial agreements with suppliers.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. With respect to the rating agency, I can confirm we had our annual review meetings with them. We  presented to them our case the disposal program in much more detail the progress we're making on the efficiency  enhancement program, the progress we are making with respect to the gas-to-oil spread in more detail, and I  share the view which I just explained, but that is also based on their public comment that they are looking a bit  more rigorously on the sector overall. But that is all what I can share with you at this point in time.

texts.speaker: Martin C. Young
texts.profession: Analyst, Nomura International Plc
texts.text: And then secondly, in relation to the gas compensation issue, I appreciate you're not going to give any specific  numbers on that. But is the level of compensation that you've managed to achieve so far are positive relative to  Rolf Pohlig  Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG  A With respect to the first question, as you assume, it's immaterial in the group's overall context. With respect –  sorry, what was the – what we actually achieved in compensation was very close in line to that what we had  originally assumed, that is over encouraging that up until now all the compensations received were very close to  what we call the probability-weighted expected outcome of arbitration and that makes us rather confident with the  future proceedings either in arbitration court or in commercial talks.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: If I counted correct, that's altogether I think five questions. But let's assume one with respect to hedge ratio. I  understand there maybe some misunderstanding misperception market. The hedge ratios, we are providing to the  market are the overall hedge ratios. So, it does include the outright hedge position, it does include the semi  outright position with respect to lignite and it does include the spread position with respect to clean dark spreads  as well as to clean spark spreads. The thing that maybe methodologically a difference to that what this other  company is providing information to the marketplace. And only to give you a little bit more flavor, if we have  hedged roughly 60% of our German plant generation volume, then you can argue that's all the new – and almost  all the lignite production have been hedged and that means that by far the bulk of the margin has been locked in.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: 2014 is 30% and that means that nuclear more or less is hedged and we are in the process of hedging lignite. And I  think we have educated the market for some time that at current price levels, the clean lignite spread is at a very  healthy region. What is also important to understand is that our overall hedging policy follows a rather straight  rule. So, almost on an semi-automatic basis, every second week, we rollover position from our generation units in  Germany to our supply and trading arm. And then it's up to the prop traders to form a view to what extent they  think it's more advantageous directly to sell the markets to pre-sell or even to hold a position for some time if they  do expect the favorable price develop – may develop. Of course, this is only within the limits we have given to  them. Perhaps remember that we provide to the market over global VaR limit which is given to our supply and  trading organization. So, the figures you see with respect to the hedge ratio, they are less volatile over time, there  may from time-to-time be some liquidity issues in the market, but taking a view on the marketplace on the price  development that is up to the prop traders and of course their positions are not disclosed for the market.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The business development in the first quarter of 2013 was in line with our expectations. EBITDA and operating  results were slightly down on previous year while recurrent net income was on par with Q1 2012 mainly due to a  lower tax rate. One of the major strategic milestones in the first quarter was, of course, the decision to evaluate  potential exit routes for Upstream Gas & Oil Division, RWE Dea. Since the establishment of liquid gas markets in  Europe, the access to own physical gas sources no longer has strategic value for our core business. In addition, to  develop the attractive resources and reserves of RWE Dea in the coming years, significant investment is needed.  We are currently preparing the search process, please understand that we can't be more specific at this point in  time.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: In the first quarter of 2013, we were also successful with further disposals. The biggest step was the agreement  with Allianz and the Canadian infrastructure group, Borealis, for the sale of our Czech gas transmission operator  NET4GAS for total value of €1.6 billion. On the basis of a normalized earnings contribution in the coming years,  this is equivalent to valuation multiple of 9.4 times enterprise value over EBITDA.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Furthermore, we made additional smaller disposals, which add up to a total of approximately €0.4 billion. This  was, among other things, the sale of minority shares in our UK offshore wind farm, Rhyl Flats, and onshore wind  farm, Little Cheyne Court. The main purpose of these disposals is to improve our leverage situation with the aim  of having access to long-term financing at attractive conditions at all times. In the current environment, that is  still the case. In the first quarter of 2013, we issued several bonds with a total volume of approximately €1 billion  at very favorable conditions. There was a huge demand by the market. Last but not least, we see that the  development in the first three months of the business year confirms our outlook for the year as a whole. I will  come to that point in a minute.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me give you a brief overview of the business performance in the first quarter on page four. Our operating  results declined by 4% as expected. This is mainly a result of lower earnings in our Conventional Power  Generation Division driven by the effect of full CO2 auctioning and the decline in generation margins.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On our recent road shows, we have talked to many of you. One of the most intensive discussed questions has been,  what we are doing with our cash negative power plants? texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: However, there were also positive offsetting trends. This was mainly the recovery of earnings in our Trading/Gas  Midstream Division. texts.text: ...keep in mind that the P&L effect you see now is reflecting the fact that we have – that we had basically bought  carbon certificates much earlier at significantly higher prices and these are now becoming only P&L effective,  yeah?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: So it's not the mark-to-market value of the carbon consumption that you have.

texts.speaker: Ahmed B. Farman
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn Partners LLP
texts.text: Hello, good afternoon. Thank you for taking my question. Sorry for going back to hedging, but you indicated the  hedge outright prices. Can you also tell us the corresponding hedged carbon prices for 2012 to 2015, so we can sort  of get an idea about sort of the hedged lignite spread?

texts.speaker: Ahmed B. Farman
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn Partners LLP
texts.text: Secondly, I'm just wondering, sort of, given the recent further weakness in the German power price, you're still  confident that the measures you have in place are enough to secure your investment grade credit rating? Thank  you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Yes. With regards to your first question, we won't provide the carbon price – the average carbon prices for the  hedged outright positions in advance. So forward-looking, this is something to look forward once we provide the  actuals for the respective periods and you would also see what the carbon cost of the respective production.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: That was actually three questions, but anyway, okay. On the half-year numbers and the half-year analyst  conference call with regards to messages on plant closures, the overall question of further asset impairment is  more – but it's driven by the overall price development against the full cost of production whereas the question of  plant closures it's driven by the price development against – or the spread development, generation spread  development against the development of avoidable cash cost. These are, of course, not unrelated, but they are not  identical, yeah? So we can't see all combinations that all that are there. If the power prices deteriorate significantly  further, we could see impairments on plants which are not closed. We could see closures on mothballing our  plants, which are not impaired. Usually, of course, they would only be not impaired because they are already fully  written-off, yeah? I mean the first – the old plants are the first victims. So this is why there is no – there is – of  course, there is some quarterly, but this is not a one-to-one relationship we see there.

file: RWE - Q1 2014 Earnings Call 14May2014 900 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 14-May-14.pdf

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Our performance in the first quarter of 2014 is in line with our expectations. EBITDA and the opera ting results are  down by 16% and 18%, respectively. In addition to the weather effects, we suffered from the erosion of margins in  the Conventional Power Generation business.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Furthermore, the figures reflect the deconsolidation of natural gas as of August 2013. Our recurrent net income  was down by 36%, in addition to the trend of the operating result, our tax rate for recurrent net income increased  from 25% to 34%.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: A further milestone at the end of February was the commercial settlement with Gazprom on our long -term gas  supply contract. As a result, there will be no further exposure to the gas-to-oil spread until the next regular price  revision in summer 2016. Until then, we are confident we will find an amicable solution for the open issues so that  the gas-to-oil spread problem will be solved once and for all.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: We now expect EBITDA to be in the range of €6.4 billion to €6.8 billion, and the operating resul t between €3.9  billion and €4.3 billion. With this, we confirm our previous outlook adjusted for the numbers of RWE Dea. In  other words, the commercial settlement with Gazprom and lower operating depreciation on the positive side and  the weather effect and further margin pressure in the gas storage business on the negative side are more or less  offsetting each other. The outlook for recurrent net income now includes the interest on the purchase price of  RWE Dea instead of the businesses' income contribution. Assuming a deconsolidation by the end of this year, this  results in a range of €1.2 billion to €1.4 billion.

texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG

texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: In terms of your question with regards to growth and do we still see that despite the decline in volumes, clearly  yes, because the growth perspective that we have is of course one which relies on normal weather patterns and is  average result, these fluctuations.

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: And secondly, on the UK business, would you be able to quantify how much of the deduction is because of the eco  charges you were mentioning versus the impact of the weather? Thank you.
