file: RWE - Q1 2015 Earnings Call 13May2015 600 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 13-May-15.pdf

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Let me start with a brief summary of the main political challenges we are currently facing and the latest update on  where we are. We can divide the whole political discussion to three main topics. First, the possible introduction of  carbon penalties for older coal plants. Second, the discussion about nuclear provisions and whether they should  be externalized. And of course, third, the discussion about the new market design for power generation in  Germany.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: So let's start with the proposal of an additional CO2 levy for old power plants. According to this proposal,  conventional power plants should only be allowed to emit a specific amount of carbon free of additional penalties  as soon as they are 20 years old. It starts with a limit of 7  million tons related to a plant size of 1,000 me gawatt at  an age of 20 years. It will go down to 3 million tons after 40 years.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: In case of emissions above those limits, an additional penalty of €18 to €20 for any additional ton would be  charged. The aim of the government is to further reduce carbon emissions by 22 million tons by 2020 to fulfill the  40% carbon reduction target the German government has set itself for 2020 versus 1990.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: The problem with this proposal is that it would not lead to a gradual reduction in carbon emissions but would  make the operation of all of our 11-megawatt, 300-megawatt and 600-megawatt blocks uneconomical in one go.  This is due to the fact that most of our fixed cash costs are related to the lignite mines and only by closing the  mines could we also reduce our fixed cash cost accordingly. This would take approximately 7-gigawatt out of our  total 10-gigawatt lignite-fired power generation out of the market.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Now, to the second topic, the discussion about the nuclear provisions. There's no official movement by the  German government on this issue, but every once in a while, there are e xperts quoted who argue that perhaps the  provisions are not high enough or that they should be externalized, as it might not be certain that the utilities  would be able to provide the cash flows once they are needed.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Let me emphasize. We have built the provisions in line with our general prudent financial approach. Secondly, the  decommissioning of the research reactor [indiscernible] (04:14) and the works on Mülheim -Kärlich support our  view that we are in line with our original expectations on decommissioning costs.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: With regards to the discount rate of 4.6%, it's important to see that the real discount rate, i.e., the difference  between the escalation in the discount rate is only in the order of 1%. This is fully in line with the current low  interest rate environment. But of course, we are not protected if politicians decide on new burns, for example, in  the context of looking for a new final storage facility.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Let me also remind you of our prudent approach to set aside financial assets for all our long-term provisions, the  non-funded pension obligations, the mining and nuclear provisions. We have more than 10% of those additionally  covered by financial assets on top of our physical assets.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: From what we can see at the moment, the introduction of a straightforward capacity market looks unlikely. It  seems more likely that the government will opt for a reform of the energy-only market in combination with the  tender of reserve capacity, which will then not be available for the energy-only market.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: The intended reserve capacity would be in the order of magnitude of 4 gigawatt at the beginning. We would expect  power plants in southern Germany, which are part of the current grid reserve, to be eligible to participate in the  auction.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Last but not least, let me update you on where we are with regards to the court cases on the nuclear fuel tax. We  were informed by the European Court of Justice that they will announce their verdict on 4th of June 2015. We still  don't have a fixed date from the German Federal Constitutional Court, but we still expect the decision in 2015 or  early 2016.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Now, back to the first quarter. The key performance indicators on slide 4 show a mixed picture. EBITDA and  operating result are down by 3% and 5%, respectively, mainly as a result of further deteriorating realized margins  in the Conventional Power Generation business. This was partly offset in our retail business units on the back of  normalized weather conditions.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Slide 6, gives you the development of the operating result by divisions and the main value drivers. The biggest  effect is the decline in Conventional Power Generation, mainly driven by a further deterioration of realized  generation spreads. But there's also some light at the end of the tunnel, as in the Renewables business. We are  starting to reap the benefits of our investments of the past years. Operating result of RWE Innogy is up by 56% to  €151 million.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: The decline of cash flows from operating activities on slide 7 does not come as a surprise. In March, we explained  to you the new procurement policy for CO2 emission certificates. While until 2013, we purchased most of the  certificates in the same year as the CO2 was emitted, we shifted the timing for the purchase of the certificates we  needed for 2014 to the beginning of 2015, the year we have to submit them. As a result, total cash flows from  operating activities in Q1 2015 is €0.5 billion lower than previous year's cash flow.

texts.profession: Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Y eah. Morning, everyone. Two very simple questions. The first one is there are several places in the statement  where you referred to the impact of the weather, let's call it, improvement in Q1 2015 versus Q1 2014. Can you  quantify the operating result or the EBITDA level, what the impact of weather was compared  to last year?

texts.speaker: Vincent P. Gilles
texts.profession: Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And the second question is reading Reuters, Bernhard, you seem to have said that by the end of 2016, the total  spending on nuclear fuel tax could get up to €2 billion, which is higher than the number that most people already  have in mind. Can you confirm you really said that and explain to us the potential increase versus the €1.4 billion  to €1.6 billion everybody seems to have in mind? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Y eah. Hi, Vincent. It might strike you a bit lower  than what you heard last year, but in 2014, we compared a very mild 2014 against the very cold 2013. 2015 now is  a normal year so far, weather-wise at least. And therefore, this is the number for the first quarter.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: On the nuclear fuel tax, there is no new evidence on the numbers. What I said in the press conference is that it's  below €2 billion. So, as we always said before, most likely, in the range of €1.8 billion to €1.9 billion at the end of  2016 will be overall tax expenses out of this tax. Nothing new.

texts.speaker: Vincent P. Gilles
texts.profession: Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And that is assuming that you're not shutting down the nuclear assets before the end of the [indiscernible]  (12:29)?

texts.speaker: Bobby Chada
texts.profession: Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: And secondly, you spent a fair bit of time walking through the CO2 levy and some of the potential impacts. Is there  anything that you can quantify for us, whether that's the size of the restructuring costs the mine closures and staff  layoffs would trigger, whether it's the impact on your lignite provision, or the impact at the operating result level  of the closures that you outlined at the start of the call?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Y eah. Hi, Bobby. On net debt, we are expecting it to be at the same order of magnitude roughly at the end of 2015  that we saw at the end of the first quarter. On the climate protection proposals by the German government, there's  no specific numbers we would like to give out at this point in time. But given the potential size of the cuts to our  operating business in lignite, 17 out of 20 power station units and two out of three lignite mines, we already said in  the first press statement end of March when these ideas came up that we would be talking about  an overall  economic impact in the €1 billion range, yeah. But this is not to say that this all goes straight through P&L. It  would also include restructuring cost, provisioning effects and all like that.

texts.speaker: Peter A. Bisztyga
texts.profession: Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: Y eah. Good morning. Another question on the carbon levy. So I'm presuming that you guys have got an alternative  proposal for how Germany should achieve its target of 22 million tons of power generation emissions reduction by  2020. So can you provide us some details as to what you're suggesting to the government as an alternative? So  that's my first question.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Y eah. Hi, Peter. First on the carbon levy, we have not been so far party to any official discu ssions or negotiations  around alternative solutions on this carbon levy. And so – but we always said also via industry groups that there  are economically and – for energy politics much more efficient ways to achieve these goals than going via this  proposed carbon levy. Just you know increased energy efficiency in private household heating environment, for  example, is just one example. But it's not that we had – anybody had asked us for any specific proposals there.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The next question comes from Deepa Venkateswaran, Bernstein.  Deepa Venkateswaran  Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.  Q  Thank you. I have two questions. One is on working capital and the other one is about the carbon levy. So starting  just with the carbon levy, I understand that your auditors are looking at sort of the financial position. Could you  elaborate a little bit more on what exactly the auditors are going to tell the government and how does that play  into the current alternative proposal that the government is supposed to be looking at?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And my second question on working capital, obviously, compared to the year end, there's been a huge negative  swing on working capital. Can you confirm how much of this will sort of unwind during the course of the ye ar,  given sort of the weather effects and other things? And would you expect it to sort of remain at that level or would  you expect it to unwind? That would be helpful. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Y eah. Hi, Deepa. Maybe we start with your carbon levy question. I think what you are referring to, there have been  some report in the German press that there has been a letter by Minister Gabriel or his ministry where they  ventilate the idea of what they call a stress test on nuclear provisions in the balance sheets of the utilities.

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: If I may actually – sorry. This is another article which said that the German government had asked the auditors to  look at the impact of the carbon levy. This was a separate article in the SPIEGEL about whether – are you aware of  your auditors having to do any work on trying to quantify the impact of the lignite mining closures on your  finances? That was my question.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: And on working capital, there are some, indeed, various effects why we see such a significant swing, for example,  also compared to last year on working capital. Some effects are related to what we call the swing effect out of the  mild 2014 – or the cold 2013, mild 2014 and it now goes pretty normal 2015 where we, on the retail side, we had a  positive – or I would say an excessively positive development of working capital, which is bound to swing back in  2015 once the installments we charge to our customers, on a monthly basis usually, are adapted to the milder year  2014. And so this is a kind of averaging out over several years. And, therefore, some of these effect we see in the  working capital is going to stay throughout 2015. Another effect, which is very pronounced only this year and as a  kind of one-off comparison to 2014, is the different treatment of the carbon certificates.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: So effectively, in 2014, there was no working capital movement, no cash effect through the carbon certificates  because the majority of them was already bought and paid in 2013, and the 2014 certificates were only now  bought and paid in 2015. And therefore, like-for-like, 2014 cash flow was basically carbon certificate free to some  degree, and 2015 is now back to a normal year where we have the one-year payment for CO2. But the one effect  that is seasonal is that Q1 in our business, traditionally, is a weak quarter cash-wise compared to profits.

texts.speaker: Lueder Schumacher
texts.profession: Société Générale SA (Broker)
texts.text: The second one is can you just shed a bit more light on the increase in your hybrid capital interest cost and  minorities? And the last one is just, the half one, just a follow-up on your timing, what you said for the carbon  levy. You said it should be resolved this year. Is this not tied to the white book, i.e., the general German market  reforms and as such, could we not expect to see a solution there before some operator?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: The last one is the carbon levy and the white book. You never know if politics are not going to bundle it into one  large package although, structurally, I think the two proposals or the two initiatives are addressing different  issues. The white book is about security of supply and the market regime ensuring that there will be sufficient  backup capacity available if renewables are not available.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: And the carbon levy proposal is around – well, climate protection – at least what the German government thinks  their contribution to climate protection is and there's no immediate concern on security of supply. Ultimately, of  course, in a kind of big holistic political picture, the two sides have to be taken into account simultaneously. And  as I said, we also would like to have clarity rather sooner than later. So if it happens before the summer break, we  would also be happy to have that clarity.

texts.speaker: Ahmed Bilal Farman
texts.profession: Liberum Capital Ltd.
texts.text: And just my second question, can I just confirm your earlier comment on the full year net debt? That basically  assumes nonfinancial debt as of Q1 and no reimbursement from nuclear tax. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Y eah. Starting with your second question, that's right. This outlook on full year net debt does not include a  reimbursement of nuclear fuel tax. And it includes the nonfinancial debt as we see it at the end of Q1.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Hi, Alex. May we come back with a quantification? I assume you wanted on the overall group level. We would have  to add the sums up because it's both in the UK Retail business, it's in also in the UK Renewables business, for  example.

texts.speaker: Deborah B. Wilkens
texts.profession: Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: Y es. Good morning. I was hoping you could help a bit just understanding if you've changed your hedging strategy  to reflect the risk of less lignite generation? And beyond hedging, what are you doing to prepare for potentially  having to close at least the oldest of the lignite facilities, which looks incrementally likely? Is the billion number  you've given over a certain number of years, an annual? What's the timeframe for that value?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Y eah. Hi, Deborah. On the hedging strategy, we have not adapted this for a – well, somehow enforced, hurried  phase-out of lignite power generation. Secondly, on the closing of older lignite capacity, we've already been  transparent that all the very old lignite plants are economically getting increasingly borderline. And as we said  also earlier, we are constantly watching them if they have now to be shut down, for example, when the next major  outage comes. So this is our view on that. But this is a kind of, what I would say, a gradual reduction of lignite  capacity and not a big crash event like the carbon levy proposal from Berlin.

texts.speaker: Stephan Lowis
texts.profession: Vice President-Investor Relations
texts.text: Just for clarification reasons, Vincent, on the first question, I think you're distinguishing between, let's call power  we provide for ancillary services for grid stability services, is that right?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: It was on Conventional Power Generation, and I think you are referring – or did I understand correctly, Vincent,  that you'd asked if we would be expecting a loss? And this is a P&L loss, I assume, on Conventional Power  Generation in the 2015 for the full year.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Y es. Essentially, again, I at least did not mean to say anything new that you do not know. I mean you know that  we  are, at least also from our segment guidance we gave for the full year 2015, that we – yes, we assume Conventional  Power Generation to be below 2014, but we are, on an operating-result basis, not assuming losses because we still  have the power sold at higher forward prices over the last three years than the current spot price level we would be  seeing. So this is a difficult phase-out effect of the hedges that I was referring to.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: And then you may remember this chart, which we showed in our analyst conference in March where on a kind of  like-for-like pro forma, both P&L and cash representation of our Power Generation business, we showed that  roughly speaking like-for-like with all the efficiency increases and the running out of the hedges. So fully mark-to- market, the Power Generation would be operating-result-wise, most likely slightly negative, EBITDA-wise, a bit  positive but there – and cash-wise, just marginally above the borderline. This was this chart number 8 from our  March analyst presentation. There's nothing new compared to that whatever Reuters is making out of it.

texts.speaker: Ingo Becker
texts.profession: Kepler Cheuvreux
texts.text: Y es. Thank you. Good afternoon. Also on the 22 million tons of intended carbon reductions in the sector, it  appears apparently there's a dilemma here, right, cutting emissions, jobs and maybe security of supply locally. You  said the government views this rather independently of each other which is, well, probably or maybe not the right  way of assessing it.

texts.speaker: Ingo Becker
texts.profession: Kepler Cheuvreux
texts.text: Do you in that triangle see any kind of particular emphasis the government is putting on one of those three  targets? Is it really just about the emission thing or isn't the situation of jobs in northern Australia at least equally  important to this government? And maybe from your discussions with the government just your impression on  that.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: So starting with the – hi, Ingo – with the carbon levy versus white book and the dilemma, as you put it, between  the various goals the government has: climate protection, security of supply and it's, say, in the broader sense,  economic prosperity including potential job losses. Unfortunately, I can't read their minds. And, therefore, I do  not know how they balance these three goals in this triangle off against e ach other. I hope that they're trying to  balance it because, otherwise, we achieve climate protection in a very expensive manner, as you know, in  Germany. But, ultimately, only time will tell.

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you. Just one follow-up question. This is about the financial impact of the carbon levy, so just so that all the  analysts are on exactly the same page, you said it's a billion euro range. My interpretation was it was an y number  from €1 billion to €9 billion and somewhere in that range. Obviously, I think, Deborah said €1 billion somewhere  later. So I just wanted to know is my interpretation correct.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: One of the reasons for the difficult market environment I mentioned is the political uncertainty around financing  the nuclear exit. In this respect, the nuclear commission, which were instituted by the German government,  presented its recommendation at the end of April. We believe that the distribution of responsibility between the  company and the state proposed by the commission is logical in principle and that the concept is heading in the  right direction.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: RWE AG honors the obligation it has to fulfill in phasing out nuclear energy. We had a group provisions for this  which are very conservative even when compared at the international level and, therefore, constitute a strong  financial precaution against the risk of cost increases. However, the risk premium proposed by the commission on  top of this, is an irresponsible undue burden on RWE AG. It is unfortunate that the commission has failed to take  the company's economic situation into account. What is decisive now is the manner in which th e legislature  implements the proposals.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Now, on to the development of the key performance indicators in the first quarter. Let me start on slide 4 which  shows the development of the operating result by division. The earnings increase in the first three months is  mainly due to the positive development in energy trading which supported very high profits in the Q1 period,  which was partly offset by the negative earnings trend in Conventional Power Generation mainly due to the  decline in realized generation margins. Nevertheless, earnings contribution of this division is disproportionately  high in Q1 2016. Nuclear fuel tax and higher maintenance cost will come in the rest of the year. Furthermore, Q1  benefited from one-off gains from the sale of real estate.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: First on slide 8 for the key earnings figures of the group. We confirm the earnings guidance we gave in March. The  increase we have seen in Q1 2016 for EBITDA and operating results were not sustained for the rest of the year.  Positive one-off effects in the second half of last year as the VSE revaluation and the profit from the sale of a stake  in the Galloper project are two reasons. Moreover, Q1 2016 had positive one-offs which mainly impacted earnings  development in this quarter, rather than in the full year. This is the sale of real estate in Conventional Power  Generation, the sale of grid assets and the revaluation of our participation in Westenergie in the division Grids/  Participation/Others.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Furthermore, the strong earnings improvement in our Trading/Gas Midstream division in Q1 2016 may not be  extrapolated for the full year. In addition, we expect higher costs, for example, for maintaining our power plants  and for maintaining and operating our grid infrastructure, which will impact our earnings mainly in the rest of  fiscal 2016.

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you so much. Yes, my first question is about what's your long-term expectation for the tax rate for RWE  AG? And secondly on the nuclear financing solutions, so I think in your review you said that you expect a  pragmatic and realistic solution. So, could you just basically help us understand where do you want to see the  premium go to from 35% for it to be acceptable? And maybe just one add-in, can you just clarify what's the total  amount of provision plus the premium for you. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Second question, or 2A, I might say, nuclear exit, we won't comment on any premium or red lines. We are still in  discussions and we are still analyzing the recommendations by the commission which are, by their very nature,  vague in some aspects and needs further detailing and specification. Anyway, and what I said about pragmatic  solution is that we are working towards it. So, it's still open how it will all end.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: The total amount just for – on a kind of a pro forma illustration is roughly out of this €10 billion overall nuclear  provisions, some €5 billion are affected by the recommendations for externalization directly with this interim and  final storage and if you apply 35% to it, this would be roughly €1.7 billion, so the overall fund would be €6.7  billion. But this is just a back-of-the-envelope calculation, no audited numbers.

texts.speaker: Ahmed Bilal Farman
texts.profession: Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: Hi. Morning, everyone. So, just one question. If the final nuclear deal required you to only transfer funds quickly  to the current value for liabilities, how much of nuclear do y ou think you'll have to divest to maintain a BBB, BBB-  type rating and also to manage the liquidity pressures? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Y eah. This is speculating about the future with a high number of known unknowns contained in it, like power  prices, like the overall development of the nuclear IPO. So, we don't give any precise guidance [ph] in terms  (11:36) of what if, the cause and effect logic, what we would do given any number of nuclear fund externalization.

texts.speaker: Lueder Schumacher
texts.profession: Société Générale SA (Broker)
texts.text: Good morning. Y eah, two questions. One is obviously, on the nuclear provision debate, I understand that you are  reluctant to talk about the size of an acceptable premium, but what is the way forward from here? What is the  timeline? I guess the overall idea must be to find an agreement between all parties before the summer recess in  July. But are there actually talks taking place at the moment? Are they scheduled? If you just give us an idea of the  way forward from here. That's the first question.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Y eah. Hi, Lueder. On the way forward, now on nuclear, and, again, as stated before, we are reluctant to get any  precise details, but we are in close contact with the Berlin administration on various levels, and I think broadly  speaking, we operate under the same expectations around the timeline the government aspires to. So it might be  that before the summer break, we see further detailing of recommendations from the government. Although, your  estimate [ph] is to be (15:15) quite ambitious timelines.

texts.speaker: Peter Crampton
texts.profession: Macquarie Capital (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And the second question relates to the German nuclear tax court case, any idea on timing?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Let's start with the second question. We have no update on the timing on the nuclear court case. So, we would still  expect it for 2016. But, unfortunately, the German constitutional court is not bound to our wishes for the time  line. On nuclear capacity, this one year earlier [indiscernible] (17:28) for us. It's too early to tell what it will exactly  mean.

texts.speaker: Bobby Chada
texts.profession: Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: All in all, the traffic lights are very bright and green there.

texts.speaker: Philippe Ourpatian
texts.profession: Natixis SA (Broker)

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Y eah. So I'll start with the revaluation of [ph] Best Energy (23:45), this is a small double-digit million euro  amount. On the energy derivatives and the other experts, don't get further detail on the exact numbers. Sorry. I  think there was one question still outstanding, can you repeat it? Something around deferred taxes?

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you. So I want to come back to my favorite topic on the nuclear provisions. So, my understanding is that  the €5 billion, you would need to [indiscernible] (25:40) hand over the nuclear fund at some point as for the  commission report immediately. So, is the scope of this timing also something that you will be discussing?

texts.speaker: Bobby Chada
texts.profession: Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Hi. Thanks. Could I come back to the restructuring and the set-up of NewCo. But there was some discussion about whether the bonds, the AG  bonds could possibly be moved across to NewCo. Can you give us any help, I suppose we should call it energy now  but can you give us any help with how that debt structure with energy might work?

texts.profession: Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: Y eah. Good morning. Couple of questions. First one just on power prices, I'd just be interested to know whether  your trader thing, the sort of recent recovery to kind of €24, €25 on German power is sustainable? And indeed,  whether that sort of brings your lignite business back into sort of cash-positive territory?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Y eah. Hi, Peter. So, on power prices, of course, our trader is ahead of you, but I am sure you fully understand why  I won't share it with you because they are trading on that. texts.speaker: Ahmed Bilal Farman
texts.profession: Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: Hi. Sorry for coming back to the nuclear issue again. But I think, Bernhard, you said this morning that if you  accept the proposal as it is, it will create excessive burden for the rating. Perhaps, could you, perhaps, elaborate it? texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Okay. And then to the German market. I think it was referring to an interview by Rolf Martin Schmitz, the CEO.  This was not an RWE assumption. He was citing a study by the German Research Institute, a very well known  respectable one, Fraunhofer Institute. And they were coming up with one scenario where power demand c ould go  up to the number you mentioned here in the call.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The logic behind it is Germany also wants to reach the emission reduction target in the transportation and heating  sector. The only way to do that is via electrification. And currently, there is a discussion in Germany ongoing, that  the entire burden is currently on the electricity demand. So, with all the EEG levies and so on, and especially in  heating, based on gas and oil but also on transport, there is not such a levy. So, there is a discussion whether the  EEG and all, the subsidization of renewables should be splitted among all sectors and not only on the energy  sector. And I think that was what was the interview was about.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: No. Maybe a personal comment. I don't expect that energy policy but also environmental policy will be among  those top three to five agenda items for the February election, and we have currently other topics. So, they all are  currently writing their programs, but it's more – a much more expert discussion now and not a very emotional  heated discussion in the public, which I think is also very helpful in the end to find the right solution.

texts.speaker: John Musk
texts.profession: Analyst, RBC Europe Ltd.
texts.text: Yeah. Good morning, everyone. First question would be on the provisions and the movement of the benefit that  you saw, I think it was about €350 million. Can you just remind us of the sensitivity of your provisions to  movements in interest rates, both on the pensions and the remaining nuclear provisions? And then also, what is  the best relevant benchmark for us to look at to try and track that going forward? And then, secondly, quite a  simple one [indiscernible] (28:33) answer, but is there any update on the nuclear fuel tax position?

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On the provisions, so it works like that in those quarters where we don't submit the CO2 certificates. So, in quarter  one, three and four, you see that we have a burden in EBITDA for CO2 emissions for provisioning them. So, there  you see the reversal in the bridge item, which we call delta in provisions and non-cash items. In Q2, when we  hand them into the regulator, you see working capital dropping by the €650 million to €700 million but also the  utilization of provisions for this item jumping to the €650 million. Over the course of the year, the utilization of  provisions for CO2 certificate is more or less zero because production volume is stable and we have that on a  yearly basis more or less unchanged.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On the sensitivity side, 10 basis points in nuclear provisions is around €50 million. And on the pension side, the  gross effect, so 10 basis points is equivalent to €200 million for the liability side alone. But usually, given our asset  investments here, we also see movements on the asset side. The numbers I have provided are for RWE stand- alone's, for the €200 million on the pension liability side when we see a 10-basis point movement.

texts.speaker: Mark Lewis
texts.profession: Managing Director, European Utilities Research, Barclays Investment Bank
texts.text: Thank you. Good morning. Two questions also from me. Firstly, we're sort of entering a period now where we  might get some meaningful reform of the EU ETF with the proposal that was put forward by the commission and  now both the parliament and the European councils suggesting a more radical reform. Are you able or willing to  share with us your sensitivity – the sensitivity of your portfolio to higher carbon prices? I don't know, €1 or €5  increase in the carbon price, what does that do to your operating profit on the generation side?

texts.speaker: Mark Lewis
texts.profession: Managing Director, European Utilities Research, Barclays Investment Bank
texts.text: And would you also, given that we're coming from a period where CO2 prices have been very flat for the last three  or four years, would it change anything in your hedging strategy if – it's probably still a premature question at this  stage, but if within 12 months time you're started seeing CO2 prices moving up as a result of that reform, would  that potentially change anything in your hedging strategy?

texts.speaker: Mark Lewis
texts.profession: Managing Director, European Utilities Research, Barclays Investment Bank
texts.text: And the second question just relates to German politics again. We have the result yesterday in North Rhine- Westphalia. People's expectations about the next government and potential coalitions are maybe starting to  change. Do you think there is any difference between outcomes in terms of implementation of the climate action  plan between the current configuration of the grand coalition between the CDU and the SPD on the one hand or  potentially a CDU-SDP-Green party coalition (sic) [CDU-SPD-Green party coalition] (35:01) or do you think  actually it doesn't really matter that policy will be implemented indifferently on that score?

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On the CO2 side, our CO2 position until the 2020 is financially neutral. So, we have already hedged our position  and we will take the decision, what we're going to take with the next period, from 2021 onwards, when we have all  the details available. So, any short-term price movements would potentially not change our hedging policy  because we are financially already hedged on the CO2 side.

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: Hello. Good morning. I have a question, on biomass, could you give us an update on what your latest thinking is,
texts.text: in respect of this technology? I think I noted that the Georgia Biomass pelleting plant was [ph] spun off (36:35) to  innogy, you retained the generation. How do you see your footprint in this area? Do you think this is something  you might seek to exit? Or will you be looking to grow a bit more in this technology? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. Thanks. As you rightly pointed out, the production plant is with innogy, Georgia Biomass. What we do is – I  mean of course, we are involved in biomass trading and also securing a supply for our own biomass demand.  And we were granted subsidies from the Dutch government to coal-fire biomass in our Netherlands coal-fired  power station. And they are – [indiscernible] (37:20) respect by a payment by the government. We will, of course,  invest into this business because it improves the profitability of the plant and also diversify the fuel mix. But we  have currently no plans to invest further into this field other than we get another back-up payment or capacity –  subsidy payment by government who wants that. Yeah.

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Second question really is a follow-up to the previous one on carbon. So, you mentioned that you're financial  neutral to a rising carbon price environment. Can you just explain how much CO2 allowances you actually have in  your books and what price are they reflected in? And should you need to mark-to-market, where – will we see that  and the EBITDA at some point? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And on the CO2 side, these CO2 certificates are not mark-to-market. You're going to see the effect in the EBITDA  when we actually produce the power so despite of the generation margin because it's a hedged position and not  speculated position.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: No. I mean, the question is then at what price levels have we actually bought the CO2 certificates and could we  have bought them cheaper, that it's an opportunity loss, yeah. But we have the CO2 position already flexible –  already hedged. So, it will, as you said, enter the cost of goods when we actually produce. But where you'll see  that this is a temporary effect where you see effect is in the margining. Yeah. So, variation margin because we do  them mark-to-market.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: In March, we presented the agreement with E.ON to sell our stake in innogy in exchange for a wide range of  assets, which will transform us into a leading integrated renewables and conventional power generator. The  execution of the transaction is going ahead as planned.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Ladies and gentlemen, in December 2016, the Federal Constitutional Court declared that the operators of nuclear  power plants should be compensated for damages of the early exit of nuclear power in Germany. The Court gave  the federal government the task to come up with a compensation law by mid-2018.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Recently, a draft law by the Ministry of Environmental Affairs became public, which envisages compensation. We  welcome that the government is addressing the matter following the ruling of the [ph] Constitution Court  (00:05:40). We assume that we will be compensated for stranded investments as well asset generation volumes  of our Mülheim-Kärlich plant, which we will not be able to either use in our plants or sell to other operators.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: This brings me to our current hedge position on slide 7. The strong decline in fuel spreads since the beginning of  the year had only a limited impact on our hedge position for 2018 and 2019, as we are almost fully hedged. As a  result, the hedge price for those years stayed broadly flat compared to the improved level at the end of last year.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: For 2020, we have a much higher open implicit fuel hedge position. Hence, the current hedge price is  approximately €2 lower, compared to the end of last year as generation spreads have [ph] broadened (00:08:27).  We show for the first time, our hedge position for 2021. We are hedged more than 30%, mainly via an implicit fuel  hedge. And by that, we keep the upside of improving generation spreads.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: From now on, we will provide additional information on our hedged CO2 position. The average hedge power price  for our outright position can only be understood in the corresponding hedged carbon prices taken into account. In  an environment of stable CO2 [ph] prices' (00:09:02) information was not relevant to understand the economics of  the business.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: This has changed with the recent dynamics of the carbon and power prices. The current hedge price for 2018 to  2021 of €28 to €29 per megawatt hour correspond with average hedged CO2 prices of approximately €5 to €6 per  ton.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me also remind you of our long-term carbon position, which we have financially hedged through the end of  2022. In other words, change in carbon prices should not affect our generation margins for the next five years.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On page 8, you can see the development of fuel spreads. Until the end of Q1 2018, which are relevant for our  hedge prices you saw on the previous slide. After the strong improvement of fuel spreads which peaked during  the Jamaica coalition negotiations due to anticipated coal capacity closures, they started to come down after the  talks failed. Since the beginning of the year, we have seen a further strong decline in clean dark spreads to levels  seen a year ago. We believe that spreads at current levels are fundamentally undervalued especially in outer  years and see some potential for recovery.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Now onto our distribution of the cash flow on slide 11. Reconciliation from adjusted EBITDA to distributable cash  flow is dominated by the seasonal development of the operating working capital in Q1. This is mainly driven by  timing effects since we purchased most of our required CO2 certificate in the first quarter of the year.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: This will revert in Q1, once the certificates for admissions in 2017 are delivered to the national clearing authorities.  Changes in provisions and other non-cash items are also impacted by the accounting of CO2 emissions. By the  recognition and provisions run throughout the year, the utilization takes place in Q2. Furthermore, Q1 showed a  very low utilization of our nuclear provisions. In the first quarter, we already accounted for the full-year effect of  the equity British pound hybrid payment which amounted to €60 million. Last year, this was reflected in Q2.

texts.speaker: Vincent Gilles
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Yeah. Morning, everyone. I got two questions, please, page 7 and 8 inevitably. You started helping us bridge the  slide you gave at the end of the fiscal year 2017 where 2020 was at €31 per megawatt hour – excuse me €38 per  megawatt hour, [indiscernible] (00:15:25) €29 per megawatt hour now. And basically, can you help us bridge?  You started but can you develop what you were saying on the bridge between the price we had at the end of last  year and the price we now have on outright power? Because, obviously, power prices move, spreads moved, but  it would be very helpful for us maybe to get a better grip on what we should expect for the rest of the year is  predominantly my question [indiscernible] (00:15:52)

texts.speaker: Vincent Gilles
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And the second thing is on page 8, the spreads. Okay, fine. We can see what happened. What is your  expectation of what may happen? Implicitly, what I'm asking you is what is your expectation on carbon prices in  the next 6 to 12 months?

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. Thanks for the question. So, first, I mean maybe let's spend some time on the implicit fuel hedging and you  asked to bridge the development between the €31 per megawatt you showed end of last year, and now the €29  per megawatt. I mean, actually, it corresponds exactly with page 8 because what you see here for the blended  spread for calendar year 2020 that it came down from around – over the last three months, around €6 to now  around €4.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Now, maybe the right question could be, why haven't you used the environment and have hedged the outright  position already so, sold the power at that prices. The big problem for us is that I have given the size of our  position that we have to decompose the different legs. We know exactly that we are very exposed to CO2 that's  why we hedge CO2 very early when we think that we should hedge at these price levels. That is why CO2 is  already financially hedged until 2022.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The second leg is hard coal. The hard coal markets are very liquid. So, we can protect ourselves and especially  Lignite & Nuclear for falling hard coal price by going short hard coal. To really use the power market three years in  advance is a very big constraint liquidity wise. So, the alternative would not have been selling what we turned into  a blended spread position, selling it outright, but keeping it entirely open. And that would mean we are exposed to  CO2 and also other developments.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: So, and what we said and you can see in 2019, where spreads were very healthy also. During the last quarters,  we used full liquidity to sell power, to close everything. 2020, we keep the position now open because we think  especially for 2020, the spreads – the average spreads are too low in the forward market. That is not what is  needed in the physical markets in order to bring enough capacity on line, to produce electricity which is needed.  And we are not willing to close a position at prices which we don't think are appropriate and we have seen a very  similar picture. I think one-and-a-half year ago when we started to explain the implicit fuel hedge.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Your second question on carbon prices, I mean, that is very difficult. I mean I had individual discussions with  many of you about the carbon market. It's very difficult to analyze the carbon market fundamentally because of its  more behavioral theory or game theory. What happens when you really run into this shortage, in this physical  supply shortage, that's next year. And what probably utilities will change in their hedging behavior and whether  industrials are selling, willing to selling their surpluses into the market, the question is at what price levels.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: So, we don't have an RWE house view on the carbon market but we know the relevance for our economics and  that's why, we said, let's protect the company against the downside risk for carbon. And we are very happy that  we could hedge the position until 2021 at price levels of €5 to €6 now. And maybe, one last aspect to that, I think,  that is important why we now disclose the carbon hedge.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: In the outright position, the most relevant one is lignite. And as we have made clear on our Capital Markets Day  on a full cash flow basis – cash contribution basis so including maintenance CapEx. We need power prices after  carbon of €22 to have a cash breakeven including maintenance CapEx. And if you now compare the €29 with the  €5 to €6, that was even a better hedge than keeping the position open because with €40 today but €15 carbon  and the intensity of lignite is 1.1, 1.2, the spread we have implicitly hedged here is even higher than waiting for  power prices being at €40 but especially driven by carbon prices of €15. So, lignite position is better off with  €29.550 than with €40.15. And that – to really understand it, that's why we decided to disclose our carbon hedge  from now on.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And secondly, on the hedging. So if I am looking at an open year, say that 70% of 2021 or a year like 2022,  you've given as one piece of information that you're financially hedged for carbon. But what would this really  mean? So for instance, if we stick to the €40 power price, €15 carbon, so for the open position in a year like 2020,  is it then the equivalent of saying, look, if we think you've covered, say, 40% of your carbon exposure, that means  you should take the market price of power, the market price of carbon for maybe approximately 60%. And we  have to kind of take a guess work on where you've locked in your carbon price at whatever level for the remaining  40% and guess, as to what kind of power price does that correspond to?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: So, I just want to make sure how we should reflect your carbon hedging until 2022 in this. And then obviously for  an open year like 2023, where you haven't hedged, it's whatever our guess is on carbon prices and power prices  then, I guess. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On the hedge position, more or less your understanding is right. I mean what we – it is, to be honest, it's very  difficult to assess the position for 2022 because we said we are financially hedged on the carbon side. So, if you  want to come up, obviously, your own calculation how it should look like 2022, you can only take the market  average carbon intensity when you deduct the carbon price from the outright power price because we have  already financially hedged our higher than market average carbon intensity.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The right question is, at what CO2 price? I mean, let me maybe come back or the IR team whether we are willing  to disclose that. On 2023, the entire position is open. But I also want to clearly tell you that we know how sensitive  our economics is towards the carbon price. We were not surprised by the current rally in carbon prices. So, we  are prepared, maybe we are also prepared beyond 2022, but I'm not willing to give you more details at this point  in time.

texts.speaker: Peter Bisztyga
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: Yeah. Hi there. Two questions, please. Firstly, just going back to the implicit fuel hedge, I'm just wondering if it's  adequately calibrated with respect to the bigger role that gas prices are having in setting forward power price at  the moment. So, I'm just wondering if there's any kind of basis risk we need to worry about that.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. Peter, thanks for the question. So, there are no basis risks in the implicit fuel hedge when it comes to  power prices, because the implicit fuel hedge is constantly adjusted to the price set in fuel mix. So, when the price  set in fuel mix changes, because carbon or commodity prices moves, also the implicit fuel hedge is constantly  adjusted. So, when gas becomes more price-setting, the implicit gas part of the hedge increases. So, the only  exposure we have is to that blended spread we show on page 8. But this blended spread can also change. I  mean, it can – some [ph] constellations (00:31:38) have higher parts of gas and others lower parts of gas being  price setting. But, as I said, it's constantly adjusted on a delta basis.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And I mean that these are the employees, but especially the shareholders and the majority shareholder has a  dominant part of the interest of the stakeholder groups. And it's totally clear that it's not in our interest to sell parts  of the company. Two things are excluded from that and these are the UK business, which is part of the merger  agreement with SSE and the Czech gas grid business. This is also excluded from [ph] these (00:33:08)  conditions.

texts.speaker: Alberto Gandolfi
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: Thank you. Good morning. I also have two, please. The first one is that looking anecdotally at what happened on  May 1, like 17 consecutive hours of negative prices, I was quite curious to see – I mean, this has already  happened in the past, but clearly we've grown renewables. It's going to happen more and more and more. So, I  was wondering what happened to your business on those days. I mean what happens to – clearly, your European  Power is quite obvious, but can you make money out of it from trading or we just purely see this as a negative  going forward for your business?

texts.speaker: Alberto Gandolfi
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: And the second question is, do you have any thoughts on the likelihood by the European Union to upgrade the  2030 renewable targets and perhaps stick into renewables? texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. Alberto, let me start with the second one because it's the easier one. Yes. I mean, we said we will come out  with our renewable strategy when we had intensive discussions with two renewables teams at innogy and E.ON.  But in terms of focus markets or core markets, that is not only Germany, the UK and the Benelux that includes all  of Europe and North America. So, we will also look into the other market as actually innogy's and E.ON's  renewables business already do.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On the negative prices, I mean, when power prices are negative, you don't earn any money from running  conventional power generation. That is totally obvious. You have to shut it for the time being, which we have also  done especially in these days. But you can make money from commercial asset optimization. And maybe I'll give  you a little example how that works.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On the forward markets, it's not clear even in the intra- – in the [ph] week ahead (00:35:56) market at which hours  you have negative power prices. So, you have a blended power price for a day or a week and then people start  buying and we start selling and you lock in an average margin and even it being very tiny, you don't make lots of  money from hedging. But then, you see the daily volatility. And in those hours, where power prices are negative,  you shut down your own power plant and you buy the power from the market and even getting money.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And in the other hours where prices are higher, you bring on additional capacity, where you earn additional  money. So, the higher the volatility in the market is, the more we can actually make. But the more concerning  thing is that the average load factor of the [ph] conventional (00:36:49) generation comes down. But we are  addressing that is now also expanding into renewables.

texts.speaker: Lueder Schumacher
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA (UK)
texts.text: Good morning or good afternoon. Yeah. Two questions from my side as well. The first one is coming back to the  rather popular topic of your clean-dark/spark-spread position. You mentioned that they came back or rather that  they peaked just as the talks of Jamaica coalition collapsed. But in your view, why have clean-dark/spreads come  back? And what's going to reverse that? Because the whole idea of coal closures is not off the table, it's still there.  So, in your view what are the main drivers for the clean-dark/spread going forward. And what was the reason for  the decline? And the second question is on your variation margin, your rather good cash flow number. What was  the underlying instrument there? I assume it will be carbon, is that correct?

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Lueder, thanks for the question. The first one, on clean-dark/spreads, yes, I fully agree that the topic of coal  closures is not off the table. Maybe it picks up when now the commission will start work, but it remains to be seen  when it will start. First, they need to agree on the nominations. And what we have seen under the Jamaica  coalition talks is, that the system is now becoming so tight, that when you talk about 5 to 7 gigawatts of additional  closures, spreads will go up significantly. And currently, I think the market doesn't anticipate a single closure in the  early 2020s. And that may be too optimistic on tightness. So, we think, at current spread levels, it's not worth  hedging the position.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On variation margins, I mean, in terms of instruments, I mean, clear variation margins, fully clear instrument,  which commodity it is, I will not disclose, because by that, I would disclose maybe also some things we do long- term for the company. I mean, what it shows and we said it's a temporary effect in one way that is right. In the  other way, it also means when we realize this cash in the generation margin, it is still there. I mean, it's better than  not having done the hedges. But in the line item variation margin, it will reverse by that time. But whether that was  a long position in carbon or short position and other things, I can't tell you.

texts.speaker: Ingo Becker
texts.profession: Analyst, Kepler Cheuvreux SA (Germany)
texts.text: Yeah. Thank you. Good afternoon. I had also two questions. The first on CO2, I think you said – many of us  probably [ph] shared that (00:40:17) in the past, the CO2 growth was rather behavioral than really fundamental.  And I guess many of us at the same time now wondering if that has changed.

texts.speaker: Ingo Becker
texts.profession: Analyst, Kepler Cheuvreux SA (Germany)
texts.text: And the other question – sorry to ask this as well, but also interested in your view on the fuel spread chart on  page 8. [indiscernible] (00:41:04) it's truly predominantly the coal closure debate or would you detect anything  else that might have changed in the last few months in the markets' forward assessment of the situation? Thank  you.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. Ingo, thanks for the question. I mean, on CO2, it is very difficult. I mean, to be very honest, we don't have a  view whether the €15 we see today is fundamentally right value or it should be a €20 or a €12, and where it  should go next year when we run into the physical supply shortage, because you need to make assumptions.  What has been done by utilities in terms of hedging? How will they change their hedging behavior when prices  are higher? And also, at which prices are industrials willing to sell part of their surpluses. It's very difficult. I mean,  I give you my personal view, I wouldn't be surprised that carbon goes up even higher this year and even higher  next year.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On fuel spreads, I think what you have seen now with spreads coming significantly down. This is maybe even  more than not only anticipating coal closures. texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Political discussions around nuclear energy and the entire national energy concept in Germany,  create a lot of uncertainty. texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: All our key financials were up by more than 20% compared to the first half 2009. Even without  Essent, our operating result would have gone up by 11%. texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In addition, our Central Eastern and South Eastern Europe division performed well. One important  driver in the year has been our regional gas supply business in the Czech Republic. texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We also made progress executing our growth strategy. In June RWE Innogy entered into a joint  venture with the Munich Municipal Utility and Siemens to construct and operate 576 megawatt  Gwynt y Môr wind farm off the Coast of Northern Wales. RWE Innogy owns 60% of the joint  venture.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Also in June, RWE Innogy and the Dutch technology company Topell Energy laid the foundation for  one of the world’s first industry scale biocoal pellet production plant. The plant will have a       corrected transcript

texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 2 production capacity of 60,000 tons per year and start operations in 2011. Such coal firing helps to meet stringency on two targets with the  existing thermal power stations i.e. no new build necessary.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Having signed the West Nile Delta concession agreement in July, we are on route to significantly  increase RWE Dea’s gas production capacity. texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: You can see that RWE is working hard to reach growth targets in the fields of renewable energies  and upstream gas and oil. As you can read on this  slide, the justifications for this tax are more than questionable both from a market perspective, as  well as from a legal point of view. A benefit sharing mechanism needs to be linked to a nuclear  lifetime extension. Our understanding is that, such a tax on any other profit-sharing mechanism the  so-called fund solution can only be referred to additional production volumes over and above those  set in the 2001 exit agreements.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: From our point of view, there are convincing arguments that the current draft law cannot be a  solution. Based on our expert calculations, the specific additional costs would amount to at least €22 per  megawatt hour. This is a first rough indication, but it gives you the order of magnitude. texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The public debate and the media make us forget that the government is still considering nuclear  lifetime’s extensions. I would even say for the most Cabinet Members, they are committed as laid  down in the coalition agreement.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: So we are using this as the base case assumption and are working on a solution representing a  legally binding agreement for all parties involved. texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In talks with investors, we frequently got the question who is working on this issue at RWE and at  what priority? I can assure you that I personally, my colleagues and our complete staff, plus all  other nuclear operators in Germany put the highest priority on this topic.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Just to give you some more flavor, while Pohlig is discussing solutions with the Ministry of Finance  and I have the privilege to be in talks with the Chancellor’s Office, Gerd Jäger, the nuclear, where  the Board Member of RWE Power responsible for nuclear operations is heading the council for       corrected transcript

texts.profession: Operator
