texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Shah Deniz II is estimated to have between 10 to 13 bcm per year of gas available for export to  Europe by 2016. In Northern Iraq, the Kurdistan regional government has publicly committed to up  the 15 bcm per year for Nabucco and we are investigating these volumes. Finally with regards to  Turkmenistan, we are supporting the European Commission’s initiative to facilitate the finalizing of  transit arrangements for Turkmen Gas through the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan and Georgia. We will  continue to look at all these options and evaluate as always their commercial viability.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Ladies and gentlemen, the core message of today’s presentation is, RWE is performing well  despite uncertainties around the decisions about nuclear lifetime extension and the entire German  energy concept. But before I hand over to Rolf, who will explain to you the details of our H1 results,  let me conclude my part with the outlook for 2010.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Now on to our divisional performance, let me start with RWE Power. It’s operating result improved  by 25%. Slide 13 gives you the individual value drivers as usual. We expect the positive trend at  RWE Power to continue during the rest of the year. The higher availability of our Biblis nuclear  power plant and lower costs for fuel and CO2 emission certificates will be the main reasons for this.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Let’s have a quick look at the status of our German forward selling. We have sold more than 90%  for 2010, more than 80% for 2011. We have hedged more than 35% for 2012 and we have started  selling volumes for 2013. Average realized prices are still above €60 per megawatt hour, which in  principle corresponds to a mix of approximately 80 to 90% base and 10 to 20% peak. We see an  increase in peak load exposure due to our change in power plant portfolio and the growth in  renewables in the overall system. And of course, not all of our generation volumes are exposed  purely to the out-priced electricity price. For the production based on hard coal and gas, the  development of spreads is more relevant. They have come down significantly for the last couple of  months. You can find more details on our backup slides 30 to 33.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Our sales and distribution network business area closed slightly above the previous year. The cold  winter supported our gas sales volumes and favored gas margins. This was offset by low electricity  margins. The German distribution network business benefited from the economic recovery, which  led to increased volumes. Lower costs for grid losses had a positive impact as well. In addition, the  regulator allowed higher costs for growth CapEx to be included in network price.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: On the other hand, the business areas suffered from the refunding of excess proceeds I explained  this in detail already in February. We expect the operating results to be up for 2010 as a whole.  This will be mainly due to improved earnings in the gas sales business above all because of the  absence of one-off costs by the negative gas to oil spreads incurred in 2009.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Now on to our new Netherlands/Belgium division. Numbers for 2010 are substantially affected by  consolidation. I explained the major items in the Q1 presentation. The performance of the  Netherlands/Belgium division was supported by higher gas sales due to the cold winter weather  and favored customer account numbers. Please don’t extrapolate H1 for the full year. We’ve  already mentioned in Q1 that more than 50% of the annual result is typically earned in the first  quarter. In addition, in the second half of this year we would see costs related to the implementation  of a new retail customer gas system and one-off costs partially linked to the integration of Essent  into RWE.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 6 Let me continue with RWE npower. Its operating results improved by 14% adjusted for FX effects, it  grossed by 11%. Earnings from our retail business were the main driver of the improved  performance. Earnings in our gas business were covered on the back of improved residential  demand over the winter month and slightly lower commodity costs. This was partially offset when  we lowered our gas tariffs at the end of March this year. In addition, we have seen lower electricity  margins following our tariff cut in March last year.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The performance of our generation business was down, driven by reduced spreads and lower  income from short-term position management, which was partly compensated for, by reduced  maintenance costs. We expect that lower spreads will also influence the performance of our  generation business for 2010 as a whole. This will be partially offset by the commissioning of our  new power plant at Staythorpe in the second half of this year and a reduction in station  maintenance costs.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: As the build-up of arising nuclear power continues, we are seeing high upfront costs for our UK  nuclear development program. Although the aforementioned tariff reductions in our retail business  is putting pressure on margins, we expect negative impacts from high electricity network fees. We  expect retail margins to benefit from slightly lower commodity costs. However, the benchmark  continues to be extremely challenging due to the significant increases in commodity prices over the  last month.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Our focus will remain on efficiencies to ensure competitive cost base. The €120 million program  initiated last year, they will be turned into a sustainable improvement and we are working on  additional efficiency measures, generation, retail and corporate functions or we anticipate a slight  increase out of the npower’s operating results.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We anticipate that earnings generated by this division will now be more in the order of last year  supported by positive Forex effects. The main reason for the slowdown of earnings growth in the  second half of this year is that margins in our Czech gas sales business as well as in the Hungarian  electricity sales and generation business are expected to come down again. On the other hand, we  will see higher earnings contributions from our Czech regional gas sales business.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Our renewables division posted an increase in its operating results of 13%. First time consolidation  of the Essent wind assets contributed €9 million to earnings. We explained already in Q1 that this is  less than originally expected due to the very weak wind production caused by the weather. As the  first quarter is the most important one for this business, we don’t expect to make up for low  earnings during the rest of the year.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The first time consolidation of Danta de Energias in May last year, as well as the commissioning of  the 90 megawatt Rhyl Flats wind farm also had a positive effect on our earnings. In contrast upfront  costs for our large investment program still dampened the development of Innogy’s operating  result. In addition, earnings went down due to lower realized electricity prices in Germany and  Spain, and less wind volumes in UK. As regards to 2010, we expect RWE Innogy to record higher  operating revenues. We achieved further results of our growth investment program. But upfront  costs for our projects are still offsetting most of this.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 7 In addition, Innogy will benefit from the first time consolidation of Essent’s wind activities but due to  the low wind volumes in northwestern Europe, the advantage will be less than originally expected. I  would like to remind you that the earnings improvement will accelerate in the coming years.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Upstream gas and oil reported a 48% increase in operating earnings. This is mainly a result of  higher oil prices, as well as reduced exploration costs in North Africa. In addition, we benefited from  lower royalties in the German business. On the other hand, Dea suffered from lower gas prices and  production volumes. Compared to the very weak 2009, we see significant upside potential for 2010.  RWE Dea expects to see improved oil prices. This will be partly offset by lower gas prices and  volumes as well as increasing production costs.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The operating results in our Trading/Gas Midstream division fell by 62%. The mark-to-market  performance of the trading business fell behind the high level of the first half last year. On the other  hand, we benefited from the first time consolidation of the Essent trading activities. They  contributed €68 million in the first half of this year. The steep decline is mainly related to our gas  supply activities. This is because of two major items. First, in the first half of last year, we had  successfully concluded price revisions. Secondly, gas market prices dropped compared to oil  indexed purchase contracts. This especially affected our Czech gas portfolio due to growing  competition. As a result, we’ve built a provision.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In 2010, we expect the division to close significantly below last year’s record level despite the  integration of Essent’s trading activities. Lower trading margins compared to the extraordinarily high  level in 2009, the absence of aforementioned one-off items recognized in 2009, as well as the  provisions for Czech gas portfolio are the main reasons. The current situation in the Czech gas  market might even require further provisions in the second half of this year.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Patrick Hummel>: Yes, good afternoon, gentlemen, and thanks for taking my questions.  There are two questions please. First one, regarding the nuclear regulation and basically you  indicated that you are committed to your gearing targets and imply that there is downside to your  CapEx, going forward. So I will be interested in case of you are successful to negotiate an  alternative clawback instead of a tax wouldn’t that mean the same cash flow impact and therefore  wouldn’t that mean the same 3 to 4 billion downside to your CapEx planning going forward?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Jürgen Großmann>: He was just waving obviously at me. Well, as you can see in the  German environment at the moment everything is influx. Just day before yesterday a new tax on  coal and gas input seemed to be levied, which was revoked yesterday. And there is absolutely no  certainty yet on the amount of levy that’s going to be imposed on us with either a fuel tax or the so  called fund solutions. But you are right, in the end, they are talking about money and when we are  paying this money to the government or even into a fund it will have certain impacts on our CapEx.  So I wouldn’t take anything for granted at the moment. There are still political deals to be made but  it’s clear that the CapEx will be reduced by some margin.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Deborah Wilkens>: Yes. Good afternoon. I was hoping you could help us by putting the  following in order of priority for you were, I do believe need to respond to the nuclear tax proposal.  you rating the CapEx – the gross CapEx and the dividend? That’s my first question. My second  question is whether or not you believe the rating agencies would view the two scenarios, tax versus  prepayment differently?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: I think that what I presented before that was a very balanced statement, which  we had carefully thought through before making that statement. But with respect to the response for  rating agency, I think as long as we have a very, very high certainty that the prepayment is actually  kind of investments, i.e., we can later on used them additional volumes from nuclear power  generation then I think it should be acceptable to treat this as an investment.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Lueder Schumacher>: Yes, good afternoon. Two questions, first and actually obvious one,  but can we assume that without the whole nuclear debate on fuel tax and life extensions, et cetera  that your mid-term guidance would remain absolutely unchanged, for the only thing that has  changed with is the nuclear debate.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And the second question is on the Czech gas business of course, extremely successful first half  and the guidance is just about been moved to flat which seems to me that you are expecting pretty  horrible second half there. So, could you perhaps give us an idea of what exactly the margin is in  the Czech gas business and what could possibly happen to it in the second half?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 11 <A – Rolf Pohlig>: Let me start with the first question, Lueder. I think on the one side, it’s clear that  we only once a year provide the mid-term guidance to the market and about in this circumstances  with the nuclear fuel tax not on the horizon but next door, we have to make the market aware that  we have our mid-term guidance under review. On the other side, we made also right from  beginning very clear to the market that our mid-term guidance is also based on a set of  assumptions and the most important assumptions were also disclosed to the market in the past.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And of course, the longer we have not thin prices, which were essential elements of these  assumptions especially the power forward prices as well as the gas-to-oil spread, as long as this  lasts, the more challenging – let me phrase it that way, the more challenging it would be to stick to  the original guidance mid-term, which we provided.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: With respect to the second question, I’m not quite sure whether you were referring to our mix – gas  midstream business for the Czech Republic or our downstream business in Czech Republic. I think  with respect to the downstream business there, we had a very strong fourth quarter last year, so  there is basis effect and for that reason, we do not expect that high growth rate, which we have  seen in the first half of this year to continue for the rest of this year. So it’s not horrible, but we had  last year and the fourth quarter, a very, very strong fourth quarter.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Peter Wirtz>: Okay. And second question regarding your Trading and Gas Midstream  business, you mentioned that the burn on the oil index gas contracts are persisting, can you give a  bit of guidelines regarding the further trends into that, what we can expect for the end of the year  and heading into 2011?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: That in so far is a very challenging question because a lot of assumptions we  have to make to make an assessment of whether or not the provision we built in the first half of this  year is sufficient. It’s not only the gas to oil spread, how it is reflected in the forward markets, but it’s  also what is our expectation about the further competitiveness in the local Czech market. What is  our assumption about the outcome, the actual or assumed outcome of price provisions and all that  kind of stuff has an impact on that. So I’m not in a position to give you a definitive answer to that,  but as I mentioned in the presentation, there is a risk that we will see further burns in the rest of the  year.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Operator:  Thank you. Next question comes from Benjamin Leyre of Exane BNP Paribas.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Benjamin Leyre>: Thank you and good afternoon. My first question is on the gas business,  you actually indicate that you won some customers, in Germany on gas retail. Do you actually see  this spud gas cheapness as actually an opportunity for your German gas business, which could  compensate for the Czech weakness?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And related to this where do you stand regarding your view to – for the need to renegotiate gas  procurement contracts and do you think it’ll be easier this time around to renegotiate your  procurement contracts with your gas suppliers?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And the second question, is on your, the nuclear tax. Can you please share with us, what your main  municipal shareholders are, the way they are positioned today? Are they helping you on the debate  of nuclear tax or are they actually considering getting out of the nuclear [inaudible]? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Jürgen Großmann>: Well, let me start with the second question first. Our nuclear  shareholders are helping us in this debate, I mean, that, not maybe all with the same -

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Stephan Lowis>: Municipal shareholders they are not nuclear.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Jürgen Großmann>: No. I said nuclear, I said municipal. You see nuclear is pervading my  brain, I’m sorry. Our municipal shareholders are to various degrees supporting us. Their heart is  where their money is and they know that, let’s say, that the whole prosperity of the company  depends on this. But of course this support has varying degrees of intensity and some municipal  governments who have a red-green coalition that is of course not quite as strongly supporting our –  also most of our municipal shareholders don’t have their own generating capacity. The opposition  from some municipalities in Germany mainly stems from them having relatively high cost coal-fired  power stations and they think that they will profit from the earlier exit of the nuclear power stations.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: Yes, perhaps I should add one other thing. Our municipal shareholders are not  only as all shareholders are concerned with respect to the future profitability and dividends of the  company. But in addition to that a lot of them are also the recipients of the trade tax and to the  extent that this nuclear fuel tax is tax deductible for trade tax purposes.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: They would suffer from that prospective condition and so far they have every incentive to articulate  themselves within their respective organizations, with the augment that the Berlin government is  balancing their budget at the cost of the local budgets. With respect to the German gas retail  business, yes, we increased the number our customers, but to give you the figure, it is by 14,000.  So that does not compensate for the impact you see in the Czech gas midstream business.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: So it would leave trading and other. You’ve mentioned possible provisions in trading and what type  of number are we talking about there? And what might happen in the other category? And then the  second question was a follow-up on the CapEx as you’re going forward. Appreciate that you’ve not  got the discretion until 2012, 2013. In what business lines would you have the greatest amount of  discretion? Would it just be at the renewables business and the upstream or should we be looking  in a wider sphere than that?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: I think to start with the last question. We should have a look in the wider  sphere, but I think what you have mentioned that is upstream and that is renewables. We are still in  the process of making further decisions on projects we have in the other divisions. We had already  in the past made decisions on major projects, so there is only or relatively little still to change. With  respect to Q4, I think we should have in mind, I already mentioned it that we had quite a basis  effect from the second half of last year, especially last quarter of last year where already a €0.01  was included in the figures. Hence I already mentioned that in the southeastern and central eastern  division, we also had a very strong last quarter of last year. So we should have that in mind have  this base effect. I’m not quite sure whether there was a third question 1a/1b.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: Yes. You are right. I already mentioned this that with respect to trading there is  limited growth there is quite the opposite there is that risk which we report under gas midstream in  the Czech Republic and for Essent as well there is for the second half this year, only very limited for  the growth potential. So I think that is the answer to this question.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 14 <Q – Matthias Heck>: Yes, hi, good afternoon. I have two questions for you. First one relates to  the provision in the Czech gas midstream business. Could you quantify the impact, and also  mention whether you had an option to build that provision, or whether it was an application because  obviously your position in the gas business in the Czech Republic is not unique in the utility sector?  Second question is you mentioned you expect to pay an attractive dividend also for 2010. Could  you please elaborate a little bit on that specifically whether the €3.50 you paid for 2009 this year,  are already an attractive level? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: With respect to the first question, the provision we built for the Czech portfolio  of our gas supply business that is a low triple digit figure. We are under an obligation under the IAS  rules is no flexibility, but having said that, I already mentioned that the size of that provision is  highly depending on assumptions about pricing, about price development, about customer behavior  and about the potential outcome of price negotiations, and in so far that is really depending on the  assumptions.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Ingo Becker>: Yes. Thank you. Good afternoon. I was wondering if you could provide a  breakdown of the total generating cost of 22 to 32 for fully depreciated plant on slide six. I guess  the 1b question would be if you could tell us your generation price in the first half in Germany,  which was €70 per megawatt hour last year. And finally, I was wondering if you had any insights  into the wider elements of the German energy plan on discussions right now, beyond the taxes  whether we should be expecting a comprehensive vision or action plan, or whether you think this is  largely to be a piecemeal strategy, and without a very clear framework for the next 10 years? Thank  you.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Jürgen Großmann>: Well, very simple answers to that, Ingo. The first one is that, over and  above the breakdown, which you mentioned, we will not give any further information on the cost of  the individual plant generation costs in Germany.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Ingo Becker>: It was on the energy plant, the government [inaudible]. Thank you,

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Jürgen Großmann>: Yes, we would hope for – I mean, of course I’m sorry, I forgot that  because I thought that this one was the most difficult one to answer. And the government is  employing two quite competent research and think tank institutions. Once they come out with the  long-term energy concept for Germany, the last one developed was under the Schmidt government  in the 70s – in the late 70s.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Since then, no German government has ever attempted to develop a scheme in which the  renewables have a certain role and so on. And we would definitely hold that this concept is being  developed and that the nuclear extension of costs would be piecemeal, if it wasn’t fit into this total  energy concept. So I had a couple of contacts with the Chancellor in the last week, last time I saw,  it was last Sunday evening and she was radiantly optimistic that this comprehensive and all  encompassing scheme could be put together.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: And may I add one other sense with respect to the generation cost. There is a  study available from the German Ministry for the economics, which for the average of the German  nuclear fleet, gives you, I think a 27 or €28 per megawatt hour figure. And then you have to see that  the smaller stations have higher generation costs than the big ones to lower ones. So that gives  you the 22 to 32 range and I have to stress that, they are the generation costs of fully depreciated  nuclear power stations.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Andreas Thielen>: Yes, good afternoon. First question on your forward sales. I noted that for  2012 the difference is roughly 5% versus the first quarter. Given the price development in the  second quarter with hindsight would you think that it would have been better to serve more than  that or would if – would it actually have been impossible to serve more than that? And the 1b  question to that would be on the 2013 sales, where you say that you have started to sell volumes,  who is taking the CO2 price risk there, is it you or your customer?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And the second question, very simple one, on nuclear again, can you give any indications what you  think about the potential timetable, which was given with first studies out on the 27th of August and  an agreement by something like mid-September, if that is feasible from your point of view? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Jürgen Großmann>: Well, as to the last one. That’s mine again. There are few to use RWE  language, milestones. The first one is the budget. The budget needs to be concluded by the end of  September and the budget needs certain assumptions as to what income can be derived from  nuclear. The government has told us that they would keep this kind of flexible so that until that  moment no finalization of any concept needs to be done. The Chancellor herself has told me that if  she wants to finish the whole energy concept by the end of October. Now of course, some of these  dates are, as always in the political process, are flexible.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: With respect to 2013, that really tends who your counterparty is but you will perhaps remember that  we’d mentioned in the past that we have concluded contracts covering 2013, but also following  years, we have the customers prepared to take care of this price risk. Whereas in other instances,  i.e., when we sell via the power exchange and then of course, we had to take care of the CO2 price  mix but given the banking opportunity between the second and third compliance periods that is  conceptually not such a big issue.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Bobby Chada>: Good afternoon. So, two questions, please. The first is on the renewables  business, I understand there were a number of one-off factors affecting the relatively slow progress  in profit terms this year. I just wondered, if you could confirm that on an underlying basis, you’re still  comfortable with the progress coming through in line with the budget that gets you to roughly 500  million of EBIT by 2013. And secondly on the UK business, again I appreciate that you don’t want  to give too much split quarter-by-quarter or generation versus supply. But I think it is clear the  business is lagging many of its peers.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: You have two big issues. I guess one is the out of the money hedges. The other is the power plants  under construction. Are you – can you at least give a statement that where these two things coming  through, I think the hedges roll off at the end of this year or early next year and the power plants are  up and running pretty soon that you expect significant progress and profit terms in the UK?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Now as to the first part of the question with renewables you are – let me compare this to an  agricultural business. Sometimes you have a good harvest. Sometimes you have a bad harvest.  For the last two years, we had a bad harvest in wind. And – but your question actually reached  deeper. If – and I’m not saying we will, but if we have to reduce or postpone investment for some  time in renewables I don’t think we can make the 500 million income by 2013. But let’s wait. I mean  we’re in a state of flux. I said that this conference comes a couple of weeks too early. Let’s see  when we know more figures about what our future looks like.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Jürgen Großmann>: Well, no. No, you see, we had quite a bit of setup costs. We are a big  player and we rolled out Innogy as a company that is involved in many fields. We didn’t only want to  be an offshore wind company. We looked into solar thermal, we looked into biomass. We looked  into a lot of things. We kind of, build a very wide road. We made some – well we conclude that not  all fields will be ultimately where we want to be. But I think it was necessary. We were a late starter  and it was necessary that we gained experience.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Christopher Kuplent>: Thank you, Good afternoon. Let me start with questions 1a to 1d.  Only joking, first question is, you were referring to a review – or a potential review not just of your  earnings outlook, but also your dividend policy if this nuclear tax is becoming a reality. Does that  mean you are putting under review the same as 50 to 60% payouts beyond 2010? That would be  my first question and the second one, similar to what Bobby just asked regarding your CapEx cuts  3 to 4 billion, I guess you already told that you haven’t identified project-by-project where these cuts  could come from, but I wanted to ask whether given that you’re losing earnings growth if you don’t  invest this CapEx, whether you would also consider selling assets outright?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: As to in CapEx or an outright sale of assets, we have put assets for sale like ETS oil and gas, there  maybe a few others, but our strategy in the past was that we wanted to be in a relatively dense core  area of Europe. So we don’t have anything far away in America or so that we could sell without it  having an impact on us and you mentioned it very well. If we cut in CapEx, it will also cut our future  income stream. So we are in a quite – it’s not a very pleasant process, but we will have to see how  can we improve our result and we should – we take this as an additional impetus to look at our  internal structures, our cost structures and make progress in our efficiency enhancement programs.  But I will not tell you now that we are making a major disposal of assets, that is not what I want to  tell you today.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Christopher Kuplent>: Okay. Thanks. Can I just ask for clarification on, sorry again, the  dividend? I was particularly keen to know whether you can confirm the 50 to 60% will be applied  come what May, in the years ahead whether we have a nuclear tax or a fund?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 18 accelerated in the first half, maybe you can put a number on the CRM and integration costs. And  also tell us whether this is a 2010 issue or this could also going to 2011? And the second question  on slide five, you show quite a convincing case about your potential legal position against this  nuclear fuel tax. How are you managing to leverage this and at which point, would you be ready to  press the button? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: Yes. We of course have not made our mind, which is the point of time where  we push the button for that strategy. But you see with respect to the earlier position, well there are  several legal arguments. The first one is, there is a EURATOM treaty for the European Atomic  Energy Community and there is an Article 86 in that contract, which states that, nuclear fuel is  commercially owned by the EURATOM organization. And in Article 3 of that same EURATOM  protocol, it is said that the nuclear fuel is exempt from any direct taxation of the member states. So  that’s the first legal argument from a European legal point of view.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The second legal argument from a European point of view is that there is the Energy Tax Directive,  which states that a member state can either to impose a tax on the used primary fuel or on the  generated power but not on built. But as we have in our country introduced a power tax several  years ago an additional imposition of a tax on a primary fuel would violate the double taxation then  according to Article 14 and 21 of the Energy Tax Directive. These are the two most important deal  aspects from a European point-of-view.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: From a German constitutional point-of-view, there is the issue of consumption tax. The nuclear fuel  tax in the draft law is described as a consumption tax. And the consumption tax based on the  legislation by – or the jurisprudence as expressed by the Federal Constitutional Court for  consumption taxes it is essential that in the bulk of the situations you can pass through the tax  burden to final customers. And what is interesting to see is that in the reasons to the law, the  Finance Ministry has explicitly described that this tax cannot be passed through to end-customers  due to the Merit Order, and so far that is inconsistent with the positions made in the past – even in  the more recent past by the Federal Constitutional Court.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Then of course, we have the issue of ownership rights and to the extent, already the 2000, 2001  phase out agreement impacted our ownership rights in our existing nuclear power stations tax  burden on that which was explicitly forbidden by that contract would lead to a situation, that our  constitutional rights are negatively affected. So, these are a range of different legal arguments  which would have to be followed in different ways, but let’s be very clear about that, if we have to  follow that route, that would be a lengthy process of several years.
