texts.speaker: Jürgen Großmann
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Turbulent weeks are lying behind us with all the uncertainties about the new German energy policy. Today, we  want to give you our strategic answers to how RWE will respond to the new situation. What are the major  differences compared to our situation in February? The German Government has withdrawn from the nuclear  lifetime extension but the nuclear fuel tanks stays in place. As a result, we are facing significant one-off burdens in  the current financial year.

texts.speaker: Jürgen Großmann
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Slide four gives you the operating performance of the group. EBITDA and operating results suffered by  approximately €700 million from the unexpected and hurried nuclear exit decision, plus approximately €200  million from the expected nuclear fuel tax. This is overshadowing the good performance in some of our divisions,  on which Rolf will enlarge later. But today, we don't look back and argue whether this decision makes sense or not.  We accept; we must accept the political will and [ph] to trust the (02:33) strategy accordingly. And you will see  that our general strategy we started in 2008 to make RWE more sustainable, more international and more robust,  is the right answer to this new environment, and therefore stays in place.

texts.speaker: Jürgen Großmann
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Due to the early nuclear closure, we are facing significant financial constraints. As a result, we will adapt our speed  to execute the strategy and have to ensure that our financial strength will not deteriorate in the long term. In this  context, you know about our planned divestment program after the successful sale of Thyssengas and our stake in  the Rostock hard-coal plant. The recent decision to bring long-term oriented financial investors onboard of our  TSO Amprion was a further important step in that direction. But against the unforeseen backlog of the current  environment, the financial pressure has intensified. Therefore, we will step up our disposal program and intend to  protect our solid A rating, which is important to finance long-term growth in our core markets. More details on  that later.

texts.speaker: Jürgen Großmann
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Before I start with the details of our planned measures, let me provide you with a summary of the key decisions of  the German Government on slide five. We were forced to shut down two of our five nuclear units, Biblis A and B,  with a total generation capacity of approximately 2.4 gigawatts or approximately 18 gigawatt hours per year. We  will make sure we protect the property rights of our shareholders and have already started legal action against the  moratorium decision and the nuclear fuel tax. The decision of the German Government was made at the peak of  our huge investment program to build highly-efficient conventional power plants and significant investment in  the renewables business as part of our CO2 mitigation strategy. This is an additional burden, which we couldn't  have expected at the beginning of the year. Although the nuclear phase-out will impact our CO2 mitigation  strategy, we uphold our general target. The measures we have initiated will reduce our CO2 exposure significantly.  Hence, from today's point of view, we are slightly along CO2 over the period from 2013 to 2020.

texts.speaker: Jürgen Großmann
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Please bear in mind, when we say evaluate our options it is still open whether we divest an asset fully, the majority  or a minority stake only. A good example is RWE Dea. The required contribution to support our balance sheet  might already be achieved by the sale of growth assets like, for example, our activities or part of our activities in  Egypt. Our planned joint venture with Gazprom is a further option within this program. We want to evaluate  potential partnerships in power generation. The benefit is to improve our CO2 position and to share the capital- intensive financing of such projects between two partners. This memorandum of understanding is not only an  attractive way to look for a project partner; it is an additional important chance to bring the current negotiations  on our gas contracts to a mutually satisfactory conclusion. We are still at an early stage and nothing concrete can  be added at this point in time, but it is a good starting point of further discussions in the next two months. And let  me add, both parties are willing to develop this MoU.

texts.speaker: Jürgen Großmann
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Our second building block is our CapEx program. As you know, 2011 will be the peak of our investment cycle in  mitigation strategy. This program will be more or less finalized by 2013. We expect CapEx in the next two years to  come down to less than €5 billion per annum. We see the long-term sustainable CapEx after our disposal program  at a level of about €4 billion. This includes approximately €2 billion of day-to-day CapEx, i.e., maintaining our  traditional businesses. The other €2 billion is earmarked for new projects, if they meet our strict financial criteria  for growth investments. Potential small bolt-on acquisitions are already included in this number. In 2012 and  2013, a significant amount of investments is already committed. From 2014 onwards, this will come down to a  level of 60% and lower including the day-to-day investments. This of course does not mean that we don't have  attractive investment opportunities; it is just an illustration of our flexibility to reduce CapEx, if needed, to further  support our solid A rating.

texts.speaker: Jürgen Großmann
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, RWE AG
texts.text: The aforementioned measures are accompanied by capital measures. These measures in particular will set the  stage for long-term growth and support our credit rating. Due to the loss of future cash flows from nuclear lifetime  extensions and the cash burden from the nuclear fuel tax, we can't avoid these measures anymore. We will pursue  two capital measures. First, we want to execute an equity capital measure of approximately €2.5 billion in total.  Depending on market conditions, we intend to execute this placement by the end of the year, but this is not a  must. We cannot be more specific about the details at the moment, but it will include the sale of our treasury  shares. Second, also depending on market conditions, we intend to issue further hybrid bonds by the end of 2012  to bridge the near-term financial needs.

texts.speaker: Jürgen Großmann
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Although we have a changed investment environment, we still have the financial flexibility to invest in the growth  areas, renewable energy at Eastern Europe including Turkey. We want to dedicate more than €1 billion per annum  for growth CapEx into renewables at more than €0.5 billion per annum for Eastern Europe including Turkey. We  can confirm our target for the renewables division to reach a capacity of 4.5 gigawatts by 2014 and to generate  operating earnings of €500 million in the same year. Central Eastern and South Eastern Europe promise a lot of  growth opportunities along all parts of the value chain. Of course, it will be of top priority to carefully evaluate  which are the most promising projects and what risk profile they have. Our focus therefore will be on organic  growth combined with selective small bolt-on acquisitions. There will be also a combination of renewable  investments in the region, Central and Southeastern Europe.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: On to our divisional performance, starting with RWE Power; its operating result decreased significantly by 43%.  The impact of the nuclear moratorium followed by the new energy policy played a decisive role in this  development. As a consequence, the operating result is negatively impacted by about €700 million in the first half  of 2011. This already includes the necessary adjustments on nuclear provisions. The nuclear fuel tax came into  effect and had a negative impact on our operating result of about €200 million. Overall, the total impact resulting  from the German energy policy is therefore about €900 million in the first half of this year. As we have mentioned  earlier, we have five lawsuits against the nuclear fuel tax.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: For the entire year, the expected impact of the political decisions on nuclear power is about €1 billion. On top of  that, we are burdened by €300 million of nuclear fuel tax. Compared to the result – impact of the nuclear lifetime  extension and nuclear fuel tax, which we had guided for in February this year, this is an additional unexpected  burden of about €600 million. Furthermore, we have also been negatively affected by the commodity price  development and lower realized electricity prices. For the full year, we expect higher fixed operating and  maintenance cost.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Our Sales and Distribution Network business area closed to 4% below the previous year. We benefited from the  full consolidation of the regional sales and distribution company, NVV, that has previously been accounted for at  equity. The main reason for the lower operating result is the development in our distribution networks business.  Higher temperature and milder weather conditions compared to the previous year led to lower volumes, especially  distribution grid infrastructure. The earnings in our Sales business declined, among other things, due to lower gas  volumes from the back of milder weather conditions. For fiscal year 2011, we expect the operating result to fall  below the previous year despite the first-time full consolidation of NVV. This is mainly as a result of higher OpEx  for improving the quality of our Distribution Network business. The costs for refunding excess proceeds will be  slightly lower than in 2010. For the Sales business, we expect lower gas volumes, assuming normalized weather  conditions. Last year benefited from the cooler-than-average winter.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Now, on to our Netherlands/Belgium division; as you already know, the 2011 results are substantially affected  because we now report part of the gas midstream business and Trading/Gas Midstream. The operational trends  are more or less unchanged compared to the first quarter of this year. We expect fiscal year 2011 to be significantly  below last year. The effects are listed in detail on slide 20.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me continue with RWE npower. The operating result has more than doubled. The increase is mainly attributed  to the improved operating performance of our Retail business, but also to some positive one-off effects. In the  Retail business, npower benefited from improved commodity cost management and growth in the segment of  larger business customers. In addition, our efficiency in cost reduction programs had a positive effect, in  particular on our bad debt position. The performance of our Generation business was supported by the  commencement of operation at our new CCGT plant at Staythorpe. Additional margins have been generated  despite some commissioning defects on two transformers that are currently reducing their production volume.  For full-year 2011, anticipate a significant increase in RWE npower's operating result, reflecting in particular RWE  npower's cost and efficiency programs. The second half of the year we expect to see a decline of the generation  spreads and increased commodity cost.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Operating earnings in our Central Eastern and South Eastern Europe Division reduced to €691 million, 4% below  the previous year's figure. Adjusted for ForEx effects, the division was down 8%. Pressure on earnings came from  weather-induced lower gas sales in the Czech Republic. Earnings are also impacted by lower margins in our  Hungarian business. One reason is that the Hungarian regulator reduced the allowed margins in the household  customer segment. The negative effects were partly compensated for by higher income in our Czech gas transport  business. For 2011, we expect the operating result to be below the exceptionally high number in 2010. In the Czech  Republic, we expect gas sales margins to further come down. The contribution from our Hungarian electricity  activities is also expected to stay slightly behind last year's level though less than anticipated. We expect to see  higher electricity network margins in Poland and a positive development in earnings from our Czech gas  transportation business.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: The operating result of our Renewables division more than tripled to €89 million. Improved wind conditions,  positive volume effects from our growth CapEx and high electricity prices were driving up Innogy's earnings to a  large extent. In addition, we received liquidated damages relating to the Greater Gabbard project as compensation  for lost profits due to construction delays. However, upfront costs for large investment program still weigh on the  division's operating results. We continue to expect RWE Innogy to post a strong earnings increase in 2011.  Generation volumes are set to increase due to the further execution of our expansion program and improved wind  conditions. Upfront costs for our projects will still be offsetting some of the positive effects.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Upstream Gas & Oil reported a 74% increase in operating earnings. Rising oil and gas prices, they're by far the  main factor. In addition, the division recorded high oil production volumes and lower exploration expenditures.  ForEx effects and the lower gas production, increased production costs and higher royalties in the German Gas  business had a counteracting effect. We expect the positive earnings trend to continue, resulting in a significant  operating result increase for full fiscal-year 2011.  The operating result in our Trading/Gas Midstream division turned into a significant negative number in the first  half of 2011. The performance of our Trading business has been exceptionally weak, mainly driven by the  turbulence on commodity markets caused, for instance, by the events in Northern Africa and the changes in  German energy policy. In addition, our Gas Supply business is still under pressure from the negative gas-to-oil  spread. As you all know, we are in negotiations and arbitrations with almost all of our suppliers. As a positive, the  division benefited from Gas Midstream margins which had previously been reported in the Netherlands/Belgium  division. All in all, we expect the operating result in 2011 to fall significantly below the level of 2010.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: The non-operating results increased by €799 million to minus €210 million. In the first half of 2011, capital gains  reached €315 million, mainly as a result of the disposal of Thyssengas and a 24.6% stake in the Rostock hard-coal  power plant. The impact of commodity derivatives on earnings was negligible in the first half-year but improved  significantly compared to last year's figures. Restructuring, other fell by €576 million to minus €522 million,  resulting from several items. In the first half of this year, we booked an impairment for the Essent gas and hard- coal power plant portfolio of approximately €270 million due to decreasing clean generation spreads in the  Deutsch power market. We built in provisions of about €220 million for restructuring programs for RWE Power  and RWE Deutschland to take personal reduction measures in a socially acceptable manner. This measure is a  reaction to the changing market conditions, particular to the early exit from nuclear generation in Germany. Our  financial result improved by €81 million to minus €706 million. This was mainly due to an improvement of our  net interest result. Here, we benefited from the release of provisions accrued in 2010.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Now on to our cash flow statement; funds from operations reduced by about €1 billion, mirroring our operating  performance. Our cash flow from operating activities increased by about 80% to €3.1 billion in the same period,  resulting from positive effects in our working capital. The majority of the CO2 certificates needed for the  redemption in April this year were already paid at the end of last year and therefore reduced our cash needs in  2011. Further relief comes from temporarily improved liquidity situation at Amprion. CapEx on fixed assets was  relatively stable and mainly related to the extension and modernization of our power generation fleet. Overall, free  cash flow increased considerably by €1.2 billion to €403 million. However, please bear in mind that as a result of  our large investment program this will change during the second half of the year.

texts.speaker: Jürgen Großmann
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, RWE AG
texts.text: First, the group's guidance for 2011; the expectation for the operational performance has improved compared to  February and May, but the unforeseeable German nuclear exit will lead to an even higher burden. As a result, we  now expect EBITDA and the operating result to come down by approximately 20% and approximately 25%  respectively. We see recurrent net income declining by approximately 35%. For 2013, we have now taken into  consideration the disposal of Amprion, Thyssengas and the stake in the Rostock hard-coal plant. They account for  €1.5 billion of our divestment program. The expected earnings figures before further divestments have improved  on the back of our increased efficiency program and better commodity prices and spreads.

texts.speaker: Jürgen Großmann
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Ladies and gentlemen, I started my presentation with reference to the turbulent weeks lying behind us. Dust has  settled now and we have a new and clear starting point for the development of RWE. With the package of  we'll be able to continue to finance growth CapEx, which will later on turn into profit growth. And thirdly, RWE  can weather future storms.

texts.speaker: Jürgen Großmann
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Looking forward, RWE will be – I should rather say, will continue to be an excellent operator who is active in  markets that we know and that you know. In addition, with our future investments we are focusing on markets  that we know very well. The energy market environment is changing dramatically, and RWE will be a reliable  partner playing an active role in shaping the new energy landscape. We believe that the combination of all four  actions represent a fair compromise in the interest of all stakeholders. In addition, I'm very happy that yesterday  the Supervisory Board decided early, and I should say timely on the successor to the CEO, and I'm sure that Peter  Terium – in Peter Terium we have an excellent personality whom you already know from investor and analyst  events. Hence, with our strategic measures and the management decision, we now have more or less all the  uncertainty out of the market, which dragged down our share price over the last couple of months.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chairman, Executive Board, RWE Aktiengesellschaft
texts.text: Ladies and gentlemen, the energy industry is going through a far-reaching transformation, and RWE is operating  with a challenging, competitive environment. I am delighted to have the opportunity to play an integral part as  well as take a prominent position in shaping this transformation. This situation is not completely new to me. And  I have firsthand experience on, for instance, disposal programs. One of my most challenging jobs in the past for  RWE was the execution of the disposal of the Waste Management business. Furthermore, I was the CEO of  Essent, responsible for the Essent transaction and its smooth integration, as well as its performance improvement  and delivering even more than the originally promised synergies on this transaction. Last but not the least, I have  been in charge as CEO for over four years of supply and trading by which I'm very familiar with RWE's value chain  and the management of its commodity risks and optimizing those risks. The whole management team, including  myself, will work hard to deliver all what just has been presented.

texts.speaker: Stephan Lowis
texts.profession: Vice President-Investor Relations, RWE AG
texts.text: Perfect. As we mentioned on the last slide, we've taken the June commodity prices. And if you take a look at your  Bloomberg screen and take the average of the June prices, then you are there, what we have taken as commodity  price assumptions.

texts.speaker: Patrick Hummel
texts.profession: Research Analyst, UBS AG (Broker)
texts.text: Okay. And as far as the gas-to-oil spread is concerned, do you assume breakeven in gas wholesale or what's the  underlying assumption there?

texts.speaker: Stephan Lowis
texts.profession: Vice President-Investor Relations, RWE AG
texts.text: We stick to what we said that we expect in 2012 and 2013 to become refunds from that, but the gas-to-oil spreads  we can't see a breakeven now.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Yes. There's still this negative gas-to-oil spread expectation for 2013.

texts.speaker: Peter Wirtz
texts.profession: Research Analyst, Westlb AG (Broker)
texts.text: Hello, good morning. Also two questions from my side. You've put a lot of core assets now on the table for sale,  maybe you cannot be too precise here but maybe you can shed a bit more light on the rationale here behind this  motivation to raise the figure. So especially, would you like to lower the dependence on the German market to the  overall portfolio, which means more focusing on disposals of German assets? And secondly, in terms of your  negotiations with Gazprom, would you sign a deal only if Gazprom would pick up some of your coal power  stations?

texts.speaker: Jürgen Großmann
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Peter, let me answer your question. First, Germany will continue to be our most important market but already  three, four years ago, we said we wanted to reduce the German share of sales and profits from between 60% and  70% where it stood before to approximately around 50%. Now, what we are also looking at when we are looking at  the disposal of individual assets is what is the situation as – for our financial [ph] goal (40:04) and what is the  growth in the area. Also, in some of the German assets we have very reliable and competent partners that are the  municipalities and there is a trend to re-communalize the German energy supply system. So we're taking all that  into account, but it does not mean that we are fleeing Germany. Germany will continue to be our most important  market.

texts.speaker: Jürgen Großmann
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, RWE AG
texts.text: As to Gazprom, the memorandum of understanding is basically on two levels. On the one level, this was already  alluded at in Patrick's question from UBS, we are in negotiations to revise the terms and conditions of the gas  supply agreement. On the other hand, we are checking and considering to put some assets and those are hard-coal  So, this is also partly – could be one part of our asset disposal program and would count against the  aforementioned €11 billion.

texts.speaker: Vincent P. Gilles
texts.profession: Head of European Utilities Research, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Yes, good morning, everyone. I have two questions for Rolf. The first one is on the rights issue. I'm trying to work  out what will be the trigger for you to launch the rights issue. And obviously, I'm trying to wonder about the  timing of setting treasury shares which have gone all the way from the €90 plus to €29 point something today at  the current stage, whether there's a better way maybe for you to defend shareholder value than selling treasury  shares or maybe that's something in – some sort of agreement with a potential long-term partner? That's question  number one. And question number two is you didn't – you gave us a number for the P&L for the nuclear impact,  but you didn't talk about the balance sheet and potential impact of the balance sheet; maybe you can help us a bit  with this?

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: I'm not quite sure whether I got the second question, because what we had an impact in the P&L has also then  impact and – exactly the same impact on the balance sheet with respect to the nuclear decommissioning  provisions. So, I think that – that, you see, might be the answer to the question, if I understand it. With respect to  the rights issue or the capital-raising effort, you know that we try to avoid this but in this new environment after  the new decisions by the German Government there is no way for us to avoid this. We had a very long debate in  the Board between further asset disposals and the capital raising, the diluting impact it will quite obviously have  on income and earnings per share. But at the very end, we came to this overall package which does include an  equity capital raising effort of €2.5 billion. But otherwise, with more and more details, I cannot comment and I  think you would not expect from me a more detailed answer at this point in time.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Next question comes from Benjamin Leyre from Exane BNP Paribas.

texts.speaker: Benjamin Leyre
texts.profession: Research Analyst, Exane BNP Paribas SA
texts.text: Yes. Thank you. Good morning, gentlemen. Two questions; first one on the disposals, can you be a bit more  explicit on the standing of the disposals, if it would be more front-end loaded or back-end loaded? And second  point, you announced that you would do another announcement of a new efficiency program in March 2012.  Would that have any extra impact as soon as 2013, and would that be already included in your 2013 guidance or  would that be actually having an impact after 2013? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Alexander Karnick
texts.profession: Research Analyst, Deutsche Bank GmbH (Broker)
texts.text: Yes. Good Afternoon. Thanks for taking my question. Just two short ones; in your 2013 guidance, could you give  us a little bit of an indication on what kind of a, if you want, margin impact you're assuming on the nuclear  closures; obviously you referred to the output volume of Biblis A and B? And the second question would be just  with respect to the cash flow impact again on nuclear, I mean obviously the missing volumes is included in there,  but just on the dismantling costs that we can expect, maybe a little bit your view on the timing when this starts per  year from now on; that would be very appreciated. Thank you very much.

texts.speaker: Jürgen Großmann
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Alex, first – your first part, if you can tell me what the business cycle in 2013 and what the demand will be, I'll  probably have it a lot easier to tell you how we can satisfy the demand, because we have an idea of what capacities  exist to satisfy that demand. Indeed we believe and the fall would show it that the nuclear shutdown at the  moment has moved forward, up by a little more than 10%, and there is no weakening in that visible. On the other  hand, that equation also [ph] needs (51:44) electricity imports, which are still running high. Basically, our  transmission lines from France and Czech are glowing dark red because of overload; we're importing up to 8  gigawatts at the moment. And we don't know whether that will continue, whether our partners in the EU will  indeed be in a position to supply. So while we know what the available capacity in Germany will be, know how  demand and how supply from outside of Germany will develop.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: I'm not quite sure whether I really got the second question about the nuclear dismantling. I have [ph] not the  adjusted (52:31) with me, but I think we provided to the market in the recent past a slide which demonstrate what  is the overall timeline – the generic timeline of dismantling a nuclear power station, what the active costs are. We  will ensure that this is available to you. But it's really a long-term process, overall decades, so it's not a big cash  outflow each and every year for the India power station to hand out.

texts.speaker: Bobby Chada
texts.profession: Research Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Good morning. Thanks very much for taking the question. My first question is on the CO2 position. I think,  Jürgen, you said in your speech that you were financially slightly long CO2. Would you – are you still less or are  you still more exposed than the market average emission factor and have the CO2 purchases stepped up in the  light of the very low prices? And then my second question is on the UK business. I think in the chart that you  showed, it shows the timing of your new power stations commissioning, the Pembroke CCGT appears to be  coming on in line with expectations. I've read some comments about the lack of environmental permits from the  local government and I wondered how comfortable you are with the expected commissioning timetable?

texts.speaker: Jürgen Großmann
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Bobby, first of all, as to the CO2, we had our – we basically had two targets. The first target was that with the price  setting plans and the CO2 price included, this would be more CO2 than our average emissions per kilowatt hour  generated. And that is still our target and we will achieve that, which basically means that taking into account all  other variables, that a high CO2 price is not to our detriment but will be reflected in a higher electricity price.  That's what we mean with CO2 long. On the other hand, your goal was kind of a secondary goal. We wanted to be  better than the industry average and we still want to be better, but we will not be able to meet that goal by 2020  because the nuclear production is missing. As to the UK, at the moment we see no reason why a further delay  because of non-available permissions to operate should delay Pembroke.

texts.speaker: Vincent De Blic
texts.profession: Research Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Yes, good morning; two questions. The first one is on the balance sheet. You're guiding to a slightly higher  EBITDA in 2013 excluding disposals, but at the same time you're selling more assets and you're planning to  increase capital. Can you repeat – elaborate on what metrics the rating agencies are looking at beyond I mean this  technical net-to-EBITDA, just to help us understand your discussions with them. The second point is on the  Gazprom MoU; obviously your coal and gas plants in the UK, Germany and Holland existing and under  construction is a very, very big portfolio. Can you give us an idea of the potential size of the divestments you'd be  ready to make, maybe an idea of the proceeds you would be targeting and whether the idea is to get some cash in  from Gazprom or whether there's any other potential deal? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Jürgen Großmann
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Vincent, as to the question relating to the MoU with Gazprom, now if you read carefully what we've said, that is we  are selecting assets in Great Britain, Benelux and Germany and they will not be CCGTs only. Why do we not want  to only transfer CCGTs into the possible joint venture, because this would – and that reflects to the question of  Bobby Chada before, this will deteriorate our CO2 position. Therefore, we want to sell or partly dispose our  portfolio that is our average CO2 emission. And here, the intentions of Gazprom meet ours. Gazprom wants to go  into a further value-added step. Instead of selling gas alone, they would also want to be in a position – to be  involved in the electricity market. And if they were generating – or they would have a share only in gas generation,  then the link to their kind of traditional – their main, their core product would be stronger. So here, I think we  have a mutually fruitful combination and it will not be the CCGTs alone, even though – and you're right, we do  have ample gas-based generation capacity in the UK, The Netherlands and Germany. As to the volume, it will be  quite a few gigawatts.

texts.speaker: Tanja B. Markloff
texts.profession: Research Analyst, Commerzbank AG (Broker)
texts.text: Yes, good morning. I have one question left. It's regarding the volumes exposed to the negative oil-to-gas price  spread. Could you please remind us how these volumes develop in 2011 towards 2013?

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Oh, Tanya, I have this not just before my eyes. Perhaps remember that we have always given you an overview  about the overall gas supply volume which the company has and perhaps remember, that is more or less 50 bcm a  year and that less than 50% is exposed to the gas-to-oil spread. So, the ballpark figure I have before my eyes is 20  bcm.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Yes. That is then maybe the outcome of some of our negotiations that we get a different indexation for gas  volumes that would reduce this. But that is what we have today.

texts.speaker: Karin Brinkmann
texts.profession: Research Analyst, Unicredit Bank AG (Broker)
texts.text: [indiscernible] (01:06:59) Munich; hello to everyone. I have two questions, the first one on the nuclear provisions.  Have I missed the figure for the nuclear provisions you have taken in the first half of the year? And can you help  us a little bit, will there be – will this be a one-time effect, what we expect for the nuclear provisions for the rest of  the year and for the next years? And also, what do you expect as to the impact for 2012 and 2013 from the  shutdown of the nuclear plant, as I have seen that you have only sold forward 30% of the electricity in 2013. Does  this reflect new spends or is this a normal part you had sold forward in the years before as well?

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: With respect to the hedging strategy, there's nothing extraordinary that is within the framework – the existing  framework of our hedging policy. With respect to the nuclear provisions, I can assure you, you didn't miss the  figure because I didn't give you the figures and that was intentionally so, because as you know, we have some legal  proceedings still. And for that very reason, we will at the right point in time to the right authorities identify that  exact figure. But what I can tell you is the following. We have each and every year – that was true for the past and  will be true for the future, an annual adjustment of the nuclear decommissioning provisions, simply reflecting the  fact there's discounting effects, that we're coming closer to the active point of cash outflows for dismantling and so  on. And on the other side, we have an increase by the actual inflation – cost inflation rate for this type of  construction work. So, that is an ongoing process each and every year. In addition to that, we had last year to  make an adjustment due to the fact that based on the nuclear lifetime decision – extension decision by the  German Parliament the exit cash outflows would start only later, which then led to a downward adjustment, and  this year it's the other way around. So there's one-off effect coming from that, but that is irrespective of the [ph]  annual (01:09:25) ordinary adjustment each and every year.

texts.speaker: Jürgen Großmann
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Lueder, indeed I can. The energy-intensive industries, at let's say in the summer of 2011, about – well, not quite,  but just a few percentage points below the consumption of the early summer of 2008. So, we've almost reached  the demand point of mid-2008 again.

texts.speaker: Jürgen Großmann
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Yes, and the timeframes of the various different lawsuits that we are currently putting forward is different. So  some of the easier – let's say, the nuclear fuel tax will probably be decided earlier than other lawsuits that we're  putting forward.

texts.speaker: Jürgen Großmann
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Alberto, let me add; I'm just happy that you call it a capacity payment and not, as some people in Germany do,  capacity markets because if and when such a decision should ever be taken, it would be a further move away from  energy markets. So, we are not expecting or hoping for such political decisions.

file: RWE - Q2 2012 Earnings Call 14August2012 900 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 14-Aug-12.pdf

texts.speaker: Stephan Lowis
texts.profession: Vice President-Investor Relations, RWE AG
texts.text: Before we start with the presentation, I would like to remind you of our Offshore Wind Capital Market Day on the  12 of September. Some of you might have been on holiday when we sent out the invitation. So, please get in touch  with us if you have missed it.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Deputy Chairman, RWE AG
texts.text: In renegotiation of our oil-indexed long-term gas contracts, we have made further progress. We're pleased that we  managed to find the structural solution with Statoil. This is a major milestone. There are now only two major  counter-parties left with whom we are still conducting price reviews. Rolf will provide some more details on the  current status of our gas-to-oil spread exposure.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Deputy Chairman, RWE AG
texts.text: The completion of the renegotiation of our oil-indexed gas contracts is also an important factor in achieving our  financial targets. As we have said several times, we expect the conclusion of the price reviews with the remaining  two counter-parties by 2013 at the latest. The clear goal is to agree on the structural solution. And so, far our  perseverance has paid off.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Deputy Chairman, RWE AG
texts.text: Last, but not least, I would like to come to efficiencies. The focus in the next two years will be not only to deliver  on our efficiency enhancement targets, and I will comment on the progress we're making there in a moment, but  we also need to lay the foundations for continuous improvements beyond 2014. Operating efficiency is and will be  an ongoing commitment at RWE. We therefore, kicked off the RWE 2015 project, which will strengthen the core  of our business model and identify further efficiency potential. I'm going to introduce you to the RWE 2015  initiatives shortly.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Deputy Chairman, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me add that we will need to continue to do so since our market will keep on changing. Let me give you some  examples. Take our generation portfolio, for instance, while we have one of the most balanced generation  portfolios in the sector, we are not immune to the changes caused by the growing feed-in from renewables. We  have to analyze our fleet constantly for its competitiveness. Decisions have already been taken, but will continue to  be required in relation to capacity retirements. Further action is currently being analyzed and discussed.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Deputy Chairman, RWE AG
texts.text: Current economic conditions do not allow for any new-build decision in the foreseeable future. For our nuclear  portfolio and expertise, we have decided to phase them out, in line with the German decision. Regardless of the  current weak power prices, the cluster risk for such an investment will be simply too high. Also, it does not make  sense to bring a new nuclear power station on line, the year after our last German one would have to shut down.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Deputy Chairman, RWE AG
texts.text: Another example is renewables. Certain technologies have experienced a significant learning curve with  subsequent cost reductions in the equipment, which has led to their increased competitiveness. This includes  photovoltaic, which has already reached life-cycle competitiveness without subsidization in certain regions, where  competence in this field. This does not mean that we will suddenly invest several hundred millions or divert  investments from other parts of RWE Energy to this field. In a first step, we will be looking at a few carefully  selected demo projects. This includes, for instance, the pilot PV wind project in Morocco within the Desertec  Initiative.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Deputy Chairman, RWE AG
texts.text: The energy market transformation requires a big effort by all market participants and cannot be delivered single- handedly. Offshore wind farms of several 100 megawatts require substantial upfront investments and carry  significant installation and operational risks. Networks need to be equipped to be able to manage the rising feed- in from decentralized sources. Partnerships will, therefore, become more important for future investments.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Deputy Chairman, RWE AG
texts.text: I would like to talk now about our RWE 2015 programme, which we launched earlier this year. You are already  familiar with our new efficiency-enhancement programme, which will contribute €1 billion between 2013 and  2014. But this is only one part of it. The market environment around us is changing rapidly and we have to ensure  that we're well equipped to face those changes.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Deputy Chairman, RWE AG
texts.text: This entails looking at our business model and structures rather than embarking on just another efficiency- enhancement programme. We want to lay the foundations for an organization which continuously drives for  operational excellence and efficiencies. We, therefore, have identified four fields of action, which have to be  addressed to make RWE fit for the future. And while some of them might lead to further efficiencies beyond 2014,  we will not provide any new targets beyond 2014. It is simply too early.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Deputy Chairman, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me go through them now. First, we are looking at some topics within our strategy. As mentioned before, we  are convinced that we are well positioned in terms of our general strategic direction. However, we are facing huge  challenges when it comes to the transformation of the energy system in Northwest Europe, with some challenging  our traditional business model. But rather than being part of the problem, we want to be part of the solution. We  are, therefore, working to identify the opportunities of the market transformation and how we can participate in it.  We are looking to be innovative and continue to grow. One example is the direct sale of large customers' electric  output from renewables on the wholesale market.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Deputy Chairman, RWE AG
texts.text: With RWE Supply & Trading already following a pan-European approach, we are bringing the assets in line with  their commercialization. The new European GenCo will have one single point of accountability for RWE's  challenges and capture synergies between different fuel types. We are now starting with the implementation and  are expecting to have the new generation company in place by January 1, 2013.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Deputy Chairman, RWE AG
texts.text: Slide eight now gives you the details of our current efficiency programme that we will finalize this year. We are  well on track to achieve the outstanding €400 million in 2012, to reach the cumulative efficiency gains of €1.5  billion compared to 2006. In March 2012, we introduced a new efficiency target of €1 billion for 2014, compared  to 2012. Out of this €1 billion, approximately €500 million is follow-on efficiency improvements from the current  programme.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Deputy Chairman, RWE AG
texts.text: Staff reduction is not a prime target, but in the context of our €1 billion programme, we will see approximately  €300 million per annum from a reduction of our workforce between the end of 2012 and 2014. This will be done  in close contact with the works councils and employee representatives on the basis of socially-acceptable  measures.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Deputy Chairman, RWE AG
texts.text: In addition, we expect to achieve another approximately €450 million on efficiency improvement from other cost  reductions and from margin improvements. Let me give you some concrete examples, so that you get an idea of  what we are working.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Deputy Chairman, RWE AG
texts.text: In our generation business, we're focusing on the improvement of maintenance concepts and technical  optimizations. As you know, our Continental European generation business, in particular, has been put under  pressure by increasing production from renewables and from the shrinking market share of hard coal and gas- consequence of these initiatives was the mothballing of steam parts of the Gersteinwerk over the summer, even  permanently – or even permanently. This results in cost savings of double-digit million euro amount and, at the  same time, makes sure that the station remains cash-generating.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Deputy Chairman, RWE AG
texts.text: Additionally, we are working on the optimization of technical parameters of our units by increasing flexibility and  load gradients and reducing minimum load requirements. This helps us to earn additional margins, capturing  market opportunities driven by the increased demand for flexibility due to the volatile production from  renewables.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Deputy Chairman, RWE AG
texts.text: In our Trading/Gas Midstream division, we are in the process of streamlining activities by moving all trading  activities out of the Geneva office, realizing considerable efficiency improvements between the Bosch, Essen and  Swindon by optimizing front as well as back-office processes. The whole programme takes 25% of the cost base  out in this business by 2014 and will contribute approximately €100 million to our €1 billion target.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Deputy Chairman, RWE AG
texts.text: In our German Sales and Distribution business unit, we're also working on more than 100 individual measures to  increase efficiency by approximately €100 million. In our UK division, we are focusing on technical improvements  at our power plants to increase their efficiency. In addition, we are optimizing purchasing contracts for our UK  generation fleet and improving the information management between the stations and RWE Supply & Trading.  Furthermore, we are optimizing processes at our commodity and contract management activities, which will also  result in staff redundancies.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Thank you, Peter, and good afternoon to everyone. Let me start, as usual, with an overview of our performance  indicators in the first half of this year. External revenue was slightly down by 1%. The main reason of that was the  deconsolidation of Amprion. Our EBITDA and operating results bill increased by 9%. A major contributor was the  absence of one-off burdens experienced in the first half of 2011 due to Germany's accelerated nuclear phase-out  decision. In addition, we benefited from an improved performance by our energy trading business.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: The non-operating result improved almost €70 million on last year's figure. We realized lower capital gains from  disposals, but this was more than compensated for by higher value gains of commodity derivatives. While we had  much lower provisions for personal reduction measures, we accrued risk provisions for investments and made  some an impairment €134 million with regards to the power purchase agreement with the Dutch nuclear power  plant operator, EPZ. The financial result declined by about €150 million, driven by the higher financial liabilities  and an increase in the interest accretion to non-current provisions.  Furthermore, the 2011 result benefited from the release of a provision made in relation to the new refund which  ceased to exist with the nuclear phase-out decision. The effective tax rate was 33% or a 6 percentage point higher  compared to the first half of 2011. The increase was mainly driven by lower tax-free capital gains and  impairments, which are not tax deductible. For the full year, we now expect the tax rate to remain at this higher  level.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me now explain the development of the operating result in each of our divisions. The operating result of our  Power Generation division in Germany advanced by 33%. Major contributors were the already mentioned  extraordinary burdens in the first half of 2011. The accelerated nuclear phase-out decision led to an increase in  nuclear decommissioning provisions. In addition, we had to write down nuclear fuel rods at our Biblis plant. But  we also suffered from lower realized power prices and spreads. A positive contribution resulted from the trial run  of our new lignite plant BoA 2&3 at Neurath. The plant has now entered commercial operations.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Before moving on, let me say something about the operational performance of our power plants. Of course, we are  feeling the impact of the rising feed-in from renewables, especially our gas and hard coal portfolio are  experiencing lower utilization. However, this is not a recent development. Older plants have already been running  on lower loads for some time. We're, therefore, making adjustments to our portfolio reflecting these new market  realities. Peter already mentioned the mothballing of Gersteinwerk, but we're also looking at adjusting the  operating mode as well as flexing and reducing fixed costs of power stations. Ultimately, we will decide to shut  plants which we cannot maintain cash-generative.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Our lignite plants continue to display stable utilization. Despite the persistent expansion of renewables, we expect  our nuclear and lignite plants to run base load for the time being. The load adjustments will continue to come  from peak and mid-merit plants.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Let's return to our division performance, earnings at our German Sales and Distribution Networks business unit  dropped by 7%. Lower electricity sales margins and decline in the income from investments were only partly  compensated by efficiency-enhancement measures and capital gains from the sale of networks due to the loss of  concessions.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Hence, results deteriorated by 13% despite the commissioning of our new CGT's Claus C and Moerdijk 2. Clean  spark spreads are particularly weak at the moment, probably as a result of Germany's continued expansion of  photovoltaic capacity. In contrast, cost-cutting and gas-sourcing optimization had a positive effect on the Dutch  end customer business. In relation to acquisition synergies, I am also happy to report that we will achieve them  this year, two years earlier than promised.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: The operating performance of RWE npower decreased by 9% to €319 million. The main reason is the  fire in a bunker led to lower output compared to last year and the plant was still firing hard coal. The first unit is  back in operation again and we expect the two other ones to follow by the end of this month. The first half of 2011  also benefited from one-off items relating to claims settlements.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Efficiency-enhancement measures, higher sales volumes and improved commodity cost management had a  positive impact on the UK supply business. Our CE/SEE [Central Eastern/South Eastern Europe] division  recorded a decline in the operating result of 17%. The Czech gas supply business contributed to this development.  However, its earnings for the full year should return close to the level achieved last year. Lower generation spreads  and retail margins in Hungary as well negative ForEx effect were further contributing factors.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Increased generation volumes and higher realized prices benefited our renewables business; however,  compensation payments received in 2011 for delays in the construction of Greater Gabbard did not recur. Our  Upstream business increased its operating result by 27%. Higher gas and oil prices and the appreciation of the  U.S. dollar over the euro were the main drivers.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: The Trading/Gas Midstream division closed the first half with an operating loss of €340 million. This is a  significant improvement compared to last year. The performance of the Trading business has improved  considerably by the burdens from the negative gas-to-oil spread continued to increase. However, we managed to  renegotiate a number of contracts for which we also received compensation payments.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Ladies and gentlemen, you know this chart, number 14, from our previous presentations. The gray area gives you  the reduction already achieved in the oil-indexed share of RWE's gas purchase portfolio, which represents more  than 50% of the contract volumes. Peter already mentioned that we were successful with further renegotiations on  long-term oil-indexed gas contracts.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: In June, we reached a solution on the outstanding gas contract with Statoil. Statoil is one of the three biggest  suppliers of RWE. The agreement includes a structural solution by gradually adjusting the contract price towards  the prevailing market condition. The settlement further comprises compensation for the historic period, since the  start of the negotiations which is within the range of our expectations.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: This agreement reflects that the gas market pricing structure in Continental Europe is in a transitional phase. We  have been able to structure our relationship with Statoil to better fit the market conditions going forward. We are  still in renegotiations with two gas suppliers for volume of approximately 11 Bcf. We expect the renegotiations or  arbitrations to be finalized in 2013 and to soften gas-to-oil spread exposure by then.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Slide 16 gives you the development of net debt in the first half of 2012. It increased by €4 billion to €34 billion.  This is more than we originally expected. The main reason is the adjustment of discount rates for pension  provisions as a result of the low interest rates. For the years as a whole, expect the current net debt figure to come  down again, but it will exceed last year's number.  This brings me to our divisional outlook. The good performance of our energy trading business and proven  progress in our gas supply contract renegotiations has led us to upgrade our guidance for the Trading/Gas  Midstream division. However, let me remind you that the performance can still fluctuate depending on the  development of the gas-to-oil spread for the remainder of the year.

texts.speaker: Vincent P. Gilles
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Yes. Good afternoon, everyone. Thanks for taking my questions. A very obvious question to start with. I'm  completely confused the way you're talking about on Statoil, because you're talking about a solution and then it's  gradual, and then you still exposed partly to gas-to-oil spread maybe on the 11 bcm only. But I guess, like  everyone, what I'm trying to understand is what is the nature of your agreement? I'm not asking you for numbers.  I'm asking you for the nature of the agreement. How you get out of the exposure, because you're talking about the  gradual leaving of this exposure? And whether we should assume that if the gas-to-oil spread widens again by the  end of the year, your agreement with Statoil protects you entirely or doesn't it? So, I guess that's, clearly, one  question to be generous with myself.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me start with the question to our gas price negotiations. On the one side, please understand that under  confidentiality agreement we cannot give you more details. However, we can, on the one side, share with you that  the solution we found with Statoil is a solution which leads to a fully structural solution. And with respect to the  granularity of that solution, I would ask you to have a look on slide 14, which describes nicely, step by step, how  our gas-to-oil exposure will decline over time.  Vincent P. Gilles  Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.  Q And second question is with regard to disposals?

texts.speaker: Patrick Hummel
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS AG (Broker)
texts.text: And second question on the gas contracts, in the case with Statoil, is it fair to say that the compensation payment  certain hit there? And what is your expectation for the coming renegotiations, do you think you can and obviously  did recover all the losses that have occurred in the past couple of years? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Deputy Chairman, RWE AG
texts.text: Yes. Let me start with the capacity markets in Germany. There is quite a lot of discussion around that. It has eased  down a little bit. The discussion was very fierce last year November before a winter season, which was threatening  people and was promising potentially even a blackout, but that's not happened. We have also involved ourselves in  that discussion by explaining that capacity markets, if they would need to lead to new investments, do not give you  any help within four, five or six years and therefore are not of any good for a short-term improvement of the  capacity situation. We also gave hints on how short-term problems can be looked at, cold reserves, keep old power  plants up as kind of a strategic reserve and we are currently working at a study which looks at those solutions in a  mid-term period perspective.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Deputy Chairman, RWE AG
texts.text: Therefore, the immediate eagerness to come to capacity market has somewhat reduced. There still is a  fundamental discussion in Germany, how the energy system for the future will need to look at, what will it look  like? But all options are at the table at this moment. We, ourselves, believe that a more subtle, to not say diligent  solution is better than a coast-to-coast capacity market solution. So, this is under discussion. We hope, until the  end of this year, to have something fixed with discussions with the politicians, with also a several science  institutions, and be able to evaluate not only the development of the market system in Germany, but also the  inter-linkage with renewables and the connection to the European market setup.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Deputy Chairman, RWE AG
texts.text: So, so far no immediate threat. Long term, I think there needs to be an improvement which comes from whatever,  a capacity market or select capacity payments, because I always say something has to give in to make sure that  over the long term the phase-out of nuclear power is being covered by backup capacity which is needed in  conjunction with renewables. And to Rolf on the 2013 guidance.

texts.speaker: Alexander Karnick
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank GmbH (Broker)
texts.text: Yes. Good afternoon. Thanks for taking my questions. First one, could you comment on the remaining volume of  your gas portfolio that is exposed to the gas-to-oil spread? If I remember correctly, the H1 presentation gave a  view of, I believe, 17 bcm. How this looks post the Statoil deal and could you also confirm whether the delta  change over March – over the March quarter is coming from Statoil? And second, there was a news flow that a big  North Sea wind park is again delayed until the end of 2013. Now, I appreciate you don't have the group guidance  out for 2014, but you do have a profit target for energy of €800 million. Do you see this at risk because of the delay  of the sizeable wind farm? Thank you very much.

texts.speaker: Stephan Lowis
texts.profession: Vice President-Investor Relations, RWE AG
texts.text: Alex, I'll take the first one on the gas-to-oil spread. Let's be precise, you talked about exposure, what we  mentioned on the chart is the remaining exposure which we have with the two gas suppliers which is 11 bcm. Due  to the fact that we have a gradual agreement also with Statoil, I can say that in 2012, by now, we have a total  exposure of 14 bcm, as well as in 2013, out of this 14 bcm is of course the 11 bcm. So, the remaining 3 bcm will go  out of this exposure gradually.

texts.speaker: Stephan Lowis
texts.profession: Vice President-Investor Relations, RWE AG
texts.text: And the second one, on energy, yes, that's right, we have this problem with the grid connection on Nordsee Ost.  We have received a letter by TenneT, as you probably have noticed from the press. So far, we have not a clear end  date when we are connected. And of course, in 2014 guidance, Innogy Nordsee Ost wind park was included. So,  whether what that means in terms of our guidance, we can't give you a detailed number yet, because it's also not  clear how we can – how we would get compensated for that delay. Let's wait till March next year, because then we  have done our full-year midterm planning and probably have more clear and also from the political side on the  offshore grid connection issue.

texts.speaker: Martin C. Young
texts.profession: Analyst, Nomura International Plc
texts.text: Yeah. Good afternoon to everybody. Just two questions. Firstly on relation to this provisions issue and the  discount on those provisions on the balance sheet, why haven't you had to take some kind of similar action in  respect of the nuclear provision discount rate, given that there is a degree of similarity between those and pension  liabilities in so much they're both long term? And what actions have you taken on the balance sheet side of things  to address this issue? And then, the second question was just following on from Peter's very kind comments about  giving some granularity in respect to the €1 billion efficiencies that you have identified. For a couple of the  divisions, you gave a figure for the impact of the cost reductions. I just wondered if you were able to spilt that €1  billion up across the divisions of the group. Thanks.

texts.speaker: Stephan Lowis
texts.profession: Vice President-Investor Relations, RWE AG
texts.text: Okay. I can give you a, let's say, generic answer, because we can't be too precise, but we started in Q4 2009 the  whole renegotiations with our gas – with respect to our gas portfolio, and Statoil was included in there.

texts.speaker: Bobby Chada
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Hi. Good afternoon. First question is about the Generation business. You said pretty clearly that you're still  reviewing effectively both the economics and cash generation of all of your plans over time. How frequently do you  expect to take decisions on this and are there any more decisions on the leased power stations, which  [indiscernible] and E.ON that you'll expect to take imminently? And then, secondly, I just want to try and clarify  this whole debt expectation today just a little bit. Is it fair to say that the change in your expectations for debt is  pretty much solely related to the change in your pension provision?

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Deputy Chairman, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me take your first one, Bobby. The review of our power plant system is being done continuously and it's a mix  of day-to-day decisions when we put plants on and off, and the market development and, specifically, expectation  of the market development drives mothballing decisions or temporarily outage which we're then forced to. On the  leased count – and so, naturally, we have a quarterly update of our long-term forecasts. We have once a year long- term review of our midterm planning in which we have a more, let's say, a systematic view on the mothballing of  plants or the complete closure of plants. The [indiscernible] or the lease contracts, as you referred to, are specific  one. There we are tied to contract dates. And at that contract date we will then finally review. Whether it makes  sense to take use of the option to prolong? I can only say that for today the logic that you might follow is that these  are in the German generation system plants, which are amongst the older coal power plants, therefore, the least  economical power plants. And on that basis, per today's view, it would be hard or unlikely that we would prolong  those leases.

texts.speaker: Bobby Chada
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Peter Terium  Deputy Chairman, RWE AG  A Maybe Bobby, one helpful addition, on second thought. If you look at the German power plants, the ones that are  mainly at the margin or out of the money are older hard coal and gas-fired power plants. If you look at our system,  the only older hard coal power plant, the mainly ones we have, is Gersteinwerk, which we talked about and are the  [stay out] leases. Our gas plants are amongst the more newer power plants in the German system. Therefore, some  of our competitors have move of an issue because they have older power plants in those two fuel types.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: And with respect to the second question, the very simple fact is whenever we commission new power station,  depreciation starts and you have seen that we have commissioned new power station, especially BoA 2&3 this  year, and we are planning to commission further power station the rest of the year. And then we'll not only have  the benefit of the margin but also, unfortunately, on other side, increasing depreciation.

texts.speaker: Vincent De Blic
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: And the second thing on the Trading and Gas Midstream, I know you probably can't give very precise numbers,  but could it be possible to have a rough idea of the breakdown of the increase in H1 year-on-year, which I think is  about €260 million, what is prop trading? What is, very roughly speaking, the Statoil compensation? And what is  the mark-to-market of the gas-to-oil spread as well? Thank you very much.

texts.speaker: Matthias Heck
texts.profession: Analyst, Macquarie Capital (Europe) Ltd. Germany
texts.text: Yes. Hi. Good afternoon. Most of my questions have been at least asked, not all answered. But the one which is left  is just if you could provide some more visibility on the remaining gas contract exposure for 2012, 2013 and 2014? I  understood from your initial question that your remaining exposure for 2012 is 14 bcm, right? So, could you  please give us the numbers for 2013 and 2014, please?

texts.speaker: Benjamin Leyre
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane BNP Paribas SA
texts.text: Yes. Thank you. A couple of the very small follow-up questions, please. First one is can you provide us with an  estimate of the EBITDA contribution from the auxiliary services in H1 in Germany from your power plants? And  the second point, you also mentioned some erosion in the electricity sales margins in Germany. I wonder if the  competitive situation is deteriorating more than you were expecting. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Benjamin Leyre
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane BNP Paribas SA
texts.text: Yeah. Sure. In your division of, I think, the distribution and sales you mentioned that you had some – that you set  out from some erosion of the electricity sales margins, and I wonder if this is due to a deterioration of the  competitive landscape.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: I think it's good to know that the most important of our supply companies here in Germany, that's RWE Vertrieb,  has they, only by the August 1, increased the prices for power and gas. So, that should help for the rest of the year.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Deputy Chairman, RWE AG
texts.text: We have detail looked at all the people in the nuclear division. And as per today's judgment, there is no reason to  see any link between what happened in Doel in Belgium, on that reactor, the supply that has delivered the parts  that are under discussion at the moment is a different supplier as to ones that we are using. And a system by  which it has been welded is a different approach is what we have been using in Germany. Clearly, in Germany,  they have chosen a different kind of a technique which are not – is not giving this risk that is currently appearing  in Belgium. Therefore, as far as we can judge and also on the base of questions that we have received, there's no  reason to expect that anything will result out of that for our German nuclear power plants.
