texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: However, we have also new capacity to our portfolio. At the beginning of August, we commissioned our 7 87   megawatt gas-fired power plant in Denizli, Turkey. Now that this plant is in commercial operation, there are only  two more stations to be completed as part of our conventional power plant new build program that began in 2006,  the two hard coal power stations in Hamm and Eemshaven.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: In July, we completed the construction of the Belgian offshore wind park, Thornton Bank, with a total capacity of  325 megawatt and in which we hold around 27% stake. With the recent closing of the natural gas transaction, we  have successfully implemented the final step in the disposal of this asset. We have already received the payment.  Consequently, the proceeds from the transaction will impact our net debt figure in the third quarter. We still  expect this transaction to remain the largest one for 2013.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Since March, I'm now on page 4. Since March, when we presented our update on the profitability of our  generation fleet, the situation on the power market has not improved, in fact, quite the contrary. The forward - based price for 2014 has decreased by €4 per megawatt hour over the course of the last five months. Two major  drivers are low hard coal and CO2 prices. We have also seen a new record high for solar production in Germany  which reached almost 24 gigawatt capacity at noon on a Sunday in July.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The reasons why we didn't see a corresponding low in spot market prices were that solar power plants were being  inspected at the same time only very low wind levels were recorded. Nevertheless, on that Sunday, the peak prices  printed about €5 per megawatt hour below the base price, the typical solar effect on the shape of the power curve.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: As a result of the deteriorating profitability of generation capacity, particularly of gas and hard coal -fired power  stations, German generators have recently become more vocal on real or potential power plant closures or  mothballing.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Firstly, we decided to reduce capacity, which I will explain in a minute on the next chart. The total amount of  capacity affected is about 4.3-gigawatt.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Secondly, we will intensively review additional capacity of almost 900 -megawatt in Germany, with the option of  applying one of our capacity measures. This includes the hard coal unit Westfalen C and three of our older lignite  units.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Thirdly, we will make a decision on each of our remaining contracted hard coal plants individually according to  the contractual dates. By the end of 2013, we will make a decision on a further 1.4-gigawatt of contracts. This is in  addition to the termination of the 1.9-gigawatt contracted hard coal plant as communicated in our Annual Report  2012 and the 1.2-gigawatt, which I will explain in a second.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And finally, we decided that for the time being we will continue the operation of certain plants, contracts, or  participations, despite them being cash flow negative at the moment. This also includes some U.K. power plants,  which have a better economic perspective in the medium term than, for instance, German or Dutch gas site  stations.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The reason is that some of the units carry unavoidable cash costs, which we cannot reduce at the moment. One  example for these unavoidable cash costs are long-running maintenance contracts. In these cases, we are in  negotiations with the suppliers to find solutions to reduce these costs. Another example of unavoidable cash costs  are onerous long-term power purchase contracts. Again, we have started to investigate solutions to  reduce these  burdens.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Our internal cash flow analysis, therefore, showed that continuing the operation for the time being is the least  cash burning option for these units. However, we will continue our thorough review of the remaining stations. We  will take a decision on each unit individually on whether to continue operations or to take the capacity offline,  either temporarily or permanently. A typical trigger point for such a decision would be the moment when a power  plant is due for a larger inspection, for example, if we will not commit to expenditure for repairs and maintenance  unless there's a commercially viable case for it.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Firstly, we will decommission the Dutch hard coal plant, Amer 8, with a capacity of 610 megawatt. The  decommissioning, however, is subject to the final decision on the Dutch energy agreement, the so -called  Energieakkoord by the Dutch government which is expected by the end of August this year. The Energieakkoord  contains conditions, among others, to close coal-fired power stations that were commissioned during the 1980s by  the beginning of 2016.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Secondly, we decided that certain gas units with a combined capacity of more than 1.7 gigawatt will be mothballed  long term between now and the second quarter of 2014. Please be reminded that we have already mothballed  several Dutch gas plants at a total capacity of around 800 megawatt in 2012.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Thirdly, we decided to seasonally mothball two steam turbines connected to gas plants in the north of Germany  totaling 720 megawatts. The result from our analysis showed that the optimal savings contribution at this specific  site will be achieved by a flexible approach to mothballing these two units.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And finally, we decided on the termination of three of our hard coal contracts with a capacity of 1,17 0 megawatt.  The contracts will expire between end of 2013 and 2014. The total cash savings from all of our capacity measures  and further optimizations will be in the order of €7 0 million per annum.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: As you can see, gas-fired power plants are the first candidates to be taken out of operation due to their high  variable cost, which are not covered by current power prices. Nevertheless, let me emphasize again that we are  also thoroughly analyzing the profitability of our hard coal and lignite assets as you can see from our first  responses.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me now come to chart number 6 and to the second hot topic, which is the ruling from the arbitration with  Gazprom. At the end of June, we received the final award from the arbitral tribunal related to our request for a  revision of the purchase price payable for the natural gas supplied on our long-term gas supply contract.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: In its ruling, the tribunal awarded RWE a reimbursement for payments made for the period May 2010 to May  2013. The tribunal also adjusted the purchase price formula for two components, which to a certain extent are  linked to each other. Firstly, adjusting the base price, a so -called P0-cut; and secondly, introducing gas market  indexation in the price formula. The new price formula has been applied retrospectively with effect from May  2010. The new conditions considerably reduced the price level on our contract with Gazprom. As a result, our  exposure to the gas-to-oil spread has been substantially reduced but has not been fully eliminated.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: So was it worthwhile to go the hard way? Y es, because the percentage of gas market indexation and the retroactive  payment are higher than what we think we would have been able to achieve in bilateral negotiations.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: At this point, let me quickly remind you that we reached mutually satisfactory solutions in relation to our o il index  gas supply contracts with all of our other gas suppliers by the end of last year. We have also initiated a new round  of price revision negotiations with Gazprom with effect from Q2 2013. The arbitration ruling in June relates to the  market situation in 2010 and, therefore, reflects only a transitory status of the market at this specific point in time.  Since then, the market has further developed which we take as a positive signal for our future negotiations with  Gazprom.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: I'm well aware that you are keen to learn more about the specific details of the award, for instance, the precise  share of the gas market indexation. Please understand, however, that both parties agreed on a high level of  confidentiality on all contractual terms. With regard to our future relationship, it is in the commercial interest of  both RWE and Gazprom to adhere to this agreement. Let me stress again that we are very satisfied with the result  from the award for the time being.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: From today's point of view, we expect the division to close the fiscal year 2 013 with an operating result in the  order of €1 billion. Please don't read this is as a zero contribution from our trading division. One has to keep in  mind that we will still incur some losses from the gas-to-oil spread exposure for the entire year.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: What does it all mean for the future earnings potential of RWE Supply & Trading? At current market prices, we  would assume this division to be able to achieve a normalized earnings contribution of between €300 million and  €400 million per annum, providing the gas issue is fully solved. As long as we are still facing some minor exposure  from the gas-to-oil spread, we would assume the division to earn about €200 million per annum. Please always  keep in mind that the trading arm of the division is typically more v olatile than the rest of our business.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me now give you a brief overview of the business performance in the first half of 2013 on page 7. Our operating  result increased by 12%, driven by the positive earnings contribution of our trading/gas midstream d ivision after  the arbitration court ruling on our long-term oil index gas contract with Gazprom.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: In contrast, the decline we saw on Q1 for our conventional power generation division accelerated. Besides the  burdens of full auctioning of carbon certificates, declining generation margins and the loss of margins from  closing our old lignite plants, we suffered from a one-off burden to adjust provisions for loss-making contracts,  and burdens from the change in nuclear provisions.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The latter refers mainly to the new law concerning the selection of a final storage facility for highly radioactive  waste in Germany. This law became effective on 27 th of July. We are of the opinion that according to the  constitution, any additional cost beyond the necessary cost for one storage facility do not have to be carried by the  utilities as long as it is not decided that Gorleben, the existing facility, is not suitable for the final storage of highly  active nuclear waste.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: However, we have provisioned for the net present value of the additional costs for us already in H1 2013. The  provision amounts to approximately €400 million. But as we had other offsetting elements, the total effect on our  operating result was limited to approximately €70 million. Please keep in mind that the positive earnings trend in  H1 is mainly driven by the one-off effect in our trading gas midstream division and should not be extrapolated for  the full year.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Slide 8 provides you with a reconciliation of our recurrent net income. The non-operating result declined to  approximately minus €1 billion, mainly related to a further impairment of our Dutch electricity generation  portfolio. Our financial result fell by approximately €7 0 million. The positive trend for net interest and interest  accretion to non-current provisions was more than offset by the negative development of the other financial  result. Here we had among other things less income from the sale of securities and significantly higher interest on  tax liabilities.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: With slide number 9, I would like to shed a bit more light on the development of our cash flow in H1 2013. Here  we have a special effect from the one-off payment after the Gazprom arbitration ruling on our long-term index gas  contract. We received the payment in July after the cut-off date for the H1 account. When we received the court  decision at the end of June, we booked accounts receivable against the pr ofit in the P&L.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me come finally to our outlook for fiscal 2013. We can confirm the outlook we provided on the 5th of March at  our full year analyst conference call and confirmed on our Q1 call in May. On 2nd August, 2013 we closed our  disposal of natural gas. As a result, it will only be included in our 2013 earnings numbers until that day. In the first  six months of 2013, natural gas contributed €150 million to our operating result.

texts.speaker: Vincent P. Gilles
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Y es. Good afternoon, everyone. I have two questions. The first one is actually more a request if you could develop  a bit on the capacity cuts/mothball that you've been announcing. Particularly on the cost side you say, if I  understand correctly, you're going to save, at least for 2013, €7 0 million. Due to these capacity cuts, what's the  cost associated with it? Is it all reflected in H1? Should we expect some provisioning in H2? So all these questions  around the cost. And also as a sort of second sub-question is do you expect the market to react to all the  announcements we've had over the last few days on capacity cuts?

texts.speaker: Vincent P. Gilles
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And my second question is I fully appreciate you don't want to speculate on your future rating, but it strikes me  that it's nearly impossible for you to be below or close to three times net debt to EBITDA in the foreseeable future  given the doom and gloom on power prices and you've been very honest about the situation. You said today there  will be no rights issue, but what can you really do now to make sure that the situation doesn't deteriorated  further?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Okay. But this was at least two-and-a-half questions, I would say. Vincent, hello. Starting with the capacity  development or the mothballing and decommissioning of conventional power generation capacity. The €7 0  million is an annualized cash saving which we will achieve once these measures have been effected.

texts.speaker: Vincent P. Gilles
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: No, no, no, no, no. Just to come back, my question actually is on the cost associated with the capacity reduction. It  was not the savings you will achieve. If we could get a view of how much it is going to cost to RWE to implement  these measures. Now my question on the power market is, do you expect a reaction from the power market  because there was obviously no reaction in the last 24 hours?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Y es, the €7 0 million is the gross number we will achieve when these measures have been executed. It's now too  early to use on one-off cost because we are currently negotiating with the employee representatives how this will  be effected. And this can be, just to give you an impression, this can be a pretty broad spectrum. If you take  German power plants where we often have many sites pretty close to each other, the one -off costs might be pretty  low because you can relocate the teams and substitute vacancies you have on other station sites.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On market expectations, we have obviously not seen drastic market reactions from the E.ON announcements and  our announcements over the last 48 hours on power prices, as far as I can tell. And this is not a surprise to us. We  always told that taking those power stations offline, which has been hardly running a few dozen or a few hundred  hours per year, can't have a tremendous effect on the baseload price. So we are not surprised by the lack of  visibility of any movement in forward prices.

texts.speaker: Patrick Hummel
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS AG (Broker)
texts.text: Y es. Good afternoon, everybody, and congratulations to the female colleague in your IR team. Is there any reason why we should not extrapolate  the multiple, which would be like €16,000 of savings per megawatt close to mothballs for potentially upcoming  closures? Or is there any other, yes, item that we have to bear in mind why the final cost savings in the generation  unit could actually be much larger than the number you've just indicated?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Hello, Patrick. I'm not 100% sure if I fully understood your first question correctly. So please correct me if I'm  heading off in the wrong direction. With regard to cost savings in the generation unit, I think the €7 0 million  which are the effect from the plant closures, this is just a tiny fraction of the overall cost savings we are targeting  there.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: So because – I mean, many of these plants are rather small and old gas-fired power plants which have low  operating cost anyway. That's what we always said. We always said the overall absolute amount of cash [ph]  negativity out (29:52) from these power plants is not too big. We have announced that there are further cost- cutting plans in the generation division underway but this is not at all exclusively connected to the mothballing or  decommissioning issue.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: So there will be significant cuts in technical staff, functions which are not r elated to single power plants. There will  be, what I would call, by RWE standards at least dramatic cuts in overhead functions due to the fact that  conventional power generation quite frankly as a business unit is fighting for its economic survival. And,  therefore, we are asking questions we wouldn't have been asking before.

texts.speaker: Patrick Hummel
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS AG (Broker)
texts.text: Right. Just a follow-up on that. I mean if the 4.3 gigawatt that you announced to be closed or mothballed or  handed back to [indiscernible] (30:44) and take the €7 0 million savings, I just calculate €16,000 per megawatt  capacity closed. And what you're saying suggests if you're going for further closures, the larger units, coal units, et  cetera, that multiple could be higher for future closures or would you consider the order of magnitude €16,000 or  €20,000 per megawatts of savings from closures a right ballpark estimate for what may come on [indiscernible]  (31:11) station?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The second aspect is that generally, of course, if you are moving away from gas, more towards coal into hard coal  or even lignite-fired stations at least on a like-for-like basis, yes, it is fair to assume that lignite and hard coal are  more OpEx intensive than gas. So it's not a simple multiplier, as I said.

texts.speaker: Stephan Lowis
texts.profession: Vice President-Investor Relations, RWE AG
texts.text: Patrick, also sorry for – I don't want to block all others, but very simplistic answer, if you look to the list which we  presented on page number 5, there are so-called gas topping turbines which is a gas turbine in front of a lignite  plant. I think if you do calculations like you do, that's too simplistic for such a measure. So I would say be cautious  on such a euro per kilowatt-hour multiple.

texts.speaker: Benjamin Leyre
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane BNP Paribas SA
texts.text: And my second question would be related to upstream. I understand from a specialized price that Bre agh in  upstream is facing new delays. That's just a few weeks or months, I don't know. Can you update us on your  expected volume of gas and oil production for 2013? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And also within the overall CapEx volumes, there is the so -called day-to-day CapEx. And what we see is that in  some parts of the business, for example, the generation business where the crisis is most visible, the m anagers  onsite, on the front line already start reducing their expenditure. And this is something which was not included in  the percentage value we gave you earlier in terms of how much CapEx is committed. This percentage value only  referred to discrete large projects which are underway like new power plants or new wind parks.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The second question on Breagh was generally that was only a slight delay in Breagh and it's – will be expected to  become, to go online in Q3 this year as expected and the natural gas production of RWE Dea in 2013 compared to  2012 is expected to go up by some 30% roughly.

texts.speaker: Lawson Steele
texts.profession: Analyst, Joh. Berenberg, Gossler & Co. KG (United Kingdom)
texts.text: And secondly, could you clarify or perhaps talk about the impact of German nuclear repository and how much  that's going to cost in terms of balance sheet and P&L? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On the German Standortauswahlgesetz or the Site Selection Law, it's the effect reflected in our H1 numbers is the  €400 million NPV of the additional burdens out of this law which are an increase in – or an addition to provisions  in the first half of this year. And this is reflected in the operating result of our conventional power generation  position. The nominal values in terms of future cash-outs are significantly higher and we mentioned this in quite  some detail in this morning's press conference. They are about €1.1 billion in very late years in the 2020s and  2030s of this century.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Chris, if you can give me a guarantee that the capital markets will stay in this situation of low interest rates and  abundant money for the next 25 years or the next 10 years, I would be happy to do so. But as a prudent Chief  Financial Officer, I think it's also our duty to prepare the company for potentially stormier weather in the capital  markets again as we've seen in the quarters post-Lehman. And there, we think a close look, a close eye on our  leverage sector will pay off.

texts.speaker: Alexander Karnick
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Broker)
texts.text: Now, I exercise the option. It's just the one. Y ou said on the nuclear provision, the €400 million hit effectively, but  just €100 million effective. Because there were other offsetting effects. Can you elaborate a little bit what these  other offsetting effects are? Are they directly related to these provisions or they're just positive one -offs  somewhere else?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: It's various smaller effects as you can imagine given the overall amount of our nuclear provisions just  having some  volatility in this provisioning is not an uncommon thing and we only commented explicitly because otherwise  everybody or you would rightfully ask where do I see the €400 million, yes?

texts.speaker: Deborah B. Wilkens
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: Y es, good afternoon. My questions are with regards first of all to the hard coal contract. So you've clarified that  you terminated 1.1 megawatts and that you've put a further 1.5 megawatts under review. Can you actua lly clarify  whether or not you renewed any of the 4.5 gigawatt of hard coal contracts and when the decisions are due for the  remaining 1.9 megawatts? That's my first question.

texts.speaker: Deborah B. Wilkens
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: And my second is something that was somewhat surprising in terms of the plants that you've put under intense  review is that you've included two lignite blocks, which one would have thought would have been lower cost than  some of the hard coal. Can you help us understand if there's anything unique about those facilities or if the fact   that they're on it also would have really clustered the other 300 -megawatt lignite blocks in your list?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Y es. Hi, Deborah. Y our first question with regards to the long-term power purchase agreement or hard coal  contracts we have, we have not renewed any of those contracts and the 4.5 -gigawatt you mentioned and the  remaining 1.9-gigawatt, they are a bit of a special kind because it's those contracts we – where we are more in the  role of an equity owner, at least, a minority equity interest. And therefore, the investment calculus in terms of NPV  is different from the normal hard coal fired contract. And, therefore, they are also longer -lasting. It's not – they  are not contracts with normal cancellation or termination dates.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: With regards to your second question, yes, you're spot-on with your question on the lignite blocks. These two 300- megawatt units, we mentioned they are special in some important aspect because it's the units P&Q on our  Frimmersdorf side where they are the only units remaining. Frimmersdorf used to house only 150 -megawatt and  300-megawatt blocks. All the 150-megawatt units have been closed, latest with the advent of the newest [ph] BoA  3 (48:52) unit and, therefore, it's just two 300-megawatt units left. And therefore, of course, the potential cost  savings, if you shut down the whole side, are bigger because you also save the cost for the overall site  infrastructure than if you just close units on an existing site where there infrastructure  continues to exist.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: So and the third unit is a very small one, which is in Goldenbergwerk which is below 100 megawatts. So it's very  old and that's the reason that, that is even less efficient than a 300 -megawatt unit.

texts.speaker: Deborah B. Wilkens
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: Can you give us a sense for the size of potential cost savings from the 300 -megawatt blocks?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And then, secondly, I'm still struggling to understand the exact impact of the provisioning change in the power  generation division. Could you confirm that the provision releases were also related to nuclear? And then,  secondly, what was the actual net effect of the provision increase, the €400 million, and the other provision  changes on Q2 results? And just to clarify, is this – the German Site Selection Act, is that a one-off effect? Is that  done now or do you expect ongoing effect in future years? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: With regards to the provisioning in the conventional power generation segment, yes, the release of the provisions  which was the offsetting effect against the €400 million increase from the Site Selection law. These were also  nuclear provisions. The net effect were €7 0 million increase in provision. So it was a burden on our H1 result.  And, yes, this is a one-off under the assumption that the law stays as it is, that the law holds water against the legal  challenge which the utility industry might still put up against it, and that the other framework conditions don't  change so costs skyrocket or whatsoever.

texts.speaker: Andreas Thielen
texts.profession: Analyst, MainFirst Bank AG (Broker)
texts.text: Y es, good afternoon. Firstly, I'd like to ask if could use one of the options left over by previous pe ople asking. If so,  I have three questions, two very simple ones. Firstly, from the plant closures, when would we start – I mean when  would we start to see serious write-downs or, in other words, would you be willing to share with us what kind of  your generation portfolio is what part – sorry, what share of your generation portfolio is already fully written  down and when would we see actual burdens coming through the P&L if closures continue? And are we still far  away from that point?

texts.speaker: Andreas Thielen
texts.profession: Analyst, MainFirst Bank AG (Broker)
texts.text: And thirdly, very simple, you've referred very often to November, the supervisory board, at least that's what's  stated in the press will be informed about the new cost savings plans or updated cost savings plans in September.  So should we expect an update on the cost savings of the overall outlook at an earlier point in time? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Y es. Hello? With regards to the planned plant closures, we will not provide a detailed breakdown of the book  values or the carrying value from impairment just on single entities. Most of those plants you see on the list are  old written-off power plants anyway, fully depreciated, so you didn't see any effect of this.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: But a portion of the impairment in The Netherlands, so in the Dutch generation fleet, was for example on the  newly built power plant in Essent. So this is already – as you can it's already zooming in on some of these units.

texts.speaker: Bobby Chada
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Thanks and good afternoon. My first – well, my only question left is on the impairment that you announced. I  think it was back at the full-year results you've talked about how the assets were not valued as one European  GenCo business and, therefore, you didn't see much scope for further impairments yet. Now there's been another  €800 million. Have you changed the approach or is it simply that the lower power – outright power price has  altered the values that you're attributing to the nuclear and the lignite assets? And in addition to that, should this  impairment lead to lower depreciation charge going forward?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: So you have seen an increasing divergence between the Dutch and the German power prices recently which is a  reflection of the interconnection capacity being a bottleneck. And, therefore, this is also the economic reasoning  by – for an impairment test basis. We still regard the German and the Dutch fleets separately.

texts.speaker: Peter A. Bisztyga
texts.profession: Analyst, Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Hi, good afternoon. Two questions from me. Firstly, one of your peers yesterday was pointing to a very significant  deterioration in gas storage profitability. I was just wondering if your gas storage business is seeing any similar  trends.

texts.speaker: Peter A. Bisztyga
texts.profession: Analyst, Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: And then, secondly, there was an adverse court ruling a couple of weeks ago that required RWE to compensate  some special gas contract customers. I was just wondering if this court ruling sets any kind of precedent for  further compensation claims and whether there is anything we should be worried about or wheth er we can just  ignore it. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Hi, Peter. It's – well, starting with your question on gas storage and one of our peers who yesterday spread some  doom and gloom on this business segment. Unfortunately, we can only confirm the general view that E.ON also  gave. It's a business which is currently under distress because summer-winter spreads have collapsed. And there's  certainly a risk going forward that the earnings levels in this business won't be realistic for the future.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: With regards to the Federal Court of Justice or Bundesgerichtshof decision that you referred to for this gas retail  contract, very special gas retail contract, this was a decision issued on the 31st of July 2013, and we have not  received the written verdict yet and, therefore, we cannot make any further comments at this point in time to what  extent it might also have inferences on a larger customer base. But I can assure you that we have provisioned for it  in our Germany supply distribution networks division already.

texts.speaker: Peter A. Bisztyga
texts.profession: Analyst, Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Okay. Thank you. Can I just sort of follow up on gas storage, are you able to tell us sort of how much money you're  making today in gas storage?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: With regards to your first question on our forward hedging, you know that we have now changed our  communication to give you the realized prices or communicate about the realized prices of our outright position  which is, well, by and large, a nuclear and the lignite position.

texts.speaker: Ingo Becker
texts.profession: Analyst, Kepler Capital Markets SA (Germany)
texts.text: Thank you. Good afternoon. I have a question on your nuclear economics given that the market is now at €35, €36  a megawatt hour. You have a €15 tax. That gives you a €20 to €21 net achievable price on nuclear. If I remem ber it  correctly, you stated in a presentation during the months after the tax, the fuel rod tax came in, in 2010, you put  your nuclear costs at over €30. I was wondering if you could give an indication where the point is reached that you  would start thinking about the nuclear closure. And if you could talk us or talk about the technicalities of that. Is it  – if such a point would be reached, would it be similar to closing a bigger coal plant or is this process entirely  different?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Okay. I think your memory serves you well in terms of what we said in the past or one of my predecessors said in  the past when the nuclear fuel tax was introduced. I think this also is in line with the statements made, for  example, by the CEO of E.ON recently about the profitability of nuclear. With price levels at around €35, we are –  or nuclear is on the – at the edge of profitability at a full cost level.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: This, however, does not mean that you would immediately shut down a nuclear power plant if the price drops to  €34 per megawatt hour, for example, because the – this, say, €35 per megawatt hour of full cost, average full cost  of the nuclear power plant's still running. This is the average cost over the operational cycle of a nuclear power  plant. So these nuclear power plants are reloaded with nuclear fuel rods regularly. Once you have reloaded it with  a nuclear fuel rod, it does not make sense to switch it off before the next reloading starts.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And the second is that in €35 also consider an averaged maintenance expense over the full maintenance cycle of a  nuclear power plant. So there might be years when the maintenance expenditure is significantly lower and then  every, I don't know, two, three, four years, you have a bigger outage with higher maintenance CapEx and then you  might ask yourself, if this is the point in time where you're still going to run for the next revision cycle. So the  decision logic is not that black and white, especially not with nuclear. They are very different on the chunkiness of  certain cash out is much more pronounced than, for example, in gas or in coal-fired power stations.

texts.speaker: Ingo Becker
texts.profession: Analyst, Kepler Capital Markets SA (Germany)
texts.text: Can I just inquire if there any regulatory difference in closing a hard-coal plant or a nuclear plant? Just  theoretically you would reach that point at some time in the future, apart from sticking to safety rules and so on.  But is the regulatory process of applying for getting approval for closure, is that the same?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Well, I think the overall procedure but the two aspects for all power plants, including nuclear, you have to  announce your intentions to take a plant offline to the Federal Grid Agency. This applies to all power plants, but I  could imagine that the Federal Grid Agency might be more reluctant or more critical. For example, just as a  hypothetical exercise now, if we announce that we would wanted to shut down our Gundremmingen twin unit  power plant in Bavaria. Bavaria is one of the critical spots in the German grid topography.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The second aspect is that approval for nuclear power plants exclusively, of course, we have all the nuclear  regulation issues around it as well. But there it's just an orderly process. It's not that they would prevent you from  shutting down a plant, but it's clearly nothing you can do overnight. Y ou would have to bring announcements.  There would be a thorough investigation and without wanting to feed any speculation, I could imagine that  especially our twin unit in Bavaria might deem system relevant. And then you would find other solutions to  remove any cash negative nature if it should turn out that we are cash negative.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me be a bit more explicit on what this means. It means, for me, that our operational performance and our  equipment actions are well in control. Remind you that this guidance that we are now confirming was first time  published in November of last year that confirmed in May of this year and reconfirmed right now. Despite that in  the meantime, we've had a very warm winter and various runoff effects, which we, accounting wise, to ok care of in  the first half of this year. Nevertheless, although this is actually a confident, I might even say, more confident,  without changing our guidance on the numbers as we are despite the factors I mentioned [ph] then (02:13).

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: In Germany, the new Renewable Energy Act took effect on August 1. Intension to strengthen the market  integration of renewables is certainly a step in the right direction. The prolongation of the current subsidy scheme  for offshore wind is also positive.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: First, our efficiency program, which we announced in March last year is right on track and we are confident that  we will deliver on our accelerated target of improving our operating results by at least €1.5 billion by the end of  2016. We will update you on our current program in March next year when we will also present our new wave of  efficiency measures.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Second, we reduced our capital expenditure considerably. Our future CapEx levels will mainly be driven by  maintaining our power plant fleet and fulfilling regulatory requirements in our group businesses. In addition, we  will also allocate some funds to our renewables business. The ambition for the time being is, how ever, that new  growth projects will be financed debt neutral. For instance, by taking partners on board overselling stakes and  assets.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Mid-term, we expect our annual CapEx to be in the order of €2 billion. For 2014, it was still amount to about €3.5  billion. Little more, the €1 billion is dedicated to our Group Business. Another important portion is being spent on  a completion of our hardcore power plants in Germany and in Netherlands and our offshore wind farms, Nordsee  Ost and Gwynt y Môr.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Third, our disposal program. In 2013, we completed disposals with a total volume of €2.7 billion, of which the sale  of that for gas was the largest one. This year, the completion of our €5.1 billion sale of our RWE Dea will be the  most important transaction. In addition, we are still working on disposal of Urenco, which we do not expect to  materialize before next year.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And reactive to the serious market deterioration, we took a number of measures in our generation portfolio. Slide  six provides an update of our capacity measures. As you can see, we took decisions on some more power plan ts.  The trigger points for deciding on capacity measures are events such as maintenance requirements, which go  hand-in-hand in investments, or expiry dates of long term contracts. We investigate thoroughly the economics of  potential, maintenance investments and the extension of contracts, and decide on a case-by-case basis where the  market conditions allow the operation to be continued profitably. The latest analysis showed that [ph] requiring  divestments (06:51) in three older coal plants would be uneconomical; hence, we decided the decommissioning of  these coal plants. They have a combined capacity of 1,000 MW by 2017, and in addition for the contracts with the  total capacity of some 470 MW, will expire by the end of this year. We will continue and we did it on an ongoing  basis to review our portfolio and we'll take further decisions if and when required and appropriate.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: We thought it might be helpful to look at the impact of the capacity measures on the development of our  conventional power plant portfolio. It's important to bear in mind that mothballed power plants do not influence  the actual size of our portfolio. The reason is that these plants are still connected to the grid. They can, therefore,  be ramped up again at a later point in time, if economics become more favorable. Taking into a consideration  further closures due to regulatory requirements as well as capacity additions, our [ph] stored (07:52) capacity will  decrease to about 40 GW by 2017. After a drop in 2014 due to the termination of almost  2.5 GW of contracts, we  will see an increase in capacity in 2015 due to the commissioning of our hard coal-fired power stations in Hamm  and Eemshaven. These are our last two thermal power plant projects in the pipeline. From 2016 onwards, we will  start to see net capacity reductions in our conventional generation portfolio.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me now spend some time on the trends in retail market, where we believe the energy market transition is  really happening. Our retail business is of growing importance with a combined annual contribution of almost €1  billion to the Group's operating results. In today's market, we sell our power and gas products to about 23 million  customers in Europe. It is a highly competitive business in most regions, especially the commodity part of the  business.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: However, we strongly believe energy retail markets will fundamentally change due to new customer requirements  and more efficient technology. Customers will play a considerably more active part in the energy business in the  future. They will be able to buy, to store, to save, and to produce electricity, and they will be able to manage it all  by themselves. The growing amount of household customers in Germany already produce electricity with solar  panels on their rooftops.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: However, while most of the electricity produced by household solar panels has started to the grid today, in the  future, customers will increasingly be able to decide whether to consume it themselves or to sell excess energy to  third-parties.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: In addition, more efficient devices and energy saving measures such as home automation will help them to reduce  the energy consumption. Similar trends can be observed in the business sector, where an increasing number of  customers will produce and consume self-generated energy and will actively manage it.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: We consider the changing retail market as an opportunity for us rather than [ph] asset (11:43). The development  of innovative products and new business models to go with these trends will be key. Innovation is, therefore, the  key priority on my agenda. [ph] Whereby we scored (11:54) some success in this respect with our cooperation with  [ph] Next (11:56) in UK and the RWE [ph] home power solar and storage products (11:59) in Germany.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: In the Netherlands, we offer the energy trading platform for horticultural customers enabling them to manage and  optimize the energy costs and revenues themselves, based on customer preferences and market opportunities.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Slide 12 shows the earnings development in individual divisions. All in all, we see a decline of approximately €1.5  billion. By far, the biggest effect is the absence of the one-off payment from the gas from arbitration ruling last  year. This accounts for approximately €1 billion.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: In our Central South Eastern division, the operating result held by some €240 million. This is mainly due to the  deconsolidation of natural gas, which contributed to €151 million through earnings in H1 2013. Furthermore, the  significant earnings decline in our supply in Netherlands/Belgium division is especially driven by the weather  effect and a positive one-off in the previous year. Nevertheless, the general trend of declining earnings in our  conventional power generation division was mitigated in the second quarter of this year.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Last year, we had the addition to provision for impending losses from an electricity purchase contract. This was  not the case this year. For more details, on the individual value drivers, I would like to refer you to the backup  section and our interim report.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Let's have a closer look at our cash flow from operating activities on slide 13, which show a much different trend  than our earnings. While EBITDA is down by about €1.6 billion, cash flows have increased by over €9 billion. This  discrepancy is mainly due to three reasons. Firstly, our earnings and FFO in 2013 already reflected the  approximately €1 billion, one-off payment from the Gazprom arbitration ruling. This is not the case with our cash  flows from operating activities. While the FFO include this in Q2 2013, it is offset by the same amount in working  capital as the cash payment only came in Q3 2013. Secondly, the repayment of nuclear fuel tax of approximately  €0.5 billion. After the Hamburg Fiscal Court decided in April now favor, we will refund the tax that we had paid  for our Emsland nuclear power plant. This is only cash flow relevant as within our P&L. We have to build a  provision from the nuclear fuel tax until we have the final court decision on the legality of the tax. We received a  decision for our Gundremmingen power plant in our favor from the Fiscal Court in Munich at the end of July. So  this is not yet reflected in our cash flow statement. Thirdly, cash flows improved due to high advanced payments  in the retail business as a result of price adjustments.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Looking further at the difference between the development of FFO and change in working capital, besides the  effect from the Gazprom payment I just explained, we have a second significant effect from the switch to the new  CO2 compliance period in our accounts. Typically, the certificates for the previous year have to handed to the  relevant emission authority in April of the following year; i.e. in 2013, we submitted the certificates for 2012 and  in April of this year, the certificates for 2013. With a change to the new regulatory regime in 2013 and thereby the  full auctioning of certificates, the number of relevant certificates has increased substantially . In the cash flow  statement, it is reflected negatively in FFO due to the use of provisions. Nevertheless, working capital improved by  the same amount as CO2 inventories are also coming down.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Reasons for the lower expectation are the impairment of our Markinch project, and the low utilization of our  German run-of-river power stations in the first six months. With this, let me hand over to Stephan, to start the  Q&A part.

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: Y es, thank you very much. Good afternoon everyone. I'll focus my two questions on power prices. The first
texts.text: question is, Peter, you just said that sometimes you have to put a different emphasis, depending on who you talk  to regarding future developments. Talking to these crowd of analysts here, what can you tell us on power prices in  the next two to three years? We have received old look at the forward curve, but it may not be correct and some of  your competitors have sounded slightly cheerio in the last two months, than in the past, so interesting to hear  from you guys. And the second thing is, following the announcement of further capacity cuts from you today,  when do you think, these capacity cuts will actually trigger something on the power market. Or should we  continue to expect more and more capacity cuts until a long period of time before something happens.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The second aspect is we are seeing physically that the spot prices when they occasionally turn out at a higher level  as the forward price for the next day, which means the physicality is just not able to follow the mood of the  market. It's also for me an indication that there is risk in the system. Now, when is that going to come? Capacity  can certainly have an aspect on that, but power price in the market do not only react to physicality, but also to the  emotions, which are there. If that picks up and you've seen already in the first half of this year, at least on one day,  four hours continuously quarterly prices at above €1,000 and occasionally above €2,000. That's an indication that  there is stretch in the market and as soon as the market picks it up, this could happen very quickly. But we're  talking to my view about €s and not about tens of €s. I mean they need to also manage our expectation and be  very clearly on that one because there still is a continuous high supply of solar and wind energy into the system.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: The second question I think you had was on capacity cuts. If we expect an immediate effect on power prices, I   mean, most of the power plants, of course, that are taken off the system are the ones who have had the fewest  running hours. So the effect won't be that big, although you now realize that it's this time it was about hard coal  and lignite. So it was not power plants, which were entirely off the system more or less except a few hours like it  was with the old gas one year ago, for example.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: So gradually, we think it will feed through. It's always difficult to get what people already priced in. And I would  also say that probably you will see an effect on the aspect that Peter mentioned on security of supply. So the  margin, the reserve margin just becomes tighter and this is at least as important as the immediate effect on power  prices, if we see increasing number of hours that we have severe system tightness and then somebody probably  will want to react.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: To the trough question, the infamous one, we expected that sooner or later it would come. So, I think it's a nice try  from your side. As you will remember, we have always said that the trust statement was originally given at the  then prevailing commodity prices, so back then in November, and since then quite a lot has happened. It's clear  that the commodity side has not helped. But there are also other things which have happened , especially those  which are under our own control that Peter mentioned where we are making very good progress on our  operational improvement programs and then that this is not just hollow words. You can see in our 2014 guidance,  which we kept constant despite, for example, the mild weather hitting our P&L and this was obviously  compensated by positive operational development. We are currently putting together or start putting together  now our mid-term plan in Autumn this year and as announced earlier, we will update you on what this means for  future years' guidance in March 2015.

texts.speaker: Benjamin Leyre
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane SA (Broker)
texts.text: Y es. Thank you and good afternoon. First question please on the German electricity consumption. I wonder what  is your estimate of the real electricity consumption trending Germany at the moment? It looks like DDW may  underestimate the auto production. I wonder if you have an estimate which is a cleanup for this impact.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me start with last one as I have initiated that discussion. We are – as I said more confident that we will end up  within the bandwidth as we have. If you give the guidance, there's always some risk, but I would think that some  risk has been reduced but has noted indication of where we we will end up within the bandwidth. I don't think it's  appropriate with still having five months ahead of us or five and half months ahead of us to be that accurate in  that extent. But there is as I said the other – the more months you have behind you, the less months you have to  go. The variance of deviation becomes smaller and I think we've done a good job despite, as Bernhard said, the  aspect which were against us that makes [indiscernible] (31:50) for the rest of the year. We're going to be in line  with our guidance for the total year. Then you've also – about the electricity consumption development in  Germany, that's not changing drastically overnight but in our mid-term planning, we are forecasting a slight  decrease and that's a balance of a various things. I think [ph] this industrial (32:11) consumption mainly, which is  one aspect. It is some energy savings. On the other hand, we see the further electrification of society going on to  balance off all of debt we would see as a slight decrease of energy consumption.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The next question comes from Alex Karnick, Deutsche Bank. Please go ahead.  Alexander Karnick  Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Broker)  Q  Y es. Hi. Thanks for taking my questions. First one is you've cut your energy outlook back. To me first reason will  be some call it one-off or anomalies for this year like hydro and the write-down but is there anything that you see  that could affect your 2016 targets of let's say softly around $4 million to $450 million EBIT. And the second  question is if you just look at your cash flow conversion, not year-on-year but quarter-over-quarter, it was single- digit in Q1. It was 115% or 110% if you could strip out the one-off from the receipt of the nuclear fuel tax. Could  you help me understand of where these pretty violent swings come from? Thank you very much.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me first answer please your question to the energy outlook. You're right, operationally, in terms of the assets  that are already in operation, the business is running fine. We had this – this it was weather effect in the first half,  especially on German hydro that you mentioned and the one-offs. So all-in-all, the operational development is in  line with our expectation and this would also extend into the future all more precise statements about further  years' outlook would come within March 2015 update. With regards to the cash flow conversion on a quarterly  basis, this is an analysis, which we have not offered so far and it's difficult to comment on the quarterly cash flows  as you know cash flows from operating activities, they contain with the networking capital development, a one  factor which is highly influenced by cutoff date effects. So there, these create tremendous volatility, which is  economically irrelevant, but analytically pretty mind-boggling at times. So just an example, cash flow of book  revenue can be received a few weeks later and, therefore, you would have corresponding swings in the networking  capital. Although over a longer period of time, there's no issue about cash conversion. So that's all we can say at  this point in time.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: If I might add one sentence to the energy outlook that looks on first glance drastic if you form slightly better go to  significantly less good. But if you look at the absolute numbers, I mean, in this year, energy was not forecasting a  very high numbers or any one-off of a smaller double-digit amount immediately has a big impact on our wording  on the outlook. But overall, on the longer term for energy and on the other [indiscernible] (35:59) numbers, it is  really insignificant.

texts.speaker: Alexander Karnick
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Broker)
texts.text: Now that is very clear. I just wanted to check and thank you very much for pointing that out again. I just wanted to  check whether it's something like the cutback in the renewal space in Spain sort of lower hydro price that lower  prices for hydro et cetera, a bit of maybe a big projects, Gwynt y Môr et cetera could have an effect on the future  event. Thanks very much.

texts.speaker: Bobby Chada
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Thank you. So two questions please. The first on the weather impact, I mean, you've talked for this about the 2014  headwinds from weather. Can you quantify those in a bit of detail props versus a normal year or year -on-year?

texts.speaker: Bobby Chada
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: And then secondly, just to touch again on the renewables business, I mean I  guess, if I understand correctly, your  point is that the headwinds in 2014 of being either one-off or weather related in nature, but it is the latest and a  reasonably long line of impairments or disappointments in the renewables business. Can you walk thr ough some  of the improvements you're trying to make in delivering projects, if you are that is, but I assume there is some  focus given some big projects that'll come over the next two years, three years?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Hi, Bobby. This is Bernhard. So, the weather impact on about year-over-year, we compare a cold 2013 to a warm  2014 is around €300 million, and it's of course, exaggerated in the sense that both of those years were not norm al,  and it was weighed for the 2014 numbers. If you would normalize it, the effect of 2014 against a more normal year  would be in the order of magnitude of roughly €150 million plus, minus. So and this is what we mean when we  talk about the guidance for example, yeah.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: So, on renewables, other examples for us, actually delivering it on our promises or against our expectations. There  is certainly no denying that, we've been paying some tributes to us, yeah, entering this field of business relatively  fast, and but, I think we have gone through a steep learning curve. If you look at the most recent projects like  Nordsee Ost and Gwynt y Môr, operationally, in terms of the project engineering, they are now all on track, and  Peter mentioned this morning that, for example, in Gwynt y Môr, we now have all of the turbines installed.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: The delays we have, for example, in Nordsee Ost are the ones due to the problematic situation on Germany with  regulation and transformer substations not being delivered by OEMs, so and we  are still claiming a compensation  against it. So we clearly see a pretty broad silver lining on the clouds of our renewables business.

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you. I had two questions. And the first one is on the capacity market discussions in Germany. So first, I  wanted to understand whether you thought that the energy only market to point O that is talked about. How  practical is that and what other practical limitations you see getting to this perfect energy only market. And  secondly, on the related to the same point, if you could just talk about your preferred solution, which is the  decentralized capacity market, how you think that would not end up to starting the energy market? And my  second question is on your CapEx of €3.5 billion, this year, if you could just help understand, how much of that is  day-to-day? I mean, you mentioned that €1 billion is grid CapEx, is the rest of all your growth projects or if you  can just give a further breakdown into how much of this is sort of day -to-day maintenance maybe non-grid also?  Thank you.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Y es. Let me start with the first one. I'll try to keep that in an answer which doesn't went out of the rest of the  session, because I've said, a lot of discussion going on. We're clearly in favor of a decentralized capacity market. As  we think that the energy only market is not given, given the right guidance, the right stability in time, and it will  lead to a volatility in pricing and price peaks, which will be politically and socially, at the end of the day, not  acceptable.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Therefore, the decentralized capacity market will give that stability that can be done in a market setup. As it said,  it's a decentralized capacity market. But we need to be very clear on the rules for that, they need to be technology  neutral, they need to middle market driven, the need to be non-discriminatory, and there's a very good proposal  for that which is done by the energy and its association BDEW, which we very much support. And I think even on  their website, not sure whether it's available in English, otherwise, we can supply that to you. There's a lot of  detailed material, how that setup could work.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Now, last [ph] try (42:47) to that, the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Energy has ordered quite a few studies,  and came up with the conclusions out of its studies. Unfortunately, the press picked only out that the e nergy only  market could do the job that would be better. If you look at it a bit more detail, it says it can do it, but under a few  quite risky assumptions. And, it also says the decentralized capacity market is a very good second choice. If you  then look at the difference in cost of a decentralized capacity market versus a – and it's the only market that we're  talking about €100 million a year, that is €1 per household in Germany per year, which is a very low price to get  energy security for. Because the energy only market will, as they've said, lead to increased distortions and  increased number of failures in a network, and that is socially and politically acceptable; I have my doubts as well.  That is why we have come to the very clear preference over decentralized capacity market.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The third reason for that, which is, we're not alone in the world, here in Germany. If you look around us, France  has already decided to introduce capacity markets, Belgium is doing their first auctions, and we, therefore, have to  adapt to the markets around us; otherwise, we'll get distortions within the European electricity system.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Y eah, hello. Your question – your second question referred to the composition of our CapEx of the €3.5 billion we  would expect for this year. You could say that roughly €2 billion out of it is day -to-day CapEx in the broader sense  because all the good CapEx we do is defined by us as day -to-day, and this even includes good CapEx, which  increases the regulated asset base and, therefore, is accretive to future profits. The rest is the big projects in the  conventional and renewable power generation.

texts.speaker: Peter Crampton
texts.profession: Analyst, Macquarie Capital (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Hello, this is Peter Crampton from Macquarie. I have two questions. First, if you could give us any more color on  Germany's probe into your data transaction, when we can expect them a decision there? And then the second  question on nuclear court cases, whether there'd been any new developments there?

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On retail, I have only limited nervousness as far as disconnecting customers from the grid. The two reasons for  that, if you look at the moment at photovoltaic utilization, of that photovoltaic is at something like 40%, even if  you put a battery and you're seller, you can may be increase to 50% or 60%. It still means that it's a significant  portion of time or of electricity consumption, which you cannot cover from your own photovoltaic rates.  Therefore, customers completely disconnecting, I think that would not be very logical for the time being and  looking forward.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Secondly, I think if that would happen in a grand scale then the regulator and the [indiscernible] (52:03) structure  will probably react to that. Because I think it's not socially acceptable that the people who can afford a  photovoltaic panel will disconnect from the obligation to pay for keeping the whole infrastructure system in place,  and to leave that to the socially and, frankly, less well equipped people.

texts.speaker: Benjamin Leyre
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane SA (Broker)
texts.text: Y es. Thank you. Just a couple of follow ups. First on Urenco, I wonder if you could have datas on this potential  disposal. It has been any progress made with the last few months. From the outside, he does not appear like a very  high priority for the government involved. And the second point of the nuclear tax again, following the Munich  court decision, I wonder when exactly you expect to cash in the [indiscernible] (55:27) of €32 million that you  mentioned in the report. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Ian E. Mitchell
texts.profession: Sales Associate, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: Y es. Hi, guys. Just a quick question, going back to Peter's original comments, which said, growth CapEx, debt  reduction and high dividends could all be possible when RWE becomes free cash flow positive. Just to look at   those, clearly you've got CapEx quite significantly on the growth side. I mean, would something need to change in  terms of power prices and spreads in order to consider a higher growth CapEx on that front or is there other areas  you can spend on?

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Y es. Let me start with my comment on the free cash flow positive. Any of you who've met me in person will know  that I'm pretty ambitious to come up with projects or which I can convince you, that it is best to put the trust and  the money in my or our hands to make more value for you than you can do with having a dividend than putting it  somewhere else. But as up to me is a challenge, and I have lot of fantasy in that area. I have lot of concrete ideas.  But I don't have concrete projects at this moment in time. Part of that will be depending on power price  development, surely, but not only. I think as outside of the generation area, a lot of things going on. And  specifically, the area around the customers and the residential homes is one way I see a lot of thin gs looming at  the moment, and there is lot of potential there.
