texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Our net debt improved significantly to €25.6 billion, mainly due to the successful disposal of RWE Dea. In the  second quarter, we also finalized and inaugurated our two new offshore wind farms, Nordsee Ost and Gwynt y  Môr. Their contribution is one of the reasons why our renewables business almost likely doubled its operating  result this year.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: We are continuing to expand our retail activities in Central and Eastern Europe. In June, we decided to enter the  Slovenian market. Initially, we were focused on electricity supply to households and target a market share of 10%  for 2020.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: In Poland and Hungary, where we have already established electricity supply businesses, we will start new retail  activities in the gas market. Here, the focus will initially be on industrial customers.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Over the past few weeks, policymakers in Germany and the UK have taken important decisions with regards to the  direction they want to take for energy policy. Let me elaborate in more detail on these decisions.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: At the beginning of July and after a series of intensive discussions, the German government abandoned the plans  of the Ministry of Economics to introduce a climate levy for all power plants. This levy would have had a massive  impact on our lignite operations, potentially leading to the shutdown of some 7-gigawatts out of our 10-gigawatts  and the associated open gas plants.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: The new proposal is more in line with government's desire to avoid structural disruptions in the lignite industry. It  foresees the transfer of all the lignite plants with a combined capacity of 2.7 gigawatts into a strategic reserve and  the closure after four years in the reserve. It is envisaged that the operators receive payments to compensate for  the plant's availability. However, important details of the payment mechanism have still not been confirmed, so  that we cannot yet tell you which of our plants we will put into the reserve and what the net financial impact will  be. This will very much depend on the technical, economical and regulatory aspects, which will be determined  over the next few months. It is estimated that the strategic reserve will save some 12.5 million tons of CO2.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: In addition to the shutdown of lignite plants, the government is targeting a faster expansion of CHP capacity, as  well as increased energy efficiency improvements to meet its 22 million tons of CO2 reduction target by 2020.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: The second element of the proposed change in German energy policy regards to future energy market design. In  the white book the government confirmed early indications that it does not believe that a broad-based capacity  mechanism is the most effective way to maintain security of supply. Instead, it has opted for a revised competitive  energy market design. It proposes a number of adjustments to the energy-only market, which should improve the  price formation process on the wholesale market, and the ability to respond to energy supply intermitancy.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: As with the strategic reserve, a lot of details are still missing so the assessment of the proposals is difficult.  However, we are skeptical whether this new energy-only market will be able to provide sufficient incentives to  retain our plant in the market or invest in new build capacity if it is required.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Finally, the government also outlined the further course of action with regards to nuclear liabilities. We welcome  the government's attempt to address the important questions regarding the management of nuclear liabilities. We  are aware of our responsibilities as operator and have made sufficient provisions to cover our future obligations in  respect to the nuclear decommissioning and final storage. RWE does not reject on principle the idea of a different  model to manage the nuclear liabilities, but it is imperative that the framework conditions of such resolution are  reached in agreement with the industry.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: We are open to entering into a constructive dialogue with the government to find a safe and cost-efficient way to  carry out the nuclear exit. On 7 July, the UK Competition and Markets Authority published its provisional findings  report. We welcome the findings of the CMA, in particular that there is no evidence of excessive profits in the  generation business and uncompetitive behavior in the wholesale market. Vertical integration was not found to  have an adverse impact on competition.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Let me now come on to talk about something which is more within our control than political decisions on energy  policy. In the context of our ongoing efficiency-enhancement program, the supervisory board agreed on Monday  to change the legal and organizational structures of RWE and its subsidiaries. This is a consequence of organizing  our operations around the value chain over the last two years, and also follows our management approach. It  allows us to become leaner and more efficient in running our business.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: In the course of this change, we also decided to streamline our steering model and aligned RWE AG executive  board more closely to the operating business. Chief operating officers for the future oversee conventional  generation, retail, grid and renewables. This will allow us to take decisions quicker, a prerequisite to be able to  face the challenges of the ever-changing market environment. The appointment of the new COOs will be  announced once it has been decided by the supervisory board.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: On the positive side, our retail business units benefited from normalized weather conditions. And in our  renewables business, we are now reaping the benefits of our investments of the past years. The operating result of  our energy nearly tripled to €233 million.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: On slide 13 we give you the development of our cash flow. It comes down by €1.3 billion to €0.7 billion. As  explained during our Q1 2015 conference call, this is mainly the result of a revised purchasing policy for required  CO2 emission certificates. This had a corresponding positive effect on our cash flow in 2014. Furthermore, we  have an increase in accounts receivable in our supply division, which is due to the weather affect. Again, this had a  positive counter effect in 2014.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: The UK retail market is one of the most competitive markets that RWE operates in across Europe, and this is seen  by the rapid growth of small suppliers and the increased switching between tariffs, all indicating that customers  are very engaged in selecting their energy needs. It should also be noted that in the current political framework,  we don't have a level playing field as small competitors don't have to bear the significant burdens from  government energy programs. Hence, most of the lost customers have signed contracts with the new players. This  is of course a very disappointing situation for RWE UK retail business, but we are confident that we have initiated  the right measures to turn the operation or our domestic business around, and that we will be able to return to  clearly improved returns in 2017. This assumes no further burdens from the CMA investigation.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: And your question, I think, on depreciation was why is it higher than what you would expect from just doubling  the H1 numbers. That's because we still see an – yeah, for the second half of the year, new power plants, especially  also wind farms, coming on line. And therefore this drives up the full year depreciation number to more than 50%  of what you extrapolated from H1.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: What the operating effect of it is, is that it completes the change from a country-based organization to a functional  organization. And that has already started in 2012 with the establishment of GenCo, the generation company that  has been continued last year with the establishment of RetailCo, our Pan-European retail division. And we're just  completing this move towards a functional organization, which, by the way, before 2012 already included energy  and RWE supply and trading.

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you. I have two questions. So, firstly, on npower, you mentioned that you're taking some measures. Would  you just elaborate on what measures you are taking in order to basically to get on top of the systems issue? And  secondly, I mean, just a follow-on the same one is obviously, looking at your competitors in the UK, I mean,  someone like Centrica actually reported far lesser losses and, in fact, very high margins. Obviously, they didn't  have the systems issue for the residential business. But – so I don't entirely see why you're being so  disproportionately challenged in npower keeping the systems issues aside.

texts.speaker: Alberto Gandolfi
texts.profession: UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Thank you. Good morning. I have two on my side. The first one is could you please elaborate a little bit on the  likelihood of the introduction of decommissioning nuclear fund? And is there a scenario under which you may be  asked to contribute cash right away, let's say, in the next 6 months to 12 months year-after-year? And how would  that change potentially your credit metrics in your view?

texts.speaker: Alberto Gandolfi
texts.profession: UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Second question is on your net debt to EBITDA. I mean, if we take a look at projections looking at commodity  outlook, power price scenario and the new measures on lignite and so on, net-net, on our number, your net debt to  EBITDA will be exceeding 4.5 times within a year and a half.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Alberto, maybe I start with the nuclear fund and a few words also on the net debt over EBITDA extrapolation that  you made. And I think you concluded with questions more around growth prospects and so maybe Peter wants to  chip in later.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: On the general discussions around the funding of nuclear provisions, this is ongoing. There is a live political  debate, which was obviously triggered by [indiscernible] (33:34) decision to split themselves up. And political  burden has now awoken to, from a political perspective, the threats that this potentially poses. And this brought  this slumbering debate around both the adequacy and the safety of nuclear provisions on our balance sheet back  to life.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: The indications are currently – whatever the outcome might be is that – when it comes to funding something, this  would not be a deadline where you have to completely switch from balance sheet internal funding into an external  fund within a timeframe of 6 months or 12 months, but it would ramp up over time maybe also in some  proportion to the remaining life cycle of the nuclear power plants where you know that they are about to be finally  decommissioned by 2022. Yeah.

texts.speaker: Alexander Karnick
texts.profession: Deutsche Bank AG (Broker)
texts.text: Yes. Hi. Thanks for taking my questions. Two for Peter, I think. First one is the capacity or the climate result, I  should to say, to what extent are you concerned that this could be sort of violating state aid rules by the EU? And if  that was the case – I mean, that's very speculative – but if that's the case, what's your view on the government  goes back to the, initially, very painful lignite tax or lignite levy?

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: If – and now we're getting into speculation, I rarely like to do that. But I think in this case, it's appropriate. If this  would not fly, I don't think that the return to the initial is a logic consequence because out of the discussions that  we've had, it became apparently clear or I mean, even [indiscernible] (43:09) clear that the original solution would  have been as disastrous for us as a climate levy.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: So, I don't think it will go back to something which we originally had. We don't need to go back to the  [indiscernible] (43:42) could be which something having comparable consequences what the climate reserve has  to be in place. But that's the option or the speculation, I think, with a fair chance that this is going to fly if we just  do our homework on that one.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Now, on the strategic outlook of generation where you very well spotted. On generation, we are moving from a  commodity play to a capacity play. And that's why we believe that integrated company is the right vision and the  right strategy because the capacity play from its risk profile is very close to where we set the new goals and where  we see our grid business are where we basically also see our large customer business. That's why we are not, from  a regional strategy, looking at disintegrating the group.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: The two factors or the two aspects that might influence them; one is the regulatory regime, the climate levy might  be an example of that, but that is gone. Is there any other thing that is otherwise I don't see it? But if it comes, we  are able to react to that.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: The second aspect is market development. I mean, where power prices are today, I think we can pursue the vision  of the integrated group. If it would unexpectedly go further south, and it will be significant, then we might need to  reconsider at a generation might eventually for the rest of the group into an unfavorable situation that could be a  situation where you then would call on that option. But as I've said, it's an option. Everybody can speculate on the  likelihood. We, at the moment, as we see it, disregard it as an in-case-of option.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: It does for the time being, but we're not saying about vision or strategy. I'm not talking next three years, I'm  talking basically end of the decade getting into the next decade. And I think that the white paper as it is right now  is a no regret what is in there. First, you play the energy-only market, let's see what it does to the capacity, that  might be adjusted. And let's then look at what a next design might be, but then we're talking, as I've said, end of  the decade. And – yeah. That's it.

texts.speaker: Peter A. Bisztyga
texts.profession: Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: Thank you. So, a short one, I promise. Can you just tell us what the one-off profit from the sale of your offshore  transmission grid was in renewables this year?

texts.speaker: Lueder Schumacher
texts.profession: Société Générale SA (Broker)
texts.text: Good morning. Yes. Two questions. One is on the nuclear stress test. You should get the results I think at the end  of September. What is actually the stress in the stress test? Is it interest rates, is it future decommissioning costs?  It would be quite interesting what actually it is stressing there.

texts.speaker: Lueder Schumacher
texts.profession: Société Générale SA (Broker)
texts.text: The second one is on the outlook for power prices and then coal prices. I mean, they all seem to be heading in the  wrong direction. Do the recent developments with the Chinese firms slowdown concern you at all?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: On power price, do you want to take that, Peter?

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Yeah. How many [indiscernible] (51:28) you want to have it for which year? On short term, it continues to be in  commodity and a currency play. What does coal do and what does the dollar do. On the longer term, let's say two  to three years out and maybe towards the end of the decade, it will depend on, for instance, what the government  will decide on lignite, how quickly will that go into the climate reserve. Will that be in 2019, November of that year  or will that be in February of next year or somewhere in between? And I think that will have an impact on the  capacity demand in Germany and that might then indirectly have some impact on the power price.

texts.speaker: Andreas Thielen
texts.profession: MainFirst Bank AG (Broker)
texts.text: Okay. So, firstly, on – related to the statements on gas – trading gas midstream, would you be willing to give an  indication how that is – how the operating result is split between the two? And secondly, on hedging, would you  be willing to give an indication how hedging on the outright power currently looks beyond 2017? Have you hedged  anything meaningful for 2018 already? And in relation to the hedging also, I understand the tax situation correctly  that based on hedging and mark-to-market to basically say as should not be a surprise but there will be no profits  in generation more or less for the next five years, driven by IFRS treatment.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Yeah. Hello. So, let's just do it one-by-one. Trading/Gas Midstream, we don't provide a detailed split of the  operating results there between the Trading part – the top Trading part which you see in our numbers and the Gas  Midstream part. But I think, we've also communicated earlier that the current numbers are still a bit depressed by  the overall situation in gas storage which is part of the Gas Midstream part. So, it at least a factor or force at work  that you currently see in the numbers.

texts.speaker: Lawson Steele
texts.profession: Joh. Berenberg, Gossler & Co. KG (United Kingdom)
texts.text: Yeah. Hi. I have a second question. Thank you. On the nuclear fuel tax, because you got the federal constitutional  courts sort of giving a ruling there in the coming months, but if the government were to win the case, do you think  they might consider extending the tax beyond 2016? Do you put that chance at zero or not? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: I think that's pure speculation. I mean, there's been this kind of a statement of the Ministry of Environment in the  press. It has not been taken over by any of other ministers. And I think this government, I mean if you look at the  memo of understanding or the, call it [indiscernible] (58:37) the agreement that they made on the energy policy  some months ago, it clearly states that the commission will look at the totality of nuclear issues. I mean they have  it on the table. They need to solve that. And I think it's going to be something in a total package.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: And maybe Lawson, just to add to that what Peter said and to re-enforce it from the pure economic side. I mean,  what you will probably see then is that the operators of the remaining nuclear power plants will seriously  reconsider the viability of these power plants if the tax was to be continued unchanged beyond 2016. So, you  might see similar stuff happening to it like [indiscernible] (59:34). And without giving you details, we can tell you  that we might have seen more closures unless there's a power plant who still currently expect an ease of life  without nuclear fuel tax.

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Secondly, the commission that the government is going to appoint to look at all the nuclear options. Could you  give us a little more color on who will appoint this commission, will there be any kind of industrial presentation of  any sort or would it be sort of external expert or could it be just politicians and is this – do you have any  opportunity to be represented or the industry more broadly in this commission? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: So, hi, Deepa. Let me take the second one. Not sure how much you followed the previous commission that we had  on the exit of nuclear. But it's very clear, this commission is not going to be an ethical or an ethics commission. It's  going to be having experts onboard. Yes, we'll have some politicians onboard as well to get the support and the  coverage in the German Bundestag. But the main driver will be industrial experts, independent if possibly, so not  necessarily representatives from the operators, but surely close enough to them to come to wise and decent  solutions and proposals.

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you. Can I just – and a follow-on there. I mean, if you look at all the expert reports floating around in  Germany, to the extent that they are sponsored by particular political parties, they come to a very obvious  conclusion if they're anti-nuclear, they basically conclude that your provisions are not enough. So, how would you  as the industry be confident that this is sufficiently robust and independent?

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Very simple. I would not qualify them as experts' reports. What is floating around is opinionated, very often  written down without consulting the energy companies involved. And we're trying to avoid that with the  commission is being established. So, although, they'll be presented, a few operators will be in it. They will be  consulted and they'll be cooperating with the commission very closely. So, of the material that you have seen  floating around has been written without talking to the experts on our payroll that could have given valid  information, which might have led to a different conclusion as what was in those papers.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: One of the reasons for the difficult environment I mentioned is the political uncertainty around financing the  nuclear exit. In this respect, the nuclear commission, which was formed by the German Government, presented  its recommendations at the end of April.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: On a positive note, we were able to come to an agreement with Gazprom on our long-term gas procurement  contract. At the end of May, we agreed upon an amendment of the conditions for the contract. As a result, there's  no price risk from this contract in the coming years.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Conventional Power Generation, in particular, shows a different picture compared to our full-year outlook. We  have an increase of €100 million in H1 2016, which is partly driven by positive one-offs from the sale of real estate  in the UK. Another is that the positive effect from the lower  nuclear fuel tax has already had nearly its full impact in H1.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: In contrast, Trading/Gas Midstream showed a very weak development in the second quarter. Once again, this  shows the natural volatility of the business. While Q4 2015 and Q1 2016 had in total significant positive earnings,  we have a similar negative amount in Q2 2016. On average, we still expect to be able to achieve an underlying  annual earnings contribution of approximately €200 million to €250 million. This year, we'll be, of course,  significantly below this level.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: These are the sale of real estate in Conventional Power Generation and the sale of grid assets in the division  Grids/Participations/Other. In addition, we expect higher costs, for example, due to more maintenance activities  for our power plants and for maintaining and operating our Group infrastructure, which will impact our earnings  mainly in the rest of fiscal 2016.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: On slide nine, you will find our divisional outlook. Since our last outlook update in May, we are now adjusting the  outlook for two divisions. First, for Trading/Gas Midstream, down to significantly below 2015 from significantly  above. We don't expect to fully offset the weak trading performance of Q2 in the rest of the year.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: There are other working capital optimization measures like what we did in previous years on carbon certificates  where we moved the actual payment date for those certificates, which are independent of interest rate  developments, and therefore, some of these working capital optimizations also continue into the future. The one- off from generation on real estate sales is a medium-double-digit million euro number.

texts.speaker: Lueder Schumacher
texts.profession: Société Générale SA (Broker)
texts.text: The second one is on the nuclear talks. Various statements on Bloomberg, I guess, from your press conference,  which describes the talk as constructive and that is looking quite good that a deal might be reached. Could you  give us an update there?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: On the nuke, and you know, we don't give more precise guidance on the full year cash flows and don't change  this now. On the nuclear talks, yes, we are indeed engaged in constructive discussions with Berlin, and it doesn't  look unlikely that ultimately some solution can be found, which is acceptable to all parties. But we all know it ain't  over until it's over. So we still need to see what the legislators actually make out of it.

texts.speaker: Lueder Schumacher
texts.profession: Société Générale SA (Broker)
texts.text: I'm really looking for a number there or at least a range. On trading, I mean you said the vision is of course  volatile. Yes, we can expect some losses, but so just looking back over the last three years, four years, the loss  you show in Q2 is quite spectacular, especially as previous losses were mainly related to the renegotiation of one- year to two-year gas contracts. What exactly went on there? And why should we not expect sometime this to  happen again?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: On the trading side, yeah, there are a few additional remarks I can offer you here. First of all, what happened in  trading is this is not a kind of incident. It's not a rogue trader. It's not a [ph] wild (17:19) bet gone wrong, nothing  like that we saw. For example, if [indiscernible] (17:23) a few years ago, or at UBS a couple of quarters later back  in the end of the last decade. So I mean, I think we have been very successful or others might say lucky that we  haven't seen a loss in our prop trading business on a quarterly basis, as far as I can remember since 2006, when  we had the carbon price collapse in spring. If you look at some other players who reveal their prop trading results  regularly, you will spot that there is a different pattern with some of these esteemed colleagues of ours.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: The balance sheet position on working capital, you find it in our balance sheet and, obviously, now it has moved a  bit up. So on a like-for-like basis, you would not expect the working capital optimization measures that we have  seen with their effect on cash flow in this quarter to be reversed unless, for example, the interest rate environment  changes.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: There is, of course, a macroeconomic logic behind your argument. Yeah. At least, as a simple economist, I would  struggle to see an environment [ph] with a high (23:48) inflation and negative interest rates over a very long time.  At least, I'm not sure if that's the world I want to live in, but that's a different discussion, [ph] probably be (23:56).

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Yeah, hi, Ahmed. On the adjusted net income, I think it's important to bear in mind that compared to last year,  there were significant positive one-offs in the second half of last year like the VSE revaluation and the Galloper  sale, which distorts the comparison between last year and this year if you dissect the year into its two half. And  also, as I've said before, we expect higher cost for maintaining our power plants, and also on our grid  infrastructure. On the power plant, it's simply driven by the revision cycles. Yeah, these are not spread out evenly  across the year, but there's a higher revision activity scheduled for the second half of this year than it was in the  second half of last year.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: And the operating and maintaining for our grid infrastructure, you know that we are in the base year of the  regulation or the run up for the next regulatory [ph] period (28:27) in electricity in Germany. And typically, the  spending OpEx profile, you see in the grid business, is [ph] huge (28:41) towards the second quarter because this  is much building activity, which is always just for reasons of weather, more difficult in the first quarter, and  therefore in the second half, which is usually warmer, you have more of this activity.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: On the timing of the IPO, I think we just stated or reiterated the obvious, yeah, and that's there's no neutrality  whatever, which we want to add there. We just said as far as we can judge now, we will be ready by Q4 and we  hope that the markets will be ready as well.

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: And the second question I had is, time and again there are discussions coming up in the papers about the  German Government looking at the lignite phase-out, maybe the next government. So just wanted to understand  if there would be an earlier lignite phase-out, say, by 2040 or 2050, does that have any implication on your mining  reserves or any kind of cash outflows on the lignite business, which makes you kind of cautious about your cash  situation now? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Yeah. Hi, Deepa. On the liquidity position and its relation to the potential cost of the externalization of the nuclear  provision, I think you're right to observe that we are not in a distressed seller position, we at RWE, for the  remaining shareholding of RWE in innogy. Well, the second [ph] top (31:13) question on this, I think, was around  paying now versus paying later. To some degree, this will also be driven by financial or commercial  considerations. It's still too early. And we don't comment on it to judge what the payment terms that the  government will ultimately legislate. We'll look like if and what interest would be charged for delayed payments  and this is then a trade-off, which we will then make once we have this information available. It's too early to  speculate now, but I think it maybe just important to know that we are not in short-term, in a distressed seller  position from a pure liquidity point of view.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: On the lignite phase-out, as you can see in our H1 report, one of the progresses we have seen on lignite recently  was that we agreed with the state government of North Rhine-Westphalia, which is responsible for our lignite  mines and their licenses, onto a third master plan for the overall mining operations. As already expected since a  while ago, there's a slight curtailment of one of the three mines at the very end of its technical and economic  lifetime in the 2040s, which was, I think, already known, at least as an idea on behalf of the politicians for more  than a year. It does not have any short-term impacts neither on our cash nor on our earnings position. So this is  stuff, which will happen or not happen in the 2040s. Very far out.

texts.speaker: Mark Lewis
texts.profession: Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: And the second one is, following up on the last question of the previous speaker, with regard to the lignite  operations. I mean, you've reached this agreement with the government of North Rhine-Westphalia, but the  German Government is – we're all waiting for the publication of the Climate Action Plan at some point in the  autumn. We're aware from press reports that that has been watered down somewhat, but nonetheless, the  government has a target in place for a very significant reduction and emission already by 2030, never mind 2040  and 2050, 55% by 2030. Notwithstanding the agreement, you've started with North Rhine-Westphalia. Is it not  incompatible with the broader federal government's plan to reduce emissions by 55% for lignite to remain in  operation at least at the level we're currently seeing by 2030, never mind 2040 and 2050? Thanks. Those are two  questions.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Okay. Yeah. So first one on credit rating. Well, first, we won't comment in detail on the interactions we have with  the rating agencies. Generally, if you want to get an impression of the pain points from a rating agency's point of  view on what might trigger, for example, further rating hedging on behalf of S&P and their negative outlook, I  would refer you to the statement they published back then when they came out in the second quarter of this year.  And as far as I remember, pensions – so, non-financial debt items like pension movements due to just interest  rate movements were not on their list. It was more about power prices, if they would decline even further or  especially on the nuclear funding discussion that we had. On...

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: But on lignite, you're right with your correction, but I can hopefully show you that there's nothing wrong with our  announcement so far. So if we were to continue our lignite operations in the same dimension or magnitude as it is  today into the 2030, which would indeed be incompatible with the federal plans for greenhouse gas reduction. But  I think we already mentioned before that there is a, what I call, a kind of soft landing plan for lignite anyway,  stretched out over several decades. And this, for example, means that we will take one of our three lignite mines  [ph] in the (30:09) lignite mine out of operation around 2030 anyway.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: So this brings significant reduction of carbon emissions. And there will also be, without giving you further detail, of  course, over the course of the next one or two decades, a further decommissioning of old lignite-fired power  plants with lower efficiencies. And these all contribute. So our lignite plant, including what was now [ph] with  ridges in Northern Australia on the third master plan (38:36) are fully compatible with the federal emission  reduction targets.

texts.speaker: Tanja B. Markloff
texts.profession: Commerzbank AG (Broker)
texts.text: And the second question would be on the decommissioning provisions, whether you see the need for a  revaluation of those after the waste treatment policies will be externalized?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: On the decommissioning provisions, so those provisions for decommissioning and dismantling, which will most  likely remain on our balance sheet, yes, there is a risk that towards the end of the year once the provisions for  interim and final storage have been taken out, we would need to apply different discount rates to those provisions  because the duration of those provisions is shorter than the storage provisions, and we move into the liquid panel  of corporate bonds with that.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Thank you, Gunhild, and good morning, ladies and gentlemen. We had a good start to the fiscal year after the  reorganization of RWE. This not only relates to our operating business, but also in particular to the positive  developments that have occurred in the field of our nuclear power business.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Based on the H1 results and our account expectations for the rest of the year, we can improve the outlook for the  European Power division. For the group's KPIs, we can confirm the outlook for the year as a whole and expect to  achieve a result at the upper end of our guidance.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On June 7, the German Constitutional Court published its decision that the nuclear fuel tax was not compliant with  the provisions of the German constitutional law and declared it null and void retroactively. We have already  received the refund for the [ph] paid (02:38) tax of approximately €1.7 billion and expect another approximately  €250 million of interest by year-end. With regards to our 2017 income tax, we expect an effect of around €200  million.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: In the context of nuclear energy, we can also report the successful conclusion to the restructuring of  responsibilities for nuclear waste disposal. On June 16, the new law entered into force, according to which the  government is now in charge of the handling and financing of the interim and final storage of nuclear waste. On  July 3, we transferred the relevant funds to the government. For RWE, this was €7 billion including E.ON's  minority stake in our Emsland Nuclear Plant. The economic stake for us was €6.8 billion.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: What is important in this context is the fact that we concluded the public contract with the German government.  This contract provides us with a higher level of legal certainty related to the release from the liability and also  establishes the conditions for transferring the radioactive waste to the federal authorities. Furthermore, it forms  the basis for ending numerous legal disputes involving nuclear energy-related issues between the utilities and the  government.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The only major outstanding topic in the context of nuclear energy is the settlement around the constitutional claim  to shorten the operational life span of German nuclear power plants. In this context, the Federal Constitutional  Court decided in December last year that some aspects were unconstitutional and that the utilities were entitled to  compensation for damages. This refers to generation volumes, which cannot be used as well as the loss in value  of investments which the plant operator had made on the basis of the lifetime extension set out by law in 2010.  The legislator was given until mid-2018 to formulate suitable regulations for this compensation. We estimate that  our claim will amount to a low triple-digit million euro amount. That's it on the nuclear topics.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Slide 5 provides the detail of the performance of the Lignite & Nuclear division in H1 and the outlook for this  division for the full year. Adjusted EBITDA has come down mainly due to declining realized generation margin.  This was partly offset by the phase out of the nuclear fuel tax in 2016. Last year, we had a burn of approximately  €100 million from the tax in the first half of the year.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: This brings me to our current hedge positions on slide 7. Compared to our situation at the end of March, we  almost closed implicit fuel hedged for 2018 and reduced it slightly for 2019 and 2020. Our hedge prices for 2019  and 2020 have improved by €1 per megawatt/hour compared to the end of March. As a result of our implicit fuel  hedge strategy, we could benefit from the improvement of the fuel spreads, which you can see on page 8.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The financial results we have adjusted for the effects from the changes in discount rates for nuclear and other  long-term provisions as well as the interest component on the nuclear fuel tax. In the non-controlling interest  position we adjusted for the effect of the write-on on our Mátra participation, taxes were adjusted accordingly.  Details of the reconciliation can be found in the appendix on slide 15.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: With regard to the change in provisions and other noncash items, I would like to point to the timing effects of CO2  provisions mentioned on the slide. With the transfer of the CO2 certificates to the national clearing authorities in  Q2, we have completed this year's utilization of provisions whereas the additions are only halfway through the  year. For the year as a whole, we can confirm our expectation for the change in provisions in the order of €650  million as we have guided previously.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The details of net debt are shown on slide on 12. At the end of June, it stood at €4.3 billion for RWE stand-alone,  approximately €2.6 billion below the end of fiscal year 2016. There are three main drivers. First, the positive  distributable cash flow. Second, the refund of the nuclear fuel tax of €1.7 billion. And thirdly, a positive effect from  a reduction in provisions mainly pension provisions, which accounted for an improvement of €450 million. One  reason is that the discount rate for our German pension provision increased from 1.7% to 1.9%. Furthermore,  pension assets performed well and thus contributed to a decline in pension provisions.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On slide 13, you can see the details of our outlook for RWE standalone 2017. I have already explained the  reasons why we are much more optimistic for our European Power division and have upgraded the expectation to  significantly above previous year. However, our earnings expectations for the Lignite & Nuclear division have  slightly deteriorated compared to Q1 for the reason which I explained earlier.

texts.speaker: Vincent Gilles
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Yes. Good morning, everyone. Two very simple questions. The first one is on the non-operating results  restructuring €1.4 billion and you got – of which €1.7 billion is the cash from the nuclear fuel tax, so obviously,  where does the difference exactly come from? I understand Mátra will be there, but if you can help us bridge very  precisely.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. No problem. First, to your very detailed question, I mean the answer is as simple. I mean, the major  missing effect is Mátra, where we said the valuation adjustment was around €300 million and then there are some  minor but offsetting effects, but very minor ones. So the two relevant factors are the reimbursement of the nuclear  fuel tax of €1.7 billion and Mátra minus [ph] €0.3 billion. (16:23)

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On commercial asset optimization, the European Power segment, I mean, on the overall profitability contribution  of commercial asset optimization is around €2 to €3 per megawatt hour as we have said and explained in detail at  the Capital Markets Day. And this is more relevant for the European Power segment than it is for Lignite &  Nuclear, but please understand that we will not give more details how much exactly it is per segment.

texts.speaker: John Musk
texts.profession: Analyst, RBC Europe Ltd.
texts.text: Yeah. Morning, everyone. Two questions from me as well. Firstly, in the actual interim report you talk a little bit  about changing regulations on airborne pollutants, and you seem relatively relaxed that these may be watered  down when pushed into national levels. But if they weren't, what is the scale of the risk in terms of your assets  and potential closures in Germany? And then secondly, with the – obviously the improved balance sheet post the  nuclear fuel tax rebate, how should we be thinking about you looking at tuck-in acquisitions in European  generation?

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On the balance sheet side, yeah, I mean, the nuclear fuel tax has brought down net debt significantly. Please  keep in mind when we talk about the €1.7 billion that we have promised €1 extra dividend, which equals to €650  million. So more or less it's €1 billion. We are currently looking at all options, how to strengthen our financial  situation that is on the debt side, but also measures may be to improve operating cash flow in the future, but it's  too early to speculate. It will take some time, but we will have a very cautious approach here.

texts.speaker: Ahmed Farman
texts.profession: Analyst, Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: Hi. Good morning, everyone. So just two questions from my side. I just want to make sure that I understood that  your comment around the changes to the basis of the guidance [ph] fairly and (20:46) correctly. I think on the  negative side, you mentioned the additional outages on the lignite, which if I understood correctly was a double- digit million impact. Was the reclassification of the Hungarian power plant had an effect as well?

texts.speaker: Ahmed Farman
texts.profession: Analyst, Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: And then on the positive side, I think you mentioned a double-digit effect from the commercial asset optimization.  But I think in the report, you also talk about better load factors and margins on the gas-fired fleet. Is that a  separate effect or is that included in your – the comment you made earlier?

texts.speaker: Ahmed Farman
texts.profession: Analyst, Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: And then my second question is on your energy Supply & Trading business. I think in the second half, you had a  negative EBITDA in that business – in the second quarter. Could you give a little bit more color on that and is that  something that we should expect for the second half as well? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Thank you. Let me maybe spend some more explanation on the guidance. First one for the Lignite & Nuclear  segment. It is correct, as you said, that the additional burden from the unplanned outage is double – a medium  double-digit million euro amount for the full year. I mean most of it in H2.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Now, coming to European Power. Right, in the interim result, we talk about different load factors for and margins  on the coal- and gas-fired power generation. More or less, these are offsetting factors. So, we make more money  than previously expected in gas-fired power generation, but less in coal-fired power generation. The simple  reason is that gas is more times price setting and the load factors for gas are higher given the very low spot gas  prices we currently see. So gas is more often in the money than previously assumed, but these factors are more  or less equaling out.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: With the Littlebrook sale, it will drive the results significantly above previous year's results. And please keep in  mind also, in last year, in 2016; we had positive one-off effects from the sale of real estate in the European Power  division.

texts.speaker: Lueder Schumacher
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA (UK)
texts.text: Good morning. First question is on Neurath. I think if I heard you correctly, you said that the unplanned outage  refers to unit F and G, so that would be the BoAs. What exactly is the reason for the unplanned outage and how  long is it expected to last? That's the first one.

texts.speaker: Lueder Schumacher
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA (UK)
texts.text: And the second one is on your fuel hedges, I didn't quite get what Markus was saying as he was speeding up  there, but I think you said that 2018 has now been closed, 2019 is still open. What is your general view? I mean,  2018, clean docks, depending on what efficiency you use, still don't look that attractive. Do you think 2018 is now  fairly valued and there's more upside for clean dark spreads [ph] further out the curve? (25:40)

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. Thanks, Lueder. On Neurath, yeah, so what was the situation at Neurath? So, the block F was down from  June, as you can also see from the REMIT publication, was down from June 2 to July 21. The reason was  damages with the turbine blades. The loss of production during that time was around 1.2 terawatt hours, and the  maximum capacity is also down now around 15 megawatt until the next regular maintenance stop. And we will  see – that was it on block F. Since block G is more or less exactly the same type, we will have an extended 17  days outages to also look at that in order to apply what we learn from the incident at F, also to G. And so, overall,  we already lost production. The additional cost for the work we have to do at the turbine will amount in total to the  medium double-digit million amount we mentioned.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And on hedging, yeah, I mean, sorry for being too fast here, but what I said is that we have closed our implicit fuel  hedge for 2018. So now it is more or less a full hedge of the outright position. I mean, of course, we can start  speculating what we think about spreads or at the absolute level of profitability here. As you can see on the next  slide 8, that the blended spreads – so, it's not the clean dark spread here but the blended spread incorporating all  assumed pass-through factors of the different fuel types and how often they are price setting. So in the end, there  is a summary of our own model. There you can see that calendar year 2018's spreads are quite high and already  above the level. We have seen in the outturn for 2016 and 2017. That is also the reason why we have closed  implicit fuel hedge position.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: In the longer run, I mean we have two effects on the spread side, since power prices, absolute prices are not that  relevant. The first one is what is the type that's in the market? I mean, we can also speculate about it, but what we  will see is that conventional generation will come down the capacity in Europe especially in Germany over time,  especially on the nuclear side.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And the other one, this is more difficult to predict, what is the exact price consolation on the fuel side, because  that will determine which technology is in the money, which technology is price setting, what the possible sectors  are, how much carbon you need, and so on. I mean, for us, the most relevant picture is this blended spread we  show here, we have shared with you. And there you can see 2018 is already quite rich.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On the CapEx side, we expect the path on where we see more CapEx in the second half of the year. And we still  stick to our guidance that's going to be around €350 million for this year and also the years to come. And this is  purely maintenance CapEx and some CapEx for the conversion of the Dutch plants into biomass.

texts.speaker: Sofia Savvantidou
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane Ltd.
texts.text: Yes. Good morning. Thank you for taking my questions. A couple from me as well. It looks like there have been  quite a lot of sort of small changes in your portfolio selling some assets, deciding to delay the mothballing of  others, putting others on held for sale. I was wondering are you seeing some opportunities or changes in the  operating environment in terms of how you evaluate your coal versus your gas portfolio for now and for the next  few years or these are just opportunistic adjustments that you've made that we've seen over the last quarter or so.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And we will reassess our entire portfolio given what we see on the forward market. So, what the profitability level  of these plant is. So this part is purely opportunistically. So don't read too much into it. On the broader context, we  always have – if you go for some portfolio measures, then we will go for more diversification of our portfolio to  bring it more in balance, because we all know that it's very coal heavy.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On the Datteln plant, yeah, I mean, I can just repeat what I said earlier. It is, for us, it's also a very clear case. We  contractually agree to take 450 megawatts out of the 1,050 megawatts. The commission is delayed – the  commissioning is delayed by years and markets have changed significantly. So, power today is a different product  than it has been seven years ago since we all know that you can't store it.

texts.speaker: Alberto Gandolfi
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: Yes. Hi. Thank you. Good morning. A couple on my side as well if I may. The first one is more on the industry in  general. And could you please elaborate on your outlook for carbon and particularly what are you doing in terms  of hedging and policies there, considering that we are entering in the – on the height of the debate on the MSR  and there has been ongoing talks about a carbon floor. So if you can maybe elaborate your framework around  carbon would be great.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And on the industry and carbon, yeah, let me answer the question with two aspects. There was some speculation  early summer and spring that after the election of [ph] Mr. Merkel, (36:09) we might see initiatives here. I think a  very senior politician from Merkel's party, the spokesman for energy policy had made a couple of days ago very  strong statement and some of you have picked it up for the research report that Germany will not support national  carbon floor measures. They support the ETF at least on the carbon floor side.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: We, as a company, are also seeing that the ETF is the system where the European Union had exactly what they  need in order to steer how much carbon will be – how much carbon emission we're going to see. Let's wait for the  outcome of the trilogue negotiations after the summer break where they will fix hopefully soon what exactly are  the parameters. In our view, it would not make a huge difference for which model they go. We expect a moderate  impact on carbon pricing for the years to come.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Our hedging policy, so far we have hedged the entire implicit financial carbon position we have until 2020, now  almost 2021 already. But we are currently hesitant to go beyond that tender because the [ph] road costs (37:31)  are very high liquidity, beyond 2022 is very low. And of course, we want to see the outcome of the trilogue  negotiations to have more clarity, where we think carbon prices are going. And after that is fixed, we might extend  our hedging beyond 2021 already now, but that's going to be decided after we have the outcome.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: So, I mean, if you want my summary, it's more or less on the carbon side now business as usual on European  level.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: My second question has to do with the German election. Besides the fact that there has been talks about changes  to [indiscernible] (38:53) legislation, is there anything for you to play for? Do you have anything to gain or to lose  on energy policy on the German level from the outcome of the election in September? Thank you very much.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. Thanks. Let me ask with – start with the second question, because it relates to question from the previous  speaker. The first – I mean, on the carbon side, I think I mean after the clear statement from the CDU party – that  is an European topic, so we don't expect the German government to – other than on European – on what non- European level, they will do something on national level. The question that needs to be asked by the next German  government is what will they do forth in order to ensure security of supplies?

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The next – during the term of the next government, we're going to see the phase-out of the entire remaining  nuclear fleet. And that brings us as we have discussed previously in very tight market situations and something  has to happen, because with the addition of renewables, load factors for thermal generation will come down,  profitability will deteriorate further.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: So if nothing happens, we're going to see more and more [ph] thermal (40:11) capacity leaving the market. And  we think it's not – in the end, it will not be a question of money, because transferring the UK capacity market to  Germany will maybe cost €2 billion, and it will already save a lot of cost fee, while the system suffers today from  stabilization measures.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Your other question is also a very relevant one. I will not give you much transparency of what it means for our  fleet. But it will – I mean, both base load and peak load spreads will go into our blended fuel spread, where we  take our hedging decisions. So, we run our model and we know exactly which plant will run at peak load. And so,  how [ph] often it is (41:26) the money that determines the position we have and of course, we use both products  base and peak to hedge our positions.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: So, we will gain from higher peak load prices and the higher peak load prices are also incorporated into the  blended fuel spread we have shown on page 8. And since we are not willing to give you too much details,  because that would reveal our assumption on pass-through factors and so on and so forth, which we think are  confidential information, but the relevant picture to look at is, how the blended spread, how we see them evolve  over time and that is page 8. And that gives you the best indication what it means for our fleet.  Michel K. Debs  Analyst, Citigroup Global Markets Ltd.  Q  So, Markus just to make sure I understand. If I look at your page 8 and I say, I'm taking the line that you call  calendar 2019, which currently is at €2.5 or €2.4 per megawatt hour, you're telling me that this is the number I can  plug against your megawatt, your terawatt hours to understand the profitability of both the Lignite & Nuclear  division and the European Power division in 2019 based on market conditions now.

texts.speaker: Michel K. Debs
texts.profession: Analyst, Citigroup Global Markets Ltd.
texts.text: So, you have effectively hit the bottom in power generation?

texts.speaker: Mark Lewis
texts.profession: Analyst, Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Yes. Good morning. Thank you. I have two questions as well but unrelated. The first one is, I mean you talked a  lot about carbon in the European context. But we have the German election coming up and we still have the issue  of Germany's domestic commissions target for 2020, which is a 40% emissions reduction target, which at the  moment seems almost unimaginable really that Germany can now meet that target.

texts.speaker: Mark Lewis
texts.profession: Analyst, Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Nevertheless, in the CDU manifesto of the 4th of July and an interview that Angela Merkel gave to the German  media on the 16th of July, she recommitted to that target. Do you think there is a residual risk that there will be  more stringent measures put in place after the forthcoming election in an attempt to try and meet the domestic  German emissions target? That's the first question.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On the CO2 side, or the national emission target, I think that we'll also be part of the equation. Let's see and wait  for the new government how they want to achieve that – whether they want to achieve it, how they're going to  balance it. It is not only a problem of the utility sector. I mean, the public mood is currently also, especially  focusing on the transportation sector, because the only sector where emissions are going consequently down  year-on-year is power generation and where emissions are going up in the transportation sector.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The first one, page 8 is not our production mix. It is the market, because the spreads you see depend on market  condition, not on our specific situation. So, what this is, is I mean we run a fundamental model – fundamental  supply and demand model with base load assumptions. As I said earlier, peak load assumptions, we see the  current price levels. We then have an assumption how often, which technology is price setting, what the pass- through factors are, and then we can calculate a blended, clean fuel spread of the market, which if you use  exactly our assumptions on technology mix, pass-through factors and so on, which you can currently buy in the  market. And that is what you see on page 8. But of course, that drives the profitability of our fleet. If this is higher,  we make more money.

texts.speaker: Ingo Becker
texts.profession: Analyst, Kepler Cheuvreux SA (Germany)
texts.text: Do you have a reason already into Q3 now to assume that or it's just a matter of being conservative? If I may ask  on the first one, do you find anything else in the rising trends for the fuel spreads than the change in the fuel price  differential between EEG, coal and gas or would you say that basically is it?

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On the commercial asset optimization result, no, there are no indications in Q3 that make us more cautious as a  matter of fact that we are more cautious, but especially in Q2, where we saw significant price changes, especially  in gas and coal, which then is used by the commercial asset optimization team to make an additional euro. When  they use the new price consolidation in order to optimize the portfolio even better. We don't expect this fuel price  volatility to continue for the next six months.

texts.speaker: Nicholas J. Ashworth
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Hi. Good morning, everybody. A couple of questions from me as well, if I may. On European Power generation,  you've talked a lot about the commercial asset optimization and a little bit around the better performance of some  of the thermal plant. Can you talk a little bit about the cost side of things as well and how that's moving? I know  you have the cost program and targets through to 2018. And I just want to get a bit of an update on that and  what's been delivered so far this year and if you're happy with the run rate.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: If you look at our reported figure, so not the adjusted one, there in our interest result, the €250 million interest  reimbursement we're going to get from the government is reflected in our interest. So, there is a positive effect of  around €250 million from the reimbursement of the nuclear fuel tax in the interest result, and that is the reason.  Yeah.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah, that is very easy. I mean, you have to bridge around €1.7 billion. It is €1.7 billion nuclear fuel tax. It is a  better operating performance of a couple of €100 million. And then a working capital, a positive working capital  effect, but that is especially at innogy. Bernhard has reported that on Friday, because they have seen a very  negative development last year in a more normalized, but still negative pattern this year. And that is the effect why  it changed.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The first one is, they are definitely changing from year-to-year, because we have different assumptions for the  supply and demand balance and different prices for the fuels. Unfortunately, I will not share any details, because  that would put you maybe in a position to find out what our fundamental assumptions are. And I mean, this model  is very important for us and it's definitely a company secret. So, we will not give you details on the exact pass- through factors we assume, because you could back-calculate what our assumption on demand and supply is.
