texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Further, innogy will support the preparation of the transfer of innogy's renewables business to RWE. In this  context, it will also be reviewed how the transfer of renewables businesses can be implemented as soon as  possible after the transfer of RWE's stake in innogy to E.ON. All in all, the agreement is an important step, and it  should give additional impetus to the execution of the transaction.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: At the beginning of June, the German government nominated the members of the Commission Growth, Structural  Change and Employment. The Commission is tasked to identify measures which will close the gap to the 2020  climate goal as quickly as possible and ensure the achievement of the 2030 CO2 reduction targets. In addition to  the environmental targets, the Commission should also take into consideration security of supply, affordability, as  well as social aspects and the avoidance of structural disruptions.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: In addition, the Commission shall develop a plan for the phase out of coal-based power generation, detailing the  necessary companion law, economic, social and structural measures. The Commission held its first meeting on  June 23 and is expected to present first proposals by the end of this year. We hope and expect that the  Commission will deal with the complex topics based on factual expertise and reach a consensus which will also  provide planning certainty for the companies involved. The timeline, however, where results are expected by the  end of the year looks very ambitious.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me also remind you of our long-term carbon position which we have financially hedged through to the end of  2022. In other words, the change in carbon prices should not affect our generation margins for the next five years.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: In anticipation of your questions, I can confirm that we have also already taken measures on our open carbon  position for post 2022, but please understand that we will not provide any details on our position due to the  sensitive nature of this information.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On page 8, you can see the development of fuel spreads until the end of June 2018 which are relevant for our  hedge prices you saw in the previous slide. The graph looks slightly different to the previous one as we instead of  average monthly figures we now show end of month data to bring the graph in line with our hedge prices on the  previous slide. Fuel spreads continued their Q1 decline in April and May before starting to recover strongly at the  end of June.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Let's move to the Supply & Trading division on slide 9. We saw a good trading performance which was driven by  a very strong second quarter. While our gas and LNG business posted a good performance, it lagged behind the  very high result of last year. Besides that, we had a negative effect from a value adjustment within our principal  investment portfolio. For the full year, we confirm our earnings expectations for this division of between €100  million and €300 million.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: With regards to the change in provisions and other non-cash items, I would like to point to the timing effect of CO2  provisions mentioned on the slide. With the transfer of the CO2 certificate to the national clearing authorities in  Q2, we have completed this year's utilization of provisions whereas additions are only halfway through the year.  For the year as a whole, we expect to be in line with our initial guidance of roughly €650 million.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: innogy's continuing activities, which are the renewables business, gas storage activities, and Kelag are expected  to contribute an adjusted EBITDA of between €700 million and €800 million compared to €785 million in 2017.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: We see CapEx for the continuing operations of RWE to amount to €1.2 billion to €1.4 billion. We are stating gross  CapEx here, so before proceeds from disposals or farm-downs. Out of this, approximately €0.8 billion to €1 billion  is attributable to innogy's continuing activities and will be mainly spent on growth projects into renewables  business.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: In conventional power generation, we still expect CapEx of approximately €400 million predominantly for  maintenance and modernization purposes. Furthermore, it includes more growth projects, for example the  conversion to biomass co-firing in the Netherlands. RWE Group net debt from continuing operations is expected  to be moderately below the level as at June 30, 2018, of €5.4 billion.

texts.speaker: Gunhild Grieve
texts.profession: Head of Investor Relations, RWE AG
texts.text: Thank you, Markus. Before we start the Q&A session, we just wanted to draw your attention to a slide deck we  have put together on the pro forma combined renewables business. You can find it on our IR website, and we  hope that this is going to answer the many questions we have received over the last few weeks.

texts.speaker: Alberto Gandolfi
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: Thank you, and good morning, everyone. I'll stick to the two rule question today. The first one is on renewables.  Could you please comment on the Triton Knoll farm down? I know it's technically innogy, but considering you  already own the economic interest, I was surprised not to see a price disclosed. The Asian press is talking about  £700 million just for the right to participate in 40% of the project. So, I guess the question is, is this ballpark figure  broadly okay and should we think about it as the rights to participate to the project and how would you intend to  redeploy capital in your pipeline?

texts.speaker: Alberto Gandolfi
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: And the second question is about sensitivity to carbon. You were talking about being financially hedged until 2022  previously, can, perhaps, I ask your question in terms of where do you see the profitability of your combined cycle  going in the next two to three years in terms of volumes and spreads if we go into a situation whereby carbon  goes to switching economics? So, we are not even talking about the coal commission here, it's going to be coal  shutting down production and perhaps lignite being impacted too at least for your competitors out there in the  market. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On CO2, yes, you are right. I mean, we are financially hedged until 2022. So, any movement of the carbon price  should not affect the profitability of RWE. Of course, it does not mean that it changes profitability of the different  technologies.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And your question pointing regarding CCGTs, so our expectation is that our continental CCGTs, I mean, in the  UK, the picture is already totally different. But our continental CCGTs should over the next year contribute more  than it currently contributes, but that has many factors. One is probably the price constellation, so hard-coal gas  and coal and spreads. But the other one is also a tightening of the market with the ongoing nuclear exit, and also  additional coal capacity leaving the market. So, in a tighter system, should make flexible generation, more  favorable for ancillary services, but also maybe load factors. So, we expect an increased contribution from  CCGTs.

texts.speaker: Vincent Gilles
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Yes. Thank you. Good morning, everyone. [indiscernible] (00:17:49). Two questions. The first one is on slide 7  and the hedging, 2021. Before that it's not a real surprise and I do realize its numbers to the end of June.  Therefore, there's a little uptick in power prices spread [indiscernible] (00:18:06) assumptions have not taken  place yet. But I would be interested to understand why you increased by 10%. Not a very large number, but still  not a lower number. You're hedging and what we should be expecting. I guess what I'm trying to get really to is  how long would it take before we see the impact of the current strength in power prices on this part of your  business. Sorry, it's a long question.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. Thanks for your question. On page 7, we have increased the implicit fuel hedge also in 2021. I mean this  gives us still exposure to the upside of increasing spread and we have hedged against falling coal and gas prices.  So, what we actually did is at current hard coal and gas prices we have sold fuels and we have bought CO2. Any  upside in power prices stemming from tightening markets or anything like that would still benefit this implicit fuel  hedge. And this is part of the risk management where we say, I mean, the exposure to fuel prices, absolute fuel  price levels, we're going to hedge and take out over time, because we have no directional clear view on hard coal  prices over the next three to four years.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Your second question, variation margins, let me put it this way. We don't want you to be overly excited. Of course,  it is a positive development that net debt comes down, which also shows that the position we have on which are  now fully mark-to-market were the right hedge decision because otherwise we would see a negative mark-to- market. But you should not double account the effect because we have now hedged our generation margins in  the outer years by implicit fuel hedging and also doing something more on the CO2 side. And that will, of course,  materialize in EBITDA, but that is now already upfront in the bank cash wise. You cannot double account. So it  was a wise decision on hedging. But you cannot double account when it realizes in the EBITDA in the future  years. But please, I mean, this is also sensitive information. I will give not the exact split which hedges and which  commodities drove the inflow of variation margins.

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you. So two questions from my side, first one on – now you've had some time to think about the new  structure post the integration of renewables, so I was wondering if you could elaborate a little bit more on your  thoughts on the capital structure and dividend policy for the new RWE?

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: And second question is on nuclear compensation. I think in the interim report you've mentioned that it's a  medium-triple-digit amount. What form will this take? Is it you selling these volumes to say E.ON or is it getting the  money from the government? Just some idea on when we should expect this [indiscernible] (00:23:15)?

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. Deepa, thanks. Let me start with the easier one where I don't have to disappoint you again which is the  second question, I mean nuclear compensation. We are obliged by the law that we enter into serious discussions  with our peers which probably need some additional production rights. We have done that. We are in the process  of negotiating with them.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On the new structure and dividend policy, I mean, of course, we have time. We are still discussing it. But given  that we cannot share all the detailed plans with innogy and E.ON's renewables business already because this is  sensitive information, it is still an outside in view of RWE on the details of their business. And please accept that  we will only come out with all details when we have this discussion and that cannot happen before closing one.  But you can then shortly, after closing, one expect us to present the full picture including dividend policy,  investments, and so on, also, the intention on the E.ON's stake, which is a relevant building block when it comes  to dividend policy and investment amount.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On the debt side, I mean, we think that we feel comfortable with the debt-to-EBITDA ratio of between 2.5 and 3. It  will still take some time with the rating agencies to sort out how this new RWE, which is a new [ph] animal  (00:25:29) combining conventional generation and renewables, what the business profile is exactly, and then  we're going to see whether we need to achieve the lower or the upper end or somewhere in the mid.

texts.speaker: Peter Bisztyga
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: And then the second one, just going back to the renewables business, maybe you could just give us a flavor of  how the cooperation agreement that you've signed with innogy will allow you to sort of start steering the  renewables business today. For example, I think you've already said there's going to be some provision for you to  assist in financing new projects. So, anything you can tell us there just to help us understand how you're going to  be able to move renewables forward? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Yes. Yeah. Thanks, Peter. You are right that this is probably artificially when it comes to cyclicality, but we  actually expect a higher result in the second half of the year than in the first half for the Lignite & Nuclear  segment. And the reason why this is now different than in previous years is the overhaul cycle, because we have  seen significant planned outages in the first half of the year and we have only very little ones in the second half of  the year. And in the last year, it was the other way around on the lignite side. So, we feel very comfortable with  our guidance of €350 million to €450 million, which also implies that we need a better H2 than we have seen in  the first half of the year.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: But what we have agreed with innogy and also E.ON are a couple of things. The first one is that we will now set  up joint project organization to preplan the integration process which also implies that innogy will start project  carving out the renewables, and we will also look into all potential measures to transfer the renewables business  as fast as possible after closing one.

texts.speaker: John Musk
texts.profession: Analyst, RBC Europe Ltd.
texts.text: And then secondly, on your hedging slide, I note it's only a small reduction, but in the outer years you've reduced  your volume expected from the outright production from 85 terawatt hours to 80 terawatt hours down to just 80  terawatt hours. And is that due to any assumptions you're already making around the coal commission or is that  just general market trends.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: There's no specific driver behind it. So, it's not that prices are different than and the money production has  significantly changed. We also don't have new assumptions on potential outcome of the coal commission in the  earlier years. It's more that we are now more confident that we're going to be more at the lower end of the given  guidance and that's why we decided to put only 80 terawatt hours here. Profitability wise, it will not have any  significant impact.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Since we have seen a significant negative effect last year driven by two elements, one was phasing out of  working capital elements, another one was a very mild winter and higher than usual gas storage inventories. And  this should definitely revert this year. So, we expect a three million digit lower positive effect in working capital for  the full year.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And then the second question I have is on your output and load factors and output in coal and gas. If I look to  your first half results, I see quite a significant decline in coal output, 25% year-on-year. Gas is also down 13%. Is  that largely due to underlying trends or are there any phasing effects, and if it is really down to underlying trends,  how does this fit with your view of higher contribution from spread generation and recovery in spreads? Thank  you.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On the load factors and the production, I mean, on coal, what is important to keep in mind that coal production if  you look into the detailed regional split has especially come down in the UK. And that was because we transferred  Aberthaw into kind of a reserve. It is not actively producing this year.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: That was a significant one and another one was in Germany where we closed the hard coal plant further together  with STEAG. So, it is an already announced closure. The general load factors on the hard coal plants which are  still running have not changed.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On gas, it is different. In gas, we have seen last year the special effect where we had two, three weeks of no  wind, no sun, and all existing conventional generation was producing significantly more. That has not been  repeated this winter. But we don't see any structural change in trends or anything. So, it's business as usual for  those plants which are active.

texts.speaker: Sofia Savvantidou
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane Ltd.
texts.text: And then the second question is on the coal exit committee. There was a press article today talking about some  suggestions that lignite provision should be reviewed in the same manner that we had for nuclear provisions. So, I  was wondering what would be your view on that, whether you see that as an opportunity to remove this lignite  provisions from your balance sheet, or how would you think about it and what would you want to see the  committee do with that? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On the coal exit and the discussion about the provisions, yeah, I think that was not a decision by the commission  to deal with the topic. It was more from some politicians to suggest they should also look into that. I mean, that is  now an expert topic. Let me maybe briefly explain how we think about it.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The comparison to the nuclear liabilities is totally wrong, because on the nuclear side, the decision was to review  those provisions where the government takes over the responsibility and the financing. And part of the deal with  the government to bring exactly that in line that those who can determine the cost level which are – which is the  government when it comes to final storage of the waste should also be responsible for the financing.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: We still have kept the other part of the provisions which is, by the way, 2.5 times bigger than the lignite mining  provisions to decommission our plants and do the packaging. And there are no review has happened because  everybody feels comfortable that IFRS rules, and our auditors, and all the transparency we have to create is fine.  And that is exactly the comparison to lignite.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: We are responsible for the re-cultivation. We are constantly doing it. It's not something which is going to happen  after the decommissioning. I think we have already re-cultivated bigger areas of land and we still will use in the  future. So, we don't see any comparison to the nuclear, which would, by the end, if that is really that – if that  would be done, would be the opposite which have been done on the nuclear side which would then bring  financing and responsibility in two hands and not keep it combined in one hand.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: We currently embedded, to the last part of your question, we currently see no initiative by the government or  anybody to discuss whether the government should become responsible for this task and should take also the  money. They see it as compared to the nuclear topic, a minor topic, also in terms of size of the liabilities. And they  all want to keep the responsibility with the company, and then also the financing should be with the company.

texts.speaker: Sam Arie
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you. Good morning, everybody. I would like to ask two questions, please, on your future renewables  business. And, Gunhild, as you mentioned, you published a very helpful document on this this morning, so thank  you for that. My question is – the first one is quite simple. I just wanted to ask what level of return you think will be  achievable on future renewables projects, projects you haven't secured yet in terms of project returns versus  WACC. It's a question I've been asking everybody this results season, so I'm interested in your perspective on  that.

texts.speaker: Sam Arie
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd.
texts.text: And then secondly, just stepping back a minute, when I look at the level of ambition from some of the countries  that you operate in, and, for example, I see the German regulators planning for an increase of 90 gigawatts to 100  gigawatts of wind and solar capacity by 2030, so that's what 7 gigawatts or 8 gigawatts of new renewables every  year in just one country. Well, then I wonder why the industry continues in the mode of auctioning developments  one by one within 1 gigawatt, 2 gigawatts of capacity up for grabs each time. Do you think that over time, we  might see the auction model offering significantly higher volumes to secure even greater cost reductions?

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. Thanks, Sam, for the question. I mean, the last one is a political question of the regulatory framework and I  mean, we also sit here puzzled and see how things are evolving in Germany. If they are serious on reaching their  target of 65% renewables by 2030, something needs to happen on both ends, additional renewable volumes to be  auctioned, but also the necessary investments in the grid and both is delayed.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: But if you ask me whether we see some indications especially in Germany that they want to change anything, we  don't see anything. So, maybe as you, we sit here being a bit puzzled how they really want to achieve that. But so  far, nothing is discussed in terms of different approaches to auctioning, also the entire regulatory framework  around renewables and security of supply.

texts.speaker: Lueder Schumacher
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA (UK)
texts.text: Yeah. Good morning. The first one is on clean dark spreads. Markus, you mentioned the quite strong recovery in  clean dark spreads from June. What was the driving force behind it? Is it just power prices catching up with few  commodities which have been running up quite strongly or did the market actually get tight over the summer,  perhaps coal plants struggling with supplies? Be interested in your view on that.

texts.speaker: Lueder Schumacher
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA (UK)
texts.text: And then also on the carbon topic, where do you currently see the early fuel switch and how much carbon  abatement can actually take place at that level in your view? There's also, while strictly speaking, not a third  question from me, because it's been asked already. So, I just wanted to clarify. On the volume, on the outright  output 2020, 2021, you said there's no specific reason behind it, but you are now more confident to come out at  the lower end. I just wonder what is this based on this greater confidence that you're going to be at the lower end.  Is it sort of a marginal lignite plant that was [indiscernible] (00:47:31) been taking out of the planning process or  just would be interesting to hear your reasoning behind that. What made you more confident?

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me start with the first one, Lueder. Clean dark spreads, I mean that's now pure speculation. I mean  technically, of course, power prices have increased more than hard coal and CO2 and that widens the clean dark  spread. What the driver is why the market reacted like that because it's a financial market. I don't know.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: But you would typically see some – from time to time you see that power is lagging the fuel complex. So, that coal  and CO2 move fast and then power moves a bit later, especially in the outer years where the liquidity is a bit more  constrained on the power side than it is typically on the fuel complex where you have much more liquidity in the  market. But I'm not aware of any specific argument right now widened at the end of June.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The second question is a very interesting one. What can really happen? I mean, of course, at current CO2 prices  and the fuel complex price constellation, you already see first fuel switching because they are very inefficient hard  coal plant; the old ones which are still in the system currently not economically. So, it takes place. But to have a  significant amount of CO2 abatement from fuel switching, we probably need higher prices. But it's now gradually  starting.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The interesting question, how much can really be saved or reduced by fuel switching? And that amount is  definitely not 100 million tons. It's in the two-digit-million area. So, if you see a shortage of CO2 supply in the  coming years, which is maybe a couple of hundred million tons, this can never be solved by fuel switching,  whatever the CO2 price level is. But I think this is a two short-term sighted view on the CO2 market because the  most relevant question is, what's going to happen with this surplus? And what happens with forward hedging  because, certainly, different price constellation in CO2 prices will probably change hedging behavior of industrials  and especially utilities.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And that would then bring the amount of CO2 certificates down. But this is a market which is very difficult to  analyze fundamentally. It's more, I would say, game theory what people will do and what kind of price level. But  as we have said before, we expected an increase, and I would not rule out that CO2 prices will go even higher.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The last one on volumes on the 80%, so, to be very clear, there is no new decommissioning plan or whatever that  we take out an additional lignite block and so on. So, we have always given the range because we also gave for  the other years range. Now, we have moved on in time.

texts.speaker: Lueder Schumacher
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA (UK)
texts.text: Okay. Thank you. Just one follow-up question, when you mentioned the definitely not 100 million tons possible  abatement from fuel switching but double digit, does this refer to Europe or just the German market?

texts.speaker: José López
texts.profession: Asset Manager, Millennium Management
texts.text: And the second question is your UK CCGT fleet is relatively more efficient than some of your peers. We had the  Beast from the East [indiscernible] (00:52:24) in H1 and yet – and coal output is down across the system and yet  your CCGT generated a little bit less than in H1 last year. Can you take me through what's behind that? Did you  have some statutory outage or maintenance that needs to be considered, and if we adjust for that, you would  have actually done a little bit better? Thanks very much.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: José, thanks for the questions and very well spotted on the CCGT in the UK. We could not fully benefit from the  Beast from the East because we had some minor unplanned outages in our CCGTs also weather related but,  unfortunately, especially in the period where prices were very favorable.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Of course, we could partly offset that by selling the gas which we didn't need because also gas prices were very  high. But in the end, this unplanned outage has resulted in the situation where we made exactly the money we  had hedged upfront, but we could not realize the additional upside and that is also reflected in the produced  volumes, so very well spotted.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On the batteries in the UK, yes, our expectation is that we'll see a continuous expansion of batteries in the market.  It will also bring down some of the ancillary services prices, especially the very short-term response. But on the  other hand, the additional renewable newbuilds will also make the demand for balancing the system will bring the  demand up. So, currently, on a net-net basis, we expect that we're going to keep the profitability level we currently  see for our fleet in the UK.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Yes, Nick, thanks for the question. First one on the portfolio, I mean, we do some, let's say, minor growth  investment into the portfolio. To name two of them, one is we invest in the biomass conversion of the Dutch coal  plant. We will bring Amer 9 to almost a 90% biomass firing until the end of this year. And also in Eemshaven up to  15% biomass coal firing. That is one smaller investment.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And, of course, we will now also bid into the auction clauses in Germany where the grid operators will auction grid  stability reserve which are smaller gas-fired power station in the area of 100 megawatt to 200 megawatt. And if  we get that secured, we are also investing there, but we talk about little investment there.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On the inorganic M&A side, we – if we can get a hold of, let's say, gas and hydro for the right prices, we would  add that to our portfolio in the model. But, I mean, we are investigating that now with potential sellers for the last  year. And, of course, it always needs two to agree on the price and we definitely want it for the right price, or we  keep our existing portfolio as it stands.

texts.speaker: Oscar Nájar Ríos
texts.profession: Analyst, Santander Investment Bolsa Sociedad de Valores SA
texts.text: Hi. Good afternoon. Oscar Nájar from Santander. Yes, one question regarding the hedging in page 7. Previously  you said that now that power prices are higher, if you had the light blue area, your average price should be higher.  However, we have seen that in the last quarter, in the second Q, the volume has gone from 30% up to 40%. And  the price achieved has been more or less the same [ph] €29 (00:57:57). Obviously, this has to do with the next  page, that is the spread of the red line that is coal for 2021 decreasing. But why don't – you have been fully  hedging the position with the dark blue instead of continuing the fuel hedge, and why don't you do that in the  following month because the power prices are much higher, and you have hedged [indiscernible] €3, €4, €5 per  megawatt-hour (00:58:23) higher? That's the question. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Yes, Oscar. I mean, there are two reasons for that. The first one is by converting the outright position into the  implicit fuel position, we implicitly hedged the power price level because we take out the risk of falling commodity  prices, especially hard coal and gas.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And the other aspect is that especially in the outer years, so 2020, 2021, we are liquidity-constrained if we just  use the power product. So, by using the fuels to also go short them and implicitly hedge the position, we have  access to more liquidity to risk management position. Otherwise, it would take much longer to reduce the risk of  the outright position.

file: RWE - Q3 2010 Earnings Call 11November2010 900 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 11-Nov-10.pdf

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Dr. Rolf Pohlig, Chief Financial Officer  Thank you, Stephan, and good afternoon to everyone. The title of our presentation gives you the  topic for today. We are discussing with you the first nine months of 2010 and the update to the  outlook for the full fiscal year. We know that due to the introduction of the nuclear fuel tax, a lot of  questions are still outstanding with regard to our future strategy. But as every year, we are currently  working on our strategy update. This will last into December. And as always you will get the full  strategy update in February at our full year analyst conference.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: At the end of September, the German government decided on a comprehensive energy concept  providing the framework for the energy strategy until 2015. Nuclear energy is considered to be a  bridge technology until renewable energy is able to provide the bulk of the acquired electric power.  As part of this concept, nuclear power plants should be granted to an extension of the lifetime of 12  years on average. This was approved by the lower house of parliament on October 28th.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Also in October the lower house decided to introduce a nuclear fuel tax. As you are familiar with the  general framework around the tax, we expect RWE to face an average annual burden between  €600 million and €700 million with regard to its operating result and approximately 400 million to  500 million as regards recurrent net income.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In addition we founded RWE East located in Prague. It will be responsible for our Central Eastern  and South Eastern activities with the exception of the gas transmission business. These  organizational measures will become effective as of January 1st next year. In line with these new  organization measures we downsized the number of Board seats to five as Ulrich Jobs left the  company at the end of September.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Now on to our division performance starting with RWE Power. Its operating result improved by  17%. Slide five gives you the individual value drivers. We expect the positive trend at RWE Power  to continue beyond the rest of 2010. A higher availability of our Biblis nuclear power plant and lower  fuel prices and costs for CO2 emission certificate will be the main reasons for this.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The sales business benefited from efficiency measures and slightly improved gas margins. We  expect the operating result to be up for 2010 as a whole. This will be mainly due to improved  earnings in the gas sales business above all because of the absence of one-off cost caused by the  negative gas to oil spreads incurred last year.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Now on to our new Netherlands/Belgium division. The numbers for 2010 are substantially effected  by consolidation effects. I commented on the major items in the first quarter presentation. The  performance of the Netherlands/Belgium division was supported by higher gas sales due to the  cold winter weather and stable customer account numbers. On a standalone basis, we had an  operating loss in the third quarter for two main reasons. Firstly, the seasonality that is typical  especially in the gas business, and secondly we transferred the Eemshaven power plant project  from RWE Power to Essent. The accumulated upfront cost of approximately €25 million are now  reflected in this division.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Let me continue with RWE npower. It’s operating results fell by 24% adjusted for Forex effect it  came down by 26%. The decline is mainly linked our generation business, the adverse market       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 3 condition for hard coke plants led to reduced earnings. This could only partly be offset by higher  production volumes of our gas pipelines and by lower maintenance cost. Addition, the third quarter  on its own looks weak compared to 2009 has some other things, we had some positive one-off  items last year.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In our retail business, we benefited from improved residential gas demand over the winter months  and slightly recovered gas margins on the back of lower commodity cost. This was partly offset and  reduced our gas tariffs at the end of March this year. In addition, we have seen lower electricity  margins following our tariff cuts in March last year.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In the generation business, we expect that lower spreads will also influence the performance for  2010 as a whole. But we are more optimistic for the fourth quarter based on the contracts we have  already locked in. The lower spreads will be partially offset by the progressive commissioning of the  four power plant units at Staythorpe during the second half of this year. In addition, we expect to  see a reduction in station maintenance costs.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Although the aforementioned tariff reductions our retail business are putting pressure on margins  we expect negative effects from high electricity network fees, retail margins are likely to benefit  from slightly lower commodity costs. However, the British market continues to be very challenging  due to the continued increases in commodity prices over last month, which have already led to  price increases in the market.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Our focus will remain on efficiencies in order to ensure competitive cost base. The €120 million  efficiency program initiated last year will be turned into a sustainable improvement and we are  working on additional efficiency measures in generation, retail and corporate functions. For the  years ahead, we anticipate a slight increase in RWE npower’s operating result.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Operating earnings at our Central Eastern and South Eastern Europe Division climbed by 29%  supported by positive Forex effects. Adjusted for Forex effects, division posted an increase of 24%.  Major factor was improved margins in our Czech gas sales business especially since the last  quarter of last year. On the other hand, we suffered from declining volumes of distributors.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In addition, we had a positive contribution above all from improved electricity sales margins in  Hungary and Poland. We anticipate that earnings generated by this division will be in the order of  last year supported by a positive Forex effect. The main reason for the slowdown of earnings  growth in Q4 is that margins in our Czech gas sales business as well as in the Hungarian electricity  sales and generation business are expected to come down again. In addition, there will be burdens  from the new energy tax in Hungary. On the other hand, we will see higher earnings contributions  from our Czech regional gas grid business.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The operating result of our renewables division fell short of last year by 33%. Upfront costs for our  large investment program are still dampening the development of Innogy’s operating result. In  addition, earnings went down due to lower realized electricity prices in Germany and less wind in  Germany, UK and the Netherlands.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In contrast, the first time consolidation of the Essent wind assets contributed €10 million to  earnings. We explained in our earlier calls that this is less than originally expected due to the very  weak wind production caused by the weather.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: As regards to 2010, we expect RWE Innogy to record higher operating earnings. We would see  further results of our growth investment program. But upfront costs for our projects are still  offsetting most of this. In addition, Innogy will benefit from the first time consolidation of Essent’s  wind activities, but due to the low wind volumes in northwestern Europe, the earning increase will  be smaller than originally expected.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 4 Upstream gas and oil reported a 52% increase in operating earnings. This is mainly a result of  higher oil prices, the stronger U.S. dollar as well as reduced exploration costs in North Africa. In  addition, we benefited from lower royalties in the German business. On the other hand, they have  suffered from reduced gas prices and lower production volumes. Compared to the weak 2009 we  see significant upside potential for 2010. RWE expects to see improved oil prices from the back of  a stronger U.S. dollar. This will be partly offset by lower gas prices and volumes as well as  increasing production costs.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The operating result in our trading/gas midstream division fell by 91%. The mark-to-market  performance of the trading business fell below the very high level of the first three quarters last  year. On the other hand, we benefited from the first time consolidation of the Essent trading  activities. They contributed €61 million in the first nine month of 2010.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The steep decline is mainly related to our gas supply activities, this is because of two major items.  First in 2009, we had successfully concluded price revisions and had to a release provisions  accordingly as a one-off item. Secondly, prices on the gas market dropped relative to oil-indexed  purchase contracts. This primarily effects our Czech gas portfolio due to growing competition. As a  result, we built a provision for onerous contract.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In 2010, we expect the division to close significantly below last year’s record level despite the  positive effect from the integration of the Essent’s trading activities. Lower trading margins  compared to the extraordinary high level in 2009, the absence of the aforementioned one-off items  recognized in 2009 as well as a provision for our Czech gas portfolio are the main reasons for this  decline.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Ladies and Gentlemen before I continue with the non-operating result, I would like to say few words  about the gas-to-oil spread exposure. We recognized on our recent trade shows that the market still  needs some more clarification. This chart, chart number 14 from our analyst conference in  February.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: There is additional slide on our backups on page 27, which provides some more information on the  recent gas-to-oil price development. The facts in brief are, we have a total annual gas purchase  portfolio of 50 bcm or about 500 terawatt hours. Approximately 27 bcm of this are covered by long- term oil-indexed purchase contracts, which however include different types of price revision  clauses. In 2010, we have approximately 11 bcm in oil-indexed sales contracts so that as a result, I  guess the oil spread exposure is approximately 16 bcm or 160 terawatt hours.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: This exposure is expected to grow to approximately 20 bcm due to the fact that more and more  sales contracts are renewed at market price levels. We are currently in negotiations with all our gas  suppliers. As a result, we expect this exposure to decline significantly again over the next two to  three years.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: As a result, the operating income of RWE Supply & Trading over the next couple of years will be  heavily influenced by the timing and the final outcome of negotiations with our gas suppliers. Now  please understand that we cannot disclose details of the negotiations while talks are ongoing.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Patrick Hummel>: Thank you. Thank you. So number one would be the hedge ratio for 2012  is just at 40% and comparing that with the past couple of years that’s fairly low. I know you basically  say it’s up to the customer’s behavior not so much under your control, but can you give us a bit of a  better feeling why it is so low, why you think your customers are reluctant? Or to which extent is  your bet on the market involved in that low hedging ratio. And the number two, would you be able to  quantify the actual loss that you made in the gas supply margin during the third quarter?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Stephan Lowis>: If we can say something about the loss in gas supply business. Very clear  answer, no we can’t, we don’t disclose the number because we are just as you know in the middle  of the talks with our gas supplier so that would be – would not be wise to do so. I think the main  driver behind your question is what happened in Q3 or what has happened in Q3 in the Supply &  Trading business. We had, let’s say, a weaker trading result as normal, so that was driving the  numbers little bit down and of course it was impacted by the gas-to-oil spread which we carried out  in Supply & Trading.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: I think the size of the provision which we built in summer this year will be  further effected during the rest of the year depending on what could be the gas-to-oil spread as per  balance sheet date that will have an impact on that.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Benjamin Leyre>: Thank you very much. Good afternoon. Two questions then. First one is  year-to-date have you already mothballed some power plants in Germany?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And second question regarding the contribution to the renewable funds, can you please tell us how  that will be accounted in your best guess. If it will have a negative impact at the EBITDA level or  should we able to capitalize it? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And another question regarding the burdens from renewable funding, so we will have 3.5% on top  of the electricity bill next year, is there anything which I should have in mind in terms of having a  intake on RWE’s earnings? May be timing effects or so?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: With respect to the renewable fund, I think that is something different, it’s not the renewable fund  the colleague from BNP Paribas asked for the other minute, it is the – what’s in there [inaudible].

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: The contribution for renewable energy for solar for photovoltaic for wind in  Germany and as you rightly reminded all of us that figure will increase form €0.02 per kilowatt hour  to €0.035 per kilowatt hour as per the 1st of January next year. That was announced several weeks  ago by the four transmission system operators for power in this country.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And we have today announced price increases for our retail customers in North of [inaudible] and  that price increases by €0.08 per kilowatt hour because we see on the one side this higher burden  of €0.015 per kilowatt hour on the other side they are purchasing cost for the power reduced, so  that led to this only €0.08 increase per kilowatt hour.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Vincent De Blic>: Yes, good afternoon, two questions. The first one, could you please just  come back on the number on slide five, the change in nuclear and mining provisions is €390 million  and just remind us of exactly what happened last year and what happened this year?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: I think 2009, it was mainly in the mining sector. I think we got the approval of a  different re-conservation concept for some of our mining activities in the lignite area. And as a  consequence, we had to release corresponding provisions.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Martin Young>: Yeah, good afternoon to everybody. I have just the two questions, the first  relates to disposals that you may consider in response to the impact of the nuclear tax. I think you  made it perfectly clear before that you wished to maintain the A rating. That to me suggests you do  need to make some disposals. I think we are prepared to accept that disposing of the grid in  Germany is more likely a possibility now than it previously was in the past. But what about the  prospect of selling some of the oil and gas interests you have, be interested in some comments on  that.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: Yeah, Martin, thanks for the two questions. With respect to disposals yes, you  are right. Already confirmed this in summer this year when the original plans by the government  were announced to introduce a nuclear fuel tax, but please understand that at this point in time I will  not specify that in more detail, that is subject for further discussion and we would then make  respective announcements in February next year. But you mentioned one asset the grid which was  already rumored that we are looking for co-investors in the product expansion of the power grid.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: With respect to contractual power station that is right, as you know we have several hard coal base  power stations under contract that is with respect to stay active on it and with respect to an E.ON  subsidiary. Some of these contracts are up for renewal I think next year and we have to make up  our mind to some extent later this year and to some extent also to summer next year. And as you  know in such renewables, which are an option to us, there is no well in ore to make a decision early  but only at the latest point in time when we have the maximum of information available, but that is  something we have got obviously in mind.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Peter Bisztyga>: Hi. Just one question from me. There has been a pretty rapid build out of  solar power generation in Germany this summer. Have you seen any impact already on the  performance of your fossil fuel generation fleet as a result of that? And also has there been any  impact of this growth in renewals on your – sorry, of this growth in renewables on your hedging  strategy?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: Solar power, we are not quite sure about that. It might have some impact, but  then it’s much more with respect to gas power station because as you know solar is only in position  to provide power over the late morning hours and early afternoon hours. But it has already – so it  might have an impact on what we call curve sharing. What is curve savings. But I think what is also  important on our stand is that in some of our regional distribution companies there is a need for  additional investments because the low curve distribution lines are originally not intended for this  type of power. So there is a need for example in our southern German region distribution company  Lechwerke to make additional investments. Of course, we will get the respective return on these  investments in due course as soon as the Bundesnetzagentur is recognizing this in the regulatory  asset base. But there is a kind of – we have to do investment, I think that is what we currently see.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Bobby Chada>: Good afternoon I just had one question left which really relates to the  renewables business. I know that there are a number of things affecting the relatively low result this  year so far, one of which is weaker weather conditions. I wondered if you could help us understand  what the effect of the upfront costs are on the results, so we can get a better feel for the underlying  profitability and if you are able to separate out the load factor or weather affect that would also be  helpful.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q>: Yeah, good afternoon. I would like to come to the mix of base load and peak load that you  mentioned that has changed and I’d like to know whether this is sustainable and what the  background is of this change of mix.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And the second question would be whether you could remind us on the average duration of your  own gas customer’s gas contract?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Stephan Lowis>: And the base peak as Rolf just said, we have split roughly between 80%  and 20%, 80% base load, 20% peak load. That hasn’t change much over the last – over this year  and last year. So we are always between 90/10 and 80/20, so that was no structural shift here.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Stephan Lowis>: Of course what we see is the volatility of feed-ins of renewables but that  can be also be reflected in the balancing power market.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: I think that doesn’t – the court made clear very early from the latest or this year  that after the nuclear fuel tax introduction we have to put everything under view and so far it would  be totally unwise to make a more detailed comment with respect to one or the other aspect of that.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Christopher Kuplent>: Hello, good afternoon, two questions from me. One honking back to  what Tanya just asked, I wonder whether the higher share of peak load reflects a lower load factor  in some of your, well, plants that used to provide base load electricity. I know you’ve been in the  German press highlighting how complementary nuclear power is vis-à-vis the intermittent  renewable energy supplies. Does that mean we should expect an average decline in your load  factors?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And the second question is as far as your first half result statement was concerned, when you  talked about the nuclear tax for the first time, you mentioned CapEx cuts, potential asset disposals,  and I wonder whether you within that tool box can rule out a capital increase or whether you are still  considering all these different options at this stage? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: With respect to the general trend of load factor and nuclear power station, we  assume that we had a much more production volume in the first three quarters of this year at Biblis,  so that is substantial base load. You have seen our argument that nuclear is ideally an instrument       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 13 for balancing the volatile wind power and solar power we had in this year. That is the argument  which is still in place but fortunately we had in the first three quarters of this year, I think only 10  hours with negative prices. So there was not that much need to make use of that. But otherwise we  are just checking I think there is no general trend of lower load factor at least I’m not aware of, no.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Christopher Kuplent>: So can I therefore assume that the higher peak load is actually  showing a higher load factor in some of your gas-fired power stations?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Stephan Lowis>: You can’t see that in the numbers, to be honest, if you check the numbers  which we provide on – let me just double check, page number 15 of our report you see that the gas  electricity production just increased by 0.4 points billion kilowatt hours so that is not – you can’t  read that – we have to double check, if we can give a more precise answer to you.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And secondly, I understand that you can’t provide full visibility on the current gas to oil spread and  risk given the ongoing negotiations with your suppliers, but could you give us an indication about  the magnitude of the current spread for 2011 before any impact of renegotiation, so we can draw a  kind of worst-case scenario which will most probably not materialize at the end of the day but then  we have a better feeling about that?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: So with respect to the Czech market under the own use accounting rules we have to build a  provision for owners contract. And as already mentioned that we did already in summer this year,  so there is still some volatility coming for that coming from the further development of the gas-to-oil  spread. And the size of the gas-to-oil spread we cannot quantify this our self because that would be  a competitive sensitive information, but we can give you an over impression there the – gas-to-oil  spread is based on publicly available information and there we have a slide in the backup to the  presentation. For the German portfolio that is different. That is under the mark-to-market rules and  there is no need to build a provision.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Bernhard Jeggle>: Yes, good afternoon, sorry for the technical problem I had. The first  question is on power prices. Could you elaborate a bit on your power price expectations and clean  dark and spark spreads for 2011 and 2012?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And the second one is on efficiency enhancements. Could you provide an update on the current  achieved efficiency enhancements and a rough breakdown regarding the divisions?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: Let me start with the efficiency enhancement program there we are absolutely  on track, perhaps remember that the goal for this year is 700 million out of the 1.2 billion program  overall for 2012, compared to 2006. So we are absolutely on track with respect to that.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: With respect to power price development and spread development, we are quite obviously  disappointed to see the current price environment. As you know we expected to resume to  significant higher power price environment and that which is actually materializing. So beside that  sharing with you that disappointment, if I would know absolutely what the power price would be  then I would bet all my personal fortune on that. Of course, we hope that it will come back to be in  line with a significant improvement we have seen in the German economy overall, because there is  a disconnect between that overall improvement of the German economy overall and the power  price development.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Alberto Ponti>: Apologies to spoil the party, but just one question really. Can you give us an  indication of the EBIT you do on supply of gas like E.ON has done? That would help us a lot.  Thanks.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Alberto Ponti>: The EBIT of the supply business in gas, i.e. how much you’re making on the  gas contracts, buying and selling.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Stephan Lowis>: I think that would be to tell you exactly what loss making we are doing there  and therefore we can’t do that. Because it would give – let’s say, valid argument for our gas  suppliers in the current talks against us and it wouldn’t be wise to do so.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Lueder Schumacher>: Good afternoon. Two quick questions. One on the gas contract  negotiations, and this is not just another way to try to get – ask the same question in a different way  but this one hopefully you should be able to answer. Are you actually just relying on the goodwill of  the supplies or are you actually drawing them a specific joker that would force the parties into legal  arbitration process? That’s the first question.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The second one is on the renewables business. Yes, it’s small at the moment but it’s supposed to  be big or bigger certainly but so far we’re only seeing a J curve without the upswing. Are you still  confident about your 500 million EBIT target for 2013 or is this something that is under review as  part of your new mid-term plan?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: With respect to the renewable business, we have several major windmill projects underway, and as  soon as they are ready to produce power they will then also generate the respective earnings. This  – perhaps you remember late last year we commissioned the Rhyl Flats wind farm. Right now we  are in the process of hopefully shortly commissioning the Greater Gabbard wind farm. So – and as  you know the variable costs for these power stations for this windmill power stations are relatively  low. So we expect a significant upswing in earnings.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Martin Young>: Yeah, hi. I’ve just got a follow-up question on the different accounting  treatments that you referred to in respect of the gas business. Is my understanding correct that as  far as the Czech Republic is concerned you anticipate the pain that you might take and provide for  it whereas in Germany you don’t take that hit on the business until you actually sell the gas? So  what we’ll see next year if indeed you realize negativity on the gas oil spread in Germany is that  number coming through when you actually sell the gas whereas for the Czech Republic you  possibly have taken most of the hit already. Is that a fair way of looking at it?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 17 <A – Rolf Pohlig>: Let me start with the legal action. I think the language we are using is that we  reserve our option. Right now there is no need to take a decision. And I think first of all what we  want to see is that the law will become effective. And as you know that our expectation is that this  will be the case before the end of this year. And we have to take final action only if and when we  receive the first tax bill under the nuclear fuel tax act and that is the time for final decision, but let’s  say we are preparing ourselves for that situation.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: The renegotiation of our oil-indexed long-term gas contracts, as well as the arbitration processes have developed  slightly better than our conservative plan builds in terms of timing and structural solution. We've got the first  positive news here as we made progress over the last few months in our negotiations with three major oil and gas  suppliers. These contracts are now indexed to traded gas wholesale prices or terminated early their mutual  consent that has the same economic effect, which is the removal of the gas to oil spread risk. We also  retrospectively set up contracts on a commercial basis, which is in one case still subject to the approval of the  Board of our contractual partner. With all other gas suppliers, we are in different stages of negotiation, parallel to  the ongoing legal proceedings. And we can also confirm that these discussions are on course for long-term  structural solutions. This makes us confident that our strategy is right. We are sure you will understand that we  cannot be more specific at this point in time as we are in difficult legal renegotiation processes with high values at  stake.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Finally, you are all aware of the negative impact from the new German Energy Policy. One particular instrument is  the nuclear fuel tax introduced with effect from January 1 this year. We filed a lawsuit regarding the payment of  the nuclear tax for our Gundremmingen B power plant at the Tax Court in Munich. We have serious doubts  concerning legality of the law imposing the nuclear fuel tax.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: The Tax Court in Munich passed a temporary injunction in favor of RWE on this question. The Munich Tax Court  has been the second after the Hamburg Tax Court to rule in favor of a nuclear power plant operator in this matter.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: The Munich decision led to a refund of €74 million. For the nuclear power plant at Emsland a nuclear fuel tax of  154 million was paid. We expect that this amount will also be refunded. The Hamburg Tax Court, which will be  responsible for Emsland, has already decided in favor of the operator of the nuclear power plant at  Grafenrheinfeld. Despite the first positive signals, it is however only the first step in a potentially very long legal  process. We therefore have to book refunds as tax liabilities.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: However, these positive effects are contrasted by additional burdens from provisions for restructuring measures,  from asset impairment at Essent power plants in H1 and from asset impairments on gas storage activities. The  financial result improved by 5%, mainly driven by the release of provisions and lower interest accretion to  additions to non-current provisions.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: As a result of the reduction of our operating results, net income decreased by 46% to €1.4 billion. Our recurrent  net income, which is adjusted for the non-recurrent items, decreased by 44% to €1.8 billion. The operating result  of the Group amounted to €4.3 billion, which is €1.9 billion below the comparable figure last year. This chart  number five gives you an overview of the development of the operating result by division. The new German  Energy Policy leaves its mark on the German Power Generation division with a reduction of the nuclear lifetime,  the implementation of the nuclear fuel tax and earlier closure of our nuclear power plants at Biblis.  In the period under review, we had about €1 billion of burdens from the new German Energy Policy, out of which  €0.2 billion relates to the nuclear fuel tax. In addition, the Power Generation division suffered from lower realized  spreads. These factors taken together lead to a decrease in operating result of 38% in the division.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: The second negative factor is the development in our Trading/Gas Midstream division. The division is particularly  hit by the impact of the negative gas-to-oil-spread. In addition, the performance of the Trading business has been  much weaker than usual.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Earnings at our German Sales and Distribution Networks division fell by 7%. The main driver here are higher  costs for improving the quality of our grid business. Our Dutch business, Essent, cannot repeat the excellent  results from last year, mainly due to the transfer of gas midstream activities to our Trading/Gas Midstream  division. Weather conditions were also less favorable than last year.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Our Central Eastern and South Eastern European division reports a reduction in operating performance of 4%,  resulting from decreasing Czech grid margins, decreasing Czech gas sales and from burdens from Hungarian  regulation. Our renewables business benefited strongly from higher revenues, from newly commissioned assets, in  total approximately 90 megawatts since October last year, better wind conditions and liquidated damages from  our joint venture in the wind offshore project, Greater Gabbard.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Our Upstream business almost doubled its operating result to €450 million. Increased gas and oil prices and  higher oil production are the main drivers. As usual, we explain individual value drivers and the full-year outlook  for the separate business divisions in more detail in the charts in the back-up section. These should be self  explanatory.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: I will now move on to the outlook of the Group. In August we updated our guidance for 2011 following the decision  to exit from nuclear in Germany and increased our 2013 outlook slightly due to higher expected earnings on the  back of our increased efficiency program and improved commodity prices and spreads.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: In fourth quarter, we expect the performance of the operating result to be slightly better than the EBITDA. The  reason is that we had in Q4 last year an extraordinarily high depreciation that we don't expect to repeat in Q4 this  year. We particularly expect an improvement for recurrent net income. This is mainly a result for better financial  result, which was disproportionately negative in Q4 last year. In the fourth quarter last year, we booked a  provision to compensate for financing cost from the non-interest-bearing prepayments to the renewables fund  and a high negative other financial result.

texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.

texts.profession: Chada
texts.text: Analyst, Morgan  Stanley & Co.  International Plc  Q Thanks. My second question was on the gas contracts, and hopefully you can answer this piece. So we seem to be in a similar

texts.profession: Analyst, Baader Bank
texts.text: Good afternoon, everybody. My first question would be on figures. Could you please give us the impact from the  releases of nuclear provisions? texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: With respect to the nuclear provisions, Stephan, do you have an answer on that?

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Please remember that in this line on slide eight in the backup chart, it does not only refer to nuclear provisions, it  does also refer to mining provision, that is important to have in mind, that is, our lignite mines.

texts.speaker: Stephan Lowis
texts.profession: Vice President-Investor Relations, RWE AG
texts.text: I think that's a very valid, but also difficult question. Let's split in two answers. texts.speaker: Matthias Heck
texts.profession: Analyst, Macquarie Capital (Europe) Ltd. Germany
texts.text: Yes. Hi. Good afternoon. Two questions for you. Firstly, on the nine months results of the Trading/Gas Midstream  business. Could you quantify the accumulated loss coming from oil-indexed contracts and do you expect them to  be fully refunded? That's the first question.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Mr. Heck, I will not speculate at this point in time. I can only repeat, I think that's not needed. With respect to gas-to-oil-spreads, yes, of course we are trying to get full refund of the  losses we have taken over the last years or so, and at the very end we will have to take decisions whether or not  proposals made to ourselves in commercial talks are sufficient or rather we further pursue the arbitration route.  But the goal is we have full refund of the losses we incurred.

texts.speaker: Deborah B. Wilkens
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International Ltd.
texts.text: My two questions, first of all, could you provide an update on the 4 gigawatts that should be coming online in  terms of new plant over the next six months? And the second question is just for clarity, the refund of the gas  renegotiations that you are expecting for later this year, they are already reflected in the guidance or will they  come on top?

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: It's not in the guidance, but you see we have also not -- of course I have it in the guidance. Perhaps you have seen that, only I think today or yesterday, we received a final  permit for our Pembroke power station, so that gives us more comfort that Pembroke will be fully commercially  commissioned next year. Then with respect to BoA 2 and 3, I think we can confirm that our latest expectation is  that those blocks will be commissioned at the end of January, end of February next year. That is the latest  information we have.

texts.speaker: Peter A. Bisztyga
texts.profession: Analyst, Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Hi, there. Two questions for me. First of all, could you remind us or tell us how much you paid for the 30% stake  in EPZ, please? And then my second question is on carbon. And  equally, does it mean you've been having to book mark-to-market losses on permits that you bought in the past?

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
