There is not a loss to be booked in the P&L,  but all these price differences on a mark-to-market basis are then booked in the other comprehensive income and  that we did as for the end of September, so it is booked there. And the appropriate charges will then be spread  over the years 2013 till 2020, as they are used in the individual years in that overall third combined period. With  respect to EPZ, I am not quite sure whether we disclose this at all or whether we are bound to -- we are just  checking -- give me a second to check what I can share with you on that. I will come back to that in a minute.

texts.speaker: Andreas Thielen
texts.profession: Analyst, MainFirst Bank AG (Brokerage)
texts.text: Yes, good afternoon. Just one question on the nuclear fuel tax, you show €210 million burden after nine months.  Would you be wiling to share with us what you see as a full year burden, and is there any reason to think of a  different number for next year? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: For the full year we expect, say, about €250 million, because in this month of November we had the refueling at  the Gundremmingen C Nuclear Power Plant and that will lead to an additional tax bill of approximately €15  million or so. And that is then payable, I think, next month. And, then we have the procedure that we will object  and try then to get it refunded.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: I'll come back to the EPZ question. We are very transparent, and on page 47 in the quarterly report we have all the  details. We explicitly share with you the information. That's the acquisition of ERH, which is the holding company  for that stake in the nuclear power plant, Bolsa, and worth payments totaling €754 million. And then it is even  more detailed then on page 47 in the quarterly report.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: The only antitrust investigation I'm aware of at this point in time is the recent antitrust investigation by the  European Union Commission and that referred to a gas problem, and we, as I think almost a dozen other  companies across Europe, we were affected insofar as we are counterparties to discuss our long-term gas supply  contracts. And that's the only comment I have, so I would not expect any outcome of that investigation before the  next two years or even longer.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: A green faction of the Bundestag had retained a lawfirm to write an opinion and that was an opinion referring to  the sector inquiry, which the Bundeskartellamt had entertained years ago, and early this year they had come to a  final outcome and the final outcome of that Bundeskartellamt investigation or sector enquiry was that there is no  proof at all that we are retaining capacity at a point in time when we can earn money with the capacity.

texts.speaker: Benjamin Leyre
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane BNP Paribas SA
texts.text: Yes, thank you. One question please on CO2 again, can you share with us some insights on the EU commission  approach to the price of CO2? Some believe that the EU commission could find a technical way to spot the price of  CO2. Do you agree how low does it need to go in your opinion for such intervention to happen? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: I have no view to what extent that is legally possible to start at that point. So I have no specific view on that. I  think on the other side it's important to have in mind that CO2-wise the Group overall is slightly long, which  means that the further price development of CO2 does not have such important impact on the Group overall.

texts.speaker: Stephan Lowis
texts.profession: Vice President-Investor Relations, RWE AG
texts.text: You were asking the question what was the effect on the transfer of the gas midstream business from Essent to...

texts.speaker: Bobby Chada
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Yeah. Well let's simplify the question, is your -- in the past RWE supply and trading has had a view that volatility  would be helpful and then volatility would increase because of renewables, is that still your view or has it  changed?

texts.speaker: Stephan Lowis
texts.profession: Vice President-Investor Relations, RWE AG
texts.text: I think knowing us, you know that we are out in the market to say, with all these renewables in the system we  think that the current forward has no or very slim capacity premium currently. And I think if that was the  question, we can expect that this kind of capacity might increase once we see more volatile price movements in the  spot market.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: The good story is that we have the chance to repair this. And, based on that we got a temporary permission for the  further construction work. That temporary permission is valid, I think, for nine months. And within these nine  months, we then have the opportunity to have a new permit, a new nature permit for Eemshaven, so construction  work is ongoing. And then, so far we hope that we will have no further delay coming from this permission issue.

texts.speaker: Christopher Kuplent
texts.profession: Analyst, Merrill Lynch International (United Kingdom)
texts.text: Two questions on timing for both of them. The first one is a follow-up to the question that Bobby, I think, asked  earlier regarding the JV and exclusive negotiations with Gazprom. You say there is JV talk of a combined with  your renegotiation of gas contracts. Does that mean that the exclusivity ending by the end of the year, you expect  to reach an agreement on both those items before the end of the year? And that would be the first question.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Not in legal terms or so. With respect to the exclusivity, the exclusivity refers to the JV, and if we would not come  to conclusion on the JV then of course we would nevertheless have to come to a solution with respect to the gas  contracts, either on the basis of contractual negotiations or in arbitration court.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Jeggle
texts.profession: Analyst, Landesbank Baden-Württemberg (Broker)
texts.text: Yes, good afternoon, everybody. First question is on the power generation segment. You've specified the burden  resulting out of the lower realized electricity price and lower volumes on the one side and the nuclear shutdown on  the other one to be €970 million. Would you please provide a breakdown of this amount?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Jeggle
texts.profession: Analyst, Landesbank Baden-Württemberg (Broker)
texts.text: And the second question is on dismantling costs of nuclear power plants, could you share some light of your -- on  your assumptions regarding dismantling costs of your nuclear power plants in Germany? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: With respect to dismantling cost that is relatively easy, because we have a breakdown of the nuclear  decommissioning provisions. I think it's either in the back-up of this presentation or in our Factbook, or at least in  our -- any reports where we have three lines for the nuclear decommissioning provisions. But as a general rule,  you can say that it is roughly €1 billion per 1 gigawatt, so that gives you the magnitude of the expected cost for  that.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Jeggle
texts.profession: Analyst, Landesbank Baden-Württemberg (Broker)
texts.text: Perhaps, one follow-up. I will ask this question, given the claim of the government in Lithuania for additional  grant from the EU to cover dismantling costs for its nuclear power plants in Ignalia, and here the government  stated that the cost will exceed previous estimates of €2.9 billion for two blocks here, by at least €0.7 billion. So  the total amount would end up with €3.6 billion for these two blocks. So the question is, are there big differences  you would see here or why are the costs in Germany so much below that amount?

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: I cannot comment on the situation in that country. I cannot comment on the budget of that country. I cannot  comment to what extent that country wants to gain more out of Brussels. I can only comment at, all these  decommissioning costs are based on expert judgment, they are refined each and every year, are adjusted for cost  inflation, that is not only done for ourselves, but also for the other nuclear operators. And some other people have  made comparisons of our nuclear decommissioning provisions to the nuclear decommission provisions in other  countries and then their argument is made that nuclear decommission provisions of our country on a per gigawatt  basis are much higher than in these other countries. That's the only comment I have.

texts.speaker: Vincent P. Gilles
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Yes, thanks for taking additional questions. I've got two of them. The first one would be in very general terms if  you could comment on the supply and demand situation in Europe? I think it's about a year ago that Mr.  Großmann mentioned this number of about 40 gigawatt that should get out of the system. Power prices have not  exactly gone higher in the mean time, and it would be interesting to have your views on this? That's question  number one, which may last a bit long.

texts.speaker: Vincent P. Gilles
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And if you got time left, question number two, I would be interested to hear what -- on exactly which legal basis  you actually take the government to court on nuclear, both on the nuclear tax and on the closure of nuclear plants,  if you could develop a bit for us to try and to understand how it's going to end?

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: I will start with that second one and then Stephan will provide you some insight in the first question. With respect  to the second one, we have the following issues: We have the nuclear fuel tax. We have the cross for the  moratorium. We have the overall change in the German atomic energy law, i.e. the phase-out law. And then we  have the minor issue that is the renewables fund. Let me go line-by-line.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: First of all, nuclear fuel tax, we are making the argument that this tax is illegal, because it does violate the German  constitution. The German constitution in some detail says which tax proceeds should go to which level of the state;  the federal level, the state level or municipal level. And the constitution explicitly says that so-called consumption  taxes are 100% for the benefit of the federal level. And for that very purpose the finance ministry, when drafting  the law last year said that it is a consumption tax.  However, there is jurisprudence by the Federal Constitution Court that it is essential for a consumption tax that it  can be passed through, in the majority of cases, through final customers. And given the merit order and then  nuclear power stations are in the merit order, we cannot pass through these costs to the final customer.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: There are further arguments against the nuclear fuel tax, but the tax courts in Hamburg as well as in Munich only  refer to this first reason, which we gave, making the argument this seems to be plausible. And for that very reason  they did not have to have a look on the other three arguments we also put in place. They are based on property  right law, they are based on European energy law, and they are also based on contractual law, but you should  remember, the contract utilities had with the German government in 2000-2001.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: The second issue is, the phasing-out law overall. You have heard that one other company has recently announced  that they have decided to challenge the constitutionality of the law at the Federal Constitutional Court. We are also  in the process. We have not taken any final decisions, but there I think are good reasons for going to the court. The  very point is that we are not trying to get the nuclear power stations once again on the system, but we are making  the argument that these phasing-out laws do not comprise any firm regulation about financial compensation for  the nuclear operators and their shareholders and for that reason they are not in compliance with our constitution.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: The fourth issue is then the renewables funds. Perhaps you remember that we agreed with the government  voluntarily on the renewables funds and we made our payments in the month of January, February, March this  year, altogether roughly €25 million, and then of course the basis of that renewables fund wasn't going to weigh  when some extension was canceled by the government. So there maybe later on issue to get the repayment of this  roughly €25 million. So that is the overall story where we are.

texts.speaker: Stephan Lowis
texts.profession: Vice President-Investor Relations, RWE AG
texts.text: And to your first question, let me try to answer this supply side. It's hard to predict that the demand side for the  next, let's say, five years, but the underlying drivers of the supply side and what we mentioned or what you have  questions about -- and that is new questions about the nuclear output in France and Belgium over the next couple  of years, and we have also a spread situation, which doesn't trigger currently new investments, especially in  Germany and also in neighboring markets of Germany, so therefore there is a good chance or likelihood, let's call  it this way, a likelihood that we see a tightening of supply over the next four to 5-ish years. I think that's the  current situation.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: It's a pleasure for me to provide you with the highlights of the first nine months of 2012. We have some good news  to report on although the environment overall remains challenging. First, with regard to the financial  performance, the numbers speak for themselves. EBITDA and operating result improved by 8%, recurrent net  income increased only slightly less with plus 6%.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Now, back to the current highlights of 2012. One of our major issues for RWE is how we will solve the outstanding  price revisions of our long-term gas contracts. We are still in negotiation and arbitration with two suppliers with a  combined contract volume of approximately 11 BCM per annum.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Besides the major discussions we have about the oil indexation for our gas supply contracts, we had one additional  dispute about whether we were allowed to reduce the minimum off-take volumes within our Gazprom contract  under certain conditions. Gazprom challenged our reduction rights in front of an arbitration tribunal and  requested payment for the full contractual minimum off-take volumes for the years 2008 to 2010.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: All in all, the development of the first nine months makes us even more optimistic for our guidance for the full  year. We now expect EBITDA and the operating result at least to match last year's level, the main reason is an  improved outlook for our gas supply activities within the Trading/Gas Midstream division and the positive  earnings trend in our German Generation business unit.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Let's now have a look at our key numbers for the first nine months of 2012 on page number four. Our EBITDA and  operating result both increased by 8%. A major contributor was the absence of one-off burdens experienced in the  first nine months of 2011 due to Germany's accelerated nuclear phase-out decision. In addition, we benefited from  a strongly improved performance by our energy trading business.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Furthermore, the 2011 result benefited from the release of a provision made in relation to a German renewable  fund which ceased to exist following the nuclear phase-out decision.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Turning to page number five, let me now briefly explain the major developments within our operating result. The  operating result of our Power Generation division in Germany advanced by 14%. Major contributors were the  already mentioned extraordinary burdens in the first nine months of 2011 from the new German energy policy  with the nuclear phase-out.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: A positive contribution resulted from the successful trial run and the commercial operation of our new lignite  plant, BoA 2&3 at Neurath. However, we suffered from lower realized power prices and spreads.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Earnings at our German Sales and Distribution Networks business unit fell by 4% due to lower electricity sales  margins and a decline in the income from investments. Essent result fell by 26% despite the start of commercial  operation of our new CCGT's Claus C and Moerdijk 2. Clean spark spreads are particularly weak at the moment,  partly as a result of Germany's continued expansion of photovoltaic capacity.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: In addition, the outage of our converted biomass plant at Tilbury due to the fire in a bunker led to lower output  compared to last year when the plant was still firing hot coal. Meanwhile, the plant is back in operation. Efficiency  enhancement measures, higher gas sales volumes and improved commodity cost management had a positive  impact on the UK supply business.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Our renewables business showed a weak third quarter and closed the first nine months 12% below last year's  number. Compensation payments received in 2011 for delays in the construction of Greater Gabbard did not

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Our Upstream business increased its operating result by 25%. Higher gas and oil prices and the appreciation of  the U.S. dollar over the euro were the main drivers.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: The Trading/Gas Midstream division closed the first nine months with an operating loss of approximately €400  million. This is a significant improvement compared to last year. The performance of the proprietary trading  business has improved considerably while the burdens from the negative gas-to-oil spread continued.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: At the peak of our renewable program, we have invested about €600 billion per year, a level which has never been  envisaged as sustainable in the long run. We have therefore announced that we will reduce our CapEx to about €4

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Slide nine gives you our divisional outlook for the whole year. We have changed the outlook for the Trading/Gas  Midstream division to significantly above last year's level from – in the order of last year's lever. This is mainly a  result of an improved expectation for our Gas Midstream activities.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: A further adjustment has been made to the outlook of our Renewables division. We now expect RWE Energy to  achieve an operating result in the order of last year's level. The main reason for this reduced outlook are delays in  the disposal of projects.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: With regards to Gazprom, you know that this is the one big outstanding price revision, yes, that's expected for  2013. I do beg your understanding that we cannot give any detailed numbers on this, but the effects from it are  part of the 2013 guidance.  With regards to our efficiency enhancement program, which has – €750 million announced for 2013, this is also  included in the 2013 guidance. And there are no significant delays or speed-up effects, so we expect it to come and  realize in the P&L as planned.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Yes, Vincent, hello. These answers can be pretty short, I think. We will pay a dividend according to our guidance in  2013 because we are expecting a recurrent net income in the order guided. And also, of course, from a legal  perspective, we also need the German local gas profits to be there to distribute a dividend and we also expect those  to be there. So there's no reason for us why shouldn't be able to pay a dividend in the 50% to 60% payout ratio.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Thank you. The next question comes from Benjamin Leyre from Exane BNP Paribas.

texts.speaker: Benjamin Leyre
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane BNP Paribas SA
texts.text: Thank you very much and good afternoon. Two questions, please. The first one, EBITDA industrial, if I may. On  the arbitration front with Gazprom in the Czech Republic, I wonder if this arbitration ruling fits, in your view, a  strong precedent. What I mean by that is that I wonder if in every gas market where Gazprom is selling gas  directly to consumers, one could think that local utilities would have now the right to ask for lower take-off pay  volume.

texts.speaker: Benjamin Leyre
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane BNP Paribas SA
texts.text: And my second question is related to nuclear provisions. I wonder if you could tell us or quantify to us what kind  of increase in nuclear provision one can expect at the end of the year due to likely lower utilized discount rate?  Thank you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: On the nuclear provisions, we have included our most up-to-date estimates on the discount rates in the Q3  numbers.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: And I think it's also very important, especially with nuclear provisions, to see that what ultimately drives the  change in the balance sheet position is the spread between the cost escalation rate and the discount rate. And as  far as I can see, in comparison to our competitors, we are relatively conservative in applying a low spread between  those two numbers. And only the two in conjunction do really make sense to be considered.

texts.speaker: Martin C. Young
texts.profession: Analyst, Nomura International Plc
texts.text: And then secondly, I think it's quite clear that you have managed to support your 2013 guidance based on the time  that you undertake your hedging given the base load orientation of your generation portfolio, particularly in  Germany. Unfortunately, I think you're going to experience the pricing pressure come 2014. I just wondered what  type of mitigating measures you might be thinking of to try and do your level best to keep things moving in a good  direction in 2014. Should we be thinking of plant closure? Should we be thinking of additional efforts on the  efficiency over and above what is in the plan at this particular moment in time? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Yes, hello, Martin. First to NET4GAS, we don't comment on ongoing M&A including disposal projects. On the – I  think what you were asking for is some sort of an outlook on 2014. We confirm what we have said, and I can only  say that of course we are not standing still and don't rest on our laurels for the €1 billion efficiency enhancement  program until 2014. They are further measures, some of them already on their way to implementation, others in  the pipeline.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Beyond that, we are constantly, so at least on the quarterly basis, reviewing our generation fleet in terms of  mothballing or even decommissioning and are constantly updating our plans in that respect.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: With regards to net working capital in the trading business, I think there are a few different factors which needs to  be distinguished. The one is that the – or the one thing which I can tell you is the main absorption of working  capital in the Trading/Gas Midstream division has nothing to do with the prop trading activities of ours. It  basically comes from two sources, the one is that we conduct our hedging activities of our generation long position  via the Trading/Gas Midstream units and this is done via exchange. And exchange rates and these are margins, so  whenever the prices change, there may be margin calls or receipts in a kind of cash swing. Of course, the expected  value of this would be zero but it will – in reality, it will never turn out to be zero.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: The other – and quite recently, this is not only power but as long as we still have the oil price index, gas supply  contracts, we are – have also been hedging our gas to oil spread position from these contracts. And so we have also  a significant underlying oil position in these and therefore, it's not only the power position if you try to reconstruct  the swings in working capital.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: The second effect is that in our Trading/Gas Midstream division, we also commercially optimized our storages,  both the amount of the internal storages and the external storage contracts which is mostly about gas storages. So  company engaged in the Gas Midstream business. And you see a buildup of storages or absorption of working  capital in Q2 and Q3, and you'll see a reduction when the storages are emptied in Q4 and Q1.

texts.speaker: Andreas Thielen
texts.profession: Analyst, MainFirst Bank AG (Broker)
texts.text: Yes, good afternoon. Two hopefully simple questions, firstly on the UK the guidance for the full year points  amongst others to progress in the retail margins. Can you give some more color on that? Is that coming from price  increases or what's happening there? And secondly, although the absolute number would be perfect, maybe you  could help us with the effect in Gas Midstream in the fourth quarter from the gas storage, but what is the exposed  volume roughly in the fourth quarter? So do we have to expect a significant loss from that business?

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: I think to start with the Gas Midstream question first, there are two aspects to distinguish, the economic position  and what you see in IFRS results. The economic position is the one – which is the one which we are actually  hedging. It's the one we expect to have after the expected outcome of the outstanding arbitrations have realized.  And so we – and this means that on an economic basis, we hedged the long-term gas supply contract in just the  same way as we hedge our power station. So we hedge the purchasing leg and we hedge the sales leg  simultaneously.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. Until we have resolved the outstanding negotiations, however, we are still – allow me the imprecise  precision, we are overpaying on the contracts because we are currently still paying according to the old price  regime although we expect that later these prices will be changed from hindsight, and therefore we are building up  you could call it a kind of reserve of overpayment and, therefore, we will incur losses of course on the gas to oil  spread in the fourth quarter of this year as we did in all the other years until the outstanding negotiations have  been settled for good.

texts.speaker: Michael A. Ridley
texts.profession: Analyst, Mizuho International Plc
texts.text: Yeah. Hi, good afternoon. I have one question. I was a little bit surprised to hear you talking about positive trends  in German generation. I was understanding that the buildout or the rollout of renewables is really hitting margins  in particularly gas-fired power plants in Germany. Are you saying that your lignite plants are very well in the  current situation or the buildout is not going to impact you so much going forward? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. Well, I think the positive development, I think this was more or less the expression I used was of course  compared to last year, which was of course close to an all-time low in terms of what could happen in German  power generation. So compared to that the developments were positive, and we had some positive developments  in terms – as I mentioned for example, also around the operations of our new lignite-fired block which are better  than originally expected. So we're seeing good availability which is a nice thing to have. Apart from that, I think on  a more macro level, it's fair to say that you can see in our numbers, the benefits of having a very well balanced  generation portfolio.

texts.speaker: Michael A. Ridley
texts.profession: Analyst, Mizuho International Plc
texts.text: Yeah, the fuel mix away from not heavy concentration on gas to different forms of thermal power, is that what you  were trying to say?  Rolf Pohlig  Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG  A This is what I try to say, correctly.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Thank you. The next question comes from Mr. Ponti from Société Générale.  Alberto C. Ponti  Analyst, Société Générale SA (UK)  Q Hi, just a very brief one. Are you thinking of closing any power stations in Germany as E.ON said yesterday? And  out of curiosity, I was wondering how Lingen is actually going in terms of profitability? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: We are not only thinking of closing or mothballing power stations in Germany. We have already done so. We have  either closed or mothballed quite a few power stations. We have closed all the 150 megawatts – or will have closed  by the end of the year, the 150 megawatts lignite blocks. This is basically in exchange for the new BoA 2&3 that I  mentioned. We have mothballed two old 150 megawatt hardcore blocks in our power station in Hamm in  Westphalia.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: We have terminated a couple of contracts with STIAC, also PPAs in the magnitude of 1.8 gigawatts in total. And  we have permanently mothballed an old gas-fired power station or 350 megawatt at Gersteinwerk in the rural area  and temporarily mothballed, so what we call summer mothballing two other 350 megawatt blocks on the same  site for a seasonal mothballing. And this is the result of our ongoing mothballing reviews that I mentioned earlier.  This is what we see under current marketing circumstances in mothballing requirements. If the circumstances  change, there might be further candidates.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: And on Lingen, I think it's not a secret to say that current times are not the best time you could imagine for  owners of gas-fired power stations. So it's clear that Lingen is not running the full load hours that we would like  them to run, but compared to other gas-fired power stations also to other new build, newly built or newly  commissioned gas-fired power stations, Lingen is still or is very much at the left hand end of the merit order due  to its favorable position on various gas pipelines and its special characteristics with the pipe storage installed  there, it's a competitive advantage over most other new CCGTs in northwestern Europe.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: No, no. If what I said about Lingen was read by you as a support for capacity markets and I have expressed myself  badly. No, I only said that they are in a competitively favorable position amongst gas-fired power plant but gas- fired power plants overall are having a hard time.

texts.speaker: Alexander Karnick
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank GmbH (Broker)
texts.text: Yes, hi. Thanks for taking my questions. One is, one larger competitor yesterday have basically stated to see  significant problems in there or significantly lower profitability in the value of gas flexibility in the storage  business. Is that something that you would see and that you would consider as a risk as well, would be my first  question? The second question would be to hear your opinion on this idea of you to satisfy 900 million of carbon  allowances, and whether this has any significant impact if adopted in your view. I mean we're seeing carbon really  a bit off the lows, if that sort of fits or is there a bigger chance to – for carbon rights to rise further and would that  be a threat to your lignite fleet? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. With regard to the profitability of gas storages, it's already very clear if you look at the development of  summer and winter spreads. Recently, the seasonal storage has not become more attractive. So economically, yes,  it has become as profitable – as attractive and all of this is reflected in our current guidance. Yeah, so as we hedge  our [inflation] position, we will also hedge out our seasonal storage position and [then pounds].

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: On the carbon set aside, on that part of my answer would be that as far as we know, it's a proposal by the EU  Commission. So there is still a long way to go for it to become fully effective, and we are closely monitoring what  will happen in the next stages of the legislative process as you're certainly aware of, and there are a couple of  European countries – or the enthusiasm about this proposal is mixed between different European countries.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: And overall, we think that what we're observing currently in the carbon market is not a symptom of market  failure, but it's rather a consequence of, if you want to call it, regulatory failure where different regulatory regimes  on European and national level, which are incompatible to each other produce undesired side effects. For  example, the low carbon price, which is just an expression that the carbon reductions are received by other means  that by our high carbon prices, for example, via the fixed feed-in tariff system for non-renewables.

texts.speaker: Alexander Karnick
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank GmbH (Broker)
texts.text: If I kind of follow up on that, I appreciate that and I appreciate the complexity, and there's a long way to go until  this is adopted. But given we're about I think 1.2 million, 1.4 billion tons long, what would be your take if this set  aside would be adopted? Would you be thinking this have a meaningful impact on the carbon price and therefore  would provide a P&L risk to you in, say, the outer years, I appreciate 2013 is fully hedged, or I would just being  fitted on your view sort of in an what if case? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: What if game is we can certainly do this month and as we said, we hedged for 2013 and overall, this carbon long  confirmed in the past as well, was meant to make us financially carbon neutral. So this effectively means that we  are neutralized against any effects of these specific politics should they move the price in whatever direction.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: I think just to make it very easy, Alex, we are Q2 neutral. So any rise or a decrease in Q2 prices generally doesn't  affect us. Of course in certain technologies like lignite, it has a probably dampening effect, but then the gas fleet  would benefit from that.

texts.speaker: John B. Musk
texts.profession: Analyst, RBC Europe Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Yes, good afternoon, just two questions, one very simple one, and I know you don't want to comment too much on  2014 but given the delays in renewables, is it right to assume that the one specific target of €500 million of EBIT  out of the renewables division is unlikely to now be achieved in 2014?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Okay. Starting with renewables and your question around the 2014 targets, we are, as I mentioned, currently fully  Of course, you are aware that there are currently some delays, not only for us but for others as well in German  with offshore projects due to a kind of regulatory or kind of deadlock between good operators and investors like  us, which is mentally resolved by legislation, but we will have to wait how exactly that looks like and how quickly it  will be solved that kind of backlog that is there.

texts.speaker: Bobby Chada
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Hi, I just have a couple of follow-ups. First of all, can you give any indication on when you would expect to take the  decision on the Tilbury biomass conversion? I think I read that you might take a decision this year, but I'm not  sure whether you have to take it before you run out of the running hours that you currently are burning through?  And secondly, can you give us any feel for when the next round of capacity which you contract from either STIAC  or E.ON is up for renewal or cancellation?

texts.speaker: Bobby Chada
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: But in itself, it's not a particularly large project in the context of RWE, is it?

texts.speaker: Patrick Hummel
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS AG (Broker)
texts.text: Yes, two quick ones. First one, can you just remind us of your hedged carbon price or carbon cost for 2013, is that  still the number close to €1.5 billion just to say that as a base and look further out into the future in order to get  the lignite spreads right? And second, I appreciate all your explanations around pre and post disposal 2013,  nonetheless, I'm still not sure what I exactly got what you meant to say. The €300 million, if that's already fully  factored in your €2.5 billion guidance, are you basically saying since you won't be able to sell €7 billion of assets  by January 1 that the actual number – net income number in 2013 will be higher than those €2.5 billion, or are  Stephan Lowis  Vice President-Investor Relations, RWE AG  A Okay, Patrick, let's make it very easy. What we say in the order of 2011, 2013, recurrent net income will be, which  means somewhere in the €2.5 billion full stop. Don't speculate if there's upside potential and downside potential  at this stage, I think the guidance is as it stands. Is that okay for you? I don't think so, but you have to take it.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: And then please bear also in mind that beyond the disposal programs and the potential dilutive effects, there are  still other – a few other big chunks outstanding, most notably the gas price revision with Gazprom where we have  an expectation built in. But...

texts.speaker: Patrick Hummel
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS AG (Broker)
texts.text: I hear you very well. Okay, and on the carbon?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Member of the Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: On the carbon, what we can say and what we've always said is of course that we have hedged all the carbon for the  2013 generation. We've hedged it in line or simultaneously with the power hedges. The overall volume is in the  order of magnitude of 100 million tons. So that's all we can say.

texts.speaker: Stephan Lowis
texts.profession: Vice President-Investor Relations, RWE AG
texts.text: We – sorry, Patrick, we always confirm the volume, the 100 million tons compared to 2012, so that's the  additional burden. But we didn't comment anything on the price.

texts.speaker: Rolf Pohlig
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, RWE AG
texts.text: I think, Ahmed, it's fair to say that all three growth areas have more ideas than we actually have cash in hand, so  renewables; secondly, the upstream business and thirdly, also our Eastern European business have more ideas  than we're currently in the position to fund. It can be offshore wind, it can be onshore wind. There are certain  opportunities in the northern African area for E&P business. So it would be too much time to explore all the  opportunities we have currently, but there are lots of opportunities, but we are cash constrained.
