texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Y es. Thank you, Stephan, and also good afternoon to everyone from my side. When I presented our strategy  update in March, the outlook for our generation business was not exactly encouraging on the back of depressed  commodity prices. Since then, power prices have moved even lower and put further pressure on the business. We  have made no secret about the precarious situation many of our power plants find themselves in. Therefore, we  provided you with an overview of the profitability of our fleet.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: But what does this actually mean for the overall earnings of our generation business? We want to refrain from  providing you with an outlook for any specific year as a lot can happen and we would not wa nt to constantly revise  it until then. However, on slide three, you can see how the generation business would have fared in 2013 under  current forward prices. It probably will not surprise you that the business would not show a positive operating  result without any efficiency improvements. For now, we are still benefiting from higher power price hedges.  However, they are rolling off over the next three years.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Generation business is therefore working very hard on measures to ensure it still can provide a po sitive earnings  contribution. Nevertheless, the GenCo will still be far off from earning its capital costs. And if power prices were to  stay at today's level, we will need to shut further power plants even if they were needed at certain times of the year.  We are running our assets purely on commercial grounds regardless of expectations on any kind of future political  support.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: First, we have identified further efficiency enhancement potential in the years to come. In addition to the €1  billion already underway until 2014, we are already working on another net €500 million of efficiency  improvements by 2017. The latter will provide financial headroom of some €1.5 billion. Second, we have decided  to drive our CapEx down, down to maintenance levels, for the time being. This will save another €2 billion in cash.  And third, the envisaged disposal of RWE Dea and Urenco will contribute to some extent to a reduction in debt.  However, the amount will depend on the achieved sales price.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Now let's focus on the combined €1.5 billion for now. A big part of the efficiency enhancements will come from  planned head count reductions. As part of the old program 2012 to 2014, we had announced staff reductions in  the magnitude of 3,700. Out of this, approximately 1,000 were already achieved early in 2012. So another 2,700 to  come between 2013 and 2014.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Finally, we are continuing to look for further small optimization potential in our portfolio. At REW Innogy, we see  opportunities to streamline activities even more towards the most cost effective renewable technologies. We are,  for example, targeting the sale of the offshore logistics activities bundled under the company of OLC.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Thank you, Peter, and good afternoon from me as well. Let me give you a brief overview of the business  performance in the first nine months of 2013 on page 11. Our operating result was on a par with previous year's  earnings. We have two main counteracting efforts. On the one hand, our trading/gas midstream division achieved  an extraordinary high result due to the arbitration court ruling on our long-term oil-indexed gas contract with  Gazprom.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: On the other hand, we are suffering a massive earnings decline in our conventional power generation division.  Besides the burdens of full auctioning of carbon certificates, declining generation margins and the loss of margin s  from closing our old lignite plants, we suffered among other things from a one -off burden to adjust a provision for  loss-making contract.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: In addition, earnings in our upstream gas and oil division are under pressure due to lower realized oil and gas  prices and burdens from dry wells as well as delays in ramping up our production. The earnings trend in the first  nine months does not reflect the earnings trend that we are expecting for the full year. While the positive earnings  effect from the Gazprom arbitration ruling is fully locked in, the negative earnings development is continuing  especially in the conventional power generation division.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: In addition, we had in Q3 mainly a write-down of our offshore wind farm project Nordsee Ost of some €0.3 billion  and a value adjustment on our German gas storage activities of some €0.2 billion.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me briefly touch upon our cash flow statement on slide 13. The cash flow from operating activities shows a  strong increase of €1.8 billion driven by the one-off from the Gazprom arbitration ruling. As opposed to the  development of our operating result, the earnings declined due to the full auctioning of carbon certificates is only  partly reflected in the cash flow.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Looking at our divisional outlook on slide 15, we confirm our expectations from August 2013 with the exception of  upstream gas and oil. Here we have adjusted our outlook down to significantly below last year's level from below  last year's level. The main reason is that due to delays and infrastructure -related production restrictions, we are  not able to produce as much gas from our UK gas fields Clipper South and Breagh as originally planned. In  addition higher than originally expected exploration costs impact on the result.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Slide 16 gives an overview about the main value drivers and their impact for the earnings in fiscal 2014 compared  to 2013 from today's point of view. There are two main reasons for a further decline of the operating result. First,  the absence of the one-off payment from the Gazprom arbitration ruling. Second, the rolling off of our hedges in  the conventional power generation business compared to the current much lower market prices.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Our ambitious and increased efficiency program will only compensate part of this. We expect in general a stable  trend for our grid and sales margins. Furthermore earnings in 2013 still included €17 1 million from NET4GAS,  which was sold beginning of August as I mentioned earlier.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: For Innogy and Dea we had mid-term target for 2014 of more than €320 million and €800 million outstanding.  For Innogy we now expect an operating result of approximately €200 million. Innogy's operating result will be  negatively impacted by project delays in Nordsee Ost and Gwynt y Môr as well as adverse developments of  wholesale power prices and prices for green certificates, mainly in Poland.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: RWE Dea is still targeting to grow the production volumes of their hydrocarbons to approximately 40 million BOE  from a level of approximately 32 million BOE in 2012.

texts.speaker: Nathalie F. Casali
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: So I'm sure you had this view on September 19 when you cut the dividend. So would it be fair to assume that  you've chosen to set that at €1, because you see this as a sustainable level that can be generated from essentially  your downstream businesses?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Y eah. Hi, Nathalie. I will start with the dividend issue. And we did indeed take into consideration when we issued  our statement in September this year a view beyond the year 2013. But on the other hand we also consciously  opted for a payout ratio to give us the flexibility to adjust to uncertain future conditions, which are hard to foresee  these days in energy markets.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Well there will be some slight increase potentially due to the effect that we have two major power stations in  conventional generation and one – two more wind farms offshore coming on stream, but that's it.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: With regards to further upsides beyond the next one or two years, there are certain factors we are eagerly working  on and maybe Peter can shed a bit of light on what our growth pockets are which may contribute to bottom line  growth of beyond a rise in power prices or the introduction of capacity markets which would certainly help.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: What bottom is indeed the things that you've mentioned cost cutting, getting generation business back on a  neutral basis again, what we haven't taken into account and certainly what we see beyond 2014 is on one hand a  potential at least on the power price side maybe. Y ou can have different views on that or we have at least not  planned on that. And if it comes, that would be a clear upside.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Naturally what I first said, cost cutting can never be a strategy, cost cutting is a prerequisite in order to make this  company efficient, make it lean, make it dynamic and make it able to take advantage of all the opportunities that  we see, mainly in the downstream business. It's a business which is highly competitive, but I think with the clear  skills that we have on board with RWE, we can be competitive in that area and that goes on one hand into the  renewable arena.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: We will continue to do wind, onshore and offshore, be it with external partners to finance that, but the operations  of that, we will do ourselves. We will come in our renewables business out of the project development and the  building mode into an execution mode, which will need to make money then and which will make money.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The other side, there's a lot of advantage in the downstream area. We've clearly committed ourselves to the region  that we are in, we do have 24 million electricity and gas customers. I think, we can make significantly more money  out of the customer portfolio as we are currently doing, as well as that we can deve lop our downstream business in  a decentral area.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: We have in Germany 5 million producers of electricity. We are currently having a producer for [ph] gas status  (35:18). That will have to change sooner or later. And if it does, they will need access to wholesale markets, they  would want to optimize their energy efficiency, they would want to take advantage of the potential flexibility in the  system. All of that we are used to do.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: We do have often at RWE a strong seasonal profile in our CapEx spending with relatively little CapEx in the first  quarter. For example, in all the – in the downstream businesses and even some of the generation construction  sites bad weather in the first quarter, cold weather, reduces our investment activity significantly compared to the  second half of the year. If you compare the annual profile throughout the year with 2012, you would see that it's  not implausible that the last quarter might be as strong as we forecasted to be in terms of CapEx spent.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: And if you look back to the first half of the last decade, we had a number of years as a group where our CapEx was  at a similar level. So due to the very long asset life cycles we have, you will hardly ever find a year in our business  where you have the long run average CapEx. So usually either you overspend as we did in the last couple of years  and now fading out, or you underspend over a long-term trend. But this is a long-term trend, which you count in  decades, and not in years. So on this level, of course, you would not build new power stations. So sooner or later, if  we want to maintain our asset base, but this depends on market and regulatory conditions, we would have to  spend more again, but this maybe many, many years off and depends on exogenous factors as I've mentioned.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: On 2014, if I understand your question correctly, you wondered why 2014 we are, of course, not yet fully marked - to-market on our generation earnings. This is true, but our expectation is that from 2014 onwards, the further  erosion of generation profits will be offset by the efficiency enhancements and cost cutting, and some other  benefits like for example in energy the assets coming online and becoming productive so that the net effect on  earnings overall will neutralize the negative effects. And this is just to be very explicit. This is no guidance for 2015  or 2016. This is just a direction or qualitative statement about our long-term earnings profile.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: It depends. Y eah, of course, I mean, and this is I think you know us very well. So if we for example take our new  generation units both renewable and conventional coming online, they will certainly be rather beneficial to  EBITDA because depreciation from these assets won't go in there and they will clearly be cash positive. So the  EBITDA effect will be positive there and this of course looks slightly different for the below the line items if you  deduct depreciation and tax effects from it. And Peter still wants to make another remark.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Now part of that has to do with reducing our CapEx as Bernhard complained. And if you ask do we feel  comfortable with that, I can only confirm and reiterate we do not feel uncomfortable with that. And the reason for  that is two-fold. On one hand you should take into account our power plants are lucky there, but due to the  current pricing situation are running significantly less than they did in the past. If a plant that runs less, I need  less day-to-day CapEx.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Secondly, we have significantly invested in our power plant fleet. New plants are less CapEx  intensive than old  plants are. So that's where the day -to-day CapEx on that lower level does not give me any uncomfortable feeling.  So it's not that the financial pressure has driven CapEx to that level, certainly it was also an element, but we  operationally think that this is a sustainable level with which we can continue.

texts.speaker: Patrick Hummel
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS AG (Broker)
texts.text: Okay. Can I ask – I'm sorry. I'm really sorry. Can I ask – what's the incremental cost savings in power generation  out of those €500 million total new program P&L impact?

texts.speaker: Patrick Hummel
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS AG (Broker)
texts.text: Sorry. The incremental €500 million cost savings program that you launched today or €1 billion was the net  impact of €500 million, how much is already factored in this mark-to-market chart on page three in power  generation? How much of the €500 million goes into generation? That was my question.

texts.speaker: Robert Schramm-Fuchs
texts.profession: Analyst, Macquarie Capital (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And then to my second question, just there was a Reuters article earlier today, citing coalition negations, but there  is apparently support within both the CDU and the SPD for creating a nuclear liabilities fund off balance sheet  instead of on balance sheet. And Reuters citing industry insiders that this would lead to credit rating pressure.  Could you just give your comment on this please? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On Urenco more of the same, naturally not commenting on any commercial valuation or success valuation of that  process. I mean from my national background I can say to you, as I've read in the Dutch press and sort of the more  see my public stocks that I've had, the political pressure is around getting a good governance in plac e. And with a  good governance to get also the nuclear risks of what Urenco has being well captured. That's what their worry is,  and that was part of the project. And that's why it takes a bit longer, because that's a complicated issue. But we're  sure that we can get that managed one way or another.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On the second point coalition negotiations, yes we see various things coming out of Berlin. Depending on t he hour  of the day they are one way or the other way. A lot of wishes being accumulated at this moment in time. The ones  that you're referring to is on the wish list of the environmental negotiation team. This is clearly not on the table of  the energy policy negotiation team. And with that I can only say I take it for notice at the time being.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: And Robert, maybe to add to the rating effects you've alluded to, please bear in mind that our net debt numbers  include the full long-term provisions on nuclear liabilities, on mining, and the pension funding gap of our pension  fund.

texts.speaker: Deborah B. Wilkens
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: Y es. Good afternoon. Two questions from us. One is could you just confirm that reaching your return target in  renewals implies an EBIT of €400 million to €500 million in 2016? And could you also just help us based on your  interactions with the government, what you believe is likely in terms of whether or not there will be financial  support for the older coal plants?

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: We certainly have pre-empted on our own studies in that. We haven't done it alone. We've done it with the sector.  There's a combined paper from the industry association BDEW. It is supported by the communal power plants  and energy companies [indiscernible] (55:49) and it is also being picked up by the industry association BDI.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Together we come to the conclusion that the implementation of capacity market is necessary. And that is not  additional money by default for old and existing power plants, but if scarcity comes up in the next years to come,  then certainly that scarcity will have a price within that capacity market design. And the ones who have power  plants will get the benefit of that. That's as less concrete as it is at this moment in time. We'll hope to have at least  given you bit of flavor through what is currently under discussion.

texts.speaker: Alexander Karnick
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Broker)
texts.text: Y es. Hi. Thanks for taking my question. With respect to the trough earnings sort of cash flow question, just  interested whether you could give us a view or update the information on the average achieved power prices for  2013, 2014 and 2015, considering or well aware of the fact that 2015 is 50% hedged.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: With your question on our average hedging prices in 2012, it was – this is always outright. Power was €55 per  megawatt hour; 2013, we expect €50, and 2014, 2015, for those portions we have already hedged, it's €45.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Another aspect for example is our ongoing commercial talks with Gazprom on the remaining oil indexation. A  third one is of course, the ongoing projects – construction projects, which are to be finalized over the course of  2014, depending on when exactly they will come on stream and start to become cash producing. So this is just an  illustration of various forces that work that even in 2014, made it appear prudent to us to provide rather a range  than a specific value.

texts.speaker: Christopher Kuplent
texts.profession: Analyst, Merrill Lynch International (United Kingdom)
texts.text: And secondly, on your slide four, 2000 – I think it's slide 16, you're talking about trading gas midstream returning  back to normalized earnings. Just wondered whether you can be a bit more specific, is that €300 million, plus,  minus that would be very helpful? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The impact of closings on the overall pricing level, just to mention that, which is occasionally being assumed is  rather limited. We see that our power plants are currently in a pretty flat part of the curve. And if you close a  power plant that is standing still or that is standing idle, then it doesn't have an immediate impact on the supply - demand curve, and therefore, it doesn't have any pricing impact.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Maybe just adding on what Peter said over the trading – normalized trading result, so the order of magnitude of  depression, we still carry from the long-term gas contracts is somewhere between €100 million and €200 million  on an annual basis, and please bear in mind that we also – the out of the moneyness of some of the gas storages  we hold to the extent that they haven't been impaired yet is also shown in our trading numbers. So this is a second  effect, which impacts at least for the time being, the – what we call normalized trading result. Normalized, on slide  16, mainly refers to the fact that the one-off from the Gazprom arbitration ruling is out.

texts.speaker: Andreas Thielen
texts.profession: Analyst, MainFirst Bank AG (Broker)
texts.text: Y es. Good afternoon. Firstly, on the – again on the – yeah, potential asset impairments or view on the power  plants, if I understood it correctly, you have 7 gigawatt under additional consideration. So from what you just said,  would it be fair to say that during the next three years to five years, you will only take the decision on if yo u  continue to run these plants or is that going to happen faster?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Y eah. Hi, Andreas. So with regard to the decision points on further capacity reductions, this is indeed spread over  the future, but I would say for most of these – this capacity is spread over the near future, and the decision point  always comes when there is a major cash commitment to be made. So typic ally, an outage or a retrofit at such a  power station would be the point in time when we consider closing it down or not closing it down.

texts.speaker: Peter A. Bisztyga
texts.profession: Analyst, Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Hi, good afternoon. Three questions from me, please. Firstly, could you give us an idea of what proportion of your  new net €500 million of cost savings is in the conventional power generation business, and how much of that  relates to potential capacity closures?

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And on the trough, maybe one point, just before Bernhard gives a more specific answer, you have to see that we  have some moving pictures in the next years to come. On one hand, we have the already hedged power prices,  which are rolling off. On the other hand, we have cost-cutting programs rolling in. And the balance out of that  then gives us the result, but we do not specify that very precisely and as far as the top of earnings concerned,  maybe Bernhard you want to repeat that.

texts.speaker: Ian E. Mitchell
texts.profession: Sales Associate, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: And then secondly, there's been a lot of news flow and speculation around the Hamburg court hearing which is  coming up next week. Could you just give us a very quick summary as to exactly what is going to happen there,  when you expect some sort of verdict, and if a verdict is in your favor, what exactly that means either in terms of  paying the nuclear tax going forward or indeed exploring back any of the payments that you made historically.  Thanks.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Okay. Ian, if I may, I would try to answer the second part of your question around the nuclear fuel tax, and yes,  indeed, there is a hearing next week before the Financial Court of Hamburg, where it will be decided if the case  will also be referred to the European Court of Justice. It has already been referred to the Federal Constitutional  Court of Germany. So then it would be before the highest two courts you can address from a German perspective  on this planet.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: If there is – it's not a verdict, then it's just a referral to another legal instance. So if they decide to do so, we plus  the rest of the German nuclear industry I assume would then file for stopping the tax payments and getting  reimbursed the payments we have done so far. And this of course would be a not unattractive perspective from the  cash side, because we would get some €900 million of already paid taxes back. And t he going rate is around €350  million on an annual basis for our running power plants.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: What we have done for – just a illustration, what we did in Q2 this year was an asset impairment on the Dutch  assets where we – given the fact that currently gas-fired power stations, hard coal power stations bear the main  burden of the depressed market prices and spreads, where we put those  assets into an asset impairment test.

texts.speaker: Robert Schramm-Fuchs
texts.profession: Analyst, Macquarie Capital (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you for taking my follow-up. Just one last on cost cutting. I know you didn't want to split it how much of  the cost cutting comes from power generation. But I think it would helpful for us to understand if any of it comes  from cost-cutting in Dea.

texts.speaker: Alexander Karnick
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Broker)
texts.text: Hi. I've just been struggling to understand the argument of trough earnings in 2014? And maybe I'm missing  something, but maybe you can help me with that. If I look at the hedging position, was that 80% hedged at around  €50, 20% at €45, so that gives us an average of €49. If I look at the 2016 forward curve, it's €38, so it's twice your  difference on say 100 terawatt hours of difference, so that alone is €1.3 billion hit between 2014 and 2016, saying  we are adding at least additional €500 million cost savings, maybe that's €600 million, maybe €200 million to  €300 million of growth from renewables, suggests to me still €300 million hit between 2014 earnings and 2016  earnings.

file: RWE - Q3 2014 Earnings Call 13November2014 900 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 13-Nov-14.pdf

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: This has no impact on our guidance for recurrent net income because we will include the pro rata interest on the  purchase price in the recurrent net income with the full year numbers. Please understand that we cannot be more  specific on the Dea transaction at this point in time. For the UK capacity market, National Grid announced in the  middle of October which power plants have qualified for the upcoming offering process. RWE has qualified with a  total capacity of 8-gigawatt. A list of the individual plans is provided in our backup section on page 13. The first  auction will take place in December this year and refers to the period from1st of October 2018 to September 30  [indiscernible] (2:11). You'll find more details on the process in our interim report. All in all, the UK's decision to  implement a capacity market is the right step in securing sufficient generation capacity at any given time and to  make conventional power generation economically viable again. But it is currently too early to make specific  forecast about earnings implications.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: So what is the current status of the discussion in Germany about the capacity mechanism? It is still open whether  the German government wants to go for a reformed energy-only market or a capacity market and what the  potential capacity market could or should look like.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: The timeline of the Economy Minister has the following milestone. At the end of October, his ministry published a  Green Book. It simply outlines the different alternatives and gives an indication of what the ministry is inclined  towards the present. The tendency is towards a reformed energy-only market in combination with a strategic  reserve. The Green Book will be the basis for the discussion in the cabinet at the beginning of December. It will be  followed by a White Book which is scheduled for spring time next year and which will give more clarity on the  detailed plans of the government. A further timeline is that a new law could be in place by spring or summer of  2016.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: After this brief excursion back to our milestones. At energy, we have taken a further step in line with our asset- light strategy to grow the business and exploit our project pipeline. At the beginning of September, we sold 85% in  the offshore wind projects Nordsee One, 2 and 3 to Northland Power. As part of this strategy, we are able to work  on large-scale projects without having to dedicate huge amounts of our funds to these projects. Furthermore, as  part of our renewable strategy to concentrate on coal activities, we have sold our 80% stake in the Enna biomass  project to FRI-EL Green Power. Energy will focus in future on an electricity generation from wind and hydro.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Slide 5 shows the earnings development in the individual divisions. All in all, we see an expected decline of  approximately €1.3 billion. By far, the biggest effect is the absence of the one-off payment from the Gazprom  arbitration ruling last year. This accounts for approximately €1 billion. In our CEE/SEE division, the operating  results fell by approximately €300 million. This is, to a large extent, due to the deconsolidation of natural gas,  which contributed €171 million through earnings in 2013. Furthermore, we are suffering from the deterioration of  realized market spreads in the conventional power generation business, and negative weather effects, mainly in  our supply businesses. This can only partly be offset by our efficiency improvements.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Firstly, we received a repayment of nuclear fuel tax of approximately €0.5 billion. After the Hamburg Fiscal Court  decided in April in our favor, we will refund the tax that we had paid for Emsland nuclear power plant. This is only  cash flow relevant as within our P&L, we have to build a provision for the nuclear fuel tax until we have the final  court decision on the legality of the tax.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: We received a decision for our Gundremmingen power plant in our favor from the Fiscal Court in Munich at the  end of July. But we have not yet received the payment as we are still in discussion with the authorities on how to  provide credentials or guarantees. As a result, there is not yet a positive impact on our cash flow.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Where do we stand regarding the main cases of the nuclear fuel tax? We still expect a decision either by the  European Court of Justice or by the Federal Constitutional Court some time in 2015. There was a hearing at the  European Court of Justice on the 4th of November, which still leaves the final decision absolutely open. The next  milestone will be the conclusion by the Advocate General which is scheduled for the 3rd of February 2015. But  please bear in mind, this will not be a decision and the conclusion from the Advocate General is not binding for  the European Court of Justice. So that's all on this topic, and back to our cash flow comments.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: The second reason for the different trend between cash flow and earnings is higher advance payments and the fact  that the mild weather led to a lower increase in our accounts receivable. In other words, while the mild weather is  already reflected in revenues, it's not yet to the same amount in the cash flow. As you can see from the slide, these  effects led to a significant positive free cash flow. Let me remind you that one of our prime targets is to become  free cash flow positive post CapEx and dividends from 2015 onwards.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Second, the trading/gas midstream division had quite a negative earnings development in Q4 2013, which we do  not expect this year. Third, although we have lowered the outlook for the supply UK division, we still expect the  fourth quarter of 2014 to improve compared to the fourth quarter of 2013. This is mainly driven by the phasing  effect on the ECO program and [ph] the crystallization (10:32) of our operational efficiency metrics.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Slide 9 gives the divisional outlook. The trend of the individual divisions we gave in August can be confirmed with  one exception. For oil supply UK division, we now expect earnings to be significantly below 2013. The weak  earnings development in the first nine months cannot be offset by the expected strong fourth quarter.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: I'm not sure, because the line was very bad, if this answered your question completely, otherwise you have to  check back. On free cash flow guidance 2014, we obviously have a very positive development in free cash flow, and  certainly we cannot exclude that we might turn free cash flow positive post-CapEx and dividend here already in  2014. But please bear in mind that this contains a significant spillover effect that I described due to the warm  weather where the revenues already reflect the lower earnings out of the warm weather situation whereas in free  cash flow, we are still charging the old lump sum to end customers which were determined after a pretty cool year  2013 and this is only going to catch up during 2015.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: With regards to the swing in working capital, it's basically two issues. The one is these weather phasing issue or  the spillover issue between cold 2013, warm 2014 and then being only catching up cash-wise only in 2015, which I  mentioned before as an answer to Benjamin's question. The other one is that we embarked on to a pretty  aggressive net working capital optimization program, i.e., reduction program in 2014, which, of course, improved  our numbers in comparison to last year.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: So it is a quite significant number, but please bear in mind that I mean this – as you know, how cash flow is  defined that this is a kind of one of the improvement below and you show up once in cash flow and then you have  to stay at this new reduced level of working capital every year thereafter in order to stay at the same level, but the  cash flow will only show it once. Yeah, it's – mainly the issue on the amount of the working capital optimization is  quite significant. As you can see from our balance sheet, we carry a significant amount of working capital and  some of them like, for example, carrying CO2 certificates over the year-end also is something we can optimize  quite easily. And also what we show you already in the working capital is part of which we call third wave. So I  would ask you and all the other participants to give us time until March to present the whole picture. But positive  effect is already seen or you can see in the 2014 numbers.

texts.speaker: Nathalie F. Casali
texts.profession: JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: Hi. Good afternoon. My first question is – sorry, again on the working capital. In the presentation, it's mentioned  that there's a significant impact from the reduction in CO2 inventories. Could you just explain that a little bit  more, is it really a one-off because if the switch to phase 3, is it something that could revert next year? So that's the  first question.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Yeah. On working capital, in terms of the reduction of CO2 inventories, I mean it's like the reduction of any  inventory or storage right on your balance sheet. You see it once in cash flow as the working capital improvement  and then you are on the new level like any cost of reduction or spare parts inventory streamlining. So it's – cash  flow-wise, it's a one-off. Yeah, of course, it brings the balance sheet on to a new lower level of working capital  utilization which is, of course, positive in terms of capital efficiency.

texts.speaker: Peter A. Bisztyga
texts.profession: Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: And then my second question is what do you think the outcome will be from the German decision on the 2020  climate protection action plan? There have been some headlines suggesting that some members of the  government want your coal and lignite plants closed?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Yeah. Hi, Peter. On Dea, there – unfortunately, I have to repeat again my response to Nathalie's question. So  please understand that we don't muse publicly on any alternative scenarios. As I said, we are working on both  sides to complete the deal that's, I think, the most important and most encouraging aspect that currently is  observable. And on the 2020 perspective of the German government, and the climate change prevention plans,  currently there are many ideas ventilated in Berlin and also quite opposing ones from within the same  government. So we are, of course, keenly observing what's happening there. But so far, it's far too early to draw  any specific conclusions from which way it will ultimately go. You got it?

texts.speaker: Patrick Hummel
texts.profession: UBS AG (Broker)
texts.text: Yeah. And hi, good afternoon. I would just like to follow up first thing on the German policy debate, I mean clearly  the Economy Minister doesn't seem to support any sort of mandatory coal phase out, but at the same time, I  wonder with the carbon targets miss that we will probably see in Germany for 2020, is there any realistic chance  in the still ongoing market design debate that lignite, in particular, or the older dirtier hard coal stations could  benefit at all from any sort of capacity remuneration in your view.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Yes. So this was probably two plus questions again, Patrick. But never mind. In German policy and this – I took  that your ultimate question was is there any chance or any hope left for lignite or old hard coal to participate in a  capacity market.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: And so I would say from the current indications, we have very much, so of course, it will always depends on the  assumption that there will be a capacity market, but one tendency, which becomes pretty clear also from the  Green Book in its current form, though, the Green Book prefers the energy-only market. The second best option is  the capacity market along the lines of the de-central capacity market, decentralized market as proposed by the  BDEW.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: And this is exactly a nondiscriminatory capacity market and therefore the Green Book is, I would say, clear about  rejection of all proponents, or proposals for a discriminatory capacity market. And I think policymakers at least to  some degree recognized that those power stations will really have to rely on a capacity market for a few hours in  the year to be available. The carbon footprint of those few hours that can play any role in the bigger scheme of  things anyway, yeah, even if it's an old and dirty hard coal plant. Currently, in Southern Germany, they're utilizing  Austrian oil-fired power plants, but arguably probably also not the most environmentally friendly to stabilize the  grid.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: On UK and the question if 2014 is already below 2013, if this is a trend which we're continuing into 2015, I mean  without giving a guidance now for this division in 2015 and then all your colleagues will ask for the other divisions  do you have the 2015 guidance for the group, I would say qualitatively, please bear in mind that 2014 was dragged  down by a few one-off effects that we had: A) it's also in the UK we have a weather effect; B) there were certain  obligations put upon us by Ofgem in terms of improving our customer service performance which required one-off  costs which we do not expect to recur in 2015. And therefore, this is not – you can't simply take 2014 as the one- on-one or the trend 2013 to 2014 as a trend to be prolonged beyond 2014.

texts.speaker: Bobby Chada
texts.profession: Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: And then secondly, on the Renewables business, I thought it was quite surprising that there was another write- down on the Markinch project, I think it's €75 million – €74 million, €75 million now on quite a small project. The  Renewables business has been a bit of a serial disappointment. What is it or can you tell us what you're doing to  try and improve the performance and whether you can be sure that you've drawn a line under the Markinch  problems now?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: On the Renewables Markinch, I mean this is clearly a disappointment. As a CFO, I'm the last one to paint this in  rosy colors. And I hate to see those impairments hitting our earnings line and what have we done to perform  better in the future. And this is what I mentioned in my speech, it's the concentration of the business on those  areas where we think we are really technically competent or even have an edge on some other competitors that's  concentrating on wind and hydro. And as you can see from the mix track records in our renewables investments,  biomass especially has over proportionate share of problem gets in that portfolio and that was one which we've  now sold, Markinch is another one. And yeah, so are we sure that this is definitely the end to Markinch for all  times. I mean in order of magnitude, I am very confident, but as a CFO, I am cautious enough to never say never  in that respect.

texts.speaker: Deborah B. Wilkens
texts.profession: Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: Yes. Good afternoon. Two question from me. Really following up on the Renewables business. Could you help us  with more clarity on the timing for the commissioning of the two offshore fields next year and any feeling for the  earnings contribution starting to come through there? And then also, in terms of the – I think you mentioned a  planned stake sale in Gwynt y Môr. Could you help us a little bit more details around that and if there has been an  agreed price?

texts.speaker: Alexander Karnick
texts.profession: Deutsche Bank AG (Broker)
texts.text: Right. But it does reduce 2014 significantly and then there is maybe a bit of a trend up in 2015, if I understand  correctly?

texts.speaker: Peter Crampton
texts.profession: Macquarie Capital (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And then secondly, with the UK capacity market auction one month away on the 16th of December, do you believe  that capacity payments could be high enough to kind of deal with the under earning on the UK generation fleet?  Thank you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Yeah. On the German power prices bottoming out, this was always a statement we made based on the then  prevailing fuel prices and the respective forward curves of fuel prices. And as you can see from our hedging profile,  we do have a view on power prices that – and now prevailing to – we don't see that much further down side, but  rather more upside to it, but also [indiscernible] (42:38), we don't expect a price jump of €3 per megawatt or €5  per megawatt hour in the near future although we would certainly be happy to see it come.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: On the UK capacity market auctions and what does it do to sooth the pain in our ailing UK generation fleet it – we  think that our power stations are very well-positioned in the UK generation step to benefit from the capacity  auctions, but at this point in time, especially given also the fact that the first half that this auction takes place. We  do not want to speculate on the specific outcomes and therefore we cannot speculate on the specific effects on the  profitability of our UK power plants either.

texts.speaker: Ingo Becker
texts.profession: Kepler Capital Markets SA (Germany)
texts.text: Hi, yes. Thank you. Good afternoon. I have a first question on nuclear provisions, which are being reset or re- assessed annually. In particular, what is driving your assessment of the future escalation rate and the discount  rate? I am wondering if the huge crisis that we've seen in bond deals might have a different effect on the  nominator and the denominator.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Yeah, hello. On nuclear provisions, as you know, the nuclear provisions as opposed to pension provisions, we have  two factors, it's the discount rate and the escalation rate, and the big question is always does the effect between the  two change or not. And in the current environment, we don't see an indication for any structural change in that  spread. So we clearly have low interest rates, but we also have pretty low inflation rates, yeah, in general and this  also applies to the escalation rates we applied through our nuclear provisions and please also bear in mind that  this is nothing. We can just determine at our own discretion and just as we like, but this is based also on studies by  independent engineering firms and therefore the degree of freedom there is also limited.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Okay. Two nice tries from you, Alberto. We don't guide on EBITDAs of sub-units of our divisions, and we won't  start doing that here. There was, of course, this year a negative development reflected in our trading/gas  midstream numbers out of gas storage activities. And we have guided that this is a low triple-digit million euro  amount that we took there as a hit. And this is also already mostly reflected in the Q3 numbers you have seen. In  terms of the overall outlook for the whole year, we stick to our statement and our guidance without any  qualifications or additions or specifications, it's €1.2 billion to €1.4 billion full stop for recurrent net income.

texts.speaker: Lueder Schumacher
texts.profession: Société Générale SA (Broker)
texts.text: The first one is on the MSR, I mean, very much a carbon footprint, I would have thought that you follow the  developments in Brussels quite closely. How would you view the debate and also the German stance who is in  favor of an early adoption of the MSR, that's the first question.

texts.speaker: Lueder Schumacher
texts.profession: Société Générale SA (Broker)
texts.text: The second one is on the nuclear – n-storage debate in Germany. Can you just remind us where we are there and  what are the potential implications for you?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Yeah. On the MSR – hi, Lueder, I'm sorry to say that I probably don't know much more than you do, so we follow  what we read in the press. It's pretty difficult for us sometimes to disentangle what's actually going on in the  Brussels jungle of various opinions, national interests and so on and so forth. And as you can see from some of the  recent debates even within the Berlin government, we still have obviously quite a divergence of opinions there. So  it's even a challenge to speak of the German position on something like that. So I mean I think from an overall  perspective, if you want to stabilize carbon price, this is probably one of the more prudent alternatives.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: In terms of n-storage debate in Germany, there is unfortunately not much progress we can report on, yeah, after  the ambitious goal, the policymakers have said themselves middle of last year that they want to take time until, I  think, 2031 to come up with a timing plan. They are not really what I would describe as a hurry to make  breathtaking progress there. And so there is not much happening there. I think they are still discussing how this  commission shall be staffed that basically will follow up on this n-storage search for a shoot-at-sight. And the  industry has nominated their members of this commission, but as far as I know, this has not been done by all the  other stakeholders. Or are you referring to our claims against some financial fallout from the final storage  legislation last year with regards to the [indiscernible] (51:34) intermediate storage site.

texts.speaker: Lueder Schumacher
texts.profession: Société Générale SA (Broker)
texts.text: No, I would have thought the loss reflect most nuclear losses thus tend to take forever. It was more like the n- storage debate as the decommissioning process has started, can't go on forever. There must a deadline when you  decide what to do with it. They can't remain a medium term storage at the plants forever if you intend to  decommissioning. So I just wondered if there is any kind of definite timeline by which we have to come up with  this one solution.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Okay. Yes, so I mean this is an instrument we're using on small scale where it makes sense economically, but it's  not the main driver behind the change in working capital. So the big ticket items are those that I mentioned like,  for example, carbon certificates or rock – virtual inventories and that sort of things.

texts.speaker: Ingo Becker
texts.profession: Kepler Capital Markets SA (Germany)
texts.text: And second question would be again on Renewables, could you remind us, please, of what roughly the capital  employed is at that division at this stage? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Okay. Starting with your first question, the famous, infamous earnings flow statement, yes, so I think it's  important to bear in mind that when we issued it last year, we always made it fully contingent on the then  prevailing power prices and spreads. And we will give an update to what this mean for 2015 with our March  Analyst Conference in due time. And before that, we wouldn't give any further details.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: The Renewables capital employed, I mean, you can find it in our annual report on page number 65 and there you  can see that it's in the order of magnitude of €5 billion.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: No, I mean, of course, it's growing at the one side with the completion of the last [ph] of our wind (55:58) parts, on  the other hand we have been divesting issuances or diluting our shares in some other wind parts, so net-net  balance, it doesn't change that dramatically anymore.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: First, let me give you an update on the most-important points regarding the discussion around nuclear abilities.  As you know, the whole debate on nuclear ability is split into a three phases. The first phase concluded with a  publication of the results of the so-called stress test on October 10. The most-important result is that the nuclear  provisions fully reflect future obligations and are more than sufficient compared to other European countries.  Although, this result has not been a surprise and has been communicated many times, it was seen as very positive  by the capital market.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Furthermore, it provides a solid foundation for the second phase of the process, which has recently started with  the establishment of a commission for the review of the financing of the nuclear phase-out. This commission will  provide proposals by the beginning of the next year. One of the options considered is the establishment of the  foundation financed by energy utilities. Just to be clear here, these proposals will have to be seen as non-binding  recommendations and decisions will be made in the political process that follows afterwards, which we have called  Phase 3.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: As mentioned at our Credit Day in September, it is important to see that the German Government follows the aim  to maintain the economic performance of utilities in the context of the nuclear phase-out and its subsequent costs.  This was outlined by the German Cabinet in the principles for successful implementation of the energy transition,  which was published on 1st of July 2015 and has been reiterated several times by statements by the German  Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Second, on October 23, the German Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy announced a framework for the so- called standby capacity that contributes to the German climate protection targets. Between 2017 and 2019, RWE  will gradually transfer five lignite power plant units with a total capacity of 1.5 gigawatt into standby for four years  each before being shutdown, the last one in 2023. The solution provides clarity with respect to the remuneration  for the companies and, therefore, reduces commodity exposure for the lignite plants affected.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: On top of that, positive news came at the end of September from the North Rhine-Westphalian government with  publication of an official draft document detailing the future role of lignite in our home area. This would give us, if  finally approved, the possibility to optimize all of our lignite mines for a time horizon beyond 2030.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Third, we are successfully growing our renewables business further. As you know, we do this currently, primarily  in the form of strategic partnerships. In line with this strategy, at the end of October, RWE Energy formed a  consortium for the Galloper Offshore Wind Park with three partners, UK Green Investment Bank, Siemens  Financial Services and Macquarie Capital. Construction has recently been started and we expect the wind farm to  go online in 2018.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: The earnings development in our Supply UK division has decreased by €156 million to minus €66 million. This is  mainly a result of process and system-related problems with private customer billing. Besides the operational  problems, lower energy consumption of customers, a shift from standard to non-standard rates tariffs and high  customer losses are also factors for the lower results.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: On the positive side, the operating result of RWE Energy has increased significantly. In the first nine months, we  have recorded an operating result of €280 million, which is already €100 million higher than the 2014 full-year  results. By the end of this year, we expect Energy to double its operating result compared to 2014. Furthermore,  the revaluation of VSE, as a result of its full consolidation, leads to an improvement of the operating result in our  CEE/SEE downstream business.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Slide five shows the development of our cash flows from operating activities. It comes down by €2.6 billion to €2.2  billion, mainly due to changes in working capital. First, as explained in our last analyst calls, our most-significant  working capital effect is a result of a revised purchasing policy for the required CO2 emission certificates. This had  a corresponding positive effect on our cash flows in 2014.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Second in 2014, we had a positive weather effect in our working capital. This was mainly due to the mild weather  which led to relatively low energy consumption in 2014, to a large extent lower than the basis for the advanced  payments we received from our customer. As a result, in 2015, we see a counter effect as final billing for the year  2014 shows lower amounts than the cash flows we received in 2014.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Furthermore, it is also important to recognize that in Q3 2014, a temporary repayment of the nuclear fuel tax of  approximately €0.5 billion was considered which was based on the Hamburg Fiscal Court decision. However this  money had to be paid back in Q4 2014 until a final decision is made. Latest indications suggest that a final  decision concerning the nuclear fuel tax is scheduled for 2016.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: However, there were offsetting effects like regular service cost that increased our pension provisions by 0.6%. Due  to the regular interest accretion, nuclear provisions increased by approximately €0.2 billion so that the net effect  in our provisions is currently minus €0.1 billion.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: On the asset side, as part of our mid-term planning which we typically conduct in the fourth quarter, we will  challenge our asset book values. Therefore, we cannot exclude impairments in the context of our full-year  accounting. However, we have had to make two adjustments, on slide eight, with respect to our divisional outlook.  First, we have to change the outlook for Trading/Gas Midstream to significantly below 2014, among others due to  a weaker Trading business performance than expected.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: We don't give a precise guidance for the tax rate in future years, which will be driven by many aspects we're  currently analyzing in our mid-term plan, which is work in progress. But generally, the forces at work can we be  expected to also affect future years. On our Trading business, I think it's very important to state that there are no  operational problems in the Trading business. There is nothing going wrong there, it's just not as a good trading  year as the last one was. And please bear in mind that amalgamated in these numbers are the burdens from gas  storage, yeah, which is currently not a real profit maker.

texts.speaker: Peter A. Bisztyga
texts.profession: Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: Yeah. Good morning. Two questions, please. So, firstly, I was wondering if you could provide some insights into  what your current methodology is, when you value your Power Generation assets. So, for example, do you look at  forward curves or do you use some alternative assumptions when you do your impairment tests? And also, could  you indicate roughly what your current sort of fixed assets are in Conventional Power Generation?

texts.speaker: Bobby Chada
texts.profession: Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Hi. Good morning. So, my first question is on the nuclear process from here. What input, if any, do you expect  either RWE or the industry to have, coming to some form of hopefully long-term solution? And then, the second  question is around the impairment issue again. If you can disclose the book value by division, are you able to just  confirm that there is still a meaningful amount of book value in that business, I just started up the last, I think,  eight or nine power plants that you'd built which had a total investment of €12 billion or €13 billion. I'm pretty  sure that's still largely unimpaired. So, can you give us some feel for, if not the size, just kind of order of  magnitude of that book value?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Yeah. Hi, Bobby. Nice try on the second question. I think you're right, of course, because, I mean, generally, the  newly-constructed power plants are not – generally not fully depreciated yet. We have, with the recent  impairments we have done in years before, eliminated our goodwill in our Generation division, yeah. So, there's  nothing left there. And yes, there are some – there's a – still be a significant asset base in Power Generation. Yeah.  Order of magnitude, it's clearly below €10 billion.

texts.speaker: Stephan Lowis
texts.profession: Vice President-Investor Relations
texts.text: I think the first question was on the nuclear political.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Yeah. Sorry. The first question, yeah, was on what input can the industry deliver on this process going forward,  around nuclear provisioning and funding. As you know, we are not members of this commission that I mentioned,  but we will – we have been invited to participate in some sessions of that commission as the industry saw the four  large utilities in Germany clearly be part of that process in terms of placing all ideas and answering to questions  from the commission.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: And I think there's also some – if you're interested in more detail, maybe you haven't spotted it yet there, I think,  on page 34 of our report for the first three quarters, you'll find a bit more backup to the VSE full consolidation.  And we have done similar things before, for example, in 2011, with [indiscernible] (24:32) a West German energy  supply company that was also put into full consolidation via operating result.

texts.speaker: Nathalie F. Casali
texts.profession: JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: The amount that you will get for the lignite plants that will go into the reserve?

texts.speaker: Jutta Unmuessig
texts.profession: Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Two questions on your Lynemouth biomass conversion project. First is do you have any insights regarding, when  to expect an EU State Aid decision now that you got referred to Phase 2 of the investigation earlier this year? And  then secondly, do you think that the cancelation of the Climate Change Levy exemption in the UK has impacted  the EC's view and also your view regarding the commerciality of the project? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Jutta Unmuessig
texts.profession: Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Yes. Sure. So, the second question was whether you think that the cancellation of the Climate Change Levy  exemption in the UK, whether you think that this changed the EC view or your view on the commerciality of the  project?

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Hello. Thank you. I was wondering if I could steal an extra question from John Musk as well, but in any case. So,  two questions, one is on the nuclear provisions, your inflation assumptions. Is that something that you could  disclose? E.ON disclosed the last three years inflation assumptions yesterday.

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: And second question is on dividend, I think you've not commented on dividend, and in your video, you basically  said that there are too many uncertainties around which it makes worthwhile for waiting longer. So, I was just  trying to understand what are the uncertainties that you're dealing with presently, which will resolve by March  next year given that both the nuclear stress tests and the lignite reserve uncertainty has been resolved now. Thank  you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Yeah. So, on nuclear provisions, it's 4.6% discount rate and 3.7% cost escalation rate that we apply. On our  reasons for not being more precise on the dividend, we still do think there are quite – some uncertainties around  the final outcome of the nuclear funding debate, where we will get more clarity over the next couple of months and  it also applies to the second item on lignite that I mentioned, so not the standby reserve but the mining  concessions that we have over the North Rhine-Westphalian state government kicked off the process recently for  the third, so-called, master plan around lignite, which will give us more clarity on the lifetime of the mines.

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: What would be an outer year, so 2030 or 2050?

texts.speaker: Tanja B. Markloff
texts.profession: Commerzbank AG (Broker)
texts.text: Yeah. Good morning, Tanja Markloff here. I'd like to ask you whether you could specify on the Trading/Gas  Midstream division, to what extent the decline is related to Trading and to what extent to the Midstream Gas  business? And in light of the negative gas price trend, how we should expect the Gas Midstream business develop  further this year and to next year?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Yeah. So, generally, in the decline of the Trading business, yes, as I said before there is also included the ailing gas  storage business, yeah. So, this is part of the numbers and it's part of the general trading – commercial trading  activities and other part. And we don't give you a more precise data. On the general, let's say, forces at work in the  Gas Midstream business, you can differentiate between the long-term gas supply contract and the gas storage  contracts that we hold there. Gas storage is still struggling with low levels of profitability, because the  summer/winter spreads, we're still at historical lows. On the long-term gas supply contracts, we have said before  that, with the exception of the one contract we have with Gazprom, all the others have been put on a mark-to- mark level. So, they are now ongoing losses there.

texts.speaker: Deborah B. Wilkens
texts.profession: Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: Something that you didn't mention, but could I check, if the nuclear tax case in Germany were to go in your favor,  would that impact the dividend or not?

texts.speaker: Christian Schuetz
texts.profession: Pacific Investment Management Co. LLC
texts.text: Yeah. Thanks very much. Just two questions. One is a follow-up to Deborah's question. Could you just confirm  how much nuclear tax was paid in 2015 so far? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Yeah. So, on the nuclear fuel tax, for the first nine months, and therefore also for full year, it's around €300  million. And on our efforts to, if I understood your question correctly, Christian, on making generation cash  breakeven. It's just a kind of moving target. Yeah. So, we are increasing and redoubling our efforts just as we see  power prices and clean lignite spreads decline. So, what has been an ambitious target for generation at the  beginning of the year has already been overtaken by reality and the targets for cash improvement are being topped  up. That's the general logic how it works. They are fully aware that they can't afford to be a cash loss producing as  a business on a structural basis.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: I mean for 2015, I think we were already from – at the beginning of the year when we gave our initial guidance,  clear that the cash balance for 2015 would be significantly below 2014 and most likely would be negative because  in 2014 we had lots of positive one-off such as, for example, the CO2 effect that I mentioned; such as the impact of  the mild weather which boosted our cash flows in 2014 and artificially beyond the kind of structural underlying  profit, which is now being caught up in 2015. Yeah. And of course, we fully stick to our aspiration and ambition  that going forward our cash balance is supposed to be positive.

texts.speaker: Bobby Chada
texts.profession: Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Thank you. It's really a question about the way that you assess the generation portfolio. So, my understanding is  that over the last few years, you have regularly every quarter, I think, looked at the fleet to assess whether any  plants were cash negative or expected to be significantly cash negative and you would then close them. We're now  in a position where power prices in Germany have been below €30 for quite some time and on an unhedged basis,  I think, most people would estimate that the operating result from your generation fleet will be negative at that  level.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: So, I do understand the words of your question, but I'm not sure I understand the economic logic of your question,  Bobby. I mean, what you're suggesting is that we might shut down power plants, which are maybe still checks  positive, but have negative earnings contribution. Well, I do believe the – for decision-making – managerial  decisional-making on our portfolio, the cash perspective is the right one. And of course, when we are looking at  the cash perspective, it's not just the current cash situation of the power plant, but also the way forward that we  expect, applying forward prices for the next couple of years. And also our estimations on how prices might develop  if there are more shutdowns, yeah, so this is the – this feedback mechanism is built into our considerations.

texts.speaker: Bobby Chada
texts.profession: Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: So, you're saying that you already think about the impacts on the overall portfolio whenever you think of a closure  decision?

texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG

texts.text: Hi. Good afternoon, everybody. A couple of questions from me.
