Can  you just talk a little bit about where you are in that program and where that can be developed [indiscernible]  (00:31:56). It feels like you're a little bit ahead of where you're expecting to be. And then secondly, CapEx for the  full year, ignoring what may or may not happen with the €500 million leftover, what [indiscernible] (00:32:11)  CapEx to be for the full year?

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. Thanks, Nick. Cost efficiency, we said we're going to keep €300 million until 2019. The split is €200 million  in Lignite & Nuclear, and €100 million in European Power. And our assumption is that we are slightly better than  one-third already at the end of this year. So we should expect another slightly below €200 million for 2018 and  2019. But it's too early to now discuss whether we're going to set up another program that also depends on what's  going to happen to our capacity over time. And I think it's not worth discussing the next program after having  realized the existing one. So we will discuss that and update you maybe in the second half of 2018 whether we do  more on not.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On CapEx, our full-year guidance was always €350 million to €400 million. This year, we expect more to end at  the upper end because of our investments into biomass conversion in the Netherlands which is more than pure  maintenance – CapEx maintenance. Pure maintenance is around €350 million for the full year.

file: RWE - Q3 2018 Earnings Call 14November2018 730 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 14-Nov-18.pdf

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Moving on to our decision to de-mothball the Dutch CCGT Claus C which has a capacity of around 1.3 gigawatt.  Based on the increasing market prices and spark spreads, bringing the station back on line results in significant  value versus keeping it mothballed.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Coming to the situation around the Hambach mine, we were surprised by the resolution handed down by the  Münster Higher Administrative Court on the 5th of October imposing a temporary stop of the clearance of  Hambach Forest. The final decision and the principal proceedings should be reached at the later date, possibly by  the end of 2020. The litigious point of the proceedings deals with the question of whether the Hambach Forest is  subject to the protection regime for potential flora/fauna habitat areas.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: The Commission for Growth, Structural Change and Employment has continued its work over the last few  months. As reported in the press, the commission met regularly to gain insight into various special topics in  relation to the energy system and the lignite regions.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: At the end of October, they finalized their interim findings and recommendation for measures to support the social  and structural development in the affected regions. By the end of November or the beginning of December, we  expect to see their recommendations on climate goals. These proposals will be more relevant for us than the  chapter on structural development, as it will provide some details on the recommended magnitude and speed of  the coal phase-out.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: As a reminder, the commission was tasked to identify measures which support structural change and  development in the affected regions, ensure the achievement of the 2030 CO2 reduction targets, and close the  gap to the 2020 climate goal as quickly as possible. In addition, it should set a date for the final shutdown of coal- fired power generation.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: As a sign that the coal phase-out is already on its way is the fact that we transferred two additional Lignite units,  Niederaussem E and F, with the capacity of 300 megawatt each into the security reserve at the end of  September. They will remain there for the next four years before finally shutdown. This was agreed for climate  protection reasons in 2016, and RWE will contribute 1.5 gigawatt to the lignite reserve from 2.7 gigawatt in total.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: The European Power division realized an earnings decline of €90 million. Adjusted for non-recurring items, it  nearly reached the level in the corresponding period of the previous year. Our hard coal and gas plants realized  lower margins; however, a positive effect came from income from the UK capacity market.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: The presented figures are as at 30th of September. So, the impact of the temporary stop to the clearance of  Hambach Forest is not reflected here. As mentioned at the beginning of my presentation, we currently assume a  decrease of some 9 to 13 terawatt hours per annum in 2019 to 2021 for outright generation.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me also remind you of our long-term carbon position which we have financially hedged through until the mid- 2020s. In other words, a change in carbon prices should not affect our generation margins in this time period.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Let's move to Supply & Trading on slide 9. We again saw a good trading performance in the third quarter.  Furthermore, our gas and LNG business posted a good performance, even if it lagged behind the very high result  of last year. Besides that, we had a negative effect from a value adjustment within our Principal Investment  portfolio in Q2. For the full year, we confirm our earnings expectations for this division of between €100 million to  €300 million.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Change in operating working capital was also much better than in the comparable period last year, despite an  increase in inventories due to higher gas prices. The main reason is the phasing out of working capital  optimization measures last year. For the fourth quarter, we expect a positive change in working capital due to a  typical decrease of gas inventories. Hence we confirm our expectation to end this year with a positive balance.

texts.speaker: Alberto Gandolfi
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: The first one is about Hambach lignite situation. Question here is considering the Coal Commission outcome is  expected sometime in mid, early December and the government is going to rule next year but the court case on  Hambach may protract until 2020, is there a chance to voluntarily use as a sacrificial lamb Hambach as a first –  effectively, 4 gigawatt of lignite to be decommissioned sometime maybe by 2020? And if so, would that be eligible  for stranded costs or compensation, because we are seeing that in the 1980s when the Spanish were closing –  well, were stopping nuclear, plants were being built, they received a moratorium. We are seeing [ph] ADF (14:36)  with [indiscernible] (14:37). So I wonder, why would for German legislation be treated differently any closure of  coal or lignite?

texts.speaker: Alberto Gandolfi
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: Second question is on renewables medium-term growth. Yesterday innogy told us there is more than 1 gigawatt  of projects under construction or advanced development stages for the next two years. And E.ON also gave some  indications about repowering, how much they are building. It would appear that you would be on track before  actually thinking about offshore to deliver 700 megawatts or about 1 gigawatt per year of annual addition, if I just  add up those figures from these separate activities. Do you think that's a crazy assumption to have going  forward? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: But the point you are making on compensation is definitely a very valid one. I mean, the commission has already  said clearly that they don't want to see any socially unacceptable layoffs, and that definitely comes at cost. So, I  read this an implicit assumption that somebody else and the companies have to pay for it because we would  always do it in a manner that is of course the best for the company. And on the other side, I mean, if there is a  clear interference with existing legislation and company assumptions on investment, then that should also come  with the compensation, that was always our understanding. It is now supported by two, three very strong legal  opinion which were public and published. And also, I mean, we all have the experience on the nuclear side where  it took us to the courts. But for the [ph] fund (17:10), for example, the government already decided to go for a  contract with the company, and we probably can expect something similar on the coal side.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: On renewables, I mean, I have the same public information than you have on the innogy and E.ON renewables.  And I cannot comment more than you can get from these companies.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. And then on Belgium, I mean, Claus C will come back, as I said, in 2020. And your question really was  referring to the short-term situation. I mean, of course tighter markets and higher power prices are affecting  especially the open spread position and the reserve markets. But especially the situation on Belgium, since the  interconnector capacity is always fully used and importing into Belgium at maximum, additional price increases  into the Belgium market has a very minor effect on the neighboring countries.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. Thanks, Peter. Let me start with the latter. I think, since it's all over the same topic and the topic is whether  this remaining little forest is a fauna/flora habitat area, I mean, an additional injunction on the other case would not  make any difference. I think what we need is a decision on the main proceeding which is the decision whether it's  a flora/fauna habitat area.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: All our legal assessments say we have a very strong case. We have not seen in Europe that after this list was  closed that a new area was declared flora/fauna habitat. We even have an environmental assessment and all  handed into the courts that this is – and would never have been one flora/fauna habitat area. So the only thing we  are awaiting is the final decision in the main proceeding and then that topic should be solved for us. The  unpleasant one is the injunction that we have to wait for that.

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you. So my two questions. So on the CO2 hedging, Markus, maybe I heard wrong, but I think you said that  you were hedged to the mid-2020s. I think previously the date that you said is 2022. So I was just wondering  whether I just misheard something or is there more, i.e., you've extended your hedging period.

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: And a second question on the whole coal closure. So there have been some new reports made by the NGOs  asking for an even more aggressive phase-out of like 16 gigawatts by 2022, of which roughly half and half lignite  and hard coal. So I was just wondering whether in your assessment something like 7 gigawatts, 8 gigawatts of  lignite closing by 2022 would actually be possible socially, technically and what your expectations would be if you  had to put your fair share in a compensation scenario.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Yes. Deepa, thanks for the questions. The first one I can confirm. Yes, you heard it right. We have extended our  CO2 hedging. We always said in the last calls that we did more after 2022, and I think now we can confirm it mid- 2020, and of course, mid-2020, 2025 is a good translation of that. So, we have extended that.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: And on the coal closures, I mean, this recent report, it was – there are many, let's say, environmentalists in the  Coal Commission, and more than these three. So only three of them were behind this kind of proposal to close 16  gigawatt and half lignite, half coal. And as I said to first question to Alberto, I don't want to speculate, but I can  clearly tell you that this number is totally impossible, I mean from many points of view, socially not acceptable,  security of supply, power prices. So I don't take it serious.

texts.speaker: Lueder Schumacher
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA (UK)
texts.text: The second one is on your net debt. Obviously, your net debt has benefited a lot from the variation margin which  is due to your carbon position. Could you maybe help us to get an idea of how much of the carbon-related fall in  net debt is due to the carbon position where positions will be closed by the end of this year so we can arrive at a  sort of clean net debt number that is reflective of, well, actually your net debt and not some kind of commodity  positions that will reverse upon delivery?

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Also with the [ph] back (29:27), I mean, we clearly tell you what drove it. It's also that of course part of it was  conversion into a spread position, so fuel price developments [ph] are relevant (29:35). We'll come back and  explain it in detail.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: On the net debt figure, yes, of course it's a mixture of carbon price movements but also power and other  commodities. A clean, clean net debt figure is very difficult to derive because it also depends on what in the end is  the additional generation margin you're going to earn in the following years because your hedging was right. But  we have already spotted the problem to get a right interpretation of the net debt, but I have not yet a solution to  that.

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you for taking my follow-on question. So I had two questions. Yesterday Uniper reported in their midstream  division that they're seeing – that they're booking some provisions for arbitration on the gas side. I was wondering  whether you have any such legacy issues or is your gas portfolio largely [indiscernible] (31:00)?

texts.speaker: Ingo Alphéus, Vice President and Head of Investor Relations
texts.profession: Okay, good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to all of you who’ve joined us here in Essen
texts.text: Let’s first have a brief look at the year just gone by. On performance, I am proud to say that we not  only achieved our financial targets but outperformed despite the difficult economic environment and  despite the prolonged outage of our Biblis power station. This allows us to pay another attractive  dividend in the year where not everybody is able to do so.

texts.speaker: Ingo Alphéus, Vice President and Head of Investor Relations
texts.profession: Okay, good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to all of you who’ve joined us here in Essen
texts.text: 2 Our renewables business has also come a long way. It grew its operating asset base by almost one  gigawatt. Our new-build program is bearing fruit with the current commissioning of our CCGT in  Lingen. It will be commissioned in April. The 1.7 gigawatt station at Staythorpe will shortly follow.  This will contribute considerably to the reduction of RWE’s overall carbon exposure.

texts.speaker: Ingo Alphéus, Vice President and Head of Investor Relations
texts.profession: Okay, good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to all of you who’ve joined us here in Essen
texts.text: Ladies and gentlemen, we live in uncertain times. The economic downturn has brought an  unprecedented drop in power and gas demand. Recovery looks challenging. This situation is not  helped by the continuous lack of clarity on regulatory framework conditions, neither globally – i.e.,  the failure of the Copenhagen Summit, and I guess we will have to call it a failure. We have to call a  spade a spade. It’s no use in saying we achieved something. We achieved nothing – and so neither  globally, Copenhagen, nor nationally, be it in Germany where the national energy policy will only be  unveiled in October or in the United Kingdom where similar decisions depend on the upcoming  election results. It provides an insufficient basis for investment decisions.

texts.speaker: Ingo Alphéus, Vice President and Head of Investor Relations
texts.profession: Okay, good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to all of you who’ve joined us here in Essen
texts.text: But increasing market volatility also represents further challenges for the industry. Negative power  prices and the decoupling of oil and gas markets are just the two most prominent examples.

texts.speaker: Ingo Alphéus, Vice President and Head of Investor Relations
texts.profession: Okay, good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to all of you who’ve joined us here in Essen
texts.text: One of the burning questions I was asked in Investor meetings throughout last year was about the  outlook for energy demand. The main concern was a lasting drop. Some even call it demand  destruction. Overall, the situation will remain challenging. However, we believe that the downward  trend has bottomed out. Energy demand has stabilized in the fourth quarter of 2009 and the  beginning of this year already showed first signs of improving industrial activity. A return to pre- crisis levels will nevertheless take a few years.

texts.speaker: Ingo Alphéus, Vice President and Head of Investor Relations
texts.profession: Okay, good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to all of you who’ve joined us here in Essen
texts.text: On the political and regulatory front, nothing much has changed. Political commitment to reduce  carbon emissions is not of equal strength around the world. We still lack clarity on regulatory  framework conditions.

texts.speaker: Ingo Alphéus, Vice President and Head of Investor Relations
texts.profession: Okay, good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to all of you who’ve joined us here in Essen
texts.text: Copenhagen as I already mentioned is the catchword for this. And the uncertain future of carbon  capture and storage as well as the Clean Development Mechanism and JI, Joint Implementation  are examples.

texts.speaker: Ingo Alphéus, Vice President and Head of Investor Relations
texts.profession: Okay, good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to all of you who’ve joined us here in Essen
texts.text: With regard to German nuclear legislation, there has been little visible progress yet. It is good news  that the new government considers nuclear energy a bridge technology and a part of the energy  mix for the foreseeable future.

texts.speaker: Ingo Alphéus, Vice President and Head of Investor Relations
texts.profession: Okay, good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to all of you who’ve joined us here in Essen
texts.text: However, we don’t expect details or clarity before October. This is when the government aims to  publish a National Energy Plan with nuclear strategy being part of it.

texts.speaker: Ingo Alphéus, Vice President and Head of Investor Relations
texts.profession: Okay, good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to all of you who’ve joined us here in Essen
texts.text: Please rest assured that we will not overpay for lifetime extension. A solution has to make sense for  all parties involved. While the demand side, there is an uncertain outlook, power supply is also  becoming more unpredictable.

texts.profession: Okay, good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to all of you who’ve joined us here in Essen
texts.text: 3 On this slide you can see an estimate on the flexibility of Germany’s overall generation portfolio,  when in baseload operation an additional 57 gigawatts can be fit into the grid within 12 hours. texts.profession: Okay, good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to all of you who’ve joined us here in Essen
texts.text: With the rising share of renewables, load swings are forecast to become bigger and faster, thus  making the flexibility in the system increasingly tight. This situation is not helped by the ever  growing number of canceled new build projects.

texts.speaker: Ingo Alphéus, Vice President and Head of Investor Relations
texts.profession: Okay, good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to all of you who’ve joined us here in Essen
texts.text: In the last 12 months, we’ve seen eight large power plant projects withdrawn with a total capacity of  8.6 gigawatts. Flexibility and responsiveness of power stations have therefore become a lot more  important. This makes our new build projects even more valuable.

texts.speaker: Ingo Alphéus, Vice President and Head of Investor Relations
texts.profession: Okay, good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to all of you who’ve joined us here in Essen
texts.text: But the gas market is undergoing dramatic changes too. This is similar to the situation of the power  generation market a few years ago. What we see today is a mix between a more liquid wholesale  gas market and still existing long-term contracts. There are three major consequences.

texts.speaker: Ingo Alphéus, Vice President and Head of Investor Relations
texts.profession: Okay, good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to all of you who’ve joined us here in Essen
texts.text: Firstly, supply and demand are more and more independent from each other. Like in power  generation, the supplier doesn’t have to wait until the customer asks for a gas contract. There is  also a wholesale market where the gas can be sold too.

texts.speaker: Ingo Alphéus, Vice President and Head of Investor Relations
texts.profession: Okay, good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to all of you who’ve joined us here in Essen
texts.text: Secondly, customers become more and more market price oriented, short-term market price  oriented. And thirdly, long-term supply contracts have become supply options. They can be  optimized comparable to a power plant portfolio. So much on this challenging environment.

texts.profession: Okay, good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to all of you who’ve joined us here in Essen
texts.text: The standardization of trading and risk management systems has commenced. The renewables  teams of both companies are now one. And we are cherry-picking the best wind projects on both  pipelines.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: All divisions with the exception of Trading and Gas Midstream showed at least a double-digit  earnings growth. With the conclusion of the integration of Essent, we are well on track to achieve  our synergy targets. We also progressed our plans for a more efficient organization by streamlining  the Group Center and by pooling our German sales and distribution businesses.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Our Central Eastern and South Eastern Europe division is now steered by the newly established  RWE East domiciled in Prague. Our CapEx program is well advanced. We commissioned two  CCGT plant in Lingen, Northern Germany and Staythorpe, Great Britain and started the  construction of another one in Denizli, Turkey.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: RWE Innogy has taken major steps to prepare for the construction of its Nordsee Ost and Gwynt y  Môr offshore wind farms. By the end of 2010, the first turbine had already started generating  electricity at the Greater Gabbard offshore wind farm.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Let me briefly explain our view on the current situation in Egypt and Libya. Egypt is an important  country for RWE Dea, even more so in the years to come after the significant gas findings in the       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 2 Western offshore Nile Delta. However, our exposure is limited as so far the country contributes less  than 10% to RWE Dea’s operating result. We also trust that the new government in Egypt will keep  the reliable investment in environment, not the least because our production is mainly intended for  the Egyptian market. Let me also update you the situation is stabilizing significantly and we have  begun to send back our experts to Egypt. So, no disruptive development there is to be expected.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Increasing energy demand on the back of a colder than average winter has not yet led to significant  improvement of electricity prices or spreads. The continued construction of generation capacity  above all the unexpected, perhaps even unforeseeable, expansion of solar PV, photovoltaic, is one  of the major reasons for this. In addition to this already challenging environment in the generation  market, political conditions have also become much less reliable. The German government’s  decision to introduce a tax on nuclear fuel is the most prominent example.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The decoupling of oil and gas prices resulting in a negative gas to oil spread is a result of the  demand supply imbalance mainly caused by the economic crisis in addition to U.S. shale gas  production and discoveries. While other countries are shying away from firm commitments in the  face of economic uncertainties, Europe is still committed to its ambitious CO2 targets. We therefore  have to brace ourselves for the tighter CO2 regime from 2013 onwards. But this is not new to us,  and comes as expected. However some smart, or should I say smarter, nations like the  Netherlands are introducing cost-efficiency considerations into their plan for a greener economy i.e.  how much greenhouse gas abatements can you get for each euro spent.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: First and foremost, we didn’t see any reasons why we should change our strategy. We stick to our  guns taking advantage of our regional expertise, process know-how and positioning in our existing  and growth markets. Our CO2 mitigation strategy is still key to making us more competitive.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Our organic growth ambitions will focus on renewables and upstream. Both activities will show on  average double-digit earnings growth over the next years. However, the nuclear fuel tax affects our  overall earnings and therefore also our financial headroom and investment budget. We reduced our  existing CapEx program by approximately €3 billion and stepped up our existing €1.2 billion  efficiency enhancement program by another €200 million by 2012.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In addition, we have already taken steps to make our asset portfolio more suitable to the changed  environment. Such initiatives include the renegotiation of our gas procurement contracts and the  ability to increase the flexibility of our power plants.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Our current markets offer attractive investment opportunities, Central Eastern and South Eastern  Europe present additional growth prospects which we intend to pursue in the medium-term. Most of  you are already familiar with our CO2 mitigation strategy, which remains key to the competitiveness  of RWE. We maintain our target of reducing our CO2 intensity to market average by 2020.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We are working on physical as well as financial mitigation measures to achieve this goal.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The most recent example for financial measures is a deal we signed at the end of last year with a  big industrial client. We sold 300 megawatts of lignite capacity for 15 years where the client takes  their cost for the required CO2 certificates. This deal alone hedges approximately 2.6 million tons  per annum of our CO2 procurement requirements and lowers our economic exposure significantly.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Last year, we provided you with the details of the CO2 mitigation measures.  These can be found in  the backup slides. However, the near-term challenge is full auctioning of CO2 certificates from 2013  onwards. We won’t be able to fully compensate for that financial burden stemming from the  purchase of some additional 100 million tons of CO2 certificates in 2013. However, we have laid  the foundation for growth projects, which will more than make up for the negative impact beyond  2013.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Ladies and gentlemen, from strategy, now let’s move on to execution. Let me start with our new  medium-term investment program, including the impact of planned portfolio divestments. We intend  to spend approximately €18 billion over the next three years mainly on our large power plants and  infrastructure projects. These projects are well advanced and we’re working hard to bring them on  stream as soon as possible. This is the reason, why we will see an increase in our capital spending  of up to €1 billion in the current year.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 4 power generation in North-Western Europe, as we don’t want to miss out on opportunities in our  broad areas of renewables and upstream gas and oil.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Once operational, we expect these projects to contribute approximately €1.2 billion of EBITDA and  €0.9 billion of operating results. But please bear in mind, developing offshore wind farms or new  gas fields takes time. As a response to the tougher financial environment, we have increased the  hurdle rates for new investment projects despite lower average cost of capital. This ensures that  RWE will concentrate on the most attractive opportunities.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Ladies and gentlemen, now let’s focus on the specific growth areas of RWE; one of course is our  renewables business. RWE Innogy continues with an ambitious investment program, which also  plays a major role in our CO2 mitigation strategy. The acquisition of Essent did not only bring  excellent power stations, and a solid customer base in the Netherlands to RWE, we also inherited a  well advanced project pipeline in renewables. We refocus on our development plans on some  larger fully consented projects, and postponed some smaller ones. This has, of course together  with CapEx cuts, some impact on RWE Innogy’s growth targets.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: With the focus now on offshore wind projects, which are more time consuming, we have to  postpone our [inaudible] capacity target. We now expect to have 4.5 gigawatts in operation or  under construction in 2014, two years later than originally envisaged. This corresponds to an  operating result of approximately €500 million. Let me emphasize, this is only the first milestone.  We plan for a significant further growth in the years thereafter.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: It is also worthwhile mentioning that we expect RWE Innogy’s results to exceed its cost of capital by  2016. Excluding the significant startup costs for such a young and capital extensive business –  intensive business and assuming normalized weather conditions, we expect operational projects to  make a positive value contribution in 2011.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: As a consequence, RWE Dea will achieve its production earnings targets slightly later than  envisaged. We now target oil and gas production of 70 million barrels of oil equivalent in 2016, with  an operating result of roughly €1 billion. We have good indications for further growth potential of up  to 90 million barrels of oil equivalent per year in a couple of years later.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Ladies and gentlemen, in 2010 the German market recorded a year of considerable growth in  renewable capacity. Photovoltaic, i.e., solar was an especially strong contributor to that. I don’t  want to bore you with the arguments about how uneconomical of this is. You’re all aware of the  facts. There will be even the – though there will be massive additional capacity coming on to the  system. Only very little between 10% and 20% of this capacity can be considered reliable to cover  demand at any given time. As a result, the need for conventional power plants to provide the so  called swing capacity will increase dramatically.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 5 The current system requires a good 30 gigawatts, which is covered by today’s generation fleet. But  one can expect this to grow up to 50 gigawatts in 2020, and even more thereafter. The positive  thing is, tight markets will provide good opportunities for operators who own flexible plants. This is  the reason why we have started a program to further upgrade the flexibility of our generation fleet.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We also believe that competitive markets are to be favored over regulated capacity markets.  Experience gained in other European countries is not convincing. In the existing market model,  price signals will indicate necessary investments in new generation capacity, even if renewables  continue to expand.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: These signals will trigger timely decisions by potential investors if policy makers create clear and  reliable framework conditions and do not interfere in the price formation process allowing price  spikes as necessary market signals. The strong increase in renewables will take our demand for  conventional power plants. But in times of low wind levels and no sun there has to be capacity to  back up the system.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Let me mention on this occasion that we are now in the third consecutive year of low wind levels,  30% below the long-term average. On one hand, this conventional capacity will grow by some 40  gigawatts which is going on line by 2013, 2014. Thereafter, we don’t expect any further additional  conventional and renewable capacity to be realized for a considerable time.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The last project was announced in 2008. Since then, we’ve only seen cancellations. On the other  hand, some 4 gigawatts will go out of the system in the short-term or has already left the system as  a lot of a new build projects are replacement plants. You might remember that even in RWE, our  new lignite BoA plant is replacing 16 old lignite blocks of 150 megawatts each.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: As a consequence, we have decided not to exercise the option to prolong 1.4 gigawatts of our  Steag contract. They will phase out in 2012. Of course, these plants will still be in the market until  their owner decides what to with do them.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: On the back of current market conditions, we see approximately 8 gigawatts of traditional inflexible  hard coal plants struggling hard to even cover their fuel cost. Recent debt finance acquisitions of generation portfolios should put additional  pressure on acquirers to behave with sense.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator

This will bring significant changes to our operations,  making processes more efficient and reducing the numbers of staff required.

texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Jürgen mentioned already that all divisions, except Trading/Gas Midstream as strongly contributing  to this. In addition, we experienced one-off effects in the other consolidation line mainly from the  release of provisions in the magnitude of €200 million.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Now, onto our divisional performance, starting with RWE Power. Its operating result improved by  17% to a record level of €4 billion. Slide 18 gives you the individual value drivers. For 2011, we are  less optimistic for obvious reasons. Our German generation business will be hit for the first time by  the introduction of the nuclear fuel tax. We expect to burn up approximately €400 million.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Average realized electricity prices were far behind last year’s high level of €67 per megawatt hour.  In 2011, our Biblis A nuclear power plant will be off line for approximately six months and Biblis B  for approximately three months. As a result, the earnings contribution of Biblis will fall behind the  2010 level and we have to incur costs for retrofit measures. However, the impact from the change  in nuclear and mining provisions will have a positive effect. This is mainly due to the absence of  costs we had in 2010.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Coming to our customary update in our forward selling position, at the end of fiscal year 2010,  we’ve sold more than 90% for 2011, more than 50% for 2012 and more than 10% for 2013.  Although we saw some recovery of electricity prices at the beginning of the year, current price  levels are far below the high prices we saw two to three years ago. The strong increase in  renewable volumes has particularly put pressure on peak low prices. As a result, the clean dark  and spark spreads are levels which are too low to justify operation of old inefficient power plants.  Jürgen mentioned already in his presentation that old and expensive plants might leave the system  if prices stay so low for longer.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In the sales business, gas volumes increased mainly because of the cold weather, while electricity  margins declined. We expect the operating result for 2011 to fall below the previous year. This is  mainly a result of higher OpEx for improving the quality of our distribution network business. The  costs for refunding excess proceeds will be slightly lower than in 2010. For the sales business, we  expect lower gas volumes assuming normalized weather conditions.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Now onto our Netherlands/Belgium division, the numbers for 2010 are substantially affected by  consolidation effect. The performance of the Netherlands/Belgium division was supported by higher  gas sales due to the cold winter and slightly higher customer count numbers. Earnings were  negatively affected by the transfer of the Eemshaven power plant project from RWE Power to  Essent. The accumulated upfront costs of approximately €25 million are now reflected in this  division.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 7 With regard to 2011, we expect the operating results to come down significantly. This is mainly a  result of the integration of the Gas Midstream business into RWE Supply and Trading.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In 2010, the Gas Midstream margin which was supported by the cold winter weather was still  reported in the Netherlands/Belgium division. Lower electricity generation spreads will have a  negative impact as well, however, the division will benefit from efficiency improvements and  additional synergies.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Then we continue with RWE npower, operating result was up by 10% adjusted for f/x effects, it  increased by 6%. The increase was mainly linked to our retail business where we’ve benefited from  our efficiency programs and from improved residential gas demand over the cold winter month.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: On the downside, we faced increased costs for bad debt this year. The performance of our  generation business was affected by the adverse market conditions for our hard coke plants. This  could only partially be offset by higher production volumes of our gas fired plants including our new  CCGT in Staythorpe and lower operating costs. RWE npower’s extensive cost and efficiency  programs also helped to stabilize earnings at difficult market environment. For the year 2011, we  anticipate an increase in RWE npower’s operating result due to an increased operational  performance program across all business segments.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The generation business will benefit from full contribution of our new gas plant at Staythorpe.  However, the deterioration of generation spreads will further suppress overall performance of this  business.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Operating earnings at our Central Eastern and South Eastern Europe Division climbed by 11%  supported by a positive forex effects. Adjusted forex effects, division posted an increase of 7%.  One major factor were improvements in our Czech gas network and sales business. However, we  suffered from decline in volumes with distributors. In addition, we had a positive contribution from  our Polish activities among other things due to efficiency improvements.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In Hungary, improved electricity network margins were more than offset by lower electricity  generation margins and the introduction of a special tax. For 2011, we expect operating result to be  down significantly year-on-year compared to the exceptionally high number of 2010. In the Czech  Republic, we expect gas sales margins to come down as well as earnings from gas storage  activities. The contribution from our Hungarian electricity activities is also expected to fall behind  last year’s level. However, we expect to see a higher electricity network margins in Poland.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The operating result of our Renewables Division improved by 29%. The first-time consolidation of  the Essent wind assets contributed €23 million through earnings. We explained in our earlier calls  that this is less than originally expected because of the very weak production volumes due to low  wind levels in Northwestern Europe. The commissioning of our Rhyl Flats offshore wind farm and  the consolidation of Danta de Energías for full-year had a positive effect. Upfront costs for large  investment program including higher staff costs are still dampening Innogy’s operating result.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: For 2011, we expect RWE Innogy to post strong earnings increase. We’ll see further results of our  expansion program, but upfront costs for projects including higher staff costs are still offsetting  parts of this. In addition, we assume normalized wind levels compared to the very weak conditions  in 2010.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Upstream Gas & Oil reported a 50% increase in operating earnings. This is mainly a result of higher  oil prices, a stronger U.S. dollar, as well as reduced exploration costs. In addition, we benefited       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 8 from lower royalties in the German business. However, Dea suffered from reduced gas prices and  lower production volumes.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We see significant further upside potential for 2011. RWE Dea expects improved oil and gas prices,  anticipate a higher oil production but gas volumes will decline due to the natural depletion of our  German and U.K. fields. In addition, we expect exploration costs to come down further.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The operating result in our Trading/Gas Midstream Division turned into a slight negative number in  the year under review. On the one hand, the mark-to-market performance of the trading business  was good, but fell below the very high level of fiscal 2009. On the other hand, we benefited from the  first-time consolidation of the Essent trading activities, which contributed €96 million in 2010.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The steep decline is mainly related to our gas supply activities. This is because of two major items.  First, in 2009, we successfully concluded price revisions which led to a triple digit one-off release of  provisions. Second, prices on the gas market dropped relative to oil purchase contract as slide 49  in our back-ups indicate. This is also the reason why we see the operating result in 2011 falling  significantly below the level of 2010 despite an expected stable development for our trading  activities.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Let me take the opportunity to update you on the situation for our gas supply business. This slide,  number 27, will be familiar to you but the numbers have changed slightly. Our original 27 bcm take- or-pay exposure has come down to 24 bcm as some smaller contracts phased out.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: As indicated to you in our recent presentations, the net exposure temporarily grows to 20 bcm as  more and more sales contracts have turned from oil-indexation to market prices especially in the  Czech Republic. However, with the current prices and contract renegotiations underway, we would  expect the oil-indexed take-or-pay exposure to come down significantly in the coming years.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Slide 28 gives you now about the maturity profile of our gas supply contracts and the status of our  revision talks. As of January 2011, we are in negotiations for a good two-third, or 17 bcm of our  long term supply contracts.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Although we are ahead of other midstream companies, the bulk of refund will most likely only come  in 2012 and ‘13. However, as we started the process to fundamentally restructure these contracts a  much earlier than most and have not accepted any temporary quick fixes, we expect any good  news also to show retroactive effects for part of the volumes from the years 2009 and 2010.  However, you should always keep in mind that price renegotiations and arbitration process of  market developments of seismic shifts have never happened in Europe before. And therefore,  precise outcomes are hard to predict. Please understand that as long as we are in negotiations, it  cannot be more explicit.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The non-operating results fell below last year’s number by €1.3 billion. This was driven by the  earnings impact of commodity derivatives. Please remember, that all the numbers we show in this  line are purely timing differences. Restructuring, other fell by approximate €240 million, is mainly  driven by three effects. The deteriorated market conditions for U.K. hard coal and oil fired power  plants forced an impairment of €296 million. Secondly, last year, 2009, we recognized an  impairment loss on our at-equity participation in Excelerate. And thirdly, in 2009, we still had a  positive contribution from the change in nuclear and mining provisions since 2010; these changes  are accounted for in the operating result.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We have already seen smaller deals like the disposal of Thyssengas, which we envisage to close  by the end of this month or the disposal of our 24.6% stake in the [inaudible] hard coal plant. You  also know that we are evaluating options with regard to financial investors as potential partners for  our electricity transport business.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Further assets will follow, but it’s too early to talk about details. The second measure to support our  rating was reduction of CapEx. Compared to our old program, we have reduced capital spending  for the next three years by approximately €3 billion. Nevertheless, due to the disposal proceeds, we  still have enough funds available to grow our renewables and upstream businesses.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: EBITDA and operating results are expected to come down by approximately 15% and 20%  respectively; the decline for a recurrent net income is expected to be approximately 30%. What are  our expectations midterm for 2013, earnings will be affected as a result of low commodity prices  and the full auctioning of carbon certificates. The portfolio divestments of – up to €8 billion are  expected to lower our EBITDA in 2012 and 2013 by approximately €1 billion, operating result by  approximately €0.7 billion and recurrent net income by approximately €0.3 billion.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The 2013 going forward price for base load went up by some €3 to nearly €55 per megawatt hour  over the last couple of days, which of course is helpful for our future profit. If you figure that in –  with 160 terawatt hours we are selling, 60 are dependent on the spreads, 100 terawatt hours are  just basically nuclear and lignite, and each Euro would transform into about 100 million in result,  disregarding our gas to oil spread.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We also expect that the influence on increased power generation from renewables will start  showing bigger effects. The lack of flexible capacity in conventional generation will be positive for  our business.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Seconds, the European gas market is already in a transition phase. Current negative spreads can  also not persist forever. But don’t get me wrong, these developments might need some years to  resolve but definitely not decades.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 11 For the later years, we also expect commodity prices to pick up again. Further we are confident that  our gas to oil spread exposure will be largely gone beyond 2013 as price reviews will have to bring  these long-term contracts back in line with wholesale prices. This is the core principle of contracts;  they have to reflect market realities.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: So my question is, should we be prepared for an additional EPS dilution that goes on top of the  disposals, is that a fair assumption at this point? And the second question is regarding to your  underlying assumptions in the gas trading business for year 2011 and ‘13 guidance. For ‘11, have  you incorporated basically the worst case i.e. no success in arbitration and renegotiations till the  end of this year and then 2013 are we back to zero or a small profit or what’s the underlying  assumption there? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Jürgen Großmann>: As for the result of the price adjustments with the long-term gas  suppliers, we do not assume anything for the years ‘11 and ‘12, that doesn’t mean that we don’t  want to conclude these negotiations, but that a financial income will only be from ‘13 onwards.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Patrick Hummel>: Okay, so just to be clear for ‘11, this assumes basically the worst case  that could happen in the gas business and then in ‘13 it would be back to normalized levels.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Jürgen Großmann>: Well, first of all I have been out, Peter first called us shy and now you  call us cautious, so these are all I would say positive properties, I like to be called shy and cautious.  Now, as to capacity cuts, so far we have only specified that we are not going to prolong the  contracts with Steag beyond 2012. And also, we’re looking at some hard coal capacity in Germany,  that is some older stations that are probably if we analyze the market situation, if the current market  situation prevails, that are probably redundant at that time.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: So we are not specifying what capacity cuts we will make. Just the 1.4 gigawatts that we don’t  prolong from Steag is the number that’s presently on the table. On the other hand, we will take out  of production, corresponding to the commissioning of our new lignite power plants, 16 blocks of 150  megawatts each. So the lignite capacity does not increase with the commissioning of the new  power plant.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Bobby Chada>: Hi, good afternoon. My two questions are first of all on the €200 million of  additional cost cutting. Can you give a little color as to some of the areas that may come from? And  secondly, back to the oil gas spread question I’m afraid; you seem to imply that the mid-stream gas  business would have bigger losses in 2011 than in 2010. Is that because more customers have  opted to take spot based pricing or is it simply due to your hedges that you had put in place rolling  off in 2011?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: Bobby with respect to the second question. I think I mentioned that we see an  increase of the net exposure. I think last year we mentioned that the net exposure is in the 16 bcm  range and that’s based on our assumptions is going into the 20 bcm range. And that is due to the  fact that customers are switching to pure gas prices away from oil index prices and that has an  impact here.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q>: Hi, good afternoon. I’ve got two questions. Firstly, Dr. Großmann, you pointed out that the  commodity prices are rather volatile these days. Could you please run us through the main 2013  assumptions for power prices coal, CO2 and gas? And the second question, you pointed out that –  that older hard coal stations are not profitable in the – in the current environment of low clean dark       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 15 spreads. In your 2013 guidance, do you assume a negative operating profit for your older hard coal  stations or have you already assumed that they are going to shut down a couple of these given  your clean dark spread assumptions in your outlook? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Jürgen Großmann>: Well,  Matthias thank you for those questions. Now our – as I said, we  used so to say a mark-to-market approach as per January 2011, which means that the German  electricity base price is €52 in ‘11, €51 in ‘12 and €52 in ‘13. Peak is €64, €63, €64. And the carbon  price is €15, €15, €16. That is I think what you were asking, now are you asking for oil or what?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q>: Essentially also hard coal and the gas TTF price.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q>: No, not for the plant new, but rather for the older power plants.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Jürgen Großmann>: He was asking whether – I think Matthias what we have to observe is  how the total market develops. It’s not only what we do, I think we are quite flexible and we have a  few stations where our obligation to operate them expires at the end of ‘12. So let’s see what the  rest of the pack is doing, and we can then decide at the time when that needs to decision making  comes. But we will definitely not hesitate to close down older hard coal capacity.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q>: Okay. But right now your 2013 guidance implies that you’re not yet shutting down the older  power stations under your control?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Deborah Wilkens>: Yes, yes, hi. Good afternoon. Could you help us understand the  development at Dea where it appears the CapEx has been increased but the profit targets has  been delayed somewhat. And then, separately from Dea – in your ‘13 guidance, is your effective  carbon cost the same as the €16 market price, or are you benefiting from your early action on  CBMJI, and if so, what is the actual average achieved carbon cost in that ‘13 guidance?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: 18 <A – Rolf Pohlig>: Deborah with respect to the last one, that will not be disclosed, please  understand this the figure we mentioned is the assumption for the uncovered position with respect  to CO2 and you rightly reminded us that we have some coverage out of the CBMJI as well as from  some pre purchases of CO2 certificates. But that will not be disclosed what will be the average  cost.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Jürgen Großmann>: Yeah, as to your first question, Deborah, I was trying to, maybe not in a  very clear way, alluding to that in my statements. Sometimes you have strange things happening  you –  in Norway, in two instances we found a lot more than we initially were looking for. So, the  CapEx will be higher, and the well comes on in production a little later, but total profit will be a lot  higher. So, there are quite a number of uncertainties in the Dea projections in the longer term, not  the least being the oil price, which we cannot hedge at this time and for that longer period we can’t  hedge it any way. And therefore there is – we are on a conservative way saying there is a 1 billion  profit contribution from Dea by ‘16.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Lueder Schumacher>: Hi, good afternoon, two questions. One is on the nuclear fuel tax. I’m  not quite sure I’ve caught, I forgot the number you’ve mentioned earlier, but could you just confirm  what impact you expect in 2011, and whether that’s the same kind of level we should assume going  forward from there for ‘12, ‘13, et cetera.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The second question is on the German generation market and all the capacity cuts if we are going  to see them, what kind of capacity cuts would be needed to get at least some form of tightened  spec into the market which would at least allow for rising coal prices to feed through into the power  price?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Jürgen Großmann>: Well, Lueder, that’s interesting now, the first as to the nuclear fuels tax,  we all know that the government even knows that we will try to take legal action against that fuels  tax. So, whatever we say now is just a, sort of say, worst case for us, and as you know that we  have already replaced some of the fuel elements in one of our power stations, so that we don’t  have to do it too soon next year. But we figured it 400 million for the ‘11 figures in nuclear fuels tax.  As to the let’s say redundant capacity there is approximately a 10 gigawatts of inflexible hard coal  capacity and of those only two just a little above two are presently ear marked for closure, so that’s  why an additional 8 million – 8 gigawatts, 8000 megawatts are needed to be identified according to  our calculations.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Stephan Lowis>: Yeah, with respect to the nuclear fuel tax in the following years that is in the  600 million to 700 million region a year. It is not exactly the same figure in each and every year  because it really depends on the nuclear fuel.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Lueder Schumacher>: Okay that’s very clear. And just on the capacity question, so you  reckon that if we’ve got some 8 gigawatts to 10 gigawatts of capacity were removed, this would be  enough to -- tightness to get back into the market?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: No, it does have the impact, because the operating hours for the swing  capacity become less and the demand on flexibility becomes higher. So, some of the old plants just  can’t cope with that, just imagine what it does to your boiler, when your boiler is not made for these  temperature changes, you’re ruining it at a very short time and that could be very costly.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: Well, Alex you can just add the 2 gigawatts and the 2.2 that’s 4.2.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Alexander Karnick>: Thank you very much. It’s just on the leader action against the fuel tax,  where is your status quo on that, like when can we expect something visible to – to be announced.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: We’ll also as to the 8 billion, we’ve arrived at that number on the variety of  courses, first we looked at, what we have in areas that don’t hurt us that are may be non-core and I  don’t want to mention them here, but one could be the Berlin water business and some others also  that are really not so decisive for what we need.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And the rest, I think you look at our need for capital, we said we want to continue our investment  into renewables and we want to continue our investment into upstream, and we do want to  participate in some growth markets and we need to finish the CapEx programs that we are currently  doing.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q>: Yes, I wonder if you’re assuming some of positive contribution due to some recovery or  compensation for capacity losses in 2010, 2011 into your 2013 earnings contribution of the Gas  Midstream division.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: To the letter, Chris, yes, I do think we feel comfortable achieving that eight  times because some of it is a business that is in different areas. It’s regulated; it’s not as risky and  so on. And the second one, I think we are looking at a variety of measures. There is some interest  in participating by external investors in participating in some of our big CapEx projects, buying into  newly built power stations, let say you’re a gas supplier and you’ll see that we have CCGPs almost  being finished in Great Britain. So there may be an interest in buying into that. There is some  interest of buying into German lignite and so on.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q>: Yeah, good afternoon, I have some – two questions; one is on the coal-fired to coal  production plants that you have on the contract so apart from the 1.4 gigawatts that, that will be  dissolved by the end of 2012, I see that you have both 5.4 additional gigawatts on the contract with  this other players, and I was interested in how flexible you are with these capacities if you can  withdraw easily from these contracts, and, or if they are due to expire soon.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And the second question is on the nuclear power investment needs, do you have clear visibility  meanwhile how much of additional investments the government might ask you for related to the life- term prolongation?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: Let’s start with the first question, I think you should have reminded, this is really  a portfolio of contracts, contracts which have different expiry dates, different opportunities for an  extension and also that this power stations have different efficiency factors. So really, on a case by  case situation, we have to evaluate the merits of extending a contract or simply not, and that is  exactly what happened in December last year that we decided not to work on further extension of  some of these contracts.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q>: Yes good afternoon. Two questions. The first one, could you just clarify please Dr. Pohlig  what you said on the dividend. Do you intend to pay the dividend in shares or just give this option to  shareholder I was basically – that’s the first one. And the second one, on CapEx, I was just  wondering whether the number you could prospect the sales teams for Germany so 900 for sale  and distribution and 400 for generation. Is a sustainable level or would it have to go up in the  following years just because of some potential works being pushed back and also if you could tell  us how much to include precisely for nuclear life time expansions in this years? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Stephan Lowis>: And then the second question was about the CapEx long term power  generation in Germany, I think was that right Vincent or so?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q>: Yes, I mean basically your 1.3 for Germany is it a sustainable number or are you seeing the  price pressure in the longer term basically?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Jorgen Großmann>: It goes down, for Germany I think in the thermal portfolio, there is no  more hard coal there is only replacement in lignite and that is not quite clear, because the- with all  the out dated to 150 megawatt blocks are out and the 300s and the 600s can stay in we’re just  modernizing the 600s, so there is just a question what we’re going to do with the 300s, but there  may be another CCGT somewhere in Central Europe, it doesn’t really matter whether its Germany  or elsewhere it’s our new commissioner, Mr. Ertinger  was right with Europe becoming the tougher  place, that may be a CCGT in Czechia rather than in Germany.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Jürgen Großmann>: The cost saving, the stepping up our efficiency enhancement from 1.2  to 1.4, but we already answered that, that was IT.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Patrick Hummel>: Okay fine. And the second one if I may just on the reserve margin  discussion we have to find this call. Just taking the firmer additions the new CCCT that comes from  stream in Central Europe we’re going to see a reserved margin expansion probably in the near  term and that’s fairly visible even though of course renewables are the big unknown but even if  renewables go down, it’s not going to be a tightening on the reserved margin that’s quite visible.  And then you’ve identified 10 gigawatts of potential closures all hard coal stations moving in the  reserve margin maybe it’s around 20% or to the high teens do you really think that is a game  changer for the stress you can achieve in the base load environment?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Rolf Pohlig>: I’m not sure we got the question really right because first of all what we intend  to say here on page 14 was the specific situation in the German markets with the renewables and  now you opened up more to the European level and as Bill mentioned in Europe. I think we have to  be very careful to end up only gigawatts plus gigawatts because reserved margin you have to really  look into the how what is calculated how reliable is the renewals there so on and so forth, what we  are saying is Germany needs more flexible.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Patrick Hummel>: I was actually not referring to that. I was more looking at the bigger picture  because you say the stress environment is actually not sustainable. I see that fine but the question  is just if we see 10 gigawatts of old hot coal stations disappearing from the system. If that will  already be enough not just to make money with more flexible new thermal stations, but also in  general, if that’s enough for an expansion of thermal extract from base lift.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator

texts.text: <Q – Alberto Ponti>: Yeah, good afternoon. I just have one quick question. What CO2 prices or  power prices or oil prices would be an impediment to – for you to achieve the three times in net  EBITDA in 2013? Thank you.
