texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: We have also successfully continued the renegotiation of our long-term oil-indexed gas contracts, more so than  envisaged in our initial guidance for 2012, which did not foresee a settlement with Statoil for last year. Our  solutions are fully structural and include compensation payments for past losses.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: After the conclusion of the price provision with GasTerra late last year, there is only one counterparty, namely  Gazprom remaining with whom we are still in the price review proceedings. As you are aware, these are in front of  an international arbitration tribunal and we expect a conclusion in the first half of this year. We have finalized our  2012 efficiency program which brought an accumulated €1.5 billion compared to 2006. Our new efficiency  enhancement program is also well on track with all operational measures identified and already bearing first fruits  last year; more on that in a moment.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Since most of you are following the power price development on an almost daily basis via your Bloomberg screens,  I won't bore you with the obvious, but I would like to highlight a couple of points. First, the drop in power prices  over recent weeks can mostly be attributed to the weakness in fuel prices, notably CO2 and coal.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Taking into consideration that these are the input costs of the price-setting plant in Germany, this is also the  reason why clean dark spreads stayed relatively stable. Second point, it is undeniable that the increase in  proportion of renewables in the system has led to over capacities in times of strong sunshine and high-wind levels.  This has an instant impact on spot market prices and it translates, to some extent, into forward prices. Achievable  spreads for peak capacities are particularly affected.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Third point, we can currently observe a relatively flat power curve and backwardation in clean dark spreads. This  implies that the market anticipates net conventional capacity additions in the next two years, since there are still  some power plants under construction and few firm capacity shutdowns announced so far.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Finally, renewables also have an ever increasing impact on load factors for conventional generation, especially big  power plants. Gas-fired plants have seen their running hours decline steeply over the last two years, due to the  expanding feed-in from photovoltaics during peak hours. And while many of them are no longer able to cover  their fixed or even cash costs at those reduced loads, they are still needed in times of system stress as seen earlier  this year during the cold spell in January.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: This is also not only true for old gas-fired power plants, but also for brand new ones. Take for example our Lingen  plant, which we commissioned in 2010. It only ran for some 2,000 hours in 2012, a decline of more than 50%.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Current forward prices and spreads lead to decrease in load hours and do not allow peak capacity to earn  sufficient margins. Therefore, mid- to long-term, we see the requirement for an upward correction of revenues for  peak capacities. However, while it has become clear that the current market design does not provide the required  remuneration to keep conventional capacity online to serve as backup for intermittent renewable generation, it is  far from certain how a new system might look. Regulatory uncertainty will therefore continue to make operational  as well as investment decisions difficult.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: We cannot escape the commodity price developments, but it would be wrong to just look at outright power prices.  Due to diversified fuel mix, our generation portfolio can mitigate some of the downward pressures. For example,  although lignite spreads came down from the highs at the end of 2011 and beginning of 2012, the decrease was  much more muted than the drop in outright power prices, and as already mentioned, clean spark spreads – sorry,  clean-dark spreads stayed relatively stable.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On the other hand, our gas fleet is not only suffering from low clean spark spreads, but also decreasing load  factors due to the renewable expansion. This is particularly evidenced by our new build CCGTs, Moerdijk and  generation business will be significantly down from 2013 levels. Although our outright position is largely hedged  for 2014 and to some extent for 2015, we have been selling forward into a falling power curve and our average  achieved price will therefore come down.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The forward selling of – forward selling for our spread positions is still in early stages. While clean dark spreads  have shown some resilience, spreads for gas plants continue to be extremely low. This will impact above all on the  profitability of our Dutch and UK generation portfolio.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Overall, the outlook for our generation business is anything else but exciting. However, we should not forget that  more than half of RWE's earnings is generated by businesses other than generation. Our regulated grid business  will continue to contribute stable earning streams and even show some moderate growth potential. The European  energy transition provides some opportunities to expand our energy services business and in areas such as  renewables and upstream gas and oil, we are still developing some growth projects. Do we believe that these can  compensate for all of the earnings pressure in the generation business? No, but we're doing everything possible to  mitigate these negative earning trends further, and I will come back to some of the measures we're taking in our  new European generation company.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Well, let me move on to RWE's strategic response to these challenges and how we intend to drive the business  forward. While we still believe that the cornerstones of our strategy are valid, it has become clear that they have to  adapt some of the targets in light of the new market conditions. The new targets are based on a number of our  fundamental beliefs for RWE's role in the transformation of the European energy markets.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: First, the transformation of the European energy market is not temporary, but structural. Renewables are here to  stay and play an ever more important role. Increasing energy efficiency and distributed energy solutions will have  a further impact on the future energy landscape. Second, today's business model for conventional generation,  especially for gas and hard coal fired power plants will not persist in the future. While it is not yet clear how a new  market design might look, we have to ensure our business can cope with current market realties and be fit for  future changes.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Lastly, a significant increase in RWE's operational excellence is necessary and possible. Initiatives such as the  European generation company as well as the bundling of business support functions will identify further cost  saving potential.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: These beliefs translate into the individual targets within our three strategic cornerstones: Invest in sustainable  projects which improve our CO2 intensity and support the energy market transformation, become more robust by  focusing even more on the cost efficiency of the business and improving our financial flexibility. Maintain our  international footprint while keeping our regional focus.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The implementation of this strategy will be based on three steps. Strategically positioning, here we have to take a  look at our portfolio and ask the question about the strategic rationale of owning each individual assets. Second  step, selective CapEx; given our financial constraints, we have to ensure that scarce investment funds are allocated  more effectively and efficiently. After the conclusion of our power plant replacement projects, we're looking for  less capital intensive growth opportunities.  Third step, spread the assets. I might even add, spread the organization. Finally, we have to ensure that our assets  continue to earn a positive value contribution by cost cutting and other efficiency enhancements. This holds  particularly true for our conventional power generation. While growth will be limited, we believe that we can  create long-term value along this route.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me now go into more detail on these individual steps. On the back of the fundamental changes in the  European energy system as well as our current financial constraints, we've taken another look at our portfolio to  identify assets which we do not consider core and do not add much value to the portfolio or where the ownership  structure could be optimized. A similar exercise was done for the ongoing disposal program where we have  divested assets such as Berlin Waterworks or Horizon which no longer fitted with our core activities.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: As mentioned earlier, we have already sold assets for some €2.1 billion. However, we will not achieve our €7  billion targeted by the end of this year. Our current focus is on the sale of our Czech gas transmission company  NET4GAS. In addition, we are not excluding further disposals. However, this will be opportunistic with the focus  on portfolio optimization and value enhancement. This could include stake reductions in companies or assets  where we do not necessarily need to hold 100%.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Our growth ambitions and investments have also been scrutinized under these considerations. The last couple of  years have been marked by the largest investment program in RWE's history. While the renewal and  modernization of our power plant portfolio was required, it also diminished our ability to quickly respond to the  changing market conditions.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: While we're more than ever convinced that Dea is an excellent business and provides promising growth potential,  we have to ask ourselves, if we are the best owner for this business. There's only limited synergy potential with the  rest of the group, even after considering a further integration of the LNG activities. In addition, with our reduced  financial headroom, we cannot provide RWE Dea with the necessary capital to realize their growth ambitions.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Our current investment program for 2013 to 2015 adds up to a total CapEx of €13 billion. This is approximately  20% below the €16 billion we had planned last year for the period 2012 to 2014. The program is still frontend  loaded as we're finalizing our power plant replacement program in 2013 and 2014. The longer term CapEx level  will be in the range of €3 billion to €4 billion. Our day-to-day investments will be between €2 billion to €2.5  billion per annum, nearly half of this is dedicated to our electricity and gas grids. The focus of our discretionary  investment projects will remain on renewables, mainly on and offshore grids.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Outside of traditional utility business, our upstream gas and oil activities will continue to require significant  CapEx. As we have much less financial headroom, we will concentrate even more on so called asset-light growth  projects. Let me give you some examples from our German and Central Eastern, Southern Eastern European  downstream activities.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The focus in our German sales and distribution division outside traditional grid business will be on energy  services. The German Energiewende presents ample opportunities in this field. For example, there are estimates  that de-centralized CHP generation will grow by 5 gigawatts to 6 gigawatts to approximately 10 gigawatts over the  next 10 years. Projects in this area typically provide an IRR slightly below 8% with a limited risk profile. In  addition, we are developing new products and solutions partly in close cooperation with our local municipal  partners, for example for complete energy concepts.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: For the coming years, we have a CapEx budget of approximately €100 million per annum for such growth  projects. In combination with our investments at the grid business and our efficiency program, medium term, we  see for the division the chance for moderate earnings growth in a magnitude of approximately 3% per annum from  a stable vacillated earnings base.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: In our CEE/SEE division, we concentrate on downstream activities in addition to our grid investments. Over the  last couple of years, we established significant market positions in either gas or electricity. The next step will be to  leverage on these positions by offering the respective other fuel and entering additional markets. The Czech  Republic for example, we're the market leader in the gas market. From this starting point, we have already gained  approximately 170,000 electricity customers to whom we provided 1.6 terawatt hours of electricity in 2012.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Slide 13 gives you more insight into our strategic targets for the other CEE/SEE regions. Ladies and gentlemen,  the environment for conventional generators is tough and further deteriorating. But to start on slide 14, with the  positive aspects, the current situation proves that we have followed the right strategy in three aspects.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Nevertheless, the slide shows that we're facing an alarming situation. Only about 50% to 60% of our plants still  cover their costs of capital. While some 20% to 30% show a negative cash balance at current market conditions,  this clearly is not acceptable. Our prime target for our generation activities is to solve the issue of those cash  negative plants. Our current efficiency program is already a step in this direction. Out of a total €1 billion for RWE  Group by 2014, approximately €0.2 billion will be realized in a new generation company and further measures are  already in preparation. This includes plant by plant specific actions to turn them cash flow neutral or cash flow  positive [indiscernible] (23:58) two-fold, improve the cash inflow and reduce the cash outflow.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Slide 15 gives you an overview of what we're currently working on. Let's take as an example Gersteinwerk, an old  gas-fired power plant, which we have in Germany. Last year, we temporarily multiplied the steam turbines of two  units with 355 megawatt each from April to September and we will do the same in this year. In addition, one block  is in constant cold reserve. With this and with a new operational regime, we were able to lower the cash cost by a  high single digit million euro amount.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Last December, when demand was high and renewables more or less not available, the plant was needed and  generated cash. Over the next couple of months, we will thoroughly investigate the cost structure and further  optimization potential of each individual unit. You will identify the avoidable cash costs and in cases where the  achievable margins will be sustainably below the avoidable cash costs, we will shutdown the plants. It is also  obvious that under prevailing market conditions, additional conventional new build projects will certainly not be  undertaken.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: While most of the measures in our new generation platform are still being identified, we are on track with the  implementation of our current efficiency program. In contrast to the factors driving the current difficult  environment for utilities, which are beyond our control, efficiency enhancements are one of the important  countermeasures which are within our control. We finalized the old €1.5 billion efficiency program last year. On  top of that, we already have early results from our new program. The €200 million we achieved in 2012 is partly  driven by quicker staff reductions mainly in our German businesses. Out of a total plant head count reduction of  approximately 3,700, roughly 1,000 were already realized in 2012. The achievements with our new program were  also one of the main reasons why earnings in 2012 came out better than originally expected.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Slide 17 gives you some information about where the efficiency improvements are coming from. 30% of the new  program will be coming from the German supply and distribution business. It includes mainly non-regulated  business. In our sales business, we're working on improvements by bundling functions. In the grid business, we  will further optimize our operating costs. But efficiency measures are not only focusing on plain cost reductions,  we want to improve our earnings situation with new products as well. The German Energiewende provides  chances for this and we want to be the partner of choice in this respect.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: With regards to conventional power generation, I just explained what we are working on. In our UK as well as  Trading/Gas Midstream division, IT optimization and further automation play an important role. As a result,  especially in our UK business, significant head count reduction is envisaged.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Slide 18 shows our outlook for 2013. The current expectation for the three main earnings figures confirm the  outlook that we gave one year ago. Thanks to our conservative hedging strategy, we feel quite comfortable with  this outlook as the margins in our generation business are already locked in. The biggest value bill is still the  settlement of the gas contract price review with Gazprom that we expect to conclude in the first half of this year.  Again, our guidance is after expected disposals, which is mainly the sale of our Czech gas transport business  NET4GAS.  As mentioned earlier, please understand that against the backdrop of an increasingly volatile business  environment, we refrain from giving an explicit long-term or longer term guidance. We will update you in  November with our concrete expectations for 2014. By then we'll have more clarity about our business activities.  But during my presentation I explained trends that we can see and Bernhard will mention further aspects in a  minute. So, it will be obvious that earnings will not match the 2013 level.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me start with the operational performance on slide 21, the operating result was up by €600 million, an  increase of 10%. This was mainly driven by improved earnings in our Germ Generation business unit after the-one  off burdens we faced in 2011 from the nuclear exit. Furthermore, we felt a positive effect from the start of our new  lignite-fire power plant in Neurath. The Trading/Gas Midstream division recovered by approximately €200  million. The energy trading activities showed a healthy and strong performance. Furthermore, we were able to  settle several oil indexed gas contract reviews.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Looking at the major value drivers, on the right hand side of the slide, our efficiency programs explain  approximately €600 million of the earnings improvement. Out of this, approximately €200 million were already  early achievements from the €1 billion program until 2014. Further positive earnings came from higher grid and  sales margins. RWE Dea did quite well due to higher oil prices and a stronger U.S. dollar.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: However, depreciation increased by €300 million as a result of our huge investment program over the last couple  of years. Electricity generation margins came down by some €100 million. We were able to offset the decline of  electricity prices and spreads to a large extent. This was especially due to the positive volume effects, mainly from  the start of the commercial operation for our new lignite plant, BoA 2&3. As a consequence of our disposal  program, we lost an operating result of approximately €100 million mainly from the deconsolidation of Amprion  in the third quarter of 2011.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Let's have a look on our earning numbers down to net income on slide 22. The non-operating result is dominated  by the value adjustment of €1.7 billion for our Dutch generation portfolio. The strong growth of renewable  capacity in Germany depresses electricity prices and generation spreads in our neighboring countries. There was  no need for additional goodwill impairments. The outcome and the sensitivity of our impairment tests to the  market parameters are shown on pages 155 to 156 of the Annual Report.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Summing up all the value adjustments we have undertaken since 2010, we reached a total of approximately €2.5  billion for our Dutch portfolio. The deteriorated environment is therefore reflected in the current valuation.  Our financial result declined by about €460 million driven by an increase in the interest accretion to non-current  provisions and the higher average net financial liabilities. The first aspect relates mainly to the adjustment of the  net present value of other long-term provisions as a result of lower discount rates. Furthermore, net interest in  2011 benefited from the release of a provision made in relation to a renewables fund, which ceased to exist  following the nuclear phase-out decision.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Before I turn to the development of net debt with slide 24, I would like to briefly introduce to you the changes in  the reporting of our hedge position on slide 23. This is a result of the new Conventional Power Generation  division. You were used to the reporting of the volumes for the German portfolio across all technologies: nuclear,  lignite, hard coal, and gas.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: With the establishment of the division, we have increased the transparency by providing a split between the so- called outright and spread positions of our Conventional Power portfolio. Outright includes our nuclear and  lignite capacities. One has to admit that with regards to its carbon price dependency, lignite could also be  considered a spread position. However, due to its dispatch features, it fits more into the outright position.  Generally, we hedge the next regeneration volumes forward driven by market liquidity.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me now come to the divisional outlook on slide 25. Since the beginning of this year, the new Group structure  has been in place. Our conventional power generation activities are now within one division, and in the  Netherlands and in UK, we show the supply activities separately. Therefore, we have provided you with pro forma  2012 numbers to give you our outlook based on the new Group structure. Please note that we will provide you with  a quarterly pro forma 2012 numbers a few weeks in advance of the publication of the quarterly reports, which  should help you to work on your quarterly forecasts.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: While we see a stable or even a slightly positive development in our downstream activities, our Conventional  Power Generation business in particular, will fall significantly below the previous year for the reasons explained  earlier. However, we expect positive one-offs from the settlement of the last outstanding gas price review in the  first half of this year, which together with the achieved settlements of the last year should improve the earning  situation of our Trading/Gas Midstream division significantly.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Our Central Eastern Europe, Southern Eastern Europe division would be significantly down mainly due to the  expected disposal of our gas transport operator net for gas. But even excluding this effect as pressure on earnings,  especially because of additional burdens from the tough political environment in Hungary.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: For RWE Energy and RWE Dea, we have additional longer term targets for 2014. For RWE Dea, we can confirm  the target to increase production volumes of hydrocarbons to more than 40 million barrel oil equivalents  compared to approximately 31 million in 2012. This should be in line with an operating result in the order of €800  million.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Unfortunately, the 2014 target for RWE Energy cannot be maintained. There are three reasons for this. First, the  reduced CapEx program for the Group as a whole will also impact RWE Energy. Although we expect to spend  CapEx in the magnitude of approximately €2 billion in the next three years, this is much lower than originally  planned. As a result, RWE Energy will not be able to reach its old 2014 targets of approximately 4.5 gigawatt of  installed capacity in operation or under construction.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: We now expect RWE Energy to operate approximately 3.5 gigawatts of renewable capacity by the end of 2014.  Consequently, the target for operating result has to be adjusted down as well.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Second, the 2014 operating results target of €500 million included a significant contribution from our German  offshore wind farm, Nordsee Ost. Due to the considerable delay with grid connection, the first feed in of electricity  is not expected before mid 2014, which clearly leads to a negative impact on 2014 earnings. This is before any  compensation payments as it is not yet clear how much and when we will receive compensation for lost earnings  by the delays.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And third, parts of our renewable generation capacity is not eligible to receive fixed feed in tariffs and hence are  affected by reduced market prices.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: To sum up, RWE Energy's operating result in 2014 is now expected to exceed €300 million, excluding any  compensation payments for the delayed grid connection for Nordsee Ost.  Slide 26, gives you the major value drivers for the development of our earnings in 2013. Our efficiency  improvements are substantial but will not be able to match the pressure on operating earnings especially from the  full auctioning of carbon certificates and the decline in generation margins. Nevertheless, and as previously  mentioned, we do expect a strong relief in our Trading/Gas Midstream division, once the last outstanding oil  indexed gas contract with price revision is settled.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The disposal program is expected to lead to an earnings dilution of approximately €200 million depending on the  disposal timing of natural gas.

texts.speaker: Patrick Hummel
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS AG (Broker)
texts.text: Okay. Very good. So, two questions please. First one is regarding your 2013 guidance and basically taking the page  26 earnings bridge and trying a bit to reverse engineer it in regards to the Gas Midstream business. If I take all the  other drivers together, it suggests that you expect a swing of give and take €1 billion in the Gas Midstream, so you  had a loss of €600 million in that division in 2012. Is the €600 million the right order of magnitude, and if so,  how much in that you would consider one-off, namely related to the Gazprom payment. And what's the impact on  2014? I guess we should take that down by several hundred million euros? And the second question is, the 20% to  30% of your generation capacity that you consider burning cash, you say basically that you're going to address this  with cost savings. You haven't really mentioned large plant closures, at least up to a significant extent, is it that  you refrain from plant closures because you think it will not have any meaningful impact on power prices. Are you  expecting any kind of additional capacity payments going forward or why you're focusing on cutting costs rather  than just closing the capacity?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Hello, good afternoon, Patrick. Maybe I can answer your first question with regards to what's happening in  midstream and gas midstream in 2013, what has happened in 2012 and what will happen in 2014 and the years  beyond. Please bear with me that we continue our communication policy of not giving you any precise numbers.  The only thing we can say, there is a significant one-off in 2013 and if you compare – if you would compare 2014  to 2012, of course, there would be a level shift with all the – with all the gas contracts being rebaselined pricing  wise, which also would be significant.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And your second question [indiscernible] (50:11), it's basically on a potential lignite tax. One needs to keep in  mind that about lignite, there are three elements of the discussion; one is the environmental element, CO2  emissions, which is clearly critical. The two other elements are on security of supply, for which lignite is a local  resource which is available; it's always available. And the third one is on affordability of energy, for which lignite is  a low cost option as well. The discussion currently in Germany focuses slightly more and more on affordability and  security of supply. I'm not saying that I feel comfortable with the discussion about lignite tax; I'm just saying that  there are opposite [ph] powers (50:52) as well.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Secondly, we've looked at this from a [ph] political (51:00) perspective. It's not that easy to implement a lignite  tax, as such. It would be a discriminatory tax, so there would be legal levers to protest against that. And if you  would put a kind of a concession on lignite because it is – the resource comes out of the own soil, then it would be  difficult to differentiate lignite from oil and gas, because that would be a similar treatment. So, never we feel  comfortable in our business, but I'm not that nervous at this moment in time around the lignite tax  Benjamin Leyre  Analyst, Exane BNP Paribas SA  Q Thank you very much.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The other part of the €600 million for 2012, which you're looking for, is the old program – the 2006 program,  which delivered its last €400 million in 2012. So, we have in 2012 overall €600 million, out of which €400 million  old and €200 million new program. And – so, this leaves the final, or the residual, number to be delivered in  terms of efficiency enhancements until end of 2014 at €800 million, which sums up to the overall €1 billion as  communicated before.

texts.speaker: Bobby Chada
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: And then, secondly, on the impairments, I think you said in your remarks that the impairments you've taken so far  fully reflect current business conditions. It seems there isn't any write-down for CCGTs built in the UK or  Germany, or indeed any deterioration in the value you might expect from some of the other types of generation  you've built. Is it fair to assume there is some recovery built in to your impairment tests or do you really think  you've fully impaired the assets on a mark-to-market basis?  Bernhard Günther  Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG  A Hi, Bobby. First to start with your question around CapEx, how much is committed and how do the numbers then  match up with the – or the previous statements on how much is committed with the actual forecast. Though, I  would be happy to claim it as a heroic deed of the new CFO that we slashed CapEx ruthlessly, I think it's – the  main reason is simply delays, yeah; and therefore, yes, we spend less, but it's not reducing the overall program,  yet. Although, of course, we are stepping on to the break heavily for everything which is discretionary going  forward.

texts.speaker: Bobby Chada
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Why haven't we done – or why don't we see anything of the same nature for Germany and the UK? That's a pretty  simple reason. In Germany, if you look at, for example, new built CCGTs, you will time them in a similar situation  to the Netherlands, not exactly the same, but a similar one, but you know that we do our impairment tests on a  fleet basis, so the whole generation fleet for a respective market in Germany and the Netherlands. And in  Germany, the German new built power plants with high asset values are benefiting from the profit shield of largely  depreciated nuclear and lignite assets.

texts.speaker: Bobby Chada
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Therefore, the overall fleet is not impaired. And in the UK, you must bear in mind that there is a difference that we  will have a different market situation post LCPD, when much of the coal has been switched off and we are very  confident that gas-fired power plants, new gas-fired power plants will contribute much higher load hours post  2015 because it's just physically needed to keep the lights from going out.

texts.speaker: Martin C. Young
texts.profession: Analyst, Nomura International Plc
texts.text: Yeah. Good afternoon to everybody. My first question kind of picks up on your comments there about the UK.  Could you share your thoughts on the outlook for your hard coal and your biomass plant in the UK for the next  couple of years because they generated quite significant volumes in 2012, which I guess is not going to be the case  on an ongoing basis at least not in the next couple of years?  And then, the second question gets back to the issue of the Netherlands. Could you give us the actual value that  you are placing on the Dutch generation portfolio, and what I presume is a positive impact on depreciation going  forward, what is that? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me start with the first question, Martin. If I understood that correctly, I mean under the current prevailing  regime in the UK, it is useful to convert hard coal stations into biomass. We are planning to do so in Tilbury; that  planning has not led to a final decision yet. I think one of the elements going forward will be that, if we would do  so, it is a kind of a cluster risk that we were creating there. So, one of the decision points would be to find a  partner, which will enter into that risk together with us. But so far, from a market view, under the regime, which is  just implemented there, where we see good value in converting Tilbury in this case, if that's the one you are  referring to, into biomass, I think that's a useful thing.

texts.speaker: Martin C. Young
texts.profession: Analyst, Nomura International Plc
texts.text: Yeah, what type of output are you expecting though for the next few years from Tilbury and indeed the hard coal  plant that you have, because presumably some of this [indiscernible] (01:02:30) plant is going to meet the end of  its days in Tilbury unless is relicensed will meet the end of its days as well?

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: No, we are not considering Didcot, we are talking about Tilbury and that would need a clear investment to bring  the plant up to a level to operate on biomass for the future of at least a number of years and we're considering an  investment, but that has not been finally decided yet.

texts.speaker: Martin C. Young
texts.profession: Analyst, Nomura International Plc
texts.text: Yeah, yeah, I appreciate that, but what I am trying to get at is what type of output should we be looking at in the  UK, say in 2013 and 2014 from the hard coal facilities that you have and in the Tilbury, because some of these are  not going to be able to operate going forward, are they?

texts.speaker: Andreas Thielen
texts.profession: Analyst, MainFirst Bank AG (Broker)
texts.text: Firstly, I'd like to understand the outlook for the utilization of the gas plants going forward. You talked a lot about  the reduced load factors. If I look on the load factors in Q4, I mean that – excluding UK, that suggests something  like 20%, and I just wondered if that could be seen as a guidance for the load factors going forward in the current  environment or should we expect that to come down further given the – yeah, rather negative margins which we  have in spark spreads?

texts.speaker: Andreas Thielen
texts.profession: Analyst, MainFirst Bank AG (Broker)
texts.text: And secondly, with respect to the CapEx guidance, firstly, I'd like to understand the €13 billion/€1.9 billion for oil  and gas, does that assume that there is a disposal – is the disposal of Dea built in there already? And the second  part to that question, is the €13 billion that Bernhard talked earlier about, a spillover from the €6 billion in 2012  into 2013, is that reflected in that or should we add another €1 billion then? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me start with the utilization of gas plants. The utilization factor, as such, is not a purpose on its own. We look  at cash flow and operational income break-even. So, insofar with some of the gas plants, it is clearly possible also  at a low utilization rate to still have a positive cash flow and they will continue to operate that gas plant. Example  on this is if we do a mothballing throughout the months of April till November, we keep the plant up and running  in the winter season, we certainly need to accommodate the workforce and quite a lot of other OpEx elements to  be aligned with that. Then certainly that gas plant would not be up and earning its full cost of capital, but it  certainly would be a gas plant that we continue to operate further on. So, the 20% that you've mentioned, you  cannot extrapolate that because we will have other, maybe even old, gas plants that will be possibly taken out of  duty. But even at the lower utilization, we will still continue to run some of the plants if they're cash positive.

texts.speaker: Andreas Thielen
texts.profession: Analyst, MainFirst Bank AG (Broker)
texts.text: Yeah. I'm sorry if I can just – I mean, I'm clear that that is only a helping tool but just in reality I'd rather want to  understand from the negative spreads we currently see, do you see that overall generation for gas plants continues  to go down versus 2012 or are we already at a low point?  Peter Terium  Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG  A Well, it depends on the development of the electricity price and the gas price and then adjusted for CO2 rates, and  then if you take the element of efficiency of the respective plant into account as well, then you can give an answer  to the question. What I'm saying is you can't have a simple standard development of your clean spark spreads and  we've already mentioned that. Specifically, the plants that have a high efficiency do not necessarily have a negative  clean spark spread. The clean spark spread, as such, is an average spread, which is not attributable to the whole of  the fleet.

texts.speaker: Ahmed B. Farman
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn Partners LLP
texts.text: Hello, good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for taking my question. Could you provide some color on the levers  you can pull to strengthen your balance sheet if the power price holds by another €4 to sort of €4 to €5 per  megawatt hour? And my second question is on the timing of the renegotiation of the gas contract. Is there any risk  that it can sort of slip to the second half of this year or else – are you very confident on H1 this year? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: So, on your first question, the levers to any further drop in power prices are the same as we have at our discretion  right now. So, it's efficiency enhancement/cost cutting; it's CapEx discipline; it's the divestment profile that we  have. These plans are not contingent on a particular level of power prices. On the gas price renegotiations, if you  ask me is there a risk, yes, of course I cannot exclude it. It's an arbitration tribunal that's like a court case. The  we confident that we will get it in the first half? Yes – too, because we have strong indications from the tribunal  that they want to get it solved within the next couple of months.

texts.speaker: Deborah B. Wilkens
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International Ltd.
texts.text: Yes, good afternoon. I was hoping you could help with setting out what your expectations are for the EU and/or  just German policy around carbon prices, and if you could also just remind us how you're prepared for a rising  carbon price?

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: I mean, we're currently discussing intensively with the German government directly and indirectly, also via the  various trade associations, what could be a potential future design for the power price – sorry, for the existing  market; and it has several levers, EEG and bringing EEG closer to the market is one. Certainly, a second one is the  ETS – developments on the ETS. And the third one is what kind of a regime will need to be brought in place in  order to have security of supply on a longer term safeguarded. These are three distinct items that correspond with  each other, or correlate to each other, and all of them we are currently discussing. On the ETS, we have clearly  stipulated out our position. We believe the ETS is a functioning system. The fact that CO2 prices are at a all times  low right now just confirms that it works, because we've seen staggering economical growth and 90% of the price  drop of CO2 prices is related to that and not to a malfunctioning of the system. So, if you don't like the outcome,  don't criticize the system, but criticize the input into the system, is our device, and that has to do with targets for  [ph] 2030 (1:19:08) in relationship to the development of the number of certificates being brought into the  market.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And then last but not least, a kind of back loading, but only in connection with the first two items, and then CO2  prices could rise to a different level. How we are going to react to that or what is our impact to that? What I have  said one year ago, two years ago, and three years ago, we have a robust portfolio with various technologies in there  and maybe lignite will be slightly less profitable, on the other hand gas will be further in the money. It has been  the aim of the game since quite a few years and that's the result of our investment program.

texts.speaker: Peter A. Bisztyga
texts.profession: Analyst, Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Hi. Just a follow-up from me on that CO2 point. Given your hedging position for 2014 and 2015, I would presume  most of your nuclear output is hedged for those two years. Could you give us an indication, therefore, whether  earnings in those two years would be positively or negatively impacted by a rise in CO2 prices?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: By and large, Peter, we are carbon neutral in our overall position. You know that we have built a strategic carbon  long position a couple of years ago and this basically delivers a carbon neutral profile of ours. So, the overall  earnings effect would be negligible as long as we are talking about normal price rises.

texts.speaker: Stephan Lowis
texts.profession: Vice President-Investor Relations, RWE AG
texts.text: And please understand, Peter, that we don't give a time specific CO2 position for our portfolio, which is let's say  the implicit question you're asking for. So, we're not saying in March we're CO2 long and in May, we are even  longer or short or whatever, that would too complicated also to back track this kind of things.

texts.speaker: Patrick Hummel
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS AG (Broker)
texts.text: Yes, just two follow-ups, please. To double check the CapEx number on there, on slide 12, you say €1.9 billion and  the years 2013 to 2015 is earmarked to oil and gas projects. You just said before that CapEx would drop by €1  Bernhard Günther  Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG  A No, you're right, spot on, that's day to day.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: No. So far it's NET4GAS, and that's it, we won't comment on anything else.

texts.speaker: Patrick Hummel
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS AG (Broker)
texts.text: Okay. But I got you right that you are still looking at, for example, in the renewables business that you might sell  stakes in your assets, which of course would have certain earnings impact, is that fair to say?

texts.speaker: Alberto C. Ponti
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA (UK)
texts.text: Yeah, good afternoon. I have two questions. One was, if you could give us a sort of EBITDA margin for supply of  electricity and gas in the UK and in the Netherlands. And the second question is, how do you – did you actually  spun out the generation assets from supply, i.e. is generation [ph] selling at (01:24:51) market prices and supply is  purely buying and trading electricity and gas, all the recent sort of tolling agreement between supply and  generation. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Alberto C. Ponti
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA (UK)
texts.text: Yeah, well, but phrase it differently, supply is not paying any tolling fee to generation?

texts.speaker: Benjamin Leyre
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane BNP Paribas SA
texts.text: Yeah, thank you. One follow-up please on the delayed grid connection for the Nordsee Ost wind farm. What could  be the magnitude of the compensation payments, which you are not including in your guidance at the moment?  Thank you.

texts.speaker: Stephan Lowis
texts.profession: Vice President-Investor Relations, RWE AG
texts.text: Just again, sorry for asking again a question, but you're asking about how long we take losses in the power stations  before we close it, was that the right question?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Our financial headroom in 2012 was quite positive and in line with our upgraded guidance from last November. In  2012, we also made progress with our disposal program and we have achieved €2.1 billion in asset disposals. This  was followed by the sale of our Czech gas transport company, NET4GAS, at the end of March for €1.6 billion.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Our current focus on our disposals program is on the sale of our Czech gas transmission company, NET4GAS.  Here we made good progress and announced on 28th of March the sale to a consortium of Allianz and the  Canadian infrastructure investor, Borealis. The deal is expected to close in the second half of this year. It does not  mean that we exclude further disposals however, these will be opportunistic with a focus on portfolio optimization  and value enhancement.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: I am now coming to the end of my presentation. We touched upon the major challenges we face in our generation  business in our full year call. However, we should not forget that more than half of our earnings is generated by  businesses other than generation. Our regulated grid business will continue to contribute stable earning streams  and RWE Energy is still developing growth projects.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: We are well aware of the tough environment and RWE will respond to the challenges it is facing. Taking into  account these market conditions, our prime target for the group is first to reach a balanced budget and second, to  return to a leverage of 3.0x midterm.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. Thank you. Let me answer those two questions in the order you asked them. On the disposal program, as we  said, what we have achieved last year were the €2.1 billion. We are now very confident, after the signing of the  natural gas deal, that we will close it in the second half of this year which would bring another €1.6 billion, which  would take us up to €3.7 billion, obviously. Everything beyond that, there is, of course, Dea but this is not likely to  come this year. It would come later. And everything else which might come this year would be minor disposals  which would not be game-changers in terms of size or financial impact.

texts.speaker: Alexander Karnick
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Broker)
texts.text: Sorry, but I'll limit it to two questions, if I may. It's around – Alex Karnick, Deutsche Bank – it's around nuclear  provisions. The first one – first question is just to clarify that the low interest rate environment and the hit that  you've seen on your pension liabilities would – can you confirm that this would not affect your nuclear liabilities  as your underlying inflation – cost inflation is relatively similar to the discount rates used, so if anything, that  would cancel each other out was my first question.

texts.speaker: Alexander Karnick
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Broker)
texts.text: Second question on the nuclear provisions would be, given that there is this new law which is called – in Germany,  which is called the new finding of a final storage or whatever, could you describe probably more qualitatively than  quantitatively what that could do to your nuclear provisions, if it does anything to it? Thank you very much.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. To start with your first question on a potential effect of changing interest environments or continued low  interest environment in our nuclear provisions. As you assumed in your question, the relevant number is not the  absolute discount rate for the nuclear provisions but it is the spread between the discount rate for the future  liabilities and the cost escalation rate for the cost estimates which we, of course, estimate on a current going- concern basis, and then we escalate it into the future assuming that there will certainly be future cost escalations.  And we historically have been assuming them to be also significantly above the average rate of inflation.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: So the overall spread position for the nuclear provisions is indeed very low. We compare it regularly also to our  peers and we do think that there we are on a conservative side. This does not preclude however any adjustments to  debt if the overall interest environment should change materially in the future.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On URENCO, yes, we do have the intention to dispose of this engagement as well. As you are aware, it has no  strategic value up for us any longer as we see our engagement in nuclear power fading out especially in Germany.  But you'd know also, I assume that this is a very political asset and we are only share with beyond 50% in a third  of the overall shareholding. So it takes not even two to tango but it takes a lot of more players to tango along.  Currently, signals we have received, as you read in the press, look quite promising, but I think it's too early to get  any further details.

texts.speaker: Michael A. Ridley
texts.profession: Analyst, Mizuho International Plc
texts.text: And the second one was just clarification, I wanted to check that I understood correctly that you thought your  adjusted net debt to EBITDA for 2013 post your gas sale would be 3.5 times? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Deborah B. Wilkens
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: Yes, good afternoon. I was hoping you could give us some more details on the rolling off of these hard coal  contracts. I think years ago, you had said they would come off a third, a third, and a third in 2013, 2014 and 2015.  And you've announced, obviously, those that roll off in 2013. Is the timing in the – is the split of the capacity about  right to be a third, and a third and a third over those three years?

file: RWE - Q4 2013 Earnings Call 4March2014 900 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 04-Mar-14.pdf

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Otherwise, our performance was marked by two major opposing factors. On the one hand, the deteriorating  electricity generation margins, including the full auctioning of CO2 certificates burdened our Generation business.  On the other hand, the successful revision of our gas procurement contract with Gazprom resulted in a  compensation payment of approximately €1 billion.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: In August, we finalized the sale of the Czech gas transmission company, NET4GAS, thereby deconsolidating the  business for the remainder of the year. This year's earnings [audio gap] (02:21) also be impacted by the disposal. I  am very pleased that our efficiency improvements are progressing well and ahead of schedule. The g roup has  achieved some €250 million more in efficiencies than envisaged for the year. This is partly due to the fact that cost  saving is becoming a matter of course to the business and I'm proud of that.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Conventional Generation can offer an attractive upside should markets improve again, but this is not a given,  since we cannot control commodity prices, nor do we see any clarity on the political front over new market design.  However, we see a kind of bottoming out in German wholesale power prices at the moment, but this is clearly  dependent on hard coal prices.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And this brings me straight to the next slide illustrating RWE's mid-term business profile and its main earnings  drivers. A very important business as well as earnings contributor will be the regulated distribution business. In  Germany, we have regulatory certainty until 2017 for gas and until 2018 for electricity. We see some potential for  growth arising from the energy market transformation, as well as efficiency improvements and performance.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: In Central and Eastern Europe, we operate distribution networks in four countries. Our main objective is to  stabilize earnings against regulatory downward pressure, which is particularly strong in Hungary. In the Czech gas  distribution business, we are in intense discussions with the energy regulator on the parameters of the fourth  regulatory period scheduled to start in 2015. Significant effort is also being invested into operational performance  and optimization.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On the Generation side, we have RWE Innogy, working on meeting their cost of capital by 2016. This implies  finalizing the two large offshore wind farms currently under construction. Divesting non-core activities, such as  biomass and offshore construction vessels, as well as improving overhead costs. We will continue to pursue  selective growth opportunities, more on that in a moment.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The Trading activities will continue to be an integral part of RWE, [ph] as we interface trade (08:32) wholesale  market. RWE Supply & Trading is responsible for the commercial optimization of RWE's asset base. Further, the  Trading business develops growth opportunities in new Trading markets, both in terms of new regions and  energy-related product. It also targets additional profits from principal investment activities and energy -related  projects.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: After the arbitration court ruling last June, we have come to a commercial settlement with Gazprom last week. We  cannot comment on details, but under the agreement, we expect no further negative impact from this long -term  gas supply contract on our accounts until the next regular price revision in summer 2016 can be triggered. Until  then, we are confident to find an amicable solution for the open issues, so that the whole the whole gas to oil  spread problem is solved. However, RWE Supply & Trading is currently losing money, from historically  contracted long-term gas storage capacities, due to the low summer/winter spreads, which do not allow us to earn  the capacity payments. Therefore, we see the underlying earnings potential of the division more in the order of  €200 million for the time being.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: I would now like to come back to our two generation businesses and explain in a little bit more detail what we are  trying to do here. In November last year, we showed how the Conventional Power Generation would have fared in  2013 at current forward prices. Of course, the actuals came out better, since we still benefited from higher power  price hedges. Our average realized baseload price was €51 per megawatt hour. Going forward, this will obviously  come down towards the current forward price.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Clearly, the business must ultimately earn its cost of capital again and although we are restructuring the business  to move in that direction again, we eventually also need the market to reimburse backup capacity, either through  higher power prices or a change in market design. We encourage policymakers to initiate the first steps of  implementation to just design and legislation process as quickly as possible. However, this is about long-term  viability of the market framework, hence we do not expect any commercial effect to materialize in the short term.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: In terms of portfolio measures, let me provide you with a short update on where we stand. Based on the regular  reviews of our power plant portfolio, we decided to mothball further capacity. The fewer operating hours  combined with the [ph] whole – a bit low (12:02) wholesale prices has made the operation of Claus C, one of our  most modern gas-fired stations unprofitable. Unit A had already been mothballed at the beginning of last year. In  addition, we have decided to reduce our contracted hard coal capacity by another 1,000 megawatt.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: As part of the overall efficiency program, these portfolio measures minimize the negative cash flow contribution of  the portfolio, while keeping some of its optionality. Further capacity remains under review and we will update you  once concrete decisions are taken.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Moving on to our renewable generation business, we see a muc h more positive trend. While we had to revise down  our 2014 outlook, we are confident that from next year onwards, RWE Innogy's operating result will start to  progressively grow on an annual basis and this is despite cutting back on CapEx.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: So where is the growth coming from? First, our two large offshore wind projects, Gwynt y Môr and Nordsee Ost  have crossed the halfway line and will come online with all turbines by year -end 2014 and mid-2015. Second, we  are still investing in growth projects, albeit on a very selective basis and through partnerships to reduce our capital  requirements and diversify risk. Third, the business is also working on restructuring and efficiency measures to  ensure it earns its capital cost by 2016.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Looking now at where the improvements to operating result are coming from, it is probably no surprise to you  that Conventional Power Generation accounts for approximately half of it, don't forget that the main reason for  bringing all of our generation assets under one roof was to enable us to raise efficiencies and reduce costs.  Measures include staff reductions in management and support functions to bring down overhead costs; lowering  of O&M costs and improvement of the availability and flexibility of our plant fleet.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Our German Downstream business contribute some 20%. In the regulated business, the focus remains on more  efficient operations and regulatory outperformance. As an example, this can be achieved by optimized  investments in the grid, which reduce future O&M costs, but simultaneously increasing the regulated asset base.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On slide 11, we have outlined, how the efficiency enhancements impact our total controllable cost base. In 2012,  total controllable costs stood at €10.8 billion, of which €5.3 billion accounted for personnel costs. For 2016, we  see them go down to $9 billion. Adjusted for portfolio and other effects, such as the expected sale of RWE Dea, the  operational cost savings amount to €0.9 billion, representing 60% of our total efficiency program.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Let me give you a concrete example. The Generation business was able to increase the output of our lignite fleet,  by approximately 3 terawatt hours, by improving its availability. This was partly achieved through better  management of different core qualities and the process optimization leading to shorter maintenance outages.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Y eah, thank you, Peter, and good afternoon from me as well. Let me give you a brief overview of the major aspect  of our business performance in fiscal 2013 on page 14. Our operating result was down as expected to €5.9 billion.  We have two main opposing effects. On the one hand, our Trading/ Gas Midstream division achieved an  extraordinary high result. This was due to the arbitration court ruling on our long-term oil-indexed gas contract  with Gazprom. On the other hand, we suffered a massive earnings decline in our Conventional Power Generation  division. Here, the new CO2 regime and declining Generation margins were the main drivers.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Despite the strong earnings decline in this division, there are positive signs. Peter mentioned already that we are  ahead of our plan with our efficiency enhancements. The box on the right-hand side of slide 14 shows a net benefit  of €800 million. This compares to our original expectation of just €550 million in 2013. We had early  achievements, mainly in our Conventional Power Generation division. One reason is the sustainably higher  availability of our lignite generation fleet that Peter explained earlier.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: In addition, we benefited from higher staff reductions. By the end of 2013, we stand at a groupwide operational  staff reduction of approximately 4,500 since the start of the program. For 2013, this means approximately 900  more than originally planned. In addition to the aforementioned trends, earnings in our Upstream Gas & Oil  division were under pressure. We suffered from the weaker U.S. currency as well as lower realized gas and oil  prices. In addition we had burdens from dry wells and delays in ramping up our production.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Slide 20 gives the divisional outlook. I think the general trends are not surprising. Therefore, I want to keep my  presentation short and refer to the Annual Report, where you can find all the details. Slide 21 provides the majo r  value drivers for 2014 compared to 2013. I mentioned already the general trend of declining realized electricity  generation margins, the absence of the Gazprom payment in 2013 and the dilution effect from the disposal of  natural gas.

texts.profession: Analyst, Exane SA (Broker)

texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG

texts.speaker: Patrick Hummel
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS AG (Broker)
texts.text: And the second question is referring to slide six, where you showed the EBITDA now for the first time for  Generation on a mark-to-market basis. Is it right to assume this is based on November and as of today,  that would probably have slightly deteriorated further with carbon going up and coal going down?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: And the last sub-question of your two questions was, I think about [indiscernible] (38:13), where then do all the  other offsetting effects come from. I think this is a debate we've often had before and you must just believe us that  we know what we're saying about the new normal that by and large over the next couple of years, there will be also  positive offsetting effects, which you can see qualitatively listed on slide number 22.

texts.speaker: Nathalie F. Casali
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: Hi, good afternoon. My first question would be on the medium-term view of the company that you've outlined, a  view which is much more focused on the Downstream business. On that view, do you expect the current €1 of  dividend to still be an adequate level of remuneration for your shareholders? And the second question is, just  following up on Patrick's question on slide 6, does the outlook that you give for the EBIT – for the EBTIDA level, I  understand this is after payment of the nuclear tax, could you just clarify. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Y es. Nathalie, thank you for your questions. Let me start with the second one, the outlook is indeed, looking to my  left side, after payment of nuclear tax, even if we would not cash-wise have to settle it, we still have to accrue for it,  because until the final settlement is being done, there's always the potential risk of having to still pay for that.

texts.speaker: Alexander Karnick
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Broker)
texts.text: The second is on the discount rate for nuclear provisions, [indiscernible] (42:01), there's a bit of adjustment there  probably coming closer to what you're discounting the pension provisions with, but could you also give us a  magnitude at which you're inflating the costs for nuclear provisions at this point in time. Thank you very much.

texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Hi, Alex. On cash flow, very clear statement, the 2015 target of balanced cash budget, so cash flow from operating  activities covering CapEx and dividends is not at risk. This is still fully valid and alive. And our nuclear provisions,  you're right, there was some movement reflecting the overall lower interest rate and inflation environment, but we  do not publish the escalation rates for our nuclear provisions.

texts.speaker: Alexander Karnick
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Broker)
texts.text: Okay. Fair enough. That is consistent with the past, I gave you the shot. But basically, the message is, since we do  not have seen a significant movement in the nuclear provisions, that there was partially a lowering of the  escalation rate along the same lines of the discount rate, just conceptually?

texts.speaker: Bobby Chada
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Hi. Good afternoon, everybody. First question is just, you gave a lot more detail today on the efficiencies and cost- cutting program. What is it about the specific lignite blocks, in p articular, that  would differentiate them, is it age, availability or location?  Peter Terium  Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG  A  Y eah, Bobby, let me start with the first question. It's a bit my hobby after discussion in the last few days on this  topic. We'd like to separate between the efficiency programs, which are the actual measures that people  [indiscernible] (44:51) place in order to get improvements done and what the net benefit to the bottom line of the  P&L is. The efficiency programs, so the gross line, the top level line level is €1 billion old program, with another €1  billion new program. Y ou see, however, in the next years to come, a lot of inflationary cost components coming  through in our P&L, think about contracted services, these kind of things. Therefore, the second €1 billion will  only benefit to the bottom line with €500 million net, that €500 million you can account for, that was scheduled  or planned for 2017 and is now contributing to the bottom line into our planning one year earlier at the  end of  2016.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Y eah. And hi, Bobby, from me as well. On your question with regard to capacity closures, I think you referred to  the lignite units, especially in [indiscernible] (45:47 ) and the Westfalen, old hard coal-fired unit, but there are  maybe two comments I would make to your question or two answers. One is that, usually, those decisions are  taken when these units reach a point where additional new significant cash-out has to be committed. So like  usually, at an outage or a major outage. And this of course is dependent on the outage strategy and they run our  profile that they have. So, this is the one reason why some blocks who are under review might not be  decommissioned one or two quarters thereafter because these natural break points have not been reached yet.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: The other aspect what makes for example, what makes Westfalen special, well that's the o nly old hard coal-fired  power – hard coal-fired unit that we still have. So, our fleet then does no longer contain any stations on hard coal  of that age. And on [indiscernible] (47 :00) lignite it's, that these are the two, only remaining units left at this   specific site. So, this is a different calculus than for mothballing or shutting down than you would have at a site  where there are still other units sharing the same overhead cost, for example.

texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: Y es. Good afternoon.
