texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Y eah, let me start with the second one, Deborah. We have made publicly a firm commitment some months ago in  relation to the moving of some of the villages that need to be cleared for the expansion of the next lignite phase.  That's the firm commitment that we've made. We have received from the highest institution al court, the  confirmation that our lignite mining plan, at least for the third phase, is valid and is right. And on that basis, we  are continuing to operate. There's no further firm commitment to that extent in the next few years to come.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: And hi, Deborah. With regards to your question on the whole old hard coal lignite contracts, we have not  prolonged a single one and all of them will be out of operation until end of 2015; 2015,  I think that's what you  asked. This does not mean that there are then no contracts left, but these were not for prolongation in the period  between Q2 2013 and now.

texts.speaker: Sofia Savvantidou
texts.profession: Analyst, Citigroup Global Markets Ltd.
texts.text: Y es. Hello, everyone. Thank you for taking my questions. Just one in two parts, if I may. Y ou have a target of  reducing your carbon emissions [ph] divided by (49:44) output from about [ph] 0.7 6 times (49:48) that you had  in 2013 to 0.62 [metric tons per megawatt hour] by 2020? If yo u could give us a little bit of color in terms of how  you expect to achieve that? How much of the improvement is coming from maybe closure of older plants, how  much from Renewables, how much is already sort of in the pipeline? And the second question is, if you have an  estimate of where your current carbon factor is versus, let's say the average carbon factor in the market, so versus  the average price-setting plants? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Stephan Lowis
texts.profession: Vice President-Investor Relations, RWE AG
texts.text: Hi Sofia, this is Stephan. I would like to refer you to the Annual Report, where we say where the current emission  sector is. I think if my memory serves me correct, 0.76 tonnes per megawatt hour and we also made a statement in  our outlook that, yes, we have a 2020 target out there, but due to the fact that the gas-fired stations are so under  water, so to say, that it will be harder for us to achieve that target over the time, if the market conditions beat the  market design or commodities don't change.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Y eah. We stick to that number we're working towards a target. It is clearly a combination of expansion of  Renewables, as well as increasing the average efficiency of our power stations. And that latter one is a combination  of new power plants coming on stream like Hamm and Eemshaven. But also what we expect a further utilization  of our gas-powered plants. I mean they are mostly standing idle at this moment in time. We do not foresee that to  continue until the end of this decade. And therefore, the combination of those with more renewables will lead to a  significant further reduction of our CO2 emissions. And our aim and still quite a way out, but our aim is by 2020  to indeed land at the 0.62 metric tons per megawatt hour.

texts.speaker: Sofia Savvantidou
texts.profession: Analyst, Citigroup Global Markets Ltd.
texts.text: Y es. For that question, yes. And if you could, my second question as well in terms of where you think you are  versus the [indiscernible] (52:32) plant, because we have seen obviously in recent times, CO2 prices going up but  power prices actually going down. So, if you could tell us where you think you are versus the market? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Stephan Lowis
texts.profession: Vice President-Investor Relations, RWE AG
texts.text: Y eah. Without having a concrete figure in front of me, to be honest, what we can say as a general statement, we are  still in line with our respective market as the marginal provider. But of course, there are – from a CO2 emissions  effect, better-placed utilities out there compared to us. But within our respective markets, where we are active, we  are the same kind of emissions sector where the general – where the marginal generator is.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: If I might add to that, Sofia, the 0.62 [metric tons per megawatt hour] was our original goal, would bring us  towards where the average of the market to our expectation would be. Now what we don't know at this moment in  time, how much of the announced plant closures will be ratified by the Bundesnetzagentur and we don't know how  much actually will be closed and what a new market design will do to that. So, at this moment in time, still a bit  touching into the dark as far as what the rest of the industry will be doing, but our expectation when we set up that  plant was that this brings us to the average of the industry and we're basically then CO2 neutral as far as price  impacts on our portfolio are concerned.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: The one is in the distribution business. In Germany, for example, we have now, lots of clarity because the  regulatory periods there have just started and it will be 2018 for electricity and 2017 for gas, until the  new periods  start. And until then, we have very high visibility of our future revenues and this is part of our overall statement.  And in the UK, as you know and maybe some other markets of course, retail prices are under scrutiny, either by  regulators or by the general public. So, it's very difficult to give any indication on where they will be heading post  2014.

texts.speaker: Ingo Becker
texts.profession: Analyst, Kepler Cheuvreux
texts.text: It doesn't mean that we are laying back and saying let's wait until it comes. We're still very actively working with  the regulators, with the politicians, actively working with them to explain what design a future market, a market  with a growing, an ever growing part of renewable, would need. And in that work and the studies that we've been  doing for that, it's clear that a non-discriminatory, technology -neutral, pan-German or maybe even with some  surrounding countries, but the bigger the market, the lower cost it would be for society as a whole.

texts.speaker: Ingo Becker
texts.profession: Analyst, Kepler Cheuvreux
texts.text: And all of that could even be kicked back into the end of the decade if politicians don't get their act together and  don't give this the priority. What we've seen in the last weeks and months is that the new Minister of Environment  – sorry, new Minister of Economy and Energy and its State Secretary are finding out t hat a focused, de-central  market, obviously is not the best choice to be.

texts.speaker: Ingo Becker
texts.profession: Analyst, Kepler Cheuvreux
texts.text: Focus, you need to know of the Minister in his first months on the office reign was on the renewable subsidies  scheme, the EEG. Second target that he is pushing is then ETS. And third on his line of priorities is then the  market design for the future, which will somewhere be – and it's [indiscernible] (59:41) already, but the mid of  this year, early after summer, to my view.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Well, let me start with a simple part and then Bernhard can do the more difficult half of the question. The German  government subscribes to the 40% CO2 reduction by 2030. They're fully committed to that goal. They, on top of  that or in addition to that, want to have Renewables target as well, but they've understand that the Renewables  target should not be impacting or should not be conflicting with the CO2 reduction targets. So CO2 reduction  needs to be leading and the other one needs to be supportive.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: It still is a long way to get that done, but a government has more means to play that we as a straightforward  company have. They can maybe bargain out some other elements, first the countries that are not very receptive of  the CO2 target right now. Think of Poland, Hungary, Romania, and they have more fish to fry which they can use  in order to, at the end of the day, get to a compromise where the 40% reduction target is being achieved on a  European level.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: That will naturally have a supportive effect on the CO2 price, but just to take away too much of your dreams, I  mean, we need a CO2 price of €60 or €7 0 in order to switch from coal to gas. I don't see that happening in the  short-term and therefore, we'll still have a struggle with some parts of our fleet and therefore, a capacity market  will continue to be a very important measurement in addition to the CO2 reduction and a higher CO2 price.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Y eah. With regards to the second part of y our question on what's being done or what hope is there for those plants  who are earmarked as being cash negative on page number 7 . Well, first of all, some of them have been  mothballed in the meantime. So, this is the status as you know of the world as it  was in Q2 last year. And  therefore, we have already done measures on our side. How much hope is there for short-term relief by some sort  of state aid or the grid agency supporting it, well this depends on the system relevance of these units. Most of our  units under these criteria are not deemed system-relevant at the time being. But bear in mind that sooner or later,  especially in the second half of the decade when the nuclear decommissioning continues, we will need some  additional capacity again. And then you will need a mechanism in Germany, which rewards or reimburses not just  the cash cost or positive EBIT, but the full cost of capital to conventional power plants, otherwise they won't be  built.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Y eah. Hello, John. I think the – of the order of magnitude in terms of where we want to end up at the end of the  period, shown on slide number 8, that's pretty correct. And we always – we've given the €500 million indication  already quite a while ago as a general target to cover our cost of capital. And for the renewals overall, there's a €1  billion sum left for renewable projects to be spent in the next three years including 2014. Of course, with a kind of  tapering off towards the end of the period where the level will be significantly lower. But by and large, you can say,  whatever left as discretionary spending in our CapEx budget will go into renewable projects.

texts.speaker: John B. Musk
texts.profession: Analyst, RBC Europe Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Y es. So, you're saying the underlying – when we get out to 2016 and there's no more renewable spend, are we back  at the, I think you used to say €2.5 billion of maintenance CapEx for the group?

texts.speaker: Stephan Lowis
texts.profession: Vice President-Investor Relations, RWE AG
texts.text: No. What we, if you look to our company presentation what we indicated is that the maintenance CapEx, where  the total CapEx, excluding Dea, is €2 billion and what balance of that is over the period 2014 until 2016, the total  sum for Renewables is roughly €1 billion.

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Our renewables business is on track to improve its performance by refocusing and streamlining its activities. texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Let's move to the first area of focus: growth. Since 2012, we have shown strong financial discipline. texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: We've made a virtue out of necessity. We entered into partnerships for a development of renewable projects and  sold minority stakes and some regulated assets to just the gas distribution network in the Czech Republic.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: The energy market is changing. Renewable energy will continue to grow in the quest of decarbonizing the energy  system. Smart infrastructures and balancing systems will become increasingly important to handle the  decentralization of electricity generation. And the drive towards energy efficiency and convenience products calls  for innovative customer solutions.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Our initiatives to grow will focus on the three parts of the value chain which support and enable this  transformation of the energy market and of RWE. In renewables, we will continue to expand our asset base. Due  to the commissioning of recently constructed assets, the business will show high double-digit compound annual  growth in earnings over the next three years. The focus will be mostly on onshore and offshore wind. We will  continue to enter into partnerships to realize our attractive project pipeline while reducing our capital  requirements and diversifying development risk.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: In our most recent deal in February, Statkraft agreed to buy a 50% stake in our Triton Knoll offshore wind farm  project in UK. The final investment decision will be taken in 2017.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Our distribution grids play a key role in the transformation of the energy market. Investments will not only go into  maintenance, but also the expansion of the grid, enabling the integration of renewables and decentralized  generation units. The deployment of intelligent grid solutions and smart technologies will offer additional growth  potential. We are working to deliver long-term, a single-digit earnings growth rate here, although we'll have  fluctuation in individual years.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Moving on to our generation business. It will certainly come as no surprise to you that a situation in our  conventional power plant fleet has deteriorated since the last time we showed you this slide. Base load wholesale  prices have come down from €37 to €32 per megawatt hour since then. As you can see, under recent commodity  prices, only roughly 55% to 65% of our portfolio is free cash flow positive, roughly 15% points less than 12 months  ago. We've worked hard over the last months to optimize our portfolio. While we have decided to shut certain coal  plants and limited their costs, we have opted to mothball a large part of our gas-fired power fleet. This allows us to  minimize the cash burden while maintaining the option to bring them back when they will be needed and  profitable again.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Slide 7 shows how dramatic the situation for conventional power generation is. At current levels, price levels of  around €32 per megawatt hour, the division is just free cash flow neutral. In other words, it is only able to earn  the cash flows it needs to cover the current cash-outs for provisions and the required CapEx to keep our assets  running. This is not a sustainable situation long term and a clear political framework is needed in the short term.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: The contribution along the value chain will roughly stay the same with RWE generation contributing about 50%,  and the supply and distribution business another 30%. A central point of attention when defining our additional  measures has again been the continuous improvement of our cost position. We are focusing on limiting cost  increases, for instance, the staff factor costs, as well as reducing our process costs.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Here are just two examples out of more than 100. In the generation business, we have optimized our requirements  for specific pipes in our plants across fuel types and increased the competition on the market. This leads to annual  cost savings of more than 20% for these pipes. And in the grid business, we were able to simplify technical  requirements together with our customers and suppliers which led to cost savings in the area of a high double- digit million euro amount.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Slide 11 outlines how the efficiency enhancements impact our total control of our cost base, as just mentioned, cost  reduction is of particular importance. About half of the contribution to our efficiency improvement will be  achieved by operational cost reductions.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Of the remainder, €1.5 billion to €2 billion will be mainly spent for renewable projects and to complete our power  plant completion program. Furthermore, we will spend a little bit in our retail business as I mentioned earlier in  my presentation.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: We continue to classify goodwill impairments as well as bookings and losses as the impact from the change in  certain derivatives in the non-operating result. Furthermore, we were suffering from the deterioration of realized  market spreads in the conventional power generation business and negative weather affects mainly now supply  businesses. This was only partly offset by our efficiency improvements, although we were able to realize them  faster than originally planned as Peter has already explained.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: First, we changed our procurement strategy for CO2 emission certificates in 2014. While until 2013, we purchased  most of the certifications in the same year as the CO2 was emitted, we shifted the timing for the purchase of the  certificates we needed for 2014 to the beginning of 2015, the year, we have to submit them. This general policy will  continue for the time being.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Second, in 2014, we had a positive weather effect in our working capital. Due to the mild weather and the effective  energy consumption in 2014, was to a large extent, lower than the advanced payments we received from our  customers. As a result, in 2015, we expect much lower cash flow from the final billing for the year 2014 compared  to the cash flow we received in 2014.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Let's now move on to slide 18. Due to the favorable cash flow trend including one-off, and the planned decline in  CapEx, we were able to reach our cash balance target one year early. We achieved a significant surplus of €1.1  billion. Mainly due to further margin erosion in the conventional power generation and the working capital effect  drawn by the weather, which I have just explained, we don't expect to achieve a positive cash balance again in  2015. Upside would come from potential cash contributions from a positive outcome of our court cases regarding  the nuclear fuel tax. Nevertheless, in general, we are sticking to our ambition of a positive cash balance on average  from 2014 onwards. Although due to the aforementioned volatility in working capital, this might be at risk in a  single given year.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Nevertheless, our achievements are better than the outlook we gave in March last year when we said we would  expect our net debt to be in this order of magnitude. This outlook was given under the assumption of a positive  contribution from the repayment of nuclear fuel tax of approximately €1.3 billion, as well as no impact from the  change in discount rates. Besides efficiency improvements, our efforts to optimize working capital were the main  reasons for the success.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Let me conclude my remarks with the outlook for 2015. First, on slide 21 for the key earning figures of the group.  Further efficiency improvements and growth in our renewables business will not be sufficient to stabilize earnings  in line with 2014. Hence, we expect EBITDA to decline to €6.1 billion to €6.4 billion. Our operating result will  most likely reach €3.6 billion to €3.9 billion and recurring net income is expected to be at level of €1.1 billion to  €1.3 billion.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: The main reason for the earnings decline is the further deterioration of generation margins in the conventional  power generation division. Let me also point out that our outlook for 2015 does not include contributions from a  positive outcome of our court cases regarding the nuclear field tests.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: On slide 23, you see the major value drivers for our outlook for 2015. I already mentioned the future decline in  generation margins, in addition, our supply and distribution networks Germany division had a very positive  earnings contribution from the sale of grid assets in 2014, which we won't see this year. Furthermore, we expect a  negative impact from the change in provisions.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: On the positive side, we expect further contributions from our efficiency program. For this year, we envisage  approximately €100 million.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: For our outlook, we have also assumed normalized weather conditions. As we don't expect similar value  adjustments that we saw in 2014, depreciation should be lower than in 2014. Last but not least, our renewables  business is expected to show strong growth due to the commissioning of new generation assets.

texts.speaker: Vincent P. Gilles
texts.profession: Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And point number two is on the 10%, let's call it, covering of nuclear provisions, can you tell us a bit more about  the assets you dedicated sort of the length [indiscernible] (30:02) securities and whether you are ready to  communicate to us a target of, let's call it, coverage? Thank you very much.

texts.speaker: Benjamin Leyre
texts.profession: Exane SA (Broker)
texts.text: And second question on the nuclear litigation. I'm curious to hear your latest views on the likelihood that the  judgment by the constitutional court in Germany on the nuclear tax will happen this year, and whether you are  still confident that the judgment will be favorable? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Okay. Hi, Benjamin, this is Bernhard. I will take the first question, and Peter will take the second one on the ruling  for the nuclear case. I'm not 100% sure if I got your first question totally correctly. I understood that it's related to  the impairments we now have in the operating result and which, of course, then would translate through into  returned net income as well.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Yes. And Benjamin, on the nuclear fuel tax, first of all, the procedure in Luxembourg is not finalized yet. We have  [ph] the Attorney General (34:48) who has given his advice. Mostly, the court follows that but not always they do.

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you for taking my questions. I have two questions. The first one is on the impact of the one-off and offset in  your working capital from the changing policy on CO2 procurement as well as trade payable. Just want to  understand how much of that €3.6 billion do you expect to sort of reverse in 2015?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Hi, Deepa. This is Bernard. So, the one-offs on the working capital side, there indeed the two main drivers are the  carbon effect and the weather. And the nature of the carbon effect, as you can see from the slide now, I know it's  presentation, if you net it, it is probably above €1 billion which we will see in 2015. And this is just now an  estimate for the ongoing year. And for the weather, we think it's a significant triple-digit million euro amount you  might see there as a swing.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: The difference between carbon and weather is that carbon is just a typical one-off, where you do something in  your inventories, it works once in working capital. And if you keep the new level, it won't happen – it won't  improve your cash flow again, but it also won't burden your cash flows. With weather, it's a swing, yeah. And  therefore, the effect is – the cash effect is bigger than what we've seen in earnings, yeah. It accelerated cash flow in  2014 and it will depress cash flow beyond its normal level in 2015.

texts.speaker: Patrick Hummel
texts.profession: UBS AG (Broker)
texts.text: And the second question is, I'd like to understand why you have actually started funding the nuclear liabilities  because your previous communication was more like we run the business with our operational assets, and that's  the way we generate most returns and, therefore, that's the best way of eventually paying off the nuclear liabilities.  Is that as a response to political pressure or, in that sense, could we expect you to even support the idea of a  German nuclear liability fund and just outsource the whole thing? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Okay. So, Peter switched off his mic which means that he probably expects me to answer the second question. Hi,  Patrick. The funding of nuclear liability. First of all, it's not nuclear only. We don't earmark assets against  liabilities in our balance sheet. It's just a matching of the asset side of our balance sheet against the overall  structure or profile of the liability side, if you will.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: There has been no political pressure of any kind on what we do with the Dea proceeds, to be very precise, and  what we think we'd demonstrate here is that we behave reasonably with these financial assets that offer this cash  at our disposal. And, therefore, we take rather the wind out of the sales of those who are propagating for an  externalization of the nuclear liabilities in conjunction with a straight funding of them.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Well, if you reduce it to such a narrow tradeoff, yes. But as I said, it's not put against nuclear alone; it's put against  our whole liability side, which is now more non-financial debt than financial debt and, therefore, we want to  manage it differently. And I don't believe in outsourcing these tasks to a state agency that this make things better.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Let me start with the second one and then Bernhard can give some further thought on restructuring charges. The  double-digit growth of Innogy is as it was originally planned. There's no change to the plans that we've previously  disclosed on Innogy. And if you look into that, a portion of it is that one-off charges for the rate, we've had some  negative impact from business activities that weren't as successful, which we cleaned out. Secondly, there is wind  parks coming on stream on grid and delivering their returns. That's where the growth comes for the next years to  come.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Yes. Hi, Bobby. This is Bernhard. With regard to your first question, well, on Slide 7 you see this highly stylized  numbers, which might still include some assets which are slightly cash negative. And as far as I can remember, at  least we never said that a) all cash flow negative power plants will be shut down immediately because it – the main  criterion for that is, what part of the cash negativity would go away when you close it down. And especially, for  example, on lignite, where you have this kind of symbiotic relationship between the lignite mines and the power  station, this is a more complex issue than just fuel prices and power prices minus operating cost. And the second  one is, that even some of the mothballed plants still cause slightly negative cash flows.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: With regard to your second question comparing our slides on the overall efficiency program and total controllable  cost, the gap between the two are other effects which we regard operational performance or efficiency  improvement. This is improvements in availability of power plants. This is improvements in retail margins due to  measures on our side. And this has also made improvements to grid margins, for example, throughout the  regulatory cycle.

texts.speaker: Bobby Chada
texts.profession: Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Okay. So, you could characterize some of the efficiency improvements as revenue benefits or availability benefits  rather than just cost reduction?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The next question comes from Deborah Wilkens, Goldman Sachs.  Deborah B. Wilkens  Goldman Sachs International  Q  Yes. Good morning. I will have a question for each of you. The first one is with regard to the financial debt. Post- Dea, it looks as if the net financial debt will be a very low single-digit number, so that's the end of 2015. Is there a  level of absolute financial debt you'd rather not go below? And then the second question, you said in your opening  remarks that the mark-to-market power generation free cash flow neutral is not a sustainable situation. What  does that statement actually mean? What will you do if the environment persist or are you actually expecting  something to change in the government?

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Let me start with the second one, Deborah. Not sustainable – as you call it in English, something has to give in. In  other words, lights go out. And that's a simple conclusion. What it is that has to give in is either the price or the  capacity. And we're pretty sure that either the market will price it and you get fly-ups, high price spikes and  volatility, or the government will put something sensible in place, which makes sure that you have an adequate  return on the power plants and a more secure system. Which of the two it's going to be? I think we'll get some  further clearance over the summer when the green book is being turned into a white book by the German  government.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: There's a variety of data that we could use, okay. And, I mean, just scratches and goes beyond imagination. Take  for example in the Netherlands where we used a Big Data approach by putting the plane with a photo camera in  the air, making pictures of all the houses in a certain area. We then combine that with cadastric information and  with our customer information and we make a specific individualized product offering for photovoltaic panels on  the roof of such house. It measures exactly the potential square feet that is available, the direction, whether it's  south or southeast or southwest bound, and it makes them a full specified product offering for that customer.  That's an example where Big Data has been combined with various data sources, not only from our own customers  but also from public and from own created backgrounds. That is just one example.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: If you really go into the house, there's much more than that, which you can use. For instance, the management of  when a house consumes electricity of a household, but also beyond that, you go into the area of heat and gas  consumption. I think that's another one where there's a lot of advantages in where we can really give some input  to.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: The third wave which is going to come is around the connected home. And I don't think that we already have a  very clear view or what potential will arise around the connected home. What very much is clear it is going to be  around electricity and heat and that is our core business. We know how to handle that, we know how to manage  that, and we know how to make product and product offerings around that.

texts.speaker: Ingo Becker
texts.profession: Kepler Capital Markets SA (Germany)
texts.text: Yes. Thank you. Good afternoon. Two questions. First, on your provision accounting. You left the nuclear mining  discount rate unchanged at 4.6%. I understand because you're working with long-term moving averages and those  have not yet triggered a change yet and I think we understand the relationship between discount rate and  escalation rate. But things did not change this time around. I'm wondering, can we take this off for good and  would you confirm that we should not expect action on this next year? And so this is all for good at this stage?

texts.speaker: Andreas Thielen
texts.profession: MainFirst Bank AG (Broker)
texts.text: Yes. Good afternoon. Firstly, I would like to understand the impact on the D&A from the impairments, if you  could give any direction there? And secondly, with the working capital improvement you're targeting until next  year in total, from what you explained earlier on, the weather effect in the current year is negative, so I just would  like to see if the assumption that the total €750 million improvement is potentially split something like one-third,  two-thirds for the years 2015 and 2016? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: And with regards to your second question, I'm not sure that I fully understood it acoustically. I mean, the  harmonization of those useful lives of the assets leads to overall to a lower depreciation. But on the other hand, we  have an offsetting effect because we commissioned new power stations which leads to higher CapEx, the overall  guidance is around €2.5 billion.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: And then the second question is on slide 7, and this sort of relates to Peter's earlier comment about this not being  a sustainable situation. But can we sort of – do you see this as a sustainable worst case at least from a free cash  flow perspective from the conventional generation? And even if power prices fall a little bit further, do you have  enough levers to pull to keep it cash flow neutral on a medium-term basis? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: In the Doomsday scenario, power prices dropped to a level where we stopped lignite mining. We will be in a  situation that we will have just the cash utilization of provisions in lignite and nuclear and not much cash  generation left. This leads to the innocent bystander the question of where the electricity in Germany should come  from under these circumstances which ties it back to Peter's question, something has to give, yeah.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Secondly, a lot of the people in generation are in lignite mining. It's a very intensive part of the generation  division, work-intensive part. And so far, the whole of the discussion stands or falls with what is the stepping the  hurdle by which we need to cut into the mining activities. But if that happens, I mean, then Germany is really in a  very miserable situation.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Wave 3 also includes the Generation Division. That is why we've announced that and we've also indicated that  there are further cost savings coming out of generation, but I mean, after you've done the low hanging fruit, and  the fruit hanging just above that, the eyes is going to get a bit thinner on the potential which is there to grab  further cost savings out of that.

texts.speaker: Deborah B. Wilkens
texts.profession: Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: Hopefully a simpler one. Could you just – actually just give us the clean EBITDA and operating result for 2014?  Can you just tell the one-offs for us?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Well, Deborah, on the operating result, it's quite simple, in a sense indeed because the one-offs basically balance  each other off, and so we have the – we have a few burdens, which are the asset impairments in generation both  conventional and the renewable and on gas storage. And we have a few positive one-offs and this is pure  coincidence, we have to be precise, a few positive one-offs which offset them, which is both on the change in long- term provisions. We have a slight positive movement. We have book gains from grid sales, like we mentioned, we  have compensation payments in the renewable area, and we had the Gazprom agreement, which was a one-off in a  sense that it also considered the situation till 2016.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: So and this is what you see on the operating results. So basically, the kind of clean operating result would be more  or less the €4.0 billion that we communicated on the EBITDA. I mean, we might want to leave this to you and you  can easily see that some of these aspects are contained in EBITDA, especially the positive ones, whereas the  negative ones, the asset impairments are not part of EBITDA. So the kind of clean EBITDA is therefore  considerably lower. And just as a guidance, if you clean it up, the EBITDA, you probably would see a movement  similar to the operating result compared to last year roughly, and then we would not have exceeded our guidance  by this amount that we did. This was, as we said, due to this different nature of one-off effect.

texts.speaker: Vincent P. Gilles
texts.profession: Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Yes. Thanks for taking the second question. Actually two questions. The first one is we've been on this call for an  hour and 20 minutes and you painted an extremely grim picture of last year, this coming year and the mid-term  future. That is just the way I listened to what you said. Is anything in the exogenous factors influencing your  company, be it carbon reform at the European level, I don't know, external M&A, anything that you believe on  balance could actually turn positive and help your company's growth in the future? That's my first question. Or are  we doomed to see effectively bad news and influence of commodity prices continuously influence in your earnings  offset by what you're doing very effectively?

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: We will grow with renewables. That's a very easy growth option. You've noticed and we've explained that we have  a lot of partners investing with us in renewables by only varying the portion that we take in an offshore wind park  and it does not need to go to 100%, because there's a risk-sharing element to that as well. What we can do, instead  of 15%, also 25% or 35%, that's easy growth to be fueled that we can do.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: And the third area, which we will grow is in the combination of grid and customers mainly in Germany.  [indiscernible] (1:22:08) next to all its detriments on power price has a booming effect in certain business lines,  business products, customer products at the interface between the grid and the customer.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: That is an area where we exclusively are in. That's another area where the telecoms or the Googles of this world  are in. That is something that we've been doing. We have one of the most efficient grids in Germany. We have over  300,000 renewable applications already connected to that grid to build products on the back of that is something  that we take as an advantage. And we haven't started with that only today or yesterday. If you take our Smart  Home product, it's the only feasible working product all over Germany that has been sold more than 100,000  times. But those are the seeds that we have been planting on which we can grow.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Are we seeing that already in this year? Maybe to a portion, but not fully. Is that coming next year? Yeah, most  likely. But do you know what exact the power price is going to be for next year and the year after? So making  promises at this moment in time. I've heard from one of my previous CFOs already the credo which says under- promise, over-deliver. I would rather stick to the underpromising part and maybe over-deliver rather now making  bold statements that do not come to fruition or realization.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: And just for clarification purposes, the growth, the single-digit that Peter referred to was, of course, in the non- conventional power generation part of the company. And if you want to know the net number, give me the power  price, and then we can do a back-of-the-envelope calculation.

texts.speaker: Ingo Becker
texts.profession: Kepler Capital Markets SA (Germany)
texts.text: And the second question on the upcoming photo years in gas and electricity in the DSO business in Germany. I  understand you probably cannot speculate here what the regulator will do. But I was wondering if you have any  indications or any information that you can share with us given the starting of that review now in gas and power?  Thank you.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Yeah. Thank you for that question, this would have otherwise together with the answer to the question to Vincent  Gilles, this would've been part of our closing remarks. Naturally, that what we are developing in Germany is due  and destined to be, if you would call it in German, Exportschlager. I mean, those things can be applied in other  countries, not all of them and not all of them immediately. We'll take the example of solar.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: We've used the technical development in Germany to put competitive solar products into the market in the  Netherlands. That's a very clear and simple example. There are also other examples and it does not need to go  west only. I was in Slovakia on Friday where we have a 49% participation. They, for instance have copied and  pasted some of the things that we have over here or in the UK. Take the example of loyalty card. But the only thing  they do different, they don't give the loyalty card as a kind of a cost factor their customers; they sell it to their  customers and earn money with it.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: On top of that, with the backing of the loyalty card, they, for instance have a product of ramping LED bulbs, so  kind of a sharing profit situation where if you want, you can buy LED light bulbs from us. You don't buy them. You  lease them and the lease fee is being accounted for on your energy bill, and it runs against the energy saving on a  monthly base.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: After two or three years, the light bulbs are yours and you can use them for another time, and then take the full  savings out of that. With that, it sounds a bit like twisting around the edges. We, by now, are the largest seller of  light bulbs, LED light bulbs in all of Slovakia. We sell more than General Electric or any of the other retailers of  their own light bulbs.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: There were other few arguments or a few aspects to that. One of them is, also there a energy transition in a key  vendor is taking place. Currently, some of those countries are burning more oil to produce electricity as in five or  six years from now, they will produce. But that doesn't sound like a good business model. So, they need to convert  to the new goals, maybe gas backup and they need a whole system. They need a grid. They need a wholesale  market. They need trading. All of that.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: In order to design that, it doesn't help if you can only deliver them to get and construct that. You need to have the  whole energy management capabilities that we as a company have. And it's very good news to say that as late as  last week, we have one, the tender for developing the energy concept for the city of Dubai in the Emirates. We've  been in direct competition with major consulting houses like Accenture, McKinsey and Boston Consulting but also  with major technology houses.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board

file: RWE - Q4 2015 Earnings Call 8March2016 630 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 08-Mar-16.pdf

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: First, we are establishing a new international company comprising our grid, retail and renewables business, which  will receive fresh capital, enabling it to fund growth investments. Second, we are implementing further significant  cost savings and efficiency measures to improve the cash flow situation of the company. And third, we won't pay a  dividend to holders of RWE common shares for fiscal 2015 in order to preserve cash and equity. However, let me  emphasize that this decision was not taken out of desperation, but rather as a result of prudent financial  management.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: We want to maintain flexibility when facing our future challenges. With these measures, we aim to put RWE back  on solid ground. We will be better placed to face future developments on the commodities market. We will be able  to accelerate growth in renewables and downstream businesses with the new company. We are strengthening our  balance sheet. We will be better prepared for funding our nuclear liabilities.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: In December, we informed you of our plants to bundle our grid, retail and renewables business in a separa te  company and to list a new company via capital increase. The recent slump in power prices has only underlined our  conviction that this move is necessary to secure the future of the Group.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Our downstream and renewables businesses, which will form the new company, have progressed well over the last  year and have taken a number of further growth initiatives. Our grid business continue to work on new pioneer in  technologies and solutions, which will ensure the energy system's ability to integrate the ever growing renewable  capacity. We have taken further steps to develop energy storage facilities and intelligent grid devices.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: The retail business also successfully expanded its activities. We entered the Slovenian electricity market and  started to sell gas in Poland and Hungary, where we already have electricity supply businesses. However, we also  took the decision to withdraw from the Turkish retail market where we do not see the opportunity to establish a  meaningful presence.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Our network of charging points for electric vehicles has also grown. With some 4,900 charging stations across 20  countries, we are one of the biggest infrastructure operators in Europe in this area.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Last year, we have also agreed to equip various new customers, including Daimler and Volkswagen with charging  solutions. Our renewables business made major strides in the expansion of its installed capacity. Over the course  of 2015, we commissioned two large offshore wind farms bringing our total installed capacity to more than 3.5  gigawatts.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Our operating result more than doubled in 2015 and also exceeded our internal expectations. We also laid the  foundation for further growth with the start of construction of another two offshore wind projects, Nordsee One in  the German Nordsee, and Galloper in the UK.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Let's move on to Conventional Power Generation. This business has been under persistent pressure over the last  few years and there are no signs that this is going to change any time soon, rather the contrary. The business has  worked relentlessly to take out costs and increased efficiencies. So far, we have bee n able to implement measures  with an accumulated net benefit of €1 billion to the operating results. We announced some 9 gigawatt of capacity  measures and reduced the head count by some 3,600 FTEs. However, in recent weeks, we have seen a further  dramatic drop in commodity prices, which puts many of our power plants in an unsustainable position.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: On page 10, you can see the free cash flow situation of our generation fleet by technology. At current power prices,  it should not come as any surprise to you that our lignite operations, including the mines, are no longer able to  cover their full cash costs.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: With regards to the spread positions, situation is a little bit more distinct. The recent power price moves have  largely followed price developments of hard coal, gas and CO2. Our generation spreads for hard coal have  remained fairly constant in Germany, they have slightly declined in the Netherlands, and they have deteriorated  significantly in the UK.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: However, clean spark spreads have recently improved across all our large markets and they've moved quite  considerably, making parts of our gas fleet more profitable again. Nuclear operations are still cash flow positive at  current forward prices, although only marginally. Overall, at prices of €20 per megawatt hour, the fleet is not able  to cover its cash costs.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: The generation business, therefore, continues its efforts to find additional measures to improve its cash flow  situation relentlessly, which is also one of the reasons we are stepping up our overall effic iency program. However,  the speed and extent of the recent power price decline will be extremely difficult to mitigate. The focus remains on  cash flow generation, but it will be challenging to be free cash flow positive at current power prices in the medium- term.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: This brings me to the overall efficiency-enhancement program. I'm very pleased to say that our efficiency program  continues to progress faster than expected. Despite the negative performance at RWE npower, we have delivered  €200 million instead of the planned €100 million in 2015. This brings the total efficiency improvement achieved  since 2012 to €1.6 billion. But we are not stopping here. In light of the deteriorating market conditions, we are  stepping up the program by another €500 million to be delivered by 2018.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: As mentioned before, the focus will be on efficiency improvements in the generation business. This takes the total  program to €2.5 billion net benefit to the operating result, which I believe is a significant amount in such a short - time period.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Ladies and gentlemen, this brings me to our CapEx program on slide 12. For 2016, we intend to spend between €2  billion and €2.5 billion. This includes investments in growth projects. €1.8 billion is earmarked for day -to-day  spending and maintenance CapEx. This is in line with our previously communicated intentions to bring CapEx  down to €2 billion. More than half of this amount will be spent on the regulated grid business to support our  regulated asset base. In light of the planned IPO of NewCo, we intend to step up investments in growth  opportunities. The majority of growth projects are within the renewables business.

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: When we decided to propose a suspension of the dividend for common shares for fiscal 2015, as per our dividend  policy, we took into account not only the financial situation of the company, but also the expected mid -term  earnings development of the company. We reached this decision mainly in light of the recent dramatic  deterioration of the earnings prospects of Conventional Power Generation. The current discussions around  funding of nuclear liabilities was also taken into consideration. The decision did not come easy to us as we noted  below disappoint many of our shareholders. However, it is necessary in order to strengthen the compa ny.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: The earnings development in our supply UK division has decreased by €364 million to minus €137 million. This is  mainly a result of process and system related problems with private customer billing, as Peter explained. Besides  the operational problems, lower energy consumption of customers, the shift from standard to non-standard rate  tariff and higher customer losses are also factors for the lower results. The restructuring plan for this division  means that we expect the situation to stabilize in 2016, but will only be fully solved by the end of 2018.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: On the positive side, the operating result of RWE Energy has increased significantly. In fiscal 2015, we have  recorded an operating result of €493 million. Besides underlying earnings improvements from the commissioning  of our offshore wind farms Nordsee Ost and Gwynt y Môr, this is also driven by a positive one -off, above all, from  the sale of stakes in our offshore wind project, Galloper. This alone accounts for an earnings contribution of €93  million. Furthermore, the revaluation of VSE as a result of its full consolidation, it's an improvement of the  operating result in our Eastern European downstream business.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Slide 16 shows the earnings development from EBITDA down to adjusted net income. EBITDA is at €7  billion,  clearly above our guidance of €6.1 billion to €6.4 billion. This is due to the fact that we decided not to finish Bloc k  D of our hard coal power plant in Hamm. In this context, we received among other things insurance payments.  However, we had to write-off the asset fully which accounted for €654 million. But as EBITDA as before  depreciation only the positive effects are reflected in this number, while the operating result reflects the total one- off burden of approximately €130 million.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Slide 17 shows the development of our cash flows from operating activities. It comes down by €2.3 billion to €3.3  billion, mainly due to changes in working capital. First, as explained in our  most recent analyst calls, our most  significant working capital effect is a result of the revised purchasing policy for required CO2 emission certificates.  This had a corresponding positive effect on our cash flows in 2014. Second, due to volatile commodity price  developments, we had higher variation margin payments, both as part of FFO and in working capital.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Second, keep a positive cash balance long-term. Although, as previously mentioned, due to volatile working  capital, this might be at risk in a single given year. Third, dedicate financial assets to long-term provisions. In  doing so, we have now funded more than 20% of our total mining, nuclear and the non-funded pension  commitments.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Let me take the opportunity for a brief comment on the work of the Commission for financing in the nuclear exit.  At the end of February, the CEOs of the utilities met with the co-heads of the Commission. The meeting was  meant to evaluate possible solutions. The Commission is going to continue its work in order to clarify the  outstanding issues. We are in constructive talks, however, any agreement has to be acceptable for both sides.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: For 2016, in Conventional Power Generation, the major drivers expected to be lower realized generation spreads.  The strong earnings decline, we expect for our renewables business is due to the one -offs in 2015, above all from  the sale of our stakes in our Galloper wind project. The earnings improvement for our division, Trading/Gas  Midstream is mainly due to an expected normalized earnings situation from our trading activities after below  average earnings in 2015.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: In our German grid business, we see lower earnings from the sale of grid assets and higher OpEx to improve the  quality of our grid business. In Eastern Europe, we will be mainly affected by the positive one -off in 2015 from the  revaluation of the VSE participation in the context of the full consolidation of the Group. The la tter applies to our  supply business as well. Furthermore, we expect burdens from the restructuring of our UK retail business.

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you. So I have two questions. One is about your chart 10, where you talk about cash loss=making. So my  question really is why isn't RWE being more proactive on closures, so just compare and contrast, SSE decided to  close their coal plant in the UK even though it got a capacity auction. You haven't done anything like that; instead,  you opted to take a pretty low capacity payment in the December auction. And so I want to understand why ther e  aren't more closures?

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: And second question is really what is your clean conventional generation earnings, sort of, if you take off the  impairment, take off the insurance, what's the clean underlying earning for conventional generation in 2015?  Thank you.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: I can – hi Deepa, this is Bernhard. If I understood you correctly, the line was not very good, the first question was  on our slide number 10 and why aren't there further closures. I think there is, you mentioned, explicitly coal UK  on the one hand and there is obviously a question mark around lignite. Lignite, as we have stressed before, is a  complex system, where you don't simply shut individual power plants, you can do so to a certain extent and  effectively this will happen with the [ph] five 200 (29:20) megawatt units, which will go into the standby reserve  soon.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: On coal UK, the situation is such as we understand that even the UK regulator is now becoming a bit more aware  that the UK might be structurally heading for an undersupply and, therefore, we would improve the situation to –  sorry, we would expect the situation to improve somewhat and don't see that the current capacity market auctions  need – or to be extrapolated into the future.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: The second question, if I understood correct, it was, I think, on the underlying earning situation for Conventional  Power Generation in 2015. So underlying probably refers to X one-offs and, in 2015, the major one-offs in power  generation were the non-commissioning of our hard coal unit in Hamm, which was a net effect of €130 million  negative and restructuring charges, which are recognized in operating result, which are of a similar magnitude.

texts.speaker: Bobby Chada
texts.profession: Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Hi. Good afternoon, everybody. My first question is on nuclear. Bernhard, in your speech, you said we need to find  a solution that's acceptable to both sides. Can you give any color on which side feels it's more acceptable right now  and what the remaining points for discussion are?

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: But on the other hand, there is also an issue of what can we afford. Very clearly, the Commission got both as a  working order, find a adequate solution for the financing, but also make sure that the four energy companies that  are concerned can continue to prosper or to survive whatever words you would like to use for that. And surely with  the current electricity power and power price development and with the recent announcements of the rating  agencies, the affordability has come into a slightly different light. Now, there is a gap between those two ambitions  and we need to see in the next weeks whether that gap can be closed or cannot be closed, but we will not be forced  into a deal that we, from a company and from a shareholder perspective, cannot subscribe to.

texts.speaker: Stephan Lowis
texts.profession: Vice President-Investor Relations
texts.text: Ahmed just to – because we seems to have here some bad lines. If we understood your questions correctly, I think  the main implications – what are the main implications on NewCo coming from the – let's say very challenging  situation in the Conventional Power Generation and also the pressure on the rating, was that the question is.

texts.speaker: Lueder Schumacher
texts.profession: Société Générale SA (Broker)
texts.text: The second one is again on the impact of power prices and what will happen in 2017 when most of the hedges will  have run out? I mean, you have indicated that lignite is already no longer able to cover cash costs. So my question  following up on this is what are you actually going to do? I mean you said it's complicated as bigger system to be  considered but are you actually going to stop producing or are you currently still selling forward for 2017 -2018 at  the current price, thereby recognizing that you will take cash losses.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Lueder, this is Bernhard. I would start with the second question, power prices and their impact on Conventional  Power Generation. So we don't expect to – the currently low level of power prices to fully hit our P&L before 2019,  because we have already hedged also for 2018 some volumes at higher prices. And yeah, of course, I think you also  understood that we said at the pro forma forward prices for the future, the power generation would not be cash  positive, especially lignite has turned cash negative.

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: As we said before, closure decisions on lignite are not as easy as on – in terms of telling what is the right step as  they are for other power plants. Because it always, or if you close a significant amount of plants, you also will  have  effects, negative effects on the mining operations. And therefore, we are now in a new ball game and we will have  to first analyze the situation internally and then potentially as Peter said, in the press conference earlier today,  also discuss together with politics and potentially the unions on what the implications from this analysis would be.

texts.speaker: Lueder Schumacher
texts.profession: Société Générale SA (Broker)
texts.text: And thank you very much for [ph] the €400 million (39:52). Can I just ask one on the lignite question. I mean,  you don't have to close lignite, all you have to do is not to run it, not to sell volumes and  you would still see a merit  order impact. But I say you still going to be operated and running them or the option of just not running them, but  not closing the whole station?

texts.speaker: John B. Musk
texts.profession: RBC Europe Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Y eah, morning, everybody. Sorry to come back to the generation fleet, but a slightly different question on the  nuclear plant. Typically we've seen other people or we have seen other people close down plants when you have a  big CapEx even given that these plants, as you said, are basically operating small cash losses. Is there any risk of  you shutting down any of the nuclear fleet earlier than the current plan? And then secondly, jus t is there any  clarity or more precise guidance you can give on the tax rate we should expect in 2016?

texts.speaker: Vincent P. Gilles
texts.profession: Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Y es, good afternoon, everyone. Coming back to two points on nuclear inevitably. Apparently in a press conference,  Bernhard, you said that 40% of the nuclear liabilities are covered they say in cash, but I'm not sure that's what you  said. And, obviously, you talked about 20% earmarked level. So if you could help us understand which assets have  been earmarked, discussion we had last year, obviously, but maybe more precision would be helpful.

texts.speaker: Mark Lewis
texts.profession: Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Y es, good afternoon, everybody. I had a question relating to the 2020 German Government emissions targets,  which seems to have dropped off everybody's radar recently. But as things stand at the moment, the latest reading  I've seen from the German Government is that the German Government is on track to meet its EU burden sharing  targets for 2020, but still some way short of the 40% domestic emissions reduction target.

texts.speaker: Mark Lewis
texts.profession: Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: How should we be thinking about that? Do you think the government is still determined to meet the emissions  reduction target for 2020? I mean, the gap seems to be very large. Y ou're looking at probably an extra 60 million  or 7 0 million tons of CO2 that would need to be reduced in order to meet that target. Is the government still  determined to meet in your view? And if so, does that mean there is an extra risk above and beyond the many risks  you've already highlighted on this call to coal and lignite generation between now and 2020?

texts.speaker: Peter Terium
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Y eah, hi, Mark. I don't see that much of an extra risk at this moment in time. It clearly has been a battle to get to  the agreement last year to meet the 2020 target at least on paper. Whether there is a gap or not differs from, I'd  say, who you ask and who has a look at it. There's even been out a recent report, which has been not getting a lot of  publicity, but which says with the actual programs in place you might even overachieve the reduction targets for  2020. So, so far, I don't see any political appetite, at least not from the current government to change anything to  what was – with quite a lot of efforts achieved last year.

texts.speaker: Andreas Thielen
texts.profession: MainFirst Bank AG (Broker)
texts.text: Y es, good afternoon. Two questions. Firstly, if I look on your CapEx chart, the €400 million for conventional  generation, is that the absolute bottom or would you be able, in the light of the current development, to reduce  that any further? And secondly, from Peter's comment initially on the nuclear funding discussion, is it correct to  think that, I mean, in the end it would be a proposal, which will be an agreement between the nuclear operators  and the government? Or is that the idea that the government will impose whatever they deem as the right thing on  the operators?

texts.speaker: Bernhard Günther
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Y eah, maybe to your first question on slide number 12 with our CapEx breakdown, the €400 million, which are  labeled Conventional Power Generation, that's not that we are building power stations in secret, hidden away from  the capital market, but this is the day -to-day CapEx and especially not only in the power stations, but also in the  lignite mine. There's a significant amount of expenses, which are activated on the balance sheet and the lignite  mines. As for example, the real estate, which is bought and sold again as the line moves through the landscape. So  can it be brought down? Y es, it can be brought down, because it also contains maintenance CapEx both for mining  and for generation. And as we expect, the assets there even more or so, I would expect this number to go down  slightly, yeah.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Operationally, we closed the year in line with our guidance. Adjusted net income was even slightly above the  range we gave in March, but we have significant one-off effect in our non-operating and financial result mainly  due to impairments of our conventional generation fleet and changes to nuclear provisions as a consequence of  the intended nuclear energy fund. We have the financing for the nuclear energy fund in place and will pay the full  amount of €6.8 billion on July 1. So, we no longer have to be a significant political risk linked to this part of the  liabilities.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On this occasion, I'm happy to confirm that last week, an agreement has been reached with the government on a  supplementary public-law contract. It is to be signed once the law comes into force up on receiving EU subsidy  law clearance. In this context, we have agreed to withdraw from the [ph] CARD claims (02:40) related to waste  disposal and the moratorium claim. The agreement does not include the constitutional claim, nor the nuclear fuel  tax claim. For the latter, we expect a final decision this year.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: First, the decision not to complete the second block of our new hard coal-fired power plant in Hamm in 2015 led to  compensation payments of more than €500 million. While this is reflected in adjusted EBITDA and adjusted EBIT,  the corresponding write-down of the plant of approximately €650 million is included in adjusted EBIT.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On the positive side, we will see no further burden from the nuclear fuel tax, which will by law phase out at the  end of 2016. In 2016, we paid approximately €0.15 billion. In addition, we are working on further efficiency  improvements.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Now, onto the performance of the Trading/Gas Midstream division. Adjusted EBIT fell by approximately €300  million to minus €145 million, as a result of the negative trading performance especially in the second quarter.  Although it is a high loss, it is still in the range of our expected business volatility. At the Capital Markets Day, we  will provide a comprehensive insight into the performance and management of this division.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Slide 8 shows the details of non-operating result, which is dominated by the impairment charges mainly on the  German generation fleet and the risk premium on the nuclear provisions of approximately €1.8 billion with the  nuclear energy fund.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Financial result on slide 9 also contains significant special items. It is impacted by the adjustment of the net  present value of the nuclear and other long-term provisions. Furthermore in 2016, we incurred losses from the  sale of securities, while in the year before we realized profits. In 2017, we will see [indiscernible] (09:25), a decline  of the regular interest accretion to provision of approximately €0.4 billion to €0.5 billion as a result of the lower  discount rates and the externalization of nuclear provisions into the nuclear energy fund.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Now, onto adjusted net income on slide 11. Here you see the details of the adjustments which lead to an average  adjusted net income of €777 million in 2016. Let me give you some explanations to the individual adjustments. As  usual, the complete non-operating result is reversed. In the financial result, the adjustment of the net present  value of the nuclear provisions due to the change in real discount rate is eliminated.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On slide 13, you can see the details of our net debt development. It came down by €2.8 billion since the end of  2015. The proceeds from the listing of innogy and further sales of innogy shares more than outweighs the  additional burden from the risk premium for the nuclear energy fund of €1.8 billion and the increase in provisions  due to lower discount rates.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Nuclear provisions increased by €2.2 billion to €12.7 billion at the end of 2016. This splits into €7 billion which will  be transferred into the nuclear energy fund and the residual nuclear provisions for the decommissioning of the  nuclear power plants and operational waste management. The €7 billion is a fully consolidated figure which  includes E.ON's minority stake in the Emsland nuclear power plant. The economic stake for RWE is €6.8 billion.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The residual provisions which will stay on the RWE's balance sheet amount to €5.7 billion. Here we have digested  an additional €0.9 billion from the change of the real discount rate from plus 0.9% down to minus 0.9%. This is  partly offset by the release of provisions due to lower expected decommissioning costs.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Let's now look at the liquidity position of RWE stand-alone. We have said that we want to pay the €6.8 billion into  the nuclear energy fund on July 1. On slide 16, you can see that we have sufficient funds available. The  remaining available liquidity after transferring €6.8 billion to the fund amounts to some €3 billion at December 31.  In addition, we have our commercial paper program in place, of which €0.5 billion were used at the end of the last  year. Finally, we have a committed syndicated credit facility of €2.5 billion and uncommitted bank guarantees of  €2.3 billion as additional reserves.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: We expect adjusted EBITDA to reach between €5.4 billion to €5.7 billion and adjusted net income of €1 billion to  €1.3 billion. Adjusted EBITDA would be moderately above 2016 due to improved earnings in our Trading/Gas  Midstream Division and a better expected result at innogy. This over compensates an expected earnings decline  in the generation business. Adjusted net income shows disproportionally strong increase.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: 2016 was a year of significant restructuring and heavy burdens for RWE. We have a significant liquidity  requirement in 2017 to finance the nuclear energy fund. Against this backdrop, we don't see any room for paying  a dividend on common shares for fiscal year 2016.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Furthermore, we are looking at RWE stand-alone and not the consolidated IFRS figures. This means that the  operating cash flow from joint Conventional Power Generation and Trading/Gas Midstream and the dividend that  we receive from innogy are relevant. On that basis, we have set the 2017 dividend target at a level which we can  afford mid-term from an earnings and cash flow perspective. texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Furthermore, we want to improve the general transparency of the operational part of our business. You will have a  chance to meet senior management of our operational business, Conventional Power Generation and  Trading/Gas Midstream and use this opportunity to drill deeper in these units. texts.speaker: Alberto Gandolfi
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: The second question is related to the first one, but separate in a way. What is your long-term vision?
