And here  on the generation side, we have saved around €200 million in 2016 compared to 2015. This is now without  innogy. Rest of the costs are more or less stable. And we also expect further efficiency improvements or cost  cutting for the years to come.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. I mean, I will not comment on what some of our competitors did, but what I can explain to you, what  happened here without revealing the actual positions we had. I mean, most of the losses stem from the second  quarter. What, in the second quarter happened, if you look at commodity prices, we have seen a massive drop,  let's take German base load exit proxy, but I mean, the entire fuel complex dropped in line with that to €20 in  February-March.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Now we will give you more details on the Trading division, but if you look at the comparable like-for-like results of  Trading, and I mean the division was highly impacted by the significant positive and negative one-off of the oil  index gas contract and the out-of-the-money gas storages where we have solved all problems. So from now on  you'll see clear figures.

texts.speaker: Ahmed Farman
texts.profession: Analyst, Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: Okay. And just one clarification here, the provisions you're referring to [indiscernible] (36:59) both nuclear lignite  mining and pension provisions?

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Yeah. Is that clear? Yeah. So my first question is, I noticed you've done a write back of your nuclear  decommissioning provision. Could you just help us understand what was the basis for that and whether based on  more near-term experience on the costs or what was the basis?

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Okay. Thanks for the question. The first one on the provision, we have two effects on the nuclear provision side,  the first one is the average duration of the remaining provisions are much shorter. It's around 10 years now. So,  according to IFRS, we have to change the methodology for discounting. We are now using market rates. So the  discount rate is 40 basis points and we assumed inflation is 130 basis points, which leads to negative real  discount rate of 90 basis points. This led to an increase of around €860 million in the provision.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And on the other hand, the remaining liabilities, which are decommissioning and waste treatment are much better  controllable by RWE. We have already experience in this field and we constantly review our assumptions on how  much that will cost going forward. And here, we have seen some productivity increases, efficiency improvements,  and we have factored that in and that led to release of around €460 million. So that on a net basis, provisions  increased by €400 million. Now to the net income question.

texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: So I would have thought that your remaining decommissioning provisions were around €5 billion and if you written  back around €400 million off that?

texts.speaker: Peter Bisztyga
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America, Merrill Lynch
texts.text: Good afternoon. So two questions from me, firstly, can you remind us the reasons why you've set a minimum  ownership threshold of 51% for innogy, is that a purely financial or are there any other reasons for that strategic or  otherwise? And then, secondly, just on the nuclear tax, do you have any more precise timing you can offer us,  when you expect to get final ruling?

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On your first question, cost cutting, so we don't expect any further significant dissynergies from separating the  groups. So, we don't expect build-up of costs. texts.speaker: Lueder Schumacher
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA
texts.text: The second question is, Markus referred earlier to tightness on the continent, latest when you phase out the  nuclear power plants, it seems quite a bullish statement. Apart from closing nuclear capacity, what else is driving  this tightness you're expecting?

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. I mean, let's first talk about the tightness. I mean, we have already seen in January of this year situations in  Germany where without the nuclear production, the consequences would have been very severe. So, it is  definitely there when the nukes go off. The question is now what happens until then.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: If you look at the decommissioning plans of the industry and what they have submitted to the regulator, it is quite  significantly and if nothing happens until the early 2020s, profitability especially of old plants will deteriorate  further. And if nothing happens, then the industry will take the action and we're going to see more closures. And  then especially in winter times, the capacity becomes tight earlier than in the early 2020s. Now, I think if you look  back what happened in the UK, it is maybe a good case example of what could happen also on the continent.

texts.speaker: Javier Garrido
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Chase Bank, NA (Spain)
texts.text: And the second question is more a separate question about this topic of the coverage of the cash outflows linked  to provisions. texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: I mean, the second question, I haven't seen the statement of Mr. Herdan today, but what I have seen is a  statement of our Chancellor and she said, we need to approach the coal exit very carefully due to several  reasons, security of supply, social consequences in the affected regions and so on. I think that discussion we will  have, but to be honest, I mean, what we experienced over the last couple of months and weeks is much more  muted now than it was earlier this year. It depends on the German election and then we see – and we take it from  there after the election. But I think it's not as it was a couple of months ago because everybody has realized what  the situation now is.

texts.speaker: Sam Arie
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd.
texts.text: Hi. Thank you. Yes. I queued up and came around for another question. [indiscernible] (01:04:12) towards the  end of the line. But I just wanted to come back to one of the first things you said on the call today regarding an  agreement that you've reached on a private law contract to the transfer of nuclear provisions and then giving up  some additional claims you have there.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. I think both sides, the government as well as utilities had a strong interest in having this contract for a  couple of reasons. The most relevant is, I mean, it's a highly complicated process in itself that we dismantling and  repackage the nuclear waste and then we move that over and the government is responsible for storing. So, an  exact technical specification how that interface works was in the best interest of both parties because otherwise  you potentially end up in lifelong law cases fighting what is the right specification because if there is a change in  specification, it also changes who pays what kind of element of the bill. So, there was – that we have full clarity on  what we have to transfer. That was the first one.

texts.speaker: Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Then we had a strong interest because a public contract, it's much better than a law. It cannot be changed without  the consent of both parties. The law can be changed by parliament. And, I mean, you can now say what did you  give, I mean two things. The first one is we have a lot of claims still related to storage. So, we had lot of claims  which are related to those part of the value chain. So, to say which are now with the government and that is an  awkward position that still run claims where we are not liable. So, we will withdraw all these claims and then in  addition to that, we also withdraw the moratorium claim regarding the Biblis power plant and that is more or less  the deal of the contract.

texts.speaker: Ahmed Farman
texts.profession: Analyst, Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: Yeah. Hi. Just one more follow-up question. I wanted to come back to comments you made earlier about the  power generation supply-demand balance tightening, and you mentioned nuclear shutdowns towards the end of  the second. Do you also see corporate consolidation within the power generation space has also helping the  supply-demand balance, or is that a theme or fact that you don't see much happening on in the next 12 to 18  months? If you could share your views on that, that will be very helpful. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Peter Bisztyga
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America, Merrill Lynch
texts.text: Hi, there. Just a quick one on nuclear provisions. Could you clarify what benchmarks you're using for the discount  rates and inflation assumptions? And are these now going to be updated every quarter as you do with pension  provisions?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Welcome to the RWE Conference Call on the Sale of Energy Stake to E.ON and the Business  Performance for RWE's Fiscal Year Results 2017 with Rolf Martin Schmitz and Markus Krebber.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Thank you, Gunhild, and good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Today, we cannot only look back at a very  successful first year for the new RWE, but also look ahead to an exciting future. Before I go into the details on the  sea change deal, we have agreed with E.ON that we'll very quickly highlight what we accomplished last year.  RWE's core business performed strongly last year. Supply & Trading restored its profitability. Commercial asset  optimization achieved above-average earnings contribution, and our efficiency program is well on track.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Adjusted EBITDA therefore came in above our expectations, and adjusted net income is at the upper end of the  benefits. I'm also pleased that we have restated a dividend for fiscal 2017. Both, the executive and supervisory  boards [ph] have proposed in which (00:01:46) operational dividend of €0.50 as well as a special dividend of €1  per share as part of the refund of the nuclear fuel tax through the AGM next month.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: In mid-2017, we saw the discussions on the responsibilities for nuclear waste disposal come to a successful  conclusion. We were able to transfer the full amount of €6.8 billion to the government at the first possible date  without any negative implications for our balance sheet, rating or liquidity situation. The conclusion of a property  contract with a German government also provides us with a high level of legal certainty.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: At our Capital Markets Day last year, we committed ourselves to the value maximizing management of our innogy  stake. We believe yesterday's announcement goes a step further. With the envisaged transaction we are  transforming RWE into a leading European generation company providing both clean renewable power as well as  security of supply. The combination of innogy and E.ON's renewables businesses will also create one of the  largest platforms in Europe in this field. In offshore wind, we will become the second largest operator. The scale of  the combined operations will provide scope for efficiencies and a platform for attractive growth opportunities.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Our leading trading platform will provide the commercial link between renewables and our flexible conventional  generation portfolio. As renewables become increasingly competitive and moving towards deregulation, we see  attractive opportunities to optimize the combined portfolio. The transaction will significantly enhance our earnings  and cash flow profile.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Page 6 shows the shape of RWE after the conclusion of the transaction. At that point, we will be a fully  operational company again. The combined renewables business will provide us with a strong new operating  segment, while we will also have access to an attractive portfolio of financial assets. The assumption of innogy's  gas storage supports Supply & Trading ambitions to grow its gas and LNG business. With gas gaining in  importance, the storage facilities will become more attractive again in future.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Let's now have a look at the combined generation portfolio. Together, with the two renewables portfolios of innogy  and E.ON, we will have a highly diversified and well-balanced generation mix. Over 60% of the capacity will be  CO2-free or low emission. This includes our highly efficient gas fleet. The renewable capacity will clearly de-risk  our generation portfolio with regards to carbon.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: However, I would like to briefly comment on our efforts to reduce CO2 in our conventional generation fleet. Since  2012, we have continuously reduced carbon emissions. Last year alone, we brought down our emissions by more  than 10% compared to the previous year and this at a time when CO2 emissions are stagnating in Germany. We  will continue to strive to bring down emissions, but see our conventional generation fleet with its reliable and  flexible plants as an important part of the future energy system.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The new combination allows us to provide both clean as well as reliable energy, something which will become  increasingly important as the energy transition is to be successful. Over time, renewables will have to be operated  in the wholesale market either because their subsidy schemes expire or they need to prevail in highly competitive  auctions. Our commercial asset optimization is ideally positioned to integrate an increasingly merchant  renewables portfolio with our flexible generation portfolio to extract value by optimizing this combined portfolio.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On page 8, you can see that this transaction is also transformational for the renewables business. Combining the  two platforms of innogy and E.ON will create the third largest renewables player in Europe. In offshore wind, we  will become the second largest player. The focus of the two renewables businesses is currently on onshore and  offshore wind. However, both players have ambitions to grow in solar as well as battery storage solutions and  have recently taken steps to develop their capabilities in this area.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Regionally, the combined portfolio is well balanced. In addition, E.ON's platform provides a strong operating  onshore wind platform in the U.S., a market where innogy intends to grow and has recently agreed to acquire a  development pipeline. We are convinced that the enlarged portfolio provides the scale to prevail in this  increasingly competitive market and scope for optimization. At the same time, there's a financial headroom to  develop this business further as we see attractive growth opportunities in onshore and offshore wind as well as  solar.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Slide 10 shows the key transaction parameters. Fundamentally, the transaction is an exchange of assets. E.ON  will acquire our 76.8% stake in innogy for an equity value of €17.1 billion, which equals €40 per share. The  minority shareholders of innogy will get a €40 cash offer from E.ON. This implies an equity valuation of innogy of  €22 billion and an enterprise value of €43 billion. This is equivalent to an implied EV to EBITDA multiple of 10.5  times, based on expected 2018 earnings. In exchange for the value of €17.1 billion, we will get the renewables  business of E.ON and innogy. This excludes minor renewable assets held by the different regional companies, as  well as a 20% stake in Rampion.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Furthermore, we received innogy's German and Czech gas storage business as well as its 37.9% stake in Kelag.  In addition, we will take over E.ON's minority stakes in our nuclear power plants Gundremmingen and Emsland.  We will also receive shares in E.ON amounting to a 16.7% stake post transaction. These shares are entitled to  dividend payments from fiscal 2019 onwards.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: For all the efforts we receive, especially the renewables businesses, we are entitled to the economic success  from January 2018 onwards. For technical reasons, we will also receive the innogy dividend for fiscal 2017 and  2018. Therefore, the transaction includes a balancing cash payment of €1.5 billion from us to E.ON.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Rolf already mentioned the strengthening of our financial profile. With regards to our earnings, we see a step  change as our EBITDA will double as a result of the transaction. Income from dividends will be of minor  importance in the future with over 90% of earnings coming from operational businesses. Renewables will account  for approximately 60% of pro forma EBITDA.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: In addition, we will have a higher degree of feasibility for our medium-term earning development, as  approximately 50% of our expected operating EBITDA will come from contracted businesses such as capacity  payments for conventional power generation, ROCs, CfDs, PPAs or fixed feed-in tariffs for the renewables  business. The transaction will also improve our financial position. As a result of the transaction, we will only  assume approximately €2.8 billion of debt to our standalone balance sheet.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Since we are becoming a mostly operational company, we can also look at traditional leverage ratios again, which  do not make much sense for RWE standalone now. Post transaction, we expect our net debt to EBITDA to be  between 2.5 times and below 3 times. We expect this to be in line with our current investment-grade rating which  we are strongly committed to maintain. We have the financial headroom to support all existing growth ambitions in  both renewables businesses. In addition, the financial portfolio provides additional financial flexibility.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: In the second step, E.ON will implement steps to further – to gain full control of innogy under corporate law. Once  this is finalized, the final transaction steps will take place. We will receive the innogy and E.ON renewables  businesses, the gas storage activities as well as the stake in Kelag. We currently expect the whole transaction to  be closed by year-end 2019. As you can see, the transaction is complex and will take almost two years to  complete. During this time, we will continue to steer the company with our economic view on RWE standalone,  and we will provide full disclosure and transparency on its main KPIs. This will be important, as the transaction will  have significant implications for our IFRS group results.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Before we come to your questions, let me reiterate the strong strategic rationale for this transaction and the  compelling outlook for RWE. For RWE, this is a unique combination of our existing business model of a provider  of security capacity with the growing market of renewables. Our leading commercial asset management and  trading capabilities will ensure that we can extract additional value from the combination of the combined  platforms. This will become even more important as more and more renewable assets will become merchant over  time.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: I will not go into the details of our 2017 results. Gunhild already mentioned that you can find all the details in the  usual format on our website. texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: But I mean, from our guidance, you'll see that the midpoint of our EBITDA guidance is around €1.55 billion. And  we said we expect EBITDA to double. texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: I think the market expect, if you combine E.ON's and innogy's renewables business, EBITDA to grow significantly  over the next four, five years at least 40% to 50%. texts.speaker: Deepa Venkateswaran
texts.profession: Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: And secondly, in terms of the renewables businesses, now these will be run by E.ON and innogy, so you need to  obviously make sure that these projects are done on time, well within budget, done within the deadline for the  U.S. PTC. But there are also things like offshore wind auctions coming up, FIDs need to be taken. So, how do you  ensure A, that the existing products are executed; and then, B, projects that will need FID in 2018 or 2019 are  done so that, when you acquire these businesses in 2020, you can start executing on them? So, if you can just  help explain how that will work in practice. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Just to say, first, there's no combination or no link to the profit warning. It's coming from the difference now what  renewables business is. Now, two years ago, that was a regulated business. Renewables business was regulated  and now it's much more competitive. It's an auction to organize and so on. And therefore, it's not. It does not fit to  E.ON and not really fit to innogy. That's the first point.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The second point is innogy and E.ON has seen that they cannot – that they do not have the capital power – the  financial power for all these three businesses, renewables, retail and grids. Therefore, it was to decide which will  they go further on and which we can we do further on. And we decided that we can combine good retail and good  business with E.ON and that the other partner's renewables business and so far electricity producing business  with us.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: I would say it makes very easy. If I would be in the management board of one of these renewables companies, I  would do all my best because, later on, we have to decide with whom we will go further on and that's the best  incentivization – incentives we can give.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Deepa, we have agreed that, I mean the beauty of the concept is that commercially the renewables business  assuming the transaction goes through which we currently assume, commercially it's already with us from  January 1st. So there is no incentive of – for the energy or E.ON to not do any investments on so on because we  have to pay for the investment but we also get the economic benefits of the businesses. So there's no  misalignment of incentives. And we have also agreed that to the legally – to the extent legally possible, we will  have joint investment and financing committees but only to the extent where it's allowed that we can get involved  until closing one. So we think we have done everything which is possible to ensure that business runs as it  should.

texts.speaker: Peter Bisztyga
texts.profession: Analyst, Merrill Lynch International
texts.text: Yeah. Good afternoon. Just a question on your geographic exposure. Clearly, once you've acquired the  renewables businesses, you're going to have a much broader geographic footprint. Would you consider investing  in conventional generation in those new regions? So, that's my first question. And then, the second one – just  quick one on E.ON. Is there a specific lock-up period for your 16.7% stake?

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: We will not invest in conventional generation in other areas as we are, Benelux, U.K. and Germany. We will not  go to the other markets where renewables are there. The second one?

texts.speaker: John Musk
texts.profession: Analyst, RBC Europe Ltd.
texts.text: Yeah. Hi, guys. Just one actually from me. I think at the beginning you talked around the gas storage business in  quite a positive light and the expected recovery you thought might come through there. Just wanting to get some  clarity on what you think the drivers of that will be. Your new friends at E.ON were talking up their electricity  business rather than their gas business earlier today?

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: I mean, on the gas storage business, it's a business which is now, I mean maybe definitely at the bottom in  Europe. And if we really transform and that's the political will, the entire generation business – power generation  business when it comes to security of supply, especially in Germany, to gas, because we phase out our nuclear  and we phase out over time – maybe a long period of time, coal, then it all depends on gas. And as you've  already seen this winter, especially in the UK, but also on the Continent, that flexibility in gas has increased  significantly in value given the shortage that we have seen and we think it's definitely a good idea to go long, gas  flexibility, that is nothing else you take when you buy gas storages.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And I think one of your colleagues has already published I think three or four days, an interesting piece,  discussing the potential turnaround of gas storages. Well timed.

texts.speaker: Lueder Schumacher
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA (UK)
texts.text: Hi. Good afternoon. Two questions for me. The first one is on the rationale for including the minority stakes in the  nukes in the deal given that it effectively leads to you taking on €800 million of nuclear provisions. That's the first  one. The second one is on your CO2 hedges. You mentioned that you're now fully hedged until the end of 2022. I  seem to recall that it's not too long ago that you started hedging for Phase 4. Have you stepped up your hedging,  given that CO2 just seems to be going up and up?

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: To the first question, with minority stakes, it makes it a little bit easier. We see some potential in the  decommissioning of the plant that we will not – that maybe we will not use all the provisions for that. And it was  one of the [ph] parts (00:40:15) who makes the deal easier for both sides. That's one of the reasons. And we have  the electricity [ph] contingents (00:40:29) to fulfill all the applications until the end of 2021 and end of 2022.  Therefore, we have discussed this last year before with E.ON in any way, and it was one additional part of the  whole agreement.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Yeah. Lueder, on carbon, I mean, to be clear what I meant, we are financially fully hedged. We have not covered  our entire carbon short position. But to the extent we needed that we have achieved the [ph] market type  throughout. I mean, market type throughput of (00:40:56) carbon is currently around 0.6%, 0.7%. Our intensity is  much higher, and we have hedged to the extent that we are financially carbon flat, yeah. So if carbon moves up,  power prices will move up accordingly. For the rest, we are hedged.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: And you are right, I mean, we have a much more dynamic hedged approach and you will see that we use a  different fuel and carbon [ph] mix (00:41:22) we have to hedge, maybe much more flexible than we have done in  the past with [indiscernible] (00:41:27). And one of the reasons you are speculating is that we have seen that  carbon market might become tighter was probably one of the reason why we have kept up carbon hedging, yes.

texts.speaker: Lueder Schumacher
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA (UK)
texts.text: Very intrigued. So, just one follow-up question. What is the average carbon intensity of your generation – entire  generation portfolio post the transaction, just to put this in relation to the 0.6% and 0.7% you mentioned for the  German market?

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: I cannot give you a credible number for the post-transaction one because that depends on how exactly you derive  the carbon exposure off the renewables portfolio and correlations between the different markets and the  development and so on. So, that – it's not a reliable number. I'm not willing to give it now. Let's give it another  year. For the existing portfolio we run, the carbon intensity is around 1.1%, yes, 1.1% – 1% to 1.1%...

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: No, no, no. It's too high, it's too high. That was for coal alone. I think it's lower. It's below 1%...

texts.speaker: Martin Samuel Brough
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (UK)
texts.text: Thank you. Yeah. I had a couple of questions. One was – just understanding, to the extent that you have visibility  already on the tax impact of the deal, obviously, you have a lot of tax losses which you haven't recognized on the  balance sheet at this point. Will that be used to offset any potential taxes of the transaction? Or would you expect  a tax impact there? And also, when you're bringing profitable activities in like renewables, will carry-forward tax  losses be a benefit to you?

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: I mean, on the tech side, we will have a very minor tax impact from the transaction. It will be a very low three- million-digit number, around €150 million. And on the tax losses carry-forward, we're going to decide when we  take over the renewables business what that means in accounting. But we have not factored anything in the  current transaction parameters. So, there would only be few upside.

texts.speaker: Christopher Laybutt
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: Good afternoon. Just two questions, please. One, just on dividend policy post deal closing. I apologize if I missed  it. But could you give us an idea of the impact of the renewables businesses as you absorb them on group free  cash flow and how that may play out in the dividend? And then, secondly, just in terms of farm down proceeds in  – within innogy or E.ON, if there were farm-down to occur between now and the transaction closing, what impact  that would have on the economics of the transaction? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On dividend policy and cash flow, I mean, that's too early to tell. I mean, what the renewables business will  contribute to bottom line cash flow will depend on how much CapEx we're going to see from 2020 onwards. And  that is pure speculation on how attractive the investments are in the 2020s right. So, we will come back to you  when we have more clarity maybe end of 2019.

file: RWE - Q4 2018 Earnings Call 14March2019 730 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 14-Mar-19.pdf

texts.speaker: Gunhild Grieve
texts.profession: Head of Investor Relations, RWE AG
texts.text: Thank you very much. Good morning to everyone on the phone and to those of you who are joining us via  webcast. I'm joined here by Rolf Martin Schmitz and Markus Krebber for the presentation on fiscal year 2018 and  the outlook for 2019. Rolf will give you a strategy update, focusing on the progress of our transaction with E.ON,  as well as the status of the discussions around the German coal phase-out. Markus will provide details on our  2018 financial performance and the outlook for 2019. As always, in order to focus on your questions, we have  kept it short.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Thank you, Gunhild, and hello, ladies and gentlemen. 2018 has been pivotal for RWE's future. We have laid the  foundation for the transformation into a fully operational company, again, with a strong and sustainable platform  for future growth. With the envisaged asset swap with E.ON, we are creating the leading renewables player. The  combined platform will be the third largest in Europe and number two in offshore wind globally. More than 60% of  our generation portfolio will be CO2-free or low carbon emitting. And it is also this part of the portfolio in which we  will focus our future growth efforts. The execution of the transaction is well on track and fully within our timeline.  We are also making good progress with the integration planning to ensure a swift and smooth integration of the  new businesses.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: After intensive analysis and works, the Commission on Growth, Structural Change and Employment presented its  final report at the end of January. While the Commission's proposals will have wide range in implications for RWE,  we believe that they provide a good basis to achieve mutual consent on plant closures, providing planning  certainty for our lignite operations.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Irrespective of the discussions of the goals set out, we continue with our own efforts to reduce RWE's carbon  emissions with changes to our generation portfolio. And last but not least, we decided to propose to this year's  AGM, the conversion of our preferred shares into common shares. With this step, every share will bear a voting  right, which is customary on international capital markets and called for by many institutional investors. The  proposed conversion aims not only to strengthen our corporate governance, but also to improve our shares  trading liquidity. This is in the interest of all RWE shareholders.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Let's now have a look at the progress of the transaction with E.ON. We are well on track with the execution of the  transaction and have taken important steps into integration planning. Since our last results call in November, we  have reached some major milestones. Most relevant filings with competition authorities have been submitted. We  have appointed the future renewables management team under the roof of the RWE and we have formulated a  high level strategy for the renewables business.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: On the 17th of January, we announced the future management team and presented the target operating model of  the combined renewables business. The team will be headed by Anja-Isabel Dotzenrath as Chief Executive  Officer who is currently CEO of E.ON's Renewables business. It will further consist of Holger Himmel as Chief  Financial Officer and Tom Glover as Chief Commercial Officer who will be in charge of the commercial  management of the renewable assets.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Holger is currently CFO at innogy Renewables and Tom brings his extensive expertise from RWE where he is  currently responsible for the commercial asset optimization of our conventional generation fleet. The team will be  completed by three Chief Operating Officers who will lead the operational units and be responsible for project  development, as well as construction operations. We are excited to have been able to nominate a highly qualified  and diverse management team with extensive expertise and international experience in the field of renewable  energy.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Before Christmas, we also concluded our high level strategic considerations. The transaction is going to create a  leading renewables player in Europe with a strong position in the U.S. However, our clear strategic ambition is to  take this newly created platform and build a truly global renewables player. The focus will be on the three leading  technologies, Wind Onshore, Wind Offshore, and Solar PV added by storage technologies where we continue to  cover the whole value chain from development through to commercialization.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: We see that these are ambitious aspirations, but we are excited by how the two renewables businesses have  progresses after the last 12 months, and we are confident that the new team will drive the business forward once  the transaction is closed. They will also develop and define the high level strategy further on which we will provide  more details after closing.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Let's now have a look at our current business portfolio. Slide 9 provides an overview of selected focus areas of  our three segments. Within the Lignite & Nuclear segment, we have turned our particular attention to the  decommissioning concept of our nuclear power plants. We have developed a new process focusing on end-to- end dismantling approach, Lean principles and a zero waste attitude in order to optimize the total  decommissioning costs. We've been starting this new approach this year at our Biblis nuclear power plant and  rolled it step by step out to the complete fleet.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Moving on to the European Power segment. In October, we have decided to de-mothball our Dutch CCGT Claus  C with the capacity of 1.3 gigawatt. Improved generation spreads and market perspectives led to this decision.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: We will also continue with the conversion of our Eemshaven and Amer 9 hard coal fired power stations to  increase the biomass coal firing capabilities. The current coal firing capacity at Amer 9 amongst the 50% and is  targeted to reach approximately 80% by early 2020. We are also working on diversifying our biomass sourcing  and focusing on identifying additional sources of biomass.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The focus in the UK is clearly of the management of our generation fleet during the suspension of the capacity  payments. The UK government is sponsoring the reinstatement of capacity markets. That is continuing to operate  a scheme short of making payments to ensure that capacity providers maybe eligible with deferred payments. We  continue to maintain the availability of our power plants and are in constant dialogue with relevant authorities and  other stakeholders to manage the suspension and the impact on our portfolio.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: For Supply & Trading, the focus remains on growing its global LNG business and to expand the Asian business.  In late December 2018, we signed an agreement with the Australian oil and gas company Woodside for the mid- term supply of LNG. This transaction represents another key building block in the further development of RWE's  flexible LNG portfolio.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Supply & Trading also realized further milestones in its Asian expansion. The Singapore office converted into a  principal trading enterprise, which is now concluding both physical and financial transactions in most energy and  energy-related commodities. We also expanded our presence in China by successfully establishing a wholly- foreign-owned enterprise in Shanghai and a branch office in Beijing.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Ladies and gentlemen, Germany should end coal-fired power generation latest by 2038. This, together with  significant early plant closures, was a recommendation by the Commission for Growth, Structural Change and  Employment in the final report.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: As the report did not provide specific details on which plants to close, the majority of early lignite closures are  expected to take place in the Rhenish mining area. RWE is prepared to shoulder the lion's share of some  measures until 2022. However, the implementation of these recommendations will have wide ranging implications  for our lignite operations and employees. It is therefore only right and consistent that the Commission stipulates  adequate compensation for these plant closures, and it is also obvious that compensation must be significantly  higher than the one paid for earlier shutdowns.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: In contrast to the security reserve, the suggested additional plant closures will also have an impact on our mining  operations including substantial redundancies. The Commission also expressed its desire to preserve the  Hambach Forest. We are currently analyzing the technical feasibility of this request. What is already clear is that  maintaining the forest will cause additional burden.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Having said all that, we believe that the Commission's proposal is a good basis for discussions with the  government. We have a clear chance to reach an agreement on the phase-out of coal-fired power generation in  Germany, which will be supported by a broad public consensus. It would ensure that the energy sector will reach  its ambitious climate targets and provide planning certainty for operators.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Ladies and gentlemen, RWE is fully aware of its environmental and social responsibility, especially when it comes  to climate change. We therefore have set ourselves ambitious CO2 reduction targets and our efforts are paying  off. Since 2012, there's been on a continuous path to bring down our carbon emissions. In 2018, we saw another  reduction of 10% compared to 2017. This means that we have now lowered our emissions by more than 50  million tonnes or 30% compared to 2012, which puts us fully on track to achieve our 2030 target. This  implementation of the Commission's recommendation would accelerate our emissions reduction and end coal- fired power generation by 2038 at the latest.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Coming back to the more immediate future, it is clear that 2019 will be a transformational year. We are working  full steam ahead on the execution of the transactional preparation for the integration of the renewables business.  We are excited and looking forward to become a leading renewables company as well as developing and  expanding business further.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Our hedge strategy has also shown to be beneficial in light of the recent development in spreads, as you will see  later on our hedge slide. And against the backdrop of a volatile and rising CO2 market, our strategy to hedge our  portfolio against higher CO2 prices proved to be the right decision. As part of the optimization of our capital  structure, we announced at the beginning of February that we would exercise the right to redeem the £750 million  hybrid at the first call date on March 20 this year.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Further cost improvement had a positive effect. By the end of 2018, we had reached our efficiency improvement  target of €200 million targeted for 2019 compared to 2016 for the most part. CapEx in 2018 remained on a  relatively high level. This is driven by accelerated resettlement activities in our lignite mining business. We  currently recognize an increased interest from affected residents in the mining area to move location in light of the  ongoing uncertainty. We expect a similar trend in 2019.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: The outlook does not yet include any potential impact from the proposal of the Growth, Structural Change and  Employment Commission. We have to await the outcome of the negotiations with the government, while it  remains unclear what impact the proposed coal phase-out will have on our earnings. We currently don't expect  major implication for our adjusted EBITDA in 2019.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: The European Power division shown on slide 17 realized an earnings decline of approximately €130 million. Out  of this, €80 million refer to non-recurring items in fiscal year 2017 mainly from the sale of real estate in the UK.  Our hard coal and gas plants realized lower margins. However, we saw higher revenues from the UK capacity  market, but this was less than we had originally expected. Under the UK capacity market regime, we had secured  payments of approximately €100 million for 2018. For Q1 to Q3 2018, we received payment of around €50 million.  The remaining €50 million for 2018 are outstanding as the UK capacity market was suspended in November last  year after the decision of the European Court of Justice

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: The UK government has indicated that it want to maintain the capacity market which prompted the EU to open an  in-depth investigation last month. We will have to await the EU Commission's decision to know if we will receive  the suspended payment at a later point in time. Operating cost improvements were another positive factor. Similar  to our Lignite & Nuclear division, we have already achieved our efficiency targets that we had set ourselves for  2019 for the most part. At European Power this is an annual efficiency improvement of €100 million compared to  2016.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: CapEx increased to €245 million. This is driven by higher maintenance CapEx for our generation fleet and growth  projects such as our biomass conversion in the Netherlands. We expect CapEx to stay on this level in 2019. We  will see a peak in inspection and overhauls of our gas and hydro assets in 2019. For our earnings outlook for  2019 of €250 million to €350 million, we don't assume any income from the UK capacity market as long as the  legal situation is unclear. Originally, we had secured revenues of approximately €180 million for the fiscal year  2019.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Now to our current hedge position on slide 18. Average hedge prices for our outright position in 2020 and 2021  increased by €1 and €4 respectively compared to the level we reported in Q3. The gain of €4 per megawatt hour  for 2021 is mainly due to the increase in hedge ratio from more than 60% to more than 80%. Additional hedges  were concluded at market prices which were significantly above the average hedge price. However, locked-in  carbon cost also increased to €7 per megawatt hour. This increase in carbon cost is rather moderate because the  financial carbon exposure above the market pass through factors was hedged in the past at favorable prices.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: The outright volumes showed on this slide reflect the expected production restrictions from the court decision on  the Hamback Forest. Due to optimization measures, we expect only a negative impact of approximately 5 terawatt  hours for 2019. And for 2020 and 2021, our expectation is more towards the upper end of the corridor of 9  terawatt hours to 13 terawatt hours. The slide does not yet include any impact from potential further plant closures  as a result of the proposal from the Growth, Structural Change and Employment Commission as it's still unclear  which plants will close by then. We hope to have more clarity by the end of this year.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Let's move on to Supply & Trading on slide 20. Adjusted EBITDA has held slightly short of our average earnings  level of approximately €200 million while trading closed for the year below last year's level and our principal  investment business suffered from a value adjustment. Our gas and LNG activities again showed a very strong  performance.

texts.speaker: Dr. Markus Krebber
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member of Executive Board, RWE AG
texts.text: Furthermore, the distributable cash flow is lower than we expected in Q3 2018 when we guided for a positive  change in operating working capital. This is a timing effect due to higher gas inventories as well as unusual high  net accounts receivable. We expect this to reverse in 2019 which ceteris paribus will have a positive effect of  approximately €250 million on our change in working capital for this year.

texts.speaker: Vincent Gilles
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Yes. Thank you. Good morning, good afternoon, everyone. Two questions. The first one is on compensation for  early closure of coal and lignite plants. Mr. Schmitz, you're quoted in Reuters today talking about €1.2 billion per  gigawatt to €1.5 billion per gigawatt. I get it right at the end. Question is obviously whether you really said that? It's  reported by the press, but I don't really trust them. And on which basis you can come to that number? We've seen  that number in the past, but also maybe if you can share with us why you're coming out with this number because  you have a high degree of certainty, it's reasonable or you had conversation with the government? Anything you  can share with us. That's question number one.

texts.speaker: Vincent Gilles
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Question number two is on renewables. Over the last 10 days, all of us have gone through CMD's presentations  from large utilities in Europe, and the magic number seems to be 2 to 3 gigawatt of renewable capacity per year.  I'm wondering whether there would be enough projects actually available given the number of candidates now.  But my question is how can you – or what will be your unique selling point in a way? What will you be doing  differently from the crowd that will ensure us that you will be creating value and renewables at a time of very high  competition for a limited number of assets? Thank you very much.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: Thank you for the question. First to compensation, there is no other number and there will be no other number  than €1.2 billion to €1.5 billion per gigawatt. We're just expecting the discussion with the government and these  numbers are coming from the compensation which we see for chances which you have seen on our power plants  the next years, especially these numbers come from the problems from the numbers which we need to have  another recultivation and another setting of provisions and so on in the lignite mines.

texts.speaker: Rolf Martin Schmitz
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, RWE AG
texts.text: The 2 to 3 gigawatts, yes, there are other people who try to do the same. But on the other year, we have now  [indiscernible] (00:34:31) fifth year that we have more than $300 billion investments per year. And I would say  that's enough for us, this – our small amount of 2 to 3 gigawatts.

texts.speaker: Alberto Gandolfi
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: Thank you. Afternoon. Thanks for taking my questions. I have two questions which are on the renewable  business. The first one is on this 2 to 3 gigawatt, let's say, €1.5 billion net investment, if I understand right, what  do you expect to be the IRR or the IRR minus WACC? And would it be fair to assume that you're broadly  expecting to deliver about €150 million of incremental EBITDA per year? Maybe depends a bit clearly on the  composition offshore versus solar onshore.

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Rexel SA

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Rexel SA

And assuming that this price remains constant in the second half, we estimate the  following impacts.

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Chairman & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: And actually, in view of the first half performance we detailed today, on the one hand; and the lower-than- expected copper prices and performance over the oil and gas sector, on the other hand, we expect to be at the low  end of the range represented in February. And the way we express this is that we expect an organic sales decline of  maximum minus 2% for the year and an adjusted EBITA margin of at least 4.8%. And regarding cash flow, we  stick with our at least 75% of EBITDA conversion rate before interest and tax, which corresponds to an around  40% of EBITDA conversion rate after interest and tax.

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Chairman & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: The adjusted EBITA margin target for the full year 2015 obviously represents a year-on-year improvement in  adjusted EBITA margin in the second half, building on the sequential improvement we recorded in Q2. I think  we've been very clear today about the cost-efficiency measures we're implementing, which should contribute to us  achieving that target. And on the gross margin side, we have very specific action plans in place to maintain the  momentum we've seen increasing in the first half. And our teams are mobilized and incentivized to that end.

texts.speaker: Lucie A. Carrier
texts.profession: Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: We took out head count. We took out a few management layers. We simplified the go-to-market model. As a  consequence, we could reduce head count with 273 full-time equivalents. Having realigned the branch network,  we tested all the hypothesis on the logistics network, eventually ended up with a decision not to invest in a DC in  Texas, which is also related to the oil and gas situation, and not yet to invest in a DC in Northeast Ohio because  that's mostly an industrial logistics platform. We need to support our Rockwell business and we actually can also  manage that through a network of super branches with the right inventory to serve large customers with a distinct  profile.

texts.speaker: Lucie A. Carrier
texts.profession: Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: So, there is also return on investment there on the OpEx side that we factored in. And all of that together, gives us  indeed the confidence that even with assuming that sales in North America and U.S. in particular will be down in  the second half, we think somewhere mid, even high-single digit decline due to that severe impact of oil and gas  that even with that profile, we can drive the EBITDA, the EBITDA improvement.

texts.profession: Chairman & Chief Executive Officer

texts.profession: Chairman & Chief Executive Officer

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Chairman & Chief Executive Officer

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Chairman & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: With respect to the different end markets, look, clearly, oil and gas is a big part of our industrial activity. texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Chairman & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Moreover, now there's this whole wind business that was huge last year, and in comps terms, is a bit distorting the  picture. texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Chairman & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Southeast Asia is an interesting case, where despite the fact that half of our Southeast Asia business is Oil & Gas,  with the same pressure, I mean, 20%-ish decrease, we're able to compensate 20% decrease on 50% of our  business, which is Oil & Gas with a similar increase in the non-Oil & Gas part.

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Chairman & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: So, our lighting projects do well. The acquired companies perform better than the business case. The high-end,  non-resi, larger project business in the hospitality area is doing well. So, that's a balancing act which works for us.

texts.text: In Canada, organic same-day growth stood at 7.6%, mainly driven by industrial end-market, not only in the  mining and oil and gas sector, but also by telecom and renewable energies. texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Member-Management Board, Rexel SA
texts.text: Now we believe that Rexel has a structural ability to generate organic growth that outpaces GDP growth. On one  hand, we are focusing our efforts and investments on developing more aggressively in fast-growing markets. And  on the other hand, we are further expanding our offer of value-added services notably related to energy efficiency  and projects with international customers.

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Member-Management Board, Rexel SA
texts.text: On Slide 30, as usual, we provide you with a progress report on our four structural organic growth initiatives, and  some of you know the acronym, the acronym is called SOG. Now, these four drivers represent a real or key organic  growth accelerator for the group. In total, they grew by 23% last year to €526 million. And this strong  performance was achieved despite the unfavorable base effect of photovoltaic sales in Germany that were boosted  in 2010 by tax incentives. So, eliminating this base effect, the four structural organic growth initiatives together  show a growth of 39% in 2011, and on average over the last two years they grew by 37%.

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Member-Management Board, Rexel SA
texts.text: Lighting retrofit projects posted the strongest increase with 57% growth in 2011 and 68% on average over the last  two years. The photovoltaic part of the portfolio recorded a 4% decline in 2011 due to the already mentioned  unfavorable base effect of sales in Germany, but it delivered still a solid 29% growth on average over the last two  years.

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Member-Management Board, Rexel SA
texts.text: Wind has posted a very strong 56% growth in 2011, offsetting a poor 2010, and it grew by 12% on average over the  last few years. And then, last but not least, IPG, our international organization dedicated to major projects with  global engineering companies posted a 28% increase in 2011 and a 52% increase on average over the past two  years.

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Member-Management Board, Rexel SA
texts.text: This product category of course benefited from the impact of energy efficient lighting, which represented about  one-fifth, about 20% of the total lighting sales, which is about €400 million consolidated sales. In there, as part of  the €400 million, the lighting retrofit projects which are indeed a priority area for us as you saw on the previous  slide grew by 57% in 2011.  And it's really a proof point of a vertical market approach, a very specific dedicated focus on a specific dedicated  market by implementing a sales model that is based on specific dedicated teams offering full service assistance to  customers including audits, administrative report, financing solutions and project management skills.

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Member-Management Board, Rexel SA
texts.text: It's also important to mention that lighting and energy efficient lighting and in particular, the lighting retrofit  projects do not only have an above average growth performance, but are also above average profitability  contributors, which helps to drive better performance of the group overall. So, we believe this segment remains  and should remain a priority and it will give us further upside going forward.

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Member-Management Board, Rexel SA

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Member-Management Board, Rexel SA

texts.text: And then finally, the third highlight of the year was the launch in May last year of our new company plan, Energy  in Motion, which in fact is Rexel's medium-term roadmap, which focuses on four main pillars, four strategic  priorities, four drivers of value creation.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: First and foremost, it talks about profitably growing both organically and through acquisitions notably by focusing  on promising high potential segments linked to energy efficiency, renewable energies, building automation, as  well as expanding our business with leading global customers and through international projects and developing  specific vertical markets such as oil, gas and mining.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: By country, the picture is as follows: in France, sales was down 2.1%, which, however, marked an improvement  over the 4.9% drop posted in Q3. texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION

texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: On a constant and same-day basis, sales were down 8.7%. texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION

Because of the effect of Australia, as I mentioned before, adjusted EBITA margin in Asia-Pacific as a whole fell  230 basis points to 3.3% in the quarter. Gross margin in there fell by 190 basis points due to the conditions in the  Pacific countries. So there's also a mix effect. texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board & CEO, Rexel SA
texts.text: When we actually presented our Energy in Motion company plan last year in May, we shared with you what we  thought would be the critical success factors. texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board & CEO, Rexel SA
texts.text: As far as UK is concerned, we posted sales of over €1 billion last year, up 9.3% year-on-year, which included a  positive effect of the consolidation of Wilts since March. On an organic basis and excluding both the negative  effects of photovoltaic sales and branch optimization, sales were down only 1.8%, which constitutes a very solid  performance taking into account the difficult market environment in the UK. You're all aware of the economic  situation and also taking into account the fact that 2011 figures were boosted by activity linked to the Olympic  games.

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board & CEO, Rexel SA
texts.text: So on slide 31, we give you an update on the organic growth sides. We, in fact, looked at three areas of growth:  high-potential business categories, international customers and projects, and specific vertical markets. So with  regards to the high-potential business categories comprising energy efficiency, the renewable energies and  building automation, we posted a growth of 9.5%, but if you exclude the renewable energies, which as you know,  behave very erratically and which were negatively impacted by changes in regulation in 2012 both in photovoltaic  and on the wind side, growth of this business category – of the high-potential business category was up 19.4%.

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board & CEO, Rexel SA
texts.text: So, in 2012, we acquired 12 companies that allowed us to make headway on all three of those fronts. We made two  strategic acquisitions in the U.S. with Platt and Munro, which significantly strengthens our position on the West  Coast as well as in the northeast of the U.S. and which perfectly fits our Energy in Motion strategy by accelerating  the development of energy-efficient solutions particularly through the acquisition of Munro.

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board & CEO, Rexel SA
texts.text: So let's move to the next chapter of the Energy in Motion story. We talked about accelerating in key markets. We  talked about focusing on the engines of growth. Let's now talk about a third critical success factor that was  highlighted last year, which is about enhancing our organizational effectiveness, which brings us to slide 36.

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board & CEO, Rexel SA
texts.text: So, in this position, Gonzalo is in-charge of accelerating the implementation of group and country initiatives  related to the earlier mentioned high-potential business categories such as energy efficiency, renewable energy,  building and home automation. And in that context, to make sure that category management has the – is tightly  connected with strategic supplier management. He's working on and responsible for strategic partnerships with  key suppliers to make sure that, from a marketing standpoint, we are completely aligned.

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board & CEO, Rexel SA
texts.text: So by aligning our accountability structure with our strategic priorities and also strengthening, reinforcing the  capabilities and the competencies with very dedicated and single accountable management, we think we're  creating the enabling conditions to successfully implement our Energy in Motion company plan.

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board & CEO, Rexel SA
texts.text: So she will succeed Michel who announced his decision to step down in October 2012 to pursue new career  opportunities. And Michel will remain in his position until Catherine's arrival beginning of May latest. And I'm  absolutely convinced that Catherine's management experience and financial acumen will be strong asset for Rexel  and of tremendous value in the implementation of the group's Energy in Motion company plan.

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board & CEO, Rexel SA
texts.text: Please remember that we created a new position of Group Senior Vice President Operations actually focusing on  one of the pillars of the Energy in Motion company plan, IT, supply chain management, CRM and e-commerce  and sales force automation. Peter Hakanson is in-charge of that position, and he joined us last July.

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board & CEO, Rexel SA
texts.text: And just to complete the story, as I mentioned before, we have Jean-Dominique Perret today as the Group Senior  Vice President Human Resources. So we will make sure that in terms of transition, continuity and consistency in the way we run the  company, everything is in place to do a quality job.  So let's then move to the last critical success factor I would like to highlight with respect to our Energy in Motion  company plan, which is about the drivers of operational performance. And I would like to feature three key  elements. One, on slide 41, it's related to what we call multi-channel sales development, particularly related to  what e-commerce is bringing us and can do for us going forward. I will talk about pricing and financial discipline  in a minute.

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board & CEO, Rexel SA
texts.text: And, of course, from a CapEx standpoint, this business is a low capital intensity business. So this is also reflected  in our low percentage of sales dedicated to capital expenditure, which consistently remains around 0.8% of sales.

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board & CEO, Rexel SA
texts.text: So with that overview and then having highlighted the – I would call it the four key success factors, the critical  success factors of the Energy in Motion company plan we announced last year, I think we can say that in 2012 we  lived up to our commitments. We did what we promised to do. We have traction in every area. And I'm confident  that we will be able to keep that momentum, and if possible, we'll do everything to accelerate that momentum.

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board & CEO, Rexel SA
texts.text: So let me now conclude the presentation with slide 45, which summarizes or I would say articulate – it's probably  a better way of saying it our 2013 outlook. Now, clearly, the ongoing uncertain macroeconomic climate leads us to  exercise caution with regards to 2013. Nevertheless, we target slightly positive organic sales growth for the year as  a whole. The trend is likely to remain negative in the first half. We expect to return to positive in the second half  and that in particular due to improving indicators in North America and in fast-growing countries.  From a profitability point of view, we aim at maintaining profitability levels, we aim at delivering a stable, solid,  robust adjusted EBITA margin of 5.7%. We also aim at generating free cash flow before interest and tax again  above €600 million corresponding to around €300 million after interest and tax.

texts.speaker: Rudy Provoost
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board & CEO, Rexel SA
texts.text: So what I'm trying to say is that from the U.S. point of view, looking to the trends and leading indicators, our own  performance, I feel quite comfortable without being overoptimistic. We also have to realize that actually, back to  the Energy in Motion areas of growth that U.S. was the best performer in the growth areas that we identified such  as energy efficiency, industrial automation. So, I mean, look to that as a whole, I think it gives you a balanced view  on U.S. markets. I would ask Michel maybe to comment on margin and we talk about dividend in a minute.

texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, Rexel SA

texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board & CEO, Rexel SA

texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board & CEO, Rexel SA

texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board & CEO, Rexel SA
texts.text: In the first half, we will see elections in Italy. So the jury is out there. There's elections in Germany later in the  year. The jury is out. texts.speaker: Michel Favre
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, Rexel SA

texts.speaker: Michael Anthony O'Leary
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Ryanair Holdings Plc
texts.text: In terms of outlook, we still expect Q yields to rise, despite last year's very challenging post -Olympic boosted  comparables, although we have noticed in recent weeks that yields on the close-in summer bookings have been  slightly weaker. texts.speaker: Michael Anthony O'Leary
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Ryanair Holdings Plc
texts.text: As ever though, and I think what separates us is our cautious outlook. We are only reporting the Q1 guidance. We  have some degree of visibility on Q2. We have no visibility over the remainder of the winter and therefore we  continue to be cautious, we expect market conditions to continue to be tough, characterized by recession,  austerity, high fuel costs and the spread of excessive government taxes, most recently the Walloon government, in  their idiocy, has announced a plan to levy an air travel tax in Charleroi from the 1st of January despite the  evidence that the Dutch government and the German government business have been very damaging to their air  travel.

texts.speaker: Howard Millar
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Deputy Chief Executive, Ryanair Holdings Plc
texts.text: Total operating expenses increased by 8% to €1.238 billion due to an increase in fuel prices, the higher level of  activity and operating costs associated with growth of the airline. Fuel, which now represents 47 % of total  operating costs in both the current and comparative period, increased by 6% to €57 6 million, due to the higher  price per gallon paid and the increased activity in the period.

texts.speaker: Howard Millar
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Deputy Chief Executive, Ryanair Holdings Plc
texts.text: So quarter one is slightly distorted by the fact that the comparative last year didn't include those quadrupling of  air traffic control charges and obviously we have those higher unit charges as Michael as well mentioned, which  will continue for the remainder of the year.

texts.speaker: Michael Anthony O'Leary
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Ryanair Holdings Plc
texts.text: In relation to the fuel costs and staff cost issue, yes, one of the big focuses of our – for us in the last I think two  years has been, we've begun to get very active on the fuel management side. One of the things that we have been  very good at, and unlike most other airlines, we have this kind of Formula 1 telemetry on all the aircraft, calling on  OFDM, I think it's Operation of Flight Data Monitoring, we get all the kind of height, speeds, everything else that  the planes are flying at. And we're now able to manage our flights in order to require our pilot to comply with what  we currently approved flight profile, which is the takeoff speed, the cruise speed, the  descent, the landing, all that  kind of stuff.

texts.speaker: Michael Anthony O'Leary
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Ryanair Holdings Plc
texts.text: So in essence, what we're doing is encouraging our – requiring pilots to fly slightly slower in order to make their  flying slightly safer. Y ou have less rapid descents, less rapid take-offs, and that's having a very significant – it has a  minor increase in flight times, which does have an impact on staff pay and on sector link, but a very significant  gain on the fuel side and in terms of the fuel consumption, and when fuel is running now at 47 % of – fuel is 47 % of  comps, revenues – total comps, obviously anything that reduces our fuel.

texts.speaker: Michael Anthony O'Leary
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Ryanair Holdings Plc
texts.text: Y ou have seen this raise its head occasionally. We have some of the more misguided pilot unions around Europe.  We publish these monthly fuel tables, which are portrayed by the misguided unions as some attempt by us to get  our pilots to fly with less fuel. And actually it has nothing to do with fuel loads, but it has everything to do with  essentially flight speeds and flight profiles, but it's being kind of misused by a lot and sa y, oh, this is Ryanair  skimping on fuel. We are flying with too little fuel.'

texts.speaker: Michael Anthony O'Leary
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Ryanair Holdings Plc
texts.text: Cost of fuel, they assume – they manage fuel burn and the fuel burn is not driven by whether you fill your tank full  to the brim, fuel burn is driven by whether you are driving at 140 miles an hour or 60 miles an hour, with the air –  140 miles an hour with the air conditioning on and the windows open, as opposed to driving at 60 miles an hour  with the air conditioning off and the windows closed. We will not take any bullshit from  the pilot's union. We  know they're a bit distracted at the moment agreeing pay cuts and job cuts in airlines like Alitalia and Iberia, and  so you'll continue to see some mewling and puking from various pilot representatives about our fuel league tables,  but as you can see on the fuel side, they are a very effective tool which enhances safety by encouraging and  requiring our pilots to fly the approved flight profiles and at the approved flight speeds.

texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Deputy Chief Executive, Ryanair Holdings Plc
texts.text: Y es, we're fully hedged out to the end of this year and we've extended our hedging into FY 2015 H1. So, we say we  have 70% of our fuel hedge in H1. We also have 70% of the currency, which enables us to say that, on a cost per  passenger basis, what we've hedged will fall by 3%.

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Ryanair Holdings Plc

texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn Partners LLP
texts.text: I suppose you have taken the guidance down slightly by reducing the fuel cost guidance by €30 million and not  changing the net profit guidance, was there a discussion around that?

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Ryanair Holdings Plc
texts.text: So I think caution is the proper way to approach Q1 numbers, don't waste too much time on them, it is much more  important what we'll seen in Q2. texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Ryanair Holdings Plc

texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Ryanair Holdings Plc

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director

texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
