It’s nothing of the order of 16 million, it wouldn’t even be –  I doubt if it’s even a million or two, but we completed about 80% of our program anyway and  maintained our number one punctuality. So I don’t know, I think they’re maybe just threatening  about their cost problems and looking for excuses, we don’t do that.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: I know some investors would like us to make it a forecast, it isn’t. It has always been subject to the  fuel variable and the fares being similar to where they were in 2007 and that is fuel at around – just  under $70 a barrel, and yields up at around in the low 40s.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Michael O’Leary>: Yes. But if – I think you have the – where we originally set out the target  about four years ago and it does refer to the same fuel and fares in 2007. Anyway, that’s what it is.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Was there anywhere else beyond the mix that maybe you’re starting to see a little bit of traction  economically that would have skewed the numbers a little bit? And also just if you comment on  again at a time when the yield guidance is starting to improve over the last month or so to the  extent the oil price weakened fairly considerably. So have we gotten maybe a little disconnect here  where the yield is going to be driven maybe a little bit more by the macro environment rather than  the oil price which was the expectation only a few weeks ago – few months ago?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Excluding fuel, which itself was up 37% in the quarter, unit costs rose by 8%. And, I said the small  Q3 loss is a little disappointing, as we were on track to break even, but earnings in the third quarter  were hit by a series of ATC strikes and walkouts in Europe. This was compounded by a spate of  ridiculous bad weather airport closures in December.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Although, oil prices have risen significantly in recent months, and again over the weekend, Ryanair  continues to benefit from a favorable fuel hedging strategy. While current spot prices have risen to  around $900 per tonne, we are 90% hedged for Q4 of FY’11 at $750 per tonne, and we are 80%  hedged for FY March ‘12 at an average price of just up some $800 per tonne. We’ve also hedged  70% of our dollar requirements for FY’12 at an average rate of $1.34 to the euro compared to $1.40  to the euro for FY’11.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The extraordinary scale of the ATC and weather cancellations during the third quarter brings  renewed focus on the unfair and discriminatory nature of the EU261 airline regulations. Urgent  reform of these regulations is vital since it’s inequitable to force airlines to pay for right to care or  compensation in circumstances where widespread flight cancellations are caused by ATC strikes,  airport’s failures to keep their runways open or the Icelandic volcanic ash air space closures.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Howard Millar>: I think it’s fair to say, too, Penny, that obviously we will have a headwind in  terms of fuel costs next year.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Howard Millar>: If you look at where we’ve hedged now and where we’re hedged in fuel, and  also in currency, we’ve got – we’re looking at about a €2 to €3 per passenger increase in fuel costs  from about – just below €17 to maybe €19 to €20, depends on where it pans out.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Michael Anthony O’Leary>: I think that the sensible thing is, the experience of the last two  fuel spikes has been that the flags across Europe and some of our so-called low-fare competitors  have been lorrying up the fuel surcharge as we continue to guarantee no fuel surcharges, and it  wouldn’t be unreasonable to expect if fuel surcharges rise this summer, as we expect they will  among competitors...

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Robert Pickels>: Thank you for taking my question. For some time now, you’ve had this goal  of, I believe, €800 million in profits, and it seems as though you guys are really executing well on  your strategy. And the one major issue that you don’t always have control over, or one of them, is  fuel. So, I’m wondering how you think of that €800 million goal in the context of a rising fuel  environment. Is there – is capacity tight enough where you can pass your – you can pass the fuel  cost on and still achieve that goal, or do you think it’s getting harder?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Michael Anthony O’Leary>: It depends on the economic environment. I mean, it’s – I’m  always slightly amused. Everybody will raise the 800 million profit goal and not the conditionality,  which was fuel at $45 a barrel. Fuel clearly won’t be at $45 a barrel by the time we get to the end of  2012. And – but it remains our aim, but we’re going to be trying to do it with much higher – no,  we’re not going to get there if oil is at a $100 a barrel, unless there is an enormous increase in  yields. But we have two variables here.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Our €800 million target for the end of 2012 was based on $45 a barrel oil and yields at a certain  level. The yields will be higher, oil will be significantly higher, and you don’t need a huge jump in  yields between now and the end of 2012 to get to €800 million. But much of it could be eaten up by  fuel. So, frankly, our guidance, when we get there for next year to FY ‘12, will be whatever it will be  based on our hedged fuel at that stage and our best estimate. When we get to the first – or the full- year results road show, we get to our best estimate of where we think yields will be for the full year.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q – Robert Pickels>: Okay. And just out of curiosity, why is it that you don’t include fuel  surcharges? You certainly aren’t opposed to other sort of fees outside of the base fare. So, why no  fuel surcharge? Is it --?       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Michael Anthony O’Leary>: The difference is all of our other fees are introduced not to raise  revenue, but to change passenger behavior. Every other fee in Ryanair is avoidable. So, you don’t  check in the bag, you don’t pay the bag fee. You use MasterCard prepaid, you don’t pay the credit  card fee. You don’t use – you don’t want priority boarding, you don’t have to pay for it. Whereas fuel  surcharges are simply – I mean, it’s a fare increase. They are unavoidable in BA, Air Berlin, or any  of the other airlines that charge them, and we don’t believe, if you’re a low fares airline, we should  be selling simple, low fares and not have a fuel surcharge. It’s – also, I think, it’s a very key and  important marketing tool for us during periods of fuel surcharges around Europe. We – our no fuel  surcharge guarantee, we think, is a very key selling point for us.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Now, the fact is in the last two oil price spikes, our average fares and yields have risen up behind  those airlines with higher fares and fuel surcharges. But I think it’s important. We believe it’s a key  marketing tool for us. But we are not unhappy or – we’re not afraid to let the average fares rise.  Remember, we are price takers in every market in which we operate. We will roll out the cheap  fares, and if they sell faster than we planned, we close them out, and if they are selling slower, we  open up more of them. What we try to focus on all the time is managing costs. That’s why we see  the fuel is well hedged out for the rest of this fiscal year and for both next fiscal year. And we’re still  running around lowering airport costs and getting more efficiencies into the system. But as for our  other fees, don’t confuse them with a fuel surcharge because all of our other fees are avoidable.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: The staff costs are under control, the maintenance costs are under control, our marketing costs are  minimal. So, I think we – now, clearly, what could blow all that out of the water is obviously war or  terrorism or some huge upward shift in oil prices. But our experience in the last two huge upticks in  oil is that the flakes around Europe who can’t make money in good times and need fuel surcharges  in bad times grow with fuel surcharges.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Michael Anthony O’Leary>: The answer to the question is, we don’t – well, we don’t really  know because in the last two years, we’ve only slowed down from 17% to 14%, 14% to 11%. But  the – if you look at the trend of average fares over the last 12 months, as we’ve slowed from 14% to  11%, there’s been a significant trend there associated with a period of falling oil prices.

texts.speaker: Michael Anthony O'Leary
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Ryanair Holdings Plc
texts.text: We're very pleased to report this Q3 profit of €15 million. It's slightly ahead of our expectations, but largely due to  the benign weather conditions experienced in December 2011 compared to the widespread snow closures, deicing  comps we suffered in December 2010. texts.speaker: Michael Anthony O'Leary
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Ryanair Holdings Plc
texts.text: As you can see, the EU recession, higher oil prices, the unfolding failure of the package tour operator model,  significant competitor fare increases and capacity cuts, have created enormous growth opportunities for Ryanair,  as large and smaller airports across Europe compete aggressively to win our growth.

texts.speaker: Michael Anthony O'Leary
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Ryanair Holdings Plc
texts.text: Our unit costs rose 11% mainly due to an 18% increase in fuel costs. Excluding fuel, sector length adjusted unit  cost fell 1%, as we continue to control costs despite a 2% basic pay increase, higher Eurocontrol fees, and  significantly higher Dublin Airport charges. In FY 2013, we are 90% hedged for half one at about $99 per barrel.  70% hedged for the second half at approximately $100 a barrel. We do expect to hedge out the balance of our H2  FY 2013 needs over the coming months. But at these prices, our fuel bill for FY 2013 will rise by approximately  €350 million which poses a significant cost challenge as we move into FY 2013.

texts.speaker: Michael Anthony O'Leary
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Ryanair Holdings Plc
texts.text: Our Q3 net profit of €15 million was slightly ahead of guidance due to a combination of benign weather, which  caused fewer flight cancellations and significant deicing savings, and a better performance on yields, reflecting our  planned winter capacity cuts, longer sectors, and higher competitor fares and fuel surcharges. Should these  positive Q3 trends continue into Q4, we now expect our full year profit will exceed previous guidance of €440  million and rise to approximately €480 million after tax.

texts.speaker: Michael Anthony O'Leary

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Ryanair Holdings Plc

texts.speaker: Michael Anthony O'Leary
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Ryanair Holdings Plc
texts.text: On load factor, I don't expect to close the gap with easyJet on load factor yet, although I think there's no doubt  that our load factor will rise over the next year or two. texts.speaker: Michael Anthony O'Leary
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Ryanair Holdings Plc
texts.text: I wouldn't expect there's an average load factor differentiator of about six percentage points to seven percentage  points. We're hovering around 82% and they around 89% year round. texts.speaker: Michael O’Leary
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer and Director, Ryanair Holdings Plc
texts.text: And I think it's also important – particularly for things like the CAA investing – or CAA – what is it they do – survey  that was referred to over the weekend, I mean, what's missing from this survey is yes, we've changed the way  that we are allocating seats, but that's a customer choice. texts.text: As you can see from the results, we announced full year profit rise of 26% to €400 million.  Revenues rose 21% at €3.6 billion; as traffic grew 8% average fares rose 12%. Unit costs were up  by 11% due to higher oil prices and a 10% increase in sector length. Excluding fuel, however,  which was up 37%, unit costs rose by just 3%.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: I think these were a very good set of results particularly given they cover a year in which we  suffered higher oil prices, dealt with the impact of the global recession, suffered the disruptions of  the volcanic ash in Q1 last year. As we said, fuel increased 37% to €1.2 billion as average oil prices  rose from $62 to approximately $73 per barrel. Excluding fuel, unit costs rose 3%.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: At last year, some 14,000 Ryanair flights were canceled arising primarily from three separate  incidents: the volcanic ash disruptions in April and May; the airport snow closures in the U.K. and  across much of Europe in December and January; and a total of 15 national air traffic control  strikes across Europe last summer.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: This brings into further focus the unfair and discriminatory airline EU 261 regulations which forced  airlines to pay for “right to care” expenses and compensation during these events even though  they’re beyond our control. It’s absurd, for example, that the insurance companies last year paid out  nothing during the volcanic ash crisis because it was an act of God, yet the airlines were passed on  all of those costs and the compensation.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: In terms of oil, higher oil prices continue to force our higher-fare competitors to increase fares and  fuel surcharges which are making our lower fares even more attractive. In many cases,  competitors’ fuel surcharges are higher than Ryanair’s lead-in fares. Higher oil prices will, as  previously, lead to further consolidations, increased competitor losses and more airlines going  broke this autumn. This creates further growth opportunities for Ryanair because we operate the  most fuel-efficient fleet, have the lowest operating costs and also the strongest balance sheet.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We expect to increase our market share and expand further into new markets as high oil prices  force more competitors to cut capacity or go bust this autumn and winter. In Ryanair, we’re 90%  hedged for the remainder of the fiscal year at about $82 a barrel. This is still, however, a 12% price  increase on last year but significantly below current spot prices which are trending around above  $100.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Higher oil prices next winter and the refusal of some airports to offer lower charges make it more  profitable to tactically ground up to 80 aircraft this winter compared to the 40 aircraft we grounded  last winter rather than suffer losses operating them to high cost airports such, as example Dublin, at  low winter yields.

texts.profession: Operator

Look, if we – if nothing else changes, we  got a couple of more airport deals or a couple of better airport deals, next year, if oil remains stable  at $100 a barrel, I think you will see, generally speaking across Europe, air fares and fuel  surcharges rise to reflect those higher oil prices. I would have no difficulty then flying. We might  only ground 30 or 40 aircraft next winter but we would have better airport deals, we would have  lower – we would have a better yield environment as well.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Michael O’Leary – Chief Executive Officer>: Yeah. I think that’s more accurate but I’d hate  not to describe fuel as a long-term issue, I think clearly, it is a long-term issue. But it’s fuel volatility  that really screws up our earnings. We’re in a very good hedging position this year versus the rest  of the industry, $82 a barrel. I don’t want to blow that by doing a lot of flying in the winter at $110 a  barrel. But the rest of the industry and nobody is in as good a hedging position as we are this year.  They’re all going to under significantly more pressure this winter. And we’re happy to cut back the  growth, sit aircraft on the ground. By the time you emerge into the summer of 2012, I think the  market will have adjusted to that as if oil prices have been relatively stable. As for the nightmare  scenario though, is that oil prices will slump in the short term, be cheap this winter while we’re at  $82 and then shoot back up again next summer, if there’s some kind of recovery.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: But look, oil is just something we’ve got to manage as best we can through a mix of hedging and a  mix of capacity discipline. And that’s what we’re trying to do this winter. Now that’s not to say if  somebody came along and said, look I’ve got an airport here, I’ll give you, you can have a 100%  discount plus I’ll give you some marketing monies, if you delivery me significant growth starting in  September, October. Hey, we’d talk to you, even if oil was $110 a barrel. But you know at the  moment, you’ve got to persuade us to fly these aircrafts not the other way around. We’re not  desperate to find homes for them this winter.

texts.text: <Q – Gérard Moore – Merrion Stockbrokers Ltd.>: Hi. Thanks very much for taking my question.  It’s just a couple of points of clarification, really. First of all on FY ‘12 guidance. Just to be sure, is  your guidance based on jet fuel prices of $1,100?

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: You’re right; we have no fuel hedges into FY ‘13. We have no guidance for FY ‘13. It’s far too early  to look at, at the moment. We’re too busy trying to manage FY ‘12. And yes, our FY ‘12 guidance is  based on our current fuel hedges, which is 90% hedged at about $82 a barrel, plus the balance  hedged out at current rates is about $105, $110 – but on $105 and $110.

texts.text: Going to page 6, CFM56-LEAP transition update. The LEAP is the engine of choice for airlines. texts.speaker: Philippe Petitcolin
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Safran SA
texts.text: The production ramp-up of LEAP is making progress. LEAP deliveries reached 1,118 units compared to 459 in  2017. texts.speaker: Philippe Petitcolin
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Safran SA
texts.text: Let's turn now, page 8, to Aircraft Equipment business highlights. In OE, Safran provides equipment to several  aircraft programs that are ramping up. texts.speaker: Philippe Petitcolin
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Safran SA
texts.text: Going to Aerosystems business highlights, page 10. Safran supported its customers' rising assembly rates  throughout the year. To start with, we did have an improvement during the quarter, most notably in North America where we did  have effects on business activity due to the weather conditions and so that many companies have seen in North  America. So there was a certain improvement during the quarter for Machining Solutions.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Sandvik AB
texts.text: We've had a small reclassification from COGS to A&S cost, but that's more of a minor nature. Our COGS has been  positively impacted by – the cost-saving activities and still catching up with the lower market activity that we've  seen, there's certain mix effects within business areas and between business areas which is also driving that.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Sandvik AB
texts.text: We are driving both cost savings that affect COGS, but also our admin costs. So our ambition and in our plans is to  have activities that should bring down admin costs looking at the coming years. So, yes.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Sandvik AB
texts.text: Aftermarket, we see as sequentially flat compared to the preceding quarter. And also, mining systems, we've  actually had a reasonably good order intake. So we are seeing sustainability in that business at the current level.  So I don't believe that Sandvik is performing differently in that sense when it comes to our equipment sales.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Sandvik AB
texts.text: I think Mats really answered the seasonality effect. I mean, we normally have a buildup in Q2 of inventory from an  over-absorption effect as a consequence. We will still have that effect, but we are trying when we're planning the  whole manufacturing system within Sandvik, especially then within Machining  Solutions and Materials  Technology, to have a flatter development over the year which we already succeeded with last year for Machining  Solutions. And this year, when it comes to Materials Technology, we are planning to try to compress the summer  shutdowns which will reduce the requirement for inventory buildup pre the summer shutdowns that we have in  Sweden.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Sandvik AB
texts.text: I would say also, I think as long as the demand for the metals and activity with the mining companies remains  high or even grows as many people are projecting going forward, it's likely that we're more or less at an  unsustainable level where we are standing right now because if metal outputs are going to be constant or even  increasing, the miners will need to replace equipment, spend more on after -market business and gradually also  invest in new machines. So, given that that trend continues, I think, there's some reason for optimism, maybe not  in the very near future but in the medium-term anyway when it comes to the output for the mining sector.

texts.speaker: Alexander T. Whight
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: Sure. Thanks. And the final question I had was just on Materials Technology. Are you seeing anything on nuclear  demand? We haven't heard anything from that area for some time.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Sandvik AB
texts.text: Well, it's fairly stable at this low level. We have not seen any clear picture on nuclear. We talked last year about the  potential drop in sales 2014 compared to 2013 in nuclear. We don't believe in that – that's not going to be the case,  I would say, in 2014 now because there were certain delays in deliveries in 2013. So we will see roughly a similar  invoicing level towards the nuclear sector during this year as we look at the marke t price now compared to the  preceding year. And that picture is unlikely to change because before an order is given, a project is started and so  on and we actually get to the invoicing point, that's quite a long lag there. So we know what we have in the or der  book and more or less what we're going to deliver in terms of same generated tubes during this year, which is the  main product.

texts.speaker: Daniel Schmidt
texts.profession: Analyst, SEB Enskilda (Sweden)
texts.text: Hello. Daniel Schmidt from SEB. Can I just ask you on the lumpiness when it comes to the large orders in SMT  which are quite big in the quarter? And I think you were fairly optimistic on oil and gas in your statement. What  should we expect going forward? Do you see a number of sort of awards being handed out in the coming quarters  as well in sort of same magnitude?

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Sandvik AB
texts.text: But we're continuing to look at taking more orders and booking more within the oil and gas sector, but we're  starting to build a quite considerable order stock now with this very heavy order intake that we saw in the first  quarter. So the lead times for us to be able to deliver to the customers is starting to move out on this product.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Sandvik AB
texts.text: No. Our plans are unchanged by this and we're still committed to achieving the targets that was set up. In Mining ,  I think it's important to separate that we have two plans that we've announced ongoing within the Mining  business area. One, a SEK 500 million short-term saving, which is about adaption of the organization to the  current business volumes. And we see that we've achieved that SEK 500 million run rate by the end of the first  quarter.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Sandvik AB
texts.text: If compare us out with stainless steel producers, we have fairly low share of distributor sales and often high value  products where there's a smaller element of speculation due to shifts in nickel prices. But I would not say that  there's a material effect as far as I see it on inventory buildup with customers driving this development.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: When it comes to the market, the demand continues to be fairly stable. We don't really see any big dramatic  changes in the market or our segments, with maybe the exception being the oil and gas market and especially the  onshore drilling activity in North America, which has been quite weak during the beginning of this year.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Aerospace had a positive development when it came to sales compared to the same period last year. And if you  look at the sequential trend, we do still see a slightly positive trend in aerospace. And energy, driven mainly by the  weaker oil price, has seen a negative sequential development.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Order intake and invoicing were more or less balanced. We had one order cancellation within Sandvik Materials  Technology, within the oil and gas sector in Asia. This was more – or fully compensated by other large orders that  were received, two in the oil and gas sector, and actually, we got the first nuclear order to China that we've seen  since the Fukushima accident. Yeah, and Mining Systems, I mentioned earlier as the area within mining where we  saw weakness. But otherwise, a fairly stable book-to-bill and a quite neutral market environment.

texts.speaker: Mats Backman
texts.profession: Group CFO & Executive Vice President
texts.text: We also announced the second phase of this saving program now in the first quarter, and that is including 10  units, the closure of 10 units. And we actually started the closure of three of the 10 units in the quarter. And that is  two units for Sandvik Mining, one unit in Turku, Finland, one in Nora, Sweden and one for Material s Technology  in Sheffield, UK. We are aiming for savings of SEK 600 million by it and full run rate end 2016. So all in all, the  supply chain optimization program is running according to plan.

texts.speaker: Mats Backman
texts.profession: Group CFO & Executive Vice President
texts.text: The best improvement, however, we saw actually within Materials Technology that's improved the relative net  working capital with 3% units in the quarter, partly due to continued destocking but also due to prepayments in  the energy product business. So that's something we are pushing for as well in order to improve the net working  capital.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: And when it comes to the market development, we see overall stable demand in most sectors and most  geographies with maybe the exception of the oil and gas sector which has performed weaker than what we saw in  the preceding quarter.

texts.speaker: Peder Frölén
texts.profession: Svenska Handelsbanken AB (Broker)
texts.text: Y es. Good morning. This is Peder from Handelsbanken. Could you please shed some light of the demand drop in  the oil and gas business for the [indiscernible] (17:57) but also in Varel, try to help us to quantify that. texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Y eah. When it comes to the demand development in oil and gas, we actually see a neutral book-to-bill within  Sandvik Materials Technology. texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: When it comes to the Venture business and especially Varel, they have about 40% of their sales in North America.  I would say in the rest of the world, it's been – I mean, of course some pressure downwards due to the oil and gas  prices, the drop there, but there's been a very dramatic drop in North America. And when it comes to the drilling  within the shale gas areas and the onshore equipment, they very rapidly slow down drilling activity with the low  oil price and also very rapidly ramp up again if the oil price comes back while the offshore projects in SMT, they  have a much longer time perspective and you don't stop multi-year very large investments projects just because of  a temporary drop in the oil and gas price, which does have effect in North America. So that's how we see, I mean, a  significant effect especially in the North American business.

texts.speaker: Peder Frölén
texts.profession: Svenska Handelsbanken AB (Broker)
texts.text: Is there a – most of that is, of course, according to the supply chain optimization program. So could you quantify  the Varel part of that?

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: We haven't specified that to that level of detail, but we are seeing a good healthy manning reduction as a  consequence of our ongoing programs here.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: When it comes to especially the parts side, I would say that we start to see slight positive development for Sandvik.  Our business against coal and iron ore is mainly driven by our Mining Systems business and we have very little  aftermarkets in those areas. So iron ore per se is not going to have a significant impact on Sandvik's aftermarket,  but it does manifest itself in the very low order intake we see when it comes to new projects within the Mining  Systems business. So the equipment in aftermarket business is much more driven by base metals gold, platinum  and these other minerals.

texts.speaker: Lars Wauvert Brorson
texts.profession: Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: And also, if you could, Olof, talk a little bit about the actual underlying drivers for your commentary on underlying  improvement in the aftermarket. I appreciate that coal and iron ore is mainly systems, but what are you actually  seeing within the aftermarket business that will be helpful. Thanks.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Y eah. It's quite difficult to comment on specific customers in detail but in general I would say we have a quite  limited Petrobras exposure when it comes to technically the kind of umbilicals and so, they have been using plastic  there and there's been a hope of them shifting into metallic umbilicals as they go deeper.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: We've seen maybe some slight uptick in the market. And as said the equipment and aftermarket business is a lot  driven by base metals, gold, platinum and this kind of minerals and not as much of on coal and  iron ore.

texts.profession: UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Thank you. And how big the oil and gas orders for SMT? Do you have any size that you can say with that? Thank  you.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: We don't specify the specific orders in that size. But we had two orders against oil and gas and the third order we  received was actually against the nuclear sector. So we booked the first order against the Chinese nuclear sector  since the Fukushima accident. So that was also an encouraging positive development I would say there.

texts.speaker: Andre Kukhnin
texts.profession: Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: hi, yes. It's Andre from Credit Suisse. Just a couple of follow-ups. One is I think you mentioned that you're looking  for oil and gas acquisitions in the press call. Your current exposure is quite varied. Could you comment where  you're looking and whether it would be reasonable to expect a deal this year? And the second one is just on Mining  Systems. Would the thinking of the Systems being about 10% of sales and new zero of orders, would that be  roughly right or should we be thinking about different numbers?

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Well, firstly I mean acquisitions it's difficult to speculate. We talk about several areas like SMS as an interesting  area to expand. There could be potentials within Mining but also the oil and gas sector, and of course this lower oil  price may create opportunities for us. And out of mining sales, Mining Systems was roughly 20% of those sales in  the quarter and we actually had as much as 57% aftermarket sales in this quarter. So that gives a perspective of the  size of Mining Systems.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Y eah. For SMT, we had more or less no effect from metal prices. So that didn't drive sort of the absolute price of  the product either up nor down. And so – and we had very limited, I would say, pricing movements also. So it's  not price driving the top-line development. It's an underlying volume development that you see.

texts.text: And again, we see continued strong order intake in the quarter, of course, in the company, where the environment  we're leaving in and the great uncertainty we have in the economies round ourselves, we do have a significant  readiness for changes – for potential changes in the market sentiments going forward here.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Sandvik AB
texts.text: So, there are some seasonal effects which will improve this number for the fourth quarter, but we also need to  continue to work with inventory reductions throughout the Sandvik Group to make sure that we stay below the  24% – 25% target.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Sandvik AB
texts.text: Looking then now specifically at the different business areas in the Sandvik Group. Sandvik Tooling, somewhat  continued improved demand as a business area. There is strong demand from areas like Automotive sector,  Aerospace, and also, the Energy sector is very strong.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Sandvik AB
texts.text: Looking at Mining and Construction, we see very strong activity, I would say, continued in the Mining sector here,  with very strong demand. And on the other hand, in the Construction area, where we have a more of a challenging  market situation, we saw a different business climate, which was much weaker than in the Mining sector.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Sandvik AB
texts.text: Then, looking at Sandvik Materials Technology, here we have a somewhat weaker market development. We have  some areas that are strong, like for example, the Oil and Gas sector, and also the Aerospace sector. But we have  more weakness in Consumer-related segments and also on standard or low value-added product in the Materials  Technology portfolio here.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Sandvik AB
texts.text: We have had lots of questions regarding our orders for steam generated tubes to the nuclear industry after the  Fukushima accident. We're now at the point where we have confirmation that there will be delays in these orders  from China, due to delays in their investments in their nuclear power plants. So, this will have a effect for us 2012,  2013, as we can see it today here.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Sandvik AB
texts.text: Then I think your question was, do we have structurally taken out any parts of SMT, which resulted in the lower  order intake? Well, in the comparable quarter last year, we had some large nuclear orders that were in there,  here currently. But the new SMC will be smaller. SMT will be smaller as of 1st of January when Process Systems  and the MedTech business move into the Venture business area.

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Sandvik AB
texts.text: We are looking at different ways to assist production capacity. And for them, both parts of the facilities can be  currently. So we're already doing ways that we can still utilize this capacity when we get hold due to the delays of  the nuclear orders to mitigate the fact of that.

texts.speaker: Ola Salmén
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Sandvik AB
texts.text: We don't have that level of details in terms of the Construction and Mining. But there will be costs in both those  areas, and there will also be savings in both those areas, but in relative terms, most of the savings will come in the  Construction area.

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: Yes. A follow-up on Tooling. On the raw material side, could you mention a bit how that will affect you, maybe
texts.text: coming into the fourth quarter next year, given the tungsten prices and also your integrated business model in  that sense? I guess, if you look at spot prices and so forth, we could expect a rather significant headwind on  margin there, but what are you already doing to mitigate that? And are you, in that sense, planning to maybe push  prices a bit more than you usually, at this stage of the cycle?

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Sandvik AB
texts.text: First, I mean the high [ph] vol (50:15) from tungsten prices, they impact us positively [ph] with the vol from  (50:23) business there, so we have some recovery in that sense. We – if you compare with the Material Technology  business, the raw material element in an insert is much, much smaller. So even quite large fluctuations don't  impact the pricing picture or the margins as significantly as they would, for example, in the SMT business. And we  also don't work with the model where we price our products based on additions due to raw material prices. We  want to give an offering, to our customers, of value in terms that they get a better product and better productivity  in their production, and by helping them to succeed in their business, we get a share of that in terms of the price in  our products. So we don't have a model where we're negotiating based on the movements of the tungsten price  here [indiscernible] (51:24).

texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Sandvik AB

texts.text: Yes, well, I mean I think that's been so far quite successful joint venture. We already this year announced a very  significant order that is joint venture got in China. texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Sandvik AB
texts.text: I mean metals like gold and platinum and silver are developing still I would say in a quite positive way. And the  biggest negative trends are for minerals like iron ore and coal on a global basis.

texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Board Member, Sandvik AB

texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Board Member, Sandvik AB

texts.speaker: Olof Faxander
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: But we do also have a certain exposure to more downstream petrochemical as you say. texts.profession: Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.

texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Now one question which comes naturally when you look at the market is, what is the evolution of the market, and  how do we see the production demand coming for – of services. For the new  fields coming onstream, anywhere between 45% to 50% of the new field is coming from offshore. And most of this  offshore production is coming in deepwater.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Now when we look at the opportunities of developing fields, we can see that deep water or ultra-deep water field  development can be developed between $30 to $80 per barrel. texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: In addition to that, if we look at the marginal cost of the costs associated with an FPSO, in particular, the  Generation 3 type of project, which is the large type of FPSO on which we are focusing, you can see that the  marginal cost of using an FPSO is only around $5 per barrel. So all of this give us confidence to state that the basis  of the economics of services to develop new FPSO – to develop new field with FPSO, is extremely good.

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV

texts.speaker: Bruno Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: So going to a Talisman Yme update. We have encountered a range of difficulties making the necessary progress to  meet our original target date of first oil in the first half of 2012. Poor productivity, caused by among other factors,  bad weather and an increase in work scope offshore are the main elements in slowing down the commissioning  and start up. We shall not be getting this type of facility again. But irrespective of this, I and the Board see this as  an imperative for SBM from a reputation standpoint as well as a commercial perspective to growing the project to  a successful completion with the client. As we have explained before, disputes, mainly related to cost, continue to  be the subject of arbitration proceedings with our client. But it can be categorized in saying that we are aligned  with Talisman in our determination to complete the platform for a mutual beneficial outcome.

texts.speaker: Bruno Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: On the project itself, progress is more satisfactory and remedial action has corrected the problems. However,  delays due to low productivity into the autumn and additional work on some system have required us to provide  for further cost. With productivity now understood and at the level satisfactory, delivery of first gas is expected to  be done during the summer.

texts.speaker: Bruno Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: So, when it comes to strategy, I think this slide has certain clarity. We have one focus, one purpose, one market  segment, and in concept one core product, the FPSO. SBM Offshore exists to develop complete offshore floating  production and storage solutions for the global energy industry.

texts.speaker: Bruno Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Now a few words on our FLNG position; we would dedicate our offshore experiences just to large and medium size  units. We will selectively target edge technology products for large sized units and the complete vessel and  equipment in the medium sized categories.

texts.speaker: Bruno Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: We are also working on three turrets of which one is related to FLNG.

texts.speaker: Bruno Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: The operation contract only for FPSO Serpentina was extended until August 2013, including options for three  further one-year extensions. FSO Unity operation under contract with Total in Nigeria ended in September 2011.  And lastly, the FPSO Aseng started first oil production for Noble Energy in Equatorial Guinea early November and  is under contract for 15-year lease and operate contract with further extension of up to five years.

texts.speaker: Mark A. S. Miles
texts.profession: Thank you, Bruno. Afternoon, everybody. I'm going to go through first of all the income statements focusing on
texts.text: The third bullet point on the slide, $38 million associated with revised strategic focus on core FPSO products, so  indeed that's relating mainly to LNG investments in the past and pre-investments in LNG business and  development costs, and to a much smaller extent on renewables.

texts.speaker: Bruno Chabas

texts.speaker: Michael Roeg
texts.profession: Analyst, KBC Securities NV
texts.text: Okay. And then a final question on the write-downs on the LNG projects. Could you give a bit of flavor what type  of projects are involved and whether there is still anything left in the books with respect to those projects?

texts.speaker: Bruno Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Okay. I think the best way is to answer through our strategy on the FLNG market, in reality. We want to be  present in FLNG market, but we want to be present in a manner whereby SBM Offshore could be successful. And  for us, there are two sides to it. For the extremely large FLNG project, we are going to provide some of the critical  components such as mooring system, turrets, offloading systems, operation, if need be. That's going to be the core  of our focus.

texts.speaker: Bruno Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: For the medium size FLNG, which are actually equivalent to the FPSO, the coveted FPSO-type market, then we  want to develop capacity in order to be able to provide those type of project. Why this evolution in our strategy  there on the FLNG market. I believe that as a company, SBM Offshore both on the financial point of view, but also  on an operating point of view, is not armed or capable of handling project with new built and large FLNG project,  which have a value of $4 billion to $5 billion. That's not our strength, that's not our capacity.

texts.speaker: Bruno Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: However, we have a lot of value added that we can bring to those project and let's focus on this value added we can  bring. The medium size FLNG project, they are there in line with our capacity with our operating experience and  there we need to develop more experience and be present in this market.

texts.speaker: Michael Roeg
texts.profession: Analyst, KBC Securities NV
texts.text: Okay, but for instance, I remember from the past there was this LNG hose that was developed. Is that, for  instance, part of the write-downs because that's not a critical part that you want to supply? You have not given up  the FLNG segment. You're still going to be focusing on turrets and midsized and whatever, but there are still some  write-downs here and there. So, I was just wondering what it is related to? What are you not – no longer going to  do?

texts.speaker: Mark A. S. Miles
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Yeah, so that was one of the critical elements indeed, which we have capitalized costs for in the past and those  have been partially written down. And it doesn't mean because we don't want to still supply those in the future. It's  you have to look at the opportunities which are on the market and the likely revenue generation from sales of the  products. And we've revised our assumptions in respect of what, when, and for how much and how many of these  systems will be selling and have taken an impairment calculation and written down partially those FLNG hose  product.

texts.profession: Analyst, Natixis SA (Broker)

Bruno Chabas  Chief Executive Officer, SBM Offshore NV  A Okay. so the first question is, yes, our focus on the FLNG will be in two side, but if you look at the medium-sized  FLNG project, we are looking at projects in the range of $2 billion or less, that's what we're looking at. We are not  looking at the big units that we have seen on the markets so far, which have a price tag of $3 billion to $4 billion. I  don't believe that this is the strength of the company.

texts.text: Now the turrets is equipment business. As the FPSO units are becoming larger or, in some cases, one of the turrets  we're working on, the FLNG units are becoming much, much bigger, having a system to be able to move the  floating system and to be able to load oil on every day of the year, in some cases, if there is a hurricane or typhoon,  to be able to disconnect and go away is the critical component and a critical competitive advantage that SBM  Offshore has. It's a market segment on which we have 30  years of experience, for which we are investing money in R&D and for which we're transferring the knowledge of  30 years of experience to our clients for value.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: So what is the net effect of this? The net effect, if we look on the strategy, and here our – the strategy and if we  look at the strategy there, the orange boxes, we can see a few things. First of all that the  strategy of FPSO-led is  starting to bear fruit. We have been able to secure three contracts, which really are at the forefront of what the  industry is going to require. Two for Petrobras; one for Shell. We're going to expand on this later on.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Now, the only disappointing figure, I would say, is the LTI frequency. What is an LTI? LTI is when someone gets  injured at work and cannot work for a period of 24 months. This frequency actually increase year -on-year, despite  the fact that the number of incidents overall and the number of man hours were the same. And so it's really  something that we need to work on and to improve next year, 2014. In prior to that, we are not only looking at the  impact of our health and safety on people, but also in the environment and for the past two years, we have started  to take some measures about our performance there. We're measuring our performance compared to the industry,  which is pretty good. And we're going to be able to communicate further on this in the coming few months and few  years.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Now, let's discuss about the market. Two elements which are of interest in the market. Starting from – through  2012, what we see is that the production of oil from our clients has increased by 1.8%, fairly low inc rease.  However, what we're seeing is that the cost to do this development has increased in itself by 6.8% and if we don't  adjust to inflation, it has increased by more than 14%. All those figures are on a year -on-year basis.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: This is not a business proposition which is going to last, and it's going to have an impact on the industry [ph] and  all things that are going to be structured (9:14). We're also seeing that the national oil companies are facing more  importance in the market. They have access to the resources, and some of them used to develop those resources.  Petrobras is a case in point; they are the leader in deepwater development.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: But some other national oil companies used to be much more passive. They're getting more active. They are taking  more activity in developing projects and in the operation of project. What's happening now, is it okay? So there is   a shift in the industry. There is some change and it has an impact on how we're – what we're going to see, I  believe, in 2014, 2015, and maybe 2016.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: The other element on the market is the fact that projects or new potential projects are being discovered,  by and  large, in deepwater. In fact, over the last six years more than 50% of the elephant or the big reserves being  discovered has been done in deepwater by more than 2,000 meter water depths for oil, and more than 1,500  meter water depths for gas.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: This is a good news for SBM Offshore. Deepwater is really what's driving the utilization of FPSO, and the demand  for FPSO. And we're seeing that with more discoveries in deepwater there's going to be more opportunity to  develop those fields there.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: What is the knock-on effect of that? The knock-on effect of that is that the fields to be developed are more  complex. They are more complex because they are in deeper water; they are more complex because the oil is more  complex; and because the political environment is also more complex.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: On the technical side, we have been investing for a long period of time. But in particular for the past two years, in  developing technology, which is going to help to develop fields in deepwater. Fields which need disconnectable  power for example; fields which requires a lot of pressure going through the turret; field which required topside in  the FPSO which is heavier than we have ever seen for a converted tanker. So we provide the tech nical solution.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Now looking at the E&P spending, and the E&P spending is segmented through the onshore market and the  offshore and deepwater market. I would say up to 2013, the E&P spending offshore including shallow water and  deepwater was in the range of 25% of the overall expenditure.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Over the period of 2013 to 2020 we're going to see yet an increase in the spending to be done, with the highest  increase coming from deepwater development, which is really the core market. But the net effect is – is it going in  and out? I'm sorry, is it okay now. Can you tell me if you can hear or – is it okay?

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: So with the net effect that the offshore E&P expenditure by 2020 is going to represent anywhere between 40% to  45% of all the expenditure of oil and gas company. So, we're in a market segment where the trend over the long  run is extremely good. It's extremely positive and we're well positioned in this market.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Now, our FPSO-led strategy also brought to us two new awards; one for two FPSOs for Petrobras of Generation 3.  What is Generation 3? Generation 3 is basically FPSO able to produce almost 150,000 barrels a day with a topside  in the range of 22,000 tonnes with a complex processing system, with a lot of interface with the client. All of this  needs to be done with local content, and all of this needs to be done in record time. And the client came to us  really to negotiate this, not through a call for tender, but through a negotiation for the award of this project.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: The second project is really the Stones project for Shell. In almost 3,000-meter water depth with a disconnectable  turret, it's the deepest, deepest of its kind worldwide and also, is at the forefront of where the industry is going to  go.

texts.speaker: Peter M. van Rossum
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: [ph] Here, it's (36:52) on the divestments; divestment program is continuing. We sold in 2013 two out of the three  office buildings in Monaco. The third one is being negotiated, as we speak. We sold the COOL hose technology;  that's a fairly minor overall divestment.

texts.speaker: Peter M. van Rossum
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Ratios, just want to highlight a particular ratio, which is pretty keen to us, which is the solvency ratio, where we  saw an improvement by just over 300 basis points, 27% at the end of 2012 to 30%, which is – clearly bringing us  much closer to, let's say, the green zone. But we're still quite a way away from the point where we want to be in  terms of balance sheet strength, which could also then bring us to, let's say, looking at an investment -grade credit  rating, which is still very much the [ph] costs (41:38) of the company.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: The second pillar of our strategy is the mooring technology. How do we fix FPSO, a floating object, to the sea  bottom; how do we fix system, which are going to access a lot of risers with high pressure, high temperature,  corrosive elements, going through an FPSO or through an FLNG?

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: And third pillar is really the development of new products. We cannot ignore the gas market. There are plenty of  opportunity in the gas market coming up, but we need to position ourselves in the gas market into such a way that  we can be credible and we can add value.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Our positioning in the FLNG market is basically the same than on the [ph] converted FPSO (46:18) market. If you  remember, the segmentation of our market is you have the small FPSO producing less than 60,000 barrels per  day; then you have the medium-sized or the large [ph] converted FPSO (46:31), which is our target segment,  producing between 80,000 to 150,000 barrels a day. Then you have the new build, which produce whatever  they're producing.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: The FLNG market is the same. Y ou have the new build; the new build is done by the Shell of this world; new stuff,  the Prelude project is a case in point. We are not competitive on that. We can provide components; we can provide  turret technology, but we're not going to do such a size of FLNG.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: What we can do is, we can provide a converted LNG tanker in order to produce small- to medium-sized fields, and  that's what we're developing. We're developing a concept which is called the twin hull concept o f FLNG. It's, at  this stage, we have done some design engineering; we're looking to go more into detail and developing this  technology over the coming few years.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: We are also developing technology to take into consideration the fact that oil is becoming mo re nasty. It's  becoming heavier. It's becoming more corrosive, that we need to transform gas to liquid. So, we're developing  technology on that.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: And, in some condition, you need to have a floating production system whereby the wellhead will be on the  topside rather than at the sea bottom. And the semi is really one way of doing this in deepwater. So, as you see,  we're developing a range of products also still linked to the floating production capacity.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: We want to keep investing into the large turret mooring technology. Again, there is plenty of opportunity there.  We have a lead on the market, and we want to further this lead. And we want to develop into new products. FLNG,  I expanded on this earlier on; semis, TLPs, and riser technology, in order to know how we interface the sea bottom  to our structure.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: So, yes, the oil companies – international oil company has a dilemma. They want to reduce the cost; they are  caught in the dilemma of adding more local content and they cannot do otherwise with that, even if it's more  expensive. And therefore, they need to change their business model. And we need to change our business model,  as a company.

texts.speaker: Mick B. Pickup
texts.profession: Analyst, Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: It's okay. I'll send smoke signals. I'll see you at lunchtime.  Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas  Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV  A  Okay, see you later on. Sorry about that.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: This really depends on the geology of the reservoir. Most of the reservoirs we're seeing in Western Africa and in  Brazil are, in fact, reservoirs which are spread and, therefore, you don't need to have the wellhead at the top side;  you need to have a subsea tie back, which could be fairly far away, or the subsea tie back going back to an FPSO.

texts.speaker: Quirijn Mulder
texts.profession: Analyst, ING Bank NV (Broker)
texts.text: Y eah, Quirijn Mulder again. On the FLNG story, as I remember 2007/2008, there were quite high promises from  SBM with regard to the FLNG story. As I remember, there was already a breakdown in the market between the big  ones, [ph] the preluders (1:21:10) of this world; and then the small ones, the [ph] niche (1:21:15) of this world; and  then the middle segment, where SBM was aiming for in a partnership with first, as I remember, Linde and then  Chiyoda, so – and they even invested in this activity. So what is the difference in 2014 against 2007, for example?  Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas  Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director, SBM Offshore NV  A  Okay. It's a bit difficult for me, you will understand, to comment on what has been said to you in 2007 . The only  thing I can tell you for a fact is, when I arrived in the Company, the only FLNG project we were bidding was for an  FLNG project for Petrobras, if my memory serves me correctly, which was a 3 million tonne or 4 million tonne per  annum FLNG, which was a project of almost $4 billion and which, in my view, was absolutely not in the capacity  of what SBM could deliver.

texts.speaker: Quirijn Mulder
texts.profession: Analyst, ING Bank NV (Broker)
texts.text: So, at this stage, we stopped the FLNG approach and – but recognizing that the gas market is an important  market. It's an important market which might take time to develop, so I'm not making any promise that next year,  we're going to have an FLNG project. What I'm telling you is that we're developing a strategy similar to our FPSO  strategy, with converted LNG providing a solution which is faster to the market than a new build; providing a  solution which could be an add-on to a large FLNG project, probably seeing 3 million tonne to 4 million tonne per  annum. And basically having – being in a position whereby we're doing projects of $1 billion to $1.5 billion, well in  range of what we can do. For this we have partners, and we're working with those partners in order to develop this  strategy.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director
texts.text: We can see the same evolution in terms of our environmental impact, whereby we've made further im provement  year-on-year on this side also. Having said all of these, this is a type of subject whereby we cannot be complacent.  We need to focus on them all the time. We need to make progress all the time; and is really a key indicator of our  overall performance as an organization.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director
texts.text: So what are we seeing in the market at this stage? And I mean all of us have seen that, but significant decrease in  price of oil. Y es, significant for sure, but the issue that the industry was facing were predating this decline in price  of oil. Our clients were not making enough money on the projects that they were doing. The type of projects that  we were doing and the structure of those projects had to be changed; and I would say that the decrease in price of  oil is in fact going to be a catalyst to change the structure of the industry and the ways of working.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director
texts.text: In fact, the last time we have seen such a change in the industry was probably in the mid -1980s, whereby the price  of oil decreased quite significantly and the industry changed. We went from an industry where most of the  offshore developments were done through platforms to an industry whereby the developments started to be done  subsea with FPSOs. We really believe that even though the market is extremely difficult, 2015 is not going to be a  good year in terms of order intake; it's going to give opportunity to restructure the industry, and really to help the  industry to grow over the medium and long-term.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director
texts.text: Now we also believe that the deepwater development is the place to win. 50% of the resources worldwide are in  deepwater and they all are going to have to be developed. They're going to have to be developed over the medium  and long-term, and we're well-positioned as a company in order to do that. In the medium term, we need to find  different ways of working with our clients.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director
texts.text: Now what are our clients telling us? They basically want to save cash at this stage. There is a high level of  uncertainty linked to the price of oil. What is the price of oil going to be tomorrow morning nobody has a clue. You  get forecasts ranging from $40 to $100 in the same day. Nobody has a clue. The volatility here is not good for  people to make plan. So there is – the only thing that people can do at this stage is really to preserve cash.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director
texts.text: Looking at the leverage ratio, as Bruno said, the expectation is given the current macro -environment is that the  order intake is going to be slow. That will have an impacts on EBITDA in 2015, it will have an impact from  EBITDA in 2016. 2015, we see an increase – 2014, we've seen an increase in net debt on the basis of high CapEx.  Part of that CapEx is paying off in 2015, but the full force of the cash flow contributions of the Generation 3 vessels  will only come in 2016, which means that we have seen an increase to a high level of debt. We're seeing EBITDA.  We will see EBITDA come down in 2015.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director
texts.text: What you do not see here is really all the Brownfield activity, the smaller type of project , which really is not  something that is visible in terms of large project, which really provides a lot of opportunity for us to generate  additional revenues to provide additional resources coming to our facilities. Also some FEED study, which really  are the bedrock of the future project to come. What you're not seeing also more importantly is really the Lead &  Operate portfolio of activity, which has an average life of 14 years and seven months.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director
texts.text: Now, we also have done a number of other strategic initiatives in order to position ourselves for the future. The  first part is really linked to our reaction to the market, with a drop of price of oil and the market volume, we have  had to reduce the workforce and we made an announcement on these in December, basically reducing our  workforce by roughly 12%.

texts.speaker: Quirijn Mulder
texts.profession: ING Bank NV (Broker)
texts.text: And then my last question about the transition phase, Mr. Chabas, can you maybe give some idea about the last  three years have showed we're $1.7 billion in general, can you give me some indication of what the price of these  FPSOs will be in this – after this transition period? What is the value or let me say what is the cost price of these  FPSOs?

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director
texts.text: Certainly that's the way it is. I'm still new. So for the service activity, in fact as a business we qualify a few items on  the service activity, we qualify the smaller type of project for which we really don't have a lot of visibility. We have  some order intake at this stage and some tenders which are on the go. So we're making some assumptions. And  the second side of the business is the offshore installation business for which we basically have a fair bit of  visibility for this year. We know it's going to be a slow year, but we're just making the assumption that we have  today in the $1 billion guidance for the turnkey activity. Again, I think what we're going to see during this year is a  number of smaller type projects for brownfield, for small buoy to be developed, or for offshore activity. Nothing  which is going to earth shattering, but is going to help us to reach the target of $1 billion revenue for the year on  the turnkey side. Sietze for...

texts.speaker: Michel Aupers
texts.profession: Rabobank Nederland
texts.text: And then maybe played the role that you're hinting on payments for the Turritella/Stones FPSO in 2014. I think in  the past you stated to investors that you're going to receive prepayments on first oil, $200 million for the Stones  Turritella FPSO. So basically what happened? Did the contract change...

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: Y es, thank you. [indiscernible] (01:31:45) The final question as I understand it. GEC always said with regards to its
texts.text: oil and gas division that it has received four more notifications that clients want to renegotiate contracts. Now  you've just elaborated on the cash flow conversion of your order quarter backlog, how confident are you that in  these exceptional circumstances you are actually going to convert those backlogs into to cash flow? In other words,  have you received formal indications or notifications or have you in the past had such a situation?

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Managing Director
texts.text: No, we have not had. Now let's put things in perspective. Let's speak generally. We're in the market whereby your  clients have some issues, so we need to listen to them, we need to find solution. There might be some win -win  solution to re-negotiate some contracts and to adjust with. But if we take yet another further step back, today  we're producing with a marginal cost of less than $7 per barrel. That's what it is. Unless the price of oil goes down  to $7  or $5, which I don't think even in the worst forecast we have seen, I don't foresee that we're going to be in a  position like this. Really, I don't foresee that. I foresee that we need to engage into a discussion with our clients  that we need to see what can be done, that we need to see if there are things which need to evolve, that we need to  invest more into some things and so on; and that we're willing to take, but I don't see any drastic change now.
