texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Now, let's speak about the market and the macro environment. This shot is certainly not a surprise to any of you.  We have seen the price of oil dropping significantly over the past year-and-a-half, and to a level which has not  been seen for the last decade. Now, we can focus on the short-term price of oil and get worried about this, and  there is good reason to get worried about this, but also what we need to realize is that the industry and ourselves  need to adjust to a lower commodity price going forward.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Now, if we look more at the medium and long-term fundamental, we need to keep hope on the market and on the  potential evolution of what's going to happen. From now until 2050, we're going to see a drop in population of  more than 2 billion people. We're going to see an increase in urbanization and we're going to see an increase in the  living standard. All of this means that in the coming 1 0 years, we're expecting to see a growth in gas demand by  42% and in oil or liquid demand by almost 20%.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Supply is going to have to be on the market for those demand increase. Even though, we don't want to speculate  on the price of oil, what we expect and what we have put into our plan is that we're going to see a tightening up of  the supply and demand in the period of 2018 and 2019 with a possibility of an increase in market demands for our  services.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Now, we're taking the assumption that the offshore oil and gas industry is going to be able to adapt to the new  pricing environments, and that we're going to be able to develop projects in deepwater, projects which are going to  be economically viable at oil price between $45 to $55. Taking this assumption, we 're seeing an increase – an  expected increase in demand for oil or for services in deepwater and ultra deepwater which is quite significant.  Obviously, there is other markets which are going to increase lightly and conventional, but the demand for the  deepwater services and our product is going to increase. And this demand would increase in market such as Brazil,  Gulf of Mexico, and Western Africa. But we're also seeing new emerging market.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Now if we look at the history of the number of awards for FPSO, we can see that this is tightly correlated to the  price of oil and it will not be a surprise to see with the low price of oil the historically low award market in the  FPSO market. In fact in 2015, we have seen only four FPSO being awarded, while on an average the average  demand for FPSO, new FPSO being on the market between 10 to 12 projects. So if we look at what is the market  telling us in the short-term, it's not a nice picture. The expectation two years ago was that in 2015, we would have  seen 13 FPSO being awarded. The reality has been that four FPSO have been awarded, one of which have been in  the target market of SBM Offshore.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: So it's really a relationship which goes from a vendor relationship to more a tenant type of relationship. So the way  forward for us is first of all to protect the future. We believe that there is a future for the oil and gas industry  offshore, that there is plenty of opportunity to come for the FPSO market, and when the market is going to  rebound we need to have the capacity to be able to deliver our project and we need t o have the capacity to be able  to build two FPSO per year going forward.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: This is a reduction in our capacity of more than 30% compared to two years ago and is a reduction in fact much  greater in the sense that we are simplifying our ways of working and we 're also subcontracting much more, so our  fixed cost structure has been reduced significantly more than the 30% reduction, but it's a capacity we're going to  maintain and it's an investment we're going to have in the coming two years in the Company.

texts.speaker: Peter M. van Rossum
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: The fact now that the full capacity is only reached later is actually also reflected in the average cost that we have  for declines at $7.20 which is even in today's oil price environment very attractive rates to continue to produce oil.  We had two new FPSOs. We also lost three FPSOs after end of contract and demobilization. Those were the Kuito,  the Marlim Sul, and the Brasil FPSOs that are no longer part of our operating portfolio.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Now specifically coming to your question is what we expect to see that 2016 is going to be extremely slow, really  no major decision being made. What we expect to see is 2017 none of FEED projects are going to be coming there,  FEED project which should be leading to project award by 2018 and 2019. Obviously if we were to see that this is  not the case, that if in 2017, the market is as bad as now, we're going to have to decide what to do a nd how to go  forward. But today the assumption is the one I just made.

texts.speaker: Peter M. van Rossum
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Of course, we can't give you exact numbers, but roughly speaking if you look at something like half of the  reduction that we saw in 2016, we're probably not going to be far off. We have one  installment to go on the Dutch  fine of $70 million which will be paid in December 2016.

texts.speaker: Peter M. van Rossum
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: If I look at lease and operate, we have predicted. So you have the 63% conversion rate and what we can see already  in 2015 that we're growing into this and 2016 will be another important step. So we'll be getting much closer to  that now that Generation 3 is about to be delivered.

texts.speaker: Fiona Maclean
texts.profession: Merrill Lynch International
texts.text: Okay, that's very clear. And just a follow-up question on another part of your longer-term strategy that you've  talked about over the last couple of years, you've always said that the returns that you are able as a company to  generate on FPSOs have been pretty low relative to where you would expect them to be for what you are adding to  the industry. Given every single other part of the sector is taking quite a lot of pain in such a low oil price  environment, where do you see your margins and your returns go ing when you do start winning projects from  2018 versus what you are generating today? Thank you.

texts.profession: ABN AMRO Bank NV (Broker)
texts.text: And secondly or maybe related to that, during the third quarter results you were kind of hinting in some sort of a  strategic review to be announced in February this year, i.e., now. Is that still to come or how should I look at that  or did I misunderstood your comments during the third quarter? And in terms of the FEED contracts that you  have in place, I think it's mainly the Browse FLNG things that you're doing in the Sea Lion FPSO. Are there any  other kind of FEED contracts that are in the market where you are tendering on, so not big EP Sharp projects, but  nice FEED contracts that can actually keep you guys busy?

texts.speaker: Philippe Barril
texts.profession: Chief Operating Officer
texts.text: So we'll just to name some, so that we can look at improving the water injection, the settlements of the number of  units. texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: CEO & Member of the Management Board, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: The second point I would like to mention on this slide is our environmental performance. Despite the fact that we  increased our capacity and our FEED by three new vessels, our emission decreased year-on-year and our gas  flared decreased year-on-year. This is due to a number of factor, but some of them is also linked to the fact that  we launched Internet program in order to improve and lower our emission for [indiscernible] (05:12).

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: CEO & Member of the Management Board, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Now, let's turn to the macro view in our market and what's happening in our environment. The first one, which is  not going to be a surprise for any of you, is really that the oil industry has been low in the investment and low in  the investment even further in 2016 compared to 2015 and 2014.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: CEO & Member of the Management Board, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Now, the impact of this has been across the oil industry, but in particular offshore, whereby the number of new  tree order has been to all-time low for the past 17 years with 17 new trees being ordered, compared to an  average over the past 10 years of around [ph] 350 (06:39). It shows you the magnitude of the downturn in the  industry and the fact that there is a long way before we rebuild confidence in the deepwater industry and we'll  rebuild to a level of activity, which is going to be acceptable.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: CEO & Member of the Management Board, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Now, what does it mean? It means that people need to adapt to the new reality and our clients need to adapt to  these. And a lot of work has been done in the industry in order to improve the economics of deepwater field by  reducing the specification and making them more fit for purpose by taking impact of the deflation in the industry.  And the net effect on these projects, which are being sanctioned or near being sanctioned, have decreased their  breakeven point per barrel significantly anywhere between 30% to 60%, depending on the case. It translates for  the FPSO industry into a demand we should increase. Now, it's not difficult to increase when you start from zero.  In 2016, basically, no project was awarded or no significant projects were awarded.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: CEO & Member of the Management Board, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Now, how do we position at the end of showing all of this? Basically, we have looked at the reality of our market,  the opportunities that there is no market, and the broader market, and how to transform the company and to use  the experience that we have in the floating production systems. For this we developed a program, an  improvement program based on three pillars. Optimize, to optimize the current business that we have in portfolio.  Transform, and really transform how we develop the better project to transform the economics, the quality of what  we're doing. And this, we're working on two main projects, Fast4ward and digital FPSO. And third pillar is, to  innovate. Basically, to transfer the floating solutions that we have into other markets, being gas, being renewable  and other.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: CEO & Member of the Management Board, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Now, Transform. On Transform, over the past two, three years, we really have been working significantly to  improve our ways of doing a project, to reduce the number of things that is being done on in terms of the over  specification and we need to come to solutions, which are more fit to our purpose. This is based on SBM Offshore  experience. This is based on what we have delivered over the year. And it's really a reduction which is  sustainable over the time even if we will see another increase in inflation going forward, the saving will remain.  And what we have done is basically being able to reduce our saving across our product portfolio in the range of  20% to 35%.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: CEO & Member of the Management Board, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: While, going forward, we cannot be blind to the change in energy mix, which seems to happen in the industry.  What we can see in this slide is, going forward in the period 2015 to 2040, the expectation is that the demand for  renewable energy and gas is going to increase significantly. Even though that the demand of oil is still going to  remain at this [ph] steady or (17:54) good level. And let's not forget that for oil, there is a lot of depletion of the  existing fuel. Having said that, new areas or new markets for demand is going to appear in our markets. And it's  going to be on the gas side and on the renewable side.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: CEO & Member of the Management Board, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: So, what is SBM doing about this? The first one is on the gas. And on the gas let's not forget that we have been  involved in this activity since 2005. We have been operating here Sanha LPG assets from [ph] this period (18:33).  We have been involved in the Deep Panuke assets also which is a gas plant for a number of years. We have  been involved in a number of turrets that we have – which have been involved on projects like Prelude and  Ichthys.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: CEO & Member of the Management Board, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: So, all of this shows our track record and our experience. We are building on this. We're building on that capacity  in order to see what can be done to safely develop gas fields, which are smaller and to develop them in an  economic manner. And we're involved in a number of projects on this.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: CEO & Member of the Management Board, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: The second aspect is the floating wind. As you have seen, we're involved in the FEED project for EDF in France  on the floating wind farm. Now, this is important. If we believe the forecast, we can see that there is a huge  amount of opportunity for floating wind farm. And SBM is uniquely placed with the floating solution that we have  had over the past six years to provide a solution, which is fit for purpose. So, we have been investing in those  technology for the past few years. We're planning to finalize the FEED that we have. We're looking at all the  alternative projects for this technology and we want to grow this activity going forward because it's something  which is there on the core competence of SBM Offshore and while we believe that there is a good opportunity of  growing.

texts.speaker: Dirk Verbiesen
texts.profession: Analyst, KBC Securities NV
texts.text: Yes. Good morning, gentlemen. A question on the prospects you gave for 2017 and 2018. Can you a bit more  precise there, how many of those are located in Brazil. And also, what the split is between oil FPSOs and gas  prospects in that overview?

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: CEO & Member of the Management Board, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Looking at the information we provided with regard to the market going forward, we're discussing only about  FPSO. So, oil related activity, we didn't give any view on the gas activity whatsoever. And that's the figure that  you've seen in one of the slide in the presentation. And, now we are not – and we have not been giving any detail  on where those projects are coming from, which clients and which prospect we're working on and we're sticking to  this policy.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: CEO & Member of the Management Board, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Yeah. It's a good question. Over time, maybe. But in a period of two to three years, unlikely. It's a market which is  starting. I'm speaking about the floating wind renewable market. It's a market which is starting, whereby only a  few projects and minor projects have been committed so far and only one of them developed offshore. So, we'll  see the stage, where we need to finalize the engineering to validate the concept, and all of this is going to take  between two to three years before or maybe a bit longer. But I would say once the concept is validated and once  we can demonstrate that we can reduce the cost and have the cost of energy on those projects, which is in line  with what the market is requesting, the opportunity on this market is going to be great. But over a period of two,  three years, it's not going to have any meaningful impact on our [ph] P&L (54:56).

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: CEO & Member of the Management Board, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Now, with regards to technology, what is of interest to us is really to be able to get some technology, which is  going to help us leverage our floating solution technology, and that could be on the renewable market, that could  be on the energy storage, that could in the gas market, and that could be done in a different manner. It could be  done through acquisition. It could be done through partnership and so on and so forth. So, we're looking at ways  where it would develop the technology that we're using on the floating platform in order to provide different  solution. And that's the focus that we have.

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SBM Offshore NV

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: So, from a macro standpoint, where do we stand? The first [ph] statement (00:06:13) is really linked to the oil  price. texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SBM Offshore NV

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Now, a lot of talk has been happening in the industry about the significant cost reduction we have seen year-on- year since 2015, and when we look at the cost reduction of the [indiscernible] (00:07:48) inflation we have seen in  the industry is probably can be quantified around 30% overall.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Now, all of this will not make any sense if there was no project to develop. texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Now what is the strategy in order to capitalize on the market upturn? Our strategy which have been developed  only two years ago has not fully changed. texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: We also see that there is an opportunity for the deep water field to be developed. And for this, we need to  transform the industry. For this, we have invested in Fast4Ward. texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Now, our world is evolving. Energy demand is growing. The shift in demand is changing with more demand for the  gas, more demand for the renewable. texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: Now, the Lease and Operate activity, again we're delivering 10% or we're producing 10% of the [indiscernible]  (00:16:16) deep water which is quite remarkable. texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: On the gas technology, again, the company has been involved there for a long period of time. We are involved in the feedback, and we're looking on  making progress through the coming 18 months only. And we want to leverage our experience obviously by doing  so.

texts.speaker: Bruno Yves Raymond Chabas
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SBM Offshore NV
texts.text: On the floating wind, we have had – we're on track with the FID that we're doing with EDF. We expect a full  investment decision by 2019. texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SBM Offshore NV

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: As you know that this project has been run as a sequential start up and that is a very good thing to have because  that will mitigate risk of course. texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: We've been running for 50% capacity up till now. But now from June, we will run it to 100%. But this is – I mean,  this is already finalized more or less. texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB

texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB

texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: When it comes to EBITDA, again, the biggest effect of course is the same its price/mix where we have high prices  for all major segments. texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Energy largely flat, we had probably more Energy costs, which I'll come back in the direct costs in Pulp slightly in  the first quarter offset by some other positive impacts in Energy, but overall largely flat. texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: We expect the fixed cost reduction, which will be the largest impact of some SEK 350 per tonne. texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: And then finally, we have the direct cost impact during the ramp up, which we expect to be around between SEK  100 million and SEK 250 million during the whole year due to the effect of higher costs for Energy, higher costs  for chemicals, some extra wood consumption, and a higher share of B-grade pulp during the ramp up.

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: We've added stable wood supply even if we had a strong and hard winter this year, of course, due to the fact that  we are – have a high degree of self-sufficiency, which is a good thing to have in a winter like this. texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Yeah. I mean, it's not so easy to calculate but I think that we've had maybe SEK 20 million, SEK 30 million in  extra costs. texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: It's very hard to give guidance but I think that was obviously Q1 last year versus Q1 this year. It increased to  some degree during last year. texts.profession: Analyst, Danske Bank A/S (Sweden)

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB

texts.speaker: Oskar Lindström
texts.profession: Analyst, Danske Bank A/S (Sweden)
texts.text: And my final question is, I guess also a follow-up on that is the – we're seeing a number of capacity increase  projects either already ongoing both in Sweden, Finland, and also in the Baltics, and you have this potential  project as well on top of the Östrand expansion. texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: I mean, we had the opposite situation, in the past I mean, we have seen lots of closures. And as it is just now, at  least in our region, we have a rather balanced situation. texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB

texts.profession: Analyst, Kepler Cheuvreux SA (Sweden)

texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB

texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Definitely, it's technical in that perspective. And I mean, one thing is to produce the volume. But for us, it's really  important that we will serve the market with high-quality pulp. texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Oh, it's spring also in the northern part of Sweden.

texts.speaker: Robin Santavirta
texts.profession: Analyst, Carnegie Investment Bank AB (Finland)
texts.text: [ph] But it is floods – there sort of floods are (00:46:08) flooding? Might that be...

texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: But the positive thing, we've had a lot of snow. It was rather cold in this winter. But, I mean, the snow came before  we had the coldness. texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: I mean, what we have done ourselves is that we have announced plus SEK 20 per cubic meter in both pulp and  saw logs, and that will, of course, have a positive impact on our EBIT level in the Forest. texts.speaker: Martin Melbye
texts.profession: Analyst, ABG Sundal Collier Norge ASA
texts.text: Excellent. Last question. The next 10-year Forest plan, when is that due?

texts.speaker: Björn Lyngfelt
texts.profession: Senior Vice President-Group Communications, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Okay. Thank you. That was the end of the list of questions and which means that we will now conclude this  session. And since we've had quite a few questions on Wood and Forest that will be a good  opportunity to have a deeper insight in the mysteries of the forest operations and wood supply. So, thank you and  look forward to seeing you soon again.

texts.text: If we take a look at the operating profit, it has grown by, as you can see, 10%. So a good growth. And that includes  two items here, of course, currency translation, once again, Swedish krona and British pound primarily. But we  also have an adverse impact from forest swaps. You may recall that as of January 1, 2015, we no longer take profit  or gains from profit swaps into our income statement. So of course for Q2 of 2015 there is no profit contribution  from forest swaps, whilst in Q2 of 2014, we had a SEK 175 million and that's part of the other bar that you see on  this line. So, if you take away the currency and the forest gain from foreign swaps, those two the organic or  underlying comparable growth was 9% in the quarter. And of course, most notably here, SEK 435 million negative  impact from raw material, most of this coming from  the tissue operations.

texts.speaker: Fredrik Rystedt
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: Just a few comments on the other, I already mentioned that part of this SEK 17 5 million or this SEK 240 million  that you see, relates to the gain from forest swaps, but there is also another part which comes from a wide number  of different things. Actually, we have a positive part, which is savings efficiency gains, and we have, in the quarter,  had levels of savings approximately equal to that of last year. So we continue to actually become more and more  efficient. But we also have higher A&P. We also have higher SG&A cost as – for the group as a whole. And, of  course, normal parts such as inflation, et cetera. Worth noting, however, is that A &P and SG&A, as a percentage of  sales, are not increasing. So it's just a normal continuation of the business, so to speak.

texts.speaker: Fredrik Rystedt
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: So the big swing between last year and this year is largely due to the operating cash surplus. And if you look at the  number, it's actually a much bigger swing than what you would see for EBIT. And the re ason is very simply that,  once again, the forest – or gains from forest swap is not a cash flow item. So the underlying cash flow impact is  much bigger. And the other part is pretty much about the same size is increased depreciation this year. So that's  why the cash – operating cash surplus improvement is much bigger than what you would see for EBIT.

texts.speaker: Magnus Groth
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Thank you, Fredrik. Then we'll dig into the key business areas in some more detail. And I'm very happy to, once  again, be able to state that better price mix, better volumes, and cost savings actually apply to all our three  business areas, so it's a recurring scene. When it comes to personal care, actually those three im provements have  made it possible for us to keep the operating margin at 11.3% in spite of the significant raw material headwinds  that we have also in this quarter. In personal care, we have a negative effect on the fluff pulp, from currency  mostly and the positive effect from the oil-based materials. But the positive effect doesn't outweigh the negative  effect in fluff pulp. And that negative impact on the margin was approximately 80 basis points, which is a  significant negative impact, and that we covered them through price mix volumes and cost savings.

texts.speaker: Magnus Groth
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: The innovations is a mix of things. And I actually have some of them here behind me. And looking specifically at  the Tork cleaning cloths, you could argue that what can you do with a piece of cloth. But I think, what  differentiates us from our competitors here is that we have the size to scale to really come with innovation that has  a noticeable and tangible payoff and benefit for the user. So as you can see here, we can prove that this new  product – it's this one over here, our new industrial cleaning cloth – requires 32% less time for cleaning a certain  surface than other products. It uses 40% less solvent which also has a positive environmental impact. And it uses  20% less effort, which is very important for the people who are using this product in an industrial situation, for  instance.

texts.speaker: Magnus Groth
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Finally, forest products continues to have a very strong performance both in terms of sales and operating profits.  The operating profit is very much driven by the strong dollar which is benefiting our forest products division since  we are producing these products in Sweden, especially kraftliner and pulp, the increasing demand and a good  price picture. While sawn timber, during the quarter, we experienced slightly declining prices and, overall, again,  a good performance in forest products.

texts.speaker: Magnus Groth
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: I just want to briefly say something about our three-year marketing platform, the participation of our female team  in the Volvo Ocean Race, which finished in Gothenburg a few weeks ago, reaches for global marketing platform  with the focus on women and with a strong connection to sustainability and CSR issues.

texts.speaker: Fredrik Rystedt
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: Y eah, I can – hi, Celine. I can start with that. If you look at personal care this quarter, as we have elaborated on,  we have a positive impact from oil-related products. So plastics has come down and, therefore, [indiscernible]  (00:27:21) nonwoven, et cetera. What is actually taking place in the last couple of months is that the plastics  indices has once again started to increase. This is not due to oil, this has to do with the demands or supply- demand balance. So there are not many producers of these materials and we are, therefore, expecting higher  prices than we have seen now. So from that perspective the oil-based product is actually at its lowest here in Q2  and will rise in Q3 and Q4. So now you've seen SEK 435 million. We're not giving any specific guidance, but of  course that benefit we've seen from oil is not going to be there.

texts.speaker: Fredrik Rystedt
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: No. That's – we're not providing – as of this year, we're not specifically proving numbers relating to efficiency  savings, Celine, and the reason we're not doing that is that the important thing is what – not what we achieve on  specific activities or programs. The importance is the total cost development of the group. That's why we are not  doing that, but the SEK 500 million number that you have I think it's more the sequential or maybe annualized  impact. But in reality, the actual saving was significantly lower than that.

texts.speaker: Magnus Groth
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer

texts.speaker: Oskar Lindström
texts.profession: Danske Bank A/S (Sweden)
texts.text: If I may ask, I mean you've previously – when you've had cost save programs or plans, you've actually set them  out in formalized cost save programs and guided us on what to expect. What is the reason for not doing so now?

texts.speaker: Fredrik Rystedt
texts.profession: CFO and Executive Vice President. Head of Group Function Finance
texts.text: I can maybe add there, because I think you can always – any company can produce a cost program, and most  companies will deliver on those cost programs because what you do is you set a specific number of activities and  then you calculate the benefit relatively conservative, and then you track them and off you go. texts.speaker: Fredrik Rystedt
texts.profession: CFO and Executive Vice President. Head of Group Function Finance
texts.text: Yeah. And again, we are comparing here when we talk about price movements against last year's quarter. So  we've seen a decline in solid wood products and kraftliner. texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: We've had a stable wood supply during the quarter and we also had a stable wood supply during the winter. We  had a harsh winter condition. We have had now dry and warm summer. But as we have a high degree of the  wood that we need from our own forest, we can handle that in a good way.

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: We've seen some price increases in the market, especially for imported wood. But again, as we have around 50%  from our own forest and as we also buy a lot of wood from the domestic market, we are not especially impacted  by import prices as [indiscernible] (00:06:54) now.

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: So we have also during the quarter launched a new paper category which we called Fine Wood-containing Paper.  It is a paper based on chemical pulp, and that paper will compete with wood-free paper. We have a super good  brightness, good bulk in the paper, and also good opacity. And why we'd based this quality on mechanical pulp, it  would be really cost efficient both for us as a producer but also for our customers. We have done between 5,000  tonnes and 10,000 tonnes in the market. And it has been really well-received in the market.

texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: The EBITDA in Forest was stronger in the second quarter than the first quarter. And this is largely the seasonality  with a larger delivery of wood sourced from our own forest in the second quarter versus the first quarter but also  some effect from higher prices.

texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: When it comes to the EBITDA waterfall, again price mix is the biggest effect on here. We've seen a positive effect  in all segments from higher prices. We had an effect again from the volumes with minus SKE 39 million. Raw  material costs with negative effect from some higher cost for raw materials for wood and for chemicals and here  also some effect from the Östrand start-up, the higher direct costs, so the usage of raw materials in Östrand and  the chemicals.

texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: On energy, we have a small positive, the electricity price is actually higher, now, in the second quarter, but we've  had some effects from higher price for electricity certificates, and we also had a negative effect from electricity  certificates last year, in the second quarter.

texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Just come on to a couple of more details on the Östrand project and this you've seen largely before, but just to  help you understand the affects. Production began in June according to plan. The ramp-up period is expected to  be 12 to 18 months. And that means we expect 2018 volumes to be in line with 2017, and that means also that  2020 is the first year we expect to be at full capacity. The new mill will be world class in its cost position. It will  double the soft wood capacity. We'll have a fixed cost reduction of SEK 350 per tonne, and we'll have an  improved energy balance with where we will go from being a small net consumer of electricity to a net producer of  some 0.5 terawatt hours.

texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: And we see potentially some higher wood costs from what needed to be sourced from further away. And then  particularly on the cost impact and here you've seen this table before as well, but we've updated for the second  quarter. And on the right-hand side, I just focus on the table on the right-hand side you can see the main effects  from the project here and you'd have the project-related cost where we had SEK 15 million in the second quarter.  We had the actual maintenance stop or expansion stop effect in the second quarter which was SEK 236 million.  And here, we expect SEK 256 million for the full year, so maybe we plan for some small effect in the second half.

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: EBITDA up 43%, and as we also stated that we are negatively impacted by the plant start-up cost in Östrand  which has cost us SEK 250 million, approximately. We have, during the quarter, announced the partnership  together with St1 in order to produce biojet. And last but not the least, we are now up and running with Östrand.  We are well ahead of the start-up curve and the quality is really good as it is just now.

texts.speaker: Mikael Jåfs
texts.profession: Analyst, Kepler Cheuvreux SA (Sweden)
texts.text: Yes. Hello. Good morning, everybody. A couple of questions from my side. The first one is around your Wood  products division that historically has been very cyclical and now it's doing very well, and if I heard you correctly,  there you said that you had price increases also announced going into the second half. Could you just elaborate a  little bit on that market? And then also in conjunction with that, you mentioned that raw material prices are going  up. Is that a function of rising wood prices in your areas? That's the first question. And the second question is  around Publication paper. Normally, we should see decline in demand but still we see paper price increases.  Could you talk a little bit about that and how long could we expect to see let's say a balanced Paper market?  Those are my questions. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Thank you. Well, if we start with the Wood business, I mean, as we've said, we've seen price increases now for  many quarter in the row. We know that we will have further price increases in the second half of this year. And the  reason for that is, of course, that we still have a strong consumption in more or less all areas as it is just now. In  general, inventory levels are very low and that goes the same for SCA. [ph] Summing this (00:25:08) balance  question. How long will it last? Well, it's not up to us to answer. [indiscernible] (00:25:15), but as it is just now it is  stable. It's a strong market I would say. And, yes, we've seen that the price on [ph] sole logs (00:25:26) is coming  up a little bit again as we are in a good position in the way that we take a lot of the wood that we need from our  own forests. We are quite balanced. But you're right, 70% of the cost where so many is related to the raw material  costs. But as it is just now, we've been able to compensate that increased cost.

texts.speaker: Linus Larsson
texts.profession: Analyst, Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken AB (Broker)
texts.text: Okay. Fair enough. And also cost item in relation to the Östrand ramp up. How do you see your wood sourcing  and wood cost develop that your own sourcing of wood is gradually increasing with a ramp up of the Östrand  volumes?

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: I mean, in general, we see that prices going up, has gone up a little bit, and we feel that we are in good control.  We have built up inventories now. So we are prepared for the start-up. Just now, we are well ahead of the start-up  curve and still I think that we are in good control, and we have a controlled wood supply I would say.

texts.speaker: Linus Larsson
texts.profession: Analyst, Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken AB (Broker)
texts.text: Are you looking to increase imports of wood; and if so, does that automatically increase the average cost of wood  for you?

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: It is just now we don't need to import more wood than we've done in the past. But I mean long-term, import is an  alternative, but we prefer to be domestically based in our sourcing, and the flow now from private forest owners is  quite good. So [ph] summing, (00:31:20) we feel confident.

texts.speaker: Martin Melbye
texts.profession: Analyst, ABG Sundal Collier Norge ASA
texts.text: Yes, good morning. So, I'm going to take with the questions on Östrand. Say, if the pulp price and the wood price  is flat in Q3. What would EBIT be? Because you have all these different effects impacting EBIT, maintenance,  direct cost, indirect cost, volume loss, etcetera?

texts.speaker: Martin Melbye
texts.profession: Analyst, ABG Sundal Collier Norge ASA
texts.text: All right. And these higher wood costs, when will that be visible in your Forest division? Or high wood prices.

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: I think the tricky thing now will be when we reached the design capacity and that is really hard to predict because  somewhere we will have some summer and some time we will have some bottleneck coming up. And then, we  can really test the design capacity. And I mean I think that we will have now a good startup during the autumn but  we, I think, we need – it's too early to say, if we need this 18 months or if we can do it faster. It's too early to say if  we reach directly the design capacity or if we need to do some complementary investments in the [ph] lime deal  or lime kiln (00:37:21) or in the, yeah, wherever.

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Quality is good. I mean clean, brightness, cleanest, also strength. That it's all positive things and not the list that  we already now see that we can produce a stronger pulp than we did in the old mill. The old mill was good. It was  good in the benchmark, but this is really promising I would say quality wise.

texts.speaker: Oskar Lindström
texts.profession: Analyst, Danske Bank A/S (Sweden)
texts.text: So, I mean you're selling it as you said all of the volume coming out of the mill is now being sold as prime pulp.

texts.speaker: Oskar Lindström
texts.profession: Analyst, Danske Bank A/S (Sweden)
texts.text: Right. My third question is around the forest fires. You don't mention them in the report. You have a press release  out on your webpage. It sounds as if that's not something that we should expect will have an impact on your wood  supply in any significant way in the third quarter. Is that how we should understand it?

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: I mean, as I said, on SCA land, we've been very lucky so far. And we have had productive forest land around 600  hectares that has been burnt down and that is equal to what we normally burn in order to keep the FSC  certificate.

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Of course, we now try to be as careful as we can. We don't run our harvesters during daytime. If it's dry and hot,  then we use them during nighttime. So, I mean, that kind of disturbances we see but nothing major, really. But this  isn't over yet. So, if this weather will continue, then it might be so that it will cause further problems in the region.  But as it is just now, it is controlled.

texts.speaker: Oskar Lindström
texts.profession: Analyst, Danske Bank A/S (Sweden)
texts.text: Good. My third question is around wood products. You mentioned low inventory levels in the industry, but also in  your mills. And I presume that's sort of finished product you're talking about. Can you increase volumes in your  wood products' operation further from where you are today or are there limits either to your own capacity or in  terms of wood supply?

texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Yeah. I think that's a fair comment. I mean, like you say, we don't see any dramatic change. We do see increased  costs for raw materials as we said on chemicals. But, yeah, we don't see any big trend, change or increase in Q3  versus previous quarters.

texts.speaker: Jan Christer Johansson
texts.profession: President, CEO & Independent Director
texts.text: I've talked a lot about innovations earlier and I will come back to that ones. We're having a very successful year  when it comes to introducing new innovations to the market. texts.speaker: Jan Christer Johansson
texts.profession: President, CEO & Independent Director
texts.text: Operating profits increased by 14%. If we take away the big profit we had in forest swaps last year, it's actually an  increase of 18%. Also, operating margin is going up, earnings per share up by 19%, and we also had a  very strong  cash flow.

texts.speaker: Jan Christer Johansson
texts.profession: President, CEO & Independent Director
texts.text: Efficiency program, we have been talking about that since we started it. If we look at the hygiene business in total  now, we have implemented the blueprint in all our sites. texts.speaker: Jan Christer Johansson
texts.profession: President, CEO & Independent Director
texts.text: We also more and more are using our scale when it comes to buying raw materials, et cetera, and we also, in some  areas, cooperate with other buyers like in pulps. So today, we are the biggest pulp buyer in the world and that, of  course, helps to get good terms in the market.

texts.profession: President, CEO & Independent Director

texts.speaker: Jan Christer Johansson
texts.profession: President, CEO & Independent Director
texts.text: Sourcing costs, down by 5%; logistics costs, 5%; energy consumption, 6%. So we can truly see that what we are  doing has an impact in all areas where we actually are working. We will continue with this and we still  see some interest and potential going forward. We are not going to set up a new program, but now we will do it in  the day-to-day business.

texts.speaker: Jan Christer Johansson
texts.profession: President, CEO & Independent Director

texts.speaker: Jan Christer Johansson
texts.profession: President, CEO & Independent Director

texts.text: Then going into Forest operations. They have quite a substantial improvement. Y ou can't really believe that when  you look at this picture. texts.speaker: Jan Christer Johansson
texts.profession: President, CEO & Independent Director

And then –  so, we got a four months to six months lag when you translate the plastics indices into non-woven or sap or  whatever it [ph] made actually towards (1:05:40) all those kind of things that we use. So, that meant that we had a  positive impact in Q2 of last year as you may recall.

texts.speaker: Fredrik Rystedt
texts.profession: CFO and Executive Vice President. Head of Group Function Finance
texts.text: Then prices went back up again and plastics indices started to go up in March timeframe last year and this was on  the back of – and you may remember this shortfall of production capacity. There was a force majeure in a plant in  the United States, et cetera, lots of things. So, basically supply issues.

texts.speaker: Fredrik Rystedt
texts.profession: CFO and Executive Vice President. Head of Group Function Finance
texts.text: And then we've seen during the fall that plastics indices have fallen once again and then after that, basically  stabilized on a lower levels despite the fact that oil prices have come down. So, if you look at that, we have a slight  benefit in Q4. We'll have a Q1 benefit and that will continue if everything stays as it is right now. We'll have a  slight benefit also in the following quarters.

texts.speaker: Fredrik Rystedt
texts.profession: CFO and Executive Vice President. Head of Group Function Finance
texts.text: So, unfortunately the math, the way it works is that plastics indices if that falls by 10% then we get an average of  benefit of 3%. That's the kind of relation you have. And then it's up to you to sort of define what's the relationship  between plastics indices and oil prices. They had been, over time, very correlated. But as I just talked about in the  last year or so, oil prices have come down a lot, plastics indices have not. So, the impact is much less than what it  appears to be just by looking at the oil price. So, once again, we don't know. I think we'll see some benefits  [indiscernible] (1:07:15)

texts.speaker: Magnus Groth
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: We also announced in August the potential split of the group in two listed companies, hygiene and forest  products. And as a consequence, we presented a new vision and enhanced strategic framework specifically then  for the hygiene part of the business.

texts.speaker: Magnus Groth
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Forest products had a pickup in sales in the fourth quarter. Organic sales increased by 4% behind these volumes  in pulp and in solid wood products primarily. Adjusted operating profit is down 10%, down from 14.8% to 12.9%  and this is due to higher energy and raw material costs and in spite of higher volumes and lower distribution  costs.

texts.speaker: Magnus Groth
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: And we also have us a bullet here of biological assets adjustment and Fredrik will talk more about this in a short  while. And as usual, I'd like to say something about the outlook for the first quarter when it comes to prices for the  most important products in forest products since these are global market prices. For publication paper, we foresee  stable outlook for the first quarter. Of course in the longer term, we have a bleak outlook for publication paper.

texts.speaker: Magnus Groth
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Kraftliner, a stable outlook for the first quarter even though we are starting to see some price increase  announcements coming now in the market. So, looking beyond the first quarter, maybe slightly higher prices. And  the same for pulp, slightly higher prices in the first quarter. And in solid wood products, also higher prices.

texts.speaker: Fredrik Rystedt
texts.profession: Executive Vice President & CFO, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Magnus talked about the biological assets. And I will just start by saying what this actually is. And what we do  every year is an adjustment or evaluation in accordance with IFRS in biological assets. And the way that works is  that based on the harvesting plan that we do every eight years, we haven't done that this year, but we base the  valuation on that harvesting model, what we do is we assess a starting value. And then we assess what the  inflation is both for the cost and for the wood price.

texts.speaker: Fredrik Rystedt
texts.profession: Executive Vice President & CFO, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Now, this therefore is not a market valuation, because it's completely linear and static model in the sense that we  don't estimate any potential future price increases that may come out from higher demand or perhaps more use of  biological assets for biofuel, et cetera, or other kind of things. So, we just have a static starting point for our  valuation.

texts.speaker: Fredrik Rystedt
texts.profession: Executive Vice President & CFO, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: We have historically used a 10-year model. And if you look at the graph there, below, you can clearly see that  over the last several years, because of many things, including storms and other things, prices of wood have  actually come down. So, the 10-year average, which is kind of clear from this graph, is much higher than the  corresponding spot price at this point of time. And that means that we have adjusted now, and we've gone to,  instead, a five-year model, which is kind of very close to where the actual spot prices is. The result of this is that  the average price has come down from SEK 467 million to SEK 432 million as a starting point of the valuation.

texts.speaker: Linus Larsson
texts.profession: Analyst, Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken AB (Broker)
texts.text: Linus Larsson with SEB. Can we start with the discussion around the forest value? You are in the middle of a  SEK 7.8 billion investment in a new pulp mill at Östrand and I would expect that to have, if anything, a positive  impact on pricing for wood in the region. I would expect that to have, if anything, a positive impact of any  harvesting plan that you have for your forest land. So, against that background, I must say I'm a bit surprised by  your move from a 10-year historic model to a 5-year historic model. Could you talk a bit more about that? And  also when is your harvesting plan up for review next?

texts.speaker: Olof Grenmark
texts.profession: Analyst, ABG Sundal Collier AB
texts.text: Olof Grenmark, ABG Sundal Collier. If I may continue then on the forest side. And it's – you gave us some  extraordinary costs in relation to the coming split up. If you could, first of all, please repeat what you've said in  terms of what we will get, any kind of information regarding that split up, the time line. If you could elaborate  possibly about what you will give for information?

texts.speaker: Fredrik Rystedt
texts.profession: Executive Vice President & CFO, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Yeah. I mean, as we have promised, we will present – we've said that all along that regardless of a decision from  AGM, we will present more detailed information relating to forest. So, of course you will see that in the Q1 report  as promised. So, we'll come back to the exact details on segmentation and how the P&L will look, et cetera, but  you will get much more information in Q1.

texts.speaker: Mikael Jåfs
texts.profession: Analyst, Kepler Cheuvreux SA (Sweden)
texts.text: Perfect. And then, I mean, we have seen now that pricing for recycled paper has come up quite a lot too in the  past quarter. There also seems to be signs around the pulp market. How are you thinking about raw material  inflation? And then, how are you thinking about the possibility to offset that?

texts.speaker: Magnus Groth
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Yeah. So, we have seen recycled paper prices going up. And as part of our tissue roadmap, we're also looking in  detail into them what will be our raw material supply going forward. It's not unlikely that we will see a replacement  of recycled tissue with more virgin tissue going forward. And we actually have already examples where we are  doing this.

texts.speaker: Magnus Groth
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: For instance, in Chile, in our factory, where there is an abundance of virgin fiber, we have actually been able to  reduce our costs for the first time almost ever, this is highly unusual. By replacing recycled fiber with virgin fiber  also then achieving a higher quality of refined products. So, this is part of our long-term strategy, that sourcing  part.

texts.speaker: Magnus Groth
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: We know that both recycled fiber prices and the virgin fiber prices will be very volatile going forward. So, they will  change over time.

texts.speaker: Fredrik Rystedt
texts.profession: Executive Vice President & CFO, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: We gave – normally, we gave a directional guidance, as you know, on raw material prices for the different parts.  So, if you look at just Q1, what we estimate. If you look at Personal Care, we believe it's going to be slightly  higher. This is chemicals and SAP or superabsorbent, basically oil-based.

texts.speaker: Fredrik Rystedt
texts.profession: Executive Vice President & CFO, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: If you look at the Tissue side, we believe it's going to be stable in comparison once again to last year's quarter,  and for forest, slightly higher or higher. So, this is basically our directional guidance.

texts.speaker: Magnus Groth
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Any capacity reduction has some impact even though, I think, in the big picture, this is a minor contribution. The  reason why we're doing this is because, for us, volumes are not contributing to enhancing our margins.

texts.speaker: Oskar Lindström
texts.profession: Analyst, Danske Bank A/S (Sweden)
texts.text: Okay. Thank you. And then, finally, just you mentioned this information brochure that you will distribute ahead of  the AGM. And I presume that that's the one that's going to include more detailed financials for the forest products  business. So that's the first part of that question.

texts.speaker: Fredrik Rystedt
texts.profession: Executive Vice President & CFO, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Maybe I can answer that, Oskar. The information brochure will not contain that broad information on the forest.  That will be a Q1 issue as we have stated before.

texts.speaker: Iain E. Simpson
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA
texts.text: Thank you very much. My apologies if this has already been asked, but you talked about SEK 11 billion of CapEx  this year of which SEK 4 billion is in forest. And I think you've also said that the forest spin off will have SEK 5  billion of debt. Is that SEK 5 billion of debt on spin off? And how much CapEx will the forest business carry out  post-spin off in this year? How much of that SEK 4 billion is pre-spin and how much is post-spin?

texts.speaker: Iain E. Simpson
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA
texts.text: And also, if you could just tie that back to the expansion – so the Östrand plant expansion in forest, how much of  the total cost of that do you think will be outstanding by the end of this year? How far through that does the SEK 4  billion take us? Thank you very much.

texts.speaker: Fredrik Rystedt
texts.profession: Executive Vice President & CFO, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Lot of questions. I will try to give you an answer. If I start with your question on the SEK 5 billion, what's that going  to be at spin off. First of all, the SEK 5 billion was actually at December 31, 2016 as an estimate. So, that means  that the old cash flow after that day will sort of add to that debt. And when I said add, it's because we expect a  negative cash flow from forest due to the Östrand investment. So, in fact, you can say all of that SEK 4 billion that  I just alluded to in terms of CapEx will actually affect that SEK 5 billion, if you understand. So, that I think takes  care of the question.

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: And we also, this quarter, had some extra costs related to that big investment project in Östrand, but they are,  again, according to plan for SEK 28 million for the quarter. Otherwise, the project in Östrand is running according  to plan. We have now done 70% of the investment or SEK 5.5 billion. We have just recently started up the  evaporation plant and, as you know, which is also big positive thing for this project.

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: We have a sequential start-up, so we took – the wood-handling department were up and running already in the  autumn. Now, we have taken the evaporation plant up and running from January. Now, we will have the  packaging line and also the drying machine up and running in February. And then we will have the big, big thing in  April, May where we will extend the recovery boiler, but everything, so far, is running according to plan.

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Then I walk over to our four segments and I'd like to start with the Forest part, and we have a balanced timber  supply situation. We have also had a stable price development with minor increases in our area. We can see that  in other area, prices going up just now, but we feel that we have a good control over the price development here.

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Last year, we did harvest 4.4 million cubic meters, which is according to the long-term harvesting plan. The year  before that, we were hit by the storm, so then we had to harvest a little bit more on external land, but this year, we  are back on track, so to say. We have also started to prepare in terms of wood supply for the big start-up. We'll  need between 2 million and 2.5 million cubic meters more annually due to the Östrand project, and we are  prepared for that.

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: And one thing that is worth mentioning is the timber yield. We have a situation where 67% to 70% of the cost for a  sawmill is related to the log. And just now, we have a little bit more than 50% yield in our sawmills, and we have  rather narrow stocks, so we are very happy about that and that also give a good contribution to our profitability.  That is related, of course, to some investments but also to a lot of hard work in this area.

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: I did mention the all-time high production in Obbola, which is really a positive thing. We also took just recently an  investment decision in order to increase capacity of white top kraftliner in Munksund. As I've said earlier, that will  not have an impact on the total production capacity, but it will increase the share of white with 50,000 tonnes  annually.

texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Looking here, this shows you the several year perspective per segment, and you can see if I take first the Forest  segment, the net sales are pretty stable in this segment as we've discussed before. The EBITDA margin and  EBITDA is also stable. We had a slightly higher level this year than we've had in the previous years, and some of  that is due to less effects from the storms that happened some three, four years ago, and therefore, a higher level  of harvesting from our own forest as well this year at 4.4 million cubic meters.

texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: If I go to the same picture for EBITDA and, here, you see the main factors, again, price/mix on EBITDA with a  SEK 390 million impact in the fourth quarter again for prices for Wood, Pulp and kraftliner, slightly negative  volume again. We had very small positive trend for raw material; and for energy, energy driven mainly by the one- off items taken last year. It's not driven by the general trend in energy costs, which is more flat. Currency again  was negative primarily due to U.S. dollar. And then we had a few items in the other column here. We had a larger  maintenance stop effect this year in the fourth quarter. We had more costs related to the project in Östrand this  year than we had last year.

texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: We also – apart from the project-related costs, we've talked before about there is an increase in direct costs in  relation to the start-up, which we expect, which comes primarily from increased energy usage, increased chemical  usage, higher wood consumption and also a higher share of lower quality B-grade pulp during the ramp-up phase.  We've given a range for this cost impact, some SEK 100 million to SEK 250 million. We expect it to be  somewhere in between but depending how well and how fast the start-up goes, it can be within that range. And  we expect that impact to come mainly in the second quarter and the third quarter of the year.

texts.speaker: Oskar Lindström
texts.profession: Analyst, Danske Bank A/S (Sweden)
texts.text: Oskar Lindström with Danske Bank. I have a question regarding forest land transactions and we've seen one of  your competitors or peers selling some forest land at the end of last year. Are you looking to become more active  in selling and buying, I presume, your forest land?

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: I can start with that but I mean today with buy and sell for approximately SEK 100 million per year. And I mean,  it's always of great interest for us to move the forest closer to the industry. So, that is what we have done in many  years, and that is also – we're very interested in that movement also going forward. Shall we do it more than  we've done in the past? Well, I mean you need to find good possibilities, and when we find them, yes, we are  interested.

texts.speaker: Oskar Lindström
texts.profession: Analyst, Danske Bank A/S (Sweden)
texts.text: If I may follow up, I mean would you be interested if the opportunity was there to increase your forest  landholdings?

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: But on the other hand, you have the legislation so you're not allowed to buy from private forest owner and  increase the amount that way. You need to buy from a legal person. That's the only way to do it, as you know.

texts.speaker: Oskar Lindström
texts.profession: Analyst, Danske Bank A/S (Sweden)
texts.text: I mean how important would it be that that forest land is located next to your production units? Or do you see  forest land also as an investment asset in its own right?

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: I think, as it is, just now we like to connect it in our value chain. So I mean we have our forest where we have the  industry and vice versa, and I think that is a good way to have it.

texts.speaker: Linus Larsson
texts.profession: Analyst, Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken AB
texts.text: May I also ask around wood cost? Maybe you could comment about market trends in the wood market in general,  but also more specifically in your situation given that you will increase your demand for wood by 2 million cubes,  2.5 million cubes per year or something like that within the next year or so, will that result in a higher wood cost on  average in 2018 for you or would you manage that in some other clever way?

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: We don't forecast. I mean, we need to get the wood that we need in order to supply our industries, and we've  been good at that in the past, and I think we'll be that also going forward. And, I mean, prices will vary over time  and, as it is just now, we can just say that we have a stable price in our area and that is not really the case when  we look around us. But in our area, it's reasonably stable. We have seen minor price increases when we buy from  private forest owners and so on, but on a rather stable level.

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: We are also rather well supplied as it is just now. I mean we have had the first real winter for many years now so  we have a lot of snow. We have had some problems with the railway and the infrastructure, as it always is, but we  are used to handle that kind of challenges I would say. So we have a balanced situation just now, and we think  that we can supply also Östrand with wood mainly from the region where we are.

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: But as we mentioned, I mean we will tie up some capital. Now we need to prepare for the start-up, of course. I  mean we need to add a couple of extra 100,000 cubic meters [indiscernible] (00:28:33) terminals and things like  that. But that work is ongoing now and is according to plan also.

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: I mean, normal, we try to reach the long-term level which is 4.3 million cubic meter. But then as Toby mentioned,  in 2015 and 2013, we had these big windfalls, and then we have to compensate for that. And then we do another  inventory in 10 years. Every 10 year, we do an inventory and then we set the new harvesting level, but we try to  keep it on 4.3 million during this period.

texts.speaker: Christian Kopfer
texts.profession: Analyst, Nordea Bank AB
texts.text: So, unbleached will be the same, and white-top will increase and then publication will come down somewhat or...

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: We don't forecast. But I mean as it is just now, we have just recently announced a price increase of €60 per tonne  from a very high level. So, of course, the market is tight. Definitely so. And I mean we have also seen that testliner  prices has – they have also announced some price increases and I think they will come through also. So I mean it  is a tight market, definitely.

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: If we start with €70 and, I mean, last year, we announced three times €50 for unbleached kraft, and step by step,  that was more or less implemented 100% last year. For white-top, we did two announcements, €50 per time, and  they were also implemented during last year. Now, we have announced plus €60 per tonne for both unbleached  kraft and white-top, and I mean our ambition is, of course, to reach this level and, as it is just now with the tight  market, I think that we will gradually see that coming in.

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: I think you have lack of capacity in recycled fiber. It's not easy to get access to recycled fiber. If you get, you have  to pay a lot, and the quality is not too good. Yield is going down. You have a momentum from the e-commerce, of  course. I mean fresh fiber give a better quality in the product, and that will also drive the demand. So I think if we  could produce more kraftliner in the market as such today, we could easily sell it.

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: So, I mean just now, you have, yeah, all capacity that we can perform that will be taken up by the market as it is  just now. But I think you have to some extent some changed pattern really. You have a higher demand for high- quality packaging materials which we can provide. And also, you don't easily get access to recycled fiber of good  quality.

texts.speaker: Mikael Doepel
texts.profession: Analyst, Svenska Handelsbanken AB (Finland)
texts.text: And what's the reason behind that why you don't get access to good quality recycled fiber?

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: That's also the reason why you have an increase in consumption of pulp, of course. So it's the same logic, and  yeah.

texts.speaker: Robin Santavirta
texts.profession: Analyst, Carnegie Investment Bank AB (Finland)
texts.text: Yes. Thank you. Just a follow-up on costs. So, what you're basically saying is that the chemical costs you're  seeing – for example, the transportation costs you're seeing at the moment are in line with what you saw in 2017,  now for 2018.

texts.speaker: Björn Lyngfelt
texts.profession: Senior Vice President-Group Communications, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Thank you. We have no more questions announced right now. So, I thank you all for participating in our year-end  report presentation here. We will have a presentation of the report for the first quarter in the 26th of April, and I  hope to see you all again then. And slightly after that, on the 22nd of May, we will have a Capital Markets Day that  is focused on Forest, that will be held in Sundsvall in the lovely spring forests of Northern Sweden. So, please  bring your rubber boots and come to Sundsvall on the 22nd of May. I look forward to seeing you there then.  Thank you. Goodbye.
