texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: The EBITDA has also increased this quarter in the Forest division. That's not due to the same effect because we  are harvesting around the same amount from our own forests. We are not increasing the level of harvesting from  our own forest due to this, but the price – the wood prices have gone up and Forest division is now passing those  prices through to the industries. So, we had some time lag. We didn't have that effect last quarter, but that effect  is now coming this quarter and, of course, that has an impact then on the industrial side, where they're taking a  higher wood cost also.

texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Bottom line has grown also due to the higher volumes of course. The margin is slightly down on Q3, but it's  basically the increased efficiency from the high volumes going through the mill. We had a maintenance stop in the  fourth quarter, as Ulf mentioned, which had an impact on cost and we also have higher wood costs coming  through, of course, which Östrand has to take.

texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: And then, in the Paper division, top line was more or less flat. Bottom line, we were down on the third quarter. And  the impact here has been – the biggest impact is due to the maintenance stop, as Ulf mentioned, in the Obbola  mill where we had both a longer and more expensive stop than we expected, and it was this turbine that affected  the stop and we had, yeah, no energy production. So, worst energy performance on electricity for the quarter, and  we also took more time to get back up to full volumes after the stop as well. So, we had a weaker performance  there than expected.

texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: We also have a small – there has been some smaller, slightly lower prices, but that's a small effect on bottom line  this quarter. But then, the wood costs as well impacts the Paper division where they're taking taking a higher  wood cost as well in the fourth quarter.

texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: If I then do the same for our EBITDA, you can see the impact of price mix that you saw in the sales. Variation is  the main impact driving the growth in EBITDA. Volume, slightly negative – a negative effect which you also saw in  the sales variation. Raw materials, we have some SEK 600 million impact, which is mainly driven by the higher  cost for wood raw material or wood prices. So, that's the main impact. We also do have higher direct costs during  the start-up of the Östrand mill as well. So, it's those two factors that lie behind the raw material cost that we're  now absorbing as well. Electricity balance, we do have higher electricity prices so that has a negative impact. But  that's been offset in the year by an income from selling green electricity certificates, which balances it out.

texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: We had production volumes this year. We're in line with the volumes last year. So, pretty much the same volume  in production this year as we had last year, which is what we talked about. Deliveries did lag behind, particularly,  in the third quarter and fourth quarter, because we built up this finished goods stock. But production wise, we  were very much in line with the volume last year. And then, you can see some of the assumptions further down,  including non-fixed costs and energy balance and so on. Östrand will also be absorbing the higher wood cost,  which is mainly due to price, but coming through now with prices being higher.

texts.speaker: Christian Kopfer
texts.profession: Analyst, Nordea Bank ABP
texts.text: Okay. Thank you very much, operator. Just my first question relates to the cost development in Östrand. I saw  that the cost per ton went slightly up in the fourth quarter, just could you give an update on what is the cost – how  much cost in wood should come down when you reach full volumes? Earlier, you have said around SEK 350 per  ton, if I remember, correctly. With increased wood cost, is a more reasonable number around SEK 300 or...

texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: I think like-for-like, we expect the cost to come down as we talked about before, around the fixed cost level, SEK  350 per ton. So, that's not changed, but then the way the wood cost ends up, depends on where the wood cost  ends up. So, I don't want to give any, kind of clear guidance on that. But like-for-like, we expect that then to be on  a cost benefit of SEK 350 per ton. In the fourth quarter, as I said, we had efficiency gains, but we also had the  impact of the maintenance stop, which wasn't there in third quarter, and we also had this higher wood cost coming  through.

texts.speaker: Christian Kopfer
texts.profession: Analyst, Nordea Bank ABP
texts.text: But if you assume that the current wood cost will remain, is it possible then to mention how much costs are  coming down there, you think?

texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: No. I mean, I think, you can say, overall, and year-on-year we've had more or less around 10% increase in wood  costs that you can see. But we had some time lag in the passing through of that wood cost from the forest to the  industry. There's still a bit of that time lag to go because the prices continued up in the fourth quarter as for wood.  So, that effect, there's still some lag effect to go. But, yeah, I don't want to quote a figure at you.

texts.speaker: Christian Kopfer
texts.profession: Analyst, Nordea Bank ABP
texts.text: Then, how much was the excess production of electricity in Q4 in Östrand?

texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Yeah. We had a much better electricity balance in the fourth quarter. But we're not yet at the levels we expect  once the project is fully – the ramp-up is completed. So, there's still quite a lot of that effect to come in next year.  So, the fourth quarter, we didn't have a large net surplus of electricity yet.

texts.speaker: Alexander Berglund
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: ...maybe may continue on the wood price topic. Do you understand what drives that in your industrial operations?  You will continue to see rising wood costs sequentially into the first quarter. And will that then be in your  expectation, the last quarter of rising raw material cost from wood in your industrial activities?

texts.speaker: Alexander Berglund
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: I mean, you will see, some – as Toby mentioned, we saw some price increases also during the fourth quarter.  And that will be passed through to the industry during the first quarter. But otherwise, I would say that the price  level on wood has at least, for the moment, being leveled out on the high level. And what we can see now is that  for imported wood, we see price decreases between SEK 50 to SEK 100 per cubic meter and around that. But still  in the first quarter, you will see some impact in the industry, yes.

texts.profession: Analyst, Svenska Handelsbanken AB (Finland)

texts.speaker: Mikael Doepel
texts.profession: Analyst, Svenska Handelsbanken AB (Finland)
texts.text: And then in terms of the pulp market and pulp pricing based on the comments that you made around that and  seeing the net price difference between China and Europe. That would suggest quite a significant pressure on  prices still on the European prices. Is that the way you see the pulp market right now, or how would you describe  it?

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: I didn't say anything about that. I mean, we know what difference we have now between Europe and China. We  have seen in China that some – maybe the biggest producer has stopped deliveries to China in order to put a  positive pressure on price. We'll have to wait and see what kind of impact that will have. Of course, we also see  that the suppliers now have started to ask for more money in China. On the other hand, you have, of course, the  pressure on pulp prices in Europe, so that we will have at least for February. I mean, we don't really speculate  and do forecasts. Just now, we have $1,170 for deliveries in January. That is what we know.

texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: We ended up on SEK 80 million. So it cost SEK 20 million more and that was basically the longer and more  expensive stops than we had guided and expected. And you could say I think the SEK 80 million is the cost  directly related to the stop but the fact of taking longer to get back to full volume and having a worse energy  performance had a higher impact than the SEK 80 million. Yeah. So, say, some SEK 10 million, SEK 20 million  extra impact from a weaker performance due to those factors on top of the direct maintenance stop impact, you  could say.

Ulf Örjan Larsson  President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB  A  Those we mentioned is Obbola and the biofuel project. texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: First is the guidance. So yeah, just to repeat what I just said. So we guided SEK 60 million, it ended up on SEK 80  million for the stop cost, and then we estimate SEK 10 million to SEK 20 million is what I said, roughly, for, you  could say, an effect on top of that from a worse – from taking more time to get back up to full volume and a  weaker energy balance. So yeah, in round terms, yes.

texts.speaker: Oskar Lindström
texts.profession: Analyst, Danske Bank A/S (Sweden)
texts.text: All right. My final question is around this wood inventory that you do, I think it's every fourth or fifth year that's  going on, I believe, now. texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Okay. We do this survey every 8 to 10 years but you're right, we will start up this summer and typically, it goes for  two summers in a row. And then you need some time for – I mean for analyzing things like that. And up till we  know anything else, we will remain on the level where we are just now, which is 4.3 million cubic meters counted  underbark. So that is more or less the sustainable level that we have just now.

texts.speaker: Oskar Lindström
texts.profession: Analyst, Danske Bank A/S (Sweden)
texts.text: So 4.3 million cubic meters. I think you've been above that level last year or this year?

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Yeah. But I mean, [ph] if the sum – (00:53:06) it can be, of course, volatile to some extent. I mean if you have a  year with the big [ph] wind falls (00:53:14) and things like that, then you have [ph] to take care of (00:53:16) the  wood, and that you have to adapt for the year after or the coming years. And so, I mean, it's not exactly every  year, but I mean we try to keep over a period the average, so to say. But of course, you can go up and down if  that suits you.

texts.speaker: Ulf Örjan Larsson
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: But the average I would say is 4.3 million cubic meters.

texts.speaker: Oskar Lindström
texts.profession: Analyst, Danske Bank A/S (Sweden)
texts.text: 4.3 million cubic meters. All right. Very good. Thank you. Those were my questions.

texts.profession: Analyst, ABG Sundal Collier Norge ASA
texts.text: Yes. Good morning. You gave some good questions on – or good hints on prices for Q1. texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: Yeah. We don't give a forecast again, but there is some effect still to go from this time lag effect. So, we've not  fully reflected in the fourth quarter. Basically, the prices invoiced in the fourth quarter from the Forest division don't  fully reflect where the prices ended up by the end of the fourth quarter. There's still an effect of that coming into  the first quarter. So, I think you will see an upward trend in the Forest division into the first quarter.

texts.speaker: Martin Melbye
texts.profession: Analyst, ABG Sundal Collier Norge ASA
texts.text: Yes. And where are wrong if we do the average wood price increase in Sweden times the sales numbers you  have? That is probably overshooting, but what kind of percent should we be looking for?

texts.speaker: Toby James Lawton
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Svenska Cellulosa AB
texts.text: We apply the same wood prices internally that we source from externally. So, it's the same wood prices we're  subject to and that the Wood division invoices out, what you see is the external wood prices. Then it's important  that you get the right market level because there are different levels in different – and Mid Sweden and North  Sweden have different levels to them. So, you need to make sure you have the right level. So, yeah, take the  levels for Northern Sweden, for example, you shouldn't be too far away.

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Swisscom AG

texts.speaker: Christian Herrmann
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, K+S AG
texts.text: The first quarter 2012 has passed with a strong performance in the potash and magnesium products business  segment, and more or less stable performance in our nitrogen fertilizer business segment, and as expected and  flagged a rather weak development in the salt business segment. texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Let's now proceed with the key figures of the Group, slide number two. Driven by lower salt sales volumes,  revenues declined by 12% and reached the good €1.4 billion in the first quarter. Coming from a high level, EBITDA  and EBIT decreased by 21% and 24% respectively, as planned, capital expenditure increased compared to the  previous year. The increase was, amongst others, attributable to investments in the legacy project in the package  of measures on water protection in the Hesse-Thuringia potash district as well as in the renovation of the  evaporation facility at Morton salt in the United States.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Compared to the first three months of 2011, operating cash flow decreased and reached €85 million excluding the  out financing of pension obligations. This decrease was mainly caused by an increased tie-up in working capital  due to higher inventory risk in the salt business segment as well as higher payments to BASF to nitrogen fertilizer  business segment for the very successful previous financial year. Earnings per share followed the overall earnings  development and stood at €1.01 for the first quarter, a decline of 26%.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: On slide number three, we provide you with a closer look at the changes in K+S Group's revenues during Q1.  Revenues overall decreased by around €189 million. Of this decrease, €287 million were contributed by negative  volume and structure effects particularly in the salt business segment due to the unusually mild winter in Q1 2012.  Sales volumes of the potash and magnesium product business segment declined moderately while nitrogen  fertilizers business segment slightly increased its volumes.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Slide number four. Performance of the fertilizer division and in particular the potash and magnesium products  business segment was clearly standing out while the salt business segment suffered from the mild winter and dry  weather conditions during the first quarter of 2012.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Potash and magnesium products revenues rose slightly to €580 million due to higher average prices and the  positive currency effect compensating for somewhat lower sales volumes. texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Nitrogen fertilizer revenues rose by 10% to €360 million due to positive price factors. texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Let's now move on to the fertilizer business sector in more detail. Slide number six provides, as always, a general  view on the environment of the markets we are active on. texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Moreover, winter kill resulting from rather dry and cold weather led to a postponement in the European spring  season. texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Against this backlog, at the end of the first quarter, there was an upturn in demand for potash fertilizers,  especially after the contractual negotiations with China for the first half of 2012 were concluded with unchanged  terms in mid-March.

texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG

texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG

texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Let us now turn to our Salt operations. Looking at the market environment on slide number 11, I especially want  to focus on de-icing business. The long-lasting wintry weather conditions in Europe led to demand which was  above average and significantly above the level of the last year in that region. Also, North America experienced a  normalization after the mild conditions of previous year's first quarter. Everywhere, prices remained under  pressure due to the mild winter in 2012 and subsequently, higher inventories.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Having reached a sufficient certainty on the most likely CapEx and OpEx from the results of the basic engineering,  it is our duty and ambition to inform the market about the knowledge we have as immediately as possible. We can  divide the reasons for the increase in the CapEx in two groups. One, as we should have made that clear before,  consists of investments into our own infrastructure instead of leasing it. A good example here is the port facility at  the West Coast. These measures will reduce our operating cash costs. We also found that due to modifications and  optimizations of plant components, sustainable savings, for example, in energy consumption are achievable. But  we are also facing higher cost for material and labor during construction time, which are, for example, due to  higher wages for the construction workforce and a lower productivity of those people than we had previously  assumed.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Please turn to page 16. I talked about the changes in our plants – in our plants earlier and also indicated that some  of these measures will lead to lower operating costs compared to what we expected before once the site is up and  running. We expect a decline of sustainable operating cost by CAD 10 per tonne, and you can imagine that this has  an impact on the NPV calculation given the life time of that site.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Therefore, please turn to slide number 19. We expect a tangible increase of global potash sales volumes to about  59 million tonnes for 2013 due to the policy start into the new year after the contract conclusion with Chinese and  Indian customers in January, and due to the continued attractive income levels for farmers which give them an  incentive to maximize their yield by using fertilizers.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: We still expect a slight increase in revenues and EBIT as our sale volumes for Potash and Magnesium Products are  expected to be at about 7 million tonnes, but average portfolio prices was declined, we expect a decrease in EBIT  for this business unit. However, the normalization of sales volumes in our Salt business and here especially de- icing salt should be able to more than offset this. We now expect Salt volumes to be closer to 13 million tonnes for  the full-year 2013. The other number we changed is the CapEx estimate for the group as already indicated. After  some CapEx for the Legacy Project will be postponed to the year 2014, we now expect group CapEx to be around  €820 million compared to €1.1 billion before.

texts.speaker: Joe W. Dewhurst
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Hi. Good afternoon. Just – I've got – sorry, a couple of questions on Potash One and then just one on operating  cost. But on, Potash One, I mean, with the CapEx estimate now, would you be able to give sort of the margin,  margin of area now within that estimate, given obviously that you've done a lot of the detail design? And then also  on that as well, with the operating expenses estimates as well as your AGM yesterday you said that you've now are  testing carbon, I think, underground. Does that mean that you've got pretty accurate data on the kind of recoveries  – recovery rates that you'll be able to get with the traditional mining when it's up and running?

texts.speaker: Joe W. Dewhurst
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Yeah. The total CapEx estimate then for the Legacy Projects, in fact would you say that estimate now is within  plus/minus 5% accuracy?

texts.speaker: Andrew G. Stott
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch International (United Kingdom)
texts.text: Hello, everyone. Good afternoon. Thanks for taking my questions. I've got a few actually. Can I start with Legacy  again? You mentioned your OpEx goes down, but you also mentioned in your press release a few weeks ago that  one of the factors behind the NPV and the return on capital staying similar to previous expectations is a higher  Potash price medium term. So, I'm wondering what's behind that increased confidence for the Potash price over  the long term, so that's number one.

texts.speaker: Martin Rödiger
texts.profession: Analyst, Crédit Agricole Cheuvreux SA (Germany)
texts.text: Yes. Two questions from my side. On the Potash pricing in Europe, I remember that you tried to lift Potash price  for granular grade in France, Italy and Benelux in February to at least a level of €360 per tonne, but obviously this  price did not stick. Can you explain why that was the case and Potash price in these countries came down  recently?

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: The first question to the Potash prices in Europe, I cannot confirm that prices have dropped. This is just an  assumption or provocation. And therefore, I can only say that there are some countries in Europe where we still  are not completely at the end where we have achieved our targets, and I also will not deny that the French  business is a little bit more difficult than other areas in the European framework. But we are still working on that  and I do not have any doubt that, at the end of the day, we will make further progresses there.

texts.speaker: Oliver Schwarz
texts.profession: Analyst, Warburg Research GmbH
texts.text: And secondly, on the Salt business, if I'm looking on the – in progression of the cost per tonne in Salt, I know this  is only a very rough calculation, but anyway, just to labor the point, the increase in volumes was 44%. But the  decrease in cost was only like 10%. I confess, I was looking for a steeper decrease in cost per tonne in the Salt  business. So, when you say there are, let's say, volume-related maintenance costs, they should be absorbed at least  in the cost per tonne view by the higher volume you saw. So, is there another point? Because I would have  expected regarding the more favorable contract in gas, the favorable development of the gas price in the U.S. as  well that we shouldn't see a cost level like that in Q1 after having such a favorable volume development in the start  of the year 2013, and perhaps last year. Just a very quick one, depreciation, amortization in Q1 in the Salt business  declined, is on a lower level than it was in all quarters in 2012. Is that a run rate to use for the oncoming quarters  as well? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: So, getting back to the beginning, it is certainly the case that we – sorry and then to the Salt business, so I'll  continue with that. Once again, I think we made it – I hope that we wrote it quite clearly that we had a  extraordinary or better than expected or better than planned de-icing salt winter in Europe and quite almost a  normal one in U.S. And when you look into the development of cost, you'll see that, more or less, not only the  energy system in Europe or in Germany that should be taken into account, this is what you learn about cost, is  generally that what we have to pay for gas in Europe for our European domestic potash production. The other  plants, more or less, have a mixture of gas, coal, electricity when it goes to, more or less, the network of production  type in Morton Salt, and there you cannot easily end, simply say the natural gas cost in the U.S. is lower – has  lowered. The contrary is the case when you compare the beginning of the year 2013 and the end of third quarter.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: So, this modest – it's one of the explanations that you cannot – you should not come from our remarks on our,  let's say, German gas supply contracts for the potash description to all production in the world. This is different  and therefore the cost of energy in the U.S. and in Canada in the first quarter has increased slightly, but don't ask  me for a figure which I don't have in my mind.

texts.speaker: Tony G. Jones
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn Partners LLP
texts.text: And then secondly, I wanted to go back also to Legacy Project assumptions. Can you remind us of the proportion  of your production cost represented by energy, especially natural gas, and whether in your update, whether your  price assumption or your long-term natural gas price assumption in the U.S. has increased or decreased since the  last update on costs? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Tony G. Jones
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn Partners LLP
texts.text: Thank you. Just as a very quick follow-up then. Are you assuming in your NPV any inflationary effects for energy  or wages or – and if you have a variable cost then or is it all flat?

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: And I think the final question, Julia mentions to me that I have not answered everything. About 50% of our cash  cost of production is related to energy.

texts.speaker: Heidi M. Vesterinen
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you. I have one additional question on the new CapEx budget. So, earlier, you said that you feel the MOP  price assumption that you're taking is not that different, the $400 to $450 becoming $420 to $460. And then you  said that you're taking prevailing gas prices, which is now lower. Do you think that if we use the previous  assumptions, so the $430 and the $400 to $450 for MOP, the CapEx budget would be significantly different from  what you have reported?

texts.speaker: Andreas Heine
texts.profession: Analyst, Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Yes. Good afternoon. I'd like also to come back to the Legacy Project. Is it fair to assume that the change you have  done in this energy cost and lower logistic cost and somewhat changes in the potash price level off roughly in your  NPV calculation the higher CapEx? Is that broadly what the outcome of your last model calculation was? That's  the first question.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: If I got your question correctly, you asked for the effects of the changes of the energy prices and freight prices on  the NPV. You shouldn't overestimate them. You can see the sensitivities that we gave you and you see that even  the change of 15% to 30% does not have a significant impact on the NPV. By the way, we have not changed our  assumptions. On the potash price, we just gave you another range of varying potash prices to give you the  sensitivity around our new model. And, yeah, I hope that answers your question.

texts.speaker: Andreas Heine
texts.profession: Analyst, Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Basically, the change in this energy and whatever, basically no influence on the NPV calculation.

texts.speaker: Andrew G. Benson
texts.profession: Analyst, Citigroup Global Markets Ltd.
texts.text: Yeah, thank you. Perhaps just a couple of follow-ons from questions that have already been asked. The 7.25  million tonnes of production, is that what you could possibly do this year based on running down working capital  or you got a sustainable level of output and production as well as sales? Can you talk a little bit about how salt was  developed into the second quarter as well? Because it was very cold in April and so should we be optimistic about  the second quarter or more optimistic about the second quarter about demand? Can you also talk about the price  evolution of salt and if that's got scope to go up? And lastly, just the magnitude of the one-off effect SAP and  others that impacted the first quarter would be a good place.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: So, once again, we said that we would be able to also go up to 7.2 million tonnes, 7.25 million tonnes of product in  the Potash division. This does not – this more or less goes in line with our maybe possible capacity utilization.  That at the end of the year we will then reach theoretically the same magnitude of inventories that we have had at  the beginning of the year. But this is not a decision that we are taking right now. And also if you more or less  reduce the volume of inventories maybe by 100,000 tonnes, yeah, and are still of the opinion that we can satisfy  the spring demand in 2014, then we would also be happy to – with 7.15 million tonnes.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Closer to 10 million tonnes than to 20 million tonnes.

texts.speaker: Peter J. Mackey
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Good afternoon, gentlemen. I've just got a couple of questions left, if I can, please. One, rather naïve one, I'm  going to ask it anyway. But I wonder if you can help me sort of square the circle between the trade press that says  absolutely nothing has happened in the potash market in Europe because of the dreadful weather, and I assume  they are talking about sales between distributors and farmers. Your production and sales volume in Europe was  actually pretty decent. And your comments that distributors tend to use you as the inventory holder and don't  hold inventory, it seems to me as if – or I would have thought the distribution channels in Europe at the moment  must be sitting on pretty substantial inventories. I wonder if you can comment on that, please. And secondly, it's  just the only thing in your guidance that changed was a tiny – a very subtle change to your energy cost guidance.  And I wonder if you could just give us a bit of color on that, please. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: The first question, potash in Europe. First of all, the farmers in Europe in these areas in which we are more or less  particularly strong, and have quite substantial volumes have seen a very long winter that lasted more or less up to  the end of March, which from their perspective had a positive and a slightly negative side. The positive side that  we have completely more or less, that they were completely not puzzled by winter kills. That means that with snow  on the fields covered the seeds which was brought into the ground at the end of the autumn in 2012. And  therefore, it was a positive start. And then we saw also including April that the demand was rising quickly. And we  have no indications from, let's say, our wholesaler as well as from the farmers that the application in Europe was  bad, which our people have told me just recently that so far, not only including the first quarter, but also take into  account the long winter and the April and maybe also starting into May, this was quite a nice business, not only  from us to our direct customers and also more or less from the customers into the agriculture area. So, I do not  know anything precisely about the inventories in our direct customers' area. But I would bet or would assume that  they are not that high as you might be afraid of. So, from our perspective, it was a quite good start also in Europe  into the fertilizer, into our potash business, with all more or less products, specialty product as well as MOP,  granular and standard, more or less, all over the product range.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: From us, it is also a question of the crop that you are – would like to produce. They are some of the crops which  generally are more or less fertilized only in April or even in early May. And therefore, I would not more or less  speculate too much about the continuous or structural change in January and February or in the future will be  weak month as we go into March. If the winter is there, the winter more or less and the snow has protected the  plant, and it is already over maybe middle of February, then they come. And we need to be prepared, and we will  be prepared. So, I think we should not speculate too much about this small shift from month one to month two or  from three to one. I think this is something which should not make us nervous, which does not make us nervous at  all.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: So, you also asked for our guidance on energy cost, and you're absolutely right. The change that you've seen is very  marginal. The original – the old guidance was given by our new gas supply contract for Germany, so for our,  especially for our potash production here in Germany, and meanwhile we have seen some increases marginally  higher as expected of energy cost in our foreign subsidiaries, and that was the reason for this marginal  adjustment.

texts.speaker: Elizabeth Collins
texts.profession: Analyst, Morningstar Research
texts.text: And I guess, globally, do you have the ability to produce much more than 30 million tonnes per year of de-icing  salts?

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: It depends. Generally, of course, when you have the ship transportation in between, this eats up a lot of the low  production costs in Chile. So, generally, you should try more or less to mobilize salt reserves more or less around  [ph] Chile (01:08:51). On the other hand, if there is demand which is urgent, and you are out more or less of the  binding volumes that you have under contract, of course there is the potential and we did price increases.  Nevertheless, the closer you are to the customer, the better it is.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Yeah, we would be happy if it would be at the lower end. And the first quarter was about the crop and vegetables,  so we have such a variety of products that fit into so many different areas of the agricultural system, from wheat to  rapeseed to, more or less, to corn also to vineyards. So, we think whoever has the demand for potash we are able  to supply and therefore, of course, we'll have potash [indiscernible] (01:13:55) of the sugarcane, but we're also able  to, more or less, deviate into other areas. I have not heard from our expert in the market that there is a strong  deviation or change from, let's say, cash crops to vegetables. I would not be afraid of that at least for the  development in Europe where we have been informed that it is substantial and sustainable.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Our Salt business performance confirmed that our presence on three continents pays off. The strong North  American winter has offset an extraordinarily mild [ph] white (2:24) winter in the Europe. Last but not least, Fit  for the Future is delivering first successes and not only with regards to the identification and implementation of  cost-saving measures. Q1 already contained small but solid savings compared to Q1 2013.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Here again, the 7% decline in group revenue is due to lower potash prices that could only partially be offset by  higher salt sales. This is also true for the EBIT I. The financial results declined from minus €18 million to minus  €27 million, as this quarter includes for the first time the interest expenses of the two bonds issued in December  last year. Subsequently, the net income decreased by 25% to €142 million.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Four weeks ago, the IFA expected global sales volumes of about 56 million tonnes in 2013. But recent knowledge  based on IFA data suggests that global demand was even stronger, at about 59 million tonnes. You're aware that  we include in these numbers what makes K+S unique roughly 3 million tonnes of potassium sulfate products and  potash grades with lower K2O content.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Looking at costs per tonne, we see an improvement of 6% versus last year, despite lower year-on-year volumes.  The main reason for that was besides lower energy costs the fact that we sold more products in Europe instead of  overseas, which led to lower freight costs in this quarter.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: In addition, we have also achieved cost savings as an effect of our Fit for the Future program. We are very happy  about this development. But to be very clear, that was one quarter only. Our best guess is that costs per tonne on a  full year view will remain flat about 2013. This expectation, of course, includes higher depreciation and increased  year-on-year OpEx for Legacy.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Let's move to our Salt business on slide seven. You may recall that we already showed you these pictures eight  weeks ago, but we did not find any others that describe the situation in Q1 better; strong winter in North America  and nothing worth mentioning in terms of winter across Europe. Inventories in North America are now at a very  low level. The opposite is the case in Europe. And here you see that the K+S strategy works. No winter on one side  of the Atlantic is offset by stronger winter weather on the other side. So K+S did and will continue to make use of  its production on three continents. Our European side helped out our North American customers this year and  will certainly do so when we need to renew inventories to prepare for the next season.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Even in light of the comments I just made, and of course assuming no major hiccups from now, this number is a  bit too conservative from our point of view, and it seems the difference comes especially out of the business unit  Potash and Magnesium products.

And a good portion of this decrease  on the cost per tonne segment, it goes back to the new gas deliver price, so lower energy costs.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: On the other hand, a good portion of our sales were European sales, and that, of course, is linked to the lower  freight costs. texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Let's take a look at the highlights of a really challenging quarter on slide two, please. We pre-released our Q2  result estimate on June 27 as the quarterly EBIT was significantly below the previous year and certainly below  what was expected. We regret that this caused trouble in many ways, but it was unavoidable; and why? Alongside  developments like the significantly lower average selling price in potash and the low activity in salt because of the  mild winter, there was an unforeseeable factor. In the second half of June, it became clearer that we face more  production [ph] still stands (01:31) because of the dry weather in the Werra Valley than anticipated.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: This alone cost us around €60 million in the second quarter. Three weeks ago there was an incident at our  Legacy site. During hydro testing, a crystallizer dropped. Of course, this is not insignificant; but from today's point  of view, it will not have a material impact. I will come back to that later. Finally, we expect an EBIT I range  between €200 million and €300 million for 2016.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Please turn to slide four. As I said earlier, during hydro testing for pre-commissioning on July 17, one of five [ph]  ECC (03:08) crystallizers fell. Of course, the most important point is that nobody was injured. Together with our  partners, we are currently undertaking extensive efforts to fix and evaluate the damage. What does that mean; we  can continue the gradual commissioning of the other parts of the plant. From today's point of view, production of  the first ton will be postponed into Q2, 2017. The expected 2017 production volume of up to 1 million tons will not  be achieved. No doubt this incident is serious. But the most important milestone seems not to be at risk from  today's point of view. We expect to reach a production capacity of 2 million tons per year by the end of 2017.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Now, please move to slide five. Saline waste water disposal remains a challenge. There is an ongoing review of  the application submitted by us in April 2015 regarding the continuation of deep-well injection until the end of  2021. Since the beginning of the year, production has been largely based on water flow in the Werra River. In  other words, our ability to fully produce remains highly dependent on the amount of rainfall unless the new permit  will be granted. To be very frank, the third quarter is usually drier than the second quarter and the effect from an  absent permit may hurt us even more in the current quarter.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Now, please move to slide six. The current situation is difficult but not without hope. We are working on measures  that will help us to mitigate the effect from the missing deep-well injection. The possible measures range from  additional storage in owned and third-party premises to various smaller measures. We are currently working on  implementing those requiring minimal efforts and are in talks with relevant authorities to get the necessary permits  for the others.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Beyond 2017, the situation will ease significantly, as you will then have the so-called KCF plant up and running.  This new facility will recycle [indiscernible] (05:42) from the production. This will help reduce saline waste water  and even deliver additional marketable products. Nevertheless, obtaining a new deep-well injection permit  remains crucial for dealing with salt water, especially in very dry period.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Looking at magnesium sulphate product, they are unaffected from the potash price decline at all. And this brings  us to slide eight. In Q2, we were also active in M&A. By acquiring the fertilizer assets of a Chinese producer of  synthetic magnesium sulphate, Magpower, we made an important step in expanding into Asia and strengthening  our position in specialties.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Synthetic magnesium sulphate is used as a fertilizer for oil palms, soybeans and sugarcane as well as for  industrial applications. Magpower will complement the existing K+S kieserite production by adding highly active  effective water soluble magnesium sulphate through scalable low cost production and further expand our global  coverage.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Now, please move to slide nine. Let's switch to our salt operation. After a mild winter leading to high inventories in  North America and Europe, de-icing volumes and prices are down year-on-year. A significant portion of North  American bidding is now behind us, and what we have seen in Q2 can also be applied to the remainder of 2016.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Slide 10, please. In line with our company's strategy of growth in the Salt business, we have added another  component to our Salt 2020 strategy. With the purchase of mining licenses in Western Australia, we are looking to  expand our Salt business into Asia. The project is still at a very early stage and we are currently preparing the  required documents to apply it for the necessary permit. We expect that production capacity will be 3.5 million  tons with a possible production start in 2022. CapEx is estimated at around €225 million. The salt produced in  Australia will be mainly supplied to the chemical industry in Asia, particularly to China.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Now let's come to our outlook for 2016 on slide 11. The business unit Salt may face tangible decline in earnings  due to the mild winter. The decline in potash prices remains the biggest factor. We believe in higher prices in the  long-term, but tend to remain cautious for this year. The second big factor is the situation at the Werra. Amongst  other things, we resume a normal year in terms of price fall for the rest of the year and that our counter measures  will help us to reduce the impact from the missing deep-well injection permits. If and when we receive a new  permit will impact our cost and expected sales volumes. Currently, we calculate with 6.2 million tons to 6.4 million  tons.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: Of course, when we created the €1.6 billion goal, we were in a better potash environment. For example, the MOP  price we used for the granulated product in Brazil was slightly above $300 per ton. But we always we maintained  to believe that the current potash market situation is not sustainable. We expect to see the bottom this year and  believe that we will experience positive impact from the announced production cuts in the industry.

texts.profession: BMO Capital Markets (Canada)
texts.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Good morning. So I have a few questions, first on Legacy. texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: As I indicated, we're expecting on today's knowledge, we are expecting to still keep the most important milestones  of achieving a capacity of 2 million tons at the end of 2017, full capacity of Phase 1, and that of course means that  until then we will have the crystallizer replaced.

texts.speaker: Joel Jackson
texts.profession: BMO Capital Markets (Canada)
texts.text: Okay. My final question would be on your guidance. texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board

texts.speaker: Joel Jackson
texts.profession: BMO Capital Markets (Canada)
texts.text: Was I right in extracting from your commentary that about a €25 per ton cost increase without a permit for – if you  keep doing countermeasures?

texts.speaker: Joel Jackson
texts.profession: BMO Capital Markets (Canada)
texts.text: And my – just the last part of the question I asked, and if countermeasures are successful and you have no permit  in water, I guess, rainfall is normal, is 6.9 million tons next year quite reasonable?

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Executive Board
texts.text: As you know, we give the guidance for 2017 in March of 2017, but I don't want to leave you completely without  information on that. texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Chairman of the Board of Executive Directors, K+S AG
texts.text: And now, let's get started, on page 3. I'm very proud to announce that we have the first potash volume from our  new Bethune mine in our hands and even two weeks earlier than we expected. Many of our colleagues have  been working very hard on this. Now, the first trains have started to Vancouver.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Chairman of the Board of Executive Directors, K+S AG
texts.text: We do expect about 600,000 tonnes production in 2017, which is mainly back-end loaders. We have reached our  capacity of 2 million tonnes annual run rate by the end of this year.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Chairman of the Board of Executive Directors, K+S AG
texts.text: Here we want to repeat, due to our low fixed cost basis at Bethune, we have the flexibility to adjust production for  the very first time. That means we are not flooding the market with additional potash, if it cannot be used. Please  also keep in mind that Bethune is partly replacing our depleting capacities, for instance, our Sigmundshall mine,  which is to be closed by 2020 at the very latest.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Chairman of the Board of Executive Directors, K+S AG
texts.text: Now please turn to slide 4 and let us have a look at the situation at our Werra plant. Last year, we were hit hard  by low water levels and missing permits, this has turned positive in 2017. After 25 days of production outages, we  did not have to put production on hold, with regards to waste water disposal in the second quarter.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Chairman of the Board of Executive Directors, K+S AG
texts.text: As we made good progress with our countermeasures and also the expansion of basin capacities helped a lot.  However, further production limitation in long period of low water levels in the river, Werra, as we have seen in the  first quarter, cannot be ruled out for the rest of the year. That means production cannot yet run at full capacity in  2017.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Chairman of the Board of Executive Directors, K+S AG
texts.text: This will change 2018. We are making good progress with our new KCF facility. The start is scheduled for early  2018 and we continue to expect a reduction of saline wastewater by 1.5 million cubic meters on a full year basis.  This will help us to secure production to a larger extent and will make us much more independent of water level.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Chairman of the Board of Executive Directors, K+S AG
texts.text: Meanwhile, the expansion of tailings pile capacity at Hattorf remains challenging. We are working on a solution  along with the regulator. At the same time, we are optimizing the capacity of the existing tailings pile. The  important message is we believe to solve the issue without further standstills in Hattorf.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Chairman of the Board of Executive Directors, K+S AG
texts.text: For the remainder of the year, we expect our average selling price in potash and magnesium products to move up  slightly on last year's achievement.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Chairman of the Board of Executive Directors, K+S AG
texts.text: In Q2, we built up some inventory on a generally low level. Unfortunately, we had to cover some small hiccups.  Production fell a bit short on our potential due to some logistic problems at our rail partner in Germany on the  back of stormy weather. In addition, we had hot weather and high temperatures in Germany in June resulting in a  short suspension of production at our Werra plant.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Chairman of the Board of Executive Directors, K+S AG
texts.text: Our guidance is based on the assumption that the overall product availability in the Potash and Magnesium  Products business unit will be significantly up from last year. We expect normal weather and water conditions for  the rest of the year and, again, a successful execution of our countermeasure to reduce the disposal of saline  wastewater into the river Werra.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Chairman of the Board of Executive Directors, K+S AG
texts.text: In total, we expect Potash sales in the range of 6.8 million tonnes to 7.2 million tonnes. On top of the volume  increase, we would not be surprised to see a slightly higher average selling price for Potash and Magnesium  Products compared to last year's level.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Chairman of the Board of Executive Directors, K+S AG
texts.text: On the other hand, the start of our production in Canada will burden our EBIT by about an additional €60 million  compared to 2016. We thought we expect a moderate increase in volume by selling prices, but selling prices are  soft as a result of the mild winter season at the beginning of this year. The upper and lower end of our guided  EBIT I range are determined on the still ongoing ramp-up of Bethune, uncertainties about the weather conditions  and the water levels at our Werra site. Furthermore, our guidance is based on normalized winter conditions and  the 10-year average.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Chairman of the Board of Executive Directors, K+S AG
texts.text: Finally, in 2018, our new KCF facility will help us to reduce the volume of saline wastewater by 1.5 million cubic  meters per year. This means that we will diminish the risk of production standstills, significantly another huge  tailwind and the KCF delivers additional specialty volume. At the same time, our investments will come down  significantly in 2018 and we expect our adjusted free cash flow to turn positive. 2018 will therefore be the year  when we will start reducing our financial debt and strengthen our balance sheet again.

texts.speaker: Thorsten Boeckers
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Board of Executive Directors - Member, K+S AG
texts.text: Yeah, Paul. We, different ways to look at it. I mean, we always strip out the EBIT's contribution from Bethune  because it's negative and we also strip out the effect from the lower water levels in the Werra and you know that  we expect for the remainder of the year still 30 days of production standstill. But including all, we would expect to  stay at about the level we came out in the second quarter. I mean, we are working hard internally on cost. We  always said that our Fit for the Future program will also have ripple effects into 2017 and 2018. And we have on  top of that, but not giving it another name, externally installed further cost discipline measures which we are  executing and this is the reason why you can counter the higher costs from driving away the brine from the Werra  to somewhere.

texts.speaker: Michael Schäfer
texts.profession: Analyst, Commerzbank AG

texts.profession: Analyst, Kepler Cheuvreux SA (Germany)

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Chairman of the Board of Executive Directors, K+S AG

texts.speaker: Oliver Schwarz
texts.profession: Analyst, Warburg Research GmbH

texts.text: The Werra site in Unterbreizbach is currently suffering from extraordinary low nutrient content as a result of  crossing a field with lower quality. texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG

texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Now, let's please move over to our Salt business. Slide number 12. In the Western European pre-stocking business  of de-icing salt, the above-average wintry weather conditions in the last two seasons led to continued high pre- stocking demand for de-icing salt in third quarter, too. The price level has risen tangibly for the winter season, '11  to '12.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: In local tenders at the U.S. East Coast, moderate price declines occurred as a result of lower freight rates for salt  imports. In the other, for K+S, relevant de-icing salt regions of the United States and in Canada too, the pre- stocking demand for de-icing salt improved in the third quarter in comparison to the previous year.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Earnings were significantly lower due to weather-related production losses on the Bahamas, higher costs for  demurrage charges due to the maintenance of our terminal in Chile, negative currency effects as well as higher  maintenance and packaging costs in North America.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Finally, I would like to give a short update on our Legacy project and provide you with our current outlook for the  year 2011 and 2012. First of all, this is shown on slide number 16, a short update on our Legacy project in Canada.  The review and customization of the feasibility study of Potash One is progressing according to plan. At the same  time, construction work for water connection, site preparation, roads, and drilling preparations are being done.  CapEx of almost €40 million can therefore be expected for these measures in 2011.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: This is based on a stable sales volume of about seven million tonnes in the Potash and Magnesium Products  business segment and a significant rise in average prices, based, and this is important, on the currently set and  achieved products for potash price level, the similarly positive development we see in the Nitrogen business.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: And the Salt business, the total of the good 23 million tonnes of salt products should be sold. Assuming an average  de-icing salt business in the fourth quarter in 2011, about 14 million tonnes out of this can be allotted to the de- icing salt, which is largely dependent on economic cycles.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: In the Potash and Magnesium products business segments, we expect to achieve a tangible rise in revenues with a  slight growth in operating earnings. This is based on sales volumes of about 7 million tonnes and once again, on  the basis of the international potash prices set and maintained at the present time, the tangible rise in average  prices.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: In the Nitrogen Fertilizer business segment, we expect revenues and earnings to remain largely stable in the  upcoming year. While in Salt, a somewhat lower average sales volume of crystallized salt of about 22 million  tonnes should lead to a moderate decrease in revenues. Along with the lower capacity utilization, operating  earnings will decline significantly to a normal level of between €175 million and €190 million EBIT 1.

texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG

texts.speaker: Christian Herrmann
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, K+S AG
texts.text: So, it's really, really, really easy to, let's say, deduct this €45 million to €55 million from the earnings we have in  the nine months. And then we ask why, and then the  people say, well, you're always so cautious and let's see how the winter will be. I, first of all, like to keep it. I keep it  in the same height as I saw it in 2010 and then 2011, so more than telling you that de-icing salt volumes in '10 and  '11 were clearly marked by higher wintry and better wintry weather, this cannot be extrapolated in the future.  More, I'm sorry, I think we cannot do. We just have to hope that the consensus is now factoring this in soon.

texts.speaker: Neil C. Tyler
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Yeah, thank you for taking my question. Just one point of clarification really, with regards to the point in your  outlook statement on potash volumes for 2012 at a stable level for 2011? texts.profession: No, you're right. The guidelines is €7 million in production possibility, take off 50,000 tonnes, something like this.

texts.speaker: Sophie M. Jourdier
texts.profession: Analyst, Liberum Capital Ltd.
texts.text: And the second, just a quick question on CapEx. I mean salt CapEx seemed to take a bit of a jump this quarter, at  least sequentially. Was that a sort of one-off spend in the salt division in CapEx or are we going to see CapEx being  higher going forward in the Salt business? Thanks.

texts.profession: I'll start with the CapEx question regarding Salt. We have purchased in the third quarter ship for our Australian
texts.text: shipping line in demand that is serving South America with the salts, particularly for the chemical industry. That  has replaced so far, a ship that we have sold offset at the beginning of the year. These items do not occur regularly  every year. That is to say, [indiscernible] (46:21) should also be taken into  consideration. But it's not regularly that the salt without these extraordinary acquisitions or purchases will have to  take generally over a longer period of time.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: I'll start with the second question on salt, [ph] much better (48:24). The big variances in volumes you see are  always coming from the Salt business and when we look into that we are more or less, between 5% and 10% of the  overall volume if we can get up or not get up. This moves the Salt business of everybody that is working in that  field of business very much and so that is positive and that's good.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Water softening is something, which we always tell you, frankly, it's under normal but I think the maintenance of  market shares to gain a little bit in the specialties and table salt in the United States is what we can expect. The  most important thing is that we can be margin-wise better off when we integrate all the costs. But margin – gain  of market share for something is not – that's not our goal. Number one in the salt business is.

texts.speaker: Joachim Felker
texts.profession: Member-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Okay, to answer your first question with prices, you can see in futures for wheat, for corn, what have you, I think  farmers would not go into what we have seen after the crisis of 2008 saving any kind of fertilizers. That would be  the wrong move for them because they can have a very profitable business.

texts.speaker: Andrew G. Benson
texts.profession: Analyst, Citigroup Global Markets Ltd.
texts.text: Yeah. I know on the weather, grain price is up high. But when you're seeing a slowdown in orders, there can be a  number of rational explanations for that and you say that economically that farmers shouldn't have to thrift, but  the point is agronomically, if they do thrift, is it your judgment that it would make any difference, because you  have seen two good years of high levels of application?

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: What I would like to understand that again to answer your question formally, the important part of your question  was without distorting their expectation. And when we look back to these last years, we had the situation that in  2008 and 2009 there was certainly under application. There was a filling up at the end of '09, '10, '11. But this has  not brought the soils into its quality that there is, let's say, are more than necessary – they're really necessary  potash contained there in general terms. Therefore, anticipating that also the yield in the year 2011 will generally  be good, we have a lot of hoisting of potash out of the ground again.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: And therefore, if they want to spoil their ambition, they say, if they want to say often looking for the future, having  in mind still attractive prices to be expected, then let's say I act normally and this would then mean what we say  related to the need of the soil full application of potash, this is – if you go along that route 100% rationally.

texts.speaker: Wolfgang Fickus
texts.profession: Analyst, WestLB AG (Broker)
texts.text: Okay, thanks. And one last follow-up on the CapEx actually. texts.speaker: A
texts.profession: To your question, agricultural MOP and industrial MOP, when you look over a long period of time then there's
texts.text: always a gap between these two prices. Also the price – mechanism is a little different. At present, the agriculture  prices are very close to industrial prices, but industrial prices have a longer contract period I must say. So there's  not much change. Both segments to us are attractive and so nothing new actually, to what I can tell you.

texts.speaker: Richard Logan
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International Ltd.
texts.text: And then just a question on any potential risk to the 7 million tonnes?

texts.profession: Member-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Well there will be normal production risks, which you always have. If there  are some storms in the harbors, then you have to delay cancels some bigger ships so you can postpone it for a few  days, but not from the structure, those non-operational risks you have.

texts.speaker: Christian Herrmann
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, K+S AG
texts.text: >: So Europe results 1.8 million tons in Europe last year. And on a normalized basis in Europe, you can already  hear the exact 1 million.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: We expect Potash and Magnesium EBIT 2012 to be slightly up on today's set and achieve price levels on stable  volumes, and despite tangibly higher unit costs. And we forecast on the basis of the normal winter weather salt  earnings in 2012 is significantly down and we have explained why we stick to that habit compared to the year 2011  exceptionally stronger in the year.
