texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Let's now move on to the Potash and Magnesium Products business segment in more detail, and slide number  four provides, as always, a general view on the environment of the markets we are active on. After there was  cautious early stocking-up of fertilizers at the start of the year, the demand for potash and magnesium products  developed positively during the second quarter of 2012.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: As can be seen from the graphs on slide number six, revenues reached €561 million in the third quarter of 2012  and was up above the figure of the previous year. Operating earnings EBIT I decreased by 7% to €159 million.  Currency and volume-related revenue increases could not completely make up for increased energy costs, higher  freight costs, costs related to the Legacy Project, as well as the negative currency result and the effect of a  reduction in inventories.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: As expected, unit costs increased tangibly to €238 in the quarter compared to €210 one year ago; especially  energy costs had an effect, as they still were impacted by the old energy supply contracts. Therefore, with the time  – with that time lag of six to nine months, last year's oil price increases still influence our cost accounting.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Now, let's move on to our Salt business and on slide – and we continue to slide number eight. In the third quarter,  it was not possible to achieve the very high level of the early stocking-up business of the previous year in Europe,  as a result of the mild and dry weather conditions at the beginning of this year. However, the creation of  additional storage capacities of on customer side ensured average earlier stocking-up volume. Due to the high  stock levels, prices fell slightly during the early stocking-up season and in the tenders for the winter season  2012/2013. By contrast, the contract volumes for the upcoming season stood at a good level.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Year-on-year, de-icing salt volumes were 240,000 tons lower due to the weaker early pre-season in all our de- icing salt regions. As a consequence, the average price level declined. In the non de-icing salt product groups,  volumes slightly decreased; an improved product mix and a positive exchange rate effect as well as some price  increases led to a higher average price.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Quarter-on-quarter, following the normal seasonal patterns, de-icing salt volumes increased due to early season  procurement. De-icing salt average prices improved due to a change in the product mix. Here, the bigger portion  of higher priced packaged de-icing salt relative to by-products had a positive impact on the average price. Volumes  on the other product groups decreased mainly in overseas markets, but prices increased due to regional product  mix effects.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, K+S AG
texts.text: I also would like to highlight the effect of earnings after taxes from discontinued operations, which are only  included on an after-tax level. After the closing of the sale of K+S Nitrogen on the 2 of July, €66 million of  earnings from the divestment were booked in the third quarter. This figure was almost €10 million higher than  expected.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: While demand continued to be at a good level on the markets relevant for K+S, price negotiations in these regions  became increasingly difficult due to the missing contracts in China and India. For 2012 as a whole, we now expect  global potash sales volumes of about 54 million tons. Please note that this forecast in contrast to our peers  includes potassium sulfate and other potash specialties of around 3 million tons.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Salt; as a result of the exceptionally mild weather conditions at the start of the year, the demand for de-icing salt  in Europe as well as in North America should decline accordingly in 2012 compared to the above-average year  2011. For 2013, we are assuming sales volumes to be on its multi-year average level both in the North American  and in the European markets.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: After demand was below average due to the mild weather conditions at the start of the year 2012, the sales  volumes of de-icing salt in 2013 should increase again accordingly. However, prices for tenders for the winter  season 2012/2013 are overall slightly below the level of the last season with regional differences.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: This means revenues of a good €3.9 billion and operating earnings EBIT I of about €820 million. The outlook is  based on sales volumes of 6.9 million tons in the Potash and Magnesium Products business segment and a  moderate rise in average prices. As always, we apply our customary and technical forecast policy, which maintains  the currently achieved potash price level unchanged for the rest of the year 2012.  On this assumption, revenues in the Potash and Magnesium Products business segment should increase  moderately. Due to a strong rise in energy costs, costs connected with the Legacy Project and the negative effect  from the foreign currency result compared to the previous year, we expect stable operating earnings in the Potash  and Magnesium Products business segment.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Taking into consideration the discontinued operations with the higher than initially expected income from the  divestment of K+S Nitrogen, we assume adjusted Group earnings after taxes of about €630 million; a value at the  lower end of the range of €630 million to €690 million given in August. This would correspond to adjusted  earnings per share of about €3.30.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: In the Potash and Magnesium Products business segment, we assume slightly weaker operating earnings. In the  Salt business segment on the basis of again normal winter business that follows the long-term average of de-icing  salt volumes, we are anticipating strongly increasing earnings in comparison to the probably below-average figure  in 2012. Following the already mentioned dividend policy, the dividend for the business year 2013 will decline as  Group earnings will no longer benefit from the effects of the divestment of K+S Nitrogen.

texts.speaker: Amy L. Walker
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: The second question was around your own potash inventories. What level of potash inventory did you have going  into the first quarter of 2012 and do you expect to be above or below that level going into 2013 please? And finally,  just on the financials line. Do you expect another adjustment to the discount rate and thus an increase in charges  for the mining provisions again in Q4 or are you reasonably confident that we've taken all of that through the P&L  now? Thanks very much.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, K+S AG
texts.text: First of all, there are only a few AA-rated corporate bonds in the market. And secondly, there is no duration which  things. We have to find a peer with a AA rating and we have to extrapolate these numbers. And to make a long  story short, it's hard to predict whether we will face another hit in Q4. So, again, I cannot give you a yes or no. It's  due to the environment that we will find at the end of December of this year.

texts.speaker: Sophie M. Jourdier
texts.profession: Analyst, Liberum Capital Ltd.
texts.text: Yes, afternoon. Thank you. A couple of questions please. Your guidance on volumes for next year of 6.9 million  tons, I think before you were signaling that next year we could see slightly higher volumes, as the environmental  projects sort of wind down. I wondered whether the change in view was related to the delays in CapEx there or  whether it was just you being a bit more cautious on market developments next year. That's the first question.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Okay, Sophie. You are right with the first question; 6.9 million is something that is connected that we are a little  bit cautious for the year 2013. If there is demand that we can cover, we could also do more than the 6.9 million but  – and we are generally, as we have written down, we are optimistic for the development of the market. But we  need to see where this all will come from and which party will more or less go forward to go into India, to go into  China. Therefore, the 6.9 million, from our perspective as of today, seems to be well balanced. We have potential  for more. And therefore, the answer is already given that it is not connected with environmental care in our Werra  plant.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Okay, first the Salt. When you see that in the de-icing salt, you have had a very dry and warm winter behind you  and the inventories of the customers are pretty much filled, and you go into the procurement area and timeframe.  You see that traders are coming along that have taken up some inventories of de-icing salt in order to earn on the  high levels of the previous year and now are sitting on that inventories and need to get rid of that. Then they of  course try to do it at lower prices, undercutting prices.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: The second, let's say, thing that you always observe is that those would generally have an output into the de-icing  salt sales, but primarily are dedicated to industrial salt production; once they don't see their output into the de- icing salt markets, they need to get rid of that somewhere due to the technology that apply; and therefore, they'll  also try to push that material into the industrial sector by lowering prices.

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: So this is some of the elements that you generally see in such situation as this. And from time-to-time also when  there is a long and harsh winter, you'll see the utilization of table salt there as well. texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG

texts.profession: Analyst, Baader Bank AG (Broker)

texts.profession: Analyst, Baader Bank AG (Broker)

texts.profession: Analyst, SG Securities (Paris) SAS
texts.text: Thank you. Good afternoon. A few questions. The first one relates to the visibility you have on your de-icing salt  for Q4, 2012. texts.speaker: Patrick Lambert
texts.profession: Analyst, SG Securities (Paris) SAS
texts.text: Question number two is a more general one. What could go wrong in the volumes of potash next year weather- wise? texts.speaker: Patrick Lambert
texts.profession: Analyst, SG Securities (Paris) SAS
texts.text: And also, yeah, if you can comment a little bit of what you see, particularly your forecast for 2013 on volumes?  Norbert Steiner  Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG  A A couple of questions. First to the Salt business in the fourth quarter, unfortunately, the visibility in that business  is very limited. Even from day-to-day, you cannot predict whether it will be slowing or not. And therefore, this is  the assumption that what we call a normalized or a normal fourth quarter pattern is applied for our review and  our outlook. And therefore, it is connected with all the problems connected with weather patterns, it might not be  reached. On the other hand, if the winter is very strong, then we also could exceed that volume. But once again,  the visibility as you personally certainly know is quite low, only a couple of days in advance. The second small  question was connected to the potash volumes in the year 2013...

texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah. The potash in 2013, we don't think and I have also not seen so many comments from our North  American competitors that there will be some, let's say, very late impact of the drought that we have seen in the  U.S. in the year 2012. texts.speaker: Norbert Steiner
texts.profession: Chairman-Executive Board, K+S AG
texts.text: With our standard material. So as long as the farmers are used to some kind of a balanced fertilization, it's just a  question of the efficiency and more or less also about the customs whether they apply or in the case of whether  they apply it in single fertilizers. The single fertilizer has the benefit that you can place it very, very specifically,  whilst the NPKs, they have also specific formulas for different kind of crops, do it in just one rush and you save on  work. So the farmer needs to select which kind of system he wants to run. But there is, when it comes to the  nutrients, no real competition between the K in NPK and the K as a single fertilizer straightforward.

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Chairman of the Board of Executive Directors, K+S AG

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Chairman of the Board of Executive Directors, K+S AG
texts.text: Finally – and I had the chance to discuss that already with many of you on our last roadshow – I have amended  the way to handle our pending approval procedures and ongoing disputes. texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Chairman of the Board of Executive Directors, K+S AG

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Chairman of the Board of Executive Directors, K+S AG

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: In salt, the North American de-icing business benefited from a strong pre-stocking. Compared to last year, we  increased the volume of de-icing salt by more than 500,000 tonnes.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: However, this overall positive development was overshadowed by the severe and ongoing drought in Germany.  We stopped production of two of our three Werra sites, which resulted in more than 50 outage days. Moreover,  we were forced to use additional shipment of saline wastewaters for offsite disposal. And the unusual low water  level increased freight rates substantially. All in All, the potash division had to absorb a weather-related burden of  about €80 million.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: Let us have a closer look at the market conditions in our potash and salt businesses on slide 4. Overall, the  potash market remained supportive. Demand is solid and many producers are already fully committed into 2019,  which is also reflected in current pricing.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: Bottom line, after the first nine months, potash prices have moved into the right direction. But, overall, rising cost  inflation [ph] need our attention. (00:04:32) For example, freight costs increased price-related by more than 5% in  the first nine months compared to last year. And even on a group level, we expect an increasing trend for the  quarters to come.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: Looking at Bethune, we are able to increase production quarter-over-quarter. And this positive trend continued in  the fourth quarter as we reached in October a new production record. On top of that, the seasonally lower  temperatures helped to cool down our product easier. In addition, in Q4, we are going to install a temporary  grinder pump. Both effects should further increase our output. All in all, we took very high efforts to tackle our  production issues.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: On slide 6, we would like to talk about the very unusual weather situation here in Germany. Due to the severe  drought in Germany, we had to stop our Werra production at Wintershall and Hattorf in September. To improve  the situation, we have further expanded our basin capacities by more than 10% to about 600,000 cubic meters  and also stretched our logistics for off-site disposal to a new limit. Therefore, we are able to restart the production  by the end of September.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: Just as a reminder, without the additional measures we have implemented already last year, we would have to  have stopped production back in June. And very important is the look into 2019. In 2019, we will further  significantly expand our capacity to store saline wastewater on-site, and that will make us even more robust next  half.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: Nevertheless, water levels in Germany remain extraordinarily low. The rainfall has been seen so far in the final  quarters is clearly below the five-year average. Due to all our countermeasures, we have to now secure protection  to the beginning of December. Nevertheless, we cannot exclude additional outage days until the end of 2018.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: In any case, we do expect further extensive shipments of saline wastewater for off-site disposal in Q4. On top of  that, inland shipping is increasingly impacted by low water levels and causing overall higher logistic costs across  the group.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: And what does it all mean to our full-year 2018 guidance? And therefore, please turn to slide 7. Overall, demand  in potash remains robust, and we expect the positive impact on pricing on our full-year EBITDA, increasing  profitability of our Bethune mine and tangibly higher salt volumes will also help the situation. However, the  production issues at our German mines, FX development and shaping 2030-related costs will negatively affect  our full-year result. The outage days in Q3, extensive oxide disposal on the back of the ongoing drought, and  inflated logistics costs will reduce this year's EBITDA. We expect additional wastewater volume and related freight  rates having an impact of up to €20 million in Q4.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: Bottom line, we are reducing our EBITDA guidance to €570 million to €630 million. This year's cash unit cost in  potash is now expected to be around €215 per tonne. Potential additional outage  days in December are not part of our full-year EBITDA guidance. The upper and lower end of our guided EBITDA  range is mainly determined by the weather situation in Q4 both for the de-icing business as well as for river water  levels and the implied logistics costs. The adjusted free cash flow should improve significantly compared to 2017  mainly on the back of lower CapEx.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: Finally, let me give you a first rough idea about 2019, and therefore, if you move to slide 8. We have done our  homework with respect to our several production issues. texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG

texts.text: And whether – even though I understand it's completely a non-controllable factor, I would just welcome a bit more  transparency which, in terms of, if kind of the precipitation level remains at the current volume, my understanding  is you're not able to put enough water into the river comparing with what you produce. texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: Yeah. Okay. Now, first of all, I think – I hope that everybody understands that weather – to predict the weather  effects on our production is a very, very difficult thing. texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: That means that we have bring a lot of our production saline waters into this pond. And once the ponds are full  and the river has still a low level, we have to shut down production. texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: And then it depends on will it rain in December, will we have only a couple of days then still or a longer period?  Even we cannot tell you. That's why we have to exclude that from our guidance.

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: No, I appreciate that. But that's exactly the kind of information that I was looking for. The second question I have
texts.text: And so my understanding as well is that from 2021, you have to stop doing the deep-well injection and that also  from 2021, your current agreement with the government – with the regional government is that you have to drop  the salinity content of the water by about 33%. texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: No, I appreciate that. But that's exactly the kind of information that I was looking for. The second question I have
texts.text: And so my question here is, what is the solution? texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: You have mentioned a lot of aspects of our environmental strategy for the Werra area. But the short message is  we are getting more and more robust, more and more robust. First of all, in the short term and maybe, may I also  add, this situation is so outstanding that not only K+S has problem, but much bigger companies which are  dependent on the river Rhine and other rivers are facing the same situation.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: And I also mentioned in my speech that we have already prepared a lot of measures, otherwise, we would have  had penciled of larger amount. And by the way, out of the 1 million that  we promised not to use to the [indiscernible] (00:23:18) that we mentioned, already half is done. It has been done  this year.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: We are currently negotiating with the authorities the solutions, the most probable outcome will be that we  discharge our waters not only temporarily but sustainably in the old mine areas at the Werra, and that means no  transportation costs. And once we do this discharge in the Werra  – in the old mine, we are talking about a huge volume and the possibility to run the mine until the end of the  lifetime in the 60s and sill discharge it there. Then, we are almost totally independent from situation that we have  been facing this year.

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: Got it. That's very clear. And regarding that – am I correct? I mean, I just read this on the plan that you had done
texts.text: with the authorities. Is it correct that the saline content of the – of what you're putting into the river also drops a lot  in 2021 or not?

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: Understood. And my last question, if I may, which is a bit shorter is just in terms of the logistic costs. If I
texts.text: understood correctly what you said before, you said that about – the impact on Q3 alone was about €15 million,  and that was roughly evenly split between potash and salt. texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: ...and that has nothing to do with our sale in waters transport. Another number I can give you the saline water  transport and with all these freight costs increase effects that we have on that transport as well will be roughly €20  million in Q4, and that is all in our guidance.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: Yeah. I think to answer that question, we have not started in this quarter to be very, very strict with all cost items.  We knew that we are running into a difficult year. And the roughly €100 million  is the result of a lot of small items. texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: Yeah. We stick to the number that we gave. First of all, I'm really happy and proud on that development. Now, we're working with a temporary. texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: I don't want to dig too much into detail there. To some extent, we are limited to strong increases, for example, in  gas prices because we have hedged ourselves into the – beyond 2020 even, and the biggest consumer here for  gas is certainly Bethune. We would still feel oil price increases via our suppliers for logistics certainly. When I take  everything together, I would say, on our cost basis, a cost inflation of 3% to 4% is not – wouldn't be unusual.

texts.speaker: Andreas Heine
texts.profession: Analyst, MainFirst Bank AG
texts.text: Yes. Two questions basically please from some from my side. texts.speaker: Thorsten Boeckers
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, K+S AG
texts.text: Yeah, Andreas, you're right. But we said already in the last call, and [indiscernible] (00:34:18) that we expect in  the midterm certainly number below €200 per tonne, but not for 2019. texts.speaker: Patrick Rafaisz
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS AG
texts.text: Thanks. So two questions for me as well. The first would be on the bridge into 2019. Is there any reason why we  should assume that the €80 million impact you flagged for the outage days, is there any reason why we should  assume that that doesn't reverse 100% next year?

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: No, again, the question taking into account the weather situation. I expect they will do it, and then we are very, very  robust, and then we can keep the €80 million impact. Well, we will not see that again.

texts.speaker: Thorsten Boeckers
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Director, K+S AG
texts.text: Yeah, but they do continue to increase, and last time we spoke we haven't expected that Q4 remains as dry as it  does, for example, in Germany and we talked about surcharges, freight surcharges because of low water levels. texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: To give you one example when – in the past when we have shipped our salt and we are talking salt now to  France, it was a number slightly below €10 per tonne. Now we are talking €40. We could not know this  development as we had our last call.

texts.speaker: Neil Tyler
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Hey. Good morning. Two questions for me. First of all, to clarify on the water issue, in order to be able to empty  the basins, do you require above-average river levels, or will things return into a sort of five-year average rainfall  level, fill rivers sufficiently for you to be able to do that? That's the first question, please.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: We would need a normal rainfall for this season, a normal rainfall and a normal river level but not only for a couple  of days, would be rather a couple of weeks we need.

texts.speaker: Neil Tyler
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: That, actually, two weeks of normal rainfall and you could empty the basins at a [indiscernible] (00:42:27)  currently?

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: More than two weeks. But normal weather situation for this kind of year for the next two – I cannot give you a  number precisely. But if we would see from now a normal weather, which we normally see in Germany in  December, January, February, March, we should be done with this problem.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: We have seen a good restocking in the third quarter, but it was not – in that way that we say many have bought  what they actually would buy in the fourth quarter. So we incorporated in the fourth quarter more or less normal  quarter. And, yeah, in the end, this depends on if we see cold and wet weather or not, right? This determines in  the end to take volume.

texts.speaker: Chetan Udeshi
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: Yeah. Hi. Thanks. A couple of question for myself. Number one is, do you think or is there a way for you to  estimate how much you might have seen benefit in terms of your soil business from outages from one of your  competitors in the U.S. in Q3 and even in Q4 if you see that benefit at all? And the second question is...

texts.speaker: Chetan Udeshi
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: Okay. And second question is, given the cost guidance on the potash production for next year, it seems all of the  delta maybe compared to the expectation earlier this year to now in terms of cost increase seems more in  German plants, or do you think there has been a change in terms of cost put on production targets even for your  new Canadian mine in Bethune. And can you remind me what is the target cost for Bethune? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Burkhard Lohr
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Chairman, K+S AG
texts.text: Yeah. The inflation – and extraordinary inflation items are more a German topic. As you know that we have the  biggest cost item of – cost of production in Canada is natural gas. And as Thorsten earlier said, we have hedged  this even into 2022, not the whole volume but a good portion of that. And so inflation is not a big issue in the  Bethune. But of course, Bethune has a significant positive impact on our average cost of production not only due  to the fact that second – the primary mining is cheaper than here in Germany but the secondary mining that we  start next year, that has a huge impact. But all in all, inflation volumes that we expect, et cetera, we will be slightly  above €200 million still in 2019.

texts.profession: Ladies and gentlemen we’re very happy to see so many of our analysts today here in Frankfurt,
texts.text: Norbert Steiner, Chairman of the Executive Board  Thank you from my side as well. As announced, a look at 2010, our last slide. The fertilizer  business is tangibly picking up again in terms of volume, even though on a significant lower price  level than just one year ago. And our salt business is once again profiting from a good overall de- icing salt demand in the current year.

texts.speaker: Company Representative
texts.profession: Ladies and gentlemen we’re very happy to see so many of our analysts today here in Frankfurt,
texts.text: We also see ourselves as being properly positioned in the medium and the long term. Important  global megatrends continue to remain intact: Global population growth, changes in dietary patterns  in the emerging markets and the greater importance of renewable raw materials should ensure an  increasing demand for fertilizers in the future as well.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: <Q – Martin Roediger>: Martin Roediger from Cheuvreux. Two questions only on wastewater. The  District President of Kassel started a hearing to reduce the maximum discharge of wastewater into  the river Werra down from 18 million cubic meters, down to eight million tonnes – eight million cubic  meters for the period of two years. That means on a yearly basis down from nine million tonnes to  four million tonnes. As far as I recall, you have wastewater of 14 million cubic meters and half of  that, seven million, is going into the river Werra. So, there is a gap of three million tonnes. How can  you solve that problem, especially when you take into consideration that the other part of getting rid  of wastewater, the immersion of – into the Platten dolomite, I mean underground is also, so to say  close to be exhausted? Second question is on – also on wastewater, you mentioned in the past that  there are some possibilities to get rid of waste water but some of them are not economic viable,  that means are too expensive. What is the worst case impact on earnings if politicians force K+S to  use these very expensive economic not viable solutions?

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: <A – Norbert Steiner>: First of all, this was just an announcement of the things that we do in  Kassel and this will be answered within the timeframe of four weeks that we have to prepare our  answer. So, as this has not been the final decision yet, I need to comment on a process that is  ongoing which we generally do not do and I do not speculate on the outcome out of this. What we  need to take into consideration is that we have an outflow of saline water out of the Werra  operations, which have more or less two outlets into the water, into the river, and into that what we  call the Platten dolomite and this is something which we have reduced significantly over the last  years. We try to reduce this even more with our 360 million package, and this is something which  we have compiled out of the measures that physically, ecologically and economically will help to  improve the situation.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: We have a clear commitment of all parties involved; that means the two states of Hesse and  Thuringia, ourselves and also the so-called Round Table, that we need to have the fulfillment of  certain prerequisites. That means all measures that need to be done, need to be politically  welcomed, need to be ecologically efficient, do not need to overburden the company and the fault  of, I do not know, these need to be fulfilled completely. And with that background we should be in a  situation that we should balance all that what we have on that board so far. And therefore, we have  also an obligation not only towards our shareholders but also our stakeholders that we intensively  look to that, more or less balance between ecological, social and economic questions for all  solutions that we take into account for the future.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: <Q – Jean de Watteville>: Yes, hi Jean de Watteville from Nomura, three questions. First of all on  financials in the fourth quarter, can you just quantify the non-recurring effect on the cost line on the  potash division? I understand there is a COGS effect because of reduction of inventories at the  high price as the increase of mining obligations and also provisions for rebate, if you can help us to  quantify this effect please?

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: The second question, you never quantified the inventories on the potash division, but we can  assume they’re still relatively high, so I expect 2010 will – can be a year of inventory reduction, if       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: 12 you could help us to quantify that for our working capital assumptions and also the impact on the  cost line on the potash division?

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: <A – Joachim Felker>: Well, and it’s very difficult to comment on the development of stocks at  present, but they are going heavily down. After we have announced our new price for Europe on  the 8 of January this year, we saw heavy order inflow. We were a little bit hampered by weather  conditions and non-availability of coaches from the German Deutsche Bahn. We’re sitting on high  order books, full order books and you can imagine that end of this quarter, first quarter this year  stocks will be reduced quite heavy again.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: <Q – Christian Faitz>: Yes, I’m Christian Faitz from Oppenheim. In relation to Jean’s question, do  you have any visibility on the inventory throughout the value chain up to the final farming customer,  how that looks? I mean, if there’s still tonnes of potash sitting around in a pig stable of the farmer or  something from 2008? And in – also in that relation someone mentioned the 800,000 tonnes, is that  above current and below current inventory, so your full inventory was it just above current inventory  just to clarify that? And then second question regarding the phasing, I mean lots of agrochemical  companies are talking about a potential phasing effect into Q2 and I know you don’t care too much  about quarters, but do you see because of weather conditions that there could be certain slow  sales at least sequentially from Q2 into Q – from Q1 going into Q2? Thank you.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: And the other one is slowing down and carryover from second – from first quarter to fourth quarter.  There is one very simple rule, the vegetation is also postponed. We have a hard winter so  vegetation period is also moving and we are moving with vegetation. So, it’s – at present it’s not  difficult for nitrogen products and for potash products. It might be a little bit critical for some       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: 13 consumer items in the COMPO division because there – because of very cold weather we had  some difficulties in producing turfs because the ground was frozen and there the time window  seems to be narrowing a little bit. So our supply chain in very busy in supplying the supermarkets  and the Home Depots and stuff like this.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: We have a lot of different sites: solar salt production; mines; sea salt production; and of course the  big Salar in Chile and this more or less needs to be brought into a picture that you optimize  logistical chains from that. This of course will then result in a clear-cut organization which does not  allow for inter-company competition anymore and this of course should also more or less  streamline the ways of goods to an extent that we are deriving synergies from that.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: <A – Norbert Steiner>: 35 years potash lifetime, this is still a lot and projects more or less are not  under time pressure with that – with view to that. We have been very careful and will continue to be       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: <A – Norbert Steiner>: The de-icing salt business in the first quarter generally is the strongest  quarter. Because of the fact that normally – whatever that means, normally the winter months are  month – January and February. But as the case maybe it can also start earlier and this needs to be  taken into consideration with the preparation of all that what we have on board in order to be ready  for that and the second part of the question pertaining to salt was..

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: 15 But because we have had these supply problems because of snow and frozen waterways, I think  we will only realize a very small quantity with this price increase of €12. When you’re working on  the Excel sheet, don’t forget that in Europe, we do not have only MOP 60, so the standard products  but also the lower loaded products. But the prices are in parity calculated to the lead product. So it’s  a realized price.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: <Q>: Mike [inaudible]. Three questions if I may, two to the P&M segment. First one is, you talked  about delayed vegetation periods and probably delayed application season in Europe. Given the  sliding forward curve we’re currently see and read in yesterday’s UCA figure, we can add a pinch of  salt to the optimists here. What’s the feedback you’re getting from the farmer’s side on their ability  to digest those price rounds? Is my first question. Second one, on the P&M segment on the cost  side, you’re referring to moderate cost increase in 2010. Also, looking into cost cutting initiatives  you launched in 2009. Could you just quantify the cost cutting effect you expect in 2010 versus  2009 in the P&M segment? And the third question is on the salt business. Bloomberg was quoting  you saying that 10 million tons you’re expecting on de-icing salt in 2010 given that you have sold 9  million tons already last year, would you regard this as a rather conservative figure or were you  misquoted? Thanks.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: The other return of opinion we hear is that when you look at the three major nutrients since the  beginning of this year, the price for DAP and also for nitrogen is heavily increasing; whereas we  decreased the price for potash, which makes all these three nutrients very comparable in valuation  for farmers. Which was one of the reasons they were trying to avoid too high dosages of potash last  year.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: In view to de-icing salt for the entire year 2009, we have sold almost 9 million tons including the  fourth quarter of Morton Salt only. And given the fact that we have started more or less quite similar  in our old salt world of Europe and American East Coast, this 10 million should be overcome easily.  It’s more or less moving more to let’s say 13, 14 or something like that.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: A little bit more color you said in Europe. I think that there are a lot of influences why farmers why  behaved in Europe the way they did. First of all, they were very surprised why we did not  immediately follow price decreases like the nitrogen people and partly also the phosphate people  did very early last year.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: I think you have to divide two systems. The nitrogen-based business is basically driven by  ammonia prices. So when the economical crisis started, ammonia prices fell. So you just pass on  the advantages you have in ammonia and gas price, you pass on to the market. Nitrogen prices  were falling very fast and demand was relatively normal starting already fourth quarter preparing for  this year.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: What also has happened that farmers don’t feel that potash prices are much, much higher than  other nutrients. That was playing into our cards. Our prices we decreased them in January, all the  other prices went up. So this feeling from the farmer’s potash is too expensive in comparison to  other nutrients, that has virtually disappeared.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: We also said 2010 will be a transitional year, that’s why for the time being we only say we will  confirm slightly over 4 million tons to 6, not the full capacity; because we want to wait until exactly  your question, what will the farmers do, will they really take over the product until this is finally done  and then only will we review our production activities for the second half of this year.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: 17 the soya prices, the palm oil prices remain what they are, I see no problems for us, for our company  also to sell to our customer portfolio, we have in Southeast Asia. So Europe is the key for us and  we have to wait for few weeks. Questions pertaining, sorry? Still the answer.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: <Q>: Yes, thank you again, sorry. Just following up on that question. On your experience when you  have a very cold winter like we had in Q1, what’s the effect on the next year? Do you see  municipalities being very conservative and then next year and therefore the option pushing prices  for the next season? But what I’m trying to get obviously is to see what could be the margin effect  next year if we go back into a normal volume environment on de-icing salt? And the second  question, completely another subject, it’s EuroChem. I’m just curious to know whether any talk  exists or any potential collaboration couldn’t exist given the fact that, given the production capacity  they have in nitrogen fertilizers and given the access you have on Western Europe, whether there  is room for you to extend your volume penetration in European markets for that collaboration?  Thank you.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: The question that you raised first with respect to an outlook, what will be the reaction on that winter  is just speculation. What I only can repeat is that obviously many people have thought after the  intensive winter of 2008-2009 that the next winter will not be that harsh and reduced more or less  the building up of own inventories during the summer time, which caused a part of the problems, at  least here in Western Europe.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: The political discussion on the behavior of the municipality and road authorities had not been there  since many years. And now they have seen that they are under pressure and maybe they act  differently and source more material during the summer in order to prepare for a longer winter. But  then they might think – sit back and think now we have had two harsh winters and long winters from  the standpoint of statistics, the next one will be a green one. And then they will be saying most  likely or they could say now we do not need to do more than the year before. So, I have no clue  what they might do but we will prepare ourselves again to be there when the demand arises in  winter time.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: <Q – Lutz Grüten>: Lutz Grüten, Kepler Capital Markets. There’re two questions from my side.  First of all on the Nitrogen, could you give us a trading update on that division in special regard to  the selling prices, and also on the input cost and also bit more precise on the outlook for 2010? And  on the Salt division, what’s your best guess for the combined businesses in regard to CapEx 2010  and the D&A?

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: <A>: With respect to the question of salt and CapEx, the combined entities we should be in the  neighborhood of in the salt business of about, if I’m not mistaken, €80 million CapEx and the  second part of the question was respect to salt once again?

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: We were at that time having extremely expensive raw materials; the phosphates about $1,600, now  the price is 400 roughly, and we also had some traded material from BASF where we bought too  high and sold too low, that’s the effect. The other part is that there was a small margin from the       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: 19 straight fertilizer business because the ammonia prices have been very high, when the bubble  collapsed it took some time to adjust it.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: So, the outlook is that demand will be more stable, at present I would estimate that the NPK plants  in Europe are running 90% and we have quite a good transparency in this area because we are  also a raw material supplier to other producers in the NPK field and we have sold more ammonia,  so, I think it will recover. And also the nitrogen when you see the nitrogen prices in the first quarter  for CN and which is one typical European product, it was so low that in the newspapers the people  were writing buy nitrogen now, you will never get it cheaper again and they have been right. So,  quality wise it’s recovering and price wise I think it will be all right.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: Perhaps I have one more – until they have got their numbers ready – one more addition to the  question, Europe, EuroChem coming to Europe, Jean, think about their product portfolio only partly  is suitable for Europe, their NPK program is very narrow only three or four formulas. And then they  are quite strong also in ammonium nitrate, which is used in Europe, but not as much because we  have all these all discussions about terrorism and so on. So, you need special storing facilities and  stuff like this. So, they can export to Europe but they have other markets where I think they feel  more comfortable.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: <A>: Now there’s a lot of – I do the first thing. I do the, what is behind and Mr. Steiner then is  commenting on throwing the hat or not throwing the hat. Okay? So, I think what you have to look at  over the last, I think, 18 months, we have heard a lot of discussion about energy findings, gas  findings in the States. And with the time lag of I would say one year there were a lot of speculation  what will the American nitrogen producers do because it’s a clearly U.S. based story.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: It’s about getting assets in the U.S. And one speculation was that some of these players would be  very interested because their point of view is that over the long period of time they will be very  competitive in gas prices. They would close the borders. They would not allow the Russians to  export, the Ukrainians to export into the United States of America because they feel that they are  very competitive in energy prices, again that was definitely one story.       corrected transcript

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: The other story I think is, why is Yara so much interested? I think they have strategically very good  positions in Russia with participation in Rossosh. They are good in Qatar which means they are  very close to some energy fields. But they are missing some position in the States. So, Terra would  be a good target, I think, and when you look at it – what they have, how should I say it, the bid they  took in seems quite interesting for some people outside.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: Second part or third part already of the whole issue is Agrium is very dedicated to nitrogen  business. Agrium is very dedicated also to distribution. They have spent a lot of money to  distribution, to resale and for them targeting CF Industries would be a perfect fit. I think there will be  synergies from transport in production and some others. So, for them to go for CF Industries makes  a lot of sense. CF Industries then going for Terra, that’s already a little bit of a different story. Terra  is bigger than CF in quantitative production. Some nasty people say it’s a way out to not be  acquired from Agrium, but I cannot comment on this, you have to ask Mr. Wilson. So, it’s a purely  U.S. story, it goes for assets. It has definitely to do with a long-term view of nitrogen and then Mr.  Steiner can comment on the hat.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: And secondly, you said in your presentation that you did increase some underground development,  but on the other hand that you delayed some maintenance expenditures? What would you say it’s  the net effect, did you like delayed some costs in 2010 or did you bring maybe forward some costs  due to the increased underground development which now helps them to have lower costs in  2010?

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: <A – Norbert Steiner>: The first question, to make it short, the people that are in the business that  are presently already producing potash strive more or less to increase their potential capacity by  that what they called brownfield expansion, with the only exemption of [inaudible] that has a small  production in Brazil and tries to get a bigger player in the potash business.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: All these announcements and projects are still in a very early stage, and will need the time – a lot of  time in order to more or less make things happen and to be ready for the sale of the first ton. BHP  Billiton, as a complete new player, showing up at least in the area of preparation of moving ahead  has said that the final stage of the mine that they are planning to build in Saskatchewan will be  either in 2026 or 2028. So, you see there is a lot of timeframe that is occupied by that. And  therefore, it is also absolutely premature to be open on that, to speculate about the impact on  prices. What we generally should be able to mention is that most of that newcomers have only one  mine on the production then which is a completely new mine that needs to shoulder everything, and  which is significantly different to that what those companies that are looking for brownfield  expansions or on the basis of existing production for greenfield expansions have as a benefit or as  an advantage that they can mix more or less there, their calculation.

texts.speaker: <A>: Martin?
texts.text: <Q – Stephan Kippe>: Okay. Thank you, Stephan Kippe from Commerzbank. I have two  questions with regards to potash prices, which were a big issue last year, hasn’t been talked about  so much this year. My question is as European farmers have proven to be pretty stubborn when it  comes to accepting high potash prices here in 2009, and now the relative pricing situation has  improved as you have said, do you see – how do you, maybe Mr. Felker, how do you personally  assess the willingness of farmers to maybe accept more substantial price increases during 2010  and maybe early 2011? And the second question is if I look at the guidance of your potash segment  for this year, even when using, lets say, flat pricing for 2010 is my impression the right one that  even in that scenario your guidance for the potash segment is more on the conservative side?

texts.speaker: Company Representative
texts.profession: I welcome you to the K+S annual conference of the results of 2010. Now we are on room, that’s
texts.text: Also in North America, in the Potash and Magnesium Products business segment, we took a  decisive strategic step to develop new production capacities. Through the acquisition of Potash  One, we acquired very promising license areas in the Canadian province of Saskatchewan.  Together with our existing domestic potash mines, this will significantly increase our international  competitiveness, thus benefiting the whole K+S Group in Europe and overseas.

texts.speaker: Company Representative
texts.profession: I welcome you to the K+S annual conference of the results of 2010. Now we are on room, that’s
texts.text: The highest earnings growth was noted by the Potash and Magnesium Products business  segment, which achieved its second-best result so far. The Nitrogen Fertilizer business segment  too, achieved positive earnings following last year’s painful loss, whilst the Salt business segment  even attained a new record, of course the first time inclusion of Morton Salt for a whole year  contributed to this.

texts.speaker: Company Representative
texts.profession: I welcome you to the K+S annual conference of the results of 2010. Now we are on room, that’s
texts.text: Ladies and gentlemen, let us now take a closer at significant events and developments in our core  business segments in 2010. As announced, I would like to begin with the Salt core business sector.  The past year saw an extraordinary high level of ice control business in Europe. Maybe you  remember that the winter of 2009/2010 had already set the new standards for the European  producers of de-icing salt. But the winter that came over the continent in December 2010, clearly  exceeded even the previous year’s experience.

texts.speaker: Company Representative
texts.profession: I welcome you to the K+S annual conference of the results of 2010. Now we are on room, that’s
texts.text: While the long-term sales volume average and therefore the normal sales budget for our European  subsidiary esco is about 2 million tonnes of de-icing salt. In 2010 here alone, more than double that  amount was sold. Although our German rock salt sites had consistently and with extra personnel  been working at full capacity since December 2009, and we had considerably increased our  warehouse capacities, de-icing salt remained a very scarce commodity for many weeks in view of  the enormous demand.

texts.speaker: Company Representative
texts.profession: I welcome you to the K+S annual conference of the results of 2010. Now we are on room, that’s
texts.text: There was much complaining about the German salt producers, and much talk about a national salt  reserve. My statement is, if all the purchasers of de-icing salt had done their homework, the  situation would have been different. Last summer, the conference of the ministers of transportation  recommended that they should build up reserves early and establish adequate warehouse  capacities in good time, and they explicitly re-confirmed this in October.

texts.speaker: Company Representative
texts.profession: I welcome you to the K+S annual conference of the results of 2010. Now we are on room, that’s
texts.text: But apparently not enough had happened since then, at least by far not everywhere. According to a  sample survey by the Dusseldorf-based newspaper Rheinische Post, last December only 20% of  cities surveyed had the required minimum stocks, and some municipalities did not even stock half  the recommended levels. The conclusion we draw from all this is that our storage facilities in  Europe will be stocked up with up to 200,000 tonnes within the next one or two years, and we are  curious to see what de-icing salt purchasers will do.

texts.speaker: Company Representative
texts.profession: I welcome you to the K+S annual conference of the results of 2010. Now we are on room, that’s
texts.text: The winter in North America in 2010 was different. In the U.S. the first quarter was relatively  normally and Canada even experienced very mild weather. Therefore, the position of suppliers on  the East Coast taking part in tenders was made difficult by the relatively high stocks. The relative  late start of winter in the final quarter nevertheless improved demand in relation to the weak  demand the year before. However, it remained below the average.

texts.speaker: Company Representative
texts.profession: I welcome you to the K+S annual conference of the results of 2010. Now we are on room, that’s
texts.text: Two factors are mainly responsible for this. First, at the start of the year 2010, there was a large  backlog demand from the trade sector in the northern hemisphere to replenish the very low stocks  in time for the spring season. And second, agriculture to a large extent reverted to sustainable  consumption patterns and during the course of the year again, displayed a high readiness for a  balanced application of mineral fertilizers.

texts.speaker: Company Representative
texts.profession: I welcome you to the K+S annual conference of the results of 2010. Now we are on room, that’s
texts.text: From a farmer’s angle, this return to normality was necessary because the major reduction in the  use of fertilizers in 2009 had reduced the nutrient content of the soil and thus increased the yield  risk of future harvests. In addition, the strong increase in the international prices of agricultural  products started in the second half of 2010 and the resulting improvement in income and farmers  provided an additional boost to fertilizer demand.

texts.speaker: Company Representative
texts.profession: I welcome you to the K+S annual conference of the results of 2010. Now we are on room, that’s
texts.text: If we take a look at the world potash market, the effects of this development are obvious. World  potash sales last year rose from 31 million tonnes to an estimated 57 million tonnes, just under 2  million tonnes less than in the record year 2007. Against this background and in view of clearly  declining stock levels, utilization of capacity of most potash producers again reached a relatively  high level during the year.

texts.speaker: Company Representative
texts.profession: I welcome you to the K+S annual conference of the results of 2010. Now we are on room, that’s
texts.text: Potash prices did not remain unaffected by this. Prices bottomed out and later in 2010, prices again  rose moderately. However, there is no rapid return to the potash prices experienced in the boom  year of 2008. From our point of view, a sustainable price policy is more important than drastic price  increases that could jeopardize market balance.

texts.speaker: Company Representative
texts.profession: I welcome you to the K+S annual conference of the results of 2010. Now we are on room, that’s
texts.text: 4 However, one should bear in mind that in the same period in the previous year, that the same –  period in the previous year, was still affected by the world financial and economic crisis, in other  words, the previous year provides a rather low point of departure. In 2009, our potash sales had  fallen to 4.35 million tonnes which we only – and we only used half our production capacity. In  2010, we sold about 7 million tonnes of potash and used our capacity almost to the full in the  business segment.

texts.speaker: Company Representative
texts.profession: I welcome you to the K+S annual conference of the results of 2010. Now we are on room, that’s
texts.text: This slide was presented for the first time at our Capital Markets Day in Berlin in last December. We  have updated it, so that it should provide you with rough indications of the cost structure of the  potash and magnesium product business segment and the development of selected cost items.  Rising energy, personnel and freight costs, as well as lower sales volumes need to compound  annual growth rate in total unit costs of approximately 10% over the last three years. Unit costs are  expected to rise moderately in 2011, with the exception of energy costs. The major costs items are  expected to rise moderately while sales volumes are forecasted on the stable level.

texts.speaker: Company Representative
texts.profession: I welcome you to the K+S annual conference of the results of 2010. Now we are on room, that’s
texts.text: Ladies and gentlemen, the nitrogen fertilizer business developed positively last year. Because of  the recovery in demand, already in the first half of the year, European production sites for nitrogen  fertilizers producers at a high capacity again and in the second half of the year even at full – we’re  running at full capacity. Therefore prices rose very markedly over the year, also on account of rising  input costs.

texts.speaker: Company Representative
texts.profession: I welcome you to the K+S annual conference of the results of 2010. Now we are on room, that’s
texts.text: In such a market environment, it comes as no surprise that we achieved a turnaround with our  Nitrogen Fertilizers business segment last year, with which we are of course very satisfied. After a  negative value of €108.1 million in 2009, operating earnings EBIT I rose to a positive €55.7 million  in 2010.

texts.speaker: Company Representative
texts.profession: I welcome you to the K+S annual conference of the results of 2010. Now we are on room, that’s
texts.text: Apart from higher sales, it was attributable to price increases of straight nitrogen fertilizers and  ammonium sulphate, which were more than – which more than made up for increases of raw  materials, as well as to a clear decrease in the input costs of complex fertilizers. The fact that in the  previous year, one-off effects influenced our results must also be taken into consideration.

texts.profession: I welcome you to the K+S annual conference of the results of 2010. Now we are on room, that’s
texts.text: 5 Ladies and Gentlemen, as you know, we obtain most of the business segment’s products from  BASF’s manufacturing plants. On March 1st of this year, BASF announced that they intends to sell  a major part of their fertilizer production assets by the first quarter of 2012.

texts.text: Based on this assumption, we expect annual growth rates of 3% to 5% in the coming years. The  capacities of potash producers will therefore continue to be used to a high degree. I have  mentioned Potash One, our new big potash product project in Canada already in my initial remarks.

texts.profession: I welcome you to the K+S annual conference of the results of 2010. Now we are on room, that’s
texts.text: Those of you who have known us for longer are aware that in view of the increasing world demand  for potash, we have been striving since long to expand our potash capacity in the medium term. The successful takeover of that company took place in February with the tendering of  over 90% of all the shares and the squeeze out process for the taking over of the remaining shares  should be completed by mid-May at the latest.

texts.text: Potash One holds several potash exploration licenses in the Canadian province of Saskatchewan,  including the legacy project, an advanced greenfield projects to establish a solution mine. This  technology, which is not applicable everywhere due to geological reasons, allows a faster  production launch, a more flexible starting curve of production and the mining of deeper deposits  than conventional mining methods would allow.

Based on available resources and the environmental permit that has been granted, the Legacy  Project has the potential to gradually increase the potash output notably in excess of 2.7 million  tonnes of potassium chloride per year.

And the charming effect behind that is  that we have started our food grade potassium plant in Zielitz plant in 2010, huh? 2009, 2010 and  we are increasing more or less the production there, so another two-pillar strategy in small terms.

So,  it’s a question we are just in discussions with the big clients in this field, what happens in the next  six months. And as you know that the availability of products worldwide is quite low. I think that  again also there you will see a time effect in price development. So, if it’s a little bit decoupled, it’s  not the same mechanism. Is that okay for you? Or do you get it?
