texts.speaker: Christopher Kirk
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Just addressing your Environment and Life Science concern, and I know you do mention it every time. I think  these businesses fundamentally belong inside SGS. The Life Sciences business is a testing business. It's a business  that we understand from a testing perspective. The laboratory aspect of Life Sciences, we fundamentally  understand. We know how to run laboratories. We're not absolutely sure how to run clinical research, still , and we  still do it. And I mentioned earlier that we will no longer grow that part of the business, but we will grow the  laboratory part of the business, preferably organically. But if we can find interesting acquisitions in the laboratory  testing part, we will do them.

texts.speaker: Christopher Kirk
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: In terms of the Environmental business, I think fundamentally, it should be part of the SGS Group. I mean it just  should be. It's embedded there anyway. There are very few Environment – correct me if I'm wrong – there are  very few Environment laboratories within the SGS Group that can be stripped out, for example, and sold. Most of  them are embedded in existing multi-labs, as we call them, where you will have Minerals and OGC and  Environment and Agri and a whole host of different testing. So it would be difficult for us to pull it out and stop  doing it.

texts.speaker: Christopher Kirk
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: I think as far as I'm concerned, we've just been through the budgeting process. I think you'd be surprised on both  counts in terms of Environment and Life Sciences, particularly, already, we  know how well Environment's going  to grow because we just finished two acquisitions that make it grow very, very rapidly already in 2015 at a much  higher profitability. Now, I'm lost after that. Do you have a...

texts.speaker: Christopher Kirk
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: There was a question about CapEx in Oil & Gas.

texts.speaker: Carla De Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, SGS SA
texts.text: So, with respect to the CapEx in the Minerals there, I mean, it's clear, given the decline that you are experiencing,  that we try to limit the CapEx investment to replacement investments. That is, I think quite a, yeah, logic  consequence of what we have been seeing.

texts.speaker: Jean-Philippe Bertschy
texts.profession: Bank Vontobel AG (Research Firm)
texts.text: No problem, back to the first question that was asked during the presentation, the impact of Peru and oil price on  the top-line and at the bottom-line. So, if you're going from your guidance 4% to 6% including this impact of oil  price in the Peru, if we go down 2% to 4%, for instance, how should we understand that? And as well on the  margin, you're guiding for flat margin, and – as well not specific impact on currencies. As well, I want to  understand why you don't have any impacts on the margin from currencies as you have seen in 2011 and in 2014?

texts.speaker: Christopher Kirk
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: The mix effect in Oil, Gas, and Chemicals has been large. The – as I said – mentioned earlier, the petroleum – the  Plant and Terminal Operations business is quite a significantly dilutive part of the Oil, Gas, and Chemicals  business.

texts.speaker: Christopher Kirk
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Further to that, in certain parts of the world – and I mentioned, Australia during the presentation, we have seen  the upstream part of the business, which is a high-profit part of the business. We've seen that reduced quite  significantly as a direct consequence of the oil price and the gas price. And then, in that case, I was talking  specifically about one of our clients, a large client in Australia, onshore Australia that had – all of those things  have had a large impact.

texts.speaker: Christopher Kirk
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: And the rest, there's nothing – I mean, there's just nothing systematic, because I think that says, the oil price hit  everybody – it just wasn't that case. It was just, we had pockets of problems here, there, and everywhere.

texts.speaker: Mourad Lahmidi
texts.profession: MainFirst AG (France)
texts.text: And the second one is about the margin of the business going in 2015 with the PTO going well and upstream likely  to slow down with oil prices. Are we going to see further margin decline?

texts.speaker: Mourad Lahmidi
texts.profession: MainFirst AG (France)
texts.text: Okay. Thanks. And another one on oil prices, are you seeing your trade-related activities going – picking up  because of lower oil prices or does it have anything to do?

texts.speaker: Paul D. Sullivan
texts.profession: Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Hello. I'm all right. How are you? Can I just follow up on a few a few divisional margin questions. So, firstly, just  on your last point about OCG (sic) [OGC] margins. So, you're saying you don't expect further decline in OCG (sic)  [OGC] in 2015, even though upstream is going to be impacted – yeah, I'm sorry...?

texts.speaker: Marco Sormani
texts.profession: Varenne Capital Partners
texts.text: Just one more question. So, Marco Sormani, Varenne Capital Partners. So, do you – we only talked about negative  impact of oil low price. Do you see any positive impact on – of a low cost of oil and of energy on some industry  some other...

texts.speaker: Christopher Kirk
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Marco, you're a man after my heart. My own heart. You and I have talked about good things together many times.  If you listen to the World Bank, if you listen to anybody else who's – knows anything about apparently, the oil  price, every $10, you get a 20 bps – 0.25% – 25 bps rise in global GDP. If it's down $40, that's 1% rise. SGS has a  minimum – tries to grow at at least – everybody inside SGS, some grow much more – but, at least twice GDP.

texts.speaker: Christopher Kirk
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: So, if you're – we're expecting – we should be getting, and by all means criticize me if you want to, upstairs, we  should be getting at least a 1% rise in global GDP, although I see World Bank or somebody said yesterday that the  world's going to go even further – slow down even more. There has got to be a positive effect. Every company in –  nearly every company in the world has a cost of logistics. Logistics require fuel. Fuel's going to be X percent  cheaper.

texts.speaker: Christopher Kirk
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: On the other side, just mere energy utilization is high for every company. The cost of energy is going to be less. So,  there has to be – I'm not saying it's a complete balance there in terms of our upstream Oil & Gas business or o ur  upstream Industry business, but there is some positives coming from it. The cost of petrochemicals, the feedstock  reduces significantly. So, cost of plastics should be less, so the cost of consumer goods should be down. You know  – and on this page, I really – I think there are some big positives onwards. We have this argument on a daily basis  – so there's some upside.

file: SGSN - Q4 2016 Earnings Call 23January2017 800 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 23-Jan-17.pdf

texts.speaker: Carla D. F. de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: Our revenue growth of 6% is solid, considering the fact that the energy-related markets remained a challenge  during the year. Our organic growth amounts to 2.5%, mainly as a result of the strong growth in non-energy  related businesses. We improved the adjusted operating income by 2.4% despite continued pricing pressure in  the energy-related businesses. In an effort to offset the pressure on the margin, we identified unproductive assets  and unprofitable businesses, and we implemented a restructuring plan.

texts.speaker: Carla D. F. de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: Secondly, our Minerals and Energy-related businesses continue to operate in a volatile market, resulting in  pressure on the volumes in our Industrial, Minerals and OGC business. And thirdly, we invested in our growth,  transformational and efficiency projects, in line with our strategic plan which will allow us to grow the top line and  improve the bottom line going forward.

texts.speaker: Carla D. F. de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: I will now break down our top line growth. Year-on-year, the company grew its revenue by 6%, of which 2.5%  organic and 3.5% inorganic. The orange part of the chart reflects the organic growth, which is driven by the  continued strong performance in the non-energy related businesses which is exceeding 6% for the full year.

texts.speaker: Carla D. F. de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: The non-energy related businesses amount to 53% of the revenue and the growth is more than offsetting the  decline in OGC, Industrial and Minerals. The dark-gray part of the chart reflects the effect of the acquisitions  made in 2015 and 2016, as this is on a 12-month rolling basis. The inorganic effects on the top line amounts to  CHF 203 million, representing a year-on-year growth of 3.5%. We acquired 21 companies, including two minority  stakes in promising technology companies as AgFlow and Transparency-One.

texts.speaker: Carla D. F. de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: This graph breaks down the importance of our line businesses from a top line perspective. And the change in the  relative rate versus last year is indicated as a percentage point change. All non-energy related businesses  increased or maintained their relative rates in the portfolio as a result of the very strong performance throughout  the year, and this at the expense of the energy-related businesses. This is in line with our strategy to reduce the  overall importance of the energy-related business in our portfolio. The relative rate of the energy-related business  declined by 2% year-on-year.

texts.speaker: Carla D. F. de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: The first one is Environmental, Health and Safety. Environmental, Health and Safety achieved a stellar double- digit growth driven by strong inorganic growth through the six acquisitions contributing more than CHF 60 million  of revenue. Next, to the inorganic growth, Environmental, Health and Safety is also star performer in terms of  organic growth, which is driven by strong performance across the whole portfolio of activities.

texts.speaker: Carla D. F. de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: Our strong growth of 6% was delivered by 92,269 colleagues around the world representing an increase of 4.9%  versus last year. As said before, the organic growth relates mainly to the non-energy related businesses, while a  big part of the restructuring is touching on the energy-related businesses. Under the new restructuring plan of  2016, we are planning to reduce the head count by another 600 FTEs.

texts.speaker: Carla D. F. de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: Similar to the trends in the revenue, the relative rates of the non-energy-related business increased or remained  stable, while the relative rate of the energy-related business decreased by 2.5%. The only exception is  Transportation, whose profitability mainly in the second half of the year was impacted by start-up costs for new  contracts such as the Uganda statutory inspection contract as well as impacted by increased investments in  development of new testing activities.

texts.speaker: Carla D. F. de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: Industrial suffers the most from a margin perspective, as it continues to face difficult market conditions in the  energy-related activities, which has partly been compensated by the restructuring benefits. And the weakening of  the margin in Environmental, Health and Safety is mainly related to the Accutest acquisition and the margin  pressure in the Australian market.

texts.speaker: Carla D. F. de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: During 2016, we spent CHF 288 million of CapEx, representing 4.8% of sales which is in line with last year. And  our primary CapEx investments were made in Consumer/Retail services and the Agriculture, Food and Life  business which are, together with Transportation, the most capital-intensive businesses in 2016.

texts.speaker: Carla D. F. de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: In Asia-Pacific, the biggest part of the CapEx is spent in China and Hong Kong – Hong Kong, given the strong  relative rate of the Consumer/Retail business and the solid growth in the region. And the relative importance of  the Americas decreased as a result of the decline in the capital-intensive energy-related businesses. You can see  from the chart, at the right bottom part, the CapEx is slightly below the depreciation due to the reduced  investments in the energy-related businesses.

texts.speaker: Carla D. F. de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: Looking at the revenue growth for the second half, there are two key messages to highlight. Firstly, our organic  growth slowed down in the second half of 2016 and amounts to 1.6%, and this as a result of the further decline in  OGC and Industrial, as well as a slowdown of our organic growth in Environmental, Health and Safety and the  Consumer/Retail services.

texts.speaker: Carla D. F. de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: The growth slowdown in the Consumer/Retail services is only related to the decline in the wireless activities. And  the weaker growth in Environmental, Health and Safety is related to the increased competition in Australia and the  fact that we completed some major European projects.

texts.speaker: Carla D. F. de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: During the second half of 2016, three businesses realized double-digit growth: Environment, Health and Safety,  Transportation and GIS. While the Environmental, Health and Safety is mainly driven by inorganic growth  resulting from the Accutest and AXYS acquisitions, the Transportation and GIS business is mainly driven by  organic growth.

texts.speaker: Frankie Ng
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SGS SA
texts.text: So if I start with Agriculture, Food and Life, the performances for 2016 was really good and we expect that to  continue in 2017 with an improved trade activities. For your information, the activities in terms of trade was slow in  the second half of the year also because of bad weather [indiscernible] (47:55) of crops that has reduced the  number of transactions. So this should be improving in 2017.

texts.speaker: Frankie Ng
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SGS SA
texts.text: Oil, Gas and Chemicals market condition remains challenging, and we are cautious moving into 2017. There are  trade activities expected to improve in the second half of the year, while the upstream explorations will remain  under pressure throughout the year. However, we have won a new contract with our North American team in the  petrochemical sector, and our refocus on the upstream service on the production and market will support our  growth momentum.

texts.speaker: Frankie Ng
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SGS SA
texts.text: And also, on the upstream, the exploration is weak. The maintenance of projects onsite, there are still  opportunities. I mentioned to you in the first half result that we had won contract in New Zealand in these  production activities and also won some additional contracts in the Middle East in the second half of the year. So,  this will help us to keep some kind of growth momentum in the oil and gas sectors.

texts.speaker: Frankie Ng
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SGS SA
texts.text: To give an example, we have bundled a suite of services to support the textile and footwear industry in the  coming months towards a zero discharge of hazardous chemicals. This suite of services include testing chemical  risk assessment on nine chemical database, product testing and wastewater screening and with close analysis.  This is a quite fast-growing market, as the textile and footwear industry is pushing really for a better use of  chemical in their product as this is a haphazard for the consumer as well as for the environmental. So, there's  quite a large portion in the industry to resolve these issues and the volume of activity should increase over time.

texts.speaker: Frankie Ng
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SGS SA
texts.text: Certification and Business Enhancement. The deadline for the transition to the new ISO 2015 standard will  support the growth momentum of CBE in 2017. In fact, if you look at the current conversion rate from the old  standard to the new standard, it is still rather low. If you look at it, we're still one year close to deadline of 2017 –  2018, so we should expect an acceleration of the request for those audit being transitioned into the new standard  in 2017 as the deadline is in 2018.

texts.speaker: Frankie Ng
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SGS SA
texts.text: Industrial services, difficult market condition expected in 2017, especially related to the oil and gas sectors. We  see limited volume in the CapEx-related activities, and we see increasing competitions and pricing pressure in the  OpEx maintenance-related activities due to excess capacities. Although the picture is slightly different, we have  more pressure in North America, Australia and South America and we're actually seeing some growth in China,  Middle East and Africa.

texts.speaker: Frankie Ng
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SGS SA
texts.text: If I move to Environmental, Health and Safety, growth momentum will carry on in 2017, driven by increasing  laboratory testing associated to persistent organic pollutant, toxin and all the hazardous substances. So regarding  Environmental, it is becoming stricter and we are seeing market demand increasing with our customers.

texts.speaker: Frankie Ng
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SGS SA
texts.text: So, this is our last business line. And if I go into the outlook 2017. Overall, we expect the market conditions to  remain challenging for the energy-related business lines, especially Industrial, because of the market condition of  oil and gas, CapEx and some of the infrastructure and construction sector. And then, to a lesser extent, OGC, we  see the market conditions to improve, as I mentioned.

texts.speaker: Denis Moreau
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Hello. Denis Moreau, UBS. Two questions. The first one regarding the guidance, to clarify a little bit, what you  mean by solid organic growth because it sounds a little bit like the guidance given by Intertek. So I'd like to check  if it's as well something between 0% and 2% organic growth that you have in mind or something stronger than  that and also what your assumptions actually behind this guidance for the energy-related activities.

texts.speaker: Frankie Ng
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SGS SA
texts.text: In terms of our assumptions, the assumptions remain that the Industrial sector will be still under pressure while  we'll probably see an improvement in the mineral activities and a kind of flattish, kind of, oil and gas services. The  oil and gas activities is where we're a little bit cautious. So, these are fine recovery. But on the other hand, for the  last two years, we've seen a lot of activities. So, this is why we need to be cautious on our projects into the oil,  gas and chemical activities for 2017. Besides that, the rest of the activities will be growing steadily in line or better  than what we've seen in 2016.

texts.speaker: Carla D. F. de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: On the CapEx. Yeah, indeed, we have now two years in a row in a pretty low CapEx as a percentage of revenue,  but it is directly related to the fact that we are under pressure in the energy-related businesses, and these are the  more capital-intense businesses.

texts.speaker: Nicholas de la Grense
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: Organic growth in the second half. Again, at the Investor Days, you had suggested that the slowdown in the  second half or at least the slowdown versus where you're expecting to finish the year was mostly energy related.  But I noticed that the non-energy and energy-related divisions both slowed down by the same amount in the  second half. Was one slightly better and one slightly worse than you're expecting or is it just...

texts.speaker: Carla D. F. de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: No. I think the – well, I think the energy-related business, they're definitely a bit worse. So, that is especially the  Industrial in the second half. And in the non-energy related business, it is on top of, I would say, the energy- related business is mainly the Consumer/Retail services as a result of the decline in the wireless activities and it is  the Environmental, Health and Safety...

texts.speaker: Frankie Ng
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SGS SA
texts.text: As well as that some of those are precision farming activities that we have, for example, in Africa, where we have  a quite big base on the precision farming. With the current weather conditions, which drought is going on in South  Africa, this obviously has slowed down significantly our activities in the second half of 2016. But, again, the  market conditions, we hope that – and especially weather conditions, hopefully, will improve in 2017, and we are  expecting a more regular pickup of these activities.

texts.speaker: Frankie Ng
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SGS SA
texts.text: Yes. We're quite optimistic about the government businesses in the sense that the, first, the scanning business is  still is growing. We have incurred most of the cost now, so we need the [indiscernible] (01:08:22) this way, as well  as we also have a couple of addition of new services we are putting in place like the e-waste program that the  team is putting in place, where we are looking at helping government to collect the tax they pay for those waste in  the European countries. For example, where they ship the goods and this tax on the waste recycling after we  collected them, so we're helping the government to do that. First, the recycling aspect, and we have a partner to  do that.

texts.speaker: Toby W. Reeks
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Secondly, Frankie, could you talk about your pricing strategy in the energy businesses? Have you held on to  prices with volumes dropped? And is it the same across all the different energy businesses or is that different?

texts.speaker: Frankie Ng
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SGS SA
texts.text: For your second question, for the pricing, these are quite high pricing pressure on some of the activities, as I  mentioned, especially on the CapEx, OpEx activities including OGC. Oil and gas for the international services. We  are very cautious. I mean, it's really a question of tactical strategic evolution for us; and some of those contract,  we just walk away from the fact that the customer is asking us prices that we believe is beyond what we feel is the  right level and is going to undermine our margin, we just walk away and let some of our competitors to take on  those projects.

texts.speaker: Frankie Ng
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SGS SA
texts.text: We are certainly monitoring the situations, but I would say it's a bit too early for me now to make exact comment  about which businesses would be affected enough. Obviously, from the new government in the U.S. there was,  for example, talks about infrastructure investment. So we're monitoring these sectors, whether this would be an  upside for our testing activities, material testing, as well as supervision.

texts.speaker: Frankie Ng
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SGS SA
texts.text: On the other hand, we talked about issues, the EPA with – lesser regulations for the Environmental Protection  Agency, but at the same time we're talking about a relax on the regulations for requirement for drilling. texts.speaker: Josh G. Puddle
texts.profession: Analyst, Joh. Berenberg, Gossler & Co. KG (United Kingdom)
texts.text: And then the second question, could you give us the exit rates of your oil and gas business within the Industrial  segment? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Frankie Ng
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SGS SA
texts.text: Your other question was the exit rate of the Industrial oil and gas business.

texts.speaker: Jean-Philippe Bertschy
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank Vontobel AG (Research Firm)
texts.text: Yeah. It was about in coal chemistry the samples were like – volume were like up 17% in H1, and now you  reported 11% in H2. So, implying like a sequential slowdown to 8% in H2. Is there like some base effects or if  there was like a deterioration in coal chemistry in the second part of the year?

texts.speaker: Frankie Ng
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SGS SA
texts.text: So, what we say is if there's margin given away in the Greater Asia Pacific region, it would be mainly on the  Australian side and, to a lesser extent, Malaysia, which is two affiliates that is quite highly linked to the oil and gas  industry, I would say.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: Now in terms of acquisitive growth, the green part, as I mentioned earlier, the 24 green bits. I'm not going to run  through all of them. And the two other divisions that are picking up the most of the  acquisitive growth are industrial and NV.

texts.speaker: Christopher Kirk
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SGS SA
texts.text: Agricultural, the Agricultural business, our Seed and Crop services, which is field trials, feed trials, crop trials,  precision farming, that business grew by as you see there, nearly 14% of which 13.3% was organic, which is really  quite spectacular. Our Seed and Crop services grew by 40% amongst that, and that's really an exceptionally high

texts.speaker: Christopher Kirk
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SGS SA
texts.text: But the balance of Seed and Crop services will also be very, very good. We're expecting to grow in Asia, in Africa  and in South America. And to that point, we just acquired a company in Brazil called Gravena. Gravena is  probably the market leader in Brazil for Crop services. Just out of interest, one thing I did miss in terms of the  trade services, this growth was achieved while we had one of our biggest agricultural countries in the world under  water. It just stopped for several months, while the  place dried out. But it should bode well for the second half of the year [indiscernible] (21:02).

texts.speaker: Christopher Kirk
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SGS SA
texts.text: Our geochemistry businesses, we have insufficient capacity right now. So we haven't got the capacity to be able to  analyze the samples that our customers give, actually, a little bit ashamed of that. But when you think that we now  analyze in our geochemistry business in excess of 10 million samples a year, you will be able to understand that  ramping up is not the easiest thing in the world. We opened new laboratories this year in Liberia, in Turkey, which  is now becoming a major exploration market. And we set up neutral services in northern Queensland, which has  been the major exporting coal area for Australia.

texts.speaker: Christopher Kirk
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SGS SA
texts.text: Oil, Gas and Chemicals, we had very, very strong revenue growth in upstream oil and gas, which is really good.  This is an area that Aleem and his team have been investing in for the last two and a half years. And that's been  very, very good. Our oil condition monitoring, which is checking the metallic components in used oil has been  very, very good, as has been our port – sorry, plant and terminal operations.

texts.speaker: Christopher Kirk
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SGS SA
texts.text: The plant and terminal operations where effectively we've moved products around inside plants and terminals is  driven by most of our customers wishing to outsource their work. So in so doing, they give us the responsibility for  moving products in their plants and their terminals, and we take it from there, again, continues to grow  significantly. The margin was impacted. As you know, we had some refinery closures here in Europe. We also had  some refinery closures in the Caribbean. And of course, because the upstream sector is brand new to the SGS  Group, we had some initial establishment costs that have in fact impacted the margin.  All of our existing businesses will continue to grow. And Aleem? We have a training session and his answer is –  everybody just says or if I say, they won't grow, will they not? But some of the new innovative services – Aleem  and his team have developed this thing called the attic. Is it a big concern? I think it's about a poet sitting on top of  an attic, somewhere writing poetry. But in fact, this [indiscernible] (24:11) Advanced Technology Innovations  Center, which we've established in Houston. These are a group of gentlemen, very highly qualified engineers who  are allowed to play with toys and money, and they invent things. They invented the [indiscernible] (24:26), the  [ph] mini gor (24:27) that we talked about historically. And the most recent innovation they have come up with is  the thing called [ph] Gaspro. (24:34) You'd be crazy if – or if you don't read the newspapers, unconventional gas –  shale gas, coal bed methane, all of these new forms of gas are obviously of significance. texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: One of the key takeaways, as we look at the graph that breaks down the importance of each of our nine  businesses from a revenue perspective, is that we continue to deliver on our strategy to grow the overall  importance of the non-energy related business in our portfolio.

texts.speaker: Carla D. F. de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: Environment, Health and Safety revenue declined of minus 1.4%, which is mainly driven by the benefit of a  commercial contract that was completed in the first half of last year. And in addition to the solid growth in the  lab services, we believe that the foundations are in place for our Environment, Health and Safety businesses to  continue to grow moving forward.

texts.speaker: Carla D. F. de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: The first half of 2017 represents the first time that OGC has also experienced a positive growth since 2014. Additionally, we achieved strong growth in sample management, oil condition  monitoring and stock measurement. We expect the growth in the second half comparable to the one of the first  half.

texts.speaker: Carla D. F. de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: Last but not least, the only business that was – which was in decline in the first half was Industrial, and the reason  is twofold. texts.speaker: Carla D. F. de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: China's very strong growth is across the portfolio and particularly driven by the recovery of the Electronics and  Electrics. texts.speaker: Carla D. F. de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: Acquisitions were the main drivers behind the Americas' positive growth, related mainly to the acquisitions we  made in Industrial, Transportation, AFL and Environment, Health and Safety that have been made last year.

texts.speaker: Carla D. F. de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: The growth in the head count in Europe, Africa, Middle East is mainly driven by the organic growth in Agriculture,  Food and Life, and Environment, Health and Safety, and the staffing of new Industrial and Mineral projects in  Russia. texts.speaker: Carla D. F. de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: The relatively low flow-through of the incremental revenue can be explained by the four developments I outlined  before. texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA

texts.speaker: Carla de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Finance Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: Three clarifying points regarding this uptake of the margin: First, the market recovery in minerals and the  efficiency gains in GIS; CBE; and Environmental, Health and Safety positively impacted our margins. And thirdly, we  benefited from the recovery of the bad debt provision we accounted for in the first half 2017 in GIS, and which  was of course related to a number of GIS contracts.

texts.speaker: Carla de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Finance Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: Most activities in the mineral portfolio experienced double-digit growth. Trade saw robust demand in Energy  Minerals, and the Geochem saw a strong increase in sample volumes, while the Metallurgy business achieved a  big performance, particularly in Canada and Australia with a higher demand for pilot plant testing.

texts.speaker: Carla de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Finance Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: Environmental, Health and Safety realized a strong growth of 6.1%, mainly driven by double-digit growth in the  Health and Safety services, and this was complemented by mid-single-digit growth in field and monitoring  services and a key contributor to the Environmental, Health and Safety growth is regulation enforcement around  the world, accentuated by the new push in developing geographies.

texts.speaker: Carla de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Finance Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: Acquisitions made in Industrial, Agriculture, Food and Life, and CRS helped the Americas region to achieve a  growth of 7.2%, of which 5.9% organic. And the organic growth in  North America is mainly driven by a double-digit growth in Agriculture, Food and Life, OGC, and Environmental,  Health and Safety. The total inorganic growth relates to the North America region, which remains a focus area for  future acquisitions.

texts.speaker: Carla de Geyseleer
texts.profession: Chief Finance Officer & Senior Vice President, SGS SA
texts.text: Environmental, Health and Safety margin improvement by 210 basis points resulted from improved performance  in the U.S. as well as increased volume in health and safety work in Europe and ongoing operational efficiency in  Asia Pacific and Europe. Our Minerals colleagues were successful in accelerating the top line growth, while  increasing the margins by 150 basis points. The team continued to work successfully on improved lab utilization  and lab operational efficiencies. And in addition, they continued to add a number of profitable contracts to the  portfolio.

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, SGS SA

On the overall is the pickup of Upstream and the pickup of PTO, and in other parts of  portfolio expect the second half margins to be back in line with the second half of 2017.

texts.text: Hi, Ben. Good morning, everyone. Let me start with the obvious topic here in Q1, which is the Transmission wind  connection charges, which, as you know, have been booked at €203 million. I mean, over the – it doesn't do any  good to anyone to now start finger pointing who didn't do the job right in terms of specification and execution and  who was involved in the lack of decision making on what the spec would be and the whole nine yards. I mean, we  are focusing now on working together, cooperating with the different stakeholders in that matter. We still do  continue to believe that this is a unique opportunity for Germany to shape the change in the energy mix going  forward, and that's obviously the most attractive topic here on a general note.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer and Executive Vice President, Siemens AG
texts.text: Now, very specific, when those projects have been awarded, we're obviously – we are working together with our  customers, also with the authorities, about what will exactly that platform look like. Will it be more classified as a  ship or will it be more classified under the legislation as an oil platform? And that's been basically the first major  hiccup here that this discussion is still ongoing. And there are massive material ramifications to that. As you  know, we have been installing quite a number of those operations already in the U.K., or in the greater U.K. area,  and that has actually worked out very well.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer and Executive Vice President, Siemens AG
texts.text: On the Renewables side, similar matters, onshore has always been quite a challenge as compared to offshore. And  that what is what you now see in the Wind, that we had, first of all, somewhat light revenue number, it was close  to €900 million. That's actually too light in order to make some profit and cover the fixed cost structure. And on  top of that, we saw relatively more onshore revenues as offshore, reason being that we needed to rush finishing  some regional wind parks, mostly also in the U.S., due to the exploration of some benefits which have been given  by the government.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer and Executive Vice President, Siemens AG
texts.text: Yeah, thanks, Simon. On Transmission, I mean, obviously, this is an area of disappointment, not just in terms of  the short-term challenges on getting our joint act together on the German renewable energy agenda, but,  obviously, also those adverse matters we had discussed a year ago on order intake on transformers and high- voltage substations have not really gotten any better and we see in major parts see the fallout of those order  intakes now in the P&L.

texts.speaker: Peter J. Reilly
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Prime Brokerage)
texts.text: Good morning, Joe. I've got two questions, please. Firstly, can you update us on your strategy in the Wind Turbine  markets? On the one hand you're saying that you've got very aggressive pricing in the onshore market. You said in  the past that offshore pricing is also deteriorating. And at the same time, you're taking large orders for onshore  projects in North America. I mean, are those projects in North America, are they at acceptable prices or are you  taking on very low-margin contracts just to win market share and grow in line with the business, with the market?

texts.speaker: Peter J. Reilly
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Prime Brokerage)
texts.text: And then secondly, I've got a slightly more high-level question on Siemens and large flagship projects. Last year  we had the problems at particle therapy, this year we've got the problems of the Wind offshore grid  interconnection, and these are both areas where Siemens is taking very big, very risky contracts, very large  prestigious projects. I mean, is this Siemens taking on board excessive risks for prestigious contracts because you  see a big opportunity or because you think it's good for the public image of Siemens?

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer and Executive Vice President, Siemens AG
texts.text: Thanks, Peter. I hear your obvious frustration as far as it comes to projects not going as well as we would have  wished for. We are not managing the company for good luck or bad luck. We are managing the company for value  increase. So now, I mean, we have extensively talked about the Transmission topic. The orders have been taken  based on the assumption that this company has done it many times before in the U.K. environment and has  always managed to do very decent profits in the Transmission division. Secondly, we do believe that the German  renewable energy policy offers a lot of opportunity to also serve as an example for many other economies to get  the energy mix right.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer and Executive Vice President, Siemens AG
texts.text: Thirdly on the Wind, the strategy in general hasn't changed. We do believe that Wind can be a decent business  because it offers a significant amount of synergies together with our Energy Turbine business. Now, obviously,  what we have seen, I respect that those 14%, 15%, 16% profit on Wind in the last three, four, five years has been  water under the bridges. But I mean, obviously, we are not managing the company for a quarter, we are managing  the company also for the mid and long term.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer and Executive Vice President, Siemens AG
texts.text: Maybe one last remark on those big, great projects, which, chances are that people believe it is some marketing. I  mean, look, if you look at the Fossil division, this is where the biggest projects are and, I mean, obviously, the  numbers suggest that we are able to do it if it is well-focused and well executed on.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer and Executive Vice President, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, I am with you that there is some frustration here on Wind, which, by the way, goes all the way through the  company this time, it's Wind as a division itself. It is the adjacent transition connection and it is also a weak point  in the Drive Technology margin, which I'm sure you have noticed. We have the Mechanical Drives business that's  also somewhat feeling the heat and the challenge of the associated Wind customer base. So, we are aware of that.  There is an underlying scheme of weakness in Wind, we expect that to be a fall-out of consolidation and we  actively need to manage through it.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer and Executive Vice President, Siemens AG
texts.text: Well, we certainly will not buy excess capacities which later on need to be restructured. And, obviously, the  company is, obviously, as we see reasonably busy to get its own Wind exercise done, so therefore, I would be  somewhat reluctant on any greater ideas to be an active capacity consolidator of that matter. If there is some local  value creation by taking over some installed base here or there which helps us utilize our footprint, maybe, but  that's pure speculation.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer and Executive Vice President, Siemens AG
texts.text: And the second is that we have been, and that was exactly our intention, we have been very, very active and, for  the most part, successful in supporting projects in our industrial sectors, like Energy and Industry and in part  Healthcare, to act as an incubator and as a catalyst to make projects possible that can then have incremental  margin on the business. So, that is within our expectations. As I said, it was a bit steep for the quarter, but we  expect that to ease out and the speed of that will significantly slow down.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We'll take our next question from Olivier Esnou of Exane BNP Paribas. Please go ahead, your line is  now open.

file: SIE - Q1 2013 Earnings Call 23January2013 230 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 23-Jan-13.pdf

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Thank you, Mariel. Welcome and good morning to everybody. Thank you for joining us to discuss the first quarter  results of 2013. In a nutshell, our start into the new fiscal year and towards our Siemens 2014 target was solid in a  still difficult macroeconomic environment. Despite the clear stabilization in the financial markets in the euro  zone, the recession in a number of countries continues and leads to an overall subdued investment climate. The  U.S. economy has stabilized, yet the ongoing discussions about raising the debt ceiling and pending decisions  about budget cuts result in a certain reluctance to invest.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: As discussed during Q4, a key lever of Siemens 2014 is focusing our portfolio, where we made good progress.  during the Capital Market Day Industry at the Hannover Fair in April, we will give you an in-depth view on our  well established capabilities in industrial software design and simulation capabilities. Second, we signed the  acquisition of Invensys Rail to further strengthen our Rail Automation business. And third, we have started the  divestment process for the recently announced disposal of our Water Treatment, Postal Automation and Baggage  Handling businesses. All of them are currently still reported in continued operations.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: For the solar activities which are currently held in discontinued operations, we had to record a further loss of €150  million this quarter, mainly due to €115 million pre-tax impairment charges mostly as a result of ongoing  challenges related to a major project in Spain.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Let's have a look at some key developments in each of the sectors. First sector, Energy. The book-to-bill ratio in  Energy is back at a very healthy 1.13. Orders were down 3% mainly due to a sharp decline in the U.S. Wind  business and more selective order intake in the Transmission business.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Fossil order intake was up significantly by 16% due to a number of large solution and service orders such as  Lausward in Germany. Some of the project awards were earlier than expected, so we will see some normalization  during the next quarter.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: First quarter revenue was stable on the conversion from Energy's strong order backlog with significant growth in  the Americas and driven by an increase of 23% in the Wind business completing all wind farms ahead of the old  BTC expiration. We are currently evaluating details and impact of the newly announced BTC scheme in U.S. based  on the new triggering event, start of construction until end of 2013. We are confident that we will see renewed  interest from our customers in the U.S.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: On profitability, Energy delivered a mixed picture. Fossil delivered a healthy 19.6% profit margin, continuing its  excellent project execution in the solution business and a seasonally strong earnings contribution from the service  business. Wind Power achieved 4.6% profitability through higher revenues and positive effect in connection with  the settlement of a claim related to a major wind farm project in Europe. On the downside, Oil & Gas faced a sharp  decline in profitability due in part to €46 million in charges, resulting from further Iran-related legal and  regulatory matters. The impact of these sanctions may also affect the division's operational margin going forward.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Power Transmission is executing on its restructuring program called transform to win and works through the  Greek connection projects to offshore wind farms. Profitability was held back by €28 million in project charges  related to these projects and the conversion of lower-margin projects from the order backlog. As indicated in  December, during the Capital Markets Day, the energy sector expects transformation charges for the full year in  the magnitude of €300 million.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Profitability in Industry Automation declined moderately by 40 basis points due to lower volume, while Drive  Technologies lost 90 basis points, impacted by weaker demand for higher-margin short-cycle products and lower  contributions from its renewable offerings. With the closing of the latest IA acquisition in the integration of LMS  in the software business of Industry Automation has started, industry expects around €400 million further  transformation charges as part of Siemens 2014.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: Maybe before we basically start answering the question of Ben, let me maybe summarize the way I've seen the Q1  developing. We believe, overall, it's been quite an uneventful quarter, which we like at this time because obviously  there's some uncertainty out there. And we are overall satisfied with the quarter and there have been quite a series  of excellent achievements if you just talk about Fossil, Industry Automation and also Imaging. The other goal is to  recognize there are areas that we need to step up our efforts. We've been somewhat slow on the transformation  charges which in a way would suggest that we are also slow in ramping up the productivity which, as a matter fact,  is not true.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: As many of you know that Siemens conservatively books the charges, mostly LMV, if there's an agreement with  the workers' representatives. So, one should not assume that the slow start of transformatory charges would  suggest any delay in our efforts to step up productivity and costs out.  Now, obviously, we do know that there are some areas where management will be focusing on since they continue  to trend unfavorably. That is the Transmission area. That's the grid access in the North Sea. There is some  challenges in Solar and, obviously, we deal with the trains. And as I said in the summary, we are satisfied with the  quarter, and we work diligently on improving our profitability as we move along.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, is that sustainable? Well, I mean, the overall market conditions in that area have not changed. It is a  complicated market from both the operator as well as the OEM. NSN's got the window now because they've been  ahead of the curve in terms of cost reduction and this is what NSN needs to use to foster its position.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: This is somewhat different if it comes to Transmission. Some of you might as well be saying that we believe or I  believe that Transmission will not be a great place to be for several quarters in a row. That's 30 volts got to do with  our challenges in the wind grid access in the North Sea, where we are operating at, obviously, gross margin zero,  so that's real dilute earnings as we move along until the orders are being fully finished.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: And the third topic, obviously being mid- and low-voltage, and that's predominantly the area where you can  expect most of those charges happening as we move along.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: Flat revenues, flat profit, that's just about the run rate, and that's what we have achieved in Q1. And we just need  to continue to work on our plans and then the guidance will be fine if there is no massive and noticeable material  change in the short-cycle environment, which obviously would change the world, but we talk about it once we see  it and not now.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: On the discontinued operations, we obviously do have OSRAM as a major impact and there is also the Solar  business as a major impact. Everything else is more immaterial. Now, on Solar, we obviously have quite a number  of issues which we need to deal with, and that's mostly related to a big project in Spain which does not quite  perform and develop the way we would have expected it to. That also provoked another €150 million of write-offs,  mostly long-lived assets, and also provided the maturity of the losses on the operational level, and that continues  to be in focus and it continues to be a complicated matter. So, therefore, I would not be too surprised if there'll be  more losses coming along associated with that project. At this point in time, however, we booked what we could  reasonably book.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: Now, if you go on the underlying performance of Oil & Gas, one needs to know that the Oil & Gas division is about  60% on industrial turbines and about 40% on process industries, oil and gas obviously is having a major part of  that being this business with that country. And we do see some seasonal weakness on the industrial turbine space,  and that has also caused the underlying temporary weakness in the division.

texts.speaker: James A. Moore
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn Partners LLP
texts.text: Good morning, everybody. It's James at Redburn. I've got three questions, if I could. Thank you very much for the  help on the charges by sector. I wondered if you could help us a bit more on the savings by sector and the timing. I  think at the Energy Capital Markets Day you talked about €3.2 billion of the €6 billion productivity savings  coming out of Energy. I wondered if you could break down the other €2.8 billion across the other three sectors  and just give us some sense on the timing as to how these numbers come in 2013 versus 2014.

texts.speaker: James A. Moore
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn Partners LLP
texts.text: Secondly, the Fossil orders have had a second good quarter. I wondered if that's a trend or just an aberration, and  how you see the outlook for the power-gen demand environment.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: Fossil had quite a decent quarter really in terms of margin, predominantly resulting from the fact that we had a  very, very, even seasonally, very high impact on Fossil services. So, from a time window there was a lot of service  going on in that particular timeframe which obviously helped the margin.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, generally, we reiterate our guidance that the Fossil margins could deteriorate down to 16-ish, 17-ish from what  we have achieved in Q1 and also in last year. So, that continues to be our assumption. If we deliver better, then we  obviously take that also. But generally, one should assume there is some underlying – there will be some  deterioration on margins down to 250, 300 basis points from the level which we had in 2012 and also in Q1.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: Energy has done that with examples on how on how this breaks down to divisions. Industry will do that in April  when we meet at the Hanover Fair and they will lay out their plans on how they get the settings done and what  margins they are going to achieve and then comes IC. And Healthcare pretty much is done with the Agenda 2013.  So, please bear with me that if we do not – now from corporate side, do not release any savings numbers, that will  be done when the sectors' head of division talk about their actions and how they achieve it.

texts.speaker: James A. Moore
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn Partners LLP
texts.text: Thank you very much, Joe. Can I just come back on Fossil? The question was about orders and demand, more  than margins. You've had two good quarters of orders and demand. Do you have a view on the current demand  outlook in Fossil? Is it better, as the numbers might suggest?

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: Well, as you said, I mean, Q1 was great with a 16% underlying order growth. That was already taking into account  some orders which were expected in Q2. So, I would not be too surprised if there was a normalization of order  intake in fiscal Q2 kind of compensating for the strong demand in fiscal Q1. So, generally, underlying, we do not  see any top-line growth on Fossil in fiscal 2013 based on the assumptions which we have in the United States, as  well as in Europe.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: We'll take our next question from Gaël De Bray from Société Générale. Please go ahead.  Gaël De Bray  Analyst, SG Securities (Paris) SAS  Q Thank you very much. Good morning, everyone. Two questions, please. Could you first elaborate on the rationale  behind the creation of the Power Grid division a couple of years ago and the rationale behind the combination of  the low-voltage and the medium-voltage businesses? What kind of synergies and what kind of complementarities  are you seeing in such a combination? I'm obviously trying to judge how core the low-voltage business is for the  group. And if you could give us an idea on the two businesses' respective margins in Q1, that would be great.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: Hi, Gaël. Thanks for the questions. I assume if you talk about low voltage, mid voltage and smart grid, I assume  you talk about the I&C sector. I mean, look, we've been combining assets in the company and put it in the Cities &  Infrastructure because we wanted, first of all, to fix the product base. And then, secondly, once we have done that,  also by focusing the spectrum there, then we are going to add the capabilities the company has in projects, in  financing, in integration, to make meaningful service offerings for urban centers. So, that's the strategy, and there  will be more to that when Roland Busch gives his presentation and the divisions on the sector. And that's what we  are doing.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: And you might have seen from our actions in Q4, in fiscal Q1, that the first priority there is focusing the portfolio  towards having a [ph] strong [indiscernible] (48:53), and one area where we've been focusing was rail automation,  and that's obviously something which we like. Another area of focusing is the space of smart grid, mid-voltage  services that we also do believe we have quite a decent footprint, especially on energy automation, where we are  very, very good at not only by market penetration, but also by margins. So, those are the two focus areas in that  space.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, on DT, I mean, obviously, the diamond in the rough, so to speak, on the DT business is the motion control. Did  I talk about diamonds? The CFO always looks into the profitability first and foremost. And so that's actually the  somewhat slow in fiscal Q1, and that's been also driving the deterioration of profitability along the side that we  have ongoing capacity adjustments to make on mechanical drives due to the fact that some of those mechanical  drives are not only much in demand, but also are approaching end of life due to the fact that the wind turbines go  more on gearless. So that's been – that's the story on Drive Technologies and those areas are also being addressed  as part of the transformatory charges which we had been reserving for in Industry.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: A bit more soft on two other topics, that's Transmission and Solar. Solar, obviously, being in the discontinued but  still has got to be paid at some point. Transmission, not so much about the execution itself and the preparation  which we have done to fulfill the order; it's more about the fact that those grid access projects in the North Sea are  operating in the meantime at gross margin zero. So, whenever you've got gross margin zero, which I'm going to  tell you, that any little change from the assumption will automatically lead into a new charge if it's a southward  trend.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: The second topic also is similar, that's Solar, which as you know is up for sale. We've been writing off all the long- life assets so there is not a single long-life asset anywhere in the book, but there are still, obviously, the operating  floating capital. And there is still the challenge to finish and operate and dispose of the projects in Spain. So, that's  where we are, and we'll take it from there.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: On the disposal of the announced assets, as you know, we've announced the disposal of Solar, of Water, Postal  Automation and Airport Logistics. Solar's been – already been moved to discontinued as of 9/30. We are currently  working on the carve-out of Water business, as well as Postal Automation and Airport Logistics. And depending  on the progress of that carve-out, we will decide, first of all, whether or not to move them into discontinued. That's  got to do with the fact how material it is and whether it's a stand-alone unit which is not integrated into the  business itself.

file: SIE - Q1 2014 Earnings Call 28January2014 130 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 28-Jan-14.pdf

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: As far as the operational business is concerned, we are making satisfactory progress toward the productivity and  cost reduction goals we set for 2014. But we prioritize – and in cases of doubt, securing business process and  project implementation is given priority over cost reduction.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: A look at the key figures from the first quarter shows that we can, all in all, be satisfied with developments even if  the new charges related to offshore wind connection projects in the German North Sea at the Energy Transmission  Division serve as a bitter reminder that these legacy projects, as we call them, that is to say, the North Sea  projects, our train projects, and the power plant Olkiluoto in Finland will likely to be latent material charges for  years to come. I repeat, for years to come.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: We won several large contracts, especially for rail projects and wind farms, which will take several years to be fully  executed. 41% of our orders came from emerging markets. This demonstrates that alongside industrialized  nations, our business is no longer conceivable without these growth markets.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: The energy sector saw a moderate increase in new orders and a moderate decrease in revenue. Energy contributed  the most to total sectors per the profit, with earnings of €506 million.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: We are very pleased to note that in the energy sector, we had really good order intake. We've been capable of  landing its largest onshore installation order-to-date for five wind farms and an order for two combined-cycle  power plant blocks in Pennsylvania, which we will equip with our H class turbines.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: We have also been chosen as a supplier for the country's first large offshore wind power plant. Orders like these, in  a land where competition often limits opportunity, are of course especially gratifying, and we are proud to have  won these contracts.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: We are a respected partner in the energy transition made in the U.S.A., which distinguishes itself from less well - executed approaches in other countries by its hitherto discipline d approach.

texts.speaker: A
texts.profession: Thank you, Mr. [ph] Hefner (23:29). Now, of course, we are looking forward to hearing what the investors will
texts.text: The company has not grown for some years and there we have to see – we have to look for growth possibilities and  we have to look at the value chain in the electrification, efficient use of electric energy, and we'll have to see what  effect the digitization has, what changes will come, what consequences that has for us and I can also say  something.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: What do I mean by the statement? The debate about the so-called fourth sector does not need or has never met  our real priorities. It's all about the definition of the content mobility, low-voltage building technology. All these  contents have to be addressed in a way that we reach tangible improvements. This is what the sector has been  focusing on and this is what has been announced by our colleagues.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: The other question with regard latent material charges, of course, we wish that all projects have been finally  dealt  with. But this is not the case unfortunately. Think about the power plant in Finland. This is a project in which we,  with our conventional power, that is to say steam turbines, have made good progress. But we are part – members  of the consortium, so we have to wait until the steam reaches our turbine.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, our partner who is in charge of the nuclear part must be capable of supplying the steam. So, within – there's  still some insecurity in this business. The same thing is true for the high-speed trains. Y ou may know that after a  couple of delays, we now can supply the German Velaro version or version of the Velaro train, more supplies will  follow. But we still have to wait and have to apply for the European operational approval.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, we are waiting for approval for the tunnel between France and the UK. So, that is to say there are some latent  risks which cannot be quantified in all detail. But we should draw your attention to the existence of these risks.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: The same thing is true for the offshore wind power connection to the grid. We had good – can make one platform  but three of the platforms are still lacking. And many things depend on the weather situation. So, even if we have  proven with the first platform that it's technically feasible, we have no influence on the weather situation.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Well, good morning, [ph] Ms. Myer (34:36). Now that was a whole range of questions. Well, the project timelines,  these range from relatively short-term issues for the next platform in the North Sea, which could happen in  spring, depending on the weather. And we should conclude these connections by 2016. Now, this is a timeline  which goes or stretches across or beyond several fiscal years. And the same goes for the Eurostar, the European  trains. And we have a major milestone in 2015. This means that we hope we will not have to reevaluate the  situation, but of course, we're working on the approval and everything. Now, we have a plan for this, of course. So,  it's not that we're planning for any problems, but of course, you should learn fr om experience. And especially  when more parties are concerned, it's not always easy.

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: Good morning. Threefold questions. You have said that record level of order intake will stabilize the job situation.
texts.text: Does that mean that after Siemens 2014, no more jobs will be melted down? Y ou have talked about less successful  approaches with regard to the energy situation. Did I interpret you correctly that you'd refer to Germany? What do  you think about Germany's plans?

texts.speaker: A
texts.profession: Thank you very much, Mr. [ph] Fetter (38:07). Stabilizing payroll situation does not exclude structural changes in
texts.text: My remark that America has a very reasonable approach to ecological restructuring of the energy supply has been  made intentionally. The so-called [indiscernible] (39:33), the restructuring of the energy  supply sector always  takes place in a given economic environment and has an impact on the gross national product, so – to gross  domestic product. And energy plays a major role for every given national economy and GDP. So, a migration  towards a new situation with reasonable mix of conventional energy and the new energy sources can be a solution  because you have to take care of peak demands.

texts.speaker: A
texts.profession: Thank you very much, Mr. [ph] Fetter (38:07). Stabilizing payroll situation does not exclude structural changes in
texts.text: America shows how we can do this in a reasonable way. They have moved away from coal rather swiftly towards  gas and is blending solar and wind energy to add it to the energy supply mix. This is how things should have been  done in Germany. So, we've been more ambitious in Germany because – due to the fact that the new act on energy  input really fueled solar panels on consumers' roofs and did not really fuel innovation. No, our consumers are not  to blame but the design fault was that you – the development has been fueled not to develop innovation but to  develop consumption. So now, we subsidize jobs in China with German tax payers' money because they make solar  panels now. In other words, I would say that sustainability is not only to be respected in ecological terms, but also  in economic terms.

texts.speaker: A
texts.profession: Thank you very much, Mr. [ph] Fetter (38:07). Stabilizing payroll situation does not exclude structural changes in
texts.text: So that – of course, there are problems with regard to our constitution because the trust of the consumers who  have invested in the solar panels has to be respected. But we have to address the situation because in that case,  risk-free capital investments are rewarded with 7 % to 8% of interest of return on capital. So this is – so you see  that there's a broad corridor of corrective actions, broad margin for corrective actions. And that is to say we must  be able to cut into existing subsidies without losing protection of investors, without jeopardizing protection of  investors. So, the change – now – well, the wrong decision to subsidize companies who need a lot of energy, a lot  of power.

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: Two short questions, please. The first one on deflation. Some economists are concerned about deflat ion in the
texts.text: Eurozone. The question is what can the company do to limit those risks? What has to be done or should be done  there?

texts.speaker: A
texts.profession: Thank you very much. No. The deflation in Europe is something I'm less worried about. Now, geographically
texts.text: So, I think when you look at the European situation, it's more than just a question of the UK, but we are quite  successful in the UK as a company. So, I wish we would be as successful elsewhere or everywhere as in the UK, not  just in the energy division. So we would like to do what we've done.
