texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Now let's have a look at some key developments in each of the sectors. First, the book-to-bill ratio in Energy was at  a very healthy 1.25x. Orders were up 3%, entirely due to a doubling of orders in the Wind business, where we, for  example, recorded the largest onshore order ever from MidAmerican Energy for five projects in Iowa totaling to  448 wind turbines.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Beginning of fiscal 2014, the new combined Power Generation division started, a merger fro m the former Fossil  and Oil & Gas divisions. Orders were 12% lower across all regions due to less volume from large orders.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Overall, the market environment for energy remains highly competitive and should not change any time soon.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: First quarter revenues were down 4% with growth in Wind and lower revenues in Power Generation driven by less  solution and gas turbine business. On profitability, Energy  showed an improved performance year-over-year.  Power Generation achieved an excellent 16.6% profit margin continuing its stringent project execution and a  seasonally strong earnings contribution from the service business. As indicated before, we expect th e division to  have a normalized margin of around 15% going forward. Wind Power reached 4.8% profitability, supported by  higher revenues also from the expanding service business and adversely affected by a seasonally lower share of the  offshore revenues.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: On the downside, Transmission faced continuous project execution challenges, resulting in charges of €67  million,  mostly related to the North Sea offshore grid connection. Above and beyond obviously on the offshore grid  connection, we do continue to have our focus on Transmission because what we see in the underlying  performance is not what we like. So, actions going forward are imminent.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Power Transmission is executing on its restructuring program, Transform the Wind, and continues to work  through projects with very low margin throughout the rest of fiscal 2014. So we do not expect a significant  improvement in 2014. This will be reserved for 2015 and beyond. And as you will remember, we have said that on  various occasions that Transmission needs time in order to fix the business as we move along.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: In January 2014, we closed the divestment of our Water Technologies business to AEA Investors for a purchase  price of about €600 million. We do not expect significant effects on income from discontinued operations from  this transaction.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Last but not least, the sector Infrastructure & Cities showed a clear improvement driven by its transformation  efforts, which the sector reported on during its recent Capital Market Day.

texts.speaker: Ben E. Uglow
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Question number two, obviously I haven't completely disaggregated margin effects in Oil & Gas and Fossil Power,  but what I am curious to understand is, is the underlying margin in the formal Fossil Power business, is that  continuing to improve? If so, why? And what is the basis in your view for the margins going from 16.6% back  down to 15%? I'm trying to reconcile what looks like a robust margin performance in Fossil Power with a lower  forecast?

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: On EP, which is Energy, Fossil including service, and the Oil & Gas Products, so to speak, I mean, we wanted to  emphasize two matters. First, we had a very decent quarter in Q1 which was predominantly related to the fact that  the service component in the total mix was rich, so was the margin, and that actually helped us drive to the 16.6%.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Going forward, in the oil organization, we said a normalized margin for Fossil including services would have been  16% plus. Now with the integration of the industrial turbine, that new normalized margin that I wanted to guide  the market with is more in the neighborhood of 15%, so that's just for your orientation.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Thanks, Gaël. Well, look, I mean, the solid macro data has been driven by the housing market. And we know that  once housing does fine, then comes consumption and then there will be industrial CapEx -driven expenses again.  So that's the chain. Unfortunately, we are not in the early cycle of this recovery. We've done some work in Building  Technologies, as well as the drives and instrumentation as it relates to the oil and gas fracking sector, but you  obviously also do see that now the weakness in U.S. revenues comes from the fact that there were nearly no order  intake from Wind in 2013.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: If you now look forward into the bookings of the United States business, you can see that we had a very strong  underlying booking for the U.S. business of 28% plus, mostly driven by Wind orders which we are also going to  execute on during the course of 2014.

texts.speaker: James A. Moore
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn Partners LLP
texts.text: Y es. Good morning, everybody. I've got three questions, please. I wonder if you could talk about pricing. We've  seen your U.S. competitor talk about order pricing deteriorate in the gas and steam turbine business. I wonder if  you could talk about that, please.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Now, but on a more serious matter, the pricing topic for gas turbines, I mean, obviously is a topic, pricing has  been becoming more challenging in a market where obviously every order counts. We have in particular been  seeing quite an active pricing behavior in the Middle East where this was about reallocating market shares over  time. I would not however see this challenging pricing environment for gas turbines all across the board. The big  question will be whether or not a competitors outside the euro currency will use that deterioration of the currency  for competitive access. That's a question we – it's still too early to tell, but that could further accelerate the pricing  debate on the gas turbine space.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: And with that, I hand it over to Ralf to give you a little more flavor on the productivity environment which we have  planned for at this time.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Hi, Simon. Power service was good all across the board except Europe. And this should not really come as a  surprise, obviously, due to the fact what operations the gas turbines do these days. And obviously Power service  being seasonal, you could also see and feel its impact on the respective quarters.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: We are looking into the space. Is not going to be earth shattering of any kind. There could be bolt-on acquisitions  if we believe timing and environment is right, but we are not an active buyer at this time.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Now, secondly on the pricing, as I mentioned, we do have selective pricing aggression to regain market shares and  so on and so forth from other competitors. We've seen that in the space of emerging economies, predominantly in  the Middle East. We do not feel inclined to open up that behavior. On the other hand, obviously, it goes wi thout  saying that gas turbines, among other things, are also important to have in terms of installed base because the  service fees together then makes meaningful sense to access this installed base, and this might have also been the  motivation of some competitive thinking.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Other than that, if you look at Indonesia or other emerging economies in Asia are doing pret ty well in both energy  as well as infrastructure. Middle East, you might have heard it when I talked about order intake, very robust, very  enthusiastic about mobility management and the likes. Wind in the United States, it's been fine, but then again,  we do see quite a lot of signs of life in the multiyear order environment and the short -cycle still provides a  potential upside if they recover as quickly as many others in the space believe they would.

texts.speaker: Mariel von Drathen
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: Okay. So we have a Power backlog question and a Drive Technology question.

texts.text: Since I'm sure that the potential impact of oil prices is on everybody's mind, let me upfront give you our take on  the oil price development. texts.profession: Head of Governance & Markets, Siemens AG

texts.profession: Head of Governance & Markets, Siemens AG

texts.profession: Head of Governance & Markets, Siemens AG
texts.text: On the positive side, we expect to benefit from higher investment in infrastructure due to lower energy bills, in  particular emerging economies such as India and increased demand from automotive and downstream customers. texts.speaker: Mariel von Schumann
texts.profession: Head of Governance & Markets, Siemens AG
texts.text: Revenue was up by 3% on growth across all divisions, except for Power and Gas, due to lower orders in previous  quarters as flagged before. Main growth drivers were in Mobility and Wind Power as well as a strong, sh ort-cycled  business in the Digital Factory Division.

texts.speaker: Mariel von Schumann
texts.profession: Head of Governance & Markets, Siemens AG
texts.text: Above and beyond the operational business, we have made material progress in strengthening our portfolio. texts.profession: Head of Governance & Markets, Siemens AG

texts.speaker: Mariel von Schumann
texts.profession: Head of Governance & Markets, Siemens AG
texts.text: At 5.4% profit margin, Wind Power is within the target range, supported by increasing revenues and rising  contribution from the service business. [ph] The limitation  (10:10) of technical difficulties with main bearings and plates progresses as planned.

texts.speaker: Mariel von Schumann
texts.profession: Head of Governance & Markets, Siemens AG
texts.text: In Energy Management, there is strong order flow across all businesses, with a clear focus on margin quality and  risk profile. texts.speaker: James A. Moore
texts.profession: Redburn (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: If I could just follow up on one question. texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: So we are not depending so much on the weather anymore, whether or not to take out and to ship out the  platform. We are on platform. texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer

I mean, obviously, I do agree with the majority of the assessments, the  9.5%, which is just about underlying, maybe a few basis points up on underlying. It's a bit light. However, it's not  been unexpected. So, it doesn't really catch us by surprise.

texts.speaker: James A. Moore
texts.profession: Redburn (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Secondly, could you talk about the strong margins that you saw in Energy Management and Mobility, and  Healthcare? To me they seemed to be three of the surprises in the reporting period. Could you just talk about how  sustainable those better numbers are throughout the balance of this year?

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: And if I may, just one final comment relating to Energy Management and Mobility. Having said that, we are very  pleased with the development, and that those divisions will grow and improve margins going forward is one thing.  By the same token, though, if divisions, which are below the 10%-plus average of the company, grow faster than  others do, that obviously helps growing the profitability and thus the earnings per share but do not necessarily  help improving the marginal growth. I think that's very important to remember is people think about why EPS  grows and margins may be still in the range which we have been saying they would be in December.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: So to speak, with regards to being accretive, I mean, what we have been telling you two years back is that  whenever we acquire a target, we look into the industry-specific environment and also conclude on what is an  acceptable and an aggressive plan in terms to get the payback done.

texts.speaker: James E. Stettler
texts.profession: Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Y es. Good morning, all. Thank you for taking the question. Quickly, just – could you give a comment on pricing  across the portfolio? And what's interesting is how your view differs from your U.S. competitor on the gas turbine  side, which would be interesting to hear why.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: James, maybe for the sake of clarification and making sure that we answer and address your question well, did I  hear you say that there is a different view on gas turbine pricing in the market or is there a different view in terms  of what gas turbines are all about in terms of, yeah, potential, in terms of growth and market development?

file: SIE - Q1 2017 Earnings Call 1February2017 230 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 01-Feb-17.pdf

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: We had a strong start into the fiscal year across all our businesses. I'm very proud of our teams, who worked  really hard to deliver another strong showing for many quarters in a row now. However, we do not only perform on  the financial targets. Our holistic efforts on sustainability were recognized by the research company Corporate  Knights, which placed Siemens as number one amongst the world's most sustainable companies, well ahead of  our competitors. We more and more do experience that a company, which is responsive to society and  environmental needs, resonates well with preferences of the best talent all over the world.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Now, let me briefly touch on some key developments in the first quarter. As expected, comparable orders were  down by 14% on tough comps, due to a significant amount of large orders in fiscal Q1 2016. However, our base  business was stable in the first quarter. And we do see a good order pipeline for the second quarter in  Renewables, Energy Management, as well as Mobility. For example, we just recently announced a significant  project win such as 1.2 gigawatt power plant project in Thailand, or a frame contract for 200 locomotives in  Austria.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Book-to-bill [indiscernible] (4:58) remained above 1. With revenues up 3%, we continued at our path of  comparable organic revenue growth. And among other things, this was driven by the energy project businesses  as well as Building Technology and Digital Factory.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Free cash flow surged to a positive €740 million. I think we need to go back many years to find a similar topic,  which provides us a positive swing year-over-year of more than €1.4 billion. This was mainly due to improved  working capital performance in Energy Management, Mobility as well as Wind Power. Finally, we recorded a  significant decrease of €2.6 billion in provisions for pension and similar obligation due to higher discount rates for  future liabilities.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Now, let's look at the key developments in our divisions. The market environment in Power and Gas continues to  be tough due to slow demand and continued overcapacities in the market. The team continues to be focused on  the opportunities in the market, and our new H-class design is very well under way. In total, we recorded 11  orders for large gas turbines, and delivered 12 turbines during the quarter. Revenue growth was mainly driven by  backlog execution, in particular, from the Egypt project. PG achieved a margin improvement of 230 basis points to  11.8%, due to a smooth project execution and reliable contribution from the service business.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Energy Management continued to be a reliable contributor and inched out a few improvements in almost all  business areas. Profitability was at target range on the back of stronger profit contribution from the high-voltage  businesses and the transmission solution area.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Process Industries benefited from a strong order in Wind Power components, which was still more than offset by  weaker demand from the commodity related industries. PD executed the structural program as planned. But since  a material part of the resource alignment is in Germany, this may take time beyond fiscal 2017 to convert into P&L  savings.

texts.speaker: Andreas Willi
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: And the second one on the Renewable – on the Wind business, in terms of the market share in the U.S. in the  last quarter, maybe you could comment on that in terms of the PTC orders that maybe others have secured, and  you had a weaker market share in the U.S. in a critical quarter given the PTC qualification. And also, in terms of  the Gamesa deal closing hopefully soon, if we adjust your current profitability for the adjustments you are going to  make ahead of the contribution to Gamesa, what kind of the level this business route goes into the new company  in terms of margins then? Thank you very much.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Andreas, hi. On the Renewable market share, I mean, absolutely right, the quarter Q1 in the year was a bit weak.  On the other hand, as you know, this is a large-scale project business. We had quite a decent order intake in  fiscal Q4 in the U.S. and [indiscernible] (27:08) intend to significantly increase order intake in Q2 and Q3 as  compared to Q1. So, we just won a 600 megawatts onshore business in the U.S. So, we actually feel pretty good  about this. We have a solid market share and expect that to hold.

texts.speaker: Michael Hagmann
texts.profession: Analyst, HSBC Bank Plc
texts.text: And then the second one, if you look at the guidance, if you look at the windfall of €172 million, if you look at the  very strong results in CMPA which I'd also consider a windfall, one could argue, look at those numbers, post-tax,  and that gives you already €0.50 per share. So, I'm trying to work out a little bit what are the risks. And here, you  have been highlighting specifically CMPA that kept you from raising the guidance even further. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Ben E. Uglow
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Just on the step-up in the margin, can you talk a little bit more around what you're seeing in Power Service that  took my attention this morning? So, that was issue number one. Issue number two, I don't know how much  visibility you've got over the course of the year, but how should we think about the kind of sequential evolution of  the Power and Gas margin? Are there drivers in there that might lead to a higher margin by year-end?

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, Ben, you can see that there is a lot going on on the operational side. We are very close to this obviously  important and, obviously, also attractive business, because the world still needs a lot of electricity.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: What you do see in the mid- and long-term run, is that things are changing there. There is a significant shift from  mono-sourcing to multi-sourcing of energy, which means from central [ph] big (41:37) to de-central flexible. You  can also see, if you look at [indiscernible] (41:42) the amount of gas large turbine market in 2016, there was about  flattish assets. I know there are some more optimistic views out there, but the facts are what the facts are.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, we are looking much more into things which are changing in trends. So, we do see, in the long-term, there's  more flexible machines associated with renewable energy. Combining them with an optimized mix, we do see that  there's more and more ICPs out there who are after the business model of the established utility model. We see  more and more guaranteed outcome rather than how great any percentages and efficiencies are. Who cares if the  outcome is not secured?

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, we learned a lot in Egypt, by the way, on what proven machines are really all about. In 18 months, we've been  providing 4.8 gigawatts, which is actually 10% more – 400 megawatt more than originally committed based on a  outstanding reliability of our machine and the site condition. So, it doesn't do a lot of good to produce a lot of  paper about ISO conditions. You need to go where customers are and take your machines to where conditions  are. So, we are very close to it. We look at customer benefits, and this is what matters most to us. So, we feel  comfortable in what we do. It's not a simple business, but no one said it would be simple.

file: SIE - Q1 2018 Earnings Call 31January2018 230 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 31-Jan-18.pdf

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: The growth momentum of the global environment seems to be strong in most economies. And our investment in  key businesses and sectors is paying off. Our focus on digitalization and innovation shows clear results. The  Digital Factory division leads the way into what we call Industrie 4.0.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Furthermore, the structural challenges in the fossil power generation market will continue. We have initiated and  will take decisive steps to adjust our capacities accordingly. Meanwhile, the dialogue with the employee  representatives have also started in Germany.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Energy Management developed sideways in the quarter with lower volume from large orders. The profit margin  was at the lower end of the target range, impacted by extraordinary adverse FX effects in the magnitude of 80  basis points.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Process Industries and Drives achieved strong order growth of 10%. However, we saw diverging end customer  trends. While commodity-related end markets showed further stabilization, the demand for mechanical  components particular in the wind business was weak. Profit margin improved by 90 basis points despite  significant currency headwinds. This was driven by record-high profitability in the process automation business.

texts.speaker: Ben Uglow
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Good morning, Joe, Ralf, and Sabine. I had a couple not surprisingly around power. So, big picture question, you  made the comment in the opening that the performance was quite different from your competitors. Joe, can you  explain that performance differential a bit? What do you see or what is actually happening in your business that's  different to your largest competitor? Is it something to do with the way that others have accounted? Is it something  to do with your regional mix? Is it even something to do with the actual gas fleet? So, why are you seeing such a  disparate performance from what others are reporting? So, that's question number one.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Hi, Ben. Well, obviously, commenting on other people's challenges is not appropriate because we have enough  on our own on that matter. I mean, the reason why I made that comment earlier was that people who are not so  familiar with the matter, especially in the general public, so people understand that this is not a Siemens problem,  but a general issue in the industry, which shouldn't come as a surprise because, obviously, if renewable energy  grows, something else needs to obviously decline.

texts.speaker: Simon Toennessen
texts.profession: Analyst, Joh. Berenberg, Gossler & Co. KG (United Kingdom)
texts.text: Yes. Thanks very much. Good morning, Joe, Ralf, and Sabine. Firstly, on Power and Gas, can you talk a bit more  about the trends you're sort of expecting by products? And I know it's sometimes difficult to quantify, but I think  the expectations for large gas turbine demand this year being quite weak is quite well understood. But do you  think you're gaining share in particularly the small, medium aero business right now given we've seen a very weak  performance here from your bigger competitor?

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: On the PG side, I think Joe has been discussing already that the large gas turbines, they still have a downward  trend from the market's perspective. Everything we know from [ph] McCoy (31:36) and alike is rather suggesting  that the trough may be even a bit lower than we saw it last year. So it's hard to tell what market shares you may  win or not win in that area before. You also have the big picture on more than one or two quarters.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: On the small gas turbine side, you mentioned that some of the competitors see a very intense market. We agree  upon that. It was a very slow market development for the first quarter. And also from the statistics that we have at  fingertips, we would assume that that was a further decline in demand on the market side.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: And the compressors being part of the value chains of the process industry's customers, that's right statement.  However, they are also lagging in terms of the lead time that you would normally see. So there wasn't the same  momentum being created as we saw that in the PD portfolio where, as we have been pointing out, had an  extraordinary good development with 10% new order growth even though the wind market with mechanical  components is fairly slow and still contracting.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: So actually, this mechanical drive environment, if it comes to wind is, so to speak, a victim of innovation where we  have the benefits elsewhere. That's when we comment a bit on weaknesses in the wind area, it's not so much  about pricing issues. I mean, everyone looks at other people's backyards which is the supplier. But this is not the  issue. The issue is that there is a segment which used to be a growth segments which now is being affected by  innovation elsewhere, and we deal with it. And if people speculate, you sell it or everything else [indiscernible]  (36:12) want to comment on it.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Thank you. We will now take our next question from Jonathan Mounsey from Exane BNP Paribas.  Please go ahead. Your line is open.

texts.speaker: Gaël De Bray
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (France)
texts.text: Thanks very much. And good morning, everybody. I have a couple, actually. The first one is related to, well, some  of your competitors' issues right now. I mean, did you see some early signs of some of the group's activities  starting to benefit from the windfall effect of GE current issues and perhaps with some of your customers now  more willing to deal with you than in the past?

texts.speaker: Gaël De Bray
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (France)
texts.text: And the second question related to Energy Management. Margins have been sliding down here for the past few  quarters now despite the good top-line development. So could you elaborate a bit more on these please? What's  going on there? And because it seems that the margin gap with some of your peers has actually expanded  relatively rapidly. Thanks.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: And we're absolutely convinced that they are going to make progress with their programs and their growth pattern  in particular. 5% revenue growth in Energy Management is quite something to achieve. We are quite happy with  that and also the fact that our product business is developing. Low-voltage product business in particular is  developing quite nicely that's also an area in the portfolio where we see a good margin conversion taking place.  So also, in that business, we saw that there's quite some momentum being created in the short cycle business.  And from that, what we see, the visibility in that market, we are also quite positively looking ahead for the quarters  to come.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Also, our Energy Management division, which sort of disappointed on the bottom line performance, also appears  with a very strong bookings record. texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Thank you, Joe, and also good morning from my side. Power and Gas continues to face tough market conditions.  However, service remains a very stable contributor to top and bottom line. This quarter, Power and Gas booked one large H- frame gas turbine in Middle East, one large steam turbine, and 36 small and medium gas turbines, a particularly  decent achievement which deserves being mentioned.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Energy Management achieved a strong and broad-based pickup in orders including Moray East, the grid  connection project, in the UK Joe mentioned before and the large HVDC order as part of the ULTRANET project,  one of the crucial North-South grid connections in Germany.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: However, the margin development was not satisfying mainly due to negative effects from grid control projects  which we closely monitor going forward. In addition, lower revenue and profitability [Technical Difficulty]  (00:08:17) impacted margin in the first quarter.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Process Industries and Drives achieved excellent and broad-based order growth of 15%. Commodity-related  industries such as mining or oil and gas continued their CapEx-related recovery. We like to see that PD's  profitability increased and the resulting efforts are paying off.

texts.speaker: Andreas Willi
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: Yeah. Good morning, everybody. I have a question on the Energy Management division there. texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: On the product side, I may not have been precise with my wording, it was not a grid product, it was the high- voltage power transmission product area where we had seasonally weak new orders in the past. We described  that before. So, perhaps, we are not running on the ideal level, that will level out throughout the next two, three  quarters again. And we also have clear visibility on the backlog.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Yeah. I wouldn't – Andreas, ladies and gentlemen, I would not overrate the hiccups we had here in the EM  division. This is a – this is in the digital grid area, which we know very well. We typically – we have revenues  there, annual revenues north of €1.5 billion, typically double-digit margins. texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: But you are right, we need and intend to improve in terms of performance. Already in the second quarter, we have  been talking about Energy Management and they have been taking measures which take us to the conclusion  that they will rapidly improve again in terms of margin levels even though, as I said, they are going to approach  the target margin corridor from the south over the course of the year. They also have for many years a  seasonality that makes the fourth quarter the strongest one. Obviously, you rightfully have been stating that the  late cycle impact of the Process Industries and Drives. We see the business developing quite nicely from the top- line perspective for a couple of quarters already, which is now finally also hitting the bottom line.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Now, on the revenue side, typically, the PG orders are big projects, sometimes even EPC contract-related ones,  they go pretty long in the time where you see notice to proceed and subsequently revenues.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: I do not expect that the cool-down of a global economy will lead to a reduced demand on energy and, therefore,  less service. I don't think it's way too early to go down that route. But we could be around of what you said, would  be satisfactory if it's a bit less than what you hope for, it's probably also in the ballpark. So – but around that area,  we also believe that this could turn out to be for 2019.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: By the way, if you look at the August presentation, there have been quite a few areas where we said that cost  savings need to materialize. If I remember it correctly out of the top of my head, we said we would have at least  20% of efficiency improvements in selected – in areas in scope which is mostly related to corporate support  environments. We said that we are going to install an effective service organization which, once completed, will at  least bring 10% to 20% efficiency improvements in that area.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: When you look into the geographies, China and the environment there, China, [ph] nominal (00:43:44)  manufacturing shipments still expand with a clear growth rate but have been losing a bit of momentum throughout  the last years. Machinery, they are still with moderate increases, but below the manufacturing average.  Automotive I already discussed. So there is lower dynamics but still relevant in terms of materiality on a global  basis. I think everything is said about the U.S. already. And in Germany, manufacturing is still in a modest growth  path, even though in lower ranges, and machinery still is reporting also a moderate increase. So it's only  automotive that is declining.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Gaël, thanks for the question. It's hard to keep apart the footprint and the growth impact, of course, because the  footprint change is facilitating growth opportunities which come from the market. And what we see is that in the  commodity-related businesses on our customer base, we saw some stabilization in their investment pattern just  lately. Also, the demand for renewable energy and wind power has been increasing again. And what you probably  heard from the disclosure of Siemens Gamesa yesterday also the pricing in their end-markets is getting a bit more  stable, which is good news for the suppliers into those businesses obviously.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: From a strategic perspective, we continued our selective approach to do bolt-on acquisitions. For example, we  strengthened our portfolio in Industrial Software through the acquisition of RuggedCom, a specialized Canadian  company providing communications solutions for harsh environments, such as in electric utility substations, oil  refineries and rail applications. In Oil & Gas, we complemented our subsea power grid offering by taking over the  Connectors and Measurement division of Expro Holdings.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: In Energy, the comparables were particularly tough in Germany where we won three major orders for offshore  wind parks a year ago. But also in emerging markets like the Middle East where we booked a major Combined  Cycle power plant order in Saudi Arabia in Q2 of last year.  The U.S. showed strength both in orders and revenue in a better-than-anticipated economic environment. Our  sales growth was very broad based with particular strength in emerging markets, such as in India with remarkable  48% growth or Brazil achieving 18% increase. For the second quarter, this resulted in a further shift of our  revenue distribution towards emerging markets with a share of 31%b up one percentage point over the second  quarter of fiscal 2011.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: What were the key developments in each of the sectors? First, sector Energy. As already mentioned, orders in  Energy went down substantially by 36% due to a broad-based decline of large projects in all divisions. The Energy  market remains highly competitive but our sales funnel for the coming quarters looks promising. And we expect a  book-to-bill ratio above one for the full year.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: Intentionally, we were more selective on orders and walked away from low-margin businesses. The sector's  backlog was at a healthy €56 billion at the end of the quarter. A major highlight in Q2 was the order for the 834  megawatt Combined Cycle power plant in Ansan in South Korea where we will deliver, among other equipment,  two world-leading H-class turbines to Posco.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: Second quarter revenue rose by 10% on the conversion from Energy's strong order backlog with substantial  growth in Asia, Australia, and a sharp increase of 42% in the renewal business. I want to point out that besides the  challenges in Transmission, the sector Energy delivered a very solid quarter regarding profit and once again  proved that our position as the only integrated energy company is fully intact.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: Fossil delivered 17.5% profit margin and continued its excellent project execution in the solution business, also  achieved a strong earnings contribution from the service business. We were very pleased to see Renewable Energy  rebounding from the weak Q1 and also taking up profitability sharply to 8.2%, which was basically volume and  top-line-driven.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: Our clear number one position in Offshore Wind gives us a competitive advantage since we achieved a healthy  revenue mix of around one-third of Offshore and two-thirds on Onshore businesses in the first half of fiscal 2012.  We are working hard to maintain the lead in Offshore Wind and stay competitive in Onshore to be successful in  the expected difficult market conditions ahead. Besides ongoing pricing pressure and expected industry  consolidation, this is mainly caused by the uncertainty over the extension of the U.S. tax benefit scheme beyond  2012.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: Power Transmission reported a significant loss of €169 million in the second quarter, major factors were  additional charges of €278 million we had to take, mostly related to the grid connections to Offshore Wind farm  projects in Germany.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: During the second quarter, we conducted a very detailed and thorough review of all of our offshore grid  connection projects in the North Sea. As a consequence, we had to rework our installation schedule for BorWin2  and HelWin1 platform, whose installation dates are anticipated to be delayed to 2013.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: I don't want to sound like providing an excuse, but this kind of offshore grid installations have not been done  before. An 800-megawatt platform has a weight of up to 19,000 tons in around 70 meters water depth and 100  kilometers off the coast. The timeslot for installation work is restricted to the period from May to September  because of weather conditions. And for all this – those reasons, it's also much more complex compared to existing  AC offshore platforms we have successfully installed already in the U.K.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: It is fair to say that we now have a better understanding of the situation and have put a lot of effort into measures  to mitigate and to contain the risks. One example is the set-up of a joint working groups with the authorities, with  the grid operators and our peers to work on the standardization of the regulatory environment and the approval  processes. In addition, we have massively ramped up our resources in the offshore grid competence center in  Hamburg. We feel we get this major mistake step-by-step under control and can learn from these experiences for  future tenders and future projects.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: In particular, in Europe, there will be a number of further tenders of offshore wind grid connections and other  HVDC projects similar to the recently awarded Western Link between England and Scotland. We want our fair  share in this attractive market but with a clear focus on risk control and profitability. If a project does not meet  these standards, we will have the discipline to walk away.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: First, as a clear sign of accountability, we decided to change the leadership of the division. Yesterday, we  announced that Karlheinz Springer will take over the divisional CEO role with immediate effect. He is a very  experienced manager who was previously responsible for the excellent development of Instrumentation &  Electrical business unit in the Fossil division. He has experience in project management and project execution and  will be of great help in this regard.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: And finally, I want to briefly highlight the key developments in the sector Infrastructure & Cities. Order volume  for the sector declined by 8% due to fewer large rolling stock orders. Nevertheless, Rail Systems was again able to  win a contract for 20 Desiro regional trains in the U.K. for the customer London Midland for around €170 million.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: If we take a look on the free cash flow development, you should see here as a green line, then I guess there are a  couple of things I want to mention. First of all, in the first six months, we have significantly increased our  inventories by €1.5 billion, and also accounts receivables by almost €600 million in order also to reflect the  continued revenue growth and expected growth also in revenues for the second half. And there has been a  material decline on the prepayments including the biddings in excess, and that amounts to €700 million for the  first half of fiscal 2012. And the ones who have been following us for a longer period of time already know and  remember that it's been consistently mentioned in that item that there is some behavioral change if it comes to  bigger, or especially from the public sector as far as prepayments are concerned.

texts.speaker: Frederic Stahl
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: The second question is I've understood from some of your customers that there's a trend now from among buyers  and grid operators to split up or separate the tendering process. For example, you would have a tender for the  substations, you would have a tender for the cables rather than just have one large tender for the whole package.  Is that correct and is that – well, is that something that you're seeing in your markets right now?

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President, CEO & Head-Corporate Communications, Siemens AG
texts.text: Yeah. Let me make one thing very clear. I mean, this is – if you remember, first of all, Siemens has not project  issues across the board because obviously one concern could be – is Siemens now having not learned enough from  the – if you remember 2008 when we talked about the fossil power issues. Clearly, when you talk in terms of  execution of big projects, we are doing extremely well, and if we take learnings from the Fossil Power division, one  of the reasons why this business has actually accelerated in terms of earnings power was not just the mix effect,  but also in terms of how it is executing.

texts.speaker: Martin Prozesky
texts.profession: Analyst, Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.
texts.text: Good afternoon. Martin Prozesky from Bernstein. Two questions on energy sold, please, but in different divisions.  Can you give us a bit more guidance on Renewables? I knew Renewables has been very volatile. And what I  understood was that mix has been very important, solar versus offshore versus onshore in terms of the  disappointing margins we saw in Q1. Now, this margin was much stronger. Can you give us a sense, is it mix? Is it  execution? Is it better projects being booked in the quarter, and does it mean margins are going to be volatile from  here on or is it going to be at a higher level?  And then the second, in terms of the Fossil, for Q1 which I understand or Q1 calendar, which is quite a big service  quarter. The margin was a bit weak. Is that because there was more turnkey in that mix or – and how should we  expect the margin to develop for the rest of the year? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President, CEO & Head-Corporate Communications, Siemens AG
texts.text: Yeah, thank you very much. Look, I would like to counteract your key argument to say the Fossil Power margins  are weak. I mean, you go back into – this is a cyclical business environment. Go back only a couple of years where  we would be extremely happy to having achieved the double digit, or a 10 to 12 or whatever the margin used to be.  And we have actually had now a period of time where we have actually – where we were able to execute  exceptional margin quality.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President, CEO & Head-Corporate Communications, Siemens AG
texts.text: And you heard me saying a couple of times when we were talking about the 20-plus or whatever it was, the 21  actually, that all stars were aligned to really make this possible. So, it was clearly execution, product mix, and  obviously you have a margin quality in the Fossil business of 17.5% is an extremely good margin. So, the key focus  right now is how do we sustain the margin quality, because at the same time, we gained market share. So, this is  not – actually, so this is a combination of gaining market share, having the right technology, having a good mix  and, between Q1 and Q2, there was always the slight mix effect and this went in, and therefore we have targeted  overall to say we want to have one-third solution, one-third products and one-third services. And you have the  combination of it. So I would say this was a pretty good performance of the Fossil business.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President, CEO & Head-Corporate Communications, Siemens AG
texts.text: In terms of pricing pressures, you have highly competitive Chinese player now going global. I mean, you have an  onshore environment in the United States, which is now benefiting from the PTC [Production Tax Credit], and the  key question is when and how long will PTC last? Should PTC not being continued, you would have a totally  different dynamics in the United States for this type of business. And so, therefore, we as a company being in this  business, we have to prepare ourselves for different scenarios because there is no clear-cut answer and nobody  knows exactly will it continue, won't it continue, so you have to prepare yourself for different scenario.

texts.speaker: Ben E. Uglow
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Ben Uglow, Morgan Stanley. I have three questions. One was from Friday last week, GE on their conference call  sounded extremely enthusiastic about their gas business for the first time in a while. I think the quote was, "All  roads lead to gas." Can you just talk very generally about tendering activity that you see at the moment? And over  what timeframe could we begin to expect some improvement in the pricing environment for Fossil Power? So, that  was question number one.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President, CEO & Head-Corporate Communications, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, I'll start with the first one. I'm not commenting on, obviously, on other companies. But statements all roads  lead to gas is – and this will be an exciting environment. This is certainly what we also share for sure. And for this  reason, we have actually globalized our footprint. If you remember now, we have the benefit that we have a U.S.  operation. We can access export/import financing from the U.S. for overseas market. And this is now a platform,  which we can use not just for the United States, but also for overseas markets.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President, CEO & Head-Corporate Communications, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, in the United States, shale, gas and everything else, I mean, the key question is only how quickly will the  economy pick up and the reserve margin which exists in the United States be lowered, because currently – I mean,  this is a major determining factor. But that this business will, for example, in the United States, is picking up in  the near future. It's no time. The question is actually when.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, that basically means now is delivery time. And we expect the business to show us the money from what we  have allocated in terms of resources. That's as easy as that. And if there is something on top of it which changes, if  all roads lead to gas and that the road is not that long, then we may as well continue to invest selectively as we'll be  picking our – we'll be picking our places where we continue to invest and increase the OpEx.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President, CEO & Head-Corporate Communications, Siemens AG
texts.text: Now, on the short-term basis, how is the environment for our business? We see an extremely – overall, you have  the numbers in our books. So, you clearly see also that our orders are down, reason being – main reason being  that obviously the Rail Component business is today very different than it used to be last year, with all the reasons  which you probably know as good as I know. So, we see certainly a slowdown in the Rail environment in China.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: The unknown, obviously is that when are we going to receive the steam because that needs to start earlier than our  steam turbines so there is a certain unknown here. On the other hand, in judging the timeframe, we've been  somewhat more conservative in our current reserves as the ones who had still the obligation to build it.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: In contrast, revenues were down 6% due to weakness in short-cycle businesses and on the back of tough comps in  Energy, where we benefited from the U.S. wind boom and from a higher amount of turnkey solutions in the  previous year. As a consequence, our book-to-bill ratio reached a strong level of 1.19. The order backlog increased  to a very healthy level of €101 billion and profitability was burdened by further charges of €84 million, mainly for  the German offshore grid connections in Power Transmission and €161 million for further delays for the high  speed trains, Velaro D and Eurostar.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: A number of businesses such as Healthcare, Fossil or Oil & Gas delivered strong profit margins, while the  industry's profit margin declined significantly due to lower volume in the high margin short-cycle businesses, a  less favorable product mix and continued weakness of the renewable offerings.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: Invensys closing is taking place as we speak, and we are looking forward to create a leading rail automation  business. The integration teams are ready for implementation. We will update you on the progress accordingly.  The exit from the solar business proves to be more difficult, while the whole industry continues to suffer and  technical challenges remain in our project in Spain. There's no high probability for a trade sale anymore. Thus, we  integrate the assets into the Energy sector, and it remains our clear intention to exit the Solar business. If the  assets cannot be sold, we will ramp it down in due course.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: From a regional perspective, for orders and sales in the second quarter, also a mixed picture order growth in  Europe was driven by two very large offshore wind orders in Germany and the UK as well as two large rail orders  in Germany and Austria.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: The base business across all sector was flat, with some positive momentum in Energy and Healthcare and  weakness in Industry. We also saw good order momentum in emerging markets, with a comparable growth rate of  25%. China was up 3%, driven by Healthcare and Energy balancing the industry business. And Russia, plus 107%,  Africa and the Middle East with an increase of 40%, and Brazil plus 25%. Emerging markets accounted for 32% of  total orders. The decrease in revenues was regionally broad-based in the U.S. The main driver was a sharp decline  in wind power, driven by the PTC uncertainty and compared to an exceptionally strong quarter a year ago, though  in emerging markets, we had some pockets of growth such as Russia and Africa both growing above 50%.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: Let me now briefly highlight the key developments in each of the four sectors. First, sector Energy. Overall,  continued strong performance was backed by Fossil and robust service. As already mentioned, orders in Energy  went up sharply by 45%, largely due to the highest quarterly order intake ever in Wind with €3.3 billion.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: I want to specifically mention the €700 million Butendiek wind park order for a total capacity of 288 megawatts.  It is the first offshore order with a 10-year long-term service agreement and supported by an equity stake of 22.5%  from SFS, an excellent example for our unmatched comprehensive offering in this field. We expect the PTC  extension in the U.S. to have a positive impact on orders in the course of the second half of this calendar year, too  late though to show a significant impact in our revenue in fiscal 2013. Fossil showed strength in orders, with  several large service awards and we booked orders for 12 advanced gas turbines, well ahead of our competition.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: The sector backlog was at a solid €58 billion at the end of the quarter. Second quarter revenue decreased by 9%,  mainly due to a lower volume of turnkey solution projects in Fossil and the weak Wind business in the United  States.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: On profitability, Energy shows a heterogeneous picture. Fossil delivered again a strong 17.6% profit margin,  despite lower volumes and supported by a strong earnings contribution from the service business. Wind Power  achieved 5.1% profitability, down from last year's extraordinary strong quarter, due to lower revenues and some  adverse mix effects. After some weaker quarters and charges from legal and regulatory matters, Oil & Gas  returned to a profitability of 9.8%.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: Power Transmission executes as planned on its restructuring program Transform To Win. More than 40% of the  planned head count reduction by 8% until 2015 has already been achieved. But Transmission faced, again, charges  of €84 million mainly related to the execution of grid connection projects to offshore wind farms in the Northern  Sea. We expect continued challenges in coming quarters related to the transport and installation of those  platforms. As mentioned, Solar was moved back to the sector level and posted a loss of €21 million pre-tax this  quarter. We expect a full-year loss of approximately €300 million post-tax. Sector energy recorded €20 million in  transformation charges for Siemens 2014 and expects a significant increase in the second half of fiscal 2013.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: Finally, I want to highlight key developments in the sector Infrastructure & Cities. Order volume for this sector  increased by 34%, due to two large rail orders, one from Deutsche Bank for an ICx extension contract and the first  order for 100 local and regional trains worth around €550 million from the frame agreement with Austrian  railway provider ÖBB.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: The Transportation & Logistics division posted a loss due to the above mentioned charges of €161 million, which  severely impacted profitability. As in previous quarters, the revenue mix was less favorable due to lower margin  associated with large long-term contracts from prior periods. Power Grid Solutions & Products delivered steady  margins of 6.8% with favorable mix in smart grid business, while low and medium voltage was seasonally weaker.  Building Technologies saw a profit decrease by 100 basis points, mostly due to a revenue decline of 5%.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: Let's talk now about the status of our Siemens 2014 program. The whole organization is fully committed to  achieve and deliver this program. First of all, as you may have seen also in the Flash slide distributed this  morning, we have restated our 2012 starting pace by including the Solar business. As discussed already in detail  during the Capital Market Day's Industry & Energy, the impact of the transformation measures is rather back-end  loaded and still around 45% of the 2013 productivity target is already P&L effective, with a large portion coming  from procurement.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: The additional measures required to achieve €2 billion in 2013 are well on track. Also, a significant part of those  measures, which will be effective in fiscal 2014, are already in implementation. They are particularly in design to  cost area as well as footprint measures, where we are in intense discussions with the employee representatives.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: Finally, let me complement the missing pieces to the four sector bridges. Assumptions are fully aligned and  broken down to the sectors. You saw already the Energy and Industry bridge during the respective Capital Market  Days. We have updated Energy where we need some additional productive to cover a slightly higher price erosion.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: Infrastructure & Cities is also planning to compensate with volume integration for price erosion effects of slightly  less than 2%. The required productivity is €800 million over two years under the assumption of reliable project  execution in fiscal 2014.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Head-Corporate Finance & Controlling, Siemens AG
texts.text: Now, if you look into the Lighting business itself, this is quite a paradigm shift which the asset has been going  through. We do see a massive decline of the basic elements of Lighting, such as light bulbs, but also the so-called  energy-saving lamps and what we see growing and that's what the equity story will be mostly focused about, that's  about the solid-state Lighting. That's about LED and the industrial application of LED.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: Charges associated with the Siemens 2014 program in the sectors, I expect it to total up to €4.9 billion for the full  fiscal year and given this developments and financial results for the first half, we expect income from continuing  operations in fiscal 2013 to approach the lower end of our original expectation. €4.5 billion before impacts related  to legal and regulatory matters and significant portfolio effects, which we expect to burden income by up to €0.5  billion, due primarily to the Solar business.

texts.speaker: Mark A. Troman
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: And finally on charges, what visibility do you have in terms of how these might evolve? You talked about  challenges on the installation of the offshore platforms. Are the worse of these charges behind or should we –  what sort of run rate should we expect going forward for charges? Thank you – project charges that is.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: And so, whatever small thing happens, as we know, will obviously find its way immediately into the P&L. This is  just one other reason why we do everything what we can to ensure successful completion, but we have to bear in  mind this are – quite frankly, before this huge monsters of steel are not pulled out of the water, 120 kilometers off  the shoreline of Germany, you simply don't know what will happen.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Head-Corporate Finance & Controlling, Siemens AG
texts.text: On the short cycle environment, I mean, that's obviously the big question which is not only material for the whole  industry, but also material for our P&L, since the short cycle environment in Industrial Automation, in Drive  Technologies and in parcels on the low mid-voltage environment, that has a significant impact on the P&L, either  if it goes up and if it goes down.

texts.speaker: Frederic Stahl
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Yes, hi, it's Frederic Stahl here from UBS. Can I ask you about the offshore wind market, if you can update us on  the tender activity right now, how you see competition and profitability that developing in that marketplace?  That's the first question. And the second question, similar, but on Healthcare, if you can tell us what you see and  talk a bit about what you see in Europe and in the U.S. over the next few quarters? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: When it comes to Wind offshore, Wind offshore for us is obviously a very important one. We continue to see this  also from a margin quality being holding up, despite the fact that this also becomes more competitive. We have  now more companies trying to enter. And then you have to talk about which projects behind which customers.  Obviously in France, you have a slightly different environment. Then, we have a good company like Dong. But  here, we are really benefiting from the over 20 years of experience from the innovation leadership which we have  there. And this is, for us, very important and we continue to be quite active in – we see an active activity in this  area is shifting a little bit towards East.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: China is becoming much more difficult in terms of the overall wind environment, because you see consolidation in  China, you see the clear intention that companies like Goldwind and others trying to position themselves. But  despite all of these, we have I think a good footprint there. We have a good position there. But from a penetration  perspective, it will be an environment where Chinese players will go global and continue to go global.

texts.speaker: Andreas Willi
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: It's Andreas from JPMorgan. I have three questions on the energy business, particularly Fossil. You had a good  performance in the profitability, despite the top line that came down quite a bit. Your U.S. competitor noted a very  weak service business in Europe and had a big hit on earnings because of that. Maybe you could comment a bit  what you're seeing in that business in terms of the good margin resilience in the quarter, but then the top – the  weaker top line, was that also due to a step-down in service by European utilities, and how you see that developing  in the next couple of quarters, also in terms of the profitability?

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: Andreas, let me start with the – with your Fossil question in terms of profitability. A, number one, we see a solid  service development in this area. We have the mix issue in terms of – I tried to highlight it in terms of more  solution business last year versus this year. The markets are solid. Obviously, what we see aggressive pricing  behavior in some project from some competitor. I would not say this is an overriding industry behind all projects,  but you can clearly see that certain projects are highly contented.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: And the environment is actually, I would say, continues to be regionally, no change what we have always discussed  over the last couple of quarters. 2015, we expect an uptake probably in the U.S., but this is what we have  highlighted versus others we are sometimes talking about 2014. So the reserve margin is still high enough, but it  will be a good gas market in the United States for sure. In Europe, basically, the activity has basically come to a  standstill, I would say. I mean, we have singular projects which are happening. And this is simply due to the fact  that there's the uncertainty, the German situation is a specific one, but there's also no really capacity build out.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: And then, we have also productivity issues. I mean, to make it very clear, we are spending too much engineering  hours for the train. There's a specific program for this division. It's called Rail on Track, with clear productivity  measures, much closer interaction, bringing down engineering hours, linking manufacturing footprint much  better in terms of also linking it back into supply chains. And we must become here much more competitive from  this standpoint, also footprint development, because the projects which are currently happening are happening  not in our historic markets. So we talk about Russia, for example, where we have already a good footprint there, a  project there. We have now projects in the Middle East when I talk about tender activities going forward. So we  have to have a smart footprint policy. We have to ensure that we leverage much more platform and design  development. So this is a clear productivity program in itself, which the division has focused on.

texts.speaker: Ben E. Uglow
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Yes, it's Ben Uglow from Morgan Stanley. I had really a follow on to Andreas' question about Fossil. What we have  been hearing is that service contracts in Europe may be coming under a little bit of pressure, i.e., the E.ONs, the  RWEs of this world are exercising their desire to lower the cost of those operation and maintenance contracts and  given where load factors are in gas at the moment, that's an understandable debate.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: The wind business offshore was actually always, relatively speaking, not a bad business for us. It was actually a  good business. We have not yet had big execution issues around offshore Wind, I mean. This is not the  transmission aspect of it. This is the wind turbine aspects of it. So – and the underlying rail business, as I said, is  an industry which is an industry that has to evolve, but I would not expect out of the contracts what we have now  highlighted, two offshore wind projects, have not obviously the quality of – and I do understand your remark,  Healthcare or Fossil. But within the Wind business, it should be the upper end of what Siemens is able to deliver.

texts.speaker: James E. Stettler
texts.profession: Analyst, Canaccord Genuity Ltd.
texts.text: And finally, sorry, another question on Fossil. But when you hear about E.ON and RWE talking about mothballing  and shutting down gas fired plants, is that just a warning? Are they being serious about that? We've also had Gaz  de France shutting down 2.5 gigawatt in gas. Is that a real risk you see or is that just a political sort of issue?

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: No, this is an absolutely real question. I mean, as we speak, actually, you have now an example, I'm not – GDF, I  cannot comment on that, but I can give you a good example because it was just announced in Germany. Our most  advanced gas turbine in Germany called Irsching, they have now signed – E.ON has signed a contract with Tenet  to find an agreement which allow them to continue to operate. I mean this is – we are now at the – this is a very,  very serious issue in Europe where you have the following situation.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: You have now buildup of massive renewable on one side. For example, in Germany it's out of – it's over 51 giga –  it's roughly 51 giga out of an overall of 85 giga, 90 giga, what you have. So it's more than – so it's over 50% and  then, you have a situation that old coal plants are continuing to operate profitably. And the gas in-between is  squeezed, so you have now a situation in Germany, for example, where the government has spent €200 billion for  51 giga delivering 5% of base load.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: Chairman-Management Board, President & CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: The old coal plants continue to operate, because they are written off. Gas plants are now operating, I mean, this  Irsching plant is now down, I think, initially it was actually over 4,000 hours. It's now down to 1,600 hours a year,  obviously, has this difficulty in providing profitability and this year, too, emissions are going up. So this, indeed is  a – this one of the debates what we have kindly in Europe, how do we ensure that base load capacity is provided  profitably against the backdrop that nuclear in some parts of Europe are actually ran down. So absolutely  happening, without any doubt.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Head-Corporate Finance & Controlling, Siemens AG
texts.text: However, if you look at the big ticket items on Healthcare, as well as in parts of the Fossil turbine new business,  then you can clearly tell that some competitors operating in that space obviously do have some tailwind from FX.  And now, the question is, are they going to use for competitive pricing or for a higher amount of profit? So that's  something where we have seasonal dynamics.

texts.speaker: Olivier Esnou
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you. Olivier Esnou, Exane. Two question, please. Coming back on the Power business, so it's been a very  difficult quarter for order intake. You mentioned competitor – some competitors being more price aggressive on  the thermal side. At the same time, Siemens is actually strongly outperforming in terms of gas turbine order  intake, so how do you make sure that Siemens is not the one in the marketplace being the most aggressive on  prices and is booking good projects? How do you monitor that?

texts.speaker: Gaël De Bray
texts.profession: Analyst, SG Securities (Paris) SAS
texts.text: Thank you. Good morning. Gaël De Bray from Société Générale. Two questions, please. The first one is about the  losses related to the portfolio effects. You mentioned total losses of €500 million, out of which €300 million  would come from the Solar reclassification. But where are the extra €200 million losses coming from?

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Head-Corporate Finance & Controlling, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, what has been the assumption? Well, first of all, it's been about €300 million on the solar reclassification. This  is gross for net, the tax impact is nil. Then, we do expect up to €100 million, maybe a bit less, of legal and  regulatory matters, which mostly have to do with an economy in the Middle East which we have decided not to  continue to supply. And the remaining items are coming from M&A-related topic. Remember, we also said that  impact from M&A for bigger material M&A-related topics are also not part of the guidance. So if you look at the  Invensys closing, which is happening today, there will be some integration one-offs very quickly, because the team  is all ready to go, and you will see that also in the actions which secure our synergies and then, if it's going  forward.
