It's important. We've seen quite a comeback yet  in the market, but obviously the cost effective is crucially important.

texts.speaker: Mariel von Drathen
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations
texts.text: If we go towards the Wind and Renewables business, obviously that's clearly disappointing. We believe that we  have fully understood what needs to be done. We also see that the actions are well underway. It may still take  some time till we can fully improve the efficiency of the supply chain in the division. We are well underway in the  innovation pipeline. But obviously, we need a significant improvement of the operational reliability going forward.

texts.speaker: Mariel von Drathen
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations
texts.text: On Energy Management, we clearly do see a significant progress in turnaround. Margins have been up quite a lot.  We do see the swing from a minus 7 .6% in fiscal Q2 2014 up to now, 3.3%, 3.4% in the division and counting. So  we are right on the way as to what we said we would do, and we continue the restructuring as a turnaround in the  Energy Management division.

texts.speaker: Mariel von Drathen
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations
texts.text: We have a different picture obviously in the Process Industries and Drives. This is the division which has been  falling victim for the most part on the oil and gas topic, especially oil price obviously, but also on the geopolitical  issues have been a huge backdrop in Russia on both LNG, oil and gas, and also what I call the secondary effects of  a weak oil if it comes to the income statements of those countries. So we do expect continued weakness on the top  line. Although we expect that the margin impact going forward will be more favorable as what we have seen in our  fiscal Q2.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: SFS delivered an extraordinary strong profit of €195 million, also benefiting from gains through selling equity  stakes in renewable energy projects. During the second half of fiscal 2015, the SFS performance is expected to  normalize on prior year's level. Centrally managed portfolio activities recorded a gain of €1.4 billion on the  disposal of Siemens' stake in BSH. As indicated, we saw a negative impact of around €200 million due to the  funding related to our share in Unify.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: For the second half of fiscal 2015, we are cautious on CMPA since we expect some negative impacts related to the  remaining businesses like Unify, Postal & Baggage Handling, Metals and Solar. Please note that CMPA includes,  as of Q2, also the solar business which was transferred from the Wind Power and Renewable division.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Net income all-in benefited from major gains of around €1.8 billion of successfully completing the sale of the  hearing aid and hospital information system businesses within discontinued operations. For the second half year,  the impact from DO will be rather limited. Having said that, I would like to focus on the clearly weaker free cash  flow development year-over-year in the second quarter with a minus of €241 million. There are two major reasons  for this development. First, power and gas as well as wind power significantly increased the net operating working  capital. Power and gas mainly lifted its inventories for an intentional increase in stock units for fast track projects  as Joe has been indicating before.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Wind power faced a weak quarter regarding large milestone payments. Secondly, there was also a significant  negative impact in corporate treasury mainly related to settlements from hedging instruments as Joe said. For the  second half of fiscal 2015, we expect a material improvement from the industrial business with regard to cash  flow. With regard to liquidity, we continue to have a very sound position of €9.9 billion, fueled by the inflows from  our recent divestments.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: To make this more tangible for you, currently, we have 14 major projects in our pipeline where technical risk  assessments were conducted by very experienced experts, so-called silverbacks of which we have identified around  60 globally in our company. During the first half year, we executed our projects in a solid way without major hits  on the bottom line. In addition, we made significant progress in delivering on our legacy project. Between January  and April, for example, we handed over three out of four North Sea offshore grid connection projects to our  customer, TenneT for commercial operation. And the fourth project, HelWin2 is on schedule to be put into  operation in the coming weeks. The percentage of completion in this project is above 85% now.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: We discussed matters like compressors. We obviously have our challenges, our economic challenges in  transmission. And it's also a matter which we have addressed such as mechanical drives. There is a series of  actions, which we have been discussing and agreeing upon is the management team of those businesses. Then we  discussed the business plan. And now, we've got a clear view on how to fix those businesses. The fix will, among  other things, will include a footprint optimization, which predominantly also relates to businesses like the  transformer business within transmission.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: So by doing that, we'll create about €1 billion incremental profit for that business and about €400 million to €500  million incremental EVA. Obv iously, we also have to keep all our options open on the way to achieving those  goals. That's how we do it, that's how we execute, and that's how we are going to narrow the scope on those  businesses which needs to be fixed from an economic perspective. Now obviously, let me close and wrap it up with  the outlook for fiscal 2015. Now, obviously, we do have a lot of weakening indicators, and I've heard of course also  the questions from the market. What will that do to the guidance? We do have oil-price-related matters, which  obviously we all know about. We do have secondary effects from this oil price development if it comes to income - related issue of those economies.

texts.speaker: Peter Reilly
texts.profession: Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: Good morning. It's Peter Reilly from Jefferies. Two questions, please. Your statement, you talk about massive  price erosion in the power generation, but you've had actually quite good order intake in Power and Gas. Y ou've  got some large orders you haven't booked yet in Egypt. In the old days, Siemens is happy to take orders at low   margins when demand was weak. So can you talk about what's happening with the current level of orders you're  booking? What the margin and the backlog looks like? What sort of assumptions you're making about cost  reductions? I think you have some confidence about pricing in the backlog.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Y eah. Thank you, Peter. Obviously, it is quite a competitive market if it comes to the Power and Gas market, and  that's relates first and foremost to the LGT business, large gas turbine business. We've seen some price erosion in  the market, first and foremost, due to an extremely aggressive behavior to get the pie, which obviously has become  a bit smaller than it used to be. So this is all about cost reduction, right.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: So if you ask me about the second half, and not speculating on any oil prices and what have you. There's been a lot  of speculation on this one already. I believe, from a structural point of view, there should be some ease on the  second half of the fiscal, if it comes to the homemade topic that we clearly see, but have a pretty good grip on. But  obviously, the CapEx-related topic in the market that remains a concern. So we'll likely have seen the bottom in  that business by end of 2015. That's what we are currently planning.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Now obviously, was the margin light on DF? Absolutely. Was it fully unexpected? Absolutely not. Are we  concerned about PD falling victim of all those geopolitical and structural topics around oil and gas? Absolutely.  But we've seen that and we need to get the costs down. Wind, clearly is a disappointment, but again we know what  we do. To fix the operational challenges and the innovation pipeline especially on low wind onshore distributor is  important. Going forward, this looks pretty good.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Look, we've come to the conclusion that our customers want systems. They have a problem that they need to move  people and goods in a reliable way. They have the issue that this is costly, unreliable and in part even just scattered  around air and car and fleet and rail and commuting and city. And they want solutions to help to get the costs  down. The revenue is up, and the reliability effectiveness up in terms of rate of how many people can move from  place A to place B. And more and more we see that this integration impact make the difference in getting orders  for those type of management.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Y eah. Thanks, [ph] James (53:00). On a global level, pricing is pretty much in the ballpark of what we have been  guiding the markets during November, no really significant topics. If you go like -for-like, not taking into account  the currency options, which obviously give some leeway there eventually. We do see fierce competition on the  whole large gas environment. Definitely, pricing have come down significantly in parts even materially. So it is all  about getting the cost out of the system and it's exactly what we do.

texts.speaker: Ben E. Uglow
texts.profession: Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Good morning. Ben Uglow, Morgan Stanley. So inevitably, my first question is about the dreaded Power and Gas  topic. Joe, could you say a little bit about the underlying margin trend at the moment in Power and Gas? The press  release cites sort of project execution. Are there specific project guidance, are there specific project gains and ar e  those going to be sustainable going forward? So that was question number one.

texts.speaker: Ben E. Uglow
texts.profession: Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Related topic is just power service. I know that you've made some comments and you actually see power service, if  anything, stabilizing a bit. And I wondered if you could elaborate on that.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Thanks, Ben. All important question. Over to Power and Gas, I mean, we've come a long way from almost 18%,  20% environment. We've always said at the time that would not be sustainable, and at the time, we are kind of  guiding 300 basis points, 400 basis points to be our performance, which made in 2016 then we've guided the  market in May last year that for the time being, a margin corridor would be between 11% and 15% and we had a  reason to do so because we kind of have been talking to our customers, did see competitive be havior,  consolidations and the likes.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Now, obviously, if you analyze the topic, we continue to push innovation because that's the differentiating factor at  the time. We do see trends from highly centralized mono-sourcing of power generation to more decentralized  power generation from wind, from solar and so and so forth. So the focus shifts more from big high -end type of  machines to a more mid-lower sized flexibility. Also, for the back half of the volatility challenges on renewables,  you've seen that one and one specific outcome which has been that we've been closing gaps especially in that area,  with the acquisition of our derivatives for specific markets as well as Dresser-Rand, which was all the way down to  engines. So that's the one thing.

texts.speaker: William Mackie
texts.profession: Kepler Capital Markets SA (UK)
texts.text: The second question relates to the discussion of cost out versus pricing. I've heard you a number of times highlight  that the competitive pricing environment needs to be addressed with cost out. When we look at the savings  program, should we look at that as a net-net zero, or should we – from the top down, think about as a drop- through of some of those gains which you're chasing? And lastly o n the Wind division, you described there's some  way to go with regard to the margin turnaround and securing the value chain. Could you highlight where you  think that will develop in the next one to two quarters? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Is it about incentives? It's about incentives in a way. But first and foremost about getting the job done. So it's  accountability in the first place and get the reactions out. On PG, on cost out versus pricing in Power and Gas, it's  clearly – the program. PG 2020 is clearly designed to have a net drop-through in profitability. So what I see today  in that area is that for example we get the cost down on large gas turbines and associated matters, double-digit,  okay? Double-digit cost, double-digit percentage cost. Now, this is not just about taking care of pricing. This is  about a net drop-through and return to profitability and those which we have seen as a normal in the past. Not our  performance, but as a normal in the past.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Wind, as I said, the growth in wind has given us some particular challenges, which we still need to optimize in the  supply chain. We expect to have seen operationally, for the operational business, we expect to  have seen the  bottom in fiscal Q2, we expect the second half to be recovering based on operational performance. Would not rule  out that there are a few corrections to be made. But in terms of a greater performance, we expect fiscal – the  second half of fiscal 2015 to be in better shape than what we've seen in the first half.

texts.speaker: Wasi Rizvi
texts.profession: RBC Europe Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Oh, hi. It's Wasi Rizvi from RBC. Just a couple of questions from me. I was interested in your comments on the  inventory in Power and Gas. Now, you mentioned it was – you saw some opportunities in fast-tracking projects, is  that that you are seeing some pockets of activity in Power and Gas or is it more that inventory is a differentiator  and a way of winning the few projects that are out there?

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Now on the inventories, first and foremost on PG, reason being that more and more we do see that economies,  governments, public areas struggle to see the demand happening ahead of time. Think about the drought issues in  Brazil which has been relying heavily on water, hydropower generation. Well, now, obviously, there is no water,  there is no power. People say can you help us? Say, yeah, but it takes a while because our suppliers need to be  notified first. We've seen that in many areas. And one of the reasons why we have been able to kind of get this  successful development in Egypt was that we are ready to go when we were needed. And there is more  of those  areas and I would not be too surprised if you see more of those pockets coming in the next quarters in terms of  bidding and channel and funnel.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: The other proof-point, of course, is you know closer to the markets means that people need to be close to  customers and that is footprint reallocation and that's exactly what we do in the structure of this job reduction,  bring people closer to the market. So it's footprint.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: But it's also just right-sizing the business. Think about, for example, transformers. It's been huge overcapacities in  both utility-related, high-voltage as well as distribution transformers and we'll go fix that one, too.

texts.speaker: Andre Kukhnin
texts.profession: Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Y es. Thank you. It's Andre from Credit Suisse. Just one question, R&D ramp-up in gas turbines that you  mentioned you're going to spent €100 million more there. Could you give us some color on what you're going to  do there and on the phasing of that spend?

texts.speaker: Andre Kukhnin
texts.profession: Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And then maybe somewhat related to that, in gas turbines, as you mentioned, your market share was boosted to I  think 35% in Q1 according to [ph] McCoy's (01:21:41). Do you think you can hold on to this type of market share  gains this year looking at the pipeline of the projects that you see for the rest of the year?

file: SIE - Q2 2016 Earnings Call 4May2016 415 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 04-May-16.pdf

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: We're in the middle of executing on our Vision 2020, and we are executing well. We are building a leading and  highly adaptive company along the value chain of electrification, automation, and digitalization. That's all based  on a, what we call, powerful ownership culture. The system of EAD – electrification, automation, digitalization –  is unique. And it matters, matters to our customers, matters to our employees, our shareholders, since it provides  a unique value proposition.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: As you can see in our financials and also in other areas of our Vision 2020 concept, we delivered what  they  promised, and they achieved a convincing – at least what we believe convincing – top and bottom line  performance compared to both the previous year and the industry. Orders continue to grow and were up 10%  excluding currency effects, driven by obviously some major orders. Major contributors came from Power and Gas.  They booked the remaining two combined cycle power plants in Egypt for about €3.1 billion. And also secondly,  Wind Power, we recorded a €1.2 billion order from an offshore wind farm project in the United Kingdom. And I'll  give you more details in a minute.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: As indicated, we accelerate revenue growth to 7% excluding currency effects and 5% on a pure organic basis. Wind  Power and Power and Gas delivered double-digit growth, while Mobility and Healthcare also showed strength in  growing their business. The Industrial profit margin was at 10.9%, which obviously was up 190 basis points year  over year. That was driven by what believe strong showings in most businesses, particularly in Wind Power and   also in Energy Management.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Now maybe we should have a look at the regional trend. We already mentioned large energy -related orders drove  growth in the Europe and Africa region, while Germany and the Americas were down on tough comps from a year  ago. In line with a particularly difficult macroeconomic environment in those regions, we saw continued order  weakness in Russia and Brazil, while order intake in China actually looked good and we took advantage from our  competitive position in efficient gas, decentral generation, and HVDC while, short-cycle demand was still  reasonably weak.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Then I'll give you maybe some information on two major orders in the first quarter. As you know, we've won a  mega-deal order in Egypt for a three combined-cycle power plants with a total 24 H-class turbines, including  service. That's all now fully in our books. Closing for the financing of Burullus and New Capital projects took place  during the second quarter. We are lining up all our resources to execute those mega-projects in time, in the  money, and also support our customer with a comprehensive training scheme for future operation.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Just a few days ago, we announced the East Anglia ONE project with ScottishPower Renewables, our largest  offshore order ever, regarding the capacity volume. This is about a 7  megawatt direct drive turbine, which receives  quite a strong acceptance in the market. And we'll deliver this project out of the manufacturing places in Hull,  here in the UK, as well as Cuxhaven, and both facilities are being built as we speak.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Now, let's have a look at some key developments in the divisions. As mentioned, Power and Gas operates in a very  competitive market environment, and the team continues to drive productivity, cost-efficiency, and focus on the  opportunities in the global marketplace. In total, we shipped 16 large gas turbines in the quarter – among those  five H-class turbines – and we continue to grow our market share. We have sold 78 H-class turbines now and  improved our own world record to 61.5% efficiency at 603.8 megawatts electrical output at our Lausward plant.  Above all, our fully operational H-class turbines have now received more than 200,000 operating hours,  demonstrating a unique – a real-life – day-by-day performance and reliability.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Wind Power has a very robust sales pipeline resulting from abundant backlog of almost €15 billion. Strong  conversion of exactly the backlog drove revenue growth in both onshore as well as offshore. Significant process  and progress in our efforts to optimize our operational excellence and a strong project completion and execution  helped drive an exceptionally strong profit margin of 9.4%. Although this may not yet be sustainable for the  quarters to come, we expect Wind Power to deliver within the target margin range for the remainder of the year.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Energy Management continued to improve its performance, approaching the target margin r ange on the back of  stronger profit contributions from solutions, transformer, and high-voltage projects in the business. In the  transmission solutions businesses, we continue to have a very clear backlog focus on quality of the backlog,  including risk and margin.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: As laid out previously, Process Industries and Drives faced further weak demand from commodity -related  industries, which were only partially offset by order growth in Wind Power-related businesses. As a consequence,  we announced a restructuring program to adjust capacities and the line footprint on demand structures. For 2,500  jobs and other assets which are affected by the restructuring, we expect severance charges of about €200 million  to €300 million probably impacting fiscal Q4.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: In the second quarter, the divestments of Unify and Sivantos, that's the former hearing aids business in Siemens,  were successfully closed. Clearly ahead of our original schedule, we closed the acquisition of CD-adapco, a  simulation specialist for fluid dynamics, for $170 million, in early April. CD-adapco is being integrated in our PLM  software business, and you already heard a very convincing joint appearance at the Hannover Fair, which  obviously left a lot of customers impressed about our digital strategy in this area. And we are also looking into  strengthening sustainability evolution and long-term visionary innovation. A good example for efficiency driving  is the sustainability agenda which we write with the formation of a 50/50 joint venture with Valeo, to provide  high-voltage powertrain for electric cars.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: As for the longer-term aspects, we have also announced a collaboration agreement with Airbus where we joined  forces to electrify aviation through hybrid electric propulsion systems, drastically reducing the emissions in  aviation. Until 2020, about 200 employees from both companies will develop prototypes for such drivetrains, and  we want to demonstrate the technical feasibility. Together, we will invest a mid-three-digit million euro R&D  amount until 2020.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Secondly, the reason why we said early signs of recovery. If you had seen it in our business a lready, there would  have been signs of recovery. And the reason why we said "early" was because we are also talking to the customers  of our customers, and they seem to be more encouraged by the environment they see. So what that means is they  need to place the orders to our customers, the machine makers and tool makers, and then hopefully follows  through to do the same with us. So that's how you should look at it.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: China. I mean, obviously, I've been there a few weeks ago in the China Development Forum ther e. A few company  leaders were discussing the five to 35 years plan with the Chinese government. And if you look at the five years  plan and the way the discussions went, there's a very clear dedication from the government to make this work in  both adding productivity in the labor market, but also looking to renewables and air pollution, as well as building  out infrastructure. So that kind of almost reads like a description of business with Siemens. That's good news.  Although I still sense that the progress on reforms, which in that case means restructuring of the old-world  overcapacities – shipbuilding, metals, mining, cement – is still considerably slow. And then as you've seen in our  company, too, if you want to add to the progress, you also need to let go on the tail end of technology. So that's  why I believe it may take some time to see noticeable upticks in the industrial capital goods environment.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Service Europe, stable on a base which is obviously lower than average of the last years due to the fact there are  not too many gas turbines running full steam these days. On Dresser – and when we refer to whole – we'll call it  Dresser only, it's the oil and gas business, but predominantly upstream and others. So if you look at oil,  downstream is obviously just really slow – I mean really slow. Midstream, oil is still being transported no matter  what the oil price will be, so that looks actually well. And this is also good for service. And downstream obviously  is not much related to the acquisitions which we made on both Rolls-Royce and Dresser. So therefore it's had no  big impact.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: So when you were quoting me about being positive on service, the answer I guess I would have is it's all relative.  So that's what it is. So the industry is struggling. We support our customers as much as we can to help them get  the cost out, and they are good areas there. We are very active on LNG, where we, I believe, provide quite a good  opportunity for them to reallocate their productivities. So we are making progress, but the environment is not   exactly supporting the CapEx spend.

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: Thank you. First question is on acquisitions and balance sheet. You're at the upper end of the leverage target. It's
texts.text: temporary probably, given it's Q2 and you've paid the dividend. But you mentioned in the press call or an  interview this morning that Siemens is the one to drive industry consolidation. Could you maybe elaborate a bit on  that in terms of both where you are in terms of leverage and your ambition to drive industry consolidation and  where? And the second question on Process and Drives in terms of the order pattern and where we  are in the cycle  there, because you have the wind component business there, which occasionally helps, where are we in terms of  where we used to be at the peak just for the more industrial-related business within that division?

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: So, if I recall the press meeting this morning, the comment was related only to wind, nowhere else. So I think  that's important in that context as far as the industry consolidation is concerned. On the PD, you want to take that  one?

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: So in terms of the industrial piece of the seasonality – that was your point, of course – we are benefiting to a  certain extent from the wind business being up in that field. The real challenge is related to the  commodity and  raw material industries around the globe, where large drives are playing a major role. And in that field I think it  would be too early to say that we have been seeing the ever-low, but with regard to our own contribution and our  self-help potential, what we can do, we have been starting to take cost out consistently. We are addressing the  workforce, and we have been doing that, I think, quite consistently, what you have been taking from media  throughout the last couple of weeks. I think we didn't shy away because it was necessary to act consistency in that  field. And the adjustments resulting from that will not be seen in the current fiscal year obviously.

texts.speaker: James E. Stettler
texts.profession: Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: The German energy reform, there's a draft document out there.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: And on the draft on the energy policy, I mean, Germany is an important country. But in fiscal Q2, for example,  Germany was about 10% of our orders. So that also obviously relates to wind. I mean, it is a global business. And  the other reason why we also have been investing right in front of the ocean [indiscernible] (40:08). So we see   that. There is some debate going on, on what to do with offshore next. But then we are a globally acting company,  and we have a lot of opportunities in that sector. So we are not honestly overly concerned about any impact that  might have.

texts.speaker: Peter Reilly
texts.profession: Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: Good morning. It's Peter Reilly from Jefferies. Two questions, please. Firstly, coming back to wind. It's been a very  bumpy ride. You've suffered from low profitability, technical problems. You've now had a very high margin in one  quarter. You've got a rising backlog, I guess, with more and more offshore. So can you help us understand whether  we're now on a sustainable path, whether the [ph] pollen's (41 :11) behind us, or whether you still see some further  issues in the future?

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: What is important for us is that the way we see the competitors act, there is not anything that would widen the gap  in any regard. So talking about the wind business and why was it that strong in particular in the second quarter,  there were no major one-offs – positives, releases of provisions or something. I think it would be too early to say  we have found new normal and steady state, but we have been addressing for two years now in our discussion s  with you that we have been intensively working on stabilizing our supply chain processes. We have been admitting  that industrialization hasn't – did not have reached very mature level in the past. And we have been also  addressing internally many different areas on which we have been working on, and it looks like we are now  gaining ground also in tangible outcomes. I mean, if you look at the yield – the first-part yield, past yields, in the  blade factories, that it has been improving by more than 20%, whic h is substantial obviously for that kind of  capacity utilization, which is then driving higher absorption of cost of course because the output is higher.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Well, what it also shows is, if you have the right management team, and have a consistency of view on what ne eds  to be done, things happen over time. So I have to say I'm very pleased with what I see there. And it shows us of  course there's good profit pull also in new business. It is a young business, so it's got a quite some opportunities.  And coming back, James, to what you said earlier in Germany, I mean, there's still the policy that offshore will  grow from 16 to 22 gigawatts through 2022. Secondly, and that's also something one should not underestimate,  there's a huge install base in onshore at very good locations for wind but at very bad efficiencies of the turbines. So  what you in essence look into is to replace the turbines at that place with more efficiency so that you gain more  outcome. And being concerned about policy drafts is one thing, but I also think the policy makers ought to be  concerned about their jobs now going if they don't get it right. So there's a lot to lose on both sides.

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: So a couple of questions. First for Joe, in the U.S. I think we've seen a number of companies this quarter have
texts.text: Question number two, depending on FX or whatever, but the base level of orders in Power and Gas looks  stable- ish. Just generally, what are your impressions at the moment of the tendering environment? Not for the mega - projects, not for Egypt, et cetera. But are you seeing any change at all in the underlying demand environment in  fossil power? So that's question number two.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: All right. So maybe – Ralf talked about the short-term outlook or the short cycle in the United States, so it is what  it is. But if we look a bit further, I believe that the outlook for automation PLM to be put together in industrial  suites will actually see its best yet to come. So why is that? First of all, if you look at this industry, it's all about cars  in the United States. There's hardly any big country in the world where the oil-price decline has arrived as quickly  and as directly at the pump station. So that in turn triggers a massive demand on cars. And you see that already, if  you look at pickup trucks – there haven't been that many pickup trucks sold a long time than they are now.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: So now, with the underlying demand environment, where almost every project becomes power generation, maybe  about 65 or 80 megawatts is a busy place. And so, it's not this thing anymore, there's a mega -project that everyone  participates and everyone else is being first-come, first-served; those times are over. And so you have to have good  teams who can convince your customers that you're the better choice. And that's what we've been focusing for the  last one and a half years in the total market, and if we look at what the market shares do without sacrificing  margin and risk, we feel good in what we do.

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: Good morning, everyone – Joe, Ralf. Maybe firstly on savings. You mentioned the move to €850 million, €950
texts.text: million. I wondered if you could say, as this is the biggest year of shift, where we are at the end of the first half. I'm  really trying to think about when is the best quarter year on year for that specific program. And within savings, the  underperformer plan we haven't talked about much today. Could you perhaps say where we are on that and which  units are running ahead or behind? On wind, I'd just like to get back to your comment that there's no provision  release and understand why you singled out main bearings in the press release this morning. And also, where are  we on onshore and offshore mix? Because that was often a big part of the margin story. And has that also helped  this number today? Finally, on FX, a bit of housekeeping, I wonder if you could say what the basis point impact  was to this quarter and what you might expect at current rates in the second half, please?

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Let me just quickly correct myself if I was misleading with regard to Wind Power. I didn't say that there wasn't  anything with main bearings. What I said is there was no material impact that was shaping the picture of the  9.4%, but the bigger impact was coming from continuous improvement of stabilizing our supply chain  management and also the quality of the supply we bring to the process. As we have been pointing out a couple of  time of times before, this is an industry that was still gaining maturity in terms of stabilizing industrial processes  on a high level. That's why we very much look into the development of our first-pass yield. I gave you the example  of the blades, which have been improving substantially more than 20% in terms of first-pass yield over the course  of last month. And then the same is applicable obviously for the nacelles. So, in total, it's more driven by getti ng  nonconformance costs out of the system than by one-time effects. Nevertheless, there was an impact from the  main bearings.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: So priorities in M&A – we have a very clear view about where we want to allocate our resources. In general, we  have the five strategic priorities. It's about areas of growth. It's about profit pull. It's about the competencies which  we can add. It's important that this asset or this investment capital use adds synergies to the greater good.  Otherwise, you're better off going it alone. And the fifth one is do we see paradigm shifts which subsequently will  change the business model of any sort of player. That's how we look at it. And the outcome was clear – we said  decentralized energy is important. We did not acquire the companies we acquired or the assets we acquired in the  last 18 months, [ph] because – of fractionality (1:03:59), we acquired them because we believe to make a  meaningful contribution to decentralized energy concepts, which we believe will happen, alongside renewables.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: We believe that, and we have a lot of supporters on our customer base that we are leading the path on digital  enterprise, not just how many connected devices someone has and all that nice read. It is about a comprehensive  offering on electrification, automation and the digital world. That's what matters. Bringing that all together in  design, to cost, in time to market, in flexibilizing – I don't know whether that word exists – flexibilizing – it exists  now – flexibilizing basically -

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: Thank you. Good morning. A couple of questions. If we could come back to Energy Management, right? The
texts.text: growth there limited in the first quarter. Perhaps you could touch on your views of the outlook for growth in  Energy Management. But more specifically, you've been successful with your transformation program, the fruits  of that coming through. And you mentioned the discipline on the order intake side. How should we anticipate the  margin developing through the rest of this year for Energy Management?

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: All right. Energy Management, I mean, if you look at where they come from on both margins, charges, confusion,  lack of focus, we've come a long way, all right? I mean, that goes by the numbers. The team is very focused on  getting things done one at a time. And that's why they sometimes also are not overly aggressive in going after  growth, especially not in the area of solutions like high-voltage solutions and associated matters, which typically  drive top line orders and top line growth at little value, which we add. So therefore they're a little bit picky about  what they take and what they don't, rather than optimize their staff.

file: SIE - Q2 2017 Earnings Call 4May2017 400 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 04-May-17.pdf

texts.speaker: Sabine Reichel
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: Let me walk you through some highlights. The acquisition of Mentor Graphics took place at the end of the second  quarter while the merger of our wind power business with Gamesa closed at the beginning of Q3. The teams are  working intensively on the integration, and I will provide you later with a first view regarding the financial impact for  fiscal 2017.

texts.speaker: Sabine Reichel
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: Let's have a look now at a selection of some large orders we received in the quarter. We saw very strong order  development in Germany, up by 94% year-over-year. It was driven by the €1.4 billion order for the Hohe See  offshore wind power plant solution for EnBW. We will connect 71 of our 7 megawatt turbines to the grid by 2019  followed by a five-year service contract.

texts.speaker: Sabine Reichel
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: Power and Gas was very successful to gain share in the distributed generation area, and will supply 12 industrial  gas turbines with the total capacity of 690 megawatts in Argentina. These orders come with a 10-year long-term  operations, maintenance and service agreement centered on our comprehensive digital service portfolio.

texts.speaker: Sabine Reichel
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: Now, let's look at some key developments in the division. Power and Gas operates in a very competitive market  environment. Global energy trend towards renewable continued to put pressure on customer demand for fossil  power generation. This results in decline in new unit business and corresponding price pressure. Due to project  shift particularly in the Middle East, we expect a decline in the large gas turbine market in fiscal 2017. In total, we  shipped 11 large gas turbines in the quarter. Among those, five H-class turbines.

texts.speaker: Sabine Reichel
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: Energy Management accelerated top line growth, improved profitability, and gained market share, supported by  several major orders. The two largest contracts alone, one in the Middle East and the already-mentioned HVDC  order in India, add up to around €1 billion.

texts.speaker: Sabine Reichel
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: Mobility delivered again industry-leading margins and significant top-line growth, clear positive evidence of our  vertical integration strategy. Successful project execution and a largest share of the high-margin rail infrastructure  business drove profitability.

texts.speaker: Sabine Reichel
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: Let me now walk you through the line items below Industrial Business, where we saw quite some movement, and  I will also give you some guidance for the second half of fiscal 2017. SFS again delivered a very strong profit of  €207 million, driven by an equity business, including a mid-double-digit million gain from selling a stake in an  offshore wind farm.

texts.speaker: Sabine Reichel
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: Our push to roll out our state-of-the-art cost and value engineering approach across all divisions is ramping up  quickly. We want to achieve cost-optimized design solutions in a very early phase, provide cost transparency and  unveil savings potential along the entire supply chain.

texts.speaker: Sabine Reichel
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: For example, we were awarded a large order in Bolivia to significantly expand the three power plants with 14  SGT800 turbines. We used the CVE methodology combined with the e-bidding to substantially optimize the cost  position for the heat recovery steam generators during the bid process.

texts.speaker: Sabine Reichel
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: A few weeks ago Energy Management announced with SAP that our Meter Data Management solution, EnergyIP,  will be combined with SAP software suite for utilities and SAP will sell it to its customers. This will significantly  broaden the customer base and bring them a high level of intelligence to make data actionable in a more and  more distributed energy landscape.

texts.speaker: Andreas Willi
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: And the second question on the wind business, just to clarify the 10% margin you've shown for the quarter, that's  still on a Siemens accounting in that sense. So, prior to the stand-alone adjustment benefit that we will see and  prior to a change in capitalization of R&D and also where will the €121 million stand-alone adjustment reappear  within Siemens if that's taken out of the wind business going forward? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Well, thank you, Andreas for these questions. Let me start with Wind Power. Yes, there is no impact yet in the  second quarter from the stand-alone adjustment of the €121 million in that what you call Siemens accounting. And  you will see, of course, the benefits from that now in the merged company which we will fully consolidate starting  with the third quarter.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, with that, I believe Wind Power and with also really strong final quarter, if you will, before merging has been  reaching a strong value proposition in which – with which it is entering now into a really exciting business  environment. I mean, just imagine 75 gigawatts of installed base. This is not only providing the Siemens Gamesa  renewable energy business with plenty of business opportunities also in the aftermarket and service environment  to come, but is also allowing Siemens to tack on customers which we didn't have access to in the past.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Also, that's why I indicated that, also in my speech, that productivity after that strong development in the last year,  which has been benefiting from [ph] One by 2016 (30:04) obviously does not go down substantially and we clearly  will be in the area of above 4% across the board. I mean what changed there, we have been discussing that in  the past while in prior years, say last decade, we more have been focusing on the factory environment. When we  have been talking about productivity we have been expanding our view even into corporate governance  processes. And so, the full cost base is covered with that, and what's happening now in the third year of that after  the initiative has been launched is we see momentum kicking in that the different owners of the cost base are  driving productivity by themselves instead of waiting for corporate initiative, and that is making things not only  sustainable, but it's getting them into a continuous improvement mode.

texts.speaker: James Alexander Moore
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Yes. Thanks. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for taking my questions. I've got three. I wonder if I could  start with the Power and Gas business. You talk about the tough energy trends globally declining unit price  pressure. And, previously, you talked about the shift to decentralized power. Can you perhaps elaborate a little on  your strategy, either organically or inorganically, and whether you believe Dresser-Rand access the decentralized  world sufficiently or whether you need to add new technologies or different power ranges to address it?

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: And the shift to de-central, I mean, on the one hand side, of course, with our H-class, we are still one of the  leading providers, and we do also have a very, very strong offering with regards to distribution. What can be  accomplished, I think, was impressingly shown in the Egypt mega orders and the fact that we have been  executing within 18 months from scratch, literally greenfield – or it wasn't even green, to be honest, to an  operating access to the grid that was even 10% higher than originally planned for in January. I think that's quite  impressive, and that is making us confident that we are able to compete in a very tough market because we c an  deliver, and we have a strong showing in the marketplace.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: The expectations for the large gas turbines that have been kind of indicated by some of our competitors in the  past, we don't see that at the moment. But we also do have a strong offering with regard to those turbines that are  rather in the area of 20 megawatts to 60 megawatts. And that is one of those areas that is addressed with the  decentral power generation approach.

texts.speaker: James Stettler
texts.profession: Analyst, Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you. Good morning, all. Two questions for me. Just excluding Power and Gas, can you talk a bit about the  pricing trends you've seen, and how they interplay with raw material inflation?

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: In a nutshell, we did our homework. We have been taking cost out, we are continuously looking at high levels of  productivity. We have been eliminating the project charges, and we are happy that we could report the sixth  quarter in a row without net impact from that area, and we are addressing the underperforming businesses. As I  said before, or as we said before at several stages, we cannot and will not share with you who they are, we have  been spelling out some of them. And therefore, you do know that in the former – in the energy management, there  used to be critical areas in the past where we have been substantially improving, and we said that – you also  heard us saying that Ultrasound is not in a leading role yet. Therefore, there is also an element in that  environment.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Now, in terms of pricing in the marketplace, I already mentioned that Power and Gas is definitely one of the  toughest places in the market to be. Also, Wind Power and Renewables have been on pretty much the same  levels.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: So now, after two, three years of consistently allocating resources and addressing the right patterns and the  meaning I described, there seems to be a very steady development now in that business that is showing a very  consistent growth path. Also extraordinary element like funding and earning out models for energy efficiency in  the U.S. has been playing a major role.

file: SIE - Q2 2018 Earnings Call 9May2018 300 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 09-May-18.pdf

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Now, let me walk you through some highlights of the quarter. We were pleased with a healthy book-to-bill ratio of  1.11 times and the new record backlog of more than €129 billion in the Industrial Business with a solid gross  margin quality. Comparable orders were slightly lower 1% due to a substantially higher volume from large orders  in the energy-related businesses one year ago. Base orders below €50 million were clearly up 9% on a nominal  basis. Organic revenue was overall flat with growth in most divisions driven by an excellent short cycle  performance offsetting weakness in Power and Gas.

texts.speaker: Lisa A. Davis
texts.profession: Member-Management Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: Looking at three of our main markets, the pattern has been very similar since fiscal 2015, sharp unit demand  declines combined with significant price erosion. The good news is that we have significantly increased market  share over the last four years in both our large gas and small, medium, and aero derivative gas turbines. Looking  forward, based on our project funnel for large gas, we expect to see less than 100 turbines being awarded in the  industry in fiscal 2018, and there are no signs of midterm recovery to higher levels.

texts.speaker: Lisa A. Davis
texts.profession: Member-Management Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: On the other hand, we expect a bottoming and moderate recovery in the small and medium gas turbine segments  as well as in compression. A higher oil price above USD $70 is beginning to support investments in upstream and  pipelines. However customers are very cost-sensitive and competition is fierce. As I already mentioned, the  measures to drive cost-out are in place.

texts.speaker: Lisa A. Davis
texts.profession: Member-Management Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: Let me also give you an update on our service business. Our installed base is a great asset and our service team  is doing an excellent job to make it even more valuable for our customers. From the current backlog of €31 billion,  around €25 billion are related to large gas. And we expect to increase the backlog even further. The service- relevant fleet continues to grow as our previously sold units reached their first major outages. This includes our H- class units, for example, in the U.S. and Asia, as well as our fast-growing base of SGT-800 units in Latin America  and elsewhere. We rigorously track our outage activity and utilization to ensure constant visibility. As you can see  from the charts, gas turbine utilization so far has been moderately up in 2018 and our balanced distribution across  the many regions helps to handle any fluctuations.

texts.speaker: Lisa A. Davis
texts.profession: Member-Management Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: I want to reiterate that customer proximity and innovation remain our key success factors. In the second quarter,  we sold six large gas turbines among them are the first two H-class turbines on the China Mainland, which will be  part of the most efficient gas-fired power plant in China. We have sold now 88 H-class turbines, of which 65 are  already in reliable operation. A key technology for our business is additive manufacturing. We will invest a further  €30 million to expand our 3D printing factory in the UK, fully equipped with software and automation from our  Digital Factory colleagues.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Process Industries and Drives is making good progress on its restructuring program and achieved clear order  growth of 6%. However, we saw diverging end customer trends. While commodity-related end markets showed  further stabilization, the demand for mechanical components, particularly in the wind business remained weak.  Profit margin improved by 60 basis points despite significant currency headwinds of 50 basis points.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: The PLM software business is very well on track to achieve its €3.4 billion revenue target in fiscal 2018 on strong  profitability despite significant invest in MindSphere and Software-as-a-Service solutions. Energy Management  showed broad-based improvement across its businesses with clear revenue growth and a margin well in the  target range. Large orders were lower on tough comps. We have seen some push-outs of HVDC solution projects  into fiscal 2019.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: The recent MAKE study on global market share developments in the wind industry confirmed the compelling  industrial logic of the merger. Siemens Gamesa took the lead in 2017 with 8.8 gigawatt new installations and 17%  market share, an increase of 3.3 percentage points.

texts.speaker: Mark Troman
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: Maybe one for Lisa, on Power Generation, with all the restructuring measures that you've announced, how much  capacity reduction in effect will there be for the large turbine business that you have? Or is it – is a better way to  think about it about just fixed cost reduction? So, I'm trying to get an idea of the impact of the measures you were  taking on your capacities or fixed cost?

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: So from that angle, the new order development has been pretty much based on that one. On the other hand, we  continue seeing a lot of pricing pressure on the mechanical drives environment, which is mainly occupied by  customers from the wind industry, which as I said before are also adjusting the consolidation phase – pricing in  the market. It's getting tougher due to more and more countries shifting their models to auction from feed-in.

texts.speaker: Lisa A. Davis
texts.profession: Member-Management Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: I'll jump in Mark on the PG question to the question on restructuring and whether we should look at it as percent  of capacity reduction or fixed-cost reduction. We do look at it very much as how we're reducing the cost base of  the business. If we were to look at it on a percent of capacity, it varies by product line, obviously, depending on  what's required in the market, so it gets a bit complicated. But on an overall cost reduction, that's really what we  focus on with respect to the restructuring we've announced.

texts.speaker: Andreas Willi
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: The question on Energy Management, obviously a much better margin this quarter after some mixed quarters.  What drove the improvement versus the last quarter? It's been kind of a bit up and down in that division and how  sustainable is the 9% margin there now and what do you see as an impact from raw materials in that division in  the coming quarters given some of the exposure to steel you have?

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Before I leave it to Lisa to answer the PG question, let me just make quickly one remark on the new business in  Power and Gas. I mean, after Lisa's presentation, I mean, it's obvious that we have a massive and also  sustainable impact from the market when it comes to the quantities out there. We said just citing an example that  most likely we won't see more than 100 new units large gas turbines per year in the current fiscal, not at all, and  maybe this is also kind of new normal.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: The second piece of your question around Energy Management, typically a long-timer like you knows that the first  half of the fiscal is fairly slow in that business. I try to understand that for more than a decade now, I have to  respect the fact it is that way, but it also was always the case that in particular the third and the fourth quarter of  the fiscal year was fairly reliable. Then when it comes to volume, we see the margin clearly on that level. And  from historical experience, the fourth quarter typically was even stronger than the second and the third quarter.  So, everything we know from backlog and everything we also know from the momentum generated in the different  businesses, there is quite underpinning that we will continue seeing Energy Management on those margin levels  maybe even a bit above. Raw material pricing is going to have an impact. You can hedge only for a certain period  of time and that has negative impact, but not material for the profitability of the division as such.

texts.speaker: Simon Toennessen
texts.profession: Analyst, Joh. Berenberg, Gossler & Co. KG (United Kingdom)
texts.text: Yes. Good morning, Ralf, Lisa and Sabine, and thanks for taking the questions. Starting with a two-folded  question in PG. You're guiding for, I think, mid-single digits to high-single digits underlying margins for the next  sort of couple of years, including 2018. Can you share maybe the assumptions with us, how you can get to the  low and the high end within that? And then, a more general question on PG. I guess the outlook for small and  medium turbine looks a bit better, and there might be some upside from the compressor business recovering i.e.,  the Dresser-Rand bit. But if we look beyond the restructuring measures, what are your arguments as to why  financially you would hold on to this business in the long-term? Then, the next question on Vision 2020+, it looks  like you're making some good progress on the Power restructuring. So, is it fair to say that we could expect an  announcement as early as August with results with regards to Vision 2020+?

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Simon, thank you very much for really broad portfolio of questions. So let me start with Vision 2020+. The way  you have been asking your question has been taking the Power restructuring aspect pretty close to Vision 2020+,  which is not the case in the way we look upon it. I mean, we made that very clear when we started to discuss and  indicate the magnitude of the need to restructure the footprint and address excess capacity in the market. And  maybe it was just coincidence that at the same time, we said that we start thinking about and developing beyond  Vision 2020, which we then called as a working title Vision 2020+.

texts.speaker: Lisa A. Davis
texts.profession: Member-Management Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, let me address your question, Simon, on the, I guess, future attractiveness of the PG new unit business. And  maybe I'll break it down into three distinct areas because there are three distinct markets within the business. The  first, on small and medium gas turbines, really, this business is driven very much by Decentralized Energy  Systems and the growth in Decentralized Energy. And so, we do see this still being a very attractive business  going forward for the use of small and medium gas turbines. They have a natural home in Decentralized Energy  Systems of the future.

texts.speaker: Lisa A. Davis
texts.profession: Member-Management Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: If we look at the compression business, really, this is a bit of a discussion about oil and gas. And as you've seen  in some of the comments, we do see this business starting to find stability and recover, and we do see this market  very much intact longer term. We also see quite an opportunity in the oil and gas business around our ability to  bring digitalization into an industry that has not advanced nearly as much as other sectors or other verticals have.  So, an opportunity that's unique to Siemens to be able to leverage our digital capability with our rotating  equipment in that industry, so a growth opportunity there as well.

texts.speaker: Lisa A. Davis
texts.profession: Member-Management Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: And even in the large gas turbine business, even though this has obviously gone through structural change and  will be a smaller market going forward, we do see a need for large gas turbines in the energy systems of the  future, if not for anything else, but for security, the ability to bring large volumes of Power into the system quickly.  And for this reason, we do see a large gas turbine market going forward, albeit much smaller than what we've  seen in the past. And, therefore, the need for us to really restructure and right-size our business to match that  market of the future. So, all-in-all, still some optimism around all three key areas of the business and the business  overall going forward.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Thank you. Our next question comes from James Moore from Redburn. Please go ahead. Your line is  now open.  James Moore  Analyst, Redburn (Europe) Ltd.  Q  Yeah. Good morning, everyone. I wonder if I could focus on Power and Gas. Firstly, could you comment whether  the service margin was stable year-on-year in the first half? If you already did, apologies. And secondly on that,  could you say how low the Dresser margin has got? You gave a number of high single digits two years ago. I just  wonder now that we've had the oil pain, where are we, has it bottomed, what's the potential?

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
