texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: We have seen quite a cooling down in demand in important end markets that are driven particularly by the  export-oriented German industry, as you can also see from the current IFO level or VDMA numbers. The  investment climate in a number of Western European countries remains very weak due to the ongoing austerity  measures and restricted access to and high cost of capital.

texts.speaker: Mariel von Drathen
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: Profitability clearly exceeded the prior-year level which was substantially burdened by the Areva arbitration  decision and the Particle Therapy reevaluation. Fossil and DX delivered strong earnings. However, profitability  was impacted by higher OpEx in all sectors and a significantly lower contribution from the Industrial sector.

texts.speaker: Mariel von Drathen
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: As for OSRAM, we stick to our original plans to deconsolidate the asset but changed our primary plans. Since  market conditions continue to be highly volatile for an IPO, we decided to pursue a spin-off to our shareholders as  the most probable part of divestiture. This option requires shareholder approval at the next AGM in January 2013  and Siemens still intends to remain an anchor shareholder in OSRAM. Though our strategic intent remains the  same from an accounting perspective, this results in a significantly negative non-cash P&L effect in discontinued  operations through a so-called cumulative catch-up of depreciation and amortization related to OSRAM.  For the record, here is the overview of the key figures for the third quarter. These challenges are reflected in our  regional split of orders and sales in the third quarter, the lack of large orders, particularly in Energy and the Rail  business, compared to a strong prior-year weighted on growth rates in Europe and also the U.S. Major driver  behind the 28% order decline in the U.S. was the expected expiration of the U.S. tax benefit scheme on  renewables, which led already to a sharp decline in new Wind orders.

texts.speaker: Mariel von Drathen
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: What were the key developments in each of the sectors? In sector Energy, as already mentioned, orders in Energy  went down substantially by 33% due to a broad-based decline of large projects in all divisions. The Energy market  remains highly competitive with some postponements of projects and competitive pricing in the market.

texts.speaker: Mariel von Drathen
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: Those of you following our news closely probably have noticed our recent order announcements, such as  Lausward, the next H-frame power combined cycle power plant for the Stadtwerke Düsseldorf with our second H- frame sold in Germany and 15 in total. We plan to achieve for the first time an efficiency level of above 61%. The  Panda Temple Power Project in Texas in the U.S. with an order volume around $300 million and the large-frame  agreement with DONG Energy to deliver 300 of our new 6-megawatt direct-drive turbines which will strengthen  our market leadership in offshore wind. And this largest offshore order ever adds another 1,800-megawatts to our  installed base of 2,700 megawatts.

texts.speaker: Mariel von Drathen
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: For Energy, we expect a strong rebound in orders in Q4 and the book-to-bill ratio for the full year likely just shy of  1% – of 1. The sectors backlog remained at the healthy €56 billion at the end of the quarter. And second quarter  revenue rose by 8% on the conversion from Energy's strong order backlog driven by a substantial increase of 35%  in the renewable business.

texts.speaker: Mariel von Drathen
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: Fossil continued its excellent project execution and delivering once again a strong margin of 17.6%. The product  and service business contributed significantly to this performance. Unfortunately, the strong top line growth in  renewable energy did not adequately convert into profitability. The reasons were supplier-related provisions of  €32 million and the €20 million charge for capacity adjustments weighting on profitability in the Wind business,  while the Solar business posted higher losses year-over-year.

texts.speaker: Mariel von Drathen
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: As previously indicated, Power Transmission reported a weak margin of 3.2% due to the conversion of lower- margin contracts and further charges of €22 million mostly related to the grid connections to offshore wind farms  in Germany. I will give you more details in a minute about the progress we have achieved to bring Power  Transmission back on track.

texts.speaker: Mariel von Drathen
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: As already mentioned, industry faced headwinds particularly in the short-cycle businesses of Industry Automation  and Drive Technologies, and in addition the sector's renewable offerings were held back by the difficult market  environment. Revenue in the sector was down 2% year-on-year while orders went down moderately by 4%, yet  supported by contract wins in the metals business. Profitability in Industry Automation was down 260 basis  points compared to the last quarter, mostly due to a significantly unfavorable product mix and also high OpEx  spending.

texts.speaker: Mariel von Drathen
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: The drop in profitability of Drive Technologies to 8.6% is largely due to a weaker margin in the short-cycle motion  control business and continuous challenges in the Renewable Energy offering of Drive Technologies.

texts.speaker: Mariel von Drathen
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: Finally, I want to walk you through the key developments in the sector Infrastructure & Cities. Revenue for the  sector was slightly up, 1, driven by an increase in the Power Grid Solutions & Products business. Profits in the  Transportation & Logistics division achieved 4.2%, 100 basis points below the prior-year level due to lower  revenue and some impact from lower margins in the long-term contracts.

texts.speaker: Mariel von Drathen
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: And third, we put a strong emphasis on stabilizing and mastering the offshore grid access project in Germany. The  resource ramp-up is almost done and each of the project is staffed with a very experienced project director. Our  team is collaborating closely with the customer, suppliers and regulatory bodies to resolve the outstanding  challenges. By this program, Transmission will achieve by 2015 30% cost savings, 8% profitability and grow faster  than the market after a consolidation phase.

texts.speaker: Mariel von Drathen
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: And finally, mastering the offshore grid projects successfully is a crucial cornerstone for Transmission, and since it  will be the reference for further projects to execute the so-called [indiscernible] (14:58) in Germany and  elsewhere.  Now I would like to hand over to Joe for some more background on the financials.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: The only one significant volatile here is our so-called asset retirement obligation. That's a construction matter of  some nuclear remains in Hanau. As you might know from our filings. It is a €2.7 billion liability up to 2075. And  alone from those numbers, you can see how heavily those future liabilities will be impacted in terms of net present  value by the discount rate which is used. So it was positive in Q3 with the plus €44 million, but that could also  change course if the discount rate turns smaller.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: If we move now on the margins, I mean, obviously, Energy is pretty close to where our bandwidth is. There's been  some weakness in the so-called Renewables which is predominantly affected through solar. Wind is actually  developing according to our expectations and produces decent margins compared to competition, at least. The  solar matter obviously is being affected by some structural changes in the global environment of that industry, and  that also means that we need to take close attention on what that means in Siemens.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: And as far as the Transmission is concerned, there's a program underway which looks promising. On the same  The reason being that the majority of the backlog on those wind projects in the North Sea, obviously, is now  running with zero gross margin and will ultimately dilute the P&L, which actually should not come as a surprise  because if charges are being made that means that gross margin will be zero as we move along. Good news is we've  been on the cap of liquidated damages here, so any potential unforeseen delays would not materially affect any  provisions as they relate to liquidated damages going forward.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: Infrastructure & Cities; I mean, obviously, it's been not exactly there where we want it to be, and where it needs to  be. On the other hand, we always made it pretty clear that the whole city infrastructure has its long-term  potentials and in the short term still needs to take some efforts on getting the product margin in order.

texts.speaker: Andreas Willi
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: And the second question on Renewables, you have announced a small capacity reduction in the quarter and took a  charge. What should we expect going forward? You have expanded capacity in a number of regions. Where are you  cutting back and kind of what's the plan for the next few years in terms of how big you want to play in wind?  Thank you.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President, CEO & Head-Corporate Communications, Siemens AG
texts.text: On Renewables, Andreas, I mean, they are – I think what you should expect is that, for us, size doesn't matter so  much. There were times where our leaders would have said that it's important to be number one or number two in  wind. I think it's much more important to focus on profitable capital-efficient growth. Therefore, our focus on  offshore wind as we have said, selective playing on the onshore and ensuring that we actually play projects which  are profitable. And therefore, in this environment, we are currently working on a couple of scenarios because  nobody really knows in the U.S. So, how we have to adjust on the PTC? How will the PTC, the Production Tax  Credit, going forward look like, so we are prepared for several scenarios there.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President, CEO & Head-Corporate Communications, Siemens AG
texts.text: We are clearly focusing on driving actually operational efficiency in our existing plants. So we have just increased  on the turbine part, actually the throughput of our turbines significantly through actually modular highly efficient  production techniques, what we have introduced there. We will play in China as we have said through the joint

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President, CEO & Head-Corporate Communications, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, clearly, Andreas, it should help us to stabilize this. We have a good order backlog, more than €8 billion. And in  the current environment, we are clearly selective in terms of which type of orders we are taking in so to ensure  that we absolutely stay as a margin – as a quality margin company in a consolidating more difficult wind  environment. So, relatively speaking, we should be able to outperform key competitors on profitability.

texts.speaker: Ben E. Uglow
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: And then final, just sort of big-picture question, in terms of the cost-savings plan, is this a genuine cost-cutting  plan, i.e., that you will be putting out a sort of cost-savings target, or is this more of a control-of-OpEx plan?  So,  are you actually looking to reduce absolute costs, or are you looking to control your OpEx spend?

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: On the gearbox environment, obviously, we've taken some actions already. We will have a few more to make sure  that our capacities and resources are being adapted to what we expect going forward. So, we do not expect that  division to kind of go – come closer to the cliff. We actually would expect in Q4 to be of similar-margin  environments underlying, as in Q3. And much of what Peter has been highlighting in terms of the efficiency  program 2013 would also be obviously related to the topic, how do we deal with the pretty significant changes in  the whole renewable environment as subsidies are short and public debt obviously is still not fully under control  in Europe.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: That brings us to Infrastructure & Cities. I mean, in order to, I guess – answering that question which just need to  go one step back and try to understand again why have we actually been founding that sector. It was the notion  that the underlying trends in the everywhere we are looking, this is about mobility, about infrastructure control  and a decent and efficient deal with Energy resources in urban environments.

texts.speaker: Mark A. Troman
texts.profession: Analyst, Merrill Lynch International (United Kingdom)
texts.text: Are you going to try and react quickly with cost cutting, or is the idea to keep investing and keep committed on the  cost base to take some market share, especially in the light of your Chinese comments? Because Peter, I think you  were saying you might expect a better 2013 than 2012, so I'm curious on how you're thinking about managing  Automation – the Automation businesses through this soft patch?  And then secondly, just a question on pricing. Obviously, the environment is weak as we all can see. Have you  seen any sequential price weakness either in Energy, which is usually – the Energy business, which is usually well  flagged for price issues, or indeed in the Automation, which has just seen weakness now? Thank you. Or recently.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President, CEO & Head-Corporate Communications, Siemens AG
texts.text: On the second one, Mark, in terms of how the pricing environment looks like on the Energy side, I would say  sequentially, pretty much the same thing. I mean, the first key assessment what we have is that it has continued to  be a price-sensitive environment. So, I would not – we don't see sequentially a major difference, but we do see, for  example, in – what we have already flagged in the Transformer businesses where we have overcapacities on the T- side, continued to be quite price-aggressive offerings. We see the HVDC projects contested.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President, CEO & Head-Corporate Communications, Siemens AG
texts.text: On power generation, it's rather a question of, for us that we see a shift in terms of different regions. Almost no  projects, for example in Europe where we used to have a pretty much – a solution scope. The exception probably  being right now what we have adjusted this order out of Dusseldorf a couple of weeks ago, but the rest pretty  quiet. The U.S. not yet picking up because of the reserve margins, what we see over there. So, the shift is moving  towards Asia and the Middle East which, historically, has always – are markets with a different price point.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President, CEO & Head-Corporate Communications, Siemens AG
texts.text: The Renewable business, as we have seen, no difference, no change in terms of the pricing strategies. So, we  continue to see capacity adjustments, overcapacity, and therefore a continuous pricing environment as we have  seen at the last time. So, no deterioration but certainly also no reason to believe that pretty soon we will see a  positive development here. And therefore, we are clearly preparing for this one also.

texts.speaker: Peter J. Reilly
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Prime Brokerage)
texts.text: Hello. Good morning. I'd like to come back, please, to Infrastructure & Cities. Two questions. Firstly, Joe, you  referred to the need to fix some of the products. Can you be more specific? I assume you're referring here to  Building Technologies. But we've been told for years that the product offering needs to be improved at Building  Tech. And I thought that process had largely been done, so maybe you can explain what you mean by the need to  improve the offering?

texts.speaker: Peter J. Reilly
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Prime Brokerage)
texts.text: And secondly, coming back to the rationale for the creation of the business, and the idea was to offer a one-stop  shop, particularly for cities, but since then obviously a lot of cities around the world have been cutting their  budgets. Has there been any positive experience from the creation of Infrastructure & Cities, or have you just seen  an increase in cost and complexity by adding another layer of overhead on the existing businesses?

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, the pressure has been clear as always. Look, I mean, be more specific on the products. We have areas here,  which are products business which got some cost of capital where we need to heavily improve the margins, and  that's obviously related to the low-voltage environment. This is a – this is actually a good place to be at because,  obviously, the profit pool is huge, if you look at what others are able to deliver in the markets. And that's why the  and they are rolling that out as we speak. So, that's the first place. Here we need to see a very clear progress  because, obviously, that's been promised for quite some time.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: The potential definitely here is on the Rail Automation side as well as on Energy Automation because both have  good profit pools and we have a good competitive standing in the market. So, those are the two focus area where  we ought to see tangible improvements in 2013. And I'm sure that Roland will – and his management team will be  even more specific in terms of how to get there at the I&C Market Day.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: Now, what is the rationale of Infrastructure & Cities? I mean, obviously, short term, there is no meaning of  dancing around it. We've been increasing our costs. There is some added complexity because if we have four  sectors, that's 33% more than three. I mean, that's clear and we know that. On the other hand, we truly do believe  that the mid- and long-term rationale is intact. So why is that?

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: Well, if you look at urbanization, if you look at big cities, the downside is that all those communities, those big  cities and urban centers, they've got actually no money but they've got an ever increasing demand because people  are coming to the cities, and they want to be there and that's called urbanization.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, what do you target at? You target at making the cost per infrastructure or the infrastructure cost of capital less.  That's what the focus area is with Infrastructure & Cities. This is not about selling more or buying more by  bundling and go to the mayor who usually doesn't have any decision power anyway on the infrastructure. This is  not what we are targeting after. What we are targeting after is to make the infrastructure needs – every urban  center, every city and every county in a way has cheaper per capita, and that's what the focus is.

texts.speaker: Peter J. Reilly
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Prime Brokerage)
texts.text: Yeah. I understand it will take time. But I'm wondering whether you actually need your customers to change first.  You mentioned that mayors have got often very limited power. And it's no good having a fantastic energy-saving  opportunity if you've got no one to talk to. Do you need your customers to change before the business really  works?

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: Hi, James. So, let me – I think that was Solar, right, you've been referring to?

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: Well, obviously, look, the Solar business in general and also in Siemens in particular didn't turn out to deliver  what we would have wished for and what have been expected. So therefore, there's got to be some material  structural realignment on that segment. And we are in the middle of doing that. There's been some already in Q2  and there will be more in order to realign expectations and reality, which by the way, the whole industry is right in  the middle of doing. So, obviously, it's completely immaterial to the company and to the sector, but the revenues  is more about realigning than any small numbers at this point in time. And there's a lot of explanation to that on  projects and what have been promised versus what governments were willing and able to deliver.
