texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board & Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Another good example for good order intake is a large order which we have been getting for an LNG project in  Yamal which will deliver our latest gas turbines to a power plant feeding one of the most ambitious natural gas  project in Russia.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board & Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: In Energy, the oil and gas division and fossil power generation showed quite a decent underlying performance. In  transmission, the first two grid access projects in the North Sea achieved a major milestone by successfully  installing the base frame on the platform. During the fourth quarter, we are going to install the top side of the  platform, which obviously is a critical milestone for delivering the project in the planned timeframe, and obviously  also in the subsequently planned cost frame.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board & Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Given these developments and financial results for the first nine months, we do expect income from continued  operations of about €4 billion in fiscal 2013, including the Solar business as well as the gain from the transaction  of NSN, and Solar, obviously being adverse in the neighborhood of about €300 million. The outlook excludes  other significant portfolio effects and obviously also legal and regulatory matters in the fourth quarter.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board & Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Hello. Well, thanks, first of all, for the good wishes. We definitely do need it, as you all know. As far as 2014 is  concerned, what we've been always thinking was that the whole 2014 recovery of growth would be related to the  recovery of short-cycle business, which all is true in a way. However, we in the meantime, also do see that the mid  and long cycle environment, especially Energy, Energy fossil for example, is still lacking the growth perspectives  in 2014 going forward. So there will be a dip also in the longer cycle environment which we need to clearly address  by incremental productivity actions.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board & Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: As far as the portfolio optimization is concerned, I hope you can mostly agree with us that there has been progress.  Well, just think about the water business, the airport logistics business, Osram and finally also NSN, which doesn't  necessarily relate to the sector, but still is a significant improvement in terms of risk management and protect the  downside. So there has been progress, and that progress will continue and everything else, please bear with me.  I'm still the CFO today and tomorrow I'm starting that other job, and you can be rest assured that we will look at  everything which we have in order to grow this company, not just in revenues, but particularly also in value.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board & Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Yeah [indiscernible] (23:35) backlog – on the backlog, obviously what we have to just keep in mind is that the very  nice and also favorable development in orders in Q2 and also Q3 comes with the tack that this is going to be  diluting in terms of margins compared to the average business in the company. So, as you are very well aware of  that, this is true with rail and this is also, in parts, true with wind.

texts.speaker: Andreas Willi
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: Yeah, good afternoon, everybody. First question on the fossil business you had weaker orders there and you  mentioned also weaker service business. But profitability was quite strong. In the past you gave quite precise  guidance on the fossil margin. Maybe you could update that on us – update that. Also, given that obviously some  of the utilities in Europe are no longer using turbines as frequently as they used to, and therefore are inclined to  try to renegotiate the long-term service agreements they have with you.

texts.speaker: Andreas Willi
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: And then just a clarification on what you said on backlog dilution. These orders in Wind and Rail, are they diluting  also relative to what these divisions currently already earn? Or is that just a result of the overall mix, if those  businesses grow faster than the rest of Siemens? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board & Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Here, fossil business, we continue to expect fossil, including service, to be in the neighborhood of about 16% to  17% just to be [ph] try (27:09) of what we've been seeing in the last fiscal quarter and that's expected to continue.  As far as this whole service method is concerned, and I know there's a lot of talk about it, I just want to give you a  few – a bit of a flavor in where our businesses are located at.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board & Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: The European service business is about 15%, 17% of the total. Germany's very small. You could probably – if you  estimate about 5%, you're not too far off. So it really is not that mattersome if the German energy change will  eventually kill the gas turbine business here. It really doesn't matter much, in terms of impact, because the U.S.  portion in our service is north of 40%. So if you look at that, we do see some, obviously, weakness in Germany,  some slow environments in Europe. But the real mattersome topic is still little contained.

texts.speaker: Andreas Willi
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: Thank you very much. And these – the percentages were for just the fossil service business, or for the overall  service business?

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board & Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: That's Energy service, but this obviously is being driven by fossil.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board & Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: [indiscernible] (29:15) in the fossil margin of 16% to 17%.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Our next question comes from Olivier Esnou of Exane BNP Paribas. Please go ahead.

texts.speaker: Olivier Esnou
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane Ltd.
texts.text: Oh, okay. So let's restart. Okay. So first question was about there's a visible strong quarter-over-quarter  improvement in the EBITDA of both oil and gas and imaging in IT, I mean, Healthcare ex diagnostic. On my  numbers, EBITDA is up by as much as the sales improvement quarter-over-quarter. So I was wondering if there  you have any more details about some specifics one-offs or whether this improvement you see that as sustainable  or not going forward.

texts.speaker: Olivier Esnou
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane Ltd.
texts.text: A third question, probably a bit boarder as well, I was listening to the press conference this morning. And several  times you were mentioning the topic of Siemens being on the electrification chain and that Siemens need to  structure itself along this electrification chain. So if you think over the mid-term, we could put a lot of things into  it, but I mean, you decided Osram was not part of this electrification chain and it's probably a fair question to ask  if Healthcare in the medium run is part of that chain. So are you able to maybe bring some light about what you  see – how electrification is going to structure Siemens in the medium-term? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board & Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Thank you, Olivier, and again sorry for interrupting. The strong performance on both oil and gas and imaging, it's  got mostly to do with the structural product mix. On oil and gas, as you know, there is the process industry,  services and there is the industrial turbine business. And we've seen quite a strong development in industrial  turbine and that's supposed to be just about similar in Q4. So that's matched to this one. And you may as well, in  the next couple of day, will also notice some structural improvements related to oil and gas and also how we  position it into the fossil environment. So that's something which is just about to be discussed and we'll keep you  updated there. This action will be targeted at further improving profitability and productivity in the fossil turbine  environment.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board & Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: If I talk electrification, obviously what I do mean is that this company is – almost no one else is so well positioned  along the electrification chain; Starfish Energy generation, T&T, efficient use of energy in Industrial Automation  and drives in building automation in mobility management and of course also in Healthcare. And obviously,  Healthcare also needs power and electrification. So I would not really jump to any conclusions in the short-term  about whether or not any material sector is part of Siemens or not. So please, as I said, please give me some  patience here to outline the priorities of the company, which we will be re-visiting and re-discussing during the  course of the next weeks and months and get out to you again in November.

texts.speaker: James A. Moore
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn Partners LLP
texts.text: And then finally, I see the gross margin's fallen 110 bps year-on-year and I think it fell something similar the year  before. And we can't see the split of one-offs by OpEx versus COGS from the outside. Without hard numbers, can  you say anything qualitative about the underlying gross margin development in the quarter, please?

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board & Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Yeah. Thanks Fredric. Look, on the discussion of GDP versus our own business, I'd rather look at our businesses  in our space and in our customers' environment, because GDP sometimes does not always necessarily reflect the  spectrum of our business. The reason that we've been slower than some in China is that we've been having our ex  mostly in the manufacturing automation. And thus CapEx related environment, whereas others might be more  associated with the process industry environment including, also of course, the oil and gas and the Energy  efficiency space.

texts.speaker: Mark L. Fielding
texts.profession: Analyst, Citigroup Global Markets Ltd.
texts.text: And then secondly, maybe briefly just talk about in the context of Drive Technologies, the sensitivity of that  business to particularly the wind market, and what impact pick-up from a [indiscernible] (53:01) low base might  have on profits going forward.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board & Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: In terms of other ongoing disposals though, I need to caution you that this is not going to bring us to billions of  cash which one would love to see. All the businesses which we have been talking about, that is water, airport  logistics and post automation, may not really be that billion near type of capital returns. It is just the focus on  streamlining our business and have the spectrum which we need to push forward. So NSN, I understand, and the  other disposals I would – as I said rather caution you about the impact of this one.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board & Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: On wind relate – as it comes to drive technology, obviously this is a significant method to us because if we look at  mechanical drives, this has been traditionally – the wind business traditionally has been the growth engine for  mechanical drives due to the fact that drives have been needed. Now – and over the years have been needed and  now with the technology changing into high performance 3.5 megawatt up to 6 megawatt machines, they all run  with the gearless spectrum. So that actually means that we need to continue to understand and act on mechanical  drives because this is going to go down further over time.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board & Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: So – and if we look at it from the Q3 perspective, revenues have been down 17%. In that wind related aspect in  NDTs and we do not expect any recovery. So that is a structural topic which we are addressing in the course of our  transformatory charges and actions going forward.

texts.speaker: William Mackie
texts.profession: Head of Capital Goods Research, Berenberg Bank
texts.text: Yes, good afternoon, Joe, Mariel. Thank you for taking the question. Actually I – just a couple of housekeeping. In  the context of a lower growth outlook, do you envisage that the company should begin to flex the investments for  innovation and R&D and CapEx against lower growth expectations and as a tightening exercise with regard to  solar within the Energy sector should – how should we expect that to impact the charges for the full year? I mean,  I think previously you've said about €300 million at the bottom line. Is there any change to your thoughts around  the solar exit?

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board & Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: As far as China, for example, is concerned, we do believe this is temporary in nature. As far as the whole tool  making, automotive environment in Germany is concerned, we expect – and also in the U.S., by the way, we  expect that to be temporary in nature, so you would not really materially cut the R&D and engineering part of it.  What we would do though if that was structural, like for example, the mechanical drive matter which we just  discussed, or the inverter topic, it becomes the solar sub-deliveries from the industrial business to the space.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board & Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: If – as far as our solar business is concerned, we obviously have two topics here. One is the company, the Solel  company itself, that actually has been pretty much handled already. There's very little to expect going forward as  far as any charges or other topics are concerned.

file: SIE - Q3 2014 Earnings Call 31July2014 300 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 31-Jul-14.pdf

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Supervisory Board, Daimler AG
texts.text: As for the third quarter, we delivered a good performance with progress in most areas. Continued challenges in  the energy business held back an even stronger profit improvement for Siemens as a whole. As for the full fiscal  year 2014, we are on track to deliver our outlook. The macroeconomic picture continues to show a heterogeneous  regional development.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Supervisory Board, Daimler AG
texts.text: In this environment, the order intake remained on the same level year-over-year on a like-for-like basis. Across  the sectors, we saw significant shifts. Large orders in the Energy sector such as the €1.6 billion Gemini offshore  wind-farm project in the Netherlands compensated for sharply lower rolling stock orders such as the €3 billion  [indiscernible] (04:34) contract which we booked about a year ago.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Supervisory Board, Daimler AG
texts.text: Sector profit was driven by a higher contribution from our short cycle businesses in Industry sector, as well as  from solid project and productivity execution in the Infrastructure & Cities sector. On the other hand, the Energy  sector is facing operational challenges that held back further profitability improvement and will require some time  to get fully fixed.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Supervisory Board, Daimler AG
texts.text: Now, let's take a look at some key developments in each of the sectors. First, the Energy sector. Let's start at the  bright spot at the beginning. Orders were up sharply with growth in all businesses and geographies, however on  obviously relatively easy comps in the quarter last year.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Supervisory Board, Daimler AG
texts.text: In Power Generation, we were able to catch up successfully and sold 16 advanced gas turbines in a very  competitive market, multi-connection with turnkey contracts. The global advanced gas turbine market, in our  view, is likely to be smaller in 2014 as compared to 2013.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Supervisory Board, Daimler AG
texts.text: On Power Transmission, we've booked the fifth offshore grid connection platform which we call BorWin3,  however, at this time, on a strongly improved – and I repeat that it was strongly improved -- first management  concept. Looking ahead, we expect the market environment to remain highly competitive for our Energy sector in  mostly all business areas.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Supervisory Board, Daimler AG
texts.text: Wind Power reached only a 2.7% margin, already well below its earnings potential, for several reasons. While the  revenue and mix was less favorable, with a lower share of the higher margin offshore business, also new product  launches, and a steep capacity ramp-up in production led to higher cost associated to the production ramp-up.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Supervisory Board, Daimler AG
texts.text: Power Transmission continues to deal with a broad-based challenge arising from legacy issues such as the wind  access, good access in the North Sea, but also some other legacy projects which we reported on in Canada and the  likes, and had a loss of €188 million in the third quarter. As I said previously, there is no quick fix on this matter.  The division's new leadership team is working hard on the remedy since the Transmission business is a key  element of the value chain of electrification.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Supervisory Board, Daimler AG
texts.text: But there's also operational progress. Meanwhile, we installed four offshore grid platforms in the North Sea. The  average completion rate is about 80%, and commissioning will take place over the remainder of 2014, and into the  first half of calendar year 2015.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Supervisory Board, Daimler AG
texts.text: The Energy sector in its current set-up, and you know we are going to change the set-up as of October 1, has  several legacy matters such as Olkiluoto, the North Sea project, and others which do pose further financial risk  potential going forward.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Supervisory Board, Daimler AG
texts.text: Thank you, Ben. Look, on the Power and Gas performance, I mean, it has a reason why we were mentioning the  sector specifically above and beyond the challenge – the ongoing challenges in Transmission, which is mostly  related to solutions, by the way. The transformer recovery is going well and restructuring shows first results. They  are truly also bright spots, but still that needs to be fixed to go back where we ought to be and where we have been.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Supervisory Board, Daimler AG
texts.text: Now, on the Power and Gas, it's a mix of a few items. We do expect order intake and top line still to be weak going  into 2015 out of the weakness in order intake in 2014 and in part even from 2013. Secondly, obviously the  European service environment is not set to improve at any given point in time, also in a way affected by, for  example, German energy policies, on continuing to subsidize wind and solar rather than look at the backup on  efficient gas. So, there might be some challenges here on the top line affecting the obviously highly profitable  service environment.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Supervisory Board, Daimler AG
texts.text: But the single most – the biggest impact on our guidance of 11% to 15% has been that we are going to invest  significantly in boosting our technical performance of the gas turbines all across the board because we believe that  at the end, competitiveness comes from innovation and efficiency. So there will be some investment in R&D and  engineering which obviously gets down the profitability for a period of time. So...

texts.speaker: Martin Wilkie
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Broker UK)
texts.text: Yeah, good morning. It's Martin at Deutsche Bank. Just a couple of questions, going back to Power Transmission.  You mentioned that it could take some time to fix some of these problems. I was wondering if you can put some  sort of framing around what you mean by some time, and whether or not from an engineering perspective, you  now know how to implement these projects and it's really factors outside your control, whether it be suppliers or  other things, that gives that uncertainty as to [indiscernible] (34:47).

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Supervisory Board, Daimler AG
texts.text: It's unfortunate, and we've seen it in Canada where we've been let down by most everyone who has been in the  area in terms of construction and soil removal and what have you. And we do see similar developments now in a  project in the UK.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: So first of all, we have been very intensively looking into the whole process and especially into the contract and  how much value-add can we really give in that project. So we found partners that are fully responsible for their  area of responsibility, means those parts which are not naturally driven by the electrification chain which we own.  So having taken all these learnings from the other four projects, we came to clear no-gos on the T&Cs.

texts.speaker: Olivier Esnou
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane Ltd.
texts.text: And also, when you mentioned the new structure of Energy going forward, you mentioned that it would be some  legacy projects in it. Obviously Olkiluoto, North Sea, plus others. And I just wanted to make sure that the others  were just a summary for what we already know -- UK, Canada and the like -- or if you have something in your  mind about new areas of risk that we haven't fully heard about yet.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Supervisory Board, Daimler AG
texts.text: Secondly, the legacy projects, I can also rest assure you, those are exactly the ones we meant. This is about the –  that's about Olkiluoto, that's about the North Sea, and that's also this Canadian/UK-type of high-voltage  substation turnkey project.

texts.speaker: James A. Moore
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Yes. Good morning, everyone. I've got three questions, if I could. On Power Transmission and Power Generation,  can you help us a little more understand the size of the risk profile for further charges into next year on North Sea,  LL3, and other?

texts.speaker: James A. Moore
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Secondly, on the underlying Energy margin you talk about the Power Generation challenges next year, but maybe  PT and Wind could be up. So the big question for me really is, overall 2015 underlying Energy profit, could that be  down?

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Supervisory Board, Daimler AG
texts.text: With Olkiluoto, for example, we are actually done with our conventional island, so it's not us anymore who holds  up the process. But as long as we don't have any steam, we cannot run our turbines. And that's the sort of issues,  what I'm kind of referring to.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Supervisory Board, Daimler AG
texts.text: But the likelihood that there's going to be earth-shattering news on this one is rather low. Same is true in the  North Sea. We have shipped them out, we are in the middle of commissioning. 80% of the total work of all those  four has already been completed. So that gives some comfort about what much can happen again.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Supervisory Board, Daimler AG
texts.text: On Wind, I mean the things we need to improve there are actually coming over on the positive side. We've been  very successful in developing our market share in offshore. We've been growing the business rapidly over the  years. Now we do see that the transformation from some, [indiscernible] (53:34) handcraft type of production to  industrial flow production takes some time. But we need to have this because productivity opportunities of the  essence to bring the cost curve, then we go back down.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Supervisory Board, Daimler AG
texts.text: So, now will the underlying Energy profit will be down in 2015, that's a very good question, and I ask you to bear  with me until we are done with 2014. And when we lay out the guidance for 2015, I'd be happy to come back to  this in more detail to see what the guidance would be for 2015. It's way too premature now because there's a lot of  opportunities and some risks which we need to quantify going forward.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: Member-Supervisory Board, Daimler AG
texts.text: Hi Gaël. On the vision, I believe your – I have a lot of sympathy for your assumption that during the significant  progress, the incremental risk or the residual risk is actually rather low compared to what we've seen in the past,  reason being that platforms have been shipped out. They have been adjusted to the place where they are going to  operate. And that's been the single-most compelling impact on those charges of this one – I think €120 million,  because we were dependent on the weather.

file: SIE - Q3 2015 Earnings Call 30July2015 300 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 30-Jul-15.pdf

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: First, we made a recent agreement with the workers' representatives for comprehensive measures to improve  productivity and simplify structures in the support function areas. Implementation of these measures across the  organization is now in full swing to drive our performance towards 2016 and onwards. In total, you'll recall the  €274 million severance charges, €173 million of which is in the industrial businesses. Negotiations with the  workers' representatives for the recently announced actions on footprint optimization as well as fixing the  underperforming businesses are in well-advanced stages.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Second, we strengthened our core and closed the Dresser-Rand acquisition, giving us a significantly strengthened  offering and footprint, in particular for distributed power generation, including the oil and gas industry.  Integration has started and initial customer feedback is very encouraging, although the depressed oil price  remains a concern in the short term.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Now let me highlight some key developments in the third quarter. The product and service business delivered  healthy order growth. However, compared to the same quarter a year ago, we saw some significant lower large  order volumes in Power and Gas, Wind Power as well as Process Industries and Drives, adding to an overall order  decline of 5% like-for-like.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Revenue was down about 3%, mainly driven by the project businesses, but Healthcare, Digital Factory and Energy  Management showed their strength in growing the business.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Now let me take a closer look at some key developments in the division and the Industrial Business. Power and  Gas is diligently implementing its growth and productivity program, PG 2020, to improve its market and cost  position by footprint optimization and accelerated innovation. The environment remains challenging with global  overcapacities and aggressive competitive behavior.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: In the third quarter, orders were down on tough comps due to fewer turnkey projects. However, we succeeded  well in the market by selling 17 large gas turbines particularly through increased demand in the United States as  well as in Mexico.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Wind Power managed to swing to profit and delivered a margin of 3.6% including a strong contribution from the  service business. We expect the fourth quarter to be very robust in terms of orders, since we have already booked  some of those orders in July.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: We like what we see on this slide with a lot of green color and I'm talking about Energy Management. The division  reached a profit margin of 3.7%, making steady progress across the businesses. The restructuring program,  Transform to Win, is well on track and will drive underlying profitability going forward in the quarters to come.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Process Industries and Drives faced lower volume from large orders from tough comps and ongoing weak demand  from commodity-related industries including metals and mining as well as oil and gas. Margins came back nicely  Q2 over Q3 towards the lower end of the target range. The challenges in oil and gas and other verticals remain in  place and, therefore, further measures to optimize the footprint and to reduce cost are underway.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Hi, James. Quite a spree of questions. On pricing environment, the good news is it's unchanged. The other news is  that, yes, there are pockets of aggressive behavior in the market, mostly due to overcapacities in areas such as  large turbines. In parts, you also do see some pressure on the imaging field. On the other hand, I think we can well  handle the issue on imaging, and we're doing what we have been describing on the power turbine environment.

texts.speaker: Andreas Willi
texts.profession: JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: Good morning, everybody. I have two questions on Energy, please. The first one, if you could elaborate on your  strategy regarding Shanghai Electric, your partner in various energy businesses. You recently sold some shares in  the listed Shanghai Electric company, Shanghai invested in Ansaldo and may also get into the gas business more if  Alstom has to dispose some of the assets to them as speculated recently. So, how do you plan to work with them  going forward now that they become more of a direct competitor?

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: On Shanghai Electric, look, the disposal of shares doesn't really have anything to do with the strategic outline of  the business. We've been working together for a very long time as a partner. We continue to work together in the  area of steam and wind. As you know, we actually have been streamlining our wind value chain together with  them, make sure we are more effective in the market. That's been done now, and you can already see that this  group's much better than it used to.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: So, Joe has already been elaborating on the microenvironment. So the growth dynamics for the global industrial  production has been weakening during the last month; you could also see that from what our competitors have  been perceiving in that area. So, there are currently no indications that it will significantly gain momentum in the  short term. So, our expectations still remain cautious on an overall picture.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: China, growth momentum of industrial production remains soft; as said before, especially investment-driven  industries like machinery show weak growth only. In the U.S., the consequences of the oil price plunge appear  stronger in the recent production data that we saw, as originally expected. So, especially parts of machinery are  under pressure, while motor vehicles, automotive, remains stable. And we expect that growth dynamics will  remain slow but still impact in the U.S.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Europe, dynamic is currently on a slight upward path and should continue to gain a bit of positive momentum  from low interest rates and weak euro support. However, environment remains fragile there also for political  tensions as you have been hearing before. So, Germany's key industries still are on a modest growth path, but  there are no significant opportunities deriving from the global environment in short term. So, that's our view.

texts.speaker: Fredric Stahl
texts.profession: UBS AG (Sweden)
texts.text: And then secondly, on Renewables, or Wind, how should we think about the comparable growth rate in the  coming quarters? I mean, we've had two quarters now weak revenues, but I still think you have a pretty sizable  backlog. So a bit of help there would be welcome. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: For the mid-term, focus is on innovating the onshore turbine environment. Siemens, as you know, has been quite  strong in offshore – actually, very strong, with some shortcomings on onshore that's been historically developed  out of where we come from. And we've been spending quite an effort on the onshore flow wind technology, where  we're making quite what I believe decent progress comparing that with the environment. So, that's where the  focus is.

texts.speaker: Peter Reilly
texts.profession: Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: Good morning. I've got two questions, please, both on Power and Gas. Firstly, can you give us a bit more color on  the €106 million of project charges? This is obviously an older project. We have been going through a period of  much lower project charges. So, is this just a sort of one-off accident from the past or is there something we should  be concerned about in the backlog for Power and Gas?

texts.speaker: Peter Reilly
texts.profession: Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: And then secondly, I was pleasantly surprised by the order intake in Power and Gas, book/bill of 1.1x. You've made  a few comments that the large project business has been weak, but also you've been selling some more gas  turbines. So, maybe you can talk about the quality of the backlog in Power and Gas and whether you're having to  offer competitive prices to have this rate of book/bill or whether you've actually got a decent quality backlog  because it's more small ticket items and, therefore, a bit less price competitive than the larger projects.

texts.speaker: James A. Moore
texts.profession: Redburn (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Firstly, the oil price is now nearly back to $50. Could you help us with the outlook for margins next year for the  Process and Power and Gas businesses? Now with Rolls and Dresser, the old oil and gas is nearly half of Power  and Gas and I'm just wondering whether we should expect margins to progress in 2016 or decline. I know you  have internal actions but I guess there's book-to-bill short lead-time business that could continue to suffer from  the oil environment.

texts.speaker: Gaël De Bray
texts.profession: SG Securities (Paris) SAS
texts.text: The first one is for the Energy Management division. With all four North Sea grid connection platforms now  delivered to the client, I guess visibility has improved for that business. So, what do you need to get back to the 7%  to 10% margin range at Energy Management?

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Hi, Gaël. On Energy Management, there is obviously quite a visibility because obviously has mostly large projects  if it comes to transmission. There is much lesser visibility if you go to areas like low voltage and the likes because  that's a more distribution-driven business. So, it's a mixed basket. We understand that some competitors which  are more in the transmission area have their comment, but if it comes to our Energy Management, it's a mix  between distribution and transmission, and first of all, that's important to know.

texts.speaker: Gaël De Bray
texts.profession: SG Securities (Paris) SAS
texts.text: Well, the first question was for Energy Management and whether the 7% [ph] was on margin range [indiscernible]  (53:14).

file: SIE - Q3 2016 Earnings Call 4August2016 345 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 04-Aug-16.pdf

texts.speaker: Sabine Reichel
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations
texts.text: Above and beyond our operational strengths and reliable execution, we will further accelerate our innovation  excellence and strengthen our portfolio in smart ways. In June, we announced the planned merger of the  Siemens Wind Power business and Gamesa. We intend to own 59% of the merged entity. We do have  substantial growth potential, highly complementary strength and a strong value proposition towards our customers  to help them get their cost down and revenues up.

texts.speaker: Sabine Reichel
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations
texts.text: Industrial profit margin was at 10%, up 130 basis points year-over-year, with hardly any support from FX for the  company. Eight out of nine divisions are in the target margin range, with margin expansion in most divisions ,  particularly in Power and Gas, Energy Management and Wind Power.

texts.speaker: Sabine Reichel
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations
texts.text: We shipped 16 large gas turbines in the quarter, among those 7 H-class turbines. Our Egypt megaproject is  progressing well as planned, with 11 H-class turbines and 11 generators already at the foundation on site. This  ramp up was a major driver for a convincing revenue growth of 22% in the quarter. However, we expect revenue  growth to soften in the fourth quarter on tougher comparables in the divisions. As already mentioned, Wind Power  has taken in major orders including a €1.4 billion order from the Beatrice Offshore Windfarm in the UK. The  division increased its backlog to almost €16 billion. Strong backlog conversion and good service turns drove  revenue growth in both onshore and offshore.

texts.speaker: Sabine Reichel
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations
texts.text: With €1.7 billion, we achieved the highest quarterly revenue ever in the wind business. The division is making  excellent progress in optimizing its supply chain and pushing for productivity on all levels. This and the better mix  help to drive the profit range beyond the target margin range to 8.3%. I would have to say the Wind Power team  has built a very solid performance track record and is ready for contributing a strong business into the world's  strongest wind enterprise together with Gamesa.

texts.speaker: Sabine Reichel
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations
texts.text: We also like what we see from the Energy Management team who executed well on their plan and continue to  improve performance across most businesses, in particular transmission solutions and high-voltage products.  Also like the progress of the transformer business, which has been one of the, what we called, underperforming  businesses in the space. There's a profit margin of 8.3%. Energy Management is back on the target range and we  now expect the division to be in that range also for the full year in 2016 and counting.

texts.speaker: Sabine Reichel
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations
texts.text: The negotiations with the employee representatives regard to planned capacity adjustments and footprint  alignments are progressing reasonably well, and we do see a good chance to have an agreement by year-end  already.

texts.speaker: Andreas Willi
texts.profession: JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: Yes. Good morning, Joe, Ralf and Sabine. My first question is on Wind Power, which had another good quarter  ahead of the deal with Gamesa. Did it already benefit from the adjustment to the structural costs, basically the  reduction in cost you allocate to that business on real estate and other matters, or was it just an underlying  improvement? And if it's the second, then it looks like the Gamesa side gets a much better deal in terms of the  much higher Siemens profitability you contribute to the asset to the combined company.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO
texts.text: Hi, Andreas. Let me, maybe, quickly go to Wind Power. Obviously, the team has been doing its job there in  getting the supply chain in order and drive productivity. We also introduced the new generations of turbines in  both offshore as well as onshore, so that is a good underlying improvement. We also mentioned that there's been  a structural mix also contributing to the improvements, so it's been a bit of both.

texts.speaker: Ben E. Uglow
texts.profession: Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Yes. Good morning, Joe, Ralf and Sabine. I think probably a few of the questions are going to be quite similar  around the phasing and getting to the backlog conversion in energy. I guess my question is similar to Andreas's. If  we strip Egypt out, you've actually had some very significant order wins outside. So even in the quarter, I look at  the U.S., [ph] H-frame (23:11), Israel, Bolivia, China. And my question is as we look forward into 2017, ex the  Egypt effect, should we be thinking that this business is growing mid-single digit, low-single digit, high-single digit?  Can you give us a frame of reference for thinking about the fossil power business revenue conversion or the  backlog conversion into 2017? So that's issue number one.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Yeah. Thank you, Ben. Let me start with the last part or the second question you have been raising. I mean if you  take exchange rate of the equation, I mean we had a very strong quarter in China in terms of growth rates when it  comes to Power and Gas, but also Energy Management has been benefiting a lot. So, these two were  outstanding, if you will, in terms of growth rates. So, Joe has been commenting already that the equipment  business in our Healthineers business has been developing quite nicely, highest teens. And also, Building  Technology has been picking quite favorably with double-digit growth rate.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: So, therefore, most of these projects that we have been winning lately in the Power and Gas space will have their  impact on next fiscal year. But bear in mind that the strong margin service portion will most likely kick in at a later  point in time than fiscal 2017.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: And with regards to what do we expect for 2017, just roughly in terms of giving you an understanding of what we  expect in the relevant backlogs being converted in PG, Wind Power and Mobility, that is in the area of 20%, yeah.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: On top of that, there always needs to be short-term book-and-bill projects that roll over into revenue fairly quickly.  And I have been mentioning the service contracts in most of these major deals anyway. So, in total, next fiscal  year will benefit from project business in that field, but that also means that the revenue mix is going into the  direction of Wind Power, Energy Management, Mobility and PG.

texts.speaker: Peter Reilly
texts.profession: Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: Secondly, on the Wind business, you've had two quarters of very strong growth and we were told at the Capital  Markets Day, you've been deliberately holding back the growth rate because you had a lot of efficiency and  supply chain issues to work through. I'm just wondering, with the record backlog, whether we're now, if we ignore  Gamesa for a second, at the start of a period of much stronger growth as you can convert the backlog more  quickly.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Thank you, Peter. Let me start with BT. I mean, when we talk projects in BT, this is not close to being comparable  to other projects like we have them in Energy Management and the like. So, BT is very selective in projects and,  therefore, very well balancing between service, product and project business in terms of solutions. They do that  on a very selective basis and very balanced, as I said. I don't – I would not expect any incremental risk being  derived from the fact that growth in the third quarter was driven by that, the project in that particular quarter. Of  course, this is a result of quite a long preparational phase, and it very much depends on when they are mature for  signing. So, I wouldn't call that untypical. It just happens to be quite condensed in the third quarter.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: With regards to Wind Power and the second quarter in a row with really very impressive results, I think you have  been hitting the nail there. It is about conversion and utilization of the existing capacities. And for quite some  times, we have been reporting back to you guys that they are still in the late stage of industrialization of their value  chains. They get – they have been getting a firmer and firmer grip around those areas, including in and outbound  logistics, which are playing a major role in that field as you can imagine.

texts.speaker: Simon Toennessen
texts.profession: Joh. Berenberg, Gossler & Co. KG (United Kingdom)
texts.text: And the last question on Process and Drives, I mean with the oil price back in the low $40s, and we've heard quite  a lot of management teams at this quarterly results season talking about no oil and gas demand recovery before  the second half of next year, and thus this could be for you even the first quarter of your fiscal 2018. How do you  feel about the current cost measures you're doing in PD, obviously in relation to you getting back into the margin  corridor? If I just do my math on the additional headcounts you're doing, I'm still not quite getting there in terms of  the bottom end of the margin guidance that you're trying to achieve for in terms of the profits that we need to  achieve. Just a bit more clarity there would be very helpful. Thank you very much.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO
texts.text: So, the third one is PLM piece, so product lifecycle management, and this now is mostly about decisions. And  that's what the whole method is all about today in discrete factories. The whole world is not so much about CapEx  and expansion. It is about efficiency, gaining efficiency, gaining productivity, gaining energy efficiency. And that's  why the PLM piece is starting to take off so much even in countries and regions where one would have said well,  you know, on a scale from industry 1.0 to industry 4.0, they are just making the transition maybe from 1 to 2.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO
texts.text: On the question earlier of CD-adapco. That's mostly also to discrete car manufacturing. You might remember  when we talked about a deal, about the time of announcements, almost 70% is car industry. It's flow control and  air flow optimization. So, that's actually similar customers but different labs. And that's actually the beauty of it. So  we are combining the bits and pieces, the silos, so to speak, of that industry into a totally integrated automation  portal. And that's what Siemens is what up to and all about. So, we do win new customers and we do win new  orders on the back of completing our spectrum. And that's what we are continuing to work on.

file: SIE - Q3 2017 Earnings Call 3August2017 400 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 03-Aug-17.pdf

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: For example, we were rewarded the order for the DolWin6 offshore grid connection from TenneT. Free cash flow  of €941 million was below prior year mainly due to the net working capital build-up at Siemens Gamesa.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: As indicated, Power and Gas continues to operate in a very challenging environment with declining markets. This  resulted in a sharply lower large order volume in the third quarter. In addition, the demand from oil and gas  customers is still sluggish. The fight for every single order is really fierce, and we see continued price pressure  due to over capacities. Lower order intake in previous quarters led to a revenue decrease of 11% particularly in  large gas turbine and compression businesses.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Combined with lower capacity utilization, this resulted in a margin decline of 140 basis points. Key focus of PG is  on adjusting their cost space, driving productivity, innovation and project execution. Our philosophy is to deliver  on our commitment. A good example is the Megaproject in Egypt where all 24 gas turbines have been delivered  within the agreed timeframe.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Already 12 gas turbines are in regular operation. After we had to catch up in turbine efficiency in the past years,  we are gaining now speed to drive technological upgrades and competitiveness. We improve our entire fleet with  new coatings, new materials, additive manufacturing and digital solutions to optimize output and life cycle cost.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: The HL family is paving the way to the next-generation of gas turbines entering into new performance levels north  of 63% with a clear roadmap to 65%. In this context, Duke Energy and Siemens have entered into a strategic  partnership to test and validate advanced gas turbine technologies.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Orders in the quarter were slightly down on tough comps in the transformer business. However, we expect a  strong order intake in the fourth quarter among others driven by the recently announced DolWin6 offshore grid  connection project with TenneT.

texts.speaker: Michael Sen
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: I'm going to spend a few moments to share some first conclusions and to give you an update on the areas that I  have responsibility for overseas. One area is Global Services, which encompasses IT, real estate, supply chain  management, and shared services. IT, for example, is a very crucial function, particularly when you look at  digitally transforming the enterprise and stirring up organizational agility. The two other areas are our Healthcare  business, Siemens Healthineers, and our renewable interest in Siemens Gamesa Renewable Energy.

texts.speaker: Michael Sen
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: It is primarily Siemens Healthineers and Siemens Gamesa Renewable Energy that I will be focusing on today.

texts.speaker: Michael Sen
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: We also continue to strengthen our portfolio with bolt-on M&A; the recent agreement to acquire Epocal from Alere  will make Siemens Healthineers the only company that covers blood-gas analysis from high volume, all bench-top  analyzers, all the way down to handhelds.

texts.speaker: Michael Sen
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: Now, let me move to Siemens Gamesa Renewable Energy. Last week, we have all seen the numbers and let me  be very clear from the outset, the business did not live up to its potential. As the major shareholder, our  expectation towards the leadership is clear. We expect a leading position in the industry and sustainable value  enhancement of our interest in the company.

texts.speaker: Michael Sen
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: As I've gained experience in this industry from the customer/utility side, I can tell you that there are three things  that are decisive to win in this market. First, it's cost. Second, it's cost. And third, it's cost. To be precise, it's the  cost for megawatt hour of electricity.

texts.speaker: Michael Sen
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: The question is who is most efficient in reducing the levelized cost of electricity more significantly and faster. The  Dutch Borssele offshore developments provide a case in point. DONG Energy, won the auction with a bid far  below the previous benchmark of €100 per megawatt hour. A few weeks ago, DONG Energy issued an awarded  letter for Borssele 1 and 2 to Siemens Gamesa 750-megawatt project, which makes me personally very happy. I  had also looked into this project from the utility side. And therefore, I'm particularly happy on this customer win.

texts.speaker: Michael Sen
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: Important initial integration steps have been announced. The combined organization is taking shape, portfolio  decisions are being taken. As an example, we expect to hear more about Adwen in the near future. Footprint  decisions are being prepared and taken such as the closing of the Tillsonburg blade factory in Canada.

texts.speaker: Michael Sen
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: To sum up, we put Siemens Gamesa Renewable Energy on track to win in the changing renewable market. And  they have the independence, size, scale, and financial strength to do so. Now, it's all about execution.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, Thank you, Andreas, for the question. Let me begin before I hand over to Michael for Siemens Gamesa with  the PG question you're raising. What I said and what is something we, of course, have been thinking about  diligently and more than onetime is that for PG, as we go, we see them in very challenging environment. We also  see that from the competitors' figures being disclosed that this is not only on us. So, the pressure of the market  will not go away any time soon, that's for sure. In particular, when it comes to the large gas turbines, therefore, we  determined to do two things. I mean, first of all, we of course, are taking cost out and making sure that productivity  is making good as much as possible for that challenging market situation.

texts.speaker: Michael Sen
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, this is a markets-driven topic and not a company-driven topic. And therefore, it is obviously attributable to  onshore, which is part of what have been Gamesa in the past, but that also doesn't make sense because today  it's Siemens Gamesa Renewable Energy. And if you look at the profit margin and the makeup of the profit margin  the 6.1%, is what we would call an underlying and it was held up – held back from transaction and M&A related  costs in the neighborhood of 130 basis points which would indicate to a margin of 7.4%.

texts.speaker: Michael Sen
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: Now on offshore, I think the management also commented publicly that went very nice and I even gave you a  precursor, which not in the order intake yet, the award letter from DONG Energy on Borssele 1 and 2.

texts.speaker: Mark Troman
texts.profession: Analyst, Merrill Lynch International
texts.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Good morning, Ralf, Michael, Sabine, and Joe for getting back for us. Thank you very  much. Firstly, a question on Process and Power divisions. I guess if we look at this quarter, it's quite clear,  obviously, Power and Gas, I guess, was flat, but Process Industries looked a bit weaker than perhaps many of us  thought and Energy Management as well, of course. What is the capacity – across those divisions, how quickly  can Siemens adjust its cost base or remedy if you like some of the margin shortfall? How quickly can that be  implemented is question number one.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: On EM, Energy Management, Q3 has been a bit of in the mixed topics. So, I would not expect that to continue. I  actually expect the division to finish strong in Q4. I always want them to be a billionaire on underlying profit, and  it's about time to deliver. So, I would actually tick that off as a temporary matter going forward. The more structural  topic which needs much more reflection on is the Power Generation market, especially in the larger segment of  the industry.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: There is an ongoing trend that the turbines, the 500 megawatts are a market which is actually on it's down  trending. We do seek decent potential on the mid-sized elements, which goes along with the distributed energy  story, which also is driven by renewables.

texts.speaker: Simon Toennessen
texts.profession: Analyst, Joh. Berenberg, Gossler & Co. KG (United Kingdom)
texts.text: Secondly, I'd just like to get your thoughts a bit more on the long-term positioning in Power and Gas and I guess,  to a certain degree, in Energy Management as well and your positioning here. I think it seems probably pretty  clear that over the next, let's say, five years, storage solutions, micro grids are going to take up quite significantly  here probably at the expense of large gas turbine investments.

texts.speaker: Simon Toennessen
texts.profession: Analyst, Joh. Berenberg, Gossler & Co. KG (United Kingdom)
texts.text: So, how do you see your positioning in this equation? Do you need to invest a lot more significantly into storage?  Do you need to do more partnerships? Also, what could be the financial impact here for the overall Power and  Gas division? I think your U.S. competitor talked about on the call or at least didn't rule out the large gas turbine  market to decline again in 2018. So, just how we see that whole equation in this business. Thank you.  Josef Kaeser  President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG  A  So, let me start with the Digital Factory, Simon. I mean, the good news is and therefore I can be brief, it was really  a broad-based growth momentum that we saw in the portfolio of Digital Factory, I have been commenting already  on the impressive growth rates for our software business, PL, with China and neighborhood really leading in that  environment with a growth rate of more than 23% and the U.S. double digits, European environment 8% up and  Germany 5% up. We also have been reflecting the fact that there was a heavy focus in the software business on  license, more than 20% which is also quite attractive in terms of margins.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: So on the long-term positioning, on power generation in a broader sense, I mean, you remember when we laid  out Vision 2020, we said that the power market is going to change. We do expect that the amount of large  turbines will go down, and it's more about flexibility centralized energy systems based on renewable and a flexible  backup pico system.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: So what that – this has actually been materializing now. We did discuss it at a time when many others said that  amount of gas turbines are going through the roof in the future. So just for the record. Then, what we've been  building was the Energy Management division which is transmission distribution and smart grids around it. The  reason why we did that – including, by the way, storage. The reason why we did it, we said that if we have a  multiple source of energy coming from many different sources like wind and sun and others, the stress is going to  go to the grid.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: So the grid management and distribution management will be of the essence in decentralized system. As I see  Michael nodding from his former life at the utility company. So that's what the purpose of Energy Management is  all about going forward, to build exactly that ecosystem.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: And that's what the long-term positioning will be. So, this is about a symbiotic solution and ecosystem of smaller  turbines for pico systems. It's about storage which will be the ultimate goal. And this will be a smart grid energy  management based on distribution and perhaps, of course, also the grid because there will still be high voltage  lines needed if the water or the wind and the sun is in a different place, then the demand for power is actually in  the end.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, very clear strategic alignment as to what we see happening, and this will also go along with product and  solution development. There is no need for inorganic major areas there, definitely not. We do see there are some  areas where we need to be mindful about if it comes to the sun as one of the major areas of renewable energies.  But in terms of how we position ourselves from decentralized, we have very clear view on what needs to be done  in the mid- and the long-term.

texts.speaker: Martin Wilkie
texts.profession: Analyst, Citigroup Global Markets Ltd.
texts.text: Yes. Thank you. Good morning. It's Martin at Citi. The first question coming back to the Power and Gas business.  You talked about service still having a robust model. And, obviously, you talked about some of the paradigm  changes inside large gas as it relates to the OE business. There are some concerns that, over time, as gas is  utilized less, particularly in Europe that that's also going to be a drag on servicing. I'm just wondering if you could  comment about – if you do see a sort of paradigm shift in the service of your installed base or if you feel that can  be robust for the foreseeable future.

texts.speaker: James Alexander Moore
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And finally, thanks, Joe, very much for your comments on Power Service, very helpful on the next 18 to 24  months. I wonder if you could just shed some simple light on how the revenue growth is developing in service at  the moment, because one of your – or your U.S. peer talked about planned outages being down high single digits  as gas turbine utilization has fallen with the increased intermittency associated with renewable bigger turbines  and I wonder whether you see that gap between service shutdown stretching, whether that's an issue for the  business or really not an issue at all?

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: On power gen, I mean if we talk about bookings of a quarter, this is always a very short period of time in terms of  long-term project assets. So, therefore, I believe, you'll see it in a more broader content for a year or maybe rolling  four quarters.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, we've seen a few delays on projects which are actually due out to come. What you also do see is there is  actually quite decent demand in some areas of the world which needs power, yet due to fiscal policy constraints  associated – among other things, associated with the oil price, less income on the budget is quite a few push-outs  in some areas. It's only a matter of time till they come, so we may as well, at some point in time, see some sort of  a peak because things need to be finally done. But the trend – the general trend definitely goes into the south  direction, I would say, around 120, 130 of larger turbines, which we consider to be above 100 megawatt. And  that's what we obviously are well aware of.

texts.speaker: Daniela Carlos Rodrigues Costa
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: And then the second thing on sort of the upcoming nuclear closures in Germany and the big connections, north to  south, the so-called Sudlink project, if you are seeing already some activity for that and what are your  expectations for that?

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Sure. And on the third one, Daniela, what is it about the transitional lines from north to south?

texts.speaker: Daniela Carlos Rodrigues Costa
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: Yeah, yeah. No, it was about the upcoming – the nuclear plant closures in Germany and there is this project to  connect the sources in the north...

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Yeah. Then, we got it right, so I just want to make sure that I'm not answering a different question. Well, that's  imminent because there's a lot of affordable-type electricity being produced in the south, and there is a lot of wind- produced electricity in the north and still some conventional power plants in the east, northeast such as still coal- fired steam. And they all really need to be connected, obviously renewable being volatile, so there's got to be  some backup on fossil which, so far, people have chosen to use coal-fired ones. That may not prevail in the long- term, but that's what we need to take in the next five years. So, the answer is yes, those lines are being built.  There are still some debate about where exactly they need to be because, obviously, out of legal and regulatory  matters, but this is a viable project.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Actually, a series of projects because there is a north – south link that is a middle corridor to connect the east into  the grid and there need to be some sort of backup grid capacity if the wind blows in the north and the sun shines  in the south. There is excess capacity which needs to be held in the grid, which comes back to what I said earlier  about the importance of energy management on grid and distribution.

texts.speaker: William Mackie
texts.profession: Analyst, Kepler Cheuvreux SA (UK)
texts.text: Yes. Good morning and thank you very much for taking the questions. Just some follow-ups really. Within Power  and Gas, could you give us a sense of where you see the demand cycle developing within your oil and gas  business which is nearly a third of activities? And within P&G staying there, to what extent is there a necessity  against a weaker longer-term outlook for large turbines to adjust the capacities in the business?

texts.speaker: William Mackie
texts.profession: Analyst, Kepler Cheuvreux SA (UK)
texts.text: And then, lastly, within Energy Management, it's good to have the confidence that you hope to be close to €1  billion for the year underlying. But are you able to throw some more color on the development between the  projects business typically in high voltage versus the performance of the medium or low voltage business within  the division? Thank you very much.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Yeah, with regard, where are we on the demand cycle, in particular in the oil and gas related environment, I  mean, it's obvious that each and every quarter of the last year has been looking like hitting rock bottom, and then  it wasn't. So we need to be careful in that one.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: All right. That brings us back to the topic of Energy Management. If you look at what we expect the business to be  in the fourth quarter in terms of, like, bookings, we do expect strong order intake, obviously, in the solutions area  since we have already been announcing the DolWin project. We also expect some strength in mid-voltage and  the transformer environment. That's how we see the growth coming in fiscal Q4 on bookings of EM which we  expect to be meaningfully double-digit.
