texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, Siemens AG
texts.text: Okay, maybe I'll start with the pressure – pricing matters. Obviously, we've got four sectors. And we had about 3%  on average last year and expect that to be slightly less, I mean, obviously, it's not that big of a difference to be  between 2.5% and 2.8%. I also said earlier that we do not expect an improvement or benefit in Energy and  Healthcare. Those markets remain to be extremely competitive. So, that should not be a sign here that Energy like,  for example, Transmission or Wind would be any easier to sell and to win as it was in 2011.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: And James, on the Fossil, the 45% of the incremental growth, I mean it's clear that we are benefiting from the  breadth of our Energy portfolio and I would say across the board, there will be growth. But obviously, in terms of  – if you start, for example, with what Joe was just highlighting, the importance of building installed base for the  Fossil business, so continue to build market share and be successful in the Fossil area is a very important one. This  then as a consequence will then drive service growth going forward.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: The Renewable business is a very important one with, at this point in time, quite different dynamics between  Wind and Solar. Wind, the opportunity right now is to industrialize and to globalize or to regionalize the business  extremely well and the Solar business is currently impacted by the overall environment, what we see in terms of  cuts or subsidies and the uncertainty what we see. But medium term, it will be an interesting business  opportunity, when we talk about the transmission, HVDC, so the oil and gas. I mean they are nascent fields in  there, which we will continue to drive subsea electrification, for example, is a very interesting area for us.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, there is current strong businesses and then there are very specific technology areas, which we will continue to  drive and to build. But overall, across the spectrum of Energy, I mean the energy demand will double. Is – the  question is, will it be in 2030, or it will be in 2040? And there is no other company who has the comprehensive  portfolio what we have and this is what we leverage in terms of footprint, also global footprint and take advantage  of it.

texts.speaker: Daniela Costa
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you. Two questions, one regarding the change in the prepayments profile, the slight negative headwind that  is on page 11. Does this in any sense comes as a reflex of actually the regional mix changing and customers in  emerging regions being less willing to give large prepayments? And the second question on Transmission, the  German electricity regulator has been stressing that the upgrade of the grid is quite urgent. What is the timeline  you see in terms of that upgrade actually coming through in terms of orders and could that be beneficiary to  pricing in any sense? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, Siemens AG
texts.text: Well, look, upsides are always welcome, but by the same token, we only can take it very seriously once they have  arrived as orders. So, I would not jump too quickly to positive conclusions. This is opportunity and those  opportunities are needed in Transmission. There is – it has been for quite some time, some oversupply, some  weakness in transformers and also some very competitive pricing environments in substations, so that segment  definitely would need some incremental demand which ease the minds of the suppliers.  So, we welcome any insight and any way of the regulator understanding that energy generation is something, but  it also needs to be put to where it is needed, and that means the industry. So, of course, we support it. We have the  solutions and we definitely like to hear that. But then again, it has not arrived in any pre-order discussions at this  time. But the sentiment is positive.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, Siemens AG
texts.text: That also, by the way, is true due to the fact that if you want to have renewable energy like Wind, that just happens  to be the north of Europe but most of the energy is needed in the south of Europe. So, there's a natural follow- through to that question on how we generate energy for Germany in the future. And that's relevant to  Transmission.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, what do I mean with that? For example, if we participate in equity for wind parks or likes, that will help  finance the project. That will help basically that we get incremental orders, so what we do is we look into the risk  assessment of the financial logic as any financial or decently run and controlled financial institution does and then  we combine what the incremental gross margin on the order looks like and look at what the risk and opportunity  profile is.

texts.speaker: James A. Moore
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn Partners LLP
texts.text: And secondly, on Fossil, your first nine-month margin of 22.5% dropped 700 basis points to 15.5% in the fourth  quarter and you signaled that there would be some impact there, but I wondered if you could help us a little  understand what proportion service was of sales in the quarter versus the first nine months? And how much of  that first nine-month margin was provision release? Because I suspect there's an element of that in there.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, Siemens AG
texts.text: There is enough time to correct matters if the environment changes or think about the incremental OpEx, which  actually has been slightly accelerating as compared to the OpEx spend in 2011. The beauty of that is, it's still a  plan. So, if we, for example, see some incremental front end here, we still can say, well, we are not just growing  like that. Maybe we get a little slower. It's much better than you have to correct your cost structure because that  usually costs you twice at the time when you decided, it means restructuring. So, that's something we, of course,  we always keep in mind as we move along because all the times are uncertain.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, Siemens AG
texts.text: On Fossil, obviously, we have been continuously saying that those margins which we really liked a lot because they  were different a few years ago have included kind of an over-performance as we call it of about 300 plus base  points. That came in part from the release of some reserves that we didn't dare to be that optimistic on our  execution, and it also was like a real good [audio gap] (01:29:28) beyond our contingencies, which we have been  planning in the order intake calculation. So, that will be the 350 base points. We really look forward to see that  again, but obviously, this is something we do not calculate with and, at some point in time, this will normalize on  that area.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, Siemens AG
texts.text: And the Q4 impact, which was somewhat light, was predominantly due to the fact that we do see now that much in  seasonal impact for the Service business which happens at times, especially during the summer season, when the  utilities need every kilowatt in order to cool down the houses. They don't let your service guy into the turbines and  that, obviously, took its toll on the combined margins.

texts.speaker: Jay Cooper
texts.profession: Analyst, Wellington Shields & Co Llc
texts.text: Jay Cooper is my name with Wellington Shields in New York. I have a question about your Renewables business,  what I see is sort of a competition arising between PV Solar and what you've concentrated most of your efforts on,  it seems to me, the Concentrating Solar, CSP. So, I find in talking with your people recently at industry  conferences that you have formed a new vertically integrated sales organization to contact – to drive specifically  PV Solar business. And I'm wondering where this is going? How important it is? Does it mean that you're trying to  balance CSP versus PV Solar in your portfolio? And that's about it, if you can answer that. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Jay, if I give you – I mean obviously we looked a couple of years back also in terms of how do we see the different  technologies. We at that point thought that actually CSP has an advantage because we have the storage facility and  actually we did not anticipate the price level what we currently see with PV. So, if you just looked in the last two  years in terms of the glut which exist in terms of PV, the PV capacity, which is installed and the demand which is  currently happening, there's obviously a massive price decline on PV. So, the – we believe both technologies are  viable going forward. It will be in different applications.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: In some instances, obviously, when you go for big, big megawatt plants, the CSB has clearly its advantage but it  has to be developed, and most recently, we have seen that even CSB projects are converted back into PV, for  example, in the United States. And the overall environment is such that both technologies are currently seeing a  slowdown because we see the subsidy picture around the world being more constrained and the tax incentives are  coming down. So, it will be very important to reach wholesale grid parity in terms of – and I think at this point in  time, this is not a mature technology field. So, as a company, you have to basically make a couple of technology  bets and then at the end of the day, we will see which applications with which technology will actually increase  further.

texts.speaker: Olivier Esnou
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you, Olivier Esnou, Exane BNP Paribas. Two questions. I'd like to have a feel for the flexibility you have in  AIDT, can you give us an idea of the use of temporary worker you have right now, please? And secondly, on the  Renewable business, Wind and Solar, it's difficult to see why the performance should improve next year from  where I stand. Can you give us some comfort of – I mean, basically what you're looking for, and what we should  wait for, is it an improvement from here? I mean on an underlying basis, of course, if we exclude the write-down,  should it get better or is it more likely to get worse next year? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, Siemens AG
texts.text: Then on the Renewable, I mean, obviously, the Solar matter has been discussed now back and forth and over  backwards, so let me focus on Wind. The Wind Energy is in the middle of becoming a global Industrial business,  that's been moving from a handcraftsmanship with a few limited areas into a broadly accepted means of  renewable sources. There's been a lot – a lot of new market entrants. There have been a lot of incumbents which  have been struggling along when capacities were shooting up and when prices were coming down and we see that  continuing.

texts.speaker: Colin N. Campbell
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA (UK)
texts.text: Hello, yes, it's Colin Campbell at SocGen. Just given that you've highlighted your very under-leveraged balance  sheet and sort of require to be maybe more shareholder friendly given the D rating, when might you consider  special dividends or share buybacks in this climate, please?

file: SIE - Q4 2012 Earnings Call 8November2012 930 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 08-Nov-12.pdf

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: However, let me start with a couple of key takeaways and financials of the fourth quarter of 2012. Orders were  moderately down by 4% year-over-year due to continued softness of the global economy impacting many of our  businesses, while Energy boasted organic growth due to a large number of orders, mainly in Fossil and Wind  Power. Revenue growth eased to 1% year-over-year, driven by strong backlog conversion in Energy and strength in  Healthcare.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Mostly due to the strong operational finish in the fourth quarter and positive impacts from below the fixed items,  we reached the lower end of our guidance for the full year. Revenue growth for the fiscal 2012 reached 3%, while  the book-to-bill ratio was at 0.98. Income from continuing operations came in at €5.2 billion, including significant  adverse effects from legal and regulatory on the lower right-hand side of the charts, and benefiting from  discontinuing the Solar business.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: The underlying business in Fossil and Oil & Gas was again healthy, with a strong product and service business. I'm  sure you saw our announcement with regard to the planned divestment of the Solar business, and therefore we are  reporting only Wind numbers instead of renewable, and moved our Solar activities to discontinued operations as  of Q4. Our Hydro activities, mainly the equity share in Voith Siemens Hydro, are now held at the Sector Energy  level.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Diagnostics is on schedule with its competitiveness program, while profitability was temporarily slightly lower. In  its short-cycle businesses, Industry delivered a solid performance in an increasingly volatile market. We are  cautious for the next quarter since we currently see a cooling down in important end markets such as automotive  and machine tool builders. Profitability was weaker due to the renewable offerings of the sector, such as wind  gearboxes and solar inverters. The sector took action to adjust capacities and optimize the portfolio in this area.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Industry is also rigorously executing on further focusing its portfolio with the acquisition of the Belgium software  company, LMS International, and the subsequent divestment of the Water business, which I will touch upon in a  few minutes in more detail.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Let's move on to Infrastructure & Cities. Orders were down on a lower volume of large rolling stock orders, while  revenues were supported by strength in Americas. Profit margins saw in particular in the Power Grid Solutions &  Products business a nice upswing supported by strong earnings conversion from higher volume in low and  medium voltage. Building Technologies delivered again a seasonal strong profitability, driven by good demand for  its energy-saving solution and positive impact from cost reduction actions.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: SFS, obviously be coming in at €100 million-plus, which was well above what we had been hoping for, reason  being that this has also been positively impacted by a few favorable one-offs. But what you also see in Q4, and we  expect that to be continuing, is that some credit hits are showing off along the lines, most of them coming from the  renewable environment. This is not a default, but we could clearly see that there is some stress in the system,  which we carefully watch. We don't expect major adverse impacts in 2013, but this is something which we see  coming. It could also be serving as an early indicator that matters are cooling in terms of economic impact.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: First, with Siemens 2014, we are stepping up our efforts in improving our cost position, and in this area we will  also see the vast majority of our activities. The single-largest lever for optimizing the cost base is our supply chain  management, where we see further potential to generate productivity gains of, in total, at least €3 billion in the  next two years, and Joe will elaborate this in a minute. A second major lever will be continuously to optimize our  global capacity and footprint with a business-by-business approach. For example, we have announced in recent  weeks several measures, such as the market-driven capacity adjustments of 600 people in U.S. Wind factories.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: As a third topic, we see significant potential to further improve process efficiency and quality, such as improving  the projects' execution excellence in the Projects businesses, in our large Infrastructure businesses, and  particularly in the Sectors Energy and Infrastructure & Cities. And as I said, this second lever, strengthening our  core activities, is of significant essence, and you can see further proof in today's announcements. We'll work with  rigor to improve our portfolio and strengthen the strongholds, but also fix underperforming businesses or find  sustainable solutions elsewhere.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: In terms of, as you can see from a series of examples, we are already well underway to execute on Siemens 2014,  particularly in the cost reduction portfolio area, and we will give you continuous updates on the various topics  over the coming quarters and also deep dives and proof points during Capital Market Days and investor  conferences. The first one coming up will be Energy, and then Infrastructure & Cities in March next year.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: A few weeks ago, we announced the divestment of our solar activities, where the framework conditions have  obviously significantly deteriorated, and as you all know, the solar market faces substantial overcapacities, strong  price pressures in the photovoltaic area, whereas CSP, the concentrated solar power, has remained more of a  niche technology. Solar was moved to discontinued operations, and delivered around €200 million in sales and  even bigger losses, including an impairment charge of €150 million in Q4 2012. We are in discussions with  potential buyers, and we will update you accordingly.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Going forward, our renewable offering is focused on Wind and Hydro. Today, Sector Industry announced also the  acquisition of the Belgium software company, LMS International, a well-established provider of CAE software for  simulating and testing mechatronic systems, mainly in the automotive and in the aerospace industry.

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: However, Sector Industry is further focusing their portfolio and allocating resources to the most promising  businesses. The water treatment actives which have been part of the Industry Automation division will therefore  be divested. We thoroughly assessed the options and came to the conclusion that there are too limited synergies of  the water treatment activities with our core automation drives and industrial software businesses. After a  successful restructuring over the last 18 months, we have put this mainly U.S.-based business, with more than €1  billion revenue, up for sale.  And Joe will go now into the details of the other Siemens 2014 levers, so over to you, Joe.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: As far as the operational topics are concerned, you'll see one each from the four sectors. And it's not really helpful  for everyone to go through the technical details of it, but if you only look at them on what they get us in terms of  savings, you can see the design-to-cost matter in Fossil frames get to the €250 million to 2014. The consolidation  of mechanical drives in the Sector Industry, which is a somewhat sensitive matter because you talk about  manufacturing footprint here, and manufacturing footprint and consolidation always means that there is some  sort of value-add to a consolidation, but that also will provide us a meaningful three-digit number on savings, and  you will see a series of those topics especially related to Industry and Infrastructure where there is a majority of  manufacturing plants around the world.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: So if you take all that together there, all those four examples, what you'll see here already accounts for about €600  million out of cost reductions or productivity. That's only a few examples, and you will see more of those in a deep  dive when we do have the Sector Capital Market Days, the first one, as Peter mentioned, starting with Energy in  December 2012.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: And obviously it's not just about purchasing being the biggest, the best lever; it is also about the area where you  best put it. It's sustainable, because it involves everything, it gives a sustainable value, also to the suppliers that  are negotiating, and then one's a dollar short, the other one is a dollar long, and the moment the power changes, it  goes the other way. So there is very little restructuring involved. It goes quick. The savings are quicker. About 40%  – four-zero – 40% of the total cost of the company is about purchasing of services and bill of materials. So you can  clearly see how huge the impact is, and this is what we're going to go about. Now, obviously the design-to-cost  element is nothing which is for the short term; this is more related in its impact to 2014.

texts.speaker: Michael A. Hagmann
texts.profession: Analyst, HSBC Bank Plc (Broker)
texts.text: Michael Hagmann, HSBC. If you look at the portfolio optimization, we have now seen some smaller steps with  Solar and with Water. Obviously, within the portfolio, there are quite a number of businesses which have sub- average margins and relatively high execution risk. So the question is, if we look forward, do we see higher or  larger disposals, or do you think we'd be rather looking at portfolio optimization in the range of businesses with  €500 million to €1 billion of revenues?

texts.speaker: Peter H. Löscher
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Andreas, let me start with the head count first because it's important. As you know that this is certainly one of the  key levers what we are able to pull, and we have it clearly on a business-by-business, where you have to look at this  issue. So the overall number, certainly, there's a very clear and tight focus on this number to pull, of course, as  part of this lever. And other one is we have to have targeted programs on the issue – where do we see structural  issues, and with structural issues we have to adjust also employment. A good example is the 600 people what we  have taken action on, on the Wind business in U.S., as the PPC basically ran out, out of the 1,600. Joe has also  highlighted an example in terms of how we actually adjust on the gearboxes for the wind industry. So, but it has to  be really around the issue where do we have issues basically where we can manage through the cycle, and then we  have to use the flexibility aspects what we have created together with the employee representatives already in the  last downturn. And where we have structural issues, and this would be focused, targeted initiatives, they will be  discussed, they will be agreed with the employee representatives, and they will be executed.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: Another topic, for example, has been low/medium voltage. There are companies which have medium and high  voltage together. Others have medium on their own. Others have low and medium together. Obviously – and  maybe to a degree, unfortunately, and we will be looking at it – our low-voltage and our medium-voltage business  is a different world each if it comes to marginal capabilities, and the more mid-voltage you have in the mix, the  better the profit is. The more low-voltage we have at this point in time – especially the commodity part of low  voltage, not the MCC piece – the bigger impact, of course, the mix is. So we will be seeing that over time that we  have this type of volatility based on volume and mix, and we will be reporting about it what the impact has been –  very favorable, by the way, in LMV, because there was a lot of mid-voltage in Q4; to a lesser extent, low voltage.  That may normalize again in Q1, for example.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: But then again, if you look at the new hurdle rates in terms of cash return, that LMS is pretty close. It's in the  ballpark of what we have. And I'll give you one example which is obviously also important for rating  considerations and the like. The cash drain, if we dispose of Water, will be pretty compensated by the free cash  flow already of the acquisition. So you can see, if you look at cash rather than some PPA-related return on capital  employed, you just can see that this is something good for us.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, Ben, on the pricing, look, if that turns out to be conservative, it's great because then we've got upside already  on the right-hand side, if nothing else, or a buffer for some which may go south. So that's – the answer is we don't  know at this time. We've been looking into the backlog, which has been scheduled already for 2013. We pretty  much know what this will look like in terms of pricing. That's [indiscernible] (1:19:44) longer-term related aspects  on project businesses, but we pretty much know that, like Wind, like Fossil, or even some Transmission topics  which we've got in there. We pretty much know what the pricing will be. So therefore that is transparent, and  that's why, in terms of potential upside, that leaves us with the short-cycle environment, and that's mostly  Industry, that's in part IC, and to a less probable part in Healthcare. Now, within Healthcare, it's very little that  pricing will ease because it isn't just a matter of competitive pressure, but also about how much the customers are  willing or allowed to pay, based on their budgets and their public environment.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Member-Managing Board, Siemens AG
texts.text: Obviously, now, the sensitivity, the sensitivity of anything material happening to the short-cycle environment,  basically its profitability is so high that we felt compelled to mention that as a important need-to-know factor for  the guidance. Because you can expect every €1 billion Industrial Automation or motion control, which is that  technology, every €1 billion this business is short of is about €500 million to €600 million to the bottom line, like  this. Don't even think about changing your costs because it goes quicker than a wink. That's a fact. So that's why  we are highly sensitive on that one. And that's why we are so close, as close as we can be to early indicators on the  automotive discrete spectrum, as well as the toolmaker's environment is also highly related to automotive, in the  end, like [indiscernible] (1:25:18) or what have you, all those suppliers providing tools to automotive in Germany.  And if you look at the carmakers, especially in Germany, the premium carmakers, they have been very successful.  There are on a very high level. They seem to be the last one to be affected by a general weakness in the global  environment.

texts.speaker: Mariel von Drathen
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, Siemens AG
texts.text: Okay. Well, thank you very much. As I said, we will be road-showing in the course of November in a number of  locations. You'll find this in the financial calendar on the slide deck, page number 28, and then we're very much  looking forward to seeing you in our Charlotte location in the U.S. December 10 and 11 for the Energy Capital  Market Day.

file: SIE - Q4 2013 Earnings Call 7November2013 930 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 07-Nov-13.pdf

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: So we ended the fiscal year at €4.2 billion, profit from continued operations after tax including a gain of about  €400 million through the disposal of NSN and about a reclassification of the solar business which accounts to  about €300 million. So all-in-all, this is also a sort of a like-for-like guidance.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: We've seen quite a strong Healthcare performance, which is on the top end of the EBITDA margin band. We like  what we see in both growth as well as profitability. Other areas have some work to do. That is true for energy as  well as for industry and predominately for the Infrastructure & Cities Sector. I would expect all those sectors to get  significantly closer to where they should be in terms of their margin bands in 201 4.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: If we go quickly on the regional aspects of our business, as it comes to fiscal Q4, as what I said fiscal 2013, later on  you can clearly see that the Americas have been quite, quite active in terms of order growth. That's  of course due  to the fact that we have seen a resurgence of the tax benefits associated with Wind. So we've been booking a lot of  orders in both Wind, as well as the associated areas if it comes to gearboxes and the likes. We also do see decent  order behavior in Fossil in the United States, and we expect that to continue also into the year of 2014.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Energy, it's been a decent development in 2013 given the aspects of transformatory charges as well as our  challenges which we have in the Power Transmission, that's been the area that has a lot of work to do and we  continue to execute on our turnaround program. It will take time and there are, of course, uncertainties if it comes  to legacy projects such as the access offshore as Olkiluoto and minor other things. So those aspects are also and  those uncertainties are also considered to play a role in the 2014 outlook.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Other than that, we will also combine the Fossil products together with the Oil and Gas products in order to make  sure that we see the full range of turbines from the lower end all the way up to 560 megawatts, 580 m egawatts on  our H-frame 8000 so we do expect synergies coming from that combination by the year 2015. So we continue to  accelerate and use all our opportunities, which we still do see in a last but not least attractive Energy sector going  forward.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: If you look at the numbers, Wind power's been weak in terms of orders but that's project-based so that does not  mean there is underlying weakness. We've seen quite the strengths for the quarters which we had in 2013, thanks  to the renewed tax credits in the United States and that will also play, as you can see, a major role in our revenue  development going forward.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: If you go to the area of Below Total Sectors, it's always been an area which has been calling for volatility. One of  the most volatile aspects from the recent quarters and recent years we've been solving by the sale of our NSN  stake. So we are basically left with some areas there like Bosch Siemens Appliances, as well as some parts of the  Enterprise PBX business. So if you expect a €100 million contribution per year in 2014 that should actually carry  your model in a meaningful way. Siemens Energy Services and Centrally Managed Portfolio Assets should just b e  about what we had in 2013.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: As far as the quite remarkable amount of disposal has been concerned, we've been completing Turbocare by  selling it to the Wood Group. TLT is sold. Oncology ramp down has been completed. Water, we just announced as  late as yesterday.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Well, first of all we do expect markets to be still not coherently up. If it comes to energy we do see some weakness  in fossil in the European environment. This is true for both new orders, new projects as well as service to servi ce  part of it due to the fact that utilization is somewhat volatile, talking about Europe. There is work to do in the  transmission area to fix our division and this is important to us as well as getting it back to where it belongs to be.  Wind should be fine in terms of delivering steady merchants.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: And last but not least, we obviously have been seeing that for quite some time, that process industries is an  attractive area to be at. You should also know that Siemens got a bunch of very, very good products to serve that  market. And that's why we have been announcing a corporate project, which will be led by Mr. Herweck, who used  to be the Strategy Officer of Siemens, on how to better penetrate the Process Industries market. We believe this is  important. We believe we've got opportunities, and the project will reveal those opportunities on how we are going  to access that environment, among other things, in the industry space.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: On the portfolio, look, this is an assessment about the value chain of [indiscernible] (43:57). This is an assessment  about what digitization does to certain areas of that value chain. Think about smart grid in energy. Think about  PLM and supply chain moving closer together in industrial automation. Today, manufacturing plants are being  designed, including the manufacturing processes where you not have even gotten to the groundbreaking yet.

texts.speaker: Ben E. Uglow
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Question number two is on the sales guidance of no growth. Is that a general comment, i.e., you're worried about  just the – how shall I put it, the global macro? Or do you have something more specific in mind and in particular  I'm thinking about the Fossil Power Division? Is there something that you see coming up in fossil or any one  division that would take the group down? So that was number two.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: All right. Thanks, Ben, on the look on the guidance. I mean, we've obviously seen the 2% to 6%, by the way, this  afternoon on the – one of our U.S. competitors and we obviously don't know whether that's got some currency  impacts, whether it was like-for-like or maybe just being helped by a somewhat weak greenback.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Secondly, and that's more important topic because this is something to learn strategically and technically going  forward. If I look at those areas like particle therapy or the wind issues in the North Sea if it co mes to connecting  the grid to land, this is not so much about project management, this is about market entry of new applications.  And this is what we have been reacting on and this is now by corporate technology, the so -called corporate  memory gets involved if the first question on an order or on a [indiscernible] (55:26) is have you done it before  and the answer is no. Then we do not leave it up anymore to the divisions or whether or not it sounds attractive  and this is a corporate matter. And it goes to Corporate Technology, the corporate experts who've been there and  done that before. And that's a significant change in the way we basically go about projects and is also a significant  change on how we make sure that the company applies what it knows.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: We take projects because we believe we can make money, And that's a bit more important, secure an installed  base. If you look at the models like energy for example, this is all about building a power plant for the service to  come. So one needs to always consistently look into the project, be it the greenfield project and the adjacent  service, which you get out of the installed base. And that's why this is important to see. And obviously, if you talk  rail or even wind, the service component becomes an ever more important topic.

texts.speaker: Fredric Stahl
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Investment Bank (Sweden)
texts.text: Hi. Fredric Stahl from UBS. I remember at the Energy Capital Markets Day, which is I think about a year ago, you  flagged pretty clearly then that the mix would shift within Wind to get more offshore and the higher margins. But I  didn't foresee it to be 11%. So my question to you is, is the current mix and the current level of profitability in  Wind the new normal for the foreseeable or for the last few quarters? That's the first question.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Well, Wind, obviously, if we look at the last quarter in Wind Power, it's been a decent development. And it's been  favorably impacted by a bigger portion on offshore, the reason being that in summer, it's easier to install offshore  wind machines than it is, obviously, in the current quarter. So what will be seeing is quite a decent mix effect in  fiscal Q4 and quite a seasonal effect in the current fiscal quarter where obviously, times are tougher to install  offshore. That's the first.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: The other topic, of course, in wind is also about what would the service model be? How can we install a decent  amount of service by installing also wind turbines? Because at the end, this is about installed base. This is about  demand response. This is about the proactive maintenance, and this is about uptime. So we will very much focus  on service models in wind. We've got some decent experience to that, also some recent successes on how to go  about it, and that will continue and count going forward that. In general, as you know , the onshore market is  actually the market which provides the bigger growth potential, also the bigger installation. So I would not feel  compelled to just say offshore wind is our thing and everything else would even out. So we focus on the wind  business on its own and get the cost down close to the grid parity because the last thing I want in the mid and long  term is to make my business dependent on government subsidies because elections change opinions and also  people. But I can't just remove my manufacturing to someplace else once we have built it.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: So therefore, it's got to be an economically feasible case. This is the challenge and the opportunity in wind to get  the costs down to a meaningful way of producing energy in the energy mix in the respective regions. Healthcare, I  look at statistics about how companies have been doing. Why don't we just leave it up to third parties to touch  about how you we've been doing. We feel pretty comfortable about the comparison, and with that, I actually would  leave that one alone.

texts.speaker: Michael A. Hagmann
texts.profession: Analyst, HSBC Bank Plc (Broker)
texts.text: Michael Hagmann with HSBC. Just on the merger between oil and gas and fossil. Can you give us a little bit more  insights on what triggered this reorganization? And also, if we look back at another big reorganization of the past,  it was healthcare, it was sold initially as a reorganization which wouldn't lead to any charges. How do we have to  look at potential charges coming out of the merger between fossil and oil and gas?

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Okay. The rationale on putting the Oil & Gas Division together with fossil and name it fossil products has come  from the fact that about half, if not 60% of the total of what we call Oil & Gas Division was industrial turbines. And  the other half, or if not 40%, has been the process-related work on oil and gas engineering work. Now obviously if  you look at the industrial turbines, which have a spectrum of 5 megawatts to up to 65 megawatts, and the other  turnkey, the turbines in fossil which are from 100 megawatts up to 580 megawatts combined cycle, 8,000, then it  goes without saying that there is quite an amount of synergies that will take car e of the whole spectrum. Think  about platforms, processes, manufacturing environments and what have you. That has been the rationale to put  them together. We expect savings to be up to €100 million over 3 years, so by 2015 we will have accessed those  €100 billion – €100 million, excuse me. And on the way to there, there might be some restructuring that was  going on which I included in the guidance as well as in the numbers for 2014.

file: SIE - Q4 2014 Earnings Call 6November2014 500 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 06-Nov-14.pdf

texts.speaker: Mariel von Drathen
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations
texts.text: While Joe will give the overview, Lisa will provide more details on the energy business, and Ralf will illustrate the  financials. After that, we have time for Q&A with Joe, Ralf, and Lisa. And with that, I would like to now hand over  to you, Joe.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Unfortunately, the challenges in the Energy sector accumulated throughout the year and led to a full-year EBITDA  margin of only 8.1%, which obviously is well below our own aspirations and strongly weighing on the operational  and, of course, also, overall results. And Lisa will talk about this in more detail later.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Now, let's have a quick look at the regional aspects of our business during the fourth quarter. While Europe and  Middle East was the order growth engines in Q4, United States and China were a stronghold in regional revenue  growth. In Europe, we benefited strongly from several large offshore wind orders in the UK, in Germany, as well  as in The Netherlands. We did see excellent success in the Transportation business in the United States such as  the large light rail order in San Francisco worth about €483 million.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Now, as far as Energy is concerned, I'd like to hand it over to Lisa and talk about the opportunities and challenges  we have in Energy. Lisa.

texts.speaker: Lisa Davis
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board
texts.text: All right. Thank you, Joe, for the introduction, and also, welcome and good morning to everyone from my side.  Looking at the fourth quarter performance in our Energy sector, we clearly saw the impact of a very competitive  market on our order books with an organic decline of 5%. This was mainly driven by fewer power generation sales  in the Americas. Our book-to-bill ratio was just shy of 1 with 0.99, and we have a strong order backlog of €58  billion.

texts.speaker: Lisa Davis
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board
texts.text: Power Generation delivered a solid margin of 13%, albeit lower than one year ago. While the service business held  up well, we saw the impact from the competitive large gas turbine market in our margins as well.

texts.speaker: Lisa Davis
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board
texts.text: Wind Power has been strong in orders due to a number of large project awards, although even with this,  profitability was disappointing. The primary factors for the significant profit swing were charges totaling €223  million for two key topics.

texts.speaker: Lisa Davis
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board
texts.text: First, charges for inspecting and replacing main bearings due to the early degradation of these bearings for a  certain onshore wind turbine type. These issues appear to be related to recent batches of bearings, and we are in  close discussion with our supplier.

texts.speaker: Lisa Davis
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board
texts.text: Second, we had to take significant charges for blade repairs caused by harsh weather conditions, both offshore and  onshore. This is a topic which we see across the industry and where we have already successfully implemented a  design change for leading-edge protection in our manufacturing facility. We'll also roll out a similar retrofit at  affected locations.

texts.speaker: Lisa Davis
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board
texts.text: On the positive side, the four offshore grid connection projects are now installed in the North Sea, and  commissioning takes place. Two of them are already in trial runs, and overall percentage of completion is now  above 80%.

texts.speaker: Lisa Davis
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board
texts.text: As Joe mentioned, I want to give you a brief overview on the action plan we have put in place to address the  challenges in Power Generation and Wind Power. In recent years, we have seen some fundamental shift in the  new equipment market, particularly for gas turbines. Demand for large gas turbines is clearly lower than expected,  while the market for smaller turbines and decentralized generation has been growing significantly, and this shift  will continue. This development holds particularly true for Europe where utilities are reluctant to invest due to  high uncertainty about the payback, as we have seen soft demand and overcapacity in the market results in market  consolidation and price and margin pressure.

texts.speaker: Lisa Davis
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board
texts.text: Wind business is operating an attractive market and we have great opportunities due to our leading position in a  fast-growing offshore market and a rapidly emerging service business based on our installed fleet of more than 25  gigawatts. As already mentioned, moving from a handcraft production to industrialized structures along the entire  value chain is causing some friction.

texts.speaker: Lisa Davis
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board
texts.text: We have a comprehensive set of actions in place to bring margins back to the industry level. First, we put  additional resources in place with a strong focus on improving engineering processes and quality management.  Second, we work continuously on further cost out and industrialization to drive down the levelized cost of  electricity. And third – our third focus is bringing new products to the market with higher performing turbines  also for low-wind locations and rapidly developing a strong service business in the installed base.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Please keep in mind that Unify, remaining metals projects and our Postal & Baggage Handling business are  undergoing significant structural changes which may have an impact on the CMPA result. SRE is, as usual,  depending on disposal gains, but we see them lower than in fiscal 2014.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Power & Gas and Energy Management will be the biggest contributors to achieve a book-to-bill above 1. Pricing  should be down by around 2.5% of revenues overall, with Wind Power, Power & Gas and Healthcare being affected  the most.

texts.speaker: Andreas Willi
texts.profession: JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: And it reminds me a little bit, maybe a bit different, but still of OSRAM in 2007 when you very early on talked  about the potential impacts from LED, but then actually, OSRAM wasn't really prepared that well for it when it  was spun off.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Now, on Healthcare, obviously, I mean, we had a reason why we have been flagging the fact that Healthcare is  different as to the closer value chain of electrification from energy generation all the way to its efficient use in –  down to Building Technologies and Mobility. But then again, Healthcare at this point in time, returns very good  margins. It returns extremely good cash from -it returns the cash from acquisitions, which the company estimated  earlier. So, there is no reason at this point in time to not give the shareholders of Siemens that free cash flow.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: On the other hand side, we are well aware that paradigm shift can change business models, and that's why we start  building the prerequisite for this unit to be proactively prepared. Sometimes – we decided to make Healthcare  stronger also operationally because they will focus their go-to-market on their priorities. They will focus their  cost-efficiency programs and their priorities not on being part of the overall efforts of a greater scheme of things in  the company.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Andreas, maybe I can add a bit on the margin development for next year. Because when we say flattened  mentioning these investments into sales and R&D, we also need to bear in mind that we had these extraordinary  negative impact on EM and also on wind business in 2014. Of course, we will substantially improve that situation  and plan so for the next year to come.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: You're right about the procurement easing that's coming now after several of the political and commercial reforms  about who makes decisions in which area. But then again, there is this topic of localization and tighter scrutiny on  multinational environment.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: So, all in all, China is, according to our expectations, with some significant upside on Energy Management due to  the fact that electricity procured in east and needs to be transported from the north to the south and west to the  east. And that's where see major growth areas. The Mobility business is picking up quite strongly. And obviously,  also, it becomes a distributed generation given the national structure in China. This is also an area of growth  where we expect significant opportunities as we move along.

texts.speaker: Fredric Stahl
texts.profession: UBS AG (Sweden)
texts.text: Yeah. Hi. Good morning, guys. I wanted to start with a question on – you spoke a bit about decentralized power  generation and the Smart Grid opportunity. And my question is, do you think that this is a – let's call it a  traditional hardware opportunity, or is it more of a software/information opportunity? How do you view it?

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Well, that is the reason why in our new organization as of October 1, we have been creating a division called  Energy Management, which is the traditional T&T, but then surrounded by the Smart Grid Energy Management  operations.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: And what we see is that the world is also changing, not just in distributed – or decentralized distributed energy,  it's also changing from a single, one-source generation to a multi-generation environment. In old times, there was  a nuclear power plant or a 1,100 or 1,200-megawatt gas or combined-cycle gas power plant. And then just starting  the transmission and then there was a substation and what have you.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: In the new times, you have generation from gas, from nuclear, from renewable like wind and solar. And that's all  coming to a grid at a time which is also not always necessarily containable because it's about the weather and the  wind – or the sun and the wind. So, therefore, this will increasingly also become a software-driven component in  terms of growth to manage exactly that volatility to the grid.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: So, if you talk to me on China, that's still mostly hardware. That's high voltage AC/DC transmission. But if you  look at the general opportunities in Energy Management, it is also about software-driven, managing the grid, and  the utility-based operations.

texts.speaker: Fredric Stahl
texts.profession: UBS AG (Sweden)
texts.text: Okay. Understood. Can I also do one more question just on – I'm just curious here. So, you have, let's say, €150  million to €200 million of costs relating to a faulty bearing in your wind turbines. Can you – is it possible for you  to recoup that cost at a later stage from your supplier?  Ralf Peter Thomas  Chief Financial Officer  A  Obviously, we are just in the middle of just understanding which responsibility they have and which we have. And  as Lisa mentioned in the press conference this morning, we are busy investigating that and if there's any chance  for us to recover anything, be rest assured that we will go for that.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Yeah. Before maybe Lisa goes on that route, I intend to give answer to your question, it's actually simply yes. So,  it's related to pure Power & Gas. Everything else is stable and there's even some pockets of growth here and there,  although reduced with that one. And it could be in a way anticipated over time because of the fact of the order  intake.  Ben E. Uglow  Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc  Q  Okay.

texts.speaker: Simon P. Toennessen
texts.profession: Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Yes. Thank you. Good morning, everyone. My first question is on charges going forward. You said earlier that you  expect lower charges outside the legacy projects and issues. What would you classify as charges outside the legacy  projects in 2014? And is the current issue in Wind Power that you're seeing a legacy project? And what are you  expecting going forward? And maybe as a last point on that, in your margin guidance for next year, could you  maybe give us a bit more guidance what level of charges you are implying in that?

texts.speaker: Simon P. Toennessen
texts.profession: Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And a last point on the news we had out of Germany and T&D this week where it seems Germany is pushing  through with the HVDC investments and also quite a lot on modernization of the grid against some of the  concerns flagged throughout the year. There's an investment value stated of €22 billion over 10 years. Can you just  maybe comment on that? What are you seeing? What are you expecting from this going forward? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Well, Simon, let me start off with the first question about the charges. I mean, it's a very valid question because we  try to be as precise as we can in that field. When we said project charges, that was very much related to those  projects that we have been discussing as legacy projects in the past, including the grid connection in North Sea  and so on.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: As Lisa has been describing, the problems with industrialization of the wind industry, that is not in particular a  project charge as such, therefore we said these are project-related charges in terms of project business. And what  it goes to is it's actually that we need to substantially improve our supply chain, the make process in total, and  understanding the impact of material like eroding materials under rough weather conditions, for example.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: The T&D, look, there's a lot which is written in daily newspapers, which occupies news in tomorrow's fish wrap.  We know there is a strong demand for bringing together the renewable energies in the South, which is mostly  photovoltaics and wind which is up in the North, together with the more baseline services of gas and then steel,  coal-fired power plant.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: On the other topic of breaking even at Transmission and Wind, I mean, obviously, the answer is yes. And target  margins, Transmission is not yet a division anymore, it's part of the Energy Management, so it's hard to really give  that answer straight. But Wind definitely is something which got good opportunity to get back into where it  belongs to be and that's the margins we have set out further in Mexico.

texts.speaker: James A. Moore
texts.profession: Redburn (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Hi. Good morning, everybody. I have three questions. On the 2015 guidance, please could you give us the  assumptions of disposal gains? Are we talking a four-digit-plus number? And, Lisa, as you're here, I wonder if you  could help us understand the underlying dynamics in the Power Generation business, and how much of the  aftermarket deterioration is behind this or how much we still have to go? So, specifically, I'm thinking about the  Fossil Service business, which is a big profit driver. Could you give us a feel for how much the utilization of your  turbines in the field have come down? And where do you think that number materially worsens going forward as  renewable continues to take more of the mix? Or do you think that that decline has now all happened? And then  finally, Joe, maybe you could help us with the Healthcare growth environment in 2015?

texts.speaker: Lisa Davis
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board
texts.text: So, maybe to respond, James, to your comment – or your question on the dynamics in the Energy business and  specific to the aftermarket. Before I comment on the aftermarket, just a comment on Energy overall. Obviously,  we continue – or we still – we see continued growth in the Energy market, especially in the need for electricity or  the demand of electricity. This will be based largely on renewables and gas going forward, so we see quite a  demand for both areas of Energy supply.

texts.speaker: Lisa Davis
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board
texts.text: In terms of the aftermarket, we have seen a decline in our Service business in Europe predominantly. We do think  that that has reached a level of no further change in a sense, so it's bottomed out if you could say. We've been able  to shift our service capability to other markets to offset that decline in business in Europe. So, we still see the  service business or the aftermarket, as you phrased it, as quite a positive contributor to the business and, in fact,  an area of growth going forward for both the gas turbine business as well as the wind business.

texts.speaker: James E. Stettler
texts.profession: Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Secondly, this whole phase, which is a lot of inward-looking restructuring, how do you ensure that you not lose out  in terms of protecting your market share and, in certain cases, even gaining? And then finally, if you look at all the  changes happening in the Wind industry, do you still think longer term that can be an attractive business? And if  so, how important is service going to be going forward to really drive the margin?

texts.speaker: Lisa Davis
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board
texts.text: And then the last one with respect to Wind, we do see this as a longer term growth area, both onshore and  offshore. So, we do – and we are investing in new technology in this space and reducing our cost to make sure that  wind is not just the most competitive renewable, but a competitive energy source in the future so that it does  continue to grow on its own. So, we do see this as an area that we continue to invest and grow quite a bit.

texts.speaker: Olivier Esnou
texts.profession: Exane Ltd.
texts.text: Question number two, coming back to the Wind business, there's a very high backlog and I had high growth  forecast for this business going forward. I was just wondering with the execution issues, how we should think  about the growth outlook for that business, please? Maybe sort of guidance for 2015 here?

texts.speaker: Olivier Esnou
texts.profession: Exane Ltd.
texts.text: And, thirdly, the order intake showed good performance in Wind and Transport, large projects. I was wondering  to what extent they benefited from your new process of the internal memory team reviewing potential large risk  contracts. Could you maybe tell us to what extent they've been reviewed and they're good margin business really?  Thank you.

texts.speaker: Lisa Davis
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board
texts.text: And I can also address, Olivier, the question on growth in Wind.

texts.speaker: Lisa Davis
texts.profession: Member-Managing Board
texts.text: We do see strong growth in the Wind business in general. As I mentioned, the Industry, on the onshore side  anywhere from 3% to 4% per annum. And on the offshore, a much higher growth rate of about 20% per annum.

texts.speaker: Olivier Esnou
texts.profession: Exane Ltd.
texts.text: And if I may follow up, that means in your sales plan for Wind, you should be aiming for double-digit 2015, yes?

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: On the areas of fast and slow, I have been talking a lot about the updates now on the regions. United States, we  believe, is going to be the motor and the locomotive of global industrial growth in 2015 out of several reasons.  Energy methods, very important. Oil & Gas, still a major mid and long term growth locomotive, that's not only  about drilling more holes. It's also about the optimization and productivity to bring the average cost down per  barrel which we get out of the ground.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: You may, for example, be interested in the fact that in 2012 and into 2013, the average cost per barrel could be  taken out of [indiscernible] (01:15:16) conventional and unconventional was $70. Now the average has gone $57,  which has all been provided by the Oil & Gas service providers and productivity matters most going forward.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: If we look at again on the stronghold what we expect 2015 for us to be, in the U.S., obviously, this is about the  propulsion system drives. As I've said, it's also about Building Technologies, we do believe that commercial  buildings will make some meaningful efforts to get energy efficiency to where it needs to be. So, we do see actually  good areas. Slow definitely will be Wind in the United States because due to the fact that we have really large  orders in 2014 and it remains to be seen what the tax incentive scheme will be in 2015 and 2016. Germany  definitely will see some recovery of Healthcare, which we like. Mobility is good and we also expect our Wind  Power and Renewables business to be able to show good growth out of the existing backlog as Ralf has already  been alluding to.

texts.speaker: Josef Käser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Now let me highlight some key developments in the fourth quarter. Orders as reported increased by 15% and were  clearly up by 6% organically on the back of many large orders in all power-related businesses such as the Power  and Gas, Wind and Energy Management.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Revenues as reported increased by 4% organically. It was moderately down by 4%. As we have obviously expected,  driven by the project business, while Energy Management, Building Technologies, Healthcare and Digital Factory  showed strength also in growing the business.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Let's now have a quick look at the regional aspect of our business during the fourth quarter. Europe and Middle  East, the order growth engine in Q4, United States delivered a solid and a broad-based revenue growth. Germany,  we benefited strongly from the large offshore wind order called Veja Mate which is about a 400-megawatt wind  project coming together with a 15 years of service agreement.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Bookings were significantly up due to some large order wins. And in total, we are able to take about 10 large gas  turbines into our books, which helped increasing our market share for the full fiscal year from about 20% to 25%.  As expected, profitability in Power and Gas was impacted by low margins in the large gas turbine and solution  business, while the service business remained very solid. We also benefited from a project settlement adding  about €55 million to the bottom line.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Wind Power delivered a strong finish in most aspects. While orders came in high as previously forecasted.  Revenues were primarily down on lower onshore revenues. Margin improvement to 4.8% delivered a decent  turnaround just a bit shy of the targeted range. The division executes well on its comprehensive productivity and  quality program and will continue so in 2016, although, it will take time to show the desired result.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: As promised, Energy Management delivered an excellent performance, especially comparing to where we come  from in all metrics and reached a profit margin of 7.5% for quite some time. The first quarterly performance was  in the target margin range, and we really do like to keep it that way. Main reasons were higher revenues in the  transformer and smart grid businesses and strong profit contribution from the solution business. Free cash flow  was impressive with €1.1 billion in the fourth quarter.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: We also did make substantial progress in working through the legacy project, for example, in Canada, and saw  also some positive completion effects elsewhere. The Energy Management transition program is well on track to  steady drive progress in profitability and growth going into fiscal 2016.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Building Technologies again has quite a seasonally strong fourth quarter with what we believe was a decent  revenue growth particularly in the higher-margin product and service business. Just to give you one example on  how excellent our customer relationship and the customer proximity in the BT business has been shows our new  strategic technology partnership with Credit Suisse environmental real estate fund where we evaluate and  optimize the CO2 footprint prior to their investments into their buildings. In addition, the stringent execution of  productivity measures helped to mitigate the effects from the appreciation of the Swiss franc which still weighs on  the business.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Now, what are our main assumptions for the items below Industrial Business for fiscal 2016? As I said, we'll  continue to operate on a similar operational level as in fiscal 2015. Centrally managed portfolio activities contain a  number of assets, such as Unify, until its closing, remaining metals project, ramping down of solar, and the Postal  & Baggage handling business. These assets are undergoing further structural changes and, therefore, we expect a  negative impact and some volatility going forward.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: This quarter included also inflows of €2.2 billion from a significant decrease in operating net working capital,  mainly from lower inventories in the energy-related project businesses. In addition, the Egypt orders had a  significant positive impact of around €0.5 billion on advances received. Other than in previous years, we saw for  advances and billings in excess in fiscal 2015, a positive impact of around €900 million.

texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: First of all, we have set a clear target to lower project-related charges through improved risk mitigation. The  improvement was significant, since project-related charges in the Industrial Business declined to around €200  million in fiscal 2015. Furthermore, we accelerated the cost savings related to our functional cost reduction  activities, which we had been guiding conservatively. texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Former Siemens' compressor unit has been integrated as of July 1 into the new Dresser-Rand business. We expect  significant synergies by combining those units. texts.speaker: Ralf Peter Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Now, the landmark order is a combined 18-year service contract for both aero-derivative gas turbines from Rolls- Royce and the related compressors from Dresser-Rand. Putting this together, we see stabilizing orders but a book-to-bill ratio below one due to the challenging  market environment.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: 2015, our R&D intensity increased by 30 basis points to 5.9% of revenue. Our R&D investment will grow further to  around €4.8 billion in fiscal 2016. Our innovation is not  about input, it is all about outcomes.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: And the ones who already visited our electronics factory in Amberg or the twin factory in Chengdu certainly  became an impression how the Internet of Things look like other than hear a lot of stories about it. texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: There is huge demand in the market for digital services. For example, our 40 data-drive flex long-term term  service contract has been sold cleverly by our power generation services. texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: However, we do see plenty of opportunities to chase in all part of the global world. We'll find them, we'll take them  and we execute. Pricing should be down by slightly 2% of revenues overall with Power and Gas, with power and  healthcare being affected the most.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Supporting our midterm growth agenda, for businesses, such as Wind Power, Digital Factory or Energy  Management, CapEx investment will be going up substantially in fiscal 2016. Although, we are excited about our  energy efficiency program for our buildings and factories to cut the carbon footprint in half by 2020, at least this  year to neutral by 2025.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: We'll be the first company in our space and our size which steps up and show the way for an economically sound  environmental CO2 concept. In the case of the current levels of the euro United States – U.S. dollar exchange rate,  we see only modest tailwind on the Industrial Business margin going forward.

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Now, if you assume for a while and that communicates to your second question, if you assume for a while and look  at the profit margins of wind and mobility in 2015. texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer

texts.speaker: Joe Kaeser

texts.profession: JPMorgan Securities Plc

texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer
