texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: Now, let's have a look at the key developments by division in the fourth quarter. Power and Gas is swiftly  executing its measures to strengthen go-to-market productivity and enhanced technology to counter aggressive  prices behavior. These investments will significantly strengthen our competitiveness. We are making good  progress to improve our footprint and deliver cost savings.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: Overall, the market, especially on the large turbine environment, remains challenging with sluggish demand on  the back of global overcapacities. Bookings are down in Q4 on tough comps due to a sharper lower number of  large orders. We at least recovered several large orders in the year, including several hundred million euros for  the make-up project in Egypt. Revenues were significantly up on strong backlog conversion and a material  contribution from the Egypt orders. In total, we delivered 16 large gas turbines in the quarter.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: The team is working hard and did a great job to gain market share from about 25% a year ago to now close to  30% in large gas turbines. We also saw material market share gains in the small and medium gas turbine  segment, and we do intend to continue that path. Also, Dresser-Rand integration has progressed very well. The  business achieved a margin improvement of 140 basis points year-over-year, excluding transformation costs. The  ramp-up of synergies is ahead of plan. We already realized about €70 million in fiscal 2016.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: Wind Power delivered again an excellent performance with 8.3% profit margins on the back of strong growth  conversion and significantly improved execution. After nine months of very strong order growth, bookings were  down in Q4 on lower large orders volume. The prior year, we booked, among other things, the €1.2 billion  offshore order, Veja Mate. The division has built a sustainable execution track record and announced a number of  few new turbine models during the Hamburg wind fair, a strong foundation to enter into the planned merger with  Gamesa.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: As promised, Energy Management delivered an impressive performance in all metrics and reached profit margins  of 8.4%, which is well within the target range and with improvements in most of its business. And there's more to  come due to further productivity measures and innovation. Top-line, we clearly outperformed our competitive  environment. Orders are up in the high voltage products and digital grids businesses, as revenues are driven by  the solutions and transformer business.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: Building Technology had, again, a seasonally very strong fourth quarter with double-digit margins on tough  comps. Order growth was mainly driven by a strong base business and contract wins for energy efficiency  projects mainly in the United States. We did make very good progress to drive a digital transformation and  increase the number of connected sets by 28% in fiscal 2016. The number of connected data points reached  almost half a million items.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: Process Industries and Drives continue to be affected by ongoing weakness in oil and gas and other commodity - related markets with sign of finding a bottom. As expected, the profit margin turned negative due to about a €200  million in severance charges to execute necessary structural realignments and capacity adjustments.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: First of all, we further accelerated the functional cost savings measures and achieved the €1 billion savings target  ahead of plan. We have further substantial measures across the company in place to deliver on a sustainable  basis our 3% to 5% productivity target. The team has a tight grip around the measures which are executed based  on a stringent operating model.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: In fiscal 2016, we made further substantial progress in risk management and project execution. There was no  negative net effect. Project-related charges or cost overruns were compensated by reversals due to improved  delivery in other projects. To illustrate this positive development, I've picked two examples. Mobility has achieved  in a number of crucial projects such as Velaro Eurostar, ICE4 and Thameslink important milestones on time.  Power and Gas mega project in Egypt to build three combined-cycle power plants with 14.4 gigawatts is on track  to deliver first power to the grid by the end of this calendar year. We will see around 40% of revenue recognition  of the solution-related project value of €3.6 billion in fiscal 2017 from them.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: We're building on our leading global number one position in automation across our domains and drive  digitalization and enhance our integrated offering, electrification along our, what we call, EAD strategy,  Electrification, Automation, Digital enterprise.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: A key element of Vision 2020 is the continued ambition to strengthen our portfolio along our strategic imperatives.  As you can see, we made further decisive moves and continued progress. The announced merger with Gamesa  to create a leading wind power player received a fabulous approval of the Gamesa shareholders with 99.75%.  Scheduled to achieve closing is on track and we expect to consolidate the financials of the new entity as of fiscal  Q3 in 2017.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: The existing cooperation in Digital Factory and Process Industries and Drives will be significantly expanded  across all Siemens domains, such as energy management, mobility or building technologies. With strengthened  ties, we have also invested around €70 million in secondary shares under a company program that will continue  until such a time as Bentley Systems stock is publicly traded.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: Secondly, we do drive industry-specific approaches across all the divisions or verticals such as food and  beverages, oil and gas, chem-and many other interesting areas, including a more process-oriented specific  design in discrete industries.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: A recent success was the award of a front-end engineering and design contract from LNG company, Cheniere, for  a midscale liquefaction project to us and our partners. In many of our businesses, the customer journeys are  changing. We do see customers who educate themselves through social media and to also expect highly efficient  transactions through digital channels with our suppliers. Therefore, we're currently developing a new B2B platform  to take these changes into account and further expand our digital sales volume.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: Next assumption is that negative pricing should be around 2.5% of revenues overall with power and gas and wind  power being affected the most. Regarding productivity, we do expect to be in the range of 3% to 5% and the  meaningful assumption would be just the midpoint to that.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: First, we further drive some actions and initiate some actions now which help us to be more flexible, to get it  started than we used to be, the one thing. And it has a range of associated actions with that. And secondly, this is  also more about the environment. If you look at healthcare, there is obviously customers, there is competitors,  there is our employees. We have a very stringent agenda on both the Vision 2020 in general and healthcare in  particular.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: Yeah, thank you, Mark. Also thanks for the feedback on especially Digital Factory. I'll make a general comment on  this and then Ralf will give you some more supporting flavor. And obviously, we also do read the numbers from  our competitors. And it's very clear that our efforts and the strategies has been paying off, and we intend to  continue that path. I think the system of electrification, automation, digitalization, discrete-event simulation  software, just clearly, clearly is the right formula. And still, we need to execute and bring that together.  MindSphere will definitely help us with that. But it's also a highly competitive market, so we need to be mindful  about the environment. A clearly good performance.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Of course. And, Mark, as I do know how important the environment and the underlying assumptions are for you,  as well as for us to kind of get your own models built and for us in terms of guiding the business and steering it  effectively. I would take an extra minute to take you through the macro environment, how we see it at the  moment.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: The other thing is whenever you are at that point, that crossroads that you do something like wind turb or the  healthcare carve-out, you need to determine, of course, how much you can afford in terms of central costs and  how much investment, if you will, in regulatory and rulemaking activities, governance at the end of the day you  intend to happen. We are particular in that field continuously asking ourselves, not only what do we need to do,  but what can we afford also for the way forward.

texts.speaker: James A. Moore
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And then maybe specifically, if I could, on Power and Gas. Your margin, if we exclude the inventory effects, has  been hovering around 10%, 10.5% in the last couple of quarters. And I get the sense that Egypt is going to be a  bigger year next year. I wonder if you could help us with how we should see PG develop in 2017 and how will the  Dresser-Rand margin within that develop.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Let me start with the last one on pricing and inflation. I mean, we saw something between 2% and 2.5% price  erosion in fiscal 2016, and that may slightly increase with a heavy focus in PG and also in Wind Power. But  overall, there is no huge change expected in 2017 over 2016 in terms of price erosion. When it comes to cost  inflation, especially with regard to personnel, you should take the same assumption as we had in prior year. 2016  was about 3.5% cost inflation and that would also be a pretty good assumption for fiscal 2017, I think.

texts.speaker: James E. Stettler
texts.profession: Analyst, Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: And then secondly, could you just give a bit more color on what's going on in Power and Gas in terms of the OE  versus service business and how you see that developing in 2017? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: The Digital Enterprise is just at the beginning of being built. So, there will always be activities, and this will be a  combination between what I said earlier EAD, electrification, automation, digital enterprise. I really feel  comfortable to predict everyone who doesn't have that vertical integration will have a tough time to make a  meaningful difference in that space. But we've seen that all over. And that's what we do. We look into  electrification fields. We look into automation, where we are obviously very strong already. Simulation, we connect  the dots and the bits and pieces, so it's almost like doing a puzzle. You just need to know what the end result  ought to look like, and then we'll find our way. And that's exactly what we do.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, back to PG or Power and Gas, very, very solid backlog in terms of quantity and quality on service. Also, very  solid understanding on that. The service portion has kind of reached a bottom in Europe in terms of service  utilization. Decent backlog on the new business environment. Some very encouraging progress in the LNG field  with what I mentioned in my speech, nothing more than that. Very encouraging innovation in building what we call  ELNG or electric LNG, which is pretty unique in the marketplace, benefiting from what we have done in our  investment in the oil and gas environment.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: There is a lot of space. There is a lot of emission. It's highly attractive and a lot of interest in that space, and a lot  of other capacities in addition to the environment of everything, which is about [500] megawatt. So, that's the  situation and we make the best out of it. So, very encouraging methods, but also constant struggle. We are up  against the best companies in that space and we have a lot of respect, but we also know how to be successful.

texts.speaker: Andre Kukhnin
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Secondly, related to Power and Gas, we see electricity prices up sharply in Europe, 20%, 30%. Is this actually  starting to help your service business over there that it's driven by nuclear issues? And also, with the coal-to-gas  switch economics, if they're quite favorable?

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: Thank you. Let me maybe try that what I will consider to be a difficult question. I mean the large projects are very  transparent because all the big three players are going after them. And so they're very clear and there is  opportunities everywhere in the world. Apart Middle East, it's about Latin America, it is about the United States of  America and China, less other business – anywhere, Indonesia. The good thing is any society anywhere in the  world needs electricity and there are still a lot of people out there who don't. So, that's why it is essentially not a  bad business to be in. The question is, which source is going to produce which electricity, renewable or gas or  steam or nuclear. So, that's why I think there are a lot of opportunities out there, and we'll always be the same  competitors fighting for winning the project, which is natural. So if I give you now the expected market share we  intend to achieve, I'm afraid we pass the impression to my competitors, you will end up in a market higher than  100%.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: On electricity pricing, true. Obviously, you see that, too. I mentioned earlier in one of the questions that service in  Europe, which has been a concern about how much service do we actually need if the turbine turns around, that  has been – you've seen that bottom. We do see some activity about increase and improvement of efficiency, but  yet the jury is still out on how much that would move the needle going forward.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and CEO, Siemens AG
texts.text: Europe is not exactly the most dynamic region at this time where business happens in the gas turbine  environment, but it's more about the Middle East. It's more about Asia, especially China, Indonesia and the like.  Talking about fossil and also of course Latin America and the United States themselves, they have about 100  gigawatt of coal-fired power plants still somewhat operating or stand-by. If you only take that out of the way to  help the planet to be a bit more sustainable would be a massive infrastructural activity, which the new president  could actually do for his country to make it even greater and also more sustainable.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Organic revenues grew moderately by 3%, while book-to-bill was at 1.3 (sic) [1.03]. Industrial Business margin of 11.2% was up 40 basis points year-over-year and reached  the increased target corridor of 11% to 12%. Although, we have been challenged for some market, as well as  internally-driven topics, which we need to take care of in the Siemens Gamesa Renewable Energy environment.  Earnings per share grew 10% to €7.44 compared to fiscal 2016 and well within the raised guidance.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: As a key pillar of Vision 2020, we achieved major milestones in strengthening our portfolio during the course of  2017. We expanded our leadership in the digital enterprise through the Mentor Graphics acquisition, which  actually has turned out to be quite favorable as to what we were originally thinking. So, very valuable asset  integrating the physical, mechanical design together with the electrical design going forward. It already shows  now that this was a very important move to complete picture in the environment of simulation. The three important  steps in the portfolio like renewable energy, mobility and healthcare, we set strategic directions to give them more  independent, going to market innovation and obviously also resource allocation.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: We continuously expand our data analytics and application capabilities to offer leading digital services, which  makes customer pay for because they get the value for it. A good example, outside Digital Factory which is  always being named is Mobility where we just have implemented digital service projects with more than 50 real  customers. It clearly shows us that our EAD system, electrification, automation, digital enterprise, is working. It is  the winning formula in the marketplace. However, obviously, one of the key areas and priorities for fiscal 2018  which we have and will tackle are the structural challenges at the Power and Gas division. We'll do that in a  prudent yet consequent way going forward.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: We expect a further decline in the large gas turbine markets by around 40% for the period of 2017 to 2020 if we  compare that to the 2016 levels. And as a consequence of overcapacities and other behavioral aspects, prices  have come down significantly. We have thoroughly analyzed the market situation and our footprint and are close  to coming up with a comprehensive concept for a future-oriented setup at Power and Gas, mostly associated with  the area of larger turbines going forward.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: So, thank you, Joe, and also good morning from my side. Let me highlight now the performance of the divisions.  As we have pointed for quite some time Power and Gas continues to operate in a very challenging environment.  Global energy trends towards renewable lead to declining markets for new units across the portfolio. In addition,  the demand from oil and gas customers remains at low levels. This unfavorable environment, we booked orders  for 11 large gas turbines and 23 small and medium gas turbines.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: For fiscal Q1, we expect revenue to be clearly below prior year, which will have a corresponding negative effect  on the profit margin. Profitability recovered from the weaker previous quarter  due to a decent performance in our product and system businesses.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Digital Factory's margin is a strong 20.5%, excluding severance impact from Mentor effect as well as expenses for  advancing the MindSphere platform. Process Industries and Drives showed again order growth up 9% after oil  and gas and commodity-related markets are stabilizing, while on the other hand, demand for wind power  component business fell substantially; main driver was the business in China with a sharp increase.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: China will see further industrial expansion, but on a more moderate level. Reflecting on Siemens, we expect the  mixed picture in our market environment in fiscal 2018 ranging from robust markets for our short-cycle businesses  to unfavorable dynamics in our energy generation markets, as well as geopolitical uncertainties that may restrict  investment sentiment. Negative pricing impact is expected to be around 2.5% of revenue.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Now, let me explain the outlook for our Industrial Business. As already mentioned, some of our businesses are  operating in a very difficult environment. Related measures to address capacity adjustments are still in progress.  But one thing is very clear, we will take decisive steps to strengthen our business and we will look at necessary  footprint adjustments.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: We believe this is ambitious. Let me explain you why. Most of our businesses, such as Energy Management,  Mobility, Building Technologies, the Healthineers and Digital Factory are extremely well underway, just to name a  few. They will compensate for significant headwinds, which we expect next year.

texts.speaker: Mark Troman
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: And then secondly on the sort of why the restructuring outside of Power and Gas, Process Industries and Drives  obviously has a few issues, but could you outline what you need to do in terms of capacity adjustments in other  divisions outside of Power and Gas. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Thank you, Mark. Before Ralf goes into the question two, maybe I'd give you my take on the Power and Gas. I  mean obviously, profits have been falling not as much as everywhere, but still we need to have a serious  environment, decline is forthcoming not unexpected. With the capability of Renewable Energy to capture  economically feasible territories and we do expect today that capacities in the market for large turbines, large gas  turbines might be as much as 400, 420 units a year assuming we are at 110, 120 a year, obviously there is a  significant demand for the right sizing.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Hi, Mark. Ralf, speaking. So, you have been also asking about the wider picture. You have been calling it  restructuring. I mean, of course, the dominating piece is going to be around capacity adjustments in Power and  Gas as we have been pointing out. There is still, and I tried to address that also in my speech, a need to look into  Process Industries and Drives. So the big picture there looks like, from a commodity markets and oil and gas  perspective, it looks like we may see the trough or may have seen the trough. So, there's positive momentum also  on the top line already in the fourth quarter and the third quarter of last fiscal year that we could sense. Is it  sustainable, we need to watch very carefully. But there is also quite heavy impact from the fierce fights in the  renewable energy environment where the wind power components that our large drives division is delivering is  still quite under pressure not that much on quantities, but rather on pricing, so we need to be very careful there.

texts.speaker: Andreas Willi
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: Yeah. Good morning, Joe, Ralf and Sabine. I have two follow-up questions on power on the details. On the  service business, you gave a relatively robust assessment there compared to GE which cut substantially there  and also MHI which reduced guidance in service. Maybe you could give us a little bit more information around  what you're seeing there and to what degree is this difference to other companies may be driven by the treatment  of accounting and advanced gas parts upgrades?

texts.speaker: Andreas Willi
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: And what do you see in the outlook? You say for the foreseeable future it looks or the near-term future it looks  fine. But we're hearing that new gas turbine service contracts are agreed at 20% sometimes even 50% below old  contracts. When is this going to translate into margin pressure, which given that probably equipment is loss- making and staying there for a while is obviously the key question going forward. And maybe also on Dresser- Rand, where we finished the year, is the book-to-bill now above 1, so the business can stabilize and how the  integration is going given also you're now on the third CEO of that business this year?

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Yeah. Thank you, Andreas. Maybe I'll start with the topic of Power Generation, and obviously, service business in  particular. We do not know what our competitors do and how they assess the situation at their customer base. All  we know is from certain data-based sources is that we have quite a full pipeline in that area. Maybe this has to do  with the geographical correlation between demand and service.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: I can't, as I said, I'm going to comment on our numbers and not to answer made by somebody else. Definitely, we  do not need accounting flexibility to drive anything, we've never done that and if I just look at the environment, I  think it was a wise idea to focus more on the business than on accounting and the reporting. But what I can tell  you is for the foreseeable future, we see a very robust business there, we do a lot in terms of demand response in  digital using our digital capabilities in the service area. And so, I believe we should be okay assuming that there is  no disruptive way of doing some matters differently.

texts.speaker: Ben Uglow
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Good morning, Ralf, Joe and Sabine. Thank you for taking the question. I guess we're all sort of looking at the  same puzzle around power and, to some extent, it was already addressed. But just on Power Service, I guess I'll  ask the previous question a slightly different way. Your competitors are seeing some pressure from lower outages  and lower fleet utilization rates. Are you seeing the same pressure on utilization but you're actually able to offset  it, so that somehow you're not seeing the same degree on the margin line? So, that's question number one.

texts.speaker: Ben Uglow
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Question number two, I realize this is slightly unfair and, Ralf, but you gave us nicely an indication on the margin  in oil and gas. Is it fair for us to assume that the oil and gas margin should, if anything, be getting a little bit better  in 2018, i.e. that this 2017 will have been a trough level for the Dresser and other businesses?

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Very clearly, first half 2018 is the targeted timeframe to go to market. And obviously, we are speeding up to be  ready as quickly as we can. So, on the – again, maybe one word on the Power and Gas, just want to remind you  there's more businesses in Siemens, and obviously, maybe not that volatile ones at this time. As I said, all I can  tell you is our view of the next 18 months, and I think that has been said with Mark and Andreas.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Obviously, there is a lot of power demand and there is a lot of turbines, which are either crude oil fired or have  heavy fuel and this and that. When the oil price collapsed, the Kingdom's budget was in trouble. So they needed  to cut subsidies and all that good stuff, which was obviously not well received. To tell you now, in order to get the  income and costs matter in order.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: What they did is they've been raising taxes and cutting subsidies. Days after that the energy demand was  massively dropping, which obviously has a lower rate of utilization for the power plant. Now depending on who  owns those power plants or service system has a lesser utilization. So that's why it's very hard to discuss that on  an overall industry level. I really do believe it's got to be done in a regional context. And then maybe there is more  clarity on who is affected more or less, needless to say, for example, just to give you another example on the  other side of the coin.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Now, with Europe, obviously, doing reasonably well based on easy comps. In the economy, there is more power  demand. And now if you got more power demand you may need more service. So, if you have a strong footprint  in Europe, well obviously you may be a bit more optimistic about things [indiscernible] (52:51). So, I think, that's  seeing along the lines how you probably need to think of or get just more clarity from the ones who are a bit more  concerned about this topic.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Ben, Ralf speaking. With regard to your question on oil and gas I need to be honest, I'm not that optimistic in  terms of margin development. I mean, what we see in the market is that top line, we should have seen troughs in  most of the commodity and commodity-related markets in 2017.

texts.speaker: Ralf P. Thomas
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: But there, price pressure will not go away anytime soon. I'm absolutely sure because overcapacities need to be  eliminated first, and then we will see the new normal. So, I'm prepared. We are prepared for the same level of  pricing pressure in fiscal 2018 when it comes in particular to large gas turbines for the next couple of quarters.

texts.speaker: Josef Kaeser
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: In the old days, a standalone Spanish company and a Siemens division, just to give you an example, both have  developed both the same low-wind turbine capacity as they do now for one and they would still at some point in  time, a Spanish company would still have try to get enough knowledge, capabilities, competencies and  experience to execute on the offshore opportunities in France. Now I guarantee you it's much simpler for a  combined entity which has the market leader in offshore with 20 years of experience on how to do that as part of  the game. And I could go on and on and on and I think in the interest of time I stop here and maybe get the last  one to ask a question and especially get it answered.

texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG

texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: The Mendix acquisition now closed on October 1, and we are starting to use – massively use the low code  platforms to speed up our application development, which obviously again in turn provides customer solution  which are – make customers willing to pay for a benefit there.

texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc

texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: Thanks, Andreas. I mean obviously, we agree with you that the power generation market will be impacted quite a  lot by issues of rebuilding the economies, which have already been suffering from a lot of external impact.

texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Siemens AG

texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Siemens AG
texts.text: And that's only a natural – that's only a matter of time [indiscernible] (61:34) that building, operators are  determining when they need service and not the product OEMs telling them when they need to pay another  horrendous amount of money for people coming in and do a job which the others could actually determine. texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: And a second one is now also waterproofing, but this time it's for new buildings. It's basement waterproofing. We  developed a new exciting membrane solution to seal off the concrete basements in houses, buildings, and  infrastructure.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: This new system, traditionally you're using a bituminous solution to seal the concrete against water. And now we  are doing this with a membrane. texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sika AG

texts.speaker: Jan Jenisch
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sika AG
texts.text: We have different trends also for other materials. The modern car is not a steel car anymore. texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sika AG
texts.text: Similar exciting is the life-cycle concept we have in construction. You see here three lines, you see the  infrastructure, that's the first cycle in an emerging market. texts.speaker: Jan Jenisch
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sika AG
texts.text: And so, this gives us the opportunity to come into these markets very early, and then we get ready for the second  cycle, which is market education and building standards, so that high-performing Sika products we see in the  global infrastructure projects will then come into the general market and they will start to use our additives, they  will start to use our mortars and so on, and that's the second life-cycle we focus on. texts.text: <A – Tom Johnstone>: If I then go to the customer area, we are in close contact with all of our  customers and trying to understand exactly what impact they could have. The area with the biggest  risk is, of course, the car and light truck industry, and to a lesser extent the heavy truck industry.  And that is due to both components such as the engine-based components, air flow sensors, also  into ECUs, which, as you know, is something like a truck. I don’t know, is it 35, 40 or so ECUs in  them. So the areas like that, in cars, of course, significant number to look at what could be the  impact there.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <Q>: Hi, thank you for taking my questions. Just have a quick question on our operating margin.  Note that our industrial division, have a great margin this quarter. But then I note that like the wind  market in China is actually suffering right now. I mean, the wind turbine markers and the  component makers there because of the wind turbine price decline. Are we going to see some  margin pressure on that front going forward, meaning are we going to sacrifice some of the margin  for growth there? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: <A – Tom Johnstone>: Yes. I would say, our wind turbine business or renewable energy business  in China continues to develop very positively even in this quarter. And that is due also to the fact  that we have set new technologies we’ve been bringing in to that industry. And then also when we  combine towards that the acquisition of a Lincoln, where Lincoln has a leading position in supply to  wind turbine manufacturers, I think we’ve weighed into our technology offer to the wind turbine  business. And of course depending how things develop going forward in the wind turbine, we  expect to be able to continue to outperform the market in that area. Will it give a margin pressure?  The wind turbine business is a good business for SKF, but as I said there, there also we see wind  turbine business in Europe looking a little bit better towards the – going through the rest this year.  So I think that will continue to develop with it. So I don’t think that will have any impact on the  industrial margins.

file: SKF.B - Q1 2012 Earnings Call 19April2012 300 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 19-Apr-12.pdf

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: We gained a number of new businesses, some of which we were able to announce and highlight in the report, such  as the new business for the wind industry with Vestas, the new business for railway with Siemens, and the wheel  end and transmission bearing business with Scania, which will mean that we will start manufacturing these  bearings in Brazil which will -- for Scania, which were previously imported there. This will help support Scania,  but also support our other prop customers there.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: But we also did very well in the Industrial business, with good sales growth in virtually all our major industries in  North America. Energy grew for us, both traditional and renewable. Off-highway was strong, as was Aerospace  and our Lubrication business. We also saw a very positive development in our sales to our industrial distributors.  North America in total has been very positive for SKF during last year, and this has continued this year.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: In Europe, the development was very much as expected. The Industrial business had the best growth, with sales to  renewable energy, aerospace, railway and our Lubrication business developing very well. Sales to industrial  distributors also held up very well, despite the uncertain market sentiment. As expected though, we saw a major  decline in our sales in the Automotive business. The car industry, heavy truck industry and vehicle service market  all suffered.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: Moving over now to look at Asia. And here, we saw the biggest decline in our business and our sales in Asia were  much lower than expected. This was driven by significantly lower sales in our Industrial business and particularly,  our business in China. Although I must say that even though January was weak, and even if I discount the Chinese  New Year, China was weak, we saw some improvement in our business as we went through the quarter in Asia.  So, let me start now by saying a few words about China and what we saw for our business there. Our decline in  sales was mainly in the Industrial businesses, with a continued weak renewable energy business and a weak  railway business, which we have commented on before. I would say we still expect to start to see some recovery in  our sales to renewable energy in the second half of this year.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: So as I look at it overall, what you saw in China was weaknesses in our renewable energy, our Railway business,  our sales to industrial distributors, which was into general market and our Automotive business, which is specific  to the car business. Other industries down there developed quite well.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: Turning over to India. Here in India, our sales were relatively flat year-on-year. And that means it didn't  developed as positively as they had done before. It was quite broad-based in India, I've got to say. There was some  segments up a little bit, some down. For example, in Automotive, cars were better, but trucks were a little bit  down. In our Industrial businesses, our sales to off-highway in India were better, but to renewable energy were a  little bit down, et cetera. So it was a mixed picture in India and I think our development was very much in line  with what's happening in the marketplace.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: Let me turn over now and look a little a bit at raw materials and what's happening in raw materials at the moment.  I'd say all the main contracts now are completed and show some ups and downs, but overall, the base prices are  slightly up for the group this year compared to last year. If we look at specifically the second quarter, then we will  face slightly higher raw material costs than the second quarter last year and that's due to the surcharges.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: Because if you look at it just now, today's surcharges are slightly lower than the average of last year. And they're  lower, of course, than what we saw in the second quarter last year. But what we see in the books in the second  quarter this year is what we had is surcharges from the early autumn last year. So, that will have some impact on  us year-on-year. So raw material will up a bit on last – compared to last year in the quarter.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: So what are we doing about it? Well, we're continuing to work with sort of three actions. One, sourcing, to do what  we can do in sourcing, to see what we can do to offset the increase. Secondly, we're working in cost reduction, as  we always do. But thirdly, we're working on price increases. And at this point, I'd like to comment that we've  announced list price increases of around 4% in both Europe and U.S.A. and these will come into effect from the  beginning of July. And these price increases in these two major regions will help offset the higher input cost that  we are facing.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: I mean, it seems the Automotive guys go through these things on a regular basis. Now you had the tragedy in  Japan last year, then the floods in Thailand, and now you have this there. But we don't see anything specific on us  just now.

texts.speaker: Benjamin G. Maslen
texts.profession: Analyst, Merrill Lynch International (United Kingdom)
texts.text: And then just coming back to pricing, there seem to be quite a few pricing investigations going on in the industry.  I know you maybe can't talk about those, but can you just talk about the environment that there is in terms of you  wanting to put through prices? Is that more difficult now because of these investigations, or they're not really  having any impact? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: Our sales to renewable energy is strong there. Their off-highway sales is strong, etc., so Germany is quite good and  Sweden and Northern Europe is quite good for us there. So there is a different picture, as you put it. So I'd say  from the first quarter, what we saw, a very big drop-off in South Europe, but seems to have found a base. East  Europe developing okay for us and moving CIS, Russia, et cetera. Turkey doing very well for us. Germany, okay,  but its Industrial. Automotive is down quite a bit and up the north, somewhat – or Sweden will have somewhat  better.

texts.speaker: Benjamin G. Maslen
texts.profession: Analyst, Merrill Lynch International (United Kingdom)
texts.text: All right. Okay, thanks.  Tom Johnstone  President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB  A Welcome. Oh, pricing. Sorry, Ben. On pricing, there, no. I think the environment, it is always tough to do things  and move prices there. These investigations don't impact it. We've got to run the business and we run the business  there and what we do is make the judgment calls on what we think is right for SKF to do. And the fact that we've  now announced some profitability spreads is why I can comment to you there. Nothing beyond that. We just run  the business as is, Ben, there. So nothing different than that.

texts.speaker: James A. Moore
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn Partners LLP
texts.text: Good morning, everyone. I've got a few questions. Tom, if you can pay your pure price, excluding mix, to raw  material impacts, kind of time series over the last year and looking forward, without the numbers, could you help  us on where the best or worst point was? I'm just trying to understand really whether the next quarter's raw  material hedges is tougher than it's been or whether it's easing.

texts.speaker: Colin D. Gibson
texts.profession: Analyst, HSBC Bank Plc (Broker)
texts.text: Thanks very much. Hi everyone. It's Colin Gibson at HSBC. Three questions, please. First of all, just looking at  Chinese growth rates, clearly your core scenario is that these perhaps start recovering already in Q2, can recover  perhaps a bit further in the second half. What do you think – how big do you think is the downside risk to that  scenario? And I'm thinking particularly, you've talked a little bit about winning orders in rail, for example. But  renewables, it sounds like it's still pretty slow.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: Regarding renewable, I mean, it's clear that renewable is something that has been an important part of our  business development in China, and actually, the first half of last year was at record levels for renewable business  in China. And then, it hit the wall in the third quarter or end of the second quarter and the third quarter, if you  remember there.

texts.speaker: Guillermo Peigneux
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Okay, thank you. And a follow-up, can you comment a little bit on utility prices and energy prices?

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: In terms of U.S.A., I mean, we see a good development in the U.S. businesses. We've been running now all through  2011, in fact, 2012. I'd say in Automotive we see production going up year-on-year. We have a new business in  Automotive. We've gained some new business for the light vehicle business in North America. And that's why we  are performing better than the marketplace there. When it comes to the Industrial business, we do see traditional  energy. Traditional energy – energy in North America is doing well for us. It's more traditional energy than  renewable there. Of course, longer term in renewable, we need to see what happens with the [ph] BTC (45:37) and  other things there's a lot of questions on.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: It was a, if you take Drives out of it, I would say, if you take in total, the areas that were down, particularly  renewable and rail out, Automotive was down, carbons  were down for us, and Industrial Distribution. They were  the two main major areas that were down for us there. The Drives business, that went up for us in China, with us  there. And they were both clearly important, not the same amount each of them, but especially the distribution   was fairly important for us there.

file: SKF.B - Q1 2013 Earnings Call 17April2013 330 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 17-Apr-13.pdf

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: We gained in the quarter a number of new businesses, as you can see in the report, with companies like Pratt &  Whitney for main shaft bearings for the aircraft engines, with Nordex for both bearings and lubrication systems  for wind energy, and for a very big and important steel producer where unfortunately I cannot give you the name.  I can tell you though this is a very important long-term contract covering nearly all our technology platforms and a  very good [ph] business (3:18) the team have done.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: At the start of this quarter, we attended the Hannover Messe, one of the largest industrial fairs in the world. At  that Messe, we launched a number of new products, some of which joined the BeyondZero portfolio such as the  Extended Life spherical plain bearings, which are used in industries such as construction, farm and forestry. We  launched a new magnetic – permanent magnetic motor and active magnetic bearing package for irrigation  blowers and wastewater plants. And both of these, the Extended Life spherical plain bearing and the permanent  magnetic motor will give our customer really, really great energy savings.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: We're working with pilot customers in wind energy, railway and the steel industry just now, and then we will go  out to other industries. As I said, this is a new breakthrough and we've now made our bearing not only the heart of  the machine but also the brains.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: We see an improving demand picture in China when I talk about renewable energy customers, which, as you  know, have been weak for us since mid-2011. Our railway business was down in the first quarter in China, but that  was basically due to no major contracts going through on freight cars. This should improve in the coming quarters  as new tenders will come out. Sales to industrial distribution also, which as you know has been weak for some  time, has stabilized there. So, overall for China, when you look across it, I would say we see a more stable business  and some positive signs that that will develop positively – better as we go through the year.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: In India, however, we still have some concerns. Basically all major industries in India showed declines, with the  biggest drop being in renewable energy, but also industries off-highway and the general industry were weak in  India. Sales to truck industry and cars were down in India, but the sales to the Vehicle Service Market and to our  two-wheeler business were – developed positively. I think India will take some time to recover. It's not showing  the same recovery as we've seen in – or strength as we've seen in China.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: If I look sequentially though, what you can also see though is that we had some improvement, some 1.2 percentage  points, again, if I clean them both from one-offs. And this was influenced and as a result of, of course, slightly  higher manufacturing volume, but also the cost reduction activities which we have. Cost reduction activities are  starting to give us some benefit. And my estimate is in the first quarter this year we had around SEK100 million of  benefit from our cost reduction activities that we've already taken. And that, if you compare it to last year. A little  bit less if you compare it to the fourth quarter, but SEK100 million if you compare it to last year.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: From an industry viewpoint, basically, aerospace is expected to continue to develop positively as will two-wheelers  and electrical. And you can see that energy which is renewable energy, we expect a positive sequential  development and that is driven by China, whereas I said earlier, we're now able to see in addition to a lot of things  you could see an improving activity in renewable energy in China.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: Before I close, I'll turn to raw materials. Raw materials actually are slightly lower at the moment, the cost for raw  materials compared to last year. And I think that will remain the same in the second quarter, and that is generally  due to lower surcharges that was seen in the business. So, we'll get a little bit benefit from raw materials.

texts.speaker: Klas H. Bergelind
texts.profession: Analyst, Nomura International Plc
texts.text: Yes. Good morning, Tom. Good morning, Marita. My first question is on your wind business, you're obviously  guiding higher on energy. We have seen some positive news flow recently both in the U.S. and in China on  extensions of tax credits, new approvals and so forth. How do you think this will impact margins? I assume your  capacity utilization here must be pretty low. So [ph] positive for (45:17) margins and how quickly could you ramp  up here in terms of capacity?

texts.speaker: Klas H. Bergelind
texts.profession: Analyst, Nomura International Plc
texts.text: The second question is on Automotive. Looking at sort of big-picture macro, it seems like the incremental  weakness currently is in Germany with the premium manufacturers starting to cut production. Your volumes  obviously weaken much earlier, suggesting that you are more exposed to the volume end. I'm trying to understand  the mix here. Should we assume that we have passed the trough from the volume side and we're less exposed to  the premium side, that we shouldn't get worried as we go into the second quarter?  Tom Johnstone  President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB  A  Very good question, both of them. Let me take the renewable energy. First of all, as you rightly point out, in North  America, the PTC has been extended. It was late in doing that, which means that the renewable energy business  was very weak at the start of the year. But to be quite honest, the absolute level in 2013 will still be very, very low  compared to what it was in 2012 because there was a lot of activity level underway in 2012 ahead of the ending of  the PTC. So you're still going to see a big drop off, absolute volumes, 2013 versus 2012 in North America. And I've  got to say renewable energy in North America is not a huge business for us. It's more for our lubrication business a  little bit more than it is for our bearing business.

texts.speaker: Klas H. Bergelind
texts.profession: Analyst, Nomura International Plc
texts.text: When we go to China, yeah, we're seeing positive signs in China. And that is good. We're starting to increase the  shipments into our renewable energy customers in China. Will it have benefit? Yes, we will soon hear it will have  benefits in manufacturing. Not so much in the second quarter. And the reason being is that [ph] we can set  (46:53) them some inventory for some time in renewable energy because of the fact that it actually hit the wall in  2011 – mid 2011. So the first thing we'll do is to run with inventory that we've got. But manufacturing will start to  move in that during the second quarter. So as you go into the second half of the year, you'll see some benefit from  that in terms of manufacturing. And of course that is a better business for us.

file: SKF.B - Q1 2014 Earnings Call 15April2014 300 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 15-Apr-14.pdf

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: Maybe let me make some comments on Kaydon right now. They've started the year very well indeed with very  good growth and they also gained some important new businesses. Operating margin also improved year-on-year.  Of course, they are impacted by PPA and the fact that the fuel savings expected this year have not kicked in yet,  but excluding this, we still improved margin. You can also see in the Specialty Business area that even PEER and  GBC saw strong growth in the quarter.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: From a country viewpoint, very good growth in China, driven by cars, sales to passenger rail, renewable energy,  but also in China, general industry developed okay for us. Indonesia was up. Here, two-wheelers were the driver.  India also showed some slight growth in the quarter. However, we still see weakness in Southeast Asia and  Australia. Our industrial distributors development was also slow in the quarter in Asia overall, although somewhat  better in China.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: Turning now to look at raw materials, they are slightly lower compared to last year at the start of this year and will  remain so in the second quarter. We are facing some pressure from our suppliers for higher prices, but our  purchasing cost reduction program is working and we expect a similar development this year as we had last year  from our purchasing.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: So in closing, I think we made a solid first quarter. We've taken some important new orders. Our cost reduction  program continues to deliver results even if we have some negatives offsetting these.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: No. The cost reduction is not SEK 0.5 billion year-on-year. We had cost reduction during last year. I think the fuel  cost reduction from our cost reduction program last year, I think the gross savings was around SEK 800 million  for the full year. We had, in the first quarter, a certain amount, it was a low amount. As you remember,  restructuring ramped up as we went through the year [indiscernible] (13:51). I estimate that if I adjust out at the  moment with the purchasing situation, with the cost reduction, et cetera, we probably had something like SEK 140  million or so benefit first quarter this year versus first quarter last year.

texts.speaker: Erik Golrang
texts.profession: Analyst, ABG Sundal Collier AB
texts.text: Thank you. Follow-up on the mix there. I mean, I know pretty well what are the good and bad mix in the Auto  division, but could you remind us now what are the good and bad divisions are sort of in the industrial division?  What are the major margin differences? It used to be rail and wind; that was good, but has that changed now?

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: Yeah. Rail and wind overall from a group viewpoint are good margins, but at the moment, with the situation still, I  mean, although Asia is ramping up in renewable. If I look at it in total, the mix between the regions is much more  an issue than the mix between the businesses.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: And of course, we'll see a much stronger ramp-up in Asia in both renewable and rail. We still have a little bit  higher cost in that area because operations that they're not fully utilized yet. So, as we go through that, we'll get  back to better margins, but it's a regional mix and that industry mix has impacted them at the moment.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: On the contrary, on other side, we expect areas like energy to be strong development going forward quarter-on- quarter. So it's the combination of all these pieces together gets us relatively flat.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: And I don't think you can just blame the weather. I think lots of other issues around investment in the general  industry arena. And if you strip out energy over there, both traditional and wind, if you strip out aerospace, if you  strip out railway, then you see the big heavier industry just not coming through. I think it's just the cautiousness of  the people and it has gone on. It's a good point you raise. It has gone on longer than one will expect, but it is that  cautiousness that is out there. And so from that viewpoint, I'm as – I don't have any better answers than you've  got on that one at all.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: And just a general feeling is that with weather dropping out with other factors, they kind of continue to like PMI.  So from the indications we've got from our organization and from the discussions I've had, and I'm going to U.S.A.  next week as well, it looks a little bit better into the second quarter, but not a dramatic change there in total. In the  Automotive, no, nothing than pure price slippage following the EU investigation at all.

texts.speaker: Alexander S. Virgo
texts.profession: Analyst, Joh. Berenberg, Gossler & Co. KG (United Kingdom)
texts.text: Yeah. Morning, Tom. Morning, Marita. Thanks for taking the question. Just a quick one on the energy comments  actually. Wondering what – so if you can give us a little bit of color around what's driving the sequential strength  in both Europe and North America.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: Yeah. For the energy in total, I mean, energy, we've had a very good development at the end of last year and in the  first quarter. I mean, we must remember, first of all, we'll take North America. North America we're down  dramatically during last year.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: I think there was underlying demand improvement in the market as well, if I listen to some of the comments  coming out from some of the wind turbine producers, but I think we performed better than the market.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: Kaydon is a little bit less than that after PPA in the quarter at the moment. And it will improve as we go through  the year, the Kaydon one, but it's a little bit behind. And that's because of the fact that in order to get that straight  level of figure, we need to get the fuel cost saving program in place.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: And if I remember, I told you that roughly, this year, we should have 40% of our targeted cost saving in the  bottom line this year, but that ramps up as we go through the year. So it's a little bit lower than that.

texts.speaker: Benjamin G. Maslen
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: And then on just your comments on March, you said that growth was very good. Do you think that reflects an  acceleration in the markets or is that Easter timing, more working days, U.S. weather stabilizing kind of short- term practice that maybe then reversed in the second quarter? Thank you.

file: SKF.B - Q1 2015 Earnings Call 17April2015 300 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 17-Apr-15.pdf

texts.speaker: Alrik Danielson
texts.profession: President and CEO, SKF Group and President, Industrial Market
texts.text: Thank you very much. Welcome, ladies and gentlemen, here. We are in Sweden, a wonderful spring day, sunny  and warm and a lot of pollen in the air. So if I'm a little bit – if I sound a little bit different today, it's because I  have starting to feel it myself.

texts.speaker: Alrik Danielson
texts.profession: President and CEO, SKF Group and President, Industrial Market
texts.text: Well, today, we released our report for the first quarter of 2015. As always, we were very busy in the quarter. We  took a lot of new businesses across many industries, as you can see in the report, in rail, renewable and  automotive to name a few. We've also launched several new interesting innovations, some of which we have  included in the presentation material.

texts.speaker: Alrik Danielson
texts.profession: President and CEO, SKF Group and President, Industrial Market
texts.text: Our profitability excluded one-offs has also come in according to expectations. Henrik will come back to this.  During the quarter, we also became one of the first organizations to achieve the energy management ISO 50001  certification on a global scale. The group's energy management system is deployed across 38 manufacturing  facilities around the world, covering more than 90% of the group's total direct energy use.

texts.speaker: Alrik Danielson
texts.profession: President and CEO, SKF Group and President, Industrial Market
texts.text: As mentioned many times, one of the key activities going forward is the continued step-up of relevant technical  development to be able to differentiate, create value to our customers and to be cost competitive. Once such  initiative just announced is the investment of SEK 300 million in two large size bearing test rigs in Schweinfurt,  Germany. One is to be dedicated to bearings for wind turbines and the other for a wide range of application  segments such as marine, mining, construction and steel. In these rigs, real-life running conditions can be  replicated.

texts.speaker: Henrik Lange
texts.profession: Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: In North America, our sales were lower than we thought going into the quarter. This is due to three main reasons.  First and foremost, on the industrial side, the direct and indirect effects of the lower activity in mining, farm and  forestry, and oil and gas had a negative effect on our sales to customers serving those industries. And the parts of  the industrial business, which developed well in North America were energy and industries outside of mining,  farm and forestry, and oil and gas.

texts.speaker: Alrik Danielson

We'll supply them to projects in turbo gas  expanders and two new gas projects in Australia. And by the way, we are the world market leader in supply and  manufacture of magnetic bearings.

texts.speaker: Marita Björk
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, SKF AB
texts.text: Another new business was the business we gained from our BeyondZero portfolio solutions, one of them is SKF  Bus Door Actuator. We talked about that back in May that we had been doing testing on that, and now we've  gained the business on it, and we will supply that to Volvo Bus starting early next year.  And we gained some important business in bonded piston seals, where we have a very good technology there, and  this will be used in automatic transmissions for Mazda in Japan. So, a number of good businesses in the quarter,  these are the ones we can talk about. There were many more businesses we gained.

texts.speaker: Marita Björk
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, SKF AB
texts.text: Our industrial business, however, did not develop as positively as in the first half. Sales – our sales to general  industries such as pumps, compressors, small gearboxes, et cetera, were down slightly in the quarter. Our  business to off-highway was okay in the quarter, but it's weakening and we can see that – a weakening trend,  especially from an orderbook viewpoint there. And our sales to renewable energy were down a lot in North  America. But that, a you know, is not such a big market for us.

texts.speaker: Marita Björk
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, SKF AB
texts.text: If we look at it from an industry viewpoint, then – and in fact with the industrial market, if we exclude aerospace  and renewable energy, who both grew in the quarter, then all other main industries declined year-on-year and  sequentially. Aerospace, as you know, is going pretty well. Renewable energy is due to the fact that we've gained  some new businesses, it's not that the market itself is developing well.  In the other industries we saw declines in general industry such as pumps, compressors, gearboxes, as we saw in  USA, and in heavy industries, such as metal, cement, and paper. And we also saw industrial distribution going  down for us.

texts.speaker: Marita Björk
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, SKF AB
texts.text: In China, our decline in sales remains mainly in the industrial businesses. Renewable energy continued to be  weak. We thought it would get better as we went through the year, but it's remained very, very weak. The railway  business was weak a little bit for freight cars. What that means it didn't grow for freight cars, both the new tender  was delayed, and the announced stimulus for the railway industry has not really had any impact.

texts.speaker: Marita Björk
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, SKF AB
texts.text: In India, our sales declined in the quarter. We faced a very weak development in the industrial market. Renewable  energy was down, general industry, et cetera: really quite broad based, down, in Indian market, as well as our  sales to industrial distributors was down there. From an automotive viewpoint, I'd say mainly the highlight was  the sales to heavy trucks, which were down a lot as well.

texts.speaker: Marita Björk
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, SKF AB
texts.text: Turning now to look at raw materials. I would say, raw materials, they will be relatively unchanged to what –  compared to last year, but a little bit better than the third quarter. This is due to lower surcharges, not a big  change in the base prices.

texts.speaker: Marita Björk
texts.profession: Head-Investor Relations, SKF AB
texts.text: Looking forward, we're working with our suppliers to finalize the contracts for next year, so it is too early to give a  view on that yet. But be sure we're working on that now. When I look at the macro environment, although, I must  say I expect some improvement in our purchase prices as we go forward into next year.

texts.speaker: Benjamin G. Maslen
texts.profession: Analyst, Merrill Lynch International (United Kingdom)
texts.text: Secondly, just on the inventory reduction, you said you're destocking Q4, but I guess the longer term objective is  to get to 18%. Does that mean that you're going to keep reducing inventories as we go into next year?

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: So, they wash out. So the 20% is a pretty good figure of where we are. We're not going to do hard push to get to  18% next year. But we will under produce a little bit as we go through next year as well to bring our inventories  down there.

texts.speaker: James A. Moore
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn Partners LLP
texts.text: Secondly, I wondered, if you could give us what the clean inventory reduction for the third quarter was, excluding  FX? And was that all finished goods and work-in-progress or was some of it raw materials?

texts.speaker: James A. Moore
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn Partners LLP
texts.text: That's what I'm sort of driving at. I'm wondering do you see it getting to zero in the next couple of quarters or not?

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: If you remember, we placed three initiatives to drive our margin. One was growth, profitable growth in our  business, which was focusing on elements of the BeyondZero portfolio, taking full advantage of our platforms and  on the service business.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: Secondly, we said in order to get there we must continue to reduce cost and eliminate waste in our business. So  that is an important element for us as well, of course, as invest in growth, which I'll not talk about just now.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: And that's why, as I say, we're emphasizing our 3C program in SKF, which is spend more time with the customers:  BeyondZero portfolio which would be better for us in terms of our ability to get margin. At the same time, let's  find way to taking cost out. Cost of doing business and manufacturing costs and become more efficient and  effective.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: In Asia, we had a growth of 5% in our sales which was broadly in line with our expectations. texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: Elsewhere in Asia we had good sales in Indonesia with two wheelers of course being the main driver and also in  South Korea. However, sales in countries like Malaysia and Thailand were weak. Looking at India, t he largest –  the second largest market in the region for us, we see a slight improvement but only slight, mainly from  automotive, renewable energy and general industry.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: Let's go to North America and here we did not see the expected development. I still believe in the medium term  and long term development in North America, but just know with all that's happening politically, it's influencing  demand, especially in the industrial arena. Our distributors are very cautious and they are destocking. Off- highway, especially related to mining was weak also. However, we do see good growth in aerospace and in railway.  Our energy business both traditional and renewable developed well, but it is relatively small in the big picture.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: From a regional and a business area viewpoint, we see all of them staying at around the same level as they are just  now except for Asia where we expect a slight sequential improvement and this is driven by the end markets we  serve in Asia. Cars and light vehicles which we expect to continue well, renewable energy, railway, two -wheelers  we expect these ones to continue well and improve sequentially and that brings Asia up sequentiall y.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: And in terms of the decoupling, that's a good question you raised there. I mean I think there is still some,  especially in industrial arena, some cautiousness in the market but I don't use that word a lot. But I thin k there are  people who are looking in many leading indicators, if you look at PMI et cetera and moving to the more positive  thing. And if all that comes through, it should mean some time going forward we should obviously see a better  environment. But at the moment, we're not seeing that.

texts.profession: Analyst, ABG Sundal Collier AB
texts.text: Thank you. Few questions from me. First one on China, if you could talk a bit more about the trends there are  outside of wind and rail, maybe you touched upon it but it would be great if you could address that again?

texts.speaker: Erik Golrang
texts.profession: Analyst, ABG Sundal Collier AB
texts.text: When do sort of the next steps up comes in terms of cost savings?

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: The finished goods inventory is not bad overall. But remember if we're going to be able to hit an 18% target over  the next few years, then clearly we can't keep running the total inventories around the 21%, 21.3%. Even if we take  raw material components, we still have to address the finished goods inventory over a longer period of time. So I  can't say I'm happy with the absolute level. It's not bad with what we are doing just now. But overall, we need to  take inventory down as a total and some of that will be raw material and some of that will be finished goods. But  it's not something we're going to slam the brakes on to do it; it's something we'll do over a longer period of time.

texts.speaker: Tom Johnstone
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SKF AB
texts.text: Chinese competitors locally, no big change. In fact, I would say SKF has been quite successful in getting business.  And if you look at mainly the businesses we've gained in automotive, which are with the local Chinese car  manufacturers, we're gaining more business in the renewable energy arena, not just with the big ones but with  other ones as well. So, I would say, generally, we are developing in a positive way in the Chinese market relative to  the local players. In terms of the Japanese, there is always the question vis-à-vis how they would use or how they  can use the currency, et cetera. It's tough fighting out there with them, but I cannot say it's currency related; i t's  tough particularly in the Asian region. It's a tough competition we're facing.  Andre Kukhnin  Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.  Q  Thank you very much for your time.

texts.profession: Analyst, Joh. Berenberg, Gossler & Co. KG (United Kingdom)

Thanks.
