texts.speaker: Alasdair Leslie
texts.profession: Société Générale SA (Broker)
texts.text: Okay, thanks. If I could just have a follow-up then, and you kind of alluded to it earlier in your – in one of your  responses. But, we've kind of heard of end users downgrading equipment specification in certain areas like oil and  gas and mining, et cetera. I was wondering for you, whether it's just – whether you've seen this in those kind of  isolated end markets or whether it's going to be more broad-based on the, i.e., in some of your general industrial  markets?

texts.speaker: Alrik Danielson
texts.profession: President and CEO, SKF Group and President, Industrial Market
texts.text: Yeah. It's, of course, a – there are two, I think there are two trends if you really look at it, what happens in a  situation like this. On one hand, there is the trend of maybe some of our customers feeling that they are under a  competitive situation, which makes them feel prone to look at a downgrade, yes. But on the other hand, there is a  definite need for many of our customers to look at reengineering of the products as well. And I'd tell you, I really  feel an increase in the interest for many of our customers to work with them on reengineering of their product  portfolio, because, of course, if you honestly – if you look at it, what you can do to – what kind of cost reductions  you can do through reengineering, of course, it takes a longer time, it's something that doesn't materialize  immediately. But the kind of cost reductions that you can do through reengineering is, of course, much superior to  actually sourcing a cheaper component for a deal that you are doing. So I see these both trends. There is a certain,  sometimes, propensity to sort of look at, if I can lower my cost to a different product in this specific component, or  – and on the other hand, I need to review my product portfolio and upgrade to be more competitive. So, right  now, we – I think we see both of these.

texts.speaker: Alrik Danielson
texts.profession: President and CEO, SKF Group and President, Industrial Market
texts.text: And one of these things that we're showing is with this new investment, we're doing Gothenburg with the state-of- the-art production life for spherical roller bearings, of course. Then as you can understand, in this kind of climate  we are now, it's more of understanding where do we have the best manufacturing units, leverage on them as I then  try to rationalize part of the footprint to get the better cost base and that is actually what in the short term we're  focusing on.

texts.profession: Group Managing Director, Smiths Medical
texts.text: Number two, a large portion of our business, especially the consumables volume, is, in fact, tight to procedure  growth. So that's just sort of obvious. texts.text: Peter, thank you for that. Moving now to the operating performance and outlook for each of our businesses. texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc

texts.speaker: Philip Bowman
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc

texts.speaker: Philip Bowman
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: Developing new products and services is also expected to drive medium-term growth. texts.speaker: Philip Bowman
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: While still early days for Jeff at Smiths, I've given him four initial priorities: one, to improve the competitiveness  and vitality of the portfolio with a continued focus on new product development and better marketing. And four, to further improve product quality and, importantly, on-time delivery to customers. And  Jeff will be updating me on progress against those challenges on a regular basis ove r the coming months.

texts.speaker: Philip Bowman
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: Construction sales rose 10% buoyed by improved demand for HVAC ducting and flexible gas piping products, and  supported by a 7% rise in single family home starts. texts.speaker: Philip Bowman
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: Looking to the second half of the year, we expect the positive trends to be maintained. And margins will benefit from higher volumes but will face  pressure as we further increase investment in research and development.

texts.speaker: Philip Bowman
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: Despite the cash demands of our legacy liabilities, our strong balance sheet allows us to fund acquisitions and  returns to shareholders. We continue to further strengthen the management teams, bus iness development  processes, and information systems. And the senior leadership continues to be transformed as we strive to raise  the talent bar. While cautious about sectors such as defense and healthcare, we remain well-placed to benefit from  a range of positive market dynamics. These include growth in energy demand, the ever-present need for improved  security, the requirements of new fuel-efficient aircraft, and increased U.S. residential construction.

file: SMINL - Q2 2015 Earnings Call 18March2015 500 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 18-Mar-15.pdf

texts.speaker: Philip Bowman
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: John Crane delivered a resilient performance which benefited from its focus on aftermarket services for our  rotating equipment customers. texts.speaker: Philip Bowman
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Turning now to our safety and environmental record, we have made good progress over recent years in delivering  improvements to key safety metrics. Although the recordable incident rate rose slightly in the period, largely due  to a number of incidents within John Crane, more than 80% of our sites have been incident -free since the  beginning of the year.

texts.speaker: Philip Bowman
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: In terms of environmental metrics, we have again recorded further improvements on energy, greenhouse gases,  water, and waste. We're targeting a 15% reduction in these by the end of FY  2018, except for water where the  target is 10%. In general, we are making good progress in all of these metrics, with the exception of energy, where  consumption in the first half was adversely impacted by lower winter temperatures, particularly in the northeast  of the U.S.A. We expect to make further progress as we continue to simplify our manufacturing footprint, and we  continue to invest more in enhanced manufacturing processes and more energy-efficient plant.

texts.speaker: Peter A. Turner
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director
texts.text: We also had a £13 million gain from the changes we made in August last year to the U.S. pension plans, as I  described in the year-end presentation back in September. And in addition, we have a £26 million goodwill impairment charge for John Crane Production  Solutions, the small upstream business that supplies products and services for artificial lift. This impact has been  triggered by the significant drop in oil prices, which has adversely affected our upstream customers and their  investment plans.

texts.speaker: Peter A. Turner
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director
texts.text: Philip mentioned that our Fuel for Growth program is on track, and this slide presents the costs and savings by  division. texts.speaker: Duncan Gillis
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, John Crane, Inc.
texts.text: In total, aftermarket revenues grew 3% on an underlying basis. However, an upstream – when upstream oil  services sales are excluded, revenues rose 7%, illustrating the strength of our rotating equipment business. Global  energy demand has remained robust, and many refineries are operating at full capacity. The business continues to  renew and win large contracts. A couple of recent wins include a global agreement with a major Saudi  petrochemical company and a gas seal reliability management contract in Singapore.

texts.speaker: Duncan Gillis
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, John Crane, Inc.
texts.text: Upstream oil services, which represent a relatively small part of our business and ar e reported as part of our  aftermarket business, declined as the low oil price put pressure on upstream customers. Underlying sales of First - fit original equipment decreased 2% as market pressures in Europe were only marginally offset by demand in  North America.

texts.speaker: Duncan Gillis
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, John Crane, Inc.
texts.text: Although we're seeing some delays or cancellations, we continue to increase our share of new downstream  business. These included an exclusive agreement for part of Kuwait's clean fuels project to upgrade two refineries.  This is one of the largest projects John Crane has won in the past 10 years.

texts.speaker: Duncan Gillis
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, John Crane, Inc.
texts.text: John Crane's strong focus on the aftermarket should support a continued resilient performance in the current low  oil price environment. The predictable revenue from our installed base supports an aftermarket that now accounts  for almost two-thirds of total sales. Our customers continued to depend on us for services and repairs provided by  our aftermarket business. Furthermore, our bias towards mid and do wnstream applications in oil and gas also  helps with refineries and petrochemical plants running at full capacity because of the low priced stocks,  feedstocks.

texts.speaker: Duncan Gillis
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, John Crane, Inc.
texts.text: In addition, we have a relatively limited exposure to upstream application, which has been hardest hit so far by the  low oil price. We also have experienced with managing the business through cyclical downturns and have already  identified a comprehensive action plan to preserve margins in this challenging environment. These plans include a  cost reduction program to address discretionary spend in overheads.

texts.speaker: Duncan Gillis
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, John Crane, Inc.
texts.text: John Crane is prepared for the ups and downs of the business cycle. While we're not immune, I believe our robust  business model means that we're better placed than many to endure a lower oil price environment. At constant  currencies, trading performance in the second half may be slightly lower than last year as our upstream segment  contends with the difficult market conditions caused by weak oil prices. But I expect mid and downstream orders  to show resilience and our cost saving initiatives should help to underpin operating profit margins.

texts.profession: President-Flex-Tek, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: Fluid management revenues rose 1% on growth in commercial airframe and automotive applications. Construction sales rose  4% supported by improved demand for HVAC ducting and flexible gas piping products as well as an increase in  single family home starts.

texts.speaker: Tedd Smith
texts.profession: President-Flex-Tek, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: Revenues from heat solutions rose 13% on the back of increased sales of specialty heating elements and  improvements in the household appliance sector. Flexible solutions saw revenue decline 2% mainly because of a  very strong year comparator period when new sleep apnea products were launched. Floorcare, on the other hand,  remained weak.

texts.speaker: Tedd Smith
texts.profession: President-Flex-Tek, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: Our increased R&D investment, up 23%, is proving highly effective at gaining approvals and products for next  generation airplanes and new heating technologies. Sales opportunities for our  specialty heating elements continue to emerge in higher margin markets. Our investment in additional sales and  marketing capabilities is effectively complementing the proven strength of the business and management.

texts.speaker: Tedd Smith
texts.profession: President-Flex-Tek, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: Looking to the rest of the year, U.S. residential housing should show steady improvement. Commercial aerospace  demand will remain muted until the new programs that need our fluid management products begin to ramp up  again. A general improvement in economic conditions is expected to benefit heat solutions while floorcare is likely  to remain weak. Overall, I believe we'll continue to make steady progress.

texts.speaker: Philip Bowman
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Over the past seven years, value engineering, site rationalization and organizational change have all helped drive  operational efficiency across the companies within the group. And most of the projected £60 million of savings, I would reiterate, are earmarked for funding  investment associated with the initiatives to accelerate revenue growth.

texts.speaker: Philip Bowman
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: In terms of outlook, we expect to deliver improved underlying performance in the second half. Smiths Detection  will benefit from a soft prior-year comparator which, of course, was affected by a number of non-recurring  charges. John Crane will probably see a slight easing in trading as upstream customers adjust their expenditure to  the lower oil price, and there's a potential risk of deferral of some OEM projects. The growth rate at Smiths  Medical was slow versus the strong first half performance. Smiths Interconnect expects some recovery but, as  Roland said, will not achieve the revenue and profit of last year, and Flex -Tek should continue to perform well.

texts.speaker: Andrew Reynolds Smith
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: We are seeing people looking at potentially delaying refinery retrofits for example, where they would go through a  midlife upgrade and move more towards an extended preventative maintenance program. texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION

texts.speaker: Rob White
texts.profession: Interim Chief Financial Officer, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: Philip mentioned that our Fuel for Growth program is on track. And this slide presents the costs and savings by  division. The two columns on the left-hand side set out the costs and annualized savings incurred to date and the  expectations for the whole program are on the right. The overall expectations of savings and costs remain  unchanged, although we delivered slightly ahead of our original plan this year with £33 million of annual savings.

texts.speaker: Duncan Gillis
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, John Crane, Inc.
texts.text: Key renewals and new aftermarket service contracts were signed with customers across the diverse mix of process  industries we serve including pulp and paper, chemical, food and, of course, energy services. Despite the  challenging markets, we're able to realize modest price increases in our aftermarket business.

texts.speaker: Duncan Gillis
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, John Crane, Inc.
texts.text: Underlying sales to first-fit customers fell 9% as market pressures caused by the fall in energy prices affected both  volume and pricing across most geographies. While we continue to see delays globally in oil-and-gas projects  which have not yet secured funding, John Crane's overall project win-rate is higher than in the previous period  reflecting our concerted effort to expand our installed base.

texts.speaker: Duncan Gillis
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, John Crane, Inc.
texts.text: First-fit sales were also affected by declines in the upstream business due to especially severe conditions in this  market. However, tight cost controls helped soften the impact on margins. You'll note from the slide that we've  reclassified revenues for the upstream oil services business from aftermarket to first-fit. The upstream business  demonstrates cyclical characteristics that are more closely aligned with the first-fit business.

texts.speaker: Duncan Gillis
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, John Crane, Inc.
texts.text: We increased investment in innovation by 17% underlying our commitment to address future market needs  through engineered solutions and technology advances. The AURA 220 gas seal was introduced representing the  next generation of advanced gas seal technology.

texts.speaker: Duncan Gillis
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, John Crane, Inc.
texts.text: Customer trials are under way for our new Predictive Diagnostics System, which represents a significant advance  in technology for our customers. The system is designed to reduce customers' operational costs by predicting their  maintenance needs and minimizing operational disruption. We also unveiled an advanced fiberglass sucker rod  that increases production output, improves load strength, and reduces lifting costs for oil producers.

texts.speaker: Duncan Gillis
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, John Crane, Inc.
texts.text: John Crane's strong focus on the aftermarket, which generates 56% of total revenue, should support a continued  resilient performance in the current low oil price environment. Our bias towards mid- and downstream  applications in oil and gas also helps with refineries and petrochemical plants running at full capacity because of  the low-priced feedstocks.

texts.speaker: Duncan Gillis
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, John Crane, Inc.
texts.text: We plan to continue investing in growth drivers aligned with our long-term strategy with a focus on commercial  excellence, innovation and IT infrastructure. We will, of course, also continue to review commitments based on  the market outlook. While not immune, I believe our robust business model means we remained better placed  than many to endure a lower oil price environment.

texts.speaker: Duncan Gillis
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, John Crane, Inc.
texts.text: Looking ahead, we expect global energy markets to remain challenging for the coming year with depressed oil  prices and significant market uncertainty. Absent any improvement in conditions, and despite the strength of our  order book at year-end, revenue is expected to decline further. At this time, we believe that it's more probable than  not that full year margins will be able to remain in the lower half of our previously disclosed target range.

texts.speaker: Jeffery A. McCaulley
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Smiths Medical
texts.text: Lastly, we'll continue to pursue investments in COGS and SG&A. And while we anticipate improving our operating  margins, some of the savings will continue to be reinvested in additional growth drivers for the future.

texts.speaker: Tedd Smith
texts.profession: President-Flex-Tek, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: Construction revenue was up 6% supported by growing demand for HVAC ducting and flexible gas piping  products, as well as an increase in single-family home starts. However, sales of gas piping products slowed in the  final quarter reflecting a change in product mix. Revenues from heat solutions rose 8% in the back of increased  sales of specialty heating elements with China showing strong growth. This more than offset the flat demand in  the appliance sector.

texts.speaker: Tedd Smith
texts.profession: President-Flex-Tek, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: Our increased R&D investment, up 13%, is proving highly effective at gaining approvals on products for next- generation airplanes and new heating technologies. Healthy growth in Fluid Management is generated by demand  from quieter, more fuel efficient aircraft for lightweight, ultra-strong hoses. Sales opportunities for our specialty  heating elements continue to emerge in higher-margin markets. Our investment in additional sales and marketing  capabilities is effectively complementing the proven strength of the business and management.

texts.speaker: Philip Bowman
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Thank you for those two questions. Before passing the first two to Duncan, I think I'd just make one overarching  observation in terms of John Crane. Clearly, what happens in 2016 and beyond depends very much on what  happens to the oil price, given the extent of John Crane's exposure to the oil and gas industry.

texts.speaker: Philip Bowman
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: I don't think it's our task here today to try and second-guess what the oil price is going to be. There are an  enormous number of experts out there who produce forecast. Most of them have actually been proved to be pretty  wrong over the last year. And I think from that perspective, I would simply say that our crystal ball is still in the  repair shop.

texts.speaker: Duncan Gillis
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, John Crane, Inc.
texts.text: The other thing I'll say is following the global financial crisis, I think as most of you know, oil prices spiked back  up pretty quickly. So, depending upon your assumption for what oil prices will do come January of 2016, that 5%  number could be quite different.

texts.speaker: Duncan Gillis
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, John Crane, Inc.
texts.text: And the pricing. So, here's the back story. Last year, we made a decision in May of 2014 to take a large price  increase reflective of cost increases that we're seeing primarily around our labor. And we announced that in May  to our customers, and was effective in August, and that was prior to any significant downturn in crude oil prices.  So, we're able to realize pretty good price increases.

texts.speaker: Andrew Carter
texts.profession: RBC Europe Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: The second one, I think the interim stage I think you talked a little bit about pipelines being reasonably active.  And I wonder if you could give a bit of an update on that. Maybe there's been some change there. And then the  final one, I guess this is going to be slightly difficult to answer but, obviously, there's a bit of pressure on the diesel  industry over the last couple of days. And I was just wondering you have seen...

texts.speaker: Andrew Carter
texts.profession: RBC Europe Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: ...a couple of share prices seem to have [ph] moved out. (75:13) But I mean I was wondering whether the move  from petrol to diesel – I mean has that possibly been a benefit to John Crane in recent years and do you think that  it could kind of go the other way?

texts.speaker: Duncan Gillis
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, John Crane, Inc.
texts.text: Pipelines, I think the last time we spoke, I talked about pipelines and gas lines primarily in the United States and  they continue to be built out. The main trunks are now done. So it's a lot of the branches going off of the trunk so  it's still quite good business and haven't seen many changes there.

texts.speaker: Duncan Gillis
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, John Crane, Inc.
texts.text: In terms of gas to diesel, it doesn't really have an impact on our business and so I don't expect it's going to matter  either way for us as long as there's something used to keep the engines running.

texts.speaker: Robert J. Davies
texts.profession: Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Second one is around the growth targets you originally set out at 4% to 6% for that business. How do you think  about those targets in a low oil price environment if we're lower for longer as we head into 2017 and beyond?

texts.speaker: Duncan Gillis
texts.profession: President and Chief Executive Officer, John Crane, Inc.
texts.text: On the growth targets, as I said, the markets are very unpredictable, very difficult to sort of look out without  having a sort of view on oil prices. And so, it's a little hard for us to say right now where we'll be relative to those  growth targets over time without making a lot of assumptions around oil prices which I know, no matter what  assumption I make, I do know it'll be wrong. I just don't know which direction it'll be wrong.

texts.speaker: Jeffery A. McCaulley
texts.profession: President & Chief Executive Officer, Smiths Medical
texts.text: No, it's really those things that don't fit nice and neatly clinically. So, in infusion, it's a very sensible grouping of  products. In vital care, it's predominantly airway management and temperature management, and then vascular  access are the vascular access devices. So, what's left? What's left is our in-vitro fertilization, the Wallace product  line; our veterinary medicine line, basically BCI; our emergency medicine line, which is our Pneupac product line,  and then our patient monitoring product line.

file: SMINL - Q4 2016 Earnings Call 28September2016 400 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 28-Sep-16.pdf

texts.speaker: Andrew Reynolds Smith
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: Against the backdrop with some of the toughest global energy markets in many years, John Crane's margin  declined but to a still very resilient 21.9%. Despite the tough headwinds, John Crane remains our highest margin  division and I'm pleased that the quality of this business continues to show through in this year's results. Overall,  the group headline operating profit margin was 17.3%, down 40 basis points.

texts.speaker: Andrew Reynolds Smith
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: Now, let me take you through the performance of each division during the year. John Crane's underlying revenue  declined 10%, primarily driven by challenging conditions in global energy markets. Oil and gas represents nearly  60% of John Crane's revenue with 40% coming from other sectors like pharma, chemical and paper. This gives  us a broader range of exposures and increasing this focus in other sectors and verticals is a key focus for the  business in the future.

texts.speaker: Andrew Reynolds Smith
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: Key wins in first-fit including Mitsubishi, Siemens and Weir, and after a large project order last year, John Crane  delivered 600 seals and systems for the massive Clean Fuels Project in Kuwait. However, we do continue to see  delays in first-fit oil and gas projects globally.

texts.speaker: Andrew Reynolds Smith
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: You'll also have seen that on Friday, we announced the disposal of our Artificial Lift business. This provides  sucker rods for onshore upstream oil and gas. It's a good little business but suffering from tough market  conditions. It has little synergy with the John Crane business overall, and limited potential to differentiate from a  technology perspective and achieve market leadership. I'm convinced this business will progress in its new home.  Just as I expect, there will be other examples of this approach across the portfolio as we actively manage and  focus ourselves to position better for long-term growth and market leadership.

texts.speaker: Andrew Reynolds Smith
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: And, finally, moving to Flex-Tek, it delivered a solid performance over the year. Underlying revenue was flat, with  Fluid Management revenue down 1% due to a softening of aerospace orders. Heat Solutions revenue was down  5%. In contrast, 3% revenue growth in Construction showed the benefits of our exposure to the U.S. housing  market. 1% growth in Flexible Solutions was driven by increased demand in medical. Operating profit fell 3% on  an underlying basis, largely due to the transition to a range of new gas tubing products. However, we saw  margins improve in Heat and Flexible Solutions.

texts.speaker: Andrew Reynolds Smith
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: We continue to see good sales growth in China and we focused our R&D spend on specialty heating elements,  gas tubing, and aerospace products to meet the requirements of the next generation of more fuel-efficient aircraft.

texts.speaker: Christopher O’Shea
texts.profession: Finance Director & Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: Yeah. I mean, I think that you defined and John Crane as Andy mentioned, we have had the [ph] clear option to  (58:16) service a very cost-conscious energy customer, this customer base over the last 30 years. So, it's not like  many companies that are focused on the upstream business or on mining where costs don't matter until you have  a huge downturn and cost are all that matters.

texts.speaker: Andrew Reynolds Smith
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: And just a couple of observations, I think, in Crane, in the area of first-fit, it's been a really pressured year. A lower  number of projects, more mouths to feed, so to speak. So, that wouldn't surprise you at all. However, on the oil  refining side, which is largely the aftermarket service side, demand remains at 92 million barrels a day, and they  need to keep the refineries running. So, you tend to see less immediate pressure.

texts.speaker: Andrew Reynolds Smith
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: We've got Glen right at the back as well after.

texts.speaker: Robert J. Davies
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: And just on the head count reductions that you already done in Crane, how much more scope is there and how  are you thinking about your sort of cost base? I guess, how far are you sort of cut in that business already?

texts.speaker: Andrew Reynolds Smith
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: Just to give you a feeling of it, the 60% that's in oil and gas and the 40% in other verticals, the pharma, the  chemical. If you ask me to assess today how the management focus was, I'd probably say it was nearer to 80/20  or 90/10. So, it has been very oriented towards the oil and gas. And we're using this opportunity to redeploy  people as well into the other verticals in a much more formal way.

texts.text: Now just to talk a little bit about the divisions. texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: We've got over 200 John Crane service centers globally that respond and anticipate what the customer wants  wherever he is. texts.speaker: Andrew Reynolds Smith
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: On to Flex-Tek, another strong performance. Sales were up 3%, with good growth in most segments and in  particular heating solutions. texts.speaker: William C. Seeger
texts.profession: Interim Chief Financial Officer & Non-Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: John Crane fell 4% as a result of challenges in the global oil and gas markets. Although down year-on-year, we  are seeing some stability in the oil and gas OE markets and an improving aftermarket now 64% of our business.

texts.speaker: William C. Seeger
texts.profession: Interim Chief Financial Officer & Non-Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: Smiths Detection improved 4%, with particular strength in air transportation. Our largest segment increased 9% in  the year. Flex-Tek grew 3%,  reflecting strength in our Heat Solutions segment, which increased 12% in the year.

texts.speaker: William C. Seeger
texts.profession: Interim Chief Financial Officer & Non-Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: Looking to 2018. The progress we have made in executing our strategy through portfolio repositioning and  organic investment supports a return to growth in 2018. We expect the gradual introduction of new products  during the year to support an improvement in Smiths Medical. In Smiths Detection, we anticipate a strong second  half driven by our air transportation business, which should generate good growth for the year as a whole.

texts.speaker: Andrew Reynolds Smith
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: If I think about that remaining piece, the 25%, that's the – I mean, I've said it couple of times before that, well, just  don't hold me to the absolute precision, because we're constantly assessing which businesses we think we can  improve organically and which we just say, let's send them somewhere else. But if you thought about that roughly  in half-and-half terms as far as those that we think will get there in that organic and nonorganic parallel path.

texts.speaker: Andrew Reynolds Smith
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: As far as margin going forward there, we've got a strong margin. We continue to make progress in that margin,  but we also need to step up the investment. So, I've mentioned last time around that we were investing much  more heavily in the digital stuff in Crane. And particularly in some of the ultra-high performance products, because  as stuff is renewing – a refinery, for example, runs at much higher temperatures and pressures now, it's got much  higher demands on the product itself, so the nano coatings that I mentioned in the speech there, those sorts of  things become crucial, plus developing some of the specific products for non-oil and gas like pharmaceutical is  going to be a big focus for us. texts.text: [indiscernible] (01:11:12) of the hurricane. What are potential H1 implications [indiscernible] (01:11:14)...

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc

But inevitably, when you're bringing up a multi-billion-dollar installation – I  mean, they don't shut these things down at the end of the week for the weekend. These things run hard and long. texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: And coming back to the sort of weather in the U.S., with Flex-Tek, I mean, they do a lot of AC-related things, [ph]  flexible (01:15:41) houses, and given the devastation to homes, is that an incremental opportunity for the near  term?

texts.speaker: William C. Seeger
texts.profession: Interim Chief Financial Officer & Non-Executive Director, Smiths Group Plc
texts.text: So, I mean, we highlight that in part because of the breadth of the product and the capability of the technology. texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: Our strong financial performance, increasing order book and broader portfolio has been achieved despite some of  the most challenging economic environment that we have operated in. And we responded to that changing climate  in 2011 by doing the following: Firstly, by focusing on operations, which we know, strengthens our customer  relationships and provides us with the incremental growth that is a hallmark of our company. Secondly, we  launched our BPO division, which we have been building for a number of years. Thirdly, we took the opportunity  to review our UK structure as well as our wider global cost base in order to maintain our competitiveness in these  challenging times.

texts.speaker: Christopher Rajendran Hyman
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Serco Group Plc
texts.text: The environment was such that the entire federal contracting market experienced significant delays in decisions  contracts and even cancelled or reduced scope of many contract or task orders. Because the government could not  enact any of the 12 normal appropriation bills, it functions under continuing resolutions and faced the frequent  threat of a complete federal shutdown, bringing uncertainty and unpredictability into the market during the year.

texts.speaker: Christopher Rajendran Hyman
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Serco Group Plc
texts.text: In the Middle East, ridership on the Dubai Metro has tripled, as I mentioned earlier, and the green line opens in  September. Our Aviation business successfully rebid for air traffic control services at the three international  airports and the General Civil Aviation Authority in the UAE. And we completed the full transfer of the U.S.  military to the Iraqi authorities of its air traffic control services for lower air space in that region.

texts.speaker: William J. Vanderpump
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: So it is mainly head count reductions, some management head count reductions or just in substance what actually  has that been?

texts.speaker: Christopher Rajendran Hyman
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Serco Group Plc
texts.text: The second point I think you're absolutely right. Certainly what we've seen is, you posed the question, is any  continue resolution good. Clearly, it not good because it slows the market down and therefore, you get, even if it's  the same thing you get, you're getting it a bit later. You don't really want that. What we are absolutely seeing in a  sort of bizarre way, there's a restriction and funding, if you go back to whether its Australia, the states, the UK  over the last 20 – 20-odd years, whenever we've seeing a slowdown in economy or a recessionary climate emerge,  we have had more opportunity than less, because they are under pressure to deliver the same service with less or  use the same money to deliver more service. So that's the time, ministers, it's not a luxury, ministers and civil  servants tend to have to go to someone who could do it cheaper, so from that perspective, yes, these continue  resolutions do cause a pent up demand and I can tell you now the difference between our – what we call the  economic buyer in America, where actually, the people would pay treasury, whilst they are going through this, the  people on the ground, are screaming for the services, so the generals that we would serve and the other senior  directors of organizations like the CIA, the FEMA, wherever they are, National Security Agency, they really need  the subs because they have to deliver that to the customers, so I think in the long term, we will find that, hence my  to deliver a certain amount of our services, but they will find they will have no money for it, and so they have to go  to the private sector, and that's been the model, that's not in question in America, policy of outsourcing is older  than this country.

file: SSAB.A - Q1 2012 Earnings Call 27April2012 330 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 27-Apr-12.pdf

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: SSAB EMEA's contract prices or price contracts for Q1 were on a lower level compared to Q4. We took the Q1  contract during November and December when prices were going down. So, we knew that would happen. The  cost-efficiency program we talked about last time is – within SSAB EMEA is proceeding and running according to  plan. The commissioning of new quenching capacity is ongoing and proceeds well also that according to plan, and  I will touch that a bit in a few slides. Sales, just above – or slightly above SEK11 billion, with an EBIT of SEK479  million for the first quarter. EBITDA per tonne, just below SEK1,000 per tonne, and in the – at the same level as  we saw in Q1 2011.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Mining, I would say fairly strong in all regions, with maybe one exception, and that is [ph] energy (04:43) coal  mining in North America slowed down a bit during Q1, and that is of course a combination of a very mild winter in  North America and lower gas prices in North America as well. But apart from that, I would say the Mining sector,  as we see it, develops fairly well.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Energy, also an important segments – several segments, remains on a decent level. Wind tower demand is still  steady, but we haven't seen any extension of the production tax credit yet. So, this could be – we could see a  slowdown here after the presidential election in North America or going into 2013. So, we have to wait and see if  they will extend those production tax credits.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Taking a more broader look, global steel production increased with 1% and amounted to 377 million tonnes in Q1,  so in line with what we saw in Q1 last year. We saw and we see a continued recovery in the North American steel  market, but no surprise, the macroeconomic outlook in Europe remains uncertain. Demand in Q1 was, as I said,  impacted by some replenishment of the inventories among customers following pronounced destocking during  Q4. The strongest segments for us remains Material Handling, large Construction Equipment and the North  American energy sector. Spot prices in general turned up during Q1 and – after a downturn in Q4.

texts.speaker: Marco Wirén
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: A couple of words about the raw materials; iron ore prices for Q1 went down about 12%, but due to the inventories  it didn't give any major impact in Q1, but this impact will come in Q2. We haven't settled any prices for Q2 yet.  That negotiation is ongoing, and we'll get back to you when we have settled thee prices as well. Coal we buy – as  you may know, about 40% is coming from North America and 60% from Australia. Due to the winter inventories,  we haven't received any deliveries during Q1 although we have settled about 75% of those annual contracts with  American coal suppliers and the price went down about 30% compared to last year's contract. But that will not  give any impact in Q2 either due to the inventories we have. So from Q3 and Q4, we will get that impact. And in  North America, we buy scrap on continuous basis to our mini mills. And prices have moved quite a lot sideways  actually. It's slightly decreased compared to year-end or last quarter. But last week, the prices have been quite a  lot sideways.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Thank you. So as said, the recovery in Americas continued and is expected to continue. In Europe the market, due  to the financial situation, the macro economic outlook, the market remains uncertain whereas the outlook for, as  we see it, SSAB APAC is stable. European price contracts for Q2 will be on somewhat higher levels than in Q1. We  will see the impact, as Marco mentioned, of lower iron ore costs or prices in Q2 and the impact of lower coking  coal prices in Q3. The startup of the blast furnace in Oxelösund, the large one, was done in early March. And we  are planning to idle the small one in beginning of May, early May. The SEK800 million efficiency program that we  launched the beginning of Q1 is proceeding according to plan and we will continue to deliver on that one.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: In this example we, with our steel and our design, managed to decrease the weight of the dumper body with 50%  and roughly doubled the life length. So instead of using 6-tonnene, we were able to produce a dumper body like  this with only 3 tonnes of steel. That is of course extremely beneficial for the end user, the owner of the truck or  the driver of the truck. It gives that person or that company possibilities to increase payload or decrease fuel  consumption or a combination on that. But I think this is – this example is interesting in another aspect as well. I  mean for the producer of the dumper body, this of course is also extremely interesting. I have a number of KPIs  here, a number of components. If you compare the old design with normal steel, we were able to take down the  number of components from 100 to 27 in this example.

texts.speaker: Christian Kopfer
texts.profession: Analyst, Nordea Bank AB (Broker)
texts.text: Finally for me, on the cost efficiency program, did you take any cost of that in Q1?

texts.speaker: Julian Beer
texts.profession: Analyst, SEB Enskilda (Sweden)
texts.text: Great. Iron ore, are you now planning to move to a quarterly contract pricing basis?

texts.speaker: Marco Wirén
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: There's no major differences between those two quarters.  Alexander Vilval  Analyst, Carnegie Investment Bank AB  Q Okay. And second question regarding – you said that you plan to idle the small blast furnace in Oxelösund as of  May. What kind of effects do you expect from that, coming into the summer?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Well, if we – when we close that blast furnace, and if we do that early May, we will keep it closed until – at least  over the summer stop. And we will see, I guess, a smaller effect than we saw in Q1 when we started the [ph] bigger  (33:39) blast furnace in beginning or mid-March.

texts.speaker: Sampsa I. Karhunen
texts.profession: Analyst, DNB Bank ASA (United Kingdom)
texts.text: Okay, thank you. Then just regarding the U.S. operations, have you seen – or what is the contract types you have  for the energy cost in the operations there, and have you seen a change in the energy price currently?

texts.speaker: Sampsa I. Karhunen
texts.profession: Analyst, DNB Bank ASA (United Kingdom)
texts.text: And what is the contract term you have in the electricity prices in U.S.?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: We have long-term contracts in North America valid until, I think, it's 2016 and 20-something. So we have long- term contracts, so we're not affected. But – I mean my example was just that we potentially could see a shift here  in North America due to shale gas and everything. So what we saw during Q1 was more the customer segment, so  to say, energy, coal, mining, that they reduced their output from the mines. And that was a combination, I would  guess, of the mild winter we saw in North America this year and also gas prices coming down from previously $8  Sampsa I. Karhunen  Analyst, DNB Bank ASA (United Kingdom)  Q True. I was basically trying to capture the effect from some of the other players using natural gas that have...

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Well, you should probably ask someone else because we are not using natural gas. We buy electricity on long-term  contracts. So, we use electricity and scrap.

texts.speaker: Sampsa I. Karhunen
texts.profession: Analyst, DNB Bank ASA (United Kingdom)
texts.text: Okay. But do you see that there is a risk in the change of the competitive position in that – that some of the players  are using, or see a decline in energy cost in their operations in U.S.?

texts.speaker: Marco Wirén
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: Yeah. When it comes to mix, mix is referring to different segments within the products that we are selling. And I  hear your wishes to get more information and disclose of – understanding of that. When it comes to crude steel  production, I said it's 80-plus in EMEA in – during Q1 and that's the whole EMEA crude steel production  including Oxelösund and Luleå.

texts.speaker: Vincent Lepine
texts.profession: Analyst, Barclays Capital SAS
texts.text: Okay. But if I look at quenched steel again in Q1 and Q2 last year when you were running at about 950,000 tonnes  per quarter, if you had 80-plus in Q1 2012 then that would have mean – that would have meant, sorry, that in H1  last year you would have been at 95-plus.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: With the exception of the small blast furnace in Oxelösund. But apart from that, yes, enormous summer  shutdowns.

file: SSAB.A - Q1 2013 Earnings Call 25April2013 330 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 25-Apr-13.pdf

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: In general, with some ups and downs, our contract prices were stable in Q1 compared to Q4. And we also saw the  effect of lower iron ore and coking coal in the P&L during Q1 and the effect of that is roughly SEK170 million  compared to Q4.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Mining, fairly stable, with the exception of the East Australia and Indonesia, and coal mining slowing down a bit.  But apart from that, no big changes what we have seen. And as you know, US energy coal market has not been  doing extremely well for the last couple of quarters, the last year. So I would say no major changes as we see.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Energy, fairly good segment. There is, in the market now, some large multiple-year line pipe projects being  discussed, some of them fairly big. So this continued to be a strong market in North America. And the  transmission tower business continues to be fairly solid given the market sentiment.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Americas, on the other side, we don't – we run at decent volumes. Here, the problem in the North American steel  market is the difference between ordinary plate and scrap, and that difference has been sliding downwards during  the second half of last year and is now an all-time low. So if it is, call it, a volume issue in EMEA, it's a margin  issue in the first quarter in Americas.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: The demand from the energy and heavy transport segments increased during the quarter and during the end of  the quarter, but construction machinery or yellow goods is still on a fairly low level compared to historically.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: In Europe, capacity utilization among the steel industry is still on a low level. In February, it was 73% which is  quite low, I would say. When we look into the supply chain, we say, overall, but the inventories are at normal  levels after the modest restocking. So we don't expect any restocking or destocking effects in the near future. The  European strip spot prices have been under pressure from late March, April. As you know, we don't sell anything  on spot. We have contract prices. But spot prices have been somewhat under pressure.

texts.speaker: Marco Wirén
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: A couple of words about raw materials. As you know, we had a contract with LKAB for purchases during Q3 and  Q1. And that price went down 23% compared to the earlier contract. This will give an impact in Q1 and Q2 due to  about one quarter lag that we have in iron ore. So steel in Q2, P&L-wise, we will get the same prices in raw  materials, what comes to iron ore, as we had in Q1.

texts.speaker: Marco Wirén
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: Coal, we buy from Australia about 60% to 70% of our needs. And that's bought in a monthly basis. And here as  well, you have seen the prices have gone down. The remaining part of coal is bought from US. And that's an  annual contract. The annual contract ended at the end of March. The new contract, starting from 1 April, same  here, as I said in LKAB contract, we don't know yet the price. We don't know yet the contract length. We are in  negotiations with our suppliers.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: We talked about the recovery we have seen in the beginning of the second quarter for US plate prices. And the  completion of the efficiency program within SSAB EMEA will start to affect the quarterly results from Q2. And the  full-year effect will be seen 2014 year-over-year. But quarter-over-quarter, sequentially, we'll see that already in  Q2.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Another explanation could be that the North American plate market is not getting worse in any direction and the  opposite. And I talked a bit about energy driving this market, the big line pipe projects and some other areas that  are looking fairly okay. So it's – and you're right. There was problem for the steel industry in North America to get  the steel prices to stick. But what we have seen, so far, with the price increase is they seem to stick.

texts.speaker: Alexander A. Haissl
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: The strip steel business, the ordinary steel business, was it above 70%?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Well, when we launched the project or the actions, we said that SEK500 million out of the SEK800 million would  be sustainable cost savings and SEK300 million would be flexibility. So SEK500 million is there and we – they are  sustainable. We'll be seeing them. And SEK300 million out of the SEK800 million will be dependent on capacity  utilization.

texts.speaker: Fredrik Agardh
texts.profession: Analyst, Svenska Handelsbanken AB (Broker)
texts.text: Not much at all. Okay. And then turning then to your raw materials, what's the – what were the Swedish krona  impacts from iron ore scrap and coal sequentially, the change in the quarter?

texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: Depends, of course, where you compare with. And now, the US dollar is about SEK6.6 or something. And when we  signed the contract, that's when we actually know exactly what we're going to have and what kind of contract we  will have. But as you know, we buy all coal and iron ore in US dollars, so, of course, that would have an impact if  it's SEK6 or SEK7. It totally depends which period you're comparing and also when we signed and what levels  we're going to have in that case.

texts.speaker: Fredrik Agardh
texts.profession: Analyst, Svenska Handelsbanken AB (Broker)
texts.text: Yes. But they have – in Q1, this quarter that you just reported, how much have you gained or lost in coal, iron ore  and scrap?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: We haven't specified exactly how much of that is raw materials.

texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: We will have a normal summer outage this year and we will stop the blast furnace for, I think, it's two weeks as we  always do. So you should expect  that we build up the slab inventories before we close down the blast furnace, but in that case, somewhat lower  compared to last year.

file: SSAB.A - Q1 2014 Earnings Call 25April2014 330 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 25-Apr-14.pdf

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Automotive, fairly a good demand in EMEA, especially in Germany, continued okay demand in North America,  even though one or two of the big producers in North America have problems to ship cars due to the severe winter  weather. But the underlying demand fairly stable and quite okay.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Energy continues to be fairly okay and stable, and especially wind tower activity has increased during Q1. In  Europe though, from the energy segment, we get some mixed signals.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Market environment, the global steel production increased during the first quarter with 2% in the European  Union or EU28 increased by 7 %. In North America, only by 1%, and all of the North American steel producers  were affected by the extreme weather conditions, and production in China increased by 2%.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: We saw a demand from several segments increasing, and my conclusion is that our shipments increased more  than the underlying market demand. So we have been taking in Q1 market shares. Prices increased by 3% for  standard steel, and that was only a mix effect. We were selling due to the warmer winter, more [indiscernible]  (06:27) and more galvanized. So I would say contract prices more or less unchanged. And for high strength steel,  they fell by 1% compared to Q4 in local currencies. And high strength steel accounted for 41%, 2 percentage points  lower than the same quarter last year.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Americas, shipments increased by 8% versus Q4. And here we had problems with – and we had an EBIT of SEK  126 million. We had problems with the weather. We had problems to get hold on railcars. We had higher scrap  prices than normal. We had higher electricity cost than normal due to the weather situation.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Demand from automotive and construction machineries strengthened during the qua rter, and the prices of  standard steels were up 7% during the quarter. And for high strength steel, prices were up 3% compared to Q4.  And I said the weather didn't only affect our shipments, it also affected our costs.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Executive Vice President, Chief Financial Officer, SSAB AB
texts.text: Then we had a negative impact from the variable cost of goods sold, and this is primarily rather only due to  Americas. And as Martin mentioned, the higher scrap costs also the weather-impacted higher electricity costs, and  we also had some production disturbances during the first quarter due to the extreme weather. And scrap prices  now in U.S. are on a significantly higher level than they were, for example, in September last year. And then we  had a positive impact of other – here we have for example some fixed costs and we have Tibnor there as well. So  all in all, an improvement of a little bit more than SEK 300 million and the short summary is that better prices in  Americas, better volumes in EMEA, somewhat offset but higher cost in Americas.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Executive Vice President, Chief Financial Officer, SSAB AB
texts.text: We also have lower variable COGS and here this is also EMEA while Americas actually are slightly higher. But in  EMEA, some raw material prices impacted better and also production efficiencies and then we have some negative  on others for same reason as previous page. And all in all, that gives the improvement of SEK 162 million.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Executive Vice President, Chief Financial Officer, SSAB AB
texts.text: Finally, from my point, some words on raw material prices. For iron ore, our prices were 7% lower than they were  in Q4. On the other hand, they were actually 3% higher than they were in Q1 last year. We have not yet signed a  new price contract with LKAB. The one we had expired at the end of Q1. We are, of course, still getting the  volumes from them, but we are in the negotiation on signing the new contract.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Executive Vice President, Chief Financial Officer, SSAB AB
texts.text: For coking coal, which we buy then both from Australia and from the U.S., our price was 6% lower than in Q4, and  actually, 29% lower than in Q1 last year. Coking coal has, over the last few years, been on a downward sliding  trend.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: The maintenance stop in Mobile was moved a bit, and the reason for that was to be able to ship material to our  customers. So, we were first expecting outage to be half of it in March and half of it in April, we had to move it due  to closing down Mobile for three days due to the weather and also problems getting hold on railcars. So we moved  it to the May; majority of that outage has been done in beginning of April.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: The typical mix effect you see is that we – during the summer have more volumes of painted material compared to  – I mean, the toughest quarters for painted is always Q4 and Q1. We had a somewhat milder winter than normal,  and then we had a small effect of the bit more painted material. But the mix effect, as always, that will help the  profitability. The mix effect is niche and standard. I mean increasing the niche part. We were running at 80%  capacity utilization in Q1, which is fairly low.

texts.speaker: Ola Södermark
texts.profession: Analyst, Swedbank AB (Broker)
texts.text: Y ou mentioned that you had lower iron ore pricing in Q1. Are we going to see them affecting the P&L in Q2 then as  normal?

texts.speaker: Carsten Riek
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Thank you very much. I have just few questions; let's start with the Americas. Could you quantify the EBIT loss  you had in Americas due to harsh weather conditions? That's the first one.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Okay, given my memory then, I'll start with the second question. I mean as we said, we were taking down  inventories in Q1 as well. And you're correct. I mean according to World Steel Association, the production in  Europe or EU28 increased with 6% or 7 %. When we look – I don't have a very close or insight in other steel  companies in that aspect. But when we look on our customers and in the supply chain we ser ve, we can't see any  massive stocks or any overstocks or any major re-stocking taking place during Q1.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: And then we had effects. I call it higher than usual effects on scrap prices due to the winter, but also electricity  prices. And then as I said, we had to close the mill in Mobile for two or three days due to winter storms and they  had, for the first time in almost 30 years, ice storms in Mobile and they had no possibility  to take away the snow.  They had to wait for the sun. So the Governor went out and closed down factories and so on. So that affected us as  well, but we haven't an immediate effect to quantify that, but it's a combination of a lot of things.

texts.speaker: Bastian Synagowitz
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank (Suisse) SA (Broker)
texts.text: Okay, got it. And then, again on the one-off effect from the weather, which you think you can quantify and the way  I would look at it was would be there could be if you can tell us the utilization rate in the second quarter will be  roughly stable, I guess more or less, at least, the whole impact should be or should have been roughly in line with  SEK 150 million you expect from the plant maintenance. And then looking at how your margin will progress going  forward, is it fair to assume that we can expect average ASPs on a like -for-like basis to pick up roughly $120 or  even $130 per ton considering the lack in the price increases you have already put out, and the one you put out on  Wednesday evening?

texts.speaker: Bastian Synagowitz
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank (Suisse) SA (Broker)
texts.text: And so how much will U.S. and Europe be combined for the maintenance, outage impact from U.S. and Europe  combined in the second half?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: I would say some of our competitors had production problems in Q1, so did we due to the weather. So I would say  average, no difference compared to us than competition. Price increase, as well you know, prices – or margins I  would say have been on a very low level the last year, on a historical low levels. And what we expect and what we  have been saying the last six months is that we expect – it's not normalized, but a gradual normalization of  margins over scrap.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: No. I see that as a combination of the growing underlying demand and the better – driven by the better economy  in U.S. and [indiscernible] (44:17) I would say. But also, I mean, we are very much, and especially for a standard  plate, very much into the energy segment, and the build out of gas pipelines and pipelines and so on. So, that is  also, I mean, of course, fueling the economy, but also, I mean, the low energy prices. So, it's a combination of these  two.

file: SSAB.A - Q1 2015 Earnings Call 27April2015 330 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 27-Apr-15.pdf

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: If we look at the segments, I would say pretty much as expected. Heavy transport developed during the quarter  fairly okay in Europe and U.S.; Automotive, overall a good demand; Construction Machinery, stable at low levels  in the Europe and the U.S.; Mining, slow demand or low levels in all markets; energy, wind towers and  transmission towers in North America, quite okay, low activity in the pipeline sector; Construction Material,  seasonally slow; and then Service Centers, very slow during Q1, and if any surprise maybe a bit slower than  expected and the destocking phase will take slightly longer than we expected when we released the Q4 report.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: So, what have we done? Well, we have done [ph] easy part of the easy stuff (05:51). We have lower purchasing  costs. We have renegotiated purchasing agreements. We are sourcing more internally to Tibnor instead of doing it  externally. We are shipping coking coal from Oxelösund to Raahe instead of buying it externally. And we have  lower administrative costs.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: We have a positive volume impact coming from both SSAB Europe and SSAB Special Steels. We also have positive  impact of variable COGS. This is related to lower raw material costs, but also that we have been running the  production well in the European system, and also some of the synergies are impacting on variable COGS.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: If we starting compare Q1 to Q1, we had almost zero Q1 last year, plus SEK 34 million. And here, we have a drop in  price of around SEK 400 million. This is excluding currency movements, and it's mainly coming from SSAB  Europe. Volumes basically no impact, and then large impact on variable COGS. And it's the same factors as with  Q1 to Q4, but here the raw material impacts are larger where all three of them, if you say, the big one, iron ore,  coking coal and scrap were lower now in Q1 than Q1 last year.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: Moving then to the raw material side, starting with iron ore and coking coal. In U.S. dollar, we saw both iron ore  and coking coal decreased during Q1 and we have, on the growth rates, from the beginning of 2014 where iron ore  started on almost $140 and is now down at – well, right now it's $58, but it was actually down even below $50 a  few weeks ago. But these are the spot prices for funds. And we buy pellet and our pellet prices decreased with 12%  in U.S. dollar, but actually increased with 1% in Swedish kroner compared to Q4.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: Coking coal has during the same time period, also decreased but not that all as much as iron ore. And for us, in Q1,  our purchase prices were down 3% in U.S. dollar, but actually 13% higher in Swedish kroner. And for our raw  material purchases, we are hedging the same length as the – we're hedging the U.S. dollar the same length as the  contracts. Usually, it's a quarter. And we have now seen the strengthening of the U.S. dollar, but we will continue  to see that also going forward for our purchases.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: For scrap, scrap prices in U.S. then also fell quite sharply during Q1, and they were down 24% compared to the  end of Q4 and actually 35% compared to the end of the same period last year. And we saw especially in February,  there was a big drop but since then, they have been pretty stable. It's important to remember though that despite  this drop now in Q1, scrap prices has not at all dropped as much as we have seen iron ore prices dropped. And  historically, they have been very much co-related but so far, scrap prices have not followed the iron ore drop yet.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: Finally, then from my side, some words about relining that we're doing now in Luleå during the summer. We will  start in the beginning of June. It will continue for three months. We will and we are currently doing them,  replacing this 500,000 tonnes of slabs. So we started up this small blast furnace in Oxelösund during Q1, and we  will continue to run that until the big one in Luleå is up and running again.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: There will be some extra cost associated to this on top of the capital expenditures of between SEK 150 million and  SEK 200 million. This will mainly impact Q3, but somewhat also now in Q2. And it will also differ a bit between  the divisions because for Special Steels, which are now running the small blast furnace again, they will actually  benefit from this because they will have lower under-absorption while Europe, which will be standing down with  the big blast furnace for three months, that cost will be burden on Europe.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Then over to something completely different. A week ago, we launched our new brand name for structural steels,  for steels above 600 megapascal, and the name of that brand is Strenx Performance Steel, and that will be instead  of Domex, Weldox, and Optim, but this is not just a change of a brand name. We also launched this together with  much better guarantees when it comes to workshop properties like weldability, bendability, surface cleanliness,  and so on, and this has been received very positively.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: It depends. I mean, if you take – as forecast showed, scrap prices during March has been fairly stable but if you  look at the – I mean, as Håkan also pointed out, the co-relation between scrap and iron ore is always very, very  high and we haven't really seen that. So my expectation is that scrap prices will continue to move down and  especially now with the season as well. And also given the currency, there is no room for exporting scrap out of  U.S. – my guess would be without knowing 100% that the scrap export out of U.S. is fairly limited. So I think we  should continue to see reduced scrap prices.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: There were some associated to that. On the other hand for Special Steels, we also had some extra cost associated  with starting up the blast furnace. So all in all, in Q1, the impact wasn't – for Special Steel wasn't that – net impact  wasn't that positive.

texts.speaker: Jean-Baptiste Devevey
texts.profession: Exane SA (Broker)
texts.text: Yeah. Okay. Sorry for that. Technical issues, I guess. Quick question on your variable costs that went down in Q1.  Can you explain a bit further given that you explained that the raw materials, and notably the iron ore and the coal  prices, whereas in Swedish kroner versus Q4? texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: Okay. If we start with the first question, the FX part is removed from the variable COGS, that part of the FX  bucket. And even though prices would have  gone up in Swedish kroner during Q1, those are our purchase prices, and that's not – normally, we simplify it and  say that we have a quarter of lag or something. So what you see that we buy in Q1, you normally we'll see hit the  P&L in the subsequent quarter.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: And on the synergies side, and if I got your question right, well, we said we have a net – we have an impact of SEK  100 million now in Q1. And you can find it a little bit everywhere. You find it partly in fixed cost, and you find it  too partly also in the variable COGS. So the positive impact you see on variable COGS contains the synergies as  well.

texts.speaker: Jean-Baptiste Devevey
texts.profession: Exane SA (Broker)
texts.text: [ph] So that's (26:54) SEK 85 million. And how much do you think would be in the variable COGS part in the SEK  275 million?

texts.profession: Exane SA (Broker)
texts.text: Okay. Thank you for that. And just coming back on the first question, so, you said, you were talking purchase  prices. So should we expect the – I mean, could you please give an indication on how you see your raw materials,  P&L impact going into Q2?

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: If we take the iron ore which is on the majority part, we say that if you simplify it, you can say what we buy in one  quarter is hit in the P&L in the coming quarter.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: That's mainly the automotive business. I don't know how many. That's roughly 300,000 tonnes or a bit more than  300,000 tonnes a year. So...

texts.profession: UBS Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: 10%. Okay. Thank you. The third question I have is Oxelösund, you said the small blast furnace is ramping up  again in order to replace to some extent Luleå. What happened to the small blast furnace once Luleå is actually up  and running again?

texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Mostly very limited number, because, as said, we are building up the slabs' inventories now to meet the relining of  the blast furnace in Luleå.

texts.profession: Deutsche Bank (Suisse) SA (Broker)
texts.text: And then my second question is whether there are any, say, effects from your product mix to work to the better  which we should have firm in mind going into the next quarters? texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: In the U.S., we don't – I'm not sure really what you meant if you meant hedging prices or hedging the scrap costs.  But the answer would anyway be that we don't hedge either on the price side or the scrap cost. We turnaround the  scrap fairly fast. So if there's a quarter lag usually on the iron ore, you see the scrap impact going in during a  month or a month-and-a-half basically.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: And then on the contract side, for floor prices, well, as Martin mentioned, we have changed. On the service center  we are selling more at the spot prices while the end-user we are selling more at the contract prices, which are then  typically in the range of three months. And now, this quarter, we have been selling more to the end-user side than  we'll be selling to the steel service center.

texts.speaker: Bastian Synagowitz
texts.profession: Deutsche Bank (Suisse) SA (Broker)
texts.text: Yeah. No, that's [indiscernible] (41:52) I guess not that much. Okay. Perfect. And then just on the last question or  regarding the synergies, so why would the – basically, shipments of coal from Oxelösund to Raahe give you any  benefit or not quickly about that.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: Well, before, Ruukki used to buy coking coal on the external market. But now, since we can do this internally  instead, we save that extra cost.

texts.speaker: Bastian Synagowitz
texts.profession: Deutsche Bank (Suisse) SA (Broker)
texts.text: Okay. And so Oxelösund simply buys the coal cheaper or...

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: No. Oxelösund produces the coking – they produces the coking coal and then they can send that to Raahe, because  Oxelösund has excess coking capacity.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: The important part is the margin of the scrap. And if scrap – if prices have a pressure downwards, selling prices,  my expectation is that we will see lower scrap cost as well.

texts.profession: ABG Sundal Collier AB

texts.profession: Danske Bank A/S (Sweden)
texts.text: Yes. Hi. Thanks for taking another question from me. texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: Well, the under-absorption that was shown in the bridge was not – you're relating to the slab buildup in ahead of  Luleå relining.
