texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: So what I'm saying – and net in Q1, it was basically close to zero-sum game, because we had some of additional  start-up cost in Oxelösund when bringing that blast furnace online. But what I am saying in total is that, yes, the  positive under-absorption you get in Oxelösund and potentially a little bit in Raahe by running those blast  furnaces at a slightly higher level, that will be taken out by that we're standing in Luleå for three months, and the  net impact is this SEK 150 million to SEK 200 million. It's not only under-absorption. Actually, it's a mix of cost as  well associated with it.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: Well, if you take the – if you isolate the blast furnace part, well, you will have the small blast furnace in Oxelösund  running the whole quarter. On the other hand, you will be standing or we will be standing with the big blast  furnace in Luleå for one full month. So maybe up slightly, but not a huge impact.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: No, I can't divide it by 2020, 2025, and compared to – what's the question, compared to aluminum. Well, we have  some steel rates, especially within automotive, where we can compete and outperform aluminum. We can be on  par when it comes to energy absorption and weight, and we can be – we can produce sincerely to a much more  cost effective compared to aluminum. So we have examples where we have been able to take market share for  safety details from aluminum with Docol 1700 and Docol 1800 martensitc steel cold form.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: For this year, we have the PCI coal injection in Raahe, which also when you look in the report, that's the main part  of the strategic CapEx, and that's a fairly big investment. But that's so far the only big one that we have decided  and communicated on.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: However, we entered Q4 on a clearly higher price level than we entered Q1 and we also have, in all our three steel  divisions, a contract structure with some things on spot, some on three-year contracts – three months, some on  six months, which means that, on average, we got a negative impact from lower prices in Q1 versus Q4.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Another segment in the U.S. that has been developing in Q1 fairly well, it looks to be developing well going  forward as well, is the wind towers segment.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Thank you, Håkan. So, what are we then going to do? This is an updated picture with the target of c ost savings.  And as said, synergy program will be finalized during this quarter and will be met. When it comes to the Ruukki  Construction restructuring, all the actions are taken, and that will now onwards be seen in the P&L. What we call  selected efficiency investments, the PCI and the water treatment plant in Alabama, done, up and running.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: This is what we always going to focus on. This is what we always have focused on. But this is what we are going to  continue to focus on. The global market for advanced high-strength steels and Q&T where, we especially within  Q&T are the global leader. Our two important home markets, flat carbon steel and tubes in the Nordic region  where we today have a market share between 45% and 50%. So, higher than before the combination with the two  companies separate and then in North America where we today have a market share within heavy plate of 25%.  So, we have been able to increase that market share as well.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Sustainability is an important part of SSAB, and it's actually our business model because what we do is actually  helping end users to reduce weight, increase payload, increase life length, and reduce fuel con sumption. And that's  how we sell our steel and our steel products. So, that is the sustainable offering. This is one good example of many,  and I've said it many times before, but we – typically when we look into an application, we can typically double the  life length. We can typically reduce the weight between 30% and 50%, and by that then, increase payload, reduce  fuel consumption or a combination of that.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: We are today the most carbon dioxide steel producer – carbon dioxide effective steel producer in the world in our  mill in Luleå. After the PCI investment in Raahe, we are on par with Luleå. So, we have, in that aspect, very good  measures. In U.S., we are 100% scrap based. We only use recycled materials. So, that is important.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: But a couple of weeks ago, we launched a new project together with LKAB and Vattenfall, where we are  determined to look into the possibilities to produce iron without any carbon dioxide as a great product. Today,  when you produce iron, you use iron ore and coal, and you get iron and carbon dioxide. We are looking into a new  process and it's not only theoretically possible. It's also possible in small-scale development tests to use hydrogen.  And then, you would produce iron sponge, and the residual would not be carbon dioxide, it would be water. So, we  are now determined to look into this and try to make it in a full-scale, cost-competitive industrial project. And that  project has been started a couple of weeks ago.

texts.speaker: Hjalmar Ahlberg
texts.profession: Kepler Cheuvreux SA (Sweden)
texts.text: Okay. And then, a question on results on Americas, which was quite good in my view, was there some kind of lag  effect or timing effect where you have more benefit from low scrap prices and price increases? Or is that some  kind of sustainable level or even better level going into Q2?

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Well, as Martin said, for Q2, we have done a number of price increases which we believe will go through. If we see Americas, prices are also moving up. However, at the same  time, we see scrap also moving up. So, there will still be pressure on the margin there. But we have increased  prices more than what we have seen scrap move.

texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: We also saw a strong growth within Automotive. Automotive premium volumes were up 20% year-over-year. texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Americas, I would say continued good demand from the energy segment. We saw higher prices. We saw the  Mobile outage, as we talked about. We also saw higher scrap cost. And this typically hit us a bit earlier than this in  the P&L due to the lead times and the lag.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: Volume also contributed positively, not that much, but around SEK 300 million, and this is Europe and Special  Steels especially. And then we had a negative impact on variable COGS. It's also some impact in variable COGS  and also the negative impact in fixed cost from the Oxelösund breakdown from the Mobile outage.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: Clear volume improvement coming from Special Steels and also from SSAB Europe, while Americas roughly on  the same level. And then variable COGS is, to a very large extent, raw material driven. Slight improvement in  fixed cost basically because we have the large planned maintenance outage in Special Steels in Q4, which we did  not have now in Q1. And we actually had quite a big negative impact from FX mainly due to a weaker Swedish  kroner during Q4. And other further losses then driven by under absorption – or improvement in under absorption  that we run in the mills at a high level.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: If we move then into raw material here, there's definitely more changes. We have seen in the P&L in Q1 and we  will see also in the next quarter increased raw material prices for iron ore and coking coal especially. This is a  new type of graph that we are using from this quarter on, it's our own purchase prices, but it's indexed. So, started  from $100 then at the end of 2015.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: And in this quarter, our coking coal prices – the purchase prices were up 2%. That's obviously very undramatic.  But if we would have added what they were up one year ago, they were up 162%. So, coking coal has moved  enormously. And as most of you probably have followed, we saw a spike in Q4 when it was about $300, then it  went down, almost down $250. And then in the last few weeks, there has been this cyclone in Australia causing  railways to break down, et cetera. So, now it's up around $300 again. At least we don't see any underlying  demand that would trigger this, but it's really much about the supply. So, we would expect that this peak would  come down again during this quarter.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: For our pellet prices, prices were 15% higher, our purchase prices in Q1 than Q4. If we were compare one year  ago, it's obviously not as dramatic as for coking coal, but they are still up 57% compared one year ago. So, very  strong increase on the raw materials side.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: We did during the quarter sign a new contract with LKAB. It's a one-year contract. So, from 1st of April to end of  March 2018. And it's now based on monthly pricing. It used to be quarterly, now it is monthly. And when we move  into this contract now, what we have also seen is pellet prices – the premium for pellets have moved up lately, so  we will in Q2 have a higher cost for the pellet premium as well.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: So, my last picture will be something completely different. It will be the four finalists in Swedish Steel Prize that we  will have in May. And these are four good examples of applications where you can have a lot of benefits by using  advanced high-strength steels or, Q&T. And these are also very good examples of what we work with in our daily  life, working together with customers, helping them to reduce weight, increase life length, increase safety, reduce  fuel consumption and emission.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: I would say we will see prices up in U.S., in North America, and we will see the majority of the raw material costs  going up in Special Steels and in Europe, so in the Nordic business, so to say. And the total delta, we say  mitigated and it's plus/minus something, but what we are trying to say is that you shouldn't expect any major  margin increases overall.

texts.speaker: Johannes Grunselius
texts.profession: Analyst, Handelsbanken Capital Markets
texts.text: Basically, the message is that we should expect sort of a neutral effect on the Steel margins or the conversion  prices overall or...

texts.speaker: Ola Södermark
texts.profession: Analyst, Swedbank AB
texts.text: Ola Södermark, Swedbank. You are saying that you see several of the end segment in Special Steels improving.  Is it mining and energy that's down south or which [indiscernible] (25:44)

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Well, Automotive is still a small part of SSAB and also a small part still of SSAB Europe. We see a strong growth  in automotive mainly because of a number of new products, 1,700 and 1,500 megapascal martensitic material  that is typically very good or developed for cold forming. So, we can compete with aluminum with the same  weight, much better energy absorption and at a completely different price. And we can also compete with press- hardening, the same weight, the same energy absorption but at a more effective price, so to say. So, that's why  we are growing Automotive.

texts.speaker: Seth Rosenfeld
texts.profession: Analyst, Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: In your case, was the disappointment purely just due to the materials flow as you were offsetting Special Steels  weakness, or was there something else there with regards to your scrap purchasing, for example? And then can  you just give us a bit more color on what scale of metal spread catch-up we could expect into Q2, assuming the  Special Steels situation is now resolved? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Seth Rosenfeld
texts.profession: Analyst, Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: And on top of that, if you can give us a bit more color, I know you've talked in the past about because of  seasonality, you essentially pre-buy coking coal in Q3, ahead of the closing of waterways over the winter. To what  extent was that the case this year and would we see something of a snapback in coal cost going into Q2? Thank  you.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: What you see on that slide is our purchase prices, although indexed, as we said, but it's our purchase price. And  then, yes, there is a lag until you see it in the P&L. We simplify and say that iron ore is slightly less than a quarter  and for coking coal it's slightly more than a quarter. But then you're obviously right that we have this for the  northern mills, not for Oxelösund, but for Raahe and for Luleå, we have that we buy more in Q2 and Q3 to build  up the stock ahead of the winter, and then we don't so much in Q4 and Q1. I wouldn't call it a snap maybe, but,  yes, we will see increased coking coal cost going forward as well. Yes.

texts.speaker: Bastian Synagowitz
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank (Suisse) SA
texts.text: Okay. Okay. Got it. Then secondly, I'm just trying to reconcile your margin trend in the U.S. and also in Europe.  So, starting with Europe where your margins have widened by a massive $40 versus Q4, as Johannes pointed  out already, could you please help us to quantify how much financial tailwind roughly there was from still having  this low-cost coal inventory which you bought in late Q3 and early Q4, please? And this is the main reason why  you feel that the second quarter margins could be squeezed because coal is really catching a little bit up with  market trends.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: I would say for second quarter, it's not only coal, it's also iron ore where both underlying iron ore fine price have  gone up. But I've said also, we will have a higher pellet premium in the second quarter than we had in Q1, so it's  both those factor. Then overall, the development of SSAB Europe's result, it's quite many aspects there. It is the  increased prices, of course, that we looked at. It's also clearly increased shipments. And we did not have the  outages in the European division in Q1 that we had in Q4. So, it's coming from a bit of everything but definitely  also from better margins, yes.

texts.speaker: Bastian Synagowitz
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank (Suisse) SA
texts.text: Okay. Just one last quick follow-up. You said you're going to hit the SEK 10 billion net debt reduction target, and I  guess that you should definitely be on the road [ph] to that (40:34). Just want you to confirm, you plan to do this  without [ph] M&A – a sale (40:37) at this point? So, this is just pure organic net debt reduction getting to the SEK  10 billion?

texts.speaker: Alessandro Abate
texts.profession: Analyst, Joh. Berenberg, Gossler & Co. KG (United Kingdom)
texts.text: Martin, what is your target until year end? Basically, the exit run rate of the total flat steel shipment to the  Automotive by year-end? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Alessandro Abate
texts.profession: Analyst, Joh. Berenberg, Gossler & Co. KG (United Kingdom)
texts.text: And the question related to the U.S. market, energy and mining.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: There seems to be a positive sentiment in the U.S. market when it comes to energy and mining going forward, so  it's probably and hopefully moving in the right direction.

texts.speaker: Carsten Riek
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you very much. Most of my questions have been answered. Just one follow-up on the European  performance, because I'm still trying to reconcile it and I struggle. Because if you say 15% higher iron ore, 2%  higher coking coal cost across the board, so, I would guess it happens to Europe as well, but the cost per tonne  decreased by 5%, that means you must have had lower cost elsewhere of more than 10%, 15% in order to make  it to that result.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: So, I would say there was not anything very strange in Q1. But on top of that, as Martin said before, we were  running production at a very high and stable level. And then typically, we don't need as much maintenance costs.  We get much better energy usage, better yield levels, et cetera. So, running production the way SSAB Europe did  now in Q1, that basically gives much better cost per tonne.

file: SSAB.A - Q1 2018 Earnings Call 20April2018 330 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 20-Apr-18.pdf

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: The result was up compared to last year, higher prices, higher volumes, but last year we had the maintenance  outage in Mobile in Q1 and Q2 which we didn't have this year. We also saw higher scrap costs, but we saw  margins gradually improve during the first quarter. Tibnor, for lat products, I would say, decent development what  we suffered from both building-related products or building-related volumes where we had the lower shipments  during the quarter compared to one year ago or compared to the fourth quarter. And the Ruukki Construction  affected by the harsher winter than we had a year ago, so if there is a lot of snow, there are no roof repairs and so  on. So, we definitely felt that during the first quarter, and sales were lower than one year ago when we had a  milder winter.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: So, when we sum up, we see lower volume and lower margins, but this is, I mean, call it, an accelerated  seasonality then due to a lot of snow, especially in the Nordic region. Håkan?

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: On the volume side, it's a zero there, but it's some pluses and minuses. Higher volumes in Americas and Special  Steels offset by lower volumes in Europe, Ruukki Construction and Tibnor. On the variable COGS side, we had a  negative impact on more than SEK 1.1 billion. If you only take the raw material part of that, it's actually SEK 1.2  billion. So, basically offsetting what we have seen so far on the price increase side. Then, we have the higher  fixed cost in this quarter compared to last year. Some higher activity level in the downstream operations, also  general salary increases. What I think is important to mention I think I did that last time as well is that in terms of  fixed manning, we are actually at exactly the same level that we were after we had finalized the redundancy  programs at the end of 2016.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: Higher prices compared to Q4, all three steel divisions, Americas, Europe, Special Steels, biggest increase in  Americas. Volume moving upwards in Special Steels. Europe moving in the right direction, but Rautaruukki  Construction [indiscernible] (00:11:35) going down compared to Q4. And on the variable COGS side, we see  actually a higher increase than we see on the price side, given that the raw material has – I'll come back to that –  but has increased quite a lot.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: So, coming back into the raw material as I talked about in the bridges, we have seen overall purchase prices have  increased, and we start with the main components for the Nordics operations, then iron ore and coking coal. Our  purchase prices both increased during the quarter, iron ore, 18%; coking coal, 23%. And for iron ore, part of the  increase that we get on purchase prices during Q1 will also impact the result in Q1, and that's mainly for the  operations we have in Luleå where we don't basically have any stock of iron ore, but we get it on a daily basis  from LKAB, and then it also quickly hits the P&L. If you compare with Oxelösund the raw, we will see the impact  of the price increase for us coming more into Q2 instead.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: Purchase price of a coking coal increased actually percentage-wise more during the second quarter – sorry first  quarter for us. However, the main purchases for coking coal we do in Q2 and Q3 given that we have this winter  stock in Luleå and in Raahe, but also that we will see an impact of the higher raw material cost in the second  quarter.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: When we look at spot prices and this chart is spot prices. We actually also see that in April, scrap prices are  continuing moving upwards, and this long trend of increased scrap prices from basically beginning of Q4 and up  until today, it's actually quite unusual. Typically when the spring season comes, it's easy to collect scrap, prices  usually moves down, but we have not seen that, so far, this year. And the main and the logical reason for that is  that EAF steel producer just like us are running at high capacity utilization then increasing demand for scrap.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: I would like to end with this picture talking a bit about our Project HYBRIT. The way we try to figure out how to  produce steel without carbon dioxide. We close the prefeasibility study in Q1 2018 and we have found nothing in  that prefeasibility study that makes us believe that this is not possible. I would say quite the opposite.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: So we have decided to start to build a pilot plant together with LKAB and Vattenfall in a joint venture. We will have  the first groundbreaking – the groundbreaking ceremony during the summer and we will build this during – take 1  1/2 year and then we will start to do bigger trials and then we are planning to build the production plant or  demonstration plan from 2025.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: So, so far, so good, and we have also in laboratories and in tests produced the first steel according to this  method. And we will now, as said, start to build the shaft, the hydrogen generation and also the hydrogen storage  in a pilot scale up in Luleå and Norrbotten.

texts.speaker: Johannes Grunselius
texts.profession: Analyst, Svenska Handelsbanken AB
texts.text: Good morning. It's Johannes here, Handelsbanken. I have two questions. The first one is basically on Q1 and  pricing and you indicate that prices are up. And at the same time, input costs like coal or iron ore is also up. Could  you perhaps talk a little bit about those two moving parts together? I mean, basically, I'm after the EBIT or [ph]  return on margin (00:21:19) or so and so forth. Thanks.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: If you take the Nordic operations then or the production using iron ore and coking coal, there was a sharper  increase on the iron ore side than we had expected. And that come – you can say that came after we had  negotiated the Q1 contract. So in that sense, we got a bit of a margin squeeze in Europe especially, I would say,  because that's also where we get the quicker impact from the higher iron ore cost.

texts.speaker: Johannes Grunselius
texts.profession: Analyst, Svenska Handelsbanken AB
texts.text: Got it. Is it fair to say that most of the higher iron ore prices, coal prices are in the books or in the P&L in Q1, and  we should see more of an effect, but less effect on a sequential basis in Q2?

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: I would say you will see if you take our iron ore and coking coal again, you will see a higher cost in the Q2 as well,  but not as much if you compare Q2 to Q1, what we see right now it shouldn't be as much as it was Q1 to Q4 if you  understand.

texts.speaker: Tom Zhang
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Okay. Thank you. And also with the iron ore contract, I see that the LKAB contract is now completed. Has that  been renewed? And can you share any details on how the pricing is determined both with respect to the iron ore  and the pellet premium?

texts.speaker: Carsten Riek
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd.
texts.text: I was just hinting on the 200,000 tonnes you have to rebuild in your inventories, which definitely don't go  unnoticed, I would guess, in your inventory buildup.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: But if you take – if we take the problems that we have with the rail transportation, we were actually still producing  the slabs. We only have problems getting them from Luleå down to Borlänge. It took longer time. We didn't get  them in the right sequence. So, we actually have those slabs in the company. It's just that we couldn't get them to  Borlänge and roll at the time when we wanted to.

texts.speaker: Carsten Riek
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS Ltd.
texts.text: Even in – absolutely and I'm just trying to actually tie the knots here because you said it's a two weeks outage in  the blast furnace which you can't produce material, but you still managed to produce the material. I'm just getting  a bit [indiscernible] (00:35:09).

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Over time, you should look at the investments within SSAB that we are moving from coke oven batteries and blast  furnaces over time into electric arc furnaces being fed by HYBRIT to DRI or what you called it was sponge iron.  From a pure SSAB perspective, that will mean two things. That will mean lower investment levels because we  don't have to reinvest or rebuild blast furnaces and coke oven batteries, which is typically very expensive. And,  secondly, this will mean better flexibility because, as you know, blast furnaces are built for running 24/7 without  any stoppages for 15 years and then you do a relining and then you continue for another 15 years.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: If you exaggerate a lot, you can say that an electrical arc furnace is a red than a green bottom. So, you're – and  when you run, you push the green one. And when you don't run, you push the red one. So, from a pure SSAB  perspective, over time lower investment costs and the better flexibility. On top of that also, we did prognoses for  emission rights and so on. I would say, also a better cost position compared to continue over time running blast  furnaces and coke oven batteries.

texts.speaker: Cedar Ekblom
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: The second question relates to spreads in your European business. If we assume that we add back the costs  associated with the issues on production and logistics in the first quarter and we normalized for currency, I'm only  getting about SEK 10 per tonne improvement in your margin in that business year-on-year and steel prices year- on-year on average were flattish in Q1 of 2017 and in Q1 of 2018. But you've had quite a big tailwind from lower  raw material prices, both iron ore and coking coal, if I look at the year-on-year difference.

texts.speaker: Cedar Ekblom
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: I'm just trying to understand, is there something in the business that we should be aware of as it relates to your  sensitivity to steel and raw material prices on a spot basis where your reported improvement and profitability  seems to fall a bit short of sort of spot improvement in profitability. And also on the downside, when we saw the  downturn in 2015, reported margins held up better than where spot margins traded to. I'm just trying to  understand the operational sensitivity or leverage to the price trends that we're actually seeing in the spot market  and how optimistic we should actually be on the potential for those improved margins to come through in steel  companies' bottom-line? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Okay. If I try to answer the first question, then, of course, there is always more to do within cost effectiveness in  all areas, and that includes Ruukki Construction. So, I think what we saw in Q1 was a stronger seasonality call it  like that with a lot of snow in the Nordic region and so on. And I expect to see enormous seasonal pattern when  the spring and the summer comes. But having said that, of course, we're working with costs and we're working a  lot with continuous improvements in Ruukki Construction. Then, when it comes to keeping the whole or parts of  the Ruukki Construction, there is no update. We will come back if and when we decide to do something.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: And on to the second question on the spreads in SSAB Europe, I think there are two things to consider there. One  is that if you only look at spot, I would assume maybe you look at fines for iron ore. And we are 100% pellet  producer using pellets, and actually the pellet price had moved in a different direction than the iron ore fines. So,  pellet premium I mean is quite a lot and that will also have an impact on our spreads. So, that's one thing when  you compare Q1 to Q1 in Europe.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: The second one I would say is that for Q1 2017, we negotiated the quarterly and a half-year contract around  November time 2016. And that was actually when the coking coal was at the highest price and also iron ore was  fairly high. So – and then we set the contract for the first half year and then raw material prices went down. So, at  that time, we were a little bit lucky in terms of timing of raw material versus our sales prices.

file: SSAB.A - Q1 2019 Earnings Call 25April2019 330 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 25-Apr-19.pdf

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Americas, 23% EBITDA margin in the steel industry. I think that's good. I think it's very good I think solid  performance. We had slightly lower shipments and the reason for that was that we had severe weather in  Midwest in Montpelier where we have one of our facilities for a bit more than a week. We had more winter storms  more than minus 50 degrees Celsius, some problems to get trucks and trains, and so on. So that's why shipments  came down compared to Q1 2018. But apart from that, a very good performance, and we are the market leader in  heavy plate in North America, but they are also clearly the cost leader. They are the most cost efficient plate  producer in North America, and that's why we see these kind of margins when the market are strong.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: Then we have higher variable COGS. Raw material is the main part but on top of that we also have higher  maintenance costs partly driven down by the standstill in Raahe. That also implies that we have to ship slabs from  Luleå or from Oxelösund to Raahe and then we get high transport costs as well. Fixed cost is somewhat higher  than Q1 last year, SEK 270 million. We had higher maintenance cost in this quarter. We have an overall salary  increase year-over-year and also when we are running production and result as we are in Americas, their salary is  – we call it fixed cost, but their salaries is actually to a large portion variable depending on the performance. So  we're paying out higher salaries in Americas given those results.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: When we have to lower volumes in Europe, given the Raahe incident, we obviously cut the lowest priced volume  first, which means that we actually had a fairly decent price development in Europe. Volumes better than Q4, and  in Q4, we had maintenance outage in all three steel divisions. And this is mainly coming from Special Steels from  Europe. Variable COGS is, well it's almost zero, but it's somewhat positive. Despite the raw material increases,  but in Q4 with the maintenance outage, we started up the second blast furnace in Oxelösund. We had a lot of  different small variable COGS that added up. So despite raw material increase, we actually basically are net  them, compared to Q4.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: Finally from me on the raw materials side and starting with iron ore and coking coal, we have seen these prices  continue to increase and especially iron ore have increased quite a lot during Q1. If we look at our purchase  prices, they have increased with 50% in Swedish krona and they increased at 14% in dollars. And iron ore, partly  or maybe even mainly because of the wall accident during Q1, iron ore prices have really spiked during this  quarter.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: We have also seen coking coal prices increase, not as much but they have increased with 8% of our purchase  prices during Q1. And as Martin said, in Luleå, we basically don't have any iron ore inventory. We get transport by  train from LKAB on a daily basis. So, there we have already started to see the impact of these higher costs in the  P&L. The other Nordic operations and including the coking coal, the higher raw material impact will mainly hit the  P&L now during the second quarter.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: For our U.S. operation and for scrap, the situation actually looks quite different. Over time, iron ore and scrap  typically follow each other but they have not done so far now. Our purchase prices were relatively stable during  the quarter or they were 3% lower than in Q4. And we have actually also seen in April that scrap prices have went  somewhat downwards in April, which will obviously then impact our performance during the second quarter.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Construction Machinery, slightly lower momentum but at a very high level. Material Handling, we see continued  high activity within mining in several regions, and it's both investments and maintenance. Energy, solid demand in  wind energy in U.S. We see also high activity in U.S. oil and gas sectors. So, overall, in these segments, strong or  healthy demand in Q2. Construction, yes, good underlying demand but some hesitation especially in residential  building in Scandinavia or the Nordic region. And then as always, the Steel Service Centers, they are in a wait  and see mood. On the other hand, month on hand for Steel Service Centers are not at any high level. So,  eventually, they need to start to buy. But we call it healthy underlying demand, but there's always some swings in  the apparent consumption.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Prices in Q2 somewhat lower for Europe and the Americas and stable for Special Steels and Håkan pointed out,  we will see higher raw material costs especially for iron ore that will be visible in SSAB Europe and in Special  Steels, and that in the beginning of the quarter, slightly lower scrap prices in North America.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Another important project is the HYBRIT project that is moving on. And as you all know, this is our project to  produce steel without carbon dioxide. And here you can see a recently taken picture up from Luleå

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: and you can see the ice still on the Baltic Sea. But we are now in the phase of erecting the pilot plant. I just have to try in  understanding of what perception is for the U.S. going into next year, because out of those two end markets, we've  seeing quite a bit of weakness in terms of demand, particularly energy and mining CapEx. texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: As said regarding energy, we have a seen a slowdown on line pipe inquiries, but there are still a lot of projects out  there. So I don't really know where that will go in 2013. I'm not that pessimistic when it comes to line pipe. When  it comes to wind tower, which is one or many important segments, I mean the tax credits will probably as I heard  at least, expire during this year and that will of course affect the demand from that sector during 2013.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: When it comes to mining, we haven't seen – I mean, we are a small supplier in a big world, and we see a lot of  opportunities, I would say especially in Latin America, which is part SSAB Americas. As said, we have seen a  slowdown when it comes to energy coal. It's not an extremely big taker of our products, but still it affects us.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: But where the mining CapEx will go in Latin America, I'm not sure about the exact figures, but still even though  our abrasive-resistant steel takes longer time to wear out, it will still wear out. So as long as it is mines up and  running and working, there will be possibilities for us to sell abrasive-resistant steel.

texts.speaker: Cedar Ekblom
texts.profession: Analyst, Merrill Lynch International (United Kingdom)
texts.text: Okay, just a follow-up question. Is there anyway that you can quantify out of those end markets that you have  mentioned sort of what percentage of sales you think is exposed to the wind tower sector and the mining CapEx  sector in North America. That's obviously the areas where demand looks to be softening. So we can get an  understanding, is it 20% of sales where demand is softening or is it 50% of sales where demand is softening?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Out of QT, which is part of the sales we have in Americas, I would guess mining related 15% to maximum 20%.  Cedar Ekblom  Analyst, Merrill Lynch International (United Kingdom)  Q Okay. And then in the wind tower market, do you have any data on that?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: That's a bit more tricky because that is mainly and/or I would say only ordinary steel and that goes directly to  producer, it goes via service center. So I can't give you an exact figure, but its not. My guess would be it's not as  much as 15%. I would say below 10%.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: It depends where scrap prices goes, of course. But typically, the way it works is, when scrap prices go down, that  put pressure on ordinary steel prices, so to say. And there is a lag effect of a couple of weeks when we consume out  of our scrap inventories. Then of course, if scrap prices flattens out, then steel prices normally flattens out and  then margin flattens out. If I mean steel prices or scrap prices go up, steel prices goes up and then initially you'll  see a margin expansion. So it depends where scrap prices will go. But everything else equal, we will see somewhat  in the beginning, somewhat better margins, yes.

texts.speaker: James F. Gurry
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Hi guys. Thanks for taking my question. Most things have been addressed, but I've just got a couple of things on  the iron ore side of things. I think, probably since you signed the annual contract, spot process for iron ore have  probably come off 10% or 12%. We know that last year, you were able to re-negotiate the contract. Do you think  the same will happen again this year? And just further on the outlook for the rest of the year, you said it's going to  be tough, is there any prospect of doing emission right sales again, like we saw last year?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: To start with the raw material question, that will be – the future will give the answer, so to say. We have exactly  the same set-up as we had last year with the [ph] Corridor (40:42) or [indiscernible] (40:45) or LKAB has the  possibility to re-negotiate the pellet prices, depending on where the prices for spot iron ore goes. So we will see.  When it comes to emission rights, well, if we are not – if we are producing less than full production, so to say,  there will obviously be some excess emission rights. What we decide to do with them well, that will be – in that  case, that will be a later question.

texts.speaker: Bastian Synagowitz
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Prime Brokerage)
texts.text: Yes, good morning gentlemen and thanks for taking my questions. I've just got two brief ones left. To follow-up on  the comments you've already made on the quenching lines in Borlänge and Mobile, when should we expect a  notable margin contribution from these projects? You mentioned that, that would be very gradually, but when will  we at least see that reflected also in the margins? And then secondly, again on raw material prices, obviously, it's  very difficult to say where steel prices will go from here, but if we just assume that they would remain stable  around where they are today. Would your margins still remain stable in this quarter versus – third quarter versus  Q2? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: I can take the first question and let Marco answer the second one. But I mean, we have not been very specific  when it comes to the ramp-up plans of QL6 and QL7. We are not filling up that capacity in a very short period, it's  a gradual ramp up, and as said, we are introducing a combination of steel that we previously also produced in  Oxelösund. So we are trying to optimizing, call it, it sounds extremely ambitious, but just to give you an idea,  trying to introduce call it a global production system, to produce different types of gauges and widths for  quenched and tempered, where it's most cost effective.

texts.speaker: Marco Wirén
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: We can't assume raw material prices and their impact on our price setting. As Martin mentioned, on standard  steels, we have higher correlation between raw material costs and our price setting, while in niche steels, we have  different price setting. And of course, if prices are stable on raw materials, then we might see, or should see, less  volatility on stainless steel pricing as well. Of course depending; if something drastic is going to happen on the  market in general, that will of course unbalance that correlation. But in going forward in longer-term, that should  be the case.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: As mentioned, the lower coking coal price will affect us from Q3 and onwards. I mean so far or up until the end of  Q2, we have used coking coal from our inventories and those inventories were bought during end of last year.

texts.speaker: Marco Wirén
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: Yeah, I would say a little bit longer, even that due to the effect before we get raw material price increase or  decrease the impact in our P&L and that's about same effect we get in our hedges as well, due to a fact that when  we buy the raw materials, we used hedge those as well, and the same time we hedge also the sales for that raw  material consumption in our P&L. So I would say to leave a longer impact than two to three months.

texts.speaker: Alessandro Abate
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Good morning. Most of my questions have been already answered. Just a little one on CO2 emission rights. Can  you please explain a little bit the mechanism of your possibility of selling the rights or in case you decide not to sell  if there is any kind of carry forward effect into next year? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: I mean, we're obviously not running the production in Europe or Sweden at 100% and that everything else equal  gives us some excess emission rights. We have not seen yet what kind of emission allowance we will get for the  coming years. So, I mean, at the end it's up – we need to decide if we are going to sell excess emission rights or if  we are going to save them for the future. So to say depends also what we will get for the coming five years and we  don't know that yet.

texts.speaker: Julian Beer
texts.profession: Analyst, SEB Enskilda (Sweden)
texts.text: So as a starting point, could I use the straight line from zero, the end of Q1?

texts.speaker: Julian Beer
texts.profession: Analyst, SEB Enskilda (Sweden)
texts.text: Okay. Do you have any script to catch up on the niche production from after the Oxelösund gas line incident by  limiting your down time Q3?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: But that is the net effect, just about 10,000 tonnes.

texts.speaker: Julian Beer
texts.profession: Analyst, SEB Enskilda (Sweden)
texts.text: Okay. But if I remember correctly, the scrap spot prices actually fell about two to four weeks ahead of the plate  prices in Q2. So I'm a bit of a lost to understand why this has had a margin impact in Q2?  Marco Wirén  Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB  A Just as Martin said, there is lag on depending when you buy and how much you buy? And especially when you see  that, we said that – we said, we saw weakening in the end of the quarter two. When you see weakening and you  still have purchase the scrap prices for another volume that you actually are delivering, then you have purchased  too much for coming volumes and then the lagging is even longer and that's what's we've seen in American  operations.

texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB

texts.profession: Executive Vice President, Chief Financial Officer, SSAB AB

texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB

Martin Erik Lindqvist  President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB  A  Well, we saw some big producer being out yesterday increasing prices for strip and we have seen some signs, but,  yeah, we'll see.

texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: Moving then to raw material, we have seen a decline in iron ore and in coking coal. And during Q2, we saw that  this decline stabilized, and was not changing so much. texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: In Q2, the net impact was between SEK 60 million to SEK 80 million. And in Q3, we expect it to be between SEK  100 million and SEK 120 million. texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director

texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: The biggest event or the most important event during the second quarter was the groundbreaking ceremony of  our HYBRIT project. And we have decided to invest SEK 1.4  billion in a pilot plant up in Luleå for this. We have, as part of the financing, got SEK 528 million from the Swedish  Energy Agency in financial support, and we are now starting to build this pilot plant. It will be up and running 2020  and then we will start to do trials, and then we are planning to build a demonstration plant which is really a full- scale production plant.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: And the reason why we do this that during the pre-study and everything, we have learned we are getting more  and more convinced that this is actually possible to produce the steel without any carbon dioxide emissions. And if we are successful with this, we will be  able to take away 10% of the Swedish carbon dioxide emissions and more than 10% of the Finnish carbon  dioxide emissions. So, that was according to me, at least, and according to SSAB the most important event during the second  quarter. texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: When it comes to your first question, quenched – prices of quenched and tempered heavy plates typically behave  differently compared to standard prices. Standard prices for plate in North America follows the scrap prices very  much.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: For Q&T, there is a different pricing mechanism and there's a different, call it, market for quenched and tempered.  So we expect prices regardless of where scrap goes to be much more stable. When it comes to ordinary products,  as said, they typically follow scrap prices, and we don't sell one single kilo anywhere in the world of quenched and  tempered via distributors. We sell it directly to end users. And the way we sell it is by doing customer development  projects and selling it out of a more, call it, a life cycle discussion kind of price setting than any extras on hot- rolled coals or extras over scrap. So it's a different pricing model. That's why they don't follow each other.

texts.speaker: Marco Wirén
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: If we take blast furnaces, as you know, we have been – we had one of the blast furnaces idle, and we have been  running the other two blast furnaces at reduced speed. But in Oxelösund, we were more running at call it 80% or  80% plus in the Oxelösund system. So the big hit in volumes and under absorption was in the strip system.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: To start with the first question, the cost efficiency and flexibility program is to run the strip system and that is  Borlänge and Luleå at breakeven at 70% and Oxelösund system at 80%, which are very low capacity utilization  rates. That program will be finished during Q1, and as we said, you will – you should expect the effects of that to  be seen gradually during 2013.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: I'll start with that question. What we see right now, we see no – we don't feel it necessary to open the small blast  furnace in Oxelösund. And then when it comes to cost cutting, I think if we – to reach breakeven at 70% in a  process industry, it's quite a good target and that we will deliver on. Then I mean being more cost effective is never  ending work. That's a lot about continuous improvement and not necessary big programs, but – so we will never  stop trying to be more and more effective.

texts.speaker: James F. Gurry
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Okay. Great. And if I just might follow up, what's the chance that you might have more carbon emission sales in  the final quarter?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: We haven't discussed that. I mean carbon emissions for us is something that we – I mean, we haven't decided  that.

texts.speaker: Alexander Vilval
texts.profession: Analyst, Carnegie Investment Bank AB
texts.text: Yes. Good morning. Alexander Vilval, Carnegie here. I have a question concerning the inventory release, and you  mentioned regarding coal purchases, that that has reduced your working capital by or capital need by SEK500  million. Is that in the third quarter numbers, and is that compared to the Q2 result or is that something that will  show in your inventory figures going forward?

file: SSAB.A - Q3 2013 Earnings Call 25October2013 330 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 25-Oct-13.pdf

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: If we take a look at the segments and this is sequential Q3 over Q2, I would say no big differences with a few  exceptions. Heavy transport, heavy equipment demand has been weak due to uncertainty in the business climate.  On the other hand, heavy equipment in U.S. booked at slightly improved levels in Q3 compared to Q2.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: And in mining, we saw a continued slowdown during Q3, compared to Q2. Energy, during Q3, a fairly okay  segment with tank cars, pressure vessels, pipelines and wind towers. Service centers continued to buy what they  need and only what they need during Q3 and inventory levels of service centers on low levels. During the  sequential outlook for Q4, I would say that we see some bright spots in these, some of the segments compared to  Q3.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: There is currently, a positive momentum in the market. We expect the plates or the steel consumption and the  plate consumption to continue upwards according to the market or the general development. We introduced the  price increase last week of $30 per tonne. And we have, effective from today, introduced another price increase for  all new orders of $20 per tonne effective from today. The reason why we do that is that we have a strong order  book and a good order intake. And we will continue to, as a market leader, increase the margin over scrap and  help the market to do that.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: We offset this by higher volumes and better utilization rate in the mill, which means lower under absorption cost,  better variable COGS, which is both due to raw material prices, but also due to the efficiencies we have done in  terms of production.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Finally, I will mention some about the trends in our raw material prices. We mentioned in our report last quarter  that we have signed a new agreement with LKAB ranging from 1st of April this year to end of March last year and  where the prices are set on a quarterly basis. For Q3, our iron ore prices increased with 6% versus Q2.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: And as we have said before, there is roughly one quarter lag from when we buy the iron ore until we see it in our  P&L. So this will be seen then in the fourth quarter.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: On the other hand, our price for coking coal decreased with approximately 11% during this quarter compared to  last quarter. And then finally, our U.S. scrap buy, the scrap has been fairly volatile during the quarter, but ended  up in the third quarter 2% higher than it was in the end – sorry, in the beginning of the quarter.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Thank you, Håkan. So what we do see then? We expect steel demand in Europe to be fairly stable in Q4. Of course,  as always, if the momentum trends upwards into Q1, we will see better apparent consumption at the end of the  quarter and if the trend is downwards, we will, of course, see lower apparent consumption. But the underlying  demand is expected or we expect to be fairly stable.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: We expect the Asian steel consumption to continue to grow and in North America steel demand will increase in  line with the economic recovery. As said, we have, together with other producers, recently announced price  increases and as said, we have from today announced another price increase for the North American plate market.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Executive Vice President, Chief Financial Officer, SSAB AB
texts.text: No, probably not more and not zero. So yeah, somewhere between there.

texts.speaker: Johan Sjöberg
texts.profession: Analyst, Carnegie Investment Bank AB
texts.text: You probably said that. Okay. SEK250 million. The final question here also. Europe seems to be screaming for  some profitability improvement and you're taking actions, of course, with your cost-cutting progress. But you're  also guiding that you will see higher iron ore costs in the fourth quarter whereas you're referring to flat prices. I  mean, if you compare it with the U.S., sure, in the U.S. you have a market-leading position here and in Europe  you're a small producer. But what can go – I mean, what can you do basically in Europe?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Continue to be very active on the market. Continue to describe all the possibilities by using our steel. Continue to  be cost-effective, more cost-effective, more productive. Continue with all the programs we are running when it  comes to different parts and then, yeah, continue the way we're working.

texts.speaker: Stephen Benson
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: Hi, there. I just wanted to come back to the mining CapEx side of things, can you tell roughly what proportion of  your volumes or percentage of your volumes head towards the mining industry? Am I correct in thinking, it's  around 10%?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Well, I don't have the exact figure, but a lot, as you know, of the yellow goods producer are shipping machines, like  the Caterpillar, to mining related facilities and that of course. So for us I mean yellow goods and mining goes more  or less hand-in-hand, but I would say within quenched and tempered that segment is more than 10%.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: I don't have the exact split, but the clear focus for us is OpEx with the Wear Service Business. But also, I mean, all  these machines needs to be repaired. You need to change buckets. You need to change damper bodies. And even if  you're not opening any new mines, you will buy new machines, excavators or big trucks. But, I mean, OpEx is  important for us and will be gradually more important.

texts.speaker: Stephen Benson
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: Okay. But there's still, I mean, there must still be a decent chunk of CapEx volumes there? I mean, I'm no expert  on the mining side, but I know the forecast here is for mining CapEx to be down 20% to 30% maybe next year  globally. So I'm just wondering what you see offsetting that potential volume decline, but what positive signals are  you seeing out there to kind of replace those volumes that are likely to not be there next year?  Martin Erik Lindqvist  President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB  A  We are not seeing any extreme positive signals. But our conclusion is that at least, the time we can overlook is not  getting worse. Then what will happen during the second half of next year, we don't have that visibility.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: We don't give that specific number, but you're right about the increase in iron ore. On the other hand, you can also  see we had a decrease on the coking coal.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: We feel that we are not over with all the things we can do. This is for us a gradual and focused work. We can be  better when it comes to optimizing the production flow and flow efficiency. We can be much better when it comes  to reducing waste. We still see opportunities to continue to reduce the working capital structurally.

texts.speaker: Stephanie Bothwell
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: And then secondly, just on scrap prices. How do you see that evolving as we move into the latter half of the year?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: When it comes to scrap, the normal seasonal pattern is that scrap seasonally goes up during the winter season  because of the more, call it, problematic scrap collection process or something. But typically, you'll see that  seasonal patterns going up during the winter and then coming down during the summer. But apart from that,  we're not seeing right now at least any big or extreme changes.

file: SSAB.A - Q3 2015 Earnings Call 22October2015 330 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 22-Oct-15.pdf

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: One and a half week ago, I was at the World Steel Association meeting in Chicago and it was an interesting  meeting and most of you have probably read the short-term outlook. And as you know, they downgraded the  outlook for 2015 and they also downgraded slightly the outlook for 2016. So there will be in 2015 a small increase  of apparent steel demand in Europe and a reduced apparent steel demand in North America and China had a big  decrease of steel consumptions.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Markets, I would say, as expected with one exception. Heavy Transport and Automotive, stable on high levels.  Construction Machinery and Mining stable on very low levels. Energy is kind of rough in North America divided  market, everything that is oil related is slow. But wind tower is one example where we see very good demand.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Of course, they are benefited from not having a summer outage this summer and also running the small blast  furnace in Oxelösund the full third quarter. That is now closed. We closed it in beginning of October. But during  Q3, due to the relining in Luleå they were running the small blast furnace.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: And now, as said, the blast furnace is relined and up in running. We lost two and a half weeks for – it's already  explained the reasons, but now it's delivering according to plan. We managed to do it cost wise within budget. And  now – this is important because this was – now gave us the opportunity to that flexibility which was a key part of  combining SSAB and Ruukki. So now we have the blast furnace fleet that – where we can flex and produce in a  much more cost effective way, we'd almost like to say, regardless of market situation, and that can be done now  since end of September.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Americas, as said, mainly prices explaining the drop and not compensated at all fully or at all by lower raw  material prices. What has happened in the beginning of Q4 or in October is that scrap prices has come down  additionally $50 to $60 per tonne. And what we have suffered from is non-existing correlation between scrap and  iron ore. And now since beginning of October that correlation is back to where it has been all the time. So scrap  prices for the October buy is down between $50 and $60 per tonne.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: During Q3, they have also invested in coal injection in Raahe and I would say that, that is mainly or partly due to  environmental reasons and partly due to cost reasons. Now that is up and running, so we will go from oil  injections to the coal injection. We will have a much better, call it carbon dioxide effectiveness in the blast  furnaces. As I said before, our blast furnace system in Luleå is the most carbon dioxide effective system in the  world, and now, after this we will be on par with Luleå in Raahe as well. But on top of that, going from oil injection  to coal injection will, at current oil prices as we have today save us on yearly basis another SEK 200 million  compared to where we stand today.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: So when we sum this up – and I take the starting point, September 1, when we got the new organization in place  and the two companies together, we will with these actions reduce the yearly costs – run rate mid-next year of the  SEK 2 billion with these three areas; synergies, Ruukki Construction, and coal injection in Raahe.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: Then we have a big positive impact of COGS, variable COGS and also fixed cost. It's coming from lower raw  material cost. It's coming from more synergies realized and it's also – or fixed cost is coming from a – between Q3  and Q2, [ph] regularization (12:57) impact, when you have the summer [ph] vacation (12:59) reserves they sold in  the Nordic regions.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: Some word on the cash flow development, where I've said we had a negative operating cash flow in the quarter,  very much impacted by high maintenance expenditures, which out of the SEK 600 million, approximately SEK  300 million were for the Luleå relining. If we look at it where we are year-to-date, we have the net cash flow down  of more than SEK 800 million positively and that's I would say despite high level of maintenance CapEx, but also  we have fairly high strategic CapEx this year, which is the largest single item here is this PCI coal injection that  Martin mentioned before. But , all in all, still after three quarters net cash flow positive SEK 800 million.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: Moving then to raw material, and starting with iron ore and coking coal, the prices were fairly stable during Q3,  both for iron ore and coking coal, they dropped slightly in July, but since then been fairly stable actually. Iron ore  now at around [ph] $65 (18:11) per tonne, coking coal at around $80 per tonne somewhat.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: For us, our prices for iron ore was down 1% in Q3, what we were buying, compared to Q2, both in U.S. dollar and  SEK. And what we also did in Q3 is that we signed a price agreement with Severstal for continued deliveries, and  these deliveries will be both to Raahe and but also to Oxelösund. Given the logistical setup we have with  [indiscernible] (18:41) Luleå, we will not use the Severstal pellets in Luleå. For coking coal, prices were down a  little bit more, they were down with 8% in U.S. dollar and 5% in Swedish kroner. So all-in-all, both iron ore and  coking coal, slightly down, not as dramatic as we've seen before, but still somewhat on the downward trend.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: If we move to scrap then, the situation is quite different actually, where we saw sharp price declines during Q3,  and these have also continued now into Q4. The spot prices, and we buy scrap for our use operations in the spot  market, they were down 30% in Q3 versus the beginning of Q3, and when you compare year-over-year, they were  down as much as 46%. And as you can see here on the chart, they have continued going down somewhat in  October. And that brings us to the correlation between iron ore that not been talked about before, where we have  been suffering and we've been a bit frustrated in our North American operations that scrap hasn't followed iron  ore, which it has done historically.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: If we look at this chart, it's an index starting in the beginning of 2012, and for two years, you can see that iron ore  being the black one and scrap being the grey one, they were basically following each other. But then here  something happened in the beginning of 2014, where iron ore went down shortly, but scrap did not really follow.  But what we see now in beginning of October, it has actually converged again, the scrap prices and the iron ore  prices.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: If you look at the segments, I would say no big changes from Q3. We expect Heavy Transport and Automotive to  be stable on high levels and Construction Machinery and Mining to be stable on very low levels. We expect to see  the same pattern in the Energy segment as well. Construction Material will typically go down seasonally in Q4,  and we don't expect any major changes in Steel Service Centers either. The destocking will come to an end. Yes.  When? I don't really know. I was pretty sure last time, I don't give you any prognosis of that this time, because  then I run the risk to be wrong once again and I really don't like that.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: My last picture is about Swedish Steel Prize 2015 and these are the finalists. Facil System from Brazil, TEREX  Cranes from Germany, Ponsse from Finland and the Milotek from South Africa. And what they have in common is  that they are using advanced high strength of steels, either to increase productivity or to reduce weight or to  reduce – or increase payload or reduce fuel consumption or energy consumptions.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: I think these are very good examples on how you can utilize advanced high strength steels and in lot of these cases,  also you see fairly big environmental benefits. And I think that is also important and it was discussed also during  the meeting in Chicago with World Steel Association, the increasing importance of doing the right things  environmentally.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: So, this I think is probably the most, the best contribution we do when it comes to reduce emissions and reduce  fuel consumptions and so on, on top of being the most carbon dioxide effective producer of steel in the world. But  by these customers and other customers using our products and reducing weight and reducing emissions and  increasing payloads and typically doubling life lines, I think this is the real contribution that SSAB can do in that  aspect.

texts.speaker: Olof Grenmark
texts.profession: ABG Sundal Collier AB
texts.text: Another question then please on this new iron ore agreement with Severstal. Could you please indicate roughly  how much of your iron ore purchases in SEK that now come from Severstal?

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: It will be – I said it will not be at all to Luleå and it will be – both for Oxelösund and for Raahe, it will be below  half of the production that will be Severstal pellets.

texts.profession: Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken AB (Broker)
texts.text: On the PCI savings, which are savings calculated based on an old CapEx program, is the SEK 200 million  annualized savings compared to the prices that you are paying in Q3 2015, or is it based on the oil prices that  persisted back in 2014?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: But what we're doing there. The PCI investment is up and running, but we had inventory of oil, so the use up that  because we will not need it in the future. So we'll do that during Q4 and then from – it will be fully empty the  inventory of oil beginning of end of this year, beginning of next year and then we will go over 100% to PCI.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: No, but – and actually when the decision was taken, the oil price was high. So this asset is at current oil price.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: But it's not only saving cost as I said, it's also you could call it environmental investment, because this will also do  a lot to that, to the emissions.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: I'll start with the blast furnace, we have had it closed for fairly long-time or either I will say. And then, when it comes to [ph] measures (35:02) in North America against the  plate import, I know there is a lot of discussion, but at the end, I guess it's a political process and – political  processes at least for me are very hard to give any predictions on.

texts.profession: Okay. And the question on the Borlänge, closing the [ph] savings effect (36:33), is that mostly [indiscernible]
texts.text: (36:36) reduction or are there fixed costs coming down on top of that as well?

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: That depends actually a lot if it's iron ore based or if it's a scrap based and...

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: ... given what another, how much this scrap has changed recently and how much iron ore has changed recently.  And I don't have that figure, we have it actually in our [indiscernible] (38:52), but I don't have the figure in my  head. I can check it for you afterwards.

texts.speaker: Andreas Koch
texts.profession: Director-Investor Relations
texts.text: Yeah. But yes, the scrap or iron ore are about the same magnitude, the scrap a little bit more earlier, but they are  more in par with it.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: What we see is that there are some pipelines projects out on the market. When they will materialize and how they  will materialize is a bit too early to say. But we see – yes, we see some pipelines – pipeline projects now for – on  the market for beginning of 2016.
