texts.profession: ABG Sundal Collier AB
texts.text: Okay. All right, cool. And then, on Europe then you talked about iron ore and coal being flattish basically, and at  least, if you look at spot steel prices that have been sort of falling in Europe, so – and that comes through to your  [indiscernible] (54:19) did to the contracts, but are you then seeing sort of a realized lower margin over input costs  going forward, do you think?

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: If I take the other two then, Bastian, starting with maintenance, yes, you are correct, the maintenance is – we have  idled the blast furnace now, and that will then, compared to Q3 will give a negative impact for Special Steel, and  on top of that there will be a maintenance outage where we will stop the production in rolling and downstream for  approximately two weeks, and that's the SEK 100 million that you are referring to.

texts.speaker: Oskar Lindström
texts.profession: Danske Bank A/S (Sweden)
texts.text: Thank you. I have four questions. The first one, just – I couldn't quite hear what the answer was before, but was  the positive impact on Special Steels from the Oxelösund blast furnace in Q3, was that SEK 50 million?

texts.speaker: Oskar Lindström
texts.profession: Danske Bank A/S (Sweden)
texts.text: And the other three questions then; first of all, the steel imports into Europe, we hear about them, but how is that  affecting your markets and segments now, and how do you see that developing in 2016? And then the other  question would be, you mentioned that volumes in Q4 could be impacted by, or would be impacted by price  expectations for Q1. And it seemed as if you were saying that if customers expected prices to increase. Are there  any signals that prices could or should rise in Q1?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: If we take them one by one. To start with the last question then, I mean it's too early to say where the price  sentiment will be for Q1, but that was more a general comment that is valid for every year I would say. You  typically see a seasonal slowdown in Q4 or in December and then apparent steel consumption will be, as always,  very dependent on the price sentiments going into Q1. And that is nothing special for this year; that is valid, for I  would say, every year during my 17 years in the steel industry at least and probably before that as well.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: This is not a new cost save; this is an effect of this investment and at current oil prices. So shifting from oil  injection to a much more energy and efficient system as coal injection. And we have coal injection today in Luleå  and in the blast furnaces in Oxelösund. And so this is a recalculation of what we will actually have in terms of  lower costs, given the current oil prices.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: No, the only change in this investment I would say then is that oil prices today are a bit lower than when the  decision was taken, but it's still a very good investment, not only for the cost of sale, but also for the energy  efficiency.

texts.speaker: Nitesh Agarwal
texts.profession: Citigroup Global Markets India Pvt Ltd.
texts.text: Hi, thanks a lot for the call. I have one question on scrap prices in the U.S. They had been quite resilient in third  quarter versus the fallen steel prices. Would you be able to quantify the impact from higher scrap in the third  quarter? I mean, if you can give an approximately figure or a range, and also what the impact, if any, you expect in  the fourth quarter? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: Not fully sure if I understand, but I'll try to answer that. The scrap prices as you said are clearly down in Q3, and  they have been going down month over month, and for us to turn the scrap from when we buy them or from when  you see the market spot prices into the P&L, that is approximately a month, month-and-a-half before we see that,  depending a little bit on how much we have – scrap we have in stock. So you can expect that our cost for scrap will  of course also be lower in Q4 than in Q3. All of the big drop that happen now on the market in October, we will not  see in our books. In October, we will see it – rather in November or in December. Would you, say, from a simple  point of view, you can look at the market-based spot prices for scrap and then put the delay on a month-and-a-half  on so on it.

texts.speaker: Nitesh Agarwal
texts.profession: Citigroup Global Markets India Pvt Ltd.
texts.text: Okay. But would you be in any way be able to quantify the impact, because in third quarter at the beginning the  scrap prices were quite resilient compared to the steel prices. Steel prices were – have been going down since. And  if you could quantify to some extent what the impact was – negative impact was from that?

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: I think you see that in the result in SSAB Americas. If you compare the Q2 result with the Q3 result, you see a big  negative [ph] derivation (01:08:52). And that's basically coming from, as you said, the scrap – sorry, plate prices  dropping more than the scrap prices have dropped. Now what we have seen during the last month-and-a-half is  actually scrap prices dropping more at least so far than plate prices have dropped on market. And if that holds,  well, then we would see a margin expansion again.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Well, the plan B is the plan A. I mean, as I said when I presented also the realigning of the blast furnace, we have  now much more flexibility to – if that would be needed, idle blast furnaces without stepping out of any profitable  business, which we as a standalone old SSAB had come to an end. But we have the big blast furnace in Luleå and  the big one running in Oxelösund. Now, we have, as I think I showed a couple of times also when we announced  the combination, we have a much more possibilities to gradually flex with the production. And the toughest part of  flex with is always the [indiscernible] (01:12:53) and especially blast furnaces. In U.S. it's different because – I  mean it's practically a red and a green button; you either start the electric arc furnace and – or you keep it closed.

file: SSAB.A - Q3 2016 Earnings Call 28October2016 330 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 31-Oct-16.pdf

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: No major change on variable COGS. On fixed cost, we see Q3 versus Q2 a very positive development of SEK  380 million. Here, I think it's important to point out that around SEK 300 million of those SEK 300 million (sic)  [SEK 380 million] (09:45) is coming during Q3 because we are dissolving vacation reserves. So, that's a typical  Q3 effect which we did not have in Q4 and we will not have in – or sorry, we did not have in Q2 and we will not  have in Q4 either.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: Finally, on other here, it's also here, it's the underabsorption that's playing a big role. Last year, we were not  running the Luleå blast furnace during the whole third quarter when we had the relining. And this year, we've been  running it. And that's a large portion of this SEK 193 million.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: Moving then into the raw material, and of course, the big item is the coking coal development. Coking coal prices  during Q3 really spiked and took off in a way I don't believe anyone had foreseen. And this one ends here at the  end of Q3, but actually even after Q3, we have seen additional increases on the coking coal side. For us, this is  the purchase price for us, not the consumption price. But the purchase price for us during Q3 was 25% higher in  U.S. dollar versus Q2, and 34% higher in SEK.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: The main impact of this coking coal increases will come from Q1 and onwards, but we will already in Q4 start  seeing the impact of the higher coking coal in our P&L, especially for the Special Steel division. For Europe, we  build up winter stocks up in Luleå and up in Raahe because the big boats cannot go there when there is ice. So,  there it will come more in Q1. But for Special Steel, we'll start seeing it already in Q4.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: On iron ore, well, it hasn't been very dramatic. It's slightly up versus Q2, but not at all in the magnitude of how we  see coking coal develop.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: Then for scrap, which is obviously what we use in our U.S. operation, well, the scrap price has been moving  down. During the quarter, they're down 17%, in the end of the quarter versus the beginning. They're still actually  slightly higher than what they were one year ago. But I think this is quite interesting because iron ore being flat,  scrap slightly moving down, and coking coal then going like this, it means for us as a scrap-based plate producer  in the U.S., we will definitely compared to the integrated players have a competitive advantage.

texts.speaker: Johannes Grunselius
texts.profession: Analyst, Svenska Handelsbanken AB (Broker)
texts.text: And then my final question here, and that's a follow-up on Christian's question, on the relative stable prices in  Europe. At the same time, coal is moving up now and you say that will be seen in the fourth quarter, but should  we see that as a – that it will be a slight sort of negative push on the conversion margin for you now in the fourth  quarter or can you give some color on that?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Well, we are not setting the price in Europe, I mean overall for spot prices in Europe. We are setting prices  on the  most advanced steel products globally and we are part of setting the prices. We're the leader when it comes to  heavy plate in North America. But in Europe, we are one among many players, so we are not setting the price  momentum. This is our outlook as we speak.

texts.speaker: Olof Grenmark
texts.profession: Analyst, ABG Sundal Collier AB
texts.text: Olof Grenmark, ABG Sundal Collier. Three questions if I may. First one on steel prices, the second on net debt  and the third on the outages, the maintenance stops. Regarding steel prices, you guide for flat or stable steel  prices in Europe at the same time as we should see a negative effect in America due to the lag effect. Isn't there a  lag effect in Europe as well? Shouldn't we see a positive effect then?

texts.speaker: Olof Grenmark
texts.profession: Analyst, ABG Sundal Collier AB
texts.text: So, it's more on the positive side then if you say roughly?

texts.speaker: Ola Södermark
texts.profession: Analyst, Swedbank AB (Broker)
texts.text: Ola Södermark, Swedbank. Just to go back to raw materials and coal prices that are spiking right now, you said  you are building inventories to Raahe and Luleå. Are you done with it for winter or are you still building  inventories?

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: No, we have bought everything we need for the winter.

texts.speaker: Ioannis Masvoulas
texts.profession: Analyst, RBC Europe Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Hi. Good morning, gentlemen, and thanks for taking my questions. Just a first question on coking coal. Could you  possibly provide some indication on the realized cost increase during Q3 quarter-over-quarter, because, I think,  you only provided the average purchase price for the quarter? And maybe a split between quarterly and monthly  price purchases for coking coal. And that will be the first question.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: Basically, in Q3, there was no impact of the rising coking coal. As we showed on the purchase price, we had an  impact. But on the P&L impact, it was virtually zero. So, that is still to come. On the second question, on the  contract structure, we have decided actually that for competitive reason, we don't want to give out a split of  monthly and quarterly contract.

texts.speaker: Ioannis Masvoulas
texts.profession: Analyst, RBC Europe Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: Okay. Thank you. And then maybe just a last question on the U.S. business. Some of your peers have been  cautious on scrap pricing in the short-term. Could you elaborate whether you see a potential for further destocking  in the next couple of months, and our scrap prices start recovering maybe from early Q1 2017, you then see  some positive trends in terms of restocking? Could that be a potential scenario that plays out?

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: Yeah. Maybe I was a bit unclear then. What I meant was that the underabsorption effect we get from having the  outages.

texts.speaker: Bastian Synagowitz
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank (Suisse) SA (Broker)
texts.text: Yes. Good morning, gentlemen. I've got three questions left  and my first one is again following up on coal. You  said already that you bought your winter needs for Europe and costs would therefore be stable in the fourth  quarter. But I remember that you used to buy physical coal even until the end of the first quarter to be really  hedged throughout the entire winter in the past. Has this changed or does this mean that we will only see the 35%  increase in coal cost until the end of Q1? And maybe you could also let us know whether you are hedged against  the appreciating U.S. dollar for the raw materials.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: We have finalized the contracts, but I don't believe that we have received all the coking coal coming into the mills  yet. But as I said before, you will see – in Europe, you will see a small impact during Q4. You will see more impact  in Special Steel. And then, going into Q1, you will see even further impact in both Special Steel and within  Europe.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: And it has not changed. I mean, what we do both in Raahe and in Luleå, we need to bring on in the coal before  the ice comes because then, it's not possible to bring in those big ships because they are not ice class. So, we  need to do that before the winter. So, there is no change in the pattern.

texts.speaker: Bastian Synagowitz
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank (Suisse) SA (Broker)
texts.text: And the price, basically, the basis for the prices which you get on exactly those volumes which you bring in right  now to be hedged for the ice period, is this the 35% you mentioned?

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: We are hedging both coking coal and iron ore. So, we hedge basically in line with the contract structure we have.  So, for iron ore, we typically hedge it a quarter at a time the U.S. dollar. And for coking coal, since we have a mix  of quarterly and monthly, we hedge it a little bit shorter. And then, we hedge the corresponding sales in euros, so  we kind of try to lock in the margin there in between. So, yes, you can say it is hedged, but it's on a short-term  basis. So, if you look at it one, two quarters ahead, it will basically even out.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: There is always a seasonal mix effect for us. I mean, during fourth quarter and first quarter, we typically sell less  of the color-coated material, so that's mix effect. In that way, you can say we have a thinner mix when it comes to  price, and that is always the case. If the winter is mild in the Nordics, it can last for a longer time in Q4. And if we  get a tough winter, there will be seasonally no consumption, or lower consumption of color-coated material.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: But that's in yearly effect that we see every year and it could be stronger in a tough winter and less strong in a  mild winter.

texts.speaker: Luc Pez
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane SA (Broker)
texts.text: Hi, gentlemen. Two follow-ups. So if I may, first of all, with regards to your guidance on the working capital  requirement, could you explain how you manage to reduce it in Q4 while the raw material cost charge will rise,  talking coking coal in particular, but maybe iron ore as well? That would be my first question.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Okay. No. But to answer that one then, what we did during Q3, we were building up slab inventories in front of the  outage in Oxelösund. And so, we'll have the blast furnaces standing still for a slightly longer time than the rolling  mill. So, we will eat up that slab inventory during Q4 and that's the reason for us being sure of working capital  reduction.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Ruukki Construction, decent market, good sales. We have not been able to fully compensate for increased steel  prices in our selling prices. So, a bit of a margin squeeze in Ruukki Construction. But I would say, all in all, a fairly  decent quarter.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: We saw spot – plate prices decreasing. During the quarter, we saw scrap prices going up and down, fading off a  bit and decreased at the end of the quarter. So, no dramatic changes compared to previous quarter, a bit more  wait-and-see maybe in U.S.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Americas shipments, 21% higher than Q3 2016. So, good demand in the Energy segment, but as I said, wait-and- see from Steel Service Centers in Q3.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: And then, Ruukki Construction where we typically see seasonally higher demand in Q3, and I would say that  demand is higher in most markets compared to previous year. This is what changes it a bit. We haven't been able  yet to fully compensate for higher steel prices in the Ruukki Construction business. But I would say also a decent  performance during the quarter.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: Volume-wise, SEK 370 million positive impact. This is mainly coming from Special Steels with a good volume  increase, but also coming from Americas. Then, we get the negative impact on the variable COGS, SEK 840  million. And here, we actually saw higher cost for compared to last year iron ore, coking coal and scraps, all the  three main raw materials had a high cost this year.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: Somewhat positive on the variable COGS side. We had lower costs for iron ore and coking coal, on the other  hand, mitigated by higher cost for scrap during the quarter. Then, we have a quite large positive impact from fixed  cost. And for those of you who have been around a few years, you know that every third quarter, we have a  seasonally positive impact, where in the Nordic operations and given that such a large portion of our employees  are in the Nordic, we have this [ph] dissolvement (00:10:57) of vacation reserves that typically happen in the third  quarter. So, when we look into fourth quarter, it's more likely that fixed cost will be more similar to the second  quarter than to what we see now in this third quarter.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: So, that's it on the balance sheet side, and I will now move into raw material. We could see in the quarter that our  purchase prices for iron ore and scrap went down quite a lot – sorry, iron ore and coking coal. If we start with  coking coal, they were down as much as 25%. In Swedish krona, 19% in U.S. dollar in Q3 versus Q2. I think it's  important to remember though that given that we have winter stocks for coking coal in Luleå and in Raahe, we do  the majority of our yearly purchases in Q3 and in Q2. And that means that what we consume and what will hit the  P&L in Q4 is more likely to be what we bought in Q2 than what we bought by now in Q3. Q3 buys will more  materialize later on in Q1 and Q2 next year.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: For iron ore, we also saw a decrease, not as much as for coking coal, but it was down 15%, our average  purchase prices in Swedish krona, but only 8% in U.S. dollar. And there we have a faster turnaround, so that's  more likely then to have an impact in Q4. We buy the majority of iron ore from LKAB. We also buy from Severstal.  And with LKAB, our contract is valid until end of March next year, but prices there are adjusted on a monthly  basis. So, we do see an impact also during the quarter when the spot prices fluctuate.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: What we can also see on this chart is that in October, scrap spot prices have decreased quite a lot actually in  Americas. They're down around €30 per tonne to €40 per tonne for the October buy. So, moving into outlook.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: My last picture, we posted new sustainability objectives today, I think. And, when I think about this, I mean, the  steel industry has always been regarded to be a big part of the [ph] program (00:18:50). In SSAB, we have felt  that with our products, the lightweighting, taking out weight, increasing life length, reducing fuel consumption,  helping customers to reduce emissions, we have seen ourselves as part of this solution.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: I think with these new objectives, where we state that we will be among others, fossil-free, completely fossil-free  2045. I think, we take another step in showing that we are not only part of the [ph] program (00:19:17), but we are  definitely part of the future solution. Of course, HYBRIT is one important part in this promise, but there are other  things as well where we need to continue to work with fuel-related emissions.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: We also have what we call sustainable offerings. We say at the latest 2025, we should help our customers to  reduce 10 million tonnes of carbon dioxide during the user phase of their application, and that is the equal to what  we emit today, emit roughly 10 million tonne of carbon dioxide, and that's a lot, of course. But, as you all know, we  are also the most carbon-dioxide-effective steel producer in the world.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: So, you could claim, and I'm not probably allowed to say that, but you could claim that, 2025, we should be  carbon neutral, and 2045, we should be completely fossil-free. We're also raising our ambitions in what – within  what we call responsible partners. So important for us to say in a clear statement for the future.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: Okay. It hasn't – so far it hasn't impacted materially on – this will be a special impact on, let's say, the Americas  where we have the scrap-based production. We haven't seen that impact yet. And what we have done is, we have  secured, so we know that we will have the volumes needed for 2018, but we haven't yet agreed on the price level.  It's still moving a lot like this up and down, so it's a bit too early to say how much it will impact, but it will most  likely have an impact on the cost in 2018 in, as I said, the Americas.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: Well, it's not substantial in the level of how much scrap can turn up and down, but it's substantial, given that it has  not actually had a major impact before. It's been fairly stable before, but now it is moving up and it will have an  impact on cost in Americas, yes.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: But, I think, if you take Americas as such, you see there's its scrap and we consume it very fast. We saw  downturn now in October on that. And usually scrap goes up in the winter season. That remains to be seen. In  Europe then for Special Steels mainly as well, we saw that, yes, iron ore have gone down. That will have a  positive impact, if it's stays on that level.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: On the other hand, as I mentioned on coking coal, we bought quite a lot there in Q2 at a reasonably high level. So  even though coking coal purchases were down in Q3, the costs will basically be what we bought for in Q2, so no  major changes on the raw material side, I would say.

texts.speaker: Johannes Grunselius
texts.profession: Analyst, Handelsbanken
texts.text: And if I can recall it right, I mean, you need to grow something like 7%, 8% per year to reach the target for Special  Steels.

texts.profession: Analyst, Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken AB (Finland)
texts.text: Okay. Great. That's pretty clear. Then a second question, also relating to U.S., you highlight the large energy  order. Could you give us some kind indication how large was the order? texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: It was around 50 ktonne and there are always orders and when activity around in the market and when activity in  the energy segment, I mean, there are orders like this in the market, they are not – this wasn't an extremely bad  order. texts.profession: Analyst, Jefferies International Ltd.
texts.text: Is there any chance you can give us a sense of how to quantify that shipping costs perhaps [indiscernible]  (00:37:56)?

texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.

texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB

texts.speaker: Bastian Synagowitz
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank (Suisse) SA
texts.text: Got it. Thank you. Then, my second question is just again following up on the situation around graphite  electrodes. I appreciate that we don't have the final number on costs and I've been hearing from some players  that cost could be up by around $40 to $50 even for the contracts on a per-tonne basis. But, say, given that part  of your competition does not face this amount of cost increase, because they produce via the blast furnace route,  how confident are you that you can fully pass this on to customers given that we, at least currently have an  environment, where prices obviously has been drifting?

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: One reason why both inventories and payables moved up is what I was talking about before that during the  second and third quarter, we increased our purchases of coking coal. You saw that and especially in the third  quarter, and that has an impact on inventories going up, but it also has an impact on our accounts payable for  these coking coals. I would say that was the main reason you saw those two increases.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Plus we can't bring in coking coal during the winter to either Luleå or Raahe as we need to build the seasonal  stock as always, because the ships are too big and they are not ice class. We can't bring them in during – from I  would say end of November until end of March.

texts.speaker: Robert Redin
texts.profession: Analyst, Carnegie Investment Bank AB
texts.text: Yeah. Hi. Three questions, if I may. This large order in energy in Q3 in North America, is there anything like that in  the order book for Q4?

texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: We have some interesting possibilities for cold-formed steel solutions when it comes to battery protection and so  on. And I mean, of course, we can't have 28% every quarter, quarter out and quarter  in, but we will meet the target, 2020 at the latest.

texts.speaker: Oskar Lindström
texts.profession: Analyst, Danske Bank A/S (Sweden)
texts.text: But in 2018, the problems relating to the Oxelösund breakdown should no longer have an impact?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: No. And having said that, knock on wood, but no, it shouldn't.

texts.speaker: Oskar Lindström
texts.profession: Analyst, Danske Bank A/S (Sweden)
texts.text: Yeah. Thank you. My final question regards your new sustainability objectives and I'm mainly sort of interested in  will this have any implications for your CapEx or investments in coming years? And will it lead you to – I mean, if  you're choosing – if you're looking at capacity expansion, will you favor scrap EAF over BOF?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Over time, what their aiming for is with this new hybrid projects to come up with a completely new way of  producing iron, liquid iron, and instead of emitting carbon dioxide, emitting pure water if you put it bluntly. And, of  course, that will require investments. On the other hand, I mean, keeping coke [ph] oven and battery (00:57:45)  alive or blast furnace realignings are also extremely expensive exercises.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: So, I would say, over time, it will require some probably higher investments, yes, over time. On the other hand, we  believe that and hope that emitting carbon dioxide will also become more expensive over time. So, when we have  looked into this, we have done it like, call it, an investment case even though it's not just an investment case. But  financially and environmentally, this makes sense for SSAB and that's why we have taken this decision.

texts.speaker: Oskar Lindström
texts.profession: Analyst, Danske Bank A/S (Sweden)
texts.text: I know your final sort of deadline is 2045, which is quite far away, it feels like, but – or it is far away. But when  should we – any kind of indication of when the technological shift for that you were describing will happen?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: I don't have the exact time plan on the top of my head. But, so far, we haven't come into anything that makes us  believe that this is not possible. And then it should be finally up and running full speed at the latest 2045, and then  it's a lot of steps, I mean, we need to – we will definitely then, of course, not invest in re-lining of blast furnaces in  Oxelösund, and we will not invest in a new coke coal and that refurbishment of the coke coal, in that we need to  some other immediate investments and so on. But this is a long-term plan, which we believe in the end will be not  only very good for the environment but also financially very good for SSAB.

texts.speaker: Operator
texts.profession: Operator
texts.text: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Luc Pez of Exane BNP Paribas. Please go  ahead. Your line is now open.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: But, for us, we don't have any center plants left, so we are 100% pellet-based. And in the longer term, yes, if that  difference between pellets and fine would increase, that would have a negative impact on our competitiveness  versus producers only using or using to a majority, fines.

texts.speaker: Cedar Ekblom
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: Can you talk about what's actually happened in the scrap market and why that seems to have moved in an  opposite direction to the healthy environment for steel prices that you seem to suggest are setting up in the U.S.  market right now?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: It was a lot of different things. I mean, you had these weather problems in Houston and in other areas that made  scrap collection a bit tougher. It's also a matter of the strength of the U.S. dollar. When you see weak U.S. dollar,  you typically see a lot of scrap export. There is seasonality in scrap collecting as well. So, if one would guess  then, so if – I mean, what – the terrible thing that happened in Houston with the weather, with the storm, the  hurricane, and what happened in Florida and other places during the third quarter might have tightened up the  scrap collection short term and will give some extra scrap mid-term. So, there's a lot of moving parts here.

texts.speaker: Cedar Ekblom
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: Okay. And then, if we just go back to the European market, can I ask you how you think sentiment is shaping up  in terms of pricing? If we look at the price hikes that steel mills announced over the summer period, some of that's  being secured, but not all of it. And over the same period, we've seen iron ore weaken quite substantially and I  just wonder if you're looking at the sentiment in the European market, has there been a shift at all when you're  talking to your buyers? Are they pushing back on price increases because of the move in raw material cost? Is  that factoring into conversations at all? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Cedar Ekblom
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: Okay. When you are talking about prices with your customers, do they look at the raw material price?

texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB

texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: So, I will not spend more time on this, but I will move into raw material side instead. For iron ore and for coking  coal in Q3, prices are very stable, I would say. texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: What we have seen now in the beginning of Q4 is that especially on coking coal, but also in iron ore, spot prices  have started moving upward somewhat. texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: To start with – we are focusing on this tiny part of the automotive steel market, I would say, somewhere around or  below – just below 5%. texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: So, I mean, we are – it is important for us SSAB Europe, it is important for us, but we have very good products,  the martensitic steel, that are excellent for cold-rolling. texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: So, we see structurally that the interest for these kind of advanced steel grades due to lightweighting and safety  and fuel efficiency and so on is increasing. texts.profession: Analyst, Nordea Bank ABP (Broker)

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB

texts.speaker: Alexander Haissl
texts.profession: Analyst, Crédit Agricole Cheuvreux SA (Germany)
texts.text: The next question is on the efficiency program. What is your overall target to bring down breakeven? Is it implied  in some kind of normalized world with no lagging effects for raw material costs to see prices you could be  breakeven between 70% and 75% here?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: To start with the second question then – no, to the first question, I mean capacity utilization in Europe going  forward, I wish I could answer that one for the whole steel industry, I don't know, to be honest, but we are seeing  our capacity utilization going up somewhat, but we still have one blast furnace idle. So, as said, I mean the  situation in Europe is a bit uncertain. So, the total capacity utilization, I have no clue where that will go.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: And then working capital, I mean the biggest part in the working capital reduction is inventories and we are on  good levels and we expect those levels to stay.

texts.speaker: Marco Wiren
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: We right only just taking down the inventory, but also seeing that we worked in a better way, so it's – it should be  sustainable going forward as well.

texts.speaker: Cedar Barnes
texts.profession: Analyst, Merrill Lynch International (United Kingdom)
texts.text: Thanks very much. Good morning. I've got one question on your iron ore agreement. We've seen spot iron ore  prices, pellets and [ph] fines (38:00) coming off sort of 20% from the peaks that we saw during Q3. texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: What comes going forward, I believe that in general in the steel market, you might see some rebound after a heavy  destocking during Q4. And, of course, what kind of mix we're going to have depends totally on our customers'  demand going forward as well.

texts.speaker: Julian Beer
texts.profession: Analyst, SEB Enskilda (Sweden)
texts.text: So, what was included – if you don't switch on that idled Oxelösund furnace during Q1 similar fixed cost issues?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Well, we'll have at least under absorption as long as the blast furnace is idle, yes.

texts.speaker: Julian Beer
texts.profession: Analyst, SEB Enskilda (Sweden)
texts.text: Okay. [indiscernible] (43:46). Lastly, then emission rights sales, do you expect some more in Q1 given you have a  shutdown furnace?  Martin Erik Lindqvist  President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB  A I had a problem to hear there.

texts.speaker: Julian Beer
texts.profession: Analyst, SEB Enskilda (Sweden)
texts.text: Yes. Do you expect further sale of emission rights in Q1 given the shutdown furnace?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: I mean, it depends how long the blast furnace will be shutdown, but we haven't thought much about that.

texts.speaker: Neil S. Sampat
texts.profession: Analyst, Nomura International Plc
texts.text: Hi, there. So, I think now question might have just been answered, just to clarify because of the blast furnace at  Oxelösund stay idled during Q1, does that mean you still get a kind of offsetting benefit from those CO2 emission  sales?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: We haven't decided when to start exactly the blast furnace. Right now, it's still idle and we haven't said when we  start it. It's going to depend on market conditions and what we see going forward. But, I mean, as long as it stays  idle, we will not use all the emission rights we have.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: As said, I mean, we haven't discussed that or even given it any thought. So, we did that during Q4, because it was  obvious that we had the blast furnace idled for the second half of last year. Then we take that decision when we  need.  Neil S. Sampat  Analyst, Nomura International Plc  Q Okay. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Well, I guess, from time-to-time there is input pressure on plate prices and all steel prices in U.S., but we'll have  some the coming weeks or months or quarters, I don't really know.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: I mean spot prices is a good indicator where contract prices and prices for standard steel are heading. And then, of  course, there is always a lagging effect, but when spot prices are under pressure you could expect prices,  everything else equal, on standard material to follow the same direction.

texts.speaker: Christian Kopfer
texts.profession: Analyst, Nordea Bank AB (Broker)
texts.text: Okay. Thanks. Just finally from me then, the startup of the final blast furnace in Oxelösund; as you're seeing a  little bit uncertainty there, does this mean that if you're not starting that up, you will see – you will gradually  phase out the standard products on the benefit of the new quenching capacity then?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: We will do that regardless of it – if we startup the blast furnace or not. I mean, we are currently selling 37% of the  volumes within our defined niches, and the target is, as said 2015 to have 50%. So, regardless of blast furnace  capacity, we will phase out standard products.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: It's, I would say, a fairly – time wise compared to a greenfield or anything fairly short investment and a very cost  effective investment. And we could potentially take up the capacity with another 200,000 tons.

texts.speaker: Oskar Lindström
texts.profession: Analyst, Danske Bank
texts.text: Yes. Oskar Lindström at Danske Bank here. Two questions about the emission rights. First of all, the emission  rights that you sold during the fourth quarter, were they relating only to lower production in the fourth quarter or  was it actually, sort of, an accumulated lower production during the latter part of last year?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: I mean, we have – had blast furnace idled since this summer. So, it was not only Q4.

texts.speaker: Oskar Lindström
texts.profession: Analyst, Danske Bank
texts.text: So, you were actually selling second half 2011. Were you also selling sort of part of the emission rights that you  would have used for the beginning of this year?

texts.speaker: Oskar Lindström
texts.profession: Analyst, Danske Bank
texts.text: Okay. So, you haven't sold those. And I read in your report that the emission rights that you will be given for the  period of 2013 to 2020 will be lower than for the previous period although the final decision will come later in this  year. Could that result in you having to have sort of a continual expense of buying additional emission rights  compared to what you've had previously and then could you put a number on that or...?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Mining I would say, with a few exceptions, is the more stable business, both in Australia and China and in the  Nordic region. The exception is coal mining. And there is a possibility on the east coast in Australia that we could  see improved demand with higher coal prices.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Energy, we see continued activity and saw a continued activity within line pipe, an important segment for us. And  we have taken orders for deliveries during the first half of this year. texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Local prices decreased by 3% for niche steel and by 8% for standard steels versus Q3 2012. And we also sold  roughly 100,000 tons of slabs externally, which we typically do from time to time over the years.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: So the market environment and outlook. Global steel production according to World Steel Association fell with 2%  in Q4 versus Q3. Capacity utilization for the overall steel industry in Europe for Q4 was 67% but in December, it was below 60% for  the European steel industry in average. Demand affected by destocking and prolonged outages among customers  in December and early January was clearly felt by us as well and other steel companies.

texts.speaker: Marco Wirén
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: And then in the others, if you remember in 2011, the fourth quarter we also sold emission rights and the amount  was about SEK275 million. That gives the impact – the difference between these two quarters.

texts.speaker: Marco Wirén
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: A couple of words about the raw materials. As we mentioned last time as well, we signed a new contract with  LKAB, [ph] which accounts (14:02) to iron ore pellet deliveries. texts.speaker: Marco Wirén
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: When it comes to coal, we purchased about 60% to 70% from Australia and the residual from the North America.  And the consumption that we had in Q4 was about 10% higher compared to Q3 and that will give an impact in Q2  and later on.

texts.speaker: Marco Wirén
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: And when it comes to U.S. coal purchases, the contract period ends in the end of March as well and then we will  have a new contract. When it comes to scrap, we buy scrap for North American facilities on a continuous basis and  during the quarter, prices by the end of quarter were actually a little bit higher than end of Q3.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Thank you. So the outlook, well, we expect volumes in Americas and APAC to improve compared to Q4. We say  that the trend in Europe continues to be uncertain. We expect though apparent demand to be a bit more positive  compared to Q4. We see that steel prices appear to have stabilized or bottomed out. We will have a positive effect  or impact from lower iron ore costs that will affect earnings in Q1 and Q2 compared to Q4.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: As said, we have a planned outage in Montpelier that will affect Americas in Q1, end of Q1 beginning of Q2. And  the efficiency program and the flexibility program runs according to plan and will be delivered.

texts.speaker: Joakim Ahlberg
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Agricole Cheuvreux Nordic AB
texts.text: Okay, thanks. Okay, on the inventory level to start with, Joakim Ahlberg, Cheuvreux, by the way, and you're  talking about the sustainability here going forward so this is on the level of inventories you are talking about and  not anything to do with the prices of coal and iron ore et cetera?

texts.speaker: Gustav Sandström
texts.profession: Analyst, Erik Penser Bank AB
texts.text: Great. And finally, you mentioned that there will be no substantial investments going forward. But given the  current gas price in the States and what seems to be an economy recovering over there, in what scenario would  you consider increasing capacity by DRI or something like that?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: And to start with that, yes, there are always possibilities, of course, and we have done some things. We have closed  some lines, one galvanizing line and there are some other options, minor options available of course. But I mean,  we have the structure we have with two blast furnaces running and there are no big things that we can do  structurally.

texts.speaker: Alexander A. Haissl
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Okay. The next question I have is on the steel prices, you indicated that we see more or less a stabilization but the  hikes didn't stick in the market. Is it more for the standard grade products for the strip steel or is it for the niche  products? What you are seeing right now?

texts.speaker: Julian Beer

texts.speaker: Julian Beer

texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Prime Brokerage)

texts.speaker: Neil S. Sampat
texts.profession: Analyst, Nomura International Plc
texts.text: Good afternoon, a couple of questions from my side. Firstly – sorry, good morning. texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB

texts.speaker: Stephen Benson
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International
texts.text: Hi, there. I just had a question around inventory. So we see LKAB contract that will be renegotiated again in April,  is it fair to assume that you will be carrying maybe eight to 10 weeks of the lower priced iron ore into the second  quarter?

texts.speaker: Alessandro Abate
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Plc
texts.text: Hi good morning to everybody, just one question related to the energy segment in the U.S. You're speaking about  continuous activity in line pipe we [indiscernible] (36:51) for H1, and optimism for wind tower. texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: You should not overestimate the optimism within wind tower because as you know the last two quarters, Q3 and  Q4 that market has been more or less dead but when they decided to extend the tax credit we have seen positive  signs but some I would say (37:26) CRO at (37:26) very low levels. When it comes to line pipe, that is, of course,  driven by the energy boom or whatever you call it in North America with shale gas and everything. And we have  seen already in Q4 an increased demand for those kind of steels that you produce line pipes of.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Yeah, in U.S. dollars we hedged the long-term purchasing contracts like the U.S. coal purchasing and LKAB  purchasing contracts from the same date when we signed those contracts.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: If we look at our key customer segments and these are the important segments for us. And if we look at the trend  in Q4 versus Q3, I would say fairly flat with the exception of the U.S. energy segment that started to pick up late  Q3 and was picking up in Q4.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: If we look at the sequential outlook Q1 versus Q4, I would say that we see more or less the same trend in heavy  transport, not getting worse. Automotive picking up, constructio n machinery on the same level, mining in our  segments bottomed out and somewhat stronger market compared to Q4 in energy. And we see also for the first  time in a long period that service centers still are cautious, of course, but they're buying at slightly  higher levels  than we have seen during 2013 and the inventories in the service center system is not on the high side and that  goes for inventories in the full supply chain, they are normal or below normal.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Americas, better shipments than in Q3 and compared to Q4 last year. Demand from heavy transport segment and  service centers increased. Demand from the energy segment remains strong throughout Q4 and into Q1.  Unchanged prices in local currencies in Q4, so the price increases have not been seen in Q4. And we have so far  announced $130 per short tonne which will have a gradual impact from Q1 then.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: What we saw and what we have seen is the seasonally higher scrap prices in Q4, we typically see that every year,  but this winter season has been fairly tough with cold weather and even snow in Alabama. texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: The scrap prices have moved up with $70 per tonne, and that is somewhat more than normal during the winter  season and the weather is still – or the winter is still fairly strong, so maybe it will take some extra weeks before  we see the normal downturn in scrap prices as we always see.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Executive Vice President, Chief Financial Officer, SSAB AB
texts.text: Finally from my side, some words on our raw material prices. Iron ore, we have a yearly delivery contract with  LKAB, however, the prices are set on quarterly basis. texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Executive Vice President, Chief Financial Officer, SSAB AB
texts.text: Then Martin mentioned this briefly before on the scrap. texts.profession: Executive Vice President, Chief Financial Officer, SSAB AB
texts.text: I think on a P&L basis for Europe, there was no – if you combine the two, iron ore and coke, there was no major  difference between the quarters. texts.speaker: Julian Beer
texts.profession: Analyst, SEB Enskilda (Sweden)
texts.text: The variable improvement wasn't really due with raw materials, it was due with other...

texts.profession: Analyst, SEB Enskilda (Sweden)

texts.profession: Analyst, SEB Enskilda (Sweden)
texts.text: Okay. texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: It's a good question. We don't – of course, we have an idea. But what we see, typically, is scrap prices moving up  during the winter season because of harder to collect it. With the weather this year, with very cold weather in  Midwest and also cold weather at south, with even snow down in Southern U.S., scrap prices have mov ed up a  little bit more than normal, and that typically levels off when the bad weather goes away or when the weather  normalizes, so to say.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: So, what we are expecting is scrap prices to come down from these seasonally higher levels during, I would say,  year-end or beginning of January.

texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: Do you see more volume upsell in the first quarter from slabs into Turkey, because clearly the Turkish mills are  scaling down scrap purchases and rather buy billets and slabs externally. texts.profession: Executive Vice President, Chief Financial Officer, SSAB AB

texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: I wouldn't say necessarily mining, but we need to see a recovery in the segments consuming Q&T, both structural  steels, the high-grade welders like big mobile cranes and equipment like that. texts.profession: Analyst, Carnegie Investment Bank AB

texts.profession: Executive Vice President, Chief Financial Officer, SSAB AB
texts.text: ...market price level at the moment, I think, is the best indicator. And what you can see on iron ore prices so far,  they have come down quite a bit during January and the beginning of February.

texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: I think to understand it – I mean, one good approximation is to take a look at the Cat's report and the other  reports from the yellow goods producer. texts.text: So, I'll just take them one by one. The first one is on the finished steel price development, have you seen any signs  of recovery in Q1 and what is your expectation looking into Q2, particularly for commodity plate?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: But I've said many times, in U.S. we have seen a clear improvement in standard steel prices. In Europe, we saw  during Q4 prices going down and the momentum into Q1 is, I mean, at least for spot prices positive.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Construction Material, Q4 is always a seasonal slowdown, and we saw that this year as well. And we are expecting  a seasonally better demand in Q1. texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: The market for energy, transportation and railcars expected to be strong in 2015. And that is due to the order  books for those customers. But we see some negative effects related to delayed investments in pipeline projects.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: And if you take SSAB's sales in North America, it is less than 10%, including what goes via service centers, that  goes directly to the oil and gas sector. And we have currently a fairly limited exposure to big pipeline projects.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: What have we done then? Well, what we have done so far and what is in that SEK 300 million is lower purchasing  costs, new suppliers, new contracts and [ph] combining best of growth (10:08). We have in-sourced material to  Tibnor that previously was bought externally, that we can produce ourselves now. We are taking coking coal from  Oxelösund to Raahe instead of purchasing externally. We have also announced some actions with later impact. As  said, we will close the galvanizing line and the color-coating line in Borlänge and that will affect to start with 210  employees. We have closed or we will close the Ruukki headquarter and reduce staff functions not only in Finland,  but in the full Europe. And we will consolidate service centers in Tibnor. And we will continue then to do things  during this year according to the initial industrial plan.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: We had slightly higher volumes, especially than in the European division, since we had the summer outage in Q3.  Negative impact of price, partly in Americas, but, actually, mainly in Europe, given the mix effect. And then  variable COGS also a slightly negative impact where we had positive from the raw material, but on the other hand,  we had the outage in Montpelier, which impacted negatively. And in the other SEK 50 million, it's, for example,  foreign exchange, it's Tibnor and fixed cost.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: The other big item then between the two quarters is variable costs. And here, it's both production efficiency has  been improved, but it's, of course, also the lower raw material cost mainly due to iron ore. And then, once again,  we have the same items in the other bucket. So, all in all, it's an improvement of a bit more than SEK 400 million  from Q4 2013 Q4 to 2014.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: Then, I would like to say some words about the relining of the blast furnace in Luleå. This is our largest blast  furnace. It has a capacity of 2.3 million tonnes. It's now 50 years since it was built, so it's definitely time to do the  relining. We will do it this summer. And we will have it closed from June until August. The capital expenditure for  the relining itself is around SEK 700 million.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: However, at the same time when the blast furnace is closed, we will anyway do some other investments, which is  good timing to do when you don't have production. So all-in-all, we will spend around SEK 800 million in Luleå  this year.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: What we will also need to do is, we need replace approximately 500,000 tonnes of slabs, and we will do this by  starting build-up slab inventory in Luleå. And we have also started up the small blast furnace in Oxelösund, that  has been idle for some time. And we will also build up slabs and ship them from Raahe.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: On top of the investment, we will have an extra cost for this, for example, transport of the slabs, start of the blast  furnace in Oxelösund. And we have estimated, the extra costs will be between SEK 100 million to SEK 150 million.  Some of them in Q1, but most of it Q2 and Q3.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: Finally, from my part, some words on the raw material prices, where in general, we see clearly lower prices year- over-year. Our iron ore price was 7% lower in Q4 versus Q3 in Swedish krona, but 29% lower when we compare  with Q4 last year.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: For coking coal, we saw coking coal prices go down significantly already in 2013. What we see now is that in  Swedish krona, they were actually somewhat higher in Q4 than in Q3. In U.S. dollar, they were fairly even. But  when we look one year back, we can see that the prices are still 13% lower.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: And what we see on scrap prices is, as you know, iron ore prices have been going like this, scrap has been fairly  stable so far. But right now, we haven't seen the normal uptick that we see in the winter season, and for March,  scrap prices are expected to decrease rather significantly.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Then, I will show you something beautiful. This is the world's largest mining dump truck, also the winner of  Swedish Steel Prize 2014, this is with a loading capacity of 450-tonnes, produced by Belaz, developed by Belaz  with the help of SSAB. And of course, there is Hardox in the dumper body. But what is interesting with this one as  well, that axles and the chassis and frame is also developed by SSAB Steel. I think it's a huge and fantastic  machine, requires a lot of steel as well.

texts.speaker: Oskar Lindström
texts.profession: Danske Bank A/S (Sweden)
texts.text: All right. Thank you. One more question. You mentioned in your presentation that the Heavy Transport end use  segment is looking slightly better, both in Americas and also in Special Steels, if I recall correctly. What is this and  how much of that is related to tank cars in North America, or are there other heavy transport segments which are  pulling that...

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: As you know, we have a quarterly lagging and piles prices and iron ore prices have been going down during big  part of 2014. On the other hand, the U.S. dollar has strengthened. So – but we have seen some effects of it during  2014 and then it all depends where the iron ore price will go. But currently, I think the piles price is around $60 or  something per tonne which is obviously much lower compared to a year ago.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: And then scrap has been not developing this year. I mean, the correlation between scrap and iron ore is, over time,  very stable, and we haven't seen that. We start to see that effect in our scrap prices coming down, but we haven't  seen that correlation up till now.

texts.speaker: Christian Kopfer
texts.profession: Nordea Bank AB (Broker)
texts.text: And for pellets, are those coming down in line with the piles?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Well, pellet is priced from piles prices and then a defined pellets premium. And we have the same – the pellets  premium we have for one year from April 1 to end of March, we have the same pellets premium.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: I don't know the percentage. But I think we sold to the automotive segment last year approximately 700,000  tonnes. It's a fairly decent chunk of business. And then we have some other volumes regarding being high- strength steel but below 700 megapascal. But in special steel, it's hot-rolled volumes above 700 megapascal, an  abrasive-resistant steel, Q&T.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: And other reason I would add why the lead times are going down is because we talked about scrap prices  expecting to go down rather significantly, and Martin mentioned service centers sitting on high inventories. There  is no point for them to buy today, when they believe that scrap will go down and then they think that the prices  will go down. So, I think we're seeing service centers sitting on the sideline just in a wait-and-see mode, and then,  of course, you've got the lead time impact on the mills.

texts.speaker: Jean-Baptiste Devevey
texts.profession: Exane SA (Broker)
texts.text: Devevey from Exane BNP Paribas. I had a question on the U.S. and the impact from the lower oil and gas prices  [audio gap] (47:29 – 47:47). Would you expect any negative impact on the mix side? [audio gap] (47:50 – 48:08) I  appreciate that oil and gas-related end-markets are not a huge share of your sales. I think you said a bit less than  10%. But are there some margin impact that should lead to some margin conversion in the U.S., given what we see  in oil prices right now?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Well, I think you can look at it in two ways. Of course, the lower energy prices will also be positive for the North  American economy and drive, call it, re-industrialization, and higher production rates and so on in U.S. So mid- term, I would say, it's probably also very positive. But short-term, of course, it affects the demand. And as I said,  for us, it's somewhere between – just above 8% or 8% directed to that sector. But the secondary effects could, of  course, be freight producers being more exposed to it or trying to find business somewhere else. So I think it's  hard to predict exactly what – where this will end up. But I would say over time, I guess, for the U.S. economy and  the steel consumption, this is fairly positive.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: The costs that we said was SEK 175 million, and those are the actual cost for the outage. So, if you would take the  total P&L impact which you're alluding to, then – due to lost shipments, yes, then it would be a bit higher.  Bastian Synagowitz  Deutsche Bank (Suisse) SA (Broker)  Q  Could you give us just a rough picture of how that would have looked like, just considering the volume loss and  lack of fixed-cost dilution would not have happened?

texts.speaker: Cedar Ekblom
texts.profession: Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: Thanks very much. Two quick follow-up questions. On the U.S., you mentioned that your direct exposure to  Energy is only about 10%. But can you talk more about how you could see plate prices across the board being  depressed even in non-energy markets as volumes that were previously directed to Energy, now find their way  into the spot market. Just trying to understand that – or to understand the extent which you might not have a  direct exposure to Energy, but which small falling Energy CapEx in the U.S. can actually impact other markets  there. And...

texts.speaker: Cedar Ekblom
texts.profession: Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: In terms of domestic production, have you seen any tonnes yet that were being sold on a contract basis by  domestic producers into the Energy end-markets being displaced into the distributor markets. I understand that  imports go into the distributor market. But what I'm trying to understand is if they actually risk that domestic  tonnes, which no longer are not demanded by Energy end-users getting to the distribution markets as well,  because we're seeing that in strip products, I understand. I wonder if we're seeing it in plates yet.

texts.speaker: Cedar Ekblom
texts.profession: Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: The book value. Okay. Fine. That makes sense. I understand that. And then just the one final question. In the  synergies slide, you mentioned that one of the synergies or savings you were able to capture was selling or  transporting coal Oxelösund to Raahe, I mean, that's a one-off, I assume, right?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: No. It's, we produce coking coal that was previously bought on the open market.

texts.speaker: Cedar Ekblom
texts.profession: Bank of America Merrill Lynch
texts.text: Okay. The coal factory is fine. That's fine. Okay.  Martin Erik Lindqvist  President, Chief Executive Officer & Director  A  So it's not a one-off.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: You could argue that way. You can also argue that part of it will have hedge for the next year. And we also – it also  depends on the profitability we have in the U.S. business. So, it's not that – and at the same time, the raw material  prices have come down, which means we will buy them for less U.S. dollars. So, it's a bit too easy to only add 20%.  There's lot of other variables in that equation.
