texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: I will start with this picture, not to give you a lection in geography, but China is very important for the global steel  industry and impacting the global steel market a lot. What we have seen in the last 10 years is China going from a  net importer of steel to a net exporter of steel. China has built up a massive steel production capacity as well. And  the demand increase the last number of years has been huge in China. But now, when it's plateauing out, China is  having a lot of excess capacity of steel.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Well, we try to concentrate on the things that we can influence ourselves, of course, being very active on the  market, reducing lead times, increasing delivery performance, safe guard, and if possible, increase market shares  in the Nordic region, the whole market for flat carbon steel in North America for plates and globally for Q&T and  other niche grade.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Synergies, as we see it, is due to the combination of Ruukki and SSAB. On the top of that, we need to do additional  efficiency measures like all the other steel companies to keep up our cost position. So, if this is a relative change in  cost position, this is to keep up with the pace in the steel industry.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: So, at the end of this year, we will be approximately 15,500 people, a reduction of 14% or 13.6%-something, which  is with – if you measure it tonnes per man hour, quite an improvement in productivity.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Americas, sharp price drops, lower volumes, partly offset by lower costs, and the declining volume is due to  destocking among steel service centers. Heavy Transport started to slow down a bit in Q4, while demand for wind  towers and some other segments remained strong. You'll also hear, we don't have any synergies here, but we have  a strong focus on cost efficiency. We do, twice a year, benchmark study to check the cost position compared to  other plate producers. We have recently done that. And we keep our leading quality and cost position compared to  other plate producers.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: On the positive side then, we had positive impact from variable COGS, to a large extent, that the scrap prices in   the U.S. decreased very much, but it's also here where we see some of the synergy impacts coming.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: We're compensating the huge drop in prices heartily by variable COGS, where raw material, all three main ones,  iron ore, coking coal and scrap, are down quite a lot year-over-year. But it's also here we see our own action in  terms synergies and also other cost improvements. But despite that, clearly, we are not compensating the variable  COGS with the drop in prices.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Energy, oil-related segments will continue to be demanding. We expect to see a continued strong demand from  wind towers. Construction Material, we typically see a seasonality in Q1. Q1 is, very often, stronger than Q4 due to  seasonality. We expect to see that pattern this year as well.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: One example of that, I mean, we gave now we are closing together Oxelösund and Borlänge an d moving  production to Hämeenlinna. That will reduce work in progress. It will reduce finished goods. We are specializing  lines now, I mean, focusing Borlänge more on high-strength steel and so on. And that gives longer sequence  lengths, less working capital, less finished inventories. And that is also part or related to the combination of the  two companies.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: In some small signs, I mean, the cold-rolled in Europe, which is a fairly important market for us, we have  approximate – what could it be – 350,000 tonnes and there has been leakages about that and we have seen a  slightly different behavior because when they do this, it will be retroactive and the one importing the volumes will  be the one paying the dumping duties.

texts.speaker: Julian Beer
texts.profession: Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken AB (Broker)
texts.text: And these are the famous facilities which currently don't have any covenants attached to them, which some have  found surprising for any steel sector company. You're renegotiating all – sorry, your maturity on those I think the  first one is Q1 next year.

texts.speaker: Robert Redin
texts.profession: Carnegie Investment Bank AB
texts.text: Y eah. Hi. Can I start on your outlook for the other segments in the U.S.? Y ou're saying Heavy Transport is sort of  expected to slow down; Construction Machinery, under pressure; whereas Wind is expected to be – to stay at a  good level. Net-net, what would you say when you're talking to your customers in the U.S.? Y our end markets  segment, is there sort of a negative, stable or upward pointing arrow in the U.S.?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Then the second question, idling capacity. We have one blast furnace in Oxelösund idled. We will permanently  close the galvanizing line during Q1 in week eight, I think it is. And move that production to Hämeenlinna. We  have permanently closed the color-coating line in Borlänge and we have now, after the relining of the blast  furnace, also possibility to idle further blast furnace capacity if the market would require so.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President
texts.text: And for the first question, we have said that there will be no additional costs for this further reduction – planned  further reduction.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: It depends a lot on markets and products, but, I mean, we have contract prices of 50% of the volumes and we have  some spot volumes and we have half-year prices. So, for standard steel we are following the usual steel market in  those regions where we are active.

texts.speaker: Julian Beer
texts.profession: Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken AB (Broker)
texts.text: And could you see any arrangement whereby a Nordic steel producer could engage in that?

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: Looking at the cost position, as said, we move into 2017 with a structurally lower cost base of SEK 3 billion, or just  above SEK 3 billion compared to the time when we merged the two companies. The majority is, of course, as we  have talked about before, synergies and the synergy realizations. We have done efficiency investments up in  Raahe. We have gone from oil injections to coal injections. That gives us SEK 200 million. SEK 200 million on the  restructuring of the Ruukki Construction. And then other cost savings, a big part of that being in Oxelösund. So, in  total, SEK 3 billion.

texts.speaker: Martin Erik Lindqvist
texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB
texts.text: If we look at the outage, we were, during the outage, changing or replacing the control system for the power  supply of the rolling mill. And there was a design error in the control system, and that resulted when we started up  the 15 of December in a damaged transformer. That had to be rewinded and sent to Norway for rewinding. We  got it back and did a second attempt during January 8. Then we blew two transformers. And then we said that we  would be up and running again early February, and we are up and running again, full speed since early February.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: Lower variable COGS to a large extent due to a lower realized cost of scrap, consumption cost, and also that we  had the maintenance outage in Mobile in Q3. Then on the fixed cost side, it's quite negative here in Q4 versus Q3  with SEK 400 million. But this is, if you remember when we talked about Q3, we had a very good improvement  versus Q2. It's a seasonal thing because in the Nordic operations during the third quarter when most people take  vacation, we have dissolvement of vacation reserves. So, we look at this, when we compare Q4-over-Q4, you will  see a totally different picture. So, it's not Q4 that was high, it's more Q3 that is seasonally low.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: If we instead compare Q4 to Q4, we get the much more positive picture where we had a very tough Q4 last year  when EBITDA minus SEK 800 million and now then slightly above SEK 100 million, so more than SEK 900 million  improvement year-over-year. Somewhat at the price, this is almost exclusively coming from SSAB Europe.  Volumes, we see positive development in all three steel divisions and also Tibnor having clearly high volumes,  Q4, this 2016 and 2015. Variable COGS, somewhat positive and this is despite that on the raw material side, we  have a very negative – big negative variation 2016 versus 2015 of roughly SEK 150 million. But, again, our own  actions there have given us the positive improvement.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: Slightly positive development from volumes, and this is mainly Special Steels volumes. Clearly, positive  development on the variable COGS. Roughly half of that is coming from raw material or actually less than half,  and the rest of it is coming then from our own actions.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: Then moving over to the raw material side. And here, we have seen quite a, call it, interesting or at least bumpy  development over the last year, especially for coking coal where we had an enormous peak here during the fourth  quarter where the coking coal price was actually above $300 per tonne, coming from being here around $100 or  below $100 previously. It was a quite short peak, and we are now below $200 again, it's at $175 or something like  that. And for us, it implied that in Q4, our average purchase price was up 65% U.S. dollar and 75% in Swedish  krona. So, it's quite amazing the high figures when you compare only Q4 versus Q3.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: Then we actually don't buy that much in Q4 because for [indiscernible] (22:51), we have – we need to take the  material in earlier to have winter stockage. We do buy steel [indiscernible] (22:56), but the main coking coal buys  we do in Q2 and Q3. We haven't so far seen the cost impact. We've seen a little bit of it, but the most of it will  come during the first half 2017.

texts.speaker: Håkan Folin
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Vice President, SSAB AB
texts.text: On the iron ore side, it doesn't look as dramatic here, but that's just because the coking coal is extremely  dramatic. texts.text: Olof Grenmark, ABG Sundal Collier. Well, if I only have to limit myself to one question, it would be regarding the  overall market situation. What's the net effect? Are we seeing higher profitability as we speak?

texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB

texts.profession: President, Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSAB AB

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: At the start of 2011, SSE established a management board to lead the operation of the business. It's made up of the  three executive directors here and a number of managing directors. And also with us today are Lady Susan Rice,  our Senior Independent Director, Chariman of Rem Comm. And Susan, where are you? Right at the back there.  We've got David Franklin, who is Managing Director for Energy Portfolio Management. David, here at the front.  Paul Smith who is MD for Generation, and Alan Young who is Managing Director – Corporate Affairs at the back.  You'll have a chance to talk to all of them at the end of the session.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: Having said that, this is not a straightforward time in which to do business, with economic uncertainty across  much of the world, and turmoil in the global energy markets, SSE's half year results reflect a number of these  issues such as the high wholesale cost of gas. Nevertheless, subject to the normal caveats, we expect to be  reporting moderate growth in adjusted PBT the full year.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: Looking at our businesses in turn, the main half-year issues were in generation and supply where operating profit  fell by 71% to £58.8 million. This was driven by four issues: higher wholesale gas prices, with summer prices  almost 40% higher than last year. Spark spreads, which were more than 60% lower than in the same period last  year, falls of 4% and 16% respectively in wholesale consumption of electricity and gas and the decision to help  customers by delaying retail price increases until mid-September.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: There was however one very positive aspect of performance in generation supply, the 55% increase in output from  renewable energy. This reflects some new operating capacity from our investment program and more favorable  weather conditions. That's more favorable for us at least.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: There was operating profit growth of 9.5% in Energy Networks which accounted for just over 70% of our operating  profit in the first half. Two things stand out. First, as a result of the progress made in the investment program,  now gathering momentum. Second, SGN performed particularly well with profit growth of 16%. Additional  revenues have come through this year and there have been continuing cost efficiencies.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: Across the other businesses segment as a whole, there was profit growth of 16.6% to £77.2 million. This was  despite falls in operating profit for Telecoms and for Contracting, Utility Solutions and Metering, which face tough  trading conditions. Growth was driven by the first contribution over a half-year from gas production of £17.3  million, and the increase in operating profit in gas storage partly due to the new capacity coming through at  Aldbrough. Our investments at Aldbrough and in transmission upgrades are now starting to deliver revenue.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: I also said earlier that the increase in output from renewable energy was due in part to new operational capacity,  with more new assets from our investment program coming on stream. Delivering returns from investment has, of  course, become our key means of securing dividend growth over the long term, and you can see the progress of our  major wind farm projects on this slide.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: Investment and capital spend totaled £796.9 million during the six months. You can see the detail in the  statement, but I draw out three points: first, major progress has been made at a number of key projects such as the  wind farms at Clyde and Griffin. All of the large wind farms you can see in this slide other than Gordonbush have  now started to earn revenue. And we expect first-generation at Gordonbush to start shortly, with more to come as  all the projects near completion.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: The latest indicative split of the spend is set out on the slide. It is made up of economically-regulated electricity  distribution investment plus essential maintenance of other assets. Economically-regulated spend on  transmission upgrades and spend that is either committed or could be committed to development of new assets  like wind farms or CCTTs to support dividend growth.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: Across SSE, we've got a lot of opportunities to choose from. There's transmission, CCTT, solid fuel, pump storage,  and wind farms. The breadth of these opportunities will allow us to reject projects with questionable returns and  choose projects with good returns from investment, quite simply, good returns mean growing dividends.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: The management reasons are fundamental. Clear dividend targets provide a simplicity and transparency and  make management genuinely accountable. The focus on dividend drives a disciplined, consistent, and long-term  approach to operations and investment. The value of our long-term approach has never been greater. Our goal is  to offer shareholders a degree of certainty in what is a fast-changing energy sector. From Prime Minister's  questions to Question Time on the BBC to questions from friends in the pub, the whole of my sector is having  criticism piled on it. And alongside the colorful language, we've got yet more legislation and regulation. We have  RIIO, electricity market reform and retail market review in Britain and market harmonization in Ireland.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: Our energy networks are a case in point. Within the SSC model, they matter for three key reasons. First, they give  us a financial backbone and operational focus. Second, they are central to our commitment to sustained real  annual dividend growth. And third, they provide us with significant investment opportunities. Their combined  regulatory asset value has now reached £5.5 billion, £400 million higher than a year ago, and the opportunities to  build on this are significant. I'd first roll out three points on distribution.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: First, 18 months experience of the new price control in electricity distribution shows we have the capability and  efficiency to deliver a post-tax real return in excess of 5% between now and 2015. Indeed the latest indications  show we're still at the efficiency front here.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: Second, we're making significant progress on smart grids. Ofgem has announced a funding package for our  Shetland project with 85% spend going on the RAV. The project features heat and electricity storage to manage  intelligently the demands for electricity generation in Shetland. And that will allow more renewable and energy  capacity to be connected. It also features new active network management solutions.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: The main project currently is of course our part of the Beauty-Denny upgrade, for which Ofgem has now a funding  of £539 million in 2009/2010 prices. Work on removing and replacing the old pylons have started and the whole  project should be finished around 2014.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: In addition to Beauty-Denny, we're also building phase 1 of the transmission upgrades in the North of Scotland.  The £200 million group of projects included the Knocknaegael substation. Work on the Beauty-Mossford upgrade  is also underway. These projects are on-time and on-budget, with the first one due to complete early in the New  Year.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: The planning issues that have been tackled means that the Beauly-Denny upgrade has been nine years in coming.  Interesting you compare that to energy supply, where nine hours can feel like a long time. So I'm going to get  Alistair to give you some perspectives on that.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Executive Director & Director-Energy Supply, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: Thank you Ian, good morning, everybody. Shortly after our results in May, Ofgem said that in a period of rising  prices, suppliers have to transform the way they deal with customers. Ofgem was right and we believe we've  responded faster and with more commitment than any other company in the sector. Five important decisions  illustrate the point. In July, we became the first leading supplier to drop commission-based doorstep sales in GB.  We've frozen our retail prices until August next year at the earliest. We've helped to transform volumes the day- ahead electricity market with our initiative to improve transparency and price discovery. We've removed  online/offline price differentials and called for an end to predatory pricing by other suppliers. And we've set out  initial plans to tackle tariff complexity, improve cost transparency and promote a better relationship with  customer all around.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Executive Director & Director-Energy Supply, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: We've set out 10 different proposals to build trust and we're working to implement them all before the end of next  year. We believe the net result will be reduced political and regulatory risk, a new and distinctive proposition in  the energy supply sector and most importantly of all a fair deal for customers that is sustainable over the long  term.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Executive Director & Director-Energy Supply, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: From that position, we need to move forward. That means going from the retailing of electricity and gas and the  legacy of complexity, to providing a wider but much simpler range of smarter products and services. This will get  extra impetus with a roll out of smart meters and the launch of the Green Deal.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Executive Director & Director-Energy Supply, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: The smart meter rollout is a job we have to do well. But fundamentally, it's part of doing business not a profit  driver. Green Deal is different. We have specific obligations as a collection agent, but it does provide business  opportunities as well and we're looking at these very closely. Throughout, we're taking a disciplined and pragmatic  approach.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Executive Director & Director-Energy Supply, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: SSE is first and foremost a customer-facing business. David Franklin's job is to source energies so we can supply  customers, our investment in renewables is a hedge against volatility in fossil fuel markets and is an increasingly  important source of energy.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Executive Director & Director-Energy Supply, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: Indeed in the first half of the year, output from our Hydro schemes and wind farms gave us the equivalent of £95  million therms of gas. To provide more diverse sources of energy, we bought North Sea Assets from Hess. This  was a good, disciplined deal, and the assets have performed well in this six-month period with good output and  profitability.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Executive Director & Director-Energy Supply, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: Through this and the 5% stakes secured in Faroe Petroleum, we've fulfilled a longstanding SSE ambition to enter  the upstream gas sector. We've done it in a measured way which has given us a new source of primary fuel and a  hedge for our gas generation supply activities.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Executive Director & Director-Energy Supply, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: We hope to build our presence in the sector over time with a focus being on mature, producing, gas-weighted  assets with no operating role. Our approach to potential assets will be consistent with our financial principles and  that will be pursued only where fair value can be secured.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Executive Director & Director-Energy Supply, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: We've also added to our long-term gas supply through the 10-year contract with Statoil for the annual supply of  500 million cubic meters of gas. Fuel supply contracts play a key part in helping us to meet our customer needs  and they contribute to the long-term stability of our energy portfolio.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Executive Director & Director-Energy Supply, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: Stability is something the politicians believe that greater gas storage capacity can give the UK and they're right.  Our investments in the facility at Aldbrough is nearing completion. Our option to extend it is probably the best in  the country. But in the absence of adequate returns, we see no prospect of investing in it in the foreseeable future.  Our overall fuel position is however evolving in a careful SSE-type way. And I'm optimistic that other  opportunities will emerge and allow us to continue to add to our mix of natural gas assets and contracts.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: Thanks, Alistair. Our plans to build trust in energy supply reflect the fact that in this decade and beyond, energy  needs to be about three things. The customer, as Alistair has talked about, plus capacity in carbon. And it's  capacity in carbon that the Electricity Market Reform is focused on. And it's still work-in-progress. There are two  key questions for SSE. Will policy changes have any negative impact on investment decisions already made? And  secondly, what will the impact of policy changes on investment decisions be that have yet to be taken?

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: On the first point, committed investments, we are comfortable with the political and policy commitment to  protecting value. That was illustrated yet again by the recent ROC banding review. If implemented, it will not have  any impact on our assets under construction. Longer term, we believe the combination of ROCs and the carbon  price support make – it represents a fair package of support for on and offshore wind.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: The good news is that construction work continues to make solid progress. A total of 122 turbines have now been  installed and 83 of these have exported electricity. This means that all 140 turbines should have been installed as  planned before the end of next year. The bad news is that our investigations into the turbine foundations suggest  that around one-third of them don't meet the standard required by the contract signed by the principal contractor,  Fluor. The onus is currently on Fluor to determine how it plans to meet its contractual obligations with regard to  these foundations. We hope it will do this in a satisfactory way but if necessary a very substantial claim will be  issued against Fluor.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: In the meantime, the construction focus is – and it is on installing the remainder of the turbines. Despite the  difficulties with some of the foundations, Greater Gabbard should be generating significant amounts of power this  winter and beyond.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: There's good news and bad news at Glendoe, too. The good news is that the repair work scheme is currently going  well. The bad news is that that work is extensive and we've decided that around half of the entire tunnel should be  lined. Taking those two factors together, we're confident that electricity generation is on-course to resume towards  the end of the first half of 2012.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: The second bit of good news on Glendoe is that we have significant insurance and legal options available to us to  make sure there's an appropriate settlement by the contractor of the costs incurred in respect to tunnel repair. The  bad news however, it is likely to take some time to resolve.  Our next spend on Glendoe will represent less than less than 3% of the total CapEx program over the period since  the original construction program started. The strategic nature of the asset is -- has value that will be realized as  the UK generation portfolio changes. That change is underway, which is why we've made it such a priority to get  Glendoe back into service as quick as possible.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: If you take £100 million as the threshold, we have four major wind farm projects in construction at the moment in  addition to Gabbard. Here the news is all good. We're seeing a growing momentum as the portfolio takes major  steps forward. The 130-megawatt South section at Clyde was finished earlier than expected and the rest of that  project is on course to be finished next year.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: Turbine installation at Griffin is nearly finished and the whole farm should be operating earlier than planned by  Christmas. Turbine installation at Gordonbush is now well underway and first electricity generation should take  place very shortly. Phase 1 of Walney has operated successfully since the summer and we've just had first  electricity from Phase 2, which should be fully commissioned in the first half of next year. In addition to these  specific projects, we've got a number of smaller onshore wind sites under construction in Scotland and England,  together with the project at Keadby we bought in May. Work on these is on time and on budget.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: On time and on budget are not phrases normally associated with the nuclear industry which partly explains our  decision to pull out of the NuGen consortium. We could have spent many millions of pounds and a lot of  management resource to keep the option open but we preferred to make a clean break.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: So our ambitions now are as a non-nuclear generator and our investment plans go well beyond on and offshore  wind. We've got extensive options for new CCGT at sites around the country starting with Abernedd. Solid fuel is  important too and we have an opportunity to build a significant business in multi fuel, working with our new  partner, Wheelabrator and starting at Ferrybridge. The detail on that project is in the statement.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: We also have Europe's biggest post combustion carbon capture trial at Ferrybridge and it should begin operating  later this year. And we're considering building on this experience at Peterhead. Our ambition at Peterhead is to  build a full chain post combustion CCS scheme on the back of one of the gas turbines. It is however dependent on  securing enough of the available government funding be it in UK or European level to make it possible to proceed  with the project. Making progress in securing that funding is what lies behind the joint development agreement  with shale that's been announced today.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: CCS is a complex area, but for more than six years, we have felt that the UK's best location for our first CCS  scheme is Peterhead. And then applying CCS to a gas plant is vital for the long-term of the UK. We still believe  both those factors still to be true.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: For the avoidance of doubt however, let me be clear about one thing; for SSE, CCS has to be an economic energy  project, not a value-destroying vanity project. As such, it has to be consistent with our six generation principles;  compliance, capacity, diversity, availability, flexibility and sustainability. Through these principles and the  experience and knowledge Paul Smith's team has build over the years, of managing our generation assets, we're  able to make the right decision about operations and investment in generation.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: In networks, we've decided that transmission is a core asset and its RAV will growth dramatically. In supply, we've  decided to change the way we retain and gain customers and show leadership in building trust. And in generation,  we've decided to be non-nuclear focusing on technologies and fuels where we have skills and experience.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: SSE's core purpose is to provide the energy people need in a reliable and sustainable way. Providing energy is a  long-term activity. SSE is a company that aims to do the right thing and make decisions for the long term. It's not  always straightforward. You have to anticipate change, influence change, respond to change.

texts.speaker: Martin S. Brough
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Prime Brokerage)
texts.text: And if you're looking at gas, existing gas fields as further potential for acquisitions, obviously they'd be very  significantly earnings enhancing in the short term and produce a lot of cash near term. Would you see those as a  complement for the sort of backend-loaded cash flows of the growing networks? And if you do go through further  gas acquisitions, how do you kind of value the back-end, of decommissioning liabilities associated with them?

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: Well I think on finance ability for the networks, it's key that we will have an appropriate settlement that covers the  finance ability issues particularly for our Transmission business where we have a significant growth in  expenditure compared to our underlying RAV and cash flows will be key to that. And that's part of our discussion  with Ofgem. And you've no doubt have seen our submission to Ofgem in terms of transmission. I think, we can't  link the gas production and say that cross subsidizes the cash flows from the regulatory business. That is just not

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: And on the decommissioning point, we factor that into the net present values as you would expect based upon the  best available evidence. But the minute you own the asset you then work with the operator to try and delay, defer  that decommissioning liability and that is one of the sources of value creation. But we don't factor that  opportunity into our assessment. It is one of the many upsides that you potentially can get when you're actually in  the projects.

texts.speaker: Mark A. Freshney
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Hi, it's Mark Freshney from Credit Suisse. Just a question on the guidance for the current financial year, I mean,  you've already given an indication that retail supply margins will be flat year-on-year last month. You've got a lot  more renewable output, which is extremely cash flow generative. So why is the guidance only for moderate PBT  growth? What else is going on within the asset mix to offset that?

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: Yeah, but do you want me to give you every number? I mean, it's interesting that you complain we don't give you  guidance, and then when we give you guidance, you want us to give you guidance on every individual line item in  the P&L account. We've given guidance, we've said that broadly, we would expect profits in energy supply to be up  around the same level as last year. At that point, we were making a very clear statement that the Ofgem number  was way off beam, and we set a far more reliable guide to profitably supply as what we earned last year than the  Ofgem number. It was – will make it a different point. That was not earnings guidance, it was, get the debate in  the right territory.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: The reality is that there are a whole raft of different issues going on and we've encapsulate that into the word  moderate, and for those – the next question you're going to ask is what does moderate mean, well actually, the  English language doesn't change as often as energy policy does. We used moderate I think three years ago, I think  it was three years ago. And at that point, we though moderate meant 2% to 5% growth, and we delivered 2.9%. I

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: Two questions. The first one is concerning the structures at price Gabbard, and I just wanted to understand the 52
texts.text: structures where you found defects. Does that mean that they cannot be operational and they have to be fixed or  are you just feeling that they're not quite up to the standard that's required and you could retroactively change  them as such? And the second thing is on predatory pricing and supply? I'm sort of interested in the comment  around that and I wondered if you could perhaps give us a bit more color? I mean, obviously EDF have talked  about potentially using profits from nuclear to cross-subsidize on energy supply. Would that be an example of  something that you're thinking of?

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: Okay. Two quite different issues Greater Gabbard. First thing I need to explain is the foundations come in two  parts. There's a monopile which, a great big 600-ton bit of metal that sticks in the sea, and then there's a  transition piece which is like a cap on top of that monopile, and then you put the turbine up. There are pumps in  the wells on 52 of the transition pieces, and I think it's around 35 of the monopiles because some of the monopiles  were fixed. Those they can operate, to answer your first question, I think all of them have operated during the  commissioning phase, some are operational today, some are not. The issue is life. And the issues are different  between the monopiles and the transition pieces because of the where the stresses lie.

texts.speaker: Lakis Athanasiou
texts.profession: Analyst, Evolution Securities Ltd.
texts.text: I'm Lakis Athanasiou, Evolution Securities. Three questions, first on nuclear, interesting your pullout, can you say  to what extent your decision was made without the government was going to go on a fixed-priced rather than the  P-fit? Secondly on rocks and grandfathering, to my mind grandfathering works because they're moral hazard. If  government pulls out in the future, you stop investing. But let's say we come to 2018, we've got a new  contractually-based system, new government comes in, slashes rock, existing rocks, and says well it won't affect  your investment because that's contractually; we can't do anything about contracts, therefore new investment will  continue. So can you comment on that? I mean, you seem to have seen comfortably what government's doing on  EMR re grandfathering. I can't quite see it myself. And last question on CapEx, that £1.7 billion and you gave a  split different way, that presumably includes [indiscernible] (52:35), if we take in rubbish that goes in to CapEx as  well about £100 million something like that?

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: If I could take the nuclear question, what was behind our decision to pull out? Firstly deal with the timing, why  did we do it? There was a budget approval process in the JV for next year, and when you approve a budget you're  on the hook for that budget for years, and that was in September. So that was the catalyst as to why we made the  decision when we made it in September. So then, why, there were three reasons, and the essential question was  one of three reasons. When we look at the EMR process in the fixed price, we are saying, we are not -- firstly, as an  energy supplier, we do not need to be in nuclear because the government takes the price risk. And secondly, as a  nuclear generator, we weren't convinced that it was in your interests as a developed to sign a fixed-price contract,  given that the chances of cost overrun, and the chance of delay, as we're seeing in today's FT, yet another delay at a  finished project, in another year, 2014, now, so I think that's five years late.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: The second one was we looked at what are SSE's competencies and capabilities, and we said to become an  intelligent client in nuclear, to rank alongside what we know and understand, say, in gas and solid fuel renewable  would have cost us quite a lot of money, on top of the development of the project, we would have to have built a  team, and spend quite a lot of money, and nothing in nuclear comes cheap, we would be competing for resources,  and actually, as a team, Paul, there as well, we didn't have the appetite to do that.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: But our job is to assess that risk and our view is the risk of a sort of change in the future applied retrospectively is  very, very low. The UK does not have a history of retrospective change. And not just in energy but – we typically –  the, just a sense in the – we talk a lot about things in the UK about risk and change and political uncertainty. We  actually don't – knee jerk and change as much as other countries and talk less about it. And we wake up one  morning and find all the German nuclear plant being closed early.

texts.speaker: Verity Mitchell
texts.profession: Analyst, HSBC Bank Plc (Broker)
texts.text: Verity Mitchell, HSBC. I just got a follow on for your on-time in budget. I seems to be that gas, seems to be  emphasized a bit more, gas power. Are you pushing very hard for that to be a greater part of the mix, a more  affordable part of the mix and saying, well, we are ready with our consented power stations if you give us this  support?

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: I wouldn't say push. I mean it's a realization of the SSE team probably over the last three years that gas is going to  be a bigger part – is and can afford to be a bigger part of the mix in the UK energy over the next 10, 15 years than  we have previously thought. And it is principally the shale gas sort of revolution in North America. Time will tell  how much it changes the gas markets outside of North American.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: But whenever you go to Houston Calgary you can see the impact that the shale gas and unconventional gas has.  And as there is that sense that actually you can afford gas to be in the mix for longer. So – and therefore, you are  absolutely right. There is a greater emphasis on gas in our CapEx programs. And how we talked about our CapEx  programs, and then are we pushing what we're pushing the government to say? You've got to think about capacity  as well as carbon in your design of EMR, and if you just think about carbon, then who will actually build the fossil  plants that the UK will need for our generation, if you like. And one of the problems we said that the government  is you're trying to solve the problem in 2050, but if you don't get 2030 right, but if the lights do end up going out  between 2020 and 2030 because you've tried to solve the problem for 2050 too aggressively and too early? You  will never achieve 2050. So in a sense, we're not pushing gas, we are pushing capacity. We happen to believe that

texts.speaker: A
texts.profession: The emergent issues that is very simply asset life-related. We were doing planned outages. We opened up the
texts.text: time to fix. And that required us to do more workarounds than we've anticipated. So that obviously lost us  availability and that's what that refers to in terms of emergent at Ferrybridge, and at Fiddlers Ferry, there's an  industry issue with what LD 66 blades on LP turbines and again its an asset life-related issue due to the number of  starts, and again, we've done more engineering work there, changed out some blades and some of the other 100- megawatt stations have also – units have got to do that, so more engineering work.

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: Hi, good morning. [ph] Gary Menshoff (01:03:06) from Liberum Capital. Just a quick question on biomass to
texts.text: Fiddler's Ferry and Usmuth. You mentioned this morning the options for those coal plants finding rock banding,  would you be able to elaborate on what conditions you think you need to see to move towards enhanced coal-firing  or conversion, and also, where that would leave your JV with Fourth Energy?

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: Okay. Two – just on the enhanced co-firing, obviously, it's a new band. That gives us an opportunity principally at  Fiddler's Ferry to effectively invest a relatively small amount of capital. We don't yet know what that is, but tens of  millions, not hundreds of millions sort of number, to effectively get Fiddler's Ferry to in the enhanced coal-firing  band. We think that that is feasible. It's not yet a project that we've put in our plans, but we've got a project team  already set up on that. And ask now if we have a plan to do a full station conversion, it looks like that is not  economic at one rock for a full conversion. So we are looking at whether there is an enhanced co-firing  opportunity around Usmuth. That's going to take a little bit longer to get our minds around as is Ferrybridge.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: So, effectively, what the conditions – the question about our conditions was we've taken the rock banding as what  we expect to happen, all though its technically concentration, we're not expecting to see change in that biomass  and we're saying, what's the engineering cost of meeting those, can we make money? So for that's that, on the  Fourth Energy, we need to look what's going on in Scotland where there are tweaks to the rock banding in terms of  more heat-led and potential capacity – what we've agreed with Fourth ports, is that we will sit down and review all  four of those projects to see which ones we think are worth continuing with, which ones maybe either dropped or  need to be redesigned to be heat-led.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: So we have opportunity we weren't expecting at Fiddlers. We have a changed opportunity at  Alfsralph and we  have a changed opportunity at Fourth. Net, net, we feel quite comfortable with whether biomass shifting around,  probably a bit more opportunity to invest in earnings than we have pre the rock banding.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: The biggest single issue is the weather. And if you get weather patterns like last week, you get low gas demands,  which means that Alistair's retail business struggles. Lower volumes and potentially bought gas and low gas  prices. Paul's generation business, I mean, last week Hydro output was double budget. It rate, typically when it's  mild it's wet and windy in Scotland. Paul's benefit is not enough to offset Alistair's problem. So typically, milder  weather is the bigger challenge facing, I think, all energy companies in this coming winter.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Scottish & Southern Energy Plc
texts.text: And today, October and first half of November have been very mild. But I think the forecast for next week is  colder. And December is seasonal, normal, whatever. So that's probably the biggest single challenge, the weather.  If it is – the worst conditions are mild, dry and still, we don't typically in the UK see them. Cold, still and dry is ok.  Mild, wet and windy is a little bit of a problem. Hence, a range.

texts.speaker: Shai L. Hill
texts.profession: Analyst, Macquarie Capital (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Hi there. Shai Hill from Macquarie. It is a bit of a general question actually and it's just maybe asking you to look  forward, let's say, to the start of 2013. To what UK gas and electricity supply might look like? Obviously, it's  become in the last three months alone the conservative, labor parties, even Ofgem seem to have decided that  obviously margins and profits are too high and I realize that you dispute that. But I'm just asking you to look  forward to 2013 and what might it look like. For example, if you're selling all your output on the wholesale market,  isn't that going to force you to split generation and supply in terms of profitability because the wholesale revenues  and the cost of the supply business will have to be reported in the accounts separately for example. And through  that that will make the margin on supply very apparent. Ofgem for example Ian, seems from the statement you  referred to say that £125 a household or a high single digit margin is evil.

texts.speaker: Shai L. Hill
texts.profession: Analyst, Macquarie Capital (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Are you going to see some kind of regulatory frame work to keep supply margins down in the mid to low single  just finally, just – are you going to see more price competition? Are you going to see people, as you alluded to  earlier? People like EDF you think they have cheaper generation power sources using that basically to try and win  share with cheaper supply prices?
