texts.speaker: Richard D. Gillingwater
texts.profession: Chairman
texts.text: From this work, two key things are clear. First, there is a significant value in operating and investing in a balanced  range of energy assets and businesses. And second, within those businesses, we have a wide range of opportunities  to develop new assets on the one hand and new customer propositions on the other. This means that we're  confident that the foundations for continuing dividend growth are well laid.

texts.speaker: Richard D. Gillingwater
texts.profession: Chairman
texts.text: We believe that policymaking should take a long-term view, should be clear and transparent, should respect  committed investments and have effective transitional arrangements where that is deemed necessary. We believe  strongly in a constructive engagement with policymakers and regulators. And that's the approach we'll maintain  as we work to achieve a long-term framework for the energy sector that benefits both investors and customers  alike.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: In the first half of this year, there has been high output of renewable energy benefiting Wholesale and relatively  good performance in Energy Supply. This is in marked contrast to the position a year ago when operating profit in  Wholesale was exceptionally low and Energy Supply reported an operating loss. As we said in September, this  means slightly that we've earned over one-third of our full year adjusted PBT in the first six months compared  with around a quarter last year.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: We've always focused on full year results and we manage our business, including the energy portfolio and phasing  of costs, accordingly. In addition, we're continuing to manage a wide range of issues across our Retail and  Wholesale activities, including the continuing negative trend in commodity prices and the generally challenging  outlook for market conditions.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: Looking now at our three business segments. In Wholesale, operating profit has recovered to £159.6 million on  the back of a 38% increase in the output of renewable energy, reflecting wetter and windier conditions in Scotland  and Ireland during the spring and summer months. The relatively dry and still weather in October, however, saw a  fall in renewable output of around 50% compared with the year ago.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: And in Retail, the operating profit of £101.5 million reflects a return to profitability in Energy Supply compared  with a year ago. It follows a strong focus on operating cost and a better performance in the I&C sector. As I said  earlier, we manage business across the financial year as a whole. We still expect to report a decline in profit in  household Energy Supply at the year-end.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: Last month, S&P affirmed our A-/A-2 rating, albeit, with a revised negative outlook, reflecting its opinion of the  impact of energy and commodity prices on the sector. As usual, we'll continue to engage actively with both  agencies and remain committed to maintaining a strong balance sheet and remain focused on the current criteria  for a single-A credit rating. We're confident we'll be able to mitigate the recent action by S&P on the treatment of  some of our hybrid securities, which will allow us to reinstate the 50% equity content.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: When it comes to investment decisions on new assets, we'll continue to recycle capital from disposals to stay in  line with the targeted net spend for the period of 2018. In line with our established value programme, we currently  expect to secure financial benefits in excess of £1 billion from the disposal of non-core assets and businesses and  from the sale of onshore wind farms on-developments.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: We've already sold and reached agreement to sell assets with a total value of just over £600 million. And the main  disposal programme on wind is now underway. This will enable us to recycle capital from current assets where  greater overhead value can be secured from investing in new ones, especially in the context of the renewables  obligation. As I said earlier, we have a strong and diverse asset base. That's where we wanted to stay and that  means retaining the ability to optimize what we build, what we own, and what we operate.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: Investment in Distribution was £113 million which helps keep the lights on for customers. And that's our first  priority. We have, for example, what we believe is the only machine in the UK which allows tree felling to take  place without the need to switch off power lines, reducing both costs and the inconvenience experienced by our  customers.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: This example of innovation in our Electricity Distribution illustrates a wider point. The business is adapting to the  changing needs of customers and changes in the way in which electricity is produced. That will be a key theme for  us for the duration of the new price control. The price control that came in effect in April will, amongst other  things, deliver an underlying reduction of over 15% in the distribution part of the average household bill in our  Southern and Scottish areas.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: Transmission's price control is now over two years old. This business is continuing to grow in a strong and  sustainable way and its RAV is now over £2 billion. This investment in the asset base is driving the sustained  growth in profitability, illustrated by the 44% increase in operating profit we've reported this morning.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: Work is also well underway on the Caithness-Moray link, following Ofgem's approval of capital funding last  December. We invested £163 million in the project in the six months to September. Construction is progressing at  seven major substations and converted stations and has reached an important milestone last month with the start  of the installation of the HVDC land cable.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: As the RO example illustrates, policy and regulation loom large over our Wholesale businesses. Their role is to  provide energy and related services for energy market participants in GB and Ireland. And they continue to be  affected by macroeconomics, commodity prices, and the impact of decarbonization on how energy is produced  and used.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: In this environment, results for any six-month period need to be treated with caution. In the first six months last  year, our Wholesale businesses contributed an exceptionally low amount of £26.7 million to operating profit. This  has recovered to £159.6 million this year with the main factor being the 38% increase in the amount of renewable  energy generated.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: In terms of gas production at £14.1 million, first half operating profit slightly higher than year ago, although, the  outlook for the second half is more challenging. The economic environment for gas storage facilities has, however,  been persistently difficult, although, there has been some recovery in operating profit to £3.7 million through cost  savings.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Between them, the UK government, the National Grid and Ofgem have responsibility for security of supply, a  point affirmed by the Energy Act 2013. Last week's NISM demonstrated again that they have a range of tools and  options in place to keep the system running. The role of a company such as SSE is to ensure the generation plant is  available to generate in response to contractual obligations and at times when electricity demand is highest.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: In Peterhead, Medway and Keadby, we have three flexible gas-fired power stations which can contribute  significantly to the stability of the electricity system. Peterhead secured a one-year contract from National Grid to  provide electricity reserve capacity totaling 750 megawatts under the 2015/2016 SBR. Medway has continued to  perform well in response to market requirements with a good level of availability to generate. And we've recently  broke Keadby after deep mothballed and secured transmission energy capacity. And so it should be in full  commercial operation before the end of the year.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: These three stations have benefited from significant investment to boost their reliability and flexibility. They  should play an important part in the country's energy system in the next few years. In doing so, they'll have the  opportunity to take part in the capacity market. So, while we're optimistic about the prospects for existing gas- fired power stations, the economics in new plants are different all together.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Our commitment to financial discipline means we have no plans to develop or build any new gas-fired plant in the  foreseeable future. In Ireland, however, our new CCGT at Great Island has completed six months of full  commercial operation. This has confirmed its position as the cleanest, most efficient and reliable gas power plant  on the Irish grid and a natural complement to our portfolio of renewables.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: The future of coal-fired power stations, which are increasingly expensive to maintain and subject to major  environmental legislation and regulation, is clearly time-limited. As we said in May, it costs over £50 million a  year simply to keep a large coal-fired power station open. Environmentally, they're major emitters of CO2. Coal- fired generation at Ferrybridge will, as you know, end in March.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: In terms of Fiddler's Ferry, the majority of the plant there has a capacity contract for a year from October 2018.  It's our intention to submit the plants into the forthcoming auction for providing capacity from 2019. We'll  reassess the options for the future operation of the station after the outcome of that auction is known. Including  Fiddler's, we successfully prequalified 6.1 gigawatts of de-rated capacity to take part in the auction.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: In the meantime, in the coming months, we'll seek to operate as well as possible capacity at both Fiddler's Ferry  and Ferrybridge. And we'll also aim to use stations coal in the most efficient manner as well. The gradual end of  coal-fired generation is being accompanied by major changes in the way power is generated. At SSE, we're playing  our part in three key ways.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: First, we demonstrated through our joint venture our ability to develop and commission multi-fuel plant. The new  £300 million 69 megawatt plant at Ferrybridge uses a range of fuel sources derived from Yorkshire and the wider  area and is a sustainable energy solution in every sense of the word. I'm pleased we've secured consent to develop  a second plant of up to 90 megawatts, also at Ferrybridge, and expect the final investment decision to be taken in  2016.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Second, we're working with Shell in the development of the world's first full-scale gas carbon capture and storage  project and are close to completing the feed stage that started early in 2014. There will have to be a satisfactory  outcome for the government's CCS Commercialization Competition funding process. But we believe this is a  project with a strong environmental case that is worthy of the right level of economic support to ensure the  opportunity it represents can be realized.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: The third feature of the progressive change in generation is renewables. SSE has developed a quality portfolio of  renewable energy assets across the UK and Ireland with hydro, onshore wind and offshore wind and with assets in  Scotland, England and Ireland. Since April 2010, we've invested £2.8 billion in renewables and completed around  800 megawatts of new onshore wind and 350 megawatts of offshore wind. In addition, Glendoe has been fully  operational since 2012 taking our conventional hydro capacity to 1,150 megawatts.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Looking ahead, we have almost 600 megawatts of onshore wind farm capacity under construction at six sites in  Scotland and Ireland. Subject to the outcome of the judicial review, we also hope to be able to complete  Stronelairg as a result of the proposed growth periods. This means we're on course to add significant additional  capacity in Scotland and Ireland before the RO comes to an end.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Looking offshore, the Beatrice project, in which we currently have a 50% stake, already has an early CfD. And  we're continuing to do the engineering, environment and procurement work that's needed to maintain progress  towards a final investment decision in 2016. The phasing out of ROCs for new projects and the introduction of  competition for support through CfDs will change the way projects are developed and constructed.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: There are, however, three things that we need to take account of in considering the place of renewables in our  generation portfolio and in our investment plans overall: the cumulative impact of changes in the way electricity is  being produced and the potential for market harmonization and interconnection; our disciplined approach to  capital investment and in particular our planned net spend of £5.5 billion for the full years to 2018; and our  commitment to maintaining a balanced portfolio of businesses and assets within Wholesale and between  Wholesale and other main businesses.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: For these reasons, we're selling existing onshore wind farms in-developments in order to recycle capital. We've  already sold wind farm assets and projects for a total consideration of over £100 million. As part of our disposal  programme, we've invited bids for further assets and are planning to recycle capital where we believe greater value  can be secured from investing in new assets across the business. This should help to take the total financial benefit  from our overall value programme to in excess of £1 billion.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: We've been involved with gas production since 2010. And in line with our focus on maintaining a balanced range  of energy businesses, the acquisition we completed in October was part of a well-established strategy. It also  completes SSE's portfolio of gas production assets for the foreseeable future. Production from the newly acquired  assets is expected to continue until the early 2030s making them a long-term investment and include the Shetland  Gas Plant critical pieces, state-of-the-art industry infrastructure.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Amongst other things, investment in gas production assets help secure energy for customers and customers are  rightly at the heart of the energy related debates currently taking place in the UK and Ireland. Over the last couple  of years, we've seen particularly competitive market conditions. And our customer count numbers have fallen in  the first six months of the financial year to 8.41 million. We have, however, maintained a strong focus on  operational and financial efficiencies.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: This, combined with better performance in the I&C sector, helped Energy Supply to return to profitability in the  first six months, having sustained an operating loss in the same period last year. Nevertheless, we manage our cost  base and our NG portfolio across the full financial year and continue to expect domestic Energy Supply operating  profit to fall over the financial year as a whole.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: To develop our Energy Supply business further, we've launched an industry-leading offer on broadband in line  with our commitment to offer customers more Home Services, actively apply the principles of treating customers  fairly with clear industry leadership in complaints management, taking a series of other substantive steps to  improve customer service, invested in delivering new systems to help customers such as our Home Services  business, invested in a fundamental overhaul of digital channels for our customers, and added to the positive  profile of our brand through sponsorships of arenas at the Hydro, Wembley and Belfast and the SSE Women's FA  Cup.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: The investment in digital communications, along with the smart meter rollout, has required considerable  investment across the six months. We spent around £70 million on Energy Supply and related services in what  amounts to a significant modernization of the business. We believe this plan will put us in a strong position to  retain and gain customers as the shape of the retail energy market becomes clearer over the coming year and as  the rollout of smart meters begins to make an impact.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Clearly, the shape of the market is going to be influenced by the conclusions of the CMA. While it means that the  degree of uncertainty about the final shape of the Energy Supply market remains, the decision of the CMA to  extend this investigation is, as I said earlier, prudent because it implies appropriate degree of caution about any  recommendations.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Retail includes the B2B Enterprise business which contributed £16.5 million in operating profit in the first six  months of the year. The business is just over 18 months old. But as customers' energy management and  infrastructure requirements evolve, we believe we've created a business that has a potential to achieve significant  and sustainable growth. To do this, we will have to integrate products and services further, keep pace with changes  in energy production and consumption, and achieve excellence in customer relationship management.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: In the last six months, we've delivered solid results on EPS and PBT and, most importantly, delivered our  dividend growth target. We've also made significant progress in terms of our key priorities in the first half of the  financial year. In Wholesale, we've completed the multi-fuel plant at Ferrybridge, developed enhanced roles for  Peterhead and Keadby power stations, acquired new gas production and infrastructure assets and began the  disposal of onshore wind farm assets.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: We'll retain that constructive approach as the CMA completes its investigation and as the government takes  forward its energy policy programme. And in a changing and challenging sector, we'll take the operational,  financial, and investment decisions necessary to ensure SSE is well placed to deliver for investors and customers  alike over the long-term.

texts.speaker: Dominic C. Nash
texts.profession: Macquarie Capital (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Hi. Yeah. It's Dominic Nash, Macquarie. Sort of three-ish leading questions all from coal, if that's okay, please.  Obviously, the dark spreads are pretty subdued at the moment and there's no short-term money being made.  Could you just give us some color on what your cash cost or your cash profitability in the coal-fired power stations  going forward are?

texts.speaker: Dominic C. Nash
texts.profession: Macquarie Capital (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Yeah. You got me now. And the leading question from there is obviously your shutting. What are you doing about  your coal inventory management and will you be running for cash and sort of why – or losses but just winding  down an inventory to give some cash generation? And, finally, leading on to capacity, if they're cash flow negative  and you've got to hold it open for four years in order to get to enjoy the capacity payment, is it possible – would  you consider transferring the capacity to your prequalified CCGTs and shutting your coal early?

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: So I'll do the sectors and, Gregor, you can do the first one. So inventory management, yes, you would imagine that  on something like Ferrybridge where we're intending to close the plant and really, really drive capacity probably to  a reasonably high pile of coal that's out there, which is driven by tax reasons around the carbon price flow  basically. We're probably going to see us and other people in the country running coal plant pretty hard over the  winter to reduce – to have written-down coal price to essentially to try and burn as much of it there. So you don't  have to dig it out. So I think that is the reality for us in the other two large stations that are closing.

texts.speaker: Dominic C. Nash
texts.profession: Macquarie Capital (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: It is possible to transfer out of coal and into one of your island in Keadby?

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Right. Okay. Right. So, I'd say, that I haven't looked at in detail. So, in theory, you've got an obligation to provide  capacity at a particular time but whether you allow to transfer the obligation or there's an actual mechanism  existing within the legislation and/or the rules to do it, I'm not sure. So, we would have to go around that. I think  there's probably a bit of work to be done on understanding how that works. In theory, I think you can. But when  you go through the detailed legislation, I don't think there's actually a mechanism in place for doing it. So,  therefore, that will perhaps have to be sorted out if anybody decides to do that. And then – sorry. Coal profits.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: I mean, basically, for starters, you'd expect with 0.6 terawatt hours as our output, we'd be making losses, low tens  of millions. And, going forward, for the rest of the year, we expect to make a small loss in the coal plant. And then  for the following year, with the carbon tax coming through, et cetera, and where Wholesale prices are, you'd  expect cash losses to be well into the tens of millions.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Martin and then a couple others. Martin Brough.  Martin S. Brough  Deutsche Bank AG (Broker UK)  Q  Hi. Thanks. Martin Brough from Deutsche. A couple of related questions really. One is on the wind disposal  process, obviously, since you announced the disposals, power prices have come down about 20% in forward curve.  The LEC benefits have been removed. Do you think that's going to have an impact on the value that you can  extract from those? And is there a scenario where the bids come in and you say, look, this isn't really good value  for us at the moment given – if there's an element of cyclicality in quantity prices, maybe it doesn't make sense.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: And then the second the question to that. You mentioned in your release the review – the government is looking at  how the carbon price flow works in the 2020s. And given the sheer amount of interconnection that may be coming  on the system, it's a little bit hard, I guess, to sustain very high UK carbon prices where Continental European  carbon prices aren't really at those levels. So, do you worry, again, about the impact of that on clean generation?

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: The carbon price floor post-2020 is something that we're clearly trying to engage with government about at the  moment. I think it's not clear exactly where they're going. I understand the point that you make around the  interconnection to Europe and whatever. I suspect Paris – although, there might be nothing particularly  conclusive, we're heading in to Paris. People have put a lot more work in pre-Paris. You've obviously got a lot more  coming out of the China and America in terms of how they want to push that forward.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: So, you would hope that between spending review, policy reset that they want to do and then going into Paris after  or going into the new year, we'll then have a bit more clarity. Is there a will or a desire to set a sensible carbon  price in Europe going forward at €20 to €30 a tonne or something like that into the 2020 to 2030 and then push  that trajectory up going beyond? That's what we think we need. And then we don't have to have the arguments  about Hinkley or onshore wind or offshore wind or whatever. So, that's the line that we're clearly pushing with  government.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: They've not indicated to us if they think that's stupid or irrelevant or not worthy going. It's just they're going  through their process of what they want to do and it all centres around, I think, what treasury is doing first. So,  I'm hopeful that we can get there. We have got a bit of time, fortunately, between now and, let's say, over the next  year or so to try and get some clarity on that. But a long-term stable, sensible carbon price is clearly what we're  arguing for. I don't think there's too many people arguing against it, to be honest. So, that's probably the best I can  do at the moment, but I expect you may come back with that again in May.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: I've got these gentlemen here and then back and then forward.  Gavin Kennedy  Sanford C. Bernstein Ltd.  Q  Thanks. It's Gavin Kennedy here from Bernstein. I just have three questions, if I may. The first is on the Retail  business. And I suppose, just given your very impressive customer satisfaction numbers, just wondering your  thoughts on why your customer attrition numbers have been slightly higher than some peers. The second on the  Laggan acquisition. If you could perhaps please give us some more color on the strategic rationale for the  acquisition and I suppose the breakeven gas prices that you've assumed in terms of breaking even on an NPV  level. And, finally, just on the renewables business. So you've got a very strong performance in the first half. Just  curious of the onshore and offshore capacity that has contributed to these results, what percentage has been  earmarked for sale? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: On the Laggan acquisition, the strategy behind that was quite simple. There were a number of assets came to the  market over the summer in Norway and the UK Continental Shelf. There were probably four big disposal  processes. We had a look at them. We picked one of them. It was Laggan. We bid for it. The others were obviously  bidding for the other ones. For us, I think, it makes a whole bunch of sense because it was relatively at that point  in time that, clearly, prices have come down since a low point in recent times in terms of gas prices. It was a long- term asset and, therefore, complemented our business. We have a long-term business and a long-term need for  gas. Even now, our total gas reserves would burn through in a couple of years basically. So, it came out together  but the fact that it's very long-term attracted us.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: And then finally, the big investment in the Shetland Gas processing facility. So, a big part of the acquisition price  was to buy a unique piece of infrastructure that will be operating for many, many years to come and earning  money as long as West of Shetland continues to produce economic gas that gets shipped into the UK. So, for us, it  was a long-term commitment. It was there at that time. Yes, it might have been nicer to buy it three months later  but it didn't have to be for sale three months later. And it probably would have been sold to somebody else and we  wouldn't have got it right now. And we think, for us, it was the right sort of asset for our portfolio. And then,  Gregor -

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: Yeah. I mean, in terms of wind and offshore wind on the Wholesale profitability, it would be more than what our  hydro contribution would be. So, most of the contribution in Wholesale was renewables. So we have more than  50%. You can look at that on the output measures where we're at 2.2 gigawatts of output from onshore wind and  offshore wind. And in respect of specific assets, I'm not going to get into the specific details because there's a  combination of assets that we look to sell. But I would say that the megawatts that we're looking at, I think, they're  kind of 200 megawatt to 300 megawatt range. And you combine that with the investment that we're putting in at  the moment of 600 megawatts of new construction, you can see there's an incremental increase in our overall  portfolio going forward.  Alistair Phillips-Davies  Chief Executive Officer & Director  A  Okay. The gentleman there, go ahead. And then we'll come to [indiscernible] (53:04).

texts.speaker: Ashley M. Thomas
texts.profession: Société Générale SA (Broker)
texts.text: Thanks. It's Ashley Thomas from SocGén. Clarification on Energy Supply and a question on electricity  transmission. On Energy Supply, the guidance that domestic Energy Supply profits are likely to be down year-on- year, can we take from that the UK domestic Energy Supply margins, that last year was 6.0%, are likely to be down  year-on-year?

texts.speaker: Ashley M. Thomas
texts.profession: Société Générale SA (Broker)
texts.text: On electricity transmission, just on the Scottish island links, you've said in the statement that there is sort of  uncertainty on timing. But just in terms of your expectations, sort of, what are you planning for in terms of when  do we get EC state aid clearance and when should we get the CfD allocation for the Scottish island onto your wind  CfDs?

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: Yeah. I agree with that. And the longer it goes on, less clarity we're getting from the UK government, the more  uncertain it becomes. But we're still pushing on that. I mean, on domestic Energy Supply, we'd expect margins to  be just slightly lower than last year, so slightly under the 6% level.

texts.speaker: Edmund Reid
texts.profession: Lazarus Partnership
texts.text: Edmund Reid from Lazarus. On domestic Energy Supply, so it look like domestic electricity volumes were down  over 3% in the first half. I was wondering if you can talk through why that's happening and what your assumptions  are going forward. And the second is on potential efficiency saving in Electricity Distribution from smart grids. I  think Ofgem assumes some, I guess, aggressive savings from smart grids. Sort of retrospect or with time do you  think those are now attainable?

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: I mean, basically, smart grid assumptions from Ofgem will play optimistic in our view. We said that very publicly.  We took – the whole deal was a package I think it's far too early to say whether some of those savings will come  through. But if we look at the package that we got, we still expect to outperform. Our specific business plan noted  meter ED1 requirements. We've supplemented the management team and changed one or two things there. And I  would expect us to still be able to earn on a post-tax basis close to over 5%. So, we look at it as a package. But I  agree, the smart grid will be challenging.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Just on the consumption piece, yeah, the number is on page 47 for the eagle eyes amongst you. So it was a little bit  colder over the first six months. And, therefore, gas was up by a little over 12%. Electricity was down a little bit.  I'm not sure we exactly know why, if I'm absolutely honest. I don't think you're seeing demand destruction at that  level. So, I think, it's difficult to tell.

texts.speaker: Lakis Athanasiou
texts.profession: Agency Partners LLP
texts.text: Hi. Lakis Athanasiou, Agency Partners. Just a few questions on CapEx, please. Firstly, on electricity transmission,  looking at your regulatory reporting pack, you've still got around £1 billion in [ph] 2009/2010 (57:53) prices of  volume driver CapEx in ET, which was the same number you had in 2014 and in 2015. Could you say if you're in  time when that pack came out to take fully into account government's change in policies on that or do you actually  expect your volume driver CapEx to be below that eventually?

texts.speaker: Lakis Athanasiou
texts.profession: Agency Partners LLP
texts.text: On also CapEx, if I did my sums right, you're saying probably 25%, 30%. Could you give a percentage split  between E&P and generation? The number just feels a bit low. And a hard question. You seem to be suggesting  £350 million of other/Retail CapEx. And in the past, you've been doing quite high CapEx on Retail. It just feels too  high for just maintaining systems and integrating with the smart grid. I don't know if I've been mistaken or not.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Smart metering will have probably driven some of that, I suppose, if you look at year-on-year because we haven't  refinanced a whole bunch of the smart meters yet. So there might be another £50 million, £60 million of the  smart meters that we've got in the balance sheet that we would expect to push back out and refinance. So, that  might be part of it. But I think we'd have to wander up and down the number. And it is what it is and we don't  have any particular concerns. And, clearly, we are spending more on Retail. Smart metering IT systems, we've put  in probably about £20 million on our system – on the new to the billing service – integrated billing service,  mobility system for the hydro services business as well. And total spend of that would have been £20 million in  the six months.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: Well, most of that is generation. The E&P, we will have some additional spend coming through from the West of  Shetland project and then some additional spend within our existing activities in E&P. But I would expect that to  be less than £100 million.

texts.speaker: Peter J. Atherton
texts.profession: Jefferies
texts.text: Yeah. Morning. It's Peter Atherton from Jefferies. Couple questions. A quick one that you can probably answer  straightaway with a no. Any interest in taking part in the bidding for National Grid's gas assets?

texts.speaker: Peter J. Atherton
texts.profession: Jefferies
texts.text: Interesting. And just on the thermal loss, back to the sort of coal point. Last year, in your segmental count, overall,  thermal made a loss. I can't remember the numbers. I think £50 million or something like that maybe. £50  million around -

texts.speaker: Peter J. Atherton
texts.profession: Jefferies
texts.text: Are you expecting a sort of similar number this year given gases are a bit better but coals are going to get a bit  worse?

texts.speaker: Peter J. Atherton
texts.profession: Jefferies
texts.text: Just on the wind – sort of selling wind farms today and recycling, obviously, the value of that wind farm depends  on the price you sell it. But also I think in – there must be sort of an element of – you're going to get better returns  in another bit of your business from the existing wind farms. I'm just wondering. If you take money out of existing  wind to put it to work in one of your businesses, where do you think you'd get the best value for that recycled?

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Obviously, we've done over – or the disposal programmes gone very well, to-date. We're over £600 million now I  think in total from that. We've done over £100 million of wind, the kind of people just came to us and bought a  couple of packages of assets that were sold at great prices. And we still feel we need to – we should be looking  actively at doing a bit more to make sure we fund that. So, it's really more wind-on-wind stuff as we would see. I  think it's all a bit fungible at the end of the day but what we felt was we had quite a little wind. We're still adding to  capacity, but we need to take some money out of that part of business, I think.

texts.speaker: Peter J. Atherton
texts.profession: Jefferies
texts.text: Sorry, just one final question on the cost of new onshore build. What sort of pound per megawatt would be a good  rule of thumb these days given the cost of the pound will come down?

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: I think it kind of depends where you are. If you're doing incredibly well, you're probably at £12.50. If you're in a  more challenged side, you maybe are more challenged on grid like you can be in parts of Ireland. You might be up  at £17.50. So I think it's quite a big difference. For us, we try and judge the through-life cost of producing a  megawatt hour of energy, the upfront cost and/or the O&M and everything else, against what the yield is from the  wind on that particular site. And that's certainly something that we put a lot of effort in and the guys have got  pretty much a 20% reduction in terms of what our cost base is against where we were a couple of years ago. So, I  think, the new assets coming on are a good deal cheaper in terms of their through-life cost and that's what we'll be  measuring.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Yeah. Because originally when we take Clyde, it was kind of spec'd for 500 megawatts and the most economic  turbine was 350 megawatt wind farm, essentially, with the turbines available that time, the wind resources and  everything else. We obviously were able to come back and do – stick another 175 megawatts on there, but,  essentially, the connections infrastructure was already there. So, therefore, you had a much lower CapEx and  therefore much more attractive return for something like Clyde extension.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Okay. Sure. Right. So I have no idea what Amber Rudd spoke to the other big energy bosses. Hopefully, she got all  18 of them. And she didn't speak to me. It was a pertinent conversation. She asked a number of questions around  prices, direction of prices, how we set prices, what our views were and all that. And we had a reasonable  conversation. I think she went away as far as I can tell reasonably happy with the answers that she got.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: Yeah. I mean, basically, the consultation has come out, as you know. We've been very kind of upfront with Ofgem  and the Scottish government that we believe the island links, if they ever happen, should be part of our existing  business, not going to competition. I think with some of the renewable spend coming down later this decade,  whether there's competitive process, it's going to be that attractive for Ofgem, time will tell. But I think it's  important that we have a business that is capable of competing in that market. And I think that would be post  2020. By that time, we will have some significant innovative projects, including Caithness-Moray, which will give  us a lot of capability to compete in that market when it opens up.

texts.speaker: Mark A. Freshney
texts.profession: Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Hi. It's Mark Freshney from Credit Suisse again. CMA – they came out earlier this year with a potential remedy as  to safeguard variable tariff. There was a lot of pushback to that tariff. And now, I think, two of your competitors  have proposed ending Evergreen tariffs. What's your view and what do you think the most likely outcome to CMA  is?

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: I think in terms of a backstop tariff, ending of Evergreen tariffs or whatever, that maybe that BG and SP think  they've got systems that cope with that better than some of their competitors. So they're maybe looking for a bit of  competitive advantage there. Equally, I think, the key thing is that – I had this conversation already with two  people earlier. It's how you deal with, one, possibly vulnerable customers, and two, those customers who are  disengaged. I think a lot of the market is highly engaged and, therefore, we've got to be quite careful about being  sort of nanny state or whatever on those people.

file: SSEL - Q2 2017 Earnings Call 9November2016 400 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 09-Nov-16.pdf

texts.speaker: Richard D. Gillingwater
texts.profession: Chairman, SSE Plc
texts.text: In May, we said there was an emerging policy and regulatory framework, within which we could do business  successfully in the years ahead. The EU result doesn't necessarily change that and we are encouraging ministers  to provide stability by maintaining the policy framework that has emerged over the last few years. And that now  includes retaining the ability to access and trade with European electricity and gas markets.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Our half-year results are in line with what we set out in our pre-course statement in September. In Wholesale, the  fall in operating profit to £121 million was mainly the result of lower output of renewable energy compared with a  year ago, partly offset by an improved contribution from the thermal portfolio. Gas Production was affected by  commodity prices and challenging market conditions continued to prevail in Gas Storage.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Operating profits in Networks saw an expected decrease in transmission due to the phasing of CapEx and  revenue, which was more than offset by increases in both Electricity and Gas Distribution. Operating profit in  Retail fell to £60.5 million as a result of increasing non-energy cost and the lower number of customer accounts in  Energy Supply, and there were lower operating profits in both Energy-related Services and Enterprise where the  focus is on investing for long-term growth.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: The Stronelairg onshore wind farm represents such an opportunity for the SSE group. After meeting transaction- related costs, we plan to donate around £100 million of the proceeds to supporting the Stronelairg investment and  return around £500 million to shareholders by way of an on-market share buyback. We would expect to execute  that by the end of 2017. Thereafter, the ongoing EPS impact of the sale and how the proceeds are used should  be broadly neutral.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Since April 2010, excluding our share of SGN's CapEx, we've invested around £10 billion across the SSE group.  Around £7 billion of this was in Electricity Networks and Renewables. In 2010, including [indiscernible] (09:33), we  had 2.3 gigawatts of renewable energy capacity in operation and an Electricity Networks RAV of £3 billion. As a  result of our investment and our renewables capacity in operation should be almost around 50% greater at around  3.6 gigawatts, at the end of this financial year. And our Electricity Networks RAV should have doubled to £6  billion.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: In this financial year, we've already invested £782.4 million and with the Stronelairg opportunity, we're on course  to invest around £1.85 billion for the year as a whole, which would be our highest ever. Next year, we expect to  invest around £1.75 billion. This is part of our full year CapEx program that is now likely to total closer to £6 billion  when it is completed in 2020. Economically regulated networks and government-mandated renewables will  account for around two-thirds of this expenditure.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: I'll now turn to Networks. Although the shape of our Networks business is evolving, it's clear that the relative  stability of the returns from them and their index-linked RAV and revenues continue to bring balance to SSE as a  whole and support our target for annual dividend growth. The index-linked point is particularly important given  some economists forecast for inflation. And as Alistair will point out, it also applies to renewable energy support  schemes as well.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Before the sale of the SGN stake, we were looking at total Networks' RAV of around £10 billion by 2020.  Following the sale, the total RAV of our Networks business is now £7.4 billion until it's well placed to reach £9  billion by 2020. At £3.2 billion, Electricity Distribution remains the biggest single part of our RAV. As expected, this  business assume the benefit of revenue arising from under recovery and incentives from 2 years ago. And  despite more challenging weather conditions in the spring and the summer, it is continuing to perform well in  terms of the number and duration of power cuts.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: This is allied to further investment in network resilience including additional automation, other innovations and  targeted tree cutting. This means that the Distribution business remains on course to achieve the performance as  targeted for the period of the price control.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Thank you, Gregor, and good morning, everyone. While the UK, and to some extent Ireland, focuses on the  economic, political and social consequences of the Brexit vote, it's easy to lose sight of the extent to which there's  been continually continuity in the overall direction of policy and regulation over the last few months. The UK  government has accepted the fifth carbon budget proposed by the Committee on Climate Change. They've  confirmed the forms of the capacity market and CMA's final remedy confirming its two-year market investigation  were as expected.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Also this morning, for the eagle-eyed amongst you and not too bleary-eyed amongst you, government has also  announced further CfD auctions in April of next year for offshore wind and consultations around coal and Ireland  CfDs. All of it is welcome. However, this is not to suggest that we foresee a benign period with no political or  regulatory risk. It is a fact of life in energy. With a political cycle increasingly built around autumn statement and  spring budgets, there's always some uncertainty and always a need for us to be politically aware and engage  constructively with politicians and regulators.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: But two key points continue to stand out for me. First, while there's always change, the sector continues to feature  robust economic regulations for network, a remuneration framework for providing generation capacity and a  competitive retail market. Second, SSE is focused on maintaining and investing in a balanced range of  businesses that's not only designed to realize opportunities across the energy value chain, but manage the risks  associated with it as well. In the current environment, this is illustrated by the fact that the majority of our forecast  earnings for the full financial year have a link to RPI inflation.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: The principal of strength to diversity applies to the SSE group and to our Wholesale businesses as well. These  businesses continue to be impacted by a number of key issues, including an uncertain macroeconomic  environment, the ongoing transition to a low carbon economy, and shift in commodity prices. In EPM and  Generation, the diversity of our assets and contracts mitigates the volatile power market conditions we've seen in  recent weeks which could have wide-ranging impact.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: While in the first six months, the impact of lower output from our renewables is being partially offset by improved  contribution from our thermal portfolio; those power stations operate in a very complex environment. They derive  revenue from a number of sources including a variety of contracts and operate in the context of a wider set of  energy portfolio management decisions. All of this means changes in spark and dark spreads may not always be  reflected in the financial performance of our generation plant.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: In terms of Gas Production, commodity prices remained a key issue. Even so, we're pleased with the  performance and output from our assets since they were commissioned. An improvement is expected in the  second half of the financial year.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Gas Storage remains a very challenged business and we've taken the decision to mothball two of the nine  caverns of Atwick. This was a difficult decision, but in terms of maintaining our financial discipline, the right one.  The Atwick facility is already fully impaired.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: As I said earlier, we welcome the UK government's endorsement to the fifth carbon budget and of the planned  reforms for the capacity market. At the same time, the market and framework within which it operates are always  subject to change and we have to monitor and manage continuously the shape of our portfolio of assets and  contracts accordingly.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: The next key market milestones are the capacity auctions in December and January. The results of  prequalification clearly demonstrate the range and diversity of existing assets that we have to offer the country's  electricity system. As you know, we've also secured prequalification for a potential second gas -fired power station  at Keadby. These are competitive processes, but in keeping with our overall approach to financial discipline, I can  say that we'll always take a rational approach to our participation in auctions.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: And as we demonstrated with Fiddler's Ferry earlier this year, we'll always take a responsible approach  considering options for the future operation of assets. The benefits of that approach are clear. An important time  when the UK electricity market is fundamentally changing as can be seen in the graph on this slide, Fiddler's  Ferry remains an important shorter-term option for the GB electricity system and for SSE. As the market features  significant volatility with high and low prices on the same day, the importance of a diverse and flexible portfolio of  assets has never been greater.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: At the same time, the Clyde disposal earlier this year showed the value of renewable energy assets have never  been clearer and with high inflation forecast, it's important that the renewables obligation is linked to RPI.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Looking further ahead, we retain other options in on and offshore wind and if future CfD auctions or other  developments provide the opportunity to deploy the capability we've built over the last decade, then we'll look to  do so. This could include other pro-wind jurisdictions.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: As I said earlier, we expect Gas Production's results to improve in the second half of the financial year. And we  remain confident about the long-term prospects for this business. Our new assets are fully commissioned and  operating well.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Looking to the 5 years to 2021, the Greater Laggan Area acquisition is expected to mean an average annual  volume of gas produced will be around 500 million therms of liquids in addition to that. Naturally, they'll benefit  from higher commodity prices that have prevailed since the acquisition. They represent a substantial collection of  assets that contributes to the overall balanced nature of the energy businesses in the SSE group. On top of that,  the Shetland Gas Plant is a critical piece of state-of-the-art infrastructure that will generate a return for SSE into  the 2020. Overall, these assets are a natural complement for a company that operates gas-fired power stations  and supplies gas to customers.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: As I've said before, everything SSE does is ultimately paid for by customers. And as a group of energy  businesses, we must always remember how important it is that people can afford to pay their bills. Today's results  were a reminder of the competitive nature of the markets in which all of our retail businesses operate. In fact,  although we made a profit in energy supply as a whole, we recorded a small loss in supplying household gas and  electricity.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: As far as energy supply as a whole is concerned, we have three clear priorities. The first is to build our presence  in the I&C market. To do that, our Business Energy team is transforming what it offers customers in the  commercial sector and the associated services it provides.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: The second is ensuring we offer customers what they're looking for in terms of products, service and value. The  net loss of customer accounts slowed in the first half of the year. Part of the reason for that is that we competed  successfully for over 350,000 new customer accounts across energy supply and related services in the first half.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Both smart metering and the CMA remedies have financial consequences across the sector and put the onus on  us to take cost out of the business, which we are doing. Excluding the meters themselves, we have so far  invested over £250 million in the smart rollout and the PPM price cap will have an estimated revenue impact of  over £40 million per annum. But we have to go [ph] with a grain (26:52) in areas such as this. That means doing  our best to implement what is expected of us while working with the government and Ofgem to be clear about the  challenges and their potential impact on customers.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Looking at Energy-related Services, our Home Services customer account numbers have continued to rise. At  440,000, they're up 10% since the start of the financial year. This represents a positive step forward in delivering  our strategy and diversifying the range of products and services we offer to customers. While operating profit is  down in the first six months, progress has been made in this business. We've launched market-leading boiler  cover propositions as we move closer to completing the national expansion of our Home Services business, and  we've introduced a range of market-leading and well-subscribed tariff in broadband. At the same time, delivering  these service and propositions has to be supported by good customer service. And I'm optimistic that our long- term plan to build scale in this business will bear fruit.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Capital investment will, however, continue to be a major engine for growth over the next few years. Over the 4  years to 2020, we now expect CapEx to be closer to the £6 billion mark. The reason for this is that we intend to go  ahead with the 225-megawatt Stronelairg onshore wind farm following the ruling in favor of the project from the  Court of Session in July. Although it's not without its challenges, the Windfarm project should secure accreditation  under the renewables obligation, and we're expecting investment in it to total around £300 million.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Including Stronelairg, we now have a net total of over 1 gigawatt of wind farm capacity at various stages of  construction. In addition to seven onshore projects, the Beatrice Offshore project, of which our share is 235  megawatts, is also now well underway and on course for completion in 2019. We're also building a second multi- fuel plant at Ferrybridge.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Okay. So, we've got the Blackhillock contract this year. We have a capacity market contract for it a couple of  years out, as well. I think, while the station was very challenged earlier in the year, it's certainly in these volatile  market conditions, I think, doing a little better. And therefore, we probably expect to see earnings from it, being  better that we'd anticipated at the start of the year because of that volatility. And I'll have to look through what you  said this morning, BEIS has said this morning. I have not seen the detail on coal but I think it's pushing things out  to 2025. If there's nothing else in there, I think we would hope that that station had a reasonably good future  between now and at least later in the decade, and we'll be able to honor all the contracts that we have on that  station.

texts.speaker: Mark Freshney
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Hi. It's Mark Freshney from Credit Suisse. Two questions if I may. The first one is just regarding very high power  prices in the spot market and what that means for your energy operating book, and also prices for customers.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Okay. I'm sorry, as they say in America. Exactly. I think there are three things. As long as your thermal plant –  flexible thermal plant operates and you get the opportunity to take some of the particularly high prices seen, then  that's a positive. Obviously, if that plant comes off unexpectedly or trips, I think than can be a significant cost. And  I think there were one or two plants we saw last week that came off. I think that you're in danger of losing a few  million pounds in an afternoon if they come up with a wrong time.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: But by and large, it should be positive for thermal generation. I think it does give problems for the retailers,  hedging that super peak over the 4:30 to 6:30 kind of timeframe is tricky and those prices are very high. So, I  would imagine Retail business is losing money over that period on some days.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Also, depending on how wind businesses or renewable businesses are hedged and some of our wind farms are  certainly hedged in this way. If you hedge forward on an average output basis, you'll struggle to make money on  those days and/or if the wind isn't blowing, you could take significantly losses trying to cover your power position.  So, I think fundamentally it should be a positive thermal generation but a negative for retail, domestic retail, and  potentially for renewables. So, that would be the trading book.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Retail customers, I think there were two parts to that. We are clearly seeing increases in cost there. I think you've  got commodity costs are up, 30% or 40% from their lows, and that is going to provide pressure to everybody.  You've also got non-energy cost as well going up into next year probably of the order of £40, I would say, per  annum. Those are all going to provide pressure for all of us.

texts.speaker: Fraser McLaren
texts.profession: Analyst, Merrill Lynch International
texts.text: McLaren from Merrill. Good morning. A couple of questions on wind, please, if I may. First of all on Stronelairg,  can you speak a little bit more about the challenges for securing ROCs there, please, and how you protect your  downside risk in the event that that becomes hard to achieve?

texts.speaker: Fraser McLaren
texts.profession: Analyst, Merrill Lynch International
texts.text: And then secondly, you mentioned international expansion in wind. How large a component was the U.S. in that  thinking?  Alistair Phillips-Davies  Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc  A  Okay. I'll take this quickly. On the ROCs, we expect to get ROCs on Stronelairg. It's just we have to get the thing  built. And so, if we've got particularly poor weather, we might struggle. And I think it is not beyond the realms of  possibility that no matter what we did, poor weather would frustrate us there. Those two issues, there's  a grid  connection side of it and then there's obviously constructing the wind farm.

texts.speaker: Fraser McLaren
texts.profession: Analyst, Merrill Lynch International
texts.text: And so, I can't guarantee that we can get that done in that time. We are highly confident that given a reasonable  set of wind conditions, a reasonable wind window, we'll get that done. We won't know for sure until a few months  before the station is fully commissioned or – sorry, the wind farm is fully commissioned basically. But we are very  confident that we have everything in place to deliver that. But I can't guarantee it to you. So, that's just why we put  that there.

texts.speaker: Ashley M. Thomas
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA (Broker)
texts.text: Ashley Thomas at SocGén. Two questions connected to the announcements from BEIS this morning. Firstly on  coal and the carbon price floor, so, the government's reaffirmed its target of 2025 for unabated coal to come off.  Just your thoughts on sort of the policy purpose of the CPS after coal goes. National Grid said recently that when  they look at interconnector investments, they assume post-2021 prudently no CPS. Having made a bid recently  on Stronelairg on a ROC, sort of did you do any stress testing on sort of longer term CPS prices?

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Okay. I'll do the first, Greg will do the second. So, yeah, obviously, trying to predict the energy prices  [indiscernible] (46:04) rates, volatilities and a hundred other things that go into figuring out whether you're going to  make money out of what sorts of generation technologies, open cycle, restive engines, through [indiscernible]  (46:16), through wind farms. There's an awful a lot of things in there. So, whether they would meet your criteria for  a stress test or not, I don't know, but we certainly look hard at the range of possibilities when we take on these  investments.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: And there's no surety of what the carbon price will be. I think it is apparent to us that carbon doesn't get talked  about as much as perhaps securities supply, and particularly consumer prices at the moment, two of the three  things that are out there. It doesn't seem the most important piece to government and regulators. But I think it's  still there, and I don't detect any sense of [ph] banding in (46:57) any policies on that. It's just challenging times.  People are bound to worry about cost and bound to want to make sure that – want to make sure that we  absolutely have adequate energy supplies for the entire country.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: So, we've run the test, and I know we've run our probabilities and all the rest of it. Carbon price floor, some of it is  priced in, but the fact that it might be changed whether it's 23rd of November this year or some future autumn  statement that that's possible, but we're definitely very comfortable for moving forward with what we think is very  strong investments at Stronelairg.

texts.speaker: Iain Turner
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane Ltd.
texts.text: And, secondly, you talked about revamping your I&C offering. And I wondered if that – if you'd look to the water  market at all and whether that figured in your thinking.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Okay. So, the easiest one of those to answer, I think, is the I&C water market. Yes, we have and we may do  something there. I think the issue for us is what can we – or how can we quickly and easily stand up a robust  billing system to provide a sensible service, and therefore, how many customers or what type of customers could  we go after, but that is something that we will look out. Whether we'll definitely do it or not is another matter.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: We've got some big projects out there. Caithness-Moray is one of our biggest projects. Was our biggest project  that we've ever done at £1.1 billion. We've got a lot of expertise in managing those projects. And clearly, if  projects become available in the rest of UK, we will look at them. And if we think we can do it, we'll put a  competitive price in for that. But I think it's a bit early. There's not that many projects available and I think there's  one big nuclear connection that's potentially there, but there's not that many big ones there at the moment. It's  probably more post 2021 for the next price control.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Yeah. And well, that one's got some challenges in it because I think it's laying big cables through a tunnel that's  going to be drilled under the [indiscernible] (52:59) somewhere. So, that one certainly looks quite tricky one. I'm  not sure it'd be the first one I'd choose to have a competitive tender around a big nuclear project to be honest,  given there's probably a few challenges of those as well.

texts.speaker: Lakis Athanasiou
texts.profession: Analyst, Agency Partners LLP
texts.text: Second on Stronelairg, the transmission link, the timing you showed in the slide looked a bit odd. Is that the  allowance or your actual spend? Because it seemed to coming in quite early before you actually fitted the wind  farm. And is the cost a bit socialized, I mean, I think it goes through your volume drivers. Will ultimately you as  SSE separately end up paying for it or does the cost get socialized across the whole transmission system?

texts.speaker: Lakis Athanasiou
texts.profession: Analyst, Agency Partners LLP
texts.text: And the timing on the slide, you're starting the construction before you've fitted the wind farm very early. If you  look on the slide, the CapEx on the transmission link seems to start like in mid-2014 or mid-2015 or something,  slide 13.

texts.speaker: Edmund Reid
texts.profession: Analyst, Lazarus Partnership
texts.text: Edmund Reid from Lazarus. Three questions. The first one is on embedded benefits. I'm just wondering where  you sit in that debate. Obviously, you've got both Distribution and Transmission-connected assets. And then, the  second question is around battery storage and whether you've got any plans to invest in that area both, I guess,  to help your generation business and also if government changes its views on some things on the distribution  network.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Okay. Embedded benefits, I suspect overall there is a discussion about the way that people look at transmission  charging and why the [indiscernible] (04:00:23). But that's been a perennial issue for 10-plus years, I suspect. But  I think there's a possibility there might be a wider review of transmission charging given that the nature of the  network and the nature of the generation on the network is different. I think the embedded benefits point is one  that ultimately we'd probably support. I'm sure there is a place on the grid for [ph] lubricating (01:00:49) the  engines, diesel plant or whatever but possibly not quite as many as bidding into the capacity auctions.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: And I think there's a real risk that there'll be no new CCGTs getting built any time soon while that many open  cycle plants are bidding in. They have an inherent advantage I think around bidding into the capacity mechanism.  I think – I believe that is understood by government and Ofgem, and I believe they're working on it. They clearly  have a place but it's whether – it's just how big that place is and it's just whether we think we do need combined  cycle gas plant. I just bet [ph] the country (01:01:27) will do it in the next few years. And so, therefore I think it's  important that in some way, shape or form, the playing field is leveled between combined cycle and open cycle  plant.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: And on battery storage, we didn't get our bid taken in the recent grid auction where they took a couple of hundred  megawatts off the top of my head of sort of battery-type storage. I think we're expecting to see more battery  storage on the bars over the next 10 years. And it's something that will be of interest for us. But I think we need  the economic projects, so I think we felt we bid that project relatively aggressively.
