texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Then if I can turn to the regulatory business, all the regulatory businesses, the transmission, distribution, gas and  electricity would have been over 5% post-tax real on a project-return basis. And if you look at return on regulated  equity, they would be in the kind of low-double-digit type return other than transmission maybe kind of – in the  kind of slightly higher 9% to 10%, that number doesn't get kind of firmed up until later on this summer.

texts.speaker: Martin S. Brough
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Prime Brokerage)
texts.text: Hi. Martin Brough from Deutsche Bank. I was just wondering whether Ian had any advice for incoming energy  regulators that might face being abolished within a couple of years under Labor party policy. So, do you expect the  energy regulators to just stick to a steady course and focus on trying to reassure investors and attract capital at  acceptable rates or is there a danger that for political survival, they have to be seen to be pandering more to the  politicians' concern?

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: My advice to an incoming energy regulator or an incoming civil servant or an incoming politician is the start at the  Hippocratic oath, and I can't remember the Latin, which you're probably not surprised. The start says a doctor will  first, do no harm. And the risk that we suffer and I see a lot is interventionitis. I think that might be a word I've  made up, but we have to be doing something, so we can have a new package of measures to do this, to do this, to  do this, and the more complex the measures, and boy, are some of them complex, the more unintended  consequences that you get so you have an intervention to promote spending on fuel poverty which pushes prices  up, which pushes more people into fuel poverty. So you then say, well, we need to spend more on alleviating fuel  poverty. So you get this unintended consequence and the policy response is frequently more initiatives.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: And I think that there's a need to step back and say, we've lost sight of the simple things we're trying to do. We  want a reliable, affordable, clean energy system. And actually if you just – that's what we're trying to achieve, I  think you'd start getting rid of quite a lot of the intervention. And that would start actually to restore confidence.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Deputy Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Achieved sparks, they'll clearly be positive because we wouldn't want to run our plans otherwise, and we do have  sufficient flexibility in the plant and where the markets probably in, I think, 11 out of the last 12 months of the year  just gone, it has actually seeing negative base load sparks. We would have expected to achieve probably something  in the range of £3 to £6 a megawatt hour and it's probably running peak sparks, you'll be £3 or £4 a megawatt  hour. And you will clearly get more out of the balancing mechanism because you can then charge maybe £20 or  £30 a megawatt hour, but you're just not necessarily getting – taking in huge volumes. It's just you're obviously  running a lot more risk there. But we would only dispatch plants when you're getting £2 per megawatt hours out  of it in the current environment.

texts.speaker: Dominic C. Nash
texts.profession: Analyst, Macquarie Securities
texts.text: Hi. Dominic Nash from Macquarie. Two questions, please. Firstly, on generation, you obviously had a wholesale  review of your generation plants and then shutting down some of your older, less efficient gas plants. You're not  the only market participant with old and inefficient gas plant. Is there a risk that you are going to face a business  dilemma here where your competitors are not going to be following suit trying to tighten up the market in the  short term albeit with a disaster waiting to happen further years down the road?

texts.speaker: Dominic C. Nash
texts.profession: Analyst, Macquarie Securities
texts.text: And the second one is on RIIO, have you had a chance to look at the assumptions that the regulator have given  you, where you can outperform and where you think in range of the ROREs you can operate your transmission  and gas distribution?

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: In terms of gas distribution, one of the things that we've really focused and the team has really focused on is  getting the cost base down. The RIIOmax is an extension of efficiency program. So, we're pretty confident that  we'll be able to outperform some of the things like some of contractor positioning we'll bring in-house, getting  more efficiencies there. I can give you some examples of what we're doing out in the field. So, I would – and we're  in pretty good position going forward over the next couple of years to see good outperformance.

texts.speaker: Jamie R. Tunnicliffe
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn Partners LLP
texts.text: Yes. Do you think there's much chance that it could be changed? It seems quite an expensive way, for example, to  reduce carbon.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Deputy Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Okay. Well, CERT and CESP, I think, delivered quite a lot. CESP given that it was a little lighter and a little hurried  in its implementation, it's probably cost quite a lot, costs us roughly twice what the government impact  assessment was in order to deliver it. CERT which has been a longer running program, I think people were more  in the swing of what they were doing. Big issues for us on ECO, I think, are around the fact that governments have  created this great new market, and that's fine, but the problem is that the market is very large between ECO and  Green Deal and it's all rather new.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Deputy Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: At the moment, we're seeing through the auction process that they've got – that the costs are probably 40% to 50%  higher than the impact assessment. That would be the initial view. Also, the individual measures like installation  measures are probably costing around three times as much as they were under the previous scheme. So, that's  clearly going to be a worry for us, particularly because that will impact on consumers bills if we're paying three  times as much to get basic insulation measures done.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Eventually a cap on the total cost and then thinking about, well, if that caps the volume, what happens to those  volumes. So, we get the balance between affordability and energy efficiency in a better place than it looks like it is  currently.

texts.speaker: Peter J. Atherton
texts.profession: Analyst, Liberum Capital Limited
texts.text: It's Peter Atherton from Liberum Capital. I was sort of interested in how you would play the future if the energy  bill is actually a success in terms of what the policymakers are trying to achieve. So presumably the energy bill will  go through consumer capacity market is introduced which is okay, and let's assume that the CFD mechanism is  introduced and the strike price that's being offered are pretty generous. And the whole point about this, of course,  is the sort of get us through towards the pathway outlined in the forthcoming budget down towards the 50-grams  target by the end of the next decade.

texts.speaker: Peter J. Atherton
texts.profession: Analyst, Liberum Capital Limited
texts.text: Well, the assumption is the energy bill is introduced successfully.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Yes, but let's also assume that engineering labor is in plentiful supply, capital markets remain buoyant, equity  price – equity markets continue at an all time – it's actually quite difficult to – I'm giving him time to think. But  it's – I mean it's genuinely – the reality is you will need to make the decisions in light of the environment at the  time. And that will be, my guess, at least a year before you guys will be able to say, well, we now understand what  the energy bill means and those aren't assumptions anymore, they're starting to be interpretation of facts. And the  rest of the world will look different in a year's time. Anyway, you've got chance to think now? Good.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Deputy Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: I have, Ian. Thank you. So, look, I think you paint a pretty rosy outcome from the energy bill actually, Peter. And if  that comes to pass, then we've got an awful lot of seabed there where we could build offshore wind if there are  attractive returns for that. We've done well at Gabbard to get that through. And Jim and Jim who went through  the process of funding talks and about mediation that they went through very successfully there to get us the  result, that's gone well for us and its operating well. So great, if people are willing to offer us returns that get  around that double-digit post-tax real, then there's 4,000 megawatts of stuff to be built, notwithstanding finance  issues I'll come back to. And I suspect Gregor may want to comment on that.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Deputy Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Equally, if there's a capacity market there, it'll underpin some of our risks to building a generation plant. We've  got six to eight sites waiting. And I named the one, two and three basically that sat there today.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Deputy Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: We've also got the opportunity to bring back Keadby, to bring back Peterhead as well into that market. So, I think  that will be a great prospect for us. And the fact that we've got opportunities to spend £1.5 billion plus at those  returns, great. Clearly, we would not look to overstretch ourselves, and it actually goes back to that point that the  two Ians discussed briefly earlier about the investment opportunities in the UK and what it was like 10, 15 years  ago compared to what it's like today. I fear myself that we will not get anywhere near as much clarity after the  energy bill, and we may indeed have a situation come to pass where we've got more issues and risks to think  about.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Deputy Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: I believe that as analysts know, I read recently that said something about maybe politicians reneging on things. I  think it might have come from your company, actually, Peter. And that's clearly the issue for us going forward is  how comfortable can we be with the policy mechanisms, and what the market is telling us in terms of committing  large amounts of capital to what are potentially quite expensive investments. I think gas is definitely needed.  Onshore wind is clearly attractive because it's a relatively cheap form of low carbon and renewable energy. The  offshore wind is rather more tricky at the moment, but we'd be delighted to see a mechanism that gave us the  opportunity to build out Galloper, Beatrice and then move on to some of the projects we've got on Dogger Bank  and in other places. But I think on financing, we would have to be careful. I'll probably leave our cautious people  at the perch next to me to comment on that.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: If the returns are there, we'll look at it. But it's not about market share for us, it's about returns and it's about  discipline and we will work within our balance sheet. I do think in offshore wind, it will come down to how much  finance is going to be available for equity, not debt. It's the equity, and you're seeing one or two players at the  moment not playing in that game. Hopefully, we'll see the Green Investment Bank starting to come in, which I  think they are talking about doing. And ultimately...

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: ...and ultimately, offshore wind, as we go out, costs aren't going down at the moment, they are going up. And  seabed conditions aren't getting easier, they're getting harder. So, returns have to reflect that and if returns reflect  that, then the government will attract not just capital from us but capital from other financial providers and trade  players.

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: The next question is, is your decision to put the coal plant into the TNP rather than opt out, now it sounds to me
texts.text: that perhaps says that you're fairly confident that your SCNR approach is going to work, therefore, you won't be  limited on output on the TNP if there was nothing there compared to opt out? And secondly, as an option value as  well, the carbon tax disappearing and no administrative constraints placed on coal plants looking post 2020, is  that a correct reading of that decision?

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: The reality is no decision yet has to be made. You opt into the TNP, but you have until the end of this year to walk  back out. So, we have not made an irrevocable decision. And actually, the way that TNP works, as long as the  SNCR is even partially successful because it reduces the level of NOx, which gives you more running, so it doesn't  have to get all the way down for it still to be useful, and we will have – they will have the results of that probably  October-November in time to make the decision. So at the moment, Lakis, it's all around optionality on the coal  assets, and decisions start to have to be made later this year. But actually in some cases, the other advantage of the  TNP, you can make some decisions quite late, 2017-2018, because you can come back out. So, at this stage, it's all  about optionality and don't read too much into particular returns we have to get to regulators at this stage.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Deputy Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: So, you can get issues in that market, but it's reasonably attractive and I don't see that market getting worse  simply because the capacity crunch comes in. I think you're going to – it's the I&C customers that are going to  suffer that never paid the capacity fee and they're the ones who are going to struggle to get the power.

texts.speaker: Harold C. Hutchinson
texts.profession: Analyst, Investec Bank Plc (Broker)
texts.text: It's Harold Hutchinson from Investec. Forgive me for being parochial but just two questions on Ireland, if I may.  The first is on Great Island. It seems to me there's plenty of conventional capacity in Ireland. There's going to be a  fairly strong growth in wind power as well. I'm just wondering how confident you are that the capacity mechanism  that's in place will actually stay in place there in the years ahead? And then secondly on supply business, I can see  the jump in your overall Irish supply numbers. I was just wondering can you give us an update on Phoenix itself  since you've acquired it? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Deputy Chief Executive Officer & Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Well, Great Island, the Irish capacity mechanism actually is a capacity mechanism that we think works well. It  remunerates old plant and remunerates most efficient the best. We've been seeing the Irish energy minister in the  past with various issuances. I think really a good efficient plan will be necessary for Ireland to deal with the wind  capacity that's coming through. So, I don't have any concerns on that capacity mechanism not remunerating the  plant.

texts.speaker: Ian D. Marchant
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: On the supply side, yes, the integration of Phoenix has gone well. We've been out to cross-sell to the gas customers  there with electricity customers. That's obviously a regulated business essentially but at some stage, it will  hopefully come out and it's a competitive market, but it's earning the sort of returns that we expected to when we  bought it and where...

file: SSEL - Q4 2014 Earnings Call 21May2014 400 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 21-May-14.pdf

texts.speaker: Hon Robert Smith
texts.profession: Chairman, SSE Plc
texts.text: In a challenging external environment, it's vital that companies have a clear purpose, strategy, and financial  objective. SSE has all of those. Our core purpose is to provide the energy people need in a reliable and sustainable  way. Our strategy is to deliver the efficient operation of and investment in a balanced range of economically  regulated and market-based energy businesses in the UK and Ireland. And our financial objective is to increase  annually the dividend payable to shareholders by at least RPI inflation.

texts.speaker: Hon Robert Smith
texts.profession: Chairman, SSE Plc
texts.text: That's why we are listening to and helping customers with the GB market's longest-ever household energy price  freeze. It's also why we're taking forward well-defined plans for net investment of around £5.5 billion in the next  four years in maintaining, upgrading and building the electricity assets customers depend on. And to support both  of those things, we're undertaking a value program to streamline and simplify the SSE business. So with this focus  on value, investment and customers, we believe we're in a very good position to deliver our financial objective – an  annual dividend that keeps pace with inflation.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Exceptional items of £747.2 million are mainly non-cash. Around 70% relates to the continuing impact on our  Wholesale businesses of the challenging sector conditions we faced in recent years. Coal-fired power stations,  offshore wind and gas storage account for well over half the total. The other significant element is the cost  resulting from the implementation of the value program we announced in March.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Looking now at our three business segments, operating profit is up 9.3% in Networks due to investment in  transmission in particular. Operating profit is down 28.6% in Retail due to higher wholesale cost and lower energy  consumption particularly due to the mild weather in the second half of the winter. Operating profit is up 24.8% in  Wholesale due to higher output from renewables and our new Sean gas production asset, which had brought in  around £90 million of additional operating profit.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Looking ahead, we'll continue to use adjusted EPS and monitor financial performance over the medium term. We  expect that EPS in this new financial year will be around or slightly greater than the £1.234 we reported this  morning. As we said in March over the wider energy sector issues like difficult market conditions for thermal  generation or potential legislation and a price freeze could mean our ability to increase EPS is subject to greater  risk in the two years from April 2013.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: This covers three main categories. Committed spend, including regulated networks projects, and construction and  maintenance; expected spend, which is the £1.3 billion transmission link we believe will be required between  Caithness and Moray, but which is currently out for consultation; an optional spend, which is currently  uncommitted, but that we may choose to spend to build new assets such as onshore wind farms that we're still  developing.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: When it comes to optional spend on new assets, we'll recycle capital from disposals of existing investments and  assets. This is entirely consistent with our commitment to financial discipline. As I said in March, we expect to  secure financial benefit of around £1 billion from a combination of the disposal of non-core assets and businesses  and the sale of existing onshore wind farms in order to recycle capital.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: We've made some progress on the disposals since March, and we're targeting the autumn for completing the sale  of the PFI lighting contracts, non-regulated gas pipelines, and the data center at Fareham. In the case of our  onshore wind farms, we're confident we've achieved excellence in development and construction and have good  opportunities to build more before the renewables obligation deadline in 2017. To enable us to do this, we'll  continue to sell operating wind farms, we believe greater value can be secured from investing in a new one, with  the next disposals likely to be in 2015-2016.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: To put the benefit of this in context, the RAV of our Networks has increased by 45% in five years and is now £6.82  billion. At £3.05 billion, Electricity Distribution remains the biggest single part of our RAV, and had a solid year.  Revenue was essentially flat, and storm-related costs had to be incurred. So there was a slight reduction in  operating profit at £507 million. The Networks ended the year in an over-recovery position of around £25 million.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Last autumn and winter, however, presented us with eight exceptional weather events. We're still very grateful for  the dedication of the engineers, tree-cutters, and customer service advisers who work tirelessly, and for the  patience of our customers. This sequence of exceptional weather events has contributed to the increased political  scrutiny of the Networks businesses and their costs.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: A revised business plan for the 2015-2023 Price Control has cost efficiency and customer service at par. It's  designed to keep us at the frontier of efficiency while preparing for what might happen in energy use between now  and 2023. While Ofgem has reduced its central estimate of the load base effect, return on equity, that's just one  part of a wider package of measures, and we're confident that our revised business plan should lead to a Price  Control package that's fair to customers and investors alike.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Transmissions Price Control is now in its second year, and this business is continuing to grow in a strong and  sustainable way. In just five years, its RAV has more than trebled to £1.33 billion. This continuing investment in  the asset base is driving the growth in profitability, illustrated by the 47.6% increase in operating profit we  reported this morning.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Good progress has been made with the four major projects under construction. Key driver for these, and for the  projects under development, like the Caithness-Moray link, is the need to accommodate renewable energy  developments in the north of Scotland. While there's no consulting in our proposed solution for Caithness-Moray,  Ofgem's view is that there is a need for a reinforcement of the transmission systems in Northern Scotland. The  combination of existing network constraints and wind farms recently completed or in construction means there is  a huge amount of work for our Transmission business to do over the next few years.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: A total of £321.7 million was invested by SGN as a whole in the period, taking our share of the RAV of the business  to £2.44 billion. SGN is one of the best gas distributors in the country. It has a clear focus on safety, reliability and  minimizing the disruption for customers and communities arising from its capital works. That clear focus,  together with the further efficiencies to come, mean it's well placed to deliver good results in the coming years. I'll  now hand you over to Alistair.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: Thank you, Gregor. Good morning, everyone. With Networks, Retail and Wholesale businesses, assets, customers,  SSE's activities reflect the broad structure of the energy sector across Scotland, England, Wales, Northern Ireland  and the Republic of Ireland. I believe that this gives us sector-wide understanding, a broad revenue base, lower  risk from any one business, and the ability to secure cost synergies and apply best practice in key areas from safety  to large capital management projects.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: With this focus, we're closer to our customers and our markets, and better connected with the politicians,  regulators and other stakeholders who will shape the energy sector across these islands in the years to come.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: In March, we set out our plan for making sure SSE is well positioned for the period to 2020 and beyond in what is  a challenging business, market, regulatory and political environment. We're simplifying our business and securing  efficiencies, focusing on value and investment decision-making, easing the burden on bill payers through our price  freeze to 2016 and our campaign on green levies, and showing our appetite for reform and our commitment to  having a voice and a debate around energy market and policy.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: Ofgem said in March that they believe that referring the energy market to their Competition and Markets  Authority offers the opportunity once and for all to clear the air. We must make sure that this opportunity is not  missed. In our response to Ofgem's referral consultation, which we've published this morning, we said we should  not pass up what could be a once-in-a-generation opportunity to reach a new, lasting settlement on the energy  market that commands broad regulatory, political and public support. That's why we believe that the CMA  investigation should go beyond the energy market for household customers and reach everything that is not  economically regulated. It should extend to small businesses and to the industrial commercial sector and cover  gas storage and electricity and gas production as well.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: In summary, we want to achieve lasting political and regulatory stability for the GB market for the benefit of both  customers and investors. Companies need to back up words with actions. Through our price freeze, we've taken  action that would make a difference for our customers. As you know, it comes at some financial cost with Energy  Supply profit margins unlikely to recover to their March 2013 level of 4.2% before 2016-2017. In the year to March  2014, the Energy Supply profit margin is 2.9%. This reflects a fall of almost one-third in operating profit to £246.2  million. The fall resulted from the high cost faced by this business and the lower demand for energy from  customers.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: The increase in bad debt followed the increased energy consumption during the prolonged colder period at the  start of 2013, combined with continued pressures on disposable income. We aim to get in touch with customers  with arrears as early as possible, but this proved more difficult last year when we had other operational challenges,  and there will be renewed focus on this in the coming financial year.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: In what has been a very competitive market, customer account numbers have fallen by 3.9% to 9.1 million. Even  so, we have a good Energy Supply business, and the early response of customers to our price raise has been  positive. That's because it's a clear step towards restoring stability and trust for the long-term.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: Long-term, an important point. Sales of our core products, electricity and gas, are on a decline last year against a  falling consumption by our customers. This means our Retail business has to evolve if it is to prosper.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: We'll start with some strong foundations. SSE has been ranked first for customer service in the Annual uSwitch  Report for eight years running. On top of this, we've led the drive to higher standards. We're bringing an end to  cold calling, and implementing two sector-leading guarantees on sales and on customer service. In addition, I  believe our campaigns to take social and environmental levies of bills, and our price freeze has started to position  us as a company that will take action to make a difference for customers.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: We're building our brands for our sponsorships at the Commonwealth Games. The SSE Hydro, which many of you  hopefully will have seen on TV this morning, is hosting Sports Personality of the Year Award, the SSE Arena,  Wembley and the SWALEC Stadium. This is about engaging with customers in a completely different way  rewarding them for their loyalty for us. We'll also be continuing our campaign to ease the burden on bill payers of  social and environmental levies.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: Over time, we believe that all this should help us to create a brand that people trust and from which they're willing  to buy a wider range of products and services so that SSE is regarded as the leading energy provider and a leading  provider of other services as well. The net result of this should be a sustainable Retail business for the long term.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: If any business should be long term, it's power generation. We're maintaining and developing a resilient and  sustainable Wholesale business. And you can see that in the 24.8% increase in this segment we reported this  morning. The increase has come largely as a result of the £127.6 million acquisition of the Sean assets last April.  In Gas Production, this has helped take output from 184 million therms to 414 million therms and operating profit  from £39.6 million to £130.2 million.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: We also have increased output from gas-fired power stations and from renewable energy. The closures of Units 1  and 2 at Ferrybridge and Uskmouth, however, clearly means our total output from coal-fired stations will never  again return to the levels seen in 2012-2013.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: Despite the closure of Ferrybridge and Uskmouth, we still have 11.6 gigawatts of capacity, the most diverse fleet in  the market, flexible [ph] plant (23:42) and a strong engineering capability to maximize plant availability. We'll be  adding to our capacity and operation later this year when the 460 megawatt CCGT at Great Island in County  Wexford is commissioned. All of this gives us a Generation portfolio with a real long-term value.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: In GB, however, the sustained impact of plant closures and difficult market conditions mean there is a continuing  debate about security of supply. There's no doubt, as Ofgem puts it, that the risks to the security of supply over the  next few winters have increased. That said, the Energy Act 2013, which enjoyed broad support across the political  spectrum, effectively gives the UK's Department of Energy and Climate Change clear responsibility [ph] and hold  (24:32) the security of supply, including the creation of a mechanism to support generating capacity.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: Looking at our thermal plants in GB, we've wholly owned thermal assets that can play an important part in  keeping the lights on. Fiddler's Ferry where all four units continue to operate; Ferrybridge Units 3 and 4; next to  which we're also building our first multi-fuel plant, Medway, which has benefited from a £48 million investment  in reliability and flexibility; and Peterhead which has just entered into a voltage response contract with National  Grid.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: In addition, the investment in Keadby in 2012-2013 means that if it should be brought back to generate electricity  in the future, it will be out to operate in a more flexible and efficient way. In saying this, I don't want give DECC,  National Grid or anyone else any grounds for complacency because there aren't any. Both the supplemental  balancing reserve and the capacity market has to be introduced in an effective and timely way. In the meantime,  we'll do everything we can to make sure that Fiddler's, Ferrybridge, Medway and Peterhead are all available to  operate as and when needed in the run-up to the next winter.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: Our renewable assets have a part to play in security of supply as well. We have 300 megawatts of pumped storage  at Foyers and over 1,000 megawatts of flexible hydroelectricity. The energy contribution of wind farms is  important as well. In 2013-2014, for example, Greater Gabbard on its own produced a total of 1.9 terawatt hours  of electricity.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: Our capital spend on renewables peaked at £852 million in 2011-2012. And since then, we scaled back spend to  focus our development work on the best available projects, delivering the greatest amount of energy. We currently  have onshore wind projects under construction or nearing completion totaling 250 megawatts. In addition, we  have projects totaling over 600 megawatts at advanced stages of the planning process. All of these, however, come  into the optional category and will be financed at least in part by the asset disposals we described in March.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: We've also scaled back our ambitions in offshore wind and our decision to focus on the 664-megawatt Beatrice  project has been vindicated by DECC's announcement that it has been successful in securing an early Contracts for  Difference. This decision means we can continue to work through the issues on Beatrice and advance to the final  investment decision in 2016, by which time we don't expect our stake in the project to be any more than 50%.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: Our approach to renewables is an example of our wider approach to managing the business as a whole, simplifying  what we're doing to focus on what's important. As an energy company, SSE has huge responsibility. We're  entrusted to deliver the best possible service to customers and invest into our assets for the future energy needs of  the country. By doing this, we're able to pay dividends to the shareholders who invest in us. To maximize our  ability to pay dividends, we maintain a balanced range of businesses, operational and investment efficiency and  strong financial management. I believe we demonstrated in March and again today that delivering the right  decisions to the customers now puts us in a better position to deliver the dividends that investors are looking for  in the future.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: The energy sector has undergone massive changes since the first year on this chart. In each of the 15 years since  1999, we've delivered a real dividend increase. We acknowledged in March that dividend growth in the next few  years may be a bit slower than it was in the past, but be in no doubt that we're still focusing on delivering growth  that at least matches RPI inflation and thereby giving shareholders a fair return on the investment they're making  in the future energy needs of Britain and Ireland. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Jamie R. Tunnicliffe
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Thank you. Jamie Tunnicliffe from Redburn. Could you just explain the rationale behind in part linking the  impairment on the Generation, the thermal generation asset to the introduction of capacity market?

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: I think, Jamie, you're referring to – it's only one part of five or six kind of issues that [indiscernible] (29:51) that  we had impairment. Bigger factor is the carbon price [indiscernible] (29:55) and the impact that has on coal plant.  Additional factor of the age of the plant and the cash cost of keeping that plant running have an impact. So I  wouldn't read too much into the capacity market. It's one factor, but it's not one a significant factor. I think if you  look at impairment as an accounting definition, we have to justify the good value that we have in the balance sheet  with good calculation. And really, the coal plant has taken a fair [indiscernible] (30:32) of the sort of impairment  charge that we have taken this year.

texts.speaker: Mark A. Freshney
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Hi. Mark Freshney from Credit Suisse. Back at the end of March, you announced the price freeze through to at  least early 2016. And at the same time, you acknowledged you'd hedged out a lot more of your fossil fuels than you  might otherwise do to provide certainty over the positive margins. Since then, I think the forward curves have  come down pretty substantially or certainly the spot has come down pretty substantially, should I say. Are you  finding that's putting you at a disadvantage versus competitors? And are you finding that you're continuing to lose  accounts as [indiscernible] (31:20)?

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: We are continuing to lose accounts. So, we're seeing a steady trickle of people away. I think you're right in your  assertion around the market. Short-term prices on the back of mild weather and high storage across the Europe  have been relatively low. We've seeing gas prices drop off more than we'd expected. But against that, we're  providing longer-term certainty, and indeed quite a furor that one or two companies created by going several  thousand pounds a few weeks ago, within two weeks ago, they put their prices up last week. We've seen a couple of  smaller companies put their prices up.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: They've got clear price pressures. I suspect at least from the future in the wrong direction and gas prices might go  in a very, very different place. We clearly acknowledge what we did, which we thought was right for consumers,  and we acknowledge that there were some risk if energy markets traded down, and we ended up with more  competition.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: In the shorter term, we are in the competition, a bit more competition. People have been able to buy slugs of gas,  but at least this summer, more slugs of gas at slightly cheaper prices, and that's the challenge that we'll have to  meet, I suppose going into a CMA process and looking at the number of customers that we've got in the market as  you think it's healthy to have a reasonably vibrant smaller part of the market that's growing from less than 1% of  domestic customers to 5% or 6%. And overall, I'm not worried about or not currently worried about the level of  losses that we're seeing.

texts.speaker: Dominic C. Nash
texts.profession: Analyst, Macquarie Capital (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And secondly, could you just – do you have the breakdown what CCGT loss is this year, and is it still what you  expect from cash flow?

texts.speaker: Hon Robert Smith
texts.profession: Chairman, SSE Plc
texts.text: Yes, well, I'll let Gregor do the detailed figures, that whether we've got the CCGT loss to hand or, when he said –  he's seriously calculating now, I suspect, or hopefully. Sorry.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: If we look at Electricity Distribution last year, the Price Control, we'd expect to be around that kind – just under  the kind of 10%. And as a real number, we're going to use the numbers that National Grid [ph] use, we use (35:04)  quite often use. And remember, Ofgem themselves says good, efficient operators should have the capability of  making double-digit RORE returns.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: Transmission will be a bit higher than that, and Gas Distribution with further efficiencies coming through, will be  a bit higher than that, in a  low double-digit RORE. And as you'd expect, that's what you'd expect for efficient  operators.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: In terms of the CCGT loss, it's more of a complex analysis, because we [indiscernible] (35:38) and from Seabank  and Marchwood, we've got – we had Peterhead last year in the balance in market, really got Keadby mothballed  and [indiscernible] (35:50) come back. I would say it's in the high tens of millions. Not going to give you a  number.

texts.speaker: Martin S. Brough
texts.profession: Analyst, Deutsche Bank AG (Broker UK)
texts.text: Hi. Martin Brough from Deutsche Bank. Just in terms of the scope of the CMA inquiry, you say, on the  competitive side, it should be a relatively broad scope and address all of the relevant issues. But does that mean  that you don't want Ofgem to make the reference [ph] executive state (36:15)? Because if Ofgem makes the  reference, it is purely going to be focused on competition issues. They're not really going to be explicitly able to  take into account issues around climate change, environment, security of supply, vulnerable customers. And your  submissions really will have to focus on just the competition issues. Are you happy with that scope, or would you  rather broader public interest issues are put into the mix on the terms of reference?

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: No. I think we'd be perfectly happy with that scope, but the key is to actually get into, not only residential  customers, but all customers in the UK and also look at the competitive markets that are feeding into that, to  things like storage, gas production, generation and all the rest of it. That was the point that we were making, not  necessarily that we have to look at every public interest issue, because I think sometimes that's best left to  [indiscernible] (37:05) politicians and they should clearly put that in one plate. But it's just not the focus. I don't  think it's right just to focus on, let's say, nine or 10 suppliers. We should look at the generators as well.

texts.speaker: Ashley M. Thomas
texts.profession: Analyst, Société Générale SA (Broker)
texts.text: And two follow-up ones. Drax has been downbeat on the outlook for ROC prices for the current compliance  period. Are you anticipating any future weakness in ROC prices?

texts.speaker: Hon Robert Smith
texts.profession: Chairman, SSE Plc
texts.text: Gentlemen, just to the right then I'll come to you. Robby, go ahead.  Bobby Chada  Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc  Q  Yes. Sorry. Bobby Chada from Morgan Stanley. On the capacity market, I know it's, in many ways it's early days.  But also, the first option is not that far away. So do you have a feel for which part of your thermal fleet you will feel  comfortable bidding into the capacity market given the penalty regime and the higher price taker threshold that  was just set?

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: So therefore, I do have a genuine concern which I'll pass it on to the government and the regulator around the  capacity market or capacity auctions happening in December. They're very committed to that timeframe because I  just wonder whether that'll be effective. And I think that's the concern that they're slightly surprised about – but –  and you would expect this from this particular treasury manager to say when he said [ph] risk that priced it in  (41:42). I'm just not sure that in the same way this country appears to have done on nuclear. We just sort of throw  more money at the [indiscernible] (41:50) to price in additional risk.

texts.speaker: Peter J. Atherton
texts.profession: Analyst, Liberum Capital Ltd.
texts.text: And what did you make of Centrica's decision to put its three large gas fired power stations up for sale? Do you see  this as a sort of shakeout of the market that ultimately will be helpful or perhaps unhelpful because it might  fragment ownership even more and are you considering bidding for them?

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: No. Absolutely not, Robert. Absolutely not. So Centrica, right, so Centrica have their own strategies, their own  things, I think they feel like – or to me, they look they feel like they're not – have not done too well as investment  in the UK, it's all about gas storage, it's all about offshore wind. They're not naturally so much of a generator. They  appear to be moving more into the E&P space. That's my feeling. But obviously, most of their board will have  probably left by the end of this year. Most of the board who were there 12 months ago will have left by the end of  the year. So therefore, what their strategies going forward, I don't know. The new people coming in will probably  determine that.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: So them selling out the gas-fired power stations, obviously, Gregor said earlier in answer to question, despite  mothballing, we're still losing money on gas-fired power stations. We do remain committed to generation in the  UK. We do believe in it in the long term. We do also believe it's a key part of what we play in the security-of-supply  debate, and we do believe they'll be valued.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: In terms of whether we'll be bidding for it or not, I'm not entirely sure who's selling it or what the process is. We  are probably – we will probably think about whether there is anything of interest there for us, but we haven't  made any decisions on that yet. But I wouldn't discount the fact that we will look at whatever is there, if there's  something that makes sense for us strategically. But we've not signaled to anybody that we're going to do that.  This will be the first time we've commented on the matter. But something [indiscernible] (49:28) in the energy  market in the UK as core business, we'd probably think about it.

texts.speaker: Lakis Athanasiou
texts.profession: Analyst, Agency Partners LLP
texts.text: Second question on efficiency trend in GB domestic in electricity and gas, very difficult, obviously, to unravel the  weather impact, but it seems to me there might be an acceleration in electricity and slowdown in gas, is that what  you're seeing and what should [indiscernible] (50:20) also on the gas figures, could you confirm that we are pretty  much in line or even slightly above normalized weather of the gas over 2013-2014?

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: On efficiency trends in GB market, and I'll make a couple of comments, and then Gregor can probably correct me  if I get my numbers wrong, yes, I think we're continuing to see energy efficiency driving down, on a weather- corrected basis, the best we can tell. Consumption, I'm not sure whether electricity is accelerating. Electricity has  gone down as well probably a bit more than we might've thought, and I think gas is continuing – I think gas when  we look at it to try and understand what the gas numbers are, a lot of it's gas boilers and thing like that, and you're  just continuing to see gas boilers and insulation and things like that move it forward. We've clearly seen warmer  weather for 2013-2014, the first part of calendar 2014, which is obviously our last quarter and indeed April, which  I presume is partly right, then it should come out from another downgrade, but clearly, being warm, and that was  part of the reason why our Retail numbers were down. So, we've definitely seen warmer weather. And 2013-2014  overall was definitely warmer overall than 2012-2013.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: On an underlying basis if you look at the chart, the assumptions on a normalized basis was pretty close to  normalized, but the spacing was significantly different, which has an impact of – the last three months of the  winter was particularly warm, and that had a distorting effect on the numbers. Yes.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: So, no, there's no factor like that as I currently see affecting the guidance that we gave on the 26th of March, and  that we essentially reiterate, or don't change sitting here today. But I suppose we're seeing a lot of competition in  the market over short-term fixes, because people are buying [ph] flex system again, (54:14) particularly the  smaller companies. I'll take 25,000 customers on with a slug of cheap summer gas because the price is £0.50,  whereas it was £0.55 not very long ago. And you do see, we were obviously trying to at least offer something to  people around some of those [indiscernible] (54:33). But we have no reason to believe currently on what we're  seeing, and the trends we're seeing, that would change our guidance [indiscernible] (54:40).

texts.speaker: Iain S. Turner
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane Ltd.
texts.text: Thanks. It's Iain Turner from Exane. Let me ask you a couple of questions. Firstly on, again on your write-downs.  You've taken a write-down against Gas Storage. Is that Hornsea or Aldbrough or both? A little bit more color on  that?

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director, SSE Plc
texts.text: The Gas Storage rates are related to Hornsea, mainly because you've got that winter-summer differential has been  [indiscernible] (57:38) big impact. And bear in mind, we've seen an £8 million reduction in profitability of the Gas  Storage business and it's going to be broadly flat for 2014-2015. You would expect us to be taking an impairment.  There's an argument as to whether that impairment could have been bigger. But we believe these assets  strategically are important for SSE, and strategically important for the UK as a whole. We think value will come  back at a later date.

texts.speaker: Jamie R. Tunnicliffe
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Yes. Jamie Tunnicliffe from Redburn. Are you worried about the perverse incentive of a capacity market, in that it  may mean unprofitable thermal plants stays on the system longer in the hope of being bailed out? And are you  seeing any evidence to support or contradict that?

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive, SSE Plc
texts.text: So I think there's quite a bit of uncertainty at the moment over how you make future investments, and yet people  are probably balancing up short run cash losses on plants versus, can I get enough out of the plants going  forward? That's quite difficult as well, with something like the carbon price support mechanism in place, which is  clearly a tax and which is limited uncertainty, I think that would force coal plants to close. It doesn't necessarily  incentivize people to go and do renewables.

file: SSEL - Q4 2015 Earnings Call 20May2015 400 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 20-May-15.pdf

texts.speaker: Hon Robert Smith
texts.profession: Chairman
texts.text: Through capital investment of over £12 billion in the last 10 years, we've transformed SSE's asset base and  extended it to Ireland, all the while maintaining the balance streams of energy businesses that have been SSE's  hallmark from day one.

texts.speaker: Hon Robert Smith
texts.profession: Chairman
texts.text: Now, politics and legislation have loomed large throughout my time as Chairman. No fewer than eight energy  ministers and seven energy-related acts of parliaments since I took the Chair in 2005. And throughout that time,  SSE has been a constructive and progressive contributor to energy policy debates. And I am very proud to have  been associated with a company that's a living-wage employer and, officially, a [ph] fair tight spear (01:39)

texts.speaker: Hon Robert Smith
texts.profession: Chairman
texts.text: In a challenging business environment, it's vital that companies have a clear purpose, clear strategy and a clear  financial objective. SSE has all of these. Our established core purpose is to provide the energy people need in a  reliable and sustainable way. At its heart our strategy is to deliver the efficient operational and investment in a  balanced range of energy businesses in the UK and Ireland.

texts.speaker: Hon Robert Smith
texts.profession: Chairman
texts.text: Now whatever way you look at it, 2015 will be an important year for energy businesses with the new UK  government taking forward its energy policy commitments and the Competition and Markets Authority ma king  progress towards the conclusion of its market investigation.

texts.speaker: Hon Robert Smith
texts.profession: Chairman
texts.text: The combination of these events is not without risk. But it does mean there's an opportunity for the emergence of  a more coherent and enduring framework for the energy sector, and I know that SSE will continue to be a positive  contributor to the work of the UK government and the [ph] CME (4:45)

texts.speaker: Hon Robert Smith
texts.profession: Chairman
texts.text: 2014-2015 financial year was expected to present a number of major challenges and it sure did. Intervention in  Wholesale, regulation in Networks, and competition in Retail and in Enterprise. Despite these challenges, we've  maintained our record of annual dividend growth. We've delivered a solid performance on adjusted earnings per  share and profit before tax. We've invested £1.48 billion in assets in the UK and Ireland, and we've extended our  household energy price freeze having cut prices twice in the last 15 months.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: The exceptional charges relate mainly to businesses in our Wholesale segment, with 46% of the total being  impairments relating to Ferrybridge and Fiddler's Ferry, 24% being impairments relating to the Aldbrough gas  storage facility, and 15% relating to our E&P assets. We did, however, benefit from exceptional credits relating to  £7 5 million of gains from assets held for sale on 31 March 2014.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: Looking now at our three business segments. In Wholesale, operating profit is down by around a quarter to  £47 3.8 million mainly through tough market conditions, lower electricity output from coal and wind, and lower  day ahead prices for gas production. This also provides some context for the difficult decision on Ferrybridge  which we also announced this morning.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: In Networks, operating profit is up almost 2% to £936.8 million with the drop in electricity distribution [ph] being  (8:00) more than offset by the benefits from our long-term investment in transmission. And in Retail, the  operating profit of £456.8 million reflects a strong focus on performance and cost efficiencies, which helped  return energy supply and profit around the level reported in 2012-2013. It equates to £69 for a typical dual fuel  customer. Retail profit also includes £88 million attributable to our enterprise and our energy-related services  businesses.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: Our asset base benefited from capital and investment spend in the year of £1.48 billion, with Networks accounting  for just over half of that. This company has always had a strong and diverse asset base. And over the la st five  years, we've added to it with an increase of $2.4 billion in the RAV of our Networks, completion of almost 800  megawatts of new onshore wind, completion of 350 megawatts of new offshore wind, and completion of the new  CCGT in Ireland.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: We expect that our capital and investment spend in this new financial year will be around £1.75 billion before  proceeds from disposals. We also expect the trend towards Networks to continue, with them accounting for  around half of the total. While the exact phasing and value of CapEx and disposals could vary, we're still looking at  a CapEx program of around £5.5 billion net across the four years to March 2018. This includes committed spend  on maintenance, projects in construction and regulated networks like Caithness and Moray. And optional for new  assets under development such as onshore wind farms that will be committed if [ph] turns out (12:42) clearly  greater than the cost of capital.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: In addition, we have a strong portfolio of projects at earlier stages of development. When it comes to optional  spend on new assets, we will recycle capital from disposals to stay in line with the targeted £5.5 billion net spend.  In line with our value program, we currently expect to secure financial benefit of just over £1 billion from the  disposal of non-core assets and businesses which has already secured £475 million and the sale of existing  onshore wind farms in development.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: We've already agreed to sell 16 megawatts at Langhope Rig before the main disposal program is even underway.  This will enable us to recycle capital from current assets where greater value can be secured from investing in new  ones.

texts.speaker: Gregor Alexander
texts.profession: Finance Director
texts.text: Investment in distribution was £328 million, and the total for the five-year price control to March 2015 was just  over £1.4 billion. This follows spend of just under £1.3 billion in the previous price control. Investment like this  helps keep the lights on for customers, and that's our first priority. One example of this is our investment in smart  fuses to improve fault detection and supply restoration. And in March, we achieved the fastest ever restoration of  supplies following a Category 2 weather event in the north of Scotland.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Our goals over the last year have been to deliver good operational performance for customers, deliver solid  financial results for investors and ensure SSE is well-positioned to succeed in a changing sector. Much change is  driven by politics and regulation. And we've been contending with the combination of Ofgem's distribution price  control process, as Gregor had described; the first ever auction for generation capacity; the CMA energy market  investigation; and the extended buildup to the UK general election.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: This means that 2015 will be an important year for energy businesses, with a new UK government taking forward  its energy policy commitments and the CMA making progress towards the conclusion of its market's investigation.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: As Robert said, the combination of these events is not without risk. But it means there is a good opportunity to  create a more coherent and enduring framework for the energy sector. SSE will continue to contribute positively  to the work of the CMA and the new UK government. The interim findings of the CMA are not now expected for  another month or so. And it's important to remember, they will then be the subject to more analysis and  consultation before the final report is published around the end of this year.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Our goal is to secure a coherent and enduring framework for the energy sector on the basis that they are soundly - based, right for the industry and its investors, and most importantly of all, customers. It's encouraging that the  new UK government is committed to supporting the CMA.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Much of the political and regulatory debate will continue to focus on energy supply. Over the last couple of years,  we've seen particularly competitive market conditions and our customer account numbers fell by 5.7% over the  year to £8.58 million. We have, however, maintained a strong focus on operational and financial efficiencies. And  this helped operating profit in Retail recover to the level seen two years ago.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Looking at Energy Supply, our profit margin was 4.6%, equating to £69 for typical dual fuel customer. We think  this is a reasonable return for an efficient operator and the lowest cost base among the leading suppliers. Last  month's cut in household gas prices however, means we expect Energy Supply operating profit to fall in this new  financial year.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: With a dynamic market and more than 20 competitors, we expect customer numbers to continue to decline in the  short-term, but we have a clear plan to help us achieve stability and trust for the long-term. It's based on  providing customers with value for money, peace of mind and sector-leading service. In support of this plan, we've  cut household prices twice in 15 months, extended our household energy price freeze until at least July 2016.  Started a long-term brand-building program, launched an industry-leading offer on broadband in line with our  commitment to offer customers more, actively apply the principles of treating customers fairly, taking a series of  substantive steps to improve customer service and invest in the fundamental overhaul of digital channels for our  customers.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: This, along with the smart meter rollout, has required investment amounting to £109.6 million during the year to  enhance customer service and install smart meters. We believe that this plan will put us in a strong position to  compete effectively as the shape of the retail energy market becomes clearer over the coming year. We think it's  the right plan for the long-term.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Retail now includes the B2B enterprise business. It's just over a year since we brought together SSE services in  competitive markets for industrial, commercial and public sector customers under the leadership of Jim  McPhillimy. Bringing together these businesses, supported by dedicated relationship management function,  complemented by the energy solutions business we acquired last summer, gives these customers one point of  contact for their energy and telecom's needs.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Including a disposal gain, the business earned £70.4 million in operating profit in the last financial year. As  customers' energy management and infrastructure requirements evolve, we believe we've created a business that  has a potential to achieve significant and sustainable growth.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: I'll now turn to Wholesale. Our Wholesale businesses provide energy and related services for energy market  participants in GB and Ireland. And in recent years, they've been impacted by long-term trends including an  uncertain macroeconomic picture, volatile commodity prices, increasing competition, government intervention  and the continued drive to a low-carbon economy.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: This has affected thermal generation and gas production assets, in particular, and contributed to two features of  this morning's results: a fall of 25.3% in operating profit in the Wholesale segment, and exceptional challenges of  £685.9 million relating to coal-fired power stations and gas storage and gas production assets.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Our thermal generation assets were again loss making during the year. And the trends I describe d plus our  commitment to value meant we had no alternative but to review them. We have to ensure that SSE retains the  right balance of assets, contracts and auctions for future development. These trends have had a particular impact  on our coal-fired power stations, which are increasingly expensive to maintain and subject to major  environmental legislation and regulation. Against this background, we've concluded that we should not reopen  Unit 4 at Ferrybridge, where equipment was badly damaged during last summer's fire. We've also concluded that  Unit 3 should be closed by the end of the current financial year, which will mark the end of coal-fired generation  at the station.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: This was a difficult decision to take because of its impact on the people who work at the station and their families,  but it was also the right decision to take. Financially, it costs over £50 million a year simply to keep a station like  Ferrybridge open. Environmentally, it is a major emitter of CO2, and therefore, a contentious source of electricity.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Ferrybridge will, of course, remain an active electricity generation site with the forthcoming commissioning of the  £300 million multi-fuel plant. The financial and environmental issues also apply at Fiddler's Ferry. But unlike  Ferrybridge, the majority of the plant there has a capacity contract for a year from October 2018, and it's our  intention to submit the plans into the forthcoming auction for providing capacity from 2019. We'll reassess the  options for Fiddler's Ferry after the outcome of that auction is known.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: All of this is consistent with our long-established strategy of moving towards a lower carbon generation portfolio,  weighted towards gas and renewables. Although gas-fired generation has struggled financially in recent years, it  will play an increasingly central role in meeting the company's electricity needs.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: SSE's gas-fired power stations have underlying quality and value in which we've continued to invest. They're  supported by a strong engineering capability, which can maximize plant's availability and flexibility. In terms of  our wholly-owned plant, Peterhead is undergoing a £15 million investment program that will improve its  flexibility, allowing it to operate in the market at up to 400 -megawatts from this winter. And it's also benefiting  from voltage contracts with National Grid.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Medway and Keadby have benefited from a combined investment of over £100 million to boost their reliability  and flexibility. And we've recently decided to bring Keadby out of deep mothball, so it have the option of returning  to service in the coming winter. The future looks more positive for Keadby and Medway, which both secure  contracts to provide capacity in the 2018 realm. And for Peterhead as well, where the Carbon Capture and Storage  project is also making good progress.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: New CCGT development is another issue, however. And our commitment to value means we don't intend to  commit any further investment in the projects at Abernedd, Keadby and Seabank unless they're successful in the  future capacity market auction process.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: SSE had developed a quality portfolio of renewable energy assets across the UK and Ireland with hydro, onshore  wind and offshore wind and with assets in Scotland, England and Ireland. As Gregor said earlier, in the last five  years alone, we've completed just under 800 megawatts of new onshore wind and 350 megawatts of new offshore  wind.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: The net result is that we have a renewables portfolio that is diverse in terms of technology, location and  jurisdiction. There are, however, three things we need to take into account, our disciplined approach to capital  investment, and in particular, a planned net spend of £5.5 billion for the four years through 2018; avoiding over- dependency on particular fuels or technologies, especially where they required government-sponsored support;  and the introduction of competition for support through CfDs which will change the way projects are developed  and constructed.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: For these reasons, we're selling existing onshore wind farms and developments in order to recycle capital. And  we've already agreed to sell 16 megawatts at Langhope Rig before the main disposal program has got underway.  We're targeting at least £500 million of proceeds from that program and we're planning to recycle the capital  where we believe greater value can be secured from investing in new assets.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: In the meantime, we have over 280 megawatts of onshore wind farm capacity under construction at four sites in  Scotland and Ireland. This means we're well placed to add new capacity before the  RO deadline of 2017 and well  placed to compete for CfDs there afterwards.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Looking offshore, the Beatrice project, in which we now have a 50% stake, already has an early CfD, and we're  continuing to do the work needed to maintain progress towards a final investment decision in 2016. Whatever the  support mechanism and however the government chooses to phase out our support for onshore wind, the test for  all our projects is the same. Can they earn returns that are clearly greater than the cost of capital and  can they be  funded within the capital program we defined last March.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: One asset that has already passed these two tests is the new CCGT at Great Island. The plant is now in full  commercial operation and completion costs have out-turned close to £125 million over the three years since the  development was acquired. And while capacity is constrained to 431 megawatts for now, it will be the cleanest,  most efficient and reliable gas power plant on the Irish grid.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Like GB, the market in Ireland is already undergoing significant change, with planned reform of a Single  Electricity Market being published in September. We have a Dublin-based team that is fully engaged in the  regulatory and policy processes. And while change always brings both risk and opportunities,  we're comfortable  with the reform process so far.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: It's now five years since SSE first invested in gas production assets and the time since then, we've built up a  portfolio of assets with estimated reserves in excess of 2.2 billion therms at March 31 this year. Clearly, lower  wholesale gas prices have taken their toll on profitability with operating profit down to £37 million. But as we said  at the interims, we'll look at gas-weighted opportunities to increase our reserve base in line with our investment  criteria and financial discipline.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Financial discipline is key because the business faces continuing challenges. By the end of this financial year, we  will have the outcome of the CMA's look at the distribution price control, start of implementation of the  new  government's energy policies and provisional findings and potential remedies in the CMA market investigation.  They all present a degree of uncertainty, but they also provide an opportunity to achieve a stable policy and  regulatory framework that give consumers confidence, allows regulators to regulate and encourages investors to  invest in the energy market. In such an environment, there will be significant opportunities for growth.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: On top of this, we've successfully commissioned the CCGT at Great Island. We focused our distribution business  on its customers, secured Ofgem approval for the Caithness-Moray link, extended our price freeze to GB  household customers, invested in the modernization of our energy supply business, launched our integrated B2B  business Enterprise, maintained a strong pipeline of options for future investments, and reduced the level of our  net debt and its cost with the issue of hybrid capital securities.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Working with Richard, we'll continue to be focused on delivering annual dividend growth that at least matches  RPI inflation and taking the long-term decisions so that shareholders continue to receive a fair return on the  investment they have made and are making in the future energy needs of Britain and Ireland. Thank you .

texts.speaker: Iain S. Turner
texts.profession: Exane Ltd.
texts.text: Thanks. It's Iain Turner from Exane. Can I just ask where you think we are in terms of onshore wind now with the  new government? Obviously, they've got this policy to not do any more or not subsidize any more, and how that  relates between England and Scotland as well? And then, if you look forward to, sort of, two years or three years,  what do you think you'll be investing in assuming there is a [ph] lock (36:55) on onshore wind? Is it just networks  or is there something else you'll be investing in? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Y eah. I think onshore wind Conservatives have clearly got a mandate on that. And they're going to come out with  some sort of policy. I think we've got to help them work through that. Onshore wind itself is attractive low cost  form of renewables. I think there were targets that they want to meet by 2020 and possibly beyond. And so,  they're going to have to think about how they phase in the policies that they want to put in place. So we'll clearly  be interested in that. We've got a strong pipeline over the next three years or four years to build out that we think  we'll still be allowed to go through because we received planning information, and it's clearly there [indiscernible]  (37 :35) awarded a CfD.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: Beyond that, we'll have to see. I think you make an interesting point about England and Scotland, what's the  policy there to essentially try to stem any build in England, but actually with the S&P having such a strong  position in Scotland and being very, very committed to renewable, is there any differentiation in policy around the  regions of the UK, Scotland, Wales, England, Ireland, et cetera, it'll certainly be interesting to see. We don't know,  but we'll certainly be engaging positively with government on that deck as we go forward.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
texts.text: I think on the second question of other investments, as I said, I think we have a strong pipeline currently for the  next few years. Networks, again, is a strong pipeline. At the end of this decade, it'll be interesting to see what the  energy system needs in this country. Clearly, on the generation side, government is controlling who's building  what. They're awarding CfDs whether that'd be for nuclear, onshore wind, now offshore wind. And we'll have to  work with the current government, I think, to see what those opportunities are.

texts.speaker: Alistair Phillips-Davies
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director
