texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: I will begin with our quarter highlights, Ricardo will present our third quarter financial results and I will then  conclude with an update on our renewables strategy and business outlook.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: We achieved total vessel utilization of 85%, our highest quarter since 2014. The third quarter is usually our  busiest operationally due to favorable weather condition in the North Sea. However, the weather at Offshore  Germany has been more challenging than expected causing some delays on the Borkum II wind farm project. We  announced four awards in the quarter resulting in $800 million of awards and escalation and book-to-bill ratio of  0.7.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Seven Seas, Seven Pacific and Seven Eagle have finished their campaigns with only Simar Esperança remain in  country to complete her scope. In Australia, the Cooper Sole project has commenced its offshore phase with  Seven Oceans transporting 64 kilometers of 12-inch pipeline. Skandi Acergy will install the associated umbilical  later in the year. The Greater Western Flank project, also in Australia, made good progress too.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: We announced the award of the Aerfugl project, Offshore Norway, late last year and also offshore operation do  not done until 2019, good progress has been made in upgrading our [indiscernible] (03:45) base to accommodate  Electrically Heat Traced Flowline, one of the new technologies developed by Subsea 7.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Offshore Germany, the EPCI Borkum II project continued with monopod installation, but progress was hampered  by adverse weather. 17 of the 32 pipes were installed in the quarter with Seven Borealis intervening after the  quarter-end to accelerate operations and mitigate the impact of challenging weather conditions. This is a very  good example of the versatility of the fleet between SURF and Renewables business units which is one of our  competitive advantage.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Offshore UK, the final 6 jackets and 33 inter-array cables were installed on the Beatrice wind farm project, which  was substantially completed in the year. Commercial discussion with our client on this project have also been  successfully completed.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Within our i-Tech Services business unit, good progress was made in the quarter on our Life of Field contract in  the North Sea and Offshore Azerbaijan. One of our technology focus area is on autonomy and remote ROV  operation. Our new onshore pilot centers will be soon operational in Stavanger and Aberdeen. This will enable  offshore ROV operation to be piloted by onshore personnel. It will not only have a significant impact on cost  reduction for our clients, it's also one of the key components of our sustainability program which aims at reducing  emissions and the potential impact of offshore operation on climate change.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: The four new projects announced in the third quarter illustrates the wide range of solutions that Subsea 7 can  provide to its clients. The Buzzard Phase 2 project, a bundled solution of Offshore UK was awarded by Nexen.  Also, of the cost of the UK, the Triton Knoll wind farm projects was awarded to Subsea 7's Renewables and  Heavy Lifting business unit. We have also announced the award of a substantial conventional project. However,  due to contractual obligation, we are unable to share any further detail on the award at this time.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Net operating income was $17 million, which included allowances for additional weather-related installation delays  on the Borkum II contract. This adversely impacted profitability of the project and the business unit in the quarter.  A $3 million loss was reported in the corporate business unit.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Capital expenditure of $74 million included a milestone payment of approximately $50 million relating to Seven  Vega, our new reeled pipe lay vessel which is under construction. The vessel is due for delivery early in 2020 in  time to meet the increased demand for reeled pipe lay campaigns already booked in our backlog.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: We expect absolute adjusted EBITDA to be lower than 2018 inclusive of the uplift of between $100 million and  $110 million applied to 2019 as a result of the implementation of IFRS 16. The forecast reduced adjusted EBITDA  reflects the impact of lower pricing on projects signed in the downturn and minimal contribution from Renewables  and Heavy Lifting following completion of the batteries and Borkum II projects.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Thank you, Ricardo. Turning to slide 12, I would like now to provide further insights into our Renewables and  Heavy Lifting business. Offshore wind projects follow similar contracting models of the oil and gas industry. Most  contracts can be categorized as either an engineering, procurement, construction and installation contract, EPCI,  or the transport and installation contract, T&I.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Historically, the predominant model has been T&I, but we expect to see more EPCI contracts in the future. This  quarter, the Beatrice project was substantially completed. This multiyear EPCI project was the largest to be  executed in the North Sea by Subsea 7 at over $1 billion. Its success was confirmed by our clients, achieving first  power as scheduled in July.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: We hear from our clients that our ability to project, manage and derisk this last projects, while ensuring on-time  delivery, is one of the key differentiators of Subsea 7 in the renewable market. The outlook for 2019 is  challenging. For various reasons, the last project awards to market have been delayed and we do not currently  expect to be active offshore on any large EPCI renewable project next year.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: There are some prospect next year for T&I projects, but we are forecasting much lower revenues compared to  recent years and low EBITDA. As we have shown previously in our oil and gas business, we are proactive and  plan to reduce our capacity in renewables to adapt to this near-term market conditions.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Capacity and cost reduction will be achieved while protecting our capability and expertise. This approach will  position our renewable business well to capture opportunities when the activity increases in the not-too-distant  future, and I remain optimistic regarding medium- and long-term prospects as we are seeing momentum on  projects, in particular in the UK, France and Taiwan.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: In our business model, we anticipate signing one large EPCI project every couple of years. The composition of  our reported revenues and profits will fluctuate depending on the type of work we are executing. New EPCI  awards won in 2019 are most likely to be executed offshore before second half of 2020.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Moving on to slide 13, the offshore wind market is growing at a healthy pace with double-digit average growth  forecast to Europe and worldwide supported by the lower levelized cost of energy. The 7 megawatts wind turbine  generator, which is the size we installed on the Beatrice field, will be superseded by a 10-megawatt turbine that  will be available to market in a few years, and even larger turbines under developments.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Larger turbine sizes require larger foundations. With a top lifting capacity of 5,000 ton, our fleet is well positioned  to take advantage as the enlarged scale of this turbine foundation differentiating Subsea 7 from our competitors.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: I will conclude with a review of our outlook. We have seen continued momentum in tieback projects being  awarded to the markets throughout 2018. Volume is recovering, and we expect this trend to continue in the years  to come. Looking into 2019, larger greenfield market awards are expected to complement this brownfield  development project. Improved utilization will follow 12 to 24 months after these awards when the offshore phases  commence, which will translate into pricing and margin improvements.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: In SURF, we have greater visibility on the timing of greenfield awards as invitations tender our receipt. Expected  awards to market include Mero, Sepia and Buzios project Offshore Brazil, SURF Golfinho and Rovuma Offshore  Mozambique, and the Bonga Southwest Project Offshore Nigeria. We also expected award to the market of some  large tiebacks project in 2019 including the Ichthys 2, Scarborough and Julimar project Offshore Australia. We  anticipate the next tranche of commercial projects Offshore Saudi Arabia to be awarded to the market in the next  two quarters.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: To summarize, Subsea 7 is well positioned for the cyclical recovery of the offshore oil and gas market later in  2019 and for the structural growth in offshore renewables. We provide our clients with first-class all-in  engagement and engineering to enable them to take profitable investment decision. We have successful alliance  and partnership to enable us to win more work on a negotiated basis. And our bespoke technology and efficient  cost base enable us to be competitively and win our fair share of markets award.

texts.speaker: James Evans
texts.profession: Analyst, Exane Ltd.
texts.text: All right. Good afternoon and thanks for taking my questions. Jean, thanks for the update on your offshore wind  strategy. Obviously, you've talked about pricing being under pressure, particularly in the SURF side. Just  wondered how you see things developing on the renewable side given the low activity. It seems like some of your  Dutch competitors have been relatively aggressive so far. So, should we think about pricing also being a little bit  trickier when we get these awards first coming through?

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Thanks, James. To answer your question on renewable, as we said, I mean, 2019 would be a transition year. And  there are may be some pressure on T&I tenders initially. But while the markets -- more project being awarded to  the industry, I'm confident that we're going to see the same thing as we see on the SURF side, which is a gradual  improvement over time.

texts.speaker: Robert Pulleyn
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: And then lastly, if I could just ask on this issue of tiebacks, obviously, the one's not awarded. How much visibility  do you have on when they're actually going to come? I understand the greenfields, these tenders come out a long  time in advance, but are these tiebacks also a long time in advance or are they relatively short notice as it were. If  you can add some color on that, that would be fantastic. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: I will take the first question and I will let John answer to the two other questions. What we are expecting on the  margin is fully in line with what we said previously. I mean, to have the margin improving, we need to see an  increase number of project to come to market. We are seeing that in tiebacks. We expect that to continue on the  tiebacks. We have more visibility on the greenfield.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: So when the greenfields are awarded to market and we expect more of these projects being awarded in 2019, we  will see an improvement at the margin. I would say overall the trend is going in the right direction. We need more  market award to accelerate the trends of improvement of margin, but it's going in the right direction.

texts.speaker: Michael Rae
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Yeah. Hi there. Two questions on Renewables, if I could. The first is just what's the expected cost of the capacity  reduction in that division both in cash terms? And if there are going to be any write downs there?

texts.speaker: John Evans
texts.profession: Chief Operating Officer, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Borkum is a EPCI contract in Germany, in shallow water in Germany. The engineering is complete, the  procurement is complete, and there are 32 monopiles and transition pieces to install. We have, as of midnight last  night, installed 26 monopiles. The main issue is the weather. The weather is leading to us finding it very slow  progress. So we've also taken the Borealis out there to have two big large heavy lift vessels. We can not only one  put the pile in, but the other one can to put the transition piece in.

texts.speaker: John Evans
texts.profession: Chief Operating Officer, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: We do expect to be complete at the end of the fourth quarter, but we are at the mercy of a deteriorating weather  window. So generally, we can put a pile in every day and we can put a transition piece in every day. So when the  weather windows open up, we are there and that's the reason we increased the fleet size, so when the weather  windows come, so we would expect by the time we release our quarter four figures, hopefully, to have this project  behind us.

texts.speaker: Michael Rae
texts.profession: Analyst, Redburn (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Okay. Okay. That's clear. And just to go back on the capacity reduction, it's just that if this happened in the SURF  side of the business, which is obviously much larger, it feels like you would get quite a lot of granularity in terms of  head count reduction and so on. But should I interpret what you're saying as it's not really big enough for that, it's  not material, it's not really big enough for a split in the model, et cetera, the cash cost?

texts.speaker: John Evans
texts.profession: Chief Operating Officer, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Yeah. I think this is a discussion purely by the Renewables and Heavy Lifting business. We did our adjustments,  as you well know, to the SURF business a long time ago. I think it's just too early to call it at this stage. Our  message I think is that, as you know, we adjust to market trends and we will adjust accordingly at the right time.

texts.speaker: Kevin Roger
texts.profession: Analyst, Kepler Cheuvreux SA
texts.text: And the second question, related. If we move outside the Renewables and that we focus ourself on your  traditional activity, the SURF and Conventional, it seems that, basically, you expect an increase in your revenue  for 2019 compared to 2018. I was wondering if you can give some granularity regarding your net operating  income for 2019 compared to 2018, just looking at this business line, please.

texts.speaker: John Evans
texts.profession: Chief Operating Officer, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: So, I'll do Beatrice first, Amy. Yes, we are physically complete offshore. We have some minor punch-list items  which we've agreed with the client that we will sort out in quarter two next year when the weather starts again to  be suitable. That doesn't need any of the big heavy construction vessels, just crew boats to do some minor  punch-list items. So, there is nothing substantial left to do on Beatrice as we stand here today.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Yes. And I will comment – I mean, regarding our expected improvement of margin over time post-2019 is based  on what we mentioned before. It's a combination of the existing ongoing work and growing work on the tiebacks;  the pickup of the conventional, in particular in Africa. We see sustain operation in – or increasing operation in  Middle East; and the number of projects or greenfield projects which will be in execution in 2021-2022 in our view  from what we know of the market here.

texts.speaker: Jean Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Regarding the impact on the project in Renewable in Q4, we are not giving specific information on projects. I  would just say that we said that the guidance is unchanged for the full year 2018 revenue and adjusted EBITDA  present margin for the group. So that give you an idea of where we will be.

texts.speaker: John Evans
texts.profession: Chief Operating Officer, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: As you said, Jean, it all starts with the flow of the large greenfield projects, which then takes up utilization which  then allows the margins to adjust. So, the discussion for each contractor for each project has to go through those  cycles with a view of how does it fit with the utilizations. And then from there, then the margin moves.

texts.speaker: Michael J. Alsford
texts.profession: Analyst, Citigroup Global Markets Ltd.
texts.text: And then just secondly, we've obviously talked a little bit about the good fleet utilization in the quarter. But I guess  if you look back at 1Q of this year, battery utilization was really low given the sort of the seasonal impact of North  Sea work. And I just wondered if you can give us some sense as to I guess how bad could it be in 4Q and 1Q  given that I guess that environment and given where we are in terms of utilization levels across the industry.  Thank you.

texts.speaker: John Evans
texts.profession: Chief Operating Officer, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: In terms of seasonality, Mike, we have quarter four, quarter one are the lowest seasonality periods for us. The  weather we've discussed that is impacting the industry at the moment. And the North Sea in particular means that  spot work is being delayed by certain clients. But the DSVs, we have [indiscernible] (51:34) working at the  moment. So what you normally see quarter four is that clients see opportunities where the weather is reasonably  okay and might get some inspection of their maintenance work done. The big greenfields and the big CapEx  contracts are all behind everybody for the year. So I think we'll see a seasonality like we normally see in, which is  quarter fourth, quarter one being relatively quiet.

texts.speaker: John Evans
texts.profession: Chief Operating Officer, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: [indiscernible] (53:35) question here I think, James, on the question about which will come back sooner rather  than later, well, I guess we see a more solid pipeline of SURF-related type projects through the early engagement  that we do the discussions we're having with clients. As we've mentioned many times, Renewables is quite a  lumpy business. These are quite large transactions which have a lot of local politics and permitting issues to get  through. So they're quite lumpy. And we're also seeing opportunities in the U.S. and Taiwan opening up, but  again the speed at which these new markets open up. So the view we have is that SURF has some clarity as to  all that's recurring. And renewables, we do see that there are opportunities for an epic award next year for work in  2020 and 2021.

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: So, what did happen in 2011? We progressed very well the engineering testing and procurement of the system. We  are pleased that we are building what we set out at the tender stage with full approval from our clients. But we  relied wrongly on the information we had from the authorities regarding the award of the environmental license  for Paraná spool and logistic base. You may remember that we got a preliminary license late 2010. This should  have lead to an automatic award of the final license. It did not happen. So, spooling operation will now be  performed in the Ubu base in 2012 and 2013, but at a higher cost, and with a negative impact on the project  schedule. All that has been including in the losses that we provisioned for in the $50 million.

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: We are working well with Petrobras to develop the best option. The new executive management of Petrobras, in a  meeting we had in Rio two weeks ago with José Formigli, made very clear that they consider Subsea 7 as one of  the key solution provider for their ambitious subsalt development plans.

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: In the Gulf of Mexico, the recommencement of the award of drilling permits should see an increase of activity with  contract award to the market in late 2012 and execution in late 2013 and 2014 in a market which remains  competitive.

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Turning now to Asia-Pacific, this is, as you know, a diverse territory from a geographical perspective. It is a market  which has had high expectations for many years and 2011 saw the award of the first of this large gas-driven project  Australia and Malaysia, I expect it in 2012 in a market, which remains competitive. We will remain selective on  the project we tender to ensure that we achieve the right returns.

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: In Brazil, we continue to see more opportunities ahead. In traditional deepwater in the Campos Basin as well as  with pre-salt developments. We expect to see further PLSV contracts award to the markets both for existing  contract renewal and new vessels to be built in Brazil. More largely, big project for pre-salt developments are  likely to come to award – to the market in 2012 and beyond.

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: We have in house today the next pre-salt tender which covers up to four fields. This is expected to be awarded to  the industry in the second part of 2012 with operation in 2014 and 2015. After which, a further run and tenders for  the next pre-salt development is expected to be issued by the client in late 2012. We believe that the buoy system  that we have designed for Guará-Lula and the experience acquired on this project positions us well to submit  competitive proposal with a right margin and acceptable risk level.

texts.speaker: Mick B. Pickup
texts.profession: Analyst, Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Okay. Can I just ask one very quick follow-up? I know Technip announced the other week a contract for gas  injection pipes on Guará-Lula. It looked to me as if that was part of your scope on there. Is part of the scope being  moved from you or am I getting this wrong?

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Yeah, I mean I heard the same comments from Technip. Just to give you some insight on that, I think it's a good  example of how we work with Petrobras. What happen is that Petrobras had to change the characteristic of the  fleet coming from the reservoir based on their latest information that they had or data that they had. So, the rigid  gas line design has to be modified.

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Petrobras has asked us to develop a long-term technical solution with the design of the buoy. And while we  perform this additional engineering work, they have moved forward with a temporary short life fix and both on  flexible gas riser from Technip. All that is obviously covered by operation order on our side. And when this new  design is finalized, we will reinstall rigid line on the system at a later stage.

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Yes, okay. I mean regarding the Montara project, it's a project, which is been executed by our joint venture, I mean  the SapuraAcergy. All the operation, the pipe-laying operation have been completed by the joint venture and is  based on the review of this operation that we recognize a loss in Q4, which was a small loss. The project is ongoing  with I would say more bread and butter operations with the Rockwater 2 and that will be with positive margin,  although it is not a very large project. So, altogether I'm not concerned with the future of this project and the  impact that it will have.

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Regarding Brazil, again we've been disappointed with a local problem we had in Brazil and the impact it had on  the schedule. I think one of the things to see for the future work is first we are going to be disciplined in the  number of jobs that we're going to bid and that will be based on our human resources and vessel availability and  part of the world and in particular our Paris organization for the EPIC contract. So, I'm comfortable that we have  what we need to bid these projects with an acceptable risk level.

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Regarding the North Sea backlog – yeah, I'm sorry I'm looking at-it's very similar to previous – go ahead, go  ahead.

texts.speaker: Simon Crowe
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: It's very similar to the previous years, there's nothing unusual about it. I think that was your question. So, we are  in a good place. And as we said, we've got some positive views on the North Sea for 2012, activity there is picking  up and bidding is – we're very busy. And the nature of the work is changing a little to more large scale and EPIC  type projects both in the U.K. and Norway.

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Another difference for the North Sea in 2012 and even more in 2013 is that we are phasing out of our backlog, the  project which were won before 2011 at lower margins. And so there are less and less of this project and they will be  mainly phased out in 2012.

texts.speaker: Henry M. Tarr
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International Ltd.
texts.text: One of the – a point to highlight on that, that at the same time, it has delayed the execution of the project and  therefore the progress has been slowed down. So, this work which will be executed a bit later, and while we are on  waiting on whether, it's good for the utilization of the vessel because we are paid for the waiting on weather, but  we don't have the added value of the project. So, that has to come a bit later too. So it's a combination of Deep  Panuke and very good utilization of the vessels being well protected by our contracts during the winter period in  the North Sea.

texts.speaker: Henry M. Tarr
texts.profession: Analyst, Goldman Sachs International Ltd.
texts.text: Okay, and thanks very much. Could I just add very quickly, you mentioned higher dry-docking this year. Are there  any major vessels out for dry-docking and what sort of impact could that have?

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Well, we have more dry-docking in 2012 than 2011. In terms of the major vessel, the Polaris, it's going to have dry- docking in South Africa for – I mean, almost three months. And then it's a combination of different vessels around  the world, in particular in Brazil, which obviously has an impact on the PLSV activity.

texts.speaker: Frederik Lunde
texts.profession: Analyst, Carnegie Investment Bank AB (Norway)
texts.text: Okay, but you would be able to target the Barents Sea SURF works with the existing fleet?

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: No, I think, I mean there is still plenty of competition in this market in all the area of the world including the  North Sea. And we are – we have seen a couple of young players coming in. We believe that what the clients are  looking for is company like ourself for the more complex projects, the larger projects and then maybe some of the  competition will be on low aspect vessel activity and some smaller projects. So, I don't see that as a big threat into  the environment. We are well positioned in the market we are in and there is a market in – with lower  specification for some of this.

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: I would like now to provide some additional color on the outlook. Slide 13. Levels of tendering remain strong with  improved pricing. texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: The Seven Oceans will be transferring from the North Sea to Brazil in 2013, where she will operate on the Guará- Lula project. This redeployment will reduce the available Subsea 7 fleet in the North Sea. Q1 results will also be  impacted by a number of planned dry-docks.

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Finally, in Brazil, we expect tendering activity to high, but Brazil remains a challenging environment.  Our Brazilian business is in two parts. We expect this market to grow in the coming years as  Petrobras needs more vessels for flexible pipe installation, both for their pre-salt and post-salt projects.

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: On the riser system, the pipe production in Germany is complete, and coating is under way in Brazil. Our  spoolbase at Ubu is ready to commence production of the riser system in early Q2.

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: I mean, regarding Guará-Lula, I mean, we're getting – regarding Guará-Lula, we're getting ready to start  operation in Q2 offshore. We reached 43% of operational completion. texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: And when you look at the program of Petrobras and what they need, not only for pre-salt, but post-salt, I think  there is a strong possibility that there will be a shortage of PLSVs, rather than oversupply of PLSV in the years to  come.

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: What I find – I mean one point I want to highlight is that even when the decision is to develop some fields with  flexible pipe, it's not bad news for Subsea 7, as the last contract that we just signed with the Seven Seas shows. texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA

texts.speaker: Rob J. Pulleyn
texts.profession: Analyst, Morgan Stanley & Co. International Plc
texts.text: And then secondly, I know you've already mentioned and given a lot of color regarding the first quarter, and  obviously the impacts of North Sea weather and dry docking. And how we  should think about margins within the first quarter? Thank you very much.

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: There is still the issue of the PIB and the tax law, which probably will delay further announcement of a deepwater  project in Nigeria. We've been quite pleased to see Erha North being awarded to us in the first part of 2013, and  that shows that things are moving.

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: Now, in terms of utilization, we're going to see a lower utilization for Subsea 7 and for the market that we've seen  in – compared with what we've seen in Q1 2012. We're back to historical good numbers. I mean, it's not that it will  be lower than 2012. In terms of the margin of the North Sea, we see the margin going in the right direction,  because of the activity there and the tenders. There is one point to take into account when you look at overall  margin of the project is the trend towards EPIC large projects that we start to see in the North Sea.

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: One other point that I mentioned in my comments is that the Ocean will not be in the North Sea in the second part  of 2013, because she will be operating on Guará-Lula. And, therefore, there will be no push-through of the Ocean  in the North Sea during the 2013 summer.

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Subsea 7 SA
texts.text: In some cases, it can postpone some of the projects of the operator without having any impact on Subsea 7. But  some projects are pushed to the right. The costs are going up. And  the risks associated with the supplier exist on all EPIC projects. And that's why we need to have the organization  that we have, the resources that we have to assign to mitigate this risk.

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: So let's turn to slide 21. I would like to offer some comments on the market condition we are experiencing today. This fall in the oil price has introduced a new period of unce rtainty for the  Subsea sector and our ability to help our clients find cost effective solutions is key to winning new work.

texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: We are not anticipating a near-term improvement and our plan for the near- or medium-term are based on this  assumption. texts.speaker: Jean P. Cahuzac
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: As set out on slide 23, we have already taken action on our cost base. We identified the softening of the market in  late 2013. This alone with other restructuring effort  worldwide has reduced our overall head count to around 13,000 people by year -end from 14,000 in 2013. texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director

texts.text: Segments like upstream Oil & Gas production are on a growth path again, and pricing pressure is decreasing at  this point in time. texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: So, if we talk about notable price pressure, it would be in the Hydrocarbon Processing and Power Generation  segments. texts.speaker: Ton Büchner
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Coming to Pumps, the growth is indeed taking place in the upstream oil and gas production and transport. So, it's  oil production and pipeline transport that is showing the growth. texts.speaker: Fabian Haecki
texts.profession: Research Analyst, Vontobel Equity Research AG
texts.text: The second question is related to bioplastics. You said that at Chemtech, you had in the process business, you had  a swing in orders, two large orders. texts.speaker: Ton Büchner
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Going to your first question, subsea pumping. The oil and gas industry is a pretty conservative industry. Basically,  they want you to show the competencies to manufacturer and test before they actually join you in the provision of  orders. What we've done is, we've built a test bed. It's finished. We have built a pump that is a subsea pump at our  own expense. That pump is in that test bed at this point in time being tested, and we've got lots of customers  standing around this test bed dying to see how this thing goes, and it's going very well.

texts.speaker: Ton Büchner
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: So, overall, we have not yet received a major order for subsea pumps, but the interest level is high. The pipeline of  quotations is already there, and customers are looking at the live pumps performing in the test bed, which makes  us believe that there will be successes going forwards.

texts.speaker: Ton Büchner
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: And as a result, we believe there is a significant potential. That test bed investment cannot only be used for subsea,  it can also be used vertical pumps. So, it's a multi-functional test bed, where a multitude of products of Sulzer can  be tested in. It's not dependent on one single product line.

texts.speaker: Ton Büchner
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: The bioplastics, I said we are supplying in two parts of the value chain. One is we're supplying the manufacturers  of lactides. They take sugar or corn, and they make a lactide. And we supply equipment to them from Sulzer  Chemtech. On top of that, we supply equipment to the plant, the modules to the manufacturers of the plastic. So,  that's actually a plastic manufacturing module, and those manufacturers are basically the ones that are trying out  these bioplastics.

texts.speaker: Ton Büchner
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: The margins certainly into the raw material suppliers with the equipment that supports the manufacturing of  lactides are going at margins similar to the rest of Sulzer Chemtech. And the bioplastic equipment that actually  makes the plastic is such an early-market segment that I couldn't give you an average margin because there's only

texts.speaker: Ton Büchner
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Again, we are a living corporation, which continuously adapts footprints and places. We invest in places, we  reducing places. Normally, we don't even largely discuss as we don't really largely discuss this Chemtech  restructuring at this point in time because it's really quite a small one. I call it regular course of business.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: But to be clear in oil and gas, we're not seeing the light at the end of the tunnel at this point. Upstream is still  dropping quite a lot. If you look, once again, at the projections of most observers, about 20% of CapEx drop for oil  and gas as a whole and about 40% for upstream this year. So, that light at the end of the tunnel is not here yet,  and therefore, we're sticking to the way we're giving guidance.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: We're proceeding according to plan, if not faster, on all our footprint adaptations. So, essentially, closing factories,  that's happening as per what we've announced. We probably will have a few more adjustments to make that we're  considering. And everything that we'll launch will be launched before the end of this year. So, I think on that one,  bear with us a little bit.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: In terms of the sales level, yeah, the sales level is healthy, but it's healthy also because it's been helped  somewhat by segments like the water segments where we – some of the segments where we have good volume.  But you have to keep in mind that we have the engineered, pre-engineered and configured pump factories. So,  we've got three groups essentially.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: And the part where we're really suffering in terms of load is on the engineered side of things. Essentially, it's the  pumps for oil and gas and power. So, power is helping us pick up the slack to some extent, but power for us is a  much smaller segment than oil and gas was. Therefore, net-net, we're still experiencing significant under- absorption in our engineered pump factories.

texts.speaker: Wasi Rizvi
texts.profession: RBC Europe Ltd. (Broker)
texts.text: And then following on from that, so the gross margin of the backlog was going up and you've got some hard cost  savings coming in indirect cost, so when should we expect the margins to start going up? And if not, so what are  the offsets we need to have in mind when we think about what might stop happening?

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: It's P&L impact. The run rate impact of the actions that we have ongoing is much more significant than that, as I  said, because I told you that 75% of the CHF 200 million is already secured to actions that are already launched.  So, essentially, the run rate of the actions that we've got launched is north of CHF 150 million. But the P&L impact  in H1 was CHF 36 million. We're expecting another – we're expecting CHF 60 million to CHF 80 million for the full  year.

texts.speaker: Thomas J. W. Dittrich
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: So, again, China is moving in the right direction but – now comes the big but – it's a really, really low base. For  instance, if you take our Chemtech business in China over the last couple of years, that was cut by three and,  therefore, their base is really low. But it's certainly going in the right direction. But again, from a very low base,  we're making progress.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: And the second aspect of it is some of the stuff that we have left to announce are things that we'll be only in a  position to do in the later part of the year because either for social considerations or because they target facilities  where we still are working through some of the backlog that we have. So, some of that impact will mostly – will  really translate more in 2017 in terms of P&L impact despite the fact that the actions will be launched in 2016.

texts.speaker: Michael Inauen
texts.profession: MainFirst Schweiz AG
texts.text: And you mentioned in one of the slides, the oil and gas, that you would expect the earliest recovery in H2 2017.  And I think, Grég, you mentioned you've got some indications they're may be from the client base. Maybe you  could elaborate a little bit so that we can understand where you got that better feeling for H2 2017, that would  probably help. Thank you.

texts.speaker: Thomas J. W. Dittrich
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer
texts.text: Sure, Michael. You'll find that in our notes to the financial statement actually on page 28 where we basically say  that the plan amendments we have recognized as past service cost. They had this positive impact of CHF 35.4  million on the P&L, of which CHF 8.2 million were recorded as COGS, cost of goods sold, and CHF 27.2 million  SG&A. So that's where you find it.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Oil and gas rebound in the second half of 2017, we're saying it the other way around. We're saying there's not  going to be a rebound before the second half of 2017 and, yeah, we spend a lot of time with our customers and  some of them give us more reasons for hope than others. But, really, at this point, we're I guess not alluding to  our CFO, but doubting Thomas, we'll believe it when we see it. And all we're saying is don't expect a market  upswing in pump oil and gas before second half of 2017. We're certainly not expecting it.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer
texts.text: Well, D&M has a big exposure to two markets, the UK and Australia for historical reasons. Australia is depressed  because metals and mining is down as a market but, really, the most important path for us is the UK. It's not a  Brexit issue because it's actually a lot of – a lot of it is UK for UK. D&M was a business that was doing a lot of  work in the oil and gas sector in the North Sea, and that work is currently beyond depressed.

file: SUN - Q2 2017 Earnings Call 27July2017 300 AM ET CORRECTED TRANSCRIPT - 28-Jul-17.pdf

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: If I move to water, orders in the water market have come down a little bit, but the market is still very healthy. The  downwards trend for H1 in orders in water is really mainly due to a very high baseline for engineered water in H1  2016. Engineered water, these are bigger projects and when you get one, it kind of moves the needle We did  lower order intake – we generated lower order intake in engineered water in H1 2017, but once again, a high  baseline in 2016 and the municipal water market continues to be very healthy.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Moving to power. The power market developed well for us despite an already relatively high base in 2016 and  aggressive competition as a result of low project activity in oil and gas. Asia-Pacific remains the most active part  of the world in power. On gas turbine side, which we also report as part of power, the increase of the installed  base in renewables results in gas turbines being used for peak rather than load. This means that the turbines are  running less hours, but they are also cycling more, which shortens the service intervals. The market is healthy.  The price pressure is significant. And this is mostly driven by the OEMs that are very, very aggressive currently in  this market.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Moving to oil and gas. The market continues to be challenging. The lower-for-longer scenario is clearly prevailing  at this point. CapEx expectations for big oil companies show stabilization at a low level, but no meaningful  rebound so far. Downstream and CPI are picking up. Upstream continues to be very difficult.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: There are some signs of life though in upstream. I mean if I give you data points, there are seven offshore  projects that are planned to pass the final investment decision second half of the year. I think the equivalent  number for last year was zero. So things are shaping up but you can't really see that in our pipeline, and you can't  see that in our order intake at this point. Downstream will remain difficult for a while. As I said, upstream will  remain difficult for a while, my apologies. Downstream and CPI are more active as I said. There, we see early  stages of recovery in the U.S. and activity in Asia-Pacific. And the – okay.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: In H1 2017, we were able to fully compensate the market impacts, the headwinds that we're facing in oil and gas  and power to a certain extent, fully compensate that with the SFP cost savings. We would expect that to continue  in H2 with SFP cost savings above market headwinds contributing to a net positive to the bottom line.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Let's go to page 8. The savings, SFP savings per category, there are two. What you see here is that the Sulzer  Full Potential plan in Chemtech and RES, pretty advanced. Both of them are mostly done with their plan. We still  have some work to do in procurement and SG&A and in Pumps Equipment.

texts.speaker: Thomas J. W. Dittrich
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: I explained the drop in sales volume in Pumps Equipment a minute ago. And on this slide, you see the impact of  that lower sales volumes and competitive pricing in the oil and gas market on the operational EBITA margin of  Pumps Equipment. Those two things hang together. With higher volumes in the second half of the year, we would  expect Pumps Equipment to breakeven for the full year, which when you think about it, for a new equipment  business in our industry at the bottom of the cycle is quite okay for now.

texts.speaker: Thomas J. W. Dittrich
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Moving on to slide 14, I'll walk you briefly through the operational profitability bridge from H1 last year to H1 2017.  As you see, savings from our Sulzer Full Potential program of 2 percentage points more than offset the market  headwinds of about 1.5 percentage points. The market headwinds come in two forms. First is a volume effect of  CHF 33 million due to the lower order intake in oil and gas in 2017, resulting from the lower backlog at the  beginning of this year. And secondly, the lower sales volume also results in under absorption in our factories  shown here as other costs.

texts.speaker: Thomas J. W. Dittrich
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Candidly, overall, I feel we have done a decent job balancing pricing pressures to maintain order win rates versus  cost of under absorption in the factories. We've been thoughtful and decisive on where and when to give in on  price to sell our factories. The margin column is positive as our water and pumps services businesses  compensated for the margin deterioration in oil and gas and power.

texts.speaker: Pascal Furger
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank Vontobel AG
texts.text: Good morning, gentlemen. Three questions from my side. So maybe starting with oil and gas. So here, you  mentioned your Pumps segment that if you reported a growth in order intake, so my question is to what extent?  And when comparing growth versus the first quarter, has this accelerated in oil and gas? And then, also with  regard to pricing here, you mentioned that pricing has further deteriorated when comparing the decline versus the  first quarter, has this ever become smaller?

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: All right. Thanks a lot, Pascal. Thanks for the questions. We'll try to answer them. Oil and gas to start with that,  the Q1 number is lower than the Q2 number. So there's a – well, I mean, to be quite direct, if I take Pumps  Equipment and I look at oil and gas for Q1, order intake was CHF 68 million and if I look at Q2, order intake was  CHF 79 million.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Frankly, I wouldn't read anything into it, because these things, they kind of go up and down. And we have a few  bigger orders can swing the needle from one quarter to the next. It could have been the other way around, frankly.  So I could give you the answer of Q2 as CHF 10 million higher than Q1 for oil and gas order intake for Pumps, but  the reality is that it could just easily have been the other way around.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: The pricing part of your question, the price pressure has actually intensified this year, because I mean, I'm not  telling you anything that we weren't telling you last year. We have always said that the volume would bottom out  and start rebounding well before pricing would start improving. We think the prices will start improving about a  year after the volume starts rebounding. And right now, we're kind of at the bottom of the barrel and everybody is  fighting for load that makes people very aggressive. And I would say that in H1 of this year, the price pressure, if  anything, has intensified in oil and gas comps.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: That sums your first question in oil and gas. The second question, you want to take the GEKA question, Thomas?  GEKA – I'll take the GEKA question. GEKA is lower profitability that are historical APS business. We gave you  numbers on that last year. There really hasn't been anything that has changed the indication we were giving you  early on, if any. Actually, GEKA has been more profitable than what we had in our business plan. So GEKA is  performing in terms of volume and margin at a higher level than our investment case, and our historical Mixpac  business is also doing really well.

texts.speaker: Fabian Haecki
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS AG
texts.text: Yes. Good morning, gentlemen. A few questions. So first, on RES. You were mentioning the pricing pressure on  the service business, particularly on the gas turbines. And if you look at the RES development, flat sales and  margins actually did not move much, stayed at 12.4% EBITA. Is this now kind of the price pressure basically  eliminate all the progression on the cost savings front? Is this something kind of a margin we also have to expect  going forward? And also, how incrementally did the pricing pressure increase? I mean there was always tough  sides with the OEMs. Maybe you can elaborate a bit on that one.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Okay. All right. Thank you, Fabian. We'll try to answer your questions. I'll start with the last one, then I'll go to RES  pricing, and then, Chemtech, Thomas will take that one. So why is our guidance up for the year on orders? It  really isn't linked to any market development that we've seen. I can't go back to you and say the markets that  we're in have actually ended up being better than we thought.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Actually, when we do our market assessment, we were seen by some of you guys as the purveyors of gloom and  doom when talking about oil and gas at the end of last year. We said we weren't expecting anything very helpful  this year and we were reserving our hopes for 2018.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Actually, the scenario ended up being even a little bit more negative on upstream that what we've anticipated. So  if anything, we revised our oil and gas market [ph] to do (36:08) slightly downwards and not upwards. The other  segments, they've been healthy, but they haven't had a growth rate which is beyond what we were expecting. The  guidance position mostly has to do with the fact that we performed well in H1 and we had good momentum and  we actually benchmarked pretty well against the internal targets that we had. And when we look at where we are  at the end of the first half to stick to our original guidance would have meant to essentially tell you guys that H2 is  going to be significantly down in terms of orders versus H1. And we don't necessarily think H2 is going to be on  the same level, but we don't think it's going to be down to the extent that sticking to our original guidance would  have indicated.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: I'll go to RES pricing. RES pricing, yes, margins are holding up. We're competing well in that business, which is  the mix of different things. As you know, it's the pump service, it's the electromechanical service, and it's the gas  turbine and other rotating equipment service. My comment was specifically on gas turbine service where we  compete with the big OEMs with GE and Siemens, and we compete quite well. We're a former OEM. We have a  level of technicity. We have a level with engineering which is really comparable to what the OEMs have. And I  know because I used to be in OEM. I worked for GE and Alstom. So we're seen by customers as a very good  alternative to the OEMs.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Now, it's always been quite a competitive market. But if you look at companies like – well, if you look at the big  OEMs, they make pretty much all of their money on the parts and service and none of it on the new equipment for  gas turbines, so very little of it on the new equipment. And that competition has intensified over the last two years.  Funnily enough, it was General Electric that was leading the raise towards low prices by trying to acquire market  share at sometimes surprising pricing, if I can put it that way, which surprisingly because usually the market  leader doesn't do that, but that's what was happening.

texts.speaker: Fabian Haecki
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS AG
texts.text: Yeah. Yeah. Thank you. Maybe just to follow-up on the RES side and the market.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: So the cost sales in RES is mostly behind us and we don't see an improvement in the pricing environment in the  market. So therefore, the uplift of the margin will be linked to the volume rebound. That might give a little bit of a  mix effect, because if I look at our portfolio in service, pumps, electromechanical and gas turbine and other  rotating equipment, I'd say no pricing improvements on the gas turbines, actually probably a pricing decrease on  the back of what I've explained about the OEMs.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: I'd say electromechanicals we are currently improving. Our business was a little bit struggling last year because  we have a lot of exposure to the North Sea in the UK and we were restructuring and mitigating and that's heading  in the right direction. And on the Pumps side, there's no pricing environment improvement. It will mostly improve  as the volume picks up.

texts.speaker: Jörg-André Finke
texts.profession: Analyst, HSBC Trinkaus & Burkhardt AG
texts.text: The second question relates to your comments on the M&A pipeline, which I sort of think is filled and we could  expect some news in the second half. Could you comment more generally on whether that would be rather within  oil and gas or outside oil and gas?

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Okay. I'll start with the M&A question. I don't want to give indications on segments where the M&A would happen.  What I would say is that if M&A ends up being oil and gas related, it's going to be for geographical reasons, i.e., to  strengthen or to establish a position in a significant market where we don't have the right geographical coverage.  And there's a lot of markets around the world for oil and gas that are quite protected and nationalistic, if I could put  it that way.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: So national oil companies, countries that have strong ambitions in terms of localizing. And increasingly, if you look  around the world, if you don't localize, you don't get to play in the big oil and gas markets. So if there's anything  M&A related that's linked to oil and gas, it will be for geographical reason. It's not going to be for scale reasons.  We have, at this point, all the scale that we need.

texts.speaker: Alessandro Foletti
texts.profession: Analyst, Octavian
texts.text: Yes. Good morning, everybody. Thank you for taking my questions. I have three questions actually. On upstream  oil and gas, the oil price is around – CHF 50 is quite higher compared to the bottom where it was [indiscernible]  (58:58) is increasing as well. And oil production, okay, is not booming but is also growing. What must happen in  that industry for the order to come back? I would expect at some point a rebound here. But what must happen  really in the industry for that to start growing again strongly?

texts.speaker: Alessandro Foletti
texts.profession: Analyst, Octavian
texts.text: A similar question to the midstream. Again, oil production has not declined despite the CapEx cycle. So, oil must  be moved from place to place through the pipes. Why there is no investment there and what must happen for that  to come back?

texts.speaker: Alessandro Foletti
texts.profession: Analyst, Octavian
texts.text: And then my third question on Rotating Equipment Services, the pricing environment that you're experiencing, is  there a connection with the oil and gas situation or is that fully disconnected in your view? So, [ph] this will drive...  (59:59)

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Alessandro, your third question is what we're describing on the gas turbine service pricing connected to oil and  gas, is that the question?

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: So, I'll start with that one. It's not connected at all. Oil and gas is linked to essentially fixed cost. You've got a lot of  people like us that have factories and service centers and there's lower volume and there's a moment where  people start looking at contribution margins instead of gross margins and try to – you can only restructure so fast  and you can only cut so deep. So, it's about keeping these businesses afloat and that makes people at times  pretty aggressive in an industry that has a very significant cost takeout drive. If you look at our oil and gas  customers, they all come out with announcements saying that they've managed to cut their costs by 30%, 40%,  and we're on the receiving end of that. So, that's the oil and gas dynamics.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: The gas turbine stuff, it has to do with the way gas turbines are being used in this market. Once again, they're  being used for peaks rather than for loads, so it's a different type of usage. And it's a market that is in terms of  installations not growing as fast and it's a market in which conservation has gotten to be pretty high. If you look at  the combined market share of GE and Siemens, you're certainly well above 50% and probably north of 60%. So,  if one of those guys is looking to acquire market share for whatever reason, that leads to a pricing environment  which suddenly comes under a lot of pressure, and that's what was happening over the last 18 months.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: So, really different dynamics. They're not related. What is related though is the pricing impact in pumps. This is  only pumps. When I look at oil and gas pumps and power pumps, the power market is healthy in terms of volume,  but the pricing is being impacted by the oil and gas market. And that's because these pumps are both engineered  pumps and they're made in the same factories. And when you don't have the load from the oil and gas guys, you  try to get the load from the power guys, and that negatively impacts the pricing because people fight harder on  these opportunities.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Midstream. Midstream, yes, there is a need. Yes, there are significant oil and gas flows. There is activity in Asia  and there is activity in the Middle East, and there's a lot of stuff [indiscernible] (01:03:41) on a holding pattern. And  if you take North America for example, I mean there's projects that were on the shelf that are being dusted off. But  these projects are still very significant, and they still have environment ramifications and regulatory ramifications,  and they haven't come to market yet. But there are signs of life. We think the market will pick up, but it's not going  to pick up right away.

texts.speaker: Alessandro Foletti
texts.profession: Analyst, Octavian
texts.text: Do you need to see like oil production at CHF 100 million, let's say, for that market to pick up [indiscernible]  (01:04:19-01:04:24) let's say, to acquire a new investment [indiscernible] (01:04:27)?

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: No. I think midstream, it's really – the environment is supportive to some new projects in terms of potential needs.  And you see that there are projects being studied. I don't think these things are necessarily on hold because of  level of oil prices because it's mostly linked to the volume that has to be transferred, and these volumes exist.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: So, I don't see midstream necessarily being driven by – I can't give you an answer of if oil prices were $10 higher,  what that would have as an impact on our business. So I think there's a backlog already of things that has to get  cleared up, and then, afterwards, we'll see.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: It's a danger of indicators. The rig count is up but actually, for this, in upstream, you really have to separate  conventional and non-conventional. So, if you take the worldwide production, which is under 96 million barrels  [indiscernible] (01:06:00) something like that, there's about 4.5 million barrels of that which is non-conventional  shale related in the U.S. And that work is booming currently because these guys are all independent companies.  They're not in OPEC and non-OPEC deals. They usually have a lot of leverage and they have debt to service.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: And they're trying to essentially get production online because they want to service their debt. So that market has  taken a lot of cost out. They're more competitive than they were before at lower prices, and these guys are going  full speed ahead. So, if you're seeing rig counts, the shale-related rig counts, the rig count is actually up pretty  significantly to the point that you hear the market that one of the bottlenecks is getting additional rigs because  operators are reluctant to [ph] lease back (01:06:55) some of the rigs that were stacked unless they get better  pricing from the oil companies.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: So, the boom in upstream is happening in the fracking related world and Sulzer does not do positive displacement  pumps. So, our exposure to that markets on the upside and on the downside is actually limited. Really, we're  more about the conventional oil market, which is everything else, the other, whatever, the other 91 million barrels  a day worldwide. And that market is still licking its wounds, essentially.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: So, what will it take for orders to go up? Well, if you guys follow some of the companies that are involved in the  fracking pumps market, you'll see an order pick up in this current environment and upstream. If you follow a guide  like us that are more conventional oil-related centrifugal pumps, you're not going to see anything positive in  upstream anytime soon. I mean I see that despite the fact that our order intake in upstream in H1 was actually  pretty good. But I don't see that as a market indication. I see that as maybe a reflection of our competitiveness  and commercial drive. At these prices, nothing of significance is going to happen in terms of market rebound in  upstream. The market, if anything, will level off at the bottom this year and if anything happens in terms of  increase, they'll be at best next year.

texts.speaker: Patrick A. Laager
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities Europe Ltd (Switzerland)
texts.text: Chemtech remains a very lumpy business, currently improving, but very erratic development. New equipment in  pumps equipment is lucky to remain, let's say, a low margin business going forward. So, I mean there is no easy  fix for this, but why not exiting the oil and gas business or at least the new equipment part of your oil and gas  business and trying to expand more aggressively outside of oil and gas.

texts.speaker: Patrick A. Laager
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities Europe Ltd (Switzerland)
texts.text: Probably I should ask this question to Viktor but – Viktor Vekselberg, but my feeling is basically there's no big  future here. You are putting a lot of effort outside of oil and gas and you did very, very well here and you're also  reducing your cost base significantly, which is good, but at the end, you remain very dependent on the oil and gas  business. So, what is – I mean, probably there is no answer here, but maybe there is a comment at least.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: So, now, let's go back to the rest of your question. Yes, oil and gas is really challenging. But oil and gas is – I told  [indiscernible] (01:12:01) I started my professional career as a drilling engineer. And I was a drilling engineer in  the early 1990s when the barrel was at, what, $8. And I lived in Aberdeen, which was the most depressing place  on earth at that time, and the people were saying, oh, that market is bad, there's no future, and so on. And then  we ended up at $120 a barrel and people were printing money and advertently wanted to be in oil and gas.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: And nobody saw shale coming and then the market goes down and everybody wants to exit again. It's kind of a  boom and bust type of thing. If oil and gas were not a market in which you can make money, Schlumberger would  not exist. And there's some really good companies out there that make their living in oil and gas equipment and  services and make a good living. And I don't see why Sulzer would be different.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: I agree with you that oil and gas right now is super challenging. I agree with you that it's not going to get easier  any time soon. I mean I see it best of volume rebounds starting next year, and I see it best of pricing rebounds  starting in 2019. And I say, at best. So, that means that if you're a Sulzer investor, you've got to accept that that's  going to be challenging for a while. But what you shouldn't lose sight of, if I take the pumps business – I'll give you  a few data points. If I exclude the fracking pumps, once again, non-conventional, which is 4.5 million barrels  maybe out of 96 million barrels of production worldwide.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: If I exclude the fracking pumps and I look at the conventional markets, if you look at third-party sources, Frost &  Sullivan for example, Sulzer is actually the market leader in oil and gas pumps worldwide. The last Frost &  Sullivan study I think had us at 13% market share and had Flowserve at 12% market share. You said we compete  with the big OEMs, which is true for gas turbine service. But if you take pumps, pumps is populated by mid-sized  companies like us. The biggest animal in this market is Flowserve and Flowserve is not that much bigger than we  are in pumps. They also have a valves business and a seals business. But in pumps, they're not much bigger  than we are.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: So if you take the pumps business, oil and gas, we're one of the biggest guys out there in the market, which is a  boom-and-bust type of market and in a market where there's still a lot of technology and a lot of differentiation. I  mean we invested in subsea pumps. We're in partnership with FMC, now TechnipFMC.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: These pumps are pretty incredible from technology perspective. And this is not a commoditized market in any  way, shape, or form.. That market currently is dead because not too many people are investing in subsea. But  there's only one thing you can be sure of in the oil and gas is that it will rebound and it will rebound because  people will hold off on investment so long that there's a moment where the supply and demand curves will have  crossed, and there's a moment where everybody will be playing catch up and that will be to once again price  inflation.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: You see that right now in the tracking market. These rigs are stacked and suddenly the market is hot and people  are fighting for capacity. So [indiscernible] (01:15:11) what I can't tell you is that I can make the oil and gas  businesses Sulzer non-cyclical. Nobody can do that. What I can tell you is that we can make it less cycle sensitive  by being more variable in our costs and being a bit smarter in the way we organize ourselves.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: It's an attractive market over time, because there is a lot of technology that goes into that. And once again, shale  and fracking is a good example of that. It's a market that did not exist that was driven by technology, vertical  drilling and different fracking techniques. Technology plays a role in oil and gas. The market is cyclical, it will  rebound, will be less cycle sensitive. We are the market leader, and there is technology and innovation in there.  And once again, we're in a world where conventional oil depletes by 5% to 7% a year, where shale oil depletes by  maybe 11% to 12%. If you don't invest as an oil company, I mean, gravity catches up with you.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: And we're not a fair weather type of navigator here. We look at these businesses and we see what the value is in  the long term and we're ready to write it out and reinforce the business during that period to reemerge as a  stronger player when these markets pick up. But they're all in different ways attractive markets.
