Now, I think the number we showed last year was 13%, and  we said we've been growing in water. Actually, we did a little bit of reallocation. Companies have this tendency to  kind of redo their allocations from time to time to say, well, this business is more like this and not like that. So, the  reality is that the comparable number for last year was 11%. This year is 12%. So, water is going up in terms of  the part of Sulzer that it represents.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: I would maybe add one thing, which is that order intake 53% aftermarket. Last year's number was 53% also. So,  your question could be, well, your new equipment business in oil and gas is eroding. Why isn't the aftermarket  going up? Reason for that is that our Tower Field Services in Chemtech counts significantly in the aftermarket  number. And Tower Field Services is an aftermarket business, but it's an aftermarket business which is unusual.  It's very lumpy, so it's outages, customers don't want to do an outage or turnaround. And it's a business with costs  that are mostly variable. So, our business kind of goes up and down, depending on whether customers are doing  outages or not.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Let me go to the next page. Next page is an overview of the markets. So, for those of you following online, this is  page 5, and it's our non-oil-and-gas markets. So, the 55% of Sulzer, if you include CPI, that's not oil and gas. So,  power, water and general industry. What you see on this is, I guess, a lot of green. All three of these markets  were up in 2016.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: In power, we saw a good level of activity that was driven by China and India. Europe, Middle East and Africa is  still slow, but we've seen investments in gas in the U.S. The challenge that we're facing in the power market is  simple. The market is healthy, but because from a pump perspective, these are similar pumps or at least made in  the same factories as the oil and gas pumps.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Most companies that are involved in pumps for oil and gas are also involved in pumps for the power industry.  Because these companies were not getting the volume they need to load their factories from oil and gas, what  they do is they have a tendency to be very aggressive commercially on the power side of the market. So, power is  a bit contradictory, because it's a healthy market that is under a lot of price pressure because of the oil and gas  downturn.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: In water, we've seen a solid municipal waste water markets in the U.S. and in China, and continuously active  desalination segments in the Middle East and in Southeast Asia.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: If I take general industry for pumps, we were up despite the fact that the pulp and paper market was a little bit  down. And the final point is we have an electromechanical service business, where we – which counts in general  industry and it suffered a little bit in the UK last year. It has a big presence in the UK and we're suffering the  impacts of the changes in the British industrial landscape, to put that in an elegant way. So, that's the non-oil-and- gas markets in 2016. As I said, positive, growing, and we had some good successes in those.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: If I go to the next page, page 6, that's the oil and gas picture. Now, the oil and gas picture is less rosy, as you  guys would expect. Our order intake in 2016 was down 11% versus 2015. 11% is in many ways a reasonable  number. You'll see on the next slide that the market itself – CapEx market itself was down something like 24%.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Why were we down only 11%? Because oil and gas is spilt in upstream, midstream, and downstream, and the  part that is really hurting today is the upstream markets. The upstream market was down in 2016. It will be down  again in 2017, by the way. Our customers invested less in this area. Fewer projects means higher competition,  and therefore, a lot of price pressure. That is significant, because you have to keep in mind that our orders in oil  and gas in 2016 become more sales in oil and gas in 2017. So, therefore, we are subject to that price pressure.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: That is changing. You guys saw that the oil prices went up in year 2016. What that means is that refining spreads  have gone down, and therefore, we have customers that were not stopping for anything in 2016 that are telling us  that in 2017 they will arbitrate in favor of some of these outages that need to happen. So that will be good for our  aftermarket business and downstream.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: So, overall, 2016 was another tough year in oil and gas. 2017 is not going to be much better. The downstream  market will continue to pick up somewhat, but the upstream market, in our view, will continue to drop in 2017  towards a trough that will happen sometime during that year. We expect to rebound in 2018, but we don't expect  big news in upstream in 2017. So, rebound in 2018, another tough year in 2017. But the light is there at the end of  the tunnel. Supply and demand will rebalance in the second half of the year, and that should mean good  commercial opportunities for Sulzer. Once again, not in 2017, but in 2018.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: That's what you see in the slide 7, which is – it's Bloomberg data. It's not Sulzer data. It's the CapEx disclosed by  the top 300 publicly traded oil and gas related companies worldwide. What you see is – I think there's a lot of  information that's interesting on this slide. What you see is that the market dropped from 2014 to 2015 CapEx by  24%. From 2015 to 2016 it dropped by 26%. Now, our oil and gas order intake was down only 11%. This counts  everything. This is CapEx. We were down 11%. Now, what we've tried to do is to break it down for you a little bit.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: If you look at the box at the top, you see the Sulzer oil and gas order intake. If you take pumps new equipment,  we were down 32% from 2014 to 2015, when the market overall was down 24%, we were down 24% from 2015 to  2016, roughly in line with the market. Now, the market numbers, they include everything. They include – it's all the  CapEx. So, it's not only new equipment, obviously.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: But just to give you a feel of how our new equipment behaves, how the business behaves when the market is  down. Once again, down 32% two years ago, down 24% this year. That's the pain that we're experiencing in  terms of factory load for these oil and gas pumps. Now, if you look at the aftermarket for pumps, which if you were  to look for the numbers in Sulzer, you find most of that in RES next year. But in 2016, you had some of it in RES,  you had some of it in Pumps Equipment, because our parts business was still in Pumps Equipment.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: And then if you look at Chemtech, now Chemtech, we took the Separation Technology business. We didn't add  the TFS business, because the TFS business, as I said, it's an aftermarket business that's lumpy. If I look at the  ST business, the Separation Technology, that's a business that has a combination of new equipments and  aftermarket. We didn't separate them. We just gave you the numbers as they are.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: All right. So, let's go into an update now on the Sulzer Full Potential plan. I'm on page 9 now. Page 9 is the –  there's a chart, which the top of it is the savings and the bottom of it is the costs. So, the short version of this slide  is we're ahead of schedule and ahead of targets on SFP. We're delivering as much or more than what we were  expecting, and we're doing that quicker than we expected.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: So let's go to page 10. That's the breakdown of the SFP savings, indirect procurement, SG&A, and then the three  divisions that we have in 2016. What you see on here is that we're at CHF 124 million of P&L savings since  inception. That is ahead of the plan, and it's more than halfway towards our CHF 200 million number.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: What you also see on there is that we've made a lot of progress in Rotating Equipment Services and Chemtech,  where we've delivered most of the plan. Still have a little bit of work on the Pumps Equipment side, because we're  still – we've announced a lot of things. Some of these measures are under social consultation currently; and  therefore, we have to give that due process, but we'll make up for that in 2017.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: The reason why we have not included that in the SFP number is that usually what happens is if you take any  comparable plan – you look at other companies, most of them actually do include the direct procurements within  their saving plans when they have to do something like this. And usually direct procurement is about a third of the  number. I benchmarked that in my previous job, because we were trying to see whether we're aggressive enough.  It's about a third usually, 30% to 40% roughly.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: These companies are direct comparables. They're not all a perfect fit for Sulzer, because some companies don't  have the same portfolio we have. Some companies are not present in the same markets. If you take a pump  company that is mostly water, they'll behave differently from a pump company that's mostly a sort of mining and  fracking, to give an example. But still, as a population, there's enough of them on this page to give you some feel  for where we are.

texts.speaker: Thomas J. W. Dittrich
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Looking at the quarterly order intake development here on slide number 14, you really see a two-part story. The  first part is 2015, where we saw a clear downward trend in orders as a result of weak oil and gas demand, and  you see it here on the slide on the left-hand side. The second part is 2016, where we have bottomed out  commercially at an average order level of around CHF 700 million per quarter, including acquisitions.

texts.speaker: Thomas J. W. Dittrich
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: And in Q4, we saw a nice rebound. Q4 orders came in 19% higher than Q4 2015, and the driver of the order  increase in Q4 compared to a year ago was oil and gas, which was flat in Pumps Equipment and up in Rotating  Equipment Services and in Chemtech. Q4 also was 14% up sequentially driven by oil and gas, which was up 18%  for Sulzer overall and driven by Geka.

texts.speaker: Thomas J. W. Dittrich
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Notable achievement for our Rotating Equipment Services division, which was able to limit its profitability erosion  to 30 basis points versus the prior year in a tough oil and gas market setting. Chemtech, it's here the bright spot at  an 11.4% opEBITA margin compared to 10.1% last year, helped by increased profitability at Sulzer Mixpac  Systems and underlying profitability improvement in all other Chemtech business units due to the Sulzer Full  Potential initiatives that Torsten and his team have carried out. On top of that, Chemtech profitability clearly  benefited from the consolidation of Geka in here.

texts.speaker: Thomas J. W. Dittrich
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Now, let me comment on the headwinds, which come in three forms. First, as a volume effect of about CHF 18  million due to the lower order intake in oil and gas from the year before. Second, in the margin column, here right  in the middle, you have a CHF 52 million price effect, as pricing has been under pressure across the board in oil  and gas and in power, mainly in the new equipment space, but also in the service and aftermarket space. And the  third effect of this challenging down-market is underabsorption in our factories, shown here as other costs of CHF  56 million.

texts.speaker: Thomas J. W. Dittrich
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: And then lastly, on the right-hand side of the chart in green, you see the effect of our Sulzer Full Potential self- help program. We have accelerated our SFP program for an CHF 88 million favorable P&L impact in 2016, and  that's nicely ahead of the CHF 60 million to CHF 80 million savings range we had initially guided for. We are able  to accelerate SFP savings mainly in the indirect procurement and selling and admin categories, as Grég  mentioned before, as well as in Chemtech, Pumps Equipment, and headquarter group functions.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: If I go to another change that we made for the beginning of 2017, we announced to you last year that we were  taking our parts business for pumps that was still in the Pumps Equipment division and putting it in the service  division in RES. Now, why did we do that? We explained it last year, we had already moved the field service and  the workshops to the RES division, and it was kind of strange from a customer perspective to essentially have a  customer that wanted parts and service to be talking to one Sulzer division for the service and one Sulzer division  for parts. It wasn't very efficient.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Another acquisition that we're excited about, but we haven't closed yet, Rotec, Rotec gas turbine service, haven't  closed yet because we're still tying up loose ends. It's more of a regulatory aspect, but it's planned for the end of  Q1. Hopefully, we can keep that to that timing. There's no particular difficulty. It's just we're closing a deal in  Russia and takes a bit of time.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Rotec gas turbine, it's the gas turbine service part of Rotec. There's a larger Rotec business that does other  things, like EPC and software that has nothing to do with us. They also do steam turbines, nothing to do with us.  We're buying the business that does gas turbine service. It's CHF 35 million of sales. As you see from there, it's  20% EBITDA. It's a very similar business to our turbo service business that's in RES.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: What it does for us is that it increases significantly our presence in one of the exciting markets for gas turbine  service. And the gas turbine service is really competitive these days. It's competitive mostly because the market is  down a bit, because utilities were not running their gas turbines as much because of the beneficial aspects of  renewables. That has led into a bit of a price war that's driven by the big OEMs, so the GE and Siemens  essentially, to name them.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: But we have a good position in this space as a large independent. Our customers value the fact that we're  independent. They also want us to be local and to have a footprint. And by buying this business, we get full  localization in Russia with the business that's based in Moscow, but the workshop – that blade workshop in  Ekaterinburg. So, our business in Russia for gas turbine service goes from being CHF 5 million to being CHF 40  million, which is significant, and we think we can grow from there.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Last acquisition that we announced right at the end of the year, actually we closed already because it was a  simpler one to close, is this Vessel Internal Electrostatic Coalescer, VIEC. It kind of rolls off the tongue, as you  can see. We're marketing geniuses. It's a complicated name, but it's a good business. It's – really we're buying a  product range that was developed by Wärtsilä. It's a product range to separate oil and water in the upstream  markets. It's inline separation. It allows us to do that very effectively with a smaller footprint. It has lot of upstream  applications for the oil and gas sector, where you're trying to get these equipments fitting into a smaller space to  save space on rigs or vessels or these types of installations.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: We expect that the oil and gas market will rebalance, rebalancing between supply and demand sometime in the  second half of 2017. I know some observers were saying earlier, our read is second half. But if we keep could  predict the oil and gas market in a really accurate way, Thomas and I would be rich. So, take it as an indication,  it's a conservative indication versus what some other people are saying.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: In power, we see that the gas market should develop positively. But there's, as I said, a lot of competition on the  service side driven by the OEMs. Coal is still substantial, but it's decreasing with the exception of Asia. And we  expect that price pressure that's carrying over from oil and gas to continue in power in 2017.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Water, we see active markets in municipal and desalination. And general industry, general industry at Sulzer is a  sum of different things. If I take APS, we believe everything will grow in 2017, dental, beauty, industrial adhesives.  If we take our general industry market for pumps, for example, we think that pulp and paper will be healthy. We  think that metals and mining will remain challenging, but that the commodity cycle is turning and that business will  start to improve slowly. And that's our view of the market for 2017.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: So, we had a very successful Q4 in a difficult market. I think Q1 is going to be softer from a market perspective  and softer from a Sulzer perspective. We expect the Q1 in terms of orders to be somewhere around the 2016  level. It doesn't change anything to our guidance for the full year, 5% to 8% up, but we're just wanting to manage  you guys' expectation so that you don't think that the storm is over and everything is linear from now on. The oil  and gas market strongly is not linear currently, and Q1 will be soft for everybody, I think, in oil and gas for the  reasons that I've mentioned, certainly for Sulzer. But still, order intake 5% to 8% up on the year for 2017.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: I'm moving now to our last slide on page 33. It's a summary slide, so I'll repeat things that I've already said. Oil  and gas headwinds will continue in 2017. That market will continue to be really challenging. Upstream will be  down. We think downstream will be up a little bit. We think the price pressure will continue to be significant. We do  expect a rebound for Sulzer in oil and gas in 2018.

texts.speaker: Thomas J. W. Dittrich
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: And, you know what, when you're doing turnarounds, you better make sure you are guiding in a way that is  something you can live with next year, and I would leave it at that and say that we have done our math on it. But  we are also anticipating the pricing pressure will continue in oil and gas and power, the spillover effect that's  there. And we are driving what we can drive. That's our self-help program. But how much then really gets to the  bottom line – look, we are already showing you in a tough market environment, an uptick from 8.3% reported this  year to 8.5%. Could that be more? Could that be a little bit less? One shall see. But we are certainly controlling  and driving all the elements that we drive and we can control.

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: Yes. But when you think of that and also keeping – yeah, taking into account that you already exploited or
texts.text: achieved [ph] a large of (01:18:26) the savings from this program, it's pretty low margin [ph] operations here  (01:18:31). What is the structural margin profile in the midterm and how you're going to achieve that? And also, in  that context, from a longer-term perspective, how do you see this Chemtech business within Sulzer portfolio? Are  there enough big synergies with the oil and gas business you have in other divisions or do you target to develop  this on a stand-alone basis?

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: We like the Chemtech business a lot. We fully intend it to remain part of Sulzer for long-term. The synergies, there  are some commercial synergies because it's oil and gas and CPI downstream. Our Pumps business also sells to  oil and gas and CPI downstream quite a lot. When we make some of these acquisitions that – like Ensival, that  has a chemical presence, that also reinforces that trait. So, there are some synergies.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: The cost-cutting, you're correct to say, is quite advanced, so Torsten doesn't really have that much to pull out of  his hat going forward in terms of taking more cost out. But as you also saw on one of the early slides – as you  also saw, the market has rebounded for that – here we go. Let me just – I'm doing it backwards, which is – here  we go. It's here. As you see here, the Separation Technology business, which is the heart of that Chemtech  business, is up year-on-year 2015 to 2016. So what we think we'll see is, we'll see volume coming back and we'll  see a pricing power coming back also.

texts.speaker: Thomas J. W. Dittrich
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Yes, the second part on the 2017. Look, in the backup you have a bridge that shows how the restructuring costs  split out in 2016, and it gives you a good indication. The large portion is Pumps, and then Chemtech, and you  have a little bit in RES and in the others. For next year, I would say you would, again, see – for next year, you'd  see a more balanced picture. Clearly, Pumps Equipment being the largest portion, showing large share of the  restructuring costs. RES, not much; Chemtech, a little bit less than this year. And then you will also see some of –  an increase in others, which is actually the headquarter functions that go beyond the divisions. So that's the  profile I would predict for next year.

texts.speaker: Pascal Furger
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank Vontobel AG (Research Firm)
texts.text: No, perfectly answered. Thanks. Just maybe on the impact, you mentioned 9% [ph] underlying FT (01:26:32)  reduction. And so, if there is still more potential in this regard and can you share with us what the impact from the  closing of the Oberwinterthur factory will be in 2017? Thanks.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: So, buying a service business in gas turbines for 4 times EBITDA is unheard of. I challenge anybody in this room  or on this call to find a multiple that's anywhere even in that ZIP code in gas turbine service transactions. It's a  really low multiple. The Renova guys did that because they understood there was a conflict. They wanted to help  us resolve it, and at the end of the day they felt that it was in the interest of Sulzer.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: What we're looking for? We're looking for businesses on the Pumps side that will continue to round out our  portfolio. It's either businesses that are really a good fit for something that we don't have or businesses that have  or could have a high aftermarket content. That's the kind of things that we're going after. We are looking at – we  continue to look at technology, mostly in Chemtech. And on the service side, we think there could be opportunities  to round out some of our service businesses where we've got the footprints. If you can load that footprint a little bit  more, it's very beneficial to the bottom line.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: But we're not being much more precise than that. We're just guiding on two things essentially. The fact that the  year is going to be back-loaded commercially, because anything oil and gas-related is going to be back-loaded,  and the fact that after – in a year that's back-loaded after a strong Q4, likelihood that we have a soft Q1 is high,  that's it.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: So I think that, in many ways, you can look at the return on capital employed – if you're looking at a comparison  with WACC, you can look at the return on capital employed of PE and RES together, because RES is not only  pump service. But, roughly, it's an indication.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: We're in no danger of asking ourselves questions as to whether we should be in the pumps business. The service  business is a very good business. And the equipment business will get better as oil and gas recovers. It's just the  margins have been hammered. Hence, the [ph] nominator (01:51:31) of the ROCEA that's in a world of pain  currently.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: I worked for Alstom and for GE, General Electric. I mean, it's – I'll probably get sued if I make comments on  General Electric's numbers, because you're not allowed to. But if you take any gas turbine business, GE, at  Siemens, anywhere else, if you start looking at your WACC and you look at the return on capital employed of the  equipment side of the gas turbine business, you'll scare yourself, because more than 100% of the profitability is in  service.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: So it's – what Thomas said about razors and razor blades, if you want to get closer to home, gas turbines kind of  the same. So, yeah, in 2017, the numbers for Pumps Equipment will look worse than they did in 2016, because  we're taking out a really profitable business and putting it somewhere else in Sulzer. That has an implication at  top line level, at profitability level, at ROCEA level. But for Sulzer overall, it'll be beneficial.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: No. No, we don't. We don't, because there is such a thing as, sort of, the spiral of death. There is a moment  where the more you cut, the more you have to cut. We've cut quite a lot and we get to the point where we have a  footprint that we're really happy with. I mean, we still have to implement some of the things that we've announced.  So, it's not done yet. Some of it is still under consultation. But still, when we look at what our footprint will be if we  managed to implement all of this beyond the consultation that's ongoing, we think that's a good footprint.

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: We also think that there isn't much meat left on the bone in terms of doing anything more significant from that  perspective. And we also think that the market will rebound, as we said, probably in 2018. So, if you look at our  water business, our water business is doing well. The power business is healthy. The part that's struggling for  Pumps is oil and gas. Oil and gas is cyclical. We've cut quite a lot, but if we want to be able to ride that rebound  and benefit from that rebound, we have to be careful that we don't commit irreparable harm to that business. So  you're not going to see much more from that perspective for those reasons.

texts.speaker: Fabian Haecki
texts.profession: Analyst, Bank Vontobel AG (Research Firm)
texts.text: I mean, it doesn't look much better in oil and gas, yes. But, say, what do you see as a downside risk on the pricing  side for new projects that will or could result in another pressure in 2018 for revenues? And is it really just that the  customers are harshly negotiating on prices or is it also that some competitors are lowering prices in order to fill  capacity? So, what is the [ph] full dynamics (01:57:48)?

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Oil and gas companies, they don't like standard products, historically, because they like to design very specific  equipment to maximize extraction. But if you do the cost benefit calculation, sometimes you can live with a bit less  recovery, if you can be faster and more cost effective. So, I think these tradeoffs will be more prevalent, and that  will boost prices. But there isn't anything that Sulzer is not sort of tackling in terms of how we adapt the business,

texts.speaker: Grégoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: But we don't have any money burning our pockets. We don't feel the obligation to do that. And what we do feel  the obligation to do is to deliver on those targets that we've outlined to you today. And continue improving Sulzer  as a business and getting it ready for that oil and gas rebound, which will happen, once again, not in 2017, but will  happen in our numbers sometime in the near future.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: What you see on here is that order intake in 2017 is back to growth in Pumps Equipment even organically as oil  and gas starts to recover from its lows. On the other hand, the power markets, the power segments for us suffer from fewer projects for  new power plants especially in China. If we take oil and gas and power together, if you want to call that energy,  the order intake was essentially flat is plus 0.6%.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: If I look at the other segments over Pumps Equipment activity, the municipal water segment for us was growing  steadily by around 3%. And in pulp and paper we also had a very successful year. Usually, we report general  industry and pulp and papers within general industry. We broke it out because actually pulp and paper is half of  general industry. So, I think it's valuable information.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: We also announced in December the acquisition of a business called JWC in the U.S. It's grinders and shredders  for wastewater. It's a significant acquisition in the sense that it's $250 million of enterprise value. But it's a  significant acquisition mostly because it's the first acquisition we make in our water business in what I would  describe as post turnaround.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: As you remember, we bought Cardo Flow a few years ago. We had a few hiccups with that integration right after  [ph] the effect (00:10:32), an impairment down the road. But as I explained over the last two years, our water  business has been improving steadily, and we're quite satisfied with how it's performing today. So, we've opened  up the checkbook again for that activity. And the JWC acquisition is a good illustration of that.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: It will allow us to grow in the key U.S. municipal wastewater market, in which JWC has very good distribution  channels. And the Sulzer platform will allow JWC, which is quite a U.S.-centric business at this point, to grow  internationally. So, it's a really good fit from a product perspective, and it's also a really good fit from a growth  perspective in terms of commercial access, both for JWC and for the existing Sulzer businesses.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Order intake in RES, I'll split it in the various segments. I'll start with the turbo service segment, which as you guys  know is mostly service for gas turbines and compressors and various other rotating equipments, but a lot of it is  gas turbine service, a market on which a lot of things have been written in the last few months given  [indiscernible] (00:13:06) reporting.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Despite lower organic sales and price pressure from the OEMs, the operational profitability, operational EBITA  margin increased in 2017 in RES on cost savings and on the positive contribution of Rotec gas turbines. The  acquisition of Rotec, which I mentioned a minute ago June 29, 2017, it allows us to build a really strong platform  in Russia. We're certainly the strongest independent in Russia for gas turbine service.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: And in terms of footprint, we have local capabilities that I think even outweigh some of the OEMs. So that is a lot  of gas turbines in Russia and this business was very successful for us in 2017. Rotec, the integration was  smooth, and commercially, we had lots of successes. The business made significant contribution to RES in order  intake in sales and in operational profitability in 2017. So, good acquisition, good timing for us, and we continue to  see good market prospect for that business in Russia.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Some companies will have valves and we don't have valves, some of them will have seals and we don't have  seals, some of them won't have oil and gas exposure and we have oil and gas exposure, some of them are pure  water-pump companies and – it's a very different market. It's really hard to have a long-term comparison. But  that's the indicator we chose, so we continue to try to walk you through it. What we said three years ago is that we  were middle-of-the-pack in about 730 basis points below the market leaders. What we are showing on the right is  that we're getting closer to the leaders and our gap is now 350 basis points. Same gap as last year roughly.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Why am I not a fan of the slide? I'm not a fan because of something that we've added on here to help you guys.  We don't give company names because it's always awkward to comment the performance of your competitors  and the objective is to talk about Sulzer. But we've added color coding. What you see in blue here are the  companies with oil and gas exposure, sorry. So, these ones, and what you see here is that maybe three years  ago, when we started using this indicator, it was interesting because it showed Sulzer was middle-of-the-pack  whether we compared ourselves with companies that have oil and gas exposure or not.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: What you see on the right is that we've improved our operations, we've taken cost out and we're a better  performing company. But what you also see is that out of the four companies that perform better from a  profitability perspective, performed better than Sulzer, three of them don't have any oil and gas exposure. So, now  that we've improved the business, now that we've become more cost effective, now that we've become more  competitive, the slide essentially becomes a proxy for oil and gas exposure, which I'm not sure is a very useful  tool at this point. But, you know, it is what it is.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: For a full disclosure, the only company that performed better on an adjusted profitability perspective than Sulzer in  2017 and does have oil and gas exposure is – it starts with a W, and ends with an R, and the letters in between  are E and I; I think Weir. These guys are cyclicality on cyclicality, right, mining and fracking. So, a very different  play from Sulzer. It's – I don't think you shareholders for the same reasons, but that's our comparison.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: So, hopefully, that explains to you that we have improved, we're doing well, we can't make the fact that we've got  45% oil and gas exposure go away. By the way, we're not trying to make that go away because we think that in  the next few years, that's going to be very virtuous for Sulzer, as the market recovers. But that's the way our peer  group pans out at this point of our development.

texts.speaker: Thomas J. W. Dittrich
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Moving on to slide number 16, I'll walk you through the operational profitability bridge from 2016 to 2017. You  know that slide we have been showing it to you every six months. And as you can see savings from our SFP  program of 2.2 percentage points in green more than offset the market headwinds of about 1.7 percentage points.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Okay. So, the first slide is the market outlook. You see the split of Sulzer according to end markets: we're 30%  general industry; we're 11% water; we're 16% power, and 43% oil and gas. What you see on here is that we  expect growth everywhere except in power. Power is going to be challenging for 2018. We expect the market in  power to decline because of the, what we mentioned about the gas turbines. The gas turbine market and gas  turbine service market with volume and price pressure. And also on the pump side, we see fewer power plant  projects especially in coal and that has an impact on our – on our Pumps Equipment business.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: So, power will be depressed. Nuclear actually will be – will show some interesting opportunities but nuclear is very  lumpy. Big projects in some specific countries like Russia, China and therefore is a lot harder to predict. But  power overall is going to be a drag for us and everything else is going to be, is going to be positive. Oil and gas,  we expect the downstream market to continue on its 2017 trend. And in upstream, we're seeing a notable  increase in inquiries. It doesn't mean that they'll translate into orders in 2018 but clearly the level of inquiries is up  significantly and our customers were back at evaluating projects and trying to decide where they're going to invest  their money and those are good signs.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Our working assumption at Sulzer is just that that upstream recovery will not lead to significant order upswing in  2018 but will lead to good things in 2019 but as I've said, downstream already rebounded in 2017 and will  continue to rebound in 2018.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: We have a cautious view on that. We don't think that oil and gas, the recovery in upstream is going to be a big  contributor to order increases in 2018. We see that as a more significant contributor in 2019. That's our working  hypothesis. I mean, I don't have a crystal ball, but that's on the basis on which we built this. Some of you will look  at our guidance from last year and say, well, you've increased it twice during the year for order intake so you have  a track record of being on the conservative side.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: People don't start adjusting their pricing policy until they feel that their factories have filled up to close to – to a  level where they've mitigated a lot of their under-absorption. Otherwise, people are still pricing based on  contribution margin to a large extent. So, our working assumption is that the pricing effect in 2018, certainly, in oil  and gas is going to continue to be negative, not positive.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: The one-off that we talked about, I don't want to make it too specific, but there's a moment about three-and-a-half  years ago where Chemtech had a strategy to expand beyond the tower and expanding beyond the tower meant  essentially – I mean on paper, it sounds great but in practice, it means doing contracting work or EPC work on  refineries or chemical plants.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: And Sulzer is not a EPC company and Sulzer is not a contracting company and we don't aim to be. In Chemtech,  we aim to be the tower specialist and separation specialist and that's what our mandate is. So, we've stopped  pursuing projects like that. These extend the scope projects that if you try to track that to Sulzer disclosures, you'll  see that there were some big projects booked in Tower Field Services at the very beginning of 2015.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: We've closed the tap on that, and we're just working our way out of these projects and stopping that side of the  business. What it means in terms of growth for Chemtech is that the growth will continue on the same momentum  for separation technology which is 70% of the Chemtech business.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: And then, we decided to be more market-focused, and we said, well, we're going to have a sales team for oil and  gas and a sales team for power to give you an example. It's a great idea except that we implemented this idea  right at the moment where the oil and gas market collapsed. And where we ended up two years into this is that  there are countries where you've got a power market and an oil and gas market that are big enough to justify  having specialized teams, and there are countries, a lot of them, which, where frankly, the volume doesn't justify it  and the skill differentiation doesn't justify it either.

texts.speaker: Fabian Häcki
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS AG
texts.text: I just have another one. On RES, I mean, what kind of downside risk do you see on the pricing front? I mean it's  quite kind of negative and there's news out in the market particularly for European gas turbines maintenance  business and so on. Clearly, becoming more and more of a battlefield now, greenfield projects and so forth,  extended maintenance cycles; and do you see any – so, first, what is risk on volume and pricing?

texts.speaker: Fabian Häcki
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS AG
texts.text: And secondly, do you see some kind of fields to mitigate like pushing more the electromechanical business which  has always been kind of a small business? So, why hasn't it grown? What keeps you from expanding into such  adjacent fields?

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Okay. A very interesting question. The RES division is three businesses: there is the pumps service, in which  we're an OEM; there's the turbo services, in which we're an ISP, an independent service provider; and there's the  electromechanical business, where we're also an independent service provider. The difference between  electromechanical and everything else is that everything else is a global business and electromechanical is a  local business. What I mean by that is, there are virtues to having a pumps service presence around the world;  you benefit from some of the technology developments as an OEM around the world.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: So, there's not going to be – the aim is not necessarily to grow very fast in electromechanical, it's not to add  geographies, it's – there's no significant M&A planned and we will only invest probably in the markets we're  already on, and just strengthen ourselves in these markets we are on. So, that's why the dynamics are a little bit  different.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: If I look at the pumps service business, which is more than half of our RES division where we're an OEM, our  challenge has been that because people have been buying less pumps, that we've been generating less  momentum for future service and parts sales. So, you've got two ways to fight against that.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: The turbo service story, for those of you who follow Siemens and General Electric, is a very challenging story and  a very challenging market at this point. The gas turbine market, worldwide, went from something like 440 turbines  to 120 turbines or something like that over the last couple of years. I'm no expert or I'm no longer an expert, but  you read up on what GE and Siemens have been saying; I mean, these guys essentially are the market makers.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: And I guess that that tells you what our assumptions are on the price contribution. Maybe we're being overly  conservative on believing that price pressure will continue to be significant in 2018. But as I said, our theory is that  the pricing will continue to drop even in places like oil and gas and will only recover in 2019. So, you can probably  kind of work it backwards. Thomas, you want to add anything more to that?

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: Yeah. Once again, there's no smoking gun anywhere. It's just a reflection of our assumptions on pricing for part of  the business. Part of the business has good trends on pricing and anything related to power is going to be quite  negative. And anything related to oil and gas – once again, our theory is that the volume will take a bit longer than  what people think to actually materialize and the pricing is about a year after that. We don't have certainties but  that's what's in our thinking and in our guidance.

texts.speaker: Fabian Häcki
texts.profession: Analyst, UBS AG
texts.text: And then also you as a former oil and gas engineer, what do you think is driving this increased confidence and  quotation? Is it just purely the level of the oil price that has recovered so much or is it more the, kind of, the  imbalance of supply demand that is driving investments?

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: If I try to answer your question as a former drilling engineer, I think what's driving the sort of the increased  buoyancy of the market, the renewed investment drive in the oil and gas market, I think it's a few things. It's, as  you said, the oil price level is certainly a contributor, but more than the absolute oil price level, I think it's the  stability. Once people start getting comfortable with the band, then they can define their investment policy and  that leads to things actually happening.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: I think the mitigating factor for all this, sort of, newfound enthusiasm, where I'm probably shocking you guys by  how positive I am, given my track record, I think the mitigating factor is that a lot of these majors are actually  saying that they're staying away from the large "trophy projects" of the past. Nobody wants to invest in something  that is a plan where first oil is 10 years out. If you look at how they're shifting their capital allocation, a lot of them  were shifting that towards stuff that has a kind of shorter payback in terms of first oil, and some of the oil majors  are saying that they'll invest more in shale rather than some of these offshore big projects from the past.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: And if you look at the Sulzer portfolio, we're not a fracking company. We don't do positive displacement pumps.  So, whenever a customer says, you know what, I'll do less conventional oil and more shale, that's not good for  Sulzer. So, I think there's an element of where the capital allocation will go, but overall, I mean overall, it's a  positive trend for us. It's just I'm mitigating that enthusiasm because I think that the lag time between inquiries, it's  like newfound signs of life, and things that you can actually measure in an order book is always longer than what  people think. At least that's my view.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: It's a good question, one that I can't or won't fully answer because I think the secret to my survival is to try not to  give guidance two or three years out at this point. The market is still somewhat uncertain. We're very comfortable  describing what our plans and our views are for 2018. Anything that's further out, I think I'll limit it to some of the  comments I've made earlier, which is that we do see a recovery of the oil and gas markets, especially – and the  one that was slowest to recover, upstream.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: We don't believe these impacts will be very significant in 2018 in terms of orders, but we believe these impacts  will start being significant in 2019. And if you look at our – the sales to – the orders to sales conversion from past  years, kind of adjusted for mix a little bit, but you have it per division, so you can do the adjustment for mix. The  only way it will change is in, I guess, in the shorter cycle. What I mean by that is – I mean, the reason why I say  that is, if I take oil and gas and my comment a minute ago about the large projects for first oil is a long way out. I  think this will be a less significant part of the capital allocation of our customers and the stuff that is more  immediate will be more important. So, I think that goes towards shorter lead times.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: And also, if I take a historical view of how the – certainly, my read of how the oil market recovers as a former  major oil company executive, the tendency is people sit on their decision until the last minute and then they want  everything tomorrow. So, we think that orders may take time to materialize, but the lead times we'll be asked to  fulfill are going to be shorter.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: When you take the RES business, the Pumps Service lead times and the Electromechanical Service lead times  are short. The Turbo Services lead time is a bit longer because, in Turbo Services, you've got some long-term  service agreements, where you take an order, but it's got multi-year delivery. So, that mix is also between the  various elements of RES you have to look at. And even within Turbo, you've got to look at the flow business  versus the LTSA business.

texts.speaker: Gregoire Poux-Guillaume
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer, Sulzer AG
texts.text: And if I take pumps, I've got two vastly different parts of the business. Anything that is standard or configured,  essentially the water or the general industry business, it's pretty short lead time. The water business, it's – we  don't produce for – we produced the stock. We produced in water. We send everything to distribution facility and  we delivered through that distribution facility. If you take the engineering part of the business, we produced orders  and we've delivered recently the pumps for – subsea pumps for Brazil and I think – the lead time on that was  probably two year. So, it's the mix makes it too complicated to fully answer the question.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: I'm pleased to say that we're performing in line with expectations. We've made good progress in making the  additional investment we announced back in May, and we're delivering the resultant improvement in many of our  operational areas. Striving for continuous improvement, so far this year we're seeing that in a number of areas  such as supply interruptions, security of supply. We're on track to deliver improvement in our serviceability on  our water distribution networks. On our non-regulated side, we're making both operational improvements and  exiting the Metering Installation business and our Severn Trent Laboratories business.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: Group PBIT, pre-exceptional charges, was down modestly at 2.6%, and that's a result of the higher infrastructure  expenditure that we announced earlier this year and depreciation at Severn Trent Water. And in addition, we have  some costs of course this time around additional costs related to private drains and sewers. Severn Trent Water  turnover and PBIT we'll talk about in a little moment.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: The third driver was the impact of measured consumption. And this period has been down 2.8% due essentially to  the wet summer with commercial consumption, and in particular, agricultural consumption much lower than we  expected. And this resulted in an £11.4 million decrease in turnover compared to the previous period.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: Hired and contracted costs were lower in the period falling by £3.4 million, and this was due to the scaling back of  work following the big focus we had in the second half of last year on leakage reduction, which was largely  successful. Tony will come back on the leakage question later.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: Power costs have increased by £3.7 million in the period due to higher consumption, mainly caused by the wet  weather, and we've got some of that today and higher strike prices on our energy cost hedging compared to the  previous year.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: Even though the operating environment we would still classify as difficult, we have seen some improvements in  the current period, in contrast to the weaker performance we saw a year ago. Like-for-like turnover increased by  9.5% while PBIT increased just under 2%. And this has been led by significant growth in disinfection products  within water purification, particularly gas feed and electrochlorination, and as well as the launch of our BALPURE  product, which contributed £2.5 million of sales, and we have about £3 million in orders. Early days but  nonetheless we have £3 million of orders for BALPURE on our books.

texts.speaker: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.profession: MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION SECTION
texts.text: So Group outlook for the rest of the year 2012 and 2013, as Tony highlighted, we believe we are on track to deliver  our expectations. Within Severn Trent Water, OpEx is expected to be higher year-on-year due to the increased  investments on networks, higher input costs and higher taxes, partially offset by some efficiency savings that we  continue to deliver.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Turning to some of the key operational functions now, we are delivering improvement in critical areas. Looking at  which looks at interruptions greater than 12 hours, and it's a key component of the serviceability assessment at the  end of the year. That's benefited from our increased infrastructure investment and something like a 50%  reduction so far there.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Compared to our performance in September – sorry, comparing our performance to September this year to the  position at March, we've also improved high water quality, enhancing our water treatment processes, something  I'll touch on in a little more detail. And on leakage, we've now achieved a further 4% reduction since March and  we're on plan to meet our Ofwat year-end target of 468 megaliters.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: So overall, an improving picture but with those three deteriorations and just very quickly, the first one of those is  higher greenhouse gas emissions. Very straightforwardly, we have used more energy this year with our less than  average weather causing us to spend more energy in pushing water and waste through the networks. And the  other two areas are internal floodings and pollution incidents. What we're seeing there is the additional numbers  coming through that we're experiencing with the advent of the private drains and sewers adoption. But in both of  those areas, we are such – from the higher base, we are showing an improving trend.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Moving on to our investment program, in May, we announced that we would be investing an additional £150  million over the rest of the AMP period to improve some of our network performance metrics and critically to  deliver stable serviceability in our water distribution network.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: As you've seen from our performance on interruptions, that is working. For example, we've invested an additional  £6 million addressing trunk mains renewals. We've been resurveying the whole of our 5,500-kilometer network of  mains to see where there is additional remedial action that we could take.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: We've trained over 150 people – of our people in improved incident management techniques and we've made  more tankers and pumps available to be on standby for deployment not only when a mains burst but you've seen  some of the flooding going on around the UK at the moment, but in deployment of our field activities to handle  that.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: We've also been enhancing our water treatment works installing more ultraviolet disinfection. For instance, at  three boreholes, we've three more to do. That's a much more sustainable solution for improving water quality.  With UV, there are no chemicals involved and the whole life treatment cost is actually lower. We've accelerated  our refurbishments on some of the filters of our larger surface water treatment works and we're re-engineering  our disinfection processes at one of our largest treatment works in Birmingham.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: All of these investments are helping us to deliver water to our customers which, as they tell us, they wanted always

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Turning to the non-regulated activities, during the first six months of the year, we had a number of changes and  some positive operational trends. We formed our new company, Severn Trent Costain, with Costain Group PLC to  provide water and waste treatment services to high volume commercial and industrial users as that new retail  market now starts to develop in the UK, and I'm pleased to say that we were able to land the first national  customer switch in the UK.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: In operating services, overall, we saw a solid performance. In the U.S., we've increased our contract base, and in  the UK, our MOD contract delivered good performance. In products, revenue and PBIT were both up period-on- period led by significant growth in the disinfection products, particularly gas feed electrochlorination as people  are starting to build again, and as Mike has already mentioned, orders now for our Ballast Water Treatment  product BALPURE.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: First, to limit the degree of flexibility that Ofwat is seeking, and we've suggested that that could be done by  limiting that flexibility to removing retail sludge processing and water resource management from wholesale  controls. Alternatively, we suggested that could also be limited by reducing the limit on the revenues from  wholesale to be exposed to competition to 20% rather than 40% in the proposal.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: In line with Ofwat's proposals, what will set out there will be a series of outcomes that we could deliver and that  will then be an opportunity for our stakeholders to seek to influence how we balance those outcomes. You may  also have seen recently our published joint report with National Grid changing course through sustainable  financing options to encourage equity financing in the water and the energy sectors. And we have copies of this  outside. If you don't have one, please do take one, and watch out for a forthcoming publication that we have  commissioned from KPMG and titled Financing Infrastructure in the Water Sector Beyond 2015.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Now, a new and the key part of the PR14 process is something called the Customer Challenge Group that Ofwat  Buckland, who is also the National Chair of the Consumer Council for Water. And the members of the panel are  drawn widely from our statutory regulators of the DWI, Environment Agency, Natural England from CCWater,  Citizens Advice Bureaus, interest groups like the NFU and the CBI, and local authority representation from across  the East and West Midlands.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: So in summary, we have delivered again on our commitment. We're delivering the investment program, and we're  seeing the consequent operational improvements in the areas that we've targeted. We're making good progress  developing our processes and plans for the next price review, PR14. And we remain supportive of the principles of  reform of the water industry and we believe we're well positioned to benefit from those opportunities.

texts.text: Okay. Two questions on, first of all, on the operational performance where we would be. texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: I didn't quite catch the second, but let me have a go. I think it was floods and what's going on there.
