Is that really just a reflection  on what's been happening with the weather? And I guess what I'm kind of groping towards asking is, was the first  year ODI high performance kind of a little bit lucky?

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: The financial, the numbers, sewer flooding does have a big contribution.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Yeah, they are an expensive business. But at the same time, if the other measures haven't been green, then I'd  agreed with you, we had a good [indiscernible] (34:39) measure. But the fact, that across the piece, we had  almost all of them already are green. It shows that we're making operational improvement performance across the  piece. Emma, anything you want to add? Yeah [indiscernible] (34:49).

texts.speaker: Emma FitzGerald
texts.profession: Executive Director & MD-Wholesale Operations, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Yeah, actually, I've said. I mean, we've improved across a number of different metrics. Although sewer flooding is  a big driver and pollution's performance is another big driver as well where we will actually saw 30%  improvements. We have to continue to see those sorts of improvements to be able to deliver the same reward.

texts.speaker: Emma FitzGerald
texts.profession: Executive Director & MD-Wholesale Operations, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: I think the other thing that we're doing, let's talk about variability [indiscernible] (35:12). We need to make sure  we've got really robust processes for weather events. And frankly this week with some  of the weather that we've had, it's been a good test of those processes. So you can be assured that we are  thoroughly ready.

texts.speaker: Nigel Hawkins
texts.profession: Analyst, Hardman & Co
texts.text: And my other question was on energy supply, possibly for the Chief Executive to deal with. Given that your retail  customer base is one of the largest in the UK and you are now generating more electricity, do you rule out  entering the energy supply market, especially if the supply businesses of heavily indebted E.ON and RWE come  up for grabs and particularly since E.ON is particularly strong in The Midlands?

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Thank you very much. So I'll answer the second one, [ph] make James the company (36:44) on the first one. So  on the second one, and as it stands now, our plans, our growth opportunities are firmly ahead of us as being a  really fantastic company in the water sector. We're obviously continuing to make a good progress in our  renewables agenda, but I don't think right now is the time to talk about a multi-utility strategy.

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Severn Trent Plc

texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Severn Trent Plc

So you should expect that's going to be spread through the  next few years of the AMP period. And, effectively, that becomes real money, so it just gets spent against totex  [indiscernible] (42:35).

texts.speaker: Edmund Reid
texts.profession: Analyst, Lazarus Partnership
texts.text: One of the things that Ofwat let out was the potential to reduce bad debt, and I think they compared water to  energy. Do you think that's a valid comparison? I think there's been some issues around here.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: I've never worked in energy, so I'm probably not best-placed to comment on an energy [indiscernible] (44:59)  comparison. James hasn't worked in energy either, so we can't help you.

texts.speaker: Sarah Bentley
texts.profession: Chief Customer Officer, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Yeah. So I think it's worth pointing out that 1.8% hasn't come out without quite a lot of effort. Somebody  mentioned about the energy sector earlier, and I think it's worth pointing out that in water, there is no opportunity  for recourse. So if somebody doesn't pay their bill, we are legally not allowed to turn them off. So 1.8% comes  with a huge amount of effort, and I wouldn't want to encourage anybody to think that we've got any aspirational  targets beyond that given the challenges we've got in forcing people to pay.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Our vision remains unchanged, to be the most trusted water company by 2020. And we believe by doing the right  thing, we will deliver really strong benefits for our colleagues, our customers, our communities, and our  shareholders. We're halfway through the five-year regulatory period. We feel that we've made good progress in  the first two-and-a-half years. We're in good shape for this time and also to move seamlessly into the next time to  come.

texts.speaker: James Bowling
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: On our excellent performance on Waste means that we're now expecting to reach the cap on Waste ODIs for this  AMP. Underlying basic EPS is up 7.7% due to the growth in underlying PBIT and a lower effective tax rate, which  more than offset the increase in financing costs. In May, we uplifted our ordinary dividend policy to growth of at  least RPI plus 4%, which means our interim dividend increased by 6.2% year-on-year.

texts.speaker: James Bowling
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Turning now to our Regulated Water and Waste Water business, for this year, we'll be showing Dee Valley  separately to allow like-for-like comparison with the prior year. In Severn Trent Water, revenue has increased by  £16.9 million for the RPI and K-factor allowance, and £12.9 million from the ODI net outperformance payments  earned in the first year of the AMP. These were offset by £12.1 million of WRFIM adjustments for billing in excess  of the Final Determination in that same year. Other movements of around £5.5 million included the impact of new  connections, meter optants and the management of voids. So, after including the additional £12.5 million of  revenue from Dee Valley, our turnover for the year is up 3.2%.

texts.speaker: James Bowling
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Turning to our underlying PBIT for Regulated Water and Waste Water, we've delivered an increase of £9.5 million  or 3.5% for the half year. In Severn Trent Water, we've maintained good control over operating costs, which have  increased by just 1.2% year-on-year. Our net labor costs increased by £2.6 million following the annual pay award  and an increase in head count as we in-source more activity. This in-sourcing has helped to lower net hired and  contracted costs, which are down £3.7 million with the comparison also benefiting from £1.8 million of setup costs  for non-household retail separation last year.

texts.speaker: James Bowling
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: As I guided in May, we've seen the impact of a sector-wide increase in electricity pass-through costs, which we've  offset through reducing usage by around 1%, despite a 2% increase in water into supply. Also, we believe we  have the lowest imported unit electricity costs in the sector, even so our gross power costs were up £4.4 million or  11% year-on-year. And as a group, we're able to hedge some of this increase through self-generation, which is  reported in our Business Services segment.

texts.speaker: James Bowling
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Now turning to Business Services, and as you can see here, we're delivering top and bottom line growth as  promised. In June, we sold our U.S. operations and together with our Italian business sold late last year, we've  reported this as a discontinued operation. Our Operating Services division now generates 95% of its revenues  from the UK and is up £2.9 million in turnover and £1.4 million in PBIT, driven by higher commission income and  additional work awarded on the MoD and Coal Authority contracts. Our Renewable Energy business increased  turnover by £3.1 million and PBIT by £1.6 million. And we're now producing the equivalent of 38% of our energy  needs and are on track to hit our target of 50% by 2020.

texts.speaker: James Bowling
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: In 2015, we committed to investing £190 million in our Renewable Energy business over the course of this AMP.  We've now invested £116 million of this, with 60% in our non-regulated assets, including a newly operational  Roundhill food waste plant and a third plant in Derby which is under construction.

texts.speaker: James Bowling
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Finally, let's turn to our technical guidance for the full year. I'll leave you to read through the details, but there are  a few changes I want to highlight. Firstly, with our strong start on customer ODIs this year, we're confident that  we'll beat our performance last year and earn at least £50 million in net outperformance payments. Most of our  ODI outperformance to date has come from our exceptional Waste performance. The total AMP capped for Waste  ODIs is about £190 million gross of tax. So, the £75 million we earned in the first two years leaves £115 million  available for the remaining three years. Based on our performance trajectory on key Waste commitments, we now  believe it will hit this cap.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: We believe right now is the right time for the societal impact of this strategy. We've got the backdrop of a housing  shortage in our region. We've got customers with affordability challenges, wanting lower bills, and we've got  population growth. We think this strategy delivers against all three of those areas and helps all of those  stakeholders. And we think it's another example of what it is that we're doing creatively as a senior team to look  for innovative ways to keep bills low for the future, whether it's cost efficiencies, whether it's the bill smoothing of  the ODI impact, or whether it's the property strategy, all of them add up towards really understanding that keeping  bills in good shape is important for our future.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Let's talk about our performance operationally. You'll recall the swingometers, we traditionally use these, and  we're proud of the first six months of our operational performance. On the most of the customers care about most,  which is internal and external sewer flooding, the hard work of my colleagues has delivered a 48% year-on-year  improvement, which is fantastic. If we look at the two of the other big, I guess, rate-making items, it will be  leakage, which you can see has gone down by 4 million leaks a day, and it'll be category 3 pollutions; again, both  of those are ahead of our regulatory targets.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: On supply interruptions, we also have had really strong underlying performance. We have had a couple of recent  events, which have moved us into our deadband territory on that particular matter. Over the last couple of years,  we've talked a lot about water quality complaints. It's been our challenging measure, and I'm really pleased that  the business improvement activities, the investment, the focus from us across the piece has really begun to move  that needle. And you'll see that we're 12% better year-on-year and we're confident of that continuing through the  remainder of the AMP.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: If I were to draw out just two, I think they've got some really fantastic methods in their water quality arena. So,  their mains cleaning techniques have been great for us to learn from. It helps them deliver the sector-leading  mean zonal compliance performance, and that's helped us improve this year. It's also been super-helpful for us  on our water quality complaints performance.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: If I were to call something else out, it will be their SIM performance. They are properly upper quartile on SIM.  They're first place on billing. They're fourth place on water. That's helped us as we continue our ambitions to  move and continue to improve against SIM. If you look at all the benefits that we've been able to help with, they're  a heap. There's technology. There's innovation. There's R&D. There's the opportunity for us to help shape their  vulnerable programs, which they've not really got in shape. And, of course, there's the whole cost savings arena.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: And if you take one example, which I guess would be electricity contracts, by moving them onto the way that we  purchase electricity and onto our contracts, we've been able to make double-digit percentage improvements on  the price that goes into electricity price for the Dee Valley customers.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc

texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: To set ourselves in good shape, we've got a challenge group, a customer challenge group called the Water  Forum who are fantastic experts and are really going to test our plan. texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: At the same time, we're not resting on our laurels. We're doing two big concrete things to get ourselves in great  shape. The first is investment. texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: And the second thing we're doing is making sure that we've got the right operating structure. We recently trialed in  Staffordshire a new operating model. And what came out of the trial was enhanced asset  management, the opportunity to make sure that we deliver more commercial savings, the chance to get our  sludge data which for us is a key measure, and to make sure there's an organization we were primed to be more  commercially aware and to drive towards success in what is a new and competitive market for us. texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: And to give you just a couple of examples of how we think this is in our DNA, it's inbred within us, I would say look  at the partnerships that we do across the piece. texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield

texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer and Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Yeah. Thanks, Liv. So I think it's worth bearing in mind that going into the summer we're in a really strong  position. texts.speaker: James Bowling
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer and Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: We've got an extensive plan for resilience in AMP7 and that's building our current resilience profile that we've got  today. texts.profession: Group Commercial Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Yes. texts.profession: Analyst, Hardman & Co.
texts.text: And the second there, your WACC [indiscernible] (00:42:22) Dee Valley acquisition. texts.profession: services business and whether you can outline the rationale for keeping that business within the
texts.text: On our Position Paper on water trading in particular, let me start from – not from Severn Trent  actually, let me start from any institution that you care to go to, to look at the effects of climate  change and the impact that that has on water scarcity for the UK. texts.profession: services business and whether you can outline the rationale for keeping that business within the
texts.text: It seems self-evident that we are going to need to redress that balance. texts.speaker: <Q – James Brand>: Hi, it’s James Brand from Deutsche Bank. The first question just on the
texts.profession: services business and whether you can outline the rationale for keeping that business within the
texts.text: <A – Tony Wray>: The – as we did point to in our Changing Course document, we think it is  almost inevitable that there will be some consolidation. texts.text: On energy, as I mentioned, we’ve increased our renewable and we plan to continue to add to that  portfolio. Our plans are on track, and indeed, we’ve now been granted our first planning permission  for a significant wind turbine at Wanlip in Leicestershire at one of our largest sewage treatment  works. In addition, as we previously reported, we have hedged the vast majority of our wholesale  energy requirements for the remainder of the AMP delivering around £20 million saving versus the  final determination over the AMP.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray, Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.profession: Okay. Good morning, everybody, and thank you for bearing with us with slight logistical interruption
texts.text: A couple of examples here, just to give you a flavor of the type of things that are coming out of that  supply chain working to drive the efficiency. At our Derwent Valley aqueduct scheme and that’s  increasing capacity on our main spine network for transportation of water north to south. The  improved modeling that we’ve applied has identified solutions that avoid us having to lay about 26  kilometers of new main; have smart reuse of some assets that we’ve got and that’s saving us  around £4 million on the planned £31 million spend for that part of that scheme, around a 13%  saving. And that’s the kind of thinking that we’ve got driving on through our schemes.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray, Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.profession: Okay. Good morning, everybody, and thank you for bearing with us with slight logistical interruption
texts.text: Another example on the water treatment works at Tack Lane where we’re introducing a new  technology for Severn Trent, but tried and tested in the broader world for treatment of pesticides  and it’s a technique known as air stripping, rather than the technique that we would usually use of  using granular activated carbon. Again, that’s given us a capital saving on the project but actually  we’re finding it’s also a lower cost operation and on that particular site alone will save us about  £10,000 a year in operating costs.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray, Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.profession: Okay. Good morning, everybody, and thank you for bearing with us with slight logistical interruption
texts.text: Looking forward then for Severn Trent Water in 2011-’12, our goal clearly is to continue to deliver  on those performance improvements and the efficiencies that are now planned. On our CapEx,  we’re guiding to a range of £450 million to £470 million net and within that, £120 million to £130  million of infrastructure renewals, higher than last year as we catch up from some of the weather  impacts on our program just last year. Our operational expenditure will show an increase year-on- year in ‘11-’12 driven by inflation, rising import cost, quasi taxes, including the carbon tax offset by  our ongoing efficiency programs.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray, Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.profession: Okay. Good morning, everybody, and thank you for bearing with us with slight logistical interruption
texts.text: Just a few words on our approach of the adoption of private drains and sewage. We have already  leveraged the expertise of our supply chain partners, and we already have in place the resourcing  model and the processes to keep our fixed cost to a minimum. We expect the transfer of assets  now to take place on the 1st of October. And in our release this morning and in the appendices to  this presentation, we’ve included our initial estimates of the potential impact in the current year ‘11-  ‘12.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray, Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.profession: Okay. Good morning, everybody, and thank you for bearing with us with slight logistical interruption
texts.text: In water purification, though, it was a tale of two halves, growth in the first six months and then a  falloff in the second half of the year, principally on sales of our high margin electrochlorination  products as well as the impact, I think as Mike said, is the Gulf coast drilling moratorium and the  political and the social unrest in the Middle East, which was delaying funding and shipments.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray, Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.profession: Okay. Good morning, everybody, and thank you for bearing with us with slight logistical interruption
texts.text: Looking forward for services with the fundamental market drivers remaining strong, we remain  confident in our opportunity for sustained future growth in Severn Trent Services. Our base  business in operating services and water purification is expected to deliver continued growth,  particularly in the second half of the year. At the PBIT level, we expect those base businesses to  deliver a continued growth, but offset by the investment we’re making in the new opportunities such  as building our market and technology, for example, resources to support the launch of our ballast  water and ultraviolet disinfection product lines BALPURE and MicroDynamics. So those  investments which we plan to be around £5 million will support the growth over the next five years.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray, Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.profession: Okay. Good morning, everybody, and thank you for bearing with us with slight logistical interruption
texts.text: 8 Just a few comments on regulatory developments. Since our publication of our changing cost report  back in April, we’ve been very pleased with the response on the engagement that it’s generated  across many stakeholder groups. Clearly, there are a number of ongoing reviews in the sector, the  Gray Review, the White Paper, and what we’re seeing in there, we’re very encouraged, we’re  seeing our ideas and views on sustainability, financeability and better optimization of water  resources being incorporated into those debate. In particular, we look forward to the planned  Government White Paper later this year.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray, Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.profession: Okay. Good morning, everybody, and thank you for bearing with us with slight logistical interruption
texts.text: Most recently, we were encouraged by, of course, publication of the preliminary model highlighting  a number of things, in particular, protection of existing investments, driving the right behavior for  each part of the value chain by putting in place appropriate incentives and the potential to place a  value on water and introduce upstream competition. Our strategy of continuous improvement and  focus on high standards, lowest charges for our customers, great people in Severn Trent puts us in  a strong position to take advantage of those opportunities should they arise.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray, Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director
texts.profession: Okay. Good morning, everybody, and thank you for bearing with us with slight logistical interruption
texts.text: And just a very quick plug for a new publication from Severn Trent which we will be putting out in  June. In Changing Course, we raised the prospects of water trading and our publication coming  forward, Changing Course through water trading, sets out our ideas on how we believe we could  integrate water trading into the existing process for the development of 25-year water resource  management plans. So, please do look out for that one in the coming weeks.

texts.text: <A – Anthony Wray – Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director>: Okay, thanks. Let me  deal with the leakage, first of all, and be clear there. We  were one of only a small number of companies that put into our funds a leakage reduction. We did  that because we think that’s the right thing for us to do and the most effective way of us delivering  the water balance.

texts.speaker: <Q – Pinaki Das – Merrill Lynch International Ltd.>: Good morning. Pinaki Das from Bank of
texts.profession: America Merrill Lynch. Two questions; one is on leakage, and the second one is on private sewers.
texts.text: So, despite the tough winter, we believe we delivered a good performance. We certainly kept our  leakage rolling three-year leakage moving down, which is the ultimate test on this. We moved very  quickly, and we’ve restored our leakage reduction. And we have ensured that in our planning going  forward, we’ve taken the best account that we have for that. We have not planned on having  average winters.

texts.speaker: <Q – Pinaki Das – Merrill Lynch International Ltd.>: Good morning. Pinaki Das from Bank of
texts.profession: America Merrill Lynch. Two questions; one is on leakage, and the second one is on private sewers.
texts.text: Just by way of little background, for the last three years in our region, three years ago, we had a  one-in-10 winter that was followed by a one-in-30 winter. And so, we’ve already made the move in our forward plans on, for instance, our resourcing 4,  5, and 6 on leakage for our infrastructure renewals on a more severe winter than normal. I’m as  confident as I can be, given that I don’t have control of the weather going forward.

We’re not trying to be a GE or a Siemens,  what we know is filtration and disinfection. We have leading technology and products there, and  wherever you go in the world, the core processes of treatment that you have of filtration and  disinfection.

texts.text: <A – Anthony Wray – Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director>: On the leakage, first of  all, no, I don’t expect any intervention from Ofwat. So, we have the leakage, but equally, we didn’t have any  hosepipe bans last year as security of supply index is in the right place. And we’re carrying on with  that, so I don’t expect any noise from Ofwat from that.

texts.speaker: <Q – Pinaki Das – Merrill Lynch International Ltd.>: Good morning. Pinaki Das from Bank of
texts.profession: America Merrill Lynch. Two questions; one is on leakage, and the second one is on private sewers.
texts.text: <A – Michael McKeon – Executive Director & Finance Director>: Yeah. Most of it is catch-up,  but not all of it. None of it has paid us; none of it. And the reason for that is that what this winter  has exposed in terms of extreme temperature, low temperatures has exposed some of the assets  that need probably to be dealt with earlier than we originally thought. So, we don’t think, overall,  that’s going to change it over five years, but we do think we’re going to have to make more effort  this year simply because it’s exposed some of these assets that need to be looked at earlier, and  that would be where are.

So now clearly that has to go through the full Ofwat assessment and  review process, but we believe we’re moving in the right direction.

If the weather continues to be the drought-like conditions, we can’t rule out  usage restrictions. We’re not in that position yet. If we get average rainfall, we won’t be needing to  do that.

texts.text: <A – Michael McKeon – Executive Director & Finance Director>: And just add to that, we have  about 30% meter penetration on the domestic side, so that gives you an idea of what the impact  would be on the metering side.

texts.speaker: <Q – Pinaki Das – Merrill Lynch International Ltd.>: Good morning. Pinaki Das from Bank of
texts.profession: America Merrill Lynch. Two questions; one is on leakage, and the second one is on private sewers.
texts.text: 15 <Q – Verity Mitchell – HSBC Bank Plc (Broker)>: Verity Mitchell, HSBC. Is that because you’re  abstracting more from rivers? Is that, Andy, a function, sorry, of your way that you get your water  supplies?

texts.speaker: <Q – Pinaki Das – Merrill Lynch International Ltd.>: Good morning. Pinaki Das from Bank of
texts.profession: America Merrill Lynch. Two questions; one is on leakage, and the second one is on private sewers.
texts.text: <A – Andy Smith – Executive Director & Director-Water Services>: In order to manage the  supplies, roughly a third of our water comes out of reservoirs; a third, we abstracted directly from  rivers, and a third from groundwater. So, we are increasing the groundwater take wherever we can.  The major rivers in our region, the River Severn, the River Avon, the River Derwent, have all been  in regulation. What that means is that we have agreements on abstraction from the environment  agency depending on the flow of the river and we can only take a certain amount out. So we  balanced those supplies in the best way that we can, and so it is a trade-off to make sure that we  can deploy our resources in the right way. Okay.

texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Severn Trent Plc

texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Severn Trent Plc

In leakage, we're  delivering more repairs per team per day, as well as significantly reducing the average time to repair the leak. And  this is on the back of our previous investments of things like our SAP, computer systems, our improved leakage  management systems, alongside our people working on driving operational excellence and continuous process  improvement. Finding and fixing leaks quicker is good for customers. It's good for our water resource position,  and, of course, it's good for cost control.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Thanks, Mike. So this morning, I'm going to focus on a few things: our operational performance across our KPIs
texts.text: Where we need to improve further is our water below ground assets. So that's the pipes in the ground. Now,  within this, our measures of performance and the key determinants are reducing mains bursts – we're on track  and we're doing well on that – reducing instances of poor pressure – we're on track and we're doing well on that –  and the thing that I've already highlighted that we need to continue to improve is our unplanned interruptions  performance. And that remains our focus in that area for this year.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Thanks, Mike. So this morning, I'm going to focus on a few things: our operational performance across our KPIs
texts.text: Now, as Mike mentioned, we've announced today that we are investing an additional £150 million of investment  delivering even fewer unplanned interruptions for our customers, more reliable performance of treatment from  our waterworks and our waste treatment works, and even fewer pollution incidents.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Thanks, Mike. So this morning, I'm going to focus on a few things: our operational performance across our KPIs
texts.text: Now, with an eye to the future and continuing to build further resilience and flexibility in our water network as a  component of our future water trading, one example of where that additional investment will be made is in the  renewal of some of our biggest pipes, our trunk mains, to give us greater security and some new valving to give us  greater options for switching our network.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Thanks, Mike. So this morning, I'm going to focus on a few things: our operational performance across our KPIs
texts.text: In Water Purification for products, our market conditions were very mixed. The US saw limited investment by,  again, local municipalities, but we did see activity picking up in the Gulf of Mexico. In our emerging markets, Asia- Pacific, Middle East, North America, they also grew. And in the UK, with the second year of the regulatory cycle  for the water companies kicking in and the capital investment plans really starting to pick up, we saw a pick-up  there. And as Mike mentioned, our BALPURE project is already finding customers ahead of our expectation.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Thanks, Mike. So this morning, I'm going to focus on a few things: our operational performance across our KPIs
texts.text: As I mentioned earlier, there was encouragement for water trading such as abstraction incentive mechanism,  reducing abstractions where it's environmentally damaging, deregulating bulk water trading, stronger obligations  on companies to consider imports and exports when planning water resources.  Where we are focusing our attention for all of those things that we like, on those things that are not clear yet, it's  in areas such as the balance between rewards and penalties on incentives and how Ofwat's proposed totex  approach might work.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Thanks, Mike. So this morning, I'm going to focus on a few things: our operational performance across our KPIs
texts.text: So, in summary, we've delivered again on our commitments to our stakeholders. We've beaten our leakage target.  We've reduced supply interruptions. We continue to forecast no water restrictions in our region for this year. And  we've maintained the lowest average charges to our customers. Our strong balance sheet and delivery of capital  efficiencies enables us to increase our investment program to improve further service for our customers. It also  allows us to provide an additional return to our shareholders.

texts.speaker: Q
texts.profession: [ph] Iain Sutter (0:35:21) from Exane. I suppose the acid test is, if you weren't doing the special dividend, would
texts.text: you still be doing the CapEx?  Anthony Paul Wray  Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc  A Mike said it. We thought long and hard about this and the right thing for us is to keep the balance right. We look  at the long-term challenges on our service and service provisioning networks. We look at the priorities that our  customers tell us about. And time and time again, our customers confirm their chief priorities are security of  supply for water and the waste water taken away and they don't have to deal with it.

texts.speaker: Harry P. Wyburd
texts.profession: Analyst, Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: Hi. It's Harry Wyburd from Barclays. I think you've answered the main of my questions. So just a couple more  housekeeping-wise. Firstly, on your private drains and sewers expenditure, could you let us know roughly how  much of that is going to be classified as infrastructure renewals expenditure?

texts.speaker: Harry P. Wyburd
texts.profession: Analyst, Barclays Capital Securities Ltd.
texts.text: And secondly, the restructuring charges, the one-off restructuring charges in the water business, could you give us  an idea as to what they were related to, what the benefit will be and how sort of one-off they are or whether you  think there might be some more next year? Thank you.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: On the restructuring, essentially what was happening last year was around – we remodeled the sewerage  operating model, so the waste water operating model. And the reason for that was we had to get ready for the  adoption of private drains and sewers. And in doing so, we took a view that we needed a much more flexible  model. That is to say that we actually transferred a number of people out into the supply chain. We regrouped  around three key suppliers in the supply chain. That's why in part some of the hired and contracted costs have  gone up. But what we're essentially doing is now we've got a much smaller fixed base against which we're  operating this model, and part of that was related to getting from that position to the position we have now.

texts.speaker: Edmund Reid
texts.profession: Analyst, JPMorgan Securities Ltd.
texts.text: We've maintained stable, as I indicated, across all three of our key categories. We've been marginal on our water  infrastructure. We believe that this last year we've gotten ourselves back to stable. The conversation we had with  Ofwat was, well, that's fine, but we want to see you do that for another year. That's what we're on target to do.

texts.speaker: Michael J. E. McKeon
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Let me answer that question. We expect hired and contracted costs to come down next year. We don't expect  employment cost to replace them particularly. Part of the reason is what I answered earlier about in terms of  restructuring, how we operate the waste water commercial model. So we have actually moved to a lower fixed cost  base and we are operating a much more flexible, variable cost base. So, depending on the activity levels, and again,  that may in part be related to PDaS because some of that cost will now be through the hired and contracted  network. So depending on the level of those costs – level of those activities, we could have higher or lower costs to  where we are. But we don't anticipate that our fixed cost – our employment costs will rise dramatically beyond  where they've been.

texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Severn Trent Plc

Fourthly, the impact of new properties and meter optants increased turnover by a  modest £1.1 million and with other net movements contributing a negative £4.5 million. This leaves turnover for  Severn Trent Water for the year at £1.511 billion, an increase of £53.5 million or 3.7%, as I said.

texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: As I said before, this is the first full year that we've seen the costs associated with private drains and sewers. And  we saw an increase of £5.7 million year-on-year to an annual cost this last year of just over £10 million.

texts.speaker: Michael J. E. McKeon
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: And moving on to those costs where we believe we have less control, we've been able to keep the bad debt charge  stable at 2.2% of turnover. There's also been a higher strike price on our energy costs when compared  to the previous year.

texts.speaker: Michael J. E. McKeon
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Quasi taxes increased by 4.9% (sic) [£4.9 million] and that includes the carbon reduction commitment and  following the announcement last year of additional capital expenditure of £150 million, expenditure on  maintaining our network and infrastructure network increased by £18.8 million in the year. Finally, depreciation  increased by £14.4 million year-on-year due to the higher level of previous additions. So overall, that brings us to a  PBIT of just over £500 million, which as I said is broadly flat year-on-year.

texts.speaker: Michael J. E. McKeon
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Like-for-like turnover increased by 5.3%, driven primarily by the strong performance in water purification  products, which saw its revenue grow by 13.4%. This improvement was driven by strong demand for disinfection  and filtration products, principally in China and the Far East, while we also saw growth in demand in Brazil and  Malaysia for electro-chlorination products due to the increased oil and gas exploration in those markets.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: On leakage, we've delivered a further 5% reduction this year. That follows on from a 7% reduction last year. So we  beat our Ofwat year-end target, and as one of the few companies that put a leakage reduction target in throughout  our AMP5 plan, we're on track to deliver our AMP5 target.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: And then finally turning to asset serviceability, our key focus for the year was improving serviceability in our water  distribution network. And, as you can see with our targeted mains renewal program, reduction in supply  interruptions, reduction in leakage, we've achieved that, so we now have all four asset classes rated as stable.  That's important in the context of PR14 as it's this year that Ofwat makes its assessments on the state of all  companies' networks.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Turning now to Ofwat and their KPIs, this chart shows how our performance has progressed since last year. We  have 10 KPIs that have improved since the last year, three that are stable, and one that has deteriorated. So  overall, a very strong improving picture, but with the heavy rainfall last year, as Mike mentioned, and the flash  flooding we saw widely across the region, we did see internal sewer floodings rise. Now despite that, we were still  able to make the network improvements to protect the further 228 properties from the risk of sewer flooding, and  we now have the lowest ever number of properties on our homes at risk of flooding register.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Moving on to our capital investment, and RCV growth, as I said earlier we're on track with our additional £150  million investment announced last year. So for instance, we've invested an extra  £17 million finding and fixing leaks, delivering our lowest ever leakage in 20 years.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: We've invested an additional £8 million replacing trunk main networks, and improving our incident management.  That's been a significant contribution to our interruptions of supply performance improvement. On the waste side  of our business, we spent £12 million on critical assets at our treatment works, and our environmental compliance  is at our best ever level in 15 years and we've invested an additional £4 million, reducing the number of sewer  blockages in the 49 most worst performing drainage areas in our territory.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Now as part of our commitment to continuous improvement, we are always encouraging our teams and our supply  chain partners to innovate. And that's alive and well in Severn Trent, and here's just one example I'd like to share  with you of the sort of things that our people invent. This thing is a thing called a Lontra Blower and you won't  know what these are, but let me tell you there are 280 blowers installed across the Severn Trent network. And  what these things do, they provide aeration in a critical part of the sewage treatment process. Now the important  thing to notice, these blowers last year consumed over 182,000 megawatt hours of electricity. That equates to an  electricity bill of about £9 million per annum.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Our teams working with Lontra – they're a clean-tech start-up and they develop energy saving compressors for  engines in the UK. We've developed a blower that improves efficiency by 20%. Now rolling that out across our  entire fleet will obviously help reduce our operating costs by reducing our electricity use and cost, but also help  reduce our carbon emissions by about 19,000 tons of CO2. That's about 3% of our total emissions, so innovation is  alive and well in Severn Trent.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: In products, revenue and PBIT grew year-on-year led by significant growth in Asia and Brazil in particular, as well  as the first contribution from sales from our BALPURE ballast water treatment projects. We're also seeing growth  in our disinfection and electro-chlorination lines.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Looking at other opportunities for value creation, our plans are on track to install this year our first four wind  turbines. That will move us further towards our target of 30% of our gross energy needs produced from our own  renewable sources. And we're about to start our first food waste anaerobic digester program, which will push us  on beyond that limit. We also continue to have property development opportunities, in particular, developing  some of our surplus land for industrial and commercial use.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: We expect final methodology for PR14 from Ofwat in July now, and our business plan will then be submitted in  December along with the independent report from our customer challenge panel, the Severn Trent Water Forum.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Our AMP6 capital program, we expect to reflect the ongoing requirement for certainly maintaining the services  and the standards from our networks that our customers already enjoy. We will have to deal with the new quality  standards, such as the Water Framework Directive, and in addition, address customer's requirements now for  security of supply certainly of water resources and protection from the effects of flooding.

texts.speaker: Anthony Paul Wray
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Severn Trent, as Mike covered, has a strong, flexible, sustainable balance sheet, the structure of which you know  we keep under constant review. We maintain our clear focus strategy focused on water. That means continuing to  drive operating performance, improving customer service levels in Severn Trent water, and being ready to exploit  the opportunities that regulatory reform and non-reg provides us. Finally, we are committed to our dividend  policy of growth of RPI+3% until March 2015.

texts.speaker: Michael J. E. McKeon
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: In COPI, we're now down to roughly around about I think just over £200 million is the adjustment. And what  we've always done is we've managed our forecasted CapEx program to our anticipated level of COPI-adjusted  investment. So we started off with a number north of £400 million, that's gradually come down, partly because  governments have changed the way they calculated COPI, but progressively that number has changed.

texts.speaker: Michael J. E. McKeon
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: We're not increasing our CapEx to get to a COPI number. If anything, we're probably reducing it against what we  originally would be allowed, because effectively, the COPI is a negative number, you'll have to reduce it. So what  we're trying to do is to match our capital program to our COPI adjusted number. But, of course, the COPI-adjusted  number changes all the time. So that's what we're trying to achieve.

texts.speaker: Michael J. E. McKeon
texts.profession: Executive Director & Finance Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: No, no. We think the number we've got there is the best estimate we can come, COPI adjusted. That's what we  think. I will check that, but that's what I believe.

Anthony Paul Wray  Chief Executive Officer & Executive Director, Severn Trent Plc  A  Water Bill, we know and I think what we know in some detail what's in the Water Bill. texts.profession: Executive Director & Director-Customer Relations, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: In terms of products, the electro-chlorination business is doing particularly well in the emerging markets of – in  China and as Tony mentioned in the oil and gas exploration offshore markets as well. So all in all, things are  looking quite encouraging for us.

texts.speaker: Guy Mackenzie
texts.profession: Analyst, Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: And secondly, obviously, the Water Bill recently received Royal Assent. They're talking about eliminating  automatic referrals with CMA [Competition and Markets Authority] for mergers. And also, obviously, putting  forth more competition in the non-household retail and allowing for non-household retail exit. Do you envisage  consolidation in the sector on the first point, and would that potentially be a part of your strateg y? And secondly,  would you be able to talk through your strategy in non-household retail from April 2017 ?

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive Officer & Director, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: In terms of question two, it was all around Royal Assent in terms of the Water Bill. So, the three kind of sub- questions there is one, what does that mean for us in terms retail competition? And I think, we're currently testing  our toe in the Scottish market to get a sense of that, it's the only place where it exists now.

texts.speaker: Anthony J. Ballance
texts.profession: Executive Director, Director-Strategy & Regulation, Severn Trent Plc
texts.text: Y eah. Thanks. We've had ongoing discussions with Water Forum, the customer challenge group for some time  now. Obviously, since getting the feedback from Ofwat, those discussions have carried on.  So, we've been looking  again at our package of ODIs, having the discussion, going through line by line through each of the ODIs with the  Water Forum, but also doing that in parallel with discussions, ongoing discussions, with Ofwat. So, I think, we're  comfortable with this, a lot of challenge, a lot of rigor in that process that will ultimately lead to our resubmission  by June 27 .

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director
texts.text: And the last thing we've done in terms of the highlights from last year, is refocused our Business Services division.  As you would have seen, we did a turnaround of subsequent sale of water purification and that now get the  Business Services team focused on our core competencies which is water, waste, retail and renewables.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director
texts.text: Now, you'll see that seven of these are green and that means good strong year-on-year performance  improvements. And there's a couple of those that we think are ac tually quite big ones. They're the ones which are  quite large on the ODI's number going forward. So particularly proud of it. And I'll [ph] turn (02:50) your  attention, for example, to internal sewer flooding. And the reason we think this is actually critical, if we just ask  our customers – and as you know, we did as part of getting ourselves ready for this next period of time – what the  things they most care about, our customers shared the thing they most care about is internal sewer flooding. It's  one of the largest ODIs for that reason and we're proud of our year-on-year performance improvement of 20%.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director
texts.text: Another area that's had a significant uplift in the year is around overall provisions. And these are categorized by  the EA. And this particular measure is around category one, two or three pollutions. Y ou might recall that a year  ago, I shared with you that in 2013/2014 we've been the only four-star rated company by the EA, so it's an area  that we are quite strong at. So, if you see a further 18% performance improvement year-on-year; again, it's a really  strong performance. That said, we have a couple of red ones here as well and let's talk about those next.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director
texts.text: So actually on serious pollutions, whilst our overall performance on pollutions is much better year-on-year, we did  have two individual more serious pollutions in the last year than we had in the year before. [indiscernible] (03:50)  for us, and we'll be striving to get ourselves back to our best ever performance rates and get ourselves back to the  top of the leader board across all of those pollutions categories.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director
texts.text: The second area you see on here as a threat is around the particular basket of measures, and it's only one measure,  as you'll recall, is the same measure we talked about last year. And you remember that we had a discussion last  year regarding coliform reductions. Now, we've made a 33% performance improvement year-on-year on this  particular measure. Nonetheless, it still manages to make that basket red because it's just at outside the Ofwat  reference point. So, even though it's a significant improvement, nonetheless, it's not enough to get us inside the  Ofwat reference point. We did flag that last year that we thought it takes two years to get ourselves back on the  [indiscernible] (04:29) Water Purification and in terms of this particular water quality measure, just wanted to  share that with you up front. There's the two [indiscernible] (04:35) on the high standards we set for  [indiscernible] (04:37). We're pleased with the progress we've made and we're looking forward to the new climate  that is ODIs.

texts.speaker: James Bowling
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Thank you, Liv, and good morning everyone. I'm delighted to be presenting these, my first set of results. It's a  great time to be part of the Severn Trent team. I knew the company well by reputation and as a thought leader in  the sector before I took the role. What has really struck me since joining is how aligned and  focused the whole  company is on its customers, on community and environment and on delivering the cost efficiencies and other  challenges of AMP6.

texts.speaker: James Bowling
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: There are lots of valuable commercial opportunities to go after, and I've been pleased to see the high energy and  determination focused on a wide variety of projects, whether it's efficiency improvements through digital  technology in our core wholesale business, maximizing the value of our property portfolio, or in renewables,  where we'll be increasing our self-generation levels to over 50% and achieving some solid low-risk, double-digit  returns on the £190 million investment we communicated in March.

texts.speaker: James Bowling
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: The company has spent the time ahead of AMP6 valuably by getting the business in the best possible shape and, as   you'll hear shortly from Liv, we're already well up the curve on securing the planned efficiencies and have  outperformance very much in our sights. This forward thinking hasn't stopped with the beginning of AMP6. We're  planning for the next industry challenges such as sludge and water trading and more near term, how the non- household retail market will pan out from 2017 and how we can be ahead of the pack. It's exciting time to join.

texts.speaker: James Bowling
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: We also decided to increase contractor spend in the second half of the year by just under £7 million on projects  that get us in the best place to start AMP6. During the year, we've continued to focus on o ptimizing and refining  debt recovery initiatives such as customer risk segmentation and Water Direct payment plans, which have helped  to improve our credit management performance by £3 million in the year and resulted in a bad debt charge of 2%  of revenue, that's down from 2.2% last year. Power costs also fell due to increased renewables generation and our  continuing drive to reduce energy consumption.

texts.speaker: James Bowling
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Turning now to our non-regulated business, the focus hasn't just been on AMP6 this year. We committed to you  last year that we would turn around the Water Purification business, and we've done this. And our decisive actions  drove the business from a loss position last year to an operating profit of £4.9 million this year. And as you would  have seen in our announcement on May 13, the deal with the DeNora valued the whole business at $99 million,  which represents an EBITDA multiple of around 8 times.

texts.speaker: James Bowling
texts.profession: Chief Financial Officer & Executive Director
texts.text: Turning now to the continuing operations in the Severn Trent Services, which exclude the Water Purification  business. We grew revenue year-on-year by just under 5% by contract wins in the U.S. and new business in the  UK. Profit for the year was impacted by investment in our business development capabilities in the U.S. and year- on-year performance was also affected by some one-off favorable items that benefited our 2013/2014  comparatives.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director
texts.text: And last of all, we remain excited about the renewables opportunity. We've been leader of the pack for a while in  terms of self-generation of energy. But nonetheless, we believe there is more. That's why we have chosen to spend  £190 million. And getting to the point where we generate over half of our needs in terms of equivalent energy  generation, it will be a great addition and that's what we'll do between now and 2020.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director
texts.text: The second thing we've been working on is around the Birmingham Resilience scheme. We've been working on  lots of our capital programs, but the one I thought I'd give you the update on is the largest of the capital schemes  certainly for us, but also for the sector, which is the Birmingham Resilience scheme. And it's a number of smallish  activities which add up to progress in this space.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director
texts.text: So for example, we've been purchasing the key land points, the particular pumping station point is now bought  near Southport. That's done. We've also been looking at the pipeline land for making sure that we get focused in  terms of planning permissions and also making sure we get the extraction permissions we need. That's in addition  to securing the correct contracts right at the start of phase 1. So we believe that overall, we're in good shape, which  is the largest of our capital programs.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director
texts.text: The second thing I want to say on ODI is that quite rightly, the regulators set very high target before you get into  the reward zone. And I want to bring that to light so you can see that year one on most of the ODIs, is the big step  change here. And what you can see here is for water quality complaints that in the first year to get into a reward  territory, you've got to do about a 17% improvement. In years two or three, it becomes a more manageable 8% or  9%, and then, as you can see, it's flat thereafter. So the key thing is – I know lots of you asked me questions about  what do I put in the model in terms of ODIs, and I guess the only guidance I can give you is it's a slow burn, right?  It's not an instantaneous moment, one, because there is this big first off year where quite a few of measures, you  have to do a big improvement.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director
texts.text: So to bring Coalport to life, and I guess I will probably give you an example, every one of these results say going  forward, but to bring Coalport to life, we're talking about sludge treatment works. And what we would naturally  have done and within the FD plan, is that we would straight replace our digesters which had come to the end of  their natural life cycle in terms of 30 years old, and are ready for replacement.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director
texts.text: What we did as part of our chief engineer creative testing solutions is looked again at options, and the solutions  we're now going with is actually to build a dewatering plant and actually it's a tanker to a nearby site using  efficiency more at nearby site and not spending on the asset financially. When you look at the configuration of our  network, we have another option available to us. That actually saves us 30% of the plant's totex spend which is a  fantastic achievement, and that's an example of totex thinking. So, you can see that saved us £4.9 million, which is  just great.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director
texts.text: And in terms of where that's come from, as you can see down on the slide, 60% of that £100 million, £60 million  come from new supplier contracts and broadly it's based around two. So one of which is a chemicals contract,  which Helen actually alluded to at Capital Markets Day, and the second of which is a new contract we've got with  Amey, which is our partner – we had two partners in our wastewater business. We've now moved to a single  supply contract with Amey and renegotiated a really contract with them which is in line with some of the activities  that are linked to ODI payments but likewise as equally helps us in terms of savings.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director
texts.text: We're also actively involved in making sure that as Open Water gets set up, that would contribute towards the  creation of that competition model in industry. We believe it's important to have people from Severn Trent  seconded on some of these key industry programs, but currently, we've got people seconded into the DWI and also  seconded into Open Water. We're actively working with Welsh as part of the Silk Commission reforms and  contributing to that discussion. We'll make we're listening and also adding value in that.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director
texts.text: Now, there's one area that we're less enthusiastic about, and that is the proposed changes from Ofwat in terms of  the CIS reconciliation and in terms of midnight adjustments in 2020. We don't agree with that at all. We've made  that clear. We've submitted our points to Ofwat. I guess we now await their decision, but it's worth being clear  that's one area that we are less keen on. And with that, maybe we'll talk something we are more keen on, which is  renewable.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director
texts.text: So, renewables. So, we mentioned to you guys – let's just jump next slide to renewables, if that's okay. Well, we  mentioned to you guys at the Capital Markets Day that we saw an opportunity for us to continue to spe nd in the  space. We currently have 28% of our energy this year equivalent [indiscernible] (31:26) self-generated. And we  want to switch that to around 50% by 2020.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director
texts.text: We shared with you before, there were a number of technologies, and it's a portfolio plan. So it's a mixture of AD  spend in sludge, also in crop and also in food waste, and then in solar. And that's what we've been doing over the  course of the last while and we shared that with you in March, just getting ourselves ready to begin to make this  happen. And we've seen some good early successes. So we've seen actually the last self-generation entirely from  our current assets improved slightly towards the tail-end of the year, and we exited at about 30% per month self- generation.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director
texts.text: The second bit of good news is having decided that we're going to do solar. And we've now got ourselves ready for  the first solar array, we'll actually go live in July. So quite a short time window. It's actually six weeks when you've  got the site ready and everything is commissioned – and everything is bought, but actually commissioning is a  very tight time window. So six weeks, so the first of those will go live in July.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director
texts.text: And we continue to make progress in our AD agenda, with the second of our food waste plants now clear in our  minds as to where it can be located and beginning the progress towards securing the contract for that and  beginning to build. So, good solid progress. As you know, we believe this is a good economic case for us. It's good  for our customers, we believe it's good for as a company. It's always something we are going to need is energy, and  we think this gives us a good opportunity to get ourselves over 50%, and as such is a natural hedge for us going  forward, and more volatile pricing.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director
texts.text: And it includes educating our people to become conversant and almost second nature talking about totex and  ODIs. It means making sure that our Business Service division best sorted for the future and that meant the sale of  WP and we are refocused and ready to focus on our core skills, which is water, waste, retail and renewables. A nd  it's also about putting customers right at the heart of our strategy because we believe fantastic customer  experience helps create long-term shareholder value. And that, of course, is the great discussion of the day.

texts.speaker: James Brand
texts.profession: Deutsche Bank AG (Broker UK)
texts.text: Second question is on mergers. Ofwat has obviously signaled potentially an increased willingness for mergers. I  was wondering what your viewpoint was on that? There's obviously one small water-only company that's in the  middle of your territory. I'm sure not expecting you to comment specifically on that, but how do you think a bout  mergers more broadly?

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director
texts.text: And in terms of the first one, in terms of regulatory reform, then I think you're right that Tony and team has done  a really good job in the past of commenting openly on where we think reform might come. I think we believe the  competition that we've set for a long time, we think the competition is healthy and is the right thing and great  companies will succeed in a moment of competition. We believe that could open up to other areas. At the moment,  it's retail. We believe that sludge trading is a good example of an area where competition might move into it. We  likewise believe that water resourcing is an area that it might enter into down the line through their conversations.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director
texts.text: And consumption at domestic usage situation can be a very dry spring. We will get excited about barbecue season  and then we begin to get our gardens in better shape for the summer. So things like that can drive consumption.  And from a regulatory perspective, the numbers are set for the next five years. So to some extent, if you have lower  or higher consumption, it's your problem to deal with. So that is where the world is in terms of the regulatory  effect.  Dominic C. Nash  Macquarie Capital (Europe) Ltd.  Q  [indiscernible] (39:12).

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director
texts.text: Let's do the easy ones first then. So, the £190 million is the number that we said we're going to spend over AMP6.  We've been a matter of weeks into AMP6, but we have, as I said, got some solar arrays going live in July. So, yes,  we are obviously spending that money now. We're not going to give you how much we spent over the last eight  weeks. But, yes, we're live spending that money now sinc e April 1.

texts.speaker: Guy Mackenzie
texts.profession: Credit Suisse Securities (Europe) Ltd.
texts.text: Hi. It's Guy Mackenzie from Credit Suisse. Just one more question from me on the debt. I mean, you obviously  showed that your net debt to RAV went up to about 61%. But I guess your key constraining metric on your credit  rating is actually FFO to debt, at least on S&P's BBB+ rating. So just wondering if you can give some guidance on  where you are on your FFO to debt right now and where you would be next year given you expect debt to increase.  And on that, how important it is to retain that BBB+ rating at the regulated water company level and the BBB- at  the PRC level?

texts.speaker: Philip Maton
texts.profession: Santander Global Banking and Markets
texts.text: Hi. Philip Maton from Santander again. Y ou briefly said about CPI and the potential of change to CPI. I know, it's  something that Ofwat projected previously but there is increase in tailwinds from electricity generation and power  generation, in particular. Could you comment on any, how advanced those discussions might be and what you see  as the time scales around that.

texts.speaker: Olivia Garfield
texts.profession: Chief Executive & Executive Director
texts.text: Leakage is another measurement at the top 10. We've seen very strong performance of a 10% improvement over  the five-year ramp on that. Likewise, water quality complaints is also one of the top measures. [indiscernible]  (50:52) to improve 17% to get there. So I'm definitely not giving you a prediction for the end of year one. What I'm  saying is I'm very confident over the five years of performing very well against the ODIs but there will be a slow  burn towards that, actually beginning to be monetized on the basis as a mixture of some of those. Is that fair  enough?
